title: Appendix A — Glossary
text: This glossary consolidates the terms defined in the eighteen chapters. Where two chapters used one word in different senses, this edition gives each sense its own name, and the entry says which word belongs to which idea. Each entry ends with links to the sections of the full text in Reference where the term is defined or used; the chapters’ own glossaries in Reference keep the fuller chapter-specific wording. The six chapters new to this edition ( Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture , Chapter 8; The Middle , Chapter 11; Arc and Theme , Chapter 12; The Reveal , Chapter 15; Series and Genre , Chapter 17; and The Structural Edit , Chapter 18) add their own terms, each linked to the chapter’s full treatment; where a new chapter uses a word already defined, its sense is added to the existing entry. A Absent opposition — A failure pattern: the opposing force disappears for long stretches of the middle, so the protagonist’s moves have no price. Ch 11 · full treatment . Absorption — The operation of folding a prologue’s material into Chapter One, or relocating it to its proper place in the main timeline, and deleting the label. The standard remedy for a unit that earns its existence but not its exteriority. Ch 10 · 1.2 , Ch 10 · 7.0 . Access — The domain of purpose in which a grant buys presence at events the existing vantage cannot attend. Ch 13 · 4.1 . Accessus ad auctores — The medieval schoolroom’s standard prefatory apparatus, supplying an author, subject, intention, manner, order and utility before the text was read. The ancestor of the orientation functions now distributed between prologue, blurb and genre shelf. Ch 10 · 3.4 . Accumulating middle — A shape of middle that gathers knowledge, with an investigator in the broad sense as its protagonist and the reader’s question as its pressure. Ch 11 · full treatment . Achrony — Genette’s term for an event whose position in story time cannot be fixed from the text. Ch 8 · full treatment . Act Two — The screen form’s name for the middle, which brings the three-act model with it; it suits many novels and not all. Ch 11 · full treatment . Action beat — An action inserted between turns in place of an attribution; called simply a beat in the first edition. The most efficient object in an exchange when it carries a second function, and a tag with extra words when it does not. Distinct from the beat of The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1) and Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2). Ch 3 · 5.3 . Adjacency pair — A two-turn sequence in which the first part makes a particular second part conditionally relevant: question/answer, greeting/greeting, offer/acceptance-or-refusal. Sacks, Schegloff and Jefferson. Its importance for fiction is that the absence of the expected second part is itself an event. Ch 3 · 3.2 . Advance mention ( amorce ), or seed — Genette’s term for an apparently insignificant detail whose significance becomes visible only in retrospect. The unit of fragmentary closure. Ch 10 · 6.2 , Ch 10 · 6.6 . Advance notice ( annonce ) — Genette’s term for an explicit announcement of something to come. The unit of the choric or proleptic prologue, closed by arrival rather than by recognition. Ch 10 · 6.2 . Aftermath — Everything between the climax and the last word. The Ending ’s neutral term (Chapter 16), preferred to denouement because it presupposes no shape. Ch 16 · 2.3.1 . Alignment — Whether the reader learns a withheld fact with a character, ahead of one, or after. Ch 15 · full treatment . Allocation and arrangement — Rung 2 of the revision ladder: the viewpoint grant, the threads, the order of times, the prologue and the book’s form. Ch 18 · full treatment . Allocation problem — The Viewpoint Shift ’s term (Chapter 13) for the structural decision about how a finite quantity of reader attention and identification is distributed across a cast. Ch 13 · 1.1 . Anachrony — Any discordance between the order in which events occur in the story and the order in which the narrative presents them. The genus of which analepsis and prolepsis are the species. Ch 7 · 3.1 . In Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture ’s sense (Chapter 8): any discrepancy between story order and text order (Genette). Ch 8 · full treatment . Anagnorisis — Aristotle’s recognition : a change from ignorance to knowledge. At an ending, the mechanism by which existing information is reorganised rather than new information supplied. Ch 16 · 3.3 , Ch 16 · 6.2 . Analepsis — Genette’s term for narration, after the fact, of an event earlier than the point in the story at which the narrative currently stands. The formal name for what Backstory and Flashback (Chapter 7) calls a cutaway. Ch 7 · 3.1 . In Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture ’s sense (Chapter 8): an anachrony that goes back to an event earlier than the present of the narrative; external, internal or mixed according to whether its extent lies before, within or across the start of the main narrative (Genette). Ch 8 · full treatment . Analogy (Levin) — A relation between plots in which the secondary action repeats the primary action’s pattern in a different key. Ch 14 · 3.2 . Anchor — The first concrete cue after a gap that answers when , where or whose vantage this is . Its function is not to inform but to stop the reader continuing in the abandoned frame. Twelve types are tabulated at Ch 5 · 6.3 . Anchor position — The number of words after a gap at which the anchor arrives. A measurable revision variable; thresholds at Ch 5 · 6.2 . Anchored order — An architecture that shows or announces one event early and tells the book towards it. Ch 8 · full treatment . Animator / author / principal — Goffman’s decomposition of the “speaker” role: the one producing the sounds, the one who composed the words, and the one whose position the words express. These can come apart, and a character who separates them is deflecting responsibility. Ch 3 · 3.3 . Announced arc — A failure pattern: a change reported as a realisation rather than shown in a decision. Ch 12 · full treatment . Answer map — Arc and Theme ’s tool (Chapter 12) for theme: the book’s question, and each major character’s criterion rewritten as an answer to it. Ch 12 · full treatment . Anthology — A series whose volumes share a premise, title or frame and nothing else. Ch 17 · full treatment . Arbitrary arrangement — A failure pattern: a departure from story order for interest the departure does not produce. Ch 8 · full treatment . Arc — The course, across a whole book, of the rule by which a character resolves dilemmas. Ch 12 · full treatment . Arrested ending — A close that stops mid-action, before the outcome. Strategy 12 at Ch 16 · 6.4 . Articulated time — Dames’s term for the experience the chapter, as a unit of the book, produces: reading divided into intervals with edges, so that a life or a history is felt as a sequence of episodes. Ch 6 · 3.1 . Asterism — The typographic mark ⁂, three asterisks in a triangle, historically used as a section divider. Ch 5 · 6.6 . Attack — The point in the story’s chronology at which the telling begins. A dramaturgical term; distinct from the opening pages, which are the text that results from the choice. Ch 9 · glossary . Attention tax — The cost, in reader attention, of any material that diverts from the chain carrying the reader’s primary investment; coined in The Subplot (Chapter 14) as the formal counterpart of The Viewpoint Shift ’s empathy budget (Chapter 13). The ending is where the refund falls due. Ch 14 · 1.2 , Ch 14 · 3.8 , Ch 16 · 7.1 test 6. Attribution (tag) — The identification of a speaker: he said , she asked . Its density, its verbs and its replacement by action beats are all craft variables with a documented history. Ch 3 · 3.5 , Ch 3 · 7.1 test 9. Authority domain — The Prologue ’s proposed sixth domain (Chapter 10): the prologue that establishes how the book knows what it tells, and on whose authority — by provenance, an intermediary, an authority claim, or an acknowledged limit. Distinct from the epistemological domain of The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13), which concerns what no single vantage can know. Ch 10 · 4.6 . Axes of distance — The four dimensions along which a prologue may be separated from the main narrative: time , place , viewpoint , register . One is normally load-bearing and the others incidental. Ch 10 · 6.1 . B Backstory — The past told : conveyed by summary, implication, report or dialogue, without the reader living through it. One of the two registers into which the fork at Ch 7 · 6.2 divides. Beat — Two related senses. In general use and in The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1), the smallest unit of change in a scene: one exchange, one action, one shift in the balance; the term comes from acting and screenwriting practice. In Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2), one of the six named functions of the scene–sequel pair (goal, conflict, disaster, reaction, dilemma, decision), a job done rather than a quantity of prose, so that a beat may occupy a page or a subordinate clause. The action inserted between turns of dialogue is an action beat . Ch 1 · 2.4 , Ch 2 · 2.4 , Ch 2 · 4 . Belatedness — In trauma theory, the property by which an overwhelming event is not fully registered at the time of its occurrence and returns afterwards, intrusively and out of sequence. Caruth (1996); contested. Ch 7 · 3.7 . Book map — A table with one row per scene of a draft and columns for position, story time, place, viewpoint, goal and decision, thread, change, what is learned, deposits and promises, from which the other chapters’ instruments are read. Ch 18 · full treatment . Bounded grant — A viewpoint grant held for one chapter or section, with no return. The cheapest form of a later grant. Ch 13 · 6.3 no. 6, Ch 13 · 6.6 . Braid — An architecture that alternates two or more strands, each chronological within itself; converging when the interval shortens until the strands meet in time, parallel when it holds. Ch 8 · full treatment . Braided middle — A shape of middle in which two or more lines of action alternate and the pressure comes from their crossings. Ch 11 · full treatment . Braiding — The interleaving of two or more chains in discourse time: how often the narrative changes thread, at what points, and in what proportions. Ch 14 · 6.1 . Braiding rhythm — The pattern of crossings across a whole book: even, accelerating, decelerating or interrupted. Ch 14 · 6.6 . Bridging object — The Transition ’s proposed sixth technique (Chapter 5): a physical thing continuous across a gap, whose recurrence does the anchoring by identity rather than by resemblance. Distinguished from the match-cut at Ch 5 · 4.6 . In Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture ’s sense (Chapter 8): at the scale of a book, an object present in two strands whose changed condition or custody measures the interval between them; a means of convergence by identity (proposed in The Transition , Chapter 5, adopted at this scale with that condition in Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture , Chapter 8). Ch 8 · full treatment . Broken back — A failure pattern of the turned middle: a midpoint so large that the second half reads as a different book. Ch 11 · full treatment . C Capitulum / kephalaion — Latin and Greek for a “little head”: a division of a text, originally created as a finding aid, usually with a summarising heading. The ancestor of the modern chapter. Ch 6 · 3.1 . Cascade — The failure in which a repair changes a fact that other units depend on and the consequence goes unchecked. Ch 18 · full treatment . Catalogue — A list whose order is doing work — geographical, social, causal, formal. Distinguished from an inventory by being shuffle-variant. Ch 4 · 6.3 , Ch 4 · 8.1 . Category detail — A detail true of the type rather than of the instance: a kitchen with a stove, a forest with trees. Orients cheaply; establishes nothing. Ch 4 · 7.1 , test 3. Causal chain — The relation by which a scene’s disaster produces the following sequel’s reaction, and that sequel’s decision produces the following scene’s goal. Ch 2 · 3.7 . Chain — A sequence of scenes linked by causality in the sense established by Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2), such that each descends from the one before. The defining requirement of a subplot. Ch 14 · 2.1 . Chain structure — A recognisable arrangement of scene–sequel pairs across a narrative, with characteristic benefits and costs. Twelve are tabulated at Ch 2 · 6.3 . Chapter architecture — The pattern a book’s breaks and larger divisions make as a whole, considered as an object of design. Ch 6 · 6.6 . Chapter break — A structural boundary placed deliberately within the stream of scenes and sequels, whose position determines what a reader carries with them if they stop. Ch 6 · 2.1 . Character compression — Woloch’s account of the effect of restricted character-space on a character’s presentation: flatness, the type, the repeated identifying tag. Not an absence of depth but the visible mark of depth excluded. Not to be confused with compression in Scene and Sequel ’s sense (Chapter 2). Ch 13 · 3.3 , Ch 13 · 7.1 no. 10. Named so in this edition to keep it apart from Scene and Sequel ’s compression (Chapter 2) of page-space against story-weight. Character zone — Bakhtin’s term for the field around a character in which the narration itself becomes contaminated by that character’s speech habits, so that the boundary between narration and quoted speech becomes porous. Ch 3 · 3.4 , Ch 3 · 9.4 . Character-space — Woloch’s term for the particular and delimited position a character occupies within a narrative, and the friction between an implied person and the room afforded them. Ch 13 · 3.3 . Character-system and plot-system — Woloch’s term for the arrangement of many character-spaces into one structure of distributed attention ( Ch 13 · 3.3 ); The Subplot (Chapter 14) extends it to the distribution of chains across a cast, the plot-system ( Ch 14 · 3.5 ). Characterisation — The observable sum of a character’s traits, as distinct from the character revealed in choice (McKee). Ch 12 · full treatment . Cheat — A failure pattern: a passage before a reveal that supports only the first reading and is stated on the narration’s own authority. Ch 15 · full treatment . Circularity — Closure by returning to the beginning’s language, image or situation. Torgovnick’s category; strategy 1 at Ch 16 · 6.4 . Circumstantial particularity — Watt’s term for the specificity of time, place, name and object that constitutes the novel’s formal realism. Ch 4 · 3.1 . Cliffhanger — An ending on visibly unresolved danger or crisis. The most expensive exit available and the fastest to fatigue. Ch 6 · 4.1 . Climax — The last major confrontation or disaster; the peak of conflict. A part of the ending, not a synonym for it. Ch 16 · 2.3.1 . Clock — A deadline or limit in the middle, known to the protagonist, whose remaining time visibly shortens. Ch 11 · full treatment . Closing reveal — A reveal in the last part of a book, with no successor question inside it. Ch 15 · full treatment . Closing the distance — The point, or points, at which the main narrative catches up to, recontextualises, completes, or deliberately refuses to close what the prologue opened. Four modes: total closure, fragmentary closure, recontextualisation, deliberate non-closure. The return of Backstory and Flashback (Chapter 7), the point at which a cutaway ends, is a different term. Ch 10 · 6.5 . Closural allusion — Herrnstein Smith’s term for content that signals ending by association rather than by structure — night, sleep, departure, death, silence — and so lends a chapter’s or a book’s close a borrowed finality. Free closure, and dangerous for that reason. Ch 6 · 3.5 , Ch 6 · 8.10 , Ch 16 · 3.2 . Closural strategy — A named shape an ending can take, with characteristic purchases and costs. Sixteen are tabulated at Ch 16 · 6.4 . Closure — The reader’s felt sense that the book has arrived rather than stopped. Distinct from resolution , and separable from it in both directions. Ch 16 · 2.3.2 . Coda — A short final movement in a changed key, continuous with the narrative. Distinguished from an epilogue, which is displaced. Ch 16 · 2.4 . Cold open — A scene begun in motion with framing deferred. A gambit available to any chapter, frequently and wrongly labelled a prologue. Ch 10 · 2.3 . Cold read — A reading of a revised draft by a reader who has not read an earlier one, or by the writer after an interval long enough to have forgotten what she meant. Ch 18 · full treatment . Companion — A book set in a series’ world whose question is unrelated to the series question; it makes no promise across volumes. Ch 17 · full treatment . Completing analepsis — An analepsis that fills a gap the narrative previously left open; it arrives into a slot the reader already has. Contrasted with the repeating analepsis. Ch 7 · 3.3 . Complication — Anything that stands in the protagonist’s way in the middle: an obstacle, a refusal, a delay. Ch 11 · full treatment . Compression — The setting of page-space against story-weight for a given beat. The principle is that the two should track each other; the failure is a default register applied regardless. The Viewpoint Shift ’s effect (Chapter 13) of restricted character-space is character compression . Ch 2 · 5.1 . Conflict — The resistance a goal meets, whose function is to change the goal’s shape rather than merely to postpone its achievement. Ch 2 · 4.2 . Congruence — Torgovnick’s criterion: whether an ending emerges from the novel’s own logic or is imposed on it from outside. Ch 16 · 3.5 , Ch 16 · 8.12 . Connotation — The mood, class signal, judgement or thematic freight a detail carries because this true thing was reported rather than another. A second-order signification, culturally supplied and historically volatile. Ch 4 · 6.1 . Consequence — The property of a reveal that changes what a character does or what the ending means. Ch 15 · full treatment . Constant — Something visibly unchanged in a character against which a change can be read (from The Ending , Chapter 16). Ch 12 · full treatment . Contained middle — A shape of middle that holds its protagonist in a fixed situation, confinement, waiting or illness, so that its engine is time and the arrivals it brings. Ch 11 · full treatment . Contextual frame — Emmott’s term for the reader’s running mental representation of a specific episode’s context — who is present, where, and when — maintained across sentences and bound to persons. A transition must recall a frame or switch to a new one; failure to bind characters to a frame produces the unanchored opening; a prologue builds a frame and immediately suspends it. Ch 5 · 3.2 , Ch 9 · 8.8 , Ch 10 · 3.9 , Ch 10 · 6.2 . Contract (narrative) — An obligation the opening pages create in the reader, which the remainder of the book must honour. Used in The Opening Pages (Chapter 9) as a diagnostic category rather than a formal-critical claim. Ch 9 · glossary . Contrast (Levin) — A relation between plots in which the secondary action inverts the primary one. Ch 14 · 3.2 . Contrast (viewpoint domain) — The domain in which a grant buys access to a materially different way of seeing. Distinct from Levin’s contrast between plots in The Subplot (Chapter 14). Ch 13 · 4.3 . Controlling idea — McKee’s term for a theme stated as a value and the cause by which it is won or lost. Ch 12 · full treatment . Convention — A feature readers expect of a genre, semantic or syntactic. Ch 17 · full treatment . Convergence — The relation a secondary chain eventually bears to the primary one. Literal convergence is intersection in event; thematic convergence is relation without intersection. Ch 14 · 6.1 . In Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture ’s sense (Chapter 8): the point at which strands meet: of times, when one strand catches up with another; by cause, when an act in one produces the situation in another; by identity, when a person or object is found in both. Ch 8 · full treatment . Convergence by coincidence — A failure pattern: strands joined by a link that carries no cause and changes no meaning. Ch 8 · full treatment . Convergence point — The page at which deleting a thread would break the main plot’s causal logic; the moment at which the subplot’s kernels become the main plot’s. Ch 14 · 3.4 , Ch 14 · 7.1 test 5. Conversational implicature — Grice’s term for meaning generated beyond what is said, computed by the hearer on the assumption that the speaker remains cooperative despite a visible breach of a maxim. The identification made in The Dialogue Exchange (Chapter 3): subtext is conversational implicature. Ch 3 · 3.1 , Ch 3 · 6.2 . Conversion arc — An arc in which the criterion changes once, at a single priced decision. Ch 12 · full treatment . Cooperative Principle — Grice’s overarching maxim: make your contribution such as is required, at the stage at which it occurs, by the accepted purpose of the exchange. Its four attendant maxims are quantity, quality, relation and manner. Ch 3 · 3.1 . Copy-edit — The check of a text’s correctness and of the continuity of its facts. Ch 18 · full treatment . Core promise — The convention whose breach a genre’s readers treat as a breach of contract: solution, union, the threat met, the kept rule or significance. Ch 17 · full treatment . Count norm — The conventional number of descriptive elements used to establish a place or person in a given period. Currently two or three; in 1835, hundreds. Ch 4 · 3.6 , Ch 4 · 7.1 test 8. Coy narrator — A failure pattern: a narration that announces its withholding without feeding it. Ch 15 · full treatment . Criterion log — Arc and Theme ’s tool (Chapter 12) for arc: a character’s largest decisions in order, with the options, the choice, the rule and the cost. Ch 12 · full treatment . Crossing character — A character with business in two or more chains, whose crossings are motivated rather than convenient. Not to be confused with the hinge of Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2). Ch 14 · 5.3 . Called the hinge character in the first edition; renamed because Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2) keeps hinge for its own term. Curiosity — Sternberg’s term for the interest generated by uncertainty about the past , as distinct from suspense (the future) and surprise (a past gap the reader did not know existed). Ch 7 · 3.4 . Curiosity reveal — A reveal that answers a question the reader knew she had (after Sternberg’s curiosity). Ch 15 · full treatment . Cutaway — Backstory and Flashback ’s cover term (Chapter 7) for any passage in which the narrative leaves the temporal position of its present action for earlier material, in either register. Ch 7 · 2.1 . D Decision — The sequel’s terminal beat: a commitment to a new concrete objective, which becomes the following scene’s goal. Ch 2 · 4.6 . Decision (carrier of theme) — The choice at the hinge, read as the book’s verdict on its question. Ch 12 · full treatment . Declared decline — A convention declined with a sign inside the book early enough to be believed, a replacement promise that the book keeps, and the declined question kept in view. Ch 17 · full treatment . Declined convention — A convention a book invokes and does not pay. Ch 17 · full treatment . Declined reveal — A book’s refusal, kept visible to its end, to disclose a fact or to adjudicate between accounts; at book scale, the form of The Viewpoint Shift ’s epistemological domain (Chapter 13). Ch 15 · full treatment . Decoy reading — A first reading supplied by a character with a reason to believe it, so that the reader’s error is attributable. Ch 15 · full treatment . Defamiliarisation ( ostranenie ) — Shklovsky’s term for the artistic device of making the habitual perceptible again, chiefly by describing an operation and withholding its name. Ch 4 · 3.3 . Deferred answer — The failure of a series that holds its question open across volumes without advancing it. Ch 17 · full treatment . Deferred decision — A sequel whose reaction and dilemma are shown but whose decision is withheld past a break, and later paid. Ch 2 · 6.2 . Denotation — The literal referent: what a detail names, plainly. Ch 4 · 6.1 . Denouement — The untying; the classical aftermath, with the implication that entangled facts are being separated. Ch 16 · 2.4 . Descriptive pause — Genette’s term for discourse during which story time does not advance. The structural form of description’s cost. Ch 4 · 2.2 . Desis and lusis — Aristotle’s tying and unravelling. The division falls at the turning point, which makes the aftermath structurally half the work rather than an appendix. Ch 16 · 3.3 , Ch 16 · 6.6 . Dialogue exchange — A passage of spoken interaction between two or more characters, each pursuing a want through what they say, in which the balance of information, power or feeling is measurably different at the end than at the start. Ch 3 · 2.1 . Diegetic threshold — The Prologue ’s term (Chapter 10) for the prologue’s constitutive hybridity: typographically paratextual (labelled, set apart, skippable) and ontologically diegetic (part of the story). The boundary Genette’s system does not quite accommodate. Ch 10 · 3.1 . Digression — Non-narrative material occupying a subplot’s page-share; has no chain and cannot be assessed by The Subplot ’s tests (Chapter 14). Ch 14 · 2.4 , Ch 14 · 8.11 . Dilatory space — Brooks’s term for the narrative middle, which resists the ending it desires. The theoretical form of deferral. Ch 2 · 3.2 . In The Middle ’s sense (Chapter 11): Brooks’s term, built on Barthes’s hermeneutic code, for the middle as the stretch in which the end is postponed; its detours are what keep the action from reaching its end too soon. Ch 11 · full treatment . Dilemma — The weighing of options each of which carries a real cost, none obviously correct. Ch 2 · 4.5 . Dimension count — The number of situational dimensions (time, space, protagonist, causality, intentionality) a gap changes. The Transition ’s best single predictor (Chapter 5) of how much orientation a gap requires. Ch 5 · 3.3 , Ch 5 · 7.1 test 2. Dinkus — A small typographic ornament, commonly three spaced asterisks, used to mark a section break where a blank line would be lost at a page boundary. Ch 5 · 6.6 . Direct linkage (Levin) — A relation between plots in which the secondary action affects the primary one causally. Ch 14 · 3.2 . Disaster — The scene’s terminal state: worse off, or a success whose cost exceeds its value, or a success revealed to have been the wrong goal. Ch 2 · 4.3 . Disclosure map — The Reveal ’s tool (Chapter 15) for timing: a row for each withheld fact and a column for the reader and each character, recording when each learns it. Ch 15 · full treatment . Disnarrated — Gerald Prince’s term for what a narrative reports as not having happened: the imagined, feared, rehearsed or explicitly denied event. The basis of the subjunctive scene. Ch 1 · 6.3 (mode 13). Displaced sequel — A structure in which the disaster belongs to one character and the reaction to another. Ch 2 · 6.3 . Dispreferred response — In conversation analysis, a second pair-part that declines what the first proposed. Systematically marked by delay, hesitation, token agreement, an account and mitigation — which is how skilled novelists write reluctance. Ch 3 · 3.2 . Distance — How far a prologue sits from Chapter One, measured along the four axes. Ch 10 · 6.1 . Distinguishability test — The diagnostic that exchanges the contents of two viewpoint sections and asks whether a reader could tell. Ch 13 · 7.1 no. 4. Distributed exposition — Sternberg’s mode in which antecedents are dispersed throughout a narrative and never gathered. Ch 7 · 3.4 . Domain of purpose — A register in which a unit of narrative can do work. The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1) sets out four — plot, character, theme and texture — and each later chapter applies them at its own scale, usually adding one: for a detail the domains are plot, character, world, theme, texture and temporal; for an ending, plot resolution, character-arc completion, thematic closure, emotional catharsis, the final image and formal closure. The proposed additions are the relational ( The Purposes of a Scene , Chapter 1; The Dialogue Exchange , Chapter 3), silence ( The Dialogue Exchange , Chapter 3), temporal ( The Descriptive Detail , Chapter 4), structural ( Backstory and Flashback , Chapter 7), authority ( The Prologue , Chapter 10), epistemological ( The Viewpoint Shift , Chapter 13), temporal counterpoint ( The Subplot , Chapter 14) and formal closure ( The Ending , Chapter 16) domains, each with its own entry. Ch 1 · 4 , Ch 4 · 4 , Ch 16 · 4 . Dormancy across volumes — The absence of a carried thread from one or more volumes, measured in volumes and in the reader’s months. Ch 17 · full treatment . Dormancy interval — The number of pages between consecutive appearances of a thread. The maximum interval, not the average, is diagnostic. Ch 14 · 6.6 . Double ending — Two endings supplied, or the choice between them exhibited. Strategy 15 at Ch 16 · 6.4 . Double plot — Two chains of comparable weight, neither clearly subordinate; the object of Empson’s and Levin’s studies. Ch 14 · 2.4 . Double reading — The reading of a passage twice, under the understanding before and after a reveal. Ch 15 · full treatment . Double-reading table — The Reveal ’s tool (Chapter 15) for preparation: every passage bearing on a reveal, with its first and second readings. Ch 15 · full treatment . Dramatic irony — The domain in which a grant buys the reader knowledge a character lacks. Ch 13 · 4.2 . Dramatisation — Rendering an occurrence such that narrative time approximates story time. Defined in The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1) by duration rather than by the presence of dialogue, action or sensory detail. Ch 1 · 3.3 . Drift — A deliberate delay of the anchor, used to reproduce a character’s disorientation. Distinguished from an orphaned cut by the criterion that the anchor still arrives, late and on purpose. Ch 5 · 6.5 . E Early reveal — A reveal in the first third of a book, which turns curiosity into consequence. Ch 15 · full treatment . Earned — Of an ending: resting only on material the book already deposited (Claim 1), and answering a pressure the book built (Claim 2). Ch 16 · 6.1 . Echo close — An ending on a resonant image, gesture or line, carrying thematic rather than plot charge. Ch 6 · 4.4 . Economy of the repair — The notes a repair answers set against the tests it reopens and the words it adds. Ch 18 · full treatment . Edit by addition — The failure in which every note is answered by adding material, so that the draft grows, slows and states what it should show. Ch 18 · full treatment . Edit by committee — The failure in which several readers’ prescriptions are partly adopted, so that the book moves towards no reader’s book and away from its own. Ch 18 · full treatment . Edit list — The record of each note and failing test: where it was felt, the rung of the symptom and of the cause, the repair, the tests reopened and the status (mended; kept and defended; passed to the line edit). Ch 18 · full treatment . Ekphrasis — Extended verbal description of a made object, especially a work of art. The oldest descriptive set piece; Homer’s shield of Achilles is the founding case. Ch 4 · 6.3 . Ellipsis — Genette’s duration category: story time elapses while discourse time is nil — a stretch of story passed over in silence. Classified as explicit , implicit or hypothetical ; as definite or indefinite ; as qualified or unqualified . It is what a completing analepsis later fills. Ch 5 · 3.1 , Ch 7 · 2.4 . Empathy budget — The Viewpoint Shift ’s working metaphor (Chapter 13): reader identification as a finite pool divided among viewpoint characters. Formalised by Woloch’s character-system ( Ch 13 · 3.3 ) and criticised at Ch 13 · 16 . Enactment — The confirmation of a new criterion by a situation the book has shown before, answered differently. Ch 12 · full treatment . Ending — The final unit of a novel, distinguished by having no subsequent scene to correct it and by being the material through which the reader retroactively re-reads the whole. Comprises climax and aftermath. Ch 16 · 2.1 . Endless edit — The failure of an edit with no stopping rule, which continues on the lowest rung and moves the book away from its first conviction. Ch 18 · full treatment . Entrelacement (interlace) — The medieval romance technique of following one thread to a point of suspension, announcing the departure, and taking up another. Ch 14 · 6.2 . Episodic middle — A failure pattern: sequences joined by a constant and not by cause, which could change places without loss. Ch 11 · full treatment . Episodic series — A series whose volumes close everything and carry only the hero, his world and his rule. Ch 17 · full treatment . Epistemological domain — The Viewpoint Shift ’s proposed sixth domain (Chapter 13): a vantage granted to demonstrate that no single vantage can know the events. In The Prologue (Chapter 10), the prologue that establishes on whose authority the book speaks is the authority domain . Ch 13 · 4.6 . Inventory — An unselected list; shuffle-invariant; without a governing principle. Ch 4 · 8.1 . Kind — A genre with its full repertoire of features, as distinct from a mode (Fowler). Ch 17 · full treatment . Ch 5 · 5.3 , Ch 5 · 7.1 test 3. Lie, the — Weiland’s term for the false belief a character holds at the start of an arc. Ch 12 · full treatment . Middle — The long stretch between the commitment that ends a novel’s beginning and the movement that begins its ending, usually half the book or more, and the part of a draft that most often loses its readers. R Range — The set of passages a reveal recasts, by reinterpretation or falsification; distinct from the reach of Backstory and Flashback (Chapter 7). Ch 15 · full treatment . Rate — The story time a strand covers per page. Ch 8 · full treatment . Re-entry — The opening of a later volume, which must serve a returning reader and a new one. Ch 17 · full treatment . Reach ( portée ) — How far an anachrony goes from the present moment of the first narrative: the size of the leap. Ch 7 · 3.2 . Reaction — The character’s registration of the disaster, which converts an external event into the internal state a decision can issue from. Ch 2 · 4.4 . Reality effect — Barthes’s term for a detail that signifies nothing within the narrative’s economy and therefore comes to signify reality itself. Ch 4 · 3.4 . Rearranged book — The failure of reordering a draft without a reason on rung 1. Ch 18 · full treatment . Recap at the door — The failure of a later volume that opens with summary of the earlier ones. Ch 17 · full treatment . Recasting close — Proposed in The Chapter Break* (Chapter 6).* An ending whose final sentence changes the meaning of the chapter just concluded rather than pointing forward, so that the reader looks back. Not to be confused with the hinge of Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2). Ch 6 · 4.6 . Recency effect — The better recall of items at the end of a sequence; the counterpart to primacy. Robust for lists, and applied to novels only as a general claim about the privilege of boundary positions. Ch 16 · 3.6 . Recognition — Aristotle’s anagnorisis : a change from ignorance to knowledge, which may precede a hinge. Ch 12 · full treatment . In The Reveal ’s sense (Chapter 15): a character’s change from ignorance to knowledge (Aristotle’s anagnorisis ); the reveal received on the page. Ch 15 · full treatment . Recontextualisation — A mode of closing in which the narrative never reaches the prologue but changes what it meant. Ch 10 · 6.5 . Recursive sequel — A sequel containing scenes within itself, each generating further reaction rather than resolution. Ch 2 · 6.3 , Ch 2 · 9.1 . Referential illusion — Barthes’s term for the impression, produced by the reality effect, that the text is transcribed rather than constructed. Ch 4 · 3.4 . Reflector — James’s term for a character through whose registering intelligence events are refracted without the character narrating them. Ch 13 · 6.2 . Refused arc — An arc in which the character reaches the hinge, sees the new rule’s decision, and chooses by the old. Ch 12 · full treatment . Refused ending — A text that declines to conclude and marks the refusal. Strategy 16 at Ch 16 · 6.4 . Register of the past — Backstory and Flashback ’s term (Chapter 7) for a recognisable way of putting past material on the page. Fourteen are tabulated at Ch 7 · 6.4 . Reinstatement cost — The attentional expense of recalling a dormant contextual frame or thread. It rises with the interval since the frame was last primed, falls with how distinctive the thread is, and is higher when the thread was suspended mid-question. The empirical form of the prologue’s problem of distance and closing, and of the subplot’s problem of dormancy. Ch 10 · 3.9 , Ch 10 · 6.2 , Ch 14 · 3.7 , Ch 14 · 6.6 . Relational domain — The state of a relationship — trust, power, obligation, intimacy, debt, hostility — considered as an independently shiftable value. Proposed in The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1) as a fifth domain of purpose and adopted in The Dialogue Exchange (Chapter 3), where dialogue negotiates standing, permission, intimacy and obligation between speakers. Ch 1 · 4.5 , Ch 3 · 4.3 . Relay series — A series that keeps a world and passes the centre to a new protagonist in each volume. Ch 17 · full treatment . Relocation — Moving a prologue’s material to the point in the main timeline where it happened, as an ordinary scene, and deleting the label. With absorption, one of the two outcomes short of keeping a prologue separate. Ch 10 · 2.1 , Ch 10 · 7.1 , test 2. Rememory — Sethe’s term in Beloved for a past that persists as a place in the world, which another person can enter. Ch 7 · 3.7 , Ch 7 · 9.5 . Reopened tests — The tests on lower rungs that a repair can make wrong for the units it touches. Ch 18 · full treatment . Repair — The correction of trouble in talk, with a strong structural preference for self-correction. Other-correction is rare in life and therefore aggressive on the page. Ch 3 · 3.2 . Repeating analepsis — An analepsis returning to material the narrative has already covered, in order to recolour it. The most expensive structure in Backstory and Flashback (Chapter 7) and the one that produces several of its greatest novels. Ch 7 · 3.3 . Reported reveal — A failure pattern: the truth delivered as information by a character or the narration, rather than found. Ch 15 · full treatment . Reset — An architecture that tells one span of time more than once, each version starting again from the same point. Ch 8 · full treatment . Reset hero — A series hero whose change in one volume is undone in the next without a scene. Ch 17 · full treatment . Resolution — The answering, or legible declining, of the plot’s dramatic questions. A domain, not the ending. Ch 16 · 2.3.2 , Ch 16 · 4.1 . Retold order — An architecture that tells one event several times from several vantages. Ch 8 · full treatment . Retroactive lens — The Ending ’s first principle (Chapter 16): the ending is the position from which the whole book first becomes available as a whole, and the reader’s final interpretation is performed upon everything, not only the last pages. Ch 16 · 1.1 , Ch 16 · 3.10 . Retrospection, anticipation of — Brooks’s term for the reader’s forward motion in expectation of a moment from which the whole will be legible. Ch 16 · 3.4 . Retrospective reframe — A late disclosure that changes what the whole book was. Strategy 13 at Ch 16 · 6.4 ; Ch 16 · 8.10 . Return — The point at which a cutaway ends and the first narrative resumes. Backstory and Flashback ’s requirement (Chapter 7) is that the present be changed , in knowledge, understanding, question or action. Ch 7 · 6.6 . Reveal — A disclosure of a fact the reader lacked that changes her understanding of what she has already read. Ch 15 · full treatment . Reveal from outside — A failure pattern: a disclosure whose source lies outside the book’s causal system. Ch 15 · full treatment . Reverse order — An architecture that tells events backwards, unit by unit. Ch 8 · full treatment . Revision ladder — The order in which a book’s decisions are checked and repaired, in five rungs, from the promise to the scene and its materials. Ch 18 · full treatment . Revoked arc — A failure pattern: a return to the old criterion after the hinge, because the plot needs it. Ch 12 · full treatment . Rules of notice — Rabinowitz’s tacit conventions determining which textual elements readers treat as significant. Ch 9 · glossary . Rung — A level of the revision ladder. Ch 18 · full treatment . Rung-up rule — Before repairing a failure, check the rung above for its cause; treat a failure found in several places on one rung, or recurring after repair, as caused above. Ch 18 · full treatment . Running arc — A line carried across an episodic series, advancing a step per volume while each volume closes its own question. Ch 17 · full treatment . S Satellite — See kernel and satellite . Scene — A unit of story in which a character pursues a concrete immediate objective against resistance, rendered in approximately real time, such that the state of the story is different at its close. Ch 1 · 2.1 . Scene (narrow sense) — The goal–conflict–disaster half of the pair. Distinguished throughout from the loose workshop sense used in The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1), and from Genette’s sense of a duration relation. Ch 2 · 2.3 . Scene and its materials, the — Rung 5 of the revision ladder: scenes, sequels, exchanges and details, followed by the line edit. Ch 18 · full treatment . Scene break — The typographic signal that a gap exists: white space, dinkus, ornament, chapter division. Not the transition, which is the narrative material on either side of it. Ch 5 · 2.3 . Scheduled arc — A failure pattern: a change predicted from the first chapters and delivered on time. Ch 12 · full treatment . Seed — The appearance of the new criterion before the hinge, usually in another character. Ch 12 · full treatment . Segmentation — The division of a continuous text into units. Dames’s central category, and The Chapter Break ’s subject (Chapter 6). Ch 6 · 3.1 . Selection principle — The statable logic governing which facts a passage reports. Its absence is the mechanism of the inventory passage. Ch 4 · 7.1 , test 10. Self-revelation — Truby’s term for the moment the hero sees the truth about themselves. Ch 12 · full treatment . Semantic and syntactic elements — A genre’s building blocks, and the relations and order among them (Altman). Ch 17 · full treatment . Sequel — In Swain’s model, the reflective half of the scene–sequel pair: reaction, dilemma, decision. Treated in full in Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2). In this book the word never means a follow-up volume; see series hook . Ch 1 · 6.6 , Ch 2 · 2.1 . Serial — One story published in volumes, each closing a stage. Ch 17 · full treatment . Serial reveal — A chain of reveals, each recasting the last. Ch 15 · full treatment . Series — A sequence of separately published works sharing characters, a world or a continuing story, which invite reading as related. Ch 17 · full treatment . Series hook — A deliberate non-closure creating appetite for a further volume; called the sequel hook in the first edition. In this book sequel has only Swain’s sense, so the follow-up volume is never called a sequel. Ch 16 · 8.11 . Series instalment — A later volume of a series; this edition’s term for what is elsewhere called a sequel. Ch 17 · full treatment . Series question — The question that runs across a series’ volumes and is closed, if at all, by the last. Ch 17 · full treatment . Sermon — A failure pattern: a theme answered one way by every character and left to statement. Ch 12 · full treatment . Shape, the — Rung 3 of the revision ladder: the arc, the middle, the schedule of reveals and the ending, checked together. Ch 18 · full treatment . Short circuit — Brooks’s term for an action that reaches its end too soon, without the detours of the dilatory space, and so arrives at the wrong end. Ch 11 · full treatment . Significance fatigue — What a reader experiences when every join in a book is doing conspicuous double duty: the loss of any plain surface against which emphasis can register. Ch 5 · 5.4 . Silence domain — The Dialogue Exchange ’s proposed sixth domain (Chapter 3): what is not said, who does not speak, and who is excluded from the exchange. Ch 3 · 4.6 . Simultaneity — Two threads occupying the same story time. Prose has no grammatical form for it; readers default to sequence unless told otherwise. Ch 5 · 8.10 , Ch 5 · 7.1 test 8. Situation model — In discourse psychology, the reader’s mental representation of the state of affairs a text describes, tracked across the dimensions of protagonist, space, time, causality and intentionality. It is sparse rather than complete, which is why a few chosen details can furnish it. Ch 1 · 3.5 , Ch 4 · 3.5 , Ch 9 · glossary . Skip test — The diagnostic derived from Genette’s observation that the preface is a book’s most easily bypassed zone: what happens to a reader who skips this? The intended profile is nothing incomprehensible, and something lost . Ch 10 · 7.1 , test 8. Soft landing — An ending on a settled, resolved beat, making the exit free. The type that makes the others legible. Ch 6 · 4.2 . Staged arc — An arc in which the criterion changes in steps, or is recognised at one point and acted on at another. Ch 12 · full treatment . Stalled sequel — A sequel expanded past the point at which new considerations arrive; repetition mistaken for depth. Ch 2 · 8.5 . Statement (carrier of theme) — A character or narrator saying what the book means. Ch 12 · full treatment . Stations middle — A shape of middle: a sequence of encounters joined by a constant rather than by cause, such as a road, a voyage or a series of trials, as in the picaresque. Ch 11 · full treatment . Steadfast arc — An arc in which the protagonist’s criterion holds under pressure and the change happens to others. Ch 12 · full treatment . Stopping rule — An edit is finished when a pass down the first three rungs changes nothing below them, every kept failure is defended, and a cold read produces notes that do not cluster above rung 5. Ch 18 · full treatment . Story order and text order — The sequence of events in the world of a book, and the sequence in which the book presents them (the Formalists’ fabula and syuzhet ). Ch 8 · full treatment . Strand — A line of the telling set in one time, continuous within itself, that the book leaves and resumes, and that runs on a question of its own. Ch 8 · full treatment . Strand table — A table giving each strand its question, span, page count, rate, viewpoint, markers and meeting. Ch 8 · full treatment . Structural domain — The proposed sixth domain: a cutaway used as an architectural device rather than for its content, to control the shape of the whole book. Ch 7 · 4.6 . Structural edit — The revision of a complete draft at the level of the decisions that span more than one scene. Ch 18 · full treatment . Structural pacing — The domain in which the alternation of vantages is itself a rhythm instrument. Ch 13 · 4.5 . Structural shift — A deliberate change of focaliser at a scene, section or chapter boundary. Ch 13 · 2.1 . Subplot — A secondary chain of causally linked scenes with its own goal, conflict and consequence, running alongside the main plot and competing with it for page count and attention. Ch 14 · 2.1 . Subtext — The want, fear or withheld fact driving a line, legible to the reader through context, contradiction or omission but rarely stated by the speaker. Ch 3 · 6.1 . Successor question — The question a reveal leaves the reader holding in place of the one it answers. Ch 15 · full treatment . Summary bridge — Connective narration that covers the interval itself, and the only technique that can put content in the gap. The natural home of distributed exposition. Ch 5 · 4.4 . Surprise reveal — A reveal of a gap the reader did not know existed (after Sternberg’s surprise). Ch 15 · full treatment . Suspense and curiosity — Sternberg’s distinction between uncertainty about the future and uncertainty about the past. A proleptic prologue trades the first for the second. Ch 10 · 3.7 , Ch 10 · 8.6 . Switch — A passage from one strand to another. Ch 8 · full treatment . Syllepsis — Genette’s term for the grouping of events by a kinship other than time, of place or theme. Ch 8 · full treatment . Sympathy engineering — The domain in which a grant complicates a verdict the reader would otherwise reach from outside. Ch 13 · 4.4 . Synecdoche — Naming a whole by one of its parts. Ch 4 · 6.3 . T Tangent — Closure by swerving to something apparently unrelated. Torgovnick’s category; strategy 3 at Ch 16 · 6.4 . Teller rule — A reveal may falsify only passages a teller in the book could have shaped, and only if it names the teller and gives a reason. Ch 15 · full treatment . Temporal counterpoint — The Subplot ’s proposed sixth domain (Chapter 14): a thread running on a different clock, whose function is to make the main plot’s pace legible and to let the book hold a duration it could not otherwise contain. Ch 14 · 4.6 . In Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture ’s sense (Chapter 8): at the scale of a book, a difference of rate between strands that a crossing makes visible; a property of the arrangement (proposed in The Subplot , Chapter 14 for threads, adopted at this scale in Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture , Chapter 8). Ch 8 · full treatment . Temporal domain — Proposed in The Descriptive Detail (Chapter 4): the register in which a detail delivers duration, decay, repurposing, seasonality or interruption, carried chiefly by aspect, wear and maintenance. Ch 4 · 4.6 . In Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture ’s sense (Chapter 8): the work a detail does in establishing duration, sequence, decay, repurposing, season or interruption; at the scale of a book, the domain of orientation (proposed in The Descriptive Detail , Chapter 4, adopted at this scale in Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture , Chapter 8). Ch 8 · full treatment . Terminal modification — Herrnstein Smith’s device: a pattern established across the text is altered at its final instance, which signals that it will not continue. Ch 16 · 3.2 , Ch 16 · 4.6 . Termination — Simply stopping. Herrnstein Smith’s contrast term for what closure is not. Ch 16 · 3.2 , Ch 16 · 7.1 test 7. Text (in the two-channel sense) — The literal content of a line: the words a court reporter would transcribe. Ch 3 · 6.1 . Thematic alibi — The unfalsifiable defence of a functionless thread on the ground that it “explores the same themes”. Ch 14 · 8.13 . Theme — A question a book tests rather than a proposition it asserts. Ch 12 · full treatment . Threshold of a strand — The point at which recurring material from another time acquires a question of its own and becomes a strand; what the structural domain proposed in Backstory and Flashback (Chapter 7) named (rejected as a domain of the cutaway in Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture , Chapter 8). Ch 8 · full treatment . Threshold problem — The Opening Pages ’s term (Chapter 9) for the structural asymmetry by which the opening pages must generate reader trust without any accumulated investment to draw on. Ch 9 · 1.1 . Tick-tock — Kermode’s minimal model of plot: the listener supplies a beginning and an end to an undifferentiated series, and the interval between them becomes a duration with a shape. Ch 16 · 3.1 . Time-stamp — An explicit statement of elapsed time or temporal position at the head of a new unit; the cheapest reliable orientation available, and the most commonly defaulted to. Ch 5 · 4.2 . Total closure — The mode of closing in which the narrative reaches the prologue’s moment and completes its frame. Ch 10 · 6.5 . Transition — The narrative material, however brief, that carries a reader across a gap in time, place, viewpoint or scale. Ch 5 · 2.1 . Transition inventory — The manuscript-scale audit at Ch 5 · 5.5 : every join listed with its technique, dimension count, anchor position, ellipsis type and second job. Transportation — Gerrig’s, and Green and Brock’s, term for the absorbed state of narrative engagement; a threshold phenomenon with a start-up cost. Ch 9 · glossary . In Arc and Theme ’s sense (Chapter 12): Green and Brock’s term for a reader’s absorption into a narrative world. Ch 12 · full treatment . Trigger — The element in the present scene that motivates a cutaway. Ten kinds are tabulated at Ch 7 · 6.6 ; the requirement of one is a consequence of narrative distance rather than an independent rule. Turn — One speaker’s contribution, bounded by the transitions on either side; the unit of conversation analysis and the smallest constituent of an exchange. Ch 3 · 2.2 , Ch 3 · 3.2 . Turn reveal — A reveal near the middle that changes the book’s engine. Ch 15 · full treatment . Turned middle — A shape of middle organised around a single turn near its centre, so that its first half asks one question and its second another. Ch 11 · full treatment . U Undated strand — A strand whose instalments are placed in time by headings alone. Ch 8 · full treatment . Undeclared decline — The failure of a book that invokes a core promise and declines it at the end without a sign inside the book. Ch 17 · full treatment . Undone ending — A conclusive ending in one volume reversed by a later one. Ch 17 · full treatment . Upward discovery — The finding, while working on a lower rung, that a higher decision is wrong; it sends the writer up the ladder before work continues. Ch 18 · full treatment . V Value shift — McKee’s term for the movement of a charged value from one pole towards its opposite across a scene. The Purposes of a Scene ’s central diagnostic (Chapter 1), and a test that any unit earning its place, an exchange of dialogue included, must pass. Ch 1 · 3.7 , Ch 3 · 1.3 , Ch 3 · 2.1 . Value-shift log — A record of the middle, one line per sequence, giving what is true at its start and no longer true at its close, with the stakes; it finds neighbouring sequences that repeat each other. Ch 11 · full treatment . Variation — Keeping a genre’s core promise while changing a convention: new semantics on an old syntax, a varied obligatory scene, or a scene performed by someone unexpected. Ch 17 · full treatment . Variation (carrier of theme) — Other characters answering the book’s question differently. Ch 12 · full treatment . Varied repetition — Repetition in which one parameter — the object’s state, its relations, its context, or its naming — has changed, producing a differential the reader can read. The mechanism by which motifs accrue meaning. Ch 4 · 6.5 . Viewpoint architecture — A whole-book shape of viewpoint allocation. Thirteen are tabulated at Ch 13 · 6.3 . Viewpoint grant — The allocation to a character of access to the reader’s identification: to whom, how much, beginning when, ending when. Ch 13 · 6.1 . Vocative — A name or title used to address someone. Rare and marked in real speech; therefore conspicuous in fiction when used on every turn. Ch 3 · 8.7 . Volume — One work of a series. Ch 17 · full treatment . Volume question — The question a volume is built on and must close. Ch 17 · full treatment . Volume table — A table with a row per volume of a series, recording its question and where it closes, its step on the series question, the threads carried, the hero’s criterion, the re-entry and the last page. Ch 17 · full treatment . Volume that owes its question — The failure of a volume that leaves its own question open at the last page to bring the reader back. Ch 17 · full treatment . W Want and need — What a character consciously pursues, and, in the manuals, what they must change; in Arc and Theme (Chapter 12) the need is a criterion not yet held. Ch 12 · full treatment . Withholder — What keeps a truth from the reader until its disclosure: a vantage that does not know, a teller with a motive, or an arrangement. Ch 15 · full treatment . Withholding viewpoint — A failure pattern: paralipsis without a reason in a narration that follows a mind which knows the fact. Ch 15 · full treatment . Z Zeigarnik effect — The finding that interrupted tasks are recalled better than completed ones; the usual psychological explanation of the cliffhanger, with a mixed replication record and heavy moderation by motivation. Ch 6 · 3.6 . Zero focalisation — See omniscience . Ch 13 · glossary . Zero-context problem — The condition under which the opening pages operate: all contracts must be opened using only their own resources. Ch 9 · 3.7 . The Craft Behind the Story — Appendix A, Glossary.

title: Appendix B — Symptom Index
text: Readers report symptoms, not causes. They say that a book drags in the middle, that they could not tell the sisters apart, that the twist was obvious or the ending a cheat, and they are usually right about what they felt and often wrong about where it came from. This index starts from the report. Each row gives a symptom as a reader or a writer might put it, the failure pattern that most often produces it, the diagnostic test that finds the pattern in a draft, and the place to look first before repairing it. The patterns and tests are those of the eighteen chapters, each linked to the chapter’s Failure Patterns and Diagnostic Tests parts, where the mechanism, the remedy and a published exception are given. The index is arranged by where a symptom is felt, using the five rungs of the revision ladder set out in The Structural Edit (Chapter 18): the promise (what kind of book this is and what question it asks), allocation and arrangement (whose book it is, how many stories it tells, in what order of time), the shape (the middle, the arc, the reveals, the ending), the joins (transitions, chapter breaks, cutaways, the opening pages) and the scene and its materials (scenes, sequels, dialogue, detail). It begins at the bottom, with the scene, because that is where most reports are made. A last section lists the symptoms of a revision that is going wrong. The column Look first applies The Structural Edit ’s rung-up rule (Chapter 18): a symptom felt on one rung is often caused on a higher one, so before repairing a scene, check whether the decision above it is settled. The entry is a first guess, not a verdict. Where it says Local , the cause usually lies on the rung where the symptom is felt, and the instrument named is the one to use. A report that fits no row closely can be matched by its rung: find the rung where it was felt, and read that section’s rows for the nearest pattern. Felt in a scene These are the reports a reader makes about a single scene, exchange or passage of description: that nothing happens, that the talk is flat, that the description tells her nothing. The table draws on The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1), Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2), The Dialogue Exchange (Chapter 3) and The Descriptive Detail (Chapter 4). Another quarrel on the same terms; “we knew that already” The redundant scene Redundancy, test 6 Rung 3: the value-shift log of the middle ( The Middle , Chapter 11) Characters ask what they would already know, and one explains fluently The expository scene in disguise Pressure, test 9 Rung 3: when the reader needs the fact ( The Reveal , Chapter 15) The drive, the queue, the waiting room; the business comes at the end The errand scene Entry and exit, test 8 Rung 4: the transition ( The Transition , Chapter 5) She wants it and gets it, at no cost The unresisted want Resistance, test 2 Rung 3: the option list ( The Middle , Chapter 11) The scene ends in unmixed success The clean win Disaster, test 3 Rung 3: the option list ( The Middle , Chapter 11) Disaster, a break, a new goal, and nothing between The skipped sequel Descent, test 2 Rung 4: the chapter ending ( The Chapter Break , Chapter 6) A choice whose right answer is obvious The false dilemma Dilemma, test 7 Rung 3: the criterion log ( Arc and Theme , Chapter 12) Reaction and weighing, then a change of subject The sequel without a decision Reversibility, test 9 Rung 4: the chapter ending ( The Chapter Break , Chapter 6) Every scene ends worse, and the stakes stop mattering The escalation treadmill Criterion, test 8 Rung 3: the criterion log ( Arc and Theme , Chapter 12) and the middle ( The Middle , Chapter 11) Characters tell each other what both know As you know, Bob Cost, test 4 Rung 3: when the reader needs the fact ( The Reveal , Chapter 15) “They all sound the same”, or all sound like the author The ventriloquist exchange Transcript, test 7 Rung 2: the grant ( The Viewpoint Shift , Chapter 13) Everyone says what they mean, or explains their own psychology On the nose Implicature, test 6 Rung 3: is the change dramatised or announced? ( Arc and Theme , Chapter 12) Quick, clever lines, forgotten a page later The tennis match Want, test 2 Rung 3: does the shape need the exchange? Respelled dialect that readers find hard going Phonetic dialect Transcript, test 7 Local: the line edit A list of accurate furniture The inventory passage Inventory, test 10 Rung 2: whose attention selects ( The Viewpoint Shift , Chapter 13) The same charged detail, in the same words, scene after scene The static motif Recurrence, test 7 Rung 3: what the motif should measure ( Arc and Theme , Chapter 12) A detail no one present could have noticed The unfocalised detail Focalisation, test 5 Rung 2: the grant ( The Viewpoint Shift , Chapter 13) The broken clock at the right emotional moment The symbol announcing itself Denotation and connotation, test 2 Rung 1: is the theme a question or a statement? ( Arc and Theme , Chapter 12) Everything is seen; no smell, touch or temperature The sense monoculture Modifiers and senses, test 9 Local: the line edit Most of these symptoms point upward. A scene in which nothing changes is often a scene the shape does not need, and characters who all sound alike often signal that the book has granted more minds than it can distinguish, so the higher rung should be checked before the scene is rewritten. Felt at a join These are the reports a reader makes about the movement between units: that she was lost after a break, that the book is relentless or slow when no scene is at fault, that she skimmed the flashbacks or put the book down in its first chapter. The table draws on The Transition (Chapter 5), The Chapter Break (Chapter 6), Backstory and Flashback (Chapter 7) and The Opening Pages (Chapter 9). ( Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture , Chapter 8) A long visit to the past before the end of chapter two The second-chapter flashback Placement, test 8 Rung 2: the arrangement ( Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture , Chapter 8); rung 1: the contracts ( The Opening Pages , Chapter 9) The present resumes as if nothing had happened The untethered return Return, test 5 Local: the trigger and the return ( Backstory and Flashback , Chapter 7) One childhood scene explains the adult The childhood-explains-everything cutaway Removal, test 3 Rung 3: the arc ( Arc and Theme , Chapter 12) The book opens with someone waking up The waking-up opening Momentum, test 3 Rung 1: what the opening promises History and world before any character The info-dump opening Zero context, test 5 Rung 2: the arrangement, or a prologue ( Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture , Chapter 8; The Prologue , Chapter 10) The gripping start the book never returns to The borrowed hook Promise, test 6 Rung 1: the promise inventory ( Series and Genre , Chapter 17) The narration coyly withholds what the character knows The withholding tease Contract, test 1 Rung 3: who withholds, and why ( The Reveal , Chapter 15) “It starts on page four” Throat-clearing Abandonment, test 10 Local: the scene test ( The Opening Pages , Chapter 9) A join is the place where a reader notices the arrangement, so its failures are often failures of rung 2 seen from the page: a flashback skimmed may be a strand that has no question, and a reader lost after a break may be a reader who was never told the book has two times. Felt in the shape of the whole These are the classic reports on a full draft: the middle drags, the protagonist does not change, the twist was guessed or felt like a cheat, the ending fell flat or was too tidy. The table draws on The Middle (Chapter 11), Arc and Theme (Chapter 12), The Reveal (Chapter 15) and The Ending (Chapter 16). Report Failure pattern Test Look first “Nothing happens in the middle”, though much does The plateau Value-shift log, test 1 Rung 1: is the want urgent? The middle’s sequences could change places The episodic middle Reorder, test 3 Rung 1: the book’s question The opposition vanishes while the protagonist prepares The absent opposition Opposition, test 5 Rung 2: the threads ( The Subplot , Chapter 14) The middle waits for an event scheduled at its end The holding pattern Option list, test 2 Rung 1: is the want urgent? The second half reads as a different book The broken back Midpoint, test 4 Rung 1: the promise ( Series and Genre , Chapter 17) “She doesn’t change”, or “I was told she had changed” The announced arc Hinge, test 2 Rung 1: the governing question ( Arc and Theme , Chapter 12) The change comes when the old rule has nothing left to defend The free hinge Price, test 3 Local: the criterion log ( Arc and Theme , Chapter 12) Readers predict the change from the first chapters The scheduled arc Seed, test 4 Rung 1: the governing question ( Arc and Theme , Chapter 12) After the change, she chooses by the old rule again The revoked arc Enactment, test 6 Rung 1: does the change answer the question? “Lectured” The sermon Answers, test 8 Rung 1: the answer map ( Arc and Theme , Chapter 12) “Felt cheated” by the twist The cheat Teller, test 2 Rung 2: who tells the book ( The Viewpoint Shift , Chapter 13) “Guessed the twist” The giveaway Double reading, test 1 Rung 2: the grant ( The Viewpoint Shift , Chapter 13) The largest truth arrives in a line of dialogue The reported reveal Recognition, test 7 Local: the disclosure map ( The Reveal , Chapter 15) The twist surprises, and nobody cares The idle reveal Consequence, test 6 Rung 1: the book’s question “Convenient”: a letter, a stranger, a coincidence The reveal from outside Source, test 8 Rung 2: the cast and the threads ( The Subplot , Chapter 14) “Unearned”: the rescue comes from nowhere The unearned rescue Earned, test 3 Local: the plant audit ( The Ending , Chapter 16) Someone sums up what it all meant The explained ending Domain, test 5 Rung 1: the theme as a question ( Arc and Theme , Chapter 12) Every thread tied off with equal care The tidy-everything ending Proportion, test 6 Rung 1: what the book declines ( Series and Genre , Chapter 17) A death solves the problem Death as resolution Earned, test 3 Rung 3: the arc ( Arc and Theme , Chapter 12) The open ending reads as evasion Ambiguity used as evasion Domain, test 5 Rung 1: the declared decline ( Series and Genre , Chapter 17) The shape depends sideways on itself, so a symptom here can lie in a neighbouring decision on the same rung: an ending that falls flat is often a middle that did not narrow, and a twist that is shrugged at is often a reveal that answers a question the book never made urgent. The Structural Edit (Chapter 18) orders the checks on this rung as middle, arc, reveal and ending. Felt in the arrangement These are the reports about whose book it is and how it is laid out: that the viewpoints were indistinct, that one timeline was skimmed, that the subplot was the better story, that the prologue promised another book. The table draws on Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture (Chapter 8), The Prologue (Chapter 10), The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13) and The Subplot (Chapter 14). Report Failure pattern Test Look first Hard to follow, yet easy to retell in order The arbitrary arrangement Necessity, test 1 Rung 1: what the order is for “I didn’t know when I was” The lost reader Orientation, test 3 Local: the orientation marker ( Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture , Chapter 8) “Skimmed the past timeline” The explaining strand Strand question, test 2 Rung 1: does the strand serve the question? Two good timelines, and the book is monotonous The lockstep braid Rate, test 5 Local: the strand table ( Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture , Chapter 8) The timelines meet by a birthmark or a shared house The convergence by coincidence Convergence, test 7 Rung 1: the book’s question The prologue could be headed Chapter One Chapter One in disguise Label, test 3 Local: the double test ( The Prologue , Chapter 10) The prologue promises a different book False advertising Genre contract, test 9 Rung 1: the promise inventory ( Series and Genre , Chapter 17) An unnamed victim dies, and the detective’s book begins The anonymous-victim cold open Higher bar, test 1 Rung 1: the promise inventory ( Series and Genre , Chapter 17) The prologue gives the ending away The prologue that spoils Higher bar, test 1 Rung 3: the disclosure map ( The Reveal , Chapter 15) The prologue’s gap is never closed The unresolved distance Closing, test 6 Local: closing the distance ( The Prologue , Chapter 10) Minds change inside a scene Head-hopping Scene integrity, test 9 Local: the declaration ( The Viewpoint Shift , Chapter 13) A viewpoint that exists to fetch information The information mule Necessity, test 1 Rung 3: the disclosure map ( The Reveal , Chapter 15) “Hard to get into”; too many viewpoints The diluted ensemble Page-share, test 5 Rung 1: whose question the book asks A new viewpoint at two-thirds, and readers skim it The unearned late arrival Late grant, test 7 Rung 3: the shape The villain’s chapter tells the reader the answer The antagonist chapter that spoils its own suspense Necessity, test 1 Rung 3: the disclosure map ( The Reveal , Chapter 15) One thread is read impatiently Parallel play Convergence, test 5 Rung 1: the book’s question “Preferred the subplot” The main-plot hijack Promotion, test 10 Rung 1: which question is the book’s? ( Arc and Theme , Chapter 12) A thread from nowhere decides the climax The late-arriving thread Dormancy, test 8 Local: the thread’s appearances ( The Subplot , Chapter 14) The threads converge because the characters meet Convergence by encounter Convergence, test 5 Local: the convergence test ( The Subplot , Chapter 14) A love story beside a plot it never touches The romance bolted on Analogy, test 4 Rung 1: the governing question ( Arc and Theme , Chapter 12) Arrangement is decided once for the whole book, so a repair here moves whole stretches of text and reopens the joins and scenes inside them. That is the reason to check the promise first: an arrangement can be faultless and still serve a question the book is not asking. Felt in the promise These are the reports that a book was not what it promised, or that a series did not keep faith with its volumes. They are made late, often at the ending, and they are the hardest to place, because the reader feels them at the last page and their cause lies before the first. The table draws on Series and Genre (Chapter 17). Report Failure pattern Test Look first Liked it until the end, then felt cheated The undeclared decline Declared decline, test 3 Decide on this rung Readers of the genre call it slow or evasive The genre in costume Core promise, test 2 Decide on this rung “Nothing was resolved; I have to buy the next one” The volume that owes its question Volume question, test 5 Decide on this rung The series’ long-awaited answer is too small The deferred answer Series step, test 6 Decide on this rung Returning readers skim the opening; new ones are lost The recap at the door Re-entry, test 7 Rung 4: the opening as written ( The Opening Pages , Chapter 9) The promise is the top rung, so a symptom here is decided rather than diagnosed. The writer chooses what the book is and what it declines, and then declares the choice early enough for a reader to stake on it. The one exception in the table is the recap at the door, whose decision is made at the top and whose repair is made in the opening pages of the later volume. Symptoms of the revision itself These are the reports a writer makes about her own revision: that each pass makes the book longer, or produces new contradictions, or answers the same note again. They are failures of the order of the edit, not of the book, and they are treated in The Structural Edit (Chapter 18). Report Failure pattern Test Look first The opening is the most revised part, and the least like the book The page-order edit Opening last, test 6 Rung 1, then down the ladder Cuts resisted; the best prose is in scenes that change nothing Premature polish Map, test 1 The book map ( The Structural Edit , Chapter 18) The same note on every draft, in new words The local repair Rung-up, test 3 The rung above the symptom Each revision makes new contradictions The cascade Reopen, test 4 The reopened tests ( The Structural Edit , Chapter 18) Each draft longer, slower and more explained The edit by addition Economy, test 5 The economy of the repair ( The Structural Edit , Chapter 18) A writer who recognises one of these should stop revising scenes and build the book map, since every one of them comes from making repairs in an order the book’s decisions do not support.
