title: Appendix C — Master Checklist
text: Every chapter ends with a revision checklist, a set of questions to put to a draft once the chapter’s tests have been understood. This appendix gathers the eighteen checklists in one place and in one order, the order of the revision ladder set out in The Structural Edit (Chapter 18): first what the book promises, then how it is allocated and arranged, then its shape, then its joins, and its scenes and their materials last. A writer who works down the list in this order makes each decision after the decisions it rests on, so that a later repair does not undo an earlier one. The questions are copied from the chapters without change, under each chapter’s own headings, and the chapter title above each set links to the chapter. Where a question uses a term, the chapter defines it, and the glossary gives it too. A question that cannot be answered is not a failure in itself: it usually means the decision it asks about has not yet been made, and the chapter says how to make it. Before the edit: the order of the work The structural edit’s own checklist comes first, because it governs the order in which the others are used: build the map, sort the notes by rung, and keep the record of what each repair reopens. The Structural Edit (Chapter 18) Before any repair Have I built a book map from the draft, not from memory, with the change column filled for every scene? Can I write the book’s promise and its governing question in two sentences, and do my first and last chapters answer to them? Have I put every note and every failing test on an edit list, with the rung where it was felt? The order For each note, have I checked the rung above the one where it was felt, and recorded the rung of its cause? Am I working downwards: the promise, then allocation and arrangement, then the shape, then the joins, then the scenes? When work on a lower rung showed me a higher decision was wrong, did I stop and make that decision before going on? Am I leaving the opening pages, the last page and the line edit until rungs 1 to 3 have settled? Each repair Have I changed the map before the text, and listed the tests the repair reopens? Have I rerun those tests before making the next repair? Does the repair answer at least as many notes as it reopens tests, and could I move or cut instead of adding? For every addition I keep, have I found something of equal length to remove? Stopping Does a pass down the first three rungs now change nothing below them? Is every failure I keep defended on the edit list in a sentence? Has someone who has not read an earlier draft read this one, or have I left it long enough to read it cold? Do the new notes avoid clustering above rung 5? Rung 1: the promise The top rung asks what kind of book this is, what it promises and what it declines. The governing thematic question, which also belongs here, is checked with the arc under rung 3, and the contracts of the opening with the joins under rung 4, since their checklists are written for the pages. Series and Genre (Chapter 17) The genre declared Where would a reader of my first chapter shelve the book, and does my last chapter belong on the same shelf? What is the core promise of the genre my opening declares, and where do I keep it? Does my jacket copy, or my pitch, promise anything the book declines? Conventions kept, varied and declined Have I listed every convention the book invokes, with the place it is first invoked? For each declined convention, is there a sign inside the book within the first quarter, and a replacement promise that I keep? Is every declined question kept in view to the end, so that the decline reads as design rather than forgetting? Which convention do I vary, and is that where the book’s meaning lies? Will a reader of my mode read any detail as a clue that I never meant to answer? The volume Can I write this volume’s question in a line, and is it closed inside the volume? Is my last page spent on this volume’s ending, with any step on the series question after the close? The series What form have my first volumes declared, and does this one keep it? What step does each volume take on the series question, and could a reader name it? How long has each carried thread been dormant, counted in volumes and in the reader’s months? Does my first chapter serve both a returning reader and a new one, with recap delivered as present consequence? Is my hero’s criterion where the last volume left it, or does this volume show it moving? Rung 2: allocation and arrangement The second rung asks whose book it is, how many stories it tells, in what order of time, and whether anything stands before it. The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13) The architecture Can I name the book’s architecture, and does the page-share confirm it? Is the right to move between minds inside a scene established, and exercised consistently, or never used? Each grant Can I name two domains for each viewpoint character, one of them not access, with a passage as evidence? Which cheaper instruments did each grant displace, and why were they rejected? Did the reader know what this character wanted before the first grant? Distinguishability Could a reader assign an unheaded paragraph to its viewpoint character? Do the vantages differ in what they notice, appraise, cannot know and call things, and not only in voice? Timing Is the book’s plurality declared before the reader’s first deep investment? Is every grant after the opening movement bounded, or paid for by a payoff no report could deliver? Does any vantage stop without the reader knowing it has stopped? Those outside For each named character without a viewpoint, who explains her motives, and does she have a repeated tag instead of a mind? What would a reader conclude the book believes from the shape of the allocation alone? The Subplot (Chapter 14) Is it a plot at all? Can I state the thread’s goal, conflict and consequence in three sentences without mentioning the protagonist’s goal? Does it have at least two branching points, moments at which it could have gone another way? If it is a recurring character rather than a chain, have I said so and sized it accordingly? What it supplies Can I name its domains, and does at least one supply what the main plot cannot by its nature? If it supplies only relief, have I looked for the second job it could do in the pages it already occupies? Can I complete the sentence because this thread exists, the reader understands that the main plot’s situation is qualified in this way , and name the two scenes between which that understanding is produced? Convergence At what point would deleting the thread break the main plot’s logic rather than thin it? Is the convergence a consequence, and not a coincidence or a meeting? Was the object or fact that converges the threads planted before the reader knew to look at it? Proportion and rhythm Have I counted every thread’s page-share, and does the distribution match the book I think I have written? What is each thread’s longest gap, and is the thread left mid-question when it is suspended? Does a thread that converges at the climax appear in the quarter of the book before it? Do the crossings fall where the material needs them, and not where a rotation demands them? Rank Have I asked the promotion question, and recorded the answer rather than defended the plan? If the book has three or more co-equal chains, does it declare that early and let the relations carry its argument? Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture (Chapter 8) The arrangement Have I written the book in story order in a page, and listed what my order adds? Which architecture does the book use, and do its parts serve that architecture’s work? What frame does the reader build from the first pages, and is it the one I want? The strands Can I write each strand’s question in one line, and do the other strands leave it open? Is every strand declared by its second instalment, within the first fifth of the book? Does any recurring material from another time lack a question of its own, and should it be cut to cutaways? Do my strands move at different rates, and where does a crossing show the difference? The markers and switches Does every instalment tell the reader its time within two sentences, using the strand’s own material first? Are the markers strongest where the strands share a place, a cast or an object? Is each strand left on an open question, and entered at a point that pays at once? Is the rhythm of alternation regular, and is every break in it deliberate? The meeting Where do the strands meet, in time, by cause or by identity, and what does the meeting change? If an object joins two times, does its condition or custody change between them? Does the order withhold anything that a character would have told, and does the book give a reason? The Prologue (Chapter 10) Position Can I complete “This must sit outside the main narrative because…” with an impossibility? Have I tried absorbing the material into Chapter One, and relocating it in the main timeline, and listed what broke? Would anything change if the prologue were headed Chapter One ? Distance Which axis carries the load, and are the others costing more than they buy? Does the main narrative close the distance on that axis, by the means the axis requires? If the distance stays open, is that the book’s policy, its subject, or an oversight? Domains Which domains does the prologue serve, and which of them require exteriority? If the authority domain is served, does the book honour the frame it installs? Plants Which specifics recur, and on which pages? Does the first fragment return within the first quarter of the book? Is the last sentence a held note, or a portentous half-line? Contract Do the prologue, pages 40 to 60 and the last chapter share pitch, pace, mode and scale? Can a reader who skips the prologue follow the whole book while still losing something? Rung 3: the shape The third rung asks how the middle narrows, where the protagonist’s change is located and what it argues, when each fact is disclosed, and what the ending spends. Its four checklists are given in the order The Structural Edit (Chapter 18) recommends, since the ending depends on the other three. The Middle (Chapter 11) Boundaries and turns Can I name the commitment that ends my beginning and the sequence that starts my ending, and say what share of the book lies between them? Is there a turn near the centre, and can I say whether it changes the goal, the protagonist’s knowledge, their mode or their fortune? Does the first half’s question get answered, or visibly carried, at the turn? Sequences Written as a value-shift log, does any sequence repeat its neighbour’s shift at the same stakes? Could any two sequences of the middle change places without loss, and if so, what links them other than a constant? If I delete the weakest sequence, does the ending lose anything I can name? Forces Does the opposing force act in every quarter of the middle, on the page or through a consequence? Is there a clock, does the protagonist know it, and does it shorten? Does at least one event narrow more than one line of action? The reader Is the protagonist’s option list shorter at the midpoint than after the beginning, and shorter again at the start of the ending? Is the question a reader carries at 60 per cent different from the one at 40 per cent? Is there any stretch longer than about a sixth of the book in which nothing closes? Arc and Theme (Chapter 12) The arc Can I write my protagonist’s rule for choosing as a short imperative, at the first large decision and at the last? If the rule is the same at both, is that the book’s design (a steadfast or refused arc), and is the rule put under real pressure? Is there a stretch of a quarter of the book or more in which my protagonist makes no decision? The hinge Can I name the decision at which the rule changes, and is it on the page, in scene, made by an act? What does that decision give up that the old rule valued, and has the reader watched that cost grow? Where is the new rule before the hinge: in another character, or in a moment my protagonist set aside? After the hinge, does any decision go back to the old rule because the plot needed it? The confirmation Is the new rule confirmed by a situation the book has shown before, answered differently? What about my protagonist is visibly unchanged at the end? Have I deleted every sentence in which the character, or the narration, explains the change? The theme Can I put my book’s theme as a question, and not only as a topic or a thesis? Does each major character’s rule answer that question, and do at least two answers differ? Does the opposing answer succeed at least once, or cost my protagonist something to reject? Who states the theme, where, and would the ending still argue it if the statement were cut? The Reveal (Chapter 15) The preparation Have I listed every passage that bears on my largest reveal, with a first and a second reading for each? Is there a passage that only the second reading explains, or that the reveal makes false on the narration’s own authority? Are the clues spread through the book, and is at least one early clue strong enough to be pointed to afterwards? Have I cut every if she had known and every phrase that announces a secret? The withholding What keeps the truth from the reader: a character who does not know, a teller with a motive, or the order of telling? If a character who knows is followed by the narration, where is her attention instead, and does the book show it? If the reveal falsifies anything, is it inside a teller’s account, and does the reveal name the teller and the reason? The timing Does the reader learn each withheld fact with the characters, ahead of them or after, and did I choose that? For a reveal before the end, what question replaces the one it answers, and is the second half built on it? Does any scene give the reader two new disclosures at once? If the book declines to reveal something, is the question kept visibly open to the end? The arrival Is the truth received by a character, in scene, in an act? Does someone act differently because of it, or does the ending mean something it would not otherwise? Does the disclosure come from inside the book’s causal system, by a character’s choice? Is the explanation after the recognition, short, and as far as possible left to the reader? The Ending (Chapter 16) The whole book Can I trace every element the ending rests on to an earlier planting, with chapter and page? Does anything new and load-bearing arrive for the first time in the ending? New material is allowed; new load is not. When I reread five earlier scenes with the ending in mind, do they read as intended? Where they do not, have I decided whether the scene or the ending is wrong? Does the ending answer a pressure the middle built, and not only a question it asked? Climax and aftermath Can I point to where the climax ends and the aftermath begins, and say what the aftermath does that the climax could not? Does the aftermath end within a page of the last decision anyone takes? Is each thread’s resolution proportional to the space it took? Domains Which domains does the ending deliver, which does it gesture at, and which does it refuse, and does each delivered domain have a passage a reader could point to? Does at least one carrier serve more than one domain, and is there some material that means nothing? If the book declared a frame, a pattern or an apparatus, does the ending close or modify it? Questions and ambiguity Is every question the book raised answered or visibly declined, and none merely dropped? Can I state any deliberate ambiguity in one sentence, and say what resolving it would cost? Has the book ended rather than stopped, and can I name the device that tells the reader so? The last page Do the last page and three passages from the middle belong to the same book? Does anyone, character or narrator, explain what the book meant? Does the final paragraph do work the paragraph before it does not, and do I know why the last word is the one it is? Rung 4: the joins The fourth rung asks how each unit meets the next: where the chapters break, how gaps are crossed, how the past is entered and left, and what the opening pages promise. The opening comes last, after every decision it must promise has been made. The Chapter Break (Chapter 6) Use the checklist on one chapter ending at a time, after reading the last paragraph and stopping. Each item is a question to answer in a sentence. The chapter What did this chapter propose near its start, in one sentence a reader would use? Does the ending resolve, escalate, hold open, recast or exchange it, and which? Is there an internal seam that would make a better ending than the present one? The ending What type of ending does the last sentence create, and was it chosen? If it is a cliffhanger, has the book already given the reader a reason to care about the danger? If it is a pivot, could the reveal come later, at the very end, and what are the pages after it doing? If it is a question close, can the question be stated without the word somehow ? The price Is stopping here free, moderate or expensive, and what did the two previous breaks charge? What does the next chapter have to spend on orientation because of where this one was cut? The manuscript Read down the ending types of eleven consecutive chapters: is there more than one gear? Plotted in order, do the chapter lengths make a tempo curve, and does it match the book’s movement? Do the Part boundaries fall where the book changes, and does the heading scheme run from the first chapter? The Transition (Chapter 5) Use the checklist on one join at a time. Read it cold when a reader has stalled there or you suspect a problem. Each item is a question to answer in a sentence. The gap How many of these change across it: time, space, protagonist, causality and intentionality? What happens inside it, and will the reader later need any of it? Does the mark on the page claim the right size of gap, and would the join survive the mark being lost? The departure Does the last sentence before the gap name a place, a person, an object or an intention the arrival can pick up? If the departure simply stops, could two words aim it? The arrival At what word can a cold reader say when, where and whose vantage? If the anchor is late, is the uncertainty the character’s, is it bounded, and is something else supplied meanwhile? At what word does the new unit’s own business begin, and what before it could the reader have inferred? Is the reader oriented twice, or reminded of what she has just read? Technique Which of the six techniques is this, and was it chosen? If it is a time-stamp, is it definite where the interval matters and event-relative where an event is available? At a handoff, does the text say whether this comes after the last unit or alongside it? Second jobs Is there an object, an echo or a tense already available that would carry the crossing and mean something? Is this one of the joins that should only orient? The manuscript Does one technique account for more than two out of every three joins? Do the joins cluster, several in a few pages and then none for forty? Backstory and Flashback (Chapter 7) Use the checklist on one cutaway at a time, after reading the page before it, the cutaway and the page after. Each item is a question to answer in a sentence. The decision What present question was open when the narrative left, and how hard was the reader pressing on it? Had the book already made the reader want this past, or does the cutaway arrive unasked? Would it cost less, and recolour more, thirty pages earlier or later? The register Written out as one sentence and read in place, does the cutaway lose anything the later pages need? Has the material been tried as a clause, and as an iterative sentence, before being given a scene? If it is a scene, does someone in it want something, meet resistance and end changed? The crossing What in the present triggers the departure, and is the narration close enough to need one? Which of the four changes has the present undergone by the return: knowledge, understanding, question or action? Is there a sentence stating the cutaway’s significance that could be deleted? The manuscript On one sheet, what are the reach, extent, register and domains of every cutaway, and what pattern do they make? How much of the book is in the past, and does its declared structure say so? If there is a second timeline, is it declared by its second or third instance, and does each strand progress? The Opening Pages (Chapter 9) Use the checklist on a finished draft of the first chapter, after reading the opening and then pages 30 to 40. Each item is a question to answer in a sentence. The scene Who is trying to do what in these pages, and what is in the way? How many words pass before the first verb of intention or change? What small deviation tells the reader that today is not like the others? The contracts Which words open each of the six contracts, and is each deferred contract deferred by choice? Is any information delivered that no character would say, to anyone, for any reason? Does the narration withhold anything the viewpoint character plainly knows, and is that gap in her or in the author? The page Which detail carries the most contracts, and could the page be built outward from it? Read aloud, where does the breath fail, and which sentences are rests? Which details are placed in the first two pages, and which of them are redeemed later? The book Do pages 30 to 40 belong to the same book as the opening, in tone, pace and stakes? If the book uses several viewpoints, timelines or documents, on what page does the reader first learn that it does? If read without its title, cover or blurb, does the opening still say what kind of book it is? Rung 5: the scene and its materials The last rung asks what each scene changes, how scene and sequel link, what each exchange does and which details are named. The line edit follows. The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1) Run each scene of a finished draft against this list before deciding that it stays as written. Each item corresponds to one of the diagnostic tests or failure patterns ; an unticked item is a question to answer, not a verdict. Engine I can state in one sentence what the viewpoint character wants in this scene, right now. Something is in the way, and getting past it costs something I can name. If the want is granted at once, the granting is itself the problem. Change I can write the two parallel sentences: what was true at the start, and what is no longer true at the close. The value moved is one the book has already made the reader care about. The reader has not already been given this shift elsewhere. Domains I can name each domain the scene serves (plot, character, theme, texture, relational) and annotate it with the specific change. The scene serves at least two, or I can say why it should serve one (a rest, or a normal a later scene needs). The relational change, if any, happens in the room, not in a sentence that states it. Mode I have asked whether this material should be a scene at all. I have tried it in at least one other mode (summary, ellipsis, iterative, reported) and know what that version loses. Habitual material is told iteratively, not dramatised as a single day. Execution The scene begins at the first moment the want is in operation. It ends on the last moment the value moves, not on its explanation. Information in it arrives under pressure, from someone reluctant to give it. Book scale Removing the scene would cost the reader something identifiable, or leave a later scene unearned. Its line in the reverse outline is written in the language of consequence. It is in the register (action or reflection) that this point in the book requires. Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2) Run each scene–sequel pair of a finished draft against this list. Each item corresponds to one of the diagnostic tests or failure patterns ; an unticked item is a question to answer, not a verdict. Goal and resistance I can state what the viewpoint character wants at the start of the unit, with a verb of pursuit and an object. I can point to the decision that produced the goal. Each obstacle tells the character, and the reader, something new. Disaster The unit ends in a sentence I can write with but or worse . I can name what the character paid, and in what currency. The disaster arises from the action, not from outside it. Sequel The reaction is carried by the body and the attention, or a retrospective narrator’s naming is doing work. I can state both costs of the dilemma in one sentence each, and a sympathetic reader could choose either. The decision names a place, an object or a person, and closes some door. Any decision withheld across a break is paid, visibly, later. Chain Written as bare events, each of three links would not have happened without the one before. My three-connective outline has no run of three and then s, and contains at least one but . Weight The space each sequel gets follows the weight of the disaster it answers. The book’s largest sequel follows its largest disaster. Arc I can name the decision at which the protagonist chooses on grounds they did not hold before. Where a beat is missing, the absence is deliberate and the reader can cross it. The Dialogue Exchange (Chapter 3) Run each exchange of a finished draft against this list. Each item corresponds to one of the diagnostic tests or failure patterns ; an unticked item is a question to answer, not a verdict. Engine I can say in one sentence each what both speakers want from each other before the exchange ends. Something is different at the last line: a fact passed, a point conceded, a form of address changed. The exchange starts at the first turn I could not cut and ends at the last. Cost and status Every fact that passes costs the speaker something, or sits in narration instead. I can name the currency of status, and some of it changed hands or was contested and held. Any relational change happens in an act (a name, a correction, a position, an exit granted or refused), not in a statement about it. Two channels Each speaker keeps something back, and I know what it is. The reader can work out what each evasion is evading. The gap closes plainly no more than once or twice in the book, and late. Some turns do only one thing, so that the oblique ones register. Voices With every tag and action beat stripped, I can tell who is speaking from the speech alone. The principals differ in sentence length, in their relation to questions and in their default way of not saying things. Dialect lives in syntax, idiom and vocabulary rather than in respelling. Apparatus and room Most tags are said or asked , and fewer than half the turns carry one once the speakers are established. Each action beat does something besides identify the speaker. I know who else is in the room, and what their silence is doing. The Descriptive Detail (Chapter 4) Use the checklist on one descriptive passage at a time, after a reader has flagged it or you have begun to suspect it. Each item is a question to answer in a sentence. Selection Can you complete these details, and not others, because … with something other than “they were there”? Does the passage lose anything if its details are shuffled? Is each detail specific to this place, or only to its kind? Perceiver Whose attention chose each detail, and what does the choice show about her? Would she, wanting what she wants, in her present state, notice this? Is any detail something nobody present could have registered? Domains and density Which domain is the passage’s principle of selection? Does any detail carry plot, a relation or a date as well as texture? Is there at least one ordinary detail, and one that simply exists? Implication Can you write a second sentence saying what each key detail implies, distinct from what it shows? Is any implication so loud that the object has left the room? Does any figure of speech have an owner in the scene? Time and return Does the passage say what has happened to the place, through aspect, wear or maintenance? Where else does each charged object appear, and what has changed each time? Is the first appearance of a planned motif unemphatic? Count and senses How many details are offered, and how many do you want kept? How many modifiers stand on a single noun? Which single non-visual detail would carry most? The checklists are written for a draft that exists. A writer planning a book can use the first three rungs as a plan, answering each question with the decision she intends, and come back to the last two when there are pages to revise. The Craft Behind the Story — Appendix C, Master Checklist. Introduction · Glossary

title: Appendix D — The Household Novel
text: Every chapter of this book revises one invented novel, and this appendix gathers what the chapters establish about it: the book’s form, its people, its objects, the order of its events in story time and in the telling, the plants and their payoffs, and what is left open. It is a summary, written for a reader who meets the household in a chapter’s case and wants to know where the material came from. Where a fact rests on a revision that a later chapter proposes rather than one the earlier chapters already contain, the appendix says proposed and names the chapter, since those revisions are argued for in their chapters and left for the author to confirm. The chapter that treats each fact is given by number; each chapter’s household case is in its Worked Analyses part, and in full in its Reference text. The book The household novel is a contemporary literary novel of family life, quiet and domestic in register, set in an unnamed British town with a ring road. Its subject is what a family withholds from itself, and the question it runs on is not what happened? but what do these three do with what they can reconstruct? ( The Ending , Chapter 16). Arc and Theme (Chapter 12) proposes that the themes the chapters name in passing (what the living owe the dead’s silences, ritual as a way of not quite facing loss, records outliving the people who keep them, counting set against unmeasured time) are aspects of one governing question, first put in The Dialogue Exchange (Chapter 3): what the members of a family owe each other in the way of truth. Each member of the household answers it differently, and the ending answers it by arrangement, three people reading one record, rather than by a statement. Series and Genre (Chapter 17) proposes that the book is a standalone: a literary family novel in the mystery mode, which keeps the mystery’s promises about who wrote in the ledger after 9 March, who took the ledger and what the father knew, and declines one, why the locks were changed, and declares the decline. There is no second volume, and nothing on the last page points to one. The form is fixed by the chapters’ cases. A prologue is told from the father’s viewpoint on his last ordinary day ( The Prologue , Chapter 10). The main narrative is close third person, past tense, divided between Elena and Nadia ( The Viewpoint Shift , Chapter 13; The Subplot , Chapter 14). Dov is seen only from outside except in one bounded chapter, the evening of 9 March, near the climax ( The Viewpoint Shift , Chapter 13). The mother is never given a viewpoint. The narration keeps a small retrospective gap over its characters, as in is what she’d tell people later ( Scene and Sequel , Chapter 2) and He would remember, later ( The Prologue , Chapter 10), which lets it see past a character’s rationalisations without leaving her head. The book’s English is British: a flat, the till, Ma . The people The father is never named, nor is the family’s surname. He kept the shop’s ledger for eleven years in a careful slanting hand with crossed sevens, recording prices and repairs and the ordinary arithmetic of keeping a small shop alive. He used the good pen, a fountain pen, for the ledger only, and kept it by the till in its case; he lost it twice in the year he died. He hooked his thumb into his left cuff before he spoke, a habit Ma called thinking with his hands , and wore the cuff through; he wore the coat behind the counter every winter, over the ledger ( The Descriptive Detail , Chapter 4). He was ill, wrote the illness into the ledger (dates, a doctor’s name misspelled twice and corrected once, and a list of what needed doing if he ran out of time), and told nobody. His last entry is dated 9 March and breaks off halfway along its third line. He died in March. His line, said to Nadia the second time he lost the pen, when she asked why a stock count needed it, is “Because someone should write it down properly. In case anyone ever needs to check” ( Backstory and Flashback , Chapter 7); she thought he meant the shop. On the prologue’s day he thinks only In case , and could not have said in case of what ( The Prologue , Chapter 10). The mother , Ma, changed the shop’s locks in March and never says why. She has no scene of her own and speaks once, at a remove, through Dov in the doorway: “She said you’d ask that” ( The Dialogue Exchange , Chapter 3). Whether she knew of the illness is not established, and the book keeps it so. Her silence is the novel’s one deliberately open thread: no chapter explains it, gives her a viewpoint or gives her an account of herself. Elena is the investigator. She drives a truck, has had a key to the shop since she was twelve, thinks in questions and notices locks. She learns in Dov’s doorway, across town from the shop, that her key no longer fits ( The Dialogue Exchange , Chapter 3); in the truck afterwards she thinks of telephoning her mother, decides against it, and drives to the shop ( Scene and Sequel , Chapter 2). At the register drawer she smells fresh biro ink and finds the ledger; it falls open near the back, she sees without reading that her father’s hand stops at 9 March and a looser hand goes on, and she turns back to the first page to read from the beginning ( The Transition , Chapter 5; The Chapter Break , Chapter 6). Her reading is interrupted before she reaches the illness entries. When she comes back the drawer is empty, because Dov has taken the ledger home ( The Subplot , Chapter 14). The Middle (Chapter 11) proposes that she decides then not to ask him who took it, because she had asked him once ; Arc and Theme (Chapter 12) proposes that she keeps her suspicion from Nadia with “I’d tell you” , and that at the convergence, when Dov brings the ledger to the shop, she lays her palm on the cover, does not open it, and rings Nadia. Her rule changes there from find out for yourself to what concerns the three of them is read by the three of them , and it is not extended to her mother. Nadia counts things, and counting is how she manages grief. Seventeen months before the novel opens she left the flat over the shop for one with heating. When the book opens, four months after March, she has stopped answering Dov’s calls and is counting register receipts that nobody else thinks need counting ( The Opening Pages , Chapter 9). She has learned not to touch the coat, and knows how many days it takes the dust to show again on its shoulders between brushings ( The Descriptive Detail , Chapter 4). About two-thirds of the way through the book she puts her hand into the coat’s pocket, the coat still on its hook, finds the good pen and remembers her father’s line ( Backstory and Flashback , Chapter 7); The Subplot (Chapter 14) proposes her reason, Dov’s request that the flat be cleared by the end of the month. At the end she goes up to the flat, takes the coat down and puts it on, gathering the sleeves so that they do not drag ( The Ending , Chapter 16). Dov , the brother, is seen from outside. In the doorway he gives Elena the new key and withholds the reason: “She said you’d ask that. She didn’t say I had to answer” ( The Dialogue Exchange , Chapter 3). On the evening of 9 March he found his father’s broken-off entry, looked for the good pen, did not find it, and wrote the date and the count with a ballpoint from the drawer; he has kept the ledger in that way since, a looser hand at first and then not ( The Viewpoint Shift , Chapter 13). He did not know his father was ill and does not know why the locks were changed. The Reveal (Chapter 15) proposes why he never learned: in eleven years he had never read a page of the ledger, since reading it back had been his father’s business. His subplot is a chain ( The Subplot , Chapter 14): he wants to sell the shop; the buyer wants the building emptied by the end of the month; he clears the register drawer, taking the ledger home, asks his sisters to clear the flat without saying why, and signs the sale without telling them; at the convergence he brings the ledger to the shop and says “It’s all there. From March, it’s mine” ( Arc and Theme , Chapter 12), without knowing what is there. Others. A boy about the age Dov once was knocks on the shop window about the sign in the prologue and is waved off. The buyer is never named. Objects The household’s objects carry most of its plot, and each is fixed with its particulars and the place it lives. Object Particulars Where it lives The ledger Leather; eleven years of the father’s hand; crossed sevens; the illness entries and the list near the end of his pages; Dov’s looser hand from the evening of 9 March, date and count only The register drawer, until Dov takes it home; held back from the sale until the convergence The good pen Fountain pen, for the ledger only; kept by the till in its case; nib replaced twice that year Pocketed in the coat on the prologue’s day; found there by Nadia The register drawer Sticks on the K; comes free on the third try The shop The coat Army green gone the colour of dishwater; left cuff frayed through at the thumb; shoulders brushed every week since March by someone who is not Nadia On the hook by the door of the flat above the shop The keys Elena’s old key, held since she was twelve, no longer fits; Dov gives her the new one Elena lets herself into the shop with it The sign Never turned to CLOSED on the prologue’s day; reads OPEN over the locked shop until, as The Middle (Chapter 11) proposes, Elena turns it at the empty drawer The shop window The stool Elena sits on it to read; Nadia sits on it at the end Behind the counter The table holds every object a later chapter may need, and a writer extending the case should add to it rather than invent a particular that contradicts it. Story order and book order In story time the events run as follows. Eleven years before his death the father begins the ledger. Some seventeen months before the novel opens, Nadia leaves the flat. In the year of his death he loses the pen twice and says his line. In early March comes the prologue’s last ordinary day: the till counted twice, the boy waved off, the sign left on OPEN, the pen pocketed. On 9 March his last entry breaks off and Dov begins writing. Later in March the father dies and the mother changes the locks. From March to July someone brushes the coat every week and Dov keeps the ledger. The novel’s present begins in July, four months after the death, and runs to the buyer’s end-of-month deadline, so nearly all of it falls within a few weeks. The book tells these events in a different order, and the positions below are those the chapters give, as fractions of the book. Position Scene Chapters Before the main narrative The prologue: the father’s last ordinary day The Prologue (Chapter 10) Opening Nadia, the unanswered calls, the receipts; then Nadia in the flat with the coat The Opening Pages (Chapter 9), The Descriptive Detail (Chapter 4) First chapter break The doorway exchange (proposed as the first chapter break) The Dialogue Exchange (Chapter 3), The Opening Pages (Chapter 9) About a quarter Elena’s sequel in the truck; a hard cut to the register drawer; the ledger and the changed hand; the chapter ends, and the next cuts to Dov Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2), The Transition (Chapter 5), The Chapter Break (Chapter 6) About 30 per cent The buyer’s deadline, in Dov’s thread, from outside (proposed) The Middle (Chapter 11), The Subplot (Chapter 14) About 38 per cent The empty drawer; a second boy at the glass; the sign turned to CLOSED; Elena decides not to ask (proposed) The Middle (Chapter 11) About half The midpoint: Dov’s message asking for the flat to be cleared (proposed) The Middle (Chapter 11) About 54 per cent Elena helps Nadia begin to clear the flat; “I’d tell you” ; the brushing declined with a sign (proposed) Arc and Theme (Chapter 12), The Structural Edit (Chapter 18) About 58 per cent Dov signs the sale (proposed) The Middle (Chapter 11), The Subplot (Chapter 14) About two-thirds Nadia finds the pen in the coat and remembers the line Backstory and Flashback (Chapter 7) About 78 per cent Dov’s chapter, the evening of 9 March, headed with that date (the heading proposed) The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13), Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture (Chapter 8) The ending The convergence; the three read the ledger in the shop; Nadia puts on the coat Arc and Theme (Chapter 12), The Ending (Chapter 16) Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture (Chapter 8) charts the arrangement: the novel is an anchored order whose anchor, the prologue, is also the first instalment of a March strand of two instalments, the second being Dov’s chapter, with Nadia’s memory of the pen as a cutaway between them. Plants and payoffs The ending relies on material deposited across the book, and the table traces each element to the chapter that plants it and the chapter that pays it. A dash in the last column means the element is not paid, by design or because it carries no load. The full audit, with the chapters that maintain each element between planting and payment, is in The Ending ’s Reference case, section 9.10.8 (Chapter 16). # Element Planted Paid Note 1 The good pen, pocketed on the last ordinary day 10 16 2 In case anyone ever needs to check 10, 7 16 The thematic payload 3 The ledger as an object 4 16 4 The changed hand after 9 March 6 16 5 Dov’s decision to keep writing 13 16 Contextualised, not disclosed 6 Dov’s silence: the key given, the reason withheld 3 16 7 Dov’s sale, signed without telling his sisters 14 14 Whether it completes is not stated 8 The coat on the hook 4 16 9 Nadia has learned not to touch the coat 4 16 The character payload 10 The frayed left cuff 4 — Present, never named 11 The doctor’s name 13 16 12 The list of what needed doing 16 16 The one element first seen in the ending 13 The drawer that sticks on the K 10 5 14 The smell of fresh biro ink 5 13, 16 15 The leather faintly warm 6 12 Proposed 16 The stool 6 16 Furniture 17 Nadia’s counting 9 16 The constant against which she changes 18 The weekly brushing of the coat 4 — Declined with a sign; proposed in 18 19 The till counted twice 10 — A seed only 20 The changed locks 3 — Declined by design 21 The boy at the glass 10 11 Paid by rhyme; proposed 22 The sign never turned to CLOSED 10 11 Proposed 23 The father’s last entry, broken off on 9 March 6 16 24 Wool that wasn’t going to be worn again 9 16 A belief the ending reverses 25 The empty register drawer 14 14 26 Dov’s request that the flat be cleared 14 14, 16 Proposed 27 Elena’s decision not to ask Dov 11 14 Proposed 28 Elena’s “I’d tell you” 12 12 Proposed 29 Nadia lets Dov’s calls ring out 9 12 Proposed 30 Dov never reads back 13 12, 16 Proposed 31 The date 9 March 6 13 Proposed 32 Elena does not telephone her mother 2 16 A sign of the decline; proposed Read down the Planted column and thirteen of the sixteen chapters of Parts I to III appear in it, which is the sense in which the ending is built by the whole book. Read down the Paid column and nothing load-bearing is paid by material that appears first in the ending, except the list (row 12), which the book keeps there because no earlier chapter could show it without a sister reading the illness entries or Dov reading back. What the book leaves open Some questions are left open by design, and a writer extending the case should keep them open. The mother’s reason for changing the locks is never given, and the book declares that it is declining the question: Dov refuses it in the doorway, and Elena decides three times not to ask (in the truck, at the empty drawer and at the convergence). Who brushes the coat is never said; The Structural Edit (Chapter 18) proposes a sign that the sisters do not ask, and records that the sign makes the mother the likeliest brusher by elimination. Whether the sale completes is not stated. And the ending gives the father the last word through his own phrase, not through a scene. The chapters also leave a set of problems unsolved, and say so in their cases: whether the prologue’s In case is a hair too large; whether paying the boy at the glass and the sign in one scene reads as arranged; that the convergence carries more payments than any other scene; that the move from the shop to the flat in the last paragraph is made in a clause; and that every proposal above still waits on the author. Drafts are not facts. The rejected drafts in each chapter’s The Problem and in each Version A, among them the solicitor’s letter and the mother’s account in the first draft in The Ending (Chapter 16), the father’s dated strand in the draft in Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture (Chapter 8), and the mother’s ringing on the last page in the draft in Series and Genre (Chapter 17), exist to be diagnosed, and nothing in them binds the novel. The Craft Behind the Story — Appendix D, The Household Novel. Introduction · Glossary

title: Appendix E — Short Forms
text: The chapters are written for the novel, and most of their instruments assume its length: room to plant and pay, to establish what is ordinary before departing from it, to let a thread go dormant and bring it back. This appendix says what the instruments become in the two shorter forms of prose fiction, the short story , a narrative of roughly two to eight thousand words that a reader finishes at one sitting, and the novella , a narrative of roughly twenty to forty thousand words, long enough for a novel’s range of feeling and too short for its machinery. The twelve chapters revised from the first edition each treat the short forms in their Reference text, in a section on the unit across forms, and the appendix draws its account of those chapters from there, with a link to each. The six chapters new to this edition do not treat the short forms, and what the appendix says of them is its own application of their instruments, marked as such. Two forces Two forces account for nearly everything the chapters say about the short forms, and a writer who keeps them in mind can work out the rest. The first is proportion. Most units of a novel carry a fixed cost and a benefit that grows with the length of the book that follows. A prologue’s doubled start, a transition’s forty words, a cutaway’s suspended question and a viewpoint’s cold start cost about the same in any book, but they are repaid over the pages after them, and a short story has few pages after anything. A forty-word bridge is a fraction of a per cent of a novel of ninety thousand words and one per cent of a story of four thousand, and a story may have six of them. The arithmetic is the reason the chapters keep finding that a unit a novel can afford is unaffordable in a story. The second is the absent baseline. A novel teaches its reader what is ordinary in its world, how a character usually speaks, what a room usually holds, before it departs from the ordinary, so that a deviation registers. A story has no time to build that reserve. Every detail is read as significant from the first line, every exchange must carry its subtext without a history of the speaker’s habits behind it, and the reader leans on the conventions of the form, which a story’s writer must know she is borrowing. The novella meets a third problem, which the chapters state in nearly the same words each time: it is usually written by novelists. It has a novel’s range of feeling and a fraction of its length, so a novelist’s habits, a three-page approach to a scene, a five-thousand-word chapter, three viewpoints, a six-scene subplot, consume it. Its characteristic solution is concentration: one place described fully and everything else bare, one transition system held throughout, one viewpoint or a frame, a subplot two scenes long. The Death of Ivan Ilyich (1886), which opens on the announcement of its hero’s death and then retraces his life, is the chapters’ model case, and it recurs because its design solves several of the form’s problems at once. Part I: the scene and its materials The scene ( The Purposes of a Scene , Chapter 1). In a story a single scene may be a third of the whole, so there is no room for scenes that establish the normal; the normal is established inside the scene that breaks it, usually by iterative clauses ( every Sunday he would… ) set in the scenic narration. The novella’s solution is the compressed scene, rendered dramatically but with heavy internal ellipsis, so that the reader has the texture of a full scene at half its cost. Scene and sequel ( Scene and Sequel , Chapter 2). A story usually holds one scene and sequel pair, and often only its second half: the disaster happened before the text begins, and the story is the sequel. The decision beat carries a disproportionate weight, since the form’s characteristic ending lives there, a decision taken and made irreversible or refused and left visible. The novella’s characteristic shape is one disaster and a long sequel; its characteristic failure is a novel’s chain squeezed into a novella’s length, pairs that are all scene and no absorption. The dialogue exchange ( The Dialogue Exchange , Chapter 3). A story has no baseline of a character’s habits, so its subtext must be legible from the first exchange, and it gets there by convention: the reader of a literary story already knows that a conversation about hills is not about hills. Two speakers are the norm, phatic and ritual talk cannot be afforded, and the closing of the gap between what is said and what is meant, which in a novel is a climax, is often the story’s ending. The novella wants exchanges that begin at their second or third turn. The descriptive detail ( The Descriptive Detail , Chapter 4). With no baseline every detail reads as chosen, so a story tolerates less unmotivated detail than a novel, not more, and a motif must make its three appearances in a few pages, with sharper variation between them. The form’s classic way of letting in air is a single concrete object given no explanation. A story’s title often supplies the world detail a novel spends a paragraph on. The novella’s natural solution is one dominating place or object described more fully than a novel would allow, which is why so many novellas are remembered by a place. Part II: the joins The transition ( The Transition , Chapter 5). A story has few joins, and each is in a privileged position, read as meaningful. It cannot establish a system of transitions, and the reader has not lived in any frame long enough to recall it cheaply, so every switch is a construction. The hard cut is the story’s default and the summary bridge its greatest risk, and the white space between a story’s sections is read as structural, closer to a stanza break than to a novel’s scene break. The novella can do what neither other form can: hold a single transition technique across its length, so that what would be a metronome at ninety thousand words becomes a form at thirty. The chapter break ( The Chapter Break , Chapter 6). A story is read at one sitting, so its section breaks offer no permission to stop and are priced by nothing but what happens across them; The Transition (Chapter 5), not The Chapter Break (Chapter 6), governs them. Numbered sections announce a formal seriousness. The novella works with many short chapters, which give it the pulse of a long poem, or with none, a single continuous movement; what fails is the middle course, five or six chapters of novel length, which make a short book feel like an abbreviated long one. Backstory and flashback ( Backstory and Flashback , Chapter 7). A story cannot amortise the cost of a cutaway over the fifty pages after it, so the return must come at once, and a dramatised flashback of eight hundred words in a story of four thousand gives a fifth of the whole to the past. The registers that suit the form deliver the past without stopping the story: a clause of implication, a participial aside, the iterative, and the corrected assumption. The last is the form’s advantage, since a reader holds a whole story in mind and a final revelation about the past recolours every sentence before it. The novella can make the retrospect its whole design rather than an interruption, as Tolstoy does, because the reader’s investment in the present has not yet become something to protect. Non-linear and multi-timeline architecture ( Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture , Chapter 8; the appendix’s application). The chapter’s instruments shrink rather than vanish. A story told in two times usually has no room for strands with questions of their own, so its second time is more often a cutaway, judged by Backstory and Flashback (Chapter 7), and its order chart has a handful of rows; what remains essential is orientation, which in a story must work within the first clause of each section. The novella can carry two strands, and its brevity makes a short interval between them easy to hold, which is one reason the frame, a present telling of a past, suits it. Part III: the architecture of the whole The opening pages ( The Opening Pages , Chapter 9). A story may open at its central situation rather than approach it, and its opening is also its middle, so contract work and plot work must happen in the same sentences, with nothing deferred. Its length is itself a formal declaration, and its title is often a working part of the opening. The novella can open on its ending, as The Death of Ivan Ilyich opens on the death and the colleagues’ reaction, declaring its moral apparatus in the first pages with no approach at all. The prologue ( The Prologue , Chapter 10). A story has, in the main, no room for a prologue: the costs are fixed and the benefits have nowhere to accrue. Where a story uses a separated preliminary unit, it nearly always serves the authority domain, a found letter, a frame narrator, an editorial note, because that payoff is immediate, and its title often does a prologue’s work in a few words. The novella should compress the schedule on which a prologue’s distance is closed, with a first fragment in the first tenth rather than the first quarter and two fragments rather than four or five; or it can open a frame and never return to it, as The Turn of the Screw does, because the interval is short enough for a reader to hold an unclosed frame without strain. The middle ( The Middle , Chapter 11; the appendix’s application). A story has no middle in the novel’s sense, no long stretch between commitment and ending in which options can be narrowed by stages, so the option list collapses to a single narrowing, usually the story’s one turn. The plateau, the chapter’s first failure, is the story’s characteristic failure in miniature: a second scene that restates the first at the same stakes. A novella’s middle is short enough to hold one turn at its centre and not two, and its clock is usually shorter than a novel’s, a day or a season rather than a year. Arc and theme ( Arc and Theme , Chapter 12; the appendix’s application). A story seldom has room for an arc located by a run of decisions, so it more often shows the single decision at which a character’s rule for choosing changes, or the moment at which she refuses to change it; Scene and Sequel ’s finding (Chapter 2) that the decision beat carries the story’s ending is the same observation from the other side. Theme in a story is carried by fewer answers to its question, often one character’s and the world’s, which makes the sermon, every answer pointing the same way, easier to fall into and easier to see. The viewpoint shift ( The Viewpoint Shift , Chapter 13). The story’s default is a single fixed viewpoint, and the default is close to a requirement: a second vantage consumes an investment the story cannot rebuild, two shifts read as instability rather than pattern, and the story is very often about what one person cannot see. The exceptions are the story told from two vantages in sequence, the second reframing the first, and the story that widens at its end, as “The Dead” moves from Gabriel Conroy’s mind to the snow falling over Ireland. In a story every character but one is minor, so allocation is nearly all character compression. The novella works with one fixed viewpoint or with a frame, which gives it two positions and a listener at the cost of one additional vantage, and which is why so many novellas are frames. The subplot ( The Subplot , Chapter 14). The short story is the form in which a subplot is nearly always wrong: at fifteen per cent of a story it is too little for a chain and too much for a motif, it cannot go dormant without breaking the story, and a second chain implies a second value shift competing for the ending. Stories use a compressed analogy instead, a second situation glimpsed rather than narrated, or a story told inside the story. The linked collection is the exception, each story a thread and the book the braid, with relations of analogy and contrast rather than cause. In the novella the rule is to prefer a second chain two scenes long, one early and one late, over one six scenes long; the reader builds the middle of it at no cost. The reveal ( The Reveal , Chapter 15; the appendix’s application). The short forms favour the closing reveal, because a reader holds the whole text in mind and a late disclosure can recolour every sentence before it, which is the corrected assumption of Backstory and Flashback (Chapter 7) at the scale of a whole story. The double-reading table is short and its rows close together, so a giveaway is easier to commit and a cheat easier to find. The early reveal is rare in a story, which has no second half for a successor question to drive. The ending ( The Ending , Chapter 16). The story’s ending has fifteen pages of deposit to spend rather than four hundred, which is the worst ratio of context to closural demand in prose. Almost no aftermath is available, plot resolution is often waived for the terminal image or incompletion, the title is often part of the ending, and the last sentence may be the only closural device. The epiphanic close, a recognition rendered as an image in the last paragraph, has been the default since Dubliners , and a writer should choose it against alternatives rather than inherit it. The novella is the natural home of the arrested ending and of death as a structural terminus, both of which discharge the most pressure in the least space; its aftermath should be about half the proportion of a novel’s. Part IV: beyond the book Series and genre ( Series and Genre , Chapter 17; the appendix’s application). A story keeps or declines its genre’s core promise as a novel does, and its brevity makes a decline harder to declare, since there is less room for the early sign. The series has its short-form counterpart in the linked collection and the story cycle, in which recurring characters or a place carry the reader’s promises from story to story; each story should close its own question, as each volume of a series should, and leave open only what the collection has shown to belong to the whole. The structural edit ( The Structural Edit , Chapter 18; the appendix’s application). The ladder holds, but its middle rungs come close together. A story’s book map may have a dozen rows, its allocation is usually settled by the single viewpoint, and its shape is one turn and an ending, so a revision of a story reaches the joins and the sentences sooner, and the sentences carry a larger share of the work. What does not change is the order: what the story promises and asks comes first, and its last sentence, the most revised in most stories, is revised last. The forms at a glance The table gathers, for each chapter, the instrument’s chief change in each short form. It is a summary of the sections above and of the Reference sections they draw on. Chapter Unit In the short story In the novella The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1) Scene The normal set up inside the scene that breaks it The compressed scene Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2) Scene and sequel One pair, often only the sequel; the decision carries the ending One disaster and a long sequel The Dialogue Exchange (Chapter 3) Dialogue Subtext legible at once, by convention; two speakers Exchanges that start at the second or third turn The Descriptive Detail (Chapter 4) Detail Every detail read as chosen; one unexplained concrete object One place or object described fully The Transition (Chapter 5) Transition The hard cut by default; breaks read as structure One technique held throughout The Chapter Break (Chapter 6) Chapter break Breaks priced only by what crosses them Many short chapters, or none Backstory and Flashback (Chapter 7) Cutaway Immediate return;
