title: Appendix F — Test Index
text: Every chapter turns its account of a unit into diagnostic tests. Each test asks a question of a draft, explains what a failure usually means, and gives a published exception in which the work fails the test but succeeds. This appendix lists every chapter’s tests in the order of the chapters, with the question each asks, so that a writer can see a chapter’s tests at once and compare tests across the book. The chapter title above each list links to that chapter’s tests, where each test’s usual failure and its exception are given. Elsewhere the book cites a test by its number within a chapter, as in test 3 (Withholder) of The Reveal (Chapter 15), and gives its name after the number so that it can be recognised without looking it up. The tests are for revision, and each chapter’s page says in what order to run them and how to read their results together. The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1) # Test The question 1 Want What does the viewpoint character want in this scene, right now, in one sentence? 2 Resistance Complete: “___ wants , and is in the way.” What did getting it cost? 3 Value shift What is true at the start that is no longer true at the close, in two parallel sentences? 4 Extraction Remove the scene. What would the reader fail to learn, feel or expect, and which later scene becomes unearned? 5 Domain count Which domains does the scene serve, as distinct from occupy? 6 Redundancy Has the reader already received this shift? 7 Summary substitution Rewrite the scene as three sentences of summary. What is lost? 8 Entry and exit Does the scene start as late and end as early as it can? 9 Pressure Does information arrive under pressure, or is it delivered? 10 Register Is the story due for an action unit or a reflective one, and which is this? Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2) # Test The question 1 Goal What does the viewpoint character want at the start of this unit, in one sentence with a verb of pursuit and an object? 2 Descent Which decision produced that goal, and can I point to the sentence? 3 Disaster Can I state how the unit ends in a sentence containing but or worse ? 4 Cost What did the character pay, and in what currency (time, money, trust, an ally, a self-image)? 5 Chain Written as bare events, would each of three links still have happened without the one before it? 6 Three connectives Outlined with only and then , but and therefore , how many and then s are there? 7 Dilemma Can I state each option’s cost in one sentence, and would a sympathetic reader disagree with the choice? 8 Criterion At which decision would the protagonist’s earlier self have chosen differently, and what changed? 9 Reversibility Could the character drop this decision between chapters at no cost? 10 Beat weight Does each beat’s page-space follow its weight in the story? The Dialogue Exchange (Chapter 3) # Test The question 1 Removal Replace the exchange with one written line of summary. What is lost? 2 Want What does each speaker want from the other before this ends, in one sentence each? 3 Status Who holds the upper hand at the first line and at the last, and was it contested? 4 Cost What does each disclosure cost the person making it? 5 Silence What does each speaker choose not to say, and who else is in the room? 6 Implicature Is each turn what was called for? Where it is not, what does the departure imply? 7 Transcript Strip every tag and action beat and read aloud. Can you tell who is speaking? 8 Substitution Could another named character say the exchange’s three best lines? 9 Attribution How many turns carry a tag, how many tags are not said or asked , and what do the action beats do besides identify? 10 Interruption Who takes the floor from whom, and where do interruptions cluster? The Descriptive Detail (Chapter 4) # Test The question 1 Removal Cut the detail. What does the reader no longer know, feel or anticipate? 2 Denotation and connotation Write one sentence on what it shows and one on what it implies. 3 Genericness Would it be equally true of another place of this kind in another book? 4 Substitution Replace it with two other true things. Do they imply different books? 5 Focalisation Whose attention selected it, and does the selection reveal them? 6 Plausibility of attention Would this person, wanting what she wants, in her present state, notice this? 7 Recurrence Where else does the object appear, and what has changed each time? 8 Count How many discrete details, and how many do you want kept? 9 Modifiers and senses (a) Count modifiers per noun. (b) Tally details by sense. 10 Inventory Shuffle the details. Then complete: these details, and not others, because … . The Transition (Chapter 5) # Test The question 1 Anchor Read cold: at what word can you say when, where and whose vantage? Is any delay doing something? 2 Dimension count How many of time, space, protagonist, causality and intentionality change? 3 Launch What does the last sentence before the gap do for the far side? 4 Technique fit Which technique is this, and was it chosen or defaulted to? 5 Momentum At what word does the new unit’s own business begin? 6 Gap content Write in one sentence what happens inside the gap. Will the reader need it? 7 Redundancy Is the reader oriented more than once? 8 Simultaneity Does the reader know whether this unit comes after the last one or alongside it? 9 Echo Could the join do a second job, and if it does one, will a first-time reader notice? 10 Consistency Across the manuscript, does the technique vary with the gap? The Chapter Break (Chapter 6) # Test The question 1 Proposition Can I state in one sentence the question this chapter raised near its start? Can I write its heading, In which… ? 2 Payoff Does the ending resolve, escalate, hold open, recast or exchange that proposition? 3 Permission Is stopping here free, moderate or expensive, and why that price at this point? 4 Stopped reader Close the file for ten minutes, then write what happened, what is open, what you want and how you feel. 5 Placement Moved one beat earlier and one later, can I say why the present position is right? 6 Proportion Does this chapter’s length match its weight in the book? 7 Variety Across eleven consecutive chapters, are the ending types and lengths chosen or defaulted to? 8 Re-entry How many words does the next chapter spend before its own business begins? 9 Container Is this one chapter, or two not yet separated, or one cut in half? 10 Architecture Reading only the headings, Part titles and first and last sentences, is the book’s shape legible? Backstory and Flashback (Chapter 7) # Test The question 1 Momentum What present question is the reader waiting on when the cutaway begins, and how hard is she pressing: low, moderate or at its peak? 2 Register Run the compression check: keep the scene, keep the sentence, or keep neither? 3 Removal Cut it and read the surrounding twenty pages: what is lost, and in which domain? 4 Trigger Is the departure motivated by something in the present, and if not, can this narration afford to go without one? 5 Return Cover the cutaway and read the sentence before it against the sentence after: does the present resume, or has it changed? 6 Reach and extent How far back, and how much time covered, and are they in proportion to what it delivers? 7 Chronology Could a reader at this point write the events in the order they happened? Ask one, and compare with yours. 8 Placement Name three other places this cutaway could go: would it cost less, and recolour more, at any of them? 9 Completing or repeating Is it filling a gap the reader knew was there, or returning to material already told, and if so, what does this pass add? 10 Proportion How much of the book is in the past, and does its declared structure acknowledge that? Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture (Chapter 8) # Test The question 1 Necessity Retold in story order, in a page of summary, what would the book lose? 2 Strand question Can each strand’s question be written in a line, and do the other strands’ pages leave it open? 3 Orientation Within its first two sentences, does each instalment tell the reader which time she is in? 4 Interval Does the reader know how far apart the strands stand, and does the distance change or hold for a reason? 5 Rate Do the strands move at different rates, and does a crossing show the difference? 6 Switch Is each strand left on an open question and entered at a point that pays at once? 7 Convergence Where the strands meet, does the meeting change what at least one of them meant? 8 Withholding Does the arrangement withhold anything, and is there a reason in the book besides the order? The Opening Pages (Chapter 9) # Test The question 1 Contract Can you point to the words that open each contract within the first two pages? 2 Scene Can you complete “In these pages, X is trying to , and is in the way”? 3 Momentum Within the first page, does something change or does someone want something, and after how many words? 4 Voice Could the first paragraph move into another novel, of another genre, unnoticed? 5 Zero context Given only the first two pages, can a reader say who, where and when, what kind of book, and what she wants to know? 6 Promise Do pages 30 to 40 belong to the same book as the opening, in tone, pace and stakes? 7 Inventory Of the details placed in the first two pages, which are redeemed later? 8 Density Read aloud: where does the breath fail, or a listener ask what is happening? 9 Form On what page does the reader learn the book’s structural rules: viewpoints, timelines, apparatus? 10 Abandonment At which sentence would an indifferent reader stop? The Prologue (Chapter 10) # Test The question 1 Higher bar Can you complete “This must sit outside the main narrative because…” with an impossibility, not a preference? 2 Absorption Write the material into Chapter One, then cut it entirely: what breaks each time? 3 Label Would anything change if the prologue were headed Chapter One ? 4 Axis Which of time, place, viewpoint and register carries the load, if any? 5 Register Rewritten in Chapter One’s voice, does the material survive, go flat, or become impossible? 6 Closing For each element the prologue opens, on what page does the book next touch it? 7 Plants Which specifics recur, once or more, and which never? 8 Skip Can a reader who starts at Chapter One follow the whole book, and what does she lose? 9 Genre contract Do the prologue, pages 40 to 60 and the last chapter share pitch, pace, mode and scale? The Middle (Chapter 11) # Test The question 1 Value-shift log Do neighbouring sequences repeat both the shift and the stakes? 2 Option list Does the list shrink between the end of the beginning, the midpoint and the start of the ending, and does each shrinkage have a cause on the page? 3 Reorder Swap two sequences in the summary: does anything break? 4 Midpoint What is different near the centre in the protagonist’s goal, knowledge, mode or fortune? 5 Opposition In each quarter of the middle, does the opposing force act, on the page or through a consequence the protagonist feels? 6 Clock Is there a deadline or limit, does the protagonist know it, and does the time left shorten visibly? 7 Cut Delete the weakest sequence of the middle and reread the ending: what has the ending lost? 8 Question What question is the reader carrying at 40 per cent and at 60 per cent? Arc and Theme (Chapter 12) # Test The question 1 Criterion Is the rule behind the last large decision different from the rule behind the first, and if not, does the book mean it to be the same? 2 Hinge At which decision does the rule change, and is that decision on the page, made by an act? 3 Price What does the decision at the hinge cost under the old rule, and has the reader seen that cost grow? 4 Seed Where is the new rule in the book before the hinge, held by another character or glimpsed and set aside? 5 Constant What about the character is visibly unchanged at the end? 6 Enactment Is the new rule confirmed after the hinge by a situation the book has shown before, answered differently? 7 Question Can the theme be put as a question to which two or more of the book’s decisions give different answers? 8 Answers On the answer map, does the opposition hold an answer the book lets succeed, or makes costly to defeat? The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13) # Test The question 1 Necessity Could report, inference, reassignment, document or ellipsis carry this vantage’s scenes, and what would be lost? 2 Domain Which domains does the grant serve, with a passage as evidence for each? 3 Investment Before the first grant, can the reader say what this character wants? 4 Distinguishability Swap two hundred words between two vantages, changing only the names: could a reader tell? 5 Page-share What share of the book does each vantage hold, in how many sections, from when, with what longest gap? 6 Declaration On what page does the reader learn the book has more than one vantage, and is it before her first deep investment? 7 Late grant Does the payoff cover formal surprise, attention withdrawal and cold start? 8 Knowledge boundary Does the vantage know only what it could know? 9 Scene integrity Inside a continuous scene, does the narration stay with one mind, and if not, has the book established the right to move? 10 Character compression For each named character with no viewpoint: how many scenes, whose explanation of her motives, what repeated tag? The Subplot (Chapter 14) # Test The question 1 Engine Can I state the thread’s goal, conflict and consequence in three sentences without mentioning the protagonist’s goal? 2 Kernel At each of its four or five chief moments, could the thread have gone another way? 3 Tax What does it supply that the main plot cannot by its nature? 4 Analogy What does it say about the main plot, and what would be lost if it were not said? 5 Convergence At what point would deleting it break the main plot’s logic, not merely thin it? 6 Proportion Are its pages proportional to its functions, and to its weight in the reader’s experience? 7 Page-share What share of the book does each thread hold, and does the distribution match the book I think I wrote? 8 Dormancy What is the longest gap between appearances, and what does resumption cost? 9 Removal Cut it on the outline: what is lost, in which domain, and does the loss exceed the pages recovered? 10 Promotion Would the book be better if this thread were the main plot? The Reveal (Chapter 15) # Test The question 1 Double reading Does every passage bearing on the reveal support both a first and a second reading? 2 Teller Is every passage the reveal falsifies inside the account of a teller whom the reveal names and whose motive it explains? 3 Withholder What keeps the truth from the reader until the disclosure, and can the reader see it, at the latest when the reveal comes? 4 Alignment Does the reader learn each fact with, ahead of or after the characters, and is that the alignment the scene needs? 5 Successor For a reveal before the end, what question replaces the one it answers, and is it as strong? 6 Consequence Does any character act differently because of the reveal, or does the ending mean something it would not otherwise? 7 Recognition Is the truth received by a character, in scene, in an act, or delivered as information? 8 Source Does the disclosure come from inside the book’s causal system? The Ending (Chapter 16) # Test The question 1 Retroactive Reread five early scenes chosen at random: what has the ending made of each? 2 Plant audit List what the ending rests on and trace each item to its first appearance: does anything load-bearing appear first in the ending? 3 Earned Complete the situation is resolved because… : is the blank inside the book’s causal system? 4 Inevitability Can a first-time reader predict the end thirty pages out, and can a finished reader build an alternative as good? 5 Domain Which domains does the ending deliver, which does it gesture at, which does it refuse, and does the distribution suit the book’s mode? 6 Proportion What share of the book follows the climax, does each thread’s resolution match the space it took, and how far does the book run past its last decision? 7 Termination Ask a reader of the last two pages whether anything comes after, and what told them. 8 Tonal match Read the last page against three passages from the middle third: are they the same book? 9 Reread Reread three passages the ending changes: do they now yield more? 10 Last line Could the book end on the paragraph before the last without loss? Series and Genre (Chapter 17) # Test The question 1 Shelf Where would a reader of the first chapter shelve the book, and does the last chapter belong on the same shelf? 2 Core promise Does the book keep the core promise of the genre its opening declares? 3 Declared decline For each declined convention, is the decline shown inside the book within the first quarter, and replaced by a promise the book keeps? 4 Variation Does the book vary at least one convention, and is its meaning in the variation? 5 Volume question Can the volume’s question be written in a line, and is it closed inside the volume? 6 Series step What step does each volume take on the series question, and can a reader name it? 7 Re-entry Can a reader who finished the last volume a year ago, and one who never read it, both follow the first chapter? 8 Criterion across volumes Is the hero’s criterion where the last volume left it, and if it has moved, does the volume show the move? The Structural Edit (Chapter 18) # Test The question 1 Map Is there a book map built from the draft, with the change column filled for every row? 2 Promise Can the promise and the governing question be written in two sentences, and do the first and last chapters answer to them? 3 Rung-up For each failure on the edit list, has the rung above been checked for its cause? 4 Reopen For each repair, are the tests it reopens listed, and have they been rerun? 5 Economy Does each repair answer at least as many notes as it reopens tests, and does the edit cut or move more than it adds? 6 Opening last Were the opening pages and the last page revised after rungs 1 to 3 had settled? 7 Stop Does a cold read produce notes that do not cluster above rung 5, and is every kept failure defended in a sentence? chapter: Chapter 1 · The Purposes of a Scene
title: The Purposes of a Scene
text: What a scene is for, and how to tell whether it is doing it The Craft Behind the Story (Second Edition) — Chapter 1. Part I: The Scene and Its Materials. In brief. A scene earns its place in a novel by changing something. Ask of each scene in a draft what was true when it opened and is no longer true when it closes; if the honest answer is “nothing”, the passage is setting rather than scene. The change can happen in five domains — the action, a person, the book’s meaning, the reader’s experience of the world, or what lies between two people — and a well-built scene usually moves two or three of them with the same material. The chapter’s tools are a two-sentence statement of the change, an audit of those five registers, a deliberate choice of narrative speed, and ten diagnostic questions. Use them one scene at a time when revising a finished draft, not while drafting. A scene that fails them may still belong in the book; its author should be able to say why. What you can do after this chapter State, for any scene in your draft, what changed in it, in two parallel sentences. Say which of the five registers a scene serves and which it merely occupies, and find the second job a single-purpose scene could do without growing longer. Decide whether a piece of material should be a scene at all, or a paragraph of summary, an ellipsis or a habitual passage. Diagnose a flat scene by its mechanism (no want, no resistance, no change, redundancy, wrong speed) rather than by how it feels. Recognise when a scene that fails every test is the right choice for the book. Key terms Scene, beat, sequence; summary, duration; kernel and satellite; focalisation; value shift; period convention; the five domains of purpose and the relational domain; multiplicity; the scene–summary continuum, iterative narration, substitution testing; the reverse outline. Each is defined at first use and collected in the consolidated glossary . Contents The first files build the instrument, the middle ones apply it, and the last are for use at the desk. The Problem Two drafts of one passage, and the chapter’s claim Definitions The scene, its boundaries, summary, adjacent terms How It Works Removability, duration, events and memory, and the test’s limits The Taxonomy The five domains of purpose The Mechanism The engine of a scene, multiplicity, and the choice of narrative speed Diagnostic Tests Ten questions on one page, and the reverse outline Failure Patterns Five recurrent failures, each tested against a published example Worked Analyses Three close readings , Fleabag, and the household revision case Checklist and Exercises The revision checklist and five exercises for your own draft Coda What the tests are for A writer already in revision can start at the diagnostic tests and use the checklist as the working page. The full treatment The Reference layer holds the complete chapter, The Purposes of a Scene : all fourteen modes of the scene–summary continuum, ten failure patterns, eight close readings, the scene in the short story, the novella, screen drama and translation, seminar questions and an assessment rubric, and the sources. See also: Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2), for what follows a scene; The Dialogue Exchange (Chapter 3), which adopts the five domains for talk.

chapter: Chapter 1 · The Purposes of a Scene
title: 1. The Problem: Scenery
text: Two drafts of one passage The household novel, whose drafts and revisions run through every chapter of this book, is a quiet contemporary family novel set in a British town. A father who kept a small shop died in March; his three children, Elena, Nadia and Dov, are left with the shop, the flat above it, his coat on its hook, and the leather ledger in which he recorded eleven years of the shop’s ordinary arithmetic. A draft chapter of that novel contains a passage of about nine hundred words in which Nadia climbs the stairs to the flat. She lets herself in, fills the kettle, and looks for a while at her father’s coat, army green gone the colour of dishwater, with the left cuff frayed through where he used to hook his thumb before he spoke. She remembers the habit. She washes the two cups in the sink, counts the cups in the cupboard, and goes back down to the shop. The prose is careful and the observation is good, and a reader finishes the passage having enjoyed it in the mild way one enjoys competent description. A day later the reader remembers nothing of it. Now suppose a second draft of the same passage, identical except for three sentences. Nadia looks at the coat and sees that its shoulders have been brushed: the dust that lies on the rest of the coat and everything else in the flat has not settled there. She has not brushed them. She washes the cups, counts the cupboard, and goes back down, and she does not ring anyone to ask who has been coming up the stairs. Nothing in the prose has improved. Yet the reader now holds a fact that Nadia has chosen not to pursue, a question the book has not answered, and a reading of Nadia herself, who would rather count cups than know. The next forty pages will be read differently. What the difference shows Two things follow from the comparison, and the rest of the chapter is built on them. The first is that the difference between the drafts is almost invisible while writing, since both feel like productive work and contain the same quantity of careful observation. It appears only when the passage is read as part of a finished draft and the writer asks what it did, which is why the diagnosis this chapter teaches belongs to revision and is harmful during composition. The second is that the quality of the prose is not evidence about the scene. A well-written passage that does nothing is harder to cut than a badly written one, and is cut less often, which is how manuscripts come to accumulate them. The claim The principle the chapter examines can be put in one sentence: If nothing changes, the scene is not a scene: it is scenery. The sentence is deliberately harsh. It claims that a stretch of dramatised narrative must answer for the reader’s attention and the book’s length, and that it answers in one currency, a change of state. It does not claim that the change must be large, external or visible to the characters. In chapter 42 of Henry James’s The Portrait of a Lady a woman spends much of the night by the fire and comes to understand her marriage, though little happens outwardly; the chapter is examined among the worked analyses . Nor does it claim that summary is a lesser mode: much of what a draft calls a flat scene is a paragraph of summary inflated into dialogue and stage business because the writer believed scenes are always better, and the chapter argues that they are not. Finally, it does not describe narrative in general: the preference for the dramatised scene over the narrated report is prominent in much twentieth-century Anglo-American craft advice, and its limits are set out in How It Works . Where this chapter sits Later chapters depend on this chapter’s vocabulary. The value-shift test, the question what changed? , returns in Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2), The Dialogue Exchange (Chapter 3), The Descriptive Detail (Chapter 4), The Transition (Chapter 5) and The Ending (Chapter 16). The five domains of purpose are adopted by The Dialogue Exchange (Chapter 3), The Descriptive Detail (Chapter 4) and Backstory and Flashback (Chapter 7), each of which proposes a further domain, and The Dialogue Exchange (Chapter 3) also adopts the relational domain proposed here. The cost of a scene in the reader’s attention becomes, in The Subplot (Chapter 14), the cost of a second line of story, and multiplicity recurs in every chapter. Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2) owns the rhythm of the dramatic unit, Dwight Swain’s division of it into a scene proper (goal, conflict, disaster) and a sequel (reaction, dilemma, decision). This chapter uses “scene” in the ordinary sense of any continuous stretch of dramatised action. See also: the Reference introduction ; The Descriptive Detail (Chapter 4), where the coat is worked as a detail.

chapter: Chapter 1 · The Purposes of a Scene
title: 2. Definitions
text: The working definition A scene is a unit of story in which a character pursues a concrete, immediate objective against resistance, rendered at something close to the pace at which it happens, so that the state of the story is measurably different at its end from its state at its start. Three parts of the definition carry most of its weight. The first is the concrete, immediate objective. This is not the story goal, the want that drives the whole book, but the scene goal, the want that drives the next ten minutes. Elena’s story goal is to find out why the shop’s locks were changed in March. Her goal in the doorway of her brother’s house, when he hands her the new key, is smaller and more urgent: to get the key without having to hear something she is not ready for, or to get the reason without having to ask for it twice. A reader who does not yet care about the story goal can still be carried by a scene goal, which is why the distinction matters most on the opening pages ( The Opening Pages , Chapter 9). The second is resistance. It is the component most often missing from draft scenes. A want that meets no obstacle produces activity rather than a scene, and the obstacle need not be a person: it can be the character’s own reluctance, the shape of the situation, or time running out. The third is pace. Dramatisation is not a matter of dialogue or action, which are the scene’s usual materials, but of the rate at which the telling moves relative to the events told, which How It Works explains. Where a scene ends There is no principled word count for a scene. Three units of different size are in common use, and each answers a different question. Unit Typical extent The question it answers Beat 20–300 words What is the smallest exchange in which the balance between people shifts? Scene 400–3,000 words What is the smallest unit that could be lifted out and still read as a story? Sequence 3,000–12,000 words What is the smallest unit that completes a movement of the plot? The figures are illustrative working ranges for this chapter, given only to show scale; they are not measured norms. A beat is the smallest unit of change, one exchange or action that alters the balance; the word comes from acting and screenwriting practice. A sequence is a run of scenes that together complete one movement of the plot. The working rule for the boundary of the middle unit is functional: a scene ends when the value it was moving stops moving, or when there is a break in time, place or viewpoint. Summary is not a failed scene The commonest confusion in workshop discussion is to treat summary as a scene that has not been written yet. Summary is narrated report, in which a stretch of story time is compressed into a shorter stretch of text and told rather than enacted: For the next three weeks she did not go near the shop covers three weeks in twelve words. It is a different speed with different uses, and the modes between it and the full scene are set out in The Mechanism . Adjacent terms Four neighbouring terms recur in this chapter, in the senses the table gives. Term Sense in this book Relation to the scene Sequel In Swain’s model, the reflective unit after a scene: reaction, dilemma, decision Treated in full in Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2) Set piece An extended scene of spectacle: a battle, a ball, a storm, a party A scene marked by scale and by the reader’s expectation of it; its failure mode is among the failure patterns Scene (screen) A dramatic unit in more or less continuous time and space; it may contain many shots and cuts Screen scenes often mark a change of time or place, but a cut alone need not end one Kernel and satellite Events that branch the story, and events that amplify a branch already taken The distinction the extraction test measures; explained in How It Works The prose sense of a scene is the broadest of these, and the other terms either subdivide it or describe what surrounds it. What this chapter leaves to other chapters The chapter concerns the single scene and what it is for. The rhythm of scene and sequel belongs to Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2), talk to The Dialogue Exchange (Chapter 3), and the descriptive detail to The Descriptive Detail (Chapter 4). Movement between scenes belongs to The Transition (Chapter 5), The Chapter Break (Chapter 6) and The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13), and scenes set in the past to Backstory and Flashback (Chapter 7). The allocation of scenes between plot lines is the subject of The Subplot (Chapter 14), redundancy in the long middle of a book that of The Middle (Chapter 11), and theme at the scale of the book that of Arc and Theme (Chapter 12). Opening, prefatory and final scenes belong to The Opening Pages (Chapter 9), The Prologue (Chapter 10) and The Ending (Chapter 16). See also: the Reference definitions ; Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2).

chapter: Chapter 1 · The Purposes of a Scene
title: 3. How It Works
text: Four strands of theory support the method, each given only as far as the method uses it and introduced by the question a reviser is asking when it becomes useful. Could this scene go? Removability, kernels and satellites A writer who suspects a scene could be cut needs a test that does not depend on whether the scene is enjoyable. The oldest is Aristotle’s. In chapter 8 of the Poetics (c. 335 BCE; translated by Malcolm Heath, 1996) he argues that a plot is unified by the internal relation of its parts, so that if any part is displaced or removed the whole is disturbed; anything whose presence or absence makes no perceptible difference is no part of the whole. In chapter 9 he adds that events in a plot should follow one another by necessity or probability, because rather than merely after , and he calls the worst kind of plot the episodic one, in which episodes succeed one another without either. Roland Barthes (1966; translated by Stephen Heath, 1977) separated the functions that open or close a consequential alternative from those that fill the space between them, and Seymour Chatman, in Story and Discourse (1978), gave the distinction the names writers now use. Kernels are branching points, moments at which the story could go one of several ways. Satellites amplify a path already chosen. Deleting a kernel breaks the story’s logic; deleting a satellite impoverishes the story without breaking it. The extraction test among the diagnostic tests is this distinction turned into a question a writer can put to a scene. What does “dramatised” mean, if not dialogue? Duration Writers often equate a scene with dialogue, and the equation produces scenes that are talk without event. Gérard Genette’s Narrative Discourse (1972; translated by Jane E. Lewin, 1980) offers a better criterion. He analyses duration , the relation between story time (how long the events notionally take) and text time (how many words or pages the text gives them), through four basic movements. In ellipsis, story time passes and the text gives it nothing ( three years later ). In summary, the text is shorter than the time it covers. In scene, the two are roughly equal, so that reading feels like being present. In the descriptive pause, the text expands while the story stands still. A scene, on this account, is the mode in which the telling moves at about the pace of the events it tells. Dialogue is its usual carrier, not its criterion. Screen drama can show the criterion directly: a continuous take presents action in real time, though an ordinary filmed scene may contain many cuts without a lapse in story time. After an opening montage, “Review”, the seventh episode of the first season of The Bear (FX, 2022), holds that ratio for a continuous take of about eighteen minutes. A pre-order system left switched on floods a restaurant kitchen with orders, the head chef turns on his staff, and the sous-chef walks out before opening; the sustained take denies the viewer the ellipsis that would let the service end. Prose seldom holds isochrony, the equality of text time and story time, for so long. The duration account also explains why “show, don’t tell” is a poor guide. Percy Lubbock’s distinction between “picture” and “scene” in The Craft of Fiction (1921) is one influential formulation of the underlying contrast, but the slogan can conflate three separate variables: duration, narratorial stance (presentation against commentary) and diction (the concrete against the abstract). Wayne Booth’s The Rhetoric of Fiction (1961) showed that all narrative is told and that showing is one rhetorical strategy among several. This chapter uses only the first variable. Why does a scene in which nothing changes leave no trace? Events and memory The reader’s failure to remember the first draft of Nadia’s visit to the flat, in The Problem , has a partial explanation. Mieke Bal, in Narratology (1985; fourth edition 2017), defines an event as the transition from one state to another. On that definition an occurrence that leaves every state as it was is not an event, however much activity it contains: they talked for an hour is not an event, and they talked for an hour and afterwards he would not look at her contains one. Discourse psychology offers a related account of comprehension. Rolf Zwaan and Gabriel Radvansky’s review “Situation Models in Language Comprehension and Memory” ( Psychological Bulletin , 1998) describes readers as building a situation model , a mental representation of the state of affairs a text describes, which they update along dimensions such as protagonist, place, time, causation and intention. Work on event segmentation finds that people divide continuous experience into events at points of change; Nicole Speer, Jeffrey Zacks and Jeremy Reynolds reported brain activity time-locked to such boundaries while participants read narratives (“Human Brain Activity Time-Locked to Narrative Event Boundaries”, Psychological Science , 2007). These studies do not establish that a passage without a state change leaves little to remember: readers may remember its imagery, language or mood. Using transitions as a revision test is this chapter’s inference, not a finding of those studies. Bal supplies one further term. Focalisation is the separation of the one who perceives from the one who speaks: the narration may be in the third person while what is seen is what one character sees. A change of state is always a change for someone, and a scene in which the value shifts for a character other than the focaliser is a scene told from the wrong side. The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13) treats the problem at the scale of the book. How far does the test bind? The value shift and the period convention The test this chapter applies to every scene is the value shift : a scene that earns its place moves some charged value (trust, safety, knowledge, hope, standing, intimacy) from one pole towards its opposite, so that something is true at its close that was not true at its start. The term is Robert McKee’s, from Story (1997), a book about screenwriting, where each unit is under heavier pressure than in a long novel. McKee insists that the value be charged, meaning that the story has already made the reader care about it, and that requirement is what separates a value shift from mere incident. Four qualifications follow, and they govern how the test is used. The test measures charge rather than size: a scene in which a woman notices that her husband has stopped asking about her day has shifted a value, and a car chase in which nothing is risked has not. The shift need not be visible to any character; it may happen entirely inside one mind, as in the James chapter, or entirely in the reader’s knowledge, as in scenes of dramatic irony , in which the reader knows something a character does not and so hears every line twice. Chapter 94 of Moby-Dick , examined among the failure patterns , does not advance the hunt, but Ishmael’s feeling towards his shipmates changes; it therefore fails a plot-only test, not the broader value-shift test. The test is also the instrument of a period convention , a preference that belongs to a time and a tradition rather than to narrative itself. Henry Fielding’s Tom Jones (1749) summarises months in a paragraph and reserves full dramatisation for selected occasions, giving them particular weight. Genette found a different proportion in Proust, with summary nearly absent. Both are deliberate designs, and applied without regard to period or form the test can report failures that are not failures. The test is therefore not a standard every scene must meet but an instrument that makes a writer’s choice visible, so that a scene that fails it can be kept knowingly, for a stated reason. See also: the full theoretical account in Reference , including Freytag, Barthes’s code of actions and the historical table of scene–summary proportions; The Transition (Chapter 5), on ellipsis.

chapter: Chapter 1 · The Purposes of a Scene
title: 4. The Taxonomy: Five Domains of Purpose
text: The value-shift test asks whether something changed, not in what domain, and a writer revising a flat scene needs the second answer because each domain has its own remedies. This chapter uses five domains of purpose : plot (the action changes), character (a person changes, or is revealed), theme (the meaning changes), texture (the reader’s experience changes), and the relational domain (what lies between two people changes). The fifth is this chapter’s proposal, and The Dialogue Exchange (Chapter 3) adopts it. The domains are lenses rather than boxes: a betrayal is at once a turn in the plot, a revelation of character and a statement of theme, and the model supplies five questions to ask of one scene. They are also an instrument for revision, not a target for drafting, since aiming at all five produces the overloaded scene described in The Mechanism . Plot: the action changes A scene serves the plot when it alters the causal chain: what has happened, what can now happen, what must now happen. It may advance the chain a step, complicate it with an obstacle or a cost, escalate the stakes of a conflict already running, turn it by a reversal, resolve a question the book has held open, or plant an object or a fact that a later scene will pay off. Because of planting, a scene that seems to do little may be indispensable, and the extraction test has to be run forwards as well as backwards: not only what would the reader fail to know? but what later scene would become unearned? Plot is easy to fake, because activity resembles consequence. Its characteristic under-delivery is the errand, a scene that moves a body from one place to another and calls the movement plot. Its over-delivery is the pile-up, three reversals in nine hundred words, each devaluing the last, since a reversal is legible only against a stable expectation. In Part One, chapter 7, of Dostoevsky’s Crime and Punishment (1866; in Constance Garnett’s translation), the murder of the pawnbroker is the planned turn, but the structurally decisive event is the unplanned one: her sister Lizaveta comes home and is killed too. A crime Raskolnikov had theorised becomes one he cannot explain to himself, and the rest of the novel runs on the difference. A scene’s plot value often lies in its departure from what a character planned. Character: a person changes, or is revealed A scene serves character when it alters what the reader knows about a person, or alters the person, under conditions that make the alteration evidence rather than assertion. It may reveal an existing trait through action under pressure, test a stated belief to see whether it holds, move a character a measurable step along an arc, complicate the reader’s sympathy, or show the gap between what a character says of herself and what she does. The carriers are behavioural: a choice made quickly, what someone notices, whom they lie to. The commonest error is the comfortable occasion, in which a character is given a confidant or a well-placed question and is simply herself; nothing is learned because nothing is risked. The domain’s under-delivery is the trait exhibition, a scene demonstrating a quality the reader has already accepted. Its over-delivery is the epiphany, in which a character understands herself completely, in words she would not have, at the convenient end of a chapter. In chapter 7 of Chinua Achebe’s Things Fall Apart (1958), Okonkwo cuts down Ikemefuna, the boy who has lived in his household for three years, and Achebe gives the motive in one short sentence after the act: he was afraid of being thought weak. Nothing about Okonkwo changes in that scene; the reader’s understanding of him does. Theme: the meaning changes A scene serves theme when it stages the book’s governing question in a form that produces meaning the scene does not state. Theme works better as the book’s repeated question than as a message: what the living owe the dead’s silences, in the household novel; what a marriage is for; what an institution does to the people inside it. A scene serves the domain when it puts that question to a character in circumstances where any answer costs something. Its instruments are a choice whose terms are the book’s terms, a mirror or a foil (two characters or events set side by side so that their difference means something), dramatic irony, and the recurrence of a motif under changed conditions. Its under-delivery is the name-check, one line that sounds like the book’s title; its over-delivery is the mouthpiece, a character who exists to state the theme. Counterpoint, two strands running at once without comment, does the domain’s work without either. In Part Two, chapter 8, of Flaubert’s Madame Bovary (1857; in Geoffrey Wall’s translation, 1992), Rodolphe’s seduction speech is intercut with the announcement of prizes at an agricultural show, for manure and livestock and fifty-four years of a servant’s labour, and the novel’s argument about the language of romance is produced entirely by adjacency. Texture: the experience changes A scene serves texture when it alters the reader’s sensory, tonal or temporal experience of the book: where they feel they are, what register they are in, how fast the book is moving. Its functions are to ground the reader in a place, set a tone, control pace, deliver a set piece the book has promised, and establish the normal, the baseline against which a later departure will register. That last function is the domain’s best defence. A scene that establishes what is ordinary in a world is load-bearing for a later scene, and the extraction test has to be run on the pair: remove the ordinary scene and it is the later one that loses its force. Under-delivery here is the generic room with a table in it, and over-delivery is the runaway set piece, spectacle at great length with every other value where it started. Richard Osman’s The Thursday Murder Club (2020), a comic crime novel set in a retirement village, alternates its third-person investigation with chapters from Joyce’s diary, written in the first person. By a strict plot accounting the diary chapters are the slackest material in the book: domestic news, opinions, the small politics of the village. They establish the normal life of the place against which the murders register, set a comic register that lets the book be about death without solemnity, and pace the investigation by supplying rests between its chapters. Relational: what lies between them changes Ask what changed in a quarrel between siblings over a key, or in the Hunsford proposal in Austen’s Pride and Prejudice , and the honest answer is rarely the plot and rarely either person. It is what lies between them. The chapter therefore proposes a fifth domain. A scene serves the relational domain when it alters the state of a relationship (the distribution of trust, power, obligation, intimacy, debt or hostility between two or more people) so that their later dealings must proceed on different terms. Two arguments support separating it from character. Relations change while both parties stay the same: after Hunsford neither Darcy nor Elizabeth is a different person, but both hold a radically revised view of each other, and the character domain, which records what a scene shows about one person, has no vocabulary for a change located in neither party and real in both. The carriers also differ. A relation is carried by forms of address and changes in them, by who begins and who yields in conversation, by physical distance, by who may say nothing without being asked what is wrong, by shared jokes that still work or no longer land, by who knows what about whom, and by the questions each may still put to the other. There are fair objections: a relation may be only a pair of mental states, one in each person, and so belong to character; admitting every category with distinct carriers would multiply domains until the model lost its use; and most relational shifts can be redescribed as plot. The chapter adopts the fifth domain for diagnosis on an asymmetry of error: writers who audit for four domains routinely fail to notice that no relational shift has happened, whereas writers who audit for five rarely mistake a plot shift for a relational one. The blind spot it removes is the family novel in which nothing between anybody ever changes. Sally Rooney’s Normal People (2018) is read in the worked analyses as a novel whose principal events are relational. How many domains at once A scene need not serve every domain, and the model is misused when it is read that way. The table summarises how each domain is usually established and how it usually goes wrong. Domain Established chiefly by Under-delivery Over-delivery Plot A choice that closes options; a plant; an irreversible act The errand; recapitulation The reversal pile-up Character Behaviour at a cost; the gap between account and act The trait exhibition The epiphany Theme Juxtaposition; recurrence; dramatic irony The name-check The mouthpiece Texture Exact nouns; rhythm; ritual; the established normal The generic room The runaway set piece Relational Address, turn-taking, permitted silence, the right to ask The relation stated rather than enacted Every scene a renegotiation The realistic target is two domains, occasionally three, and the allocation depends on the book and on the scene’s position. A thriller weights plot and may serve character mainly through action; a novel of consciousness may run for pages with the plot idle; a final scene usually has to close in several domains at once. The domains stay constant, while the allocation is chosen for each genre and position. See also: the Reference taxonomy , with each domain’s functions and carriers in tabular form; The Dialogue Exchange (Chapter 3), for the relational domain in talk.

chapter: Chapter 1 · The Purposes of a Scene
title: 5. The Mechanism: Engine, Economy and Speed
text: A scene produces change by a mechanism with three parts: an engine makes something happen, multiplicity determines how much the happening is worth, and the choice of speed decides whether the material should be a scene at all. The engine A scene’s engine is a want that operates now, a resistance to it, and a cost. The third converts activity into consequence: a want that overcomes resistance at no cost has the shape of conflict and none of its effects, so the useful question after any scene is what did getting it cost? The engine has one variant that looks like a failure. A want may be granted at once, and the granting may itself be the disaster. In chapter 18 of Dickens’s Great Expectations (1861), the lawyer Jaggers finds Pip and Joe at the Three Jolly Bargemen, then tells them in the parlour that Pip has great expectations and is to be brought up as a gentleman. Pip wants what he is given, but the transaction has conditions, and Joe resists Jaggers’s manner and refuses payment for releasing Pip from his apprenticeship. The cost lies in Pip’s response to the news and in the estrangement from Joe that follows. The engine also tells a writer where a scene stops: when the value stops moving, and anything after that point slackens it. Multiplicity Multiplicity is the practice of making one unit of text discharge several narrative functions at once. At the scale of the scene it is best stated as an economy. A novel has a finite number of scenes, each of which costs the reader time and takes up space in the book; a scene that serves one domain has spent a scene’s worth of attention to buy one function, and a scene that serves three has bought three at the same price. The practical instruction is not to add domains but to notice which are already latent: almost every draft scene contains an unexploited second function in material already present. The opening of Darcy’s first proposal, in chapter 34 of Austen’s Pride and Prejudice (1813), shows how much work a few phrases can do: In vain I have struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you. The speech opens on the vocabulary of defeat, so the reader learns first that this man experiences love as a failure of self-government; that is character, and because the first words are about him rather than her, it is also relational. It will not do is the idiom one uses of an unsatisfactory arrangement, applied to a passion, which makes it texture and character at once. The passive my feelings will not be repressed removes him as agent. You first appears in an instruction, you must allow me , which shapes the refusal that follows. And ardently , the one word in which feeling escapes control, collides with it will not do to open the novel’s question about feeling and judgement. Elizabeth’s answer does the same work in reverse. She tells him he could not have made her the offer of his hand in any possible way that would have tempted her to accept it, and in any possible way refuses not this proposal but every proposal from this man. The clause also closes her own options, and the rest of the book is needed to reopen them. Revision often looks for multiplicity in metaphor. At the scale of the scene the work is usually done in four humbler places. The first is the physical business, what hands do while mouths talk: a man who goes on wrapping shop stock in newspaper through an accusation supplies texture (the chore), character (the refusal to stop), relation (he will not give her his attention) and plot (a man packing a shop has already decided something). The second is the object that changes hands. A key, a ledger or a plate passed or withheld registers power between two people without a word spoken, which is how the doorway exchange in The Dialogue Exchange (Chapter 3) works, when Dov gives Elena the new key and keeps the reason. The third is what a character declines to say or ask. An unasked question costs no words, and when one sibling does not ask another where he was in March the omission does character, relational and plot work while the reader performs the inference. The fourth is placement against the reader’s knowledge: a scene the reader enters knowing more than the characters means two things in every line, so dramatic irony multiplies functions without adding text. Multiplicity has a ceiling, and the failure at the ceiling is the overloaded scene. Its symptoms are that every line is significant, so that emphasis becomes impossible; that several characters each pursue a different want in one room, so that the reader cannot tell whose scene it is; that the reader can say what is being established but not what is happening; and that every object means something, so that the reader stops believing in the room. The remedy is to let some scenes do only one thing, because a reader who is never allowed to rest cannot register emphasis. Speed: the scene–summary continuum A prior question is at what speed the material should be narrated. The scene–summary continuum is the range of modes between full scene and ellipsis; the Reference chapter sets out fourteen, and the eight below cover most revision decisions. Mode What it is It buys It costs Full scene The occasion rendered moment by moment Presence; the clearest value shift Length; flattened proportion if used everywhere Compressed scene Scene texture with hours removed at the joins Scenic force at a fraction of the length Clumsy joins read as lapses Scene within summary A summary that opens for a paragraph into one rendered moment Proof that the summary is true Repeated moments can turn a summary into a sequence of scenes Singulative summary Plain report of a bounded stretch of time Speed; the power to say this mattered less May offer less immediate experience; overuse reads as synopsis Iterative summary One narration of something that happened many times A life rather than an episode; the normal Individual occasions and choices may be less distinct Interiorised scene An occasion rendered as thought, paced by thought Deep change with no external event Needs a mind worth following for pages Ellipsis The event is not narrated; the reader infers it The reader supplies what the text withholds An ellipsis over an unguessable event is a gap Documentary rendering The event delivered as a letter, entry or report A change of state through a document Access to perception is limited by what the document maker records The mode most often missing from contemporary drafts is iterative narration, which tells once what happened many times: every week someone brushed the shoulders of the coat . One dramatised occasion can illustrate a habit, but it cannot by itself establish its duration or repetition: a writer who tries to convey eleven years of a man’s ledger-keeping by dramatising one Tuesday has shown the reader only one Tuesday. The continuum is used by substitution testing : take a scene that is not working, rewrite it in two modes as far from its own as possible (a full scene as summary and as ellipsis, say), and judge only when all three versions exist. If the summary loses nothing, use the summary. If it loses something the writer cannot name, the scene has a function nobody has identified, and the next step is to name it and strengthen it. If it loses something the writer can name at once, the scene is doing its job, and the revision is to cut whatever in it is not that job. The domain audit The mechanism can be checked across a chapter with a table. For each scene, write its length and the letters of every domain it actively serves (P, C, T, X for texture, R), and beside each letter write the specific change in three or four words: not character but she stops defending him . A letter that cannot be annotated marks a domain the scene occupies rather than serves, and is struck out. If most scenes carry a single letter, the draft is spending scenes one function at a time; if most carry four or five, the reader has no rests. A long scene carrying only X is either a runaway set piece or a scene establishing the normal, and the question that separates them is which later scene it serves. See also: the Reference treatment of multiplicity , with the full Hunsford anatomy; the full continuum of fourteen modes .

chapter: Chapter 1 · The Purposes of a Scene
title: 6. Diagnostic Tests
text: The ten tests below are for revision, not composition: several ask questions only a finished scene can answer. The output of each should be a sentence describing what the scene does, not a pass or a fail, since ten sentences describe a scene and ten ticks describe nothing. A failed test is a question about a choice, and every test here is failed by at least one scene this chapter admires. Test 1 — The want test What does the viewpoint character want in this scene, right now, in one sentence? Failure. No engine: the passage is an occasion, not a scene. Exception. Scenes of pure reception, where bad news comes to someone who wanted nothing. Test 2 — The resistance test Complete: “___ wants ___, and ___ is in the way.” What did getting it cost? Failure. Activity rather than scene; nominal resistance overcome for free. Exception. The want granted at once, where the granting is the disaster ( Great Expectations , chapter 18). Test 3 — The value-shift test What is true at the start that is no longer true at the close, in two parallel sentences? Failure. The engine idles: a want is pursued and nothing moves. Exception. Scenes establishing the normal, whose shift arrives in a later scene; run the test on the pair. Test 4 — The extraction test Remove the scene. What would the reader fail to learn, feel or expect, and which later scene becomes unearned? Failure. A satellite given a kernel’s length. Exception. A plant whose value appears only forwards, which is why the test runs in both directions. Test 5 — The domain-count test Which domains does the scene serve, as distinct from occupy? Failure. One annotated letter: under-used space. Exception. Rests and normal-establishing scenes, which should serve one. Test 6 — The redundancy test Has the reader already received this shift? Failure. The book is repeating itself, usually in its middle. Exception. Repetition as argument (Kafka’s The Trial , chapter 5). Test 7 — The summary-substitution test Rewrite the scene as three sentences of summary. What is lost? Failure. A summary inflated into a scene. Exception. Summary can carry atmosphere too; the question is what, if anything, the fuller rendering contributes here. Test 8 — The entry-and-exit test Does the scene start as late and end as early as it can? Failure. The scene opens before the want is in operation, or runs on past its last movement. Exception. A slow entry that builds the normal the shift will break (the reaping morning in The Hunger Games ). Test 9 — The pressure test Does information arrive under pressure, or is it delivered? Failure. Exposition in disguise: a briefing with stage furniture. Exception. Exposition that is itself the crisis (the Grand Inquisitor). Test 10 — The register test Is the story due for an action unit or a reflective one, and which is this? Failure. Several units of one register in a row: incident without consequence, or brooding without motion. Exception. A deliberate run of one register to produce exhaustion or stasis. The exceptions are all discussed in this chapter: the Kafka and Dostoevsky cases among the failure patterns , The Hunger Games among the worked analyses . Reading the results together Failures cluster, and the cluster points to the remedy. When tests 1 (Want) and 2 (Resistance) fail together, the scene has no engine: find the want or convert the passage to summary. When test 3 (Value shift) fails alone, the engine idles: make the pursuit cost something. When tests 3 (Value shift), 4 (Extraction) and 6 (Redundancy) fail together, they usually mark a fossil of discovery drafting, which can be cut once its one useful sentence has been moved. When tests 1 to 3 (Want, Resistance and Value shift) pass but test 5 (Domain count) returns four or five domains, the scene is overloaded and needs less. When a scene fails test 3 (Value shift), the instinctive remedy is to add an event, which treats a structural absence as a shortage of content. The stronger remedy is to find the shift already latent in the scene, which the writer has usually muffled by continuing past it (test 8: Entry and exit) or by having a character announce it. The reverse outline The tests examine one scene; the reverse outline examines a book. Go through the finished draft and write one line per scene, in order, in a single document. Write each line in the language of consequence rather than of event: not Elena and Dov talk in the doorway but Elena gets the new key and not the reason . Add each scene’s length and domain letters, then read the document straight through. A line that will only come out event-shaped marks a satellite; two lines that say the same thing mark redundancy; a run of six lines without an R or a P shows a domain gone dark; and the end of the first movement arriving at forty per cent of the book shows a problem of proportion no scene-level test can see. See also: the Reference protocol , with each test’s procedure and a table of combined failures; The Middle (Chapter 11), for redundancy at the scale of the book.

chapter: Chapter 1 · The Purposes of a Scene
title: 7. Failure Patterns
text: The five patterns below are described by their underlying mechanisms rather than their surface symptoms, so that the remedy follows from the cause. Each ends with a published example that tests the diagnosis: some are apparent faults that prove purposeful when read in the context of the book. The Reference chapter’s full catalogue adds five further patterns: the one-note scene, the runaway set piece, the meeting to decide, the scene that resolves at its own climax, and the over-polished second-draft scene. The purposeless scene Symptom. The scene occupies pages and shifts no value in any domain. It is usually pleasant and often well observed, and it cannot be summarised in the language of consequence. Mechanism. A satellite has been given a kernel’s resources. The scene exists because it was written, and it was written because the writer needed it: drafting by discovery requires passages that find the story, and those passages are scaffolding rather than narrative. The writer needed to write it; the reader does not need to read it. Remedy. Run the extraction test in both directions, then work down a ladder of remedies: compress the scene into a paragraph of summary, fuse it with a neighbouring scene that has a job, relocate its one load-bearing sentence into a scene that already exists, and cut it only as a last resort. Most purposeless scenes contain one sentence that matters. Apparent exception. Chapter 94 of Melville’s Moby-Dick (1851), “A Squeeze of the Hand”, has Ishmael and his shipmates kneading lumps out of cooling spermaceti until Ishmael finds himself squeezing his companions’ hands in a rhapsody of fellow feeling. No major plot event follows from the work, and Ahab is absent. But Ishmael says he forgets the crew’s terrible oath and feels free of ill will: his emotional state and feeling towards his companions change. The chapter therefore fails a plot-only test, not the broader value-shift test. Its texture also carries an argument: remove the chapter and the book loses a felt version of Ishmael’s alternative to Ahab’s monomania. The redundant scene Symptom. A second scene establishes what the reader already knows: another demonstration of a cruelty, another quarrel on the same terms, another refusal to answer the same question. Mechanism. The value shift has already been banked. Once a reader has registered a change of state, the state is changed, and a scene that performs the change again asks the reader to learn something twice, which reads as the book losing confidence. Remedy. Choose the better-placed of the two scenes, usually the earlier unless the later is better made, and delete the other. Differentiating them does not help: a redundant scene made more interesting is still redundant. Exception. In chapter 5 of Kafka’s The Trial (1925; translated by Breon Mitchell, 1998), Josef K. opens a lumber-room door in his bank and finds two warders being flogged on account of his own complaint about them. The next evening he opens the same door and finds the same scene unchanged, and shuts it. The repetition is the novel’s argument: with the trial’s progress uncertain and the court’s reach diffuse, the discovery that yesterday is still happening is itself consequential to K. The expository scene in disguise Symptom. The scene has the furniture of drama (a room, two people, someone pouring a drink) and exists to deliver information. Characters ask questions whose answers they already know, and one of them explains the situation with unusual fluency. Mechanism. Information is being supplied rather than transacted. It arrives without cost to the person parting with it, so the scene has no engine and the briefing has been dressed as a scene. Remedy. Put the information in the hands of someone who does not want to give it, in front of someone who should not hear it. The three components are reluctance, an audience and a cost, and any two usually suffice. Exception. The Grand Inquisitor chapter of Dostoevsky’s The Brothers Karamazov (1880; translated by Richard Pevear and Larissa Volokhonsky, 1990) is dominated by Ivan’s long account of freedom and authority, told to his brother Alyosha in a tavern. It succeeds because the exposition is the crisis: Ivan is not merely informing Alyosha but testing his faith, so the listener is at risk, and the speech exposes the speaker. Alyosha challenges Ivan at several points, then answers with a kiss; their exchange is the scene’s event. The errand scene Symptom. A character goes somewhere in order to do something, and the going is dramatised: the drive, the queue, the waiting room. The scene’s real content occupies its last fifth. Mechanism. Transitional material has been mistaken for a scene because it runs continuously into one. Its plot function is to move the character to the next place, which summary does better, so the errand scene is the plainest case of choosing the wrong speed. Remedy. Use summary ( she drove to the shop ) or an ellipsis, cutting from the decision to the arrival and letting the reader supply the road. In the household novel, Elena’s drive across town after the doorway is not narrated as a journey at all; what the truck holds is her decision not to telephone her mother, which Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2) treats as a sequel. Exception. Woolf’s Mrs Dalloway (1925) opens on an errand, Clarissa walking through London to buy flowers for her party, and the walk fills the novel’s opening pages. The errand is the occasion rather than the subject: what is narrated is a consciousness, and the walk supplies encounters and memories of Bourton that let a mind be shown. The motor car appears after Clarissa reaches the florist, and the aeroplane sequence moves among other observers; they belong to the novel’s wider opening movement, not simply to her walk. The value shifts are interior, and the errand helps deliver them. The unresisted want Symptom. The viewpoint character wants something specific and gets it, at no cost, from someone with no reason to refuse. The scene passes the want test and fails the resistance test. Mechanism. A reader’s engagement with a scene depends on uncertainty about its outcome, and an unresisted want has no outcome to be uncertain about. The scene reads as administration: something is arranged, and the book moves on. Remedy. Relocate the resistance inside the character, so that the asking costs her something she was not prepared to spend; change what is wanted, so that she comes for the key and leaves wanting to know why he would not look at her; or grant the want and make the granting the disaster, as in Great Expectations . Exception. Rachel Cusk’s Outline (2014) follows an English writer who flies to Athens to teach a summer writing course and, in chapter after chapter, listens to the people she meets talk about their lives, their marriages and their work. She asks little, the reader is seldom told what she wants, and almost nothing she wants is opposed. The book holds attention because the engine has been moved to the speakers, each of whom is trying to tell a version of themselves that the telling undermines, and because the narrator’s own situation emerges by inference from what she chooses to hear. The want and the resistance are present, but not in the viewpoint character. See also: the Reference catalogue of ten patterns ; The Transition (Chapter 5), on the drive that becomes a cut.

chapter: Chapter 1 · The Purposes of a Scene
title: 8. Worked Analyses
text: Three close readings show different parts of the instrument at work: multiplicity in a commercial novel, a relational change made offstage in a literary one, and a chapter with no external event. A short screen reading and the household revision case follow. The Hunger Games : the reaping Suzanne Collins’s The Hunger Games (2008) is a young-adult dystopian novel whose premise is launched in a single scene. The novel’s first chapter opens on the morning of the reaping, the annual lottery in which District 12 must surrender one girl and one boy to the televised Games. Katniss Everdeen wakes and goes hunting with her friend Gale, and the unhurried chapter builds the normal (scarcity, illegal hunting, the arithmetic by which Katniss’s name is in the lottery twenty times and her twelve-year-old sister Prim’s once) that the draw will break. At the end of the chapter the name drawn is Prim’s, and at the start of chapter 2 Katniss volunteers to take her place. The engine changes gear in a sentence. Katniss’s want in chapter 1 is to get through the day; once the name is read, it is to save Prim, and the resistance is the rule itself, which allows a substitute only if one volunteers, together with Prim clinging to her until Gale carries the child away. The cost is Katniss’s probable death, accepted in two words: I volunteer! Stated in two parallel sentences, the shift is this. At the start, Katniss believes that survival means keeping her family fed and her head down. At the close, she has publicly traded her life for her sister’s. Each domain is served by the same material. The plot turns. Character is revealed at the highest available cost, which is how character becomes evidence. The relation between the district and the Capitol shifts too, because when the crowd is invited to applaud, it does not; people touch three fingers of the left hand to their lips and hold them out, a gesture the novel will later use as a sign of dissent. That refusal is also where the theme enters, the book’s question about spectacle and consent, staged without comment. The second draw names Peeta Mellark, prompting Katniss to recall how he once gave her bread from his family’s bakery when her family was starving. The memory introduces a debt the Games will make her confront, and the whole sequence is built from a few objects and gestures. Normal People : the car Sally Rooney’s Normal People (2018) is built in dated sections, each headed by an interval and a month ( Three weeks later (February 2011) ), and the intervals carry much of its structure. Connell and Marianne’s relationship at school is secret, because he fears what his friends would think. In the section headed Two days later (April 2011) , Connell, having asked a popular classmate, Rachel Moran, to the Debs (the school-leaving dance), tells his mother Lorraine in the car. When she learns that he has not told Marianne, she asks to be let out. A draft would probably stage the confrontation between Connell and Marianne. Rooney places the scene’s weight on a third party. Connell’s want is small and evasive, to have his decision accepted as a practical matter; the resistance is his mother’s judgement, and it is total, since she refuses even to stay in the car with him. The value shift is relational twice over. Between mother and son, approval has been withdrawn, and his mother’s moral authority, the one he cannot argue with, is now against him. Between Connell and Marianne, a change has happened that neither of them has yet spoken about. The character domain is served by the gap between Connell’s account of what he has done (a social convenience) and what the reader and his mother see (a betrayal), which is the gap on which the whole novel turns. The theme, whether people can be themselves under the gaze of others, is staged without being stated. The next section heading jumps four months, to August, by which time Marianne has stopped attending school except to sit her exams. The rupture arrives across an ellipsis as a state already changed. Rooney’s dated headings let her move a relationship by omission: the reader measures the injury by the distance revealed when the next section opens. The Portrait of a Lady : the vigil Chapter 42 of Henry James’s The Portrait of a Lady (1881) gives most of its space to Isabel Archer’s thought rather than dialogue or outward event. After her husband leaves the room, a servant briefly attends to the fire; Isabel asks for fresh candles and continues her meditation. She has also come upon her husband seated with Madame Merle standing nearby, a configuration whose familiarity troubles her. When the clock strikes four, she rises to go to bed but pauses over that remembered image. In the preface to the New York Edition James described the chapter as a representation of her “motionlessly seeing”, and claimed it threw the action further forward than twenty incidents would have done. James’s chapter passes all ten tests. Its engine is Isabel’s want to understand what she saw, and the resistance is her own: the understanding is unbearable, and the chapter proceeds through her approaches to and retreats from it. At the start, she believes her marriage is a private failure of feeling and that her choices were her own. At the close, she knows her husband hates her, that the hatred is settled, and suspects that her freest act was arranged for her. In terms of speed, it is the interiorised scene: story time is several hours and text time is a chapter, with the pace held chiefly by thought rather than by talk. The chapter has stages, each with its own recognition, so that the reader experiences progress rather than accumulation, which is where attempts at this mode usually fail, since the thought circles instead of advancing. The chapter shows the difference between a function and its carrier. Everything the model requires is present; the usual outward carriers occupy little space. A screen reading: Fleabag , series 2, episode 1 The first episode of the second series of Fleabag (BBC, first broadcast 4 March 2019) takes place almost entirely at one restaurant dinner, held to mark the engagement of Fleabag’s father to her godmother. Several wants run at once around a single table, which is one of the symptoms of the overloaded scene described in The Mechanism . The episode stays legible because the heroine’s asides to the camera make her the focaliser throughout, so that the question whose scene is this? never arises. Its decisive change is relational. When her sister Claire miscarries in the restaurant’s toilets and the truth threatens to come out, Fleabag tells the table that the miscarriage is hers. The lie exposes her to the table’s judgement and spares her sister, and the relation between the sisters changes without either of them saying so. The episode’s opening shot, of Fleabag wiping blood from her nose, places the end of the evening first; the viewer then watches the dinner knowing that it ends in violence, which turns the episode into a sustained piece of dramatic irony. The household revision case: the ledger confrontation This case is an exercise rather than a part of the household novel’s sequence. In the novel Elena finds the ledger in the register drawer, about a quarter of the way through the book, and sees that the hand changes after the father’s last entry on 9 March. The exercise imagines a later scene in which Nadia, told of the discovery by Elena, confronts Dov at the shop. Nothing in it binds the novel. Version A (draft) Nadia had been at the shop since nine. She had counted the receipts twice, which took a while because the register drawer stuck on the K and only came free on the third try. Dov arrived at eleven with a roll of bin bags and started on the shelves. Elena had found the ledger the week before and rung her about it. Their father had kept it for eleven years, in his careful slanting hand with the crossed sevens. But after the ninth of March the writing changed. It was looser, and it was not his. Since their father’s death, things had been difficult between all three of them, and she found it hard to trust Dov the way she once had. “You’ve been writing in it,” she said at last. “Haven’t you.” Dov admitted that he had. He explained that he had not wanted to worry her or Elena, and that he had only been keeping up the accounts because somebody had to. Nadia said she understood. They finished the shelves and went out for lunch. Diagnosis When run through the diagnostic tests , the draft fails almost all of them. Nadia wants nothing until eleven o’clock; Dov concedes at once and explains fully; the value shift, from suspicion to confirmation, is the weakest available; and the one fact delivered is one the reader already has from Elena’s discovery. Only texture is served, thinly, and the relational shift is stated ( she found it hard to trust Dov ) rather than enacted. The scene enters two hours early, leaves after lunch, and delivers every fact as briefing. The prose is not bad, which is why the faults are hard to see. Version B (revision) The ledger was in the register drawer, open at the ninth of March. Nadia took it out and held it up. “You’ve been writing in it.” Dov went on wrapping the shelf stock in newspaper, not looking up. “Somebody had to.
