I knew something was wrong.” He held out his hand for it. She watched his hands, steady, too steady, and put the ledger back in the drawer and shut it, and kept her palm flat on the wood. He didn’t argue. That was the part that frightened her. At the start, Nadia expects Dov to deny it or explain it away. At the close, she knows he will do neither; she has kept the ledger from him and found that his not arguing frightens her more than a lie would have. The plot is served because a question has been opened (what did Dov see on the ninth of March that told him something was wrong?) which the novel answers only in Dov’s own chapter. Character is shown through a physical tell and through what Nadia does with the book rather than what she says. The theme, what the living owe the dead’s silences, is staged as two people negotiating over a document neither will read aloud. The wrapping of stock sets a register of ordinary business interrupted. And the relational shift, the scene’s principal transaction, has become an event with a place in the room: an outstretched hand, refused. The revision entered with the ledger already open; gave Dov one sentence that admits the small fact and withholds the large one, so that what he says increases the reader’s uncertainty; replaced a stated relation with a transacted one; turned exposition into physical business; and exited on the last moving beat. What Version B has not solved Version B is too tidy. Eighty-nine words carrying five domains, a tell and a closing line of interpretation sit close to the ceiling of multiplicity, and That was the part that frightened her tells the reader how to read the gesture instead of letting the gesture work; a more confident version would end on He didn’t argue . The redundancy is also unresolved. The reader learned of the changed hand at Elena’s discovery, so the scene’s real shift is narrower than its staging suggests: not that Dov wrote in the ledger, but that he will not defend himself. A better version would make the accusation about something else. Finally, if the scene were ever moved into the sequence, Dov’s line would have to stay vague enough not to spend his own chapter, and Nadia could not read the ledger’s later pages, which the novel keeps for its ending. See also: the Reference analyses , with eight close readings including Middlemarch , Madame Bovary and The Great Gatsby ; The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13), for Dov’s chapter.

chapter: Chapter 1 · The Purposes of a Scene
title: 9. Checklist and Exercises
text: Revision checklist Run each scene of a finished draft against this list before deciding that it stays as written. Each item corresponds to one of the diagnostic tests or failure patterns ; an unticked item is a question to answer, not a verdict. Engine I can state in one sentence what the viewpoint character wants in this scene, right now. Something is in the way, and getting past it costs something I can name. If the want is granted at once, the granting is itself the problem. Change I can write the two parallel sentences: what was true at the start, and what is no longer true at the close. The value moved is one the book has already made the reader care about. The reader has not already been given this shift elsewhere. Domains I can name each domain the scene serves (plot, character, theme, texture, relational) and annotate it with the specific change. The scene serves at least two, or I can say why it should serve one (a rest, or a normal a later scene needs). The relational change, if any, happens in the room, not in a sentence that states it. Mode I have asked whether this material should be a scene at all. I have tried it in at least one other mode (summary, ellipsis, iterative, reported) and know what that version loses. If one dramatised day stands for a habit, the surrounding narration establishes its repetition and duration. Execution The scene begins at the first moment the want is in operation. It ends on the last moment the value moves, not on its explanation. Information in it arrives under pressure, from someone reluctant to give it. Book scale Removing the scene would cost the reader something identifiable, or leave a later scene unearned. Its line in the reverse outline is written in the language of consequence. It is in the register (action or reflection) that this point in the book requires. Exercises These five exercises are for your own draft. Each produces a page of writing or a table, and none of them needs a finished book. Exercise 1: two sentences per scene. Take one chapter of your draft. For every scene in it, write the start-and-close sentences of the value shift, in the same grammatical form. Where you cannot write them, write instead what the scene is for, and decide whether that is a reason the book needs. Exercise 2: the domain audit. For the same chapter, build the table described under “The domain audit” in The Mechanism : length, domain letters, and three or four words of annotation for each letter. Strike every letter you cannot annotate. Choose the longest single-letter scene and find its latent second domain without adding more than fifty words. Exercise 3: three speeds. Choose a scene that is not working. Rewrite it as singulative summary of no more than three sentences, and again as an ellipsis (the scene before it ending, the scene after it beginning, with nothing between). Read all three versions in place, in the chapter, before deciding which stays. Exercise 4: the object between them. Choose a scene in which two characters’ relation is meant to change. Remove every sentence that states the relation. Give them one object to pass, withhold or refuse, and let the change happen through it. Exercise 5: the reverse outline. Write one line per scene for your whole draft, in the language of consequence, with lengths and domain letters. Read it straight through and mark redundant pairs, runs of six lines in which a domain goes dark, and the point at which the book’s first movement ends. See also: the Reference checklist and studio work , with further exercises and seminar questions.

chapter: Chapter 1 · The Purposes of a Scene
title: 10. Coda: What the Tests Are For
text: The chapter has offered a definition, five domains, a continuum of speeds, ten tests and five failure patterns, and every one of them has limits. Chapter 94 of Moby-Dick advances no major plot event but changes Ishmael’s feelings. The second scene behind the lumber-room door in The Trial repeats the first. The Grand Inquisitor is dominated by an argument, Clarissa Dalloway’s walk is an errand, and the narrator of Outline seldom states a want anyone opposes. A mechanical use of the tests could misdiagnose these passages. Their effects depend on each book’s larger design as well as on changes within the passage. That does not make the tests useless; it settles what they are for. A test that a great scene can fail cannot sort good scenes from bad ones. What it can do is make a choice visible to the writer who made it. Most inert scenes in a draft were never chosen at all: they were written because writing them was how the story was found, and they stayed because they were well written. The value-shift test converts such a scene from something that happened during drafting into something the writer must decide about, and that conversion is the whole of its use. Once the writer can say what a scene does, or can say why the book needs a scene that does nothing, the test has done its work, whichever answer it returned. The right question at the end of a revision pass is therefore not whether every scene passes, since a novel revised until every scene passes every test would be competent and exhausting. It is whether the writer can account for every scene that does not. See also: the Reference coda ; Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2), which takes the unit forward into its consequences.

title: Scene and Sequel
text: How one unit of a novel produces the next The Craft Behind the Story (Second Edition) — Chapter 2. Part I: The Scene and Its Materials. In brief. A scene is held in place by what comes before and after it. This chapter divides the unit of a novel in two: a scene, in which a character pursues a concrete goal, meets resistance and ends worse off; and a sequel, in which the character absorbs the setback, weighs options that all cost something, and decides. The decision becomes the next scene’s goal. Where those two links hold, each event reads as something that had to happen next; where either breaks, the book reads as a list. The tools are six named beats, a principle that page-space should follow the weight of what happened, a test for whether a character’s grounds for choosing ever change, and ten diagnostic questions. Use them on a finished draft, on a run of pages that feels busy but inert, or beautiful but static. They describe one way of building momentum, and a book that runs on another should know that it does. What you can do after this chapter Find the six beats in a passage, including the ones compressed into a clause or a verb. Trace a chain back three links and locate the point at which “because” has turned into “and then”. Price a dilemma by writing both costs before writing the options. Check whether the space each sequel gets matches the weight of the setback it follows. Find the decision at which your protagonist chooses on new grounds, or learn that there is none. Key terms Scene and sequel in the narrow sense; goal, conflict, disaster, reaction, dilemma, decision; the causal chain, post hoc and propter hoc ; narrative desire and dilatory space; the proairetic code; the motivation-reaction unit; compression and beat weight; the deferred decision; chain structure; the criterion and the hinge; the escalation treadmill. Each is defined at first use and collected in the consolidated glossary . Contents The first files set out the model, the middle ones show how it runs, and the last are for use at the desk. The Problem Two opposite drafts with one complaint, a household paragraph, and the chapter’s claim Definitions Scene and sequel in the narrow sense, the senses of “scene”, adjacent terms How It Works Causation, desire and delay, the reader’s search for causes, and where the model comes from The Taxonomy The six beats, each with its carriers, its failures and its compressed form The Mechanism The two links, compression, deferral and the hinge Diagnostic Tests Ten questions on one page, and the beat-weight audit Failure Patterns Five recurrent failures, each with a published work that commits it and succeeds Worked Analyses Crime and Punishment , Small Things Like These , The Martian , Mad Max: Fury Road , and the household revision case Checklist and Exercises The revision checklist and five exercises for your own draft Coda What the model can and cannot tell a writer A writer already in revision can start at the diagnostic tests and use the checklist as the working page. The full treatment The Reference layer holds the complete chapter, Scene and Sequel : the theory in full (Propp’s functions, Todorov’s equilibrium schema, Burke’s pentad, situation models), each beat’s carriers and failures in tabular form, twelve chain structures, twelve failure patterns, eight close readings including Jane Eyre , Great Expectations , Dune and Catch-22 , scene and sequel in the short story, the series, screen and translation, seminar questions and an assessment rubric, and the sources. See also: The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1), for what a single unit is for; The Chapter Break (Chapter 6), for where a break falls on a deferred decision.

title: 1. The Problem: Busy and Static
text: One complaint, two opposite drafts A reader’s report that “nothing is happening” is one of the least useful things a writer can be told, because two opposite conditions produce it, and the remedy for each makes the other worse. The first draft is full of incident. In eighty pages there is an arrest, a flood, a confession and a fire. Each is competently written, each is over within four pages, and then the next chapter opens somewhere else with someone doing something new. The reader says the book is busy and that nothing is happening. What they mean is that nothing lands: events arrive faster than the reader can convert them into consequence, and consequence is the form in which a reader stores an event. The second draft is full of interiority. Its protagonist suffered a real catastrophe on page nine and has been considering it ever since, in sentences that are the best the writer has produced. The reader says the book is beautiful and that nothing is happening. What they mean is that nothing is due: the character weighs options and never commits, and endless weighing is not deliberation but scenery with a mind in it. The first draft needs its catastrophes absorbed; the second needs its absorption to end in a decision. A vocabulary that calls both of them pacing problems cannot tell them apart, and the craft language in common use is lopsided in a way that makes the second harder to see. For the active half of narrative there are many words: conflict, obstacle, stakes, reversal, climax. For the reactive half there are few, and they are faintly dismissive: reflection, downtime, the quiet bit. The imbalance encourages a writer to treat aftermath as the gap between the interesting parts, when the aftermath is where a novel converts what happened into what a person will do next. The same fault in one paragraph The household novel used throughout this book shows the fault at the scale of a paragraph. Elena has driven across town to her brother Dov’s front door and learned there that their mother changed the shop’s locks in March. Dov gives her the new key and withholds the reason, an exchange The Dialogue Exchange (Chapter 3) works in detail. The first draft of what follows reads, in part: She was angry with Dov, but there was no point arguing with him when he got like that, and anyway she had what she’d come for. She then drives to the shop, lets herself in and starts on the register drawer. Every event is in place, and the paragraph is inert. The reader cannot feel why Elena goes to the shop rather than anywhere else, because the paragraph has priced the doorway as a success (she had what she came for), registered its cost with a single named emotion, and dismissed the alternative of asking their mother in six words. The doorway scene is sound and so is the scene at the drawer. The fault lies in the join between them, and the join is this chapter’s subject. The worked analyses diagnose the paragraph and revise it. The claim The chapter’s governing claim has two halves. A story is not a sequence of things that happened. It is a chain of things that had to happen next — and “had to” is a relation the reader constructs, not a property the text possesses. The first sentence is the model’s promise. A reader experiences two units as connected when the second unit’s goal descends from a decision made at the end of the first, and when each unit ends in a setback that the next must absorb. The second sentence is its qualification. Readers supply causes readily, often on evidence a logician would refuse, so the feeling of necessity can be produced by other means than the six beats this chapter describes: by pattern, by a recurring image, by plain adjacency. It can also be refused on purpose, as the picaresque and much modernist fiction refuse it. The six beats are the most teachable route to that feeling, which is a reason to learn them, and not the only route, which is a reason to use them as a diagnosis rather than a rule. Where this chapter sits The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1) asked whether a unit does a job, and answered in terms of the value shift (what is true at the end of a scene that was not true at its start) and five domains in which the shift can happen. This chapter asks a different question: does the unit’s job arise from the last one’s, and does it create the next one’s? The two tests are independent. A scene can pass the first and fail the second, as a well-made episode that could be moved fifty pages in either direction without damage. The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1) would keep such a scene; this chapter asks what holds it in place. Three later chapters build on the answer. The Transition (Chapter 5) handles how the gap between two units is crossed, and this chapter handles what must be true on either side of it for the crossing to feel necessary. The Chapter Break (Chapter 6) handles where the gap is placed, which matters most when a break falls on a decision not yet made. And The Ending (Chapter 16) inherits the chain whole, since an ending feels earned largely to the degree that a reader can trace it backwards. See also: the Reference introduction ; The Opening Pages (Chapter 9), which works with no accumulated context, as the ending works with nothing else.

title: 2. Definitions
text: The working definition In this chapter “scene” has a narrow sense, taken from Dwight V. Swain’s Techniques of the Selling Writer (1965). A scene is a unit of dramatised action in which a viewpoint character pursues a concrete, immediate goal , meets conflict , and ends in disaster : worse off than at the start, or successful at a cost that exceeds the gain. A sequel is the unit that follows it, in which the same character registers the disaster ( reaction ), weighs options none of which is good ( dilemma ), and commits to a new concrete objective ( decision ), which becomes the following scene’s goal. Swain calls the six functions beats. The word keeps that sense here; in The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1), it also denotes the smallest unit of change. Four clauses of the definition carry its weight. Viewpoint character : the model follows one consciousness at a time, which is why a novel with several viewpoints runs several chains side by side. Concrete, immediate : “get Dov to say why the locks were changed” is a scene goal, because it has an addressee, an occasion and a test of success, while “understand my father” is a theme, which no one can pursue in a room. Worse off : a disaster is defined by its job, which is to generate a sequel, and not by its size; a raised eyebrow will do. Becomes the following scene’s goal : this is the clause the model exists for. Without it the six beats describe one unit; with it they explain how units connect. No characteristic length Neither half has a typical length. A scene may be a sentence or a hundred pages. A sequel may be a single clause, she did not wait to see whether he would follow , or five of the six parts of Crime and Punishment . The beats are functions rather than paragraphs: a beat is a job done, and a subordinate clause can do it. Nor does the model predict chapters. A chapter may hold three complete pairs, half a pair, or a sequel alone, and where the beats fall and where the breaks fall are separate decisions that drafts often run together. Which “scene” Craft conversation uses the word “scene” in at least four senses, and the table separates them. Sense Meaning Where it is used Loose Any continuous stretch of dramatised action The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1), and most workshop talk Narrow The goal–conflict–disaster half of a pair This chapter Duration Narrative time roughly equal to story time, as against summary and ellipsis (Gérard Genette’s sense) the continuum of speeds in The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1); The Transition (Chapter 5) Dramaturgical A division of an act, marked by entrances and exits Stage and screen practice This chapter uses the narrow sense throughout and marks the loose one where it needs it. The duration sense is the one to keep apart with most care, because it measures speed rather than function: a scene in the narrow sense may contain summary, and a passage told at full duration may contain no goal at all. “Sequel”, likewise, never means a follow-up volume in this chapter; this book calls a later volume a series instalment. Swain’s word is kept because the model travels under it and because the alternatives mislead. Some later manuals say “aftermath”, which implies passivity, when a sequel’s job is to produce a decision. Adjacent terms Swain also describes a unit at the scale of the sentence, the motivation-reaction unit : an outside stimulus, presented objectively, followed by the character’s response in a prescribed order of feeling, reflex, action and speech. The fixed order reads today as a period style. The principle beneath it is the chain at the scale of the paragraph: nothing should arrive without a visible cause just before it. Two terms from Aristotle’s Poetics are the classical ancestors of the disaster. Peripeteia is a reversal of fortune arising out of the action itself; anagnorisis is recognition, a passage from ignorance to knowledge. Seymour Chatman’s distinction, used in The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1), between a kernel (an event that opens alternatives the story must choose between) and a satellite (an event that elaborates without branching) also maps onto the model: a disaster is nearly always a kernel, and much of a reaction is satellite material. An obligatory scene is a confrontation the chain has promised far in advance and must deliver, which is the ending’s business. A deferred decision, treated under the mechanism , is a sequel whose decision is withheld across a break and paid later. What this chapter leaves to other chapters What a scene is for (the value shift, the five domains, the economy of doing several jobs at once) belongs to The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1). How the gap between two units is crossed belongs to The Transition (Chapter 5), and where the gaps fall to The Chapter Break (Chapter 6). Whose chain the reader follows after a change of viewpoint is the question of The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13), chains that run in the past belong to Backstory and Flashback (Chapter 7), and how a second, parallel chain earns its pages belongs to The Subplot (Chapter 14). Change in a character across a whole book is the subject of Arc and Theme (Chapter 12), which takes up this chapter’s hinge at that scale. See also: the Reference definitions , with a table of ten adjacent terms; The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1), on the duration sense and the scene–summary continuum.

title: 3. How It Works
text: The model rests on four strands of argument. Each opens here with the practical question it answers, and the last says how far the model binds. Why does a caused event land harder? Aristotle and Forster A writer who asks why one sequence of events grips and another, equally eventful, does not is asking the oldest question in the field. In chapter 9 of the Poetics Aristotle ranks lowest the episodic plot, whose episodes follow one another without probability or necessity, and highest the plot whose events happen against expectation and yet di’ allēla , “through one another”. His standard is plausibility rather than proof: events must arise from what this kind of person would do in this situation. The Latin pair often attached to the idea, post hoc and propter hoc (“after this” and “because of this”), comes from logic, where inferring a cause from a succession is a fallacy. In narrative the same inference is a competence. Readers make it constantly and on little evidence, and the craft of the chain consists in supplying enough evidence for the inference to feel earned. E. M. Forster’s Aspects of the Novel (1927) gives the formulation most writers half-remember: “The king died and then the queen died” is a story, and “The king died, and then the queen died of grief” is a plot. Two words turn sequence into consequence. Forster does not dramatise the grief or motivate it; he asserts a cause in a prepositional phrase and the reader accepts it, which shows how cheaply the conversion can be bought. Why must a scene end worse? Desire and delay The rule that a scene should end in a setback can look like a taste for melodrama. Peter Brooks’s Reading for the Plot (1984) supplies the reason for it. Brooks describes reading as driven by narrative desire , the reader’s want, produced by the text, for the end that will make sense of everything before it. The middle of a narrative is a dilatory space (from the Latin dilatio , delay), a stretch of detour and postponement whose function is to stop the story reaching its end too soon. A disaster is the device that keeps the end away: each time a goal is nearly reached and turned into a worse problem, the reader’s desire is renewed instead of spent. A clean win spends it, and its damage shows in the next chapter, whose goal must then be invented rather than inherited. Kenneth Burke’s Counter-Statement (1931) states the same idea most briefly: form is “the creation of an appetite in the mind of the auditor, and the adequate satisfying of that appetite”. On that account a scene creates and sharpens an appetite, and a sequel turns an appetite left unsatisfied into a new one. Why must a goal be legible? The reader’s search for causes Writers are told to imply rather than state, but a goal cannot be so hidden that the reader cannot tell what the action is for. Roland Barthes, in S/Z (1970), called the reader’s running ability to recognise an action in progress and give it a name the proairetic code , from the Greek proairesis , the choosing of a course of action; his examples are names such as Stroll and Murder . A legible goal lets the reader name the sequence, whether the goal is stated or inferred from action. Once Elena wants the key, the reader opens a file called getting the key and measures every sentence against it; when her purpose is unclear, the reader lacks that yardstick. Experimental work supports a narrower point. Tom Trabasso and colleagues model a story as a causal network, and find that events on the chain connecting opening to outcome are recalled better and judged more important than events off it, and that the more causal links an event has, the better it is remembered (Trabasso and van den Broek 1985). Graesser, Singer and Trabasso (1994) add that readers routinely infer why something is happening now more readily than they predict what will happen next. Readers can also infer unstated character goals from action, particularly larger goals that organise a sequence (Long, Golding and Graesser 1992). The practical consequence is to make a scene goal clear early, either by stating it or by giving the reader enough action to infer it. A chain that is present need not be underlined, because the reader is already looking backwards for causes. These findings concern comprehension and memory, not literary value: the chain makes a narrative cheap to process, and that cheapness is a resource a writer may spend or decline. How far does the model bind? Where it comes from A writer should know where a tool was made before relying on it. Swain (1915–1992) wrote for the American all-fiction magazines and later taught professional writing at the University of Oklahoma, and his book codifies a market that paid by the word and bought reliably shaped stories in volume. The model’s features follow from that market. It is generative, telling a writer what to write next, which criticism never does; its units fit a reading session; and every unit ends in a state that motivates the next. Jack M. Bickham’s Scene & Structure (1993) carried it to a wider readership, and from there it passed, simplified and often unattributed, into online craft advice. It appeared when, in Mark McGurl’s account in The Program Era (2009), the university workshop was teaching nearly the opposite lessons: the image and the epiphany rather than the chain and the unresolved close. That is the model’s period convention , the set of assumptions it carries from its time and market. Agency, escalation and external goals are the virtues of one tradition, and a book that does not share them is not broken for that reason. Barthes made the deeper qualification in an essay of 1966, arguing that narrative works by confusing what comes after with what comes because of. Causality is conferred by readers rather than contained in texts, and three things follow. Adjacency does much of the work the model credits to structure, so causal signposting can usually be lighter than a writer fears. The chain can be faked in connecting sentences, so the diagnostic tests are run on events with the connectives removed. And refusing the chain is a legitimate choice: Don Quixote makes the arbitrariness of sequence part of its joke, and Catch-22 makes the absence of causal logic its argument. The model is therefore most useful as an instrument that tells a writer which kind of book a draft currently is. See also: the full theoretical account in Reference , including Propp’s functions, Todorov’s equilibrium schema, Burke’s pentad and situation models; The Purposes of a Scene , “How It Works” (Chapter 1), on kernels and satellites and on why a scene without change leaves no trace.

title: 4. The Taxonomy: Six Beats
text: The six beats are a functional taxonomy: each names a job, not a quantity of prose, so one beat may take four pages or four words, and one sentence may do two. What the taxonomy offers is a set of separate questions with separate remedies, which turns make this chapter better into something a writer can act on. Its characteristic misuse is as a template for drafting. Filled in beat by beat, it produces competent and lifeless prose, because it describes the skeleton of a working scene, and a skeleton assembled first and clothed afterwards has the proportions of a diagram. Read it backwards, on a finished draft. For each beat below the question is what it buys, what carries it, how it fails, and what it looks like compressed to almost nothing, since in accomplished fiction that is how it usually appears. Goal A goal is a concrete, immediate objective, legible to the reader before the resistance begins and specific enough that the reader can tell whether it has been achieved. It buys a yardstick. Tension comes from an outcome the reader can score rather than from danger, which is why a fight between strangers is merely fast and a conversation in which someone is trying not to cry is tense. Two distinctions do most of the work in revision. A story goal ( find out what my father was hiding ) cannot be pursued in a room, while a scene goal ( get Dov to say why the locks were changed ) can; drafts that feel unfocused often have a clear story goal and no scene goals. And a goal is something the character is doing something about now, whereas a wish is only a preferred state of affairs. The strongest carrier is descent from the previous decision, so that the goal arrives already motivated. Andy Weir’s The Martian (2011) shows the plainest form: its astronaut, stranded alone on Mars, sizes each goal to a day (make water, grow food, reach the old Pathfinder lander to talk to Earth) and logs it before he starts, so the reader can score every entry. A goal fails when the reader cannot discern it, when it is diffuse ( she wanted things to be better between them , which nothing can count against), when it is announced to someone who does not need telling, and when a paragraph of motive precedes a small objective. Compressed, a goal is an action in progress, since a character picking a lock needs no sentence of intention. The test is whether the reader could say what the character would count as success in the next ninety seconds. Conflict Conflict is the resistance the goal meets, and its job is to change the shape of the goal rather than postpone it. Resistance earns its pages when it is informative. Three locked doors in a row are one obstacle told three times; a door that is locked, a second locked from the inside and a third recently oiled are an escalation, because each yields a fact and narrows the interpretation. Stephen King’s 11/22/63 (2011) makes the principle its premise. Its time traveller finds that the past is “obdurate” and resists change in proportion to how much the change matters, so that small alterations cost little and the attempt to prevent the Kennedy assassination brings accidents and illness. Every obstacle tells him, and the reader, how large the thing he is attempting is. Internal conflict, a character resisting their own goal, is weak when it stays a mood and strong when it is converted into small external choices. Kazuo Ishiguro’s Stevens in The Remains of the Day (1989) is never slack because his reluctance keeps surfacing as a visible decision: whether to take the trip, whether to raise a subject. Conflict fails when an obstacle yields at the first push, when delay leaves the character unchanged, or when resistance is so total that the character has nothing to try. It compresses least of the six beats, since it is what supplies duration; its one legitimate compression is dramatic irony, in which a reader who knows what the questioner does not feels the resistance in every polite sentence. Disaster A disaster is the unit’s terminal state, and it buys the sequel: without it there is nothing for reaction, dilemma or decision to be about. It takes three shapes, which the table sets side by side with what each leaves the sequel to do. Shape Formula What the sequel is about Costed success Yes, but What the cost has made impossible Compounded failure No, and furthermore Shock, and fewer options than before Poisoned success Yes, and that is the problem Recognition; the dilemma concerns the self The costed success is the shape drafts tend to miss, because a character holding what they came for looks like a winner: Elena leaves the doorway holding the key she came for, and has spent trust she did not know she was spending. The compounded failure can reach backwards, as the interrupted wedding in chapter 26 of Charlotte Brontë’s Jane Eyre (1847) does when it voids the marriage and explains a year of the household’s strangeness at once. The poisoned success is the literary tradition’s characteristic disaster, in which a goal is achieved and revealed to have been the wrong goal; it lets a novel change its subject without changing its plot. The cheapest carrier is a refusal or a silence, since it costs the writer no event at all. A disaster fails as the clean win, as a cost no one registers, as inflation in which each unit must end bigger than the last, and as a calamity from outside the action. What matters is the change in the character’s options, not the size of the event. Compressed, a disaster is a single priced object, such as a coat brushed again since the last visit, which is why The Descriptive Detail (Chapter 4) is this chapter’s partner. Reaction Reaction is the character’s registration of the disaster, given room in proportion to its weight. It buys permission, since readers take their emotional cue from the text’s own pacing and a catastrophe passed over in a clause did not matter; characterisation under pressure, since reaction is involuntary and therefore more revealing than any decision; and conversion, since it is the beat in which an outside event becomes an inner state, the only form in which it can motivate a choice. Reaction is best rendered by what the body does and what the attention selects. A named emotion ( she was furious ) is a summary of the beat and does not perform its conversion. The exception is retrospective first person, where the naming is an act of the older narrator: Pip in Great Expectations (1861) names his shame at length, years after the event, and the gap between the boy’s disordered perception and the man’s naming is the book. Reaction fails when it is skipped, when every character absorbs every blow with the same brief composure, when it runs past the point of new information, and when a small setback is given a catastrophe’s vocabulary. Compressed, it is a changed verb: she didn’t wait to see if he’d follow carries the feeling in the refusal. Dilemma A dilemma is the weighing of two or more courses, each with a real cost, none obviously right. It is the only beat that invites the reader to reach a view before the character does, and a reader with a view is invested in the outcome. It has two requirements. Its costs must be comparable, so the remedy for a lopsided dilemma is to write the two costs, one sentence each, before writing the options; and its options must be available to the character, or the beat is a lament. In chapter 27 of Jane Eyre Brontë gives the option Jane will refuse the better speeches, and the departure costs something because of it. Real deliberation is uneven, since people spend most of their time arguing against what they are about to do. A dilemma fails when one option is plainly right, when neither cost is named, and when it repeats without adding a consideration. Compressed, it is one rejected option: She could have called their mother , which implies the alternative and a reason in a clause. Decision A decision is a commitment to a new, concrete objective, arising from the dilemma and specific enough to become the next scene’s goal. It buys the chain itself. A decision needs concreteness ( she would open the register drawer names an object a scene can start from; she resolved to find the truth does not) and some degree of irreversibility, since a choice the character could drop between chapters at no cost is a preference. The strongest carrier is an action taken at once, as when Jane leaves Thornfield before dawn with almost nothing. A decision fails when the next scene reveals a choice never made on the page, when it is too abstract to yield a goal, and when it is announced and then explained. Compressed, it is a verb of motion in the next sentence, since arriving somewhere is deciding to go there; but the fact of a decision cannot be compressed away. Must all six be present? No. The beats are functions spread across a sequence, not slots in each unit: a disaster may be registered three chapters later, by another character, as Septimus Smith’s death is registered by Clarissa in Virginia Woolf’s Mrs Dalloway (1925). Some beats are unavailable in some books, since a person without options cannot decide. And the proportions are a matter of register: a thriller compresses the sequel and expands the scene, and a novel of consciousness does the reverse. The question in revision is never whether a beat is missing but whether its absence is deliberate, and whether the reader has what they need to cross the gap. See also: the Reference taxonomy , with each beat’s carriers and failures in tables and a summary table of all six; The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13), on the viewpoint arrangements that put the reader ahead of a character.

title: 5. The Mechanism: Chain, Compression and the Hinge
text: The two links The model’s mechanism consists of two links, and both must hold. A scene’s disaster is the specific event that the following sequel reacts to; that sequel’s decision is the specific goal that the following scene pursues. This is the causal chain . Where both links hold, units read as consequences of one another; where either fails, they read as items on a list. The chain can be checked from either end. Forwards, every disaster should leave something for a sequel to absorb and every decision something for a scene to pursue. Backwards, every goal should be traceable to a decision on the page, which is the direction readers themselves travel, since they look for causes more readily than they project consequences. Compression The chain says what must happen; compression governs how much room each part gets. This book uses the word in this sense only: the page-space given to a beat should follow the beat’s weight in the story rather than the writer’s default register. The failure is never compression as such. It is compressing or expanding every beat by the same proportion regardless of what it carries. Compression is a dial rather than a virtue: a thriller that folds a sequel into a clause and a novel of consciousness that spends nine pages on a dilemma are both right, and each would be ruined by the other’s setting. What readers detect is inconsistency in the exchange rate. A book that pays a page for a lost umbrella and a paragraph for a lost child has taught the reader that its accounting cannot be trusted. A compressed sequel many readers will know is in chapter 31 of Mark Twain’s Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884). Huck has written to Miss Watson to tell her where her runaway slave Jim is being held, and feels washed clean. Then he finds himself remembering the river: Jim standing his watch as well as his own so that Huck could sleep. He happens to look round and see the paper. It was a close place. I took it up, and held it in my hand. I was a-trembling, because I’d got to decide, forever, betwixt two things, and I knowed it. He thinks for a minute, holding his breath, and says to himself, “All right, then, I’ll go to hell”, and tears the letter up. The memory of Jim’s kindness is the dilemma, priced in what each choice would cost rather than argued. A close place , the paper held and the trembling are the reaction, with no emotion named. The decision is executed by the hands, and it generates the next goal, stealing Jim back, without another sentence of motive. The sequel spans several paragraphs, but its decisive turn is compressed into a few sentences because the disaster before it is unambiguous: the reader knows what the letter will do. Compression is bought in the previous unit. Where compression lives Cutting a sequel rarely compresses it; usually it produces a skipped sequel. The compressive work is done in four smaller places. The first is the verb of the next action: she drove rather than she decided to drive . The second is tense: the pluperfect performs whole sequels, as in by the time she reached the shop she had stopped rehearsing what she would say . The third is the white space at a break, placed after a disaster and before a scene that opens on a new goal, which tells the reader that a sequel occurred. The fourth is a repeated gesture given a new value: if the father has twice hooked a thumb into his cuff before speaking, the same gesture made by someone else after his death is a full sequel without a word of interiority. Compression has two limits, and they fail differently. Pushed past the point at which a reader can reconstruct what was skipped, a sequel reads as arbitrary rather than fast, and readers report that they “couldn’t follow why she did that” about a book whose events are perfectly clear. Expanded past the point at which new considerations arrive, a sequel stops being a beat and becomes a condition. The difference between that failure and the long sequels of great novels is not length but yield, which the worked analyses measure in Crime and Punishment . Deferral A sequel can also be interrupted. A deferred decision is a sequel whose reaction and dilemma are shown and whose decision is withheld past a chapter or section break, to be supplied later. Having watched the weighing, the reader has usually formed a preference, and now wants the decision for two reasons: to know what happens, and to know whether they judged this person rightly. Brooks’s dilatory space explains when this works. Deferral is a tax on desire, and it can only be levied where desire exists, so a chapter that breaks off mid-dilemma before the reader has any stake in the outcome has broken off on nothing. Its one hard condition is that the deferral must be paid. A decision interrupted and never shown, with a later scene assuming a choice was made, is a skipped sequel wearing a deferred one’s excuse. Meir Sternberg’s distinction between suspense (uncertainty about what will happen) and curiosity (uncertainty about what has happened) says how the payment must be made: suspense is paid by an event, curiosity by a disclosure. Deferral is one of several chain structures , the larger shapes a sequence of pairs can take. Besides the clean chain, in which every decision becomes the next goal in order, the Reference catalogue lists twelve, among them the braided chain, which cross-cuts two chains so that each one’s waiting is spent in the other; the displaced sequel, in which one character’s disaster is registered by another; the sequel-dominant novel; and the chain run backwards, which announces the outcome first. A sequence that is not working is often the right material in the wrong structure, and the useful exercise is substitution: defer one decision in a chain that feels mechanical, or cross-cut a sequel that has stalled, and see what the change reveals. The hinge: when the grounds for choosing change The six beats track how a character’s goals change. They say nothing about how the character’s grounds for choosing change, and that is what readers mean by an arc. To resolve a dilemma a character applies a rule about which cost is more bearable (loyalty over legality, the family over the self, the truth over the peace). Call the rule the criterion . Most decisions are made on a criterion the character already holds, so the plot advances and the person does not. At a few points in a well-made novel, sometimes only one, a dilemma is resolved on a criterion the character did not hold before. That point is the hinge : the moment within a sequel, between dilemma and decision, at which the criterion changes while the options may stay the same. Huck’s All right, then is a hinge. He does not refute his moral training; he accepts its verdict that he will be damned, and chooses Jim anyway, so the old criterion is outranked rather than overturned. This chapter treats the hinge as a property that a decision may or may not have, not as a seventh beat. It is inferred rather than seen on the page; it belongs to the shape of a whole book rather than to the join between two units; and most sequels have none. But a manuscript can pass every test in this chapter for four hundred pages and still prompt the complaint that its protagonist does not change, because the chain is intact and the criterion never moves. The test for that condition is the criterion test in the diagnostic tests , and Arc and Theme (Chapter 12) takes the hinge to the scale of the book, where it is adopted as the point at which an arc is located and rejected as a seventh beat. See also: the Reference treatment of compression , with a clause-by-clause table of Huck’s sequel; the twelve chain structures ; the hinge and the case against it .

title: 6. Diagnostic Tests
text: The ten tests are for revision, not drafting: applied while writing they produce the beat-shaped lifelessness the taxonomy warns against. Run them on a pair rather than a scene, and in order, since tests 1 to 5 (Goal, Descent, Disaster, Cost and Chain) are structural and their failures make the later ones meaningless. Record a sentence rather than a verdict: “the goal is find out why the locks were changed , and it descends from the drive across town” is useful, and “passes test 2” is not. Before tests 5 (Chain) and 6 (Three connectives), strip the connectives ( and so , because of this , which meant that ), since a chain asserted in connecting sentences is not yet dramatised in events. A failed test is a question about a choice, and each test here is failed on purpose by a book this chapter admires. Test 1 — Goal What does the viewpoint character want at the start of this unit, in one sentence with a verb of pursuit and an object? Failure. No engine, or only a book-sized goal. Exception. Pure reception, where bad news reaches someone who wanted nothing. Test 2 — Descent Which decision produced that goal, and can I point to the sentence? Failure. A free goal, supplied by the plot’s needs; the fault is usually in the previous sequel. Exception. A goal descending from another character’s decision, or from a parallel chain. Test 3 — Disaster Can I state how the unit ends in a sentence containing but or worse ? Failure. A clean win, and a next goal that will have to be invented. Exception. The run of clean wins handed to the losing side ( The Count of Monte Cristo ). Test 4 — Cost What did the character pay, and in what currency (time, money, trust, an ally, a self-image)? Failure. Drama without expenditure: both parties end where they began. Exception. A deliberately weightless incident in a comic register. Test 5 — Chain Written as bare events, could each of three links have happened without the one before it? Failure. The chain has become a list. Exception. The picaresque and the episodic satire, where succession is the point. Test 6 — Three connectives Outlined with only and then , but and therefore , how many and then s are there? Failure. Three or more in a row: the chain has failed there. All therefore and no but : no resistance. Exception. A novel built on refusal of causal logic ( Catch-22 ). Test 7 — Dilemma Can I state each option’s cost in one sentence, and would a sympathetic reader disagree with the choice? Failure. A false dilemma; the reader finishes the weighing first. Exception. The dilemma false from outside and real from inside ( The Remains of the Day ). Test 8 — Criterion At which decision would the protagonist’s earlier self have chosen differently, and what changed? Failure. None: a working plot and no arc. Several close together: the arc spent too fast. Exception. A book whose subject is a criterion that cannot move ( Manchester by the Sea ). Test 9 — Reversibility Could the character drop this decision between chapters at no cost? Failure. A preference, not a decision; the sequel has not ended. Exception. Early decisions carried by momentum, where foreclosure comes later. Test 10 — Beat weight Does each beat’s page-space follow its weight in the story? Failure. The register is on autopilot. Exception. A deliberate flatness of affect that the book makes its subject ( Blood Meridian ). The and then , but and therefore test is popular craft lore rather than theory: it circulates as a formulation of the South Park writers Trey Parker and Matt Stone, and echoes Forster’s distinction between sequence and consequence. It works because it forces the writer to state the connective, which is the one thing prose allows a writer to avoid. The exceptions are discussed among the failure patterns . Reading the results together Failures cluster, and the cluster points to the first move. Tests 1 (Goal) and 2 (Descent) failing together mean scenes assembled by plot requirement: rebuild forwards from the last decision that was made on the page. Test 2 (Descent) alone means a free goal, whose cause is a missing or decisionless sequel before it. Tests 3 (Disaster) and 4 (Cost) together mean incident without cost: ask what each victory should have spent. Tests 5 (Chain) and 6 (Three connectives) mean the chain has become a list: rewrite the disaster before the first and then so that it forces the next goal. Test 8 (Criterion) alone means a working engine and a static protagonist, and the remedy is to find the one decision that should have been made on new grounds and make it. A book that passes 3 and 8 and fails 1 is probably sequel-dominant by design; confirm the register rather than repair it. The beat-weight audit Test 10 (Beat weight) is the slowest and finds what the writer cannot see, because a default register is invisible from inside. Take ten consecutive pairs from the middle of the draft. For each, count the words given to the scene (goal, conflict, disaster) and to the sequel (reaction, dilemma, decision), and rate the disaster’s weight from 1 to 5 by how much it changes what the character can do. Then compare. Sequel length that stays roughly constant regardless of the weight means autopilot: cut the sequels after minor disasters to a clause before expanding anything. Length that falls as weight rises means the writer is more at ease with small feelings than large ones, which is common and correctable. The longest sequel following a minor disaster is usually a fossil of drafting, where the writer found the book’s voice; keep the prose and move its function. Several pairs with no sequel at all mean incident without consequence. See also: the Reference protocol , with each test’s procedure and a table of combined failures; the audit’s interpretation table .

title: 7. Failure Patterns
text: The five patterns below are described by mechanism rather than surface, so that the remedy follows from the cause. Each ends with a published work that commits the fault and succeeds, because a pattern that is sometimes right has to be diagnosed rather than banned. The Reference chapter’s full catalogue adds seven more: the free goal, the stalled sequel, borrowed motivation, the passive protagonist, the deferred decision never paid, the free disaster and the named emotion. The clean win Symptom. The scene ends in unmixed success: the character wanted the thing and got it. Mechanism. A costless satisfaction spends the reader’s desire instead of renewing it, and leaves nothing for the next goal to be built from. The damage therefore shows one unit later, when the following scene’s goal has to be invented, so a clean win is rarely a local problem. Remedy. Leave the win intact and charge for it: trust, time, an ally’s good opinion, a fact the character would rather not have learned. Exception. In Alexandre Dumas’s The Count of Monte Cristo (1844–46) the hero’s schemes succeed one after another, more or less as designed, and the novel is not slack. Each of his wins is somebody else’s disaster, and Dumas gives the victims sequels, so the chain is intact and has been handed to the losing side. The cost to the winner is deferred across the whole book, as his method destroys people it should not have touched. The skipped sequel Symptom. Disaster, section break, new goal, with no reaction and no weighing between them. Mechanism. The conversion of an outside event into an inner state never happens, so the decision that follows has nothing to issue from. Readers report characters who behave “randomly” or “coldly” and blame the characterisation. Remedy. Insert one sequel, a paragraph long, after the most costly disaster in the sequence, and reread. The surrounding material often stops feeling thin without further change. Exception. Cormac McCarthy’s Blood Meridian (1985) omits the reaction beat almost entirely, and the omission is its moral argument: violence is narrated without registration because a world that registered it would be a different world. The distinguishing question is whether the missing beat is legible as missing. McCarthy’s absence is felt on every page; a draft’s absence is merely absent. The false dilemma Symptom. Two options are offered and one is plainly correct. Mechanism. The reader completes the weighing before the character starts, so every further line reads as delay, and the character, who cannot see what the reader sees at a glance, is made to seem slow merely to fill a page. Remedy. Write the two costs first, one sentence each. If one sentence is hard to write, the dilemma does not yet exist. Exception. The Remains of the Day is built of false dilemmas. Stevens weighs choices whose right answer is obvious to every reader (whether to speak to Miss Kenton, whether to leave his father’s deathbed to serve dinner) and chooses wrongly each time, at great length. The dilemma is false from outside and real from inside, and the gap between the two positions is the novel. A false dilemma fails when the narration cannot see what the reader sees, and works when it can. The sequel without a decision Symptom. Reaction and dilemma are fully delivered, and then the sequence dissolves into a break and a change of subject, as though nothing were pending. Mechanism. An appetite is created and not satisfied: the reader has been drawn into a weighing and released without payment. It differs from the deferred decision in one respect, which is that nothing is coming. In drafts it usually means the writer does not yet know what the character decides. Remedy. Write the decision, however provisionally. A wrong decision that can be revised forces the next scene to have a goal; an absent one does not. Exception. In Colm Tóibín’s Brooklyn (2009), Eilis Lacey returns to Ireland after her sister’s death, having secretly married Tony in New York, and for a long stretch decides nothing. She leaves Tony’s letters unopened and drifts towards Jim Farrell and the life her mother would like for her. The decision arrives when Miss Kelly, the shopkeeper she once worked for, lets her know she has heard about the marriage; Eilis books her passage back at once. The book succeeds because the missing decision is replaced by the return of an earlier one: the secret marriage, Eilis’s own act, comes back as the disaster that forces her hand. A missing decision has to be replaced by another engine, not simply left out. The escalation treadmill Symptom. Every scene ends worse than the last, every test of the chain passes, and the reader still reports that the protagonist does not change and that the stakes have stopped mattering. Mechanism. Two faults combine. Readers habituate to magnitude, so each disaster must outdo the previous one to register at all. And the criterion never moves: the engine works perfectly and is attached to a person who is not going anywhere. Remedy. Stop escalating size and look for the hinge. Find the one decision that should be made on new grounds, and let the disasters around it be smaller. Exception. Kenneth Lonergan’s film Manchester by the Sea (2016) refuses the hinge on purpose. Lee Chandler, named guardian of his nephew after his brother’s death, carries a guilt that cannot be outranked: years earlier a fire he caused killed his three children. Asked to stay, he tells his nephew that he “can’t beat it”, arranges for a family friend to adopt the boy and leaves for Boston, offering a spare room. The film’s subject is a criterion that cannot move, and its refusal of an arc is the argument. What it does not do is escalate: its disasters stay domestic in size, which is why the static centre reads as grief rather than as a stalled plot. See also: the Reference catalogue , with a table from symptom to mechanism; The Purposes of a Scene , “Failure Patterns” (Chapter 1), for the scene that does no job at all.

title: 8. Worked Analyses
text: Three close readings, a screen reading and the household revision case. The method is the same throughout: find the beats, name the chain structure, and judge the compression. Crime and Punishment : the sequel that fills a novel Fyodor Dostoevsky’s novel (1866; read here in the translation by Richard Pevear and Larissa Volokhonsky, 1992) either breaks the model or shows its widest application. Raskolnikov’s goal is formed and rehearsed through Part One. The conflict is his own body, the staircase, the porter, and the unexpected return of Lizaveta, the pawnbroker’s sister. The disaster, at the end of Part One, is a compounded failure of the most complete kind: he kills two women instead of one, takes almost nothing, and finds that the theory the act was meant to prove has not been proved. Five parts and an epilogue remain, and nothing in them is a scene that closes the chain. Raskolnikov forms goals (evade the investigator Porfiry, find out what his friend Razumikhin knows, discover what Svidrigailov overheard), but every one is generated by his reaction to the murder, not by a decision that ended a completed sequel. The book is one sequel with scenes inside it, the structure the Reference calls the recursive sequel. It does not stall because each part adds a new consideration to a dilemma (confess or persist) that stays fixed. Part Two brings the body’s refusal to obey the theory; Part Three, Porfiry, who has read Raskolnikov’s article and states its theory aloud; Part Four, Sonya, and the possibility that suffering is not defeat; Part Five, Katerina Ivanovna’s death; Part Six, Svidrigailov, the theory lived to its end, and his suicide. Five parts, five new terms, and the dilemma is never reweighed in the same words, because each part changes what confession would mean. Where the hinge falls is a real critical question: Sonya’s reading of the raising of Lazarus, the confession to Sonya, and Svidrigailov’s suicide are all candidates, and the epilogue insists that the deeper change comes after the novel ends. The verdict is double. The six beats are all present and in order across six hundred pages, which shows that the model says nothing about duration. And the model cannot say why five hundred pages of a fixed dilemma grip rather than bore; for that a reader needs Brooks on desire and delay, or simply the observation that the prose is doing what no diagram records. Small Things Like These : the hinge Claire Keegan’s novella (2021) is set in New Ross, County Wexford, during the months leading up to Christmas 1985, and it is almost entirely sequel. Bill Furlong, a coal and timber merchant with five daughters, makes an early-morning delivery to the convent and finds a girl shut in the coal shed, shivering. That is the disaster: knowledge he cannot unknow. It is compounded when the Mother Superior gives him tea and a Christmas card with money in it, and the girl is made to say she was hiding as a game. The reaction is carried by routine and memory rather than named feeling: the deliveries continue, the town’s preparations for Christmas go on around him, and his own history keeps returning. His mother was an unmarried girl working for a Protestant widow, Mrs Wilson, who kept her on and raised the boy in her house. The dilemma is priced by the people around him rather than argued by him. His wife, Eileen, says it is not their business and that they have their own daughters to think of; Mrs Kehoe warns him to keep quiet about the convent, reminding him how far the nuns’ influence reaches. Every cost of acting is stated by someone else, and stated reasonably, which is what makes the dilemma real. On Christmas Eve he goes back, finds the girl, Sarah, in the coal shed again, and walks her through the town towards his home. The hinge is the change of criterion beneath that act. Until then he has chosen by what keeps his household safe; at the end he chooses by what Mrs Wilson did for his mother, and the old criterion is outranked rather than refuted, since none of its warnings has been shown to be wrong. Keegan ends the book before the costs arrive. The decision is concrete and irreversible, and the reader is left holding the dilemma’s prices, unpaid. A sequel-dominant book of about a hundred pages keeps its momentum because every memory adds a consideration: this is the yield that separates a sustained sequel from a stalled one. The Martian : the clean chain made literal Andy Weir’s novel was first published by its author in 2011 and by Crown in 2014. Its structure is the clean chain in log form. Mark Watney, left for dead on Mars when his crew evacuates in a storm, records each day’s goal, works against physics, meets a disaster, and logs a compressed sequel before the next goal. The largest disaster is characteristic: the habitat’s canvas tears at an airlock, the Hab depressurises, and the potato crop on which his survival depends is killed. The sequel is a joke, a calculation and a plan, and the plan is the next goal. The comedy is structural. Watney’s wisecrack is the reaction beat compressed to a line, which keeps the sequels short enough for a thriller’s register while still registering the cost. The dilemma becomes arithmetic (calories against days), and the decision is an engineering procedure the reader can follow. A second chain, on Earth, is braided with the first, and its decisions are generated by Watney’s disasters. What the book lacks is a hinge: Watney’s criterion, to stay alive by solving the next problem, never changes. The book does not need one, because its pleasure is competence under pressure, and a reader who finds its people flat is naming the cost of that choice rather than a fault. A screen reading: Mad Max: Fury Road George Miller’s film (2015) is nearly all scene in the narrow sense, a pursuit across the desert, and screen has no cheap interiority, since a reaction that prose gives in a sentence costs a held shot and a performance. The film spends that cost once. Furiosa learns from the Vuvalini, the women of her own clan, that the Green Place she has been driving towards is the poisoned swamp the convoy crossed the night before. She walks alone into the dunes, falls to her knees and screams, in a long shot with no dialogue: the reaction beat, priced by the only stillness in the film. The dilemma follows, with the group resolving to ride out across the salt flats on the chance of something beyond them. The decision is made by someone else. Max, who has parted from them, rides after them and proposes the opposite course: to go back to the Citadel, now undefended, which has water and crops. The decision reverses the goal the whole film has pursued, from flight to return, and it is a hinge for the group, whose criterion changes from escape to taking back. It is also a decision displaced onto a character other than the one whose disaster it answers. The household revision case: Elena after the doorway The pair follows the doorway exchange worked in The Dialogue Exchange (Chapter 3). Elena learned there that their mother had changed the shop’s locks, and left wanting to know why; Dov gave her the new key and withheld the reason. The draft of the sequel reads as follows. Version A (draft) Elena left with the key. She was angry with Dov, but there was no point arguing with him when he got like that, and anyway she had what she’d come for. She got into the truck and drove across town to the shop, thinking about what her mother might say if she asked her directly. She decided it wasn’t worth it. Better to look for herself. She parked outside, let herself in, and started with the register drawer. Diagnosis The tests locate the faults in the join rather than in either scene. Test 3 (Disaster) finds the disaster weakened: “she had what she’d come for” prices the doorway as a win, and the cost (she trusts her brother less) is asserted by “angry” and never spent. Test 4 (Cost) fails, since no currency is named. Test 5 (Chain) finds the chain intact only in its connectives: but , anyway , better to . Test 7 (Dilemma) finds a false dilemma, the call to their mother dismissed in six words on grounds of convenience. Test 10 (Beat weight) finds five words of reaction, all of them a named emotion, twenty-three of dilemma, and a decision that is logistics rather than choice. The patterns present are the skipped sequel, the false dilemma and the named emotion. Every necessary item is in Version A; its fault is arrangement, since the sequel has been summarised rather than performed. Version B (revision) She didn’t cry in the truck, is what she’d tell people later, though she also couldn’t say what she’d done instead: some effortful blank thing with her hands on the wheel, the key already leaving a mark in her palm because she hadn’t unclenched. She could call their mother and ask outright, and get the same answer Dov had given her, or worse, the silence that meant she’d asked something true. Or she could go through the ledger herself, quietly, and risk finding out Dov’s silence in the doorway hadn’t been protecting their mother. It might have been protecting her. She didn’t call. She drove to the shop instead, let herself in with the key, and went straight for the register drawer that stuck on the K. The revision restores the reaction and renders it in the body: the unclenched hand and the key’s mark in the palm replace “angry”. Is what she’d tell people later installs the narration’s small retrospective gap, which lets it see past Elena’s account of herself without leaving her head; the book keeps that gap throughout. Both options are priced: calling risks the answer, and looking risks learning that Dov’s silence was protective, and a sympathetic reader could prefer either. The real disaster moves from the withheld reason to its interpretation, since a brother who is protecting her is worse than a brother who is obstructing her; the costed success has become a poisoned one. The decision is executed as it is made, she drove to the shop , and the drawer that sticks on the K, planted in the prologue drafted in The Prologue (Chapter 10), gives the next scene its first move. The beat weights are set deliberately low (reaction 44 words, dilemma 56, decision 27) against a moderate disaster, leaving room above for the heavier sequels Dov’s sale of the shop will need. What Version B has not solved Three things remain, and the six beats cannot see any of them. The decision is reversible: nothing forecloses calling their mother later, so the passage runs on momentum rather than on a closed door. There is no hinge: Elena’s criterion (find out for yourself, do not ask people who will not tell you) is the one she held in the doorway, which is right for an early chapter, but a book made of such pairs would earn the treadmill diagnosis. And the dilemma’s second option is more interesting than its first, which risks the lopsidedness the false-dilemma test warns against; whether It might have been protecting her is a turn or a thumb on the scale is an editorial disagreement worth having. See also: the Reference analyses , with eight close readings including Jane Eyre , Great Expectations , Dune , Catch-22 and The Handmaid’s Tale ; The Chapter Break (Chapter 6), where Elena’s reading at the drawer is interrupted.

title: 9. Checklist and Exercises
text: Revision checklist Run each scene–sequel pair in a finished draft against this list. Each item corresponds to one of the diagnostic tests or failure patterns ; an unticked item is a question to answer, not a verdict. Goal and resistance I can state what the viewpoint character wants at the start of the unit, with a verb of pursuit and an object. I can point to the decision that produced the goal. Each obstacle tells the character, and the reader, something new. Disaster The unit ends in a sentence I can write with but or worse . I can name what the character paid, and in what currency. The disaster arises from the action, not from outside it. Sequel The reaction is carried by the body and the attention, or a retrospective narrator’s naming is doing work. I can state both costs of the dilemma in one sentence each, and a sympathetic reader could choose either. The decision names a place, an object or a person, and closes some door. Any decision withheld across a break is paid, visibly, later. Chain Written as bare events, each of three links would not have happened without the one before. My three-connective outline has no run of three and then s, and contains at least one but . Weight The space each sequel gets follows the weight of the disaster it answers. The book’s largest sequel follows its largest disaster. Arc I can name the decision at which the protagonist chooses on grounds they did not hold before. Where a beat is missing, the absence is deliberate and the reader can cross it. Exercises 1. The three-connective outline. Outline one chapter of your draft as a list of events joined only by and then , but and therefore . Mark every and then , and rewrite the disaster before the first one so that it forces the next goal. 2. Costs before options. Take the hardest choice your protagonist makes. Before rereading it, write what each option costs, one sentence each. Then rewrite the dilemma from the costs, giving the option your character refuses its best case. 3. The beat-weight audit. Run the audit in the diagnostic tests over ten consecutive pairs from the middle of your draft. Find the largest disaster and the longest sequel. If they are not the same pair, decide which one is wrong. 4. Compress and expand. Rewrite one of your full sequels as a single sentence that carries reaction, dilemma and decision. Then expand one of your compressed sequels to a page. Read both against their disasters and decide which setting each pair needs. 5. Find the hinge. List your protagonist’s five largest decisions and, beside each, the rule by which the character chose. If the rule never changes, either find the decision that should be made on new grounds or write a paragraph explaining why your book, like Manchester by the Sea , is about a criterion that cannot move. See also: the Reference checklist and studio work , with further exercises, seminar questions and an assessment rubric.

title: 10. Coda: What the Engine Cannot Tell You
text: The six beats describe one way of building momentum, not the only one. A novel can feel inevitable through pattern, image and voice without a single goal being stated, and some of the novels this chapter reads are built on refusing the chain, because their subject is a world in which causes do not hold or a person who cannot choose. A writer who treats the beats as a law will diagnose those books as broken, and will be wrong about them. The model’s origin in a mid-century magazine market is not a reason to dismiss it. That market needed stories that held a reader across a break and through a session, and the model it produced describes a large part of the fiction written since, including a great deal its author never read. Knowing where it came from tells a writer which of its assumptions to question, chiefly its preference for agency and escalation, and which to keep. Its value in revision is diagnostic. Run on a draft, the tests do not say whether the book is good. They say what kind of book it currently is: one that runs on the chain and has a broken link at a findable point, or one that runs on something else. In the first case the tests locate the repair. In the second they put to the writer the question the chapter has been building towards: if this book does not run on the chain, what does it run on, and is that engine strong enough to carry a reader to the end? A writer who can answer that has used the model well, whichever kind of book they turn out to be writing. See also: the Reference coda ; The Dialogue Exchange (Chapter 3), which takes the chain into talk.

title: The Dialogue Exchange
text: What a passage of talk must do, and how to test it The Craft Behind the Story (Second Edition) — Chapter 3. Part I: The Scene and Its Materials. In brief. Dialogue that sounds like real talk is not thereby working. A passage of speech earns its place when each speaker wants something from the other, wants it now, and uses words to get it, so that what lies between them (a fact, a standing, a permission) is different at the end. Most of that work happens in what is not said: readers assume that speakers are cooperating, and when a character answers the wrong question, says too little or too much, or agrees in the shape of a refusal, the reader works out what was meant. The tools are six domains in which an exchange can change something, a list of twelve ways of opening a gap between what is said and what is meant, and ten diagnostic questions. Use them on an exchange that is fluent and inert, or on a cast whose members all sound like the author. What you can do after this chapter State what each speaker wants from the other before the exchange ends, in one sentence per speaker. Name the currency of status in an exchange and say whether any of it changed hands. Rewrite an on-the-nose line four ways, and choose between them as a decision about character. Strip the tags from an exchange and tell, from the speech alone, who is talking. Keep the plain, unguarded line in reserve for the place in the book that needs it. Key terms Dialogue exchange; turn, conversation and exchange; phatic communion; the Cooperative Principle and its maxims; flouting and conversational implicature; adjacency pair, conditional relevance and preference organisation; repair; face, footing and the participation framework; heteroglossia; the relational domain and the silence domain; text and subtext; attribution, the action beat and the contradicting action beat; the gap-closing move. Each is defined at first use and collected in the consolidated glossary . Contents The first files set out what an exchange is and why talk on the page differs from talk in a room; the middle files show the machinery; the last are for use at the desk. The Problem A transcript, a fluent draft, and the chapter’s claim Definitions The exchange, its scale, conversation against exchange, adjacent terms How It Works Implicature, the machinery of turns, face and footing, the contest of social languages, and the dates of the conventions The Taxonomy Five domains of purpose, and a proposed sixth: silence The Mechanism Multiplicity in four turns, the two channels, twelve subtext mechanisms, and the gap-closing move Diagnostic Tests Ten questions on one page, and how to read their failures together Failure Patterns Five recurrent failures, each with a published work that commits it and succeeds Worked Analyses Wuthering Heights, The Remains of the Day, The Road, Succession, and the household revision case Checklist and Exercises The revision checklist and five exercises for your own draft Coda What the subtext ideal is, and what it is not A writer already in revision can start at the diagnostic tests and use the checklist as the working page. The full treatment The Reference layer holds the complete chapter, The Dialogue Exchange : the theory at length, each domain’s carriers in tabular form, the twelve subtext mechanisms with exemplars, twelve failure patterns, close readings of Pride and Prejudice , the Grand Inquisitor, Their Eyes Were Watching God , Blindness , The Portrait of a Lady and “Hills Like White Elephants”, dialogue in the short story, the series, screen and translation, seminar questions and an assessment rubric, and the sources. See also: The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1), for the value-shift test and the relational domain this chapter adopts; Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2), for the decision that is made binding by being said aloud; The Descriptive Detail (Chapter 4), for denotation and connotation, the descriptive counterpart of text and subtext.

title: 1. The Problem
text: A transcript and a draft Imagine recording ninety seconds of conversation between two people who know each other well, then transcribing it faithfully. Depending on the recording, the page might contain overlapping speech, false starts, fillers such as um and you know , brief responses from the listener, or a topic raised and dropped. Those details would be accurate, yet on the page they might distract from the speakers’ wants and from what changes between them. A novelist can omit or reshape such features while preserving the social pressures that make dialogue feel lifelike. That asymmetry is where this chapter starts. A description of a room is not expected to be an inventory, and no one defends one on the ground that rooms really look like that. Dialogue alone is habitually defended on the ground that people really do talk this way. They do, and they also produce greetings, weather and scheduling that no reader will sit through. What a reader registers as realism in dialogue is fidelity to a set of social facts about talk: that people want things from each other, that they seldom say so directly, that saying and meaning come apart, and that every turn places its speaker relative to the last. A reader who says an exchange “sounds real” is reporting that the wants under it are legible, not that the words would match a tape. The common draft fault runs the other way from the transcript. It is fluent, clean and helpful. The household novel used throughout this book supplies one.
