Elena has driven across town to her brother Dov’s front door, not knowing that their mother changed the locks of the family shop in March. In the first draft Dov opens with “I know you want the shop key. I’ve been dreading this conversation,” and Elena answers that it is humiliating to have to ask for one. Within five turns Dov has explained the locks, his divided loyalty, his mother’s reasons for not explaining and his regret, and he apologises. Nothing in it is false to these people. It is inert, because every speaker says what they feel, nothing is withheld, and the reader has nothing to do. The worked analyses diagnose it and revise it. The claim The chapter’s governing claim is the following. Two characters trading lines are a transcript. A dialogue exchange is a transcript with an engine under it: each speaker wants something from the other, wants it now, and uses the words to get it, so that the balance of information, standing or feeling between them is different at the end. Three limits on the claim keep it usable. The want need not be large: I want you to admit you were wrong or I want to leave this room without answering will drive an exchange, as The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1) argues of scene goals, provided the want is legible and resisted. The want need not be conscious, since the gap between what a character pursues and what she thinks she pursues is one of the form’s resources, provided the reader can infer it. And not all speech in a novel must be an exchange in this sense. Ritual talk and small talk establish register, mark time and supply the norm against which a deviation shows; what they cannot do is carry a scene. Where the chapter sits The chapter applies the value-shift test of The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1) (the question what changed? ) at the scale of a run of turns, and adopts the fifth domain proposed there, the relational, because in talk the standing between two people moves more often than anything else. It proposes a sixth, the silence domain, for what an exchange does through what is not said. Who reports the speech, and how much of the gap between saying and meaning the narration exposes, is a viewpoint matter, handled in The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13). The household facts in play follow the canon kept for this book. The doorway is Dov’s, across town from the shop; the key is the new key to the shop door; and Elena learns there, four months after the event, that the locks were changed. Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2) picks up her drive to the shop afterwards. See also: the Reference introduction , with the claim’s qualifications in full; the Reference account of transcribed talk , with a table of the features of real conversation that dialogue omits.

title: 2. Definitions
text: The word dialogue is used for three things: the words inside the quotation marks, the technique of representing speech, and a structural unit of the novel. They fail in different ways, and this chapter is about the third. The working definition A dialogue exchange is a passage of spoken interaction between two or more characters, each pursuing a want through what they say, in which the balance of information, power or feeling between the speakers is measurably different at the end from what it was at the start. Four parts of the definition carry weight. Spoken interaction means that the unit is the interaction, not the speech: a page of one character talking at another who does not answer is a speech, which obeys other rules. Each pursuing a want means both sides. An exchange in which only one party wants anything is an interrogation or a briefing, which are legitimate forms with one engine, and the diagnostic tests will find them. Through what they say means that the talk is the instrument; if two people chat while one of them picks the other’s pocket, the talk is a layer of texture over a different unit. Measurably different is the value-shift test of The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1) at a smaller scale, and the change may be small: a fact has passed, a point has been conceded, a form of address has altered. Scale Three scales are in use, because they answer different questions. The turn , one speaker’s uninterrupted contribution, answers what does this line do that the last did not? The exchange, a bounded run of turns on one matter with a beginning and an outcome, answers has anything moved? The dialogue scene, a whole scene whose action is talk, answers does this scene earn its pages? This chapter treats the middle unit as primary, because a single turn is too small to shift a value and a whole scene can hide a failing exchange behind a working one. An exchange ends at a change of topic, a change of participants or the arrival of the outcome it was pursuing. A rule of thumb for revision follows: the exchange begins at the first turn that could not be cut without loss and ends at the last such turn. Most drafted exchanges carry a few turns of approach at the front and a couple of retreating turns at the back, which are the writer’s runway, not the reader’s requirement. Conversation and exchange The distinction a reviser most needs is between conversation and exchange. Conversation is a social activity whose function is often to maintain a relationship rather than to transfer anything. Much of it is what the anthropologist Bronisław Malinowski, writing in 1923, called phatic communion (from the Greek phatos , spoken): talk whose content hardly matters, because its purpose is to confirm that the channel is open and the relationship intact. Greetings, the weather and the ritual enquiry after health are important socially and nearly inert in a novel. An exchange is conversation under load. The difference is not one of subject, since two people can discuss the weather in an exchange and their own divorce in a conversation; it is whether anything is being contested. A conversation ends when its participants are done, and an exchange ends when someone gets something or is refused. Novels need both; the error is mistaking one for the other. Adjacent terms A monologue is sustained speech by one character, and the interior monologue, which represents thought rather than speech, belongs to The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13). Reported speech renders talk in the narrator’s words ( she said she would not come ) and is the compression any revision of an exchange must consider. Free indirect speech renders speech or thought in the narrator’s grammar and the character’s diction, unquoted; it is the boundary case, where narration and speech meet. Attribution , or the tag, identifies a speaker: he said , she asked . An action beat is an action set between turns in place of a tag: Elena held out her hand. The Reference text calls this simply a beat. This book reserves beat for the smallest unit of change in a scene, as The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1) defines it, and for the six named functions of Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2), and calls the action between turns an action beat. Subtext, the want, fear or withheld fact beneath a line, is defined with its mechanism in The Mechanism . What the chapter leaves to others The representation of thought is left to The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13), and the chapter treats thought only where the narration uses it to expose the gap between what a character says and what she means. Plays and screenplays are used for comparison, but the model is built for prose fiction, in which a narrator stands between speaker and reader; that narrator is the largest formal difference between novelistic and dramatic dialogue, and much advice imported from screenwriting leaves it out. The linguistics of dialect is a field of its own; its representation on the page is treated here as a craft and ethical problem. A chapter break placed inside an exchange belongs to The Chapter Break (Chapter 6). See also: the Reference definitions , with the tables of delimitations and adjacent terms; the consolidated glossary .

title: 3. How It Works
text: Craft advice on dialogue is mostly prohibition: cut the greetings, use said , avoid phonetic dialect, never let characters tell each other what both know, write on the slant. Most of it is right where it is right, and almost none of it comes with a reason. The reasons exist, in fifty years of research on recorded conversation that the teaching of fiction has seldom drawn on. Each strand below opens with the question a writer has, then gives the source that answers it. Why does an evasion mean something? A character asked where he was on Tuesday talks about the car, and the answer can be heard as a refusal. The philosopher H. P. Grice explained why in talks given at Harvard in 1967 and published as “Logic and Conversation” in 1975. Hearers assume that a speaker is following the Cooperative Principle : make your conversational contribution such as the talk requires at the stage where it occurs. Grice distinguished four categories of maxims : quantity (say as much as is needed and no more), quality (do not say what you believe false), relation (be relevant) and manner (be clear, brief and orderly). A speaker who breaks a maxim covertly, as a liar breaks quality, simply misleads. A speaker who breaks one openly, so that the hearer cannot miss it, is flouting it, and the hearer does not conclude that cooperation has failed. She assumes it continues at a deeper level and works out the extra meaning that would restore it. Grice called that meaning a conversational implicature . His example is a reference for a philosophy post that says only that the candidate’s English is excellent and his attendance regular: nothing false is said, quantity is flouted, and the reader concludes that the referee thinks nothing of the candidate’s philosophy. One useful correspondence follows. Conversational implicature explains one way dialogue produces subtext: a conspicuous departure can prompt the reader to infer an unstated meaning. Implicature can also arise when speakers observe the maxims, while other subtext emerges through action, narration and the organisation of turns. The categories offer a procedure for some effects, which The Mechanism sets out, but they are not a complete taxonomy of subtext. A direct, cooperative line can still imply more than it says; on-the-nose dialogue becomes inert when it supplies its own interpretation before the reader can make one. Two cautions travel with this account. The weighting of the maxims differs between communities (Elinor Ochs Keenan’s fieldwork in Madagascar in the 1970s found speakers withholding information without implying what an English speaker would infer), so a novelist must establish a community’s norm of directness before a departure from it can signify. And much indirection is politeness rather than concealment, as Penelope Brown and Stephen Levinson argued in Politeness (1987): a character who hedges may be hiding something, or protecting the hearer. Why does a hedged yes read as a no? Conversation analysis, the study of recorded talk founded by Harvey Sacks, Emanuel Schegloff and Gail Jefferson (their paper on turn-taking appeared in Language in 1974), supplies the machinery of sequence. Its basic unit is the adjacency pair : a first turn, such as a question, an invitation or a greeting, that makes a particular second turn expected. The technical term for that expectation is conditional relevance , and its consequence for fiction is that a missing second turn is itself an event, heard as meaning something. A character’s failure to answer costs the writer nothing and tells the reader a great deal. The second finding is preference organisation : the two possible answers to an invitation or an assessment are not symmetrical. Acceptances come at once, briefly and without explanation; refusals come with a recognisable package of delay, a hesitation such as well , a token agreement, an unrequested account and softening, and often with no outright no at all. That package is how skilled novelists write reluctance, and it explains why flat refusals in drafts ( “No.” “Then I’ll go alone.” ) sound stylised: they put refusing content in the format of agreement. A character who agrees after a pause and an explanation has refused something. The third finding is repair , the correction of trouble in talk. Speakers strongly prefer to correct themselves, so correcting another person’s name, date or word is rare and marked, which makes it one of the sharpest status moves a writer can give a character. When does an argument turn, and whom is it for? The sociologist Erving Goffman described talk as the mutual protection of face , the social value a person claims in an encounter. People soften, offer each other exits and accept transparently false excuses to protect even an opponent’s face, which is why an exchange turns at the moment one party stops doing so: a full name used, an excuse refused, a euphemism replaced by the accurate word. In Forms of Talk (1981) Goffman added footing , a speaker’s alignment to what she says. The person who utters a line, the person who composed it and the person whose position it expresses can come apart, as when a clerk delivers a company’s refusal; a character who moves from I think to people say to Ma said has shifted footing twice, and each shift changes who is answerable. Goffman’s participation framework completes the picture: every utterance is designed for everyone present, the addressed, the unaddressed and the overhearers, so that who is in the room but not in the conversation is a fact about the exchange’s structure, not about its setting. Why must characters sound different? The usual answer is clarity. The Russian theorist Mikhail Bakhtin gave a stronger one. The novel, he argued, is made of heteroglossia (Greek for “different tongues”): the stratification of a language into the speech of professions, generations, classes and regions, each carrying its own valuations. A character’s speech carries a social position, and two characters who sound alike occupy the same social world, which forfeits the form’s main resource. Bakhtin also distinguished novels in which every voice is finally subordinated to the author’s from polyphonic novels, his term for Dostoevsky’s, in which characters’ positions keep their independence; that is the ground for requiring that an argument staged in dialogue be left open. The conventions have dates Today’s conventions of presentation are properties of a period. Quotation marks settled into their present function only in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries; present-day craft advice often favours said over expressive tags, while he rejoined in a Victorian novel is a period convention, not an error; Austen rendered much of her social interaction in summary and free indirect report, keeping direct speech for what mattered, a ratio that a modern workshop would mark down. Studies of transcribed talk document overlap, false starts, filled pauses and abandoned sentences, with frequencies that vary by speaker and setting. Novelists can retain, omit or stylise these features while preserving structural ones: refusals marked, absences heard, footing shifted, and meanings inferred from what is said or left unsaid. Deborah Tannen’s Talking Voices (1989) found that people retelling a conversation do not quote it either; they invent and compress, producing what she called constructed dialogue. The novelist’s stylisation of speech formalises something ordinary speakers already do. See also: the Reference theory section , with the maxims tabulated against the subtext mechanisms, the period table of conventions and the sources; the consolidated glossary .

title: 4. The Taxonomy
text: The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1) sorts the change a scene makes into domains of purpose , registers in which something can change: plot, character, theme and texture, with a fifth, the relational, proposed there. Dialogue adopts all five, and this chapter takes up the fifth for a reason particular to talk. Speech is the main medium in which people negotiate status, and an exchange can leave two characters unchanged as individuals while altering for good what each may say to the other. A four-domain audit cannot see that change, and it is what a large share of memorable dialogue is doing. The chapter then proposes a sixth domain, for the work done by what is not said. The model is for diagnosing a drafted exchange, not for planning one, and the domains overlap by design. Plot: a fact or a decision changes hands An exchange serves plot when a fact passes, a commitment is made, a plan is set or broken, or a lie is caught. Dialogue is the novel’s quickest way to move information, and information transfer is its most often abused mechanism. The remedy the tradition converges on is not to remove the information but to make it cost something. Give the fact to someone who does not want to say it, so that saying it is an event; give the need to someone who already suspects part of it, so that she tests rather than receives; and let it arrive incomplete, as a fragment that raises the next question. A second plot function is less often noticed. A decision made in a character’s head can be revised in silence; a decision said aloud to another character has a witness, and the witness makes it binding, which is why the decision that closes a sequel in Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2) so often lands in speech. The limit case is a fact created by a conversation that transmits none. When Lady Catherine de Bourgh demands that Elizabeth Bennet promise never to marry Darcy, in Austen’s Pride and Prejudice (1813), Elizabeth refuses to promise, Lady Catherine reports the refusal to Darcy, and Darcy reads it as hope. Character: the speaker is revealed Speech is the one element of a novel in which, by convention, the character rather than the narrator chooses the words, which is why a false note in dialogue does more damage than one in narration. Its carriers are diction, the shape of a speaker’s sentences (their length, and whether she finishes them), what she avoids, what she claims about herself, and how she changes register when the audience changes. The last is used least often. A character who speaks one way to a superior and another to a subordinate is characterised by each register and again by the switch, and the professional target is a consistent repertoire rather than a single consistent voice. Evasion inverts the intuitive relation between speech and disclosure, since an unanswered question is heard as meaningful and the reader is licensed to interpret it. Under-delivery is the interchangeable line, plausibly spoken and attributable to anyone in the cast; over-delivery is the verbal tic, a catchphrase or dialect spelling that substitutes a label for a person. In Zora Neale Hurston’s Their Eyes Were Watching God (1937), when the townspeople call for a speech from Janie, her husband Jody answers for her that his wife knows nothing about speech-making and that her place is in the home. The refusal characterises him completely, and it characterises her by the silence it imposes. Relational: the standing between speakers changes The relational domain , in dialogue, is the balance of power, intimacy, obligation and permission between the speakers: what each may now say to the other, and on what terms. Readers track it continuously and without noticing, through who opens, who yields the floor, who may change the subject, who asks and who must answer, who apologises, who is corrected, and who uses whose first name. Three principles make it usable. Status is a change, not a state: an exchange in which the powerful character is powerful throughout has illustrated a fact, not served the domain, unless the power was contested and held. Partial shifts are more legible than total ones, so a character who yields the ground and keeps the one thing that mattered makes a clearer move than one who capitulates; the household doorway turns on this, when Dov gives up the key and keeps the reason. And the strongest moves are the smallest: a surname exchanged for a first name, a courtesy withheld that every earlier scene granted, an answer addressed to a third party. Physical position belongs here too. A character standing in a doorway controls access, and a character who must ask to pass has already lost something, so moving a person across a room is a relational move that costs no dialogue at all. Under-delivery is static status, an exchange in which nothing was contested; over-delivery is a dominance display with nothing underneath. Theme: the argument changes Dialogue is the one place in a novel where a proposition can be advanced by someone the author does not have to answer for, so a book can hold two incompatible positions in suspension because two characters hold them. The theme domain fails often, on this chapter’s reading, because its failure is so attractive: a writer gives the book’s argument to a character, who states it, and the book stops. The useful question is not whether someone says the thematic thing but whether the exchange puts it at risk, and three tests answer it. Is the opposing case made in a form its own adherents would accept? Does the narration refrain from arbitrating, for instance by tagging one speaker reasonably and the other snapped ? And does either speaker want something other than to win? The third is the one most often missed. When Ivan Karamazov tells Alyosha, in Dostoevsky’s The Brothers Karamazov (1880; trans. Constance Garnett), that he accepts God but returns his ticket, the argument is hard to bear because Ivan is trying to make his brother agree with him and Alyosha is trying not to lose his brother. Theme can also be served with no argument at all, by dramatic irony, as when a narrator’s sincere account of his own dignity is heard by the reader as a diagnosis. Texture: the experience of reading changes Dialogue changes the visual density and rhythm of a page, so every exchange offers a pacing choice. Its carriers are the length and rhythm of turns, register, the density of tags and the proportion of white space: short turns and paragraph breaks can make an exchange feel brisk, while longer turns can slow it. Register can also tell a reader where and among whom she is, through courtesies, jargon handled without explanation and what is treated as unsayable. Dialect can be carried by syntax, idiom and vocabulary as well as spelling: I don’t have but the one places a speaker without an apostrophe of elision. Under-delivery is a cast that all speaks a mild contemporary standard; over-delivery is the dialect showcase, in which respelling can slow reading to decipherment. A proposed sixth: the silence domain The five domains describe what speech does, and much of what an exchange achieves is done by speech that does not occur. The chapter therefore proposes the silence domain : the exchange does its work through what is not said, through unanswered questions, interruption, pause, characters present who do not speak, overhearers, and people excluded from a conversation about them. A commercial instance shows how little text it needs. In Lee Child’s Reacher thrillers the line Reacher said nothing recurs so often that Andy Martin, who watched Child write Make Me (2015), took it for the title of his book about the process. The phrase occupies a turn: it stands where Reacher’s answer would be, and leaves the other speaker to fill the silence. There are three arguments for the domain. Its effects do not reduce to the others: a character present and silent through eight pages produces no characterisation and transacts nothing, yet turns the exchange into a performance for an audience. It has its own failure, the exchange in which everyone says everything they think, and its own remedy. And it is where much of a novel’s serious content lives, since what cannot be said in a society, by a given person to a given hearer, describes that society. The argument against is strong: silence is a means, not a value that changes, and every unanswered question can be filed as a relational or a thematic shift. The chapter adopts the domain for diagnosis while conceding that objection, on the practical ground that writers do not look for what is absent unless something prompts them. The Ending (Chapter 16) is the place to adopt or reject it, with the mother’s unexplained silence in the household novel as its test case. The Ending (Chapter 16) rejects it as a domain of the ending, where the mother’s silence is served by plot resolution as a question visibly declined and the siblings’ silence carries catharsis, and leaves it standing here, at the scale of the exchange. The table below summarises the six domains with the carriers to look for and the two directions of failure. Domain Chief carriers Under-delivery Over-delivery Plot Information under pressure; a decision made before a witness; negotiation Nothing passes The briefing: every turn a fact, nobody resisting Character Diction; sentence shape; evasion; register shift; self-description The interchangeable line The verbal tic Relational Address; who asks; the floor; correction; position Static status Dominance display with nothing under it Theme The staged argument; dramatic irony; the error left uncorrected A line that names the subject The mouthpiece Texture Turn length; register; white space; tag density Register-neutral speech The dialect showcase Silence (proposed) The unanswered question; pause; interruption; the silent and the absent Everyone says what they think Portentous withholding One domain served fully outperforms five gestured at: ask which domain an exchange is for, and whether it moves. Early exchanges in a novel tend to lean on character and texture, because the reader needs the voices before the contests; late ones lean on relation and theme, because the accumulated history makes a small move legible. See also: the Reference taxonomy , with each domain’s carriers tabulated and further illustrations from James, Achebe, Saramago and Brontë; The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1), where the relational domain is proposed.

title: 5. The Mechanism
text: The mechanism has two parts. Multiplicity, the principle that one unit of text should do several jobs, takes a particular form in dialogue; and the two channels of text and subtext are the means by which it does so. Multiplicity under a motive Narration can address the reader, description can dwell and interiority can explain. Speech can do none of these without breaking, because every function an exchange performs must be routed through sentences that a particular person would plausibly say aloud to a particular hearer for a reason of her own. A line of dialogue has one channel of production and two of meaning, and it must serve the book while appearing to serve only the speaker. Dialogue’s multiplicity is therefore motivational rather than arithmetical: the constraint is not space but the need for every function to be discharged by a sentence someone had a reason to say. The common failure is the exchange that serves one domain, two characters trading the facts the reader needs, and the fix is never to remove the information but to make it cost something, so that the same facts arrive while a relation moves and a character is revealed by what the disclosure costs her. Four turns near the opening of Ernest Hemingway’s “Hills Like White Elephants” (1927) show the principle at full stretch. A man and a young woman wait at a Spanish railway station and later discuss an operation whose nature — an abortion — they never name. She says the hills look like white elephants; he drinks his beer and says he has never seen one; she answers, No, you wouldn’t have ; and he objects that her saying so doesn’t prove anything. Every turn serves at least three domains and none announces any of them. Her image is character (she is the one still trying to play), relation (a bid for shared attention) and theme: a white elephant can mean an unwanted or burdensome possession, a possible resonance for their situation that neither speaker glosses. His reply answers the words and refuses the invitation, which can suggest more than his literal answer says. Her retort is the status move of the exchange, and his defensiveness about proof previews the vocabulary he will bring to the real subject. No fact passes and no decision is made. What changes is permission: after the third turn they can no longer talk about the hills. In revision, multiplicity is seldom found in what characters say about large matters. It lives in four humbler places. The first is the choice of noun or idiom: white elephants , not the hills look strange . The second is the form of address, which carries relational value on every line where it appears and which most drafts leave constant for a whole novel. The third is what the answer does to the question: delivered, delayed, partly given, over-given or refused. The fourth is the action beat. A gesture in place of a tag (turning a key between two fingers, refilling a glass, not looking up) tells the reader who is speaking and carries texture, relation and character in a clause. Elaborate figures in characters’ mouths are the riskiest instrument, because a metaphor that misses draws attention to the author; Hemingway’s works because it is a dead idiom used literally, the kind of figure people do produce. Multiplicity has a ceiling. When every line is quotable and every line oblique, obliquity stops signifying; an exchange can benefit from some relatively direct turns, because a conspicuous departure has more force against an established pattern. The two channels Every working line runs on two channels. Text is the literal content, the words a court reporter would take down. Subtext is the want, fear or withheld fact driving the line, legible through context, contradiction or omission and seldom stated. In a flat exchange the two have collapsed into one. Subtext is not ambiguity: an ambiguous line is one whose meaning the reader cannot settle, while a line with subtext has a surface meaning the reader settles easily and a second meaning she also settles, and the two do not match. Nor is it always concealment. A character may know what she means and know that her hearer knows; the indirection is then a courtesy, or a way of leaving both parties an exit. Concealment tends to produce suspense, and shared, courteous indirection poignancy. A novel has two hearers for every line, the character addressed and the reader, and they need not compute the same thing. The second meaning can be shared, which produces complicity between two people managing a subject neither will name; it can be the reader’s alone, which is dramatic irony; or it can be the character’s alone for now, so that the reader knows something has passed without knowing what, which produces suspense and much of the pleasure of rereading. The narrator adds four resources a stage lacks. It can withhold interiority, so the reader stands where the other character stands; supply one speaker’s interiority and not the other’s; refuse to arbitrate when it could; or contradict the speech by reporting an action the words deny. A character who says take your time while checking the clock has been contradicted by the narration. This contradicting action beat transfers to any book, because it is available on any line and costs a clause, and a good deal of the difference between drafted and published dialogue is that published dialogue puts the counter-evidence in the room. Twelve mechanisms The gap between the channels is opened in a small number of ways, most of them a flouting of one of Grice’s maxims. The table names twelve, with the maxim where one is involved. Mechanism Flouts What happens Evasion Quantity, downward The question is acknowledged and the turn is empty The changed subject Relation The answer belongs to another topic; the swerve is the content The question for a question Relation The burden is handed back: Where were you? — Why does it matter? Over-answering Quantity, upward Far more is supplied than was asked: anxiety, guilt, an alibi The too-precise reply Quantity, manner A date and an hour where a while ago was due The delayed agreement Preference Assent in the packaging of a refusal The false agreement Quality Assent both know is not assent, given to end the exchange The third-person deflection Manner One’s own position given to someone absent: Ma said you’d ask that The ritual formula Quantity, downward A courtesy where an answer was owed The interrupted concession Turn-taking A yielding cut off before it binds The significant repetition Manner The other’s word returned flat: Did she. The unfinished sentence Manner The speaker stops; the hearer and the reader finish it The table is for substitution rather than classification. A flat exchange is often the right material in the wrong mechanism, and the productive move is to take its most direct turn and rewrite it four times, as an evasion, a changed subject, a too-precise reply and a delayed agreement. The versions imply different people, and choosing between them is a decision about character that the writer did not know she was making. Each principal character can be given a default mechanism and one she never uses. The gap-closing move Everything above concerns widening the gap. The opposite operation is rarer and stronger. Closing the gap, so that a character who has deflected for three hundred pages says once and plainly what she means, is a climactic move available once or twice in a novel and spent when used. Its power is positional: the reader has learned the gap and registers its closing as an event, so the line need not be eloquent. Darcy’s second proposal in Pride and Prejudice , in short unqualified clauses that offer Elizabeth the power to silence him for ever, is the classic instance. The prohibition on on-the-nose dialogue is therefore not a rule against direct speech but against direct speech everywhere, which leaves a book with no plainness in reserve for its climax. The move does not need both parties. In The Remains of the Day , read in the worked analyses , one speaker closes the gap and the other keeps his open, and the asymmetry is the tragedy. See also: the Reference account of multiplicity , with the four turns tabulated by domain and the domain audit; the Reference account of the two channels , with an exemplar, a gain and a cost for each mechanism and the historical drift of the subtext ideal.

title: 6. Diagnostic Tests
text: The ten tests are for revision, not composition: applied while drafting they produce self-conscious dialogue. Run them on one exchange at a time, not on a whole scene, which averages a failing passage away; and run them in order, since tests 1 to 4 (Removal, Want, Status and Cost) are structural and a failure there makes the rest pointless. Record a sentence, not a verdict: “Dov holds the upper hand at the start and a smaller share of it at the end” is useful, and “fails test 3” is not. Each test below is failed on purpose by a book worth reading. Test 1 — Removal Replace the exchange with one sentence of summary. What is lost? Failure. Nothing: the summary is the better version. Exception. An exchange kept for a voice the reader needs to hear at length. Test 2 — Want What does each speaker want from the other before this ends, in one sentence each? Failure. One engine (a briefing) or none. Exception. The interrogation, a one-engined form chosen as such. Test 3 — Status Who holds the upper hand at the first line and at the last, and was it contested? Failure. Static status that nobody tried to disturb. Exception. Status fiercely contested but held, or fixity that is the subject (Beckett). Test 4 — Cost What does each disclosure cost the person making it? Failure. A briefing in dialogue’s clothes. Exception. The naive listener, who needs what she is told. Test 5 — Silence What does each speaker choose not to say, and who else is in the room? Failure. Everyone says what they think. Exception. The climactic plain line, kept in reserve. Test 6 — Implicature Is each turn what was called for? Where it is not, what does the departure imply? What might a cooperative turn convey beyond its literal content? Failure. Every turn supplies its own interpretation, leaving little for the reader to infer. Exception. Dostoevsky’s full self-accounts, whose gap is between the said and the case. Test 7 — Transcript Strip every tag and action beat and read aloud. Can you tell who is speaking? Failure. Speakers told apart by content only, or not at all. Exception. A declared uniform register (Wilde, Compton-Burnett). Test 8 — Substitution Could another named character say the exchange’s three best lines? Failure. The line does no character work. Exception. A chorus, where interchangeability is the point. Test 9 — Attribution How many turns carry a tag, how many tags are not said or asked , and what do the action beats do besides identify? Failure. The exchange is being narrated at. Exception. Period practice, where rejoined is the convention. Test 10 — Interruption Who takes the floor from whom, and where do interruptions cluster? Failure. Formal alternation: a committee, not a contest. Exception. Ceremony, where the turn order is fixed by rule. Four refinements sharpen the tests. In test 1 (Removal), compare length as well as content: an exchange of nine hundred words that a sentence fully replaces has spent the reader’s attention on a transaction that did not need it. In test 2 (Want), the want must be directed at the other person ( I want to understand the situation is not a want from anyone) and immediate, not the story goal. In test 3 (Status), name the currency (who holds the information, the physical position, the right to end the conversation, the right to ask), since these can move in opposite directions, and an exchange in which someone gains one and loses another is doing more than one in which everything moves together. In test 6 (Implicature), do not aim for a fixed share of conspicuous departures. Look at their placement: a turn at the exchange’s crisis can carry more force when the surrounding turns have established a baseline. Reading the results together Failures cluster, and the cluster points to the first move. Test 1 (Removal) alone means a scene the writer needed in order to find out what happened and the reader does not need: use the summary. Tests 2 (Want) and 4 (Cost) together mean a briefing: give the facts to someone who does not want to say them. Test 3 (Status) alone means static status: find what one of them could concede, and make the other reach for it. Tests 5 (Silence) and 6 (Implicature) mean an exchange on the nose: apply the twelve mechanisms in The Mechanism to its three most direct turns. Tests 7 (Transcript) and 8 (Substitution) mean the ventriloquist exchange, and the instinct to make each speaker more distinctive by adding tics and catchphrases produces labels instead of people. Differentiation is structural: give each character a different average sentence length, a different relation to questions (who asks, who answers, who deflects) and a different default subtext mechanism, and distinguishable speakers follow without a single quirk. Failure on all of tests 1 to 5 (Removal, Want, Status, Cost and Silence) means the passage is not an exchange; cut it, or find the want that would make it one. See also: the Reference protocol , with each test’s procedure and a table of combined failures; the domain audit , which marks each turn with the domains it serves.

title: 7. Failure Patterns
text: The five patterns below are described by mechanism rather than surface, so that the remedy follows from the cause. Each ends with a published work that commits the fault and succeeds, because a pattern that is sometimes right has to be diagnosed rather than banned. The Reference chapter’s full catalogue adds seven more: the static-status exchange, the maid-and-butler opening, the name in every line, the attribution fault, the therapeutic exchange, the speech that answers a question nobody asked, and the one-engined exchange. As you know, Bob Symptom. Characters tell each other what both already know so that the reader can overhear: As you know, our father left the shop to the three of us. Mechanism. A character supplies more information than the situation gives them a reason to say aloud. With no motive available in the fiction, the reader notices the author’s need to convey the fact. The information may be necessary; the delivery is what fails. Remedy. Adding a plausible reason for the conversation does not help, because plausibility is not what is missing; cost is. Give the fact to someone who does not want to say it, give the need to someone who already suspects part of it, or let it arrive incomplete. Where none of these is available, the fact belongs in narration. Exception. The naive listener, who needs what she is told. Janice Hallett’s crime novel The Appeal (2021) is told entirely in emails, messages and documents, which a senior lawyer passes to two law students, Femi Hassan and Charlotte Holroyd, with no account of the case, asking them to work out what really happened. Because the students, and the reader with them, start from nothing, the correspondents inside the documents never have to brief each other. The arrangement descends from Nelly Dean telling Lockwood the history of Wuthering Heights , and its standing cost is the same: the listeners must be made interesting in their own right. The ventriloquist exchange Symptom. Every character reasons, jokes and speaks in the author’s voice. Each line sounds right, and the exchange fails the transcript test on every line. Mechanism. Writers hear dialogue in their own inner voice, which has one vocabulary and one rhythm. In Bakhtin’s terms the novel’s stratified social languages collapse into one position, and the form’s main resource is lost. The fault survives line-editing indefinitely, because it is in no single line. Remedy. Structural, not lexical: a different average sentence length, a different relation to questions and a different default subtext mechanism for each principal, then the transcript test again. Exception. Ivy Compton-Burnett wrote some twenty novels in which parents, children, servants and tyrants all speak the same lucid, formal, epigrammatic English, and the uniform register works as a convention of the form, like verse in Racine, so that characters differ by what they are willing to say. An undifferentiated register is a failure when it is unintended and a style when it is declared. On the nose Symptom. Text and subtext say the same thing throughout: I’m angry that you lied to me. — I know. I’m afraid of losing you. The variant in which characters explain their own psychology in the book’s terms ( I keep pushing you away because of what happened with our father ) is the therapeutic exchange. Mechanism. A line that states a character’s feeling directly can supply its own interpretation before the reader has had to make one, foreclosing the exchange it should open. A cooperative line can still imply more than it says. Used everywhere, explicit self-explanation also spends the gap-closing move, since a book with no gap has no climactic plainness left. Remedy. Keep the feeling and remove the statement of it, by substitution through the twelve mechanisms. For the therapeutic version, give the analysis to another character as an accusation, which its subject can refuse: a diagnosis offered by an enemy is contestable, and the same diagnosis offered by its subject is a verdict. Exception. Dostoevsky’s characters say what they think at enormous length, Marmeladov delivering his own moral autopsy to a stranger in a tavern and Raskolnikov confessing to Sonya, in novels of great psychological depth. They are still not transparent, because what they say is not the truth about them but their most forceful self-account, offered under pressure to a hearer they are trying to move. The gap in Dostoevsky lies between what is said and what is the case, and self-analysis is dramatic when it is a move and inert when it is a report. The tennis match Symptom. Quick, clever back-and-forth with energy in every line and no throughline. It is entertaining in isolation and forgotten a page later. Mechanism. Each turn does one thing, which is to be good, and the shape is an oscillation rather than a trajectory. The signature is that the turns could be reshuffled without loss. Remedy. Move three turns and see whether anything breaks; then cut to the turns that could not be moved and rebuild around them. Exception. The opening of The Social Network (David Fincher, written by Aaron Sorkin, 2010) is some nine script pages of rapid exchange in a bar between Mark Zuckerberg and Erica Albright, in which Mark jumps between the number of people in China with genius IQs, his own SAT score and Harvard’s final clubs, and Erica tells him that he says two things at once and she cannot tell which she is meant to be aiming at. It reads at first as a tennis match. It is not one, because both players want something (he wants her to recognise his standing; she wants not to be condescended to), and because the rally ends in a reversal: she breaks up with him, and her parting speech, that girls will not dislike him for being a nerd but for being an asshole, closes the gap the whole scene has kept open. The tennis match becomes structural when the reader can see what the players are playing for. Phonetic dialect Symptom. Non-standard speech rendered by respelling: apostrophes for dropped consonants, eye-dialect such as wuz , dense orthography sustained for pages. Mechanism. Three problems usually conflated. Respelling can slow reading, so long passages may turn into decipherment. Eye-dialect can use a nonstandard spelling for an ordinary pronunciation: sez for says , or wuz for a common reduced pronunciation of was . The spelling may mark the speaker as nonstandard without recording a distinctive accent. And where one group’s speech is respelled and another’s is not, the unmarked group is placed at the centre of the book’s language. The rule against the practice grew partly out of a correct perception of that asymmetry, but it has often fallen hardest on writers representing their own communities. Remedy. Carry dialect in syntax, idiom and vocabulary rather than in spelling, with at most a light orthographic marker. Exception. Douglas Stuart’s Shuggie Bain (2020), set in Glasgow in the 1980s and winner of that year’s Booker Prize, is narrated largely in standard English while drawing on local terms and phraseology; its dialogue gives different characters varied Glaswegian voices. The marking reaches across the community, though its degree varies by speaker; the book’s centre of value is inside those voices; and Stuart has said that in James Kelman’s Booker-winning novel of 1994 he first saw his own people and their dialect on the page. Hurston’s Their Eyes Were Watching God is the older case of the same structure. Phonetic dialect fails when it marks a speaker as a departure from a standard the book itself embodies, and succeeds when the narration does not stand above the speech. See also: the Reference failure patterns , with a persistence note for each pattern and a table from symptom to mechanism; the diagnostic tests .

title: 8. Worked Analyses
text: Three close readings show different parts of the instrument: the participation framework in a Victorian novel, the two channels held apart for a whole book and closed by one party, and a post-2000 exchange that does without quotation marks and tags altogether. A short screen reading and the household revision case follow. Wuthering Heights : who is in the room Emily Brontë’s Wuthering Heights (1847) often reaches the reader at two removes. Much of it is Nelly Dean’s account to Lockwood, a tenant who knows little of the household, so many exchanges are reported by a narrator with her own loyalties. A central exchange is Catherine’s confession to Nelly in the kitchen that she has accepted Edgar Linton. Heathcliff is in the room, out of Catherine’s sight. He listens until she says that it would degrade her to marry him, and then leaves, so he does not hear her say that she is Heathcliff. Nelly notices his departure and tells Catherine to hush, but does not plainly tell her what he heard. Read with the taxonomy, the exchange’s plot work is done almost entirely in the silence domain. Two silences, a departure and a withholding, set the course of the rest of the book, and neither is speech. The participation framework explains why the scene cannot be rewritten as a two-hander: Catherine’s speech is designed for one hearer and received by two, and the overhearer takes away the half that wounds. Nelly’s silence is a narrator’s silence as well as a character’s, since the woman who chose not to tell Catherine is the woman now choosing what to tell Lockwood, and the reader is left to weigh how far her account is shaped by the same reticence. The exchange fails test 2 (Want) on a strict reading, because Catherine wants nothing from Nelly but a hearing, and the failure is the point: a confession is a speech looking for a witness, and the witness the speech finds is the wrong one. The Remains of the Day : the gap kept open Kazuo Ishiguro’s The Remains of the Day (1989) is narrated by Stevens, a butler whose professional register is a status instrument: its formality lets him decline every intimacy Miss Kenton offers without refusing one. The relational value that moves across the novel is not power, since his position is secure, but permission. What Miss Kenton may say to him narrows from scene to scene, through evasions of impeccable length and no content, ritual formulas where answers were owed, and his habit of dating and placing his recollections with a precision that tells the reader what he has dwelt on. Her announcement of her engagement is made in order to be answered, and his failure to answer is the event. The novel’s end turns the two channels into its structure. Twenty years later, waiting with him at a bus stop in the rain, Miss Kenton, now Mrs Benn, closes her gap: on desolate occasions, she says, she thinks of a life she might have had with him. The narration then closes Stevens’s gap for the reader alone, in the sentence in which he admits that at that moment his heart was breaking, while what he says aloud is a courtesy that returns her to her marriage. The configuration is the reader-only one, held for two hundred pages and confirmed at the last moment, and the gap-closing move is made by one party while the other keeps his open. A writer borrowing the register should note its cost: a character who evades at this volume risks becoming unreadable rather than opaque, and Ishiguro avoids it by varying the kind of evasion from scene to scene. The Road : an exchange without apparatus Cormac McCarthy’s The Road (2006) follows an unnamed man and his son south through a burned America. Its dialogue has no quotation marks, almost no tags and few apostrophes, and is set out one turn to a line. In one exchange the boy asks whether they would ever eat anybody, and the father says no. Then: Even if we were starving? We’re starving now. You said we werent. I said we werent dying. I didnt say we werent starving. The boy then asks the father to confirm the formula they live by, that they are the good guys and are carrying the fire, the father repeats it after him, and the boy ends the exchange with Okay . The transcript test is built into the page, since there is nothing to strip, and it passes on structure alone: the speakers differ by their relation to questions, the boy asking and the father answering. The status work is done by repair. You said we werent is an other-correction, a rare and pointed move in talk because speakers prefer to correct themselves, made by a child against the father who is his only authority, and the father’s too-precise distinction between dying and starving is the answer of a man caught out. The formula that follows is a ritual one, and its meaning depends on who demands it. Here the boy holds the right to ask, makes the father recite, and decides when the exchange is over. The plot does not move. What moves is the relation: the child has become the keeper of his father’s ethics, which is the novel’s subject stated in nothing but turns. A screen reading: Succession , “Hunting” In “Hunting”, the third episode of the second series of Succession (HBO, first broadcast 25 August 2019; written by Tony Roche, directed by Andrij Parekh), Logan Roy, at a hunting lodge in Hungary and convinced that someone close to him has been talking to an outsider, interrupts dinner and makes Tom, Greg and Karl get down on the floor as boars and fight for sausages while the table watches and chants. The scene is a participation framework turned into an instrument. Logan holds the floor and the sole right to ask; the three men on the floor are compelled to perform; and the rest of the table, his children among them, are overhearers who must laugh to show they are not suspects. Nobody can refuse, because refusal is what the game exists to detect. Logan says little, and his short commands against his children’s jokes show the repertoire principle at work: the joke is a way of keeping face, and in this room only he may do without one. Before the night is out, Kendall has given Roman up, and the humiliation moves to his brother. On screen the narrator’s resources are gone, so the camera and the actors’ faces carry the subtext a novel would give to interiority or a contradicting action beat. The household revision case: the doorway Elena has driven across town to Dov’s front door. She does not yet know that their mother changed the shop’s locks in March. The first draft reads as follows. Dov stood in the doorway. “I know you want the shop key,” he said. “I’ve been dreading this conversation.” “I’ve had a key to this shop since I was twelve,” Elena said. “It’s humiliating to be offered one by you.” “It won’t fit any more. Ma changed the locks in March, right after the funeral. I’ve felt caught in the middle ever since — I don’t want to betray her, but I don’t want to lie to you either.” “Why would she do that? Doesn’t she trust me?” “She said you’d ask that. She knew you’d take it personally, and I do think she’s right that you take things personally. But she asked me not to explain, and I feel I have to respect that, even though I know it’s hurting you.” He stepped back from the door. “I’m sorry. I really am.” The tests find the faults quickly. Test 1 (Removal) fails, since Dov gave her the key and would not say why the locks had been changed carries everything the exchange carries. Test 2 (Want) passes only on the surface, because both wants are stated, which removes the reader’s work. Test 3 (Status) fails: Dov concedes the key, the fact, his own divided position and an apology, and nothing is contested because nothing is withheld. Tests 4 (Cost), 5 (Silence) and 6 (Implicature) fail together, since every disclosure is volunteered, neither speaker keeps anything back, and the exchange supplies its own interpretation. Test 7 (Transcript) fails, because without tags the two are one person, fluent in the same emotionally literate register. The patterns present are on the nose, with its therapeutic variant ( caught in the middle , take things personally ), a touch of as you know ( right after the funeral , which Elena knows) and the ventriloquist exchange. The draft holds all the necessary information and is not badly written; it runs on one channel, and it is more emotionally explicit than the revision while conveying less emotion. “You’ll want the shop key,” Dov said, not moving from the doorway. Elena held out her hand. “I’ve had a key since I was twelve.” “Not this key.” He turned it over once between two fingers before he set it in her palm, face down, like he was folding a hand of cards. “Ma changed the locks in March.” “Did she.” Elena closed her fist around it. “Did she say why.” “She said you’d ask that.” Dov stepped back into the hall. “She didn’t say I had to answer.” The revision converts every statement of feeling into an act: I’ve been dreading this conversation becomes not moving from the doorway , and Elena’s humiliation becomes a hand held out while she asserts her old right. The fact arrives inside a correction, Not this key , so that Elena is contradicted before she is informed, which makes the information cost something. The turned key is a contradicting action beat: a man simply conceding does not handle the concession so carefully. Elena’s Did she is a significant repetition, and the missing question marks mark questions that are not requests for information, because she has already drawn a conclusion. Dov’s last line is a third-person deflection, the same refusal as the draft’s with responsibility shifted to the absent mother; he is speaking someone else’s instruction, which shields him and also discloses a man who needs the instruction to be someone else’s. The registers are differentiated by two variables only, Dov’s complete declaratives against Elena’s two- and three-word turns. The relational shift is real and partial. Dov opens holding the doorway and the key; he gives up the key, keeps the reason, and ends the conversation by withdrawing into his own hall. The plot is served by a fact with a consequence Elena has not yet worked out, that she has been shut out for four months without knowing it, and the silence domain by Dov’s refusal and by the absence of the mother from a conversation entirely about her. Three things remain unsolved. The revision is conspicuously written: the card simile and the missing question marks are visible technique, and it passes the transcript test against its own draft more easily than against the shelf it will sit on. It leans on two mechanisms, deflection and repetition, in three of its five turns, and Dov is at risk of becoming a man who only ever declines. And its theme, what family members owe each other in the way of truth, is available to a reader who has the rest of the book and thin in the scene itself. Against that, it does one thing the draft could not. Dov’s reason is now a withheld object with a place in the book, which a later exchange can close, and the draft spent it. See also: the Reference worked analyses , with readings of the Hunsford proposal, the Pemberley exchanges, the Grand Inquisitor, Their Eyes Were Watching God , Blindness , The Portrait of a Lady and “Hills Like White Elephants”, and the case’s audit by domain; Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2), for Elena’s sequel in the truck.

title: 9. Checklist and Exercises
text: Revision checklist Run each exchange of a finished draft against this list. Each item corresponds to one of the diagnostic tests or failure patterns ; an unticked item is a question to answer, not a verdict. Engine I can say in one sentence each what both speakers want from each other before the exchange ends. Something is different at the last line: a fact passed, a point conceded, a form of address changed. The exchange starts at the first turn I could not cut and ends at the last. Cost and status Every fact that passes costs the speaker something, or sits in narration instead. I can name the currency of status, and some of it changed hands or was contested and held. Any relational change happens in an act (a name, a correction, a position, an exit granted or refused), not in a statement about it. Two channels Each speaker keeps something back, and I know what it is. The reader can work out what each evasion is evading. The gap closes plainly no more than once or twice in the book, and late. Some turns do only one thing, so that the oblique ones register. Voices With every tag and action beat stripped, I can tell who is speaking from the speech alone. The principals differ in sentence length, in their relation to questions and in their default way of not saying things. Dialect lives in syntax, idiom and vocabulary rather than in respelling. Apparatus and room Most tags are said or asked , and fewer than half the turns carry one once the speakers are established. Each action beat does something besides identify the speaker. I know who else is in the room, and what their silence is doing. Exercises 1. The want sentence. Choose the longest exchange in your draft. Above it, write what each speaker wants from the other before it ends, one sentence each, with a verb aimed at the other person. If one sentence will not come, rewrite the exchange until it does, or summarise it. 2. Four mechanisms. Take the most direct line in one exchange and rewrite it four times: as an evasion, a changed subject, a too-precise reply and a delayed agreement. Keep the version that tells you something about the speaker you had not decided. 3. The transcript test. Strip every tag and action beat from two pages of dialogue, and give the bare lines to a reader who does not know the book. Ask her to mark where the speaker changes and to describe each speaker in two adjectives. 4. The domain audit. Beside each turn of one exchange, write the letters of the domains it serves: P, C, R, Th, Tx, S. Most turns carrying P alone means a briefing; R never appearing means status is fixed; S never appearing means everyone says what they think; one turn carrying most of the letters is the exchange’s spine. 5. Find the plain line. List the three places in your book where a character says plainly what she means about what matters most to her. If there are more than three, choose the one the book is building towards and restore the gap in the others. See also: the Reference checklist and studio work , with further exercises, seminar questions and an assessment rubric.

title: 10. Coda
text: The model in this chapter, with its two channels, twelve mechanisms and ten tests, describes a particular and datable ideal of dialogue: compressed, indirect and heavy with subtext. That ideal took shape in the reception of Chekhov, in Hemingway’s stories and in the writing workshops that codified both, and it is a technical achievement worth learning, because it engages the reader’s inference and produces character without assertion. It is not a description of dialogue as such. Austen’s gap was social, a matter of what could be said in a given drawing room, not psychological. Dostoevsky’s characters say what they think, at length, and the gap lies between their self-accounts and the truth. Compton-Burnett’s speak a syntax no one has spoken, and Wilde’s say what no one says aloud. Each of these would fail several of the tests, and the failures are why they are read. The tests therefore identify what an exchange is doing, not whether it is good. A writer who turns their findings into verdicts will cut the passages where the conventions are under strain, which is often where the book is most alive. What survives the change of fashion is not the preference for obliquity but the social grammar underneath it, which held for Austen and holds for McCarthy: speakers want things from each other, protect each other’s face until they stop, mark their refusals, and design what they say for everyone in the room. Dialogue may be as stylised as a book requires, provided it still does what talk does. See also: the Reference coda , which develops the historical argument; The Descriptive Detail (Chapter 4), the next chapter, on the detail that means more than it names.

title: The Descriptive Detail
text: Which true thing to name, and how to test the choice The Craft Behind the Story (Second Edition) — Chapter 4. Part I: The Scene and Its Materials. In brief. A room offers more describable particulars than a page can carry, so description is a choice: the writer names a few possibilities out of many, and the reader may treat those choices as salient. A detail can earn its place by planting what the plot will need, showing who is looking, implying how a world works, measuring time, or carrying a feeling without naming it. The tools are five domains in which a detail can work and a proposed sixth for time, the distinction between what a detail names and what it implies, a repertoire of descriptive strategies, and ten diagnostic questions. Use them on a passage that feels accurate but inert, or on a draft whose description has been praised without anyone saying what it adds. What you can do after this chapter State, for any descriptive passage, the principle that chose these details and not others. Mark each detail in a paragraph with the domains it serves, and read the pattern. Rewrite a flat passage in three other strategies before editing a word of the original. Test whether a perceiver, in her state at that moment, would notice what the passage reports. Plant an object so that its later return measures a change. Key terms Descriptive detail; the infinite field; principle of selection; formal realism and circumstantial particularity; the Homeric and biblical poles; defamiliarisation; the reality effect; situation model; descriptive pause; focalisation and the plausibility of attention; the domains of purpose and the proposed temporal domain; multiplicity, compression and selection; the density ceiling; denotation and connotation; descriptive strategy, metonymy, synecdoche, the negative detail and ekphrasis; motif, singulative, repetitive and iterative narration, varied repetition. Each is defined at first use and collected in the consolidated glossary . Contents The first files set out why description is a choice and what the choice can do; the middle files show the machinery; the last are for use at the desk. The Problem An accurate hallway that does nothing, and the chapter’s claim Definitions The detail, its scale, description against imagery, adjacent terms How It Works Particularity, omission, estrangement, the reality effect, research on reading, and changing descriptive conventions The Taxonomy Five domains of purpose, and a proposed sixth: time The Mechanism Multiplicity in one sentence, denotation and connotation, twelve strategies, substitution, and the motif Diagnostic Tests Ten questions on one page, and how to read their failures together Failure Patterns Five recurrent failures, each with a published work that commits it and succeeds Worked Analyses Great Expectations, Beloved, Klara and the Sun, Parasite, and the household revision case Checklist and Exercises The revision checklist and five exercises for your own draft Coda The case for allowing some apparently incidental details A writer already in revision can start at the diagnostic tests; the short coda, on what the tests are not for, is best read early. The full treatment The Reference layer holds the complete chapter, The Descriptive Detail : the theory at length, each domain’s carriers in tabular form, the twelve strategies with exemplars, thirteen failure patterns, close readings of Madame Bovary , “Un cœur simple”, The Great Gatsby , Things Fall Apart , Moby-Dick and To the Lighthouse , description in the short story, the series, screen and translation, seminar questions and an assessment rubric, and the sources. See also: The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1), for the domains of purpose and the value-shift test this chapter takes down to the single detail; The Dialogue Exchange (Chapter 3), for text and subtext, the counterpart in speech of denotation and connotation; The Ending (Chapter 16), which spends the motifs this chapter plants.

title: 1. The Problem
text: A writer revising a quiet family novel has a scene in which Nadia, a woman in her thirties whose father died in March, goes up to the flat above the family shop where he lived. The draft paragraph reads: Nadia came up the stairs into the flat above the shop. The hallway was narrow and dim, with a worn carpet and a radiator that ticked. There was a coat rack by the door with several coats on it, and an umbrella stand, and a small table where the post collected. On the wall was a mirror in a wooden frame, and beneath it a pile of free newspapers nobody had thrown away. The place smelled of dust and old cooking. It had been like this for as long as she could remember, and it was strange to think that her father would never come through the door again. The paragraph gives the reader a plausible hallway: its light, objects and smell. It also states Nadia’s feeling about her father’s death. What remains unclear is why these particulars, rather than others, matter to her at this moment. The roughly hundred-word passage spends much of its space on an inventory before naming the feeling it might have allowed the reader to infer. The infinite field The difficulty is not peculiar to this writer. A room offers more describable particulars than a page can hold: its ceiling height, temperature, dust on different surfaces and, in some rooms, old paint beneath the current coat or a chair repaired with mismatched screws. Description can continue at ever finer levels of specificity, but a page must leave most possibilities out. This chapter calls that open-ended range of possible choices the infinite field . The draft’s problem lies in its selection, though the observations are plausible. A writer can continue adding specific details without deciding which ones this scene needs. Such a paragraph may be accurate and still feel inert; that is easy to miss when the individual sentences seem well observed. The chapter’s claim The chapter’s governing claim follows from the asymmetry between the world and the page: A detail is not included only because it could be true. It is included because of what it can do among the alternatives the writer might have chosen. The claim says that inclusion is a choice: a reader who cannot see the room may treat the chosen facts as salient, whether or not the writer intended them to be. A familiar detail, such as a stove in a kitchen, may add little unless the scene puts it to use. The claim does not require every detail to be symbolic; orientation, pace and characterisation are other possibilities. Nor must the writer know a detail’s purpose while drafting: the tests in this chapter are for revision. A detail without an obvious plot or thematic job is not automatically a fault. Barthes’s account of the reality effect, set out in How It Works , offers one explanation for how apparently incidental details can help a represented world feel inhabited. Where the chapter sits The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1) asked of a scene what is true at its end that was not true at its start, and named the domains in which the change can register. This chapter asks the same question of a single detail: what does the reader know, feel or anticipate after it that she did not before? The Dialogue Exchange (Chapter 3) gave dialogue its two channels, what is said and what is meant; description offers a related distinction between what a detail names and what it implies. A detail can also contribute without carrying a legible second meaning. The chapter also plants. The household novel that runs through this book takes several of its principal objects from the revision of Nadia’s hallway: the father’s coat on its hook, the frayed left cuff, the dust on the shoulders, and, without emphasis, the ledger he kept for eleven years, which a later chapter’s discovery depends on the reader having already met. The ending, in The Ending (Chapter 16), is a varied return of the coat, and the account of the motif in The Mechanism is what makes such a return work. See also: the Reference introduction , which states the claim’s assertions and limits in full; the household revision case , where the hallway is revised.

title: 2. Definitions
text: Craft discussion uses “description”, “imagery”, “detail”, “symbol” and “setting” almost interchangeably. They name units of different sizes that fail in different ways, so the chapter separates them before using them. The working definition A descriptive detail is a concrete, specific unit of sensory or physical information, chosen from an open-ended set of possible alternatives that go unmentioned, and included for what it contributes beyond plausibility or accuracy alone. Each phrase of the definition does work. Concrete and specific rules out judgements: the room was messy is a verdict that withholds its evidence, whereas three coffee mugs, none finished, ringed the base of the lamp is a detail, countable and particular. The workshop slogan show, don’t tell is more useful as a question about where inference happens. A detail can invite the reader to infer a judgement that an abstract label supplies directly. Chosen from alternatives that go unmentioned is the centre of the definition: a detail’s meaning may depend partly on what was not said. Sensory or physical restricts the subject to the perceptible; a reported thought may be characterisation, and a summary of someone’s finances is exposition, but the state of their shoes is description. Work beyond accuracy is the purposive clause on which the taxonomy rests, and the one the chapter later complicates. Scale The unit stretches from a single modifier to a whole chapter, and its possible failures change with its size: modifiers may pile up, a named object may decorate, a detail sentence may go generic, a paragraph may become an unselected list, and a set piece may halt the story for the author’s knowledge rather than anyone’s need. Gérard Genette, the French narratologist whose terms for narrative time are developed in The Transition (Chapter 5), calls a stretch of description during which story time does not advance a descriptive pause . A pause can be short or long, and description can also occur while events advance. The term draws attention to the relation between description and narrative time, rather than setting a minimum size for a descriptive passage. This chapter takes the detail sentence as its working unit, since that is a scale at which a choice is visible and can be revised. Description is not imagery Description and imagery are related but answer different revision questions. Imagery is the sensory and figurative texture of the prose, what the language may evoke in a reader’s senses. Description supplies information about the represented world. A page of metaphor can be rich in imagery while giving little information about a room; an inventory can describe a room without much figurative language, though its objects may still evoke images. Ask both what the reader can now picture or sense and what the passage has established. Nor is description the same as setting, which is a kind of content: a face or a meal can be described as readily as a place. Adjacent terms The terms below recur through the chapter. Each names something next to the detail rather than the detail itself. Term Meaning Relation to the detail Image A sensory impression produced by language The effect; the detail is the choice that produces it Symbol An object that stands for an abstraction One possible implication Motif A recurring detail, image or phrase whose repetition acquires significance, with or without variation A pattern extended through time Metonymy, synecdoche Naming a thing by something associated with it; using part for whole or whole for part Two related descriptive strategies Ekphrasis Vivid verbal presentation of a subject; in modern usage often a work of art (Greek, “speaking out”) Can form a set piece; Homer’s shield is an early, influential example Focalisation Genette’s term for who perceives, as distinct from who speaks Decides whose selection a detail is Objective correlative T. S. Eliot’s 1919 formulation of objects, a situation or a chain of events that evokes a particular emotion One account of how an external occasion can convey feeling Symbol, motif and ekphrasis are special cases; treating them as the norm is how description becomes over-managed. What the chapter leaves to others This chapter considers exposition delivered as description chiefly when it hinders a passage; how antecedent information can be distributed is Backstory and Flashback ’s subject (Chapter 7). The use of a descriptive pause to slow a sequence before a shock is also discussed in The Transition (Chapter 5), which examines narrative speed. The Opening Pages (Chapter 9) considers why readers may give an opening detail unusual weight. Gesture around speech belongs to The Dialogue Exchange (Chapter 3), and questions about whose perceptions a chapter can report belong to The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13). Prose rhythm matters, but this chapter does not examine it systematically. See also: the Reference definitions , with the scale table and a fuller list of adjacent terms.

title: 3. How It Works
text: The chapter needs only the theory its method uses. Each strand below starts from a question a writer asks in revision, then gives the source that answers it. Why not simply cut the description? Ian Watt’s The Rise of the Novel (1957) argues that formal realism helped distinguish the emerging novel from earlier prose fiction by presenting individual experience through particulars of time, place and person. Ordinary names, dated time, named streets and objects that are owned or worn are examples of the circumstantial particularity he discusses. These are central to the realist mode in Watt’s account. For revision, his argument offers a reason to preserve particulars that establish a book’s world. Spareness does not by itself turn a novel into a fable or parable; the effect depends on the work. Particularity can authenticate without being a faithful transcript of an actual room. How much should I describe? Erich Auerbach’s Mimesis (1946; translated by Willard R. Trask, 1953) opens by comparing two ancient texts. In Book 19 of the Odyssey the old nurse recognises Odysseus by a scar above his knee, and the poem turns aside for roughly eighty lines to explain it. Genesis 22, the binding of Isaac, gives fewer concrete particulars: it names the land of Moriah and says Abraham saw the place on the third day, but leaves the speakers’ appearance and most thoughts unstated. Auerbach calls the biblical manner “fraught with background”. The contrast offers two possibilities for a writer: extensive foregrounded description and a sparser mode that invites inference. Neither guarantees presence or depth. Auerbach treats both as successful styles rather than prescribing one of them. Why does an odd angle make a reader see? Viktor Shklovsky’s essay “Art as Device” (1917; translated by Lee T. Lemon and Marion J. Reis as “Art as Technique”) argues that perception can become habitual. In his account, art can renew perception by making the familiar strange, a process he called ostranenie , usually translated as defamiliarisation . His examples include Tolstoy’s descriptions of flogging and property as perceived by a horse. Describing an operation while withholding its familiar name is one strategy a writer can test; it may slow a passage and has a different effect when estrangement becomes a book’s sustained style. What about the detail that does nothing? Roland Barthes’s essay “The Reality Effect” (1968; translated by Richard Howard) challenges a strict demand that every detail serve plot or character. Analysing Flaubert’s “Un cœur simple” (1877), he discusses the barometer in Mme Aubain’s room. In his reading, it has no clear narrative function and can instead signify the category of the real: an apparently superfluous particular makes the text seem to report a world. Other critics may find social or historical associations in the barometer.
