His reality effect is a critical account of realism’s rhetoric, not a measured finding about what every reader needs to find a room convincing. Three replies are available. The first treats authentication as a job, though job then risks becoming too broad to guide revision. The second asks about a passage’s selection as well as a sentence’s apparent function. The third treats the demand for an identifiable job as an aesthetic preference rather than a law. This chapter works from the second and keeps the third in view. Its practical question is whether the passage has a principle of selection . Barthes supplies no required proportion of incidental details, and no fixed ratio separates a convincing room from a list. How many details will a reader keep? Research on reading describes a situation model , a representation of a text’s state of affairs along dimensions such as protagonist, space, time, cause and intention (Rolf Zwaan and Gabriel Radvansky’s 1998 review). In experiments by Zwaan and colleagues, spatial discontinuities affected reading times when participants had learned a map of the setting, but not when they read without it; temporal, causal, goal-related and protagonist discontinuities affected reading times in both conditions. A craft inference is to establish spatial relations clearly when a scene requires the reader to follow movement. These studies do not count the descriptive details in novels, establish how many a reader will remember or identify a fixed memory threshold. Elaine Scarry’s Dreaming by the Book (1999) offers a theoretical account of how prose, including descriptions of motion, can guide imagination. A writer can test that possibility by describing an object in use. Scarry’s account is not an experimental ranking of descriptive techniques. The conventions have dates Descriptive conventions vary by work, form and period. Balzac opens Père Goriot (1835) with an extended description of a boarding house; Hugo devotes sections of Les Misérables (1862) to Waterloo and the Paris sewers. These examples do not establish a period norm or what every contemporary reader wanted. Later works also vary: some introduce a room through a few details, while others use catalogues or set pieces. This chapter has no corpus from which to infer a two- or three-detail count norm , a tenfold decline or the date when a workshop convention began. Photography, film and publishing formats changed, but that alone does not establish a causal decline in descriptive length or that writers were generally paid by length. Naomi Schor’s Reading in Detail (1987) discusses an older devaluation of detail and its later reconsideration. Treat selection as a choice rather than a dated universal rule. See also: the Reference theory , which stages the collision with Barthes in a table and develops each strand; The Opening Pages (Chapter 9), on the rules of notice that make a placed detail read as a promise.

title: 4. The Taxonomy
text: The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1) names plot, character, theme and texture as domains of purpose, with a relational domain also proposed there and adopted by The Dialogue Exchange (Chapter 3). At the scale of a detail, this chapter adds world as a fifth domain and considers relational effects under character. It then proposes a sixth domain for time. These are revision lenses, not a required inventory of functions. Two possible misuses are worth naming. One treats the domains as slots to fill and revises a passage until each is represented; the other assigns a domain to a detail after the fact merely to justify keeping it. A difficult-to-explain function may be a reason to examine the passage, though readers can respond differently. Plot: the detail matters to what happens A plot detail gives the reader information the action will need. It may plant an object a later scene requires, orient the reader in space, mark a threat or material constraint, or supply a clue. Chekhov’s gun is commonly used as craft advice about conspicuous emphasis creating expectations; it is not a measured rule about how soon a detail must pay off. Research on situation models shows that readers can track spatial relations when a task or context supports doing so. In a scene that depends on movement, placing the relevant spatial facts before they become decisive may help the reader follow it. In the first chapter of Great Expectations (1861), the convict on the marshes demands food and a file from Pip. The file connects with the leg-iron Pip has seen and leads him to steal from Joe’s forge in chapter 2. In Chinua Achebe’s Things Fall Apart (1958), Okonkwo earlier fires a gun at his wife and misses; at a funeral, his gun explodes and a piece of iron kills a boy, causing Okonkwo’s exile. In both works, an object that belongs to the represented world also becomes important to the plot. Character: the detail reveals a person A character detail may reveal the person perceiving, the person perceived, or both. When a perceiving mind selects what to notice, the choice can contribute to characterisation. Two people enter one kitchen: one registers scorched milk and an unpaid bill, the other the light on the tiles. Those different selections invite different inferences. A useful revision question is whether this perceiver, wanting what she wants in her present state, would notice the detail. This chapter calls that the plausibility of attention . Hilary Mantel’s Wolf Hall (2009) opens on the boy Thomas Cromwell knocked flat on the cobbles by his father, and what he registers, dazed and bleeding, is the boot: its stitching is coming undone, and a hard knot in it has caught his eyebrow and opened another cut. A boy being kicked does not survey a yard. He sees the one object a few inches from his face, and the selection gives both his state and the novel’s habit of attention to how things are made. Relations to objects can reveal a person: what someone maintains, lets go, has mended or continues to wear. The household case uses one such carrier to show a relation. Who dusts a thing, who may move it and who has stopped touching it may characterise more than one person within a clause. World: the detail builds the setting’s reality A world detail can help a place feel inhabited and convey its practices. One method is normalisation , a term this book takes from The Opening Pages (Chapter 9): a rule appears through use rather than explanation. A character who steps round an offering bowl at the threshold without comment may imply a household custom; a narrator can also explain the custom when the story needs it. A specific noun such as awl can carry more material information than tool , provided readers have enough context to understand it. An unfamiliar cue may need context for a reader to understand its role. N. K. Jemisin’s The Fifth Season (2015), winner of the 2016 Hugo Award for best novel, introduces terms such as orogenes, comms and the Fulcrum in scenes while also providing explanation and a glossary at the back. There is no established two- or three-detail norm for familiar or unfamiliar settings. Theme: the detail carries meaning A theme detail may suggest what a book is about on its first appearance or develop meaning through a return or contrast. Eliot’s 1919 essay on Hamlet gives a well-known formulation of the objective correlative : objects, a situation or a chain of events can evoke an emotion. The term predates Eliot, though his formulation is influential. In To the Lighthouse (1927), the boeuf en daube at dinner can be read as contributing to concerns with transience and made things without standing for either as a simple symbol. Texture: the detail shapes the reading A texture detail can give a reader a felt condition: mood, pace, bodily sensation or pleasure in the prose. Its effect depends partly on placement; description may slow a moment, build suspense or interrupt an awaited answer. Prose can name smell, temperature and the feel of cloth, while film often suggests these through image, sound and a character’s response. Neither medium has an exclusive claim to nonvisual sensation. A proposed sixth: the temporal domain The five-domain model folds time into world. This chapter proposes separating it as the temporal domain : a detail belongs to it when its work is to establish duration, sequence, decay, repurposing, season or interruption, that is, not what the world is but what has happened to it. Three arguments support the proposed temporal domain. It has useful carriers, including perfect and pluperfect forms ( what had once been ), participles such as mended and worn through , habitual forms, wear, residue and maintenance. These can also serve plot, character and world; the category draws attention to effects those domains might overlook. Readers track time as a dimension of situation models. Margaret Atwood’s The Handmaid’s Tale (1985) opens with its narrator sleeping in “what had once been the gymnasium”; the phrase marks a change of use. Jon McGregor’s Reservoir 13 (2017) covers thirteen years after the disappearance of Rebecca Shaw. Its first chapter opens with the search, and New Year fireworks recur later as part of the village’s yearly cycle. The calendar can be read as one way the novel represents the community’s changing relation to her absence. The case against a separate temporal domain is substantial. Another category adds to a writer’s checklist, with no principled stopping point; one could also propose a social or bodily domain. A frayed cuff can suggest wear, household and a person’s habit at once. Distinct carriers do not by themselves prove a distinct domain. This chapter adopts the sixth domain as a prompt for noticing aspect, wear and maintenance while acknowledging that these may also be features of other domains. Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture (Chapter 8) also considers temporal orientation. Must every detail serve several domains? No. A detail can perform one modest job; another can serve several. Some apparently incidental details may contribute to texture or to the reality effect described by Barthes. No measured proportion is required. Consider coverage at the level of a passage rather than demanding several functions from every sentence. The domains are lenses, not slots: ask which helps explain the passage’s selection and whether another suggests a useful revision. See also: the Reference domains , with each domain’s carriers, under- and over-delivery, and further illustrations; the domain audit , a marking procedure for a paragraph.

title: 5. The Mechanism
text: The domains say what a detail can do. The mechanism says how one detail does several things, how a detail comes to mean more than it names, and how a detail planted early comes to mean something later. Multiplicity under a constraint Multiplicity , making one unit of text do several jobs, was introduced at the scale of the scene in The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1). At the scale of the detail it becomes a question about emphasis: which particulars should the reader notice, and which can contribute quietly? The situation-model research discussed in How It Works does not say how many details a novel contains or how many any reader will retain. One detail can serve several domains, but it does not occupy a measurable single slot in memory. The section turns on a useful distinction. Compression puts several things into a small space; it can succeed, but an overstuffed clause may call attention to the effort. Selection changes what is described, perhaps finding one object that already suggests a plot fact, a relation or a date as well as texture. In revision, compare a compressed sentence with one built around a different detail and judge which serves the passage. One sentence, six domains In chapter 8 of Great Expectations , Pip is taken into Miss Havisham’s room and reports: It was when I stood before her, avoiding her eyes, that I took note of the surrounding objects in detail, and saw that her watch had stopped at twenty minutes to nine, and that a clock in the room had stopped at twenty minutes to nine. The original sentence has forty-six words. Pip’s avoidance of her eyes directs his attention to the objects. He has already noticed that the watch and chain have not been put on, so the watch is a personal possession rather than one worn on her body. The matching stopped time suggests a deliberate act and a prior event; its precision may also support a reading of arrested time. These are possible functions of the sentence, not a measure of what every reader retains. Where multiplicity lives Multiplicity can arise in four plain places as well as in metaphor. The first is the choice of noun: chokecherry , not tree . The second is which attribute is reported: a coat’s colour may provide texture, while its frayed cuff can suggest time and habit. The third is an object’s condition and who maintains it. In Mick Herron’s Real Tigers , Slough House is described as a place where things are “either broken or mended”; that condition can also be read as a comment on the staff’s careers. The fourth is grammatical aspect: had once been , used to , still hung . A metaphor can also connect functions, but the writer should consider what its comparison brings into the scene. Multiplicity can become conspicuous. When every detail seems charged, some readers may see the arrangement more readily than the room. The chapter calls the point at which a passage begins to feel strained the density ceiling : a revision prompt, not a measured threshold. A writer can test whether some details should carry one modest purpose or remain apparently incidental. A highly charged passage may also be a deliberate formal choice. What a detail names and what it implies A detail can be considered at two levels. Denotation is what it names in context; connotation is an association or implication that may arise from that choice: mood, class, foreboding or judgement. A chipped teacup and a bone-white teacup might be the same cup, but their descriptions invite different associations, which depend on the scene and reader. The pair is a useful counterpart to text and subtext in The Dialogue Exchange (Chapter 3). In a semiotic account associated with Barthes, a first-order sign can become the signifier of a further meaning. Connotations can change across cultures and periods; neither those changes nor a detail’s effect can be ranked by a universal rate. Twelve strategies, and substitution “Choose a better detail” may be hard to act on; a repertoire of named strategies offers options. A descriptive strategy is a way of selecting and presenting a detail. This chapter uses twelve. Metonymy evokes a thing through something associated with it (Gatsby’s shirts can suggest his wealth; Charles Bovary’s cap can suggest Charles), while synecdoche uses part for whole or whole for part (a hand for a worker). An estranged detail may withhold the familiar name; a catalogue may make order do the work. A negative detail names an absence, often implying an expected state and its deviation. A comparison’s voice or viewpoint matters; a focalised detail is selected through a perceiving mind. In Barthes’s account, an apparently superfluous detail can contribute to a reality effect. Repetition can be identical or varied. Ekphrasis is vivid verbal presentation of a visual subject, often a made object in modern examples. Lessing’s Laocoön (1766) discusses Homer’s presentation of Achilles’ shield as it is made; this offers a way to test a description in motion, not proof that process always surpasses a still image. A technical register describes through a trade’s vocabulary. The repertoire can support substitution. If a passage feels flat, name its current strategy, then try a focalised detail, a negative detail or a technical register and compare the effects. The exercise changes the principle of selection as well as the wording. The motif: how a detail planted early means something late A single detail can suggest a theme; a return can develop or complicate that suggestion. Genette’s narrative frequency describes how often an event is told relative to how often it happens: once for once ( singulative ), several tellings of one event ( repetitive ), or one telling of repeated events ( iterative ). A motif is different: a detail, image or phrase recurs and gains significance, often in separate scenes. Those scenes can each be narrated singulatively. Identical repetition can itself be expressive, as Dickens’s repeated fog shows; variation gives readers another basis for comparing appearances. No fixed number of appearances makes a motif legible. Two can establish an echo; further returns can alter it. An unemphatic first appearance is one option, while a conspicuous first appearance can create anticipation. A final return may be changed or explicitly interpreted. Fitzgerald’s green light at the end of Daisy’s dock figures in three scenes: Gatsby reaches towards it before Nick identifies it; when Daisy visits, Nick comments that its former significance to Gatsby may have diminished; and in the closing passage Nick connects it with the future Gatsby pursued. The middle and final scenes both contain commentary. The object remains while its place in Gatsby’s and Nick’s understanding changes. See also: the Reference multiplicity , with the sentence anatomy as a table and the domain audit; the Reference account of denotation and connotation , with the twelve strategies tabulated, a worked substitution on the household coat, and a table of connotations that have aged.

title: 6. Diagnostic Tests
text: The ten tests are prompts for revision. Run them on passages a reader found slow or that you suspect need work. Record a sentence, not a verdict: “this detail supplies mood and nothing else” is more useful than “fails test 2”. Tests 8 and 9 can be done with a pen to make a passage’s choices visible. A feature flagged by a test may also be an intentional part of a book’s design. Test 1 — Removal Cut the detail. What does the reader no longer know, feel or anticipate? Possible concern. You cannot identify what the detail contributes, although its emphasis suggests a larger role. Alternative. An apparently incidental detail may help establish a scene or register. Test 2 — Denotation and connotation Write one sentence about what it shows and one about what it implies. Possible concern. The passage needs an implication, but this detail offers little beyond its literal report. Alternative. A plain report may be exactly what the book’s register calls for. Test 3 — Genericness Would it be equally true of another place of this kind in another book? Failure. A category detail that confirms what the name already supplied. Exception. A cheap orienting cue, used sparingly. Test 4 — Substitution Replace it with two other true things. Do they imply different books? Failure. The choice was not doing selective work; change the object. Exception. Interchangeable detail in a deliberately uniform world. Test 5 — Focalisation Whose attention selected it, and does the selection reveal them? Failure. In close narration, a detail written over the character’s shoulder. Exception. Declared omniscience ( Middlemarch ). Test 6 — Plausibility of attention Would this person, wanting what she wants, in her present state, notice this? Failure. A survey performed by someone in no condition to make one. Exception. A perceiver given a reason to wait or look. Test 7 — Recurrence Where else does the object appear, and what has changed each time? Possible concern. An emphasised appearance seems to promise a return that never comes, or repeated appearances have no clear effect. Alternative. Identical wording can itself be expressive, within a passage or across a book. Test 8 — Count How many discrete details, and how many do you want kept? Possible concern. The passage offers more detail than its intended emphasis can organise. Exception. A catalogue with an ordering principle. Test 9 — Modifiers and senses (a) Count modifiers per noun. (b) Tally details by sense. Possible concern. (a) Several modifiers obscure the object. (b) The visual emphasis does not serve the scene. Exception. Nabokov’s cumulative modifiers; Robbe-Grillet’s chosen visuality. Test 10 — Inventory Shuffle the details. Then complete: these details, and not others, because … . Failure. Shuffling loses nothing, and the answer is “because they were there”. Alternative. An apparently unselected inventory may be deliberate; test its effect in context. Four refinements sharpen the tests. In test 4, substitute objects as well as attributes: ask why the coat rather than the shoes or the shopping list on the table. In test 6, consider how fear, pain, urgency, grief or desire might direct a character’s attention; there is no fixed number of details such a character can notice. If a passage needs a wider survey, give the perceiver a reason to wait or look. In test 9(b), tally the senses actually used and decide whether another sensory detail would help; no measured share of visual detail defines a typical draft. In test 10, possible completions name a perceiver’s preoccupation, a causal argument, a temporal record or a formal order. Reading the results together Patterns across the tests may suggest a revision. If tests 1 and 10 raise the same concern, try a clearer principle of selection. If test 2 raises a concern, consider whether a different object or a plainer report would serve the passage. Tests 5 and 6 can prompt a check on whose attention governs the description. Test 7 can prompt a change in an object’s state or context. If test 8 raises a concern, choose details by their effect in the passage rather than cutting to a fixed number. If an implication seems too emphatic, try reducing its emphasis. The tests lean towards the purposeful. Applied indiscriminately, they may encourage a book in which every detail visibly justifies itself. Use them to investigate passages that seem problematic, and judge any revision in the context of the whole work. See also: the Reference protocol , with each test’s procedure and a table of combined failures; the domain audit , which marks each detail with the domains it serves.

title: 7. Failure Patterns
text: Rules against long paragraphs, adjectives, lists or weather can obscure what a passage is trying to do. The five patterns below are revision prompts rather than prohibitions. Each includes a published work in which a similar feature serves a purpose. The inventory passage Symptom. A list of accurate, unselected details: the room had a table, two chairs, a window and a rug. Furniture is listed rather than seen. Mechanism. Without a discernible principle of selection, a list can seem generic. The issue is not its length or the fact of listing, but whether its contents and order contribute to the passage. Remedy. Try choosing a principle (what this perceiver avoids looking at, what the rent explains, what nobody has touched since March) and revising the list around it. Fewer items or one object instead of a room may help. Example. Balzac opens Père Goriot (1835) with an extended description of the Maison Vauquer, including furnishings and the lodgers’ payments. Prices and material conditions help organise the social portrait; this is one way to read the catalogue’s effect. Reordering its details would change that progression. The static motif Symptom. A charged detail repeated in the same words, scene after scene, with nothing about it or around it developing. Mechanism. If each return seems to add little in context, repetition may lose its force. Exact recurrence can also be intentional, so assess its effect before revising it. Remedy. Change the object’s state or who stands in relation to it at each return, or cut the returns to two and let the second one matter. Example. The opening of Bleak House (1853) repeats fog across successive clauses while varying its location and associations. The repeated word can read as incantatory. Exact recurrence can also work across a longer text when the context gives it force. The unfocalised detail Symptom. In close third or first person, a detail no one present could have registered: what lies behind the character, what the room looked like before she entered, another person’s face while unobserved. Mechanism. If a passage has established close access to one character’s perception, an unexplained shift in access may feel inconsistent. Check whether the narration has already allowed a wider view. Remedy. Give the detail to the perceiver, by finding what she would notice that implies the same fact, or move it to a passage where the narration’s access is wider and declared. Example. George Eliot’s Middlemarch (1871–72) has a narrator who moves between minds and comments on events. Wide access is an established feature of its narration. The symbol announcing itself Symptom. A detail so plainly meaningful that the reader stops seeing the object: the broken clock, the caged bird, the dead tree in the garden, arriving at the right emotional moment and described at the right emotional length. Mechanism. If the narration stresses an object’s symbolic meaning, some readers may attend to the device before the scene. That effect may be useful or distracting, depending on the work. Remedy. Reduce the emphasis, not the meaning. Let the object appear first as ordinary world detail, give its announcement to a character rather than to the narration, or give it a plain use in the story. Example. Four episodes of Breaking Bad ’s second season (AMC, 2009) open with largely black-and-white flash-forwards featuring a pink teddy bear. The four episode titles spell “737 Down Over ABQ”, and the season later reveals the bear as debris from a collision over Albuquerque. The conspicuous image can work as an enigma with a literal answer. In The Great Gatsby , George Wilson reads the eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg as the eyes of God; the novel also gives Nick’s account of the billboard. The sense monoculture Symptom. Everything is seen. Across a manuscript, description is visual with an occasional sound, and smell, temperature, texture and the body’s own report are absent. Mechanism. Prose can name smell, touch, temperature and bodily sensation as well as sight. A strongly visual passage may be effective; the question is whether its sensory range serves the scene. Other narrative media can also convey nonvisual sensation through words, sound, performance and reaction. Remedy. Tally the senses, then consider whether a nonvisual detail would strengthen the scene. Smell can be useful when it matters to a character’s memory or judgment; film can suggest it through dialogue, sound, images and reactions. Exception. Alain Robbe-Grillet’s Jealousy (1957; translated by Richard Howard) is visual by programme: shadows measured on a veranda, rows of banana trees counted, a stain on a wall returned to again and again, and no interior life stated. The narrator never names himself and is never named. The monoculture is the position, a refusal of the interiority the novel had relied on, and the reader infers a jealous watcher from the obsessive precision of what is seen. See also: the Reference failure patterns , where each pattern also states why competent writers keep producing it; Diagnostic Tests , for the test that catches each.

title: 8. Worked Analyses
text: Three close readings, a screen reading and a revision case. The method is the same throughout: name the strategy, audit the domains, and say what the passage would lose under substitution. Great Expectations : a room made of what has stopped On Pip’s first visit to Miss Havisham in chapter 8, he enters her candlelit room and sees her yellowed wedding clothes, a watch and a clock stopped at twenty minutes to nine, and the shoe she has not put on. The daylight is shut out. The bride-cake belongs to a later visit, in chapter 11: Pip sees a decaying object on a long table, obscured by fungus and cobwebs, with spiders running in and out of it. Miss Havisham identifies it as her bride-cake. Keeping the visits separate shows how the novel adds to its picture of arrested time. The stopped watch and clock, unworn shoe, yellowed clothing and decaying cake invite a reading centred on time and condition. Dickens also gives spatial information, including the tables and the route into the room. The point is one of emphasis: a room can be described through what has happened to its contents as well as through its layout. This is one use of the temporal domain set out in The Taxonomy . Across the two visits, the details accumulate rather than forming one continuous descriptive sweep. On the second visit, Miss Havisham points to the table and says she will be laid there when she dies; she then identifies the decaying bride-cake for Pip. The table and cake can be read as part of a developing motif, but the order of disclosure matters: the death reference comes before the cake is identified, in the same visit. Beloved : a figure is somebody’s Sethe’s back is scarred from a whipping. In Toni Morrison’s Beloved (1987) it is first described by Amy Denver, the white girl who finds her on the run, as a tree, a chokecherry tree, with trunk and branches and even blossom. Sethe has never seen her own back and keeps Amy’s word for it. The strategy is the comparative detail, and the reading turns on who owns the figure. Its denotation is raised, branching scar tissue. Amy’s comparison offers an image of growth and beauty even as the scars record violence. It also tells us something about Amy’s way of speaking and Sethe’s dependence on another person’s description of a back she cannot see. Giving the comparison to Amy makes her response part of the scene; a narrator’s simile could have worked differently. When Paul D later touches the scars, he thinks of the work of an ironsmith. The different comparisons leave room to ask how Sethe’s injury can be described and by whom. The chapter’s tests reach the edge of their competence here. The removal test and the domain audit both work, and neither touches what matters: whether a figure of speech may be allowed to make a wound bearable to look at. That is an ethical question about description, and the Coda returns to it. Klara and the Sun : the estranged perceiver Kazuo Ishiguro’s Klara and the Sun (2021) is narrated by Klara, a solar-powered “Artificial Friend” bought as a companion for a sick girl. Her account of the human world can be read alongside Shklovsky’s discussion of estranged perception. Klara believes the Sun gives her nourishment and may heal the girl, and she comes to fear a street machine she calls the Cootings Machine because its pollution blocks the Sun. The reader can understand it as machinery whose pollution blocks light, while Klara treats it as an enemy. The distance between those readings is one source of the novel’s pathos. Ishiguro also makes Klara’s visual processing part of the description. Her field sometimes breaks into panels; in one scene, “that whole section of the room had become partitioned”, with the Mother’s narrowed eyes repeated from box to box. The panels appear in more than emotionally ambiguous moments, so they should not be treated as a fixed signal for one emotion. In this scene, a reader may connect the partitioning with Klara’s difficulty reading the exchange. Her distinctive vocabulary and repeated attention to the Sun help sustain the viewpoint. A screen reading: Parasite Bong Joon-ho’s Parasite (2019) makes smell a consequential detail. The Kim family have taken work in the Park household under false identities. Hidden under the living-room table one night, Ki-taek, now the Parks’ driver, hears Mr Park compare his smell to an old radish or a boiled rag and associate it with subway riders. At the garden party near the film’s end, Park recoils at the smell of the man who has been living beneath the house, and Ki-taek stabs him. Film can suggest smell through dialogue, reactions and other audiovisual cues. Here, what matters is who notices it and who hears the remark. The later recoil recalls the earlier conversation. The repeated detail can be read in relation to plot, Park’s judgment, Ki-taek’s response and the film’s treatment of class. The household revision case: the coat on the hook The draft is the hallway paragraph quoted in The Problem : Nadia climbs to the flat above the shop where her father lived, and the narration lists a narrow dim hall, a worn carpet, a ticking radiator, coats, an umbrella stand, the post, a mirror, free newspapers and a smell of dust and cooking, ending with it was strange to think that her father would never come through the door again . Run through the tests, the draft offers a broad survey of the hall and ends by naming Nadia’s feeling. Some details could be exchanged for others without much change to the scene. The revision below tries a different emphasis: it stays with an object Nadia associates with her father. A mirror could carry an expectation in some contexts, but this draft gives it no further role. These are revision judgments about a constructed example, not measured claims about which details readers will remember. The revision: The coat still hung by the door, army green gone the colour of dishwater, and someone — meaning kindness — had brushed the shoulders free of dust every week since March. He had worn it every winter behind the counter, over the ledger. The left cuff was frayed through where he used to hook his thumb before he spoke, a habit their mother called thinking with his hands. Nadia had learned not to touch it. She had also learned, without meaning to, how many days it took the dust to show again on the green, because she watched, and did not brush it herself, and told herself this was not the same as counting. The revision replaces the inventory with one object at about the same length: 114 words against 109, counting space-separated words in the quoted passages. Its principle can be stated as these details because they show how Nadia and the household have attended to the coat since March . The colour and worn cuff suggest duration and habit. Nadia’s attention stays on one object, while someone else’s regular brushing complicates her refusal to touch it. The shift is a choice of subject and emphasis, not a claim about how many details a reader retains. Several domains can be read into it. Since March gives the period of the coat’s care; the paragraph alone does not state when the father died. The ledger is named once, in a clause about where the coat was worn, before Elena finds it in the register drawer in The Chapter Break (Chapter 6). Nadia’s attention to dust and her refusal to brush the coat can suggest a way of managing grief without naming it. The cuff evokes her father’s habit, and the unnamed brushing suggests another person’s care. The past-perfect had brushed , the habitual used to hook and every winter , and the wear itself give the object a history. The ending, in which Nadia takes the coat down and puts it on, returns to it in a changed context. Several questions remain. The paragraph may feel densely meaningful when read aloud; an ordinary sentence beside it could change that effect. An apparently incidental object might also help the hall feel inhabited, but it need not be meaningless to do so. The ledger clause leaves the present hallway for the father’s habit, and a reader may ask whether Nadia would think of the counter here. The restrained close-third voice may also feel familiar; that is a question for The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13) as well as this chapter. See also: the Reference worked analyses , with readings of Charles Bovary’s cap, the Bovary wedding cake, Flaubert’s barometer, Gatsby’s shirts and Eckleburg, Things Fall Apart , the whiteness of the whale and the boeuf en daube, and the case’s audit as a table; The Ending (Chapter 16), for the coat’s return.

title: 9. Checklist and Exercises
text: Revision checklist Use the checklist on one descriptive passage at a time, after a reader has flagged it or you have begun to suspect it. Each item is a question to answer in a sentence. Selection Can you complete these details, and not others, because … with something other than “they were there”? Does the passage lose anything if its details are shuffled? Is each detail specific to this place, or only to its kind? Perceiver Whose attention chose each detail, and what does the choice show about her? Would she, wanting what she wants, in her present state, notice this? Is any detail something nobody present could have registered? Domains and density Which domain is the passage’s principle of selection? Does any detail carry plot, a relation or a date as well as texture? Would an ordinary or apparently incidental detail help the passage’s chosen effect? Implication Can you write a second sentence saying what each key detail implies, distinct from what it shows? Is any implication so loud that the object has left the room? Does any figure of speech have an owner in the scene? Time and return Does the passage say what has happened to the place, through aspect, wear or maintenance? Where else does each charged object appear, and what has changed each time? Does the first appearance of a planned motif create the emphasis you want? Count and senses How many details are offered, and how many do you want kept? How many modifiers stand on a single noun? Which single non-visual detail would carry most? Exercises The principle swap. Take a descriptive paragraph from your draft and write the same place three times, from three principles: what your viewpoint character is avoiding looking at, what has not been touched since a date that matters to the book, and what an expert in the place’s trade would notice. Keep the version that tells the reader most about the book you are writing, not the best-written one. One object instead of a room. Find a passage that surveys a room. Try replacing the survey with one object in that room, described by its state and by the person who maintains it, if anyone, at the same length or less. Compare the effects. The outside audit. Mark each detail in one paragraph with the domains it serves (plot, character, world, theme, texture, time), then give an unmarked copy to a reader and ask her to do the same. The details you credited with domains she did not find are the ones to revise. The negative detail. Describe a place in your novel only by what is missing from it, stopped in it or not done in it, in no more than eighty words. Then decide which one of those absences belongs in the finished passage. Plant and return. Choose an object that will matter at the end of your book. Draft an initial appearance and a return, then try a further return if it develops the object. Compare a quiet introduction with a conspicuous one, and decide how much explanation the final appearance needs. See also: the Reference checklist ; the Reference studio work , with further exercises, seminar questions and an assessment rubric.

title: 10. Coda
text: This chapter’s tests favour details whose purposes can be named, but applying them everywhere could flatten a book’s variety. Barthes reads the barometer in Flaubert’s account of Félicité as an apparently superfluous detail that contributes to a reality effect; that is a critical interpretation, not a measured response from readers. Dickens’s extended portraits may resist a count test; the opening fog of Bleak House repeats a word while changing its setting and associations; and Robbe-Grillet’s visual emphasis serves his chosen form. The tests should be read against what each work is doing. The tests therefore help identify what a passage is doing; they do not decide whether it is good. A page selects from many possible particulars, whether the result resembles Balzac’s catalogue or McGregor’s brief natural observations. Readers may attend to those choices in different ways, and some details can remain apparently incidental. The description of Sethe’s back is a reminder that choices also raise questions of viewpoint and representation beyond the passage’s economy. See also: the Reference coda , which develops the argument; The Transition (Chapter 5), the next chapter, on how one unit hands over to the next.

title: The Transition
text: How to carry a reader across a gap, and how much to spend doing it The Craft Behind the Story (Second Edition) — Chapter 5. Part II: The Joins. In brief. A gap in a novel — a skipped afternoon, a change of town, a move into someone else’s head — may ask the reader to update several things at once. The transition is the writing on either side that helps her across. The effort can depend on which dimensions change (time, place, protagonist, causality and goal), how much time passes, and what the reader already knows. The right amount of orientation may be a paragraph, a clause, or nothing at all. The tools are a count of what changes, six techniques with different demands, the last sentence before the gap, twelve anchor types to choose from, a test for deliberate disorientation, and ten diagnostic questions. Use them on a draft whose readers stall after scene breaks, or whose scene openings feel slow without being wrong. What you can do after this chapter Count the dimensions a gap changes, then judge which changes the reader needs help with. Choose among six transition techniques instead of defaulting to one. Rewrite the last sentence before a gap so that the first sentence after it has less to do. Locate the anchor in any join, measure its delay, and substitute a stronger one. Audit the joins in a manuscript and read the resulting pattern. Key terms Transition; join; scene break, dinkus and asterism; duration and ellipsis (explicit, implicit and hypothetical; definite, indefinite and characterizing); singulative and iterative; paralipsis; contextual frame, frame switch, frame recall and frame repair; the event-indexing model and the dimension count; distributed exposition; continuity editing and montage; the orientation budget, managed ellipsis and re-anchoring; hard cut, time-stamp, match-cut, summary bridge and handoff; the proposed bridging object; launching line; anchor, resumed object and drift; significance fatigue; the transition inventory. Each is defined at first use and collected in the consolidated glossary . Contents The first files say why a gap costs the reader something and what the cost depends on; the middle files set out the techniques and the anchor; the last are for use at the desk. The Problem A well-written paragraph at the wrong place, and the chapter’s claim Definitions The transition against the scene break, the scales of a gap, adjacent terms How It Works Ellipsis, contextual frames, evidence on processing shifts, exposition at the gap, the film analogy, and the history of the convention The Taxonomy Five techniques, and a proposed sixth: the bridging object The Mechanism The anchor, its types and timing, drift, and where a transition does more than orient Diagnostic Tests Ten questions on one page, and how to read their failures together Failure Patterns Five recurrent failures, each with a published work that commits it and succeeds Worked Analyses To the Lighthouse, Station Eleven, A Visit from the Goon Squad, Up, and the household revision case Checklist and Exercises The revision checklist and five exercises for your own draft Coda What the budget cannot price A writer in revision can start at the diagnostic tests; the short coda is best read early. The full treatment The Reference layer holds the complete chapter, The Transition : the theory at length, each technique’s textual carriers, the anchor types with exemplars, the typography of the gap, twelve failure patterns, close readings of Mrs Dalloway , “Wandering Rocks”, Anna Karenina , The Sound and the Fury , Pedro Páramo , One Hundred Years of Solitude and Bleak House , transitions in the short story, the series, screen and translation, seminar questions and an assessment rubric, and the sources. See also: The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1), for the scene–summary continuum this chapter approaches from the seam; Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2), whose decision beat is the transition’s best preparation; The Chapter Break (Chapter 6), on where a gap is placed; The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13), on who is on the other side of it.

title: 1. The Problem
text: The household novel that runs through this book has reached a join. Elena has come away from her brother’s front door with a new key to the family shop and without the reason their mother changed its locks; she has sat in her truck, thought of telephoning their mother, and decided against it. Her sequel ends on a sentence that names where she is going and what she will do there: She didn’t call. She drove to the shop instead, let herself in with the key, and went straight for the register drawer that stuck on the K. Then comes white space, and the draft’s next paragraph begins: Three days later, Elena drove to the shop. It was a Thursday, and the traffic on the ring road was worse than she had expected, so it was nearly four by the time she parked outside. The paragraph goes on for 187 words. The town has not changed; the greengrocer two doors down has put out its trestle table; the shop’s window is still full of stock their father never marked down; Elena sits with her hands on the wheel and thinks about the doorway and the key; she crosses the pavement, lets herself in, smells dust, lets her eyes adjust, and at word 178 reaches the register drawer. Every sentence would survive a line edit, and the unmarked-down stock characterises the father in a clause; readers of the finished book would find it slow without being able to say why. What has gone wrong Nothing in the paragraph is false, and nothing in it is needed. The sentence before the white space had already told the reader where Elena was going, how she would get in and what she would reach for; the paragraph after it tells her again, at the length of a small scene. The only new information is three days later , and that is the most damaging phrase in the passage. Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2) built Elena’s decision as the end of a sequel: a reaction, a dilemma, a decision made in anger and executed at once. Three days inserted between the choice and the act turn a woman who drove to the shop because she could not bear not to into a woman who thought about it over a long weekend. The time-stamp, which looks like the safest sentence in the paragraph, has quietly rewritten the character. The writer cannot see any of this, for a structural reason. For the writer the gap is not a gap. She has imagined the drive, the parking, the weather and the key in the lock, and all of it is present to her at once as a continuous world; the white space is punctuation between two things she already knows. For the reader the white space is a real discontinuity in the only world she has, which is the text. At the moment her eye crosses it, everything she was holding — a doorway, two people, a withheld reason, a key changing hands — becomes provisional, and she does not yet know whether five minutes have passed or five months, whether she is in the same town, or whose eyes she is behind. This is the join problem : the writer is the one reader who is never on the far side of her own gaps, so everything a reader needs at a join is information the writer already has and therefore does not miss. Transitions are therefore found in revision, by reading each join cold. The claim The chapter offers an orientation budget as a revision tool. A gap can make the reader update time, place, person or purpose, and the writer must decide what help this particular crossing needs. That is a question of style as well as quantity. A transition is not the white space. It manages what changes across the gap and helps re-anchor the reader. When story time is omitted, it also manages an ellipsis. The amount to write depends on this particular crossing, and may be nothing. The claim does not say that shorter transitions are better: the hard cut is one technique among six, and a manuscript that uses it at every gap can have the same fault as one that time-stamps every gap. It does not say that disorientation is always a fault, since several of the novels this chapter reads withhold orientation on purpose and are built on the withholding. Nor does it say that transitions are mere plumbing. A transition can do a second job, though some need only to orient. The household paragraph spends heavily on a gap that needs little, orients the reader three times, and delays the new scene. The revision, in the worked analyses , replaces it with two sentences. See also: Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2), for the sequel this join follows; the Reference introduction , with the claim’s two halves set out at length.

title: 2. Definitions
text: The working definition A transition is the narrative material, however brief, that carries a reader across a gap in time, place, viewpoint or scale, answering her implicit questions of when , where and whose vantage in as many words as the gap requires. It comprises the last words before the gap and the first words after it, and it may be a paragraph long, a clause long, or absent. Four phrases do the work. However brief means that a transition of no bridging words is still one: white space followed at once by new material hands the whole job to the new unit’s opening sentence, which is a choice with costs. The last words before the gap means that a join is a departure problem as often as an arrival problem, since the final sentence of the outgoing unit decides how much the incoming one has to supply. When, where and whose vantage are not an arbitrary list; with two additions they are the dimensions that readers can be shown to track, which How It Works sets out. And as the gap requires places the requirement in the gap, not in the writer’s habits. A join is this book’s general word for any point at which one narrative unit ends and another begins: a paragraph break that changes the subject, a scene break, a chapter break, a part break. Similar orientation questions can arise at each scale, from a paragraph break inside a scene to a new part that crosses decades. This chapter concentrates on scene-to-scene and chapter-to-chapter joins. For revision, one possible measure is the number of words spent before the new unit’s own business begins: none for a hard cut, perhaps a clause for a light bridge, a paragraph for a summary, and a longer bridging passage that may need to be judged as a unit in its own right. These are working descriptions, not measured boundaries. The term most often confused: the scene break A scene break is a typographic device: a blank line, or a visible mark such as a dinkus (three spaced asterisks, or a printer’s ornament) or an asterism (⁂). A transition is a piece of writing. The break signals a division; the transition helps the reader cross it. Inserting the signal alone may leave a new scene unanchored. Conversely, a break at every small shift can make the manuscript feel more fragmented than the story requires. Typography is a cue, but it does not prescribe a particular size of gap. There is a third relation, which competent writers use and rarely name: a transition can cross a large gap with no mark at all. A sentence of habitual summary — All that winter she went in on Thursdays — moves a paragraph from one Tuesday to the following spring without a break on the page. The mark and the transition are independent variables. Adjacent terms A bridge is the informal word for explicit connective prose; here it names one technique among six. A cut , from film, is an instantaneous change of vantage, and How It Works explains why the word can mislead when taken literally in prose. Anachrony , Gérard Genette’s term for discord between the order of events in the story and the order of their telling, covers the flashback and the flash-forward. Simultaneity is two threads occupying the same story time. Prose can mark it with while , meanwhile or matching time cues; without such cues, readers may infer sequence. What this chapter leaves to others The chapter assumes that each gap is where it should be and asks how to cross it. Where to place a break, and how to end a unit so that the reader turns the page, belong to The Chapter Break (Chapter 6). Which minds a novel may enter, and on what terms, belong to The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13); here the change of viewpoint is treated only as a transition with a high cost. A transition backwards in time incurs a second cost, the reader’s reluctance to invest in material whose relevance is not yet established, and the cutaway therefore has its own chapter, Backstory and Flashback (Chapter 7). The architecture of a whole book built on more than one timeline is Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture (Chapter 8). The book’s first transition, from the world into the text, has no near side and belongs to The Opening Pages (Chapter 9) and The Prologue (Chapter 10); the last, out of the text, belongs to The Ending (Chapter 16). See also: the Reference definitions , with a table of scales and a fuller list of adjacent terms; The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1), on the continuum from scene to summary.

title: 3. How It Works
text: Craft advice says that a transition must orient the reader quickly, and does not say why, how quickly, or what orienting consists of. Five bodies of work answer, each opening here with the question it answers at the desk. How large is this gap, and does the reader know? The frame is Gérard Genette’s treatment of duration in Narrative Discourse (1972; translated by Jane E. Lewin, 1980): the relation between the time an event takes in the story and the space it takes in the telling. The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1) sets out his four movements — scene, summary, pause and ellipsis — as a decision about the speed of a unit. This chapter works at the seam between speeds. An ellipsis is story time that passes while the telling spends nothing on it. When a transition skips story time, it can be understood as an ellipsis whose edges have been finished. A simultaneous shift of place or viewpoint still calls for orientation, but is not an ellipsis in Genette’s duration scheme. Genette distinguishes an explicit ellipsis , which declares the lapse ( three days later ), from an implicit ellipsis , which the reader infers from evidence (new light, new clothes, a healed cut), and from a hypothetical ellipsis , which cannot be located and is discovered only later, when something the narrative skipped comes to light. The explicit kind can be economical, though repetition risks monotony. The implicit kind leaves the new unit’s first sentences to supply evidence of elapsed time as well as place and person. The hypothetical kind is useful for thinking about the uncertain chronology of Ford Madox Ford’s The Good Soldier . An ellipsis is definite when its duration is stated and indefinite when it is not. Genette calls it characterizing when the temporal indication also gives information about the interval ( three days later, after the funeral ). Genette’s category of frequency adds a bridging tool. The singulative narrates once what happened once; the iterative narrates once what happened many times ( Every Thursday he counted the till twice ). An iterative sentence crosses a stretch of time while characterising, because a habit is a fact about a person as well as a calendar. One more term is held in reserve: paralipsis , Genette’s word for withholding information the established focalisation would ordinarily supply. A gap that hides a decisive event may be what this chapter calls a false ellipsis ; it is paralipsis only if that focalisation condition is met. The failure patterns make the distinction. What is the reader doing in the first words after the white space? Catherine Emmott’s Narrative Comprehension (1997) proposes that readers keep contextual frames , mental representations of the current episode holding who is present, where and when. Characters are bound into a frame, and the frame in use is primed. Three of her operations describe a transition. A frame switch abandons the primed frame and builds another; frame recall retrieves a frame built earlier, as when a novel returns to a thread; frame repair corrects a frame built on a wrong assumption. The consequences are practical. White space need not clear a contextual frame; without a cue, a reader may initially read new sentences into the old scene and later have to revise that assumption. A familiar name can recall an established thread, while a new setting may take more work to build. This suggests testing whether a paragraph of reminder is needed. A place with a person bound into it can anchor more specifically, so Elena let herself into the shop may do more work than The shop was cold . Why does one gap feel heavier than another? Discourse psychology offers evidence about the load, though not a fixed price for a literary join. The event-indexing model of Rolf Zwaan, Mark Langston and Arthur Graesser (1995) proposes that readers track five dimensions of a narrative — time, space, protagonist, causality and intentionality (whose goal is in play). That study used a memory task, not reading-time measurements. Zwaan’s time-shift experiments (1996) found longer reading times after an hour later than after a moment later in the tested stories. In a separate 1998 reading-time study by Zwaan, Gabriel Radvansky, Amy Hilliard and Jacqueline Curiel, time, causality, goals and protagonist showed effects; a spatial shift slowed reading when participants had first learned a map, but not in the other conditions. Multiple discontinuities could increase reading time, but the study did not establish an additive cost per dimension. The dimension count is therefore a diagnostic for asking what changed, not a measured bill or a better predictor than duration in every case. Causality and intentionality can help explain why a join that settles when and where still reads as a non sequitur. The experiments use short constructed texts in laboratories and describe tendencies in processing, not literary value. Work on event segmentation by Jeffrey Zacks and Barbara Tversky (2001), and by Nicole Speer, Zacks and Jeremy Reynolds (2007), supports the narrower claim that people segment narrated activity and show transient neural responses at boundaries they later identify. It does not establish that every literary join consolidates memory. Where can I put exposition without stalling the story? Meir Sternberg’s Expositional Modes and Temporal Ordering in Fiction (1978) treats exposition as a problem of distribution: a story conveys antecedents in a chosen order and at chosen times. A break can give a writer a place to summarise skipped events, if the reader needs them before the next scene begins. This is one possible home for distributed exposition , not a guarantee that a reader will welcome summary there. Sternberg’s distinction between suspense (uncertainty about what will happen) and curiosity (uncertainty about what has happened) suggests a question for intervals: is uncertainty about the gap something the book means to develop later? If not, a simple indication of elapsed time may serve better. Is “cut to” a good way to think? Film vocabulary can help a writer think about transitions. David Bordwell and Kristin Thompson’s Film Art describes continuity editing , including establishing shots, matches on action and cross-cutting, which have prose analogues. Sergei Eisenstein’s montage emphasises meaning created by juxtaposition; the Kuleshov effect is another example of context shaping a viewer’s reading of a shot. Neither makes the match-cut a direct descendant of that experiment. Film can present many visual cues together, while prose supplies its cues in sequence and can choose which details to name. A description of rain also directs a reader’s attention to rain, so an establishing paragraph may create expectations beyond orientation. Viewers can revisit a shot in some circumstances, just as readers can backtrack, though the usual viewing and reading conditions differ. Cut to is useful for imagining the sequence; in prose the writer must still decide what the arrival needs to make clear. The dates of the convention Narrative conventions have varied. Fielding opens the books of Tom Jones with introductory chapters, and Dickens’s narrator in Bleak House turns from Chancery, in its second chapter, to the world of fashion on the same miry afternoon. More recent fiction also uses unmarked cuts, dated headings and direct narratorial handovers. No single period has an exclusive claim on any of them. The orientation budget is therefore offered as a revision instrument: a gap may call for cues, and the writer decides how much to give. It assumes that orientation can be treated as an expenditure; the coda names novels whose effects exceed that metaphor. See also: the Reference theory , with tables of Genette’s types, Emmott’s operations and the five dimensions, and the history in three phases; The Opening Pages (Chapter 9), on Sternberg and on the reader’s rules of notice.

title: 4. The Taxonomy
text: The taxonomy names six ways of managing a crossing, so that write a transition becomes a choice among options with different demands, and the repeated use of one instrument becomes visible as a choice. The categories describe strategies, not sentences, and a single join often braids two. They are not ranked: the hard cut is not more sophisticated than the time-stamp; it leaves more of the orientation work to the arrival. They answer which without supplying a formula for how many words. The hard cut The hard cut crosses a gap with no bridging language: the unit ends, white space or a chapter number intervenes, and the next unit begins inside its own material and orients the reader in its first sentences while getting on with its business. It leaves the orientation work to the new unit’s opening, and succeeds when that opening can carry it. Two conditions can help. The first is that the launching line , this chapter’s term for the last sentence before the gap, has done preparatory work: a departure that names a place, an object or a person prepares the reader for the arrival. Scene and Sequel ’s decision beat (Chapter 2) is one version. The second is that the reader can infer or recall enough of the new frame. Counting changed dimensions can expose a difficult handoff, but it cannot set a universal limit for the hard cut. Tolstoy’s chapter-level alternation in Anna Karenina (1878) often uses names and familiar settings to help the reader cross. Under-delivered, the hard cut is the orphaned cut; overused, it can leave a manuscript feeling fragmented. The time-stamp The time-stamp states elapsed time or temporal position at the head of the new unit: Three days later. In April. By the time the shop reopened. It is a concise way to orient the reader in time, though it cannot by itself settle place, person or purpose. Its bad name comes from defaulting to a numerical stamp whether or not the interval matters. The remedy is to use its varieties. Besides the relative interval there are the absolute date, the event-relative stamp ( after the funeral ), clock time, the seasonal or liturgical stamp ( by Michaelmas ), the stamp measured on a body ( when the bruise had gone yellow ), the iterative ( all that autumn ), and the dated heading set above the prose. The event-relative form shows how a stamp can do more by saying more. Three days later, she went back to the house is nine words and delivers time. The day after the funeral, she went back to the house is eleven, and the extra words also invoke a death and a reason for returning. Some weeks later can indicate that the exact interval does not matter. A long interval may need more explicit orientation when context cannot supply it; a short interval can matter just as much when causality depends on it. Gabriel García Márquez turns the instrument against itself in One Hundred Years of Solitude (1967; translated by Gregory Rabassa), where it rains for four years, eleven months and two days: a hyperbolic event given a chronicle’s exact duration. The match-cut The match-cut , or echo transition, crosses a gap on a repetition: a word, image, action, sound or sentence shape at the end of one unit recurs, changed, at the start of the next, so that the join carries meaning. It is the only technique whose purpose is not orientation; it orients as a by-product and buys an argument, on Eisenstein’s principle that two things placed side by side produce a third that is in neither. The screen’s best-known case is the cut in Stanley Kubrick’s 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968) from a bone thrown into the air by a hominid to an orbiting satellite, which the film leaves unidentified and Arthur C. Clarke’s novel makes an orbital weapon: one cut joins the first tool to the latest and says they are the same thing. Its failure is invisibility: a reader who misses the echo has lost nothing she knows of, and the writer cannot detect the loss. Hence a floor: an echo must be detectable on a first reading at ordinary speed by a reader not looking for it, and an echo found only on rereading is a reward for rereading, not a transition. Three things raise detectability without ostentation: proximity (the echo at the very end of one unit and the very start of the next), distinctiveness (an unusual word, or an ordinary one used unusually), and difference (the same object changed, which reads as an argument, where pure repetition reads as a stutter). The most reliable form is ironic inversion, the same element with the opposite value. Dickens shows how high the ceiling of ostentation goes when his narrator in Bleak House (1853) asks outright what connexion there can be between the place in Lincolnshire, the house in town and Jo, the outlaw with the broom. The summary bridge The summary bridge narrates the interval itself in compressed form: For the next three weeks nothing was decided. Dov came in on Saturdays; the stock did not move. It can put selected content inside an interval without giving it a full scene. A break can be a useful place for that content when the reader needs it before the next scene. Summary is one way to make duration felt, and its negative form ( nothing was decided; nobody rang ) gives an interval a shape. Its difficulty is the hand-over from summary into scene; one possible repair is to end the bridge on a specific occasion. Austen’s bridges, in which a season passes or a family moves, suggest a working question: what can the reader infer, and what needs to be dramatized? John Steinbeck raises collective summary to a whole chapter in The Grapes of Wrath (1939), whose twelfth chapter renders Highway 66, the mother road, as the migration in aggregate. Under-delivered, the bridge leaves an interval that mattered crossed with nothing; over-delivered, it becomes throat-clearing or recap. The handoff The handoff changes whose consciousness the reader occupies, or where she is, or both, and it is common in novels with more than one thread. It can change several dimensions at once, though the processing cost is not a fixed sum. Three revision choices follow. Where the story allows, make time, place or an object shared across the handoff. Give a name or another clear cue early enough for this reader and this passage. And make a recurring pattern legible: an established thread can be recalled rather than rebuilt, though later handoffs are not automatically free. Paula Hawkins’s The Girl on the Train (2015) uses section headings with narrator names and dates, sometimes followed by Morning or Evening : Rachel’s first section is dated Friday, 5 July 2013, and Megan’s first Wednesday, 16 May 2012, so the headings show that Megan’s strand begins over a year earlier. A reader pulled away from a thread at its height, which is The Chapter Break ’s subject (Chapter 6), may need an arrival that quickly establishes what has changed. A proposed sixth: the bridging object One recurring practice is useful to name separately from the five. The bridging object is a physical thing that appears on both sides of a gap and can help anchor the new unit: the coat on the hook, the ledger, the key, the car in the street. A match-cut joins by resemblance; a bridging object invites recognition of an apparently identical thing. That may help recall a known frame, though recognition is itself an inference and its speed is not a measured advantage. Its carriers include the definite article, limited re-description, a changed condition and a transfer of custody. A distinctive object planted earlier can gain meaning through repetition, giving the argument of The Descriptive Detail (Chapter 4) a structural payoff. In Mrs Dalloway (1925) the motor car with drawn blinds moving up Bond Street draws attention from several characters, linking their responses to the same public event. Three objections stand. It may be a carrier, not a technique: every join needs an anchor, the resumed object is one of the anchor types in The Mechanism , and any of the five techniques can land on one. The distinction between identity and resemblance may not survive scrutiny, since the reader meets only a second occurrence of a noun and infers that the referent is the same by the route a match-cut uses. And a category for recurring objects invites one for recurring sounds, phrases and weather patterns without limit. This chapter adopts the bridging object for revision, because the advice it yields — plant it, particularise it, use the definite article, do not re-describe it — differs enough from the match-cut’s to be worth separating, and it concedes the second objection as unanswered. Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture (Chapter 8), which joins whole timelines rather than scenes, adopts it at the scale of a book as a means of convergence by identity, on condition that the object’s condition or custody changes between appearances, which answers the second objection at that scale. Must a join use only one? No. Compounding is normal; the fault is compounding a technique with its own redundancy, such as a stamp followed by a summary of the same interval, and the test is whether the second element resolves a dimension the first did not. Some gaps need no technique at all, such as a paragraph break of ninety seconds between two moments of one scene. The question is never which technique is best, but what this gap costs. See also: the Reference techniques , with each technique’s textual carriers, its illustrations and a summary table; the Reference worked analyses , on Mrs Dalloway ’s car and aeroplane and on Anna Karenina ’s alternation.

title: 5. The Mechanism
text: An anchor is the first concrete cue after a gap that answers when , where or whose vantage . Drift is the deliberate delay of the anchor, holding the reader in uncertainty for a beat before orienting her, and it differs from an oversight in one respect: the anchor still arrives. What the anchor does Emmott’s contextual-frame account suggests that a cue can help a reader identify which episode is now in view. Without it, the reader may initially assimilate new sentences to the previous frame and later revise that reading. An anchor can be a referent, a description or a heading; a familiar name may work faster than a paragraph of scene-setting. One symptom to hunt in revision is the backtrack. A cue is useful for the questions it settles: a name may identify a familiar protagonist and imply a place, while weather alone may leave both uncertain. Position matters because a delayed cue can give the reader more to reinterpret. For revision, mark where the first reliable cue appears and ask a reader to do the same. A cue in the first clause may suit a rapid handoff; a later one may serve deliberate drift. The numerical ranges used in this chapter are prompts for inspection, not measured thresholds, and the right delay depends on the prose and the frame already in memory. Twelve anchors to choose from The twelve anchor types offer alternatives for revision. Their order is a working list, not a measured ranking of how many dimensions each settles. # Anchor Instance 1 The proper name in the first clause Tolstoy’s Levin chapters 2 The place-noun, particularised Bleak House opens on “London.” 3 The time-marker The dated entries of Dracula 4 The resumed object, with the definite article and no re-description The coat; the drawer 5 The continued action, already announced before the gap A hand already on a drawer 6 The sensory cue Benjy’s honeysuckle; fresh ink 7 The somatic cue: cold, pain, a healing bruise The heat of Comala in Pedro Páramo 8 The dialogue tag in the first line The opening of “Time Passes” 9 Weather or light used as a clock The rain in One Hundred Years of Solitude 10 The social cue: a title, a form of address Tolstoy’s formal and familiar names 11 The register shift: the voice itself changes Esther against Bleak House ’s panoramic narrator 12 The paratextual anchor: a heading or date-line The Girl on the Train ’s section headings Four are especially worth testing. A resumed object can recall an earlier scene once planted. Continued action can make a seam feel slight when the departure has prepared it. A register shift can distinguish a new voice without naming its speaker, though the reader may need time to recognise it. A paratextual anchor uses no narrative words but still shapes the reading. To substitute, take a join that is not working, record its anchor and its word position, choose two other types, and rewrite the first two sentences once for each. If every version needs the time-stamp back, the interval may matter; if every version reads flat, examine the new scene’s purpose; and if nothing improves, look at the launching line. Drift Drift is a real technique and the commonest alibi for an orphaned cut, so the criterion must be stated plainly: in drift the anchor arrives late and on purpose; in an orphaned cut it arrives where the writer’s failure to notice its absence put it, or not at all. Three conditions mark drift. The uncertainty is the character’s own, as when she wakes in a strange room or is held by grief that has detached her from place and time. The uncertainty is bounded, so the reader knows what she does not yet know. And something else is supplied meanwhile, a voice, a body, a sensation, since delay plus thin prose is only thin prose. When a writer says I meant it to be disorienting , ask for the schedule: when does the anchor arrive, and what is the reader doing until then? Where a transition does more than orient A novel of ninety thousand words has, on this chapter’s estimate (a working guess, not a count), between eighty and two hundred joins. If each spends forty words on orientation alone, the book spends between 3,200 and 8,000 words on connective tissue that does nothing else (80 × 40 and 200 × 40), placed where the reader is most impatient. The remedy is selection rather than compression: the one detail that already carries orientation and a second job. It lives in four humble places. The launching line can name the destination: after She left , the arrival must say where, when and why; after She drove to the shop instead, and went straight for the register drawer , it need say nothing. The first noun after the gap is the reader’s first chance to build or recall a frame, and the drawer anchors on an object with history where the room anchors on nothing. Tense and aspect orient for free: a pluperfect after a gap ( the shop had been shut for a fortnight ) delivers an interval and its contents. And what is not re-described orients by its absence, since naming the coat without describing it tells the reader she knows it. After two chapters of a present-tense narrator ranging over London, the third chapter of Bleak House opens as Esther Summerson begins: I have a great deal of difficulty in beginning to write my portion of these pages, for I know I am not clever. In twenty-three words the pronoun settles the vantage by total contrast with what came before; have sets a present of composition against the panoramic narrator’s present of scene; beginning to write declares a retrospective document; my portion concedes that the book has other portions; and I know I am not clever gives a character and a narrator the reader must read past. Nothing bridges, and not one word is about the transition. There is a ceiling. Significance fatigue is what a reader feels when every seam rhymes and every arrival lands on a loaded object: no join is plain, so none can be felt as emphatic. A novel needs joins that only orient, as rests. As a working figure for a first revision, not a rule, fewer than one join in four should be doing conspicuous double duty. The mark on the page Typography can cue a reader to expect a change in time, place, vantage or subject, but no mark has a fixed meaning or a fixed gap size. A manuscript broken at every small shift may feel choppy; an unmarked large shift may be harder to follow. A blank line at the foot of a printed page can be missed, and some digital layouts handle blank space differently. Where a section break must remain visible, a mark such as spaced asterisks may help, while the prose should still supply any needed orientation. See also: the Reference anchor and drift , with the twelve types’ costs, a scale of drift and the typography of the gap; the Reference multiplicity , with the Esther sentence anatomised word by word.

title: 6. Diagnostic Tests
text: The ten tests are for revision, not composition. They rest on one procedure: read the join cold, covering the preceding unit and reading the transition and the next two hundred words as though the book began there, since a writer reading in sequence arrives already oriented and will never find the fault. Run tests 1 to 4 (Anchor, Dimension count, Launch and Technique fit) first, because there is no point tuning an echo at a join whose anchor never arrives. Record a sentence, not a verdict: “the anchor is a place-noun at word thirty-four” is useful, and “fails test 1” is not. On a full manuscript, run the transition inventory (in the checklist ) first, then the tests on the dozen joins it flags. Each test is failed on purpose by a book worth reading. Test 1 — Anchor Read cold: at what word can you say when, where and whose vantage? Is any delay doing something? Failure. An orphaned cut, unless the delay meets the three conditions of drift. Exception. Benjy’s section of The Sound and the Fury . Test 2 — Dimension count How many of these change: time, space, protagonist, causality and intentionality? Failure. The reader needs a cue the join has not supplied, or receives more explanation than this crossing needs. The count alone cannot decide which. Exception. A disorientation the book means. Test 3 — Launch What does the last sentence before the gap do for the far side? Failure. The departure simply stops, so the arrival carries the whole bill. Exception. A cut meant to surprise. Test 4 — Technique fit Which technique is this, and was it chosen or defaulted to? Failure. A habit: usually the numerical time-stamp. Exception. A book whose repeated document headings are part of its form, as in Dracula . Test 5 — Momentum At what word does the new unit’s own business begin? Failure. Throat-clearing: words telling the reader what she would have assumed. Exception. A narrator whose company is the point ( Tom Jones ).
