Vanity Fair , chapter 32: the battle in the white space Thackeray’s Vanity Fair appeared in monthly numbers from 1847 to 1848, and chapter 32 closed the ninth number, published in September 1847. The novel declines to narrate the Battle of Waterloo. The chapter stays in Brussels with the civilians, the rumours, Jos Sedley’s flight and the guns audible in the distance, and ends: Darkness came down on the field and city: and Amelia was praying for George, who was lying on his face, dead, with a bullet through his heart. The withheld fact arrives last, in a subordinate clause, at the end of a chapter and of a month’s instalment, so the ending is a pivot. It is also a recasting, since the same sentence makes Amelia’s prayer, and much of the chapter’s waiting, futile in retrospect; and an echo close, since the final image is a body given no commentary. In placement it is a cut just past the disaster, one beat into a reaction that is not given, so the reader supplies the grief herself, and it is the chapter-length silence: the battle falls into the white space after the full stop, and the novel never goes back for it. The omission survives because it is foregrounded. Twenty pages of listening to guns make the battle’s absence conspicuous, and the reader cannot mistake it for an oversight, which is the condition the twelfth placement needs. The Underground Railroad : the heading as a promise Colson Whitehead’s The Underground Railroad (2016) has twelve titled chapters. Five are named for states, Georgia , South Carolina , North Carolina , Tennessee , Indiana , and follow Cora’s flight from a Georgia plantation. Between them come shorter chapters named for people, Ridgeway , Stevens , Ethel , Caesar , Mabel , which step outside her experience to give the life of the slave-catcher pursuing her or of someone she has met. The scheme is declared on the first page, where the opening chapter is named for Cora’s grandmother, Ajarry , so the reader learns early that a person’s name at the head of a chapter means a step aside from the main line, and the book uses the promise rather than breaking it. The eleventh chapter, Mabel , is placed immediately before the last, The North . Cora has carried her mother through the novel as the woman who escaped and left her behind, and the reader has carried her that way too. The chapter shows Mabel, on the night of her flight, deciding to turn back for her daughter, and dying of a snakebite in the swamp. Nothing in Cora’s situation changes, since she is not told and goes on believing she was abandoned; what changes is the meaning of everything the reader has been told about Mabel. At book scale this is a recasting, and its position is chosen for the property the recasting close has at a chapter break: because it creates no pending situation, the final chapter is free to return to Cora’s flight without engaging it. The heading did half the work: a chapter titled with a name, where the scheme has taught the reader to expect a step aside, delivers a fact about the past without seeming to interrupt the ending. A screen reading: Game of Thrones and Severance An episode, like a chapter, is a segmentation set by a delivery technology and then exploited. “Baelor”, the ninth of ten episodes in the first season of Game of Thrones (HBO, June 2011), ends with Ned Stark beheaded. The season’s largest event is placed one unit before the end, a cut at the disaster at season scale, and the finale is left to reaction and aftermath, which is the shape of a novel whose climax falls in its penultimate chapter. The first season of Severance (Apple TV+) ends, in “The We We Are” (April 2022), in the middle of its action: Mark recognises the colleague he knows as Ms Casey as his wife, Gemma, and runs to tell his sister that she is alive, as Milchick tackles Dylan and shuts off the means by which the workers’ other selves have woken. Their outside selves resume as the scene cuts to black. This is the mid-scene cut, the cliffhanger at its most expensive, at the one kind of boundary where the gap is real. The second season premiered on 17 January 2025, so the cut was held for nearly three years, a much longer scheduled gap than a monthly number. What does not transfer is the fixed slot: an episode is a duration, while a chapter is a word count read at the reader’s speed. The household revision case: where to end the chapter at the drawer The chapter opens in Elena’s truck after the doorway in which Dov gave her the new key and withheld the reason for the changed locks ( The Dialogue Exchange , Chapter 3). Her sequel ends on a decision, made in anger, not to telephone their mother but to drive to the shop ( Scene and Sequel , Chapter 2), and a scene break carries her into the shop by a hard cut ( The Transition , Chapter 5). The ledger has been named once before, in passing, in a clause about the coat her father wore behind the counter over it ( The Descriptive Detail , Chapter 4). The chapter after this one cuts to Dov’s thread, the sale and the buyer’s deadline ( The Subplot , Chapter 14). Version A, the draft. The drawer came free on the third try, same as always, and the smell that met her wasn’t dust. It was ink, fresh ink, the sweetish smell of a biro, wrong for a till nobody had opened since March. — the chapter ends. Diagnosis. The proposition is clear, who has been in this drawer since March? , and the payoff holds it open entirely (test 1: Proposition; test 2: Payoff). The exit is expensive (test 3: Permission), and a stopped reader carries an anomaly, an intruder and no person, a feeling of unease without an object (test 4: Stopped reader). The placement is a mid-scene cut, before the scene’s own discovery (test 5: Placement), and it leaves a short chapter whose only event at the shop is two sentences long (test 6: Proportion). The variety test counts against it, since this would be the third open close in a few pages, after the doorway and the sequel, in a book of domestic register that can afford an expensive exit perhaps five times in all, by this case’s estimate (test 7: Variety). The re-entry test counts against it too: the next chapter must either resume the scene, forfeiting the cut to Dov, or leave the alarm ringing through a chapter the reader should be reading closely (test 8: Re-entry). And the cut to Dov answers the question by adjacency, turning the cliffhanger into a delayed caption. Version B, the revision. The drawer came free on the third try, same as always, and the smell that met her wasn’t dust. It was ink, fresh ink, the sweetish smell of a biro, wrong for a till nobody had opened since March. The ledger was in the drawer, where it had always lived. She lifted it out and set it on the counter, the leather faintly warm, as though someone had been leaning an arm on it an hour ago and not four months. It fell open near the back. Her father’s careful hand ran down the page, the same slant, the same crossed sevens, to an entry dated the ninth of March that stopped halfway along its third line. Under it someone had written the date again, and a count, in a looser hand that was not his, and the looser hand went on over the page. She did not read any of it. She sat down on the stool because her legs asked her to, turned back to the first page, eleven years back, and started from the beginning. — the chapter ends. The break has moved one paragraph later, and the sentences before it are unchanged. The payoff now partly resolves the proposition and exchanges it: someone kept writing after the ninth of March, in another hand, which answers was anyone here? and raises whose hand, and why? The price drops to moderate, a curiosity rather than an alarm, and the stopped reader carries a woman on a stool with a book she cannot put down and a dead man’s handwriting turning into someone else’s, dread with an object. In type it is a pivot compounded with a recasting, since the last paragraph turns the scene from a break-in into an inheritance. The cut to Dov now becomes dramatic irony instead of a caption: the reader watches the person she suspects go about his business, and reads everything he does in that chapter twice. A suspense that the next chapter would deflate has become a curiosity that the next chapter feeds. Version B is right because of what precedes and follows it, not because a partial resolution is better than a withholding. If this chapter closed Part One, Version A would be the better cut, since a Part boundary can carry an expensive exit and licenses a discontinuity on the far side, so that the next Part could open in Dov’s thread without the juxtaposition reading as an answer. The same two sentences are a mistake at one position and the best choice at another. The substitution test confirms the choice. A beat earlier, on the leather faintly warm , gives an echo close that raises the proposition twice and pays it never. A beat later, after Elena has read the first entries in the looser hand, gives a disclosure and a second proposition the chapter cannot pay, which is the chapter that is really two. What the revision has not solved. It moves the book’s mystery early from who to why , which suits a novel about withholding rather than crime, but a version that wanted uncertainty about Dov for another hundred pages should choose A and accept its costs. Its last sentence carries a reaction, a characterisation, a decision and a handoff, and read aloud it is crowded. Its proposition is inherited from the previous chapter, so it cannot be assessed or set as an exercise in isolation. And She did not read any of it asks the reader to accept an investigator’s restraint at the moment she has most reason to look. The sentence is motivated, since Elena means to know the ledger in order, from its first page, but it also protects the ending, in which the illness entries and the list at the end of her father’s pages must reach all three siblings at once. The book does not return to Elena’s reading until the ledger has left her hands, which The Subplot (Chapter 14) arranges; a sceptical reader may still see the author’s hand in her patience. See also: the Reference worked analyses , with readings of Bleak House , The Count of Monte Cristo , Middlemarch , Don Quixote , Moby-Dick , Catch-22 and Tristram Shandy , and the revision case with the full protocol in a table; The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13), for Dov’s chapter, which explains the looser hand.

title: 9. Checklist and Exercises
text: Revision checklist Use the checklist on one chapter ending at a time, after reading the last paragraph and stopping. Each item is a question to answer in a sentence. The chapter What did this chapter propose near its start, in one sentence a reader would use? Does the ending resolve, escalate, hold open, recast or exchange it, and which? Is there an internal seam that would make a better ending than the present one? The ending What type of ending does the last sentence create, and was it chosen? If it is a cliffhanger, has the book already given the reader a reason to care about the danger? If it is a pivot, could the reveal come later, at the very end, and what are the pages after it doing? If it is a question close, can the question be stated without the word somehow ? The price Is stopping here free, moderate or expensive, and what did the two previous breaks charge? What does the next chapter have to spend on orientation because of where this one was cut? The manuscript Read down the ending types of eleven consecutive chapters: is there more than one gear? Plotted in order, do the chapter lengths make a tempo curve, and does it match the book’s movement? Do the Part boundaries fall where the book changes, and does the heading scheme run from the first chapter? Exercises for your own draft The heading test. Write an eighteenth-century heading for every chapter of the draft: In which Elena obtains a key and no explanation. Chapters that resist the formula may have an unclear proposition. The stopped reader. Finish a chapter, close the file and do something else for ten minutes; then, without looking, write what happened, what is unresolved, what you want next and how you feel. Do it for five chapters and compare the answers. Three breaks. Take the chapter whose ending you like least and, without changing a sentence, make three versions by moving the break one beat earlier and one later. Judge only when all three exist. The chapter-length audit. Make a table of chapter number, word count, ending type in one word, and price (free, moderate or expensive), and read it without the manuscript. Lengths within fifteen per cent of one another throughout may signal a habit; a price column with no free entries may risk monotony; one with no expensive entries is a prompt to inspect whether the book has enough forward pull. The audit takes about twenty minutes. Six endings. Give one chapter six final paragraphs, one for each type, and write a paragraph on what each does to the chapter before it and the chapter after. See also: the Reference checklist ; the Reference studio work , with further exercises, seminar questions and an assessment rubric.

title: 10. Coda
text: The price model carries an assumption that should be stated rather than smuggled in: that the reader might leave, that the book would rather she did not, and that attention is scarce. Serial markets helped shape the assumption that a reader must be drawn across a scheduled gap; the model describes one literary culture, broadly the trade fiction of the last half-century, not narrative as such. The method is useful in revision because most drafts are written within that culture. It cannot describe several of the books this chapter has used. Tristram Shandy places its breaks arbitrarily, tears out a chapter and leaves others blank, in an attack on the idea that a book should carry its reader helplessly forward; its cuts are wrong by every test and right for a novel about the impossibility of ordering a life into units. A chapter read aloud at bedtime is designed to let the listener go, and children’s books are full of soft landings built to satisfy one reader and release another. The zhanghui chapter’s storyteller-style invitation to continue draws on conventions associated with oral performance, though printed chaptered fiction was generally written for reading. None of these is a fault the tests failed to catch, and none can be absorbed by widening their thresholds; they are segmentations whose value lies where the model sees only cost or waste. The model therefore survives as an instrument for making a decision visible, so that a writer can confirm it as hers. A chapter that fails four tests may be the best in the book; what the method asks is that the writer know what each break charges, and why, and be able to say so. When the tests begin to choose for her, they have gone further than their evidence. See also: the Reference coda ; the Reference reading of Tristram Shandy .

title: Backstory and Flashback
text: When to leave the present, in what register, and what to bring back The Craft Behind the Story (Second Edition) — Chapter 7. Part II: The Joins. In brief. A passage that leaves a novel’s present for an earlier point in its story may ask the reader to hold a suspended question, build a second situation and file it against the first. This chapter calls that demand a debt, repaid when the past changes how the present is read. The cost is not fixed. It can fall when the reader has already asked for the past, rise when the passage goes far back for a brief moment, and depend above all on where in the present it is placed. The tools are a choice between telling the past and dramatising it, tested by a one-sentence compression check; fourteen temporal registers, including prolepsis as a counterpoint; six domains of purpose; the trigger and the return; and ten diagnostic questions. Use them on a draft whose flashbacks readers skim, or whose past arrives as information nobody asked for. What you can do after this chapter Decide, by writing one sentence, whether a piece of past material should be told, dramatised or cut. Measure how far back a passage goes and how much time it covers, and say whether it fills a gap or repeats what the reader has. Name what a passage of the past buys, and find the past moment that buys several things at once. Choose a trigger, and write a return that leaves the present changed. Audit every departure into the past in a manuscript on one sheet, and move the ones that are in the wrong place. Key terms Cutaway, backstory and flashback; the register of the past; the first narrative; anachrony, analepsis and prolepsis; reach and extent; external, internal, completing and repeating analepsis; ellipsis and paralipsis; iterative narration; the interest deficit; suspense, curiosity and surprise; the situation model and the contextual frame; belatedness and rememory; the one-sentence compression check; the fourteen temporal registers and substitution testing; the trigger, the return and the changed question; the flashback budget; explanation and illumination; reader knowledge and the proposed structural domain; the cutaway audit. Each is defined at first use and collected in the consolidated glossary . Contents The first files say what a cutaway is and why it costs what it does, the middle files what it can buy and how to choose its form, and the last are for use at the desk. The Problem A well-written memory at the wrong moment, and the chapter’s claim Definitions The cutaway, its two registers and four scales, the first narrative, adjacent terms How It Works The reader’s cost of going back, Genette’s measures, Sternberg’s curiosity, the past that is the story, and the dates of the convention The Taxonomy Five domains a cutaway can serve, and a proposed sixth: the structural domain The Mechanism The fork and the compression check, fourteen registers, triggers, returns, and where the multiplying work lives Diagnostic Tests Ten questions on one page, and how to read their failures together Failure Patterns Five recurrent failures, each with a published work that commits it and succeeds Worked Analyses The Death of Ivan Ilyich , The Sense of an Ending , Where the Crawdads Sing , Lost and Arrival , and the household revision case Checklist and Exercises The revision checklist and five exercises for your own draft Coda The books for which the debt runs the other way A writer in revision can start at the compression check and the diagnostic tests; the short coda, which says which books the tests are not for, is best read early. The full treatment The Reference layer holds the complete chapter, Backstory and Flashback : the theory and the history of the flashback at length, each domain’s carriers, the fourteen registers with their exemplars, twelve failure patterns, eight further close readings, the cutaway in other forms and in translation, seminar questions, an assessment rubric and the sources. See also: The Transition (Chapter 5), on crossing the gap; The Prologue (Chapter 10), on such material placed before the reader has invested anything; Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture (Chapter 8), on the past as a strand of the whole book.

title: 1. The Problem
text: A memory at the drawer In the household novel used throughout this book, three siblings in a British town are dealing with the shop their father kept and the ledger he wrote in for eleven years, and about a quarter of the way through the book Elena opens the register drawer. The drawer comes free on the third try, and the smell that meets her is fresh biro ink in a till she believes nobody has opened since March ( The Transition , Chapter 5). Imagine a draft in which, at that sentence, the narrative leaves her. It goes back to the afternoon she was twelve, when her father had a key to the shop cut for her, threaded it onto a ring and told her to keep it safe. The scene runs to two pages. It has the light through the front window, the bell over the door, the cold of the new key in her palm and her father’s thumb hooked into his cuff while he talked, and every detail in it is accurate and well observed. Then a blank line, and the draft resumes: She lifted the ledger out of the drawer. The writer’s first readers say they skimmed the key, and cannot say why, because nothing in the passage is badly written. What has gone wrong is a matter of accounting. At the moment the drawer opens, the reader is holding a question, who has been in this drawer since March? , and the question is at its sharpest. The departure suspends it without answering it. It then asks the reader to build a second situation from nothing: a younger Elena, a younger father, the shop in another decade, with different ages and different people present, while the first situation stays live in memory. And it asks her to file the new material against the old, since past material means something only in relation to the present it bears on. All three operations cost attention before the past has delivered anything. The draft never repays the cost. The reader had not asked where Elena’s key came from, so the scene answers no question she was carrying; it is far back and brief, so the whole vanished context is built for one afternoon’s use and then thrown away; and when the narrative comes back to the drawer, nothing in the present is different for its having been away. Compressed to a clause, the material survives. The key she had carried since she was twelve costs the reader nothing and tells her as much. Better still, the book already has the right place for it: the doorway in which Dov hands Elena a new key because their mother has changed the locks, and the old one, held since she was twelve, no longer fits ( The Dialogue Exchange , Chapter 3). There, the history of the key is not an interruption but the measure of what has been taken from her, and it needs no scene at all. The claim The chapter’s argument can be put as a debt. Every cutaway starts in debt. Leaving the present spends the attention the reader was paying to an open question, and the past must repay it by changing the present before the narrative returns. Being interesting in itself does not repay it. A cutaway, here, is any passage that leaves the present for an earlier point in the story; the term is borrowed from film editing, where a cutaway is a shot that leaves the main action and comes back to it. The claim is harsh on purpose, and three qualifications make it usable. The debt is positional: the same material at a calmer point in the present may cost almost nothing, so the first remedy for a failing flashback is usually to move it, not to rewrite it. The debt can be paid in advance: a reader who has been made to wonder about the past receives the cutaway as an answer rather than an interruption. And the claim assumes that the present carries the book’s engine. For a substantial tradition of fiction, from Proust and Faulkner to Ishiguro and Morrison, in which the past is the subject and the present is a way of approaching it, the account runs the other way, and the coda says how. The chapter ends where the household novel’s own cutaway is revised: Nadia, two-thirds of the way through the book, with her hand in the pocket of her father’s coat. See also: The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1), whose account of the scene applies in full to a dramatised flashback; the Reference introduction , with the cost of temporal departures and the claim’s limits set out at length.

title: 2. Definitions
text: The working definition Craft talk calls a dramatised scene, a sentence in the past perfect and a whole retrospective design all flashbacks ; they have different costs, so the chapter separates them. A cutaway is any passage in which the narrative leaves the time of its present action to present material from an earlier point in the story’s chronology. It has two principal registers. Backstory is the past told: conveyed by summary, implication, report or dialogue, without the reader having to live through it. A flashback is the past dramatised: a scene in its own right, rendered moment by moment and subject to every rule that governs a scene. The term flashback was used in early cinema, though retrospective narration long predates film. The register of the past, in this chapter, is the manner in which past material is put on the page, from a subordinate clause to a dramatised scene to a found document; the difference between backstory and flashback is a difference of register, not of content, since the same material can be delivered either way. The present against which the past is measured has a technical name. Gérard Genette, whose Narrative Discourse (1972; translated by Jane E. Lewin, 1980) supplies most of this chapter’s vocabulary, calls it the first narrative ( récit premier ): the temporal level a narrative establishes as its principal one, to which it returns and against which every other level is felt as a departure. Genette’s general term for any discordance between the order of events in the story and the order of their telling is anachrony (from Greek roots meaning “back” and “time”). Analepsis (Greek, “taking up again”) narrates an event earlier than the present point of the first narrative, and is the formal name for a cutaway; prolepsis (“taking in advance”) narrates one before its time, the flash-forward, and is treated here only where it bears on the cost of going back. Four scales Advice calibrated to one scale of cutaway is often misapplied to another, so the table separates four. Scale Typical length Reader’s experience Governing question The implication A clause or phrase Barely registered as a departure Is the fact needed here? The report A sentence to a paragraph A brief change of pitch Told or shown? The scene 300 to 3,000 words A full temporal relocation Does it earn the suspension of the present? The structure A strand of the whole book The past as a second timeline Is the architecture declared? The chapter treats the third scale as its main subject, because that is where drafts most often go wrong, but the other three set its first rule of thumb: deliver the past at the smallest scale that does the job, and expect the burden of proof to rise with the scale. A clause needs no justification, a paragraph needs to be the right paragraph, a scene needs an argument and a second timeline needs a structural reason. Adjacent terms Exposition , in Meir Sternberg’s usage, is the information about antecedents a narrative must convey for its present action to be intelligible: who these people are, what the situation is, what has already happened. It is a category of content, and backstory and flashback are two of several ways to deliver it; dialogue, description, habit, documents and the reader’s inference from an unexplained detail are others. Not all exposition is backstory, and not all backstory is exposition, and heavy backstory is often better relocated than compressed: into an object, a habit or an unremarked assumption. The household ledger carries eleven years of a man’s life without a sentence of retrospect. A character remembering is not the same thing as a cutaway. She remembered the argument about the pen is an event in the present, one clause long; leaving the present to stage the argument is a flashback. Nor is retrospective narration the same as a cutaway: it tells a whole narrative from after its events, so the past is itself the first narrative, as Pip’s life is in Great Expectations ; in The Remains of the Day , by contrast, the first narrative is a motoring trip in 1956 and the 1920s and 1930s are analepses within it. Ellipsis is a stretch of story time passed over in silence, the gap that a later analepsis may fill. Paralipsis (Greek, “leaving aside”) is the omission of something the narrative’s own vantage should have supplied, a lateral gap rather than a temporal one and the usual material of a late revelation. What this chapter leaves to others The mechanics of crossing a gap belong to The Transition (Chapter 5); this chapter begins one step earlier, with whether to cross, and ends one step later, with the present on return. Where a gap falls among the chapters belongs to The Chapter Break (Chapter 6). A prologue belongs to The Prologue (Chapter 10): it often holds the same kind of material as a flashback, but comes before the reader has invested anything, so its costs run the other way. A cutaway to a scene the viewpoint character did not witness is also a viewpoint problem, which belongs to The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13). Books built from two or more timelines belong to Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture (Chapter 8); a withheld past disclosed late belongs to The Reveal (Chapter 15); and an ending that reinterprets the past belongs to The Ending (Chapter 16). See also: the Reference definitions , with a table of adjacent terms; the glossary .

title: 3. How It Works
text: The deficit claim in the problem file , which the Reference chapter calls the interest deficit (the attention a cutaway spends before it has delivered anything), is a metaphor, and a writer revises better when she knows what it stands for. Five strands of theory answer five practical questions. What does a temporal departure ask of the reader? Research on narrative comprehension gives the cost a possible mechanism. Rolf Zwaan and Gabriel Radvansky’s review of the field ( Psychological Bulletin , 1998) describes readers building a situation model , a mental representation of the state of affairs the text describes, tracked along dimensions including protagonist, space, time, causality and intention. A shift on a dimension can require an update and affect reading time. Catherine Emmott’s Narrative Comprehension (1997) adds the reader’s contextual frame , the running record of who is present, where and in what configuration, and distinguishes switching to a new frame from recalling an old one. A flashback may require the reader to keep the present available while building a past situation and then return to it. Keisuke Ohtsuka and William Brewer ( Discourse Processes , 1992) presented listeners with five differently ordered versions of a narrative and tested their grasp of event order: the canonical version was easiest, while the flashforward version was the most difficult. These findings support caution about temporal reordering, not a general ranking in which a backward shift is harder than a forward one. The experiment tested comprehension of short passages heard aloud, not the artistic value or difficulty of whole novels; it cannot predict how any particular reader will experience Absalom, Absalom! . What is the reader leaving, and how far? Genette’s first narrative answers the first half. Since anachrony is measured against it, a departure needs some temporal baseline to be felt as one. A long flashback in a book’s second chapter may leave that baseline unclear, unless the book has already established a frame or declared a multi-timeline design. The second half is answered by two measures. Reach (Genette’s portée ) is how far back the cutaway goes from the present of the first narrative; extent ( amplitude ) is how much story time the cutaway itself covers. They are independent, and the table sets out the four combinations. Short extent Long extent Short reach Yesterday’s argument, dramatised: cheap and underused The last six months of a marriage, summarised: cheap, the natural home of summary Long reach One afternoon thirty years ago: potentially expensive if it needs a new context A childhood or a war: potentially a second strand, needing an architecture A long reach with a short extent can be expensive when the reader must build a vanished context, other ages, another place, a superseded set of relations, for one scene’s use. That possible imbalance between construction and occupancy, rather than childhood itself, is a reason to question a childhood flashback. Reach can also change while a cutaway runs: a long analepsis that moves forward closes the distance to the present, as Nelly Dean’s chronicle in Wuthering Heights starts about thirty years before Lockwood’s present and runs on until it meets it, and the reader feels the closing as momentum. Genette’s further distinctions locate the trouble. An external analepsis lies wholly before the first narrative begins and may revise what the reader believed about its antecedents; an internal analepsis falls inside its span and may repeat or contradict an earlier account of those events; a mixed analepsis starts outside and runs in. Within the internal case, a completing analepsis fills an ellipsis the reader knew was there, and arrives as an answer, while a repeating analepsis returns to material already narrated in order to recolour it, and is worth the reader’s time only if the second telling differs. The Good Soldier and Beloved are built almost entirely of repeating analepses and survive because each return differs from the last, which is the warning against reading the cost model as a prohibition. Can the cost be paid in advance? Sternberg’s Expositional Modes and Temporal Ordering in Fiction (1978) answers this. He distinguishes exposition that is preliminary (delivered up front), delayed (action first, antecedents later) and distributed (dispersed and never gathered), and three interests a narrative can raise. Suspense is uncertainty about the future, discharged when the outcome arrives; curiosity is uncertainty about the past, discharged when the gap is filled; surprise is the discovery that there was a gap at all, opened and filled at once. A cutaway that answers a question the reader is already asking is not an interruption but a payment. The household novel uses this: from the drawer onwards the reader wants to know why the looser hand in the ledger begins on 9 March, so when Dov’s chapter goes back to the evening of 9 March ( The Viewpoint Shift , Chapter 13) it pays a debt the book contracted a long way earlier. Hence the rule: open the gap before you fill it. Prolepsis can do related work from the other side, since a reader told what will happen may want to know how. The Death of Ivan Ilyich uses a different arrangement: its first chapter establishes a funeral as a frame, and the second turns back to the life that ended there. When is the past the story? Paul Ricoeur’s Time and Narrative (1983–85; translated by Kathleen McLaughlin and David Pellauer) supplies the counterweight: locally a cutaway interrupts, but at the scale of the book the arrangement of past against present is the book’s meaning. Trauma theory pushes further. Cathy Caruth’s Unclaimed Experience (1996) describes traumatic experience by its belatedness : an event not fully registered when it happened returns intrusively, so that it cannot be told in sequence and possesses the present rather than preceding it. Sethe’s rememory in Beloved , a past that persists as a place someone else can walk into, is its fictional form. Caruth’s model is contested, by Ruth Leys (2000) on its clinical basis, by Dominick LaCapra (2001) on its collapse of acting out into working through, and by Stef Craps (2013) on its Eurocentrism; for a writer the upshot is the same either way. The conventions of fragmentation and return exist and readers recognise them, and a book that borrows them without the subject, fragmenting material that is merely withheld, has taken on obligations it cannot meet. The dates of the convention The term flashback has early cinematic uses, and Maureen Turim’s Flashbacks in Film (1989) examines devices such as the dissolve, the voice-over and the return to a face in film history. Earlier narrative held its past differently. When Eurycleia recognises Odysseus by his scar in Book XIX of the Odyssey , Homer breaks off for some seventy lines to tell how he got it, and Erich Auerbach’s Mimesis (1946; translated by Willard Trask, 1953) argues that nothing is suspended while he does, because Homer’s narrative has no background held in reserve. The chapter’s preferred cutaway, with a motivated trigger and a consequential return, depends on a suspended foreground. These are practical conventions for certain present-driven novels, reinforced by workshop teaching; they are not rules for all narrative. See also: the Reference theory section , with Mendilow, the historical forms of the past from the epic excursus to the oral chronicle, and the interest deficit restated with its four refinements.

title: 4. The Taxonomy
text: The domain model asks one question of any cutaway: what does it buy? It turns the instruction tighten your backstory into separable questions with separable remedies. The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1) sets out four domains for any unit of narrative, plot, character, theme and texture, and proposes a fifth, the relational domain, which The Dialogue Exchange (Chapter 3) adopts for dialogue. This chapter audits a cutaway’s relational work under character, as The Descriptive Detail (Chapter 4) does for description, and adds a fifth domain of its own, reader knowledge, because control over when the reader learns something is the cutaway’s distinctive power. It proposes a sixth, the structural domain. Its danger is mechanical application: a writer who learns that good cutaways serve several domains starts loading them until they visibly perform. Plot: the cutaway explains what is happening now The plot domain buys the causal history behind a present situation, carried by the causal antecedent, the origin, the plant, the precedent and the correction. It is the domain a writer can see a need for in advance, and therefore the one most often served thinly: a cutaway written so that the reader will understand why the shop is failing satisfies a requirement and does nothing else. Causal information compresses, so if the whole return on a scene is the shop had been losing money for years , the scene should be a sentence. The precedent, which shows that this has happened before, is undervalued: it turns an event into a pattern at little more cost than an instance. In Faulkner’s Absalom, Absalom! (1936) Thomas Sutpen’s boyhood humiliation at a plantation door is offered as the origin of his whole design, but at four removes, as something Sutpen told General Compson, who told his son, who told Quentin, who tells Shreve, so that it is explained and questioned at once. Character: the cutaway explains who someone is now The character domain buys the history behind a present behaviour, through the formative moment, the measure of then against now, the withheld justification, the recolouring and the habitual. It is the domain where the flashback register is most often right, because the gap between knowing and feeling is widest here: a reader told that a man was humiliated at fourteen has a fact, and a reader who watched it has an experience she will apply to everything he does. It is also where drafts assume a person is explained by an origin, so two things a character cutaway can do need distinguishing. Explanation answers why is he like this? and closes the question. Illumination shows something that makes the present behaviour legible without making it determined, leaving the reader to construct the relation. The difference in practice is usually one sentence, the one that draws the connection, and declining it is nearly always the better choice. Stevens’s memory in The Remains of the Day (1989) of serving at a conference while his father died upstairs is given without one sentence linking it to the man narrating, and the reader makes the link. A recolouring, which changes how established behaviour reads, has a strict ordering rule: the behaviour must already be in place, so the cutaway must come late, and Beloved (1987) withholds the full account of Sethe’s act until the reader has been inside her ordinary competence and love. Theme: the cutaway restages the argument across time The theme domain buys evidence that the book’s concern is not particular to one moment, by restaging it under other conditions: the ironic parallel, compounding cost, the lesson the present refutes. It is the domain most easily claimed rather than shown, and the test is whether the rhyme survives the deletion of every sentence that points it out. Its peculiar resource is that past and present can share a page, so the reader performs the comparison herself. The Death of Ivan Ilyich (1886) builds its whole retrospect on this domain, each episode of career, marriage and house an instance of one claim made at the outset. Texture: the cutaway shapes the reading The texture domain buys a change of rhythm, register or sensory palette set against the pressure of the present. Craft teaching distrusts it, because this flashback is here for the rhythm can justify anything, and a change of pace is available more cheaply from a short scene of a different kind, a paragraph of description, a chapter break or a sequel in Scene and Sequel ’s sense (Chapter 2). A cutaway justified by texture alone is usually the most expensive solution to the problem it solves, which is why texture appears in strong cutaways as a secondary function. Delay at peak tension is a real technique within limits: an interruption of a few lines can sharpen a peak, and an interruption of six pages replaces the tension with an engagement in other material. Measure a delay at a peak in sentences, not pages. Proust’s madeleine shows how sensory texture can carry memory and a meditation on recovering the past at once. Reader knowledge: the fifth domain The fifth domain buys not information but information timed. Like other narrative units, a cutaway can revise what the reader thinks she knows. Its particular resource is to change when she learns about earlier events, and that order can change their meaning. Its carriers are dramatic irony created or resolved, the corrected assumption, calibrated suspense and the reframed detail. Placement relative to the present scene decides the effect, as the table shows for a fixed cutaway moved through three positions. Position Reader’s state during the present scene Effect Before Knows what the character does not Dramatic irony: she watches the mistake approach During, interrupting Learns it as the scene runs Recontextualisation in real time, the highest-risk placement After Rereads a scene already read Retrospective correction: she feels her own misreading Each makes a different book, but a draft that placed its cutaway where the writer happened to think of it has usually chosen the second. The reframed detail is the cheapest member of the set: it adds no fact, but makes a detail the reader already holds mean something new, and it is worth looking for in any revision. The household novel’s pen is the case worked in the worked analyses . The over-delivered form is the reversal treadmill, in which each cutaway overturns the last until the reader stops forming beliefs, which destroys the mechanism, since a correction needs a belief to correct. In Great Expectations (1861) the novel plants a specific false account of Pip’s past, that Miss Havisham is his benefactor, and demolishes it by Magwitch’s account of his years since the marshes; the reveal depends on the belief having been specific. A proposed sixth: the structural domain The five domains so far describe what past material delivers. Some cutaways are chosen for what they do to the shape of the book. A cutaway serves the structural domain when its main function is architectural: it establishes, maintains or completes a pattern in the book’s design, and something like it would be needed at that point even if its content were somewhat different. Three forms recur. The braided timeline alternates a present and a past strand on a declared rhythm, as Kate Morton’s The Forgotten Garden (2008) moves among 1913, when a little girl is left aboard a ship departing London and later found in Australia, 1975, when Nell, who learned on her twenty-first birthday that she was that child, goes looking for where she came from, and 2005, when her granddaughter Cassandra takes up the search; in Delia Owens’s Where the Crawdads Sing (2018) a strand beginning in 1952 runs forward until it reaches the investigation of 1969. The returning frame opens a situation the book departs from and comes back to, as in Wuthering Heights and Tayeb Salih’s Season of Migration to the North (1966; translated by Denys Johnson-Davies). The recurring approach circles a withheld event, each approach nearer, as Beloved circles the shed. The case for admitting the domain is that in these structures placement is set by the design rather than the content, so a model that judges each cutaway against the present question it interrupts has no words for a departure that is expected; that the structural function has failures of its own, strands progressing at incompatible rates, a frame that never closes, a centre reached too early, which no improvement to individual cutaways repairs; and that a chapter of the past strand can be load-bearing without being locally interesting, which the content domains mark as weak. The case against is respectable: alternation may be texture at book scale, a recurring approach may be reader knowledge seen from far away, and a domain answering what does this do for the book? sits oddly among domains answering what does this deliver here? This chapter adopts the structural domain for diagnosis, with two conditions. It is unavailable before the pattern is declared, in practice before its second or third instance, so a braided book must declare its architecture early. And it is the easiest justification to assert and the hardest to check: it’s a dual-timeline novel, so this chapter belongs here is a claim about the contents page, not the chapter. Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture (Chapter 8) rejects it as a domain of the cutaway: in The Forgotten Garden and Where the Crawdads Sing the past material recurs with a question of its own, so it is a strand, judged by Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture ’s tests (Chapter 8), and material that recurs without one fails there as an explaining strand. Must every domain be served? No. Two domains are the working target, three is strong, and five is often a sign of strain; the count exists to catch the single-domain cutaway that should have been a sentence. The weighting is book-specific, a crime novel’s cutaways running on plot and reader knowledge and a novel of consciousness’s on character and texture. The table summarises what failure looks like in each domain. Domain Under-delivery Over-delivery Plot The missing antecedent: the reader feels she skipped a page The explained present: nothing may simply be true Character The unexplained refusal The psychological receipt: a documented cause for every trait Theme The decorative past, connected to nothing The illustrated thesis: a parallel the reader completes early Texture The flat cutaway: the past sounds like the present The postcard: the past out-writes the book Reader knowledge The flat reveal: a new fact that recolours nothing The reversal treadmill Structure (proposed) The undeclared pattern Alternation kept up past its purpose Read across a manuscript, the table usually shows failures gathered in one column, which says more about the draft than any single row. See also: the Reference domains , with each domain’s carriers in a table and further illustrations.

title: 5. The Mechanism
text: The fork Every novel contains the past. The decision is the register in which it is delivered, and the two errors are symmetrical. A flashback used where backstory would do reads as bloated: the reader is made to live through a moment that needed only reporting. Backstory used where a flashback was needed reads as flattened: a moment the reader should have felt arrives as a fact, and when a later scene depends on its weight the dependency fails silently, so that the writer looks for the fault in the later scene. The second error is harder to find because its symptom appears somewhere other than its cause. Percy Lubbock’s The Craft of Fiction (1921) gave influential attention to scene and picture and often favoured dramatic presentation; this chapter treats the two as a fork, not a hierarchy. A direct line from Lubbock to the later maxim show, don’t tell is harder to establish. In Genette’s measures of duration backstory sits in the summary band (much story time, little text) and flashback in the scene band (the two roughly equal). The Transition (Chapter 5) asks how much text to spend crossing a gap; this chapter asks how much to spend on the far side. A flashback is a scene, so The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1) applies to it in full: someone wants something, meets resistance, and something is different at the end. A past passage with no want and no resistance has no engine, and a flashback without a change of value is the most expensive form of summary there is. Nor is the fork a spectrum: half-dramatised past, a fragment of dialogue in a stretch of précis, has a scene’s length and a summary’s engagement, so push a doubtful passage to one end and see which version the book prefers. The one-sentence compression check The one-sentence compression check settles the fork. Compress the cutaway to one sentence of summary and read the surrounding pages with that sentence in its place. If nothing the reader needed to live through is lost, the material was over-dramatised backstory; if the compression flattens something the later pages depend on, the flashback has earned its place. Write the sentence out, because a writer imagining the compressed version imagines it carrying everything the full version carried. Read it in context, two pages on, not in isolation. And expect a third outcome: some passages compress with nothing lost at all, including any reason for their existence, and the verdict then is to cut, which in first drafts is the commonest result. Fourteen registers The fork describes only the degree of dramatisation, and a working writer needs a finer repertoire. The Reference chapter sets out fourteen temporal registers: thirteen ways of handling past material and prolepsis as a forward-looking counterpoint. The table compresses what each buys and what it costs. # Register Buys Costs 1 Clause of implication Density with little interruption Little room to make a moment felt 2 Participial aside Biography without stopping Needs a narrator licensed to comment 3 Summary paragraph Long extents cheaply Reads as a report if extended 4 Iterative habitual A whole era in a sentence; the normal Cannot carry a singular event 5 Dramatised flashback The reader lives it The most expensive unit; suspends the present 6 Embedded oral tale The teller’s bias as content; a listener Two narrators to sustain 7 Found document Authenticity; another diction Must be plausible as itself 8 Involuntary memory The past as something that happens to a character Unmotivated by plot 9 Repeating analepsis Meaning by accumulation Every pass must visibly differ 10 Braided timeline A sustained parallel argument Both strands must progress 11 Reconstructed past Reconstruction as the reader’s activity Several accounts to hold 12 Unreachable past The gap as subject; maximum curiosity Must be legible as a refusal 13 False memory corrected The reader recruited into a misreading Needs a specific false belief 14 Prolepsis The intervening book as a completion Can neutralise suspense Registers 1 to 4 are easily overlooked when a draft leans heavily on summary paragraphs and dramatised scenes. A useful discipline is to attempt each piece of past material as a clause first and promote it only when the clause fails. Genette’s analysis of frequency separates the singulative (telling once what happened once), the repeating (telling several times what happened once) and the iterative (telling once what happened many times), and the iterative is the register that establishes what was normal, without which a dramatised exception has nothing to be an exception to. Register 8 complicates the rest: Proust’s madeleine is an unmistakably sensory trigger, even though the recollection is not there to advance an immediate plot question. A rule requiring every trigger to serve the plot would misread it. Register 12 works only if the reader can tell she is being refused and why, which The Opening Pages (Chapter 9) states as the question whether a gap is in the character or in the author. The table’s use is substitution testing : rewrite a failing cutaway in three other registers, one much shorter and one much longer, and judge only when all four exist, in place. The most revealing substitution is into the embedded oral tale, because turning past material into something a character says aloud, to someone, for a reason, forces two questions a flashback lets a writer avoid: why now, and why to this person. Trigger and return A trigger is the element in the present scene that motivates the cutaway, turning an authorial decision into an event in the story: an object, a sensation, a phrase, a question asked, a place entered, a silence, a date, a document, a resemblance, or nothing at all. The object is the strongest, because it survives the return: a smell is over when it is over, but a pen is still in the hand on the far side, and the return sentence has something to work with. The requirement of a trigger is a consequence of narrative distance, not an independent rule. Close third-person narration often stays near a consciousness, so an untriggered departure may feel abrupt; confident omniscient narration has made no such promise, which is why Tolstoy can simply go. Over-triggering is a fault too: a stopped clock that recalls the day time stopped shows the machinery, and the best triggers are slightly oblique. The return is where the cutaway is paid for, and its rule is that the present must have changed by the time the narrative comes back to it, in a way the reader can locate. There are four kinds of change, in rising strength: changed knowledge, in which the reader knows something that recolours the scene; changed understanding, in which the character does; a changed question, in which the present scene now carries a question it did not have; and changed action, in which the character does something other than what she was about to do. The changed question is the most generally available and the least used, since it needs no plot event. Where the multiplying work lives Revision looks for multiplicity in a more dramatic memory, but most of the work is done in four humbler places. The trigger object exists in both timelines and can carry plot, character, theme and reader knowledge at once if it is already load-bearing elsewhere in the book. Tense and aspect are the cheapest carriers English has: He had always kept it by the till establishes in eight words a history a scene would need three hundred for, and characterises, since always is somebody’s claim. The first sentence after the return is the only one that can work on both timelines at once, and drafts spend it on re-anchoring. And the sentence not written, the one that would state the cutaway’s significance, is the commonest single improvement available, since a connection the reader makes is held more firmly than one supplied. For a present-driven draft, it can help to treat fully dramatised past scenes as a flashback budget : check whether each one earns its space, especially when a clause would have delivered the same material. The useful allowance varies with the book, and no fixed number is implied. Multiplicity also has a ceiling: when every remembered detail is significant and the return changes the present in the designed way and no other, the cutaway reads as a mechanism. A past needs some surplus, detail that is merely true; Roland Barthes’s “The Reality Effect” (1968) argues that the apparently useless detail signifies reality itself. See also: the Reference register section , with the fourteen registers and their exemplars and the tables of triggers and returns; the Reference multiplicity section , with the cutaway audit.

title: 6. Diagnostic Tests
text: The ten tests are for revision, not composition; applied while drafting they produce a writer who cannot put anything in the past without a permit. Before running any of them, decide once whether they apply to your book. They assume that the present carries the engine, and in a novel whose present is deliberately thin, a drive west, a night’s conversation, a man dying in a room, tests 1 (Momentum), 3 (Removal) and 8 (Placement) will report failures that are not faults. Run tests 1 to 4 (Momentum, Register, Removal and Trigger) first, since there is no point tuning the trigger of a cutaway that should be a sentence. Tests 3 (Removal) and 7 to 10 (Chronology, Placement, Completing or repeating and Proportion) need the manuscript, not the passage alone. Record a sentence, not a verdict; every test is failed on purpose by a book worth reading. Test 1 — Momentum What present question is the reader waiting on when the cutaway begins, and how hard is she pressing: low, moderate or at its peak? Failure. The timing was not chosen. Exception. The Remains of the Day , whose present asks almost nothing. Test 2 — Register Run the compression check: keep the scene, keep the sentence, or keep neither? Failure. Over-dramatised backstory. Exception. Lost , which used a recurring off-island strand in many episodes as part of its format. Test 3 — Removal Cut it and read the surrounding twenty pages: what is lost, and in which domain? Failure. A decorative past. Exception. Proust’s Combray, where the accumulation is the argument. Test 4 — Trigger Is the departure motivated by something in the present, and if not, can this narration afford to go without one? Failure. An unmotivated jump in close third. Exception. The Death of Ivan Ilyich , whose narrator simply goes. Test 5 — Return Cover the cutaway and read the sentence before it against the sentence after: does the present resume, or has it changed? Failure. The untethered return. Exception. “El curioso impertinente” in Don Quixote , which changes nothing. Test 6 — Reach and extent How far back does it go, how much time does it cover, and are they in proportion to what it delivers? Failure. A whole context built for one scene. Exception. Sutpen at the plantation door in Absalom, Absalom! Test 7 — Chronology Could a reader at this point write the events in the order they happened? Ask one, and compare with yours. Failure. Confusion where withholding was meant. Exception. The Good Soldier , where reconstruction is the reading. Test 8 — Placement Name three other places this cutaway could go: would it cost less, and recolour more, at any of them? Failure. The right material in the wrong place. Exception. The scar in Odyssey XIX, at the peak of the recognition. Test 9 — Completing or repeating Is it filling a gap the reader knew was there, or returning to material already told, and if so, what does this pass add? Failure. Redundancy, or a gap never opened. Exception. Beloved , some of whose returns add only weight. Test 10 — Proportion How much of the book is in the past, and does its declared structure acknowledge that? Failure. A retrospective novel organised as a present-tense one. Exception. Wuthering Heights , nearly all retrospect inside a diary’s frame. Three refinements sharpen the tests. In test 3 (Removal), perform the removal on paper and leave it out for a day, since a writer reading a passage just deleted supplies it from memory. In test 6 (Reach and extent), record whether the reach shortens as the cutaway runs; a long analepsis that closes on the present makes its own momentum, and one that stays at a fixed distance must find momentum elsewhere. In test 10 (Proportion), percentages can prompt a question about the book’s declared structure, but there is no evidenced threshold at which characters lack history or a novel becomes retrospective. Record the proportion and ask whether the present, past and framing agree with the design the book has taught its reader to expect. Reading the results together Failures cluster, and the cluster points to the first move. Test 2 (Register) alone means compressing to the sentence you wrote. Tests 1 (Momentum) and 4 (Trigger) together mean the cutaway arrives on the writer’s schedule: run test 8 (Placement) and find a place where a present question already exists. Test 3 (Removal) alone means cutting, not adding a function. Test 5 (Return) alone means rewriting the return for a changed question. Test 6 (Reach and extent) alone means finding a nearer memory. Test 7 (Chronology) alone is usually fixed by one date. Test 9 (Completing or repeating) failing as repetition means naming the difference or cutting the pass. Test 10 (Proportion) means changing the structure, not the proportions. Tests 1 (Momentum), 3 (Removal) and 5 (Return) together mean the material belongs to another book. Test 8 (Placement) carries a warning. When a cutaway fails, writers revise the cutaway, because it is the object in front of them. In the cases this protocol catches, by this book’s estimate from drafts read rather than from a count, the material is more often sound and its position wrong, and moving four hundred words is a smaller operation than rewriting them, with a larger effect. See also: the Reference protocol , with each test’s procedure and a table of combined failures; the Reference failure catalogue .

title: 7. Failure Patterns
text: Each pattern below is described by its mechanism and ends with a published work that commits it and succeeds, because the pattern fails through the mechanism, not the surface feature, and where the mechanism is absent the feature is harmless. The Reference chapter’s full catalogue adds seven more: the unmotivated cutaway, the redundant flashback, the nested flashback, the better past, the italicised memory, the prologue relocated as a flashback, and the undeveloped repeat. The momentum killer Symptom. The cutaway arrives at the most tense moment of the present and stops it, with a payoff smaller than the interruption. Mechanism. Tension is not preserved during an interruption; it is replaced. A reader given six pages of other material does not hold the earlier tension in reserve but builds a new engagement, and the old tension has to be restarted from a lower level on return. The failure is one of scale, not kind, since a short cut at a peak can sharpen it. Remedy. At a peak, measure the interruption in sentences. If the material needs more, it is in the wrong place: run test 8 (Placement). The exception. At the opening of the second part of Les Misérables (1862) Hugo interrupts Jean Valjean’s story with a long account of the battle of Waterloo, fought years before, and the interruption is defensible because the book’s subject is the relation between single lives and historical forces. A book may decide that its interruptions are its argument, and then it must make them long enough to be read as one. The info-dump backstory Symptom. Paragraphs or pages of compressed history with no scene-level engine, read as a report rather than felt as consequence, often where a family’s history or an invented world tempts the writer to deliver a whole system at once. Mechanism. Two failures together. Delivered early, exposition spends an asset that would have generated curiosity. And information is not memorable without a container: a reader given four generations of a family before she cares about anyone in it has nowhere to store the material and retains little of it. The writer, who knows the history intimately, fears the reader will be lost without it; but the reader needs to believe the writer knows the history, which confident specificity achieves, not to know it herself. Remedy. Ask of each expository sentence which character would say it, to whom and why, and attempt the material as a clause or an iterative sentence before giving it more room. The exception. Balzac’s Père Goriot (1835) opens with long accounts of the boarding house, its economics and its lodgers’ antecedents, an info-dump by any later standard. The accounts are causal: the novel’s argument is that the lodgers are what the rent makes them, so the rent must be specified before the people can be understood. A book with a determinist thesis needs its determinants on the page. The second-chapter flashback Symptom. The novel leaves its present for an extended visit to the past before the end of its second chapter. Mechanism. A departure is measured against a first narrative, and a first narrative not yet consolidated can be hard to identify. The reader may not yet have formed the model the cutaway would interrupt, so the departure can leave its relation to the present unclear. Remedy. Delay the first substantial cutaway until the reader could describe the book’s present situation in a sentence, which is usually later than it feels. The exception. Where the Crawdads Sing (2018) opens on a body found in 1969 and turns at once to 1952, to a six-year-old girl watching her mother walk away from their shack in the North Carolina marsh, and from then on moves between the two strands. It commits the pattern in its first pages and does not suffer from it, because it declares a braid instead of interrupting a present: the reader learns within a few chapters that the book has two timelines and that one is travelling towards the other. The Death of Ivan Ilyich escapes the pattern another way, by making its first chapter, the funeral, complete in itself. The untethered return Symptom. The cutaway ends and the present scene resumes as though nothing had happened. Mechanism. The deficit is never discharged: the reader paid for the departure and receives nothing where payment was due. The cutaway itself may have been excellent, and the fault may lie in one sentence. It persists because the return is written last and treated as re-entry, not payoff. Remedy. Rewrite the first sentence after the cutaway to carry one of the four changes, preferably a changed question, which is available in nearly every case. The exception. “El curioso impertinente”, the novella read aloud at the inn in Part I of Don Quixote (1605), runs across three chapters and returns the story to the state it was in. Cervantes was criticised for his interpolations, answered the criticism inside Part II (1615) and largely gave the practice up there. Cervantes’s response shows that interpolated tales were already open to criticism in his own time; his change of practice does not establish when a broader convention ended. The childhood-explains-everything cutaway Symptom. A single childhood scene, usually of humiliation, loss or a parent’s failure, is offered as the origin of an adult’s defining trait. Mechanism. Three faults at once. Structurally it combines a long reach and a short extent, which can require substantial context for one scene. Psychologically it proposes a model of personality in which one event determines a life, which readers do not recognise from experience. And narratively an explained character is a closed question. The pattern persists because it is what the phrase character motivation is usually taken to mean, and some screen stories use a single traumatic memory as shorthand for an inner life. Remedy. Prefer illumination to explanation; move the material nearer, since a recent memory usually makes the same point without the determinism; or deliver it in a register that claims no causal authority, the iterative or the clause. The exception. Tana French’s In the Woods (2007) is built on a childhood afternoon in 1984, when three children went into a wood near Dublin and one came out, found against a tree with his shoes full of blood and no memory of what happened. That boy is now the detective who narrates, working a child’s murder in the same place. The novel takes the pattern’s premise, an adult organised around one afternoon in childhood, and refuses the scene: the memory never returns and the 1984 case is never solved. The origin explains the man by being missing, which turns the device’s reductiveness into its subject. Faulkner’s Sutpen, whose origin arrives at four removes, makes the same turn by another route. See also: the Reference failure catalogue , with each pattern’s persistence and a table from symptom to mechanism.

title: 8. Worked Analyses
text: The readings run from a single sentence to a whole book’s design, then to the screen and the household case. The Death of Ivan Ilyich : the sentence that opens a life Tolstoy’s novella (1886; translated by Louise and Aylmer Maude) gives its first chapter to the funeral: colleagues calculating what the death means for their promotions, the widow asking about the pension, and Peter Ivanovich escaping to his game of cards. The second chapter opens the retrospect, which is the rest of the book, with this sentence: Ivan Ilych’s life had been most simple and most ordinary and therefore most terrible. Fourteen words do all the preparation for forty-five years. Ivan Ilych’s life declares the scope, not an episode but a life. Had been is the only signal of departure: the pluperfect tells the reader she is going back, with no trigger, since nobody in the present is remembering, and no bridging language. Most simple and most ordinary characterises the man and warns the reader off expecting event. And therefore carries the theme on a conjunction: not but , not and yet ; the ordinariness is the cause of the horror. And most terrible , placed before its evidence, turns the forty-five years from a chronicle into a case the reader is invited to test. The sentence feels blunt, not efficient, which is the usual signature of multiplicity done well. Because the death comes first, the retrospect is a completing analepsis, filling a gap the reader knows ends at that funeral, and the missing trigger is licensed by a narrator who never promised to stay inside anyone’s head. The retrospect also changes speed as it goes. It begins with years compressed into paragraphs, summary and iterative, and slows until the last days take pages, so the reach shortens while the pace slows, and the two together give a long retrospect the sense of arrival it otherwise lacks. The Sense of an Ending : the document that corrects a memory Julian Barnes’s novel (2011; Booker Prize 2011) is narrated by Tony Webster, retired, in two parts. The first is his account of his school friend Adrian Finn, of his girlfriend Veronica, and of the letter he wrote when Adrian and Veronica became a couple, not long before Adrian killed himself. The whole of Part One is retrospective narration, and the reader has only Tony’s version. In Part Two, forty years on, Veronica’s mother leaves Tony five hundred pounds and Adrian’s diary, Veronica withholds the diary, and she gives Tony a copy of his own letter. He reads it, and it is malicious in a way his memory had erased. In this chapter’s terms Part Two is a repeating analepsis delivered through a found document, and its register is the false memory corrected. Test 9 (Completing or repeating) asks what the second pass adds, and the answer is the most a repetition can add: the same event in the narrator’s own hand, contradicting his account of it. The reader is recruited into the misreading by the only means available, the narrator’s confidence, and charged for it by a document she cannot argue with. The correction works because Part One gave a specific belief to overturn, not a blank. Barnes then repeats the move at smaller scale: the novel’s last revelation corrects a second assumption, about whose child a man Veronica shows Tony is, and Tony has to revise again. The novel is useful to anyone writing the household book, whose theme is records outliving the people who keep them. A record’s authority in fiction comes from its having been made at the time, by someone with no idea of how it would be read later, which is what the father means when he says in case anyone ever needs to check . Where the Crawdads Sing : a braid whose reach shortens Delia Owens’s novel (2018) opens with two boys finding a body below a fire tower in 1969, then turns to 1952, when Kya, aged six, watches her mother leave their marsh shack and not come back. The book then moves between the investigation in 1969 and Kya’s life from 1952, the past strand advancing year by year through her abandonment by the rest of her family and her survival alone in the marsh. The investigation strand also advances, but over a shorter span; the past strand covers years. Its reach therefore shortens with every chapter, and the reader feels the past coming to meet the present, the momentum a long analepsis gains by approach. When the past strand reaches 1969 the two become one narrative for Kya’s arrest and trial. The book is a test case for the proposed structural domain. Many 1969 chapters, taken alone, deliver little, and the content domains would mark them weak; their work is architectural, keeping the destination in view so that every chapter of Kya’s childhood reads as a step towards a body. The reader-knowledge domain runs through the same design. By the trial she knows Kya’s life as the jury cannot, and the verdict is read against that knowledge. The last pages, after Kya’s death decades later, add a found document: her partner, Tate, finds a poem alluding to the death and the shell necklace the dead man wore, and the reader must reconsider earlier events. The poem is a new clue, though poetry has appeared earlier in the novel. A screen reading: Lost and Arrival The season 3 finale of Lost , “Through the Looking Glass” (ABC, 23 May 2007), relied on three seasons of a convention. Many episodes had paired the island story with scenes from a character’s past, so when the finale cut to Jack, bearded and despairing in a city, viewers could read the scenes as flashbacks. The last scene revealed them as the future: Jack has left the island, and tells Kate, We have to go back . It was the series’ first flash-forward. Denis Villeneuve’s Arrival (2016), from Ted Chiang’s novella “Story of Your Life” (1998), plays the same move on a single viewer’s assumptions: the scenes of the linguist Louise with her daughter, Hannah, are presented as memories of a dead child and revealed as the future she will choose, knowing how it ends. Both turn the convention of the register against the viewer. A cut to another time is assigned a direction by its grammar, and that assignment is itself an assumption a narrative can plant and overturn, which is the corrected assumption at its most economical: no new fact about any event, only about when it happened. In Arrival the correction also changes the emotional domain, since grief for a child already lost becomes a decision made in full knowledge. The household revision case: the pen in the coat About two-thirds of the way through the household novel, Nadia, in the flat above the shop, puts her hand into the pocket of her father’s coat, which still hangs on its hook by the door, and finds the good pen: the fountain pen he used only for the ledger and kept by the till in its case. The reader saw him pocket it in the prologue, on his last ordinary day ( The Prologue , Chapter 10). The line he speaks in this cutaway is quoted at the novel’s close ( The Ending , Chapter 16). The cutaway is the middle term between an object planted and a line returning. Version A, the draft. The draft opens a new section with Nadia at nine, helping with the stock count for the first time, on a Sunday in November with the shop closed: a radiator making its noise like something clearing its throat , two chairs at the counter, tea, a bus shaking the window, the marks made in fives and the sevens crossed. She asks why he is using the good pen, and he puts the cap on it, looks at her over his glasses, and says, “Because someone should write it down properly. In case anyone ever needs to check.” She thinks he means the shop, goes back to her column of fives, and the section ends in the past as the light goes. It runs to about 320 words. Diagnosis. No present question is open when the cutaway begins, because there is no present at the point of departure (test 1: Momentum). It compresses to one sentence, He had once told her, when she asked why a stock count needed the good pen, that someone should write it down properly, in case anyone ever needed to check , with nothing lost (test 2: Register). There is no trigger, a conspicuous gap in this close third-person passage (test 4: Trigger), and no return (test 5). Its reach is about twenty-five years and its extent one afternoon, a potentially costly combination, with a radiator, a bus and two chairs built and thrown away (test 6: Reach and extent). It contradicts the canon: the conversation took place the second time he lost the pen, in the year he died, between adults, and the draft turns it into a formative childhood scene, an explanation where the book needs an illumination (test 7: Chronology). And it spends at leisure, cushioned by tea, the line on which the ending depends. The writing is not at fault; the failure is register, placement and motivation, which is the usual case. Version B, the revision. Nadia found the pen in his coat pocket, right where she remembered him keeping it — except it wasn’t the register pen, the plain black one. It was the good pen, the fountain one he only used for the ledger, the one he wasn’t supposed to carry loose because he’d lose it. He’d lost it twice that year already, and made Ma buy a new nib. She had asked him about it once, the second time. Why he needed the good pen for a stock count nobody was going to read twice. He’d looked at her over his glasses like she’d caught him at something. “Because someone should write it down properly,” he said. “In case anyone ever needs to check.” At the time she’d thought he meant the shop. She had not thought, until just now, standing by the door with her hand in the pocket of a coat still on its hook, to ask him what he’d actually thought anyone might need to check. The revision changed the register, not the content: a dramatised scene of 320 words became an exchange of a few lines, entered through a clause, and the sentence the compression check produced turned out to be the father’s own. It attached the cutaway to an object already load-bearing, so the trigger was found, not invented, and remains in her hand after the return. It moved the exchange out of childhood, which removed the determinism, restored the canon and shortened the reach from decades to months, so that no context needs building: the reader already knows this shop. It is a completing analepsis, since the prologue showed the pen pocketed without saying why. It rewrote the return as a changed question: Nadia comes back holding a question she did not have when she reached into the pocket, and the present scene now has to carry it. And it declined the explanatory sentence: nothing says the father knew he was ill, and the reader assembles it. It reframes a detail the reader already has, the pen carried loose, from habit to decision, which is reader knowledge at its cheapest, and it opens the book’s argument about records. What the revision has not solved. The last sentence is the return, the changed question, the thematic statement and the emotional beat at once, close to the ceiling on multiplicity, and an editor might ask whether At the time she’d thought he meant the shop has already done its work. The trigger is very apt: the defence is that the aptness was established by the prologue, two hundred pages earlier, and a reader meeting the scene alone would find it neat.
