Nadia has learned not to touch the coat ( The Descriptive Detail , Chapter 4), so the scene before this one must give her a reason to put her hand in its pocket now, and that reason is not yet written. The revision in The Prologue (Chapter 10) gives the prologue a fragment of the line, In case , as the father’s unfinished reason when he pockets the pen, so this cutaway is partly a repeating analepsis, and test 9 (Completing or repeating) asks what the second pass adds: the rest of the line, the occasion, the listener and Nadia’s misreading, which is enough, though the reader will have heard the first two words before Nadia understands them. And one version was never tried: Nadia telling Elena about the exchange, which would give a listener and the chance that Elena reads their father differently. See also: the Reference worked analyses , with readings of In Search of Lost Time , Wuthering Heights , The Good Soldier , Absalom, Absalom! , Beloved , The Remains of the Day and Season of Migration to the North , and the revision case with the full protocol in a table.

title: 9. Checklist and Exercises
text: Revision checklist Use the checklist on one cutaway at a time, after reading the page before it, the cutaway and the page after. Each item is a question to answer in a sentence. The decision What present question was open when the narrative left, and how hard was the reader pressing on it? Had the book already made the reader want this past, or does the cutaway arrive unasked? Would it cost less, and recolour more, thirty pages earlier or later? The register Written out as one sentence and read in place, does the cutaway lose anything the later pages need? Has the material been tried as a clause, and as an iterative sentence, before being given a scene? If it is a scene, does someone in it want something, meet resistance and end changed? The crossing What in the present triggers the departure, and is the narration close enough to need one? Which of the four changes has the present undergone by the return: knowledge, understanding, question or action? Is there a sentence stating the cutaway’s significance that could be deleted? The manuscript On one sheet, what are the reach, extent, register and domains of every cutaway, and what pattern do they make? How much of the book is in the past, and does its declared structure say so? If there is a second timeline, is it declared by its second or third instance, and does each strand progress? Exercises for your own draft The cutaway audit. List every cutaway in the manuscript in order, with its page, reach, extent, register, domains served and the present question open when it began, writing none where there was none. Do not assess any single entry; read the sheet. Most entries serving one domain means the book is using cutaways to deliver information; many entries reading none means they arrive on the writer’s schedule; a cluster in the first quarter means the past is being spent before the reader wants it. The cutaway audit takes about an hour. One sentence. Take the flashback you are least sure of, write its one-sentence compression, and paste the sentence into the manuscript in its place. Read on for two pages, leave it a day, and read again before deciding. Four registers. Rewrite one failing cutaway as a clause of implication, an iterative sentence and something a character says aloud to another character, and judge only when all four versions exist. Three placements. For one dramatised cutaway, name three other places it could go. For each, write the present question it would interrupt there and the detail it would recolour that it cannot recolour now. The return sentence. For five cutaways, cover the cutaway and read the sentence before it against the sentence after. Where they read continuously, rewrite the sentence after so that the character comes back with a question she did not have.

title: 10. Coda
text: The debt model assumes that a reader leans forward into what happens next, and that the past interrupts the lean. For most plot-driven fiction this describes the reading well, and the tests built on it catch real faults. But it is a description of a kind of book, not of narrative, and the books it does not describe are not a margin. In The Remains of the Day the present is a drive west, a broken radiator and a walk up a hill, made thin so that the retrospect can carry the book. In Beloved the past is not visited but suffered, and the present at 124 is what interrupts it. In The Good Soldier and Absalom, Absalom! the reader’s question is not what happens next but what happened, and whether this teller can be trusted about it. In Proust the subject is the involuntary return itself. For these books forward motion is the interruption, and a writer who applied the tests to them would cut what they are for. The practical consequence is a question to ask before any test is run: which timeline is this book about? If the answer is the present, the past must earn each departure, and the instruments in this chapter say how. If the answer is the past, the present has the burden instead. It must justify its claims on the reader’s attention as an occasion, a frame or a vantage, and a present that does not know it is a frame will drag in the way a bad flashback does. A great many uncertain drafts sit between the two answers, with a past the writer cares about more than the present that carries it, and for them the remedy is neither better flashbacks nor fewer, but a decision about which timeline is the story. See also: the Reference coda .

title: Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture
text: Which time the reader is in, and why it is that one The Craft Behind the Story (Second Edition) — Chapter 8. Part II: The Joins. In brief. A book told out of chronological order uses the order of telling, not the order of events, as its main instrument of meaning. The arrangement earns its departure from chronology when the order does work that chronology could not: each strand runs on a question of its own, the reader always knows which time she is in and how far it stands from the others, and the point at which the strands meet changes what at least one of them meant. The chapter’s tools are the order chart, which sets the position of every unit in the story against its position in the text, and the strand table, which records for each strand its question, its span, its rate and where it meets the others. Use the chapter when you are planning a book set across more than one time period, when readers say they were lost or skimmed one timeline, or when a draft’s arrangement feels like chronology made harder to read. What you can do after this chapter Chart a book’s order of telling against its order of events, and say what the arrangement gains over chronology. Decide whether recurring material in another time is a cutaway or a strand, and give a strand a question of its own. Mark each time so that the reader is never lost, at the least cost in headings and explanation. Set the rates and intervals of several strands so that their difference does work, and place their meeting where it changes meaning. Diagnose an arbitrary arrangement, a lost reader, a strand that only explains, a lockstep braid and a convergence by coincidence, and revise them. Key terms Story order and text order; anachrony; strand; instalment; switch; interval; rate; convergence; convergence of times, by cause and by identity; orientation marker; the order chart; the strand table; the braid; the anchored order; the reverse order; the mosaic; the nested order; the threshold of a strand; temporal counterpoint; the temporal domain; the bridging object; the arbitrary arrangement; the lost reader; the explaining strand; the lockstep braid; the convergence by coincidence. Each is defined at first use and collected in the consolidated glossary . Contents The first files say what a non-linear book is and what a reader does with one, the central files how its times are kept apart, marked, paced and brought together, and the last are for use at the desk. The Problem A household draft that braids a second timeline through the book, and the chapter’s claim Definitions Story order, text order, strand and the terms around them, and what other chapters keep How It Works What order does to meaning, what readers do at a shift of time, and what the evidence says The Taxonomy Five architectures, and two rulings: the threshold of a strand and temporal counterpoint The Mechanism How strands are given questions, marked, paced, switched and brought together, with rulings on the temporal domain and the bridging object Diagnostic Tests Eight questions on one page, and how to read their failures together Failure Patterns Five recurrent failures, each with a work that commits it and succeeds Worked Analyses Slaughterhouse-Five , Where the Crawdads Sing , Station Eleven and Memento , and the household revision case Checklist and Exercises The revision checklist and five exercises for your own draft Coda What the model assumes, and why an arrangement is an argument about time A writer in revision can start at the diagnostic tests, with an order chart drafted for the book as it stands. A writer planning a book in two or more times should read the mechanism first, because a strand’s question and its meeting with the others are easier to design than to find afterwards. The full treatment This is a new chapter, so the Reference layer holds a single full treatment rather than a corrected original: the theory at greater length, an extended catalogue of architectures and failure patterns, the four rulings in full, the procedures for each test, further analyses ( Cloud Atlas , Hamnet , The Time Traveler’s Wife and Dunkirk ), the household order chart and strand table, a glossary of the chapter’s terms and the sources. See also: The Transition (Chapter 5), for the join between two units, of which a switch between strands is the largest case; Backstory and Flashback (Chapter 7), for the single cutaway into the past; The Subplot (Chapter 14), for threads that run in one time; The Reveal (Chapter 15), for truths an arrangement withholds.

title: 1. The Problem
text: A writer revising the household novel has been told by an early reader that the father is a ghost in his own book. The reader has a point. The novel’s present is the July after his death, when his three adult children reconstruct what he left: Elena, who learns in Dov’s doorway that their mother changed the shop’s locks in March; Nadia, who counts things and will not touch the coat that still hangs in the flat above the shop; Dov, who gave Elena the new key and kept the reason. The father appears alive only in the prologue, his last ordinary day, and in Nadia’s memory of the second time he lost his good pen. Everything else the reader knows of him comes through objects: the coat, the pen, and the ledger he kept for eleven years in a careful slanting hand, whose entries stop on 9 March. The writer’s answer is a second timeline. The draft now braids six chapters set in the father’s last five weeks, each headed with a date, through the first three-quarters of the book, alternating with the sisters’ July, so that his strand reaches the evening of 9 March just before Dov’s chapter of the same evening. The first of them reads, in part: February. He wrote the week’s figures into the ledger with the good pen, and Nadia, doing the stock count at the end of the counter, asked why it had to be that pen. Someone should write it down properly, he told her. He did not mention the letter in his inside pocket, or Thursday’s appointment. There would be time for that. The prose is clear, and every chapter of the strand is dated, so no reader is lost. The trouble is in the arrangement. The strand’s end is known from the opening pages, which tell the reader that the father died in March, so the only question it can run on is the one the book has saved for its last chapter: what he knew. The draft can answer that question in its own chapters, which spends the book’s largest truth at a tenth of its length, to the reader alone; or it can keep the answer out of a mind that knows it, which is what He did not mention the letter does, and which tells the reader both that there is a secret and roughly what it is. The strand also spends, in its first chapter, the line Nadia is meant to remember at two-thirds of the book. And its arrival at 9 March changes nothing, because the reader already holds every fact it delivers. The draft has a second timeline without a second question. The case is not an argument against telling a book in more than one time. It is an instance of a confusion that the chapter separates into its parts: the difference between material that belongs to another time and a strand, a recurring line of the book’s telling set in another time and running on a question of its own. Material from another time can be delivered as a cutaway , a single departure that ends where it began, which Backstory and Flashback (Chapter 7) treats; a book whose order of telling is organised around such departures is this chapter’s subject. The chapter’s claim is that an arrangement of times is justified by the work it does, and that the work can be named. A book told out of chronological order earns the departure when the order does work that chronology could not: each strand runs on a question of its own, the reader always knows which time she is in and how far it stands from the others, and the point at which the strands meet changes what at least one of them meant. An arrangement that fails these is chronology made harder to read. The claim has a consequence for revision. A draft whose readers are lost needs better marking of its times, which is cheap. A draft whose readers skim one timeline needs a question for that timeline, which is not; and a draft whose timelines meet without consequence needs its meeting moved or remade, which means rethinking what each strand is for. None is mended by adding chapters to a strand. The revision in Worked Analyses removes the father’s strand and finds that the book already has a second time, in two instalments and an object, and gives it one heading. The chapter also rules on four proposals that earlier chapters left to it, since time at the scale of a book is its material: The Descriptive Detail ’s temporal domain (Chapter 4), The Transition ’s bridging object (Chapter 5), Backstory and Flashback ’s structural domain (Chapter 7) and The Subplot ’s temporal counterpoint (Chapter 14). See also: the full treatment , section 7, with the draft strand charted chapter by chapter; The Reveal (Chapter 15), on the withholding viewpoint, the failure the draft’s father commits.

title: 2. Definitions
text: The working definition A non-linear book is one whose order of telling departs from the order of the events it tells by design, at the scale of the book: the departures form a pattern the reader learns to expect, not a scatter of local excursions. The definition needs two orders, and the chapter names them plainly. Story order is the sequence in which events happen in the world of the book; text order is the sequence in which the book presents them. The Russian Formalists of the 1920s called them fabula and syuzhet , and every later account of narrative time starts from the gap between them. Any discrepancy between the two is an anachrony , Gérard Genette’s term: a unit told earlier in the text than its place in the story, or later. A multi-timeline book is a non-linear book whose anachronies are organised as two or more strands. A strand is a line of the telling set in one time, continuous within itself, that the book leaves and resumes; each continuous run of it is an instalment , and each passage from one strand to another is a switch . A strand differs from a cutaway in three ways: it recurs, it advances in its own time between instalments, and it runs on a question of its own, which is the condition the chapter treats as decisive (see The Taxonomy ). The interval between two strands is the distance in story time between them at a given point; the rate of a strand is the story time it covers per page. A convergence is the point at which strands meet, and they can meet in three ways: in time, when one strand catches up with the other; by cause, when an act in one is found to produce the situation in another; or by identity, when a person or object is found to be in both. A non-linear book need not be multi-timeline. A book told backwards, or in fragments ordered by association, departs from story order without strands. The chapter covers both, and gives most space to strands because most revision problems are theirs. Adjacent terms Several neighbouring terms belong to other chapters and are used here in the senses those chapters give them. The cutaway is Backstory and Flashback ’s single departure (Chapter 7) into the past, with its reach , Genette’s portée , the distance in time between the cutaway and the present it leaves; an interval is the same measure taken between two strands, neither of which needs to be the present. A subplot is The Subplot ’s second thread (Chapter 14) with a causal chain of its own; most strands set in another time are also subplots, and a strand shares The Subplot ’s tests (Chapter 14) for its chain and adds this chapter’s for its time. The Subplot ’s structural convergence (Chapter 14), the point at which threads meet, is the convergence defined above, seen from the side of cause. The transition is The Transition ’s join (Chapter 5) between two units, and a switch is a transition that also changes time, usually across a chapter break , which belongs to The Chapter Break (Chapter 6). A strand often has its own viewpoint character, and when it does the switch is also a viewpoint shift , whose costs The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13) prices. An orientation marker is anything that tells the reader which time she is in: a heading, a time-stamp, a tense, a detail of period or wear, an object she has seen before. The term is this chapter’s, and it gathers devices that The Descriptive Detail (Chapter 4) and The Transition (Chapter 5) treat one at a time. What the chapter leaves to other chapters The mechanics of the single cutaway, its registers and its exit, belong to Backstory and Flashback (Chapter 7); this chapter begins where the cutaways form a strand or the whole book is out of order. A truth withheld by an arrangement and disclosed late is shared with The Reveal (Chapter 15), which asks whether the withholding has a reason; this chapter asks whether the arrangement has a use. A prologue set in another time belongs to The Prologue (Chapter 10), though a prologue that is the first instalment of a strand is also this chapter’s. A middle told out of order belongs here, and The Middle (Chapter 11) says what it must still do. The order of volumes in a series, and the genres that expect a dual timeline, belong to Series and Genre (Chapter 17). See also: the full treatment , section 1, on the boundary between a strand and a run of cutaways.

title: 3. How It Works
text: The theory a writer needs for arranging times answers four practical questions: what is being rearranged, why the same events mean something different in a different order, what keeps a reader going across a change of time, and what that change costs her. Each strand below opens with the question and then gives the source. What is being rearranged: two orders and the anachrony The question. When a writer moves a chapter from the end of a book to its beginning, what has she changed, and what has she left alone? The Russian Formalists gave the first answer. Viktor Shklovsky and Boris Tomashevsky, writing in the 1920s, separated the fabula , the events in their causal and chronological sequence, from the syuzhet , the same events as the work arranges them (Tomashevsky’s “Thematics”, 1925, translated by Lee T. Lemon and Marion J. Reis, 1965). Moving the chapter changes the syuzhet and leaves the fabula alone; the writer has changed nothing that happened and everything about how it is met. This chapter calls the two story order and text order. Gérard Genette’s Narrative Discourse (1972; translated by Jane E. Lewin, 1980) made the comparison precise. He called any discrepancy between the orders an anachrony, an analepsis when the text goes back to an earlier event and a prolepsis when it goes forward to a later one, and measured each by its reach, how far from the present it goes, and its extent , how much story time it covers. He also named a limit case, achrony , an event whose position in story time cannot be determined from the text, which is where a mosaic of fragments ordered by association ends up. A writer charting a draft uses the same notation without the vocabulary: number each unit by its place in the story, then list the numbers in the order the text gives them. That list is the order chart of The Mechanism . Why order changes meaning: primacy and recency The question. Why does a reader who meets the murder first read the marriage differently from one who meets the marriage first? Menakhem Perry’s “Literary Dynamics: How the Order of a Text Creates Its Meanings” (1979) argued that a reader builds a frame from what comes first and reads what follows through it, the primacy effect , until the text forces a revision, after which the most recent frame governs, the recency effect. Meir Sternberg had made a related argument about exposition in Expositional Modes and Temporal Ordering in Fiction (1978): where a writer places the facts a reader needs decides which of them she treats as the norm and which as departures. The Prologue (Chapter 10) uses the primacy effect for prologues. For a non-linear book the consequence is that every arrangement installs some frame first, and the writer should choose which. Chronicle of a Death Foretold (1981; translated by Gregory Rabassa, 1982) names the killing in its first sentence and then goes back to the hours before it; the reader reads every delay and every warning not given as a step towards the death, which is the frame Gabriel García Márquez wants. What keeps a reader going: suspense, curiosity and surprise The question. A switch takes the reader away from a strand at the moment she cares about it. Why does she keep reading? William Brewer and Edward Lichtenstein’s structural-affect theory (“Stories Are to Entertain”, 1982) explained the three pleasures of plot by the relation between story order and text order. Suspense arises when the text gives an initiating event and withholds its outcome; curiosity when it withholds an earlier event and lets the reader know it is missing; surprise when it withholds an earlier event without the reader knowing, and discloses it late. All three are made by ordering, which is why an arrangement of times is a machine for producing them. A switch at the right moment converts a strand’s open question into suspense held across the other strand; a strand set later than another produces curiosity about how the earlier one gets there. In their experiments readers judged texts more story-like when the order produced one of these effects and the outcome was finally resolved, which The Reveal (Chapter 15) relies on as well. The theory also predicts the commonest complaint about braided books: a switch made when the reader holds no question about the strand she is leaving produces no suspense, and the strand she enters must earn her interest from nothing. What a change of time costs: the evidence The question. How much does a jump in time cost a reader, and does a non-chronological book cost more? Rolf Zwaan’s event-indexing model of reading (Zwaan, Langston and Graesser, 1995) holds that readers track a situation along several dimensions, time, place, cause, the characters’ goals and the protagonist, and update their model when any of them changes. Zwaan’s “Processing Narrative Time Shifts” (1996) measured the time dimension. Sentences that opened with An hour later or A day later were read more slowly than ones that opened with A moment later , and information from before the larger shift was recognised more slowly afterwards: a shift in story time, not the number of words, made earlier material less accessible. Keisuke Ohtsuka and William Brewer (1992) compared texts told in chronological order with texts that told events out of order, and reported that readers understood the order of events less well in the second. The evidence is from short texts read in laboratories, not novels, and the chapter uses it for one modest conclusion: every switch between times costs the reader an update, and a book that switches often must pay for each with a marker she can read at once and a reason to make the effort. The convention Chronological order is itself a convention, and not the oldest. Horace advised epic poets to begin in medias res , and the Odyssey tells Odysseus’s wanderings in his own retrospective account in the middle of the poem. The realist novel’s preference for following events in sequence, with cutaways where needed, dominated the nineteenth century and was broken deliberately by modernists such as William Faulkner and Virginia Woolf. Whether multi-timeline novels are commoner now in commercial fiction than they were, as is often said, this chapter has not measured, and it treats the claim as an impression. The tools below assume a reader who reads a book once, in the order printed, which is the reader every arrangement is designed for. See also: the full treatment , section 2, with Genette’s notation worked on an example, the formalists at greater length, and Brian Richardson’s accounts of temporalities that no story order can reconcile.

title: 4. The Taxonomy
text: Non-linear books are classified here by what governs their order of telling, because that decides what a reader must hold and what the order can do for her. Five architectures recur. Two rulings follow, on proposals that Backstory and Flashback (Chapter 7) and The Subplot (Chapter 14) left to this chapter. Five architectures The braid alternates two or more strands, each told in its own chronological order, set in different times. It is the form most writers mean by a dual-timeline novel. Its variants are named by what happens to the interval. In a converging braid the earlier strand advances faster than the later one until the two meet in time: Delia Owens’s Where the Crawdads Sing (2018) runs a strand from 1952, when Kya is six, towards a strand that begins with a body found in 1969, and the strands merge for the trial ( Worked Analyses ). In a parallel braid the interval stays fixed and the strands meet by cause or identity instead: Kate Morton’s The Forgotten Garden (2008) keeps 1913, 1975 and 2005 apart to the end and joins them through a child left on a wharf, the woman she became and that woman’s granddaughter. The braid’s work is to set two times side by side so that each comments on the other, and its risks are the ones the failure patterns record: a strand the reader skims, and strands that move at one pace. The anchored order shows or announces one event early, usually its end or its crisis, and then tells the book towards it, so that the reader reads every scene as a step to a known point. Gabriel García Márquez’s Chronicle of a Death Foretold (1981; translated by Gregory Rabassa, 1982) names the killing in its first sentence, On the day they were going to kill him , and spends the book on how a town let it happen. The anchored order converts curiosity about what into curiosity about how and why , and its successor to suspense is dread. Its risk is that the anchor answers the book’s question; it works only when the book’s question was never the event. The reverse order tells events backwards, unit by unit, so that each scene explains the one before it in the text. Harold Pinter’s Betrayal (1978) runs from the end of an affair in 1977 to its beginning in 1968, and its last scene, the first moment of the affair, is played under everything the audience knows of its end. The form makes every scene a disclosure of cause and every ending a beginning, which is why it is rare at novel length: Martin Amis’s Time’s Arrow (1991) runs a life backwards to make the Holocaust’s logic legible inverted. Memento ( Worked Analyses ) combines it with a forward strand. The mosaic orders its units by association, theme or a character’s memory rather than by time, so that story order can be reconstructed, often only partly, but does not govern the reading. Kurt Vonnegut’s Slaughterhouse-Five (1969), whose hero has come unstuck in time , is the familiar case; Jennifer Egan’s A Visit from the Goon Squad (2010), which The Transition (Chapter 5) reads for its joins, is a mosaic of thirteen chapters across about fifty years. The mosaic’s work is to make the reader assemble, and its condition is that the assembly mean something. Its risk is achrony without purpose. The nested order opens one time inside another, so that the reader goes in through frames and comes out through them in reverse. Wuthering Heights (1847) goes from Lockwood’s 1801 into Nelly Dean’s account of thirty years and comes back. David Mitchell’s Cloud Atlas (2004) breaks off five stories, from a nineteenth-century Pacific journal to a twenty-second-century testimony, tells a sixth whole at the centre, and then closes the five in reverse, each narrator having read or watched the one before. The nested order’s work is containment: the inner time is held, and judged, by the outer one. Most books mix the forms. The household novel, as Worked Analyses charts it, is an anchored order whose anchor is a prologue, with a second time in two instalments: a braid at its smallest. The classification is used to say what the arrangement is for, not to file the book. The threshold of a strand: a ruling on the structural domain Backstory and Flashback (Chapter 7) proposed a structural domain for the cutaway: a cutaway serves it when its main function is architectural, establishing, maintaining or completing a pattern in the book’s design, as in a braided timeline, a returning frame or a recurring approach to a withheld event. It adopted the domain for diagnosis on two conditions, that the pattern be declared before the domain is claimed and that the claim be checked, and conceded that it might be texture or reader knowledge seen at book scale, and that it mixed what does this deliver here? with what does this do for the book? It named The Forgotten Garden and Where the Crawdads Sing as test cases. This chapter rejects the structural domain as a domain of the cutaway, and keeps what it named as a threshold. A past unit that recurs in a declared pattern, advances in its own time and runs on its own question is no longer a cutaway; it is a strand, and the question what does this do for the book? is asked of the strand, by this chapter’s tests, not of each departure. The two test cases show it. Each 1913 chapter of The Forgotten Garden advances a question of its own, who left the child and why, and each 1952 chapter of Where the Crawdads Sing another, whether Kya will survive alone and what she will become; neither is justified by its architecture, and both would fail if it were. The threshold of a strand is therefore the point at which recurring material acquires a question of its own. Below it, material from another time is a cutaway, judged by Backstory and Flashback ’s five domains (Chapter 7). Above it, a strand is judged by test 2 (Strand question) of Diagnostic Tests . Material that recurs in a pattern without a question of its own sits at the threshold and fails both, and the failure patterns call it the explaining strand. Backstory and Flashback ’s two conditions (Chapter 7) survive in that test and in the rule of The Mechanism that a strand be declared early. Temporal counterpoint at the scale of a book: a ruling The Subplot (Chapter 14) proposed temporal counterpoint, a subplot on a different clock from the main plot’s, whose function is to make the main plot’s pace visible by contrast and let a book hold a duration it could not otherwise contain. It adopted the domain on condition that a thread claiming it also show a chain, conceding that it might be a property of the telling, that it rarely appears without thematic counterpoint, and, as unanswered, that it gives every slow, inert thread a defence. This chapter adopts temporal counterpoint at the scale of a book, as a property of the arrangement rather than of a thread, which accepts the first objection and answers the third. A difference of rate between strands is something the arrangement makes, and it does work only where a crossing sets one strand’s time against another’s, so that the reader feels the difference. The claim is therefore checked at the crossings, not asserted of a thread: a slow strand that never meets a fast one at a moment where the difference shows has no counterpoint to plead. Christopher Nolan’s Dunkirk (2017) is the test case on screen. Its three strands cover a week on the mole, a day at sea and an hour in the air, intercut as if simultaneous, and they cross at the rescues, where an event the viewer has seen from the hour-long strand is seen again from the day-long one. Maggie O’Farrell’s Hamnet (2020) sets the day of a child’s illness in 1596 against about fifteen years of his parents’ lives, and the counterpoint is felt each time the long strand reaches a decision the short one is paying for. For threads in one time, The Subplot ’s condition (Chapter 14) stands. The second objection stands as well: in both cases the counterpoint carries the theme, and the chapter does not claim the two can be separated. See also: the full treatment , section 3, with three further architectures (the reset, the retold and the single day in several lives), a summary table, and the rulings in full.

title: 5. The Mechanism
text: An arrangement of times has five jobs: give each strand a question, mark each time, set the intervals and rates, place the switches, and make the convergence change something. Two documents serve all five. The order chart numbers every unit of the book by its place in story order and lists the numbers in text order, with each unit’s position in the book as a percentage; it shows at a glance where the book departs from chronology and how far. The strand table gives each strand a row: its question, its span of story time, its rate, its viewpoint, its orientation markers and the point at which it meets the others. The examples below assume both. A question for each strand A strand holds a reader across switches only if it leaves her with something to want, and a strand set in the past has a particular difficulty: the reader often knows how it ends, because the present strand is its end. The question must therefore be one the present does not answer. In Where the Crawdads Sing the present tells the reader that Kya is alive in 1969 and suspected of murder; the 1952 strand’s question is not whether she survives but how she becomes the woman the town suspects, and whether she did it, which the present cannot settle. A past strand whose only question the present has already answered is the explaining strand of Failure Patterns . The test is to write each strand’s question in one line and to check that the other strands’ pages do not answer it. A strand must also be declared early, by its second instalment and in practice within the first fifth of the book, because a reader who has invested in one time resists a second introduced late; The Opening Pages ’s formal contract (Chapter 9), the promise a book’s opening makes about its form, is the instrument. Marking the times Each instalment must tell the reader which time she is in before she needs to know, which in practice means within its first sentence or two, and the cost of a marker should match the difficulty of the switch. The cheapest markers are a strand’s own: a viewpoint character who lives in only one time, a tense or person kept for one strand, and a setting whose period shows. Headings and time-stamps are reliable and explicit; Audrey Niffenegger’s The Time Traveler’s Wife (2003), whose hero travels involuntarily in time, heads its sections with a date and both lovers’ ages, the only way to keep a reader oriented in a book where one character is in two times at once. The most economical marker is an object or a detail the reader can date. That last category is the subject of The Descriptive Detail ’s proposal (Chapter 4), the temporal domain : a detail belongs to it when its work is to establish duration, sequence, decay, repurposing, season or interruption, carried by aspect, wear, residue and maintenance. The Descriptive Detail (Chapter 4) adopted it for diagnosis, conceding that six domains are harder to hold than five and that time may be a feature of details rather than a kind, and left this chapter to adopt or reject it at larger scales. This chapter adopts it at the scale of a book, as the domain of orientation. In a book with two times the same place and the same objects appear in both, and only temporal detail tells the reader which time a passage is in without a heading: the shop in March and the shop in July differ in a sign never turned, a coat brushed weekly, a page in a second hand. That answers the second objection at this scale, because a detail can be chosen for which time it places a passage in and for nothing else, and a multi-timeline book needs many such details. Jon McGregor’s Reservoir 13 (2017), whose thirteen chapters each cover one year, confirms it: the book’s orientation is its calendar. The Descriptive Detail ’s concession (Chapter 4) on parsimony stands for the single detail. The domain’s failure at this scale is the undated strand, whose instalments could belong to any time and are placed by their headings alone. Interval and rate The interval between strands, and how it changes, is the arrangement’s clock. A converging braid shortens it until the strands meet, and the reader feels the meeting approach; a parallel braid holds it fixed and must supply its pressure elsewhere. Rate is the strand’s story time per page. Strands at different rates can produce temporal counterpoint, ruled on in The Taxonomy , but only where a crossing shows the difference; strands at one rate, crossing without variation, are the lockstep braid of Failure Patterns . The strand table records each strand’s span and page count, from which the rate is a division. The switch A switch is a transition across time and usually across a chapter break, so The Transition (Chapter 5) and The Chapter Break (Chapter 6) supply its tools, and three rules are this chapter’s. Leave a strand on an open question, so that suspense carries across the switch; enter the next strand at a point that pays at once, because the reader arrives with her interest elsewhere. Keep the rhythm of alternation regular once it is declared, or break it on purpose, since a reader learns the pattern and reads a break in it as a signal. And watch the asymmetry: a reader who prefers one strand will tolerate the other only if each of its instalments advances its own question, which makes the instalment’s opening paragraph the weakest point in most braided books. The convergence Strands meet in time, by cause or by identity, and the meeting must change what at least one strand meant, or it is a coincidence of dates. A convergence of times is the converging braid’s end; a convergence by cause discloses that an act in one strand made the other’s situation; a convergence by identity discloses that a person or object is in both. The object’s case is The Transition ’s proposal (Chapter 5), the bridging object : a physical thing on both sides of a gap whose presence anchors the new unit by identity rather than resemblance. The Transition (Chapter 5) adopted it for revision, conceding as unanswered that identity and resemblance may not differ for the reader, and named Station Eleven and the household ledger as test cases at the scale of a book. This chapter adopts it at that scale, as a means of convergence by identity between strands, on one condition: the object’s condition or custody must change between its appearances, so that the change itself measures the interval. The condition answers the conceded objection at book scale. A resembling object carries no history, so the reader can learn nothing from it about the time between; an identical object that has been worn, written in or handed on tells her how long and through whose hands. In Station Eleven (2014) a glass paperweight passes from Clark to Arthur and Miranda, back to Arthur, and on the night he dies, by way of a child minder, to Kirsten, aged eight, who carries it for twenty years; each change of custody is a link between times ( Worked Analyses ). The household ledger is written in one hand until 9 March and another after it, which is the interval made visible on a page. Without the change, an object repeated across strands is a match-cut, and The Transition ’s concession (Chapter 5) stands. See also: the full treatment , section 5, with the order chart and strand table laid out for a sample book.

title: 6. Diagnostic Tests
text: The eight tests are for revision, and they need the two documents of The Mechanism : an order chart and a strand table for the book as it stands. Test 1 (Necessity) asks whether the arrangement should exist, tests 2 to 5 (Strand question, Orientation, Interval and Rate) read the strands, and tests 6 to 8 (Switch, Convergence and Withholding) the switches and the meeting. Record a sentence for each, not a verdict. Test 1 — Necessity If the book were retold in story order in a page of summary, what would it lose? Failure. The arbitrary arrangement: order chosen for interest it does not produce. Exception. Laurence Sterne’s Tristram Shandy (1759–67), whose disorder is its subject and its comedy. Test 2 — Strand question Can each strand’s question be written in a line, and do the other strands’ pages leave it open? Failure. The explaining strand: a past told in instalments to account for the present. Exception. Citizen Kane (Orson Welles, 1941), whose flashbacks share the frame’s one question. Test 3 — Orientation Within its first two sentences, does each instalment tell the reader which time she is in? Failure. The lost reader. Exception. Faulkner’s The Sound and the Fury (1929), whose first section makes disorientation the condition of its narrator. Test 4 — Interval Does the reader know how far apart the strands stand, and does the distance change or hold for a reason? Failure. A braid with no clock: strands whose relation the reader cannot estimate. Exception. Cloud Atlas (2004), whose intervals of decades and centuries matter only as an order of succession. Test 5 — Rate Do the strands move at different rates, and does a crossing show the difference? Failure. The lockstep braid. Exception. Michael Cunningham’s The Hours (1998), three single days at one rate, where the sameness is the point. Test 6 — Switch Is each strand left on an open question and entered at a point that pays at once? Failure. A strand the reader skims. Exception. Where the Crawdads Sing (2018), whose short investigation chapters are tolerated as a clock. Test 7 — Convergence Where the strands meet, does the meeting change what at least one of them meant? Failure. The convergence by coincidence. Exception. Dunkirk (2017), whose crossings change little in meaning and much in feeling, as counterpoint. Test 8 — Withholding Does the arrangement withhold anything, and is there a reason in the book besides the order? Failure. An order used to keep a secret that a character would have told. Exception. Memento (2000), whose withholding is the hero’s amnesia. Reading the results together Failures cluster, and the cluster locates the repair. Tests 1 (Necessity) and 7 (Convergence) failing together describe an arrangement that neither needs its order nor uses its meeting: retell the book in story order and see whether anything is lost, since a book that loses nothing should be chronological, with cutaways where they serve. Test 2 (Strand question) failing for one strand while test 6 (Switch) fails at its entries is the commonest pattern in a braided draft, the strand readers skim because it only explains; the repair is to give it a question the present does not answer, or to cut it to cutaways placed where the present needs them. Test 3 (Orientation) failing alone is the cheapest failure to mend, with markers chosen from the strand’s own material before headings are added. Tests 4 (Interval) and 5 (Rate) failing together mean the strands have no clock between them; decide whether the braid converges in time, and if so let the earlier strand run faster. Test 8 (Withholding) failing is a reveal problem as much as an arrangement problem, and The Reveal ’s tests (Chapter 15) for a withholder apply: an order of telling may delay a truth, but a reader will forgive the delay only if something in the book, not the writer’s table of contents, explains it. A clean pass on all eight, with readers who still find the book hard going, usually means the switches are too frequent for the book’s markers; lengthen the instalments before adding headings. See also: the full treatment , section 5, with the procedure for each test and the household’s order chart and strand table.

title: 7. Failure Patterns
text: Each pattern below fails through a mechanism rather than a surface feature, and ends with a published work that commits it and succeeds, because where the mechanism is absent or answered the feature is harmless. The full treatment has a longer catalogue, among them the premature convergence, the frame left open, the over-labelled book and the strand that outgrows the book. The arbitrary arrangement Symptom. Early readers say the book is hard to follow, and then, asked what happens, give its events in chronological order without difficulty. Nobody can say what the order is for. Mechanism. The arbitrary arrangement departs from story order for interest the departure does not produce: chapters are shuffled to open on drama, or a strand is added because the material seemed thin in sequence. It fails test 1 (Necessity), and usually test 7 (Convergence), since an arrangement with no purpose has no meeting to aim at. The cost is all on the reader’s side, the updates Zwaan measured at every shift of time, with nothing in return. Remedy. Test 1 (Necessity). Write the book in story order in a page and list what the arrangement adds: a frame installed first, a suspense held across a switch, a meeting that changes meaning. If the list is empty, make the book chronological and keep only the cutaways the present needs. If one item is on it, rebuild the arrangement around that item. Exception. Joseph Heller’s Catch-22 (1961). Most of its chapters are named for characters and move back and forth through the war so freely that the order can be reconstructed only with effort, and many readers take it as arbitrary. It succeeds because one event, the death of Snowden over Avignon, recurs in fragments, each a little fuller, until it is told whole near the end; the apparent scatter is a recurring approach to the thing Yossarian cannot face, and the novel’s circular logic is enacted by its order. The lost reader Symptom. Readers report confusion about when a scene is happening, sometimes for pages, and some of them misread a scene as belonging to the wrong time and carry the error forward. Mechanism. The lost reader is a failure of orientation: instalments open without a marker the reader can read at once, or with markers that only a careful reader could decode, a minor character’s age, a car’s model. It fails test 3 (Orientation). Writers commit it most often by relying on the markers they know, which the reader does not yet have. Remedy. Test 3 (Orientation). Put a marker in the first two sentences of every instalment, chosen in order of cheapness: the strand’s own viewpoint character, a tense or person reserved for the strand, a detail of period or wear, an object the reader has seen in that time, and only then a heading or a time-stamp. Make the markers stronger where the strands share a place or a cast. Exception. William Faulkner’s The Sound and the Fury (1929). Its first section, narrated by Benjy, an intellectually disabled man for whom past and present are equally near, moves among more than a dozen times with only italics to warn of a change; Faulkner wished it could be printed in inks of different colours, and an edition of 2012 did so. Readers are lost, and the section succeeds because the reader’s loss is Benjy’s condition, and the later sections, each in a clearer order, supply what the reader needs to go back. The explaining strand Symptom. Readers skim one timeline, usually the past, and say they wanted to get back to the other. The skimmed strand is often well written. Mechanism. The explaining strand is material from another time delivered in instalments whose only function is to account for the present: why a character is as she is, how a situation arose. It has no question of its own, since the present is its answer, so it fails test 2 (Strand question), and its entries fail test 6 (Switch), since the reader arrives with no question to carry. It sits at the threshold of a strand ruled on in The Taxonomy , recurring like a strand and working like a cutaway. Remedy. Test 2 (Strand question). Either give the strand a question the present cannot answer, a choice in the past whose outcome the present does not show, or cut it to cutaways, each placed where the present needs it, which Backstory and Flashback (Chapter 7) treats. Exception. Citizen Kane (Orson Welles, 1941). Its long flashbacks, told by five people who knew Kane, are explanation and nothing else: each accounts for the man whose death opens the film. It succeeds because the frame lends every instalment one question, what Rosebud meant, which none of the tellers can answer, and because the tellers disagree, so that each flashback revises the last. The lockstep braid Symptom. A competently built dual-timeline book reads as monotonous, though both strands have questions and the switches are well placed. Readers cannot say why. Mechanism. The lockstep braid runs its strands at one rate, with instalments of one length and switches at one interval, so that the crossings produce no variation and neither strand makes the other’s pace visible. It fails test 5 (Rate), and usually test 4 (Interval), since a braid in lockstep has no closing interval either. Remedy. Test 5 (Rate), with the strand table. Change a strand’s rate, so that one covers years while the other covers weeks, or vary the instalments’ length so that one strand accelerates towards the meeting; then find a crossing where the difference shows, a moment in the slow strand that the fast one has already paid for. Exception. Michael Cunningham’s The Hours (1998). It braids three single days, Virginia Woolf’s in 1923, Laura Brown’s in 1949 and Clarissa Vaughan’s at the end of the century, at one rate, in a regular rotation. It succeeds because the sameness of rate is its argument, a day in three lives made equal, and because its convergence, the disclosure that Laura is the mother of Clarissa’s friend Richard, changes what two strands meant. The convergence by coincidence Symptom. The strands meet, and readers feel the meeting was arranged: a shared name, a birthmark, a house that turns out to be the same house. It changes nothing they understood. Mechanism. The convergence by coincidence joins strands by a link that carries no cause and no change of meaning. It fails test 7 (Convergence). Writers commit it when they have built two strands and need them to meet, and choose the cheapest link available. Remedy. Test 7 (Convergence). Make the link causal, so that an act in one strand is found to have made the other’s situation, or make it an identity that changes meaning, a person or object whose presence in both recasts one of them. If an object carries the link, give it a changed condition or a change of hands, the condition of the bridging object in The Mechanism . Exception. Cloud Atlas (2004). Several of its protagonists bear a comet-shaped birthmark, a link as arbitrary as any, and the novel succeeds because its working link is elsewhere: each narrator reads or watches the story before, so the strands meet by reading, and each reading changes what the earlier strand meant to the later. See also: the full treatment , section 4, with the extended catalogue.

title: 8. Worked Analyses
text: Three close readings of published arrangements, a short screen reading and the household revision case. Each reading names the architecture, the strands and their questions, the markers, the rates and the meeting. Kurt Vonnegut, Slaughterhouse-Five (1969): a mosaic with an anchor Billy Pilgrim, an American soldier taken prisoner in the Battle of the Bulge, survives the firebombing of Dresden in February 1945 in the meat locker of a slaughterhouse, comes home, marries, becomes a prosperous optometrist, survives a plane crash, and says he was kidnapped by aliens from the planet Tralfamadore, who see all moments at once. The novel moves among these times in short sections, without dates, because Billy has come unstuck in time , and a first chapter in the author’s own voice explains how long it took to write about Dresden and why. The architecture is a mosaic, and its order is governed by Billy’s involuntary travel, which is association made into a premise. Story order can be reconstructed without much trouble, and the reconstruction loses what test 1 (Necessity) asks for: in sequence, the book would be a war story followed by a life, and Dresden would be its climax; in the mosaic, the reader keeps arriving near the bombing and being taken away, and it is told at last, briefly, near the end. The mosaic’s centre is an anchor the book circles, which makes the order a recurring approach to an event that a sequence would have had to narrate as a climax and that the book refuses to make into one. The Tralfamadorians’ account of their own novels, many moments seen at once with no beginning, middle or end, is the book describing itself, and the refrain So it goes , after every death, levels the times as the order does. Orientation is carried by the strands’ own material, the prison camp, the optometry office, the zoo on Tralfamadore, which the reader learns quickly, so the book needs no headings. The mosaic has no convergence in the usual sense; its meeting is the bombing, the one time all the others lead back to. Delia Owens, Where the Crawdads Sing (2018): a converging braid The novel braids two strands. One begins in 1952, when Kya Clark is six and is left by her mother, then by her siblings and father, to grow up alone in the North Carolina marsh. The other begins in 1969, when the body of Chase Andrews, the town’s former star quarterback, is found below a fire tower, and follows the sheriff’s investigation. Each chapter is headed with its year. Each strand has its question. The investigation’s is who killed Chase, or whether anyone did; the 1952 strand’s is not whether Kya survives, which the 1969 strand shows, but how the abandoned child becomes the woman the town calls the Marsh Girl and suspects, and whether she is capable of what it suspects. The second question is one the present cannot answer, which is why the past strand is read for itself rather than skimmed. The rates differ widely: the 1952 strand covers seventeen years, the investigation a few months, so the interval shortens through the book until the past strand reaches 1969 and the two merge for the arrest and the trial. The reader feels the meeting approach as the years in the headings rise towards the investigation’s. The investigation chapters are short and thin, and a reader who preferred the marsh might skim them; the braid tolerates them because their job is a clock, putting pressure on every chapter of the past. The convergence is of times and, at the end, of cause: after Kya’s death in old age, a poem and a shell necklace found among her things recast the verdict. The arrangement withholds that truth, and test 8 (Withholding) asks whether anything in the book besides the order explains the delay; the answer is Kya, who kept it. Emily St. John Mandel, Station Eleven (2014): a parallel braid joined by objects The novel opens on the night the actor Arthur Leander dies of a heart attack on stage in King Lear in Toronto, as a flu pandemic begins that will kill most of the world. It then moves among Arthur’s earlier life, his marriages and friendships; the weeks of the collapse; and Year Twenty, when Kirsten Raymonde, a child actor in that Lear , travels the Great Lakes with a company of actors and musicians who play Shakespeare to the settlements. The architecture is a braid whose interval does not close: the strands are separated by the collapse, and no strand travels across it to meet another in time. They meet by identity, through people and objects that survive the gap. Arthur gave Kirsten two copies of a comic, Station Eleven , drawn by his first wife, Miranda; the other went to his son, Tyler, who in Year Twenty is the prophet whose cult threatens the company. The glass paperweight, passed from Clark to Arthur and Miranda, back to Arthur and on the night of his death to Kirsten, aged eight, is carried for twenty years. Clark, Arthur’s oldest friend, keeps a museum of the old world in an airport. These are the test cases The Transition (Chapter 5) named for the bridging object, and they meet the condition of The Mechanism : each changes hands or condition across the gap, so that its presence in Year Twenty measures what has been lost and through whom. The comic is the strongest case, since its changed condition is a change of meaning: a private work by a woman nobody remembers becomes scripture for one reader and consolation for another. The strands’ questions are distinct. Year Twenty’s is whether the company will survive the prophet; Arthur’s, which the opening has already ended, is what his life amounted to, which the present answers only through the objects he gave away. The book’s order delivers its theme, that what survives is what was handed on, more than any single strand states it. A screen reading: Memento (Christopher Nolan, 2000) Leonard, who cannot form new memories since an attack in which his wife was killed, hunts her killer with photographs, notes and tattoos. The film has two strands. Colour sequences run backwards, each ending where the one before it in the film began; black-and-white sequences, in which Leonard talks on the telephone in a motel room, run forwards. At the end the black-and-white strand reaches the point where the colour strand’s last sequence in story order begins, and the picture turns to colour as a Polaroid develops. The reverse strand gives the viewer Leonard’s condition: like him, she meets each scene without knowing what led to it, and learns the cause only in the next sequence she sees. The forward strand is the clock and the orientation marker in one, since colour itself tells her which time she is in, the cheapest marker on screen. The convergence is of times and changes the meaning of the whole: the first act in story order, shown last, discloses that Leonard has chosen to deceive his future self, so the hunt the viewer has watched backwards was set up by its hunter. The arrangement withholds that truth for a reason the film gives, the hero’s amnesia, which is why test 8 (Withholding) passes. The household revision case: a second timeline for the father The situation. The household novel’s present runs from about four months after the father’s death in March to the end of July. The prologue is his last ordinary day, three days before he stopped answering the phone; Nadia remembers, at about two-thirds, the second time he lost the good pen; and Dov’s one viewpoint chapter, at about 78 per cent, is the evening of 9 March, when he finds his father’s last entry broken off and begins to write in the ledger. The reader saw that entry, and the looser hand beneath it, at about a quarter of the book, when Elena found the ledger in the register drawer and saw where the hand changed without reading. Version A, the draft. The father’s strand of The Problem : six dated chapters in his viewpoint, from February to the evening of 9 March, braided through the first three-quarters of the book. Diagnosis. The strand passes test 3 (Orientation), since every chapter is dated, and fails most of the others. Test 2 (Strand question) fails because the strand’s only open question is what the father knows, and that is the book’s largest reveal: the strand must disclose the illness to the reader alone at a tenth of the book, or keep it out of a mind that knows it, which fails test 8 (Withholding) and commits The Reveal ’s withholding viewpoint (Chapter 15). Test 5 (Rate) fails, since the strand covers five weeks in six chapters and the present a few weeks in the rest, a lockstep. Test 7 (Convergence) fails, since the strand reaches 9 March just before Dov’s chapter of the same evening, two chapters of one evening from two minds, and the meeting delivers nothing the reader lacks. The strand also spends Nadia’s memory of the father’s line, and grants a fourth viewpoint against the allocation that The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13) settled. Version B, the revision. Cut the strand. The order chart of the book without it shows that the novel already has a second time, March, in two instalments, and an object that joins it to July: Text position Unit Story time Time 0% Prologue: the last ordinary day Early March March 1–25% Opening, doorway, coat, drawer; the ledger seen, the hand changing at 9 March July July 25–75% The middle; at about two-thirds, Nadia’s memory of the pen (a cutaway) July July About 78% Dov’s chapter Evening of 9 March March 80–100% The convergence and the reading July July The March strand’s question is the prologue’s in case of what , which Dov’s chapter sharpens without answering, and its rate is a few days across the whole book against the present’s few weeks, a counterpoint that shows at the crossing in the ledger, where eleven years of one hand meet four months of another. The revision adds one thing: Dov’s chapter is headed 9 March , the only dated heading in the book, written as the date stands in the ledger. The reader has seen that date on the page where the hand changed, about half a book earlier, so the heading orients her by an object she knows rather than by a calendar, and turns the date she saw into a time she now enters. What the revision has not solved. The father is no less a ghost: he lives in a prologue, a memory and his hand, and the early reader who wanted more of him will still want it; the defence is that his absence is the book’s subject, which a reader may reject. The interval between the prologue’s day and 9 March is undated, since the prologue counts from the day he stopped answering the phone and the canon does not say whether that was the ninth. A single dated heading declares an exception that must be checked against the book’s other chapter headings. And Nadia’s memory of the pen lies in a third time, the recent past, with no heading; its marker is the second time he lost the pen , which must stand in its first sentence, or a reader may take it for the March strand. See also: the full treatment , with readings of Cloud Atlas , Hamnet , The Time Traveler’s Wife and Dunkirk , and the household’s order chart and strand table in full.

title: 9. Checklist and Exercises
text: Revision checklist The arrangement Have I written the book in story order in a page, and listed what my order adds? Which architecture does the book use, and do its parts serve that architecture’s work? What frame does the reader build from the first pages, and is it the one I want? The strands Can I write each strand’s question in one line, and do the other strands leave it open? Is every strand declared by its second instalment, within the first fifth of the book? Does any recurring material from another time lack a question of its own, and should it be cut to cutaways? Do my strands move at different rates, and where does a crossing show the difference? The markers and switches Does every instalment tell the reader its time within two sentences, using the strand’s own material first? Are the markers strongest where the strands share a place, a cast or an object? Is each strand left on an open question, and entered at a point that pays at once? Is the rhythm of alternation regular, and is every break in it deliberate? The meeting Where do the strands meet, in time, by cause or by identity, and what does the meeting change? If an object joins two times, does its condition or custody change between them? Does the order withhold anything that a character would have told, and does the book give a reason? Exercises The order chart. Number every chapter or scene of your draft by its place in story order, list the numbers in text order with each unit’s position as a percentage, and mark every departure. Beside each, write in a phrase what it gains over the chronological place. The chronological retelling. Write your book’s events in story order in no more than three hundred words. Then list what a reader of your arrangement knows, wants or fears at the midpoint that a reader of the retelling would not. If the list has fewer than two items, rewrite the opening chapter in chronological order and compare. The strand table. For each strand, write its question, its span of story time, its page count, its rate, its viewpoint, its markers and its meeting with the others. Find the strand whose question the other strands answer, and either give it a new one or redistribute its material as cutaways. The first two sentences. Copy the first two sentences of every instalment of your weakest strand onto one page. Mark each opening that does not place the reader in time. Rewrite three of them using only the strand’s own material, without a heading or a date. The crossing. Find the place where your strands’ times are nearest, or where an object or person appears in both. Rewrite the scene so that the difference between the strands, of rate, of condition or of knowledge, is visible on the page, and so that the meeting changes what one strand meant.

title: 10. Coda
text: The instruments in this chapter assume a reader who reads the book once, in the order printed, and builds a single model of its world as she goes. The order chart measures how far the text departs from that world’s chronology; the strand table measures what each departure costs and gives. Both describe a reader who does not yet know the story order and is assembling it. A rereader holds the whole chronology from the first page, and for her an arrangement of times is no longer a puzzle or a source of suspense but a set of juxtapositions: this scene beside that one, this year set against that. That a non-linear book can be reread with pleasure, as Slaughterhouse-Five and Wuthering Heights are, is evidence that its arrangement was never only a way of delaying information. It was a set of claims about which times belong together. That is the chapter’s argument. An arrangement of times is an argument about time, made by placing one moment beside another that chronology would have kept apart, and it is judged as an argument is, by whether its juxtapositions say something chronology could not. The three conditions in the governing claim, a question for each strand, a reader who knows where she is, and a meeting that changes meaning, are the conditions under which a reader can follow the argument and feel its force. Where they fail, the reader receives the costs of an arrangement, every update and every switch, without its claims. The household revision illustrates the economy. It cut six chapters of the father’s last weeks and added one heading, and found that the book’s argument about time was already in place: a man’s last ordinary day at the start, his son’s first evening with the ledger near the end, and between them four months of the living, joined by a page on which one hand stops and another begins. The arrangement says that the father’s March and his children’s July are one record read at different times, which is the book’s subject. See also: the full treatment , section 8, on the limits of the model; Series and Genre (Chapter 17), for arrangements across volumes; The Structural Edit (Chapter 18), which puts the order chart into a revision order for the whole book.

title: The Opening Pages
text: What the first pages of the main narrative owe the reader, and how to tell whether they pay it The Craft Behind the Story (Second Edition) — Chapter 9. Part III: The Architecture of the Whole. In brief. The opening pages are the first stretch of a novel’s main narrative, and they are the only pages that must work as an ordinary scene while teaching a reader who has invested nothing what kind of book she has entered. They cannot draw on trust earned earlier, because nothing came earlier. The chapter’s tool is the contract model: an opening opens obligations of voice, genre, character, world and stakes, and, as proposed here, of form, which the rest of the book must keep. A page cannot give each obligation its own sentence, so the work is done by selection, by finding the details that already carry several obligations at once. Ten diagnostic questions turn the model into a revision order. Use the chapter on a first chapter that readers put down, on one that hooks and is then betrayed by its own book, or on one that holds all the necessary information and none of the pull. What you can do after this chapter Mark which obligations each sentence of a first page opens, and say whether each one left for later was deferred by choice. Find the detail in a draft that already carries several obligations, and build the page outward from it. Decide where in the story the telling begins, and find the small deviation that answers why today? Tell an opening that hooks as a by-product of its work from one that has borrowed its hook from a more exciting book. Run ten tests on a draft opening and turn their failures into a revision order. Key terms Opening pages; the threshold problem and the zero-context condition; the hook; the attack; exposition and orientation; paratext; the rules of notice and the primacy effect; the situation model and the contextual frame; the horizon of expectations; suspense and curiosity; the contract model, with the voice, genre, character, world and stakes contracts and the proposed formal contract; narrative distance and free indirect style; reliability and the reading protocol; normalisation; the immediate want; the pull-forward question; planting and withholding; multiplicity, selection and the density ceiling; in medias res and the hybrid resolution; the hairline crack; the opening gambits and substitution testing; the multiplicity audit. Each is defined at first use and collected in the consolidated glossary . Contents The first files say what the opening is and why it carries the weight it does, the middle files what it owes and how the debt is paid, and the last are for use at the desk. The Problem A book’s best scene moved to page one, and the chapter’s claim Definitions The opening pages, how long they last, the hook, adjacent terms How It Works The rules of notice and primacy, the situation model, the reader’s horizon and the paratext, the distribution of exposition, and the dates of the convention The Taxonomy Five contracts, and a proposed sixth: the formal contract The Mechanism Multiplicity as selection, the density ceiling, the attack, the hairline crack and the gambits Diagnostic Tests Ten questions on one page, and how to read their failures together Failure Patterns Five recurrent failures, each with a published work that commits it and succeeds Worked Analyses Pride and Prejudice , Everything I Never Told You , Lincoln in the Bardo , Inglourious Basterds and The Sopranos , and the household revision case Checklist and Exercises The revision checklist and five exercises for your own draft Coda Why the opening is revised last A writer in revision can start at the diagnostic tests and the multiplicity audit among the exercises; the coda, which says when the tests mislead, is best read early. The full treatment The Reference layer holds the complete chapter, The Opening Pages : the theory at length, each contract’s components and carriers with further illustrations, twelve opening gambits with their gains and costs, ten failure patterns, seven close readings (among them The Stranger in three translations), openings in the short story, the novella, braided books and series, a concordance of concepts to novels, seminar questions, an assessment rubric and the sources. See also: The Prologue (Chapter 10), on the separated unit that may come before the opening; The Ending (Chapter 16), the formal inverse, read against everything instead of nothing; The Chapter Break (Chapter 6), on later chapter openings, where the reader arrives already oriented; Series and Genre (Chapter 17), on the opening of a series instalment.

title: 1. The Problem
text: The drawer on page one A writer revising the household novel this book follows has heard that agents and editors read submissions under pressure, and that a first page must grip. She looks through her draft for its most gripping scene and finds it about a quarter of the way in: Elena, back in the shop with her new key, forcing the register drawer that sticks on the K, smelling fresh ink where nobody should have written, and finding her father’s ledger, whose careful hand stops at an entry of 9 March while a looser hand continues. She moves the scene to the front. The new first page is tense, specific and well made, and it does not work. (This version is a hypothetical draft, used to show the problem; it is not the novel’s opening.) A quarter of the way into the book the scene pays because of what the reader brings to it. She has watched the father pocket the good pen on his last ordinary day, seen his coat on its hook in the flat above the shop, and heard Dov refuse to say why the locks were changed. The smell of ink is wrong for a till nobody should have used since March, and she feels the wrongness. On page one the same sentences describe a woman she has never met, in a shop she cannot picture, smelling ink that means nothing to her and finding a book whose handwriting she has no reason to care about. Every detail is a promise she cannot yet weigh. The scene has not lost its craft. It has lost its funding, and the opening has spent the book’s best discovery on a reader who could not yet value it. There is a second, slower cost. A page that opens on a forced drawer and a secret record tells the reader what kind of book she is in: a mystery, whose question is what happened? The household novel’s question is different, closer to what do these three do with what they can reconstruct? , and its pace is set by unanswered telephone calls, register receipts and dust on a coat. A reader recruited by the drawer will reach page thirty, find herself in the quieter book, and feel that the opening was written for another one. The first cost is paid on page one and the second at page thirty, and the second is the larger, because by then the reader has invested and feels misled. Underneath both costs lies a comparison between page 3 and page 203 of any novel. Page 203 arrives funded: by then the reader knows whose story this is, what the narrator sounds like, what the world permits and what is at risk, and a scene can spend eight hundred words on someone sitting alone with a memory and keep her, because two hundred pages of satisfaction underwrite it. Page 3 has no account to draw on. Whatever it asks of the reader it must earn in the asking, and if it fails she may never reach the page that would have justified it. This difference in kind between the opening and every later stretch of a book is the threshold problem , and it is why the opening pages need a chapter of their own instead of a paragraph in the chapter on the scene. The claim An opening is not a hook but a structure that carries obligations. The first pages of the main narrative must work as a scene in which someone wants something and meets resistance, and the same words must open, for a reader who has invested nothing, the obligations of voice, genre, character, world, stakes and form that the rest of the book will keep. Because all of them fall due at once and in little space, the work is done by selecting details that carry several obligations together, not by adding a sentence for each. The claim has a consequence for the writer who moved the drawer. Her fault was not that the page was too dramatic but that it opened obligations the book would not keep and left unopened the ones it would. The opening the household novel uses, analysed in the revision case in Worked Analyses , is quieter, and it is built on an object the drawer scene would have made redundant: a coat that nobody in the family wants to touch. See also: The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1), on the scene the opening must also be; The Chapter Break (Chapter 6), where the drawer scene ends its chapter.

title: 2. Definitions
text: The working definition The opening pages are the first stretch of the main narrative: Chapter One, or whatever comes immediately after a prologue. They must work as a real scene, in which a character wants something and meets resistance, and at the same time give the reader her first experience of the book’s voice, world, genre and stakes, before any of these has earned the benefit of the doubt. Three phrases in the definition carry its weight. Main narrative means that the opening begins where the book’s primary line of time begins; epigraphs, maps, lists of characters and prologues come before it and change the conditions under which it is read without being part of it. At the same time names the difficulty, which is not that any one obligation is hard but that all of them fall due together, in a small space. And before any has earned the benefit of the doubt is the zero-context condition : the reader has no investment to draw on, no frame into which new information can be filed, and no evidence yet that reading on will be rewarded. How long is the opening? No page count follows from principle, and any number is a convention. Three spans are in use, and they answer different questions. Span Typical extent The question it answers First line or paragraph 1 to 100 words Does it arrest the reader? First page or two about 250 to 700 words Are the obligations opened? First chapter or scene about 1,500 to 4,000 words Are they honoured, and is the book’s engine started? This chapter treats the middle span as primary, because it is the span over which every obligation must at least be begun, and because it is roughly what an agent’s first look, a bookshop browse or an online preview samples. The working rule is that the obligations are opened within two pages and honoured within the first chapter. Opening an obligation means giving the reader enough to form an expectation; honouring it means confirming that the expectation was right. The hook is a tool, not the job The hook is the arresting first line or paragraph, and confusing it with the opening produces a recognisable draft: a first sentence that seizes attention and three pages that do nothing else.
