A hook buys attention, which lasts a paragraph; what carries a reader to page twenty is trust, which the rest of the opening must earn. Ford Madox Ford’s The Good Soldier (1915) begins This is the saddest story I have ever heard , and the sentence hooks, but it also sets up a narrator speaking in retrospect, an emotional register, a claim to authority and, in the word heard where lived would be expected, the doubt about his reliability on which the novel turns. Strong first sentences hook as a by-product of that other work. The reverse failure, an opening so anxious to hook that it front-loads an event the book cannot sustain, is the borrowed hook in Failure Patterns . Adjacent terms Several neighbouring words are used as if they meant the opening. The incipit , a term from bibliography, is the opening words of a text, a narrower unit useful when a first line is treated as a citable object. The attack , a term from dramaturgy (the craft of building plays), is the point in the story’s chronology at which the telling begins, and it decides what the opening pages show. Exposition is information about what came before, the backstory, the world and the situation needed to understand the present action; it is a kind of content spread through a book, not a place in it. Orientation is the reader’s state of having a stable frame, knowing who, where, when and what is normal, which exposition may or may not produce. A cold open , a term from television, begins inside a scene already running and defers all framing; it is one way of beginning in the middle, not a synonym for it. And paratext , Gérard Genette’s word for everything around a text that conditions its reading, covers the title, the cover, the jacket copy and the rest. What this chapter leaves to others The prologue, a separated unit in another time, voice or vantage, belongs to The Prologue (Chapter 10), whose standard is stricter because the reader must be persuaded that the detour was needed. The openings of later chapters, where the reader arrives already oriented, belong to The Chapter Break (Chapter 6), and the ending, the opening’s formal inverse, to The Ending (Chapter 16). Who carries the viewpoint, and when it changes, belongs to The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13); books built from several timelines to Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture (Chapter 8); and the opening of a later volume in a series to Series and Genre (Chapter 17). See also: the Reference definitions , with the adjacent terms in a table.

title: 3. How It Works
text: The theory below is limited to what the chapter’s methods use, and each strand starts from a question a writer asks at the desk. Why does a detail on page one weigh more than on page 150? Because readers treat certain positions as meaningful. Peter J. Rabinowitz, in Before Reading (1987), describes the tacit rules of notice by which readers decide which parts of a text matter. Among the strongest are the rules of privileged position: titles, epigraphs, first and last sentences, and the beginnings and ends of chapters are read as load-bearing, and whatever is placed there is assumed to be there for a reason. A writer who mentions the weather on page one has told the reader, whether she meant to or not, that weather matters in this book. Detail that would pass unnoticed on page 150 becomes on page one a promise, and unredeemed promises accumulate into a sense that the book does not know what it is about. The discipline is not fewer details but details the writer is willing to be held to, and names are the costliest case, since a character named on page one is promised to matter. The positive use is placement doing work that description would otherwise have to do. In the first chapter of Frank Herbert’s Dune (1965) the Reverend Mother holds a poisoned needle, the gom jabbar, at the boy Paul’s neck as part of a test; at the novel’s climax his sister Alia kills Baron Harkonnen with it, and the weapon needs no introduction, because the opening gave it its weight. Early material also governs how later material is read. In Solomon Asch’s experiments on impression formation (1946), the same list of traits produced a more favourable judgement when it began with intelligent than when it began with envious , and Menakhem Perry’s “Literary Dynamics” (1979) carried the finding into reading as the primacy effect : the reader builds a hypothesis from the first material and fits later material to it, resisting revision until the contrary evidence is overwhelming. For the writer this cuts both ways. An impression made by accident is expensive to correct: if page two makes the protagonist read as passive, fifty pages of agency will read as inconsistency. An impression made on purpose is a resource. Jane Austen’s Emma (1815) calls its heroine handsome, clever and rich, and says that she seemed to unite some of the best blessings of existence; most readers adopt the flattering frame, and the one verb lets the later correction be shown to have been signalled. What does the reader need before she can care? Enough to build a picture of what is happening. Research on how readers understand stories holds that they do not store sentences but construct a situation model , a mental representation of the state of affairs a text describes. Rolf Zwaan and Gabriel Radvansky (1998) propose that readers track five dimensions of it, the protagonist, space, time, causation and intention, and that each shift in one of them costs effort to process. Catherine Emmott’s Narrative Comprehension (1997) adds the contextual frame , the reader’s running record of who is present in a scene and where, and argues that texts which do not bind characters to frames early leave readers disoriented. The five dimensions correspond closely to the obligations set out in The Taxonomy : whose experience this is (character), where (world), when and how fast (form and world), what is making things happen (stakes) and what someone wants (character and stakes). The obligations can be read as a craft description of what a reader must have before a situation model exists at all. The practical inference is that an opening may withhold some dimensions to make a mystery, but must supply enough that the withheld ones are felt as absences. A named character in an unnamed place is intriguing; an unnamed pronoun doing an unspecified thing in an unspecified place is noise. Does the reader arrive with nothing? No, and the qualification governs how the chapter’s tests are used. Hans Robert Jauss’s horizon of expectations ( Toward an Aesthetic of Reception , translated by Timothy Bahti, 1982) is the set of generic, formal and thematic expectations a reader brings from earlier reading, and the opening pages are where a text confirms, adjusts or violates it. That is why genre can be signalled cheaply: the reader supplies the schema, and one well-chosen noun can orient someone who has read forty books of the kind. Genette’s Paratexts (translated by Jane E. Lewin, 1997) describes the rest of what the reader brings: title, cover, jacket copy, shelf, reviews. Yet the paratext is not the author’s to control, nor permanent, nor always present. Covers change between editions, jacket copy is written by marketing departments, and openings are excerpted, photocopied and read in workshops without any of it. So the test that asks the writer to read her opening as if she knew nothing about the book (test 5: Zero context in Diagnostic Tests ) survives as a deliberately austere idealisation. It does not describe how books are read. It isolates what the prose does on its own, and an opening that fails it has a dependency that the writer should choose knowingly. Where should the backstory go? Wherever it buys most. Meir Sternberg’s Expositional Modes and Temporal Ordering in Fiction (1978) treats exposition not as a place in a novel but as a problem of distribution: every narrative must convey its antecedents, and the variables are when and in what order. Exposition can be preliminary, delivered before the action, which gives clarity at the cost of suspense; delayed, supplied after the action has begun; or distributed, scattered and never gathered. Sternberg’s distinction between suspense , uncertainty about what will happen, and curiosity , uncertainty about what has already happened, explains why delay is productive: the reader who does not yet know why Josef K. was arrested, or what happened at 124, is pulled forward by a question about the past. Front-loaded backstory fails not because backstory is dull but because delivering it early spends an asset. Backstory and Flashback (Chapter 7) treats the cost of each later return to the past. The dates of the convention The advice in this chapter describes current conventions, not laws. Horace praised Homer for plunging his audience in medias res , into the middle of things, instead of beginning with the egg from which Helen was hatched, but Homer’s audience already knew the Trojan War, and Homer recovered the antecedents later by retrospection; the rule was about sequence, not omission. Nineteenth-century novels such as Père Goriot (1835) and Middlemarch (1871–72) favoured preliminary exposition and a narrator who surveys a society before entering a scene. Modernist novels plunged into a consciousness and distributed orientation. Contemporary openings attack faster and show their voice earlier, under institutional pressures that Noah Lukeman’s The First Five Pages (2000) describes from inside publishing, and his book is best read as an account of a filtering institution, not of an aesthetic principle. Some of the openings that have lasted longest in English would fail a modern first-page screen, and Bleak House is admired partly because of its opening of fog, not in spite of it. See also: the Reference theory , with transportation and absorption, Suvin’s novum and Delany’s account of the science-fictional sentence; the history of opening conventions .

title: 4. The Taxonomy
text: The contract model treats the opening pages as opening a set of obligations to the reader, each of which the rest of the book must honour. The metaphor comes from the older critical language of the narrative or generic contract and from reader-response criticism’s interest in the expectations a text licenses. Its value is diagnostic, since it turns make the opening better into separate questions with separate remedies. Its danger is mechanical application, which produces a first page visibly discharging obligations instead of telling a story. Five contracts are set out below, and a sixth is proposed. Voice: what it will be like to read this book The voice contract tells the reader what it will be like, sentence by sentence, to be inside the book, through distance, diction and rhythm, and reliability. Narrative distance is how close the narration stands to a character’s mind. Genette’s Narrative Discourse (translated by Jane E. Lewin, 1980) separates who speaks from who perceives, and James Wood’s How Fiction Works (2008) gives an accessible account of free indirect style , third-person narration coloured by a character’s own words and judgements. The same event can be told from far off ( The woman crossed the yard ), close ( She kept to the gravel. The grass would be soaked, and she had one dry pair of shoes left ) or from inside the mind ( Gravel. Not the grass, not today ). Each is competent, but the opening chooses, and a book that opens far off and drifts inward by chapter three has not deepened, it has wobbled, unless the drift is patterned. Reliability , Wayne Booth’s subject in The Rhetoric of Fiction (1961), is signalled in an opening not as a verdict on whether the narrator lies but as a reading protocol : take this at face value, or read it with suspicion. Herman Melville’s Moby-Dick (1851) begins Call me Ishmael , an instruction about what to call him, a name offered for convenience whose relation to the truth is left open. In Kazuo Ishiguro’s The Remains of the Day (1989) the butler calls a short motoring holiday the expedition that has been preoccupying my imagination now for some days and approaches his own intention as if it were weather he is observing; nothing is said about repression, and the syntax enacts it. Gail Honeyman’s Eleanor Oliphant Is Completely Fine (2017), a commercial novel narrated by a finance clerk in Glasgow, begins: When people ask me what I do – taxi drivers, hairdressers – I tell them I work in an office. The sentence is about how she deflects questions, and its examples, the only people who ask, show how few people ask her anything; she reports her life accurately and misreads it, and the opening teaches the reader to hear both. Under-delivery of the voice contract is interchangeable competence, and over-delivery a style so insistent that it hides the situation. Genre: what kind of book this is The genre contract tells the reader what kind of book this is, and therefore what to expect, hope for and fear: its scale, its tone, whether its world’s rules match ours, and what to watch for. It is the cheapest contract to discharge, because the reader’s horizon supplies the schema, and the cost of getting it wrong is lopsided. A reader promised a thriller and given a domestic novel feels defrauded however good the domestic novel is, while a reader promised less merely puts down a book she would have liked. The technique that works for an unfamiliar world is normalisation : the strange element arrives as subordinate information inside a sentence about something else, treated by the viewpoint character as unremarkable. George Orwell’s Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949) begins with a weather report, It was a bright cold day in April , and ends the sentence and the clocks were striking thirteen : in fourteen words the strangeness arrives in the tone of the temperature, and the reader is taught that details here are load-bearing. Margaret Atwood’s The Handmaid’s Tale (1985) begins We slept in what had once been the gymnasium , nine words in which the tense implies a before and a rupture, the pronoun a confined collective and the gymnasium a civic space put to other use. J. K. Rowling’s Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone (1997) promises the fantastic by the vehemence with which the Dursleys insist they are perfectly normal, thank you very much . Set against these, an announcing sentence such as In this world, magic was real discharges the genre contract and damages every other. Character: whose eyes, and what they want now The character contract tells the reader whose eyes she has borrowed and why she should care what they see next. Its engine is the immediate want , which is often confused with the story-goal. The goal of the book, to expose the conspiracy or survive the winter, usually cannot be felt on page one, because the reader lacks the context to weigh it; page one needs something smaller, such as getting out of a conversation, finishing the till or not answering the phone. Dwight Swain’s Techniques of the Selling Writer (1965) set out the scene as goal, conflict and disaster, and the goal can be trivial so long as it is legible and resisted. Virginia Woolf’s Mrs Dalloway (1925) opens on such a want already in motion, Mrs Dalloway said she would buy the flowers herself ; Dostoevsky’s Crime and Punishment (1866), in Constance Garnett’s translation, lets the reader infer one from a young man walking slowly, as though in hesitation , towards a bridge. The subtler half is interiority as selection: a character shows herself less by what she feels than by what she notices, the scorched milk and the unpaid bill where another would see light on the tiles. And sympathy is not required; investment is. Nabokov’s Lolita (1955) opens in the voice of a man the reader should despise and holds her by verbal seduction, so that she is charmed by Humbert before she is asked to judge him, which is the book’s ethical design. World: a real place whose rules the book knows The world contract tells the reader that there is a real place here, with rules, and that the book knows them. Ian Watt’s The Rise of the Novel (1957) made circumstantial particularity, named places, exact times, specific objects, constitutive of the novel’s realism, and Roland Barthes’s “The Reality Effect” (1968) argued that some details signify nothing but reality itself, so that three exact things outperform a paragraph of general scenery. The rules of a place are shown by what the viewpoint character fails to find remarkable. A world can be established as atmosphere, as the fog of Dickens’s Bleak House (1853) makes Chancery’s obscurity the reader’s condition before anyone suffers from it; as a system of value, as Chinua Achebe’s Things Fall Apart (1958) begins with what Umuofia esteems; as material condition, as Balzac’s Père Goriot specifies the boarding house’s rent because the lodgers are what it makes them; or as rupture, as in Atwood’s gymnasium. Strong openings usually choose one and imply the others. Stakes: why here, and what pulls the reader on The stakes contract tells the reader why the book began here and what question will pull her forward. The pull-forward question is the working form of Barthes’s hermeneutic code ( S/Z , 1970, translated by Richard Miller), the means by which a narrative poses an enigma and delays its answer. Its useful division is between planting , which creates a question the reader knows she has ( why won’t she answer her brother’s calls? ), and withholding , which conceals what the reader does not know is missing or knows is being kept from her; coy narration that declines to name what the viewpoint character plainly knows breaks the voice contract to serve the stakes contract. Toni Morrison’s Beloved (1987) begins 124 was spiteful. Full of a baby’s venom. A number stands where a name belongs, the reader must infer a house, a spite and a baby, and the withheld information is bounded, which separates it from obscurity. Franz Kafka’s The Trial (1925), in Breon Mitchell’s translation, opens on Josef K.’s arrest without having done anything wrong , and its must have been adopts K.’s own hypothesis, so that the reader receives the enigma and a warning about her guide in one sentence. Cost completes the contract: a want with no price for failure is a preference, and the price needs only to be real to this character. A proposed sixth: the formal contract The five contracts come from a realist account in which the reader’s questions concern the represented world, but readers of an opening also learn how the book is built. The formal contract , proposed here, is what the opening teaches about the book’s structural conventions: person and tense, the handling of time, the unit of division, any apparatus of documents, notes or epigraphs, and whether one consciousness or several will carry it. A late change in any of these reads as error or gimmick, and the severest case is the viewpoint: a book that spends forty pages in one mind and then moves meets resistance in proportion to the attachment it built, which is why books with several viewpoints usually declare the pattern at the first chapter break. Gabriel García Márquez’s One Hundred Years of Solitude (1967) declares its handling of time in its first sentence, which in Gregory Rabassa’s translation sets a future firing squad, a present of remembering and a remembered afternoon of discovering ice in twenty-six words, so that the novel’s loops arrive as the fulfilment of a rule. George Saunders’s Lincoln in the Bardo (2017) declares its form before its place, as “Worked Analyses” shows. Flaubert’s Madame Bovary (1857) is the doubtful case: it opens in a schoolboy’s we , which vanishes as the narration becomes impersonal, and critics still disagree whether that is a flaw, the residue of a draft or a way of showing Charles from outside before the book enters Emma. The objection is that five is enough: person, tense and distance belong to voice, conventions of apparatus belong to genre, and a sixth dilutes a model whose virtue is compactness. The defence is that readers do not experience structure as voice or genre, that its failures and remedies are distinct, and that a book which misdeclares its viewpoints has a structural fault the five cannot name. This chapter adopts the formal contract for diagnosis and concedes that the five cover most revision problems. The Ending (Chapter 16) adopts or rejects it, since its own proposed formal closure is the same contract discharged at the far end of the book, and The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13) may also rule, since the viewpoint is its severest case. The Ending (Chapter 16) adopts it at the scale of a book, as the contract its formal closure discharges, and The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13) adopts it for viewpoint plurality. Must every contract be discharged at once? No. A contract may be opened on page one by a single cue and honoured over the first chapter, and the stakes contract in particular is usually opened by a small question and honoured when the real problem arrives pages later. Deferral is legitimate when it is chosen: Austen’s Pride and Prejudice (1813) defers character behind a general proposition, as “Worked Analyses” shows. The question to ask of an absence is whether it is deliberate and whether the reader has been given a reason to tolerate it. The contracts are the same for every book; how they are weighted is a choice informed by genre. See also: the Reference contracts , with each contract’s components, more illustrations and a summary table of carriers and failures.

title: 5. The Mechanism
text: Multiplicity as selection Multiplicity is the practice of making one unit of text discharge several functions at once, and in the opening it is arithmetic, not ornament. A first page of about 250 words must open six contracts, sustain a scene and give a stranger a reason to turn the page, and it cannot give each job its own sentence. Lines that do one thing, a sentence only of tone or only of fact, are affordable at page 150 and nearly unaffordable at page one. The discipline is not compression but selection : the writer is not looking for a way to say five things in one sentence but for the detail that already carries five things because it is the right one. Compression produces density; selection produces details that keep yielding. Woolf’s first sentence shows selection succeeding. Words What they discharge Mrs Dalloway Character (who); genre (a social register); world (a married woman known by her husband’s name) said she would Voice (reported, at one remove); form (the book will arrive slightly after its own events) buy the flowers Character (a want); stakes (a day with a plan in it, the party) herself World (there are servants); character (insistence); stakes (something she must do alone) Nine words touch every contract, and no word does a job another word was already doing. Yet the sentence does not feel efficient. It feels casual, and that is the mark of selection: the reader experiences ease while the text carries density. Where the multiplying work lives Revisers tend to look for multiplicity in metaphor, on the assumption that figures are where meanings stack. In practice the work is done in four plainer places. The first is the choice of noun: gymnasium , not building , carries a history that an adjective would have to state. The second is tense, mood and aspect: had once been , must have been and was to remember imply a history without narrating one, which makes tense the cheapest worldbuilding in the language. The third is what the viewpoint character declines to explain, since the unremarked thirteenth chime is a positive signal about what she considers normal. The fourth is which three things, of the thousands available, this person notices, which is characterisation, world and voice at once. Metaphor can multiply, but it is the riskiest instrument in an opening, because a figure that misses draws attention to the author, and one tied to a technology can age: the sky in William Gibson’s Neuromancer (1984), the color of television, tuned to a dead channel , meant grey static to its first readers and may mean flat blue to later ones. The density ceiling Multiplicity has an upper bound, the density ceiling , and a page past it shows three symptoms: no sentence at rest, so that the prose has effort and no rhythm; clauses stacked faster than the main clause can carry them; and a primary action the reader can no longer name, because she can say only what is being established. The remedy is counter-intuitive: an opening needs some sentences that do only one thing. Emphasis depends on contrast, so a page on which every detail is significant contains no significant detail. Dickens’s fog paragraph is long and low in density per sentence, repeating one word until the repetition becomes an argument; it works by hammering one function, not by stacking five. High multiplicity is a technique, and the virtue it serves is proportion. Where to begin: the attack Every narrative decides where in the story’s chronology the telling begins, and every such decision trades momentum against comprehension. Beginning in the middle buys momentum, an immediate question and the impression of a book already running, and risks action without context that reads as noise. Beginning with orientation buys clarity and a frame against which later disruption will register, and risks a first page on which nothing is yet at stake. The failure of the plunge is the counter-intuitive one. Action is not interesting in itself: tension depends on caring about an outcome, which depends on knowing what is at stake for whom, and a chase between two strangers whose names the reader has just learned is fast without being tense. Most working openings resolve the trade-off in the same way, which this chapter calls the hybrid resolution : begin in the middle of a small, comprehensible action, not the book’s central conflict, which delivers voice, character and world together, and let the real disruption arrive once the reader has enough footing to feel it. The action must already be in motion, so that the reader arrives after it started; instantly comprehensible, needing no context; and characterising, so that the choice of action and the manner of it reveal the person. Clarissa Dalloway buys flowers; in Albert Camus’s The Stranger (1942) Meursault receives a telegram and asks his employer for leave; Ishiguro’s butler considers a motoring trip. The engine of each book arrives later, into a reader able to feel it. The hairline crack Whatever the attack, the opening must answer why today? , and the answer is rarely a catastrophe. It is the hairline crack , the smallest deviation from routine that signals that this day is not like the others: the telegram in The Stranger ; the alarm clock and then the rat in the one-room flat of Richard Wright’s Native Son (1940); the breakfast that does not arrive on the morning of Josef K.’s arrest. The crack must be noticeable as a deviation, which requires the routine to be sketched clearly enough for the deviation to register, and that is why an opening that is all plunge can fail: without a baseline nothing reads as a departure from it. Gambits and substitution The choice between plunge and orientation describes only the relation in time. The Reference chapter sets out twelve opening gambits , recognisable strategies with characteristic costs: the small action ( Mrs Dalloway ), the aphorism ( Pride and Prejudice ), the voice declaration ( Moby-Dick ), the panorama ( Bleak House ), the frame narrator ( Wuthering Heights ), the glimpse of a later moment ( One Hundred Years of Solitude ), the document ( Dracula ), the arrival of a stranger ( The Magic Mountain ), the rupture of routine ( Native Son ), the catalogue ( Père Goriot ), the telling that refuses to begin ( Tristram Shandy ) and the withheld referent ( Beloved ). Their use is not classification but substitution testing . A draft that is not working is often the right material in the wrong gambit, and writing the same first page as a rupture, a voice declaration and a small action teaches more than three rounds of line-editing the original. See also: the Reference account of multiplicity ; the attack and the twelve gambits , with each gambit’s gains and costs in a table.

title: 6. Diagnostic Tests
text: The ten tests are for revision, not composition; applied while drafting they produce a writer who cannot finish a first page. Run tests 1 to 3 (Contract, Scene and Momentum) first, since their failures make the others premature: there is no point tuning the voice of an opening that has no scene in it. Test 6 (Promise) needs the manuscript, not the opening alone. Record a sentence, not a verdict, because every test is failed on purpose by a book worth reading, and its job is to make a choice visible so that it can be confirmed as a choice. Test 1 — Contract Can you point to the words that open each contract within the first two pages? Failure. An omission mistaken for a deferral. Exception. Pride and Prejudice , which defers character behind a surplus of voice. Test 2 — Scene Can you complete “In these pages, X is trying to ___, and ___ is in the way”? Failure. Description or exposition, not a scene. Exception. Bleak House , whose fog is the argument. Test 3 — Momentum Within the first page, does something change or does someone want something, and after how many words? Failure. A static opening. Exception. The Stranger , whose flatness is its subject. Test 4 — Voice Could the first paragraph move into another novel, of another genre, unnoticed? Failure. Interchangeable competence. Exception. The Trial , whose official plainness is the effect. Test 5 — Zero context Given only the first two pages, can a reader say who, where and when, what kind of book, and what she wants to know? Failure. A dependency on paratext. Exception. Lincoln in the Bardo , whose title supplies the frame its first page withholds. Test 6 — Promise Do pages 30 to 40 belong to the same book as the opening, in tone, pace and stakes? Failure. The borrowed hook. Exception. Madame Bovary , whose opening narrator vanishes. Test 7 — Inventory Of the details placed in the first two pages, which are redeemed later? Failure. Too many promises, too few kept. Exception. Tristram Shandy , whose unkept promises are the joke. Test 8 — Density Read aloud: where does the breath fail, or a listener ask what is happening? Failure. A page past the density ceiling. Exception. The Benjy section of The Sound and the Fury , saturated by design. Test 9 — Form On what page does the reader learn the book’s structural rules: viewpoints, timelines, apparatus? Failure. Structure arriving as a surprise. Exception. Bleak House , whose second narrator arrives in chapter 3. Test 10 — Abandonment At which sentence would an indifferent reader stop? Failure. The opening stops performing and starts explaining. Exception. Père Goriot , whose inventory the book needs. Three refinements sharpen the tests. In test 3 (Momentum), the published openings discussed in this chapter reach a verb of intention or change within about fifty words, an observation from the examples, not a count. In test 4 (Voice), retype your first paragraph among three published openings with the attributions removed and ask a reader to describe each voice in two adjectives; clear and fine are failures. In test 5 (Zero context), the reader must be someone else, since a writer cannot unread her own blurb. Reading the results together Failures cluster, and the cluster points to the first move. Tests 2 (Scene) and 3 (Momentum) together mean the opening is description or exposition: find the action underneath and start there. Test 4 (Voice) alone means competent, undistinguished prose, to be rewritten in the character’s diction instead of the author’s. Tests 1 (Contract) and 7 (Inventory) together mean too many promises and too few kept: cut named entities and concentrate the detail. Test 5 (Zero context) alone means supplying the missing frame inside the prose, or keeping the dependency on purpose. Test 8 (Density) alone usually means over-revision, a page polished until it has no air, and the remedy is to restore some sentences that do one thing. Test 9 (Form) alone means declaring the pattern in the first chapter. Test 6 (Promise) alone means a mis-promise, and it carries a warning. When an opening and its book disagree, writers revise the book toward the opening, because the opening is the more finished object and often the more exciting one. The direction is usually wrong. The opening is two pages and the book four hundred, and the smaller object is the one to change. See also: the Reference protocol , with each test’s procedure and a table of combined failures; the multiplicity audit , which test 1 (Contract) uses.

title: 7. Failure Patterns
text: Each pattern below is described by its mechanism and ends with a published work that commits it and succeeds, because the pattern fails through the mechanism, not the surface feature, and where the mechanism is absent the feature is harmless. The Reference chapter’s full catalogue adds five more: the weather report, the overstuffed first page, the unanchored opening, the cast parade and paratext dependency. The waking-up opening Symptom. The novel begins with a character waking, lying in bed, getting up, washing and considering the day. Mechanism. Waking is a passage into consciousness, not an action within it. The character has not been awake long enough to want anything, faces no obstacle and stands in no relation to anyone, so every contract is deferred behind physical events that are the same for everyone. Nothing can be at stake in a body becoming conscious. Drafts drift towards the pattern because it is the chronological start of the day and a comfortable run-up for the writer. Remedy. Begin at the first moment the character wants something, which is often three or four paragraphs later. The deleted material is usually the writer’s warm-up, not the reader’s need. The exception. Andy Weir’s Project Hail Mary (2021), a commercial science-fiction novel, opens with its narrator half-conscious while a voice asks What’s two plus two? ; the question irritates him, and he drifts back to sleep. He wakes without his name or any idea where he is, beside two crew members long dead, and does not recover his name until the third chapter. The pattern succeeds because the waking is the disruption: his want, to know who and where he is, forms as he wakes, the obstacle is his own memory, and the question he shares with the reader drives the book. Wright’s Native Son succeeds by another route, since its alarm clock is an intrusion and what follows is not washing but a family dressing in one room, and then a rat. Where waking is the event, the pattern becomes a strong opening. The info-dump opening Symptom. History, worldbuilding or backstory arrives before any character or action: the political situation, the magic system, the family’s four generations. Mechanism. Two failures, usually together. In Sternberg’s terms, delivering the antecedents early spends an asset that would otherwise have produced curiosity. And information is not memorable without a container: a reader given a nation’s history before meeting anyone who lives there has nowhere to store it and retains little, so the dump fails even at its own purpose. The writer’s fear that the reader will be lost is real, but the reader does not need to know the world early; she needs to believe that the author knows it, which confident specificity achieves. Remedy. Turn exposition into implication. Ask of each expository sentence which character would say it, to whom and why; if no one would, the reader does not need it yet. The exception. Dune opens with an epigraph from an invented history and then a scene thick with unexplained terms, Bene Gesserit, gom jabbar, Arrakis, almost none of them defined. It succeeds because the vocabulary arrives inside a tense scene between two people, an old woman testing a boy, and because the unexplained terms work as withheld information, producing curiosity, instead of as delivered information. An unexplained proper noun is an asset; an explained one is an expense. The borrowed hook Symptom. A gripping opening, a chase, a murder, a scream, that turns out to be a dream, an unconnected flash-forward, a scene from a genre the book does not belong to, or an event the next three hundred pages never resume. Mechanism. The opening writes a cheque the book will not honour. Because of the primacy effect the reader forms her model of the novel from these pages, and everything after is read as a deviation from the promised book. Readers forgive a book that becomes more than it promised and do not forgive one that becomes less. The pressure behind the pattern is the advice to hook: the fastest hook available is an event more exciting than the book’s own material, and the mismatch is invisible to the writer, who knows what is coming. Remedy. Run test 6 (Promise). If the opening and pages 30 to 40 read as different books, change the opening. The exception. Daphne du Maurier’s Rebecca (1938) opens with a dream, Last night I dreamt I went to Manderley again , the device the pattern most distrusts, since a dream presented as waking reality voids the reader’s investment. It succeeds because the dream is declared as a dream in its first clause and belongs to the book: the ruined house it visits is the book’s loss seen from afterwards, told in the voice that will tell the rest. The same distinction governs glimpses ahead, as the firing squad that opens One Hundred Years of Solitude shows: a flash-forward that belongs to the book is a structure, and one that belongs to a more exciting book is a fraud. The withholding tease Symptom. The narration conspicuously declines to name what the viewpoint character knows perfectly well: the thing she had done that summer , what was in the box , a protagonist called only he for six pages. Mechanism. The voice contract is broken to serve the stakes contract. Close narration promises access to a mind, and a mind that circles a fact without naming it is either being coy on the author’s behalf, which shows the author’s hand, or repressing, which is a different and harder effect. Readers sense the difference, and they meet coyness with irritation, not curiosity. Withholding looks like suspense and is easy; making a question the reader wants answered is harder. Remedy. Distinguish planting from withholding. Give the reader the fact and withhold its meaning, which is nearly always the stronger structure. The exception. Beloved withholds on a large scale and succeeds, because what it withholds is unspeakable within the minds it represents, the repression is the subject and is maintained consistently, and what replaces the missing information is concentrated, disorienting specificity, not evasion. The test is whether the gap is in the character or in the author. Throat-clearing Symptom. The novel begins on page four. The first three pages are context, scene-setting, biography, or a character travelling somewhere. Mechanism. The process of composition leaks into the finished text. Writers need a run-up to find the voice, and the run-up is drafting apparatus, not narrative. It is often well written, which makes it hard to see, and it feels necessary to the writer because for the writer it was. Remedy. Delete the first three paragraphs and read what remains. If the opening improves or is unchanged, they were throat-clearing; repeat until a deletion causes a loss. The exception. Thomas Mann’s The Magic Mountain (1924) begins with a young man’s journey up to a sanatorium in the Alps for a visit meant to last three weeks, and the slowness of the approach enacts the book’s subject, the elasticity of time for those who stay. The distinction is whether an approach does thematic work or merely postpones. See also: the Reference failure catalogue , with a table relating each pattern to its mechanism and the contracts it damages.

title: 8. Worked Analyses
text: Three close readings, a short screen reading and the household revision case follow. Each reading names the contracts the opening opens, the gambit it uses and what it leaves for later. Pride and Prejudice : the contracts paid unequally Austen’s first sentence, It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife (1813), asserts a law that the reader is invited to disbelieve while accepting it as the law this society lives by, and that double stance is the novel’s mode. On a mechanical audit the sentence fails three of the five contracts: it supplies no character and no want, no place and no time, and nothing is at stake in it. It survives because the voice contract is discharged with a large surplus, the irony audible in universally and in the inversion of who is in want of whom, and because a reader of 1813 recognised the marriage plot from the content alone, so that the reader’s horizon paid the genre contract. The second paragraph narrows the law to a neighbourhood with daughters, and the third arrives at a scene: “My dear Mr. Bennet,” said his lady to him one day, “have you heard that Netherfield Park is let at last?” The character and stakes contracts then open in a rush, with a wife who wants something, a husband who resists by teasing, and a question about the new tenant that will occupy the book. The lesson is that contracts can be paid in unequal instalments, provided they are not all defaulted together. The aphorism defers character, which is the gambit’s usual cost, and buys authority, tone and theme at once. It sounds arch when the voice cannot sustain it, and a draft that copies the gambit without the voice has made an omission, not a choice, which is what test 1 (Contract) is for. Everything I Never Told You : the fact given, the meaning withheld Celeste Ng’s first novel (2014) opens: Lydia is dead. But they don’t know this yet. The first sentence gives the book’s gravest fact, the death of a sixteen-year-old, in three words. The second declares the narration’s relation to the family: it knows what they do not, and it says so. What follows is a morning, 3 May 1977, in a small town in Ohio, on which Lydia’s mother finds her bed not slept in; the family calls the police and the friends Lydia was supposed to have, and the next morning her body is recovered from the lake. In the terms of “The Taxonomy” the opening is a plant, not a tease. It gives the reader the fact and withholds its meaning, the remedy the withholding tease lacks, and it converts what might have been suspense, whether the girl will be found, into curiosity, why she died and what this family did not tell one another. In Sternberg’s terms the backstory has become the engine. The opening is also the borrowed hook’s answer: the most dramatic event in the book is on its first page, and the next three hundred pages do resume it, because the death is the book’s own material, delivered in the voice that will tell the rest. The dramatic irony of the second sentence then does the work of the hairline crack, since an ordinary morning and an unslept bed read as dread to a reader who knows what the family does not. And the formal contract opens in the same breath: a narration that can say they don’t know this yet has declared a vantage above any one character, so its later movement among the family’s minds reads as its nature. Lincoln in the Bardo : the form declared before the place George Saunders’s novel (2017) begins with a stranger. Its first words, On our wedding day I was forty-six, she was eighteen , are spoken by Hans Vollman, a printer telling of his young wife and of the beam that fell on him before their marriage was consummated, and the passage is attributed to him by name, set off from the text as a citation would be. Vollman calls the box he lies in a sick-box and expects to recover. The reader infers, before he does, that he is dead, and the withheld referent is bounded: she knows which question she has. The opening is a voice declaration, and its larger work is the formal contract. A novel that will be told by a crowd of the dead, each passage attributed, and that will intercut chapters assembled from quotations about Lincoln and the death of his son Willie, has shown its unit of division and its apparatus on its first page, so that the later chapters of citation read as the book’s nature instead of the author’s intervention. The cost is borne by the paratext. A reader with only the first page meets a man describing his marriage and has no reason to expect a president; the title supplies the frame the prose withholds, and the opening fails the zero-context test. The dependency is chosen, which is all the test asks, and the case shows how the tests are to be read: a failure that marks a decision is not a fault. A screen reading: Inglourious Basterds and The Sopranos Quentin Tarantino’s Inglourious Basterds (2009) begins with a title card, Chapter One: Once upon a time… in Nazi-occupied France , which opens the formal contract, chapters and a fairy-tale frame, before the first shot. The scene is the hybrid resolution at length: in 1941 a farmer chops at a stump while his daughter hangs washing, and a car approaches on the road. The action is small, in motion and comprehensible, and the car is the crack. Colonel Landa declines wine, asks for milk and praises it, and later asks to continue in English; why that matters is withheld until the camera finds the Jewish family hidden beneath the floor, who do not speak it. From then on the stakes contract is fully open, and every courtesy in the conversation is a threat. Only the daughter of the hidden family, Shosanna, escapes, and Landa lets her run. David Chase’s pilot for The Sopranos (1999) opens in a psychiatrist’s waiting room, Tony Soprano framed against a statue of a nude woman before Dr Melfi calls him in. The scene declares the series’ terms: a crime drama whose mode of attention is a gangster’s account of himself, given to a therapist, with his recent days shown in flashback as he describes them. The genre contract is adjusted in the first minute, and the immediate want, Tony’s wish not to be there at all, is legible before anyone has been threatened. The household revision case: the first page after the prologue The household novel opens with a prologue focalised through the father on his last ordinary day, in which he counts the till twice, waves off a boy at the glass and pockets the good pen ( The Prologue , Chapter 10). The opening pages follow it, and they belong to Nadia, four months after March. The reader arrives knowing the shop and something of the father, and nothing of his children. Version A, the draft. Nadia woke early, as she always did, and lay for a while listening to the traffic on the main road. It was going to be another hot day. She had lived in the flat for over a year now, ever since she had moved out of the place above the shop, which had never had proper heating and which she had shared with her brother Dov for most of her twenties. Their father had died in March. Since then things had been difficult between them. She got up, made coffee, and thought about whether she should call him. Diagnosis. The scene sentence cannot be completed, because she is not trying to do anything (test 2: Scene). The first sixty words are waking and listening (test 3: Momentum), and the prose could belong to any of a thousand books (test 4: Voice). Every sentence carries one function, the opposite of the density problem (test 8: Density). On the contract test, character is opened partly and world thinly, voice and genre not at all, and the stakes are stated instead of enacted (test 1: Contract). It is a waking-up opening with throat-clearing in front of it, and its emotional situation is summarised, things had been difficult , instead of performed. Yet it holds every necessary fact. Its failure is arrangement and selection, not information. Version B, the revision. Nadia had got good at the maths of it: four months since March, seventeen since she’d left the flat over the shop for one with actual heat, and a week to the day since she’d stopped answering when Dov called to ask if she’d been by to check on the coat. She hadn’t. She told herself this was because grief had a schedule and hers ran on different maths from her brother’s, not because she couldn’t stand the smell of dust settling on wool that wasn’t going to be worn again. When her phone buzzed with his name a fourth time that morning, she did what she always did lately, which was let it ring itself out and go back to counting the register receipts nobody but her seemed to think still needed counting. The audit of Version B is tabular, one row per contract. Contract How Version B opens it Voice Wry, self-auditing close third; she told herself lets the narration see past her rationalisations without leaving her head Genre A quiet, interior register: a literary family novel, and the pace the book will keep Character A small, resisted want: do not answer, do not go, keep counting; grief shown as avoidance World Contemporary, domestic, straitened: heating as an achievement, a shop, a till, an unworn coat Stakes Four unanswered calls, a coat nobody will wear, receipts nobody else thinks matter: three planted questions Form Close third, past tense, linear, and so far one viewpoint Every contract is opened inside one paragraph, and the rows share their material: the receipts are character, world and stakes at once. The revision made five moves. It deleted the throat-clearing, the waking, the traffic and the weather. It turned biography into inventory, so that the same facts, the old flat and the months since the death, arrive as Nadia’s own counting and the exposition characterises her. It found the hairline crack, the fourth call this morning, which answers why today? without an event. It replaced a summary of feeling with an object, a coat, dust, wool and a smell. And it opened the narration’s small gap over its character, she told herself … not because , which is the reliability protocol for the whole book. The result is the hybrid resolution: a small, comprehensible action, declining a call, with orientation delivered by voice and detail in the same breath, while the book’s engine arrives later. What the revision has not solved. The first sentence carries three measurements of time and four facts, close to the density ceiling, and a reader may read it twice; whether that is richness or strain is a fair editorial disagreement. The register is distinctive against Version A but recognisable against its own shelf, so test 4 (Voice) is passed only locally. Four months since March never says what happened in March: Nadia knows, and the narration does not name it, which the withholding tease’s test allows only because the gap is in her, who counts instead of naming, and because the prologue has just shown the father’s last ordinary day; read without the prologue, the month is an unexplained noun. Test 7 (Inventory) finds all but one detail redeemed. The coat is paid at the ending ( The Ending , Chapter 16), the counting returns in the sleeves she gathers there, Dov’s calls lead into his thread, and wool that wasn’t going to be worn again is Nadia’s belief, which the last chapter reverses when she puts the coat on, so the opening plants the ending without her knowing it; only the flat with heating stays idle, and it is small. The largest gap is in the formal contract. The page declares one viewpoint, and the book alternates between Nadia and Elena; by test 9 (Form), Elena’s first scene, the doorway exchange with Dov, should follow at the first chapter break, before the reader’s attachment to Nadia hardens into an assumption that the book is hers alone. See also: the Reference worked analyses , with readings of Bleak House , The Trial , The Stranger in three translations, Beloved , The Remains of the Day and Native Son , and the revision case with its diagnosis in tables.

title: 9. Checklist and Exercises
text: Revision checklist Use the checklist on a finished draft of the first chapter, after reading the opening and then pages 30 to 40. Each item is a question to answer in a sentence. The scene Who is trying to do what in these pages, and what is in the way? How many words pass before the first verb of intention or change? What small deviation tells the reader that today is not like the others? The contracts Which words open each of the six contracts, and is each deferred contract deferred by choice? Is any information delivered that no character would say, to anyone, for any reason? Does the narration withhold anything the viewpoint character plainly knows, and is that gap in her or in the author? The page Which detail carries the most contracts, and could the page be built outward from it? Read aloud, where does the breath fail, and which sentences are rests? Which details are placed in the first two pages, and which of them are redeemed later? The book Do pages 30 to 40 belong to the same book as the opening, in tone, pace and stakes? If the book uses several viewpoints, timelines or documents, on what page does the reader first learn that it does? If read without its title, cover or blurb, does the opening still say what kind of book it is? Exercises for your own draft The multiplicity audit. Print the first page double-spaced. Beside each sentence, write the initial of every contract it opens (V, G, C, W, S, F), and then read the pattern. Mostly single letters means the page spends its words one job at a time; mostly four or five means it needs rests; an empty column is a contract not opened; a sentence carrying most of the letters is the page’s spine and may belong earlier. The multiplicity audit takes about twenty minutes. Three gambits. Rewrite your first page as a small action, as a voice declaration and as a rupture of routine, using the same material. Judge only when all three exist, and look for what each version found that the original lacked. Delete three paragraphs. Cut the opening three paragraphs and read on. If the opening is no worse, repeat; stop at the first cut that loses something, and restore only that. The second-page test. Read your opening, then pages 30 to 40, and write one sentence on the kind of book each promises. If the sentences differ, rewrite the opening toward the book. The cold reader. Give the first two pages, without title or description, to a reader who knows nothing of the book, and ask four questions: who is this about, where and when is it, what kind of book is it, and what do you want to know? Each blank answer is a dependency to remove or to keep on purpose.

title: 10. Coda
text: The contract model describes how openings work under present conventions, and its tests catch real faults in drafts written for present readers. It is not a law of narrative. Bleak House fails at least three of the ten tests (the scene, zero-context and form tests in “Diagnostic Tests”) and its opening is part of what readers admire in it; Pride and Prejudice defaults on three contracts in its first sentence; Tristram Shandy spends volumes refusing to begin. The conventions behind the tests were shaped in part by the way manuscripts are filtered and books are browsed, and a writer who can say only that an opening would be rejected today has explained the market, not the book. The tests should therefore produce questions, and an opening that fails one has done nothing wrong until the writer has asked why the book might want the failure. The model does settle one question of practice, and it concerns order. Every obligation an opening opens is defined by the book that follows. Whether a genre was promised accurately, whether a detail placed on page one is redeemed, and whether the form declared is the form used can be judged only against the finished whole. An opening written first is therefore a hypothesis about a book that does not yet exist, and the familiar advice to perfect the first pages before going on asks the writer to finish the hypothesis before the evidence is in. The order that follows is to draft the opening to begin, since a book needs somewhere to start; to revise it last, when the book can say what it owes; and, when the opening and the book disagree, to change the opening, because it is the smaller object and the one written in ignorance of the rest. See also: the Reference coda .

title: The Prologue
text: What a separated opening must prove, and how to tell whether it has The Craft Behind the Story (Second Edition) — Chapter 10. Part III: The Architecture of the Whole. In brief. A prologue is a unit of narrative set apart from the main story in time, place, viewpoint or register, placed before it, and labelled as apart. Like any scene it must do work the reader would miss; unlike any scene it must also show why that work could not be done from inside Chapter One. The chapter’s tool is that double test and its consequence: a prologue that fails only the second part is not cut but absorbed, its material folded into the main narrative where it belongs. A prologue that is kept opens a distance the book must close, and the chapter argues for closing it in small instalments rather than in one late reveal. Use the chapter on a prologue that readers call unnecessary, on one that promises a different book from the one that follows, or on a quiet book that seems to need something in front of it. What you can do after this chapter Say in one sentence why a prologue’s material must sit outside the main narrative, and distinguish a sentence that names an impossibility from one that names a preference. Decide whether to keep a prologue separate, absorb it into Chapter One, or relocate it in the main timeline. Name the axis of distance that carries a prologue, and choose how and where the book closes it. Audit the specifics a prologue plants and schedule their recurrence. Run nine tests on a draft prologue and turn their failures into a revision order. Key terms Prologue; the higher bar; absorption and relocation; the cold open, the preface, the frame narrative, the epigraph and the teaser; paratext and the diegetic threshold; the rules of notice and privileged position; suspense and curiosity; prolepsis and fictions of concord; the primacy effect; the contextual frame and reinstatement cost; the domains of purpose, with the reader contract and the proposed authority domain; the unwitnessable incident; distance and its four axes; the load-bearing axis; closing the distance, with total closure, fragmentary closure, recontextualisation and deliberate non-closure (the held note); advance notice and the seed; prologue types, including the proposed last ordinary day; false advertising. Each is defined at first use and collected in the consolidated glossary . Contents The first files say what a prologue is and why it costs more than an ordinary opening, the middle files what it can do that the main narrative cannot and how the distance it opens is closed, and the last are for use at the desk. The Problem A prologue cut, restored and relabelled, and the chapter’s claim Definitions The prologue, its length, and the units mistaken for it How It Works The diegetic threshold, suspense and curiosity, primacy, the dormant frame, and the age of the suspicion The Taxonomy Five domains stated as what distance makes possible, and a proposed sixth: the authority domain The Mechanism Distance and its closing, fragmentary closure, prologue types, and multiplicity as evidence Diagnostic Tests Nine questions on one page, and how to read their failures together Failure Patterns Five recurrent failures, each with a published work that commits it and succeeds Worked Analyses Frankenstein , The Book Thief , Life of Pi and Saving Private Ryan , and the household revision case Checklist and Exercises The revision checklist and five exercises for your own draft Coda Whose test the prologue is taking A writer in revision can start at the diagnostic tests and the absorption exercise; the coda, which separates the craft standard from the market’s suspicion, is best read early. The full treatment The Reference layer holds the complete chapter, The Prologue : the history of the form from the Greek prologos to the genre prologue, Genette’s three variables and Said on beginnings, fourteen prologue types with substitution testing, twelve failure patterns, eight close readings (among them Wuthering Heights , “The Custom-House”, Don Quixote , Dracula and the “Historical Notes” of The Handmaid’s Tale ), the prologue in the short story, the series, drama and on screen, a concordance of concepts to works, seminar questions and the sources. See also: The Opening Pages (Chapter 9), on the first pages of the main narrative, which a prologue precedes; Backstory and Flashback (Chapter 7), which applies distance to the cutaway inside the main narrative; The Ending (Chapter 16), whose final note is the same contract kept at the far boundary; The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13), on the cost of moving a reader between minds; The Reveal (Chapter 15), on the single late disclosure.

title: 1. The Problem
text: A novelist revising the household novel, the book this guide uses as its running example, has been told by two early readers to cut her prologue. The prologue is one page in the father’s viewpoint on his last ordinary day. He counts the till twice, waves off a boy knocking at the glass, means to flip the sign to CLOSED and does not, and puts the good pen, the fountain pen he keeps by the till for the ledger, into his coat pocket. Chapter One belongs to his daughter Nadia, four months after his death in March. The readers’ complaint is the usual one: nothing happens, the father is not in the rest of the book, and the book should start where the book starts. She cuts it. The new first page is Nadia counting register receipts that nobody else thinks need counting, and it reads well, as an opening scene with a want in it. The loss appears two hundred pages later. About two-thirds of the way through, Nadia puts her hand into the pocket of her father’s coat, still on its hook in the flat above the shop, and finds the good pen. In the draft with the prologue the reader saw him put it there, so the discovery is a recognition: the reader knows how the pen got into the pocket and Nadia does not. Without the prologue the scene is a discovery like any other, a pen in a pocket. The dread the prologue laid over every domestic scene, the reader’s knowledge that the ordinary day was the last one, has gone too, and nothing in the main narrative can restore it, because none of the three children was in the shop that day. She restores the page and, to meet her readers halfway, heads it Chapter One . A third reader reports something different. She took the father for the protagonist, settled into his head, and felt dropped when the next chapter moved to Nadia. The label Prologue had been doing a job as well: it told the reader that this viewpoint would not be held, which let her watch the father without attaching herself to him. The novelist has learned three things by experiment. The page earns its existence, since cutting it costs the book a recognition and a dread. It earns its position, since nothing inside the main narrative can see that day. And its label is an instruction about how to read, not a title. What she could not do was say any of this before the experiment, and the chapter’s purpose is to make that saying routine, so that the decision is made by argument instead of by trial and error. The readers who said cut it were not wrong to be suspicious. A prologue asks of a reader things an ordinary scene does not. It makes her begin twice, investing in one situation, setting it down and investing again a few pages later. It asks her to hold the first situation in reserve for an interval she cannot estimate. And it occupies the position she uses to decide what kind of book she is holding. Readers who have met many prologues that repay none of this learn to resent the label, and editors who read submissions at speed learn the same thing faster. The suspicion is a reasonable response to a poor average. The chapter turns it into a test instead of a rule. The chapter’s claim. A prologue is not asking to be kept. It is asking to be kept separate , and those are different arguments. A scene that does no work the reader would miss is cut. A prologue that does real work, but work the main narrative could do as well, is not cut: it is absorbed, and its material moves to where it belongs. The rest of the chapter supplies the means. The definitions separate the prologue from the cold open, the preface, the frame and the epigraph, which are often mistaken for it. How It Works gives the reasons a separated unit costs a reader more than an equally good scene inside Chapter One. The taxonomy names what a prologue can do that the main narrative cannot, and the mechanism shows how the distance it opens is closed. The tests, failures and worked analyses turn all of this into a decision about a draft: keep it separate, absorb it, or relocate it. See also: the Reference introduction , on the two beginnings and on the chapter’s place beside the opening and the ending.

title: 2. Definitions
text: The working definition A prologue is a unit of narrative set apart from the main story in time, place, viewpoint or register, placed before the main story begins and labelled as apart, whose separation from Chapter One does work that the main narrative’s own opening pages could not do as well. Each clause carries weight. Set apart in time, place, viewpoint or register names the four axes along which a prologue can differ from Chapter One, and a passage that shares the protagonist’s time, place and vantage and speaks in the book’s ordinary voice has opened no distance, whatever it is called. Placed before fixes the position: a separated unit after the main narrative is an epilogue or an afterword, and belongs with the ending. Labelled as apart is the clause most often forgotten, and it does the definitional work. A stylised, urgent opening scene is not a prologue because it is stylised and urgent; it is a prologue because the book has told the reader that it sits outside the main sequence. The last clause builds the chapter’s standard into the definition. A passage that could be folded into Chapter One with nothing lost was never a prologue, only an opening scene wearing a label its content did not need. The definition is functional and typographic at once, on purpose. Some passages do a prologue’s work without the label: the opening chapters of Wuthering Heights (1847), in which the tenant Lockwood blunders into a story already nearly over, and the overture to Zora Neale Hurston’s Their Eyes Were Watching God (1937), a page of proposition about men, women and desire before the novel’s woman walks back into town. Others carry the label and do none of the work. Both kinds test the definition, and the tests in this chapter use both. Two operations follow from the definition. Absorption folds a prologue’s material into Chapter One and deletes the label: a memory, a paragraph, a document the protagonist finds, a line of dialogue. Relocation moves the material to the point in the main timeline where it happened and lets it be an ordinary scene. Neither is a lesser form of deletion. Both keep good material and change only its compartment, and most prologues that fail this chapter’s tests should end in one or the other. Length No length is right in principle, and any figure offered is a convention. Prologues fall roughly into four sizes, and the size changes which failure is likely. An overture of a few hundred words, such as the Prelude to George Eliot’s Middlemarch (1871–72), risks doing an epigraph’s work under a prologue’s label. A scene of up to a few thousand words, the usual size of the commercial genre prologue, risks promising a more exciting book than the one that follows. A chaptered prologue of up to about ten thousand words, such as the four letters that open Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein (1818), risks reading as a first act, so that the reader never quite accepts Chapter One as the beginning. A sectional prologue beyond that, such as “The Custom-House” before Nathaniel Hawthorne’s The Scarlet Letter (1850), risks being skipped whole. One working rule, offered as a convention and not a finding: the longer the prologue, the earlier the book must begin closing the distance it opened, because a long prologue has borrowed more of the reader’s patience. Adjacent terms Several units sit near the prologue and are confused with it, and the confusions produce most of the bad advice. A cold open begins inside a scene already running and defers the framing. It is a way of starting, available to Chapter One as freely as to any separated unit, and nothing about beginning in motion requires separation: a cold open headed Prologue in the protagonist’s own time, place and voice is a Chapter One mislabelled. A preface is discourse about the text, addressed to the reader by an author, an editor or an invented intermediary, whereas a prologue is usually part of the fiction; the eighteenth-century novel blended the two, and the blend survives in the editorial notes of later books. A frame narrative is an outer story that contains the main one, and its first panel is often a prologue, but a frame returns and a prologue need not. An epigraph is a quotation placed at a threshold, which makes its claim by juxtaposition, not by telling. The teaser is television’s pre-title sequence and the nearest screen analogue, though on screen a cold open costs almost nothing, for reasons How It Works gives. What this chapter leaves to others The first pages of the main narrative belong to The Opening Pages (Chapter 9); a prologue precedes them and changes their conditions, since the reader of Chapter One has then met the book once already. Analepsis and prolepsis inside the running narrative, the flashback and the flash-forward, belong to Backstory and Flashback (Chapter 7), which applies this chapter’s language of distance to the cutaway. Chapter titles, part divisions and the other marks that segment a book belong to The Chapter Break (Chapter 6), which treats the prologue label as one member of that family. Epilogues and final notes belong to The Ending (Chapter 16). Which minds a novel may enter, and at what cost, belongs to The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13). The single late disclosure, considered for its own sake, belongs to The Reveal (Chapter 15), and the recap or prologue at the head of a series instalment to Series and Genre (Chapter 17). See also: Reference definitions and boundaries , with a table of adjacent terms (the argument, the proem, the induction, the chorus, the dramatis personae) and the four sizes in detail.

title: 3. How It Works
text: Five strands of theory explain why a separated opening is held to a stricter standard than an ordinary one. Each answers a question a writer meets in revision, and each is used by the tests. Why does a reader treat a prologue as both skippable and significant? Gérard Genette’s Paratexts: Thresholds of Interpretation (1987; translated by Jane E. Lewin, 1997) studies the paratext : everything that surrounds a text and mediates its reception, from titles and dedications to epigraphs, notes and prefaces. Genette’s image is a threshold, a vestibule where the reader may step in or turn back, and his preface is discourse about the text that follows, the most easily skipped zone of a book. A novelistic prologue rarely fits that account. It is not commentary on the book but the book itself, beginning earlier and elsewhere: a man counting a till, a ship in Arctic ice. It sits on a boundary Genette’s system does not quite accommodate, typographically part of the apparatus and in substance part of the storyworld. This chapter calls it a diegetic threshold , from diegesis , the narratologist’s word (Greek for “narration”) for the world a story tells: a piece of the story wearing the apparatus’s costume. The reader extends to it the apparatus’s licence to skip and the narrative’s demand for meaning, which is why craft advice about prologues contradicts itself. Advice from the apparatus side says keep it short, since readers skip it; advice from the story side says it must be a real scene with a real want. Each is right about its half. The demand for meaning has a second source. Peter Rabinowitz’s Before Reading (1987) describes the rules of notice , conventions that tell a reader which parts of a text to treat as significant, the strongest of which concern privileged position : titles, first and last sentences and the openings and closes of chapters carry weight automatically. A prologue is privileged twice, as the beginning of the book and as a bounded unit with its own first and last sentences. Every detail in it is read as a promise, and a detail never redeemed costs more there than on page 100, where it would pass as texture. Why does a prologue that shows the end change the whole book? Meir Sternberg’s Expositional Modes and Temporal Ordering in Fiction (1978) treats exposition, the antecedents a reader needs, as a problem of distribution, and the prologue is the limit case of delivering them all in advance. His more useful distinction is between suspense , uncertainty about what will happen, and curiosity , uncertainty about what has happened. A prolepsis (Greek for “anticipation”), the telling of a later event before an earlier one, shifts the balance: a prologue that shows the house burning reduces suspense about whether it burns and creates curiosity about how and why, so that the whole main narrative becomes an approach to a known destination. A book whose pleasures lie in causes gains from that trade, and a book whose pleasures lie in outcomes is damaged by it. Frank Kermode’s The Sense of an Ending (1967) explains why the trade also buys patience. People make sense of time through fictions of concord , structures in which a middle is intelligible because it lies between a beginning and an end that belong together. A prologue that frames an ending promises concord in advance, and a reader who has been shown the destination will tolerate a slower approach. The promise binds, however: a book that installs a frame and never completes it has broken a commitment the reader was given no reason to doubt. Why does a mis-pitched prologue damage the pages after it? Solomon Asch’s experiments on impression formation (1946) found that the same information in a different order produces different judgements, because earlier items govern how later ones are read. Menakhem Perry’s “Literary Dynamics” (1979) carried the finding into reading as the primacy effect : readers build a hypothesis from the first material and fit later material to it, resisting revision. A prologue is the first material, and the frame it installs is the frame through which Chapter One is read. A prologue that promises a thriller makes a quiet family novel read for its first hundred pages as a thriller that has stalled. Why does a prologue fade, and what keeps it alive? Catherine Emmott’s Narrative Comprehension (1997) describes readers as building a contextual frame for each situation, a running representation that binds characters to a place and a time, and as keeping one frame primed while others lie dormant. Returning to a dormant frame requires the reader to reinstate it, and this chapter calls the effort the reinstatement cost . A prologue’s frame is built in a few pages and suspended at once, so it is the thinnest frame in the book and the one held longest. Applying Emmott’s model to prologues is this chapter’s inference, not her finding, but it predicts what readers describe: a prologue first recalled near the end of a book costs more than one touched at intervals, and some readers turn back to reread it at the moment it matters, which is the cost made visible. The Mechanism draws the practical conclusion. How old is the suspicion of prologues? The form is older than the novel. Aristotle’s Poetics defines the tragic prologue by position, as everything before the chorus enters, and Euripides filled it with a speaker who set out the antecedents directly. The sonnet before Romeo and Juliet gives away the ending; the Chorus of Henry V instructs the audience how to watch; the eighteenth-century novel opened with editors vouching for found papers; and the genre prologue of fantasy and the thriller became standard in the second half of the twentieth century. The hostility a contemporary writer meets is recent, Anglo-American and largely commercial. Its likely causes are institutional: agents and editors who decide on a submission within its first pages, as Noah Lukeman reports in The First Five Pages (2000); a sample of three chapters, of which a prologue uses part; and genre prologues so uniform that the label predicted the contents. That “readers skip prologues” is repeated far more often than it is measured, and this chapter knows of no survey that settles how many do. The pressures are real, and a writer who submits a prologue pays a tax she should know about. They are not a theory of narrative, and the Coda keeps the two apart. See also: the Reference theory , with Genette’s three variables, the accessus of the medieval schoolroom, the eighteenth century’s editorial fictions, Said on origin and beginning, and the history tabulated by period.

title: 4. The Taxonomy
text: The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1) sets out the domains of purpose , the registers in which a unit of narrative can change something: plot, character, theme and texture, with a proposed fifth, the relational domain, which The Dialogue Exchange (Chapter 3) adopts. A prologue adapts that list. Plot, character and theme keep their meanings. World, as The Descriptive Detail (Chapter 4) uses it, replaces texture, since register and scale are what a separated opening most often offers. The relational domain seldom applies, because a prologue usually comes before the relations the book will follow, and where it does apply it is audited under character. The fifth domain is the prologue’s own: the reader contract, the deal struck with the reader before the story proper begins. Each domain is stated here as what distance makes available, not as a job any opening might do. That is what turns the higher bar into an audit: a writer who can name the domains her prologue serves can usually name what the separation buys. Plot: what only distance permits A prologue serves plot when it delivers events the main narrative’s own sequence cannot reach, because they happened too early, too far away, or to someone the protagonist never meets. Four carriers do this work, and they solve different problems. The framed ending shows an outcome first and trades suspense for curiosity. The unwitnessable incident is an event the book needs and no character in the main narrative could have seen. The running clock is a threat already moving before Chapter One. Compressed antecedent is history at a scale no scene can hold, generations or centuries. The unwitnessable incident is the plot domain’s least contestable justification. If an event matters and nobody in the main narrative witnessed it, the writer can have it reported later at second hand, invent a witness, produce a document, or give it a compartment before the story starts, and the fourth option is what a prologue is for.
