The prologue of Dan Brown’s The Da Vinci Code (2003) is a clean case: the curator Jacques Saunière, shot in the Louvre’s Grand Gallery by an attacker who wants a secret he guards, spends his last minutes leaving a coded message, among the paintings and on his own body, for whoever finds him. No one in the main narrative sees those minutes, and the book’s first puzzle is what he did with them. Compressed antecedent is the carrier most likely to fail, because it is nearest to pure exposition; generational history that a grandmother could tell in the novel’s twelfth chapter does not need a prologue, only that chapter. Under-delivery is the vague portent, a figure watching and something was coming , which delivers nothing the main narrative could not deliver better. Over-delivery is a prologue holding the book’s most dramatic event, after which everything is descent. Character: the absent vantage A prologue serves character when it occupies a consciousness the main narrative cannot enter, because that person is dead, absent, unknown to the protagonist or barred from viewpoint. Its carriers are early access to a mind the reader will not revisit, dramatic irony (knowledge given to the reader and withheld from the cast), a formative scene the protagonist never learns of, and the retrospective self, a narrator placed after the events, as in the labelled Prologue of Ralph Ellison’s Invisible Man (1952), spoken from a cellar lit by stolen electricity after everything the novel narrates. The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13) shows that moving a reader between minds costs something, and a prologue spends that cost in advance, on a person the reader may never occupy again. A reader who attaches in the prologue and is moved to a different protagonist can feel Chapter One as a demotion. There are two remedies. Make the prologue’s viewpoint plainly not the protagonist’s, by a voice older, remoter or more formal than the main narrative’s. Or make the loss the point: the household novel’s father is a person the reader is meant to lose, because the book is about a family losing him. The second is the stronger move, since a prologue whose viewpoint is the one the book is about not having justifies its separation without further argument. Under-delivery is the viewpoint that is a function, a nameless watcher who exists to see a battle; over-delivery is a prologue mind so vivid that the real protagonist cannot compete, which may mean the book has chosen the wrong protagonist. World: the register shift A prologue serves world when it speaks in a mode the main narrative cannot sustain, mythic, choric, documentary or panoramic, to set scale, rules or texture before the book narrows to one person’s view. The distinction that matters is between register and information. A register shift changes how the book speaks; an info-dump is a quantity of what it says. The substitution test separates them: rewrite the prologue’s content in Chapter One’s voice. If it survives with nothing lost but length, it was information and belongs inside. If it becomes flat or impossible, because a close third person cannot say for three hundred years the valley was empty , the register was doing the work. J. R. R. Tolkien’s “Concerning Hobbits”, the prologue to The Lord of the Rings (1954), is open exposition, hobbit customs and pipe-weed and a note on sources, and it survives the test because its antiquarian voice is itself a character whose premise the book sustains. Under-delivery is heightened language with nothing behind it; over-delivery is a register the book never returns to, so that the novel reads as a falling-off from its own first page. Theme: the promise A prologue serves theme when it states the book’s central image or question in distilled form before the narrative complicates it. The domain is the cheapest to serve well, a single figure costing two hundred words and paying across four hundred pages, and the most expensive to serve badly, since a thesis stated in advance turns the novel into its illustration. Two disciplines follow. State the question, not the answer: a prologue that says the book is about how families keep secrets has told the reader what to conclude, and one that shows a man deciding not to say something has posed a question. And choose an image you are willing to repeat, because the prologue’s image is the most heavily marked object in the book. Middlemarch ’s Prelude does both in three paragraphs: Saint Theresa as a child setting out for martyrdom, then the question of what becomes of later Theresas who find no form for their ardour, a figure the Finale returns to. The reader contract: tone, patience and protocol The reader contract is the domain unique to the prologue’s position, and the one most often served alone, which is the shape readers and editors have learned to distrust. Its carriers are a declaration of tone, patience purchased, felt stakes (a dread the characters do not share) and a reading protocol (instructions about the status of what follows). Patience purchased is the most defensible and least discussed. A domestic novel whose engine takes sixty pages to start has a real problem, and one legitimate solution is to show the reader, before Chapter One, that something is coming, so that Chapter One can afford to be quiet. The household prologue works mainly in the felt-stakes mode. The opening Chorus of Henry V (1599) is pure protocol: it narrates nothing and tells the audience what imaginative work the play requires of them, which no first scene could do without breaking its fiction. A proposed sixth: the authority domain Some prologues resist all five domains. Dracula (1897) opens with an unsigned note saying how a set of papers was arranged and that they are contemporary records. Frankenstein opens with letters from a man who will relay a dying stranger’s story. Yann Martel’s Life of Pi (2001) opens with an Author’s Note in which a novelist, a fictional version of Martel, is told of Pi Patel in a coffee house in Pondicherry and promises to set the story down in Pi’s own voice. None of these sets much tone or advances a plot. What they do is make a claim about how the book knows what it tells. The chapter proposes the authority domain : a prologue serves it when it establishes on whose authority the book’s account rests, by supplying a provenance, a transmitting intermediary, a documentary basis, or an account of the limits of what can be known. Two arguments support separating it. It has its own failure, a frame narrator installed and then ignored while the book narrates scenes that narrator could not know, which readers feel as a slippage no other domain names. And it requires exteriority more plainly than any other domain, since a close third-person chapter cannot pause to explain where its own account came from without becoming a different book. The objections are serious. The domain may be world (a documentary register) and reader contract (a reading protocol) seen together; it belongs largely to a tradition running from Defoe’s editors to the Gothic and its revivals, so most contemporary novels make no such claim; and Genette’s typology of fictive and authentic prefaces already describes the apparatus more finely. The chapter adopts it for diagnosis on the ground that its failure is real and otherwise unnamed, and concedes that it is bound to certain forms in a way the other five are not. The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13), whose epistemological domain concerns who in a book knows what, rules that it is not a domain of the viewpoint grant and leaves it here, as a domain of the separated unit: the authority domain claims that a vantage suffices, and the epistemological domain shows that none does. Life of Pi is the test case among the worked analyses. How many domains? Not all six, and the model is misused when read that way. Two or three is the normal shape of a prologue that survives revision. Some domains exclude one another in practice: installed dramatic irony forecloses a book whose pleasure is discovery shared with its protagonist. And the domains carry unequal weight for the higher bar. The unwitnessable incident and the authority domain clear it almost automatically, because their work is impossible from inside; the reader contract clears it least easily, because tone can nearly always be set in Chapter One. A prologue serving one strong domain is better placed than one serving three weak ones, and the audit’s output is a decision, keep, absorb or relocate, not a score. See also: the Reference domains , with the carriers tabulated for each domain and further illustrations ( Romeo and Juliet , Rebecca , The Canterbury Tales , Don Quixote , The Master and Margarita , The Name of the Rose ).

title: 5. The Mechanism
text: Every prologue opens a gap between itself and the story that follows. What separates a working prologue from an orphaned one is whether the main narrative does something with the gap. Distance and its four axes Distance is how far a prologue sits from Chapter One, measured along four axes: an earlier or later time, a different place, a viewpoint the reader will not hold again soon, and a register the main narrative does not share. The axes open different gaps and are closed by different means, so the table below is the one place in the chapter where they are set side by side. Axis What it buys How it is normally closed Characteristic failure Time Compressed antecedent, dramatic irony, a framed ending The narrative reaches the prologue’s moment, or explains it A rendezvous the reader waits for and never gets Place Scale, an off-page threat, a second front A character reaches the place, or its consequences arrive A decorative location that never matters Viewpoint The absent vantage, access to a dead or opposing mind The viewpoint returns, or its traces are recognised in what others find A consciousness the reader attached to and lost Register Protocol, lore, documentary authority The register recurs, or its claims are cashed in the ordinary voice A book that reads as a falling-off from its opening Most prologues use more than one axis, and one of them carries the load. The household prologue is distant in time (three days before the father stopped answering the phone), in viewpoint (his) and slightly in register (a retrospective formality). The load-bearing axis is viewpoint: any flashback could cross the time gap, but nothing in the main narrative can recover his vantage. Naming that axis tells the writer what the closing must deliver. The axes also differ in what it costs to leave them open. An open register gap is often tolerable, since a reader accepts that a book had an overture; an open viewpoint gap is the most expensive, because the reader built a mind into a contextual frame and had it withdrawn. Closing the distance Closing the distance is the point or points at which the main narrative catches up with, recontextualises, completes or deliberately refuses to close what the prologue opened. There are four modes, and they are not ranked; each suits a different book. In total closure the narrative reaches the prologue’s moment and completes it: Frankenstein returns to Walton’s ship at the end, and the pilot of Breaking Bad (AMC, 2008), which opens on Walt White in a gas mask in an RV in the desert, recording a message to his family as sirens approach, goes back to his fiftieth birthday and catches up with the desert by the episode’s end. In fragmentary closure elements of the prologue recur singly across the book and are recognised each time, as the Chorus of Henry V returns before every act. In recontextualisation the narrative never reaches the prologue but changes what it meant, so that a second reading differs from the first. In deliberate non-closure , which the Reference calls the held note , the gap is held open for good, as Henry James never returns to the fireside that frames The Turn of the Screw (1898). Deliberate and negligent non-closure look the same on the page, and three signals tell them apart: the book withholds other closures too, so that open ends are its policy; the non-closure follows from its subject, as the unresolvable governess’s tale would be falsified by a return to the confident fireside; and the prologue is about something that cannot be got back. Where none of the three applies, the honest diagnosis is a distance the book forgot. Genette’s Narrative Discourse (1972; translated by Jane E. Lewin, 1980) supplies the vocabulary for the two ways a prologue can plant what it will close. Advance notice ( annonce ) announces what is to come and is closed by arrival: the event occurs. The seed ( amorce ) is a detail that passes as insignificant and acquires significance only in retrospect, and it is closed by recognition: the reader meets it again and understands. The prologue of Stieg Larsson’s The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo (2005; translated by Reg Keeland, 2008) is built on a seed. An old man receives a pressed flower on his eighty-second birthday, as he has every year since his niece disappeared, and he takes it for a taunt from her killer. The flowers return when Henrik Vanger tells the journalist Mikael Blomkvist their history, and they are closed when the investigation finds the sender: Harriet herself, alive, telling him so in the only way she dared. A reader who meets the flower in the prologue carries a question the whole investigation answers. The argument for fragmentary closure Craft advice, where it addresses the closing at all, tends to assume a single late reveal: the prologue’s meaning is held back and delivered in one place near the end. That is usually the weaker structure, and Emmott’s frame model, in How It Works, explains why. A single late reveal asks the reader to reinstate the prologue’s thin frame after the longest interval, at the point where the reinstatement costs most. Fragmentary closure inverts the schedule. A series of small returns re-primes the frame at the cost of a clause each time, confirms that the prologue is being used, makes each later recognition cheaper, and spreads the risk, since a reader who misses one fragment can catch the next. Three rules follow. Plant three to five recoverable specifics, objects and phrases rather than moods, since a reader can recognise a fountain pen and cannot recognise an atmosphere. Bring the first fragment back within the first quarter of the book, where its job is reassurance, not payoff. And vary the weight, from an unremarked mention to a noticed one to a scene that turns on the object. The single reveal is right in two cases: when the prologue’s meaning is the book’s central secret, which fragments would give away, and when the effect depends on the reader having forgotten. The conditional form is the useful one. A prologue meant to be carried, as a dread, an irony or a knowledge the characters lack, should be closed in fragments, because its effect is continuous. A prologue meant to be sprung should be closed once, and the writer should shorten the interval instead of lengthening the suspense. Most prologues, examined, turn out to be of the first kind and to have been built as if they were of the second. Types, and the test of substitution The Reference chapter tabulates fourteen recognisable types of prologue. A few recur in revision. The proleptic flash-forward is strongest when it shows an aftermath, not the climax: a narrator in exile remembering reveals that something happened without saying what, and buys concord at little cost in suspense. The victim’s last hour, a character followed until a death, works when the victim is a person and fails when the victim is a function. The frame narrator’s reception and the editorial note serve the authority domain. The false prologue relies on a misreading the reader makes, such as taking a scene for the beginning when it is the end. The chapter proposes a fourteenth type, the last ordinary day : the routine that immediately precedes a rupture the main narrative will investigate, in which nothing happens and the dread comes wholly from the reader’s knowledge that the ordinariness is ending. It contains no event to be arrived at, only objects to be recognised, so it is the type that most needs fragmentary closure. The household prologue is one. The taxonomy is for substitution, not classification. A prologue that is not working is often the right material in the wrong shape, and rewriting it as another type that keeps its load-bearing axis and its domains shows what each shape buys. Substituting the last ordinary day for the victim’s last hour suits a book about aftermath, not pursuit; substituting an editorial note for a deep-historical overture suits material that is information, not experience. Substitution often ends in absorption, which is a success of the method, not a failure of the draft. Multiplicity as evidence Multiplicity , in The Purposes of a Scene ’s sense (Chapter 1), is a unit’s doing several jobs at once. In an opening it is an economy; in a prologue it is evidence. One domain can always be explained away, since tone can be set inside Chapter One and a fact delivered later, but three domains braided into the same three hundred words are hard to relocate without scattering them across three places, and the writer can then say what would be lost. As a rule of thumb, a prologue serving one domain is suspect, two is defensible if one requires exteriority, and three is the normal shape of one that survives revision. The multiplying work lives in four places: the choice of moment (the household prologue’s three days before, not the day itself), the objects handled, the axis chosen, and the last sentence. That sentence is the final and most heavily weighted position of a bounded unit, and a prologue that spends it on a portentous half-line has wasted its strongest place. See also: the Reference treatment of distance and its closing , with all fourteen types, a table of substitutions and the historical drift of the axes; the Reference multiplicity , with Hurston’s first sentence annotated and the domain audit.

title: 6. Diagnostic Tests
text: The nine tests are for revision, and most need the finished manuscript, since the closing, the plants and the genre contract cannot be judged from the prologue alone. Run tests 1 to 4 (Higher bar, Absorption, Label and Axis) first: they decide whether the prologue should be separate at all, and there is no point tuning the register of a passage that belongs in Chapter One’s third paragraph. Record a sentence, not a verdict. The output of the whole set is a three-way decision, keep separate, absorb or relocate, and very few prologues should simply be deleted, because the material is usually good and only its compartment is wrong. Test 1 — Higher bar Can you complete “This must sit outside the main narrative because…” with an impossibility, not a preference? Failure. Real work, wrongly placed. Exception. Middlemarch , whose intrusive narrator could have asked the Prelude’s question in chapter 1. Test 2 — Absorption Write the material into Chapter One, then cut it entirely: what breaks each time? Failure. Nothing breaks, or only a hook is lost. Exception. The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo , whose flowers Henrik later explains to Blomkvist anyway. Test 3 — Label Would anything change if the prologue were headed Chapter One ? Failure. Chapter One in disguise. Exception. Their Eyes Were Watching God , whose overture works inside chapter 1. Test 4 — Axis Which of time, place, viewpoint and register carries the load, if any? Failure. No axis, or several incidental ones. Exception. The Breaking Bad pilot, distant only by weeks, on a screen where the cold open is free. Test 5 — Register Rewritten in Chapter One’s voice, does the material survive, go flat, or become impossible? Failure. Information, not register. Exception. The Da Vinci Code , whose prologue shares the book’s register and rests on viewpoint. Test 6 — Closing For each element the prologue opens, on what page does the book next touch it? Failure. A distance never closed. Exception. The Turn of the Screw , whose frame never resumes. Test 7 — Plants Which specifics recur, once or more, and which never? Failure. Unredeemed promises in a privileged position. Exception. The General Prologue to The Canterbury Tales , many of whose pilgrims never tell a tale. Test 8 — Skip Can a reader who starts at Chapter One follow the whole book, and what does she lose? Failure. Nothing lost, or something incomprehensible. Exception. “Concerning Hobbits”, skipped by many readers at a cost the book accepts. Test 9 — Genre contract Do the prologue, pages 40 to 60 and the last chapter share pitch, pace, mode and scale? Failure. False advertising. Exception. The Scarlet Letter , whose satirical essay precedes a tragic romance. Three refinements sharpen the tests. In test 1 (Higher bar), a completion that ends because it would not be as striking names a preference and counts as a failure; acceptable completions sound like because no one in the main narrative could have seen it or because the vantage belongs to someone dead before Chapter One . In test 6 (Closing), a viewpoint gap “closed” by the narrative reaching the right date is a mismatch: a viewpoint distance is closed by a viewpoint event, a time distance by arrival, a register distance by recurrence. In test 8 (Skip), the reader must be someone else, interviewed at page 100 and at the end, and the intended profile is nothing incomprehensible and something lost. Reading the results together Failures cluster, and the cluster points to the first move. Tests 1 (Higher bar) and 3 (Label) together mean a Chapter One in disguise: relabel and renumber, and nothing else is needed. Tests 1 (Higher bar) and 4 (Axis) together mean a strong scene in the wrong compartment: absorb it, using the inventory test 2 (Absorption) produced. Test 4 (Axis) alone means distance that costs without buying: collapse the prologue onto its load-bearing axis and expect to lose about a third of its length. Test 6 (Closing) alone means a distance the book forgot: build the closing, preferably in fragments, or absorb the material so that no gap needs closing, but do not add a late scene that explains it. Test 7 (Plants) alone means over-planting: cut specifics rather than inventing payoffs. A failure on test 8 (Skip) because something is incomprehensible means the book depends on a unit it has licensed the reader to skip: restate the essential fact in the main narrative, so that the prologue supplies first knowledge, not only knowledge. Test 9 (Genre contract) alone means false advertising, and it carries a warning. When a prologue and its book disagree, writers revise the book toward the prologue, because the prologue is more finished and often written last with the whole book in view. The direction is usually wrong. The prologue is a thousand words and the book a hundred thousand, and the smaller object is the one to change. See also: the Reference protocol , with ten tests (removal separated from absorption), their procedures, and a table of combined failures.

title: 7. Failure Patterns
text: Each pattern below fails through a mechanism, not a surface feature. Each ends with a published work that uses the feature successfully because the mechanism is absent. The prologue makes this easy to show, since the form’s best-known instances break its most confident rules: Romeo and Juliet ’s prologue gives away the plot, and “The Custom-House” runs to some fifty pages, opens a distance it never closes, and was republished by Hawthorne, against complaints, without the change of a word. The Reference chapter’s full catalogue has twelve patterns. Chapter One in disguise Symptom. The prologue shares the protagonist’s time, place, viewpoint and register, and was labelled Prologue because the writer was unsure the opening earned its place as Chapter One. Mechanism. No distance is open, so the label creates an expectation the material does not honour, and it tells the reader to hold at arm’s length a scene that is the beginning of the book. The label is a hedge: it feels like a structural choice and is the postponement of one. In this edition’s judgement it is the commonest pattern in draft manuscripts, which is why the blanket advice to cut a prologue so often helps. Remedy. Test 3 (Label), which is also the cure: relabel, renumber and read. Exception. Ellison’s Invisible Man has a labelled Prologue in the narrator’s own voice and register. Only time differs, since the Prologue speaks from the cellar after everything, and that one axis carries the novel’s architecture: the label tells the reader that the voice already knows where the story goes, so the young man’s naivety in chapter 1 reads as naivety. One axis is enough when it does the work. False advertising Symptom. A violent, hooky or high-stakes prologue whose pitch the book never matches: a murder before a quiet domestic novel, a chase before three hundred pages of interiority. Mechanism. The primacy effect turns every later page into a deviation from the promised book. The separation makes it worse than the borrowed hook of an ordinary opening, because the label makes the promise deliberate and the privileged position makes every detail in it load-bearing. It is the same violation as the ending’s mismatched final note, committed at the other boundary. Remedy. Test 9 (Genre contract), run on pitch, pace, mode and scale; then revise the prologue, not the book. Exception. Wuthering Heights opens on Lockwood, a fatuous tenant whose chapters promise a light comedy of manners and misjudged neighbours, and what follows is a novel of extreme violence and longing. The mismatch is the method: the distance between Lockwood’s register and what he blunders into is what the book is about. A mismatch the book uses is a structure; one it has not noticed is a mis-sold book. The anonymous-victim cold open Symptom. A prologue focalised through someone murdered at its end, usually unnamed, usually a woman, in a book about the detective who will investigate. Mechanism. The reader is asked to occupy a mind that exists only to be destroyed. With no future it has no want beyond survival and no properties worth individuating, and readers sense a demand for feeling that has not been earned. The type’s long use is a second mechanism, since a label that predicts its contents has stopped working as a device, and a writer choosing it should know that it has made a woman’s terror a standard opening unit in a great deal of fiction. Remedy. Individuate the victim, with a want unrelated to her death and a specific that returns later; or substitute the last ordinary day, which gives dread without a death. Exception. The Da Vinci Code follows its victim to his death and succeeds because Saunière is not a camera position: he acts, choosing in his last minutes how to pass on what he knows, and his acts become the book’s first clues, so the investment the prologue asks for is repaid by the whole plot. The prologue that spoils Symptom. The prologue reveals the outcome: who dies, who is guilty, how it ends. Mechanism. Disclosure converts suspense into curiosity, which destroys a book whose value lies in outcomes and serves one whose value lies in causes. The failure is conditional on what the book is for; there is no general prohibition on disclosure. Remedy. Ask which engine the book runs on. If curiosity, disclose freely; if suspense, disclose an aftermath instead, which promises a shape without answering the question. Exception. The sonnet before Romeo and Juliet gives away the feud, the deaths and the reconciliation in fourteen lines, and the play’s pathos depends on it: every hopeful line is heard by an audience that knows. Markus Zusak’s The Book Thief , among the worked analyses, does the same in a novel. A prologue may spoil anything the book is not for. The unresolved distance Symptom. The prologue opens a real gap, a time jump, a viewpoint, a frame, and the book never returns to it. Mechanism. A contextual frame is built, primed briefly and suspended for good, and the reader holds it at a cost, expecting a return that never comes. Nothing feels wrong while reading; the failure arrives at the end, as a sense that the book was longer at the front than it needed to be, which readers report as “the prologue was unnecessary”. Writers commit it because they know the connection and cannot see that it was never written down. Remedy. Test 6 (Closing), as a literal inventory with page numbers; then build the closing, preferably in fragments, or absorb the material. Exception. “The Custom-House” opens a distance on all four axes, two centuries, another building, a narrator absent from the romance and an essayist’s register, and closes none of it. It works, so far as critics agree that it does, because the essay is about a man who cannot enter the past he holds in his hands, and returning to him would assert a continuity the book denies. Whether it is design or indulgence is still argued, which is the honest status of the exception. See also: the Reference catalogue , with the info-dump prologue, the redundant prologue, the unfollowable mythic overture, the orphaned voice, the prologue written to fix a slow Chapter One, the prologue that is really an epigraph and the threshold pile-up, and a table from symptom to mechanism.

title: 8. Worked Analyses
text: Three close readings, a short screen reading and the household revision case. Each reading names the type, the load-bearing axis, the domains served and the mode of closing. Mary Shelley, Frankenstein (1818): the frame as prologue The novel opens with four letters from Robert Walton, an explorer bound for the Arctic, to his sister in England. His ship is caught in ice; his crew see a gigantic figure driving a dog-sledge across the floes; the next morning they take aboard a second traveller, half-dead, who has been pursuing the first. That stranger is Victor Frankenstein, and his story, which contains the creature’s, fills the book until Walton’s letters resume at the end, when Victor dies aboard and the creature comes to mourn over his body. The type is the frame narrator’s reception, and the load-bearing axis is viewpoint: Walton is the listener, and his letters are the only position from which the whole chain of telling can be seen. The letters serve five domains. Plot: they frame the ending, since the reader meets Victor at the end of his life before learning how he reached it. Character: Walton’s ambition, his wish to go where no one has gone, mirrors Victor’s and makes him the reader’s warning in advance. Theme: knowledge pursued past its limit is posed as a question in a man who has not yet paid for it. Reader contract: the Arctic letters buy patience for Victor’s long, undramatic Genevan childhood, chapters of family, schooling and friendship that would be slow without the ice in front of them. Authority: Walton’s letters are the transmitting record, written, he says, from the stranger’s own account. The closing is total, since the frame is re-entered and completed, and it is also what turns Walton back south when his crew demand it: the one person in the book who hears the story and changes course. A prologue that buys patience for a slow opening is the usual failure of the form; this one succeeds because it does four other things as well. Markus Zusak, The Book Thief (2005): the prologue that spoils, kept The Book Thief is narrated by Death, and its prologue, “A Mountain Range of Rubble”, is his account of the three times he saw the girl he calls the book thief: under a white sky, beside a railway line where her younger brother died on a train; under a black sky, when an enemy pilot crashed near her town; and under a red sky, when the bombs fell on Himmel Street and she was left in the rubble of everyone she loved. The book then begins with the first of these and spends the length of the book reaching the third. The type is the proleptic flash-forward, and the novel takes the riskier of its two forms, showing the catastrophe itself, not only its aftermath. By the chapter’s account it should fail as the prologue that spoils, since a reader who knows Himmel Street will be destroyed has lost all suspense about it. It succeeds because the book runs on curiosity and dread, not on suspense. The reader watches a girl learn to read, steal books and find a family on a street she has been told will be destroyed, and every ordinary scene is coloured by that knowledge, which is the felt-stakes carrier of the reader contract at full strength. The load-bearing axis is register: Death’s voice, wry, weary and given to stating outcomes in advance, is one no character in the book could supply, and it goes on disclosing, announcing deaths before they arrive, a habit readers argue over. The closing is total, since the narrative reaches the red sky, and it is extended by an epilogue in which Death meets Liesel again at her own death, as an old woman in Sydney, and gives back the manuscript she lost in the bombing. The prologue made one promise, that the three meetings would be told, and the book keeps it in the form in which it was made. Yann Martel, Life of Pi (2001): the authority domain Life of Pi opens with an Author’s Note written in the voice of a fictional version of its author. A novelist whose last book has died on him travels to India, and in a coffee house in Pondicherry an old man, Francis Adirubasamy, tells him he has a story that will make him believe in God. The novelist finds Pi Patel in Toronto and promises to tell the story in Pi’s own voice. The novel then gives Pi’s account of 227 days in a lifeboat with a Bengal tiger, broken by passages in which the novelist describes visiting the grown Pi; and it ends with a transcript of two Japanese officials interviewing Pi, who offers them a second, brutal version of the same voyage without animals, and asks which story they prefer. The type is the frame narrator’s reception crossed with the editorial note, and the domain is authority. The Author’s Note establishes a provenance (Adirubasamy, then Pi), a transmitting intermediary (the novelist, who claims to have changed only the telling), and a promise about belief that the book will test. It sets little tone and advances no plot, and the five-domain model can file it only as reader contract, which misses what it does. The closing is recontextualisation. The ending does not return to Pondicherry; it puts a second account beside the first and leaves the reader holding the Note’s promise, that the story would make her believe, as a question about which story she has chosen. A prologue that claimed no authority would have nothing for the ending to unsettle. This is the case for the authority domain as a separate category, and it also shows the objection: the Note’s work could be described as world and reader contract combined, and only the ending shows why that description falls short. A screen reading: Saving Private Ryan (1998) Steven Spielberg’s film opens on an old man walking among the graves of an American war cemetery in Normandy, his family behind him. He kneels, the camera closes on his eyes, and the film cuts to the landing on Omaha Beach in 1944 and to Captain Miller. Many viewers take the old man for Miller remembering. Miller dies in the final battle, and only then does the film return to the cemetery and show that the old man is Ryan, the private Miller’s squad was sent to bring home, standing at Miller’s grave. The type is the false prologue, which depends on an error the viewer makes; the closing is total and recontextualising at once, since the return to the cemetery completes the frame and changes whose memory the film has been. It keeps the rule for the type: the misreading is rewarded without being required, because a viewer who never took the old man for Miller still has the film’s ending. The household revision case: the prologue The household novel’s prologue is set three days before the father stopped answering the phone, in his viewpoint, in the shop. The canon fixes what it must plant: the till counted twice, a boy at the glass waved off, the sign not flipped to CLOSED, the register drawer that sticks on the K, and the good pen put into his coat pocket instead of left by the till. The main narrative belongs to his three adult children, Elena, Nadia and Dov, in the July after his death. Version A, the draft. He waited until the street was empty before he pulled the blind down. Then he crossed to the register, opened the drawer that stuck — it always stuck, it had stuck for eleven years — and took out the folded papers he had put there in March, and did not read them again, because he already knew. There had been a car on the corner for three evenings now. He had counted. A man in it who did not get out. He carried the papers through to the back, where the sink was, and he burned them one at a time over the basin, holding each until the flame reached his fingers, and when the last of it had gone down the drain he ran the tap for a long time. Then he put the good pen in his coat pocket, where nobody would find it, and turned the sign in the window to CLOSED, and stood in the dark of his own shop, listening. Diagnosis. It is competent prose and a structural failure. It passes the higher bar (test 1) for the wrong reason: nobody in Chapter One knows any of it, because none of it is the book’s material. The register is a thriller’s, surveillance and burned evidence, set before a quiet family novel, so test 5 (Register) finds a register the main voice would contradict, and test 9 (Genre contract) fails on pitch, pace, mode and scale. Test 6 (Closing) fails outright, since the papers are ash, the car never returns and the book contains no conspiracy. Test 7 (Plants) finds six unredeemed specifics in under two hundred words: the blind, the car, the man, the papers, the basin and the tap. By the primacy effect the reader builds a thriller from these lines, and reads the book through it: Nadia not answering her brother’s calls becomes a cover-up, Dov’s silence in the doorway complicity, the changed locks a security measure. And the draft spends the household’s material. The pen goes into the pocket where nobody would find it , which turns care into concealment and destroys the ending the book is built toward, and the sign is turned to CLOSED, when the book needs a man who did not finish his day. Version B, the revision. Three days before he stopped answering the phone, he stood at the register and counted the till twice, though it came out the same both times. Outside, a boy about the age his son used to be knocked on the glass, mouthing something about the sign in the window, and he waved him off without looking up. He would remember, later — if there was a later he’d know how to measure — that he’d meant to flip the sign to CLOSED and hadn’t. That the register drawer stuck on the K. That he had, for reasons he could not have explained to his wife, put the good pen in his coat pocket instead of leaving it by the till, the way he always did. In case, he would have said, if she had asked; and he could not have said in case of what. What the revision did. It changed the type, from the victim’s last hour with the death withheld to the last ordinary day, which suits a book about aftermath. It deleted the invented plot and kept what happened on the day, which the writer knew and had avoided because it was quiet. It turned announcements into seeds: a till counted twice, a boy waved off, a sign not flipped, a drawer that sticks, a pen in a pocket. It restored the pen’s meaning, care and not concealment, and gave the last sentence to the pen and to two words of a reason the father cannot finish. In case is a fragment of the line he will say to Nadia the second time he loses the pen, in case anyone ever needs to check , which the reader hears in full only in the cutaway Backstory and Flashback (Chapter 7) analyses and which closes the book in The Ending (Chapter 16). The domain audit finds plot (an unwitnessable day), character (the father’s small private dread), world (the shop’s working rhythm), theme (counting set against unmeasured time) and the reader contract (a dread carried into every domestic scene); plot, character and the reader contract require exteriority. The closing is fragmentary. The drawer returns at about a quarter of the book, when Elena works it free on the third try and smells fresh ink, and its job is reassurance. The pen returns at about two-thirds, when Nadia finds it in the coat, and the reader knows how it got there. The line lands at the end, when the three of them read the ledger together. A single late reveal would ask the reader to recall, at page 340, a frame primed for one page three hundred pages earlier; three fragments keep it warm, and each is an object or a phrase a reader can recognise. What the revision has not solved. It is quiet, and quietness is a submission risk: an agent reading at speed may not reach the second sentence, a cost imposed by an institution that the writer should pay knowingly. The retrospective He would remember, later grants the father a foreknowledge he cannot have, and a reader may take it as the author being ominous, the passage’s one unearned effect. In case is either the right size or a hair too large: if a reader hears the line coming in Backstory and Flashback (Chapter 7) before Nadia does, the cutaway loses some of its surprise and gains a recognition, and only a reader new to the book can say which. And the boy at the glass and the sign never flipped are planted in a privileged position and redeemed nowhere in the book as it stands; they stay open on purpose, alongside the mother’s silence, unless the ending decides otherwise, and an editor applying test 7 (Plants) will ask about both. See also: the Reference analyses , with Wuthering Heights , “The Custom-House”, Don Quixote , Their Eyes Were Watching God , The Master and Margarita , Dracula and The Handmaid’s Tale , and the household case with its full test table.

title: 9. Checklist and Exercises
text: Revision checklist Position Can I complete “This must sit outside the main narrative because…” with an impossibility? Have I tried absorbing the material into Chapter One, and relocating it in the main timeline, and listed what broke? Would anything change if the prologue were headed Chapter One ? Distance Which axis carries the load, and are the others costing more than they buy? Does the main narrative close the distance on that axis, by the means the axis requires? If the distance stays open, is that the book’s policy, its subject, or an oversight? Domains Which domains does the prologue serve, and which of them require exteriority? If the authority domain is served, does the book honour the frame it installs? Plants Which specifics recur, and on which pages? Does the first fragment return within the first quarter of the book? Is the last sentence a held note, or a portentous half-line? Contract Do the prologue, pages 40 to 60 and the last chapter share pitch, pace, mode and scale? Can a reader who skips the prologue follow the whole book while still losing something? Exercises The sentence. Write “This must sit outside the main narrative because…” for your prologue three times, with three different endings. Strike any that name a preference. If none survives, the prologue is a candidate for absorption. The absorption. Write your prologue’s material into Chapter One as a paragraph, a memory, a document or a line of dialogue, and separately relocate it as a scene in the main timeline. List what each version could not carry across. The list is your case for the separation, or against it. The audit. Beside each sentence of the prologue mark the domains it serves (plot, character, world, theme, reader contract, authority), then mark each I if the job could be done inside the main narrative and X if it requires exteriority. Justify every X in a sentence beginning “This cannot be done from inside Chapter One because…” . The schedule. List every specific in the prologue and the page on which the book next touches it. Choose three to five to carry the closing, cut the rest, and place the first return within the first quarter. The substitution. Rewrite the prologue as two other types that keep its load-bearing axis: a last ordinary day for a victim’s last hour, an editorial note for an overture, a flash-forward to an aftermath for one to the climax. Compare what each buys and costs before choosing.

title: 10. Coda
text: The higher bar assumes a sceptical reader, one who must be persuaded that the detour was needed and who holds the separation against the book until it is justified. That reader exists, but she is not the only reader the form has had. An Elizabethan audience expected a prologue and would have marked its absence; a reader of the eighteenth-century novel expected an editor to say where the papers came from, because a book asserting invented events with no account of how they were known was not yet a settled convention; a reader who chooses a long fantasy has, by choosing it, accepted an overture that a general reader might refuse. Change the reader and the bar moves. The standard is real but it is not natural, and the distinction matters because the two uses of the bar lead to different revisions. As an instrument, the bar makes a writer state a choice that would otherwise be made by default: why this material, here, outside. Used that way it rarely removes a good prologue and often improves one, because the statement either holds or shows where the material belongs. Mistaken for a fact about narrative, it becomes the market’s suspicion in the language of craft, and it licenses the removal of prologues such as those before Romeo and Juliet , Frankenstein and Invisible Man , none of which would survive a rule against the form. The two pressures often point the same way, since a prologue that cannot say what its separation buys is usually both a weak prologue and a submission liability. When they diverge, the writer should know which one she is answering. A quiet prologue that serves the book and costs a sale is a cost she can choose to pay or to avoid by absorption; a loud one that wins the sale and misreads the book is a cost her readers pay for her. The tests in this chapter cannot decide between those, but they can make the decision visible as hers.

title: The Middle
text: Where a book’s possibilities are narrowed The Craft Behind the Story (Second Edition) — Chapter 11. Part III: The Architecture of the Whole. In brief. The middle is the long stretch between the commitment that ends a novel’s beginning and the movement that begins its ending, usually half the book or more, and it is where drafts most often lose their readers. A middle seldom sags because too little happens. It sags because what happens leaves the protagonist’s options, and the price of each, where they were, so that the same kind of setback arrives at the same stakes again. The chapter’s tools are the option list, which records what the protagonist could still do at the end of the beginning, at the midpoint and at the start of the ending, and the value-shift log, which finds the sequences that repeat each other. Use the chapter when readers say a book drags in the middle, when its middle sequences could be shuffled without loss, or when its ending feels like one choice among several. What you can do after this chapter Say where a middle begins and ends, and find the turns inside it. Distinguish a complication from an escalation, and a delay that changes the reader’s question from one that repeats it. Name the shape of a middle and the engine that carries its pressure. Use the option list to see whether the middle narrows the book towards its ending. Diagnose a sagging middle and choose a remedy that changes the terms rather than adding incident. Key terms Middle; Act Two; complication and escalation; narrowing and price; the option list; the value-shift log; the midpoint; false victory and false defeat; the mirror moment; pinch; the hermeneutic code and its delays; the dilatory space; short circuit; the clock; the six shapes of a middle (escalating chain, turned middle, stations middle, braided middle, accumulating middle, contained middle); the plateau; the episodic middle; the absent opposition; the holding pattern; the broken back. Each is defined at first use and collected in the consolidated glossary . Contents The first files say what the middle is and why it is hard to write, the central files how a middle generates pressure and how it fails to, and the last are for use at the desk. The Problem A household middle in which a great deal happens and nothing moves, and the chapter’s claim Definitions The middle, its boundaries and turns, and the terms around it How It Works Why a middle exists at all, why readers tolerate delay, where the conventions put the turns, and what the evidence says The Taxonomy Six shapes of middle, each named for the engine that carries its pressure The Mechanism Narrowing and price, the kinds of midpoint, and the proportions of a middle Diagnostic Tests Eight tests on one page, and how to read their failures together Failure Patterns Five recurrent failures, each with a work that commits it and succeeds Worked Analyses Pride and Prejudice , A Gentleman in Moscow , The Midnight Library and Groundhog Day , and the household revision case Checklist and Exercises The revision checklist and five exercises for your own draft Coda What the model assumes, and why the middle is where a book is decided A writer in revision can start at the diagnostic tests; a writer planning a book should read the mechanism first, because the option list is easier to build before the middle is drafted than to impose on it afterwards. The full treatment This is a new chapter, so the Reference layer holds a single full treatment rather than a corrected original: the theory at greater length, with Barthes’s delays set out one by one and the screenwriting conventions compared in a table, an extended catalogue of shapes and failure patterns, further analyses ( Catching Fire , The Seven Husbands of Evelyn Hugo , the second stage of Great Expectations and Squid Game ), the household middle in full and the sources. See also: The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1), whose value shift and redundancy test this chapter applies at the scale of the book; Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2), whose escalation treadmill is the plateau’s opposite failure; The Subplot (Chapter 14), for the braided middle; The Ending (Chapter 16), which inherits what the middle has or has not narrowed; Arc and Theme (Chapter 12), for the change in the protagonist that a middle usually carries.

title: 1. The Problem
text: A draft of the household novel has a middle that runs from the register drawer, about a quarter of the way through the book, to Dov’s chapter at about 78 per cent. By then the reader knows the situation. Four months after their father’s death, three adult children are reconstructing what he left: Elena, who has learned in Dov’s doorway that their mother changed the shop’s locks in March and wants to know why; Nadia, who counts things and has learned not to touch the coat on its hook in the flat above the shop; and Dov, who gave Elena the new key and kept the reason. At the drawer Elena has found the ledger, and seen her father’s hand stop at an entry of 9 March and a looser hand carry on. The draft’s middle then does this. Elena calls at the locksmith’s to ask who ordered the new locks; he tells her it was her mother and nothing more. Nadia counts the week’s receipts again, and lets Dov’s call ring out. Elena goes back to Dov’s door and asks again, and he tells her it is not his to explain. Nadia goes up to the flat, stands in front of the coat, and comes down without touching it. Elena drives to her mother’s street, parks, and leaves without knocking. Elena comes back to the shop to go on reading and finds the drawer empty, and rings Dov, who says he will explain when he can. Meanwhile, in two sentences of summary, Dov has been talking to an agent about the shop. Then Nadia finds the good pen in the coat’s pocket, at about two-thirds, and the book moves towards its climax. Every one of these is a scene in the sense The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1) gives the word, with a want, resistance and a change. An early reader’s note on the draft still says I lost the thread somewhere after the drawer , and the writer’s first response is to add something: a break-in at the shop, a row at the funeral tea, a new character. Each addition would be another event at the stakes the middle already has, and the reader’s complaint is not that too little happens. It is that the same thing happens. Elena’s sequences end where they began, with a question put and not answered, and Nadia’s end with a refusal kept. By the fourth of them a reader can predict the fifth. What Elena could do at a quarter of the way through (ask Dov, ask her mother, ask someone else, read the ledger) is what she can still do at two-thirds, less the ledger, and nothing has made any of it cost more. The one line of action that could close a door, Dov’s sale, runs off the page and touches no one until the end. This chapter calls the stretch of a novel between the commitment that ends its beginning and the movement that begins its ending the middle , and its claim is that middles fail by this mechanism far more often than by any shortage of incident. A middle sags when its events leave the protagonist’s options and their price unchanged, however many events there are; its work is to narrow what the book can still do until the ending is the move that remains, so each sequence in it should close a way forward or raise the cost of one. The claim has a consequence for revision that runs against instinct. The remedy for a slow middle is seldom more material, and is often less: the household’s draft middle needs no new events, since the sale, the empty drawer and Dov’s silence are already in it. They are in the wrong places and have no effect on anyone. The revision in Worked Analyses moves the sale’s deadline into the sisters’ lives, turns the empty drawer into a decision, and puts a turn at the centre of the book, so that each sequence takes something away from someone. It cuts three of the draft’s sequences, and what it adds, the sale’s deadline and Dov’s request to clear the flat, comes out of the sale the draft already had. The claim also explains why the middle is the part of a novel that writers most often call the hardest to write. A writer planning a book usually knows how it starts and roughly how it ends, and the middle is drafted as a way of getting from one to the other, so its sequences are written as transit. Transit has no direction of its own: every sequence in it is equally far from the end. This is a judgement from editorial practice rather than a measured finding, but it predicts the household draft’s symptom, a middle whose parts are interchangeable because none of them was written to change what comes after it. See also: the full treatment , on the middle’s place among the book’s recurring concepts; The Subplot (Chapter 14), for the occupational thread, a subplot given work to keep it present, which is the draft’s treatment of the sale.

title: 2. Definitions
text: The working definition The middle of a novel runs from the first commitment the beginning cannot take back to the point at which the ending’s movement starts. The first boundary is a change of state rather than a page: the protagonist has chosen, or been forced, into the line of action the book will follow, and the opening’s normal is no longer available. Screenwriting manuals call it the first turning point or the first plot point, and it is the moment at which the book’s question becomes specific. The second boundary is the start of the ending in the sense The Ending (Chapter 16) gives the word, the climax and its aftermath: the middle stops where the sequence that leads straight into the climax begins. Defined by its boundaries, the middle is usually the largest part of a book. In the three-act convention of screenwriting, the middle, Act Two, takes about half the running time, 60 pages of a 120-page screenplay in the most widely taught version. Novels vary more, and a middle of half to three-fifths of the book is common, but the proportion follows from where the commitments fall and is not a target. The household novel’s middle runs from the drawer at about a quarter to Dov’s chapter at about 78 per cent, so it occupies 78 − 25 = 53 per cent of the book. The turns inside it A middle is not a level stretch between two turns. It has turns of its own, and the one that carries most weight is the midpoint , a turn near the centre that changes the protagonist’s relation to the goal. It can change the goal itself, change what the protagonist knows about the goal, change the protagonist’s mode, from reacting to what the opposition does to acting against it, or reverse the protagonist’s fortune. The name records a convention of placement, and a midpoint at 40 or 60 per cent is still a midpoint if it divides the middle into a half that asks one question and a half that asks another. Two further words describe what happens between the turns. A complication is anything that stands in the protagonist’s way: an obstacle, a refusal, a delay. An escalation is a complication that changes what the protagonist can do or what doing it will cost. Every escalation complicates, but not every complication escalates, and the difference between the two is the subject of The Mechanism . Aristotle’s word for the part of a plot before its turning point, the desis or tying of the knot, covers both, which is one reason the distinction is easy to miss. Adjacent terms Several neighbouring words describe the same stretch from other angles. Act Two is the screen form’s name for it and brings the three-act model with it, which suits many novels and not all. Rising action is the English name for the second of the five parts in Gustav Freytag’s pyramid of dramatic structure, set out in How It Works , where the climax sits in the middle of the play rather than near its end. Sagging middle is a workshop term for the reader’s experience of a middle that has stopped moving; it names a symptom and not a cause, and a sagging middle can have any of the causes in Failure Patterns . The development , a term from music, is the central section of a movement in sonata form, in which themes stated in the opening section are broken up and carried through other keys before they return. It is a useful analogy, since a strong middle mostly works on material the beginning has already introduced, which is also why the middle is where the plants of The Ending ’s plant audit (Chapter 16) are maintained. What the chapter leaves to other chapters The escalation of a single sequence of scene and sequel belongs to Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2), and the alternation of plot lines across the middle to The Subplot (Chapter 14). The inner change a protagonist undergoes in the middle is traced across the book in Arc and Theme (Chapter 12); a midpoint that is a revelation is a reveal, and its management belongs to The Reveal (Chapter 15). A middle told out of chronological order belongs to Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture (Chapter 8). The middle volume of a trilogy or series belongs to Series and Genre (Chapter 17), and the order in which to revise the parts of a book belongs to The Structural Edit (Chapter 18). See also: the full treatment , with a table comparing where the screenwriting manuals place the middle’s boundaries and turns.

title: 3. How It Works
text: Only the theory the chapter’s method uses is set out here, and each strand begins with the practical question it answers. The full treatment gives each at greater length. Does the middle have a job of its own? A writer who thinks of the middle as the distance between a beginning and an end will fill it, and the question is whether it is anything more. The oldest answer is Aristotle’s. The Poetics says that a whole has a beginning, a middle and an end, and defines the middle as “that which follows something as some other thing follows it” (in S. H. Butcher’s translation, 1895). The definition is causal, not positional: a middle is identified by what it follows from and what follows from it, so a stretch of action that neither depends on what came before nor produces what comes after is not a middle on Aristotle’s terms, however central its pages. The same treatise draws the consequence. “Of all plots and actions the episodic are the worst,” it says, and an episodic plot is one “in which the episodes or acts succeed one another without probable or necessary sequence.” The test that follows, whether two parts of the middle could change places, is the reorder test in Diagnostic Tests . The second answer comes from the theatre. Gustav Freytag’s Die Technik des Dramas (1863), translated by Elias J. MacEwan as Technique of the Drama in the 1890s, describes a five-act tragedy as a pyramid in five parts: introduction, rise, climax, return or fall, and catastrophe. The climax stands at the centre, in the third act, and everything after it is consequence. Most modern novels put their climax late, so the pyramid fits them badly, but it records something the later models keep: the centre of a dramatic action is where its direction is decided, not where it waits. The midpoint of the modern manuals is what remains of Freytag’s central climax in a form that has moved its climax to the end. Why will a reader put up with waiting? The middle withholds what the reader wants to know, for most of the book, and the writer’s question is why a reader tolerates it and when the tolerance runs out. Roland Barthes’s S/Z (1970), translated by Richard Miller (1974), reads a Balzac story through five codes, one of which, the hermeneutic code , is the set of devices by which a text raises a question and delays its answer. Barthes names the delays: the snare, which points the reader the wrong way; the equivocation, which mixes truth and snare; the partial answer; the suspended answer, broken off once begun; and jamming, the admission that the question cannot be answered. Peter Brooks’s Reading for the Plot (1984) builds on this to describe the middle as a dilatory space , the stretch in which the end is postponed, and in a reading of Freud argues that its detours are necessary: without them the action reaches its end too soon, by a short circuit , and arrives at the wrong end, one the book has not prepared. The two accounts give the craft rule that the chapter uses throughout. Delay is the middle’s medium, and the question is never whether to delay but how. Barthes’s delays differ in what they do to the reader’s question. A partial answer changes it, since the reader now knows something and wants something else, and a snare changes it by sending the reader after the wrong thing. A delay of the same kind repeated, the question put and blocked and put again, leaves it where it was, and that is the delay readers experience as stalling. The household draft in The Problem delays by the same device five times. Where should the turns fall? Writers want to know where in the middle its turns belong, and the most detailed answers come from screenwriting manuals. Syd Field’s Screenplay (1979) divided a feature film into three acts, with Act Two, which he called the confrontation, filling the middle half. In The Screenwriter’s Workbook (1984) he added a midpoint, which he said he had found while studying Robert Towne’s screenplay for Chinatown , and his later accounts of the paradigm add a smaller turn in each half of Act Two, at about pages 45 and 75, which he called a pinch , a scene that keeps the story on track; the manuals after him made it a reminder of the opposing force. Blake Snyder’s Save the Cat! (2005) made the midpoint a false victory or a false defeat , a point at which the protagonist seems to have won or lost and the stakes are raised, after which the opposition closes in. James Scott Bell’s Write Your Novel From the Middle (2014), written for novelists, calls the centre the mirror moment : the protagonist takes a hard look at what they have become, or realises that they are likely to die. The manuals converge on a turn near the centre that changes the protagonist’s relation to the goal, and that convergence is the reason this chapter uses the midpoint. Their placements are conventions of one commercial form whose running time is fixed, and they describe current practice rather than laws. The novel’s middles were shaped earlier by its forms of publication. A three-volume novel invited a turn inside its middle volume: in Pride and Prejudice (1813) Darcy’s first proposal falls in the eleventh of the second volume’s nineteen chapters. A novel published in monthly parts, as Dickens’s were, needed a turn in every part, so its middle was a chain of small turns rather than one central one. The tests in this chapter therefore ask what a middle does, whether it narrows the book, and not where its turns sit. Is there evidence? The evidence is thin. A study by Andrew Reagan and colleagues, published in EPJ Data Science in 2016, measured the emotional vocabulary across some 1,700 works of fiction from Project Gutenberg and found that their trajectories cluster into six basic shapes. The two shapes with two changes of direction, a rise, fall and rise and a fall, rise and fall, were associated with the most downloads. The measure is of words, not of events, and downloads are not a measure of reading, so the finding is consistent with the claim that readers prefer a middle that turns and does not establish it. This chapter treats that claim as a conjecture supported by editorial experience. See also: Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2), where Brooks’s account of narrative desire explains why a single scene should end in a setback; The Ending (Chapter 16), for Brooks on the retroactive reading of the whole, which is the other half of the dilatory space.

title: 4. The Taxonomy
text: Middles differ less in what happens in them than in what carries their pressure, and the six shapes below are named for that engine. Each narrows the book by a different means, and each has a characteristic way of failing, given at the end of its entry. Most books combine two, a braided middle with an accumulating one or a contained middle with a turn at its centre, and the useful diagnosis names the shape that carries the pressure in each half rather than assigning the book to a single type. The escalating chain In an escalating chain , one line of action carries the middle, and the outcome of each sequence is the cause of the next and costs more than the last. The engine is price: each step is required by the one before it, and each makes going back harder. Patricia Highsmith’s The Talented Mr Ripley (1955) is the pure case. Once Tom Ripley has killed Dickie Greenleaf and taken his identity, every later act is demanded by an earlier one, the forged letters by the impersonation and a second killing by Freddie Miles’s suspicion, and each closes a road back to the life Tom had before. The shape suits the thriller, the quest and the crime novel told from the criminal’s side. Its characteristic failure is the escalation treadmill of Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2), in which the price rises in size but never in kind, and the reader, recalibrating, stops feeling it. The turned middle A turned middle is organised around a single turn near its centre, so that its first half asks one question and its second half another. The engine is a change of goal or of knowledge. Suzanne Collins’s Catching Fire (2009), the second novel of the Hunger Games trilogy, spends its first part, “The Spark”, on whether Katniss Everdeen can placate a regime she defied at the end of the first book’s Games, by staging an engagement for the cameras and by keeping her head down. In chapter 12 of 27 the president announces that the tributes for the coming Quarter Quell will be reaped from the existing pool of victors. Every move she has tried is closed at once, since she is the only female victor her district has, and the novel’s second half is a return to the arena. The announcement falls 12 ÷ 27, about 44 per cent, of the way through the chapters. Pride and Prejudice , read in Worked Analyses , turns its middle on a proposal and a letter. The characteristic failure is the broken back of Failure Patterns , a turn so large that the second half reads as a different book. The stations middle A stations middle is a sequence of encounters joined by a constant rather than by cause: a road, a voyage, a series of trials, a list, a frame that sends the protagonist out and brings them back. The picaresque novel, from Lazarillo de Tormes (1554) to Don Quixote , is built this way, and so are many quests and novels of trials. Because the stations are not linked by cause, the engine has to come from elsewhere: from a rule that removes a possibility at each station, from a destination and a limit that make each station cost time or strength, or from a change in how the protagonist meets them. Matt Haig’s The Midnight Library (2020), read in Worked Analyses, uses all three. The characteristic failure is the episodic middle, whose stations could change places without loss. The braided middle In a braided middle , two or more lines of action alternate, and the pressure comes from their crossings: an event in one thread closes an option or sets a clock in another. The Subplot (Chapter 14) treats the braid as a structure, and calls the crossing that a subplot imposes on the main plot a supplied constraint; this chapter’s interest is narrower, in what the braid does to the middle’s pace. A braid divides the middle among its threads, so each thread’s middle is shorter than the book’s and each thread is absent for long stretches. Threads that cross keep each other moving. Threads that alternate without touching give the reader two plateaus (stretches in which nothing narrows) instead of one, which is the characteristic failure, and the household draft’s. The accumulating middle An accumulating middle gathers knowledge. Its protagonist is an investigator in the broad sense, a detective, a biographer, a child working out what the adults are hiding, and its pressure comes from what How It Works calls Barthes’s delays: partial answers that change the question, and snares that send the inquiry the wrong way. Wilkie Collins’s The Moonstone (1868) hands the investigation from one witness’s written account to the next, and each account closes some explanations of the theft and opens another, so that the question the reader carries at the end of each narrative is narrower than at its start. The characteristic failure is the plateau of interviews, in which the investigator asks one witness after another and each answer leaves the question where it was, as Elena’s visits do in the household draft. The contained middle A contained middle holds its protagonist in a fixed situation, confinement or waiting or illness, from which the plot does not let them leave. Nothing can be achieved by going somewhere, so the engine is time and the arrivals it brings: the situation stays and the people in it change. In Thomas Mann’s The Magic Mountain (1924), translated by John E. Woods (1995), a visit of three weeks to a sanatorium becomes seven years, and the book’s middle is the slow loss of the life Hans Castorp came from. Amor Towles’s A Gentleman in Moscow (2016), read in Worked Analyses, gives the contained middle a designed shape in time and a turn at its centre. The characteristic failure is the holding pattern, a middle that waits for an event scheduled at its end. Reading a middle’s shape The shapes combine, and the combination says where to look when a middle sags. The household novel’s middle is braided, among Elena, Nadia and Dov’s thread, and accumulating, since Elena is reconstructing what her family has hidden. In the draft neither engine runs: the threads never cross before the end, and Elena’s inquiries return no partial answers, only refusals. The revision in Worked Analyses keeps the braid and makes it cross, and puts a turn at the centre, so that the middle becomes braided and turned. No proposal for a further shape is made here. See also: the full treatment , with three further shapes (the mirrored middle, the interval middle and the retold middle) and a table of shapes, engines and failures.

title: 5. The Mechanism
text: Narrowing and price At any point in a novel the protagonist has a set of moves still open towards the goal, and each move has a cost. This chapter calls the set the option list : for Elena after the drawer, ask Dov, ask her mother, ask someone outside the family, read the ledger to the end. An event in the middle can do one of three things to the list. It can remove a move, which the chapter calls narrowing ; it can make a move cost more, which the chapter calls raising its price ; or it can do neither, delaying the protagonist without changing what they can do or what it will cost. The first two are escalations, in the sense given in Definitions , and the third is a complication only. The household draft’s middle is made almost entirely of the third kind: the locksmith, Dov’s door and the mother’s street each delay Elena and leave her list as it was. Narrowing and price are not equal. A raised price changes the size of what the protagonist risks, and size is relative: a reader recalibrates after two or three increases, which is why Scene and Sequel ’s escalation treadmill (Chapter 2), the disaster that is bigger every time and never different, stops working. A narrowing changes the kind of situation the protagonist is in, because the moves that remain are different moves. The strongest middles therefore escalate mainly by closing doors, and use price to make the remaining doors frightening. Narrowing also explains what the reader feels as momentum. A reader in the middle holds a set of ways the book might end, mostly unspoken, and each narrowing removes some of them. A complication that closes nothing leaves the set unchanged, and that is what a reader means by nothing happens when a great deal has happened. The account is a conjecture, consistent with Brooks’s description of reading forward in anticipation of an end, and its practical form is checkable: at the start of the ending, the protagonist’s option list should be short, ideally one move, which is why an ending that comes out of a narrowed middle reads as inevitable. The Ending ’s inevitability test (Chapter 16), in which readers propose alternative endings as good as the real one, fails when the middle never narrowed the material, and the repair is here, not in the ending. A middle may also open moves: an ally appears, a new route is found. Openings are necessary, since a list that only shrinks reaches one move too early, but each one delays the end, and in a strong middle each is paid for by a later closing. A middle that opens more than it closes is expanding, and the stations middle, whose new stations are new possibilities, is the shape most exposed to it. The midpoint The midpoint is where the narrowing becomes visible to the protagonist. Before it, options may close without the protagonist knowing, and the reader may know when the protagonist does not, which is one of the middle’s best sources of dramatic irony. At the midpoint the protagonist learns that the list has changed, and the second half is played under the new list. What changes can be one of four things. The goal can change, as in Catching Fire , where the turn replaces placate the regime with survive the arena again . The protagonist’s knowledge can change, so that the goal is the same and its meaning different, as when Elizabeth Bennet reads Darcy’s letter in Pride and Prejudice . The mode can change, from reacting to acting or from asking to acting alone, so that the protagonist begins to make moves instead of answering them. And fortune can reverse, in Snyder’s false victory or false defeat, which changes the price of every move at once. A strong midpoint usually does two of these. A midpoint that does none is an event at the centre of the book, which is a different thing, and the midpoint test in Diagnostic Tests is designed to tell them apart. Multiplicity in the middle The most economical events in a middle narrow more than one line at once. The Subplot (Chapter 14) calls this a supplied constraint when a subplot imposes it on the main plot: one act in one thread closes a move in another. In the household revision, Dov’s request to clear the flat by the end of the month advances his own chain, sets a clock for both sisters, and closes Nadia’s refusal to touch the coat, three effects from one telephone message, two of which narrow options. An event in the middle can also maintain a plant, in the sense of The Ending ’s plant audit (Chapter 16), by returning an object or phrase the ending will need: the middle is where that audit’s maintained in column is filled, and a middle that narrows by means of planted objects is doing two jobs with one sentence. The household’s empty register drawer narrows Elena’s inquiry and keeps the ledger present by its absence. Proportion A middle is long, and its length is where it is most likely to idle. The screen conventions in How It Works put a turn at the centre and a lesser turn in each half, so that no stretch of Act Two runs much more than an eighth of the film without one. A novel can carry longer stretches, but a working rule of thumb, from editorial practice rather than measurement, is that any stretch of the middle longer than about a sixth of the book without a sequence that narrows should be read with suspicion. The household revision has a stretch of 78 − 66 = 12 per cent between Nadia’s discovery of the pen and Dov’s chapter, held by the clock alone, and Worked Analyses records it as unsolved. The rule concerns sequences that narrow, not sequences that are busy. A middle can be full of event and still fail it, and a quiet middle can pass, provided its quiet stretches end by taking something away. See also: the full treatment , with a worked option list for the household novel at four points and a note on options that open.

title: 6. Diagnostic Tests
text: The eight tests are for revision, and they need a summary of the middle to work on: one line per sequence, in order, with its position in the book as a percentage. Two of them are procedures rather than questions. The value-shift log writes, for each sequence of the middle, what is true at its start and no longer true at its close, in two parallel sentences as The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1) does for a single scene, with the stakes in a word. The option list, defined in The Mechanism , records the protagonist’s open moves at three points. Tests 1 to 3 (Value-shift log, Option list and Reorder) read the sequences, tests 4 to 6 (Midpoint, Opposition and Clock) the forces acting on them, and tests 7 (Cut) and 8 (Question) what the middle does to the reader. Record a sentence, not a verdict. Test 1 — Value-shift log Do neighbouring sequences repeat both the shift and the stakes? Failure. The plateau: The Purposes of a Scene ’s redundancy test (Chapter 1) failed at the scale of the book. Exception. The Old Man and the Sea (1952), whose middle repeats one struggle for days and raises its price only by exhaustion.
