Test 2 — Option list Does the list shrink between the end of the beginning, the midpoint and the start of the ending, and does each shrinkage have a cause on the page? Failure. The middle has not narrowed, and the ending will read as one choice among several. Exception. Mrs Dalloway (1925), a single day in which little closes and the approach of the party supplies the pressure. Test 3 — Reorder Swap two sequences in the summary: does anything break? Failure. Episodic: the sequences are joined by a constant, not by cause. Exception. Three Men in a Boat (1889), whose river episodes could change places and whose digressions are the point. Test 4 — Midpoint What is different near the centre in the protagonist’s goal, knowledge, mode or fortune? Failure. No turn: the second half pursues the first half’s question by the first half’s means. Exception. W. G. Sebald’s The Rings of Saturn (1995), translated by Michael Hulse (1998), a walk with no turn, held by association. Test 5 — Opposition In each quarter of the middle, does the opposing force act, on the page or through a consequence the protagonist feels? Failure. The absent opposition. Exception. Robinson Crusoe (1719), whose opposition for most of its length is weather, illness and solitude rather than an agent. Test 6 — Clock Is there a deadline or limit, does the protagonist know it, and does the time left shorten visibly? Failure. A middle without felt time, in which any sequence could take a week or a year. Exception. The Magic Mountain , which dissolves its clock on purpose and makes the loss of time its subject. Test 7 — Cut Delete the weakest sequence of the middle and reread the ending: what has the ending lost? Failure. Nothing: the sequence was transit. Exception. Groundhog Day (1993), whose repeated wake-ups would fail this test one by one and together carry the premise. Test 8 — Question What question is the reader carrying at 40 per cent and at 60 per cent? Failure. The same question: the delays have repeated it instead of changing it. Exception. The classic detective novel, The Moonstone (1868) among them, whose question stays who took it? while its answers narrow. Reading the results together Failures cluster, and the cluster says more than any single result. Tests 1 (Value-shift log) and 3 (Reorder) failing together mean that the sequences are joined neither by cause nor by change, and the remedy is to link them, so that each sequence’s outcome produces the next, before cutting any. Test 2 (Option list) failing while test 4 (Midpoint) passes means a turn that changes what the protagonist knows without closing any move, and the second half needs consequences of the turn, not more revelation. Tests 5 (Opposition) and 6 (Clock) failing together usually mean that the opposition has no schedule: give the opposing force a deadline of its own and let the protagonist learn of it, as the household revision does with Dov’s buyer. Test 7 (Cut) failing on several sequences means the middle is longer than its material, and the remedy is to cut rather than to intensify. Test 8 (Question) passing while test 2 (Option list) fails describes a middle of snares, in which the question keeps changing and nothing closes, which readers experience as being led about. The hardest result is a clean pass on every test and a middle that still reads slowly. The fault is then probably not structural: sentence rhythm, the proportion of scene to summary, or a register held too long, which The Purposes of a Scene ’s register test (Chapter 1) and its reverse outline are built to find. See also: the full treatment , with the procedure for each test, a blank value-shift log, and the household novel’s option list at four points.

title: 7. Failure Patterns
text: Each pattern below fails through a mechanism rather than a surface feature. Each ends with a published work that uses the feature successfully because the mechanism is absent. The full treatment has a longer catalogue, among them the training-montage middle, the spectacle that turns nothing, the reset at the end of every sequence, the research middle and the second sag after a strong midpoint. The plateau Symptom. Consecutive sequences end where they began. A summary of the middle repeats its verbs: asks , is refused , asks again ; waits , refuses , waits . Readers report that nothing happens, though the writer can list a great deal that does. Mechanism. The plateau repeats one value shift at constant stakes, so the option list never changes and the reader’s sense of where the book might end never narrows. It is the opposite twin of Scene and Sequel ’s escalation treadmill (Chapter 2): the treadmill changes the size of what is at risk and nothing else, the plateau changes nothing. Writers produce it when a sequence is written to keep a situation present, to remind the reader of a question rather than to move it. Remedy. Tests 1 (Value-shift log) and 2 (Option list). Keep the strongest instance of each repeated shift and cut the others, or make each repetition close something the last left open: the third refusal should cost the protagonist a move the first did not. Exception. Samuel Beckett’s Waiting for Godot , first staged in French in 1953 and in Beckett’s own English in 1955, which Vivian Mercier described in The Irish Times in 1956 as a play in which “nothing happens, twice”. Its second act repeats the first: the same road, the same waiting, a boy with the same message. It works because the repetition is the argument and because it degrades: Pozzo returns blind and Lucky dumb, and the price rises behind a foreground that stands still. The fault is a repetition the book does not mean. The episodic middle Symptom. The middle’s sequences could change places. Each is a self-contained adventure, and the middle can be summarised only with and then . Mechanism. The sequences are linked by a constant, a road or a list or a hero, and not by cause, so no sequence closes anything for the next. Aristotle’s objection is practical as well as formal: a reader forms expectations about what comes next from what has just happened, and in an episodic middle nothing has just happened that predicts anything. Remedy. Test 3 (Reorder). Carry an outcome from one sequence into the next, a wound, a debt, an enemy, a piece of knowledge, or impose a rule or a limit that removes a possibility at each station. Exception. Cervantes’s Don Quixote (1605 and 1615), translated by Edith Grossman (2003). Many of the first part’s adventures, the windmills, the flocks of sheep, the galley slaves, could be reordered with little loss. It works because the constant is itself an engine, the knight’s reading of the world through his romances tested afresh at each station, and because the second part supplies the cause the first lacked: the people Don Quixote meets have read the first part, and a duke and duchess stage adventures for him, so that the world narrows around his delusion. The absent opposition Symptom. The opposing force, a person or an institution or a natural power, disappears for long stretches while the protagonist prepares, trains, researches or travels. The middle feels safe. Mechanism. It is usually the opposition that closes doors. Without it acting, the protagonist’s moves have no price and the option list cannot shrink, so the middle becomes the protagonist’s private project, observed. The absent opposition is common in middles built as preparation, where the writer is saving the antagonist for the end. Remedy. Test 5 (Opposition). Give the opposition a chain of its own, running off the page, and let it surface in each quarter of the middle as a consequence the protagonist feels, which is the pinch of the screenwriting manuals. Exception. Herman Melville’s Moby-Dick (1851). The whale is not seen until chapter 133 of 135. It works because the opposition acts through consequence throughout: Ahab’s leg, and the nine gams, the Pequod’s meetings with other ships, several of which bring news of the whale. The Samuel Enderby ’s captain has lost an arm to it; the Rachel is searching for a boat lost in chasing it, and her captain’s plea for help, which Ahab refuses, closes the last move by which he might have turned back. The gams are pinches in the later manuals’ sense, reminders of the opposing force, placed from chapter 52 onwards, and at each one Ahab asks the same question of a stranger. The holding pattern Symptom. The middle waits for an event scheduled at its end, a trial, a wedding, a departure, a contest, and its sequences fill the time. The protagonist’s situation is the same at each. Mechanism. In a holding pattern the scheduled event carries all the pressure, and nothing in the waiting can change it, so nothing in the waiting can narrow anything. The reader skims towards the date. Remedy. Tests 6 (Clock) and 7 (Cut). Make the waiting change the event: what the protagonist does while waiting should alter how they will meet it, or bring it forward. Otherwise cut the wait. Exception. Donna Tartt’s The Goldfinch (2013). After his mother’s death Theo Decker is taken to Las Vegas by his father, and spends a long stretch in a half-built suburb with his friend Boris, drinking and taking drugs, while the painting he carried out of the museum stays hidden. The book’s length drew what a Vanity Fair article in 2014 called some of the severest pans in memory, and Meg Wolitzer, reviewing it for NPR, praised its “rich, dense, leisurely middle”. The holding pattern works because it is where the adult of the book’s later parts is formed, and because the waiting conceals the book’s central plant: Boris exchanged the painting in Las Vegas, and the package Theo has guarded for years turns out to hold a school textbook. The broken back Symptom. The midpoint is so large that the second half reads as a different book, with a new protagonist, a new genre or a new question, and readers who were held by the first half feel abandoned. Mechanism. The turn changes goal, knowledge and protagonist together and leaves the first half’s question open, so the reader carries two questions and the book answers one. The broken back is the turned middle’s characteristic failure. Remedy. Tests 4 (Midpoint) and 8 (Question). Close the first half’s question visibly at the turn, or carry something across it, a character, an object, the old question in a new form, so that the second half reads as the first half’s consequence. Exception. Alfred Hitchcock’s Psycho (1960). Marion Crane, the film’s star and its protagonist, has stolen $40,000, and she is killed about 47 minutes into a film of 109, 47 ÷ 109 or about 43 per cent of the way through. The second half belongs to Norman Bates and to the people looking for her. It works because the film closes the first half’s question on screen: cleaning up, Norman puts the newspaper with the money in it into the boot of her car without knowing what it holds, and sinks the car in a swamp, so that the viewer watches the theft go down with it. Hitchcock protected the break by refusing late admission to screenings. See also: The Subplot (Chapter 14), for the occupational thread, the braided middle’s version of the plateau; The Ending (Chapter 16), for the proportion problem, which begins as a middle that ran long.

title: 8. Worked Analyses
text: Three close readings, a short reading of a film, and the household revision case. Each reading names the middle’s shape and runs the option list across it. Pride and Prejudice : the midpoint as recognition Jane Austen’s Pride and Prejudice (1813) was published in three volumes of 23, 19 and 19 chapters. On one reasonable reading its middle runs from Elizabeth Bennet’s refusal of Mr Collins in chapter 19, which commits her to marrying for regard or not at all, to the visit to Pemberley that opens the third volume, and its first half is an accumulating middle built of snares. Wickham’s account of Darcy’s cruelty, given just before the middle begins, is confirmed by Bingley’s sudden departure from Netherfield and by Colonel Fitzwilliam’s remark that Darcy had lately saved a friend from an imprudent marriage. Each looks like a partial answer to the question what kind of man is Darcy? , and each confirms an answer that is wrong. The reader, sharing Elizabeth’s vantage, is led by the same snares. The turn comes in chapter 34, the eleventh of the second volume’s nineteen. Darcy proposes at Hunsford and Elizabeth refuses him, accusing him over Jane and over Wickham; in chapter 35 he gives her a letter, and in chapter 36 she rereads it and says, of herself, “Till this moment I never knew myself.” The midpoint does two of the four things a midpoint can do. It changes Elizabeth’s knowledge, since the letter reverses her account of both men, and it reverses fortune, since she has closed by her own act the one move the second half will make her want. Before chapter 34 her option list towards Darcy costs nothing: she can dislike him freely. After chapter 36 the move she wants has been refused, and the second half’s question is whether a closed move can be reopened. Austen then prices it. Lydia’s elopement with Wickham in chapter 46 disgraces the family and makes Darcy’s renewed attachment improbable, and the move is reopened only by an act Elizabeth does not know of until a letter from her aunt in chapter 52: Darcy has found the couple and paid for the marriage. The turn does not break the book’s back, because it answers the first half’s question instead of abandoning it, and the second half’s question grows out of the answer. It falls at 34 ÷ 61, about 56 per cent of the chapters, at the centre of the centre volume. A Gentleman in Moscow : a contained middle shaped in time Amor Towles’s A Gentleman in Moscow (2016) opens in 1922, when a Bolshevik tribunal sentences Count Alexander Rostov to spend the rest of his life in the Metropol hotel, to be shot if he leaves. The situation cannot change, so the middle cannot narrow by place, and Towles gives it a shape in time instead. In his own account, the chapters advance by a doubling principle, one day after the arrest, then two days, five, ten, three weeks, six weeks, three months, six months, a year, two, four, eight and sixteen years, and after that point a halving principle brings the intervals back down. The book ends in 1954, 32 years after the arrest, so the turn of the chronology at sixteen years, in 1938, is the centre of its span: 16 × 2 = 32. The design makes the clock the engine of a contained middle. In the first chapters days pass slowly and the hotel is explored; in the middle, years pass between chapters and the Count’s world changes around a fixed point; in the last part the intervals shorten, so that the reader feels time running out without any deadline being named, which is test 6 (Clock) answered by the chapter dates themselves. At the centre Towles puts a turn. In 1938 Nina Kulikova, whom the Count knew as a child in the hotel, leaves her young daughter Sofia with him in order to follow her husband to a labour camp. The arrival changes the Count’s goal, from living with grace inside a sentence to raising a child, and the second half’s narrowing is all on her account: what the Count can risk becomes what Sofia can lose, and the plan that ends the book, by which she leaves the country and he leaves the hotel, is a move only Sofia makes necessary. The contained middle supplies the duration and the turn supplies the direction. The Midnight Library : stations that narrow Matt Haig’s The Midnight Library (2020) is a stations middle with its rule in plain view. After trying to end her life, Nora Seed finds herself in a library between life and death, kept by Mrs Elm, her school librarian, where every book is a life she might have lived; she may enter any of them and stays until she is disappointed, when she returns to the library. The structure invites the episodic middle, since one life could follow another in any order, and parts of the sequence would pass the reorder test badly. The book narrows it in three ways. The lives are ordered by kind: the first undo regrets listed in the library’s Book of Regrets, the pub she might have run with her former fiancé, the friend she did not follow to Australia, the swimming career her father wanted, and later lives are chosen for what she wishes rather than what she regrets, a glaciologist’s work in the Arctic, a rock star’s fame. Partway through, in the glaciologist’s life, she meets Hugo Lefèvre, another traveller who has passed through many lives of his own, and he is the plateau made into a character: he shows her the version of her journey that never ends. When the sequence threatens to become that version, Haig moves into summary, and many lives pass in a few pages. And the last life, married to a man named Ash with a daughter, is the most fully lived and the most wanted, so leaving it, when she learns that a boy she once taught the piano has gone wrong in a life without her, costs the most. Each station costs more to leave than the one before, and the middle ends when one move remains. On screen: Groundhog Day Harold Ramis’s Groundhog Day (1993), written with Danny Rubin, is the purest plateau in mainstream film: a weatherman, Phil Connors, wakes to the same 2 February in Punxsutawney, again and again. It holds because the day stays the same and Phil’s response does not. He exploits the loop, uses it to try to seduce his producer, Rita, despairs and tries repeatedly to die, and then spends the days learning the piano, ice sculpture and French and helping the town. The middle’s turn is the despair. When even death returns him to the same morning, his option list holds no exit, and the one move left is to change how he spends the day, which is the second half. The old homeless man he cannot save, however he tries, keeps that move from becoming a victory over the loop. The household revision case: the middle The situation. The draft middle in The Problem runs from the drawer at about 25 per cent to Dov’s chapter at about 78. The tests find it quickly. Test 1 (Value-shift log) fails, since Elena’s three inquiries share one shift, a question put and not answered, at one stake, and Nadia’s two sequences share a refusal kept. Test 2 (Option list) fails: Elena’s option list after the drawer is to ask Dov, ask her mother, ask someone outside the family, or read the ledger, and at two-thirds it is the same except for the ledger. The locksmith, Dov’s door and the mother’s street pass the reorder test in any order, and the locksmith fails the cut test outright. Dov’s sale, in two sentences of summary, fails the opposition test, and no clock is felt by anyone. The revision. The middle is rebuilt as a braid that crosses, with a turn at the centre. Positions are estimates. Position Sequence What it closes or prices 25% The drawer: the ledger and the looser hand ( The Chapter Break , Chapter 6) The middle begins: Elena’s question is now whose hand, and why? 30% Dov’s thread, seen from outside: the buyer wants the building, shop and flat, emptied by the end of the month ( The Subplot , Chapter 14) Nothing yet for the sisters; the reader holds a deadline they do not 38% Elena comes back to finish reading and finds the drawer empty The ledger as a source; Dov as a witness, by her own decision 50% The midpoint: Dov’s messages reach both sisters, and Nadia plays hers Sets the clock for both; ends Nadia’s refusal to touch the coat 58% Dov signs, without telling his sisters The shop itself, irreversibly 66% Nadia, clearing the flat, puts her hand into the pocket of the coat on its hook and finds the good pen ( Backstory and Flashback , Chapter 7) The coat is priced: its pockets are checked because it must go 78% Dov’s chapter, the evening of 9 March ( The Viewpoint Shift , Chapter 13) The middle ends and the climax begins The first turn of the middle, Elena’s, reads: She had left the ledger where it lived, meaning to come back for the rest. The drawer stuck on the K and came free on the third try, and there was nothing in it: no ledger, no pens, not even the rubber bands. Behind her someone knocked on the glass. A boy had tried the door and was pointing at the sign, which said OPEN, and must have said it since March. She shook her head at him and he went. Then she reached up and turned the sign round to CLOSED. Two people had keys besides her, and one of them had given her hers. On the way home she passed the end of Dov’s road and did not take it, and by the time she was indoors she had decided not to ask him, because she had asked him once. The midpoint, Nadia’s, reads: There were six messages from Dov. She played the last one standing at the sink. “Clear the flat by the end of the month. All of it. Please.” She played it again and counted the words, thirteen, and none of them was why. What the revision did. It cut the locksmith, Dov’s second doorway and the mother’s street, and promoted the sale from summary to a thread with a deadline. It turned the calls Nadia lets ring out in the opening, which in The Opening Pages (Chapter 9) are about the coat, into the carrier of the midpoint, so that the unanswered calls acquire content. It made the empty drawer a decision rather than a puzzle: Elena stops asking, which closes Dov as a witness by her own act, rhymes with the doorway, where he gave her a key and withheld the reason, and supplies what The Subplot (Chapter 14) recorded as unsolved, a reason for her not to put her question to Dov until he produces the ledger himself. Her option list now shrinks from four moves after the drawer to waiting at the midpoint, since she declined to telephone her mother in Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2), to none of her own at Dov’s chapter: the ledger must come to her, and at the convergence it does. Nadia’s moves shrink from leaving the coat untouched to having to clear the flat. And the scene at the drawer gives the prologue’s two open details their second appearance: Elena waves a boy away from the glass, as her father did on his last ordinary day, without knowing it, and turns at last the sign he never turned. Only the reader can see the rhyme. What the revision has not solved. A decision not to ask is hard to dramatise, and two sentences may not persuade a reader that an investigator would stop; the book probably needs a scene in which Elena keeps her suspicion from Nadia and it costs her something, which Arc and Theme (Chapter 12) proposes at about 54 per cent. Paying both of the prologue’s open details in one scene may read as arranged, and a reader who has forgotten the prologue meets a stray boy. Turning the sign gives Elena an act in the middle, which may answer The Ending ’s complaint (Chapter 16) that her arc completes by presence rather than by act, or may only move the act away from the ending where it was wanted. The stretch from the pen to Dov’s chapter, twelve per cent of the book, is held by the clock alone. And the order of the request and the signing, which The Subplot (Chapter 14) left open, is settled here as a proposal. See also: the full treatment , with the option lists for each sibling at four points and further readings of Catching Fire , The Seven Husbands of Evelyn Hugo , Great Expectations and Squid Game .

title: 9. Checklist and Exercises
text: Revision checklist Boundaries and turns Can I name the commitment that ends my beginning and the sequence that starts my ending, and say what share of the book lies between them? Is there a turn near the centre, and can I say whether it changes the goal, the protagonist’s knowledge, their mode or their fortune? Does the first half’s question get answered, or visibly carried, at the turn? Sequences Written as a value-shift log, does any sequence repeat its neighbour’s shift at the same stakes? Could any two sequences of the middle change places without loss, and if so, what links them other than a constant? If I delete the weakest sequence, does the ending lose anything I can name? Forces Does the opposing force act in every quarter of the middle, on the page or through a consequence? Is there a clock, does the protagonist know it, and does it shorten? Does at least one event narrow more than one line of action? The reader Is the protagonist’s option list shorter at the midpoint than after the beginning, and shorter again at the start of the ending? Is the question a reader carries at 60 per cent different from the one at 40 per cent? Is there any stretch longer than about a sixth of the book in which nothing closes? Exercises The value-shift log. Write one line for each sequence of your middle with its position as a percentage, then the shift in two parallel sentences and the stakes in a word. Mark every neighbouring pair that repeats both. For each pair, keep the stronger and cut the other, or rewrite the second so that it closes a move the first left open. The option list. List your protagonist’s open moves towards the goal at four points: after the beginning, at the midpoint, at three-quarters, and at the start of the ending. Beside each move that disappears, give the page that closes it. Where nothing disappears between two points, write the event that would close a move using only material already in the book. The shuffle. Write each sequence of the middle on a card, shuffle them, and a week later, or with another reader, try to put them back in order. Wherever the order cannot be recovered from the cards alone, a causal link is missing. The opposition’s calendar. Write the opposing force’s own timeline through the middle, off the page and dated, as though it were the protagonist. Mark each point at which it surfaces in the book as a consequence, and add one wherever a quarter of the middle has none. Two midpoints. Write two alternative midpoints for your book, a page each: one that changes the protagonist’s goal and one that changes what they know. For each, rewrite the option list for the second half, and keep the version whose list narrows furthest by the start of the ending.

title: 10. Coda
text: The instruments in this chapter assume that a middle should narrow. The option list, the midpoint test and the clock are calibrated to books that move towards a single end, and they will report as failures the contained and episodic middles of a serious body of fiction that prefers duration to direction: The Magic Mountain , The Rings of Saturn , the picaresque. When they do, the model is reporting its own assumption, and the exceptions in Failure Patterns show what such books put in place of narrowing, a repetition that is itself the argument or a constant that is itself an engine. For most novels the assumption holds, and it has a consequence that is easy to state and hard to accept. The ending is where a book’s shape becomes visible, but the middle is where it is decided. Whether an ending reads as inevitable or arbitrary depends on how many moves the middle left open, and whether the climax lands depends on what the middle made it cost. A writer who revises the ending of a book whose middle never narrowed is repairing the wrong part, which is why The Ending (Chapter 16) sends its hardest diagnosis back here. That is also the answer to the complaint the chapter began with. A middle that drags is rarely short of event, and adding event treats the symptom. The remedy is to ask of each sequence what it takes away from someone, and to cut or rewrite the ones that take nothing. The household draft is the chapter’s evidence that this is usually a matter of arrangement rather than invention: its revision cut three sequences, and everything it added came out of the sale the draft already contained, moved to where it closed a move for someone. See also: the full treatment , on the limits of the model and the forms of middle it does not describe; The Structural Edit (Chapter 18), which puts the option list into a revision order for the whole book.

title: Arc and Theme
text: Who changes, and what the change argues The Craft Behind the Story (Second Edition) — Chapter 12. Part III: The Architecture of the Whole. In brief. An arc is a change in the grounds on which a character chooses, and a theme is the question that a book’s choices answer. The chapter treats them together because they are one structure seen from two sides. A protagonist’s change becomes visible only at a decision that costs something under the old grounds, and the book’s theme is what that decision argues once it is set beside the different answers other characters give. The chapter’s tools are the criterion log, which records the rule behind each of a character’s largest decisions and finds where, or whether, the rule changes, and the answer map, which writes each major character’s rule as an answer to the book’s question. Use the chapter when readers say a protagonist does not change or changes unconvincingly, when a book’s meaning is stated rather than felt, or when you can say what your book is about only as a topic. What you can do after this chapter Name the rule by which your protagonist chooses at the start of the book and at the end, and find the decision at which it changes. Distinguish an arc that is chosen from one that is announced, and a change that costs something from one that is free. Choose among five kinds of arc, including the arcs that hold or refuse change. Put your book’s theme as a question, and see which of your characters answer it and how. Diagnose an arc or a theme that is not working and revise it by rearranging decisions rather than adding statements. Key terms Arc; criterion and hinge; want and need; flat and round characters; the lie; self-revelation; premise and controlling idea; moral argument; theme and the thematic question; motif; the five arcs (conversion, staged, falling, steadfast and refused); the four carriers of theme (decision, variation, motif and statement); the criterion log; the answer map; the seed; the mirror moment; the constant; enactment; the announced arc; the free hinge; the scheduled arc; the revoked arc; the sermon. Each is defined at first use and collected in the consolidated glossary . Contents The first files say what an arc and a theme are and where the ideas come from, the central files how a change is built and how a theme is carried, and the last are for use at the desk. The Problem A household ending in which one sister’s change is announced and the book’s meaning is spoken aloud, and the chapter’s claim Definitions Arc, criterion, hinge and theme, and the terms around them How It Works Why choice reveals character, which characters need to change, where the arc models come from, what a theme is, and what the evidence says The Taxonomy Five kinds of arc, named for what happens to the criterion, and four carriers of theme The Mechanism How a change is seeded, priced, made and confirmed, and how a theme is argued through several characters Diagnostic Tests Eight questions on one page, and how to read their failures together Failure Patterns Five recurrent failures, each with a work that commits it and succeeds Worked Analyses Emma , Gilead , A Man Called Ove and The Godfather , and the household revision case Checklist and Exercises The revision checklist and five exercises for your own draft Coda What the model assumes, and why theme is decided by arrangement A writer in revision can start at the diagnostic tests. A writer planning a book should read the mechanism first, because a criterion log is easier to draft before the decisions are written than to impose on them afterwards. The full treatment This is a new chapter, so the Reference layer holds a single full treatment rather than a corrected original: the theory at greater length, with the arc models compared in a table, an extended catalogue of arcs and failure patterns, further analyses ( Project Hail Mary , The Kite Runner and Paddington 2 ), the household arc and answer map in full, a glossary of the chapter’s terms and the sources. See also: Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2), where the criterion and the hinge are defined at the scale of a single decision; The Middle (Chapter 11), whose midpoint is the plot-side counterpart of the arc’s first failure; The Subplot (Chapter 14), for thematic counterpoint between threads; The Ending (Chapter 16), where character-arc completion and thematic closure fall due.

title: 1. The Problem
text: A draft of the household novel ends with two paragraphs that its writer added late, after an early reader said that Elena seemed to finish the book as she began it. By this point the reader knows the situation. Four months after their father’s death, three adult children have spent the book reconstructing what he left: Elena, who learned in Dov’s doorway that their mother had changed the shop’s locks in March and has wanted ever since to know why; Nadia, who counts things and has learned not to touch the coat on its hook in the flat above the shop; and Dov, who gave Elena the new key and kept the reason, and who has been keeping the ledger in a looser hand since the evening of 9 March. The three have just read the ledger together, and found in their father’s careful hand the dates of an illness he told nobody about. The draft then continues: Elena sat at the register with her hands flat on the counter and understood, all at once, what the four months had been for. She had tried to find everything out alone, the way their father had kept everything alone, and it had nearly cost her the only people left who could tell her anything. Some things, she saw now, a family could only know together. “He was protecting us,” Nadia said. “That’s what this family does. We protect each other by not saying.” The early reader’s second note was shorter than the first: Now I’m being told what to think. Both notes are accurate, and they describe one fault. The first paragraph gives Elena an arc , a change in a character across the book, by reporting it: she understood , she saw now , and the narration supplies the content of the understanding. The second gives the book a theme , the question its events are about, by having a character state an answer to it. Neither is a decision. Elena does nothing in the scene that she would not have done in the first chapter, and the reader has no way to test her new understanding except by taking the narration’s word for it. Nadia’s line closes a question the book has spent its whole length keeping open, and closes it with a proposition the reader may reject, since the mother’s silence, which is the household’s largest withholding, has not been shown to protect anyone. The writer’s instinct, faced with the first note, was to explain the change more fully, and the instinct is common enough to be the subject of a failure pattern in this chapter, the announced arc. More explanation leaves the cause untouched. Elena has made the same kind of decision throughout the book: in the doorway she asks once and is refused; in her truck afterwards she decides not to telephone her mother; at the register drawer she reads the ledger alone, from the beginning; at the empty drawer, about 38 per cent of the way through, she decides not to ask Dov who took it, because she had asked him once . The rule behind every one of these choices is the same, find out for yourself, and do not ask people who will not tell you , and nothing in the book shows her choosing by any other rule. A paragraph of understanding at the end cannot make the reader believe in a change that no choice has shown. The chapter’s claim is that arc and theme are one structure, and that they fail together. An arc is a change in the rule by which a character chooses, and it exists only at a decision that costs something the old rule valued; a theme is the question such decisions answer, argued by setting one character’s choice beside the others’ rather than by saying what it means. A change that is announced, or a meaning that is spoken, is an arc or a theme in description only. The claim has a consequence for revision that runs against instinct. The remedy for an unconvincing change is not a better account of it but an earlier price and a later decision: a scene in which the old rule costs the character something she can see, and a moment, under pressure, at which she chooses by a new one. The remedy for a stated theme is to delete the statement and make sure the question is answered differently by different people, so that the ending’s arrangement does the arguing. The revision in Worked Analyses deletes both of the draft’s paragraphs and adds two short passages of decision, about two hundred words in all, one in the middle of the book and one at the convergence before the reading. The claim also explains why craft teaching often separates the two subjects and why the separation causes trouble in revision. A writer who treats arc as a matter of character tends to repair it with backstory, a wound that explains the old rule; a writer who treats theme as a matter of meaning tends to repair it with images and statements. Neither repair touches the decisions, which is where both are made. This is a judgement from editorial practice rather than a measured finding, but the household draft illustrates it: its writer had already given Elena a reason to distrust people who withhold, and had already given the book a recurring object, the ledger, as a carrier of its meaning, and still the ending told rather than showed. See also: the full treatment , on the relation between this chapter and the character and theme domains of the ending; The Ending (Chapter 16), whose revision case records that Elena “completes by presence rather than act”.

title: 2. Definitions
text: The working definition of an arc A character’s arc is the course, across a whole book, of the rule by which that character resolves dilemmas. Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2) gives the rule its name. To resolve a dilemma a character applies a rule about which cost is more bearable, loyalty over legality or the family over the self, and that rule is the criterion . Most decisions in a novel are made on a criterion the character already holds, so the plot advances and the person does not. The arc is what the reader sees when the criteria behind a character’s largest decisions are read in order: the same rule throughout, a rule replaced by a better or a worse one, or a rule tested to the edge of change and kept. The point at which the criterion changes is the hinge , Scene and Sequel ’s term (Chapter 2) for the moment within a decision at which a dilemma is resolved on a rule the character did not hold before, while the options themselves may stay the same. The old rule is usually outranked rather than refuted. Huckleberry Finn accepts his training’s verdict that he will be damned for helping Jim, and chooses Jim anyway; he has not stopped believing the rule, he has found one that matters more. That is the general shape of change in fiction, and it explains why arcs that work rarely feel like conversions to an argument. The character keeps the old belief and acts against it. An arc defined in this way is a matter of decisions, not of feelings, knowledge or circumstances. A character can learn a great deal, suffer a great deal and end in a different place without an arc, if every choice along the way was made by the same rule. Equally, a character who ends in the same place can have a strong arc, if the last choice is made for a reason that could not have motivated the first. The definition is narrow on purpose, because it gives the writer something to look for on the page: a decision, and the rule behind it. The working definition of a theme A theme, in this chapter as in The Ending (Chapter 16), is a question the book tests rather than a proposition it asserts. It differs from a topic, which names what the book is about (grief, inheritance, a family shop), and from a thesis, which is one answer. The household novel’s topic is a family after a death; its theme, put as a question, is what the members of a family owe each other in the way of truth, a phrasing first given in The Dialogue Exchange (Chapter 3). The question form matters for revision, because a question can be answered differently by different characters, and a book argues by arranging their answers. A book that has only a topic gives the reader nothing to weigh, and a book that has only a thesis gives the reader nothing to decide. The two definitions meet at the hinge. A theme is tested when characters choose under pressure, and the criterion behind each choice is, read from the other side, that character’s answer to the book’s question. Where the protagonist’s criterion changes, the book’s argument turns. Adjacent terms Several neighbouring words describe parts of the same structure. The want is what a character consciously pursues, the goal of Scene and Sequel ’s goal–conflict–disaster sequence (Chapter 2); the need , in the screenwriting manuals, is what the character must change in order to live better, usually unknown to them. In this chapter’s terms the need is a criterion the character does not yet hold, and the hinge is where they come to hold it. Characterisation is the sum of a character’s observable traits, how they speak, dress and behave; the arc lies beneath it and is visible only in choices, a distinction set out in How It Works . Motif is a recurring element, an object, image or phrase, that carries a theme by being returned to in changing contexts; the ledger and the coat are the household’s. Premise and controlling idea are the names two widely used manuals give to a theme stated as a proposition, and the chapter treats them as one carrier among four in The Taxonomy . Two terms from earlier chapters recur. The Ending ’s constant (Chapter 16), something visibly unchanged against which a change can be read, is one of the conditions of an arc in The Mechanism . And The Subplot ’s thematic counterpoint (Chapter 14), two threads that comment on each other by analogy, is the subplot’s version of what this chapter calls variation. What the chapter leaves to other chapters The single decision, with its dilemma and its criterion, belongs to Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2); this chapter takes it to the scale of the book. Whose mind the reader is granted, and therefore whose arc can be shown from inside, is The Viewpoint Shift ’s question (Chapter 13). The completion of an arc and the closure of a theme at the last pages belong to The Ending (Chapter 16), and the midpoint at which a protagonist’s mode or knowledge changes to The Middle (Chapter 11). A change in what the reader understands, as distinct from what a character chooses, is a reveal, and belongs to The Reveal (Chapter 15). A character carried across several books, whose arc may be suspended or spread across volumes, is Series and Genre ’s subject (Chapter 17). See also: the full treatment , with a table relating the terms of the main arc models to this chapter’s.

title: 3. How It Works
text: The theory below is limited to what the chapter’s tools use. Each strand opens with the question a writer in revision is asking, and then gives the source that answers it. How does a reader know that a character has changed? The reader knows by watching choices. Aristotle’s Poetics , in S. H. Butcher’s translation, puts it in one sentence: “Character is that which reveals moral purpose, showing what kind of things a man chooses or avoids.” The Greek words are ēthos , character, and prohairesis , deliberate choice, and the claim is that the first is visible only through the second. Aristotle ranked plot above character, and the ranking follows from the definition: a character is known by what they choose, so the choices, which are plot, come first. Robert McKee’s Story (1997), a widely used screenwriting manual, restates the point as a working rule: “True CHARACTER is revealed in the choices a human being makes under pressure – the greater the pressure, the deeper the revelation, the truer the choice to the character’s essential nature.” McKee separates true character from characterisation, the observable sum of a person’s traits, and the separation is useful in revision. A writer who wants a character to seem changed can alter the characterisation, a new haircut, a softer voice, and nothing beneath it moves. A change in character is a change in what the person chooses when choosing costs something, and the more it costs, the more the reader believes it. The household draft in The Problem changes Elena’s understanding and leaves her choices as they were, which is why the reader does not believe it. Does every character need to change? No, and the clearest early account says why. E. M. Forster’s Aspects of the Novel (1927) divides characters into flat characters , “constructed round a single idea or quality”, and round characters , whose test is that they are “capable of surprising in a convincing way”. Forster defends flat characters, which are easy to recognise and remember, and holds only that round ones are needed to carry tragedy for any length of time. His test of roundness is close to a description of the hinge. A surprising decision is one the reader did not predict from the character’s earlier choices; a convincing one is a decision the reader, looking back, finds prepared. A change that is predicted fails the first condition and reads as a schedule, and a change that is unprepared fails the second and reads as the author’s convenience. Forster’s division also licenses the steadfast and refused arcs in The Taxonomy . A round character can refuse to change, and the refusal can surprise; a flat character can change other people without changing at all. Where do the arc models come from, and what do they assume? Most current advice on arcs descends from the theatre and from screenwriting. Lajos Egri’s The Art of Dramatic Writing (1946) asks the writer to begin from a premise, which he defines as “a proposition antecedently supposed or proved; a basis of argument”, and gives Macbeth ’s as “Ruthless ambition leads to its own destruction”. A play, for Egri, is the proof of its premise, carried out by characters whom conflict forces to change. Later manuals turned the proof into a sequence of named stages. John Truby’s The Anatomy of Story (2007) gives the hero a weakness and a need, a desire, an opponent and a self-revelation , the moment at which the hero sees the truth about themselves, and treats the story as a moral argument conducted through the hero’s and the opponent’s actions rather than through statement. K. M. Weiland’s Creating Character Arcs (2016) builds the arc on the lie the character believes at the start, which the story disproves, and names five arcs: a positive change arc, in which the character gives up the lie for a truth; a flat arc, in which the character already holds the truth and changes the world; and three negative arcs, disillusionment, fall and corruption. The models are useful in one respect above all. They make the writer name the old criterion before drafting, as a weakness or a lie, so that the decisions that test it can be planned. Their cost is the assumption built into them, that change is the value a story serves and that it happens once, late, to a protagonist, in a sequence that can be scheduled. These are the conventions of twentieth- and twenty-first-century screen drama and of the commercial fiction that has learned from it. The picaresque, much modernist fiction, many long-running series heroes and a good deal of fiction outside the Anglo-American tradition do not arc in this sense, and the models will report them as failures. When they do, the models are describing their own assumption. What is a theme, and how does a book argue one? Egri’s premise and McKee’s controlling idea, which McKee describes as a value and the cause by which it is won or lost, both state a theme as a proposition. This chapter, following The Ending (Chapter 16), treats a theme instead as a question, and the difference is practical. A proposition written down before drafting tends to produce characters who illustrate it, and the opposition becomes a straw figure the book knocks down. A question written down before drafting can be answered by several characters in several ways, which is what Truby’s moral argument requires. The proposition is still useful, but as the answer a book reaches, found in revision by reading what the decisions argue, not as an instruction to the characters at the start. What does the evidence say? The evidence on how stories change readers is limited and indirect. Melanie Green and Timothy Brock (2000) ran four experiments on what they called transportation , the reader’s absorption into a narrative world. More transported readers held more story-consistent beliefs afterwards and judged the protagonists more favourably, and labelling a story as fact or as fiction made little difference to either. The finding supports a modest claim, that a story’s events can move a reader’s beliefs through absorption. It does not show that a stated theme persuades less than an enacted one. That is a conjecture consistent with it, since a statement addressed to the reader may interrupt the absorption the effect depends on, and the household reader’s Now I’m being told what to think is the kind of report the conjecture predicts. See also: the full treatment , with the arc models set out in a table and the terms of each related to the criterion and the hinge.

title: 4. The Taxonomy
text: The chapter sorts arcs by what happens to the criterion, since that is what a writer can find and change on the page, and sorts the means of carrying a theme by how far each one argues. The two lists are related: the kind of arc a book gives its protagonist decides which carriers its theme can use. Five arcs The conversion arc The criterion changes once, at a single priced decision, usually late in the book. Before the hinge the character chooses by the old rule, and the cost of doing so grows; at the hinge they choose by a new one, and afterwards the old rule no longer governs. Claire Keegan’s Small Things Like These (2021), read in Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2), is a pure case: Bill Furlong chooses throughout by what keeps his household safe, and on Christmas Eve walks a girl out of the convent’s coal shed towards his home, choosing by what was once done for his mother. The conversion arc suits a book whose question can be answered by one act. Its risks are the free hinge and the scheduled arc in Failure Patterns : a conversion that costs nothing, or one the reader saw coming from the first chapter. The staged arc The criterion changes in steps, or the change is recognised at one point and acted on at another. Jane Austen’s Emma (1815), read in Worked Analyses , gives its heroine a recognition after Box Hill and an action on the new rule the next morning, and later a second recognition about herself that changes a different set of choices. The staged arc suits long novels, because a single hinge spread over five hundred pages leaves long stretches in which the character only waits for it. Its risk is the one Scene and Sequel ’s criterion test (Chapter 2) names for hinges set close together: the arc is spent too fast, and the last third of the book has nowhere left to go. A staged arc whose stages are recognitions without decisions is a refused arc that has not admitted it. The falling arc The criterion is replaced by a worse one. The descent usually proceeds by decisions each of which is defensible on the old rule, so that the character never chooses to become worse and becomes worse by choosing. Michael Corleone in The Godfather (1972), read in Worked Analyses , protects his family at every step, and the protection becomes the thing he had wanted no part of. Macbeth is the canonical case, and Weiland’s fall and corruption arcs, set out in How It Works , are both forms of it. The falling arc carries the strongest dramatic irony of the five, because the reader can see the destination before the character can. Its risk is the opposite of the conversion arc’s: a descent with no point at which the character could have chosen otherwise reads as fate rather than fall, and the reader stops judging. The steadfast arc The protagonist’s criterion holds under pressure designed to break it, and the change happens to others, who come to choose by it. The pressure must be real: the character must be offered the old world’s terms, with something to lose by refusing them. Paul King’s film Paddington 2 (2017), read in the full treatment , sends its bear to prison for a crime he did not commit, and it is the prison that changes. Weiland calls this the flat arc. The steadfast arc is the usual form of the series hero, whose criterion must survive into the next volume, which is Series and Genre ’s subject (Chapter 17). Its risk is that a criterion never truly tested reads as stasis, and the book becomes a demonstration of a virtue rather than a trial of one. The refused arc The character reaches the hinge, sees the decision the new criterion would make, and chooses by the old one. The change is in recognition, not in choice, and the recognition is the arc’s climax. Stevens in The Remains of the Day (1989), treated in The Ending (Chapter 16), sees on the pier at Weymouth what he gave up, and turns at once to the problem of learning to banter; Lee Chandler in Manchester by the Sea (2016), Scene and Sequel ’s exception (Chapter 2), is offered the chance to stay and says he cannot beat it. The refused arc recurs in literary fiction, as the cases from Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2) and The Ending (Chapter 16) show, and its condition is that the recognition be on the page and cost something, since a refusal the character never sees is a static character, not a refused arc. Four carriers of theme A theme is carried by four means, which differ in how far they argue. They are listed from strongest to weakest as argument, and the order has a reason: a carrier argues to the degree that the reader has felt a cost attached to it. The first carrier is the decision . What the protagonist chooses at the hinge, against a cost the reader has watched grow, is the book’s verdict on its question, and the reader accepts it as a verdict because they have weighed the price with the character. The second is variation : other characters answer the same question differently, so that the book’s answer is one among several and is tested against them. Truby’s moral argument depends on it, and The Subplot ’s thematic counterpoint (Chapter 14) is the form it takes between threads. Variation argues only if the opposition holds an answer the book takes seriously; a straw opponent is variation in name only. The third is the motif, which carries the theme by recurring in changed contexts, as the household’s ledger passes from the father’s hand to Dov’s and then to all three children. A motif shows that the question persists and where its weight lies, but it cannot argue by itself, since an object answers nothing. The fourth is statement , a character or narrator saying what the book means. It is the most explicit carrier and the weakest as argument, because it asks for assent rather than earning it, and at an ending it borrows the authority of the last position that The Ending (Chapter 16) calls privileged. Statement works where the narration has been stating things throughout, as in George Eliot’s Middlemarch , or where a character’s statement is one answer among several that the book goes on to test. The hinge: a ruling Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2) proposed the hinge as a seventh beat of the scene–sequel unit, and its Core chapter presented it instead as a property that a decision may or may not have. This chapter adopts the hinge at the scale of the book, as the point at which an arc is located and the place a writer looks first when an arc fails, and rejects it as a seventh beat. Three findings support the ruling. Most decisions have no hinge, so a beat that is usually absent is not a beat. The hinge is inferred rather than seen, by comparing a decision with the decisions before it, so it belongs to the shape of a book rather than to one unit of it. And two of the five arcs above, the steadfast and the refused, have no hinge by design. The objection the ruling does not answer is that a falling arc, and some staged arcs, change by erosion, a series of small accommodations none of which is the turn. Lydgate’s decline in Middlemarch is built that way, and in such books the hinge may be an analyst’s construction laid over a gradual change. The chapter concedes the objection for arcs of erosion and keeps the hinge as the test for arcs of decision. See also: the full treatment , with the five arcs related to Weiland’s in a table, a note on the disillusionment arc, and arcs shared across an ensemble.

title: 5. The Mechanism
text: The criterion log An arc can be read only by setting a character’s decisions side by side, so the chapter’s first tool is a table of them. The criterion log lists, for one character, the five to eight largest decisions in the book, in order, with four entries for each: where it falls, as a percentage of the book; what the options were; what the character chose; and the rule by which they chose, written as a short imperative ( find out for yourself , protect the family ). Reading down the last column shows the arc. If every entry is the same rule, the character has none, which may be the book’s design or its fault. If the rule changes once, the change is the hinge, and the decision on either side of it should be tested for the conditions below. If it changes several times, the arc is staged, and the gaps between changes should be long enough for each new rule to be tried. The log has a second use, which is to find decisions the draft has not written. A writer who cannot fill the rule column for a decision has usually written an event rather than a choice: the character did something without the book showing the alternative or its cost. Where the log shows a gap of a quarter of the book or more with no decision in it, the character has stopped choosing, and the arc is being carried, if at all, by circumstance. The four conditions of a change A change convinces when four conditions are met, and together they meet Forster’s test of a round character, that a change should surprise and yet convince. The first condition is the seed . The new criterion must be present in the book before the hinge, so that the reader, looking back, finds the change prepared. The usual seed is another character who already holds the rule, so that the protagonist adopts something the book has shown working for someone else. A rule another character refuses to follow can also serve as a seed. A second form is a moment when the protagonist glimpses the new rule and sets it aside. The seed should be placed far enough from the hinge that the reader does not see the hinge coming from it, and close enough to remember it when it comes. The second condition is the price. The old criterion must be seen to cost something before the hinge, and the hinge must give up something the old criterion valued. The first cost is often concentrated in what James Scott Bell, in a manual already used in The Middle (Chapter 11), calls the mirror moment : a scene near the middle in which the character sees what they have become. In arc terms it is the scene in which the old rule produces a result the character would condemn in someone else. The second cost is the price of the hinge itself, and it is what makes the decision a decision: a change that costs nothing under the old rule is the free hinge of Failure Patterns . The third condition is the hinge itself: a decision, on the page, under pressure, made by an act rather than a statement. The act can be small. It must be one the character could not have performed under the old rule, and the reader must be able to see the alternative being declined. The fourth condition is enactment : the new rule must be confirmed after the hinge by a choice in a situation the book has shown before, answered differently, against something that has not changed. The Ending (Chapter 16) calls the unchanged element the constant, and an arc without one reads as replacement, since a character who is different in every respect has been swapped for another rather than developed. The constant is often the character’s manner, their habit of attention or their want, carried unaltered into a decision made for a new reason. Where the conditions fall The conditions have conventional positions, which follow from what each needs. The seed falls early, often in the first quarter, so that it can be forgotten and recalled. The mirror moment tends towards the centre of the book, where The Middle (Chapter 11) places the midpoint’s change of mode or knowledge, and this is not a coincidence: a midpoint that changes what the protagonist knows is often the moment the old rule is first seen to cost. The hinge falls at or just before the climax, because a criterion is tested hardest when the options have narrowed to one move and the old rule forbids it. Enactment falls in the aftermath, where The Ending ’s domain of character-arc completion (Chapter 16) lives. These are conventions of placement, not requirements, and a book that hinges early must find something else to carry its second half. The answer map The theme has its own tool, which reads the same decisions from the other side. The answer map writes the book’s thematic question at the top, and beneath it, for each major character, the criterion by which they choose, rewritten as that character’s answer to the question. Three readings follow. If every character answers the same way, the book has a sermon rather than a theme. If the opposition’s answer is one the book never lets succeed or cost anything, the variation is a straw figure. And the protagonist’s hinge can be located on the map: the new criterion adopts another character’s answer, combines two, or finds one no character held. The last is the strongest and the hardest to seed. Multiplicity at the hinge A hinge scene usually serves three of the domains The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1) sets out at once. It moves the plot, since the decision changes what happens next; it completes or turns the arc; and it delivers the book’s verdict on its question, since the reader weighs the new answer against the answers the map has shown. A hinge that serves character alone, a scene of interior change that the plot does not need, tends to read as inserted. In the household revision in Worked Analyses , Elena’s decision not to open the ledger until her sister is in the room delays the plot by a page, completes her arc and gives the book’s answer to its question, with no sentence of statement. See also: the full treatment , with a blank criterion log and answer map, and the household’s log and map in full.

title: 6. Diagnostic Tests
text: The eight tests are for revision, and they need two documents to work on: the protagonist’s criterion log, defined in The Mechanism , with the five to eight largest decisions and the rule behind each, and the answer map, which writes the book’s question and each major character’s answer to it. Tests 1 to 6 (Criterion, Hinge, Price, Seed, Constant and Enactment) read the arc, and tests 7 (Question) and 8 (Answers) the theme. Record a sentence for each, not a verdict. Test 1 — Criterion Is the rule behind the last large decision different from the rule behind the first, and if not, does the book mean it to be the same? Failure. No arc, in a book that wanted one. Exception. The Remains of the Day (1989), whose rule holds at the last decision and whose recognition is the arc. Test 2 — Hinge At which decision does the rule change, and is that decision on the page, made by an act? Failure. Change by drift or by report: the announced arc. Exception. George Eliot’s Middlemarch (1871–72), in which Lydgate declines by small accommodations and no single turn. Test 3 — Price What does the decision at the hinge cost under the old rule, and has the reader seen that cost grow? Failure. The free hinge. Exception. Dickens’s A Christmas Carol (1843), where Scrooge’s change costs only money he has, and the price is paid in what the ghosts make him see. Test 4 — Seed Where is the new rule in the book before the hinge, held by another character or glimpsed and set aside? Failure. A change from nowhere, which the reader credits to the author. Exception. As You Like It , in which Duke Frederick is converted offstage by “an old religious man” and the comedy’s contract is reconciliation. Test 5 — Constant What about the character is visibly unchanged at the end? Failure. Replacement: a different person, not a developed one. Exception. Virginia Woolf’s Orlando (1928), a change of sex and of centuries whose subject is how much a self can lose and remain one. Test 6 — Enactment Is the new rule confirmed after the hinge by a situation the book has shown before, answered differently? Failure. A change confirmed only by statement. Exception. Tolstoy’s The Death of Ivan Ilych (1886), translated by Louise and Aylmer Maude, whose change comes in a dying man’s last hours and cannot be repeated. Test 7 — Question Can the theme be put as a question to which two or more of the book’s decisions give different answers? Failure. A topic, which gives the reader nothing to weigh, or a thesis, which gives nothing to decide. Exception. George Orwell’s Animal Farm (1945), a fable whose theme is a proposition and whose form exists to demonstrate it. Test 8 — Answers On the answer map, does the opposition hold an answer the book lets succeed, or makes costly to defeat? Failure. The sermon: one answer, and figures to illustrate it. Exception. John Bunyan’s The Pilgrim’s Progress (1678), an allegory in which every figure is an answer and only one is allowed. Reading the results together Failures cluster, and the cluster says more than any single result. Test 1 (Criterion) passing while test 2 (Hinge) fails means the character ends somewhere new without having chosen to: find the decision the book skipped and write it in scene. Tests 3 (Price) and 4 (Seed) failing together mean the change belongs to the author rather than the character, and the remedy is to give the new rule to another character early, as a seed, and to make the old rule cost something visible near the middle. Test 5 (Constant) failing while test 1 (Criterion) passes means replacement, and the repair is usually small: keep the character’s want, or a habit of attention, unaltered into the decision made for a new reason. Test 7 (Question) passing while test 8 (Answers) fails describes a book with a real question and only one answer in it, which readers experience as being lectured, and the remedy is to strengthen the opposition’s answer until it costs the protagonist something to reject it. Test 1 (Criterion) failing while test 8 (Answers) passes usually describes a steadfast arc, and the question is then whether the protagonist’s rule has been put under real pressure. The hardest result is a clean pass on every test and readers who still do not believe the change. The usual cause is the hinge’s position rather than its content: it has been placed in summary, or at a low point of pressure, or a chapter away from the climax that should test it. Move it into scene, and into the climax’s pressure, before rewriting anything else. See also: the full treatment , with the procedure for each test and a worked criterion log for each of the household’s three siblings.

title: 7. Failure Patterns
text: Each pattern below fails through a mechanism rather than a surface feature. Each ends with a published work that uses the feature successfully because the mechanism is absent or offset by another effect. The full treatment has a longer catalogue, among them replacement, the drifting theme, the arc for everyone, the decorative motif and the untested steadfast arc. The announced arc Symptom. The change is reported rather than chosen. The character realises , understands at last or sees now , and the narration or the character supplies the content of the realisation. Readers say they were told the character had changed and did not feel it. Mechanism. The announced arc substitutes knowledge for decision. A realisation is an event in the character’s mind, and the reader can verify it only by what the character then does differently; where nothing is done differently, the reader has the narration’s word and nothing to weigh it against. The motive is understandable: by the end of a draft the writer knows what the change means and wants to be sure the reader does. The household draft in The Problem is a clean instance. Remedy. Tests 2 (Hinge) and 6 (Enactment). Delete the realisation and find the decision it stands in for, then place that decision under pressure and make it cost something the old rule valued. If the realisation must stay, put it after the decision, so that it names what the reader has already seen. Exception. F. Scott Fitzgerald’s The Great Gatsby (1925). Nick Carraway tells the reader on the first page that he is “inclined to reserve all judgments”, and tells the reader on the last pages that he has decided to go back West, in a passage that is largely statement. The book works because Nick’s arc is the telling itself: the retrospective narrator who judges every person in the story is the change, and the reader watches it happen in the voice rather than in a scene. The free hinge Symptom. The character chooses by a new rule at a moment when the old rule has nothing left to defend. The obstacle has died, the rival has withdrawn, the money has arrived, and the change is made at no cost. Mechanism. The free hinge moves the price from the character to the plot. A decision is legible as a change only if the old rule would have forbidden it, and if circumstances have already removed what the old rule protected, the character is choosing between options that cost the same. The reader may feel satisfaction at the outcome but has seen no one choose it. Remedy. Test 3 (Price). Find what the old rule values, and make the hinge give it up. If the plot must clear the way, let it do so after the decision, not before. Exception. Charlotte Brontë’s Jane Eyre (1847). Jane’s return to Rochester comes after the plot has removed every cost: his wife is dead in the fire that destroyed Thornfield, he is blinded and maimed, and Jane has an inheritance of her own. The return has struck readers as convenient since publication. The book holds because its priced decision came earlier and was paid in full, when Jane left Thornfield with nothing rather than stay as Rochester’s mistress, and the return reads as the reward for a choice the reader watched her make. The scheduled arc Symptom. Readers predict the change from the first chapters, and the book delivers it on time. The flaw appears to exist in order to be corrected, and the climax restages an early scene with the roles reversed. Mechanism. The scheduled arc meets Forster’s condition that a change convince and fails his condition that it surprise. Arc models that begin with a named wound or lie make the schedule easy to build and hard to hide, because the writer has planned the change before the character has made any decisions, and the reader detects a plan sooner than a person. Remedy. Tests 1 (Criterion) and 4 (Seed). Keep the destination and complicate the route: let the hinge cost something the opening did not promise, place the seed in a character the reader does not suspect, or let the aftermath show that the change did not cure everything. Exception. Khaled Hosseini’s The Kite Runner (2003), a long-running bestseller. Its first chapter gives the arc away: a telephone call from Rahim Khan, an old family friend, ends with “There is a way to be good again.” Amir’s betrayal of his friend Hassan in Kabul is answered decades later by his return to rescue Hassan’s son, a beating by the man who once assaulted Hassan, and a slingshot that repeats a threat from the first part, and the last page returns Hassan’s devoted phrase, for you, a thousand times over . The design is visible to any reader. The book works because the price is heavy and the aftermath does not cure: the boy Amir rescues stays withdrawn and nearly silent through the last chapters. The revoked arc Symptom. After the hinge, the character goes back to choosing by the old rule, because the plot needs them to. Mechanism. The revoked arc breaks the enactment condition. The hinge has told the reader that the old rule no longer governs, and every later decision made on it either contradicts the hinge or empties it. Revocation usually comes from structure rather than character: a set piece planned before the arc was understood, or a comic or action climax that requires the old behaviour. Remedy. Test 6 (Enactment). Rewrite the later decisions on the new rule, or move the hinge after them. Exception. Mark Twain’s Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884). Huck decides in chapter 31 that he will go to hell rather than give Jim up, and in chapters 33 to 43 at the Phelps farm he defers to Tom Sawyer, who turns Jim’s escape into a game and has known all along that Jim was freed by Miss Watson’s will. Leo Marx argued in 1953 that this part, often called the Evasion, jeopardises the significance of the whole novel. The book has survived the argument, and some readers defend the Evasion as Twain’s satire of a freedom granted on paper; the arc’s force is great enough that its revocation reads, to them, as part of what the book shows. The sermon Symptom. Every character’s choices answer the book’s question in the same way, or the characters who answer it differently exist to be defeated. Readers report being lectured, and the narration or a favoured character states the answer. Mechanism. The sermon removes variation, the second carrier in The Taxonomy , and leaves the theme to statement. Without a serious opposing answer the book has nothing to test its answer against, so the reader’s assent is asked for rather than won. Remedy. Tests 7 (Question) and 8 (Answers). Give the strongest opposing answer to a character the book respects, let it succeed at least once, and make rejecting it cost the protagonist something. Exception. Harriet Beecher Stowe’s Uncle Tom’s Cabin (1852), serialised from 1851, the best-selling novel of the nineteenth century. Stowe breaks into the story to deliver homilies on slavery, and closes the book by addressing her readers directly. The book sets out to persuade, and by the measure of its sales and of the argument it provoked it succeeded; its sermon works because the scenes it rests on made its readers feel the cost of the answer it rejected. See also: the full treatment , for the extended catalogue; The Ending (Chapter 16), for the explained ending, the sermon’s form at the last page.

title: 8. Worked Analyses
text: Three close readings, a short reading of a film, and the household revision case. Each reading names the arc, finds the hinge if there is one, and reads the theme from the answers the book sets beside it. Emma : a staged arc and its mirror Jane Austen’s Emma (1815) has fifty-five chapters in three volumes, and its heroine chooses for most of them by one rule: her own judgement of what other people should want, exercised for her amusement. She persuades Harriet Smith to refuse a farmer who loves her and to hope for Mr Elton, who wants Emma; she imagines Jane Fairfax in an intrigue with a married man. The seed of the new rule is in the book from its first chapters, held by Mr Knightley, who tells her plainly that her management of Harriet will do harm. And the book gives her a mirror in Mrs Elton, the vicar’s new wife, who patronises Jane Fairfax as Emma has patronised Harriet, and whom Emma finds intolerable for it. The first hinge comes at Box Hill, in the forty-third chapter, 43 ÷ 55 or about 78 per cent of the way through. Frank Churchill’s game asks each of the party for one very clever thing or three very dull ones, and when Miss Bates, poor and garrulous, says she will be sure to manage three dull things, Emma answers: “Ah! ma’am, but there may be a difficulty. Pardon me—but you will be limited as to number—only three at once.” Knightley takes her aside afterwards: “It was badly done, indeed!” Emma cries most of the way home. The recognition is not the hinge, since tears change nothing; the hinge is the next decision, when she resolves to call on Miss Bates “the very next morning”, and to make it “the beginning, on her side, of a regular, equal, kindly intercourse”. The visit costs her what her old rule valued, her command of a room, and Jane Fairfax will not come out to see her. A second stage follows. When Harriet confides that she hopes for Mr Knightley, “it darted through her, with the speed of an arrow, that Mr. Knightley must marry no one but herself!” and the recognition changes a second set of choices, about Harriet and about her own heart. The constant is Emma’s energy of imagination, which the last chapters still show working, now on her own errors. The theme, put as a question, is what a person with social power owes others in the way of attention, and the answer map is full: Knightley’s responsible regard, Frank Churchill’s play and concealment, Mrs Elton’s patronage, Miss Bates’s undiscriminating goodwill. Emma’s new rule is close to Knightley’s, which is why the marriage reads as the book’s verdict rather than its reward. Gilead : a hinge made by blessing Marilynne Robinson’s Gilead (2004), which won the Pulitzer Prize for fiction in 2005, is a letter written in 1956 by the Reverend John Ames, an elderly Congregationalist minister in a small Iowa town, to the young son he will not see grow up, since his heart is failing. The letter is full of blessing, the minister’s habit of seeing the world as given, and the book’s arc concerns the one person Ames cannot bless. Jack Boughton, the prodigal son of Ames’s oldest friend and Ames’s own namesake and godson, has come home. Ames has judged him for years as cruel, since as a young man Jack fathered a child with a poor girl and abandoned them, and Ames fears his attention to his own young wife and son. His criterion towards Jack is judgement and guard: give him nothing, and watch. The seed is Ames’s own theology. He has preached grace for decades, and the letter keeps returning to it; the reader holds the new rule before Ames applies it to the man in front of him, and old Boughton’s helpless love for his son is the variation that makes Ames’s guardedness visible as a choice. Late in the book Jack visits Ames at the church and shows him a photograph: he has a wife, Della, a Black woman, and a young son, and the laws of Missouri and her father’s disapproval keep them apart. The knowledge changes Ames’s understanding of Jack. It does not require him to do anything, and the hinge is the act that follows. When Jack leaves Gilead, Ames walks him to the bus stop, asks if he may bless him, and puts his hand on his head. The blessing costs Ames his judgement and his last word on the man he feared, and it is made by the gesture the whole book has been practising for someone else, the old minister’s hand on a son’s head. The constant is the voice, unhurried and attentive to light, which is the same before and after. The theme is the question of what grace can extend to, and the answer map runs through three generations: Ames’s grandfather’s fierce abolitionism, his father’s pacifism, Boughton’s love and Ames’s own long withholding.
