The book’s verdict is given by where Ames’s hand rests, and its letter form allows Ames to state what he means without the statement doing the work, since the reader has seen the act. A Man Called Ove : the constant that carries the change Fredrik Backman’s A Man Called Ove (2012), translated from the Swedish by Henning Koch (2014), is a commercial novel whose arc shows how far a constant can carry. Ove, a fifty-nine-year-old widower, patrols his housing association every morning to check that no one has parked in the wrong place, visits his wife Sonja’s grave, and has decided to join her. He ties a rope to the ceiling; he runs the car in the closed garage. Each attempt is interrupted by a neighbour’s need, most often Parvaneh’s, the pregnant Iranian woman who has moved in nearby and who will not leave him alone, and each time Ove resolves the dilemma, die now or deal with this, by his old rule: a thing badly done must be put right. The arc is staged, and the criterion log shows something the hinge test alone would miss. Ove’s rule never changes. What changes is what it serves: the same insistence on doing things properly that makes him intolerable in the first chapters makes him indispensable in the last, as he teaches, repairs, takes in a stray cat he says he does not want, and defends the people he despised. The rule that is outranked is his loyalty to the dead, and it is outranked by accumulation, each interruption a small decision on the old rule that leaves him further from the rope. The hinge test finds no single turn, which places the book among the arcs of erosion that the ruling in The Taxonomy concedes. The constant is so strong that the change can hardly be missed, which is why one reviewer called the book predictable and why it is easy to follow. Years later Ove dies in his sleep of the heart condition the book has carried, in a house that the people he once kept at a distance have filled. The theme, what the living owe each other set against what is owed to the dead, is argued by the neighbours’ claims winning one at a time. On screen: The Godfather Francis Ford Coppola’s The Godfather (1972), from Mario Puzo’s novel, is the falling arc in its classic form. Michael Corleone, a war veteran and the youngest son, wants no part of his family’s business, and says so to Kay at his sister’s wedding. Every step of his descent is taken by one rule, protect the family. At the hospital he finds his wounded father’s guards removed, moves him to another room and stands guard outside. Then he offers to kill Sollozzo and the corrupt police captain McCluskey at a restaurant meeting, and does: this is the hinge, the first act his old rule forbade, made in the name of the new one. The constant is his calm, which the film shows unaltered from the wedding to the end. The last scenes enact the fall in a repeated situation: at the wedding he told Kay the truth about his family’s methods, and now, when she asks whether he had his sister’s husband killed, he lies; the door closes on her while his captains kiss his hand. The theme, what a person owes his family against what he owes himself, is answered by every brother differently, Sonny by temper, Fredo by weakness, Tom Hagen by counsel, and Michael’s answer consumes the self that first refused it. The household revision case: Elena’s arc The situation. The draft in The Problem ends with a paragraph of Elena’s understanding and Nadia’s line We protect each other by not saying . The criterion log for Elena, built from the decisions earlier chapters have fixed, shows why the reader does not believe the paragraph. Positions are estimates. Position Decision Rule Cost Before the drawer In Dov’s doorway, asks why the locks were changed, is refused, and leaves with the key ( The Dialogue Exchange , Chapter 3) Ask directly, once Shut out without a reason After the doorway In the truck, decides not to telephone her mother and drives to the shop ( Scene and Sequel , Chapter 2) Find out for yourself Her mother left unasked 25% At the drawer, turns back to the first page and reads alone, from the beginning ( The Chapter Break , Chapter 6) Find out for yourself None yet 38% At the empty drawer, decides not to ask Dov who took the ledger, because she had asked him once , and turns the sign to CLOSED ( The Middle , Chapter 11) Do not ask people who will not tell you Dov closed as a witness End (draft) Understands, reading with the others, that the family could only know together (stated, not chosen) None The tests find the fault quickly. Test 1 (Criterion) fails in the way the draft did not intend: the rule at the last decision is the rule at the first, and the change is in a paragraph rather than a decision, so test 2 (Hinge) fails as the announced arc. Test 3 (Price) fails, since understanding costs Elena nothing. Test 4 (Seed) finds no seed: no one in the book holds the rule Elena is said to reach. And Nadia’s line fails test 8 (Answers) from the other side: it states one answer, protection by silence, at the ending’s privileged position, and the book has not shown it to be true of the mother, whose silence is the household’s largest. The revision. It deletes both paragraphs and adds two passages, about two hundred words in all. The first is a mirror moment at about 54 per cent of the book, after the midpoint at which Dov’s messages ask both sisters to clear the flat, and before he signs at 58. Elena helps Nadia begin: “Do you know why he wants it cleared?” Nadia was folding the tea towels into thirds and counting them as she went. Elena had a box of receipts on her knees and the empty drawer in her head. “No,” she said, which was true. “You’d tell me, though. If you knew anything.” “I’d tell you.” She would remember, later, how easily it had come. The second is the hinge, at the convergence after Dov’s chapter, when Dov brings the ledger to the shop, where Elena is, before the reading that the ending drafted in The Ending (Chapter 16) begins with They read it together, in the end : Dov put the ledger on the counter and took his hand off it. “It’s all there,” he said. “From March, it’s mine.” She had wanted it since the drawer. She laid her palm on the cover, and the leather was warm from his arm, and she did not open it. “Ring Nadia,” she said. “She doesn’t answer me.” “She’ll answer me.” She rang, and Nadia answered, and Elena told her to come to the shop, and why. What the revision did. It gave the arc its four conditions. The seed is Nadia’s: You’d tell me, though is the new rule, spoken by another character and set aside by the protagonist. The price is visible at the middle, where Elena’s rule makes her do to her sister what Dov and their mother did to her, and the narration’s small retrospective gap, She would remember, later , lets the reader see the cost before Elena admits it. The hinge is an act under the greatest pressure the book can supply: the ledger she has wanted since a quarter of the way through is under her hand, and she declines it until the three of them are in the room. And the enactment is a repeated situation answered differently. Elena declined to telephone her mother in the truck, and at the empty drawer she declined to ask Dov; here she telephones, and she tells Nadia why, which is the word Dov’s thirteen-word message to Nadia left out. The constant is her want, her palm on the cover. The theme is now argued by the answer map rather than stated: Character Answer to what do the members of a family owe each other in the way of truth? The father Write it down properly and tell no one: the truth kept for later, in case Ma Silence, unexplained: the answer the book declines to test Dov The form without the content: the key without the reason, the date and the count Nadia Count, do not touch, and expect to be told Elena, until the convergence Find out for yourself; do not ask people who will not tell you Elena, at the convergence What concerns the three of them is read by the three of them The book’s answer is given by the ending’s arrangement, three people reading one record together, and Nadia’s line is no longer needed, since the reader can weigh protection by not saying against the father’s, Dov’s and the mother’s practice of it without being told. The convergence now completes two arcs in successive decisions a page apart, Elena’s at the counter and Nadia’s at the coat, so the last decision in the book is still Nadia’s. What the revision has not solved. The hinge adds a fifth discharge to a convergence that The Subplot (Chapter 14) already found crowded with four, and Nadia’s answering at once, after a book in which she lets Dov’s calls ring out, may read as arranged. Elena’s new rule stops at the three siblings: she does not telephone her mother, and the book does not say whether the rule would reach her, which keeps the mother’s silence open as the canon requires but leaves Elena’s change visibly partial. The mirror moment depends on a retrospective sentence that some readers will take as the narration underlining. And the warm leather is the third time the ledger has been warm, which may tip an echo into a tic. See also: the full treatment , with criterion logs for all three siblings, further readings of Project Hail Mary , The Kite Runner and Paddington 2 , and the household case in full.

title: 9. Checklist and Exercises
text: Revision checklist The arc Can I write my protagonist’s rule for choosing as a short imperative, at the first large decision and at the last? If the rule is the same at both, is that the book’s design (a steadfast or refused arc), and is the rule put under real pressure? Is there a stretch of a quarter of the book or more in which my protagonist makes no decision? The hinge Can I name the decision at which the rule changes, and is it on the page, in scene, made by an act? What does that decision give up that the old rule valued, and has the reader watched that cost grow? Where is the new rule before the hinge: in another character, or in a moment my protagonist set aside? After the hinge, does any decision go back to the old rule because the plot needed it? The confirmation Is the new rule confirmed by a situation the book has shown before, answered differently? What about my protagonist is visibly unchanged at the end? Have I deleted every sentence in which the character, or the narration, explains the change? The theme Can I put my book’s theme as a question, and not only as a topic or a thesis? Does each major character’s rule answer that question, and do at least two answers differ? Does the opposing answer succeed at least once, or cost my protagonist something to reject? Who states the theme, where, and would the ending still argue it if the statement were cut? Exercises The criterion log. List your protagonist’s six largest decisions in order, with each one’s position as a percentage, the options, the choice, the rule as a short imperative and the cost. Read down the rule column and mark where it changes. If it never does, write a paragraph saying whether the book means that, and if it does not, find the decision that should be made on new grounds. The answer map. Write your theme as a question at the top of a page. Beneath it, write each major character’s rule as an answer to it, in their own idiom. Mark the answer your book agrees with and the strongest answer it rejects; if the strongest rejected answer would not persuade an intelligent reader, rewrite the character who holds it. The hinge without words. Rewrite your hinge scene so that the character says nothing about what has changed and the narration reports no realisation. Keep only what the character does and what it costs. If the scene no longer shows the change, the change was in the words, and the scene needs a different act. The seed. Find the new rule’s first appearance before the hinge. If there is none, give it to another character, early, in a scene about something else, and let your protagonist dismiss it. Then check that the reader will remember it when the hinge comes and will not predict the hinge from it. The repeated situation. Find a situation from the first third of your book that your protagonist could meet again after the hinge: a call not made, a door not opened, a question not asked. Write the later version, answered by the new rule, and keep one detail of manner or habit unchanged in both.

title: 10. Coda
text: The instruments in this chapter assume that change is what a character’s story is for. The criterion log looks for a rule that changes, the hinge test for the decision where it does, and the conditions in The Mechanism for the seed, the price and the confirmation that make the change believable. They will report as failures a serious body of fiction that does not share the assumption: the picaresque hero who meets the world and is not altered by it, the modernist consciousness that is observed rather than tried, the series detective whose rule must survive into the next volume. The steadfast and refused arcs in The Taxonomy take in some of these books, but not all, and where the tools misfire they are describing their own assumption rather than the book’s fault. For books that do share it, the chapter’s argument is that arc and theme are decided by the same choices, and that both are lost by the same move, a statement put where a decision should be. The consequence runs against a writer’s training in clarity. A theme is not made clearer by being said; it is made arguable by being answered in several ways, and the reader decides between the answers. A change is not made more convincing by being explained; it is made convincing by costing something, and the explanation, if any, comes after the reader has seen the price paid. That is why the household revision could delete the two paragraphs its writer added to make the ending clear, and make the ending clearer. It added an exchange of five lines in the middle, in which a sister keeps something from a sister, and a decision at the convergence in which she does not open a book. Neither passage states what the book means. Together they place three people in one room reading one record, and that arrangement is the book’s answer to its question: an answer a reader can reject, because the book has shown the other answers working, and the mother’s, the one it never tests, remains open. See also: the full treatment , on the limits of the model; Series and Genre (Chapter 17), for the arc held across volumes; The Structural Edit (Chapter 18), which puts the criterion log into a revision order for the whole book.

title: The Viewpoint Shift
text: Who is granted a mind, how many, and when The Craft Behind the Story (Second Edition) — Chapter 13. Part III: The Architecture of the Whole. In brief. A viewpoint shift moves the narration from one character’s consciousness to another’s. Behind every shift lies a decision this chapter calls the grant: which characters the reader is allowed inside, for how much of the book, and from when. The grant is a structural decision rather than a local one, because each new viewpoint adds coverage but divides depth, and because the characters left outside are shaped by being left there. The chapter’s tool is an admission test: a viewpoint must name two jobs it does that no cheaper instrument could do, and one of them must be something other than carrying information. Use the chapter when readers cannot tell your viewpoint characters apart, when a draft feels thin although every scene is anchored, when a new viewpoint arrives late, or when you are tempted to explain a difficult character by going inside her. What you can do after this chapter Distinguish a structural shift from head-hopping, and say whether a book has earned the right to move between minds inside a scene. State for any viewpoint character which jobs the grant does and which cheaper instruments it displaced. Name a draft’s viewpoint architecture and audit its page-share. Price a late grant, and decide whether to bound it to a single chapter. Say what the allocation does to the characters who receive no viewpoint, and defend it. Key terms Viewpoint shift; the grant, with its recipient, extent, onset and termination; head-hopping, the structural shift and omniscience; focalisation (zero, internal and external; fixed, variable and multiple) and the focaliser; voice, person and narrative distance; the reflector; psycho-narration, narrated monologue and quoted monologue; character-space, character-system and character compression; the situation model; levels of intentionality; narrative empathy; the domains of a grant (access, dramatic irony, contrast (viewpoint domain), sympathy engineering, structural pacing) and the proposed epistemological domain; the cheaper instruments; the knowledge boundary; viewpoint architecture; the bounded grant; the first grant and the later grant; page-share. Each is defined at first use and collected in the consolidated glossary . Contents The first files say what a viewpoint grant is and why it is expensive, the middle files what a grant can do and how its cost is managed, and the last are for use at the desk. The Problem A household draft with too many viewpoints, and the chapter’s claim Definitions The shift, the grant, head-hopping, and the terms confused with them How It Works Who perceives, what a grant delivers, what happens to the people left outside, what a shift costs, and the age of the head-hopping rule The Taxonomy Five domains a grant can serve, a proposed sixth, and a ruling on the authority domain of The Prologue (Chapter 10) The Mechanism The admission test, where the distinguishing work lives, the first and later grant, the ceiling, and the architectures Diagnostic Tests Ten questions on one page, and how to read their failures together Failure Patterns Five recurrent failures, each with a published work that commits it and succeeds Worked Analyses Middlemarch , The Vegetarian , Me Before You , The Affair and the household revision case Checklist and Exercises The revision checklist and five exercises for your own draft Coda What the shape of an allocation says A writer in revision can start at the diagnostic tests and the page-share audit in the exercises; the coda, which sets limits on the chapter’s central metaphor, is best read early. The full treatment The Reference layer holds the complete chapter, The Viewpoint Shift : the fuller narratology, the cognitive literature and its limits, a history of the head-hopping rule, thirteen architectures, twelve failure patterns, eight close readings (among them Bleak House , Wide Sargasso Sea and Beloved ), viewpoint in other forms and in translation, seminar questions and the sources. See also: The Transition (Chapter 5), on how the reader is carried across the gap a shift opens; The Chapter Break (Chapter 6), on where the gap falls; The Opening Pages (Chapter 9), whose formal contract requires a plural architecture to be declared early; The Subplot (Chapter 14), whose attention tax is the same scarcity at the scale of a plot line; The Reveal (Chapter 15), on the disclosure a withheld viewpoint so often holds back.

title: 1. The Problem
text: A third of the way into a first draft of the household novel, the writer has given each of the three siblings a viewpoint in rotation: a chapter for Elena, a chapter for Nadia, a chapter for Dov, and round again. The rotation felt fair while drafting, since each of them has a stake in the father’s death and the shop. Two early readers have now sent notes. The first says she cannot always tell Nadia’s chapters from Dov’s when she covers the chapter numbers, because both of them count things, worry about money and resent the others. The second asks why the book never lets her inside the mother, who changed the locks and will not say why, and suggests a fourth strand in the rotation so that the mother can explain herself. The draft and the suggestion are illustrations for this chapter, not the novel as it stands; they are useful because the two readers have, between them, named both halves of the problem the chapter treats. Coverage and depth Imagine two finished manuscripts of the same length, both about this family after the death. The first is told entirely through Elena. Everything the reader learns, she learns by being present, by being told, by inferring or by being misled, and whole regions of the story are closed: Dov’s dealings with the buyer, the mother’s reasons, the father’s last months. The book is badly informed. It is also, after four hundred pages, in possession of one person so thoroughly that the reader can predict what she will notice in a room before she notices it. The second is told through all four in rotation. Nothing is closed. Dov’s negotiations are dramatised and the mother’s reasons supplied. The book is well informed, and it holds four people at a quarter of the depth each. The arithmetic is plain at novel length: in a book of 90,000 words, one viewpoint has all 90,000 words in which to become known, and four equal viewpoints have 22,500 each, about the length of a long short story, with the further cost that the reader has been asked to begin again with each change. Neither manuscript is better by construction. What separates them is a decision about how a finite quantity of reader attention and identification is distributed across a cast. That decision is made once, at the level of the whole book, and then honoured or broken at every scene boundary. Coverage is additive: each new viewpoint adds the scenes that character can attend. Depth is divisive: each new viewpoint divides the same pages and the same accumulated familiarity. A book cannot buy coverage without spending depth, and it cannot keep depth without accepting blindness. The people left outside The second reader’s suggestion points at the less obvious half. A character seen only from outside, in a book whose other characters are seen from inside, is not neutral in the reader’s mind. The mother in the household novel is present throughout, changes the locks, speaks once at a remove through Dov, and is never entered, and the reader treats her silence as the book’s standing question. Give her a strand and the question is answered, whether or not the writer meant to answer it, because a mind the reader is inside cannot keep its reasons from the reader without visibly refusing to think about them. The allocation of viewpoint is also an allocation of what stays unknown. The household novel, as the canon of this edition fixes it, settles both halves. A prologue is focalised through the father on his last ordinary day; the main narrative belongs to Elena and Nadia in close third person; Dov is seen from outside until a single chapter near the climax; and the mother is never entered. This chapter is the reasoning that reaches that settlement and defends it, and the household revision case in Worked Analyses tests it. Viewpoint is an allocation, not a technique: a distribution of a finite resource across a cast, whose shape can be read, argued over and revised, and which shapes the characters it leaves out as surely as those it lets in. The rest of the chapter states the claim’s terms, sets out the theory it depends on, names what a grant can be for, and gives the tests that turn the claim into a revision plan. See also: The Transition (Chapter 5), which assumes the far side of each crossing has already been chosen; the Reference introduction , with the strong form of the claim and its qualifications.

title: 2. Definitions
text: Talk about viewpoint is unusually prone to conflation, because “point of view” is made to carry person, distance, reliability and the identity of the narrator all at once, so that four different problems receive one diagnosis. This file separates them before the argument begins. The working definition A viewpoint shift is a deliberate change in the consciousness through which the narration is filtered, made at a structural boundary such as a section or chapter break, in a book built to hold more than one vantage. The decision underneath it is the grant : the allocation to a character of access to the reader’s identification. A shift is an event in the text and a grant is a commitment of the whole book; one grant may produce forty shifts, or one. Every grant has four properties a writer should be able to state for each viewpoint character: its recipient (who holds it), its extent (how much of the book), its onset (when it begins) and its termination (whether it ends, and whether the reader knows). Most advice about viewpoint concerns the recipient alone; structural failures occur in the other three, which are properties of the whole book and so are invisible while drafting forward and obvious in an audit. Viewpoint decisions are made at the scale of the sentence, the scene, the chapter and the book, and this chapter works at the last: who has a viewpoint at all, how many, and in what proportion. A manuscript can be sound at the first three scales and wrong at the fourth, with five cleanly anchored viewpoints spread so thin that nobody is known. Head-hopping, the structural shift and omniscience Head-hopping is workshop slang for a change of viewpoint inside a continuous scene, without a boundary, so that the reader’s access moves from one character’s interior to another’s in the middle of the action. The usual teaching sets it against the structural shift made at a boundary, and calls the first an error and the second a design. That teaching describes a convention of roughly the last century, not a property of narrative. Middlemarch , Anna Karenina and Tom Jones move between minds inside a single scene constantly, with effects nothing else could produce, and in them the movement is omniscience : narration by an intelligence with free access to any mind, exercising it. The discrimination that matters is whether the narration has a stable convention that the movement belongs to. A mid-scene change of mind is head-hopping when the book has established a limited narration and then leaks; it is omniscience when the book has established a mobile narration and then moves. The reader’s unease comes from the mismatch, not from the movement, and Failure Patterns treats the case at length. Adjacent terms Several neighbouring terms are needed throughout the chapter, and the table gives each with its relation to the viewpoint shift. Term Meaning Relation to the shift Focalisation Gérard Genette’s term for the regulation of what the narrative tells according to a perceiving position: who perceives , as distinct from who speaks (a word he chose after Brooks and Warren’s “focus of narration”) What a viewpoint shift changes Focaliser Mieke Bal’s term for the character whose perception organises what is presented The recipient of a grant Narrator The agent who speaks the narrative Often unchanged across a shift Person First, second or third Independent of focalisation Narrative distance How close the narration stands to the focaliser’s mind A change inside one grant, not a change of grant Reflector Henry James’s word for a character through whom events are refracted without her narrating The single-viewpoint architecture Two of the pairings cause most confusion in practice. Person is not focalisation: The Great Gatsby is told in the first person and mostly observes Gatsby from outside, while Mrs Dalloway is told in the third person from very close inside a succession of minds. Distance is not viewpoint: moving from She crossed the yard to Gravel. Not the grass, not today changes how near the narration stands without changing whose mind it occupies, and it is repaired as prose, while a viewpoint problem is repaired as structure. What this chapter leaves to others The crossing itself, the anchoring proper noun and the cost of each frame switch, belongs to The Transition (Chapter 5); where the break falls belongs to The Chapter Break (Chapter 6); the requirement that a plural architecture be declared early is stated in The Opening Pages (Chapter 9), and this chapter supplies its mechanism. How two narrators are made to sound different at the level of the sentence belongs to The Dialogue Exchange (Chapter 3); this chapter asks whether they notice, want and know differently. The relation between a narrating I and the younger self she remembers is a matter of time and belongs to Backstory and Flashback (Chapter 7). The cost of material that pulls attention from the main line, at the scale of a plot line, is the attention tax of The Subplot (Chapter 14), and the two chapters make one argument at two scales. See also: the Reference definitions , with the full table of adjacent terms, including Chatman’s filter and slant.

title: 3. How It Works
text: Six practical questions organise the theory this chapter uses, and each strand below opens with the question it answers before naming its source. Whose head am I in, and is that the same as who is talking? Craft advice about “point of view” often fails because it runs two questions together. Gérard Genette separated them in Narrative Discourse (1972; English translation by Jane E. Lewin, 1980): who speaks? is the question of voice , the narrating agent, and who perceives? is the question of focalisation, the position from which the narrative’s information is regulated. Genette distinguished zero focalisation , in which the narration knows more than any character; internal focalisation , in which it is restricted to what one character knows; and external focalisation , in which it reports behaviour without interiority, like a camera. He then divided internal focalisation by how it behaves across a whole text. Fixed focalisation keeps one focaliser throughout, as The Remains of the Day does. Variable focalisation changes focaliser one at a time, as most multi-viewpoint novels do, and buys coverage: each vantage sees different material and the reader assembles a wider world. Multiple focalisation tells the same events through different characters in turn, as The Sound and the Fury does, and buys doubt: the reader assembles a contradiction. The difference between those two last kinds is what separates the ordinary multi-viewpoint novel from the proposed sixth domain in The Taxonomy . Mieke Bal ( Narratology , 1985) added that focalisation is a relation with two ends, a focaliser and what is focalised. To say a chapter is Nadia’s is half a description; the other half is what Nadia is allowed to look at, and a viewpoint character pointed only at plot information is a fault that Bal’s formulation makes visible. Why do some viewpoint characters feel inhabited and others only reported? Dorrit Cohn’s Transparent Minds (1978) names three ways third-person narration renders a mind. Psycho-narration reports a consciousness in the narrator’s language: She had never trusted her brother’s silences. Narrated monologue , the mode usually called free indirect style , gives the character’s own idiom in the third person and the narrative tense: Her brother’s silences. What was she supposed to do with those? Quoted monologue gives the thought in the first person: I have no idea what he is not telling me. The modes cost different amounts of the reader’s attention. Psycho-narration reports a mind without asking the reader to inhabit it, and a book can afford it for a dozen characters; narrated monologue asks the reader to adopt a character’s judgements, and is the mode in which a viewpoint is truly held. A draft that “has five viewpoint characters” may have one inhabited mind and four reported ones, and the diagnosis is invisible until the modes are named. What happens to the people who get no viewpoint? Alex Woloch’s The One vs. the Many (2003) supplies the rigour behind the metaphor this chapter calls the empathy budget : reader identification treated as a finite pool divided among the viewpoint characters. A novel implies many people and has room to attend to few. Woloch calls the delimited position each character occupies in the narrative its character-space , and the arrangement of all those spaces, in which the attention given to one is a function of the attention withheld from others, the character-system . His most useful claim for a writer is that minor characters are not small but squeezed, and that the squeeze shows: the eccentric with one repeated gesture, the type, the walk-on defined by a job. This edition calls that effect character compression , to keep it apart from the compression of page-space against story-weight that Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2) measures. A repeated tag is what a person becomes when a book needs her to be recognisable and has no room to make her knowable. Woloch’s further point is that the distribution argues something: deciding whose interior the reader will inhabit is deciding whose experience the book treats as fully human. His evidence is the nineteenth-century realist novel, with its large cast and single protagonist, and the chapter uses the model as an instrument for noticing distribution, not as a theory of value. Why does each new viewpoint cost more than the last? Rolf Zwaan and Gabriel Radvansky’s review of research on situation models (1998), the reader’s running model of the state of affairs a text describes, holds that readers track protagonist, space, time, causation and intention, and pay a measurable processing cost when any of them changes. A change of viewpoint usually changes the protagonist and drags space, time and intention with it, which is why it is among the more expensive moves a book can make; that it is the most expensive of the five is this edition’s inference, not their finding. Catherine Emmott’s work on contextual frames (1997) supplies the remedy: once a book has declared a pattern, the reader recalls a frame rather than building one, so the twelfth alternation costs less than the first. Lisa Zunshine ( Why We Read Fiction , 2006) adds the idea of levels of intentionality , I believe that she wants him to think , and reports from earlier studies that readers manage about four comfortably. A grant turns a character from someone the reader guesses at into someone whose view of every other character must be held as well, so the load plausibly grows faster than the cast; that last step is conjecture, offered because it matches what dilution feels like. Will going inside a character make readers sympathise? Wayne Booth ( The Rhetoric of Fiction , 1961) observed that sustained inside views tend to align a reader with a mind more or less regardless of what it contains, so that a writer who grants a viewpoint has already argued for the character. Suzanne Keen ( Empathy and the Novel , 2007) supplies the limit: narrative empathy , feeling with characters while reading, is real and measurable, but the evidence that it changes behaviour afterwards is weak. The best-publicised experiment, Kidd and Castano’s 2013 report that reading literary fiction improved a theory-of-mind task, failed in a large replication by Panero and colleagues (2016). What survives is the narrower claim this chapter needs: inside views produce alignment within the book. Is head-hopping wrong? For most of the novel’s history in English, French and Russian, the default was a mobile narrator who moved between minds when the material called for it. Henry James’s prefaces (collected as The Art of the Novel , 1934) argued for the reflector, a single registering intelligence, as a gain in intensity bought by a loss of scope; Percy Lubbock’s The Craft of Fiction (1921) turned that preference into doctrine; and E. M. Forster’s Aspects of the Novel (1927) dissented at once, holding that a novelist may shift vantage if he can make the reader accept it. The prohibition then hardened in mid-century Anglo-American teaching and editing. The convention is real, and a reader trained by recent fiction does feel an unsignalled change as a wobble, so it has a cost to be paid. The cautions in this chapter describe that convention, not narrative as such. See also: the Reference theory , with Stanzel’s typological circle, Uspensky’s four planes, Palmer’s fictional minds and the historical table.

title: 4. The Taxonomy
text: The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1) taught the habit of asking what a unit of narrative is for and requiring an answer that names a category rather than a feeling. This file transposes the habit from the scene to the grant. The question is not whether a character is interesting, since nearly every character is interesting to the person who invented her, but what direct access to this mind buys that no existing vantage could deliver. The answers fall into five domains, set out below with a proposed sixth. The domains are a diagnostic, not a licence: naming one does not justify a grant, it only states the grant’s purpose so that the purpose can be weighed against the cost. Used as a checklist for building a viewpoint character, they produce a committee’s character. Access Access is the domain of a grant made so that the narrative can be present where the existing focaliser cannot be: another room, another city, a conversation held in her absence, a death she does not witness. It makes certain books possible at all, since a novel of a war or a family dispersed across a continent cannot be told from one vantage without becoming a novel about not knowing. It is also the most often invoked and least often examined justification, because it is the one a writer reaches while solving a plot problem, and its work can nearly always be done more cheaply, by the instruments listed in The Mechanism . It under-delivers when the viewpoint chapter could be compressed into a line of reported speech in the next chapter, and over-delivers when every location acquires a resident mind and the book becomes a map, fully informed and attached to no one. Tolstoy needs vantages at Austerlitz, at Borodino and in occupied Moscow in War and Peace , but nearly every one of them also does a second job: Pierre at Borodino is a civilian who does not understand what he is looking at, which is the novel’s argument about history in small. Dramatic irony Dramatic irony is the domain of a grant that gives the reader knowledge another character lacks. Meir Sternberg’s distinction ( Expositional Modes and Temporal Ordering in Fiction , 1978) is the instrument: suspense is uncertainty about what will happen, curiosity is uncertainty about what has happened, and surprise is the discovery that one’s model was wrong. A grant that tells the reader what the protagonist does not know converts curiosity into suspense, and the reader stops wondering and starts dreading. The trade is not always favourable. A crime novel that grants the killer a viewpoint has exchanged who did it? for will they be caught, and at what cost? , and a draft that makes the exchange in order to enjoy the villain’s company has spent its main asset without noticing. The quietest form is the strongest: a wife knows what her husband does not, the reader has been inside both, and every later domestic exchange has two floors. The domain has one requirement that is easy to miss, which is that the two vantages meet again; an asymmetry the ignorant party never acts on in the reader’s presence buys dread and spends it on nothing. Crime and Punishment discloses the murderer at once, and every scene with Porfiry Petrovich is legible on two levels. Contrast (viewpoint domain) Contrast (viewpoint domain) is the domain of a grant that lets the reader occupy a materially different way of seeing: another class, generation, temperament, moral framework or condition of mind. The name is qualified because The Subplot (Chapter 14) uses contrast for the commentary one plot line makes on another; this domain is that argument made at the level of consciousness. Its carriers are differential noticing (two vantages register different things in the same room), differential naming (what each calls the same person, place or act), differential explanation (what each treats as needing none), a different sense of time, and different theories of cause, so that one sees God where another sees money and a third sees luck. It is the domain most often claimed and least often delivered, because the differences drafts supply are usually differences of circumstance, of job, age and problem, while the two minds notice the same things in the same order. It over-delivers when a vantage becomes a position, the pious one or the cynical one, rather than a person. In The Sound and the Fury Benjy, Quentin and Jason inhabit different relations to time, language and cause; Benjy’s section has no chronology because he has none, and Jason’s is a running account of grievance and money. Sympathy engineering Sympathy engineering is the domain of a grant made to a character the reader would otherwise judge from outside, so that the judgement becomes harder. It is Booth’s alignment used on purpose, and it has two modes. The exculpatory mode supplies information that changes what an act was: the silence was protection, the theft was for someone else. The non-exculpatory mode supplies no such information; the act stays what it was and the reader is made to inhabit the person who did it. The second is more valuable and harder, because exculpation is a plot revelation delivered by structural means, after which the vantage has nothing left to do. Timing decides much: sympathy placed before a damaging act produces dread and complicity, and placed after it produces re-evaluation or, handled badly, the sense of an author lobbying. In Anna Karenina Karenin’s forgiveness at Anna’s sickbed makes a man the novel has let the reader despise briefly the best person in the room; nothing is excused, and the reader loses the option of contempt. Structural pacing Structural pacing is the domain of the alternation itself, the pattern of visits across the whole book used as a rhythm. A book that alternates A, B, A, B for four hundred pages has taught its reader that the sequence means nothing; a book that alternates A, B, A, B, A, A, A has said something about A’s crisis without a word of comment. The carriers are the deferral cut, the interval between returns varied by each thread’s state, a fast external mind set against a slow ruminative one, convergence, and the long stay in one vantage after a regular alternation. A cut away at a moment of tension is The Chapter Break ’s decision (Chapter 6); the question it cannot answer belongs here, which is where the reader goes instead, since a deferral into a vantage the reader is glad to see costs little and one into a vantage she has been tolerating turns suspense into irritation. Tolstoy’s proportions in Anna Karenina enact the book’s argument: Levin’s share rises as Anna’s world contracts, and Part Eight has no Anna in it. A proposed sixth: the epistemological domain The five domains above all name something a vantage supplies, and assume that assembling vantages produces a fuller picture. Some books grant viewpoint for the opposite reason. The epistemological domain is a grant made to show that no single vantage can know what happened; the incompleteness of each account is the point, and the reader is given irresolution rather than assembly. Its structural signature is Genette’s multiple focalisation without adjudication. The test that separates it from contrast is whether a reader who read only one vantage would come away believing something the book denies: a reader of Levin’s chapters alone has an incomplete picture but not a false one, while a reader of one teller in Absalom, Absalom! is misled, and the book knows it. On screen, The Affair (2014) splits each episode of its first season between two lovers whose memories of the same events disagree, a case Worked Analyses reads. The objections have force, and the chapter concedes part of each. The domain may be contrast with unreliability added, a compound rather than a new category; its examples cluster in modernist fiction, which suggests a period style; and it names what a structure means rather than what a grant buys for the story, which mixes levels. Against the second, Dracula (1897) and the epistolary novel of contradictory testimony show that it is not a modernist invention. The chapter adopts the domain for diagnosis because it names a purpose a draft can be failing to serve: a writer with three contradictory testimonies who does not know that irresolution is a legitimate destination will reconcile them and destroy the book. The Reveal (Chapter 15) adopts or rejects it at the scale of a book, since a reveal is the adjudication this domain refuses. The Reveal (Chapter 15) adopts it at that scale, as the plural-vantage form of the declined reveal, a book that keeps a question of fact visibly open to its end. At book scale contrast plus unreliability ends in a reveal that says which account to discount, and this domain ends without one, which answers the first objection; the third lapses, since what a structure means is a reveal’s own subject; the second stands in part. A ruling on the authority domain The Prologue (Chapter 10) proposed an authority domain for prologues: a separated unit that tells the reader what kind of text follows and how far to trust it, as the Author’s Note of Life of Pi does, or the note before Dracula asserting that the papers have been placed in sequence so that the facts may stand for themselves. This chapter, named to rule on it, declines to add it to the domains of the grant and leaves it where The Prologue (Chapter 10) put it. A grant made to establish standing is already one of two things the model here contains: a witness’s access, as in the log of the Demeter ’s captain, or an epistemological structure in which the frame’s claim is tested, as Dracula ’s documents test its note and Life of Pi ’s second story tests its Author’s Note. The two proposals are one pair seen from opposite sides. The authority domain claims that a vantage suffices; the epistemological domain shows that none does. The first belongs to the threshold of a book, where The Prologue (Chapter 10) measures it, and the second to the allocation inside it. A grant need not serve every domain. In the novels this chapter reads, the usual shape is two domains served strongly and a third incidentally, and the next file turns that observation into an admission rule. See also: the Reference domains , with each domain’s carriers tabulated and further illustrations from Dracula , Bleak House , Lolita and Wide Sargasso Sea .

title: 5. The Mechanism
text: The mechanism of this chapter is an economy: a grant is the most expensive instrument a novelist has, so it must be admitted on terms, worked hard once admitted, and timed so that its cost falls where the book can bear it. The admission requirement A grant commits the book’s scarcest resource, the reader’s identification and capacity to model minds, for the length of the book rather than of a scene. Its commonest justification, access, is the one for which the cheapest substitutes exist. Before granting a viewpoint for access, a writer has five cheaper instruments : report (someone tells the focaliser what happened), inference (she deduces it, from a smell of fresh ink in a drawer, say), reassignment (the scene is rebuilt so that she can plausibly be there), document (a letter, a message, a ledger) and ellipsis (the event is not narrated, and its consequences carry it). The principle of multiplicity in The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1), that a unit should do several jobs at once, becomes at the scale of the grant an admission rule. A grant should be able to name two domains, and one of them should not be access. In practice the writer completes two sentences before granting: This vantage gives the reader … that no existing vantage could deliver , and The cheaper instruments I rejected are …, and I rejected them because … . There is a good answer to the second, and it is usually the same one: report can state a fact, and only dramatisation can make a decision felt as it is taken. The threshold of two is a working rule, not a law; a grant may serve its domains across the book rather than inside its own pages, as Addie Bundren’s single section in As I Lay Dying serves almost nothing locally and reorganises the novel around it. The rule runs in both directions. A grant should do more than one job, and the character receiving it should already be doing more than one job in the book. The strongest grants go to characters who were load-bearing before they became viewpoints: Esther Summerson is the hidden centre of Bleak House ’s plot, and Levin is the counterweight of Anna Karenina ’s argument. A vantage awarded to a character who exists only to hold it reads as an appointment. Where the distinguishing work lives Revision usually looks for difference between viewpoints in voice, in dialect, rhythm or verbal tic. Voice is the most expensive place to work and the easiest to overdo, and in close third person among characters of one family it is often unavailable without making some of them sound affected. The work of a grant lives in four cheaper places. Selection is what a mind registers. Two people enter the shop; one notices that the register drawer sticks, the other that the coat still hangs on its hook upstairs, and they are now distinct at no cost in words, since the sentences were going to describe something. The idiom of judgement is what appraisal leaks into the narration: when a third-person sentence calls a room poky or a brother impossible , the judgement is the focaliser’s, and the reader knows whose head she is in before any name appears. The knowledge boundary is what the vantage cannot know, and it is a resource: a chapter that keeps its boundary produces inference, misreading and dread, and a viewpoint chapter that feels thin has usually been allowed to know too much. Naming is what a vantage calls people, places and acts: a sister who thinks Dov and a brother who thinks of the dead man as his father have been told apart without exposition, and so have a vantage that calls the sale selling the shop and one that calls it what he did . The first grant and the later grant A first grant is made while the reader’s investment across the cast is still forming, in practice within the first chapters, and it is cheap because a new vantage simply joins the field. A later grant is made after the book has trained the reader to follow fewer vantages, and its cost is the sum of three charges. Formal surprise is the reader’s discovery that the book is a different shape from the one she thought; it is reduced by declaring early that movement is possible. Attention withdrawal is the pages taken from vantages the reader has invested in; it is reduced by keeping the grant short. Investment cold start is the work of building a new mind from nothing at the point in the book where the reader is least willing; it is reduced by prior presence. The third charge yields the chapter’s most practical rule: a later grant is cheap in proportion to how long the reader has already been curious about its recipient. A character watched from outside for three hundred pages, whose silence has been a standing question, costs almost nothing to enter. That is why the bounded grant , one chapter or section given to a mind that never holds the reader again, is the standard remedy for a late grant. It pays formal surprise once, withdraws a chapter’s worth of attention, and pays no cold start if the recipient has been present throughout. Its shaping requirement is that the section read as complete in itself, not as the first instalment of a thread the book then drops. As a rough schedule, a grant in the opening chapters needs nothing; in the middle it should be bounded or carry a payoff no report could deliver; in the last quarter it should be bounded, or the book’s subject should be the insufficiency of its own vantages; and in the last pages it must read as the book’s argument rather than its author running out of alternatives. The ceiling There is no correct number of viewpoints. The ceiling rises with the book’s length, but only if the length goes into longer stays rather than more vantages; with the reader’s task, sharply if the task is triangulation and not investment; with distinguishability, since fifteen instantly recognisable minds are cheaper than four interchangeable ones; and with the legibility of the pattern. As I Lay Dying gives fifteen focalisers fifty-nine sections in a short novel and is not diluted, because the reader triangulates one journey rather than investing in fifteen people, because each voice is known at once by idiom and obsession, and because the distribution is deliberately unequal: Darl holds nineteen of the fifty-nine sections. A book can carry as many vantages as it can make instantly identifiable and as its reader’s task requires; what it cannot carry is many vantages all asking to be inhabited equally. Architectures The four properties of the grant combine into a small number of whole-book shapes, here called viewpoint architectures , and a manuscript nearly always belongs to one whether or not its author chose it. The table gives the commonest, with what each buys and costs. Architecture Shape Example Buys Costs Single fixed One focaliser throughout The Remains of the Day Depth; the boundary as a permanent engine Everything off-stage reported or inferred Roving third One mind at a time, moving without a declared pattern Mrs Dalloway Coverage at close range Minds blur without strong differential noticing Alternating dual Two vantages for the length of the book Bleak House Contrast at its clearest; a felt rhythm The reader prefers one; the other interrupts Rotating ensemble Three or more in a cycle The Poisonwood Bible A social subject Dilution; the cycle becomes a metronome Hub and spokes One dominant vantage, others brief and specific Anna Karenina (two hubs) Depth and coverage together An unequal cast, which drafts resist Bounded grant One section to a mind that never returns Addie in As I Lay Dying A late grant at a fraction of the price The reader may expect a return Documentary Letters, diaries, transcripts Dracula Authenticity; incompatible vantages Interiority always performed for a reader Mobile omniscient A narrating intelligence with free access Middlemarch Scope, irony, analysis Needs a narrator strong enough to hold it Refused grant One character kept outside throughout The Count in Dracula Inference; opacity as subject Readers supply an interior, perhaps the wrong one The architectures are adjacent regions rather than boxes, and accomplished novels braid two. Their use in revision is substitution: name the current architecture, name its two neighbours, and rewrite one chapter in the stronger. The substitution that most often helps and is least often tried is the last row applied to one character, because much of what a draft calls developing a difficult character is granting her an interior, and much of what makes such characters powerful is its absence. See also: the Reference treatment of the grant , with thirteen architectures, the signals that declare a plural book and the historical drift of architectures; the Reference economy of the grant , with the page-share audit’s interpretation table.

title: 6. Diagnostic Tests
text: The ten tests are for revision, not composition; applied while drafting they make the writer stop before every scene to ask whose head it belongs in, which is a reliable way to write nobody’s. Run them on grants, not scenes, since the unit under test is a viewpoint character across the whole manuscript. Run them in order and stop when one fails badly: tests 1 to 3 (Necessity, Domain and Investment) ask whether a grant should exist, 4 to 7 concern the shape of the allocation, and 8 to 10 concern execution and consequence. Record a sentence, not a verdict (“Dov’s vantage serves sympathy and contrast, and appears once, at 78 per cent” is useful; “fails test 7” is not), and treat every failure as a question, since each test is failed by at least one novel this chapter admires. Test 1 — Necessity Could report, inference, reassignment, document or ellipsis carry this vantage’s scenes, and what would be lost? Failure. An access grant to convert. Exception. The Demeter ’s log in Dracula , whose facts the novel also prints as a newspaper report. Test 2 — Domain Which domains does the grant serve, with a passage as evidence for each? Failure. Access only: under-employed. None: remove. Exception. Addie’s section in As I Lay Dying , which serves the book rather than its own pages. Test 3 — Investment Before the first grant, can the reader say what this character wants? Failure. A cold start; the grant reads as an appointment. Exception. “Long, Long Time” in The Last of Us , which introduces Frank and gives him the episode. Test 4 — Distinguishability Swap two hundred words between two vantages, changing only the names: could a reader tell? Failure. Two cameras, one mind. Exception. Dracula , whose similar journals corroborate one another. Test 5 — Page-share What share of the book does each vantage hold, in how many sections, from when, with what longest gap? Failure. Equal shares across five or more; a vantage re-entered as a stranger. Exception. Wide Sargasso Sea , whose Antoinette is re-entered as a stranger on purpose. Test 6 — Declaration On what page does the reader learn the book has more than one vantage, and is it before her first deep investment? Failure. An undeclared architecture; resistance rather than confusion. Exception. Me Before You , whose first chapter outside Lou comes about a fifth of the way in. Test 7 — Late grant Does the payoff cover formal surprise, attention withdrawal and cold start? Failure. An unearned late arrival. Exception. The Sound and the Fury , which turns to an outside narration for its last section. Test 8 — Knowledge boundary Does the vantage know only what it could know? Failure. Scattered: an omniscient slip. Clustered at plot points: a vantage that knows too much. Exception. The Great Gatsby , whose Nick narrates scenes he never saw. Test 9 — Scene integrity Inside a continuous scene, does the narration stay with one mind, and if not, has the book established the right to move? Failure. Head-hopping: a right exercised but never established. Exception. Anna Karenina ’s races, told among Vronsky, Anna and Karenin. Test 10 — Character compression For each named character with no viewpoint: how many scenes, whose explanation of her motives, what repeated tag? Failure. A character-system that argues something the writer did not intend. Exception. Lolita , whose single grant compresses Dolores Haze and makes the compression its indictment. Three refinements sharpen the tests. Test 1 (Necessity) asks about loss, not information, since report can always convey a fact; what it cannot do is dramatise a decision as it is taken, render a misapprehension from inside, or make a silence feel like a choice rather than an absence, and a loss of one of those passes the test. Test 10 (Character compression) is the only one that looks away from the pages under revision, and it asks three things of each outsider: whether the only character whose motives are never available is the one the plot needs to be wrong, whether a relative appears in many scenes only to make a viewpoint character feel something, and whether a whole group is present in the book without a single interior. Reading the results together Failures cluster. Tests 1 (Necessity) and 2 (Domain) together mean the grant is a delivery mechanism: convert it to report, inference or document and reassign its scenes. Test 2 (Domain) alone means an under-employed vantage: give it a want and a blind spot, or bound it. Test 3 (Investment) alone means a cold start, and the remedy is presence before the grant, not more interior inside it. Test 4 (Distinguishability) alone means a redundant vantage: repair it by what each mind notices, appraises, cannot know and calls things, and if that fails, merge the two characters, which is nearly always an improvement. Test 6 (Declaration) means the first change should move to the first chapter break. Test 8 (Knowledge boundary) clustered means replacing knowledge with inference, and the scenes usually improve, because inference is dramatic and knowledge is not. Test 9 (Scene integrity) in a limited architecture means deciding: repair to the convention, or commit to a mobile narrator from page one, not both. Test 10 (Character compression) is not a repair but a decision about what argument the distribution makes. A page-share audit that shows a beloved secondary vantage holding four per cent of the book prompts the instinct to expand it, and the instinct is usually wrong. The useful question is whether those pages are the right four per cent, and whether they should be one bounded section rather than six thin ones. See also: the Reference protocol , with each test’s procedure and a table of combined failures.

title: 7. Failure Patterns
text: Each pattern below fails through a mechanism, not a surface feature. Each ends with a published work that uses the feature successfully because the mechanism is absent. The first pattern is a rule that names a convention rather than a mechanism, and it takes more space than the others because the convention is so widely taught as a law. The Reference chapter’s full catalogue has twelve patterns, including the redundant vantage, the omniscient slip, the corpse’s-eye view and the viewpoint granted only to be killed. Head-hopping Symptom. Inside one continuous scene the narration reports the interior of more than one character, moving from what she thinks to what he thinks without a boundary. Mechanism. The usual account is that the reader, having bound the scene to one mind, must rebuild it around another without warning. That is true of one configuration and false as a general account. What produces the unease is a mismatch between what the narration does and the convention the book has set: a novel confined to one mind for eighty pages has taught confinement, so an excursion on page ninety-one reads as an accident and costs the reader some confidence in the book. Two further distinctions decide most cases. Governed movement goes somewhere to compare, correct or judge; opportunistic movement goes where the plot needs a fact the current focaliser cannot supply, and readers detect the difference without naming it. And free access needs a narrator substantial enough to be the reader’s constant, an audible intelligence with a temperament and opinions; transparent close third person has none, so when it moves there is nothing to hold. Remedy. Decide the architecture, limited or mobile, and write the decision down. If limited, replace each straying sentence with what the focaliser could observe or infer. If mobile, establish the right in the first pages and exercise it throughout, including where it is not needed. Do not do both: a manuscript limited by default and mobile at its crises fails in both directions. The rule as it should be taught is not never change viewpoint within a scene but do not exercise a right the book has not established . Exception. Middlemarch (1872). In the marriage of Lydgate and Rosamond the reader is given the same exchange from both sides in consecutive paragraphs, his exasperation and her serene incomprehension, each reasonable from inside, and the marriage’s tragedy consists in the reader’s ability to hold both at the moment each speaks; alternating chapters could not produce it. Eliot also theorises the practice, in the parable of the pier-glass at the opening of chapter 27, whose random scratches seem to arrange themselves in circles around any candle held to it: every mind organises the same events around itself, and a narration that can move the candle can show the circles are not there. The information mule Symptom. A viewpoint character whose sections exist to deliver plot information the protagonist cannot reach, a colleague who overhears or an official with the file, and who has no want of her own. Mechanism. The costliest instrument applied to the cheapest problem. The reader enters a mind and finds it furnished only with the plot, and because an inside view implies significance, she keeps a place open for someone who will not matter. Remedy. Test 1 (Necessity), then one of three moves: reassign the scene to an existing vantage; convert the content to report, document or inference; or give the mule a want that acquiring the information costs her, which turns an access grant into one that also engineers sympathy. Exception. Wilkie Collins’s The Woman in White (1860) is built largely of information mules and remains a lasting popular novel. Its minor narrators, a housekeeper, a cook, a doctor, testify once and vanish without arcs, and the structure works because Collins frames the book as evidence given as before a judge, each witness speaking only to what she can attest. In a novel of testimony narrowness is a witness’s virtue; a mule fails in a novel of consciousness and succeeds in one where the reader has been told what a narrator is for. The diluted ensemble Symptom. Five, six or eight viewpoint characters in a book without the length to develop any of them; coverage is total and investment slight, and readers find the book hard to get into without knowing why. Mechanism. The trade between coverage and depth settled by default. Each added vantage adds a set of relations to the reader’s load, and each section opens with a beat of who is this again? even when the anchor is correct, a failure of memory rather than of anchoring. Remedy. The page-share audit, then conversion to hub and spokes: most diluted ensembles are hubs whose author will not admit the hub. A second remedy, less often tried, is to shorten the visits, so that the reader samples rather than settles. Exception. Bernardine Evaristo’s Girl, Woman, Other (2019) grants twelve women their own sections, in four chapters of three, each section ranging across a whole life. It avoids dilution by not cycling: each woman holds the reader once, at length, so no section has to be re-entered, and each new section is tied by family or friendship to one already read, so that identification is cheap. The novel then gathers most of them at a party after the opening of Amma’s play, which converts coverage into convergence. An ensemble is dilute when its members compete for the same reader function, and robust when each performs a different one. The unearned late arrival Symptom. A new viewpoint character appears at the two-thirds mark or later, holds several chapters, and pulls attention from vantages the reader has invested in; the reader skims to get back. Mechanism. The three charges of the later grant, formal surprise, attention withdrawal and cold start, incurred together where the reader is least willing to begin again. Remedy. Bound the grant; or plant the vantage earlier, even briefly, so that its arrival is a return; or solve the plot problem underneath, which is usually that the climax has been placed where the protagonist cannot reach it. Exception. Jean Rhys’s Wide Sargasso Sea (1966) opens its third part in the voice of Grace Poole, a servant who has not narrated before, for a page or two, and never again. By every criterion above it should fail. It succeeds because it performs the novel’s argument in its form: the book is about who may speak of a woman called mad, and the last voice before Antoinette’s final section is her keeper’s, the person Jane Eyre used to explain her. The arrival reads as the book’s meaning, not its author’s convenience. The antagonist chapter that spoils its own suspense Symptom. A book built on a mystery grants a viewpoint to the person who holds the answer, and the reader is told what the book was going to be about. Mechanism. The trade of the dramatic-irony domain made without noticing: curiosity converted into suspense when the rest of the machinery was built for curiosity, so the investigators have nothing left to find. Remedy. Decide which engine the book runs on and allocate accordingly; if the antagonist’s vantage stays, supply a replacement question at least as strong as the one spent. Exception. Gillian Flynn’s Gone Girl (2012) commits the pattern twice and profits both times. Its first part alternates Nick’s present-tense account of his wife’s disappearance with Amy’s diary, so that the antagonist holds a vantage from the second chapter, disguised as a victim’s document. Its second part opens on Amy alive, I’m so much happier now that I’m dead , and the diary is revealed as a fabrication planted for the police. The mystery is spent at the midpoint, deliberately, and replaced by questions the first half could not ask: whether she will win, and what the marriage will become. See also: Diagnostic Tests , whose combined readings point to these patterns.

title: 8. Worked Analyses
text: Three close readings show grants made, refused and bounded; a screen reading shows multiple focalisation where the medium’s default is the outside; and the household case shows a grant being decided. George Eliot, Middlemarch (1872): a reallocation in one sentence Chapter 29 opens in the manner the novel has trained its reader to expect, then breaks off: One morning, some weeks after her arrival at Lowick, Dorothea—but why always Dorothea? Was her point of view the only possible one with regard to this marriage? In twenty-eight words the sentence performs the argument of this chapter. Its first clause is the ordinary machinery of an opening, a time and a place, set up so that the break registers as a break. Dorothea names the focaliser the reader has followed for twenty-eight chapters, and always identifies that expectation as something built by repetition, and so built on purpose. Point of view names the object under discussion in the reader’s own vocabulary, and this marriage fixes the scope: not everything, but the one subject on which two vantages will now be shown to differ. The pages that follow enter Casaubon, insisting that he has an intense consciousness and is spiritually hungry like the rest of us. The grant is bounded: Eliot takes the reader inside Casaubon for a stretch and returns, without making him a rotating viewpoint. It is sympathy without exculpation, since nothing about the marriage improves and only the reader’s licence to find him merely absurd is withdrawn. And it costs almost nothing here because it was paid for earlier: the narrator has generalised, addressed the reader and moved between minds since the first pages, so the mobile omniscient architecture already holds the right of free movement. The same sentence in a limited-third novel would be an error. A later grant to a character the reader has watched from outside for twenty-eight chapters is the cheapest kind there is, and why always Dorothea? is, in a clause, the question Woloch’s study spends its length asking. Han Kang, The Vegetarian (2007; translated by Deborah Smith, 2015): the centre refused Yeong-hye stops eating meat after a dream, and the novel follows the consequences in three parts, each held by someone else: her husband, Mr Cheong, in the first person; her brother-in-law, an artist, in close third; her sister, In-hye, in close third. Apart from a few brief dream monologues in the first part, Yeong-hye is never given a vantage, and when asked why she has changed she says only that she had a dream. The architecture is three sequential bounded grants around a refused centre, and each grant serves contrast (viewpoint domain) by showing a different appetite trained on the same woman: the husband’s convenience, the brother-in-law’s art and desire, the sister’s duty. The order moves the vantage closer in kinship and sympathy, and In-hye’s part comes nearest to understanding without entering. That is the epistemological domain at a small cast’s scale: no account adjudicates, and the reader who wants Yeong-hye’s reasons is left where her family is. The refusal also makes character compression the novel’s subject rather than its by-product. Yeong-hye is all exterior, a body seen by three people who need her to be something, and the reader is bound to their failure to see her. A draft that “solved” the novel by adding her chapter would explain her, and the book’s argument is that she is not available to be explained. The structural claims survive translation; claims about how close the narration stands to each focaliser at a given sentence belong to Smith’s English. Jojo Moyes, Me Before You (2012): bounded grants around a withheld decision The novel is narrated in the first person by Louisa Clark, a carer for Will Traynor after the accident that left him quadriplegic. Apart from a third-person prologue set before the accident, four chapters leave her: one each in the voices of Will’s mother, Camilla, his nurse, Nathan, his father, Steven, and Lou’s sister, Katrina. After the prologue, Will is never a narrator. Moyes has said that his was the one mind she could not enter, “because I wanted his intentions to be one of the central tensions of the book.” The book shows the bounded grant working in commercial fiction at low cost. Each of the four chapters goes to someone already present, so there is no cold start; each is single, so the reader learns that someone else occasionally speaks rather than that a rotation has begun; and each lets the reader see Lou’s situation from a position she cannot occupy, the mother who has agreed to her son’s request, the nurse who knows his body, the father, the sister, which serves sympathy and, where they know what Lou does not, dramatic irony. The first arrives about a fifth of the way in, after the reader’s investment in Lou is substantial, which test 6 (Declaration) would flag; the flag is answered by the single, bounded shape of each visit. And Will shows that a character does not need a viewpoint to have a mind: the most vivid person in the novel is seen entirely from outside, and the refusal keeps the book’s central decision in the one mind the reader cannot read. The household novel’s mother is built on the same principle. A screen reading: The Affair (Showtime, 2014) A camera’s default is external focalisation, so screen narration has to build interiority by voice-over, point-of-view shots or performance. The first season of The Affair , created by Sarah Treem and Hagai Levi, builds it by allocation instead. Each episode is split into two parts, one remembered by Noah and one by Alison, the lovers, and the versions of shared moments differ in detail, down to who made the first move; a police detective’s interviews, set in the future, frame the recollections as testimony. This is Genette’s multiple focalisation, the same events through different characters, and the season serves the epistemological domain cheaply because the declaration is total from the first episode. When the second season adds the perspectives of Helen and Cole, the two spouses, it makes later grants to characters the viewer has watched from outside for a season, which the cold-start rule prices at almost nothing. The household revision case: should Dov ever hold a viewpoint? The situation. Dov has been observed only from outside. In the doorway he gives Elena the new key and withholds the reason ( The Dialogue Exchange , Chapter 3); Nadia knows him through calls she does not answer ( The Opening Pages , Chapter 9); his sale of the shop reaches the reader by report ( The Subplot , Chapter 14); the ledger is first seen as an object in The Descriptive Detail (Chapter 4), and the looser hand that follows the father’s entry of 9 March is discovered by Elena in The Chapter Break (Chapter 6) without her reading it. The question is whether to grant him a viewpoint, and in what form. Version A, the draft. Dov as a rotating viewpoint from page one: Dov had been at the shop since seven, which was earlier than he needed to be and later than he wanted. The buyer’s agent was due at eleven. He had the papers in the folder on the passenger seat and had not told either of his sisters, and he told himself this was because Elena would want to argue about the valuation and Nadia would want to argue about everything else … Someone had to keep the place open. Someone had to answer the phone. He had been answering the phone since March and neither of them had asked him what it cost. Diagnosis. It fails necessity, since the sale, the secrecy, the deadline and the resentment all reach the reader from the sisters’ vantages. It serves access and a thin sympathy, and no contrast, because Dov’s words of appraisal differ from his sisters’ in subject, not in mind; swapped into Elena’s chapter with three nouns changed, the paragraph survives, so it also fails distinguishability. It passes the investment test only because nobody has investment on page one. The largest failure is character compression. A focalised Dov knows what his mother said to him, and must either think about it or be seen conspicuously not thinking about it, so the mother’s silence becomes a reported silence and the book’s one deliberately open thread is closed by the allocation. The household novel is an investigation, two sisters reconstructing what was withheld from them, and granting the withholder a vantage turns it into a study of a man with a secret, with nothing strong enough to replace the question it spends. Version B, the revision. One chapter, placed after Nadia finds the good pen in the coat pocket and before the three of them read the ledger together, at about 78 per cent of the book. It dramatises the evening of 9 March and the decision to go on writing: The last entry in his father’s hand was three lines long and the third line stopped halfway, so that the doctor’s name — misspelled, then misspelled differently, then got right — trailed off into a scratch. The name meant nothing to him. Dov sat with it for a while. The leather was faintly warm from the lamp. He looked for the good pen where it was always kept, beside the till, and it was not there, and he did not think about that then; he thought about it for years afterwards. What he used was a ballpoint from the drawer that stuck. He wrote the date. He wrote the count. He did not write anything else, because his father had not written anything else on the ninth either, and it seemed to him that the ledger had a way of being written in, and that if he did it wrong someone would be able to tell. What the revision did. It reduced the grant to the minimum that carries the payload, one chapter, and moved it to the point of greatest prior curiosity, so the cold start costs nothing. It chose a decision rather than a fact: the fact that someone kept the ledger going was delivered by the object about half a book earlier, and the grant supplies only what an object cannot, the choosing. It serves three domains: sympathy (from outside, the continued ledger reads as forgery or as the start of the sale; from inside it is filial), contrast (Dov protects by keeping quiet, as his father did, where his sisters want to expose) and dramatic irony (the reader carries into the reading of the ledger what the sisters do not know). It built distinguishability from the four cheap places: he notices the pen’s absence and the warm leather where Nadia would count and Elena would look at a lock; he appraises how the ledger is written in, a category neither sister has; he thinks his father . And it made the knowledge boundary the chapter’s engine. Dov does not know where the pen is, though the reader, who has seen the father pocket it in the prologue and Nadia find it, does.
