The name on the third line means nothing to him, and in the four months he keeps the ledger he writes forward and never reads back, so he does not know his father was ill, then or at any point before the three of them read the ledger together. He does not know why the locks were changed, and the chapter does not tell the reader. The narration’s the doctor’s name belongs to its small retrospective gap, he thought about it for years afterwards , not to what Dov understood that evening. What the revision has not solved. A single chapter that succeeds creates an appetite the book then refuses, and some readers will feel the refusal as discipline and others as a pleasure withheld; that cost is paid every time a grant is bounded. The chapter solves Dov and leaves the mother: she changes the locks, speaks once at a remove and is never entered, a defensible allocation that a reader entitled to ask why always the siblings? can challenge with Eliot’s authority. A vantage granted just before a scene in which its holder is judged looks arranged, and the defence is that it excuses nothing: Dov still signs the sale without telling his sisters, and the entries after 9 March are still, in the plainest description, someone else writing in his father’s book. And Dov’s never reading back over four months needs a reason the reader can believe; the ledger had a way of being written in begins to supply one, and the chapter may need a sentence more. See also: the Reference analyses , with readings of Bleak House , The Sound and the Fury and As I Lay Dying , Anna Karenina and its dog, Wide Sargasso Sea , Dracula , The Golden Notebook and Beloved .

title: 9. Checklist and Exercises
text: Revision checklist The architecture Can I name the book’s architecture, and does the page-share confirm it? Is the right to move between minds inside a scene established, and exercised consistently, or never used? Each grant Can I name two domains for each viewpoint character, one of them not access, with a passage as evidence? Which cheaper instruments did each grant displace, and why were they rejected? Did the reader know what this character wanted before the first grant? Distinguishability Could a reader assign an unheaded paragraph to its viewpoint character? Do the vantages differ in what they notice, appraise, cannot know and call things, and not only in voice? Timing Is the book’s plurality declared before the reader’s first deep investment? Is every grant after the opening movement bounded, or paid for by a payoff no report could deliver? Does any vantage stop without the reader knowing it has stopped? Those outside For each named character without a viewpoint, who explains her motives, and does she have a repeated tag instead of a mind? What would a reader conclude the book believes from the shape of the allocation alone? Exercises The page-share audit. List every viewpoint character with her word count as a percentage of the book, her number of sections, the page of her first and last section, and her longest gap. Draw the sections in book order as a strip of initials, so the pattern shows as a shape, and write beside each name the domains her grant serves. Then repeat the exercise for the named characters with no viewpoint, recording their scenes, who explains them, and their tags. The two sentences. For each viewpoint character, complete This vantage gives the reader … that no existing vantage could deliver and The cheaper instruments I rejected are …, and I rejected them because … . Any character for whom the second sentence will not complete is a candidate for conversion. The swap. Take two hundred words from each of two viewpoint characters, exchange them with only the names changed, and give both to a reader who knows the book. Where the passages survive, rewrite one of them at the four cheap places: what she notices, what she appraises, what she cannot know, what she calls things. The substitution. Name your architecture and its two neighbours, write two hundred words on what the book would gain and lose in each, and rewrite one chapter in the stronger. The bounded chapter. Choose the character whose silence your book depends on, and write the one chapter that would grant her a viewpoint, at the point of greatest prior curiosity. Then decide, in a sentence, whether the book keeps it, and what the decision says about whose experience the book treats as fully real.

title: 10. Coda
text: The empathy budget is borrowed from economics, and like most such metaphors it presents scarcity as natural. A budget presupposes a fixed sum and unavoidable trade-offs, and that framing has diagnostic power: the page-share audit and the admission rule could not exist without it. It also imports an assumption that much fiction refutes. War and Peace grants interiority to a great many people, including a boy the reader enters on the night before his death, and on the budget model this is profligate; on the page it produces a sense that the world is full of people whose insides are as crowded as the reader’s own. The scarcity belongs to a form, the realist novel with its protagonist convention, and forms without that convention distribute attention on other principles. Nor is attention simply conserved: a reader shown that Casaubon has an inside does not care less about Dorothea, but differently, because Dorothea now stands next to someone. What the model does reliably is turn a vague dissatisfaction into a specific question. This book feels thin becomes five vantages hold equal shares and none has a knowledge boundary , or this grant serves access only , or the one character whose motives are never available is the one the plot needs to be wrong , and specific questions can be answered. It cannot measure worth, since every empirical source it rests on measures comprehension and response. What remains, once the tests are run, is the argument the allocation makes about whose experience the book treats as fully real, and that argument is the writer’s to choose. The household novel’s choice, two sisters inside, a brother entered once and the mother never, is defensible only because the writer can say what the mother’s exclusion is for, and a manuscript whose writer cannot say that about its own outsiders has an allocation it has not yet decided.

title: The Subplot
text: What a second story costs, and what it must supply The Craft Behind the Story (Second Edition) — Chapter 14. Part III: The Architecture of the Whole. In brief. A subplot is a second chain of causally linked scenes, with its own goal, conflict and consequence, running beside the main plot and competing with it for pages and attention. It is the largest optional unit in a novel, and every page it takes is a page not given to the story the reader came for, so it must supply something the main plot cannot supply by its own nature: a counterpoint, a test of character, relief, a wider world, or a convergence in which its turning points become the main plot’s. The chapter’s tool is the convergence test: find the point at which deleting the thread would break the main plot rather than merely thin it. Use the chapter when a secondary thread feels like filler, when readers prefer the subplot, when a late convergence lands flat, or when a book with several threads cannot decide which is primary. What you can do after this chapter Distinguish a subplot from a recurring character, a digression and a motif. Name the domains a thread serves and what it supplies that the main plot cannot. Locate a thread’s convergence point, and distinguish convergence from a meeting. Audit page-share and dormancy, and price a thread’s resumption. Decide whether a thread should be cut, converted, promoted or recognised as a co-plot. Key terms Subplot; the attention tax; chain; presence is not a plot; page-share; runner, double plot and multi-plot novel; digression; contextual frame; direct linkage, analogy and contrast (Levin); kernel and satellite; convergence, literal and thematic; character-system and plot-system; the domains of a subplot (thematic counterpoint, character testing ground, pacing relief, structural convergence, world expansion) and the proposed temporal counterpoint; braiding; multiplicity; crossing character; promotion; dormancy interval and reinstatement cost. Each is defined at first use and collected in the consolidated glossary . Contents The first files say what a subplot is and why it costs, the middle files what a subplot can do and how threads are braided and joined, and the last are for use at the desk. The Problem A household thread that is present but not a plot, and the chapter’s claim Definitions The subplot, presence and plot, scale, and the terms confused with them How It Works What a second story costs, how plots that never meet cohere, where a thread joins, who gets a plot, and the history of the suspicion The Taxonomy Five domains a subplot can serve, and a proposed sixth The Mechanism Multiplicity at book scale, where integration lives, braiding structures, dormancy, and the ceiling Diagnostic Tests Ten questions on one page, and how to read their failures together Failure Patterns Five recurrent failures, each with a work that commits it and succeeds Worked Analyses The Corrections , Big Little Lies , Bleak House , The Wire and the household revision case Checklist and Exercises The revision checklist and five exercises for your own draft Coda Where the attention tax stops applying A writer in revision can start at the diagnostic tests and the audit in the exercises; the coda, which sets limits on the chapter’s central metaphor, is best read early. The full treatment The Reference layer holds the complete chapter, The Subplot : Levin, Empson and the Victorian publishing economy in full, fourteen braiding and convergence structures, thirteen failure patterns, eight close readings (among them Middlemarch , Anna Karenina , Les Misérables and King Lear ), the subplot in the short story, the novella and the series, seminar questions and the sources. See also: Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2), whose engine defines a chain; The Transition (Chapter 5), on carrying the reader across a crossing; The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13), whose empathy budget is the same scarcity at the scale of a mind; Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture (Chapter 8), which rules on temporal counterpoint; The Ending (Chapter 16), where the last convergence falls.

title: 1. The Problem
text: In an early draft of the household novel, the brother’s money troubles run through the book as atmosphere. Elena notices unopened envelopes from the bank on the shop counter. A neighbour asks Nadia whether the family is selling. Dov is short with Nadia on the telephone about “sorting things out”, misses a visit because he is “seeing someone about the lease”, and at the end, when the three of them are in the shop together, says he has been dealing with an offer. This is the neighbour’s scene: The woman from the hardware place two doors down asked her, in the tone people used for asking about illnesses, whether they’d decided anything about the shop. Nadia said they hadn’t decided anything about anything. The woman nodded as though that were an answer, and went back in, and Nadia stood on the pavement a while and counted the shutters that were down along the row. Four, out of eleven. It had been two, in March. The paragraph does several things well. It places the shop in a declining row, gives Nadia something to count, which is how she manages grief, and sets a private loss against an economic one. Nothing in the draft’s six appearances is badly written, and the writer, asked what the material is, calls it the subplot: Dov’s story running beside the sisters’ reconstruction of what their father withheld. It is not a subplot. Each appearance tells the reader that the shop is in trouble, and the sixth tells her nothing the first did not. Dov has no specific goal; he is in difficulty, which is a condition and not a goal. No moment in the six could have gone another way. Delete all of them and the sisters still find the ledger, and the ledger still says what it says. A reader finishing the draft could say what Dov’s situation was and could not say what Dov did. The draft has the information a subplot would need and none of its structure, and the fault is hard to see in a read-through because the material is short, well written and never conspicuously idle. Two adjacent chapters The difficulty is clearest in two adjacent chapters of any novel. The first belongs to the main plot. A reader arriving at it has two hundred pages of investment behind her, a question she wants answered and a character she has followed since page one, and the chapter can be slow or oblique and she will stay, because staying is what she was already doing. The second belongs to a secondary thread, and asks four things the first did not: that she suspend the question just raised, recall people and stakes last seen forty pages back, re-establish why they matter, and do all this while the live question waits behind her. The two chapters are held to different standards, and the difference is structural rather than a matter of the second being less well written. The first spends trust that already exists; the second must raise its own. Two further features make the subplot hard to revise. It is large, measured in chapters rather than paragraphs, so an error in it cannot be corrected at the level of the sentence. And it is optional in a way no other unit is: every novel has an opening, an ending and scenes, but The Remains of the Day and Things Fall Apart each run a single line, and many admired novels have no second chain at all. The subplot is the one large unit whose presence has to be argued for, and the chapter’s claim is the standard the argument must meet: Every scene spent on a subplot is a scene not spent on the story that carries the reader’s primary investment. A subplot earns that cost only by supplying something the main plot cannot supply by its own nature. The claim is deliberately harsh, and it carries an assumption that should be stated at once: that the book has one primary investment. That is true of most commercial fiction and of most manuscripts in revision, and false of Middlemarch and Bleak House , in which no thread is the plot and the relation between threads is the subject. For a book with one investment the claim is the right standard; for a book without one it is the wrong instrument, and How It Works and the Coda say what replaces it. The household novel has one investment, the sisters’ reconstruction, and the draft’s thread fails the standard. See also: the Reference introduction , on the asymmetry between the two chapters; Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2), whose goal–conflict–disaster engine supplies this chapter’s definition of a chain.

title: 2. Definitions
text: The working definition A subplot is a secondary chain of causally linked scenes with its own goal, conflict and consequence, distinct from the main plot’s, running alongside it in story time, usually sharing its characters or world, and competing with it for the same pages and the same attention. Four phrases in the definition carry its weight. Chain means causal linkage in Scene and Sequel ’s sense (Chapter 2): each scene descends from the one before, so that the thread reads as things that had to happen next rather than things that also happened. Its own goal means a separate instance of the engine, not a smaller copy of it; a thread whose only goal is to help or hinder the protagonist is main-plot machinery distributed across other people. Alongside in story time excludes material set wholly in the past. Competing belongs in the definition because competition is what makes a subplot cost anything. This chapter calls the cost the attention tax : a levy on the reader’s attention, paid by every page that leaves the line carrying her primary investment. Presence is not a plot A frequent error in diagnosing a manuscript is to mistake a recurring character for a subplot. The distinction is settled by one operation. Write down the character’s goal at the first appearance and at the last; if the two are the same goal in an unchanged state, or there is no goal to write down, there is no chain, only a person who keeps arriving. The chapter’s shorthand for this is presence is not a plot . Recurrence without a chain is legitimate, and such a character may supply information, embody a social world or provide friction against which the protagonist is defined, but cannot deliver the functions that need a chain, convergence above all. A recurring character who is nearly a subplot is also one of the cheapest opportunities in a draft: the scenes exist, and a want, an obstacle and a reversal can turn them into a thread for a few hundred words. Scale A thread’s page-share , the proportion of the book in which it is the primary business of the scene, changes what kind of thing it is. The bands below are conventions drawn from practice rather than findings, but they are stable enough to use in diagnosis. Share of the book What the reader experiences Usual name Under 3% A recurring detail; no chain is legible Motif or runner 3–8% A thread tracked but not weighed Minor subplot; the screen’s C-plot 8–20% A second story with its own stakes Subplot proper; the B-plot 20–35% Uncertainty about which line is primary Double plot Three or more threads of 15–35% each No thread is primary; the relation is the subject Multi-plot novel The first row names the runner , a term from screen comedy for a small repeated piece of business with no chain. A double plot has two chains of comparable weight, neither clearly subordinate, and a multi-plot novel has three or more, with no main plot at all. The middle band is, in this book’s estimate, where the tax bites hardest, because the diversion is large enough to notice and too small for the book to have declared itself something else. The last two rows are not larger subplots but a different form: a book in which four threads each take a quarter has abolished the category. Adjacent terms A digression is non-narrative material, such as history, essay or catalogue, occupying a subplot’s pages; it has no chain, and the tests in this chapter cannot assess it. An episode is a self-contained incident that does not build. A frame narrative encloses the main story rather than running beside it. A foil is a relation between characters, where a subplot is a relation between chains. The B-plot and C-plot of television, an episode’s secondary and tertiary lines, are useful for proportion and misleading in prose, because they assume each episode resolves its secondary lines. What this chapter leaves to others Material set before the present belongs to Backstory and Flashback (Chapter 7). A second thread running wholly in another period, braided rather than flashed back to, is shared with Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture (Chapter 8), which treats the arrangement of times across a book. Frames and prologues belong to The Prologue (Chapter 10). Which character narrates a thread is The Viewpoint Shift ’s question (Chapter 13); this chapter assumes the allocation and asks what the thread does. How the reader is carried across a crossing between threads belongs to The Transition (Chapter 5) and where it falls to The Chapter Break (Chapter 6); this chapter treats the rhythm of the crossings. Threads spanning several volumes belong to Series and Genre (Chapter 17), and the book’s last convergence to The Ending (Chapter 16). See also: the Reference definitions , with a fuller table of adjacent terms (underplot, counterplot, intercalary chapter) and the ensemble novel without chains.

title: 3. How It Works
text: Six strands of theory bear on the method, each answering a question a writer asks in revision. Like every account of structure in this book, they describe conventions of a period as well as properties of narrative, and the last strand says how far the present suspicion of subplots is such a convention. Why does a second story cost the reader anything? Because the reader keeps a model of the story, and a change of thread changes most of it at once. Rolf Zwaan and Gabriel Radvansky’s review of research on situation models (1998) holds that readers track a few dimensions, among them protagonist, place, time, cause and intention, and that a shift in any of them costs processing time. A crossing between threads usually shifts all of them together. Catherine Emmott’s Narrative Comprehension (1997) supplies the mechanism a writer can use: a scene’s contextual frame , the reader’s running record of who is present and where, is not deleted when the narrative leaves it but held in a recoverable state and recalled on return. A thread is recalled rather than re-read, and recall decays with the interval. Two inferences follow, as tendencies rather than findings. A thread with a distinctive cast, place and register is recalled from fewer cues. And a reader resuming a cold thread usually manages it but resents being asked, so the fault registers as a complaint about pace rather than about clarity. No experiment has measured how long a novel’s secondary thread may lie dormant, and the intervals given in The Mechanism are conventions informed by this research, not derived from it. Isn’t unity the rule? It was a rule for tragedy. Aristotle’s Poetics asks that a plot imitate one action whose parts are so connected that removing one disjoints the whole, and calls the episodic plot, in which episodes follow one another without probability or necessity, the worst kind. The same work allows the longer epic to take on episodes that extend it, and the novel is epic in scale; much weak advice about subplots applies tragedy’s rule to a form Aristotle would have classed with epic. E. M. Forster’s Aspects of the Novel (1927) gives the oldest defence: a novel may be held together by pattern and by rhythm, repetition with variation, as well as by cause, so a second chain may be integrated by rhyme rather than by consequence. Forster also gives the caution, that pattern pursued rigorously shuts out life. How can two plots that never meet belong to one book? Richard Levin’s The Multiple Plot in English Renaissance Drama (1971) answers from a theatre in which double and triple actions were the norm. Levin names three relations between actions. In direct linkage the secondary action changes what is possible in the primary one. In analogy it repeats the primary action’s pattern in another key, at another social level or among other people. In contrast (Levin) , so named here to keep it apart from The Viewpoint Shift ’s viewpoint domain (Chapter 13), it inverts the primary action: the same pressure, the opposite result. Levin’s central argument is that analogy can integrate a work whose actions never meet, because the relation is the work’s argument; and relations change, so that when an analogy becomes a causal link the change has a name, convergence. William Empson’s essay “Double Plots” (1935) is the strongest defence of the second chain. Set two actions side by side and each comments on the other, so that the juxtaposition produces a meaning that belongs to neither alone; the effect may be felt without being statable. Its weakness is that an ingenious reader can find such a comment between almost any two things, so a writer who defends a thread this way should be able to say where the comment is produced. The transfer from stage to page also costs something. A play is seen in one sitting, and an analogy perceptible across twenty minutes may be lost across eighty pages, so a novelist must mark analogies a dramatist could leave implicit. What makes a thread a subplot, and where does it join? Seymour Chatman’s Story and Discourse (1978), developing Roland Barthes, divides events into kernels , moments that open an alternative and cannot be deleted without breaking the story’s logic, and satellites , which elaborate and can be deleted at a cost only to texture. Applied to threads, the distinction gives the chapter its definition in working form: a subplot is a chain of events that are kernels in its own system and satellites in the main plot’s, until convergence , the point at which its kernels become the main plot’s kernels too. Convergence is literal when the chains meet in event and thematic when they never meet and comment on one another. Before that point, deleting the thread thins the main story; after it, deletion breaks it. The question this yields, where would deleting this thread break the main plot? , finds convergence where it is rather than where the writer believes it to be. Chatman concedes that the line between kernel and satellite is often arguable, so the instrument diagnoses rather than decides. Who gets a plot? Alex Woloch’s The One vs. the Many (2003) treats a novel’s characters as a character-system in which attention given to one is withheld from another, and The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13) uses it for the allocation of viewpoint. Read from the plot side, the same arrangement is a plot-system : some characters are granted goals, obstacles and reversals, and others only appearances. A plot is the stronger grant. Viewpoint confers access and a plot confers consequence, and a character can have either without the other: Dov is entered only once, near the climax, and has a complete chain throughout. The distribution of chains also argues something. A novel in which the servants appear constantly and never want anything makes a claim about servants, whether or not its author intended one. Is the suspicion of subplots a law? Largely it is a product of book length. The nineteenth-century English multi-plot novel was underwritten by publication in monthly parts, which rewarded alternation between threads, and by circulating libraries that favoured the three-volume novel. Bleak House came out in monthly numbers from 1852 to 1853, and Middlemarch in eight parts in 1871 and 1872. The three-volume format collapsed in the 1890s. A literary novel today commonly runs to between 80,000 and 110,000 words, a quarter to a third of the length of Middlemarch , so a subplot taking a fifth of it is some 16,000 to 22,000 words, a heavier cost than the same share was for Dickens. The braided form survived where length survived: epic fantasy, the family saga and long-form television, whose season reinvented the monthly number. The present suspicion is best learned as a convention of the current market, applied with full force to a book with one investment and set aside for a book built on the relation between several. See also: the Reference theory , with the Victorian publishing economy in a table, Levin’s three-level play, and the case for and against the attention tax at full strength.

title: 4. The Taxonomy
text: The domain model asks one question of a secondary chain: what does this thread supply that the main plot, by its nature, cannot? It is the attention tax in working form, and its use is that it turns this subplot feels like filler into separate complaints with separate remedies. It carries two dangers. Any thread can be described afterwards as serving some domain, so a claim of counterpoint must say what the relation asserts and what would be lost without it. And a writer who learns six domains will try to serve six, which loads a thread until it has no shape of its own. Five domains follow, then a proposed sixth. Thematic counterpoint Thematic counterpoint supplies a second treatment of the book’s governing question, conducted by other people under other conditions, so that the main plot’s answer reads as one answer rather than the only one. Its carriers are the parallel dilemma, the road not taken, the inverted outcome, the success that costs more or less than expected, the shared object or institution, and the rhyming gesture. What separates delivery from claim is the difference between analogy and duplication. An analogy restates the question in other terms, and the difference in terms informs; a duplication restates it in the same terms, and the reader learns only that the book believes what it has already said. The working test is to ask what the book asserts with this thread that it could not assert without it: an answer naming a qualification, a cost, an alternative or a limit is counterpoint, and “the same thing, again, about someone else” is not. Under-delivery is the decorative rhyme, a parallel the writer can point to but not interpret, or the unmarked analogy, whose two halves lie eighty pages apart. Over-delivery is the thesis thread, peopled by positions, or the rhyme underlined by a narrator who does not trust the structure. In Middlemarch four threads treat vocation and its compromise, and each character finds a different relation between what they wanted and what a provincial town will pay for. Character testing ground The character testing ground applies a pressure the main plot has no occasion to apply: money where the main plot has love, a sibling where it has a lover, a situation with no audience. Its value is information the main plot cannot fake. In the main plot behaviour is partly excused by the stakes; under a subplot’s smaller stakes it is unexcused. A man who is brave under fire has told the reader about the fire, and a man who cannot tell his sisters he has sold a shop has told the reader about himself. The requirement is that the trait revealed carries weight later, ideally the trait on which a main-plot decision turns; otherwise the thread is an anecdote at subplot prices. Over-delivery is the showcase, in which a character is tested and simply passes. Nikolai Rostov’s card game with Dolokhov in War and Peace is the model: the war has proved his courage, and the card table finds his shame about money and his inability to refuse a man he admires, which no battle chapter could reach. Pacing relief Pacing relief changes register, rhythm or stakes so that the main plot’s tension can be sustained without stalling. Tension is relational: two hundred pages at full pressure read as monotony, because the reader loses the contrast against which pressure is felt. Relief is not a pause, since a subplot lowers the pressure while a story continues to run; and a cut away from the main plot at its moment of greatest pressure turns relief into suspense, provided the interruption is short. This is the domain that most often appears alone, and a thread that can claim only relief has the shape readers call filler. Under-delivery is the holiday, a thread the reader can skip without losing anything she could name; over-delivery is the tonal breach, or relief the reader comes to prefer. The Bagnet household in Bleak House shows the domain at full value: a warm domestic runner that turns into plot when the Bagnets stand surety for George, so that debt reaches the one household that seemed safe from it. Structural convergence Structural convergence is an eventual intersection in which the subplot’s chain complicates, obstructs, accelerates or resolves the main plot’s. A book with a main plot cannot do without it, with two loosenings. Convergence may be thematic, Levin’s integration by analogy. And it is a gradient rather than a moment, built from a shared minor character, then a shared place, then a shared consequence, so that a thread which has never touched the main plot and then touches it decisively reads as contrivance however well it was prepared. Its carriers are the supplied object (a document, a key, a witness), the supplied constraint (a deadline or a prohibition), the supplied person, the shared secret, the collision of incompatible goals, and the revealed identity, which is the carrier most open to abuse because an identity can join anything to anything. Under-delivery is the parallel line, or convergence by proximity, in which characters merely meet. Over-delivery is the mechanism thread, which exists only to hand over an object, or total convergence, in which every thread resolves at once in one room. Zadie Smith’s White Teeth (2000) ends in total convergence. The Joneses, the Iqbals and the Chalfens are gathered at the unveiling of the FutureMouse on New Year’s Eve 1992, where Archie Jones takes in the thigh the bullet Millat fires at the scientist Archie was ordered to kill in 1945 and spared, and the mouse escapes. James Wood coined the phrase hysterical realism in a hostile review of the novel, and the ending is where the charge is easiest to see; readers who defend it argue that the convergence is the book’s comedy of connection, in which the past cannot be kept out of the room. The disagreement is a fair test of whether total convergence can be a style rather than a fault. World expansion World expansion gives access to territory the protagonist’s goal never visits: another class, institution, place, faction or body of knowledge. The nineteenth-century social novel used it for serious purposes, since a novel arguing that a society is one connected system must show more of the system than one life touches. Its difficulty is that it is the only domain that can be served without a chain, simply by describing the territory, and the description is then a digression. The discrimination is whether the territory is entered by someone who wants something there. Jo the crossing-sweeper in Bleak House has a chain, wanting to be let alone and to move on, being prevented, and dying of it, and through him the novel’s argument that Chancery and the slum are one system is made as narrative. Under-delivery is the tour, a setting without a reversal; over-delivery is research on parade, or a world more interesting than the book. A proposed sixth: temporal counterpoint The five domains are defined by content. A sixth relation between chains is one of rate. Temporal counterpoint is a subplot running on a different clock from the main plot’s, slower, faster or set in another period, whose function is to make the main plot’s pace visible by contrast and to let the book hold a duration it could not otherwise contain. A chain has one rate, and a novel about three days cannot also render three generations unless a second thread does it. Bleak House sets Esther’s months against the generations of Jarndyce and Jarndyce, and Wuthering Heights sets two generations against each other. The domain also names a failure the others cannot: a competently built, converged thread that still reads as inert because both threads move at one rate and the crossings produce no variation. The objections are serious. Temporal counterpoint may be a property of the telling rather than something a thread supplies; it rarely appears without thematic counterpoint; and it hands every slow, inert thread a defence, an objection this chapter cannot answer. The chapter adopts the domain for diagnosis on condition that a thread claiming it also shows a chain. The Descriptive Detail (Chapter 4) proposes a temporal domain for the single detail, and Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture (Chapter 8), which treats the arrangement of times across a whole book, adopts both at that scale, this one as a property of the arrangement, claimed only where a crossing shows the difference of rate, which answers the objection this chapter could not; for threads in one time, the condition above stands. How many domains? The domains are a budget, not a checklist, and three rules of thumb follow. One domain alone is rarely enough, and the first move for a thread that can claim only one is to find the second job it could do in the pages it already occupies. Two domains are the working minimum, and thematic counterpoint with structural convergence is the most durable pair, because the thread then means something and does something. More than three declared domains usually indicate a co-plot, a thread with the weight of a second main plot, and the right question is then whether it should be the main plot. Against all three stands a qualification: a thread serving one domain superbly beats one serving four adequately. The Ilyusha thread in The Brothers Karamazov would score poorly for world expansion and pacing, and it closes the novel. See also: the Reference domains , with a table of carriers for each domain and the case against temporal counterpoint at full strength.

title: 5. The Mechanism
text: The mechanism has two halves that craft discussion often runs together. Braiding is the interleaving of chains in the order of telling: how often the narrative changes thread, where, and in what proportions. Convergence is the relation the chains finally bear to each other. Braiding concerns the reading experience and convergence the story’s architecture, and a book can braid well and never converge, or converge decisively after a braid so sparse that the convergence is unearned. The two have to be designed together, and multiplicity is what joins them. Multiplicity at book scale Multiplicity , The Purposes of a Scene ’s term (Chapter 1) for one unit of text doing several jobs at once, changes character at the scale of a thread. A sentence that does three things is an economy; a forty-page thread that does one thing is hard to defend, because no single function justifies that many pages. The requirement is stronger than doing several things in turn. The discipline is not to give a subplot more jobs but to find the version in which the jobs are the same act: a thread whose convergence is its counterpoint, where the object it hands the main plot is the object the comparison was about, does one thing that means two. The chaplaincy vote in Middlemarch (chapter 18) shows how small such an act can be. Lydgate must cast the deciding vote for the chaplain of the new fever hospital. Bulstrode, who funds the hospital, supports Tyke; Lydgate prefers Farebrother, who is likeable, poor and needs the forty pounds; Lydgate votes for Tyke. The vote advances Lydgate’s chain, since his goal is medical reform and the hospital needs Bulstrode’s money; tests his character in a choice nothing forces; sets a third case of vocation compromised by money beside Dorothea’s and Farebrother’s; and plants, unnoticed, the obligation to Bulstrode that the novel later calls in. The thematic relation and the causal one are a single event at a committee meeting. Writers looking for multiplicity in their subplots tend to look at the large scenes, and it is more often found in small ones placed where several lines cross. Where integration lives Revision often looks for integration in theme, in a stated resemblance or an image repeated across threads. The work is mostly done in four plainer places. The first is a shared object or institution, a lawsuit, a hospital, a will, a shop, a ledger, which gives both chains something to do to the same thing and which memory holds better than it holds a parallel. The second is a crossing character , someone with motivated business in more than one chain. Stiva Oblonsky in Anna Karenina is Anna’s brother, Dolly’s husband and Levin’s friend, and nearly every crossing between the novel’s two great chains passes through him. Crime fiction has the role built in. In Kate Atkinson’s Case Histories (2004) three old cases, a small girl missing from a garden in 1970, a young woman stabbed in her father’s office in 1994 and a wife jailed for killing her husband with an axe in 1979, share nothing but the private detective Jackson Brodie, who is hired on all three, and a resemblance: each turns on a lost girl and a family that cannot stop looking. The cases are solved separately, and the book holds together because Brodie carries each into the others and because the resemblance is marked in every one. The third place is a repeated decision-shape: in the household novel people keep having to decide whether to say a true thing that will cost them, and a recurring kind of choice survives intervals that defeat imagery. The fourth is the placement of the crossing: a cut from the subplot’s small betrayal to the main plot’s large one asserts a relation that no sentence has to state. Structures and rhythm The Reference chapter lists fourteen braiding and convergence structures, and five cover most revision decisions. The alternating braid, regular alternation at chapter breaks, keeps threads warm and teaches the reader a pattern that can later be broken for emphasis. The block structure, long runs of one thread, buys immersion and charges the highest cost on return. Early convergence ties the threads cheaply and gives up the late payoff. Late convergence pays most and must be paid into throughout. In promotion , a thread presented as secondary is revealed as primary, as Magwitch’s is in Great Expectations . A thread that is not working is often the right material in the wrong structure, and the quickest test is to chart the book on one page, a row per chapter and a column per thread, and redraw the marks under another structure. Rhythm is governed by the dormancy interval , the number of pages between a thread’s appearances, and by reinstatement cost , what the reader must spend to resume it. The bands in the table are conventions, not experimental findings; they describe a manuscript rather than legislate for it. Longest gap, as a share of the book What resumption costs Under 5% Nothing: a name and an action 5–10% One sentence re-anchoring person, place and open question 10–20% A paragraph re-establishing the stake 20–30% A scene, in which the book is heard explaining itself Over 30% A new introduction; the thread reads as late-arriving Three refinements follow from the table. The longest gap matters, not the average: a thread seen in chapters 3, 5, 7 and 34 has a healthy average and a gap that destroys it. A distinctive thread survives about one band longer, so differentiating threads subsidises memory as well as supplying variety. And a thread left in the middle of an open question is recalled more cheaply than one left at rest (an inference from the frame research, not a measurement), so the cheapest repair is often to move a cut. A thread that converges at the climax should appear in the quarter of the book before it, and crossings that grow more frequent towards a convergence let the form announce it before any sentence does. The ceiling The limit on how many chains a book can run is not a count. War and Peace carries something like a dozen traceable chains and is not hard to follow, because its threads are anchored to families, its crossing characters are many (Pierre has business with the Bolkonskys, the Kuragins and the Rostovs), its crossings are frequent and short, and each family has a register that identifies a paragraph before a name appears. The ceiling is reached when readers can name the characters but not what any thread is trying to achieve. A book that runs three or more chains with none primary has become a multi-plot novel and inherits three duties: to declare itself early, which is The Opening Pages ’s formal contract (Chapter 9); to let the relations between threads carry its argument; and to converge or rhyme at the end. See also: the Reference mechanism , with all fourteen structures, the history from medieval interlace to the television season, and the patterns of crossing; multiplicity at book scale , with the full page-share and domain audit.

title: 6. Diagnostic Tests
text: The ten tests are for a finished draft. Applied while drafting they produce paralysis at a scale from which manuscripts rarely recover; applied in revision they are structural triage. Run them on every thread, the main plot included, since several produce information only by comparison, and run them in order: tests 1 (Engine) and 2 (Kernel) ask whether the thread is a chain at all, 3 to 5 what it does, 6 to 8 how much of the book it holds and when, and 9 and 10 whether it should exist and in what rank. Record a sentence, not a verdict (“converges only at the party in chapter 31, and nothing before chapter 27 prepares it” is usable; “fails test 5” is not). Run the protocol twice, some weeks apart: the first run reports the writer’s intentions and the second the text. Test 1 — Engine Can I state the thread’s goal, conflict and consequence in three sentences without mentioning the protagonist’s goal? Failure. Presence, not plot; or main-plot machinery spread across other people. Exception. Platon Karataev in War and Peace , a term the novel needs rather than a thread. Test 2 — Kernel At each of its four or five chief moments, could the thread have gone another way? Failure. One kernel and a long tail of satellites. Exception. The intercalary chapters of The Grapes of Wrath , general chapters between the Joads’ story, which have no kernels and carry the novel’s claim. Test 3 — Tax What does it supply that the main plot cannot by its nature? Failure. Only relief, or nothing. Exception. Middlemarch , which has no single primary investment to be taxed. Test 4 — Analogy What does it say about the main plot, and what would be lost if it were not said? Failure. Duplication, a decorative rhyme, or an analogy no reader sees. Exception. The inserted tale of the curious impertinent in Don Quixote , whose relevance the novel’s second part admits was questioned. Test 5 — Convergence At what point would deleting it break the main plot’s logic, not merely thin it? Failure. Parallel play, or a meeting mistaken for convergence. Exception. Anna Karenina , whose Levin thread never converges in event. Test 6 — Proportion Are its pages proportional to its functions, and to its weight in the reader’s experience? Failure. Padding, or an under-served co-plot. Exception. The Ilyusha thread in The Brothers Karamazov , a small share that takes the ending. Test 7 — Page-share What share of the book does each thread hold, and does the distribution match the book I think I wrote? Failure. A different book from the one the writer believes in. Exception. Vanity Fair , whose pages follow Becky and whose subtitle admits it. Test 8 — Dormancy What is the longest gap between appearances, and what does resumption cost? Failure. A re-establishing scene where a crossing should have been. Exception. The Corrections , whose long sections leave whole threads dormant for a hundred pages. Test 9 — Removal Cut it on the outline: what is lost, in which domain, and does the loss exceed the pages recovered? Failure. Nothing nameable; or a loss one scene could supply. Exception. Koznyshev and Varenka in Anna Karenina , two chapters whose removal would cost only a rhyme. Test 10 — Promotion Would the book be better if this thread were the main plot? Failure. The wrong book has been written. Exception. Great Expectations , which builds the transfer of primacy into its design. Reading the results together Failures cluster, and the clusters point to remedies. Test 1 (Engine) alone usually means presence, not plot, and the remedy is cheap: supply a goal and a reversal using scenes that already exist. Tests 1 (Engine) and 2 (Kernel) together mean texture wearing a subplot’s page-share; reclassify it as motif or runner and cut it to the size of what it is. Tests 3 (Tax) and 4 (Analogy) together mean a thread that neither does nor says anything; cut it, and check whether its one useful relation can be carried by a scene elsewhere. Test 4 (Analogy) alone is usually a braiding failure disguised as a thematic one, repaired by bringing the compared scenes nearer. Tests 5 (Convergence) and 8 (Dormancy) together mean a late convergence that has not been paid for: braid the thread into the quarter before it, or move the convergence earlier. Tests 6 (Proportion) and 7 (Page-share) point opposite ways according to the mismatch, towards cutting where share is high and weight low, and towards expanding where share is low and weight high, the remedy writers in structural revision least often consider. Test 10 (Promotion) comes last because it can overturn every other answer. When it returns an uncomfortable result, writers tend to defend the existing hierarchy, since the main plot is the more finished object and the one the book was planned around. A thread that keeps growing across drafts is evidence of where the book’s energy lies, and the two honest responses are to promote it or to recognise a double plot and stop ranking. See also: the Reference protocol , with each test’s procedure and a table of combined failures.

title: 7. Failure Patterns
text: Each pattern fails through a mechanism rather than a surface feature. Each ends with a published work that uses the feature successfully because the mechanism is absent. At this scale several exceptions are among the most admired novels in their languages, which suggests that the rules describe a present convention more closely than they describe the novel. The Reference chapter’s full catalogue has thirteen patterns, among them the vestigial subplot, the comic-relief thread, convergence by coincidence, the digression and the thematic alibi. Parallel play Symptom. Two chains run the length of the book without affecting or commenting on one another, and the reader reads one of them impatiently. Mechanism. No convergence of either kind. The second chain’s kernels never become the main plot’s, and no analogy or contrast is marked, so the reader cannot turn the diversion into meaning. The failure is not that the threads never meet but that nothing in either changes because the other exists. It survives revision because each thread is satisfying alone, and revision scene by scene cannot see it. Remedy. Establish a relation and mark it: bring compared scenes nearer, give the threads a shared object or decision-shape, let one thread’s people know the other’s exist. Or accept that there is no relation, and take the weaker chain out of the book. Exception. Anna Karenina (1875–77). Anna’s chain and Levin’s are joined causally at the start, since Vronsky’s pursuit of Anna leaves Kitty free, in time, to marry Levin, and they touch once more late in Part Seven, when Stiva takes Levin to Anna’s house and he is charmed for an evening; nothing follows. What holds the novel together is analogy in Richard Levin’s sense, marked constantly across eight parts: two households, two jealousies, two encounters with death, two people trying to live truthfully, one destroyed by the attempt. Tolstoy, defending the book’s architecture in a letter, located its connection not in the plot or the characters’ relations but in an inner linkage. The rule therefore concerns relation, not intersection. The main-plot hijack Symptom. The secondary thread becomes more compelling than the primary. Readers skip ahead to it; the writer notices that its chapters are the ones she enjoys writing. Mechanism. The book’s centre of gravity has moved and its structure has not. Investment follows interest, not outline, so the main plot’s climax lands on a reader whose investment has gone elsewhere, and an event of great significance arrives with little feeling. Two benign causes keep the pattern common: secondary threads are written with less anxiety, because less rides on them, and the subplot is usually the newer idea. Remedy. The promotion test, honestly answered. Then promote the thread, restructure the book as a double plot, or, less often, reduce the subplot deliberately. Leaving the arrangement as it stands is the one response that does not work. Exception. Vanity Fair (1847–48). Amelia Sedley is the nominal heroine and Becky Sharp the thread that eats the book; Thackeray’s attention follows Becky, and so does the reader’s. The novel survives because it makes the hijack its subject. Its subtitle is A Novel without a Hero , and the narrator’s management of the reader’s preferences demonstrates that we would rather watch an adventuress than a good woman, and that the preference is not to our credit. A hijack the book knows about is a structure; one it has not noticed is a fault. The late-arriving thread Symptom. A thread introduced in the second half, or braided in twice early and then absent for two hundred pages, converges decisively at the climax, and the convergence lands on weight the book has not built. Mechanism. Reinstatement failure compounded by an investment shortfall: the reader is asked for a feeling proportionate to an investment she had no opportunity to make. The result is not confusion but flatness at the moment of greatest intended effect. Late threads are often the solution to a plotting problem found in a third draft, and solutions arrive where the problem was noticed rather than where they need to be planted. Remedy. Braid backwards. A thread converging at the climax should appear in the quarter before it and be established in the first third; two short crossings in the dormant stretch usually cost a few hundred words. Exception. War and Peace (1865–69). Platon Karataev enters in the fourth volume with no prior existence, and Pierre’s change in the prisoners’ shed, where he meets him, answers the question the previous thousand pages have failed to answer. Karataev succeeds because he is not a thread but a term: he has no chain, and what converges is not a plot but the question Pierre has carried since his first conversations about freemasonry. A late arrival can pay off an early investment when the investment was in the question rather than in the thread, and the question is still open. Convergence by encounter Symptom. The threads converge because the characters meet: they are in one room at the end, introduced, talking. Nothing else changes. Mechanism. A meeting is not a convergence. Delete the encounter and both chains proceed unaltered, so the convergence test returns nothing. The pattern is a common false positive because a meeting looks like what convergence is supposed to be, and outlines mark it as the point where threads join. It is partly a habit borrowed from the screen, where actors sharing a frame do real work; prose has no shared frame, and a meeting must produce a consequence or it has produced only an image. Remedy. Ask what each character wants from the other and make the wants incompatible. Convergence is conflict, not contact; if nobody wants anything from anybody, the encounter is a curtain call. Exception. Love Actually (Richard Curtis, 2003). The film braids ten love stories, linked mainly by kinship and employment (the Prime Minister’s sister, Karen, is married to Harry, who is tempted by his secretary; a junior member of the Prime Minister’s household is the object of his own attention), and it opens and closes at the arrivals gate at Heathrow, where several of its characters are reunited. As plot, the closing gathering converges nothing. It works because the encounter is the film’s claim, made in the voice-over to the opening montage of arrivals: that love is visible wherever people meet. When the meeting is the argument, an empty encounter is the form of the point. Ulysses gives the case in prose, where Bloom and Stephen’s meeting over cocoa leads nowhere and is felt against a convergence that has been happening all day by theme. The romance bolted on Symptom. A love story runs beside a plot to which it is unrelated: the detective’s relationship, the soldier’s sweetheart. Its obstacles are misunderstandings, and its outcome could be reversed without changing a scene elsewhere. Mechanism. The engine test passes and the tax test fails. A romance chain is easy to build correctly because its shape is culturally familiar, and the familiarity is what makes a detached one inert: the reader recognises the shape at once and so attends to little in it. The pattern persists through commercial expectation in several genres and through a writer’s sense that a protagonist needs a private life. Remedy. Make the relationship about what the main plot is about, a site of the same conflict rather than a refuge from it. A romance whose obstacle is the value the protagonist will not give up becomes a character testing ground. Exception. Middlemarch (1871–72), the thread of Fred Vincy and Mary Garth. It presents as the most detachable thing in the novel, a courtship comedy in which an idle young man must find a respectable occupation, and it barely touches Dorothea. It succeeds because it is the novel’s control case on vocation: Dorothea wants a life of consequence and is denied one, Lydgate wants one and loses it, Bulstrode buys one with concealed money, and Fred, the least serious person in the book, is the only one who acquires a usable trade, taught slowly by Mary’s father. Mary’s refusal to marry an idler is what forces the training, and reversing the courtship’s outcome would change the novel’s argument about work. A romance is bolted on when its outcome is thematically inert and integral when its outcome is one of the book’s answers. See also: the Reference catalogue , with each pattern’s persistence and a table from symptom to mechanism.

title: 8. Worked Analyses
text: Three close readings show a family novel converging on one character’s want, a commercial novel braiding its threads towards a single night, and the classic convergence on a secret; a screen reading shows institutions converging on one boy; and the household case shows a thread being turned into a chain. Jonathan Franzen, The Corrections (2001): convergence by a want The Corrections has five threads: Alfred Lambert, retired and declining with Parkinson’s disease and dementia; his wife Enid; and their three adult children in the East. Gary is a depressive banker in Philadelphia whose wife resists every visit home; Chip, a dismissed academic, goes to Lithuania on an internet fraud; Denise, a chef, loses her job over an affair with her employer’s wife. The book is built in blocks. After an opening in St. Jude, the Lamberts’ Midwestern town, long sections follow one or two of the family at a time, under titles such as “The Failure” and “The More He Thought About It, the Angrier He Got”, before “One Last Christmas” brings everyone home and “The Corrections” disperses them. By the bands in Definitions this is close to a multi-plot novel: no child’s thread is primary, and the relation between them is the subject. What keeps the blocks from becoming separate novellas is that the convergence is itself a chain. Enid wants one last Christmas in St. Jude with all three children, and her want runs through the other blocks as recurring pressure, telephone calls, guilt and persuasion, which each child’s own chain resists. The gathering is therefore not a meeting arranged by the author but the outcome of a goal, opposed by three others; when the family assembles it has been dragged there, and the gathering is a collision rather than a curtain call. This is the remedy for convergence by encounter carried out at the scale of a book: the meeting is someone’s want, and everyone else’s wants are against it. The blocks pay their cost in dormancy. Each child is left for long stretches, and the novel survives the gaps by the means the frame research predicts: each thread is individuated in register, comic for Chip, paranoid for Gary, appetitive for Denise, and each is left with a question open, so that the reader returns knowing what is at stake. Alfred’s decline supplies temporal counterpoint, a slow clock against which the children’s crises move fast, and it turns the Christmas Enid wants as a reunion into the occasion on which the family must decide about him; after it he goes into a nursing home. Liane Moriarty, Big Little Lies (2014): braiding towards one night Big Little Lies follows three mothers of children at a beachside primary school: Madeline, resentful of her ex-husband’s new family; Celeste, whose wealthy husband Perry beats her; and Jane, a young single mother new to the town. Each has her own chain, and they are braided chapter by chapter, a common arrangement in commercial fiction. Two devices organise the braid. The chapter headings count down to a school trivia night at which, the reader learns at the start, someone has died. And at the ends of chapters come short statements by other parents and staff, given after the trivia night: a chorus of gossip that is not a chain at all, and that justifies itself as the intercalary chapters of The Grapes of Wrath do, by supplying world, comedy and a running reminder of the clock at the cost of a few lines. The convergence uses the revealed identity, the carrier most open to abuse. At the trivia night Jane recognises Perry as the man who raped her years before under another name, Saxon Banks; Perry strikes Celeste, and Bonnie, the new wife of Madeline’s ex-husband, pushes him from a balcony to his death. Two chains, Celeste’s marriage and Jane’s past, are joined by an identity, and the third by the person who acts. By the standard of coincidence the join is suspect, since one man connects two women’s secrets in one school. It holds for two reasons. It turns analogy into causality: the book has set two women’s experience of male violence side by side for hundreds of pages, and the identity reveals that the rhyme was a mechanism. And it is planted in a third chain. From the first day of school Jane’s son is accused of hurting a classmate, and the hurt is being done by one of Celeste’s sons, the child of the violence at home; the bullying thread has carried the convergence’s two halves together long before anyone in the book knows it. The countdown also settles the late-convergence problem in advance, since every chapter of every thread is, by its heading, paid into the night. Charles Dickens, Bleak House (1852–53): three systems and one secret Bleak House runs three systems: the Chancery suit of Jarndyce and Jarndyce, which has consumed generations; the Dedlock marriage at Chesney Wold; and Esther Summerson’s story, told in her own first person in chapters that alternate with a present-tense third person. In the second chapter Lady Dedlock, shown a legal document, asks who copied it and is shaken by the hand. The reader does not yet know there is anything to recognise. The copyist is the law-writer called Nemo, once Captain Hawdon, and he is Esther’s father; Lady Dedlock is her mother. Every system runs towards that fact. Tulkinghorn, the Dedlocks’ lawyer, pursues the handwriting; Jo, the crossing-sweeper Nemo was kind to, carries the infection that scars Esther; the detective Bucket follows Lady Dedlock’s flight, and Esther finds her mother dead at the gate of the burial ground where Hawdon lies. The threads converge in sequence rather than together, a convergent cascade in which each convergence raises the stakes of the next, and the structure is the novel’s argument. Dickens asks outright what connection there can be between Chesney Wold and Jo the outlaw with the broom, and the plot’s improbabilities are the answer: a society that believes itself divided into compartments is one system, through which infection, guilt and money travel freely. The coincidences that a present-day structural edit would cut are a claim about the world. For a writer the plant is the lesson: the convergence is a recognition, and it is strong because its object, a hand on a page, was set down before the reader knew to look at it. A screen reading: The Wire , season 4 (HBO, 2006) The fourth season of The Wire braids four systems in Baltimore: a middle school, where the former police officer Prez now teaches mathematics and the retired major Bunny Colvin runs a special class for disruptive pupils; a mayoral campaign, which Tommy Carcetti wins in the primary; a police department, where Lester Freamon finds the bodies Marlo Stanfield’s crew have sealed in vacant houses; and the street. Four boys, Namond, Michael, Randy and Dukie, are the season’s centre. The convergence works by passing one boy through every system. Threatened with expulsion by an assistant principal over a murder he knows about, Randy tells what he knows; the school hands him to the police; a detective mishandles him and lets slip that Randy talked; Marlo’s people spread the word that he is a snitch; and after a false call draws off the officers guarding his home, the house is firebombed, his foster mother is badly burned, and he ends in a group home. No system intends the outcome, and each passes him on by its own rules. It is direct linkage at its starkest, and it shows prose writers that convergence need not be a meeting or a revealed secret: it can be a person handed from chain to chain until chains that never share a room meet in one life. The household revision case: Dov’s thread The situation. The draft in The Problem keeps Dov’s money troubles as atmosphere across six appearances. It fails the engine test (Dov is in difficulty and has no specific goal), the kernel test (no moment could have gone another way), the analogy test (the thread says only that the family is also under financial pressure, which is information, not relation) and the convergence test (deleting it changes nothing). Its page-share is about 4 per cent, a runner’s, and its longest gap about 18 per cent. The patterns present are presence mistaken for plot, an occupational thread that gives Dov something to do between appearances, and convergence by encounter, since the siblings simply find themselves in one room at the end. The revision. The same man, shop and money, arranged as a goal–conflict–disaster chain: Beat Dov’s chain Its effect on the main plot Goal Sell the shop before another season of losses None yet; it runs beside the sisters’ reconstruction Complication The buyer wants the building, shop and flat, emptied by the end of the month Dov clears the register drawer before telling anyone, taking the ledger home before Elena has read far into it, so that she comes back to an empty drawer; then he asks his sisters to clear the flat by the month’s end, without saying why Disaster He signs the papers without telling his sisters A betrayal inside the main plot too: the place the sisters are reconstructing has been signed away Reveal He produces the one thing he held back from the sale, the ledger, and admits that the looser hand after 9 March is his Full convergence: the subplot hands the main plot its evidence, and deleting the thread now breaks the book What the revision did. It turned a condition into a goal with an object and a deadline, which is the moment a thread acquires a chain. It supplied a branching point, the buyer’s demand, at which the thread could go two ways. It made the subplot’s clock the main plot’s, the supplied constraint of The Taxonomy : the deadline reaches Elena as an empty drawer, and Nadia as a request to clear the flat, which gives her a motive the book has lacked for putting her hand into the pocket of the coat, since a coat’s pockets are checked before it goes, while the coat itself stays on its hook. One man’s secret moves both sisters’ chains before either knows it exists. It made the disaster a betrayal in both systems. And it placed the convergence on an object already planted: the ledger is first seen in The Descriptive Detail (Chapter 4), the looser hand is Elena’s discovery in The Chapter Break (Chapter 6), and Dov’s chapter in The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13) has shown the reader whose hand it is, so the reveal tells the sisters what the reader has carried for some time. The thread now serves thematic counterpoint (Dov protects by silence, as his father did, and the rhyme is produced by the reader holding two withholdings together), structural convergence (he supplies the evidence) and a character testing ground (nothing forces him to sign in secret). The object that converges the plots is the object the counterpoint is about, the ledger as both proof and parallel. Page-share rises to about 12 per cent, the longest gap falls to about 9 per cent with a crossing added in the middle stretch, and the structure becomes an accelerating repeated intersection with a late literal convergence. What the revision has not solved. The convergence carries a great deal for one scene: it resolves Dov’s chain, delivers the evidence, tells the sisters whose hand it is and lands the rhyme with the father, and four discharges at once may let the reader feel the architecture, a risk The Ending (Chapter 16) treats. The rhyme risks the redundant mirror, since a son concealing a sale and a father concealing an illness may be too small a change of key; the correction is to motivate the two silences differently, the father keeping the record so that someone could check it, as Backstory and Flashback (Chapter 7) gives in his own words, and Dov keeping the same ledger with only the date and the count, the form of his father’s honesty emptied of its content. The promotion test returns an uncomfortable answer: Dov has the most at stake, is the only sibling who acts irreversibly and the only one with a deadline, and on three of the test’s four questions his thread is stronger than the reconstruction it serves. The book has decided that it belongs to Nadia and Elena and that Dov’s opacity helps the ending work, but that is a decision, not a fact. And the empty drawer gives Elena a new question, who took the ledger, which the book must keep her from putting to Dov until the convergence, or the convergence comes early. See also: the Reference analyses , with readings of Middlemarch , Anna Karenina , War and Peace , Vanity Fair , Les Misérables , The Brothers Karamazov and King Lear .

title: 9. Checklist and Exercises
text: Revision checklist Is it a plot at all? Can I state the thread’s goal, conflict and consequence in three sentences without mentioning the protagonist’s goal? Does it have at least two branching points, moments at which it could have gone another way? If it is a recurring character rather than a chain, have I said so and sized it accordingly? What it supplies Can I name its domains, and does at least one supply what the main plot cannot by its nature? If it supplies only relief, have I looked for the second job it could do in the pages it already occupies? Can I complete the sentence because this thread exists, the reader understands that the main plot’s situation is qualified in this way , and name the two scenes between which that understanding is produced? Convergence At what point would deleting the thread break the main plot’s logic rather than thin it? Is the convergence a consequence, and not a coincidence or a meeting? Was the object or fact that converges the threads planted before the reader knew to look at it? Proportion and rhythm Have I counted every thread’s page-share, and does the distribution match the book I think I have written? What is each thread’s longest gap, and is the thread left mid-question when it is suspended? Does a thread that converges at the climax appear in the quarter of the book before it? Do the crossings fall where the material needs them, and not where a rotation demands them? Rank Have I asked the promotion question, and recorded the answer rather than defended the plan? If the book has three or more co-equal chains, does it declare that early and let the relations carry its argument? Exercises The audit. For a finished draft, list every thread, including those you have not thought of as threads, with its goal, obstacle and consequence in a sentence each, and put any that lack one of the three on a separate list headed presence, not plot . For each thread record its page-share, its domains, its convergence point and its longest gap. Then look for a thread with one domain and more than 8 per cent of the book, a thread with no convergence point, and two threads serving the same domains. The engine conversion. Take a recurring character who has no chain and give that character a goal with an object and a deadline, one obstacle and one reversal, using only scenes that already exist. Note how much new material the conversion cost. The chart. Draw the book on one page, a row per chapter and a column per thread, with a mark wherever a thread is active. Redraw it as an alternating braid and then as blocks, and note what each arrangement does to the convergence. The removal. Delete a thread on the chart, not in the prose, and write one sentence naming what is lost in the terms of the domains. Then ask whether a single scene elsewhere could supply it. The clock. Find the subplot’s deadline, or give it one, and write the scene in which that deadline first changes what a main-plot character can do before she knows the deadline exists. See also: the Reference checklist , with items on removal and hierarchy; the Reference studio work , with seminar questions.

title: 10. Coda
text: The attention tax is a good instrument for a book with one primary investment and a poor one for a book with several. Applied to Middlemarch it produces confident nonsense: that Eliot should have cut Lydgate, that Tolstoy should have chosen one family, that Dickens should have decided between Chancery and Chesney Wold. Those books are not tolerated exceptions. Their threads are not deductions from a main plot, and Empson’s argument says why: the relation between plots produces a meaning that neither carries, and a pruned novel cannot have it. The present preference for a single tightly held line is largely a fact about the length of books and the market that sets it, passed on as craft advice. The tax is still worth applying, because it is a stress test rather than a description. A thread that survives it has a function its writer can name, and a thread that fails may still belong to a multi-plot novel, provided the writer says so and accepts the duties that come with the form: declaring it early, letting the relations carry the argument, converging or rhyming at the end. In this book’s judgement the commonest structural fault in an ambitious manuscript is not a second plot but a book that has half-declared itself a multi-plot novel while keeping half a hierarchy, so that the reader cannot tell whether a thread is a co-plot to be weighed or a subplot to be tolerated. The tests cannot answer that question for the writer. What they can do is make its answer unavoidable, and the answer is a decision about what kind of book this is, which no count of pages will make. See also: the Reference coda , on the digressions of Les Misérables and Moby-Dick and what a pruned novel loses.

title: The Reveal
text: What the reader learns late, and what it must change The Craft Behind the Story (Second Edition) — Chapter 15. Part III: The Architecture of the Whole. In brief. A reveal is a late disclosure that changes what the reader understands of pages already read. It is earned when those pages bear two readings, the one the reader made and the one the disclosure makes, and when something inside the book, a character who does not know or a teller with a reason not to say, explains why the truth came when it did. It may reinterpret anything the double reading reaches, and falsify only what a teller in the book could have shaped. The chapter’s tools are the double-reading table, which sets each passage bearing on a reveal against its first and second readings, and the disclosure map, which records who learns each fact when: the reader and each character. Use the chapter when readers guess a twist early, feel cheated by it, or shrug at it, and when a book holds a secret and the writer does not know where to spend it. What you can do after this chapter Test whether the pages before a reveal support both readings, and find the passages that give it away or tell a lie. Name who withholds each truth from the reader, and why, and repair a withholding that has no reason in the book. Decide when the reader should learn a fact relative to the characters, and what question the reveal should leave in place of the one it answers. Judge how far a late disclosure may recast a whole book, and when a book may decline to reveal at all. Diagnose a reveal that cheats, gives itself away, arrives by report or changes nothing, and revise it. Key terms Reveal; double reading; first and second readings; recognition; curiosity and surprise; the four objects of a reveal (event, identity, motive and telling); the early reveal, the turn reveal and the closing reveal; the successor question; the withholder; alignment; the double-reading table; the disclosure map; equivocation; the decoy reading; the teller rule; range; the declined reveal; the cheat; the giveaway; the reported reveal; the idle reveal; the reveal from outside. Each is defined at first use and collected in the consolidated glossary . Contents The first files say what a reveal is and what readers do with one, the central files how a reveal is prepared, withheld, timed and spent, and the last are for use at the desk. The Problem A household convergence at which the book’s largest truth is spent in two sentences of dialogue, and the chapter’s claim Definitions Reveal, double reading and the terms around them, and what other chapters keep How It Works What a reader does at a reveal, what she feels before one, what makes one fair, how far a teller can be trusted, and what the evidence says The Taxonomy Four objects of a reveal, three positions, and two rulings: the declined reveal and the teller rule The Mechanism How a double reading is built, who may withhold, how disclosure is timed, and how several reveals share a book Diagnostic Tests Eight questions on one page, and how to read their failures together Failure Patterns Five recurrent failures, each with a work that commits it and succeeds Worked Analyses Atonement , Gone Girl , We Are All Completely Beside Ourselves , The Sixth Sense and the household revision case Checklist and Exercises The revision checklist and five exercises for your own draft Coda What the model assumes, and why a reveal is a debt the book has been paying all along A writer in revision can start at the diagnostic tests, with a double-reading table drafted for the book’s largest reveal. A writer planning a book with a secret should read the mechanism first, because where a truth is withheld, and by whom, is easier to design than to retrofit. The full treatment This is a new chapter, so the Reference layer holds a single full treatment rather than a corrected original: the theory at greater length, an extended catalogue of reveals and failure patterns, the procedures for each test, further analyses ( The Murder of Roger Ackroyd , The Silent Patient and Knives Out ), the household double-reading table and disclosure map in full, a glossary of the chapter’s terms and the sources. See also: Backstory and Flashback (Chapter 7), for the mechanics of returning to the past once a reveal has made it necessary; The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13), whose knowledge boundary is the commonest reason a truth is withheld; The Ending (Chapter 16), where a closing reveal falls due and the plant audit checks its preparation; Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture (Chapter 8), for truths withheld by the arrangement of timelines.

title: 1. The Problem
text: A draft of the household novel reaches its convergence about four-fifths of the way through. The reader knows the situation. Four months after their father’s death, his three adult children have been reconstructing what he left. Elena learned in Dov’s doorway that their mother had changed the shop’s locks in March, began to read the shop’s ledger at the register drawer, and came back to find the drawer empty. Nadia, who counts things, has been asked by Dov to clear the flat above the shop and has found their father’s good pen in the pocket of the coat that still hangs there. Dov, who gave Elena the new key and kept the reason, has been keeping the ledger in a looser hand since the evening of 9 March, has signed away the shop, and took the ledger home when he cleared the drawer for the buyer.
