Now he brings it to the shop, where Elena is. The draft reads: Dov put the ledger on the counter. “It’s all there. From March, it’s mine.” He kept his hand on the cover. “And before that. I took it home and I read it, Lena, the whole thing. He was ill. He’d been seeing someone since the autumn. There are dates, there’s a doctor. He knew.” Elena then rings Nadia, Nadia comes, and the three of them read the ledger together, as the ending in The Ending (Chapter 16) has them do. The draft’s writer added Dov’s last four sentences after an early reader asked a reasonable question: why would a man who has the ledger at home for weeks not read it? The question was right and the answer was wrong. A second reader’s note shows what the answer cost: By the time they opened the book I already knew what was in it, and so did they. The scene in which three people read their father’s record together, which the book has been building towards since its prologue, has become a scene in which two people confirm what a third has told them. The largest truth in the book, that their father knew he was ill, wrote it down and told nobody, arrives as a sentence of hearsay, before the reading, from the one person who has had no reason to look for it. The fault is a matter of structure rather than prose. A reveal is a late disclosure that changes what the reader understands of pages already read, and this one has three jobs. It must reach back: the till counted twice in the prologue, the father’s two words In case , the doctor’s name that meant nothing to Dov on the evening of 9 March, all of which the reader took one way, must now be taken another. It must arrive by recognition, received by the people it concerns at a moment of the book’s own making. And the delay before it must have a reason inside the book. The draft fails the third job and so loses the second: it solved the plausibility problem by spending the reveal, when the problem asked for a reason for the delay. The chapter’s claim is that every reveal makes these three demands, and that most failed reveals fail one of them. A reveal is earned when the pages before it bear two readings, the one the reader made and the one the disclosure makes, and when something inside the book, a character who does not know or a teller with a reason not to say, explains why the truth came when it did. It may reinterpret whatever the double reading reaches, and falsify only what a teller in the book could have shaped. The claim has a consequence for revision. A reveal that readers guess early has too many passages that bear only the second reading; one that makes readers feel cheated has a passage that bears only the first, stated on the narration’s own authority; one that lands without force was delivered as information rather than received as recognition. None is mended by adding clues or explanations at the moment of disclosure. Each is mended earlier, in the passages that prepare the reveal and in the reason for the delay. The revision in Worked Analyses deletes Dov’s four sentences and adds one sentence to his chapter of the evening of 9 March, just before the convergence. The sentence gives his not reading a reason and makes his It’s all there mean something he does not know. The claim also settles a question this book has carried since The Chapter Break (Chapter 6), which proposed the recasting close, a chapter ending that changes the meaning of the chapter it closes, and asked how far a close may recast a whole book. The answer, argued in The Taxonomy , is the second sentence of the claim: as far as the double reading holds, and no further than a teller’s authority reaches. See also: the full treatment , on the plausibility of withheld knowledge; The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13), whose household case recorded that Dov’s never reading back “needs a reason the reader can believe”.

title: 2. Definitions
text: The working definition A reveal is a disclosure of a fact the reader lacked that changes the reader’s understanding of what she has already read. The definition has two parts, and both are needed. The first separates a reveal from ordinary new information: most of what a novel tells the reader is new, and most of it changes only what will happen next. The second makes the reveal retrospective: after it, earlier passages mean something they did not mean before, and the reader’s mind goes back over them. A pistol produced in the last chapter is new information; the discovery that the narrator fired it in the fifth is a reveal. The retrospective movement is what the chapter calls the double reading . Every passage that bears on a reveal is read twice, once forwards, under the reader’s understanding at the time, and once in memory or on a second pass, under the understanding the reveal supplies. The first reading is the one the reader made; the second reading is the one the reveal makes. A reveal is prepared when the passages before it support both readings, and the craft of preparing one is the craft of writing sentences that are true under each. The fact disclosed may be large or small, and the reader may or may not have known there was something to learn. What makes it a reveal is the change of understanding, not the size of the fact or the reader’s surprise. The disclosure may come by a character’s discovery, by a document, by a change of narrator, or by the narration itself; and it may be shared with the characters or reach the reader alone. Adjacent terms A recognition is a character’s change from ignorance to knowledge, Aristotle’s anagnorisis . It is the reveal received on the page. Oedipus learns who he is; Pip learns who his benefactor is. A reveal can occur without a recognition, when the reader alone learns a fact (the last pages of a novel told by a murderer), and a recognition without a reveal, when a character learns what the reader has known all along. The two coinciding is the strongest arrangement and the commonest. A twist is a reveal the reader did not know to expect, the popular name for what this chapter, following Meir Sternberg, calls a surprise reveal (see How It Works ). A clue is a passage that bears the second reading for a reader who looks for it, and a red herring is a passage built to support a false second reading; both are tools of the double reading, described in The Mechanism . Dramatic irony , in The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13), is the reader knowing what a character does not, and the reveal is one of its ends: the moment the character catches up. Paralipsis , Genette’s term, is the omission of information the narration’s own vantage ought to have supplied, the mechanism of most reveals and of most cheats, and The Transition (Chapter 5) and Backstory and Flashback (Chapter 7) use it for the false ellipsis and the withheld past. A plant , in The Ending (Chapter 16), is an element deposited early for use late; a reveal’s preparation is a set of plants whose second meaning the reader did not see. What the chapter leaves to other chapters The mechanics of narrating a past event once a reveal has made it necessary, the cutaway and its registers, belong to Backstory and Flashback (Chapter 7); a withheld past disclosed late is this chapter’s. Truths withheld by the arrangement of two or more timelines, where the reveal is a convergence of times, belong to Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture (Chapter 8), which this chapter touches only where the withholding needs a reason. The prologue that discloses its ending in advance belongs to The Prologue (Chapter 10); the midpoint that turns on a revelation is placed in the book’s shape by The Middle (Chapter 11), and this chapter says what the revelation must do once it is there. A character’s change of the rule by which she chooses is an arc, in Arc and Theme (Chapter 12); a change in what the reader understands is a reveal, here, though the two often fall at the same moment. Who may know what, and at what cost to the book’s allocation of minds, belongs to The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13); the ending’s other duties belong to The Ending (Chapter 16); and a reveal held across volumes of a series, or required by a genre’s contract, belongs to Series and Genre (Chapter 17). See also: the full treatment , section 1, on the boundary between a reveal and a recognition.

title: 3. How It Works
text: The theory below is limited to what the method uses. Each strand opens with the writer’s question, then gives the source that answers it. Most of the sources describe a particular tradition, the classical tragedy, the golden-age detective story, the modernist unreliable narrator, and their rules are period conventions describing contracts that readers of those forms accepted, not laws of narrative. What does a reader do at a reveal? A writer who has a secret wants to know what the disclosure will do to the reader, and the oldest answer is Aristotle’s. In the Poetics (chapter 11, in S. H. Butcher’s translation) a recognition is “a change from ignorance to knowledge”, and the finest recognition is one that coincides with a reversal, a change of fortune, as when Oedipus’s search for the murderer of Laius discovers himself. In chapter 16 Aristotle ranks the kinds of recognition: lowest are those made by tokens and scars, or contrived by the poet; higher are those made by memory and by reasoning; best of all is the recognition that “arises from the incidents themselves”, where the discovery is produced by the chain of events the play has already set moving. The ranking is the earliest statement of two conditions this chapter uses: a reveal should be received by a character in an act that changes something, and it should come from inside the book’s causal system rather than from a token supplied for the purpose. What Aristotle describes from the stage, the reader performs in her head. The disclosure sends her back over what she has read, and the pleasure of a good reveal is the pleasure of finding the earlier pages rearranged and still whole. The double reading in Definitions names that movement. What is the reader feeling before it? Before a reveal the writer has to know what kind of interest the withheld fact is generating, because that decides how the reveal should land. Meir Sternberg, in Expositional Modes and Temporal Ordering in Fiction (1978) and later essays, distinguishes three interests produced by the order of telling. Suspense is uncertainty about what will happen. Curiosity is uncertainty about something in the past that the reader knows she lacks, as when a book opens on a body and the reader wants to know who killed it. Surprise is the discovery of a gap the reader did not know was there, which sends her back to revise what she thought she understood. A reveal answers curiosity or produces surprise, and the chapter calls the two kinds the curiosity reveal and the surprise reveal . Roland Barthes’s S/Z (1970; translated by Richard Miller, 1974) describes the same field from the side of the text: a hermeneutic code that poses an enigma and delays its answer by snares, equivocations, partial answers, suspended answers and jamming, until a disclosure. The terms are useful as a list of what a writer can do between posing a question and answering it. Alfred Hitchcock put the trade between surprise and suspense in an image that writers still use. In his interviews with François Truffaut ( Hitchcock , 1966; English 1967) he described a bomb under a table: if it goes off unannounced the audience has fifteen seconds of surprise, but if it has been shown to the audience beforehand, the conversation above it gives fifteen minutes of suspense. The image is about film and about bombs, but its lesson is general: a fact disclosed to the reader early, before the characters learn it, converts surprise into suspense. Where to disclose is a choice between the two, and The Mechanism treats it as alignment. What makes a reveal fair? A writer worried that a reveal will feel like a trick is asking about fair play, a term the detective story made explicit. Ronald Knox’s “Decalogue” (1929) and S. S. Van Dine’s “Twenty Rules for Writing Detective Stories” (1928) set out what a puzzle writer owed the reader. Knox’s first rule says that the criminal must be mentioned early but must not be anyone whose thoughts the reader has been allowed to follow; his ninth that the detective’s companion, the Watson, must not conceal any thoughts which pass through his mind. Three years earlier Agatha Christie’s The Murder of Roger Ackroyd (1926) had been narrated by its murderer, and the arguments over whether it cheated have run ever since. The rules are a period convention, and few writers outside the puzzle mystery keep them literally. What survives is their principle: the reader must have been able, in principle, to read the passages correctly, and no thought of a mind the reader shares may be hidden without a reason the book can show. The principle is the double reading and the withholder of The Mechanism . How far can the reader trust the teller? The question underneath the largest reveals is whether the narration itself can be mistaken or lying. Wayne C. Booth’s The Rhetoric of Fiction (1961) named the unreliable narrator : a narrator who does not speak or act in accordance with the norms of the work, so that the reader learns to read past what the narrator says. Gérard Genette’s Narrative Discourse (1972; translated by Jane E. Lewin, 1980) supplies the finer instrument, paralipsis, the omission of something the narration’s vantage ought to have included. Between them they mark the difference this chapter calls the teller rule: a narrator, or a character who writes or tells within the book, can be wrong or lie, and a reveal can expose it; the narration of a book that has declared no such teller cannot, and a reveal that requires it to have lied voids what it reveals. What does the evidence say? The evidence is thin and experimental, using short texts rather than novels. Hans Hoeken and Mario van Vliet ( Poetics , 2000) gave readers versions of one story with its discourse rearranged and found that adding an unexpected event raised both readers’ appreciation and their recall of the story, which the authors attribute to readers reassessing the preceding events: the double reading, measured. Jonathan Leavitt and Nicholas Christenfeld ( Psychological Science , 2011) found that readers given the outcome of short stories in advance, including stories with ironic twists and mysteries, rated them as more enjoyable, not less. Benjamin Johnson and Judith Rosenbaum ( Communication Research , 2015) found the opposite with longer stories: unspoiled readers reported more suspense and more enjoyment. A conjecture consistent with both is that a reveal’s value depends less on the surprise than on what the reader does with it, which is the claim this chapter makes on other grounds. See also: the full treatment , section 2, with Aristotle’s six kinds of recognition, Barthes’s terms, the fair-play codes and the evidence at greater length.

title: 4. The Taxonomy
text: Reveals are classified here in two ways: by what the disclosure changes, which decides how far back it reaches, and by where it falls, which decides what it leaves the reader wanting. Two rulings follow, on proposals that earlier chapters left to this one. Four objects of a reveal The reveal of event discloses what happened: a death that was a murder, a past act that explains the present. It recasts the passages that described the event’s surface, and usually the behaviour of whoever knew. In Daphne du Maurier’s Rebecca (1938) Maxim tells the narrator, after a diver finds Rebecca’s boat in the bay, that he killed his first wife and that he hated her, and every scene in which the narrator read his silences as grief for Rebecca is recast. Its preparation lies in the surface of events: an absence, a timing, an object out of place. The reveal of identity discloses who someone is: the benefactor is a convict, the stranger a brother, the dead man the narrator. In Great Expectations (1860–61) Magwitch’s return in chapter 39 discloses that Pip’s fortune was his, and every scene in which Pip assumed Miss Havisham’s design is recast. Its preparation lies in what a character is permitted to do or not to do while the reader holds the wrong identity, and its danger is that a single scene showing the character doing what the true identity forbids will void it. The reveal of motive discloses why: an act the reader has watched is given a different reason. At chapter scale it is the motive supplied last that The Chapter Break (Chapter 6) describes, Okonkwo’s He was afraid of being thought weak ; at book scale it can turn a villain or a saint inside out. Its preparation is the act itself, shown in enough detail that the second motive fits it as well as the first. The household novel’s largest reveal is of this kind as well as of event: the reader has watched the father count the till twice and pocket the pen, and learns at the end that he did these things as a man putting his affairs in order. The reveal of telling discloses something about the text the reader has been reading: who wrote it, why, or that part of it is untrue. The Murder of Roger Ackroyd discloses that its narrator is the murderer; Gillian Flynn’s Gone Girl (2012) discloses that one of its two alternating texts is a fabrication; Ian McEwan’s Atonement (2001) discloses that the novel is the work of one of its characters, and that its happiest scene did not happen. This kind reaches furthest, because it can recast every page, and it is the kind the teller rule below governs. A single disclosure often has two objects, as the household’s does, and the classification is used to find the passages a reveal must recast, not to file it. An identity reveal recasts the scenes in which the character appeared; a reveal of telling recasts the whole text the teller controlled. Three positions Where a reveal falls decides what it gives the reader in exchange for the question it answers. The chapter calls the new question the successor question . The early reveal comes in the first third and turns a book that could have run on curiosity into one that runs on consequence. Karen Joy Fowler’s We Are All Completely Beside Ourselves (2013) discloses at about a quarter of its length a fact a more conventional book would have kept for its end, and the successor question is no longer what was Fern? but what was done to her, and to the family that raised her? ( Worked Analyses ). The turn reveal comes near the middle and changes the book’s engine, usually from curiosity to suspense. Part Two of Gone Girl opens on Amy alive; the question what happened to Amy? is answered, and replaced by what will she do, and will Nick survive it? A turn reveal is one way to make the midpoint that The Middle (Chapter 11) places at the centre of a book, and it must be followed by a book that uses the new question, or the second half will feel like an epilogue. The closing reveal comes in the last part and has no successor question within the book; what it gives the reader is the double reading itself. Atonement ’s coda and Christie’s last chapter are closing reveals. Because nothing comes after, a closing reveal is judged almost entirely by its preparation and its range. The declined reveal: a ruling on the epistemological domain The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13) proposed an epistemological domain for viewpoint: a grant of several vantages made to show that none can know what happened, so that the reader is given irresolution rather than assembly. It adopted the domain for diagnosis and conceded three objections: that it may be contrast plus unreliability, that its examples cluster in modernist fiction, and that it names what a structure means rather than what a grant buys. It left this chapter to adopt or reject it at the scale of a book, since a reveal is the adjudication the domain refuses. This chapter adopts it at the scale of a book, as the plural-vantage form of a wider category, the declined reveal : a book that holds a question of fact open to its end and shows the reader that it is doing so. The first objection is answered at this scale, because it supplies the test that separates the two. Contrast plus unreliability ends in a reveal that tells the reader which account to discount; the epistemological domain ends without one, and the reader who took any single account would believe something the book will not confirm. The third objection lapses, because what a structure means is a reveal’s own subject. The second stands in part. The declined reveal is commoner in literary than in commercial fiction, though The Affair ’s first season keeps its two lovers’ memories unreconciled on screen, and Yann Martel’s Life of Pi (2001) ends by offering one teller’s two accounts of a voyage and asking which the listener prefers, the same refusal made by a single teller. The condition for a declined reveal is that the question must be visibly declined, not forgotten: the book must keep it before the reader and close its other questions around it. The Ending (Chapter 16) made the same demand of the household’s mother, whose reason for changing the locks the book never gives. Hers is a declined reveal without an epistemological structure, since no competing accounts are offered, only a silence kept in view. A declined reveal that is not visible is an abandoned thread. How far a close may recast a book: the teller rule The Chapter Break (Chapter 6) proposed the recasting close, a chapter ending that changes the meaning of the chapter it closes, and found that over-delivered it voids the chapter it closes. The Ending (Chapter 16) ruled that the category stops discriminating at a book’s last line and passed on the question it leaves: how far a close may recast a whole book. The answer distinguishes two things a closing reveal can do to earlier pages. It can reinterpret them, giving a second meaning to passages whose first meaning stays true as a description of what the reader was shown; and it can falsify them, declaring that what the reader was shown did not happen. The range of a reveal is the set of passages it recasts in either way. Reinterpretation may extend as far as the double reading holds. Falsification is governed by the teller rule : a reveal may falsify only passages that a teller in the book, a narrator, a diarist, a character telling a story, could have shaped, and only if the reveal identifies the teller and the book gives the teller a reason. Atonement falsifies its reunion scene and survives, because the coda identifies Briony as its author and her motive as atonement; The Murder of Roger Ackroyd falsifies nothing, since Sheppard’s narration omits but does not state an untruth, and its range is the whole book by reinterpretation alone. An ending that declares the book a dream, or a simulation that nobody in the book was writing, falsifies passages the narration vouched for on its own authority, and voids the book as the over-delivered recasting close voids its chapter. The recasting close therefore needs no separate category at book scale. A close may recast a whole book when every passage it recasts survives the double reading or lies within a teller’s account. See also: the full treatment , section 3, with the extended catalogue (the false reveal, the serial reveal, the reveal of world) and a summary table of objects, positions and ranges.

title: 5. The Mechanism
text: A reveal is built in three places: in the passages that prepare it, in the reason for its delay, and in its timing relative to the characters. The chapter’s two tools work on the first and the third, and the second is a question asked of each. The double-reading table The double-reading table lists every passage that bears on a reveal, in book order, with its position, its first reading and its second. Draft it for the book’s largest reveal before revising anything. A sound table has three properties. Every row has both readings filled; a row with only a first reading is a passage the reveal will contradict, and a row with only a second is a passage that gives the reveal away. The rows are spread through the book rather than bunched before the disclosure, since bunched clues read as an approach. And at least one early row is strong enough that a reader, on the second reading, can point to it and say the book told her. Five devices put both readings into one passage. An equivocation is a sentence true under both readings, whose words mean one thing forwards and another backwards; Christie’s narrator, recording the minutes after the murder, writes that he did what little had to be done, which is true. A decoy reading is a first reading supplied by a character with a reason to believe it, so that the reader adopts an error she can later attribute to someone; the decoy works best when the character is sympathetic and the error is a kindness. The clue in a list places the significant item among insignificant ones of the same kind, so that it is present and unweighted. The steer of attention places the significant detail where the reader’s attention is elsewhere, at the peak of another scene’s tension, or in the subordinate clause of a sentence about something else. And the act with two motives shows an act in enough detail that the second motive fits it as well as the first: a till counted twice reads as habit, and then as a man putting his accounts in order. The withholder Every reveal has a withholder , the thing in the book that keeps the truth from the reader until the disclosure, and the reader accepts the delay in proportion as she can see what the withholder is. There are three legitimate kinds. A vantage that does not know is the commonest: the book follows a character who has not learned the fact, and the reader learns it when the character does; the delay is as plausible as the character’s ignorance, so the ignorance must be motivated, which is where the household draft in The Problem failed. A teller with a motive is the second: a narrator, diarist or storyteller who conceals, and whose concealment the reveal explains; the delay is as plausible as the motive. An arrangement is the third: the book’s order of telling, a timeline placed after another, a chapter cut away at the moment of discovery, withholds by structure, and the delay is as plausible as the reader’s acceptance of the arrangement, which The Chapter Break (Chapter 6) and Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture (Chapter 8) price. The illegitimate kind is paralipsis without a reason: a narration that follows a mind which knows the fact, and simply does not say it. Knox’s rule against hiding the Watson’s thoughts names this case. It is not always fatal. A viewpoint character may know a fact and not think of it, if the book shows where her attention is instead, and a retrospective narrator may delay a fact he knows, if he says that he is doing so and the delay serves something the reader can see. Without either, the reader who reaches the reveal feels that the book, not a character, kept the secret. The disclosure map and alignment The disclosure map is a table with a row for each fact the book withholds and a column for the reader and for each character who will learn it, recording the position at which each learns it. It shows the reveal’s alignment : whether the reader learns the fact with a character, ahead of one, or after. Each alignment buys something different. Learning with a character gives the recognition its full force, since the reader’s change of understanding and the character’s are one event; this is the arrangement Aristotle prized. Learning ahead gives suspense, Hitchcock’s bomb under the table, and turns the character’s eventual recognition into a scene the reader awaits rather than one she undergoes. Learning after, when a character the reader follows already knows, is the riskiest, because it is the paralipsis above unless the withholder is visible. The map also shows the successor question of The Taxonomy . For each reveal, write beneath it the question the reader is left holding. A turn reveal that leaves no stronger question than the one it answered has spent the book’s engine early; a closing reveal whose only successor is was that all? has spent nothing worth the wait. Consequence and recognition A reveal is spent when it changes what someone does. In the sense this chapter uses, a reveal has consequence when at least one character acts differently because of it, or when the book’s ending means something it would not otherwise mean. The two often coincide in the recognition scene, the scene in which a character receives the truth, and that scene follows the rule of Arc and Theme (Chapter 12): a change shown in a decision persuades, and a change reported does not. The character who learns the truth must do something with it on the page, even if what she does is decline to do anything, and the reader must see the cost. Several reveals in one book Most books withhold more than one thing, and the map’s columns show how the reveals share the book. Three practices follow from it. Give the reader no more than one new disclosure in a scene, since a second arriving before the first has been received spends both; a scene may still carry several disclosures to characters, if the reader holds all but one of them already, because those she holds play as suspense rather than information. Order a book’s reveals so that each changes the reading of the last, rather than cancelling it; a twist that voids the previous twist teaches the reader to believe nothing, which is the serial reveal’s danger. And keep one reveal largest, by range, so that the book has a centre of gravity: the reveal the double-reading table is drafted for. See also: the full treatment , section 5, with the procedures for both tools and the household’s table and map in full.

title: 6. Diagnostic Tests
text: The eight tests are for revision, and they need the two documents defined in The Mechanism : a double-reading table for the reveal under test and a disclosure map for the book. Tests 1 to 3 (Double reading, Teller and Withholder) read the preparation, tests 4 (Alignment) and 5 (Successor) the timing, and tests 6 to 8 (Consequence, Recognition and Source) the reveal’s arrival. Record a sentence for each, not a verdict. Test 1 — Double reading Does every passage bearing on the reveal support both a first and a second reading? Failure. A row with only the first is the cheat; a row with only the second is the giveaway. Exception. Christie’s Murder on the Orient Express (1934), whose clues point everywhere, because the suspects planted them. Test 2 — Teller Is every passage the reveal falsifies inside the account of a teller whom the reveal names and whose motive it explains? Failure. The cheat: the narration made to lie on its own authority. Exception. Lewis Carroll’s Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland (1865), which ends as a dream and voids nothing, since it never offered its events as fact. Test 3 — Withholder What keeps the truth from the reader until the disclosure, and can the reader see it, at the latest when the reveal comes? Failure. Paralipsis without a reason: the book, not a character, kept the secret. Exception. The Murder of Roger Ackroyd (1926), whose withholder is invisible until the last chapter, by design. Test 4 — Alignment Does the reader learn each fact with, ahead of or after the characters, and is that the alignment the scene needs? Failure. A recognition the reader has already undergone alone, or suspense never built. Exception. Hitchcock’s Vertigo (1958), which shows the audience the deception two-thirds through, against advice, and turns the rest into suspense. Test 5 — Successor For a reveal before the end, what question replaces the one it answers, and is it as strong? Failure. A second half that reads as an epilogue. Exception. Muriel Spark’s The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie (1961), which tells early who will betray Miss Brodie and keeps the reader on why. Test 6 — Consequence Does any character act differently because of the reveal, or does the ending mean something it would not otherwise? Failure. The idle reveal. Exception. Atonement (2001), whose closing reveal comes when nobody can act, and makes that impossibility its subject. Test 7 — Recognition Is the truth received by a character, in scene, in an act, or delivered as information? Failure. The reported reveal. Exception. Ambrose Bierce’s “An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge” (1890), whose truth reaches only the reader, at the instant it ends the character. Test 8 — Source Does the disclosure come from inside the book’s causal system? Failure. The reveal from outside. Exception. Wilkie Collins’s The Moonstone (1868), solved by an experiment devised by a man introduced late, whose method rests on clues the book has kept in view. Reading the results together Failures cluster, and the cluster locates the repair. Tests 1 (Double reading) and 3 (Withholder) failing together are the commonest pattern in a reveal readers call a cheat: a passage gives only the false reading and nothing in the book accounts for it. The repair is usually to find a withholder first, a character who did not know, or a teller with a motive, and then rewrite the passage as an equivocation from inside that withholder’s view. Test 1 (Double reading) failing on the giveaway side while test 4 (Alignment) passes means the reader is ahead of the characters by accident rather than design; either thin the clues or make the alignment deliberate and use the suspense. Test 5 (Successor) failing alone, in a book whose reveal falls at the middle, means a turn reveal has answered the book’s question without replacing it. Move the reveal later, or find what the characters must now do that they could not do before, and make that the second half’s engine. Tests 6 (Consequence) and 7 (Recognition) failing together describe a reveal that is information and nothing else: the reader learns, and nobody acts or recognises. The repair is a recognition scene in which someone receives the truth and does something with it. Test 8 (Source) failing is rarely solved by better preparation of the outside source; route the truth through a character the book has followed. A clean pass on all eight, with readers who still guess the reveal early, usually means the double-reading table has too many rows, not that any row is wrong. Cut the weakest third of the clues and test again. See also: the full treatment , section 5, with the procedure for each test and the household’s table and map.

title: 7. Failure Patterns
text: Each pattern below fails through a mechanism rather than a surface feature. Each ends with a published work that uses the feature successfully because the mechanism is absent or offset by another effect. The full treatment has a longer catalogue, among them the coy narrator, the serial reveal, the red herring that eats the book and the withholding viewpoint. The cheat Symptom. Readers feel tricked rather than surprised. They go back over the book and find a passage that the reveal makes false, and they resent the book rather than admire it. Mechanism. The cheat is a passage before a reveal that supports only the first reading and is stated on the narration’s own authority, so that the reveal requires the narration to have lied. It fails test 1 (Double reading) on the first-reading side and test 2 (Teller). The motive is usually haste: the writer, wanting the false reading firmly held, writes it as fact rather than as a character’s belief, or writes a viewpoint character’s thoughts so that they exclude what she knows. Remedy. Tests 1 to 3 (Double reading, Teller and Withholder). Find the passage, then find a withholder for it: reassign the false statement to a character who believes it, or to a teller whom the reveal will name; or rewrite it as an equivocation, true under both readings. If the passage is in the mind of a character who knows the truth, show her attention fixed on something else, and make that something matter. Exception. The Usual Suspects (Bryan Singer; written by Christopher McQuarrie, 1995). Much of the film is shown in flashback while Verbal Kint tells his story to a customs agent, and the images, which a viewer ordinarily trusts as a camera’s record, show events Kint is inventing from the notices pinned to the office wall. The film commits the cheat on screen’s terms and succeeds because it has framed every flashback as Kint’s telling from its first minutes, so its last sequence names the teller and his motive. The screen’s authority was borrowed by a teller, and the reveal returns it. The giveaway Symptom. Readers guess the reveal early, sometimes in the first third, and the disclosure lands flat. The writer, told so, is often surprised, because no single clue seemed obvious. Mechanism. The giveaway is a reveal whose preparation contains passages that support only the second reading, or so many passages supporting both that their density becomes a reading of its own. It fails test 1 (Double reading) on the second-reading side. A common cause is the coy narrator, who signals a withheld fact with if she had known then , which tells the reader there is a fact; another is a clue described with more attention than its first reading warrants. Remedy. Test 1 (Double reading), then test 4 (Alignment). Give each clue a first reading that a reader would accept without effort, which usually means a reason in the scene for the detail to be there. Cut the weakest clues and every phrase that announces withholding. If readers will guess regardless, decide whether to let them, and make the alignment deliberate. Exception. Columbo (NBC, from 1971). Each episode shows the murder and the murderer in its opening act, so that the viewer holds the solution before the detective arrives, and the series’ pleasure is watching him reach what the viewer knows. The format commits the giveaway on purpose and succeeds because it has moved the reveal’s work from the viewer’s discovery to the murderer’s, and the successor question, how he will be caught, is stronger than the one it gives away. The reported reveal Symptom. The largest truth in the book arrives in a sentence of dialogue or a page of explanation, and the scene that should have been its recognition becomes a confirmation of what the reader has been told. Mechanism. The reported reveal delivers the truth as information rather than as recognition. A character who learned it offstage tells it, or the narration explains it, and the reader and the other characters are passive recipients. It fails test 7 (Recognition), and usually test 4 (Alignment), because the teller learned the truth before the reader in a scene the book did not show. The household draft in The Problem is a clean instance. Remedy. Tests 3 (Withholder) and 7 (Recognition). Ask why the character who reports the truth learned it first, and whether the book needs that; if not, keep him ignorant and give his ignorance a reason. Then let the truth be found by the people it concerns, in a scene, by an act: a page turned, a name read, a door opened. Keep explanation after the recognition, short, and ideally unspoken. Exception. Christie’s Murder on the Orient Express (1934). The solution is a speech: Poirot assembles the suspects and explains, and the reader receives the truth as information. It succeeds because the puzzle mystery’s contract, in the sense of The Opening Pages (Chapter 9), makes the explanation the payoff the reader came for, and because the speech contains a recognition after all, the suspects’ as they are told what they did and wait for Poirot’s decision. The idle reveal Symptom. The reveal is surprising and fairly prepared, and readers shrug. Asked what changed, they can say what they learned but not why it mattered. Mechanism. The idle reveal changes the reader’s understanding of the past and nothing else: no character acts differently, no relationship alters, and the ending means what it would have meant without it. It fails tests 5 (Successor) and 6 (Consequence). The motive is often a writer’s pleasure in a secret for its own sake, or a reveal kept from an earlier draft whose plot has since moved away from it. Remedy. Test 6 (Consequence). Tie a decision to the reveal: someone who learns the truth must now choose what he would not have chosen. If no decision can be found, ask what the book’s question is and whether the reveal answers it; a reveal that answers a question the book is not asking belongs in another book or nowhere. Exception. Great Expectations (1860–61). Late in the novel Pip works out that Estella is the daughter of Magwitch and of Jaggers’s housekeeper, Molly. He tells Jaggers and Wemmick, and nobody does anything with the knowledge: Estella never learns it, and Magwitch is told only that his daughter lived. The reveal succeeds because its consequence is meaning rather than action. It completes the book’s pattern of hidden origins, so that the lady Pip built his expectations around came from the same convict as his fortune. The reveal from outside Symptom. The truth arrives by a letter, a stranger, a confession from someone the reader has barely met, or a coincidence. Readers call it convenient. Mechanism. The reveal from outside draws the disclosure from beyond the book’s causal system, so that no character’s choice brings it about and nothing the reader watched prepared its source. It fails test 8 (Source) and usually test 7 (Recognition). The Ending ’s draft ending (Chapter 16), in which a solicitor’s letter and the mother’s account explain everything, is the household’s own instance; The Subplot (Chapter 14) describes the same failure as a convergence by coincidence. Remedy. Test 8 (Source). Route the truth through a character the book has followed, and make its arrival the result of something that character did. If a document must carry it, the document should be one the book has shown, and its finding should be a choice. Exception. Henry Fielding’s Tom Jones (1749). The truth of Tom’s birth arrives late, from Mrs Waters, who was the Jenny Jones once blamed as his mother, and from a deathbed message that Blifil suppressed. It succeeds because the comic contract has promised restoration from the first book, so that the outside source reads as Providence keeping a promise rather than as the author rescuing a plot.

title: 8. Worked Analyses
text: Three close readings of published reveals, a short screen reading and the household revision case. Each reading names the reveal’s object, position, withholder, alignment and range. Ian McEwan, Atonement (2001): a closing reveal of telling The novel’s first part, set on one hot day in 1935, follows thirteen-year-old Briony Tallis as she misreads a scene at a fountain between her sister Cecilia and Robbie Turner, reads a letter not meant for her, and accuses Robbie of a rape he did not commit. The second part follows Robbie in the retreat to Dunkirk in 1940; the third, Briony as a trainee nurse in London, who goes to Balham to find Cecilia and Robbie together and promises to undo her lie. The third part ends with initials and a place and date, BT London 1999 . A last section, “London, 1999”, is narrated by Briony at seventy-seven, newly diagnosed with vascular dementia, who discloses that Robbie died of septicaemia at Bray Dunes in June 1940, that Cecilia was killed months later when a bomb destroyed Balham Underground station, that she never went to Balham, and that the novel the reader has read is hers. The reveal’s object is the telling, and its range is the whole book. Most of that range is reinterpretation: every scene of 1935 stands as a description of what Briony, now the novelist, imagined the others felt, and passages that seemed the narration’s omniscient privilege, Robbie’s thoughts on the march, Cecilia’s at the fountain, become a guilty woman’s reconstruction of minds she wronged. One passage is falsified, the reunion in Balham, and the book survives the falsification because it meets the teller rule of The Taxonomy : the coda names the teller and gives her motive, a kindness she calls her atonement, granting the lovers in fiction the happiness she took from them in life. The double reading was prepared from the first page. Briony is introduced as a child writer with a passion for order and a play she wants performed; Part Three gives her an editor’s letter, signed with initials, criticising a novella she has written about a girl watching a scene at a fountain; and the initials at the end of Part Three put a signature on the text before the coda explains it. The withholder is a teller with a motive, and the alignment is the reader learning alone, since no character in the coda learns anything. The reveal has no successor question and no consequence a character can act on, which is the exception given for test 6 (Consequence) in Diagnostic Tests : the impossibility of action is the book’s subject, because atonement by fiction is all that is left to its teller. Gillian Flynn, Gone Girl (2012): a turn reveal Part One alternates two texts. Nick Dunne narrates, from the day his wife Amy disappears, the police search and his own growing exposure; Amy’s diary entries, beginning seven years earlier, trace a marriage in which she grows afraid of him. Part Two opens with Amy, on the day she vanished, alive and pleased: I’m so much happier now that I’m dead . The diary was written to frame her husband. The reveal’s object is the telling again, but its range is half the book, because the teller rule confines it. The diary is falsified, and it can be, since the reveal names its author and her motive; Nick’s chapters are only reinterpreted, because his narration never stated a falsehood on the book’s authority. It did conceal: he had a young mistress, and he withheld her from the reader as from the police. But it flagged the concealment as it went, most memorably in It was my fifth lie to the police. I was just starting. The flag makes Nick a visible withholder, so that when his secret comes out the reader feels the book kept faith with her, which is the difference between a teller with a motive and paralipsis without a reason. Positioned at the turn, the reveal answers what happened to Amy? and replaces it with a stronger successor, what will she do, and can Nick survive it? The alignment changes with it. For half a book the reader learned with Nick, or behind him; from Part Two she is ahead of every character but Amy, and the curiosity of a missing-wife mystery becomes the suspense of a contest between two people the reader now knows to be lying. The test of a turn reveal is whether the second half uses the new question, and Flynn’s does, by giving the reader both players’ moves. Karen Joy Fowler, We Are All Completely Beside Ourselves (2013): the early reveal Rosemary Cooke narrates as a student at the University of California, Davis, in the 1990s, and tells the reader that her father advised her to start in the middle. Her sister Fern disappeared from the family when Rosemary was five, and her brother Lowell left home after it. About a quarter of the way into the book (page 76 of one edition), Rosemary tells the reader what she has withheld: Fern was a chimpanzee, raised alongside her as a twin in a psychological experiment run by their father. A more conventional book would have kept this for its end, as a surprise reveal of identity, and earned it by a double reading of every early description of Fern. Fowler spends it early and on purpose, and the withholder is a teller who says why she withheld: being raised with a chimpanzee defined her childhood, and it is, she says, never going to be the first thing she shares with someone. The delay is therefore characterisation rather than trickery, and the reader’s experience of the delay, having taken Fern for a girl, is the experience Rosemary has spent her adult life avoiding in others. The successor question is stronger than the one answered: not what was Fern? but what was done to her when she was taken away, and what her family did and failed to do. The early reveal trades a twist for a subject, and the trade is the book’s argument, that the line between the sisters was drawn by the people who studied them. A screen reading: The Sixth Sense (M. Night Shyamalan, 1999) A child psychologist, Malcolm Crowe, is shot in his home by a former patient. Months later he takes on a frightened boy, Cole, who confides that he sees dead people, who walk around like regular people and do not know they are dead. Malcolm’s marriage seems to have cooled: his wife does not answer him at their anniversary dinner, and he cannot get into his basement office. At the end his wife, asleep, drops a ring from her hand, and Malcolm sees that it is his own: he died in the opening scene. A short sequence of earlier moments replays them under the second reading. The reveal’s object is identity, and its range is the whole film, held by reinterpretation alone, as in The Murder of Roger Ackroyd . Nothing the camera showed is falsified, because the film was built so that no character but Cole speaks to Malcolm, and every scene of the marriage reads as estrangement forwards and as a ghost’s presence backwards. The withholder is a vantage that does not know, Malcolm’s, and the alignment is the viewer learning with him, which gives the recognition its force: the viewer’s change of understanding and his are one event. It has consequence, since Malcolm, knowing, speaks to his sleeping wife and lets her go. The replayed sequence is the film doing part of the viewer’s double reading, a concession to a medium in which the viewer cannot turn back the page. The household revision case: the ledger at the convergence The situation. The book’s largest reveal is in the ledger: that the father knew he was ill, wrote down the dates, a doctor’s name and a list of what needed doing, and told nobody. The canon keeps it from everyone until the end. Elena’s reading at the register drawer is interrupted before the illness entries; Dov takes the ledger home when he clears the drawer for the buyer; and Dov, the only person to hold the book in those months, writes forward and never reads back. The convergence follows Dov’s viewpoint chapter of the evening of 9 March, at about 78 per cent of the book: he brings the ledger to the shop, says “It’s all there. From March, it’s mine.” , Elena rings Nadia, and the three read it together, as Arc and Theme (Chapter 12) and The Ending (Chapter 16) have it. Version A, the draft. The convergence in The Problem , in which Dov adds that he took the ledger home, read it, and knows their father was ill. Diagnosis. The draft’s writer was answering test 3 (Withholder), and answered it by removing the withholder. Dov’s ignorance needed a reason; the draft gave him knowledge instead, and the book lost its recognition. Test 7 (Recognition) fails, since the truth is reported by a character who learned it offstage. Test 4 (Alignment) fails in a particular way: the illness was the one fact the reader, Elena, Nadia and Dov could learn together, and the draft has Dov learn it first, in a scene the book does not show, so that the reader receives it second-hand at the same moment as Elena. Test 6 (Consequence) is damaged as well. Arc and Theme ’s arrangement (Chapter 12), three people reading one record, which is the book’s answer to its thematic question, becomes one person telling two, and the ending’s He had known. He had not told them repeats what the reader was told a few pages earlier. Version B, the revision. Delete Dov’s four sentences, so that he says only “It’s all there. From March, it’s mine.” , and add two sentences to Dov’s chapter of 9 March, after he writes the date and the count: He did not turn back the page, then or in any of the months after. In eleven years he had never read a page of it; the ledger was for writing in, and reading it back had been his father’s business, and he did not start now. What the revision did. It gave the withholder a reason in the character, a deference that fits a son who thinks of the dead man as his father and who, in the same chapter, has decided that the ledger has a way of being written in. It put the reason where the reader can see it before the reveal, so that the delay is visible, and inside the one chapter the canon grants Dov’s mind, so that it costs no new viewpoint. And it gave Dov’s line at the convergence a double reading. Forwards, It’s all there is a confession of his own hand; backwards, the reader knows what Dov does not, that he has never read what is there. The disclosure map shows why the convergence can bear its load. The sisters receive three disclosures there, the looser hand, the sale and the illness; the reader holds two of them already, the sale from Dov’s thread at about 58 per cent and the hand from his chapter, so for her the scene carries one new fact, and the other two play as suspense about how the sisters will take them. The illness is the one disclosure in the book that reaches all four at once. The double-reading table for the illness, in brief, shows the preparation the revision relies on. Position Passage First reading Second reading Prologue The till counted twice A careful man’s habit A man putting his accounts in order Prologue He could not have said in case of what An impulse he cannot explain A reason he could not say aloud About 25% His last entry stops halfway along its third line An entry interrupted An entry interrupted by what it records About 66% In case anyone ever needs to check , which Nadia took to mean the shop A shopkeeper’s scruple A record kept for this About 78% A doctor’s name that means nothing to Dov; he never reads back A son’s grief and deference Why the truth waited for all three Convergence It’s all there Dov’s confession He does not know what is there Every row has both readings. Nadia’s reading of the line in Backstory and Flashback (Chapter 7) is a decoy reading in the sense of The Mechanism : a character with a reason supplies the first reading, so that the reader’s error is hers. The mother’s reason for changing the locks has no row and no column with an entry. It is the book’s declined reveal, kept visible by Dov’s She said you’d ask that , and the revision leaves it so. What the revision has not solved. The new sentences state Dov’s motive rather than dramatise it, and they lean on the narration’s retrospective gap, then or in any of the months after , which his chapter has already used once ( he thought about it for years afterwards ); a second use may read as the narration underlining. Placed beside the doctor’s name, they tell the reader that there are unread pages, which sharpens her curiosity enough that many readers will infer the illness at 78 per cent: the ending becomes a curiosity reveal with the reader half a step ahead, which is the design, and it costs surprise. The prologue’s he could not have said in case of what survives the double reading only if said means spoken aloud; a reader who takes it to mean known will find the narration claiming an ignorance the father did not have, the book’s nearest approach to a cheat, protected only partly by the conditional. And the convergence remains crowded for the sisters, though not for the reader, so its sequence must let Elena receive the hand before Nadia arrives for the reading. See also: the full treatment , with readings of The Murder of Roger Ackroyd , The Silent Patient and Knives Out , and the household’s double-reading table and disclosure map in full.

title: 9. Checklist and Exercises
text: Revision checklist The preparation Have I listed every passage that bears on my largest reveal, with a first and a second reading for each? Is there a passage that only the second reading explains, or that the reveal makes false on the narration’s own authority? Are the clues spread through the book, and is at least one early clue strong enough to be pointed to afterwards? Have I cut every if she had known and every phrase that announces a secret? The withholding What keeps the truth from the reader: a character who does not know, a teller with a motive, or the order of telling? If a character who knows is followed by the narration, where is her attention instead, and does the book show it? If the reveal falsifies anything, is it inside a teller’s account, and does the reveal name the teller and the reason? The timing Does the reader learn each withheld fact with the characters, ahead of them or after, and did I choose that? For a reveal before the end, what question replaces the one it answers, and is the second half built on it? Does any scene give the reader two new disclosures at once? If the book declines to reveal something, is the question kept visibly open to the end? The arrival Is the truth received by a character, in scene, in an act? Does someone act differently because of it, or does the ending mean something it would not otherwise? Does the disclosure come from inside the book’s causal system, by a character’s choice? Is the explanation after the recognition, short, and as far as possible left to the reader? Exercises The double-reading table. For your book’s largest reveal, list every passage that bears on it, with its position as a percentage, its first reading and its second. Mark each row that has only one reading. Rewrite one such row as an equivocation, a sentence true under both. The disclosure map. Make a table with a row for each fact your book withholds and a column for the reader and for each major character. Enter the position at which each learns each fact. Find one fact the reader learns alone that a character could learn with her, and rewrite the scene so that they learn it together. The withholder’s reason. Name the withholder of your largest reveal. If it is a character’s ignorance, write one sentence, placed before the reveal, that gives the ignorance a reason the reader can see. If it is a teller, write the sentence in which the teller, after the reveal, says why. The successor question. If your book has a reveal before its last quarter, write beneath it the question the reader now holds. Write the same for the question it answered. If the new question is weaker, either move the reveal later or write the decision that the reveal forces on a character, and place it within a chapter of the disclosure. The recognition without explanation. Rewrite your reveal scene so that no character explains the truth and the narration does not summarise it. Keep only what is found and what someone does about it. If the reader can no longer tell what has been revealed, the preparation is too thin; if she can, cut the explanation from your draft.

title: 10. Coda
text: The instruments in this chapter assume a reader who reads forwards, once, and then looks back. The double-reading table measures what a first reading takes and a second reading finds; the disclosure map times what is learned against what is withheld. Both describe a reader meeting a book for the first time, and both say little about the reader who returns knowing everything, as every rereader of a book does. For that reader every reveal is an alignment ahead of the characters, and every twist is suspense. That a book with a famous reveal can be reread with pleasure, as Great Expectations and The Murder of Roger Ackroyd are, is evidence that the reveal was never only a surprise: its preparation was writing that held two meanings, and the second meaning is what the rereader comes back for. That is the chapter’s argument. A reveal is not a moment but a debt the book has been paying all along: with sentences that were true twice, a withholder the reader could see, and timing chosen for what it gives the reader in exchange. The moment of disclosure only shows whether the payments were made. This is why the repairs in the failure patterns are almost always earlier than the reveal itself, and why a writer who adds a clue or an explanation at the moment of disclosure is usually paying a debt in the wrong place. The household revision illustrates the economy. It deleted four sentences that told the truth and added two that kept it, in a chapter some pages before the disclosure. The truth arrives where it did before, in three people’s hands at once, and the book’s other question, the mother’s, stays where the book has kept it, declined in plain view. The Ending (Chapter 16) defended that silence as the book’s last narratable material; the classification here adds a condition for keeping it, that it must stay visible, since a declined reveal the reader can no longer see is an abandoned thread. See also: the full treatment , section 8, on the limits of the model; Series and Genre (Chapter 17), for reveals held across volumes and required by genres; The Structural Edit (Chapter 18), which puts the double-reading table into a revision order for the whole book.

title: The Ending
text: What the last pages may spend, and what they owe The Craft Behind the Story (Second Edition) — Chapter 16. Part III: The Architecture of the Whole. In brief. The ending is the last stretch of a novel, its climax and whatever aftermath the book needs, and it differs from every other unit in two ways: nothing follows it to correct what it does, and the reader rereads the whole book through it. A weak ending therefore damages the book, not only its last pages, and an ending may spend only what the book has already deposited. The chapter’s tools are the plant audit, which traces everything the ending rests on back to the place it was planted, and the last-decision rule, which ends the aftermath within a page of the last decision anyone takes. Use the chapter when an ending feels unearned, flat, tidy, abrupt or overlong, or when you cannot tell whether a deliberate openness reads as a choice or as an evasion. What you can do after this chapter Separate the climax from the aftermath, and resolution from closure, and say which one a draft lacks. Name the domains an ending serves, gestures at or refuses, and find a carrier that serves several at once. Trace every load-bearing element of an ending to its planting, and distinguish a missing plant from missing pressure. Decide how long an aftermath should be, and where it should stop. Distinguish a declined question from a dropped one, and a chosen ambiguity from an evasion. Key terms Ending; climax and aftermath; desis and lusis; resolution and closure; termination; the retroactive lens; fictions of concord; closural allusion, terminal modification and unqualified assertion; anticipation of retrospection; privileged position; the narratable; the five domains (plot resolution, character-arc completion, thematic closure, emotional catharsis, the final image) and the proposed formal closure; earned and unearned; deposit and pressure; inevitability and predictability; the plant audit; the over-determined ending; the proportion problem and the last-decision rule; closural strategy; series hook. Each is defined at first use and collected in the consolidated glossary . Contents The first files say what an ending is and why it weighs more than its length, the middle files what it owes and how it pays, and the last are for use at the desk. The Problem A household ending that arrives in the post, and the chapter’s claim Definitions The ending, climax and aftermath, resolution and closure, and the terms around them How It Works Why readers want endings they know are artificial, what makes a last line final, why the end is read backwards, and the case against closure The Taxonomy Five domains an ending can serve, a proposed sixth, and rulings on proposals from earlier chapters The Mechanism Earned and unearned, inevitability, multiplicity at the close, and the proportion of climax to aftermath Diagnostic Tests Ten questions on one page, and how to read their failures together Failure Patterns Five recurrent failures, each with a work that commits it and succeeds Worked Analyses Great Expectations , Beloved , Never Let Me Go , Six Feet Under and the household revision case Checklist and Exercises The revision checklist and five exercises for your own draft Coda What the model assumes, and what an ending gives in exchange A writer in revision can start at the diagnostic tests and the failure patterns; the case against closure in How It Works is best read before either, because the tests are calibrated to endings that conclude. The full treatment The Reference layer holds the complete chapter, The Ending : Kermode, Herrnstein Smith, Brooks, Torgovnick, DuPlessis and Miller in full, the cognitive evidence and its limits, sixteen closural strategies, twelve failure patterns, nine close readings (among them Middlemarch , The Great Gatsby , Anna Karenina , Nineteen Eighty-Four , Ulysses , Don Quixote and Blindness ), the ending in the short story, the novella, the series and on screen, the household plant audit across the whole book, seminar questions and the sources. See also: The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1), whose value shift the ending makes at the largest scale; Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2), whose sequel is the shape of an aftermath; The Opening Pages (Chapter 9), the formal inverse of this chapter; The Subplot (Chapter 14), whose attention tax the ending refunds; The Structural Edit (Chapter 18), which puts the ending’s audit into a revision order for the whole book.

title: 1. The Problem
text: A draft of the household novel ends like this. Four months after their father’s death, three adult children have spent the book reconstructing what he left: Elena, who wants to know why their mother changed the shop’s locks in March; Nadia, who counts things; and Dov, who gave Elena the new key in his doorway and kept the reason to himself. Then a letter comes. The letter came on a Tuesday, forwarded twice, and it was Elena who opened it. Whitlock & Ames, Solicitors, regretted to inform the family of the late proprietor that the deeds to the premises had been placed in trust the previous February, and that a copy of the medical report lodged with them at that time was enclosed for the beneficiaries’ attention. Elena drives to her mother’s, and the mother, who has had no scene in the book, explains everything: she had known of the illness since January, he had made her promise, and she changed the locks to keep the children out of the ledger until she had decided what to tell them. Nadia arrives at nine and Dov at eleven, and the draft closes on by midnight there was nothing any of them did not know. Nothing in the passage is badly written. Its sentences are clear, its facts consistent, and every question the book raised is answered. A reader who reaches it nonetheless feels that the book before it has been cancelled: the investigation, the counting and the ledger turn out to have been a way of not opening the post. That feeling is the subject of this chapter, and it has a structure. The ending is the best-funded stretch of any novel. Every character, object, phrase and question the book has put down is available to it, and nothing needs establishing. Two constraints follow from that position, and they pull against each other. The first is that the account cannot be added to. An ending may spend what the book has deposited and nothing more, so a firm of solicitors arriving on the last pages is a withdrawal against an account that was never opened; readers call this cheating, and what they have detected is an unfunded transaction. The second is that nothing comes after the ending. Every other unit in this book works inside a story that is still running: a slack chapter can be redeemed by the next, and a scene whose point is hidden acquires one when its plant pays off, the relation The Chapter Break (Chapter 6) calls proposition and payoff. The ending has no next scene, so whatever it does is what the book did. Together the two constraints produce a third fact, which governs the rest of the chapter: the ending is read backwards. Until the last page a novel is an unfinished object about which the reader is still forming hypotheses; at the last page it becomes a finished one, and its shape is conferred from the end. This chapter calls that the retroactive lens . Because of it, the letter does not spoil one chapter of the household draft. It reaches back and reassigns every earlier scene to a book about delay. The same mechanism works in the writer’s favour, since an ending that lands can make a slow middle read as patience and an obscure early scene read as design. The ending is the unit through which the whole book is finally read, and nothing follows it to correct what it does; so an ending may spend only what the book has already deposited, and it is judged by what it gives the reader in exchange for stopping. The second half of that claim concedes something. Closure ends the instability that made the book worth reading, and a serious tradition of criticism, set out in How It Works , holds that this makes every ending a loss. The chapter accepts the loss and asks what the reader receives for it. In the household draft the answer is a set of facts delivered from outside. The revision in Worked Analyses gives the same three people one room, one document read together and one act; most of the facts still arrive, the one the post supplied (the mother’s reason) stays unsaid, and the book’s own material, not the post, produces what the reader is given. See also: the Reference introduction , on where the ending sits among the book’s recurring concepts; The Opening Pages (Chapter 9), on the opening, which works with no accumulated context where the ending works with nothing else.

title: 2. Definitions
text: The working definition The ending is the final unit of a novel. It is made of the climax , the last major confrontation or disaster, and the aftermath , everything between the climax and the last word. Two properties distinguish it from every other unit: nothing after it can correct, complicate or pay off what it delivers, and the reader rereads the whole book through it. The definition says nothing about resolution, satisfaction or happiness, which are things endings often do rather than what they are. It also makes the ending a stretch of text rather than a sentence: usually the last chapter or two, sometimes a whole part, as in Anna Karenina . An epilogue does not escape it, since an epilogue is part of the ending and not something after it. Climax is not ending The climax is the final disaster of the final goal–conflict–disaster sequence, in the sense Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2) gives the term. Aristotle’s Poetics divides a tragedy at its turning point into the desis , the tying of the knot, and the lusis , the unravelling, and on that account the aftermath is not an appendix but half the structure. The climax discharges the accumulated conflict and usually serves plot and catharsis; the aftermath establishes what the discharge means and usually serves character, theme and the final image. A book without a climax has no engine. A book without an aftermath has had its largest value shift without giving the reader a moment of lower pressure in which to register it. The most useful way to think about the aftermath is as the novel’s own sequel, in Scene and Sequel ’s sense of the word (Chapter 2): reaction, dilemma, decision, applied to the book. That explains a pattern every editor knows. An aftermath consisting only of reaction, a character grieving for thirty pages, feels indulgent; an aftermath that reaches a decision, however small, feels complete. Resolution is not closure The second distinction does more work and is named less often. Resolution is a property of the plot: the book’s questions are answered, or legibly and deliberately left open, and a reader can list them and check. Closure is a property of the reader: the felt sense that the book has arrived rather than stopped, which can be reported but not checked. The two come apart in both directions, and all four combinations occur in published fiction, as the table shows. Closure felt Closure absent Resolved The classical settlement: Jane Eyre , Emma The hollow tidy ending: every question answered and nothing felt Unresolved The open close that closes: The Handmaid’s Tale , Beloved The deliberate refusal: Kafka’s unfinished The Castle , read as though finished Only the top-right cell is a failure by default; the other three are choices. The table also explains a common revision mistake. A writer who diagnoses a flat ending as a resolution problem and answers more questions usually makes it flatter, because the mechanisms that produce closure are largely formal rather than informational. A Passage to India (1924) answers nothing on its last page: Aziz and Fielding cannot be friends, and the earth and sky say No, not yet and No, not there . The reader still feels the book is finished, because the refusal is stated in the book’s own terms, the failure of connection, and the sentence is a negation with nothing possible after it. Adjacent terms Several neighbouring words are used loosely. A denouement (French, “untying”) implies that entangled facts are being separated, which is a nineteenth-century plot’s aftermath; a modern aftermath often unties nothing and consists only of consequence, so this chapter prefers the neutral aftermath . An epilogue is displaced from the narrative along an axis of time, voice or vantage, as The Prologue (Chapter 10) describes a prologue, and must justify its exteriority; a coda , borrowed from music, is continuous with what precedes it and changes only its key, so it need justify only its length. The last line is the final sentence considered as a citable unit. Apparatus is the notes, appendices and other matter that follow a narrative, and can close a book on its own account. A series hook is a deliberate non-closure designed to create an appetite for a further volume; Failure Patterns and Series and Genre (Chapter 17) treat it. What the chapter leaves to other chapters A chapter break offers the reader a place to stop and the ending offers the place they must, so the temporary stopping place belongs to The Chapter Break (Chapter 6). The epilogue as a separated unit belongs to The Prologue (Chapter 10), the structure of the climactic scene itself to The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1) and Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2), and the convergence of threads to The Subplot (Chapter 14). The reveal that recasts a book belongs to The Reveal (Chapter 15); the arc and the theme the ending completes are traced across the whole book in Arc and Theme (Chapter 12); the last volume of a series belongs to Series and Genre (Chapter 17); and the order in which to revise a whole book, ending last, belongs to The Structural Edit (Chapter 18). Unfinished novels such as The Mystery of Edwin Drood fall outside the chapter, since a text with no ending cannot be analysed as having a bad one. See also: the Reference definitions , with a table of the four delimitations of an ending’s length and the full list of adjacent terms.

title: 3. How It Works
text: Endings have the richest critical literature of any subject in this book. Five strands are used here, each because it answers a question a writer meets in revision; the Reference treatment adds Torgovnick’s typology of closural relations, the cognitive evidence in full and the history of the ending period by period. Why does a reader who knows endings are artificial still want one? Frank Kermode’s The Sense of an Ending (1967) starts from the observation that we live in the middest , born after the beginning and dying before the end, and make sense of the middle by positing ends. He calls the resulting shapes fictions of concord , and his model is the clock: it makes identical sounds, and we hear tick-tock , a beginning and an end with an interval that the pair organise into a duration. Nothing in the acoustics licenses the distinction; the listener supplies it. Kermode’s point for a novelist is that sophisticated readers know an ending is imposed and want it anyway. Endings are discredited but not abandoned, which is why a novel that refuses shape on principle often disappoints readers who endorse the principle. From Aristotle he takes peripeteia , the reversal that falsifies an expectation and satisfies a better one, and the craft form of it is the rule this chapter uses throughout: an ending should be inevitable in retrospect and unforeseen in prospect. What makes a last line feel final? Barbara Herrnstein Smith’s Poetic Closure (1968) separates termination , a text simply stopping, from closure, the reader’s sense that the stopping is the appropriate conclusion of the structure. Because a poem is short enough to analyse exhaustively, she could describe closural devices with a precision that transfers to prose almost intact. A closural allusion refers, at a terminal position, to something terminal (sleep, night, snow, a departing train), and is the cheapest device in the language, which is why so many endings feel right and audit badly. A terminal modification alters a pattern at its last instance, so that in a novel the last chapter that does not do what the previous forty did is read as closure even by readers who cannot name the pattern. An unqualified assertion , a short declarative sentence without hedging, closes by grammar alone. Her account of modern poetry adds a principle the chapter relies on: an open ending is a closural strategy, not the absence of one. It works by withholding devices the reader knows are available, so it depends on the reader’s competence in the conventions it declines, and reads as integrity only in a book that has taught the reader to expect it. Why does a weak ending damage the whole book? Peter Brooks’s Reading for the Plot (1984) describes reading as anticipation of retrospection : we read forward in expectation of a moment from which the whole will become legible, and tolerate the middle because we expect an end that will say what it was. Meaning is conferred from the terminus, which is why an ending can make earlier material better without changing a word of it, and why a reader who has hoped for four hundred pages that two people will marry feels cheated by a marriage the book has not earned. Readers want the ending the book requires, not the one they wanted. Peter Rabinowitz’s Before Reading (1987) supplies the interpretive half: readers follow tacit rules of notice, and the last sentence holds a privileged position , read as a statement about the book whether or not it was written as one. The cognitive evidence is suggestive and limited. Donald Redelmeier and Daniel Kahneman (1996) found that patients’ memory of a painful procedure was predicted largely by its worst moment and its last, the peak–end rule. The studies concern brief physical discomfort judged soon afterwards; extending them to a novel read over weeks is an analogy, not a finding, and the retroactive lens rests on the literary evidence without them. What does “earned” mean? Aristotle’s Poetics requires the incidents of a plot to follow one another by necessity or probability, because and not merely after , which is the test Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2) applies to every causal chain. Two refinements carry into revision. Probable is enough: an ending need not be the only possible outcome, only one the established people in the established world would plausibly produce. And the objection to the deus ex machina is to externality, not improbability: an outcome produced by something outside the causal system the play has built.
