Aristotle was arguing against a living practice; the god arriving at the end was Euripides’ signature, and later writers made its arbitrariness the point. What if closure is the problem? D. A. Miller’s Narrative and Its Discontents (1981) denies the assumption behind everything above. Narrative consists of the narratable , instability, lack and desire, and closure is the elimination of the instability, so closure ends the novel’s own condition of existence. He finds traditional endings thinner than the books they end, and written in a different register, summary instead of scene. Rachel Blau DuPlessis’s Writing Beyond the Ending (1985) adds a history: the nineteenth-century novel offered a heroine two endings, marriage or death, so a closural convention can encode what a life is allowed to be for, and a mismatched last chapter can be the sound of material forced into an unavailable shape. Things Fall Apart ends by showing the form that would have contained it, the District Commissioner reducing Okonkwo to a paragraph. This chapter accepts Miller’s diagnosis and disputes his prescription. Closure does end the narratable, and every ending is a loss; but a novel is also an object with a shape, and the shape is available only from the end. The craft question is what the reader is given in exchange. The account predicts that strong endings close the book while leaving one thing moving, and the readings in Worked Analyses bear it out. A caution about period Most prescriptions here are calibrated to Anglo-American practice since about 1960. In that tradition the unresolved close has become the house style of literary fiction, while crime, romance and thrillers keep strong resolution conventions, so an open ending no longer signals a deviation and must do the work any other choice does. Victorian wind-up chapters and Tolstoy’s eighth part show that the short aftermath is a period preference. Henry James named the underlying problem in his preface to Roderick Hudson (1907): relations stop nowhere, and the exquisite problem of the artist is eternally but to draw, by a geometry of his own, the circle within which they shall happily appear to do so . The ending is that circle, and the word happily sets its standard: the appearance must satisfy, not merely be asserted. See also: the Reference history of the ending , from the Victorian settlement to the present, with DuPlessis and Miller at full length.

title: 4. The Taxonomy
text: The domain model asks what kinds of work an ending owes the reader, so that “this ending isn’t working” becomes “it delivers plot and catharsis, gestures at theme and does nothing for character”. It is the move The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1) makes for the scene. Its danger is that the domains are read as a schedule: an action climax followed by a chapter for character, a passage for theme and a closing picture. They are registers in which an ending is heard, not tasks to be done in order, and the strongest endings sound several in one image ( The Mechanism ). Nor are they equally obligatory. A detective novel that fails plot resolution has failed, since its contract is about knowledge; a lyric novel of consciousness may resolve nothing and be complete. The weighting follows genre, not merit. Plot resolution The reader receives answers to the questions the book raised, or a visible refusal to answer them. A question can be answered, declined on the page or dropped, and only the third is a defect. The rule that follows costs a sentence to obey: a declined question must be visibly declined, by a character who asks and is not told, a narrator who notes the absence, or a document found to be incomplete. The Handmaid’s Tale (1985) never says what became of Offred, and its Historical Notes stage a conference of scholars failing to find out, which turns the gap from an omission into the subject. The domain also settles accounts with The Subplot ’s attention tax (Chapter 14): a thread that took eighty pages and receives one sentence has been under-paid, and a thread that took eight and receives a chapter misstates the book’s hierarchy. Character-arc completion The reader receives the final state of the change, or of the refusal to change, that the book has tracked. Arcs complete in behaviour, not statement, and the most reliable device is the repeated situation answered differently, which uses material already paid for and lets the reader make the comparison. In Emma Donoghue’s Room (2010), five-year-old Jack has spent his life in one locked room with his mother, treating its objects, Rug and Lamp and Plant, as companions; at the end, after the escape and a long adjustment outside, he goes back, finds the room smaller than he remembers and says goodbye to the same objects before leaving. The objects are the ones he began with, and his relation to them has reversed. Two refinements matter. An arc may complete as a refusal: in The Remains of the Day (1989) Stevens recognises on the pier at Weymouth what he gave up, and then turns at once to the problem of learning to banter. And an arc needs a constant , something visibly unchanged against which the change can be read; if everything about a character is different, the reader registers replacement rather than development. Thematic closure The reader receives the book’s final position on the question it has been testing. Theme is a question the book tests, not a proposition it asserts, and the ending’s job is to conclude the test. An ending in which a character says we can never really know the people we love delivers a proposition the reader may dispute; an ending in which three people read a document proving that the man they loved kept something from them, and none of them says anything, delivers an experience. A generalisation in the last pages acquires the authority of privileged position, which makes it the strongest carrier and the easiest to abuse. A narrator may state the theme at the end only if the narrator has been stating things all along, as Eliot’s has for eight hundred pages of Middlemarch . Emotional catharsis The reader receives the release of a pressure the book has built. Catharsis is not caused by the ending; it is a release of pressure created upstream, so a writer who finds an ending emotionally flat and adds feeling to it usually adds embarrassment, when the deficiency lies earlier, in the access The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13) calls the empathy budget. The dependable carriers are physical: people in one room who have been apart, a hand taken, someone sitting down, and silence after argument. The Grapes of Wrath (1939) ends with Rose of Sharon, whose baby was stillborn, feeding a starving stranger in a barn; nothing in the plot is resolved, and the book’s pressure, the argument that survival is collective, is discharged in one act. The final image The reader receives the last thing the book shows, which is the door they leave by. There is no neutral last sentence: a novel that ends on a character making tea has told the reader that tea is what the book was for. Four variables can be set deliberately. Scale narrows to a detail or widens to a panorama. Direction in time looks back, stays, or projects forward. Grammar closes harder when the sentence is short, declarative and ends on a stressed syllable. And presence decides who is in the last clause: Wuthering Heights ends with Lockwood at three graves among moths and heath, and the withdrawal of everyone the book was about is the closure. A proposed sixth: formal closure A reader at the last page is also finishing an artefact with a pattern of its own. Formal closure is the completion, modification or disruption of the book’s structural pattern rather than its story: the frame that returns, the repeated chapter shape altered at its last instance, the apparatus that follows the narrative. It is The Opening Pages ’s formal contract (Chapter 9) falling due, the conventions of person, timeline, division and apparatus that an opening declares. Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949) is the strongest case for the domain. Its narrative closes thematically in total defeat, He loved Big Brother , and is followed by an Appendix on Newspeak written in the past tense by a scholar for readers who evidently do not live in Oceania. No plot question is reopened, but the artefact now contains a vantage from which the regime is over, and a reader who notices the tense has been given a hope the story denied. The objection is that formal closure is a means by which the other domains are served, not something the reader receives, and that mixing ends and means weakens a diagnostic model. The defence is that it has distinct carriers, distinct failures (the frame opened and never closed, the epistolary novel that drifts into plain narration) and distinct remedies (close the frame, or remove it from the opening), and that a reader can feel a book’s form left unfinished after its theme has closed. This chapter adopts the domain for diagnosis, conceding that it sits at a different level of description from the other five; The Structural Edit (Chapter 18) has since ruled on it: rejected as a domain of the ending, since in both test cases the formal pattern carries and the payment lies in another domain (the Appendix’s past tense is received as hope, the Six Feet Under montage as the series’ theme), and adopted at the scale of the book as the form audit, a test of the book’s form that asks of every pattern it declares whether the pattern is completed, modified for a reason the book shows, or removed from where it was declared. The objection holds at the ending; the defence holds for the audit. Proposals from earlier chapters Four earlier chapters left their proposed categories for this one to judge. The Opening Pages ’s formal contract (Chapter 9) is adopted at the scale of a book: formal closure is that contract discharged, and an unclosed frame is a failure only where a frame was declared. The Dialogue Exchange ‘s silence domain (Chapter 3) is rejected as a domain of the ending. Its test case, the household mother’s unexplained silence, is served at the ending by plot resolution, as a question visibly declined, and the siblings’ silence as they read is a carrier of catharsis; here the objection The Dialogue Exchange (Chapter 3) conceded, that silence is a means and not a value that changes, holds, and the domain stands in The Dialogue Exchange (Chapter 3) at the scale of the exchange. The Chapter Break ’s recasting close (Chapter 6), the chapter ending that turns the reader back to what has happened, stops discriminating at a book’s last line, where nothing comes next and every close looks back; it remains a type of chapter ending, and the question it leaves, how far a close may recast the whole book, passes to The Reveal (Chapter 15), which answers it with the teller rule: a close may falsify only what a teller in the book could have shaped. The Prologue ’s last ordinary day (Chapter 10) is confirmed as a type of prologue: the household ending pays off the two objects of the father’s last ordinary day, the good pen and his unfinished In case , and leaves two of its details unredeemed, which Worked Analyses records as the type’s risk. See also: the Reference domains , with carrier tables, under- and over-delivery for each domain, and a table of the domains each genre makes load-bearing.

title: 5. The Mechanism
text: Earned: deposit and pressure “Earned” is the central word in talk about endings and the least examined. It contains two claims, which fail differently and need opposite remedies. The first is about preparation and is a fact about the text: every element the ending uses as load-bearing must exist in the book before the ending. Anyone with a copy can check it, and its instrument is the plant audit , which lists what the ending rests on and traces each item to its first appearance. Its failure is the unearned rescue, and its remedy is usually a sentence planted early. The second claim is about pressure and is a fact about the reader: the ending must feel, in hindsight, like what the book was moving towards. It cannot be checked, it can fail in a book where every element is dutifully planted, and its remedy is not more planting but a want, running through the middle of the book, that the ending answers. The two failures look alike from inside a draft. When a plant is missing the reader asks where did that come from? ; when pressure is missing the reader asks so what? Adding pressure to an unplanted ending produces melodrama, and adding plants to an unfelt one produces a well-documented shrug. The full statement the chapter uses is that an ending is earned when everything it relies on was already in the book and what it does with that material answers a pressure the book has built. The first is a matter of deposit, the second of interest accrued on it, and the second is also the answer to Miller’s objection in How It Works : an ending that closes the narratable by answering a pressure the narratable generated has given the reader something in exchange. Inevitable is not predictable The commonest misunderstanding is that an earned ending is one the reader can see coming. Predictability is a property of the reader before the ending, who can say what will happen; inevitability is a property of the reader afterwards, who cannot imagine it otherwise. All four combinations occur. Predicted and inevitable is the pleasure of tragedy and of the marriage plot, where nobody doubts that Elizabeth will marry Darcy and the interest lies in the route. Predicted and not inevitable is tedium. Unforeseen and arbitrary is the cheat. Unforeseen and, in retrospect, the only possible outcome is the target, and it has a teachable structure: plant the materials in plain sight and withhold the combination. Afterwards the reader can point to every component; beforehand they could not assemble them, because the assembling needed a decision, a recognition or a change of vantage that only the ending supplies. Gérard Genette’s word for the unemphatic advance notice is the amorce , a seed that passes as ordinary, and the test of a plant is not whether the reader noticed it but whether they can find it afterwards. Two corollaries follow. Coincidence may start a story and may not end one, because an opening coincidence generates the causal chain and a closing one replaces it. And the rule nothing new and load-bearing at the end forbids new load, not new material: an ending may contain a room the reader has not seen or a stranger on a bus, provided it does not rest on them. The test is substitution: remove the element, and if the ending still works it is furniture. Multiplicity at the close Multiplicity, one unit of text doing several jobs at once, is the principle of The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1) and of every chapter since. At the opening it is a matter of space. At the ending it is a matter of simultaneity: an ending that works through the domains in turn is legible as a procedure, and the reader who can watch the machinery suspects that the book was machinery too. The last sentence of Things Fall Apart (1958) shows the alternative. Okonkwo has hanged himself, and the District Commissioner, who has been thinking that the story might make a reasonable paragraph in his book, has already chosen the title: The Pacification of the Primitive Tribes of the Lower Niger . Plot, character, theme, catharsis and form are all touched, and the sentence performs no visible closing work. Achebe has not packed five things into it; he has found the one vantage from which one thing means five. Closural multiplicity lives in humble places more than in symbols. The object already in the room , established and left lying about, carries plot, character, theme and image without a word of explanation, because all four meanings were deposited earlier. A gesture the book has shown before, performed differently, carries the change and the parallel. Tense, person and the choice of who holds the last position cost nothing and alter a whole paragraph’s relation to the reader: Flaubert gives the end of Madame Bovary to the pharmacist Homais, Achebe to the Commissioner, and the assignment is the argument. Multiplicity has a ceiling. In the over-determined ending every noun means something, the weather participates and the last line answers the first, and the reader hears the book locking shut. Roland Barthes argued that details which signify nothing but reality authenticate a fictional world; an ending with no inert material withdraws that authentication when the reader is deciding whether the book was true. An ending needs something that means nothing, a bus going past or a stool somebody sits on. Middlemarch is the limit case: its Finale settles every major figure and generalises at length, and does not read as arranged, because its narrator has been doing this for eight hundred pages. Climax and aftermath: the proportion problem The largest structural decision at an ending is how much aftermath to write, and the two errors are opposite, so a writer correcting one tends to produce the other. The aftermath can do things the climax cannot: show consequences, complete a second arc, let the reader register the value shift at lower pressure, release catharsis, return a transported reader and leave a last image. It must not introduce a new question, resolve threads in order of appearance rather than weight, explain what the climax meant, or continue past its own last decision. That gives the chapter’s working rule, the last-decision rule : find the final decision any character takes, however small, and end within a page of it, since consequences are endless and decisions can be counted. The rule has two kinds of exception. Anna Karenina (1878) runs a whole eighth part after Anna’s death, about Levin’s search for faith; readers have complained since publication, and the part is indispensable, because a novel with two arcs cannot complete both at one climax. An aftermath is not too long while it completes an arc, and is too long once it only reports consequences. At the other extreme The Grapes of Wrath has no aftermath at all and is complete, because its last gesture is itself a decision. See also: the Reference account of earned and unearned , with sixteen closural strategies, substitution testing and a table of aftermath lengths by tradition; the Reference account of multiplicity , with the closural audit.

title: 6. Diagnostic Tests
text: The ten tests are for revision, not composition, and here more than anywhere: the ending is the one unit whose obligations cannot be known until the rest of the book exists, and a writer who runs the plant audit while drafting will write a book made of plants. Run them in order, because tests 1 to 4 (Retroactive, Plant audit, Earned and Inevitability) concern the ending’s relation to the book and a failure there makes the rest premature. Tests 1 (Retroactive), 2 (Plant audit), 6 (Proportion) and 9 (Reread) need the whole manuscript, and test 4 (Inevitability) needs other readers, which is why they are the ones writers skip. Record a sentence, not a verdict. An ending written first is a hypothesis about the book, and the book that got written may have falsified it: revise the ending last, whenever it was written. Test 1 — Retroactive Reread five early scenes chosen at random: what has the ending made of each? Failure. Stranded scenes; either the ending or the scene is wrong, and the choice should be explicit. Exception. The cetology chapters of Moby-Dick , which no ending converts and readers keep. Test 2 — Plant audit List what the ending rests on and trace each item to its first appearance: does anything load-bearing appear first in the ending? Failure. Unearned in the strict sense; usually mended by one sentence early. Exception. Dickens’s original ending to Great Expectations , which introduces a Shropshire doctor and a horse and has distinguished defenders. Test 3 — Earned Complete the situation is resolved because… : is the blank inside the book’s causal system? Failure. New information, a new capability or, worst, a new agent. Exception. The Threepenny Opera (1928), whose mounted messenger with a royal pardon is the play’s argument. Test 4 — Inevitability Can a first-time reader predict the end thirty pages out, and can a finished reader build an alternative as good? Failure. Alternatives come easily: the ending is one of several the book never distinguished. Exception. Great Expectations again, where the author wrote the alternative and both endings are defended. Test 5 — Domain Which domains does the ending deliver, which does it gesture at, which does it refuse, and does the distribution suit the book’s mode? Failure. A domain credited on the writer’s intention rather than a passage a reader could point to. Exception. The Grapes of Wrath , which refuses plot resolution outright. Test 6 — Proportion What share of the book follows the climax, does each thread’s resolution match the space it took, and how far does the book run past its last decision? Failure. Climax without aftermath, endless aftermath, or every thread settled at equal length. Exception. Room (2010), whose escape comes about halfway, leaving half the novel to the aftermath. Test 7 — Termination Ask a reader of the last two pages whether anything comes after, and what told them. Failure. A book that stops because the pages run out. Exception. Bleak House , whose last sentence breaks off unfinished and still closes. Test 8 — Tonal match Read the last page against three passages from the middle third: are they the same book? Failure. Uplift the material does not support, or a gratuitous darkening. Exception. Madame Bovary , which follows two deaths with the pharmacist’s medal, a change of note that is the verdict. Test 9 — Reread Reread three passages the ending changes: do they now yield more? Failure. An effect that depended on the reader not knowing. Exception. The Murder of Roger Ackroyd (1926), whose reread yields the pleasure of the concealment and nothing more. Test 10 — Last line Could the book end on the paragraph before the last without loss? Failure. The last paragraph coasts on the book instead of adding to it. Exception. Mrs Dalloway , whose For there she was means nothing alone: dependence is a last line’s condition, coasting its fault. Reading the results together Failures cluster. Tests 2 (Plant audit) and 3 (Earned) together mean an imported element or agent; plant it in the first third, unremarked. Test 4 (Inevitability) alone, with readers producing good alternatives, means the middle never narrowed the material, and the repair is in the middle. Test 1 (Retroactive) alone means the ending strands earlier scenes; decide which is wrong, and do not mend both. Test 6 (Proportion) split between a low aftermath and failing domains means the book needs its lusis, not more climax; a high aftermath means finding the last decision and ending within a page of it; uniform resolution means cutting resolutions rather than adding them. Test 7 (Termination) alone usually wants a formal signal, a returned image or a terminal modification, not new material. Test 8 (Tonal match) alone means changing the ending, not the book: the ending is twenty pages and the book four hundred. The hardest result is a clean pass on every test and an ending that lands on nothing. It is the commonest outcome of a competent revision, and the tests cannot repair it, because they audit the ending and the fault lies in the middle of the book, which has not built a want urgent enough to conclude. That is a real diagnosis, and The Structural Edit (Chapter 18) starts from it. See also: the Reference protocol , with each test’s procedure and a table of combined failures.

title: 7. Failure Patterns
text: Each pattern fails through a mechanism rather than a surface feature. Each ends with a published work that uses the feature successfully because the mechanism is absent. At the ending the exceptions carry more weight than in any other chapter, since several of the patterns are committed by endings that are among the most admired in the language. The Reference chapter’s full catalogue has twelve patterns, among them the climax without aftermath, the endless aftermath, the mismatched final note, the ending that resolves the wrong question and the last-minute reversal. The unearned rescue Symptom. Resolution arrives through something the book never integrated: a sudden power, a stranger’s intervention, a document that appears, a fact withheld from the reader until it is needed. Mechanism. The causal chain breaks at its last link. The objection, as Aristotle saw, is to externality rather than improbability: if the outcome came from outside the system the book built, the book did not determine its own ending, and the retroactive lens applies that verdict to every page. A second harm follows. A rescued protagonist has not acted, and since character is legible mainly in choice under pressure, the rescue dissolves the character domain when it falls due. Writers produce the pattern when they have painted the situation into a corner, or, most often, when they have not noticed that the resolution needs a fact the reader lacks, because the writer has it. Remedy. Test 3 (Earned). Plant the element early and unremarked, so that the intervention becomes the arrival of something the reader knew existed; or change the outcome to one the existing system produces. Exception. Jane Eyre (1847). On the point of accepting St John Rivers, Jane hears Rochester’s voice calling her across an impossible distance, a supernatural intervention at the moment of decision. It works because Brontë has built a world in which presentiment, dream and vision operate, and because the voice does not decide for Jane; it interrupts a decision she then makes herself. The rescue is unearned in mechanism and earned in preparation. The explained ending Symptom. A character or the narrator sums up what the book has meant, often in a penultimate scene and often beginning I suppose what I’ve learned is . Mechanism. The thematic work moves from the reader to the text, and a test the reader could have concluded becomes a proposition to accept or reject. The ending’s most privileged position is spent on a paraphrase of the book. Where the narration has been scenic throughout, the explanation also breaks the voice contract at the moment the book can least afford it. The motive is sympathetic: the writer cannot bear the thought that the meaning might be missed, and by the end knows it well enough to state it. Remedy. Delete the explanation and read the ending without it; in most drafts nothing is lost. Where something is, convert it into an act or an object, not back into speech. Exception. Middlemarch (1871–72). The Finale explains, generally and at length, what to conclude about Dorothea and about lives like hers. The narrator has generalised for eight hundred pages, so the register completes the book’s mode instead of breaking it, and the generalisation extends the novel rather than paraphrasing it: it tells the reader what cannot be known about such lives, a proposition the book made available and had not stated. The fault is an explanation that replaces the book with a summary of itself. The tidy-everything ending Symptom. Every thread and question is resolved with equal, mechanical thoroughness, whatever its weight. Mechanism. Uniform resolution destroys hierarchy. Emphasis is relational, so an ending in which everything is settled to the same degree says that nothing mattered more than anything else, contradicting the weighting the book spent its length establishing. It is also the place where a novel most visibly administers its own material, the shift from scene to inventory that makes last chapters read as thinner than their books. Remedy. Cut resolutions rather than adding them. Remove the resolutions of the two least-weighted threads and reread; usually the rest gain force, and where something is lost, that thread carried more than the audit suggested. Exception. The epilogue of Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (2007), “Nineteen Years Later”. On a platform at King’s Cross the surviving friends, now married, see their children off to school; Harry’s younger son is afraid of being sorted into Slytherin; the last sentences report that the scar had not pained Harry for nineteen years and that all was well. Many readers and reviewers found it too neat, and Rowling has said she wanted it to be clear that Harry had triumphed and would not face Voldemort again. It works for the series’ readers because its tidiness is graded and formal: it takes one morning and a handful of families rather than the whole cast, it returns to the train with which the series began, and its last line answers the first wound of the first volume. A seven-volume contract for a closed world is discharged in the series’ own terms. Death as resolution Symptom. A central problem is resolved by a death, usually of the character who poses it. Mechanism. Death is the most available terminal event in fiction and the easiest substitute for a decision: it is final, unarguable and requires nothing of anyone. When nobody chose it and none of the book’s forces produced it, the ending has been handed to chance, and the reader’s investment in a character’s capacity to choose is discharged into an event rather than an act. Remedy. Ask whether the central problem would be resolved if the character lived. If not, the death is doing structural work; move it before the ending, so that the ending holds a decision made in its light. Exception. Jodi Picoult’s My Sister’s Keeper (2004). Anna, conceived as a donor match for her sister Kate, who has leukaemia, sues her parents for the right to refuse a kidney, wins, and is fatally injured in a car crash on the way home; her kidney goes to Kate, who survives. Readers have argued for twenty years about whether the accident is a cheat, and the 2009 film reversed it, letting Kate die and Anna live, a change Picoult publicly regretted. The novel commits the pattern and keeps its readers because the arbitrary event lands on the book’s own question, whose body it is, and answers it with an irony no decision could have produced: Anna wins the right to refuse, and her kidney is given anyway. Ambiguity used as evasion Symptom. The book declines to settle its central question, and the refusal reads as an absence of decision rather than as one. Mechanism. An open ending works by withholding devices the reader knows are available, so it needs the withholding to be legible. Now that the unresolved close is the convention of literary fiction, it no longer marks itself: an ambiguity must be specific, so that the reader can say what is undetermined and why the book cannot determine it, or it reads as default. It is also unfalsifiable, which is why it survives revision. Remedy. Two questions. What, in one sentence, is ambiguous? An ambiguity the writer cannot state is not a design. And what would resolving it cost? If nothing, it is doing no work. An ambiguity that survives both needs a formal signal. Exception. The Sopranos , “Made in America” (HBO, 10 June 2007), written and directed by David Chase. Tony sits in a diner while Journey plays on the jukebox, his family arriving one by one, a man in a Members Only jacket going to the washroom; the door opens, Tony looks up, and the screen cuts to black and silence. Many viewers assumed their signal had failed. The ambiguity is about one thing, whether this is the moment Tony is killed, and it is the series’ standing condition made formal: a man who could be killed at any meal, watched by a viewer who finally cannot see. Chase has declined to explain it, and later said only that the scene showed Tony could die, not that he did. The cut is the most legible signal a screen has. See also: the Reference summary table , which maps each of the twelve patterns to its mechanism and the domains it damages.

title: 8. Worked Analyses
text: Three close readings of published endings, a short screen reading and the household revision case. Each reading names the domains served, the carriers that serve them and, where there is one, the disagreement, without settling it. Charles Dickens, Great Expectations (1860–61): two endings No other case lets a reader watch the plant audit, the tonal-match test and the question of imposed endings work on the same material. Pip, who believed his fortune came from Miss Havisham and was meant to win him Estella, has learned that it came from the convict Magwitch, lost the money and lost Estella to Bentley Drummle. Dickens’s first ending is brief. Years later, walking in London with Joe and Biddy’s small son, Pip meets Estella in the street; Drummle has died, she has remarried a Shropshire doctor, they exchange a few words and part, and Pip is glad to see that suffering has given her a heart to understand his. Dickens showed the proofs to Edward Bulwer-Lytton, who urged a happier close, and rewrote it. In the published version Pip returns after eleven years to the site of Satis House, finds Estella in the ruined garden in the evening mist, and they leave together: I saw no shadow of another parting from her. John Forster, Dickens’s biographer, printed the cancelled ending, and the argument has run ever since. The case for the original is congruence. The novel dismantles every expectation Pip held, and an ending that grants him the one he should have lost, in the garden where he learned to want it, concedes what the book argued; the original leaves him work, modest means and the adult capacity to see Estella’s suffering without wanting anything from her. The case for the revision begins with the plant audit, which favours it decisively: the garden, the ruin and the mists are long established, while the original rests on a street, a doctor and a horse the book has never shown. The revision also completes a pattern, the morning mists of Pip’s first departure answered by the evening mists now, and it is less happy than its reputation. Satis House is demolished, Estella calls herself bent and broken, and the last sentence reports only that Pip sees no shadow, in a novel about a man who sees wrongly. The serial text read I saw the shadow of no parting from her ; the 1862 edition moved the negation to the shadow and added another , conceding that there has already been one. What cannot be settled is a prior question, what kind of book this is: a satire on expectation wants the original, a study of two damaged people learning to perceive can take the revision. The case yields three lessons. The plant audit and the tonal-match test can disagree, and no procedure resolves them. Grammar can make an ending closed in plot and open in knowledge. And the provenance of an ending is not evidence of its quality: that Bulwer-Lytton asked for the change says why the second ending exists, not whether it is better. Toni Morrison, Beloved (1987): the phrase that contradicts itself The last chapter withdraws from scene into a choral register. Beloved is gone, the neighbourhood forgets her, and a sentence recurs: It was not a story to pass on. At its last occurrence the tense changes to This is not a story to pass on , and the novel ends on one word, Beloved , standing alone. The phrase forbids the story (do not hand it on), requires it (it cannot be passed over) and asserts that it persists (it will not pass away), and it is printed inside four hundred pages of transmission. The ambiguity is specific, which is what separates it from evasion: the reader can say which three things the sentence does and why the book cannot choose among them, since its subject is an event that must not be spoken of and must not be forgotten. The tense change is a terminal modification that turns from the characters’ past to the reader’s present. The last word serves every domain at once and is the title, so the book ends by becoming its own name, answering an opening that put a number, 124 , where a name should be. A sceptic can argue that the choral register arrives after the story to supply an effect the story did not produce; the reply is that the unattributed monologues before it have taught the register. Kazuo Ishiguro, Never Let Me Go (2005): closure without release Kathy H. has told the reader on the first page that she will stop being a carer at the end of the year, and the reader has learned what that means: she will begin the donations that have already ended Ruth’s life and Tommy’s. The novel’s question was never whether this would happen. The ending finds her driving in Norfolk, the county the Hailsham children called the place where lost things go. She stops by a field where rubbish has caught along a barbed-wire fence, torn plastic sheeting and bits of old carrier bags, and lets herself imagine that if she waited, Tommy might appear across the field. She does not let the fantasy run. She cries without sobbing or losing control, then turns back to the car to drive off to wherever it was she was supposed to be. Every domain is served by restraint. Plot was resolved before the scene began. Character completes on its constant, Kathy’s composure, with the one licensed fantasy as the change. Catharsis arrives at the size the narration has always allowed, tears without a scene. The final image is the fence of lost things, a closural allusion the book planted in its middle. And the last decision is the novel’s subject, the one readers argue about: she gets back into the car. The ending refuses the escape the reader has wanted for the length of the book, and the refusal is congruent, because no character in the book has ever run. A screen reading: Six Feet Under , “Everyone’s Waiting” (HBO, 2005) The series’ last episode, written and directed by Alan Ball, ends with Claire, the youngest Fisher, leaving Los Angeles for New York. As she drives, to Sia’s “Breathe Me”, the episode moves forward through each principal character’s death, decades ahead: her mother Ruth’s in a hospital bed, Keith’s in a robbery, David’s in a park, Federico’s on a cruise ship, Brenda’s in mid-conversation with her brother, and finally Claire’s own, in 2085, at the age of 102. By the rules of this chapter it should fail twice: it is the most total proleptic close imaginable, settling every named fate, and it continues long past the last decision, Claire’s departure. It works because the series’ every episode opened on a death, so the montage completes its formal pattern rather than reporting consequences, and because the departure is the decision and the deaths are its frame: the life Claire drives into is shown whole, which is what the series was about. The household revision case: the ending The draft. The ending in The Problem , in which a solicitor’s letter and the mother’s account explain everything by midnight. The diagnosis. The plant audit fails on four load-bearing elements deposited nowhere: the solicitors, the trust, the medical report and the February date. The earned test fails on new information and, worse, on a new agent, so the book’s causal system is bypassed at its last step. The domains are misdistributed: plot is over-served, character unserved (four people receive and nobody acts), theme is stated by the mother, and the mother, who has had no scene, receives the longest speech in the book. The last line is an abstraction ending on know . One error produces the rest: the draft makes the book’s question what happened? when it has been what do these three do with what they can reconstruct? The first is answerable by a document, the second only by the siblings in each other’s presence. The draft also spends a plant: the changed locks, an unexplained act of withholding since The Dialogue Exchange (Chapter 3), become a practical measure with a stated purpose. The revision. They read it together, in the end — Elena at the register, Nadia on the stool, Dov standing because he said he’d rather. Their father’s hand ran clean and careful for eleven years of entries, prices and repairs and the ordinary arithmetic of keeping a small shop alive, and then, three pages from the end, a different kind of entry altogether: dates, a doctor’s name misspelled twice and corrected once, and beneath it, in the same careful hand as always, a list of what needed doing if he ran out of time to do it himself. He had known. He had not told them. He had, instead, done what he always did, which was write it down properly, in case anyone ever needed to check. Dov’s hand picked up where his father’s left off on March the ninth, looser at first and then not. He hadn’t known what else to do with a ledger that had stopped making sense the way ledgers were supposed to. It was Nadia who went up to the coat, in the end. It was hanging on the hook where nobody had moved it. She didn’t ask permission. She took it down, and after a moment, so the sleeves wouldn’t drag, she put it on. What the revision did. It answers the operative question by putting the three in one room, and leaves the stated one, why the locks were changed, unanswered. It resolves by combination rather than material: the ledger has been seen only in fragments and alone, Elena’s reading interrupted before the illness entries and Dov writing forward without reading back, and now it is read whole, by all three, in the shop. Six domains are served by three carriers. The ledger carries plot (the father knew and wrote it down; Dov kept it from the evening of 9 March), theme ( in case anyone ever needed to check , now understood by everyone in the room) and form (the book’s spine, read through at last); the room carries catharsis (three people together and silent); and the coat carries character and the final image. The arc completes by a repeated situation with its terms altered: Nadia has stood before the coat since The Descriptive Detail (Chapter 4), and in Backstory and Flashback (Chapter 7) her hand went no further than its pocket; here she takes it down. The constant is in the same clause, so the sleeves wouldn’t drag , her managing precision since the opening pages. The passage ends within a sentence of the last decision anyone takes, explains nothing, and gives the father the last word through his own phrase. The first draft of this passage read Nadia was the one who found the coat ; she had not found it, having known where it was for four months, and the verb is corrected. Run as test 2 (Plant audit), the audit traces the load to its plantings: the good pen and the line to the prologue ( The Prologue , Chapter 10) and Backstory and Flashback (Chapter 7); the ledger to The Descriptive Detail (Chapter 4), maintained in The Chapter Break (Chapter 6), The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13) and The Subplot (Chapter 14); the looser hand to The Chapter Break (Chapter 6), with The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13) showing whose it is; the doctor’s name to The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13); Nadia’s refusal to touch the coat to The Descriptive Detail (Chapter 4) and the opening. One thing appears first here, the list of what needed doing, and the revision keeps it there as new material rather than new load: remove it and the ending still says that he knew and wrote it down, on the strength of the dates and the doctor’s name. The audit across the whole book is in the Reference case , rerun there across all eighteen chapters with every element the later chapters deposit, and summarised in Appendix D . What the revision has not solved. The mother is unresolved, which is a choice with a cost: the defence is that her silence is the book’s last narratable material, kept moving, and that the reader who now has an explanation of the father’s silence can extend the same charity to hers; the cost is that a reader may feel the largest question has been sidestepped. Two details of the prologue’s last ordinary day, the boy at the glass and the sign never turned to CLOSED, are never redeemed, and need a second appearance in the middle of the book or deletion. The passage may be over-determined, since every noun means something; a sentence that means nothing, placed between the ledger and the coat, is the available correction. Elena, who drove the book’s forward motion, completes by presence rather than act, defended by her decision in the truck in Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2) and still the weakest completion in the passage. And the ending is covert, with no coda or change of register to signal the last scene, so it risks test 7 (Termination); its signal is an object withheld for a book and finally taken, and the move upstairs to the flat, made in one clause, is the place a reader may stumble. See also: the Reference analyses , with readings of Middlemarch , The Great Gatsby , Anna Karenina , Nineteen Eighty-Four , Ulysses , Don Quixote and Blindness , and the household plant audit across the whole book.

title: 9. Checklist and Exercises
text: Revision checklist The whole book Can I trace every element the ending rests on to an earlier planting, with chapter and page? Does anything new and load-bearing arrive for the first time in the ending? New material is allowed; new load is not. When I reread five earlier scenes with the ending in mind, do they read as intended? Where they do not, have I decided whether the scene or the ending is wrong? Does the ending answer a pressure the middle built, and not only a question it asked? Climax and aftermath Can I point to where the climax ends and the aftermath begins, and say what the aftermath does that the climax could not? Does the aftermath end within a page of the last decision anyone takes? Is each thread’s resolution proportional to the space it took? Domains Which domains does the ending deliver, which does it gesture at, and which does it refuse, and does each delivered domain have a passage a reader could point to? Does at least one carrier serve more than one domain, and is there some material that means nothing? If the book declared a frame, a pattern or an apparatus, does the ending close or modify it? Questions and ambiguity Is every question the book raised answered or visibly declined, and none merely dropped? Can I state any deliberate ambiguity in one sentence, and say what resolving it would cost? Has the book ended rather than stopped, and can I name the device that tells the reader so? The last page Do the last page and three passages from the middle belong to the same book? Does anyone, character or narrator, explain what the book meant? Does the final paragraph do work the paragraph before it does not, and do I know why the last word is the one it is? Exercises The plant audit. List every element your ending uses as load-bearing, aiming for eight to twenty. Record the chapter and page of each one’s first appearance and of every later one. Mark anything that first appears in the ending, and anything that appears early and then vanishes for more than a third of the book, and for each marked item write the sentence that would plant or maintain it. Three strategies. Rewrite your ending twice more, as a parallel scene that repeats an earlier situation with its terms altered and as an arrested ending that stops before the outcome, a page each. Do not judge until all three exist, then write one sentence for each saying what that version makes the book about. The deletion ladder. End the book one paragraph earlier, then one scene, then one chapter, and read each version. Record where the ending is, and what the deleted material was doing for you rather than for the reader. The closural audit. Beside each sentence of your last three pages write the letters of the domains it serves (plot, character, theme, catharsis, image, form) and mark the sentences that serve none. Read the distribution: letters in blocks mean a serial ending, no inert sentences an over-determined one, and dense letters on the first page and thin ones after mean the ending has already happened. The counterfactual ending. Write a deliberately unearned ending for your own book, one that resolves by a letter, a stranger or a confession, and run the ten tests on it. Then list which of its failures your real ending shares in a milder form.

title: 10. Coda
text: Every instrument in this chapter assumes that an ending should conclude. The plant audit, the last-decision rule and the domain count are calibrated to closure, and they will report the refusals of a serious body of fiction as failures. When they do, the model is reporting its own limits. Miller’s objection stands at the end as it stood at the beginning: closure ends the instability that made the book worth reading, and a novel’s last chapter is often thinner than its middle because the thing it ends was the thing that was interesting. The answer this chapter has given is an exchange rather than a rebuttal. The reader at the last page loses the narratable and gains the whole, a shape that was unavailable at any earlier point, and the craft question is whether the shape is worth what it cost. That is why the tests can pass and the ending still fail. An ending that satisfies every audit and lands on nothing is reporting that the book never built a want urgent enough to conclude, and no repair to the last twenty pages will supply one. It follows that the ending cannot be revised as a unit on its own. It is where a writer finds out what the book was about, and the finding often sends the revision back to the middle, where the pressure is built, or to the opening, where the contracts the ending must honour were made. That is the reason to revise the ending last, whatever order it was written in: its obligations are set by everything else, and only when everything else is settled can a writer tell whether the ending is failing or the book is. See also: the Reference coda , on what the model does reliably and what it leaves open.

title: Series and Genre
text: Promises the reader brings to a book, and promises she carries out of it The Craft Behind the Story (Second Edition) — Chapter 17. Part IV: Beyond the Book and Into Practice. In brief. A genre is a set of promises a reader holds before the first page; a series is a set of promises she carries past the last. A book keeps faith with both when every convention it invokes is either kept or visibly declined before the reader has staked much on it, and when each volume of a series closes the question it was built on and leaves open only questions it has shown to belong to the series. The chapter’s tools are the promise inventory, which lists each convention a book invokes, where, and whether it is kept, varied or declined, and the volume table, which records for each volume of a series its own question, the step it takes on the series question and the threads it carries. Use the chapter when early readers say a book was not what they expected, when a draft borrows a genre’s machinery without its payments, or when you are planning a second volume or have been asked to write one. What you can do after this chapter Name the core promise of the genre a book declares, and say where the book keeps it. List the conventions a draft invokes and decide, for each, whether to keep, vary or decline it. Declare a decline early enough, and replace it with a promise the book keeps, so that the reader takes the decline as design. Give each volume of a series a question it closes, a step on the series question and an entry a new reader can use. Diagnose an undeclared decline, a genre in costume, a volume that owes its question, a deferred answer and a recap at the door, and revise them. Key terms Genre; convention; semantic and syntactic elements; horizon of expectations; core promise; obligatory scene; mode; formula; variation; declined convention; declared decline; paratext; the promise inventory; series; volume; series instalment; episodic series; running arc; serial; relay series; volume question; series question; series hook; re-entry; dormancy across volumes; the volume table; the undeclared decline; the genre in costume; the volume that owes its question; the deferred answer; the recap at the door. Each is defined at first use and collected in the consolidated glossary . Contents The first files say what a genre and a series promise and how readers hold those promises, the central files how a book keeps, varies or declines them and how a series carries its questions from volume to volume, and the last are for use at the desk. The Problem A household draft that ends on a hook for a second book, and the chapter’s claim Definitions Genre, convention, series and volume, and what other chapters keep How It Works How readers hold a genre’s promises, what a formula gives them, and what the evidence says The Taxonomy Five core promises and four forms of series The Mechanism How a promise is made, staked, kept or declined, and how a series carries its questions Diagnostic Tests Eight questions on one page, and how to read their failures together Failure Patterns Five recurrent failures, each with a work that commits it and succeeds Worked Analyses Northanger Abbey , In the Woods , the Neapolitan novels, The Leftovers and the household revision case Checklist and Exercises The revision checklist and five exercises for your own draft Coda What the model assumes, and why a convention is a promise rather than a rule A writer in revision can start at the diagnostic tests with a promise inventory drafted for the book as it stands. A writer planning a series should read the mechanism first, because a series question and the step each volume takes on it are easier to design than to find in the third book. The full treatment This is a new chapter, so the Reference layer holds a single full treatment rather than a corrected original: the theory at greater length, an extended catalogue of promises, series forms and failure patterns, the procedures for each test, further analyses ( Bring Up the Bodies , Beach Read , 61 Hours and Twin Peaks ), the household promise inventory in full, a glossary of the chapter’s terms and the sources. See also: The Opening Pages (Chapter 9), for the genre contract made in the first pages; Arc and Theme (Chapter 12), for the arc a series hero carries; The Reveal (Chapter 15), for the declined reveal; The Ending (Chapter 16), for the series hook at a book’s last line.

title: 1. The Problem
text: The household novel has found an agent, and the agent has two requests. The book is a quiet family novel set in a small British town: four months after their father’s death in March, his three adult children reconstruct what he left. Elena learns in Dov’s doorway that their mother changed the shop’s locks in March, and Dov gives her the new key and keeps the reason; Nadia counts things and will not touch the coat that still hangs in the flat above the shop; the father’s ledger, kept for eleven years in a careful slanting hand, stops on 9 March, and a looser hand continues it. At the end the three read the ledger together in the shop, learn that their father was ill and wrote it down and told nobody, and Nadia goes up to the flat and puts on the coat. Their mother’s reason for changing the locks is never given. The agent likes the book and wants a second one. Her first request is a last page that opens the door to it. The draft now ends, after the coat, with a short scene in the shop: Elena was locking up when the phone lit on the counter. MA, it said. She let it ring twice, and answered. Her second request is jacket copy that tells a browser what kind of book this is. The draft copy reads: In March their father died, and their mother changed the locks. Four months later, one of his children is going to find out why. Neither request is foolish. Series sell, a family with a living mother who has never spoken has room for another book, and a jacket that asks a question is doing what jackets do. The trouble is that both make promises the book spends its whole length declining. The copy tells the reader she is holding a mystery, a kind of book whose readers are guaranteed an answer to the question it poses. The book poses that question in its first chapter and never answers it, and it says so, through a brother who will not answer, a sister who decides not to ask, and an ending that closes every other question around the one it keeps. A reader who takes the copy at its word will read the book’s refusals as the writer’s failures. The last page then turns the refusal into a postponement: the mother rings, and the question the book had declined becomes the question of the next one, which means that this book did not end but stopped. The case is not an argument against series or against borrowing a genre’s machinery. The household novel borrows a great deal from the mystery: an investigator, a changed lock, a document in a changed hand, a suspect, a gathering at the end. It is an instance of a confusion the chapter separates into its parts, between a convention a book uses and a promise it makes, and between a question a book declines and one it defers. The chapter’s claim is that genre and series are both contracts with the reader, made partly outside the book, and that a book can keep, vary or decline any term of either, provided the reader is told in time. A genre is a set of promises the reader brings to a book, and a series a set of promises she carries out of it. A book keeps faith with both when every convention it invokes is either kept or visibly declined before the reader has staked much on it, and when each volume closes the question it was built on and leaves open only questions it has shown to belong to the series. A book that breaks a promise it never declined, or spends its last page on a question it owed, has borrowed against a contract it does not mean to keep. The claim has a consequence for revision. A book whose readers feel cheated by its ending is seldom mended at the ending. The repair is usually earlier, where the promise was made or should have been declined, and sometimes outside the text, in what the jacket says. The revision in Worked Analyses removes the last page and the question on the jacket, and finds that the book’s genre is already declared, by three decisions not to ask. See also: the full treatment , section 7, with the household’s promise inventory in full; The Reveal (Chapter 15), on the declined reveal the mother’s silence is.

title: 2. Definitions
text: The working definition A genre is a group of works that readers, writers and booksellers treat as alike, and, for a writer, the set of expectations a reader brings to a book she has identified as one of them. The second sense is the one this chapter uses. A genre is known by its conventions , the features its readers expect, and the film scholar Rick Altman divided them usefully into two kinds. Semantic elements are the genre’s building blocks: its places, objects, figures and kinds of event, the body in the library, the spaceship, the ballroom. Syntactic elements are the relations among them: who wants what of whom, and in what order things happen, the investigator who sets out to learn who did it, the two people kept apart by a barrier that falls. A book can use a genre’s semantic elements without its syntax, or its syntax in different dress, and much of what this chapter diagnoses lies in the gap between the two. Among a genre’s conventions one is decisive. The core promise is the convention whose breach the genre’s readers treat as a breach of contract rather than a choice: the mystery’s answer to the question of fact it poses, the romance’s union of the lovers. A book that keeps the core promise may vary every other convention and stay on its shelf; a book that breaks it has, for many of its readers, changed genre without saying so. A series is a sequence of separately published works that share characters, a world or a continuing story, and that readers are invited to read as related. Each of its works is a volume . The book follows its own rule, set out in Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2), of keeping sequel for the reaction, dilemma and decision that follow a scene, so a later volume is called a series instalment , never a sequel. Each volume has a volume question , the question it is built on and must close, and a series may also have a series question , which runs across volumes and is closed, if at all, by the last. Adjacent terms Several neighbouring terms belong to other chapters and are used here in the senses those chapters give them. The genre contract belongs to The Opening Pages (Chapter 9), one of the five contracts an opening makes: what kind of book this is, and therefore what to expect, hope for and fear. This chapter follows the contract past the opening to the whole book and its ending. The series hook belongs to The Ending (Chapter 16): a book that declines to close a major question in order to create an appetite for a further volume. The declined reveal belongs to The Reveal (Chapter 15): a question of fact held visibly open to a book’s end. The steadfast arc , in which a character’s criterion holds and the change happens to others, belongs to Arc and Theme (Chapter 12), and it is the usual arc of a series hero. A mode , in Alastair Fowler’s sense, is a genre’s character used as an adjective in a work of another kind: a gothic novel is a gothic work, while a family novel with a locked room, a document in a changed hand and an investigating daughter is a family novel in the mystery mode. Most revision problems with genre are problems of mode, since a mode borrows conventions without, by default, borrowing the core promise, and the reader does not always know which has been borrowed. What the chapter leaves to other chapters The genre signals of the first pages belong to The Opening Pages (Chapter 9), and the genre test for a prologue to The Prologue (Chapter 10); this chapter asks what the whole book then owes. The serial instalment’s chapter endings, Dickens’s monthly parts among them, belong to The Chapter Break (Chapter 6), since they are breaks within one story. The last line of a series, and the retroactive judgement it fires on every volume, belong to The Ending (Chapter 16), though the final volume’s load is discussed here. Arrangements of time within a volume belong to Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture (Chapter 8); this chapter takes the order of volumes, and the genres that expect a dual timeline. Market categories, publishing economics and the length a genre’s readers expect are outside the book’s scope, except where a length changes a structure. See also: the full treatment , section 1, on the boundary between a series and a sequence of independent books that share a setting.

title: 3. How It Works
text: The theory a writer needs for genre and series answers four practical questions: what a reader expects before she has read a word, why a familiar pattern pleases rather than bores, how far a book can depart from the pattern and stay on its shelf, and what holds a reader from one volume to the next. Each strand below opens with the question and then gives the source. What a reader brings: the horizon of expectations The question. Two readers finish the same last chapter, and one is satisfied and the other cheated. What did they bring to the book that made the difference? Hans Robert Jauss gave the answer a name in “Literary History as a Challenge to Literary Theory” (1967; translated by Timothy Bahti in Toward an Aesthetic of Reception , 1982). A reader meets a new work with a horizon of expectations , formed by the works of its kind she has read already, and the new work is experienced against it: it confirms, varies or breaks what she expected. Genre is the largest part of that horizon, and it is supplied before the first page by the title, the cover, the shelf and the reader’s own history. The two readers of the last chapter brought different horizons, and the writer controlled neither. Tzvetan Todorov’s “The Typology of Detective Fiction” (1966; translated by Richard Howard in The Poetics of Prose , 1977) shows how specific a horizon can be. The classic detective novel, he argued, contains two stories: the story of the crime, which is over before the book begins, and the story of the investigation, whose whole task is to recover the first. A reader who recognises the form expects the second story to end when the first is fully told. That expectation is the mystery’s core promise, and it is a promise about structure, not about corpses. Why a formula pleases: repetition and its variations The question. A reader who has read forty novels with the same hero picks up the forty-first. What is she paying for? John Cawelti’s Adventure, Mystery, and Romance (1976) called the pattern a formula , a conventional story structure that a culture’s readers know, and argued that formula fiction gives two pleasures at once: the security of a known shape and the interest of a new handling of it. Umberto Eco made the same point about series. In “The Myth of Superman” (1962; translated by Natalie Chilton, 1972) he described the iterative scheme of the comic-book hero, whose adventures begin again each time as if nothing had happened, so that he cannot be used up; in “Innovation and Repetition” (1985) he argued that a serial’s reader enjoys recognising the scheme and, if she is a competent reader of the form, enjoys the variations a writer works within it. The consequence for a writer is that a formula is not a failure of invention. A book that follows one gives the reader the pleasure she came for, and its distinction lies in what it varies. How far a book can depart: semantics, syntax and mode The question. A novel has a dragon, knights and a quest, and its author does not think it fantasy. Who is right, and does it matter? Altman’s “A Semantic/Syntactic Approach to Film Genre” (1984) separated a genre’s building blocks from the relations among them, and argued that genres change when a stable syntax takes new semantics, or familiar semantics are given a new syntax. Alastair Fowler’s Kinds of Literature (1982) made a related distinction between a kind, a genre with its full set of features, and a mode, a selection of a kind’s features carried into other works. Between them they answer the question about the dragon. A novel with fantasy’s semantic elements and another genre’s syntax is fantasy in mode, and its readers will judge it by the promises its syntax makes; whether its author uses the word matters less than whether the book tells the reader early which promises it is making. The Mechanism builds on this. What holds a reader between volumes The question. A reader finishes a volume and waits a year for the next. What has she been promised, and what does she remember? Eco’s typology in “Innovation and Repetition” separated the series, in which a fixed situation recurs and each work is complete, from the saga, in which characters age and the story accumulates. Jason Mittell’s Complex TV (2015) gave the television version: the episodic series resets its world each episode, the serial carries consequences forward, and much contemporary television combines the two, closing a case each week while a story runs across the season. Each combination makes a different promise about what a single volume will close and what it may leave open. What the reader remembers across the gap the chapter has not measured; The Opening Pages (Chapter 9) and The Subplot (Chapter 14) proceed on the working assumption that she keeps a story’s emotional shape better than its mechanics, and so does this chapter. The evidence, and the convention Rolf Zwaan’s “Effect of Genre Expectations on Text Comprehension” (1994) gave readers the same passages, telling some they were reading literature and others that they were reading news. According to the summaries the chapter has used, readers told they were reading literature read more slowly, remembered more of the wording and built a weaker model of the situation described: an expectation of kind changed how the same words were read. The study used short texts and two broad categories, and the chapter draws a modest conclusion from it: what a reader believes she is reading changes what she attends to, before any convention is kept or broken. Genres are historical. The detective novel’s rules of fair play were codified in the late 1920s, and the romance’s requirement of an optimistic ending is a definition its own writers’ association adopted. Claims about which genres sell most, or about how readers of one genre regard another, the chapter treats as impressions, and it treats no genre as more serious than another: literary fiction has conventions and a core promise of its own, set out in The Taxonomy . See also: the full treatment , section 2, with Todorov’s two stories worked on an example, Eco’s typology in full and Pamela Regis’s account of the romance.

title: 4. The Taxonomy
text: The chapter classifies in two directions. Genres are sorted by their core promise, the payment a reader is guaranteed at the end, because that is what a book must keep or visibly decline; series are sorted by what a single volume closes and what it carries, because that is what a writer must decide before the second volume exists. Five core promises Most genres a novelist works in make one of five core promises. The list is a revision instrument, not a map of the bookshop: a shelf label may cover two promises, and a single promise may serve several shelves. The promise of solution belongs to the mystery in all its forms, from the country-house puzzle to the police procedural. The book poses a question of fact, usually who did it and how, and guarantees that by the end the question will be answered from evidence the reader has been shown. Its obligatory scene , the scene its readers expect to see and miss if it is absent (the term is Shawn Coyne’s, in The Story Grid , 2015), is the exposure: the moment the answer is stated and the evidence is seen to support it. The promise of union belongs to the romance. The Romance Writers of America defined a romance by two elements, a central love story and an emotionally satisfying and optimistic ending, and Pamela Regis’s A Natural History of the Romance Novel (2003) found eight elements in the form, from the meeting and the barrier to the declaration and the betrothal. Its obligatory scenes are the meeting and the declaration, and between them the point at which the union seems impossible, which Regis calls the point of ritual death. The promise of the threat met belongs to the thriller, the horror novel and the adventure. A danger to the protagonist, and often to many others, is established and will be confronted directly by the end; the reader is guaranteed the confrontation, not the protagonist’s survival. Its obligatory scene is the hero at the mercy of the threat. The promise of the kept rule belongs to science fiction and fantasy. A world that differs from ours is declared, and the book guarantees that it will obey the rules it has declared, so that a problem is solved within the world’s terms rather than by a new power arriving to solve it. Its obligatory scene is less fixed than the others’; most often it is the scene in which the world’s rule is seen to cost someone something. The promise of significance belongs to literary fiction, which has conventions of its own and readers who notice when they are broken. The book guarantees that its particulars will add up to more than a summary of its events could hold, and that the ending will change how the reader sees what came before, whether or not it pays any of the other four. Its conventions include the open or partial ending, the domestic scale and the epiphany, and its obligatory scene is the recognition, in the sense The Reveal (Chapter 15) uses: the moment a character or the reader sees what the book has been about. The table sets the five side by side with the convention each genre most often declines while keeping its promise, since that is where a writer has room. Core promise Genres Obligatory scene Convention often declined while the promise is kept Solution Mystery, detective, procedural The exposure The detective’s survival, or the culprit’s punishment Union Romance, romantic comedy The declaration A wedding; the union may be a beginning The threat met Thriller, horror, adventure The hero at the mercy of the threat The hero’s survival, or a clean victory The kept rule Science fiction, fantasy The rule’s cost seen An explanation of the rule’s origin Significance Literary fiction The recognition Any of the other four payments The last column is the practical one. A mystery can let its culprit go free and keep its promise, because the promise was the answer, not the arrest; a romance can end on the first night of a relationship, because the promise was the union, not the marriage. A book that declines the core promise itself has done something larger, which the chapter calls a declined convention of the first rank, and The Mechanism says what such a decline requires. Hybrids, modes and the dual timeline A hybrid makes two core promises and keeps both: romantic suspense guarantees the threat met and the union, and its readers will accept neither without the other. A book in a mode, by contrast, borrows conventions without the core promise. The household novel is a family novel in the mystery mode, and its revision problem in The Problem is that its draft jacket sold the mode as a promise. One genre takes Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture ’s architecture (Chapter 8) as a convention. The dual-timeline mystery, of which Kate Morton’s The Forgotten Garden (2008) is an example, braids a present-day investigator with a strand in the past, and its readers expect the strands to converge by identity, a person in the present found to be the child or descendant of a person in the past. In such a book the braid is not a choice the arrangement must justify to the reader; it is a promise, and the convergence is its obligatory scene. Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture ’s tests (Chapter 8) still apply to each strand’s question, but the necessity test is answered by the genre before the book begins. Four forms of series Series differ in what one volume closes and what it carries forward. The four forms below are distinguished by those two things, and the form a series declares in its first volumes is itself a promise about the rest. The episodic series closes everything in each volume and carries forward only its hero, his world and his rule. Its volumes can be read in any order, and its hero usually has the steadfast arc of Arc and Theme (Chapter 12): Lee Child’s Jack Reacher arrives in a new town, the town changes, Reacher does not. Eco’s iterative scheme describes the form, and its pleasure is the variation within the scheme. The episodic series with a running arc closes its volume question each time and carries a second line, a relationship or a past, that advances a step per volume. Its volumes can be read singly but are better read in order. The X-Files (1993–2002) alternated self-contained cases with episodes that advanced its continuing story, and many crime series now give the detective a life that changes across the books while the cases close. The serial is one story published in volumes. Each volume closes a stage, not the story, and the reader must read in order; the series question is the story’s own. Elena Ferrante’s Neapolitan novels (2011–14; translated by Ann Goldstein, 2012–15) and Hilary Mantel’s Cromwell trilogy (2009–20) are serials, and J. R. R. Tolkien’s The Lord of the Rings (1954–55) is a single novel its publisher divided into three. The relay series keeps a world and passes the centre from one character to another, so that each volume has a different protagonist, often a minor figure in the one before. Anthony Trollope’s Barsetshire novels are a relay, and so is Tana French’s Dublin Murder Squad, whose second novel, The Likeness (2008), is narrated by Cassie Maddox, the partner of the first book’s narrator. Its volumes close their own questions, and what carries is the place and the reader’s knowledge of people the new protagonist barely knows. The table compares the four by the decisions a writer must make before the second volume. Form What a volume closes What carries Reading order The hero’s arc Episodic Everything The hero and his rule Free Steadfast Running arc The volume question One line, a step per volume Preferred Slow, staged Serial A stage The story Required Any, across the whole Relay The volume question The world and its people Free, with rewards for order A new protagonist each time Mixed forms are common, and the commonest revision problem in a series is a form changed without notice: an episodic series that ends one volume on an open question, or a serial whose middle volume closes so completely that the next must invent a reason to go on. Diagnostic Tests read both, and the full treatment adds the anthology and the prequel. See also: the full treatment , section 3, with each promise’s conventions listed and a summary table of the series forms.

title: 5. The Mechanism
text: A genre’s promise passes through three stages in a book: it is made, the reader stakes attention on it, and the book keeps, varies or declines it. A series adds a fourth, carrying what is left to the next volume. The chapter’s two instruments record those stages, the promise inventory for a single book and the volume table for a series. How a promise is made A promise is made by semantic signs and confirmed by syntax. A body in the first chapter, a locked room, a stranger met in the rain are signs; the promise is not made until the book sets the syntax going, an investigator who sets out to learn who did it, two people whom something keeps apart. Signs without syntax make a mode, and the reader waits to learn which promise, if any, they belong to. Syntax without the familiar signs makes a variation, and the reader, recognising the relation, applies the promise in unfamiliar dress. Some promises are made before the first page. Gérard Genette’s Paratexts (1987; translated by Jane E. Lewin, 1997) named the paratext , everything that surrounds a text and presents it, the title, the cover, the jacket copy, the epigraph, the shelf. A writer controls little of it, and a publisher’s jacket may promise what the book does not. The practical rule is that the text must declare its own genre within its first chapters, strongly enough to correct a paratext that has made the wrong promise, because the paratext cannot be revised after the reader has bought it. How a reader stakes, and when a decline is cheap A reader stakes attention on a promise in proportion to the pages it organises. A question of fact posed on page one and left open is cheap to decline if the book shows at once that it will not answer it; the same question kept in front of the reader for three hundred pages, with clues and a suspect, is expensive, because she has read every page through it. The chapter’s working estimate, which it has not measured, is that a decline of a core promise should be legible within the first quarter of a book, and that a decline first made legible at the ending will be read as a failure by most readers who hold the promise. A declared decline has three parts. The first is a sign, inside the book, that the question is being held open on purpose: a character who will not answer, a character who chooses not to ask, a narrator who says the answer is not coming, a frame that tells the end. The second is a replacement, a promise the book makes in place of the declined one and then keeps, usually a promise of significance in the sense of The Taxonomy .
