The third is visibility to the end: the declined question stays in view while the book closes its other questions around it, which is The Reveal ’s condition (Chapter 15) for a declined reveal. A decline missing the first part is an undeclared decline, the chapter’s first failure pattern; one missing the second leaves the reader with a debt and nothing for it; one missing the third looks like forgetfulness. The promise inventory The promise inventory is a table of the conventions a book invokes. Each row gives the convention, the genre it comes from, where in the book it is first invoked (as a percentage of the text), whether the book keeps, varies or declines it, and where the keeping or the decline is shown. The inventory is drawn up from the manuscript, not from the writer’s intentions, and its most useful column is the last: a declined convention with no entry there is a broken promise waiting for a reader. Worked Analyses gives the household’s. Variation is the third course, between keeping and declining. A book can keep the syntax and change the semantics, a romance set in a mortuary; keep the core promise and vary its obligatory scene, a declaration made by letter, years late; or keep the obligatory scene and change who performs it, an exposure made by the suspect. Variations cost the reader nothing if the core promise holds, and they are where a formula book’s distinction lies. How a series carries its questions A volume in a series carries two questions, and the reader must be able to tell them apart. The volume question is closed inside the volume, by its own climax; the series question advances by a step the reader can name. A volume whose last page is spent on its own question, left open to bring the reader back, is The Ending ’s series hook (Chapter 16), and its cost is the cost of an unclosed ending: the reader judges a book she has not been given. A volume whose last page opens the series question a step further, after closing its own, is doing what a series promises. Threads that run across volumes go dormant between them, and the dormancy is measured in the reader’s months as well as in pages. The Subplot (Chapter 14) set a thread’s dormancy limits within a book; across volumes a thread absent from one book has been absent for a year of the reader’s life. The second volume therefore needs a re-entry : an opening that serves a returning reader who remembers the shape and not the mechanics, and a new reader who remembers nothing. The Opening Pages (Chapter 9) gives the rule for it, recap delivered as present consequence rather than as summary. A series hero’s criterion, in Arc and Theme ’s sense (Chapter 12), must be where the last volume left it. In an episodic series it does not move, and the change happens to others; in a series with a running arc it moves a stage per volume, and each volume shows its stage. The order of volumes is a further choice. A prequel , a volume set before the others, is an analepsis at the scale of the series: its reader knows how its story ends, so it must run on a question the later volumes leave open, which is Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture ’s strand question (Chapter 8) applied to a book. The volume table The volume table has a row per volume, written or planned, and seven columns: the volume question and where it closes; the series question and the step the volume takes on it; the threads carried in and out, with their dormancy in volumes; the hero’s criterion at the end; the re-entry device; the last page, closing or hooking; and the form the volume implies. A series whose table has an empty step column in two successive rows is stalled, and one whose last-page column says hooks where the volume question column says open is owing. See also: the full treatment , section 5, with the procedures for drawing up both instruments, and section 3.4 on prequels and reading order.

title: 6. Diagnostic Tests
text: The eight tests are for revision. Tests 1 to 4 (Shelf, Core promise, Declared decline and Variation) read a single book’s genre and need a promise inventory; tests 5 to 8 (Volume question, Series step, Re-entry and Criterion across volumes) read a series, or a book that may become one, and need a volume table, which can include planned volumes when only the first has been written. Record a sentence for each, not a verdict. Test 1 — Shelf Where would a reader of the first chapter shelve the book, and does the last chapter belong on the same shelf? Failure. Genre drift: a book that changes kind without telling the reader. Exception. From Dusk Till Dawn (Robert Rodriguez, 1996), a crime film that becomes a vampire film at its midpoint, the change its own joke. Test 2 — Core promise Does the book keep the core promise of the genre its opening declares? Failure. A broken promise, or a book that has not decided what it is. Exception. Jojo Moyes’s Me Before You (2012), a romance in its conventions whose hero chooses to die, keeping the emotional payment and declining the union. Test 3 — Declared decline For each declined convention, is the decline shown inside the book within the first quarter, and replaced by a promise the book keeps? Failure. The undeclared decline. Exception. Psycho (Alfred Hitchcock, 1960), which kills its apparent protagonist and drops her story before its midpoint, and replaces it with a stronger one. Test 4 — Variation Does the book vary at least one convention, and is its meaning in the variation? Failure. The inert formula. Exception. Lee Child’s Reacher novels, whose pleasure is the scheme, kept. Test 5 — Volume question Can the volume’s question be written in a line, and is it closed inside the volume? Failure. The volume that owes its question. Exception. Tolkien’s The Fellowship of the Ring (1954), a third of a novel its publisher divided, which closes only a stage. Test 6 — Series step What step does each volume take on the series question, and can a reader name it? Failure. The deferred answer, or a stalled series. Exception. Columbo (from 1971), which has no series question and has declared that it has none. Test 7 — Re-entry Can a reader who finished the last volume a year ago, and one who never read it, both follow the first chapter? Failure. The recap at the door, or a closed door. Exception. Hilary Mantel’s Bring Up the Bodies (2012), which opens on Cromwell’s falcons, named for his dead daughters, with no summary of Wolf Hall . Test 8 — Criterion across volumes Is the hero’s criterion where the last volume left it, and if it has moved, does the volume show the move? Failure. The reset hero: an arc undone between volumes without a scene. Exception. Seinfeld (1989–98), whose writers worked to the rule “no hugging, no learning”. Reading the results together Failures cluster, and the cluster locates the repair. Tests 1 (Shelf) and 2 (Core promise) failing together describe a book whose opening declared one kind and whose ending pays another; decide which kind the book is, and revise the end that is not it, which is usually the opening, since the ending carries the meaning. Test 3 (Declared decline) failing alone, with tests 1 (Shelf) and 2 (Core promise) passing, is the commonest pattern in a book written in a genre’s mode: the book keeps its own promise and borrows another genre’s question without saying it will not be answered. The repair is a sign inside the book, early, not a change to the ending. Test 4 (Variation) failing alone is not always a fault. An episodic series can pass on the scheme alone, as Eco argued, and a writer should fail test 4 (Variation) knowingly, for a reader who wants the scheme. Tests 5 (Volume question) and 6 (Series step) failing together are a series hook that has replaced a series question: the volume leaves its own question open because it has no larger one to advance, and the repair is to close the volume and find the step. Test 7 (Re-entry) failing is cheap to mend and test 8 (Criterion across volumes) failing expensive, since a criterion reset without a scene breaks the arc of Arc and Theme (Chapter 12) in every volume that follows. A clean pass on all eight, with readers who still feel cheated, usually means the paratext made a promise the text did not; look at the jacket before the book. See also: the full treatment , section 5, with the procedure for each test and the household’s promise inventory.

title: 7. Failure Patterns
text: Each pattern below fails through a mechanism rather than a surface feature. Each ends with a published work that uses the feature successfully because the mechanism is absent or offset by another effect. The full treatment has a longer catalogue, among them the reset hero, the undone ending, the escalation ratchet and the overloaded last volume. The undeclared decline Symptom. Early readers like the book until the last chapters and then feel cheated, often angrily, and say the ending was not what the book had promised. Readers who knew nothing of the genre, or who were told what to expect, do not mind. Mechanism. The undeclared decline invokes a genre’s core promise, lets the reader stake the book on it, and declines it at the end without having shown inside the book that it would. It fails test 3 (Declared decline), and sometimes test 2 (Core promise). The reader is not wrong to feel cheated: by the horizon she was given, the book broke a contract. What she lacks is the sign that the contract was never offered. Remedy. Test 3 (Declared decline). Find where the promise is first invoked and put the sign of the decline as near it as the material allows: a character who will not answer, one who chooses not to ask, a frame that tells the end. Then name, in the promise inventory, what the book promises instead, and check that it is kept. Do not mend the ending by paying the declined promise after all, which turns a refusal into a cheat. Exception. No Country for Old Men (Joel and Ethan Coen, 2007, from Cormac McCarthy’s novel of 2005). The film builds a chase thriller around Llewelyn Moss, who has taken drug money, and the killer Anton Chigurh, and then has Moss killed off screen by other men, lets Chigurh walk away injured from a car crash, and ends on the retired sheriff telling his wife a dream. The threat is never met. The film succeeds because its decline is the subject, a sheriff outmatched by a violence that does not keep the genre’s terms, and because its last scenes keep the promise of significance with unusual force; it is also the case that a part of its audience felt cheated, which is the pattern’s cost even where it succeeds. The genre in costume Symptom. The book has a genre’s furniture, a dragon or a corpse or a spaceship, and readers of that genre find it slow, thin or evasive, while the writer is puzzled that they read it as a genre book at all. Mechanism. The genre in costume uses a genre’s semantic elements without its syntax, so that the reader recognises the signs and applies the promise, and the book then pays a different one. It is a failure of test 1 (Shelf) in a mild form: the first chapter shelves the book in one genre and the last pays another, though each chapter is consistent with itself. Remedy. Tests 1 (Shelf) and 3 (Declared decline). Either give the furniture its syntax, so that the dragon is a threat that will be met, or declare early that the furniture serves another promise, by letting the protagonists treat it as the people of their world would, as weather rather than quest. Exception. Kazuo Ishiguro’s The Buried Giant (2015). An elderly couple, Axl and Beatrice, travel through a post-Arthurian Britain in which a mist makes people forget, with an ageing Sir Gawain, ogres and a she-dragon, Querig, whose breath is the mist. Ishiguro told an interviewer for The New York Times that he wondered whether readers would be “prejudiced against the surface elements”, and Ursula K. Le Guin answered on her blog that he seemed to take the word fantasy for an insult. The book succeeds for many readers because its syntax is declared early and kept: the quest is a marriage examining what it has chosen to forget, and the dragon’s death matters because it ends the forgetting. The volume that owes its question Symptom. Readers finish a volume of a series and complain that nothing was resolved, or that they were made to buy the next book to learn how this one ends. Mechanism. The volume that owes its question leaves its own question open at the last page in order to bring the reader back. It is The Ending ‘s series hook (Chapter 16) seen from the series’ side, and it fails test 5 (Volume question). It spends the volume’s ending on a proposition, and it often reveals a deeper problem, test 6 (Series step): the series has no question of its own for the hook to advance, so the volume’s question is made to do the work. Remedy. Tests 5 (Volume question) and 6 (Series step). Close the volume’s question inside the volume, and put the reader’s reason to come back in the series question, advanced a step on the last pages after the close. Exception. Lee Child’s 61 Hours (2010), the fourteenth Reacher novel. In a snowbound South Dakota town Reacher is protecting a witness against a drug operation; she is killed, Reacher kills those responsible in an underground facility, and the book ends as fuel in the tunnels ignites and he runs for the stairs, with a woman far away watching the news of the explosion. The volume closes its question, the operation and the witness, and owes only its hero’s survival, which an episodic series thirteen volumes old could hardly withhold for long; the next volume, Worth Dying For (2010), followed within months. The hook works once because the form had been declared thirteen times before it. The deferred answer Symptom. A series poses a question in its first volume and lets it grow across the volumes, and the final volume’s answer, however clever, seems too small for the waiting, or cannot be given at all. Mechanism. The deferred answer holds a series question open across volumes without advancing it, so that the reader’s stake grows while the material stands still. It fails test 6 (Series step). Every volume adds to what the answer must repay, and The Ending ’s retroactive lens (Chapter 16), fired at the last volume, judges the whole series by it. Remedy. Test 6 (Series step). Give each volume a step on the series question, a fact learned, a possibility removed, a cost paid, so that the final answer completes a sequence rather than ending a wait. Or declare the question declined, as Worked Analyses shows The Leftovers doing. Exception. J. K. Rowling’s Harry Potter novels, which hold the question of Severus Snape’s allegiance from the first volume (1997) to the seventh, Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (2007), where a chapter of his memories answers it. The deferral works because each volume closes its own question and adds a piece of evidence on Snape both ways, so the answer completes a sequence the reader has been assembling. The recap at the door Symptom. The second or third volume opens slowly; returning readers skim its first chapters and new readers are lost in them anyway. Mechanism. The recap at the door delivers the previous volumes as summary before the new volume’s story starts. It fails test 7 (Re-entry) on both counts: the returning reader is told what she remembers, and the new reader is given facts without the scenes that made them matter. Remedy. Test 7 (Re-entry). Open on the new volume’s situation and deliver what is needed from the past as present consequence, in The Opening Pages ’s sense (Chapter 9): a character behaving in a way the previous volume explains and this one shows. Give the new reader the people before the history. Exception. The television Previously on sequence, which commits the pattern in its purest form, a minute of summary before the story, and succeeds because it is placed outside the episode, assembled from the series’ own scenes, and can be skipped. A novel can do the same with a note or a list of characters before the first chapter, which keeps the summary out of the story it would otherwise delay. See also: the full treatment , section 4, for the extended catalogue.

title: 8. Worked Analyses
text: Three readings show a genre’s promise declined with a declaration, declined with half of one, and a series’ question declined across four volumes; a screen reading shows a series that declared its decline in its title sequence. The household case follows. Jane Austen, Northanger Abbey (1817): a mode declined on its first page Austen’s novel invokes the gothic, the most widely read genre of its decade, and declines its core promise in its first sentence: No one who had ever seen Catherine Morland in her infancy would have supposed her born to be an heroine. The narrator tells the reader at once that the book will use the gothic’s conventions and not pay its debts, and the reader is given a replacement in the same sentence, a comedy of a girl who reads too much, with the romance’s promise of union running beneath it. The declaration lets Austen invoke the conventions at full strength. Catherine reads Ann Radcliffe’s The Mysteries of Udolpho at Bath and arrives at the Tilneys’ abbey expecting the gothic’s syntax: a locked cabinet, a hidden manuscript, a tyrannical father, a dead wife. Every sign is honoured and every payment refused. The manuscript in the cabinet is an inventory of linen; the late Mrs Tilney died of an illness, and Catherine’s suspicion that the General murdered or imprisoned her earns a rebuke from Henry Tilney, who asks her to remember the country and the age in which they live. The variation comes afterwards. The General turns Catherine out of the house and sends her home alone, because he has learned she is not the heiress he had supposed, and Catherine concludes that in suspecting him she had scarcely sinned against his character, or magnified his cruelty . The gothic’s exposure, the tyrant found out, is kept in a domestic key: the villain is real and his crime is money. The romance’s promise is kept too, and Henry marries her. A reader of the gothic was never cheated, because the first sentence told her what she was reading; the book’s distinction lies in the convention it varied after declining it. Tana French, In the Woods (2007): a promise kept and a promise declined French’s first novel, which won the Edgar Award for best first novel, is a police procedural with two questions. In 1984 three children went into the woods at Knocknaree outside Dublin and one came out, found clinging to a tree with blood in his shoes and no memory; the other two were never found. Twenty years later the survivor, Rob Ryan, is a detective, and with his partner Cassie Maddox he investigates the murder of a twelve-year-old girl, Katy Devlin, whose body is found on an archaeological dig beside the same woods. The volume question, who killed Katy, is answered by the genre’s terms: a man working on the dig confesses, and the book shows that Katy’s elder sister manipulated him. The second question, what happened in 1984, is the one the book has made personal, since Rob narrates it as the wound of his life, and it is never answered. Readers divided over the ending, and many said they felt cheated. The promise inventory shows why. The procedural’s core promise is made twice, once for each case, and kept once. The decline is half declared. Rob warns the reader at the start, I crave truth. And I lie , which tells her to doubt the narrator but not that the past will stay closed, and the two cases are linked by place and by evidence found near the body, which invites the reader to expect a single solution. A reader who reads the book as a novel of trauma has the replacement promise, and it is kept: the past is unrecoverable because Rob cannot recover it. A reader who reads it as a procedural has staked the whole book on the link. The series form then confirms the decline after the fact. French’s second novel, The Likeness (2008), is narrated by Cassie, and the Dublin Murder Squad became a relay series, so no later volume carries the 1984 question; the decline holds because nothing was deferred. Elena Ferrante, the Neapolitan novels (2011–14; translated by Ann Goldstein, 2012–15): a serial with a declined frame The four novels, My Brilliant Friend , The Story of a New Name , Those Who Leave and Those Who Stay and The Story of the Lost Child , are a serial, one story told by Elena Greco across sixty years of her friendship with Lila Cerullo. The first volume’s prologue sets the frame: Lila’s son telephones Elena, both women now in their sixties, to say his mother has gone, and Elena, angry, decides to write down everything she can remember. The series question is declared on the first pages, and so is the decline of its plainest form. Where Lila has gone is a question of fact the quartet never answers; what Lila was, the question the writing pursues, is the one the series keeps. Each volume closes a stage rather than the story. My Brilliant Friend ends at Lila’s wedding feast, when Marcello Solara, the man she refused, walks in wearing the shoes she designed, a sign that her husband has made his peace, and his business, with the Solaras. The volume question, whether Lila’s marriage will free her from the neighbourhood’s terms, is answered there, no, so the volume closes; the last page also opens the next stage, which is what a serial’s volume ending must do. A reader who stops after the first volume has been given a whole book. The final volume shows what a serial owes at its end. Lila’s daughter Tina vanishes in 1984 and is never found, a second question of fact declined, and the quartet ends with Elena receiving a package holding the two dolls the girls lost as children in the first volume. The dolls are a bridging object in Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture ’s sense (Chapter 8) across four books, and whether they are an insult or a reassurance the book does not say. The serial keeps the promise it declared, a whole account of a friendship, and declines the two facts it never offered to supply. A screen reading: The Leftovers (HBO, 2014–17) Damon Lindelof and Tom Perrotta’s series, adapted from Perrotta’s novel of 2011, begins three years after two per cent of the world’s population vanished at once on 14 October. The premise invokes the mystery’s core promise at the largest scale available, and the series declined it from the start: it follows the people left behind and never explains the departure. In its second season it changed its title sequence to Iris DeMent’s song “Let the Mystery Be”, a declaration placed inside the work, in the series’ own paratext, at the head of every episode. The finale lets one character give an account of where the departed went, which nobody can check, and ends with the man she tells saying that he believes her. The series question, how people live beside an event that will not be explained, was advanced in every season, and the declined question was kept in view to the last scene. The household revision case: a hook for a second book The situation. The household novel’s present runs from about four months after the father’s death in March to the end of July. Elena learns in Dov’s doorway, at the first chapter break, that their mother changed the locks, and Dov will not say why. At a little under a quarter of the book, in the truck, she weighs ringing their mother and foresees the silence that meant she’d asked something true , and drives to the shop instead. At about 38 per cent she finds the register drawer empty and decides not to ask Dov who took the ledger, because she had asked him once . At the convergence she rings Nadia, not her mother, and the three read the ledger in the shop; Nadia goes up and puts on the coat. The locks are never explained. Version A, the draft. The agent’s two additions from The Problem : a last page on which the mother rings and Elena answers, and jacket copy promising that one of the children will find out why the locks were changed. Diagnosis. Test 1 (Shelf) fails at both ends: the jacket shelves the book as a mystery, the last page closes it as one, and everything between is a family novel in the mystery mode. Test 3 (Declared decline) is the decisive failure, and of an unusual kind. The book had declared its decline, and the draft takes the declaration back: a reader who accepted the doorway, the truck and the empty drawer as signs that the question would stay open is told on the last page that she was wrong to. Test 5 (Volume question) fails, since the hook spends the volume’s last page on a question, and the ending’s privileged position on a proposition. Test 6 (Series step) finds no series question to advance: a second volume could only answer the locks with the mother’s own account, which the book’s meaning, and its canon, forbid. Version B, the revision. Cut the last page, so that the book ends where it did, with Nadia and the coat, and the mother’s silence stays in view. Replace the jacket’s question with a promise the book keeps: Four months after their father’s death, Elena finds that her key no longer fits the shop, and that someone else has been writing in his ledger. The promise inventory shows that the text needs nothing more: Convention Genre First invoked Kept, varied or declined Where shown A question of fact posed early: why the locks Mystery The doorway, at the first chapter break Declined The truck; the empty drawer at 38%; the call to Nadia; the ending The investigator Mystery The doorway; the truck Varied: she investigates by reading and decides not to ask The empty drawer The document in a changed hand Mystery The drawer, about 25% Kept: whose hand Dov’s chapter, about 78%; the convergence The suspect: who took the ledger Mystery The empty drawer, 38% Kept The convergence The secret of the dead: what the father knew Mystery, family novel The prologue’s In case Kept The reading The gathering for the solution Mystery — Varied: three read one record, and nobody explains The ending The declined row has a sign at intervals from the first chapter break to the last page, and the replacement promise, what these three do with what they can reconstruct, is kept by the gathering in the last row. The book’s genre was declared by three decisions not to ask, and the revision removes the two additions that contradicted them. What the revision has not solved. The declaration is cumulative, and the first sign, the truck, is legible as a decline only in retrospect, so a reader who arrives with a mystery’s horizon may still hold the question to the end and feel the locks as a debt. The jacket is not the writer’s to write, and the book’s genre cannot depend on it. A mystery’s horizon also makes a reader treat details as clues: the boy at the glass, the sign left at OPEN and the coat’s shoulders brushed every week by someone the book never names will be read as evidence, and the last of them is a second question of fact the book declines without a sign, an undeclared decline under the mode it has chosen. And the agent’s request for a second book is answered only negatively: the book has no series question that does not spend its own. See also: the full treatment , with readings of Bring Up the Bodies , Beach Read , 61 Hours and Twin Peaks , and the household’s promise inventory and volume table in full.

title: 9. Checklist and Exercises
text: Revision checklist The genre declared Where would a reader of my first chapter shelve the book, and does my last chapter belong on the same shelf? What is the core promise of the genre my opening declares, and where do I keep it? Does my jacket copy, or my pitch, promise anything the book declines? Conventions kept, varied and declined Have I listed every convention the book invokes, with the place it is first invoked? For each declined convention, is there a sign inside the book within the first quarter, and a replacement promise that I keep? Is every declined question kept in view to the end, so that the decline reads as design rather than forgetting? Which convention do I vary, and is that where the book’s meaning lies? Will a reader of my mode read any detail as a clue that I never meant to answer? The volume Can I write this volume’s question in a line, and is it closed inside the volume? Is my last page spent on this volume’s ending, with any step on the series question after the close? The series What form have my first volumes declared, and does this one keep it? What step does each volume take on the series question, and could a reader name it? How long has each carried thread been dormant, counted in volumes and in the reader’s months? Does my first chapter serve both a returning reader and a new one, with recap delivered as present consequence? Is my hero’s criterion where the last volume left it, or does this volume show it moving? Exercises The promise inventory. List every convention your draft invokes, with its genre, the percentage of the text at which it is first invoked, whether you keep, vary or decline it, and where the reader is shown which. Mark every decline with no entry in the last column. The shelf test. Write two sentences of jacket copy from your first chapter alone and two from your last chapter alone. If they would sit on different shelves, decide which book you are writing and revise the other end. The early sign. Take one declined convention and write the sign of its decline into a scene in the first quarter of your draft, using a character’s decision rather than the narrator’s statement. Then write, in one line, the promise the book makes in its place. The volume table. For a series written or planned, fill in a row per volume: volume question and where it closes, the step on the series question, threads carried and their dormancy, the hero’s criterion, the re-entry, the last page. Find any two successive rows with no step, and any last page that hooks on an open volume question. The re-entry. Rewrite the first two pages of a later volume so that nothing in them is summary, and every fact a new reader needs from earlier volumes arrives as a present action, a habit, a scar or a quarrel.

title: 10. Coda
text: The instruments in this chapter assume a reader who arrives with a horizon, not a blank page, and who reads a book as an answer to the expectations she brought to it. The promise inventory records what the book asks her to expect; the volume table records what a series asks her to keep expecting across the gaps between books. Both describe a reader for whom a convention is not a rule a writer obeys but a promise she was made, and who judges a book less by what it pays than by whether it paid what it said it would. That a book can decline a genre’s central payment and satisfy its readers, as Northanger Abbey and The Leftovers do, is evidence that the reader’s contract is with the book’s declarations, not with the genre’s rules. That is the chapter’s argument. A genre is a set of promises a writer inherits and a series a set of promises she makes for later, and each is kept or broken by the text, not by the shelf. A convention may be kept, varied or declined, and the third is as legitimate as the first, on two conditions: that the book says so early, inside itself, and that it puts something in the declined promise’s place and keeps that. A volume of a series may leave much open, on one condition: that what it leaves open is the series’ question and not its own. The household revision illustrates the economy. It removed a last page and a sentence of jacket copy, and found that the book had declared its kind three times, each by a character deciding not to ask, and that the question it declines is the one its subject requires it to leave open. See also: the full treatment , section 8, on the limits of the model; The Structural Edit (Chapter 18), which puts the promise inventory into a revision order for the whole book.

title: The Structural Edit
text: In what order to revise a whole book, and when to stop The Craft Behind the Story (Second Edition) — Chapter 18. Part IV: Beyond the Book and Into Practice. In brief. A structural edit revises a book’s architecture before its sentences, and its difficulty is order: every decision in a novel rests on others, so a repair made in the wrong order is undone by the next one. The chapter’s claim is that a book should be revised in the order in which its decisions depend on one another, not in the order of its pages: first what it promises and asks, then whose book it is and how its times and threads are arranged, then the shape of the whole, then the joins, and the scenes and their sentences last. Diagnosis runs the other way, from the place where a reader felt a problem up to the highest level at which its cause can lie. The tools are the book map, a table with one row per scene from which the other chapters’ instruments can be read, and the revision ladder, which puts those instruments in order. Use the chapter when you have a full draft and a pile of notes, when each revision seems to undo the last, or when you cannot tell whether the book is finished. What you can do after this chapter Build a book map of a full draft in a day, and read the other chapters’ charts and tables off it. Sort a set of readers’ notes onto the revision ladder by where each problem was felt and where its cause lies. Revise in the order of dependence, recording for each repair the tests it reopens. Diagnose a page-order edit, premature polish, a local repair, a cascade and an edit by addition, and revise them. Decide when a structural edit is finished, and defend the failures you keep. Key terms Structural edit; line edit; copy-edit; macro-edit and micro-edit; the book map; the revision ladder; rung; the promise; allocation and arrangement; the shape; the joins; the scene and its materials; order of dependence; upward discovery; the rung-up rule; the edit list; reopened tests; the economy of the repair; the form audit; the stopping rule; the cold read; the page-order edit; premature polish; the local repair; the cascade; the edit by addition. Each is defined at first use and collected in the consolidated glossary . Contents The first files say what a structural edit is and why its order matters, the central files set out the ladder and the map that serve it, and the last are for use at the desk with a draft and its notes. The Problem A household edit made in page order, and the chapter’s claim Definitions The structural edit and its neighbours, and what other chapters keep How It Works How experienced writers revise, what editors do first, what a map should record and how to read a reader’s note The Taxonomy The five rungs of the revision ladder, and the ruling on formal closure The Mechanism The book map, the order of dependence, the edit list and the stopping rule Diagnostic Tests Seven questions about the edit itself, and a table from symptom to rung Failure Patterns Five recurrent failures of revision, each paired with a work in which the same habit succeeds Worked Analyses The Great Gatsby , Never Let Me Go , Make Me , Annie Hall and the household revision case Checklist and Exercises The revision checklist and five exercises for your own draft Coda What the ladder assumes, and what no edit can decide A writer with a draft and notes in hand can start at the mechanism, build the map, and then use the diagnostic tests. A writer who has revised several times and finds the book getting no better should read the failure patterns first, since the commonest cause is the order of the work rather than its quality. The full treatment This is a new chapter, so the Reference layer holds a single full treatment rather than a corrected original: the theory at greater length, every chapter’s instruments placed on the ladder, the kinds of structural edit, the ruling on formal closure in full, further failure patterns, the procedures for each test, further analyses (the Harry Potter series, The Martian , A Little Life and the remix of Arrested Development ), the household book map and edit list in full, a glossary of the chapter’s terms and the sources. See also: The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1), whose two-sentence statement of change is the map’s central column; The Ending (Chapter 16), whose plant audit is the last test of the shape; Series and Genre (Chapter 17), whose promise inventory is the first.

title: 1. The Problem
text: The household novel is drafted from end to end. It is a quiet family novel set in a small British town: four months after their father’s death in March, his three adult children reconstruct what he left. Elena learns in Dov’s doorway that their mother changed the shop’s locks, and Dov gives her the new key and keeps the reason; Nadia counts things and will not touch the coat that still hangs in the flat above the shop, its shoulders brushed every week by someone the book does not name; the father’s ledger, kept for eleven years in a careful slanting hand, stops on 9 March, and a looser hand continues it. Dov’s single chapter of viewpoint, near the end, is the evening of 9 March. At the convergence the three read the ledger together, learn that their father was ill and wrote it down and told nobody, and Nadia goes up to the flat and puts on the coat. Three early readers and the agent have sent notes, eleven in all. The opening is slow, and it takes a chapter to learn whose book it is. One reader kept waiting to learn who brushes the coat. The middle sags somewhere between Nadia finding the pen and Dov’s chapter. At the head of Dov’s chapter one reader did not know when she was. The ending is crowded, with too much happening in the shop at once. Elena does not seem to change. The ledger is warm three times. And there are four notes about sentences. The writer does what most writers do with notes: she opens the file at page one and works forward. She tightens the opening and adds a sentence telling the reader that the book is also Elena’s. At about 45 per cent she writes a short scene in which Nadia, coming up to the flat early, finds their mother there with a clothes brush, and leaves without a word. Where the middle sags she adds a chapter in which Elena searches the flat. She puts a paragraph at the head of Dov’s chapter explaining that this is the evening of 9 March, four months earlier. At the convergence she cuts Elena’s call to Nadia, to thin the crowd, and has Nadia arrive by chance; and since a reader said Elena does not change, she gives her a paragraph of reflection on the last pages. She takes warm out twice. Every one of these repairs answers its note, and the book is worse. The scene with the clothes brush gives the mother a scene of her own, which the book has refused her from its first chapter, and answers in passing a question the book was built to decline. The search chapter repeats the empty drawer at the same stakes, which is how middles sag in the first place. The paragraph at the head of Dov’s chapter states what a heading could show. Cutting the call removes the one act in which Elena’s change is visible, and the paragraph of reflection then has to say what the act had shown. And the opening the writer polished first now promises a book whose middle and ending she has since changed. Six weeks of careful work have produced a draft whose parts no longer agree, and the notes that remain are harder to read than the first ones, because some of them are about the repairs. The fault is not in any single repair. It is in the order. A novel’s decisions depend on one another, and they depend in one direction: the arrangement of a book’s times depends on what the book is asking, the chapter breaks depend on the arrangement, and the sentences depend on everything. A writer who revises in page order makes each repair against decisions she has not yet checked, and repairs at the top of the book undo work done lower down. A structural edit revises a book in the order in which its decisions depend on one another, not in the order of its pages: first what the book promises and asks, then whose it is and how its times and threads are arranged, then the shape of the whole, then the joins, and the scenes and their sentences last, because a change at any level reopens work beneath it and none above. Diagnosis runs the other way, from the place where a reader felt a problem to the highest level at which its cause can lie, and the edit is finished when a pass at the top changes nothing below and every failure that remains is one the writer can name and defend. The claim has a consequence for notes. A reader’s note says where a problem was felt, which is evidence, and seldom where it was caused. The revision in Worked Analyses takes the same eleven notes, sorts them by the level at which each cause lies, mends four of them, keeps two failures it can defend, passes the other five to the line edit, and finds that the note about the coat, a note about a detail, is answered by a decision about what the book declines. See also: the full treatment , section 7, with the household book map and edit list in full; The Middle (Chapter 11), on why adding incident does not mend a sagging middle.

title: 2. Definitions
text: Working definition A structural edit is the revision of a complete draft at the level of the decisions that span more than one scene: what the book promises its reader and what question it asks, whose book it is and how its times and threads are arranged, the shape of the whole (the protagonist’s change, the narrowing of the middle, the schedule of disclosure, the ending), and the joins between its units. Its unit of attention is the book, and its material is the draft as it stands, read as a set of decisions rather than as a sequence of pages. A structural edit may end in a rewrite, a scene drafted again from a statement of what it must do, or in a revision, a change made in place, and it usually ends in both. The structural edit is distinguished from two later kinds of work. A line edit revises sentences and paragraphs inside a scene for sense, rhythm, economy and voice; it takes the scene’s job as given. A copy-edit checks correctness and consistency: spelling, grammar, house style, and the continuity of facts such as names, dates and the colour of a coat. Publishers’ editors call the first of the three a developmental or structural edit, and the order of the three in a publishing house, structure, then line, then copy, is itself an order of dependence: there is no point in correcting the spelling of a paragraph that is going to be cut. The writer’s own edit follows the same order for the same reason, and a writer who edits alone is doing all three jobs, which is why she is tempted to do them at once. Two further terms come from the chapter’s own instruments. The book map is a table with one row for each scene of a draft, recording where it falls, when and where it happens, through whose eyes, in which thread, what changes in it and what it deposits for later. The revision ladder is the order in which the decisions of a book are checked and repaired, from the decisions that the others depend on down to those that depend on everything; each level is a rung . Both are set out in The Mechanism and The Taxonomy . Adjacent terms The order of dependence is the relation the ladder records. One decision depends on another when changing the second can make the first wrong, and changing the first cannot make the second wrong. A chapter break depends on the arrangement of the book’s times, because moving a strand can leave a break that no longer falls where a question opens; the arrangement does not depend on the break, because moving a break leaves the strands where they were. Dependence is a property of decisions, not of pages: the opening pages come first in the book and depend on almost everything after them. Planning and editing use the same order. A writer who outlines before drafting makes the decisions at the top of the ladder first and drafts the scenes last, and a writer who drafts first and discovers the book in the drafting makes the same decisions afterwards, in the edit. The ladder serves both, as an order of decisions rather than of drafts. The plant audit of The Ending (Chapter 16) traces everything an ending rests on to the place it was planted. It is a test of the ending against the book, and the structural edit uses it as the last test of the shape of the whole. The chapter’s other neighbours are the diagnostic tests of every earlier chapter, each of which tests the text at one level; this chapter says in what order to run them and what to do with what they find. What this chapter leaves to others This chapter adds no test of the text. Every test it orders belongs to the chapter that defines it, and the instruments it reads off the book map (the order chart, the option list, the criterion log, the disclosure map, the promise inventory and the rest) are defined and justified in their own chapters. The tests in this chapter are tests of the edit: whether it is being done in an order that will hold, whether each repair has been checked against what it disturbs, and whether it is finished. The line edit and the copy-edit are outside the book’s subject, which is structure. The consolidated symptom index and the master checklist, which gather every chapter’s symptoms and checklists in one place, are in the appendices; this chapter gives a short table from symptom to rung, enough to start an edit, and leaves the full index to them. The working relation between a writer and an editor, and the questions it raises about whose book an edited book is, are touched on in the full treatment , section 8, and not otherwise treated. See also: the full treatment , section 1, with the working definitions in one place.

title: 3. How It Works
text: The method in this chapter uses four strands of theory, and each answers a question a writer meets with a draft and its notes in front of her. The strands come from research on how writers revise, from editorial practice, from the psychology of reading, and from writers’ own accounts of how they work. Why do writers revise the wrong things first? The practical question is why a writer with a structural problem spends her revision on sentences. Nancy Sommers put a version of it to two groups in 1980, twenty first-year university students and twenty experienced adult writers, and compared what each did when revising its own essays. The students revised mainly by substituting words and phrases, a strategy Sommers called the thesaurus philosophy, and they described revision as cleaning up. The experienced writers revised to find the form or shape of their argument: they added, deleted and above all reordered, worked on the whole and the parts in turn, and expected the whole to change. Sommers’s subjects wrote essays, not novels, and her finding is about what the two groups did, not about what made their texts better; but it describes the first failure pattern of Failure Patterns closely, and it locates the difference in the writer’s idea of what revision is for. Linda Flower, John Hayes and their colleagues (1986) proposed a working model of revision in three steps: detecting a problem, diagnosing it, and choosing a strategy. A diagnosis names the kind of problem, and only a named problem can be mended by a strategy that reaches beyond the sentence where it was found; an undiagnosed problem tends to be met by rewriting the passage in which it was noticed. A common gloss on the model, which this chapter adopts as a working assumption rather than as a finding, explains why a writer finds her own problems late: she knows what she meant, and reads her meaning into the text. The model is the reason this chapter separates the place a problem is felt from the place it is caused, and the reason it asks a writer to diagnose before she repairs. What does an editor do first? The practical question is which part of a book to look at before the others. Editorial practice has an answer older than the research. Maxwell Perkins’s letter to F. Scott Fitzgerald of 20 November 1924, about the typescript of The Great Gatsby , praises the book’s design and makes one structural objection, that Gatsby is somewhat vague : The reader’s eyes can never quite focus upon him, his outlines are dim. It says nothing about sentences. The editor Susan Bell, who uses Perkins and Fitzgerald as her main case in The Artful Edit (2007), divides a writer’s self-editing into the macro-edit , which reads the whole for its shape, its proportions and its sense, and the micro-edit , which works line by line, and puts the first before the second. The publishing sequence of structural edit, line edit and copy-edit is the same order at an institution’s scale. The same practice supplies the map. Shawn Coyne’s The Story Grid (2015) asks a writer to fill in a spreadsheet with one row per scene, recording among other things the story event, the value that shifts in it, the viewpoint, the time, the duration, the location and the characters on stage, and to state the whole book on a single page before revising any of it. Writers of non-fiction have long used a reverse outline, a summary of a draft paragraph by paragraph written after the draft, for the same purpose. The book map of The Mechanism is a version of both, with columns chosen so that the instruments of this book’s other chapters can be read from it. What should the map record? The practical question is which facts about each scene a writer must have in front of her to see the book. The psychology of reading suggests an answer. Rolf Zwaan, Mark Langston and Arthur Graesser (1995) found that readers keep track of five dimensions of a story as they read: time, space, the protagonist and other entities, causality, and the characters’ goals. A sentence that breaks continuity on any of them takes longer to read, and events that share more of them are more closely linked in the reader’s memory. A reader’s grasp of a book, on this evidence, is built on those five, and a map that records them for every scene records what the reader is building. The book map adds what the novel’s own structure needs: the thread, what changes, what the scene deposits for later, and what the reader learns. The Transition (Chapter 5) uses the same five dimensions to price a transition, which is the same finding at the scale of a gap. What is a reader’s note evidence of? The practical question is how far to trust a note. Neil Gaiman put the usual working answer in one of his rules for writers, published in 2010: when people tell you something’s wrong or doesn’t work for them, they are almost always right. When they tell you exactly what they think is wrong and how to fix it, they are almost always wrong. The rule is advice, not research, but it agrees with Flower and Hayes’s model: a reader detects, and seldom diagnoses. Her note is good evidence of a symptom and of where she felt it, and poor evidence of its cause, which may lie hundreds of pages from the place she marked. The Ending (Chapter 16) gives the clearest case: an ending that passes every test of the ending and lands on nothing has its fault in the middle of the book, which has not built a want urgent enough to conclude. Is the order a description of how writers work? The practical question is whether a writer who does not work in this order is doing it wrong. Kurt Vonnegut, in Timequake (1997), distinguished two kinds of novelist: swoopers , who write a story quickly, any which way , and then go over it again, and bashers , who go one sentence at a time and do not move on until the sentence is right. He counted himself a basher. The ladder is not a description of either habit. It is an order of decisions, and a basher who settles each sentence before the next has settled, in her head and before the sentence, what the book is and where the sentence stands in it; when she cannot, she stops. The chapter’s order describes dependence, which holds however the decisions are reached. The period caveat applies as it does throughout the book. The ladder assumes a novel of the kind the earlier chapters model, built on wants, decisions and causes, in which the shape of the whole can be read from a sequence of scenes. A book whose unit is the voice rather than the scene, or whose meaning lies in a pattern rather than a change, still has an order of dependence, but its rungs hold different decisions, and its sentences may sit higher in that order than this chapter puts them. See also: the full treatment , section 2, with each strand at greater length and its sources.

title: 4. The Taxonomy
text: The revision ladder has five rungs. Each holds a set of decisions, the instruments from earlier chapters that test them, and the symptoms readers report when they fail. The rungs are ordered by dependence: a decision on a rung can make decisions on the rungs below it wrong, and cannot make those above it wrong. The order is a claim about novels of the kind this book models, and The Mechanism says where it bends. Rung 1: the promise The first rung holds the promise : what kind of book this is, what question its choices answer, and what it declines to answer. Its decisions are the genre and its core promise, kept, varied or declined, from Series and Genre (Chapter 17); whether the book is a standalone or a volume of a series, from the same chapter; the governing thematic question and the answer each major character gives it, from Arc and Theme ’s answer map (Chapter 12); and the contracts the opening will make, from The Opening Pages (Chapter 9), taken here as decisions about what the book owes rather than as pages. The instruments are the promise inventory and the answer map. A writer should be able to state the rung in two sentences: what the reader is promised, and what question the book’s choices answer. A change on this rung reopens everything below it, which is why it is checked first and changed reluctantly. It fails in symptoms that readers seldom locate: an ending that was “not what the book promised”, a book that “didn’t know what it wanted to be”, and, less obviously, a middle that sags because nothing in the book’s question makes one outcome more urgent than another. Rung 2: allocation and arrangement The second rung holds allocation and arrangement : whose book it is, how many stories it tells, in what order of time, and in what form. Its decisions are the viewpoint grant of The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13) (which minds, for how much of the book, from when); the threads and their convergence of The Subplot (Chapter 14); the arrangement of times of Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture (Chapter 8), with its order chart and strand table; whether the book has a prologue, by The Prologue ’s double test (Chapter 10); and the book’s form, the person and tense of its narration, its divisions, and any frame, apparatus or repeated pattern it declares. The instruments are the admission test, the convergence test, the order chart, the strand table and the form audit described at the end of this file. A change on this rung moves whole stretches of the book, so it reopens every rung below for the units it moves. Its symptoms are the reader who could not tell the viewpoints apart, who preferred the subplot, who skimmed one timeline or did not know when she was, or who took the prologue for a different book. Rung 3: the shape The third rung holds the shape of the whole: where the protagonist’s change is located, how the middle narrows, when each fact is disclosed, and what the ending spends. Its decisions are the arc, located by Arc and Theme ’s criterion log (Chapter 12) at the decision where the character’s rule for choosing changes; the middle, narrowed according to The Middle ’s option list (Chapter 11) and checked for repetition by its value-shift log; the schedule of reveals, set by The Reveal ’s disclosure map (Chapter 15) and tested by its double-reading table; and the ending, audited by The Ending ’s plant audit (Chapter 16) and its last-decision rule. These four are one rung because they depend on one another sideways: moving a reveal changes what the middle narrows, and moving the arc’s decision changes what the ending must pay. They are checked together, in the order middle, arc, reveal, ending, since the ending depends on all three. A change on this rung reopens the joins and scenes near the decisions it moves. Its symptoms are the classic reports on a draft: the middle drags, the protagonist does not change or changes from nowhere, the twist was guessed or felt like a cheat, the ending fell flat or was too tidy. Rung 4: the joins The fourth rung holds the joins , the places where one unit of the book meets the next: chapter breaks, by The Chapter Break ’s statement (Chapter 6) of what each chapter proposes and how its ending prices stopping; transitions across gaps, by The Transition ’s count (Chapter 5) of what changes; cutaways into the past, by Backstory and Flashback ’s compression check (Chapter 7) and its rules for the trigger and the way back; and the opening pages, by The Opening Pages ’s contracts (Chapter 9) as written. The opening is treated as a join because it joins the reader to the book, and it is revised last of the joins, after every decision it must promise has been made. A change on this rung reopens the openings and closings of the scenes on either side. Its symptoms are local but global in effect: a book that readers call relentless or slow when no scene is at fault, a reader who stalls after scene breaks, flashbacks skimmed, a first chapter put down. Rung 5: the scene and its materials The last rung holds the scene and its materials : what each scene changes, by The Purposes of a Scene ’s two-sentence statement (Chapter 1) and its five registers; how scene and sequel link, by Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2); what each exchange of dialogue does, by The Dialogue Exchange (Chapter 3); and which details are named, by The Descriptive Detail (Chapter 4). The line edit follows this rung. A change here reopens nothing above it, which is the reason the sentences come last: they can be revised without disturbing any other decision, and every other decision can disturb them. The ladder in one table The table gathers the five rungs with their instruments and the symptoms that most often bring a writer to each. It is a summary of the paragraphs above, not a substitute for the chapters it names. Rung Decisions Instruments Typical symptoms 1 Kind of book, governing question, what is declined, standalone or series Promise inventory ( Series and Genre , Chapter 17), answer map ( Arc and Theme , Chapter 12), contracts as decisions ( The Opening Pages , Chapter 9) “Not what it promised”; “didn’t know what it wanted to be” 2 Viewpoint grant, threads, order of times, prologue, form Admission test ( The Viewpoint Shift , Chapter 13), convergence test ( The Subplot , Chapter 14), order chart and strand table ( Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture , Chapter 8), double test ( The Prologue , Chapter 10), form audit ( The Structural Edit , Chapter 18) Viewpoints indistinct; subplot preferred; lost in time; prologue resented 3 Arc, middle, reveals, ending Criterion log ( Arc and Theme , Chapter 12), option list ( The Middle , Chapter 11), disclosure map ( The Reveal , Chapter 15), plant audit ( The Ending , Chapter 16) Middle drags; no change; twist guessed; ending flat 4 Chapter breaks, transitions, cutaways, opening pages Ending types ( The Chapter Break , Chapter 6), count of change ( The Transition , Chapter 5), compression check ( Backstory and Flashback , Chapter 7), contracts as written ( The Opening Pages , Chapter 9) Relentless or slow; stalls at breaks; flashbacks skimmed; first chapter put down 5 Scenes, sequels, exchanges, details Two-sentence statement ( The Purposes of a Scene , Chapter 1), the six beats ( Scene and Sequel , Chapter 2), the domains of the exchange ( The Dialogue Exchange , Chapter 3) and of the detail ( The Descriptive Detail , Chapter 4) Nothing happens; flat talk; description that tells nothing Read across a row, the table says where to look; read down a column, it shows how much of the book each rung governs, which is the reason for the order. The symptoms column is a first guess, since a symptom felt on one rung is often caused on a higher one. Proposals from earlier chapters The Ending (Chapter 16) proposed a sixth domain of the ending, formal closure: the completion, modification or disruption of a book’s structural pattern rather than its story, such as the returned frame or the apparatus that follows the narrative. It adopted the domain for diagnosis, conceding the objection that formal closure is a means by which the other domains are served rather than something the reader receives, and left this chapter to adopt or reject it when it audits the form of a whole book, with Nineteen Eighty-Four ’s Appendix and the last episode of Six Feet Under as test cases. This chapter rejects formal closure as a domain of the ending and adopts it at the scale of the book as the form audit , a test on rung 2: for every formal pattern a book declares, its person and tense, its divisions, any frame, apparatus or repeated shape, the audit asks whether the pattern is completed, modified for a reason the book shows, or removed from the place where it was declared. Both test cases pass the audit, and both show why the domain belongs there. In the first chapter of Nineteen Eighty-Four a footnote declares the apparatus: For an account of its structure and etymology see Appendix. The Appendix discharges it, and its past tense, written from a time in which Newspeak is history, is received by the reader as a hope the story denied, a thematic and emotional payment. Six Feet Under opened nearly every episode on a death, and its last episode, which opens instead on a birth, ends on a montage of the principal characters’ deaths decades ahead; the pattern is completed and modified at its last instance, and what the viewer receives is the series’ theme, each life shown whole. In both, the formal pattern is the carrier and the payment lies in another domain, so the objection holds at the ending. The Ending ’s defence (Chapter 16), that formal closure has distinct carriers, failures and remedies, holds for the audit: a frame opened and never closed is a decision on rung 2 that the ending has failed to discharge, and the remedy is as often to remove the frame from the opening as to close it at the end. See also: the full treatment , section 3, with every chapter’s instruments and tests placed on the ladder and the ruling on formal closure in full.

title: 5. The Mechanism
text: The mechanism has four parts: a map of the draft made once, an order in which to read it, a list that records each repair and what it disturbs, and a rule for stopping. The book map The book map has one row for each scene and a column for each fact the other chapters’ instruments need. Its first five columns follow the five dimensions readers track; the rest record the novel’s own structure. A map of a three-hundred-page draft takes a day to build, from the draft rather than from memory, and its value lies in being built from the draft: the writer’s memory holds the book she meant, and the map has to hold the book she wrote. Column What it records What is read off it Position Where the scene falls, as a percentage of the text Every instrument that places events in the book Story time When it happens, by date or by order The order chart and strand table ( Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture , Chapter 8) Place Where it happens The count of change at each gap ( The Transition , Chapter 5) Viewpoint Whose mind, if any The grant and the admission test ( The Viewpoint Shift , Chapter 13) Goal and decision What the viewpoint character wants, and what she decides at the end The option list ( The Middle , Chapter 11) and the criterion log ( Arc and Theme , Chapter 12) Thread Which chain of cause it belongs to The convergence test ( The Subplot , Chapter 14) Change The Purposes of a Scene ’s two-sentence statement (Chapter 1), compressed The scene’s purpose ( The Purposes of a Scene , Chapter 1) and the value-shift log ( The Middle , Chapter 11) Learns What the reader learns, and which characters learn it The disclosure map ( The Reveal , Chapter 15) Deposits What it plants, and what it pays The plant audit ( The Ending , Chapter 16) Promise Any convention invoked, kept or declined The promise inventory ( Series and Genre , Chapter 17) A row that cannot fill its change column is the first finding of the edit, before any test is run. A map also gives the writer what no single chapter can, which is a view of the book at a size she can hold: three hundred pages become about ninety rows. One map, many readings The instruments of the earlier chapters are views of the same map. The order chart sets the position column against story time; the strand table groups rows by thread; the option list reads the decision column at three positions; the criterion log reads it for one character from end to end; the disclosure map reads the learns column; the plant audit reads the deposits column backwards from the ending; the promise inventory reads the promise column forwards from the opening. A writer who builds the map once can run every test in the book without rereading the draft, and when she changes the book she changes the map, so that every instrument stays current. This is the practical reason for a single map: the instruments of separate chapters, made separately, disagree with one another as soon as one repair has been made, and the seventeen contradictions found when the household novel’s cases were first set side by side, over where the ledger was first seen, who found it and what each sibling knew, began in that way. The order of dependence, and where it bends The ladder is read from the top for repair and from the bottom for diagnosis. A writer revising works rung by rung downwards, finishing the decisions on each rung before the next, because a decision on a rung can make work below it wrong. A writer diagnosing starts where the reader felt the problem and looks upward. The rung-up rule states the second direction: before repairing a failure, check the rung above it for a cause, and treat a failure that appears in several places on one rung, or that recurs after it has been repaired, as caused above it. The order bends in one way. A writer working on a lower rung sometimes finds that a decision above is wrong: a scene written to fill a gap shows what the book is about, or a cut that was meant to tighten a chapter makes a thread unnecessary. This is upward discovery , and it is common, since writers learn what their books are by writing them. The order does not forbid it; it says what to do with it. When discovery runs up the ladder, the writer stops work on the lower rung, makes the higher decision, and comes down again, because the lower work was done against the old decision and will need checking against the new one. The edit list The edit list records every note and every failure the tests find, one row each: the note and its source, where it was felt, the rung of the symptom, the rung of the cause, the repair, the tests the repair reopens, and its status. The status is one of three: mended, kept and defended in a sentence, or passed to the line edit. Reopened tests are the tests on lower rungs that a repair can make wrong for the units it touches: moving the arc’s decision reopens the option list at the midpoint, the plant audit, the chapter break nearest the decision and the scenes on either side. The list is what keeps the order honest. A repair whose reopened tests are not rerun is the cascade of Failure Patterns . The economy of the repair A scene that does several jobs with one set of material is economical, as The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1) argues, and a repair is economical in the same way when it answers several notes with one change. Repairs differ in economy by rung. A repair on a high rung often answers notes felt on several lower rungs at once, since their cause was shared, and a repair on a low rung answers one note and reopens little. The economy of the repair is the number of notes a repair answers set against the number of tests it reopens and the words it adds. Between two repairs that mend the same failure, prefer the one that answers more notes; between two that answer the same notes, prefer the one that reopens fewer tests; and between two that reopen the same number of tests, prefer the one that moves or cuts over the one that adds. When to stop The stopping rule has three conditions. A pass down the first three rungs changes nothing below them. Every failure that remains on the edit list is kept and defended in a sentence, or passed to the line edit, which The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1) already asks of a scene that fails its tests: its author should be able to say why. And a cold read , by a reader who has not read an earlier draft or by the writer after an interval long enough to have forgotten what she meant, produces notes that do not cluster above rung 5. The third condition is the one most often skipped, and the one that tests the first two, since a writer who has revised a book knows it too well to see what it now does. See also: the full treatment , section 5, with the procedure for building the map and keeping the edit list.

title: 6. Diagnostic Tests
text: The seven tests are tests of the edit, not of the text; the text is tested by the earlier chapters’ tests, run in the ladder’s order. Tests 1 (Map) and 2 (Promise) are run before any repair, tests 3 to 5 (Rung-up, Reopen and Economy) on each repair, and tests 6 (Opening last) and 7 (Stop) at the end. Record a sentence for each, not a verdict. Test 1 — Map Is there a book map built from the draft, with the change column filled for every row? Failure. The writer is editing the book she meant, not the one she wrote. Exception. A writer who settles the top rungs before drafting and drafts in one pass, as Lee Child did with Make Me (2015). Test 2 — Promise Can the promise and the governing question be written in two sentences, and do the first and last chapters answer to them? Failure. Rung 1 is unsettled, and every lower repair is provisional. Exception. A work whose question is found in the edit itself, as Annie Hall ’s was in the cutting room; the test should then fail until late. Test 3 — Rung-up For each failure on the edit list, has the rung above been checked for its cause? Failure. The local repair: the symptom mended where it was felt. Exception. A note local by nature: a wrong fact, a misspelt name, a sentence that says the opposite of what was meant. Test 4 — Reopen For each repair, are the tests it reopens listed, and have they been rerun? Failure. The cascade: a repair that breaks something the writer has not looked at. Exception. A repair inside one scene that changes nothing any other row of the map uses. Test 5 — Economy Does each repair answer at least as many notes as it reopens tests, and does the edit cut or move more than it adds? Failure. The edit by addition, or a repair on too low a rung. Exception. Fitzgerald’s galley revision of The Great Gatsby (1925), which answered one note by reopening three chapters. Test 6 — Opening last Were the opening pages and the last page revised after rungs 1 to 3 had settled? Failure. The page-order edit: an opening that promises an earlier draft. Exception. Andy Weir’s The Martian (2011), whose opening chapters were published before its ending was written. Test 7 — Stop Does a cold read produce notes that do not cluster above rung 5, and is every kept failure defended in a sentence? Failure. The edit is unfinished, or has been abandoned rather than finished. Exception. A cold read whose notes above rung 5 the writer can defend: the stopping rule is then met by the defence. Reading the results together Tests 1 (Map) and 2 (Promise) failing together are the commonest state of a first draft and are not a fault; they say that the edit has not begun. Test 2 (Promise) failing alone, with a map built, says that the writer can see the book and cannot yet say what it is for, and no repair on a lower rung should be made until it passes, however obvious the repair. Tests 3 (Rung-up) and 4 (Reopen) failing together describe an edit that is busy and getting nowhere: notes are being mended where they were felt, and each mend creates a new note elsewhere. The repair is to stop, sort the edit list by the rung of each cause, and begin again from the highest. Test 5 (Economy) failing on one repair is often right, since the repair that mends a cause on a high rung may reopen much; it is a fault when it fails on every repair, which is the edit by addition. Test 6 (Opening last) failing is cheap to mend at the end and expensive to discover after submission. Test 7 (Stop) failing with notes still clustered on one rung says where the next pass begins. From symptom to rung The table lists the symptoms readers most often report, the rung on which each is usually felt, and the rung above to check before repairing it. It is a starting point; the consolidated symptom index in the appendices gives every chapter’s symptoms in full. Reader’s report Felt on rung Check first Chapters “Not the book it promised”; ending resented 3 Rung 1: the promise inventory Series and Genre (Chapter 17), The Opening Pages (Chapter 9), The Ending (Chapter 16) “Couldn’t tell whose book it was” 4 Rung 2: the grant and its declaration The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13), The Opening Pages (Chapter 9) “Skimmed one timeline”; “didn’t know when I was” 2 Rung 1: does each strand serve the question? Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture (Chapter 8) “Preferred the subplot” 2 Rung 1: which question is the book’s? The Subplot (Chapter 14), Arc and Theme (Chapter 12) “The middle drags” 3 Rung 1: is the want urgent? Then the option list The Middle (Chapter 11) “She doesn’t change” 3 The criterion log; rung 1: does the change answer the question? Arc and Theme (Chapter 12) “Guessed the twist”; “felt cheated” 3 Rung 2: who could have told it, and why not? The Reveal (Chapter 15), The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13) “The ending fell flat” 3 The middle; then rung 1 The Ending (Chapter 16), The Middle (Chapter 11) “Relentless” or “slow”, no scene at fault 4 Rung 3: the proportion of the shape The Chapter Break (Chapter 6) “Lost after the breaks”; “skimmed the flashbacks” 4 Rung 2: the arrangement The Transition (Chapter 5), Backstory and Flashback (Chapter 7), Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture (Chapter 8) “Put it down in the first chapter” 4 Rung 1: what the opening promises The Opening Pages (Chapter 9) “Nothing happens in this scene” 5 Rung 3: is the scene needed by the shape? The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1), Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2), The Middle (Chapter 11) “They all sound the same” 5 Rung 2: the grant The Dialogue Exchange (Chapter 3), The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13) “Beautiful, but I don’t know why it’s there” 5 Rung 3: what the detail deposits The Descriptive Detail (Chapter 4), The Ending (Chapter 16) The table has one pattern worth seeing whole: almost every symptom is felt one or two rungs below the rung where a writer should look first, which is the rung-up rule in tabular form. See also: the full treatment , section 5, with the procedure for each test and an extended table.

title: 7. Failure Patterns
text: The patterns below are failures of revision rather than of the text: each describes an edit that does careful work in an order or a manner that undoes it. Each ends with a published work in which the same habit succeeds because the mechanism is absent or has been addressed. The full treatment has a longer catalogue, among them the endless edit, the edit by committee and the rearranged book. The page-order edit Symptom. The opening is the most revised part of the draft and the least like the book. Each pass slows as it goes, and the writer reaches the last chapters tired, with little time left and a list of changes that would require the opening to be revised again. Mechanism. The page-order edit revises the draft in the order in which a reader meets it. Page order is the order of reading, not of dependence, so each page is revised against decisions further on that have not yet been checked, and the opening, which depends on almost everything after it, is revised first. When a later repair changes what the book promises or how it ends, the polished opening now promises an earlier draft. The method fails tests 1 (Map) and 6 (Opening last) of Diagnostic Tests . Remedy. Build the map, sort the notes onto the ladder, and work downwards. Revise the opening pages after rungs 1 to 3 have settled, and the last page with them. Exception. Lee Child’s Make Me (2015), begun from a single sentence and written forward in one draft, without a plan and, by Andy Martin’s account of watching it written, without going back. It succeeds because the series had settled most of the top of the ladder before the first sentence: the hero, his rule for choosing and the promise his readers bring are fixed across the series. A forward draft on those terms is an edit done in advance on the lower rungs only, and Worked Analyses reads it as such. Premature polish Symptom. The writer resists cuts that the map shows the book needs, defending scenes by their sentences. The draft’s best prose is in scenes whose change column is empty, and successive revisions are small. Mechanism. Premature polish is line editing before the top rungs have settled. It costs twice. Polished pages are harder to cut than rough ones, because the work in them is visible and the writer is reluctant to waste it, so polish raises the price of every structural change made after it. And polish hides the absence of change: a scene whose sentences are good reads as finished, which is the problem The Descriptive Detail (Chapter 4) diagnoses in the description that readers call beautiful and cannot say what it told them. Sommers’s students, who revised by substituting words, show the pattern at its simplest. Remedy. No line edit until rungs 1 to 3 pass. Keep a file for cut passages, which lowers the price of cutting without changing the book. Judge each scene by its row in the map before reading its sentences. Exception. Kurt Vonnegut’s novels, written by his account in Timequake (1997) as a basher’s are, one sentence at a time, each finished before the next. His books succeed because a basher’s polish is not premature: he does not move on until the sentence fits decisions above it that are already made, and when it cannot fit them, the sentence stops the book rather than the book accommodating the sentence. The local repair Symptom. The same note arrives on successive drafts in different words. Each repair answers its note, and the reader who made it is no happier. Mechanism. The local repair mends a symptom where it was felt, when its cause lies on a higher rung. Readers report where a problem was felt, and a writer who mistakes that place for the cause repairs a page that was working: she adds incident to a sagging middle whose options have not narrowed, explains a reveal that the pages before it never made ambiguous, or gives a protagonist a paragraph of change because no decision in the book shows it. The symptom moves, or recurs in a new form, because the cause is untouched. The repair fails test 3 (Rung-up). Remedy. The rung-up rule. Before mending any note, write on the edit list the rung where it was felt and the rung above, and run that rung’s test. Sort the list by the rung of the cause, not of the symptom. Exception.
