Charles Dickens’s Great Expectations (1861), whose original ending, in which Pip and a remarried Estella meet and part for good, Dickens replaced in June 1861 with a more hopeful one at Edward Bulwer-Lytton’s suggestion, changing only the last pages. The original was published by John Forster after Dickens’s death, and readers have argued over the two since. The local repair holds because the note concerned the ending’s own decision, on which nothing else in the book depended, so that its symptom and its cause were on the same rung. The Ending (Chapter 16) reads both endings. The cascade Symptom. Revision produces new contradictions. A character knows a fact before the scene in which she learns it, an object is in two places, a date is wrong by a month, and the copy-editor’s list of queries grows with each draft. Mechanism. The cascade is the unrecorded consequence of a repair. A change to one unit alters a fact that other units depend on, and without a map that shows which rows use the fact, and an edit list that names the tests the change reopens, the consequence goes unchecked. Cascades are the commonest product of careful revision, because careful revision changes many units. The seventeen contradictions found when the household novel’s cases were first set side by side are cascades of this kind: who found the ledger, whether Dov knew of the illness, whether Nadia had touched the coat. The repair fails test 4 (Reopen). Remedy. Change the map before the text. When a row changes, read down every column the change touches, list the tests reopened, and rerun them before the next repair. Exception. Dr Watson’s wound, a Jezail bullet in the shoulder in Arthur Conan Doyle’s A Study in Scarlet (1887) and a wounded leg in The Sign of Four (1890). The Holmes stories succeeded with the contradiction, which readers have since treated as a puzzle to be explained. A cascade matters in proportion to what depends on the fact it changes, and nothing in either story depends on where the bullet went. The edit by addition Symptom. The draft grows with each revision. Notes are answered by a new scene, a paragraph of explanation or a line of reflection, and readers of the new draft report it slower than the old and its meaning more stated. Mechanism. The edit by addition answers every note by adding, because addition disturbs nothing already written and is therefore cheap for the writer. The reader pays. Each addition is a new unit with its own joins, a new claim on the reader’s attention, and often a statement of something the book should show: the explanatory paragraph at the head of a chapter, the character’s reflection on how she has changed. It fails test 5 (Economy). Remedy. For every repair, ask whether something could be moved or cut instead; for every addition that stays, find something of equal length to remove. A repair on a higher rung usually adds less than one on a lower rung, since it mends a cause rather than covering a symptom. Exception. Hanya Yanagihara’s A Little Life (2015), a long novel whose editor, Gerry Howard, first thought it would be a better and/or more salable book if 100 or even 200 pages could go , and came to think that it justified its length; Yanagihara held her ground. The book succeeds with its length because the length and the excess are its promise, decided on the first rung, rather than additions made in answer to notes. See also: the full treatment , section 4, with the endless edit, the edit by committee and the rearranged book.

title: 8. Worked Analyses
text: The three readings below are of structural edits that are documented, or of a book written without one; the fourth is a film restructured in the cutting room. Each locates the edit on the ladder: where the problem was felt, where its cause lay, and what the repair reopened. The household revision case follows. F. Scott Fitzgerald, The Great Gatsby (1925): a note on rung 5, a repair on rung 3 Maxwell Perkins read the typescript in November 1924 and wrote that the book was extraordinary and that its hero was its one weakness: Gatsby is somewhat vague. The reader’s eyes can never quite focus upon him, his outlines are dim. He suggested a repair on the lowest rung, phrases, and possibly incidents, little touches that would show Gatsby to be in some active way mysteriously engaged . Fitzgerald made a different repair, in the galley proofs. As Kenneth Eble described it, the revision brought the true story of Gatsby’s past out of Chapter VIII and placed it at the beginning of Chapter VI. The galley text before the revision was published in 2000 as Trimalchio , edited by James L. W. West III, so the two arrangements can be compared. The note was felt on rung 5, as a quality of a character, and its prescription stayed there. Its cause lay on rung 3, in the schedule of disclosure. With the whole truth about James Gatz held for Chapter VIII, where it arrives with the catastrophe, the middle of the book gives the reader rumours and no knowledge, and a figure made only of rumours is dim. Moved to the opening of Chapter VI, the truth reaches the reader after the reunion with Daisy and before the party at which she fails to be won, so that the reader watches the rest of Gatsby’s performance knowing what it is made of. The pages after the move bear the double reading of The Reveal (Chapter 15) for longer, and the narrator gives his reason for the placement at once, as that chapter’s teller rule asks: He told me all this very much later, but I’ve put it down here with the idea of exploding those first wild rumors about his antecedents. The repair fails test 5 (Economy) of Diagnostic Tests and is right. It answered one note and reopened three chapters, which Fitzgerald revised heavily in the galleys, because the note’s cause lay on a rung from which a move reaches everything below. Perkins was right about the symptom and wrong about the cure, which is the pattern of reader’s notes in How It Works . Kazuo Ishiguro, Never Let Me Go (2005): the top rung found last Ishiguro has described setting aside a novel about a group of students twice, in 1990 and again in 1995, before the book that became Never Let Me Go took shape in 2001, when, among other prompts, a radio broadcast about biotechnology suggested what the students were. He has written that at that point I suddenly felt I could see before me the entire story. The account is evidence for the order of dependence at its starkest. The material of the lower rungs existed, a group of young people, a closed community, attachments among them, and it could not be made into a book in two attempts, because nothing above it said what it was for. Once the promise was decided, what the students are and therefore what question their lives answer, the decisions below it became determinate, which is what the entire story reports. The novel’s arrangement follows from that decision: Kathy H., a carer, tells the story looking back from near the end of her own term, and the disclosures about Hailsham’s purpose are made in plain sight, half-heard, as children hear things, because the question is not what the students will learn but what they will do with what they know. The inference about drafts is this chapter’s, not Ishiguro’s; what his account shows is that a rung-1 decision made last can make the rest of a book possible at once. Lee Child, Make Me (2015): a book with no structural edit Child began Make Me on 1 September 2014, with a first sentence and, by his own account of how he works, no plot: I try to come up with a good opening sentence … and go from there. Andy Martin, who watched the book written for Reacher Said Nothing (2015), describes a single draft, written forward. The novel sends Jack Reacher off a train at a town called Mother’s Rest, where he meets a private investigator looking for her missing partner, and builds a chain of discoveries each of which causes the next. The book is not an exception to the ladder; it is the ladder with its top rungs settled outside the book. Reacher’s rule for choosing does not change from novel to novel, so the arc of Arc and Theme (Chapter 12) is decided for every volume, and the promise of the episodic series, set out in Series and Genre (Chapter 17), is fixed before the first sentence. What remains is the lower rungs and part of the shape, and for a book built as a causal chain those depend largely on what came before, not on what comes after: each link of Scene and Sequel ’s chain (Chapter 2) is the consequence of the last. In such a book page order and the order of dependence nearly coincide. Where they part is at the ending, which depends on everything planted; a writer who does not know the end must make it out of what is already on the page, which is The Ending ’s rule (Chapter 16) that an ending may spend only what the book has deposited, in its strictest form. A screen reading: Annie Hall (Woody Allen, 1977) The film was shot under the working title Anhedonia , and its first assembly ran about two hours and twenty minutes. It was built on the associations of its protagonist’s mind and included a murder-mystery strand, material that its editor, Ralph Rosenblum, thought some of the freest and funniest in it. In the cutting room Allen and Rosenblum found that the film’s centre was the romance between Alvy and Annie, and cut it to ninety-three minutes around that. The structural edit happened after the material existed, as upward discovery: the footage showed what the film was about, the top rung was decided, and the strands that did not serve it went, however good. The edit cut its best material on the evidence of the map, which is the reverse of premature polish. The household revision case: an edit in page order The situation. The household novel is drafted from the prologue to the coat, with the decisions of the earlier chapters’ revision cases in place, and three early readers and the agent have sent eleven notes (see The Problem ). Version A, the draft edit. The writer’s page-order pass: a sentence in the opening announcing Elena; a scene at about 45 per cent in which Nadia finds their mother in the flat with a clothes brush; a chapter in which Elena searches the flat; a paragraph at the head of Dov’s chapter explaining its date; the call to Nadia cut from the convergence; a paragraph of Elena’s reflection at the end; two warmths removed. Diagnosis. Sorted onto the ladder, the notes look different. The edit list below gives each note’s rung as felt and the rung of its cause. Note Felt on rung Cause on rung Repair Reopens Status Opening slow; whose book? 4 2: Elena’s viewpoint declared late The doorway at the first chapter break, Nadia in the flat inside the first chapter The opening pages; the first break Mended Who brushes the coat? 5 1: a question of fact declined without a sign, under the mystery mode A sign in the scene in the flat at about 54 per cent Promise inventory; plant audit Mended Middle sags between the pen and Dov’s chapter 3 3: no decision from about 66 to 78 per cent None — Kept and defended When is Dov’s chapter? 4 2: the second instalment of the March strand unmarked Heading 9 March , as the date stands in the ledger Order chart; the break before Mended Ending crowded 3 3: three disclosures reach the sisters at once None — Kept and defended Elena does not change 3 3: her decision at the convergence given in summary Give the decision its moment: her palm on the cover, the call in direct speech Criterion log; the convergence chapter Mended The ledger warm three times; four notes on sentences 5 5 Line edit — Passed Four of Version A’s repairs fail the rung-up rule. The scene with the clothes brush mends a rung-5 note on rung 5 and breaks rung 1, since the mother’s silence is the book’s declined question and the scene gives her a scene. The search chapter mends a rung-3 note by adding a sequence that repeats the empty drawer at the same stakes. The paragraph at the head of Dov’s chapter answers a rung-2 cause with rung-5 explanation. Cutting the call removes the decision that locates Elena’s arc, so that the paragraph of reflection has to state it, and the two repairs together are a cascade and an edit by addition. Version B, the revision. The same notes, worked downwards. On rung 1 the writer decides that the brushing belongs to what the book declines, as the locks do, and that it needs a sign. On rung 2 she moves the doorway to the first chapter break and heads Dov’s chapter 9 March . On rung 3 she checks the option list and the convergence, keeps both defended failures, and finds Elena’s decision present but summarised. On rung 4 she rereads the two breaks the moves touched. On rung 5 she writes the sign into the scene in the flat, where Elena has just said “I’d tell you” : “Dov thinks I come up and brush it,” Nadia said. “Don’t you?” “No.” Nadia folded the tea towel into thirds and put it on the pile. Neither of them asked the next question. She gives the convergence its decision in direct speech, and revises the opening pages last. Version B adds about sixty words where Version A added several thousand, and its two kept failures carry their defences: the stretch from the pen to Dov’s chapter is twelve per cent of the book, a wait before the climax held by the buyer’s deadline; and the convergence is crowded for the sisters and not for the reader, who learned two of its three facts earlier. What the revision has not solved. The sign makes the person who brushes the coat inferable by elimination, since it is not Nadia and Dov thinks it is, and that points at the mother; an act is not an account and does not explain the locks, but it gives her a ritual, which may begin to explain her, and the alternative, cutting the weekly brushing from the coat’s first scene, would cost Nadia’s measure of the days between brushings. The two defences are the writer’s, made by someone who knows the book too well, and only a cold read can test them. The edit list was built from notes on an earlier draft, so Version B itself is unread. The plant audit across the whole book is not rerun here; it belongs to the ending. And the line edit remains, with the ledger’s three warmths. See also: the full treatment , sections 6 and 7, with the Harry Potter series, The Martian , A Little Life and the remix of Arrested Development , and the household book map and edit list in full.

title: 9. Checklist and Exercises
text: Revision checklist Before any repair Have I built a book map from the draft, not from memory, with the change column filled for every scene? Can I write the book’s promise and its governing question in two sentences, and do my first and last chapters answer to them? Have I put every note and every failing test on an edit list, with the rung where it was felt? The order For each note, have I checked the rung above the one where it was felt, and recorded the rung of its cause? Am I working downwards: the promise, then allocation and arrangement, then the shape, then the joins, then the scenes? When work on a lower rung showed me a higher decision was wrong, did I stop and make that decision before going on? Am I leaving the opening pages, the last page and the line edit until rungs 1 to 3 have settled? Each repair Have I changed the map before the text, and listed the tests the repair reopens? Have I rerun those tests before making the next repair? Does the repair answer at least as many notes as it reopens tests, and could I move or cut instead of adding? For every addition I keep, have I found something of equal length to remove? Stopping Does a pass down the first three rungs now change nothing below them? Is every failure I keep defended on the edit list in a sentence? Has someone who has not read an earlier draft read this one, or have I left it long enough to read it cold? Do the new notes avoid clustering above rung 5? Exercises The book map. Build a map of your draft with one row per scene and the columns of The Mechanism . Do it from the draft in a single sitting if you can. Mark every row whose change column you cannot fill, and every column you could not fill without rereading. Two sentences. Write your book’s promise and its governing question in two sentences, without looking at the draft. Then read your first chapter and your last chapter, and write down every place where either answers to a different promise or question. The edit list. Take a set of notes on your draft, from readers or from your own reading. For each, record where it was felt and its rung, then run the test of the rung above and record the rung of its cause. Sort the list by the rung of the cause, and count how many notes share a cause. The reopened tests. Choose the highest repair on your sorted list. Before making it, change the map and write down every test it reopens and every row those tests touch. Make the repair, rerun the tests, and record what they found. The cold read. When you believe the edit is finished, give the draft to a reader who has not read it before, or set it aside for at least a month. Sort the new notes onto the ladder. If they cluster on a rung above the fifth, the next pass begins there.

title: 10. Coda
text: The revision ladder assumes that a novel is a set of decisions, that some of them rest on others, and that the dependence runs mostly one way, from what a book is for, through how it is arranged and shaped, to the joins and the sentences. The book map assumes that a book can be seen whole at the size of a table, and that what readers build as they read, a world indexed by time, place, person, cause and goal, is what a writer must be able to see. Neither describes how a book is written. Books are discovered in the drafting, often from the bottom, and the order of dependence says only what to do with a discovery once it is made: take it to the rung it belongs to, decide there, and come down again. That is the chapter’s argument, and it is the argument of the book’s earlier chapters taken together. Each of them described a unit, from the detail to the ending, and gave a test for whether it works; this chapter has added no test of the text, only an order in which the tests are worth running, since a test passed on a rung whose decisions above are unsettled can be failed again by the next repair. The order explains why careful revision so often makes a book worse, and why the cure is seldom more care. A repair is good only relative to the decisions it rests on, so the quality of an edit depends as much on its sequence as on its judgements. What the ladder cannot do is decide its own top rung. What a book promises and what question it asks are decisions, not diagnoses, and no test in this book makes them; the tests can only show that a decision has not been made, or has been made twice. The household revision shows the limit: its most consequential repair was a decision about what the book declines, and the chapter could propose it but not prove it, which is why it is left, with the book’s other proposals, for the author to confirm. See also: the full treatment , section 8, on the limits of the model; The Ending (Chapter 16), whose plant audit is the last test of the shape; Series and Genre (Chapter 17), whose promise inventory is the first.

The first edition, published in 2026 as Narrative Structure: A Textbook , had twelve chapters. This second edition, also of 2026, is revised for practising novelists and retitled. It adds six new chapters ( Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture , Chapter 8; The Middle , Chapter 11; Arc and Theme , Chapter 12; The Reveal , Chapter 15; Series and Genre , Chapter 17; and The Structural Edit , Chapter 18), an Introduction and six appendices, and it is published in two layers: Core, the reader’s edition, and Reference, the full text behind each chapter.

title: The Craft Behind the Story
text: A Systematic Guide to Structuring and Revising Fiction Second Edition. Introduction. This book is for novelists who have a draft, or a plan for one, and want to know why parts of it do not work. It treats a novel as a structure of units, from the smallest that can stand alone, the scene, through the joins between scenes, to the architecture of the whole book and its relations with the books around it, and it gives each unit a chapter. Every chapter says what its unit is for, sets out the ways in which it can do its work, and turns that account into tests a writer can run on a draft, failures a writer can recognise, and a checklist for revision. The Introduction says what the book argues, how its chapters are built, what the invented novel that runs through them is, and how to find the chapter a particular problem needs. Contents The book has four parts and six appendices. The list gives each chapter with the question it answers, which is also its subtitle. Part I: The Scene and Its Materials The Purposes of a Scene What a scene is for, and how to tell whether it is doing it Scene and Sequel How one unit of a novel produces the next The Dialogue Exchange What a passage of talk must do, and how to test it The Descriptive Detail Which true thing to name, and how to test the choice Part II: The Joins The Transition How to carry a reader across a gap, and how much to spend doing it The Chapter Break Where to cut, and what the reader holds if she stops there Backstory and Flashback When to leave the present, in what register, and what to bring back Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture Which time the reader is in, and why it is that one Part III: The Architecture of the Whole The Opening Pages What the first pages of the main narrative owe the reader, and how to tell whether they pay it The Prologue What a separated opening must prove, and how to tell whether it has The Middle Where a book’s possibilities are narrowed Arc and Theme Who changes, and what the change argues The Viewpoint Shift Who is granted a mind, how many, and when The Subplot What a second story costs, and what it must supply The Reveal What the reader learns late, and what it must change The Ending What the last pages may spend, and what they owe Part IV: Beyond the Book and Into Practice Series and Genre Promises the reader brings to a book, and promises she carries out of it The Structural Edit In what order to revise a whole book, and when to stop The appendices gather what the chapters leave in eighteen places. Appendix A is the consolidated glossary of the book’s terms. Appendix B is the symptom index, which starts from what a reader reported and leads to the chapter, test or failure pattern that explains it. Appendix C is the master checklist, every chapter’s revision checklist in the order in which a structural edit uses them. Appendix D summarises the invented novel that runs through the book, with every element traced to the chapter that plants it and the chapter that pays it. Appendix E says what each chapter’s instruments become in the short story and the novella. Appendix F is the test index, every chapter’s diagnostic tests with the question each asks, for comparing tests across the book. This Introduction The Introduction has five parts. This page is the first, and the other four are these. The Book’s Argument What the book claims, how its four parts divide the novel, and the ideas the chapters share How the Chapters Work The eleven parts of a chapter, the two layers of the book, and its conventions The Household Novel The invented novel that every chapter revises Reading Routes Where to start with a draft, a plan, a course or a single problem A writer with a problem in hand can go straight to the last part, which says where to start; the first three can be read afterwards, or not at all, since every chapter is written to be read on its own.

title: 1. The Book's Argument
text: Units and their work A finished novel is read as a continuous experience, and most of the advice a writer receives treats it that way, as a matter of pace, voice or tension felt across the whole. Revision cannot work on a whole. It works on parts: a scene cut, a chapter moved, a viewpoint withdrawn, a reveal brought forward. This book starts from that fact. It divides the novel into the units a writer can act on, and asks of each one the same question, which the first chapter, The Purposes of a Scene , puts to the scene: what is it for, and how can a writer tell whether it is doing it? The answer the book gives for every unit has the same shape. A unit is a stretch of text, or a decision about the arrangement of text, that a writer can add, cut, move or change without rewriting everything else: a scene, a passage of dialogue, a detail, a transition, a chapter break, a cutaway to the past, a strand in another time, an opening, a prologue, a middle, an arc, a viewpoint, a subplot, a reveal, an ending, a genre’s promise. Each unit costs the reader something, in attention, orientation or patience, and each must repay the cost by doing work the reader would miss if the unit were gone. The work can be done in several registers at once, which the chapters call domains , and a unit that does two or three jobs with one piece of material earns its place more cheaply than one that does a single job alone. The chapters call that economy multiplicity , and it recurs more often than any other principle in the book: the first chapter, The Purposes of a Scene , introduces it for the scene, and it appears in thirteen of the eighteen chapters. A unit of a novel earns its place by changing something the reader would miss, and it is diagnosed by asking what it costs, what it does, and whether another unit could do the same work more cheaply. That claim is the book’s governing argument. Each chapter restates it for its own unit, and each one gives it a practical form: a test a writer can run on a draft, and a table or chart on which the test is run. The four parts The parts follow the scale of the units, from the smallest to the largest and then outward. Part I, The Scene and Its Materials , treats the scene and what it is made of. The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1) defines the scene by the change it makes (the value shift , a charged value moving from one state towards its opposite) and introduces the domains and multiplicity. Scene and Sequel (Chapter 2) divides the unit in two, the scene and the reflective sequel in which a character absorbs a setback and decides, and shows how a decision becomes the next scene’s goal, so that events read as having had to happen next. The Dialogue Exchange (Chapter 3) treats the passage of talk, whose work happens largely in what speakers imply, and The Descriptive Detail (Chapter 4) the detail, whose work begins with the choice of one true thing out of many. Part II, The Joins , treats what lies between units. The Transition (Chapter 5) treats the writing on either side of a gap in time, place or viewpoint, and prices it by how many things the gap changes. The Chapter Break (Chapter 6) treats the point at which a reader may stop, and the price the last sentence before it sets on stopping. Backstory and Flashback (Chapter 7) treats the passage that leaves the present for the past, and Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture (Chapter 8) the book that is arranged in more than one time, so that the order of telling becomes its main instrument. Part III, The Architecture of the Whole , treats the decisions that shape a book entire. It begins at the book’s first boundary, with The Opening Pages (Chapter 9) and The Prologue (Chapter 10), passes through The Middle (Chapter 11), Arc and Theme (Chapter 12), The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13), The Subplot (Chapter 14) and The Reveal (Chapter 15), and ends at the second boundary, The Ending (Chapter 16). The opening and the ending are inverses. The opening works with no accumulated context and must win trust from nothing; the ending works with nothing but accumulated context, and may spend only what the book has deposited. Part IV, Beyond the Book and Into Practice , steps outside the single book in two directions. Series and Genre (Chapter 17) treats the promises a reader brings to a book from its genre and carries out of it into a series. The Structural Edit (Chapter 18) treats the revision of a whole draft, and puts every earlier chapter’s instruments in the order in which a revision should use them: first what the book promises, then whose book it is and how its times and threads are arranged, then its shape, then its joins, and its scenes and their materials last. Ideas the chapters share The chapters are written to be read alone, but they are a book rather than a collection because a small number of ideas are introduced once and used throughout. The table gives the principal ones, the chapter that introduces each, and the chapters that use it in their own instruments; it was compiled by searching the chapters’ texts for each idea, and lists the chapters whose arguments draw on it. chapter’s instruments Several chapters also divide one problem between them, and a writer who knows the division can tell which chapter a problem belongs to. Three chapters divide the gap: The Transition (Chapter 5) owns how a gap is crossed, The Chapter Break (Chapter 6) where it is placed, and The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13) who stands on the other side of it. Backstory and Flashback (Chapter 7) and Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture (Chapter 8) divide the past: a passage of past material that recurs without a question of its own is a cutaway, judged by the first, and one that recurs in a declared pattern and runs on its own question is a strand, judged by the second. The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13) and The Subplot (Chapter 14) divide the reader’s attention, the first by minds, the second by threads, and both treat attention as a budget that every addition draws on. The Opening Pages (Chapter 9) and The Ending (Chapter 16) divide trust, minted at one boundary and spent at the other, and The Reveal (Chapter 15) and The Ending divide what the reader learns late, the reveal changing what the earlier pages meant, the ending changing what the whole book meant. The models are heuristics Every model in the book is a heuristic, a rule of thumb for noticing, and none is a law. The evidence is in the chapters themselves, each of which pairs every failure it describes with a published work that commits the failure and succeeds. Pride and Prejudice opens on a general statement rather than a character; Anna Karenina runs for the length of a long novel’s part after its heroine’s death; Middlemarch has no subplot in the sense The Subplot (Chapter 14) defines, because it has four plots. A model that ruled these books out would be reporting its own limits, and the chapters say so where it happens. What the instruments do reliably is turn a vague dissatisfaction into a question that can be answered. This isn’t working becomes the voice contract is undischarged , or this thread’s turning points are satellites, not kernels , or the middle’s setbacks leave the protagonist’s options where they were . A writer who can name the question can decide whether the book should answer it or whether the book has a reason to break the rule, and the second decision is the one the counterexamples are there to teach. See also: How the Chapters Work , on the parts every chapter shares; The Structural Edit (Chapter 18), where the instruments are put in order.

title: 2. How the Chapters Work
text: The eleven parts of a chapter Every chapter is built on the same plan, so that a reader who has used one can find her way in any other. It opens with a page headed In brief , which states the chapter’s claim and its tools in about a hundred and fifty words and says when to use them, followed by what a reader can do after the chapter, its key terms and its contents. The chapter proper then runs in ten parts. The Problem opens on a draft that fails, usually a draft of the invented novel described in The Household Novel , sometimes a published book, and states the chapter’s claim. Definitions fixes the unit and separates it from its neighbours, and says what the chapter leaves to other chapters. How It Works gives only the theory the method uses, and each strand of it opens with the practical question it answers before it names the theorist who answered it. The Taxonomy sets out the kinds of the unit or the domains of its work. The Mechanism explains how the unit does what it does, and how one unit can do several things at once. Diagnostic Tests puts the chapter’s tests on a page, each with the question it asks, what a failure usually means and one exception. Failure Patterns describes four or five recurrent failures, each as a symptom, a mechanism, a remedy and an exception: a published work that commits the failure and succeeds. Worked Analyses reads three or four published books closely, usually with one film or television case, and ends with the household revision case, in which a draft is diagnosed and revised and the revision’s remaining weaknesses are named. Checklist and Exercises gives the revision checklist and exercises for a writer’s own draft. The Coda ends on the chapter’s argument, and usually on what its model cannot do. The tests are the working centre of each chapter. Their number follows the material, from seven to ten, and each is framed as a question a writer can answer from a draft without outside help. A test that fails does not prove a fault. It locates a place where the book does something the model does not expect, and the writer must then decide whether the book has a reason; the exception attached to each test, and the exception attached to each failure pattern, are there to show what a reason looks like. Two layers The book has two layers. Core , which this Introduction opens, is the reader’s edition: eighteen chapters of about eleven thousand words each, written for use at the desk. Reference holds the full text behind each chapter. For the twelve chapters revised from the first edition, Reference is that edition’s full chapter, corrected, renumbered and brought into line with this one, with its longer theory, its complete catalogue of failure patterns, further close readings, the unit across forms, a glossary, sources, further reading, and exercises, seminar questions and an assessment rubric for teachers. For the six chapters new to this edition, Reference holds a single Full Treatment of up to eight thousand words, with the extended catalogue, further analyses, the household case in full, a glossary and the sources. Core links into Reference wherever a reader may want the full catalogue, the evidence or the longer argument, and the See also line at the end of each part says where. Reference never depends on Core: each Reference chapter can be read on its own. Conventions A few conventions hold across the book, and knowing them saves a reader from misreading a term or an example. Terminology. Each technical term has one sense in this book and is explained where it is first used. Where two chapters of the first edition used one word for two ideas, this edition gave each idea its own name. A beat is the smallest unit of change in a scene ( The Purposes of a Scene , Chapter 1) or one of six named functions of the scene and sequel ( Scene and Sequel , Chapter 2); the action set between turns of dialogue is an action beat ( The Dialogue Exchange , Chapter 3). Compression is the fitting of page-space to the weight of what happened ( Scene and Sequel , Chapter 2); the effect of restricting the space given to a character is character compression ( The Viewpoint Shift , Chapter 13). The hinge is the point at which a character’s grounds for choosing change ( Scene and Sequel , Chapter 2; Arc and Theme , Chapter 12); a chapter ending whose last sentence changes the meaning of the chapter it closes is a recasting close , and a character with business in two plots is a crossing character . A sequel is always the reflective half of Swain’s scene–sequel pair, and a follow-up volume is a series instalment . The glossary gives every term with links to the places it is defined. Proposals and rulings. Most chapters propose one category beyond the established ones, a sixth domain of an ending, say, or a seventh kind of transition, and argue for it against the strongest objection. A proposal survives only if a later chapter, meeting the same problem at a larger scale, adopts or rejects it, and the ruling is recorded in both chapters’ taxonomies. The proposals are therefore not decorations; each is a claim the book tests on itself. Examples. Each chapter reads classic novels alongside recent ones: across its Core and Reference text, at least four novels published since 2000, of which at least two are commercial or genre fiction, and at least two films or television series. Genre and commercial fiction are treated as forms with their own disciplines, which the chapters describe in the same terms as any other. The examples were chosen because they are likely to stay in print and in discussion, and a reader who does not know one can follow the argument from the chapter’s description, which never depends on having read the book. Translation. Some of the novels read closely are translations. The book’s rule for them is that structural claims survive translation and texture claims do not. What happens, in what order, who knows what and when, where a chapter ends: these are the same in any competent translation, and the chapters make such claims freely. The rhythm of a sentence, the connotation of a word or the effect of a particular phrasing belong to the translator’s language, so a claim about them is a claim about one translation, and the chapters name the translator wherever they make one. Period. The conventions the chapters describe are those of the novel in English and in the European traditions most read in it, chiefly from the eighteenth century to the present. Where a convention belongs to a period, such as the Victorian ending that settles every fate or the serial’s chapter that ends on a danger, the chapter says so. A writer working in another tradition should treat the models as one tradition’s account of the novel, not as the form’s. Evidence and quotation. Claims about readers rest on published research, which the chapters cite, or are marked as conjecture. Quotation from works in copyright is brief, usually a phrase or a sentence, and longer passages are described. The book’s English is British. See also: The Book’s Argument , on the ideas the chapters share; Reading Routes , on where to begin.

title: 3. The Household Novel
text: One invented book Every chapter revises the same invented novel, so that a reader can watch the book’s instruments work on one body of material and see each chapter’s repair take its place among the others. The novel is a quiet contemporary novel of family life, British in setting and register, and its subject is what a family withholds from itself. A father kept the ledger of a small shop for eleven years, in a careful slanting hand with crossed sevens. He used a fountain pen, the good pen, for the ledger only. He was ill, wrote the illness into the ledger, with dates and a doctor’s name, and told nobody. He died in March. After his death the mother changed the shop’s locks, and she never says why. Four months later his three adult children are working out what happened from the objects he left. Elena, who drives a truck and has had a key to the shop since she was twelve, learns in her brother’s doorway that the key no longer fits, and wants to know why. Nadia, who counts things, watches the dust gather on her father’s coat on its hook in the flat above the shop and has learned not to touch it. Dov, the brother, gave Elena the new key and kept the reason to himself; he has been writing in the ledger since the evening of 9 March, when his father’s last entry broke off, and he is selling the shop without telling his sisters. The book opens with a prologue on the father’s last ordinary day, on which he pockets the good pen and cannot say why. Its main narrative is told in close third person and divided between Elena and Nadia. Dov is seen only from outside, except in one bounded chapter, the evening of 9 March, near the climax. The mother is never given a viewpoint. The book ends with the three siblings reading the ledger together in the shop, and with Nadia going up to the flat and putting on the coat. How the chapters use it Each chapter’s household case works the same way. A first draft of some passage, called Version A, fails the chapter’s tests in a way the chapter can diagnose; a revision, Version B, repairs it; and the case ends by naming what the revision has not solved. The revisions are consistent with one another because a single record of the book’s facts governs them: who knows what when, what each object looks like and where it lives, and in what order the scenes occur. Appendix D summarises that record. The cases accumulate. The descriptive-detail chapter plants the ledger as an unemphatic object near the coat; the chapter-break chapter has Elena find it and see that the hand changes at 9 March; the viewpoint chapter gives Dov his one chapter and shows whose the second hand is; the ending pays the plants off. The chapters new to this edition revise the book further. The middle chapter places the scenes between the discovery of the ledger and Dov’s chapter; the arc chapter gives Elena a decision at the convergence; the reveal chapter decides when the father’s illness reaches the reader; the multi-timeline chapter charts the book’s two times; the genre chapter decides what the book promises; and the structural-edit chapter takes a set of readers’ notes on the whole draft and sorts them by where their causes lie. Each of these later revisions is offered as a proposal, argued for and left, as an editor’s proposal is left, for the author to accept or decline. The ending audits the whole: every element the ending relies on is traced back to the chapter that planted it, to show that nothing load-bearing arrives for the first time on the last pages. One element is unresolved by design. The mother’s reason for changing the locks is never given, and the book’s later chapters treat that silence as a question the book visibly declines rather than one it forgets. A novel that closed every account would argue that families can be solved, which this one does not believe; a different novelist would write the other book, and the chapters say what that choice costs. See also: Appendix D , with the people, objects, timeline, scene order and the full table of plants and payoffs; The Ending (Chapter 16), where the plant audit is run.

title: 4. Reading Routes
text: With a full draft A writer with a complete draft and readers’ notes should start with The Structural Edit (Chapter 18). It shows how to build a map of the draft, one row per scene, and how to sort the notes by the level at which each problem’s cause lies, so that the revision begins with the decisions everything else rests on. The chapter’s table from symptom to cause leads into Appendix B , the symptom index, which takes a reader’s complaint ( it drags in the middle , I didn’t believe the ending , I couldn’t tell the sisters apart ) to the chapters, tests and failure patterns that explain it. Appendix C gives every chapter’s checklist in the order of the revision. With a single problem A writer who knows where the trouble is can go to the chapter directly. A scene that is busy but inert belongs to Chapters 1 and 2 ; talk that is fluent and empty to The Dialogue Exchange (Chapter 3); description that is accurate and tells the reader nothing to The Descriptive Detail (Chapter 4). Readers who stall after scene breaks, or call a book relentless or shapeless, need Chapters 5 and 6 . Flashbacks that readers skim belong to Backstory and Flashback (Chapter 7), and a timeline readers lose or skip to Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture (Chapter 8). A first chapter readers put down belongs to The Opening Pages (Chapter 9), a prologue they call unnecessary to The Prologue (Chapter 10), and a middle that sags to The Middle (Chapter 11). A protagonist who does not change, or a theme that is stated rather than felt, needs Arc and Theme (Chapter 12); viewpoint characters readers confuse, The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13); a secondary thread that feels like filler, The Subplot (Chapter 14); a twist that is guessed or resented, The Reveal (Chapter 15); an ending that feels unearned, tidy or evasive, The Ending (Chapter 16); and a book that readers say was not what they expected, Series and Genre (Chapter 17). Within a chapter, the quickest route is the In brief page, then Diagnostic Tests , then the failure pattern the tests point to. The theory in How It Works can wait until a test has failed and the writer wants to know why the test asks what it asks. With a plan A writer planning a book, rather than revising one, should read in the order in which a book’s decisions depend on one another, which is the order The Structural Edit (Chapter 18) sets out for revision. What the book promises comes first, in Series and Genre (Chapter 17) and in the contracts of The Opening Pages (Chapter 9). Whose book it is and how it is arranged come next: The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13) on viewpoints, Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture (Chapter 8) on times and The Subplot (Chapter 14) on threads. The shape follows, in Arc and Theme (Chapter 12), The Middle (Chapter 11), The Reveal (Chapter 15) and The Ending (Chapter 16). Parts I and II matter most once there are pages to revise. In a course A student or a writing group should read in order. Part I is the foundation of everything after it, since the value shift, the domains and multiplicity are introduced there and used throughout. The Purposes of a Scene (Chapter 1), The Opening Pages (Chapter 9) and The Ending (Chapter 16) make the strongest single sessions; The Dialogue Exchange (Chapter 3) and The Viewpoint Shift (Chapter 13) carry the most contestable material, and the Reference text of each of the twelve revised chapters includes exercises, seminar questions and an assessment rubric. A course on the short story or the novella can use Appendix E , which says what each chapter’s instruments become in the shorter forms. See also: Contents , with every chapter’s question; the glossary .

chapter: Chapter 1 · The Purposes of a Scene
title: The Purposes of a Scene
text: The Unit of Dramatised Story: Theory, Analysis and Practice The Craft Behind the Story (Second Edition), Reference — Chapter 1. Part I: The Scene and Its Materials. The foundational chapter of the book: the value-shift test set out here is used again by Chapters 2, 3, 4, 5 and 16, the four domains by Chapters 3, 4 and 7, and the account of what a scene costs by Chapter 14. All illustrative passages are quoted briefly for the purposes of criticism and study; full citations appear in §14 . Where a work is read in translation, the translator is named, and the chapter maintains the series’ distinction: structural claims survive translation, texture claims do not. Contents On this page: Chapter Abstract · Learning Outcomes · Key Terms · How to Use This Chapter Introduction: The Scenery Problem Definitions and Boundaries Why a Scene Must Have a Job The Domains of Purpose — plot, character, theme, texture, and a proposed fifth Multiplicity: The Economy of the Scene The Scene–Summary Continuum Diagnostic Method — the ten tests Failure Patterns — with their exceptions Worked Analyses — eight close readings and a revision case The Scene Across Forms · Concordance: concept to scene Revision Checklist Studio Work — exercises, seminar questions, assessment rubric Glossary Sources Cited Further Reading Coda: Against Mechanical Application Chapter Abstract The scene is the smallest unit of narrative that can be lifted out of a novel and still behave like a story. It is therefore the unit at which most structural problems in a draft become visible, and the unit at which they can most economically be fixed. This chapter formalises the working writer’s intuition that some scenes are load-bearing and others merely occupy space, and it does so by asking of each one a single question: what changed? It proceeds in four movements: Theory — why a scene must be answerable for its own existence, drawing on Aristotle’s requirement that events follow one another by necessity or probability, Freytag’s dramaturgy, Lubbock’s scene/picture distinction and its later vulgarisation as “show, don’t tell”, Genette’s account of narrative duration, Chatman’s kernels and satellites, Barthes’s proairetic code, Bal’s definition of an event as a transition between states, and the discourse psychology of situation models and event segmentation. Taxonomy — the four domains of purpose (plot, character, theme, texture), each anatomised in terms of its textual carriers, its characteristic under-delivery and its characteristic over-delivery, followed by a proposed fifth: the relational domain , argued for and argued against. Method — the principle of multiplicity , a twelve-part taxonomy of the scene–summary continuum with Genette’s duration categories as its frame, and a ten-test diagnostic protocol for revision. Application — ten failure patterns, each with a published counterexample; eight close readings of scenes from the European and anglophone novel; a revision case worked through the series’ household canon; and a full apparatus of exercises, glossary, sources and further reading. The chapter’s governing claim is that a scene is not a setting containing dialogue but a unit of change with an engine : someone wants something now, something resists, and the state of the story is measurably different at the end. Its governing qualification, developed at §3.7 and again in the Coda, is that the modern preference for scene over summary is a period convention rather than a law of narrative, and that several of the finest scenes in the European novel fail the chapter’s own central test. Learning Outcomes By the end of this chapter, a student should be able to: Distinguish the scene from adjacent units — the beat, the sequel, the episode, the chapter, the set piece, the summary and the descriptive pause — and explain why the distinctions bear on revision. Define dramatisation in terms of narrative duration rather than in terms of dialogue or setting, with reference to Genette’s four canonical movements. Apply the value-shift test to any scene, stating what was true at its start and what is no longer true at its close, and recognising where the test is inapplicable rather than failed. Identify which of the four (or five) domains of purpose a scene actively serves and which it merely occupies. Select deliberately from the twelve modes of the scene–summary continuum, rather than defaulting to full dramatisation. Diagnose the recurring failure patterns by mechanism rather than by surface feature, and articulate the conditions under which each “failure” is the correct choice. Evaluate the historical and cultural specificity of the model itself, including the period-bound assumption that scene is preferable to summary. Key Terms Scene · summary · value shift · the four domains · multiplicity · dramatisation · duration · kernel and satellite · proairetic code · situation model · focalisation · scene and sequel · the relational domain · disnarrated · pseudo-iterative · interiorised scene Full definitions appear in the Glossary ( §13 ). Terms are bolded on first substantive use. How to Use This Chapter Reader Route Purpose Student in a seminar §§1–6 in order, then §9 , then §12 exercises Conceptual grounding, worked models, guided practice Writer in revision §7 (diagnostics) → §8 (failures) → §6.4 (substitution) → §11 (checklist) Fast triage of a live draft, scene by scene Teacher or workshop leader §§4 , 6, 8, 9 for material; §12.1 for assignments; §12.3 for the rubric Ready-made teaching sequence with published examples A caution before beginning. This chapter contains a taxonomy, a continuum, ten tests and ten failure patterns. None of them is a formula. They are instruments for noticing, and their proper output is a question rather than a verdict. A protocol that produces the answer “this scene fails the value-shift test” has done nothing at all until the writer asks why the book might want it to . Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages ) makes the same warning about the contract model; the warning matters more here, because the scene is the unit at which mechanical application does the most damage. A novel revised until every scene passes every test in §7 would be a competent, exhausting and slightly inhuman book.

chapter: Chapter 1 · The Purposes of a Scene
title: 1. Introduction: The Scenery Problem
text: 1.1 An asymmetry between writing and reading Consider two passages from the same manuscript, each about nine hundred words long. In the first, two sisters clear out their dead father’s shop. They talk. One of them makes a joke about the state of the stockroom; the other does not laugh. They find a box of receipts, decide it can wait, and go to get lunch. The prose is exact. The dialogue is plausible. The reader finishes the passage having enjoyed it in the mild way one enjoys competent observation, and remembers, a day later, nothing. In the second, the same two sisters clear out the same shop, and one of them finds a page in the ledger that is not in their father’s handwriting. She says nothing about it. She goes on wrapping glassware, and when her sister asks what she has found, she says “receipts”. The prose is no better. The dialogue is no more plausible. But the reader now knows something the second sister does not, is left with a question the book has not answered, and will read the next forty pages differently. Two consequences follow, and they organise everything that comes after. The diagnosis has to happen in revision. The tests in §7 are useless and actively harmful during composition. They are for the second pass, when the manuscript has become an object rather than a process. Prose quality is not evidence. A well-written scene that does nothing is harder to cut than a badly written one, and is cut less often, which is why manuscripts accumulate them. The most expensive material in a draft is the material the writer is proud of. 1.2 The claim in its strong form The principle can be put in twelve words: If nothing changes, the scene is not a scene — it is scenery. The formulation is deliberately harsh, and the rest of this chapter is largely a matter of establishing what it does and does not claim. It does claim that a stretch of dramatised narrative is answerable for its consumption of the reader’s attention and the book’s length, and that the currency in which it answers is change of state . It does not claim that the change must be large, external, or visible to the characters. The change in The Portrait of a Lady , chapter 42, is that a woman sitting motionless by a dying fire understands her marriage; nothing else in the room alters ( §9.8 ). It does not claim that summary is a lesser mode. A great deal of what a draft calls a “flat scene” is a paragraph of summary that has been inflated into dialogue and blocking because the writer believed that scenes are always better. They are not ( §6 ). It does not claim universality. The preference for the dramatised scene over narrated report is prominent in much twentieth-century Anglo-American craft advice; eighteenth- and nineteenth-century examples show why the model must be used with historical awareness ( §3.6 , §6.5 ). 1.3 Where this chapter sits in the series This chapter is the foundation of the textbook, in the ordinary sense that later chapters depend on its vocabulary. Concept introduced here Where it is used again The value shift — “what changed?” Chapter 2 ( Scene and Sequel ), Chapter 3 ( The Dialogue Exchange ), Chapter 4 ( The Descriptive Detail ), Chapter 5 ( The Transition ), Chapter 16 ( The Ending ) The four domains — plot, character, theme, texture Chapter 3, Chapter 4 and Chapter 7 each adopt them and each propose a different fifth The principle of multiplicity Every chapter in the series Chapter 2 ( Scene and Sequel ) owns the rhythm. Dwight Swain’s division of the dramatic unit into a scene proper (goal–conflict–disaster) and a sequel (reaction–dilemma–decision) is treated there at length, including its origins in mid-century American commercial-fiction pedagogy and the reasons to be sceptical of it. The present chapter uses “scene” in the loose, ordinary sense — any continuous stretch of dramatised action — and refers to Swain’s narrower sense only where the distinction bears on diagnosis ( §6.6 ).

chapter: Chapter 1 · The Purposes of a Scene
title: 2. Definitions and Boundaries
text: 2.1 The unit under study Working definition. A scene is a unit of story, rendered in something approximating real time, in which a character pursues a concrete, immediate objective against resistance, such that the state of the story is measurably different at its end from what it was at its start. Three elements of that definition carry weight, and each is developed later. “Concrete, immediate objective.” Not the story-goal (find out why the locks were changed; get out of the marriage; win the war) but the scene-goal: get him to give me the key; get through this dinner without being asked; find out whether he already knows . Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages ) makes the same distinction for page one, where the immediate want is what carries a reader who does not yet care about the story-goal. “Against resistance.” The most frequently missing component in drafts, and the subject of test 2 ( §7.1 ). A want that meets no obstacle produces activity rather than scene; the resistance need not be a person, and is often the character’s own reluctance, the situation’s shape, or time. “Approximating real time.” This is the technical heart of the definition and is treated at §3.3 . Dramatisation is not a matter of dialogue, or of physical action, or of sensory detail. It is a matter of duration : the rate at which narrative time passes relative to story time. 2.2 How long is a scene? There is no principled word count, and any number given is a convention. Three delimitations are in circulation and answer different questions. Delimitation Typical extent Answers the question The beat 20–300 words What is the smallest exchange in which the balance of power shifts? The scene 400–3,000 words What is the smallest unit that could be extracted and still read as a story? The sequence 3,000–12,000 words What is the smallest unit that completes a movement of the plot? A scene ends when the value it was moving stops moving, or when time, place or viewpoint breaks. 2.3 The term most often confused: summary The commonest terminological error in workshop discussion is the treatment of summary as a failed scene. It is not a failure mode; it is a different narrative speed with different uses, and the relationship between the two is the subject of §6 . Summary is narrated report: a stretch of story time compressed into a shorter stretch of narrative time, told rather than enacted. “For the next three weeks she did not go near the shop” covers three weeks in twelve words. 2.4 Adjacent terms Term Meaning Relation to the scene Beat The smallest unit of change: one exchange, one action, one shift in the balance A scene is a sequence of beats; the term comes from acting and screenwriting practice Sequel In Swain’s model, the reflective half-beat following a scene: reaction, dilemma, decision Treated in full in Chapter 2 ( Scene and Sequel ); see §6.6 Set piece An extended scene of spectacle: a battle, a ball, a storm, a party A scene distinguished by scale and by the reader’s expectation of it; see failure pattern §8.5 Scene (screen) A dramatic unit in more or less continuous time and space; it may contain many shots and cuts Often narrower in time and place than the prose sense; the difference is analysed at §10.3 Kernel / satellite Chatman’s terms for events that branch the story and events that amplify without branching The precise vocabulary for what the extraction test ( §7.1 , test 4) measures 2.5 What this chapter excludes The sequel and the scene–sequel rhythm — Chapter 2 ( Scene and Sequel ). This chapter’s §6.6 gives one paragraph and a cross-reference. The internal mechanics of dialogue — Chapter 3 ( The Dialogue Exchange ), which adopts the four domains and adds a relational fifth of its own. Movement between scenes — Chapter 5 ( The Transition ) for how a gap is crossed, Chapter 6 ( The Chapter Break ) for where it is placed, Chapter 13 ( The Viewpoint Shift ) for who is on the other side. Scenes set in the past — Chapter 7 ( Backstory and Flashback ), which treats the additional burden a cutaway scene must carry to justify the interruption. The allocation of scenes between plots — Chapter 14 ( The Subplot ), whose “attention tax” is the page-space form of the argument made here about the cost of a scene. The special obligations of first, prefatory and final scenes — Chapters 9, 10 and 16.

chapter: Chapter 1 · The Purposes of a Scene
title: 3. Why a Scene Must Have a Job
section: Why a Scene Must Have a Job
text: 3.1 Unity and necessity: the classical inheritance The oldest form of the principle is Aristotle’s, and it is more exacting than its modern descendants. In the Poetics (c. 335 BCE), Aristotle argues that a plot is not unified by having a single hero — the events of one man’s life do not compose a whole — but by the internal relation of its parts. The test he proposes in chapter 8 is a test of removability : the parts of a plot should be so arranged that if any one of them is displaced or removed, the whole is disturbed. Anything whose presence or absence makes no perceptible difference is not a part of the whole at all. That is, in the vocabulary of this chapter, the extraction test ( §7.1 , test 4), stated two and a half thousand years earlier and applied to the incident rather than to the scene. Two further Aristotelian claims bear directly on the model. First, the necessary-or-probable connection. In chapter 9 Aristotle distinguishes the poet from the historian: the historian relates what happened, the poet what would happen, “according to necessity or probability”. The events of a plot must follow one another not merely after but because . Chapter 2 ( Scene and Sequel ) develops this into the causal-chain test — the requirement that each unit could be joined to the next by and so or but rather than by and then . Second, and most usefully, the criticism of episodic plot. Aristotle names the worst kind of plot the episodic : one in which the episodes succeed one another without probability or necessity. He observes, drily, that bad poets write such plots through their own fault and good ones through the pressure of competition — an early acknowledgement that structural failure is often produced by working conditions rather than by incapacity. The modern draft full of well-written scenes that do not connect is an episodic plot in Aristotle’s exact sense. Freytag ( Die Technik des Dramas , 1863) supplies the nineteenth-century engineering version. His five-part structure — introduction, rising action, climax, falling action, catastrophe — is now known chiefly as a triangle in school textbooks, but Freytag’s own concern is with the scene as the place where the play’s forces are transmitted: he analyses the individual scene as a small dramatic movement with its own exciting force and its own turn, and he is explicit that scenes exist to raise or lower the tension by a measurable degree. The modern craft habit of asking whether a scene “goes up or down” is Freytag’s inheritance. So, less happily, is the tendency to think of narrative shape as a diagram — a tendency this chapter resists in §16 . 3.2 Scene and picture: Lubbock, James, and a slogan’s decline Percy Lubbock’s The Craft of Fiction (1921) gave an influential formulation of the scene/picture distinction in English-language criticism. Lubbock, systematising Henry James’s practice and James’s own prefaces (collected in 1934 as The Art of the Novel ), distinguishes two modes of narration: Lubbock’s term What it does Reader’s position Picture (panoramic) The narrator surveys, summarises, generalises across time Listening to an account Scene (dramatic) The action is exhibited, moment by moment, apparently without a mediating teller Watching an occasion Lubbock’s celebrated formulation is that the art of fiction does not begin until the novelist thinks of the story as a matter to be shown — so exhibited that it will tell itself. James’s own instruction to himself in his notebooks was blunter still: dramatise, dramatise. The vulgarisation. By the middle of the twentieth century Lubbock’s distinction had been compressed into a three-word rule — show, don’t tell — which is now the most widely transmitted and least examined piece of advice in anglophone creative writing. What went wrong in the compression was a conflation. The distinction between scene and summary (a matter of duration) was conflated with the distinction between presentation and commentary (a matter of narratorial stance) and with the distinction between the concrete and the abstract (a matter of diction). These are three separate variables, and a rule that collapses them cannot be applied intelligently. “She was angry” is telling in the diction sense; “she had been angry for a fortnight” is summary in the duration sense; “the narrator observes that anger of this kind is always a form of fear” is commentary. Only the second is what Lubbock meant. Booth’s correction should be taught alongside the rule. In The Rhetoric of Fiction (1961), Wayne Booth demonstrated that the showing/telling opposition is incoherent as an absolute: all narrative is told, “showing” is one rhetorical strategy among others, the author’s voice is never actually absent but only disguised, and the modernist preference for effacement is itself a rhetoric with its own costs — chiefly, that a wholly dramatised narrative loses the ability to establish moral distance and can leave a reader without the means to judge what they are watching. Booth’s book is the reason a serious pedagogy of the scene cannot simply say dramatise everything . 3.3 Duration: what “dramatised” actually means Genette analyses duration as the relation between story time (the notional time occupied by the events) and narrative time (the space the text gives them, measured in words or pages). Four canonical movements exhaust the possibilities: Movement Relation Effect Ellipsis Narrative time = 0; story time = n Time passes unnarrated: Three years later… Summary Narrative time < story time Compression; the standard connective tissue of the nineteenth-century novel Scene Narrative time ≈ story time ( isochrony ) The illusion of real time; conventionally realised by dialogue Descriptive pause Narrative time = n ; story time ≈ 0 The text expands while the story stands still This gives the definition of dramatisation that the chapter uses: A scene is the mode in which discourse time approximates story time. It is not defined by the presence of dialogue, or of physical action, or of sensory detail — those are its usual carriers, not its criteria. It is defined by the rate at which the telling moves relative to the told. Proust changed the ratios. Genette’s central corpus is À la recherche du temps perdu , and one of his most striking findings is that summary, the workhorse of Balzac and Fielding, has almost disappeared from Proust: the Recherche is built out of enormous scenes and vast ellipses, with iterative narration doing much of the connective work that summary used to do. This is the single best piece of evidence that scene/summary proportion is a historical variable rather than a constant of the form (§3.6). 3.4 Kernels, satellites, and the code of actions Barthes , in the “Introduction to the Structural Analysis of Narratives” (1966), divides narrative functions into cardinal functions ( noyaux , nuclei) and catalysers . A cardinal function opens, maintains or closes an alternative consequential for the story: the telephone rings, and it will be answered or not. A catalyser fills the space between nuclei — the character crosses the room, lights a cigarette, notices the rain — and can be removed without altering the story’s logic, though not without altering its texture. Chatman , in Story and Discourse (1978), anglicises this as kernels and satellites , and adds the formulation that makes it usable in revision: kernels are branching points , moments at which the story could go one of several ways; satellites are amplifications of a path already chosen. Deleting a kernel destroys the narrative logic; deleting a satellite impoverishes the narrative without breaking it. Barthes’s S/Z (1970) supplies the third instrument, the proairetic code — the code of actions, by which the reader recognises a sequence of gestures as an action with a name (“the Rendezvous”, “the Murder”, “the Departure”) and thereby knows what completion would look like. The proairetic code is the reason a scene generates expectation at all: the reader who recognises the opening moves of a confrontation knows the shape of a confrontation and reads forward to see whether it is completed, deflected or abandoned. A scene that activates no proairetic sequence has nothing for the reader to anticipate, which is the mechanism beneath the vague complaint that a passage “has no tension”. Bal contributes the definition on which the value shift ultimately rests. In Narratology she defines an event as the transition from one state to another state . This is a stronger claim than it looks: on Bal’s definition, an occurrence that leaves every state as it found it is not an event at all, whatever activity it involves. “They talked for an hour” is not an event. “They talked for an hour and afterwards he would not look at her” contains one. Bal’s other contribution is focalisation — the separation of the agent who perceives from the agent who speaks — which supplies the question the four domains cannot ask on their own: whose scene is this? A scene’s value shift is always a shift for someone , and a draft in which the value shifts for a character other than the focaliser is a scene told from the wrong side. Chapter 13 ( The Viewpoint Shift ) treats the general problem; the local form of it is test 1’s supplementary question ( §7.1 ). 3.5 The cognitive strand: what readers actually store Discourse psychologists study how readers build a situation model , a mental representation of the state of affairs described. Rolf Zwaan and Gabriel Radvansky’s synthesis (1998) examines the multiple dimensions such models can represent; related reading studies find that changes in a narrated situation can affect processing: Dimension The reader’s implicit question Domain it feeds ( §4 ) Protagonist Whose experience is this? Character Space Where are we? Texture Time When, and how fast? Texture / Plot Causality What is making things happen? Plot Intentionality What does someone want? Character / Plot The limited inference. Readers can update representations of who is involved, where and when events occur, and what causes or motivates them. That helps explain why a change of state can be conspicuous, but it does not show that a passage without a plot transition leaves no memory. Description, language and mood can also be remembered. Bal’s definition of an event (§3.4) offers a useful comparison, not an empirical proof of the chapter’s value-shift test. A third strand bears most directly on the scene. Work on event segmentation (Zacks and colleagues; Speer, Zacks and Reynolds) finds that perceivers and readers divide continuous activity into events and that changes in a narrated situation, including characters’ goals, are associated with event boundaries. These boundaries show distinctive processing signatures. This supports an analogy between some scene boundaries and perceived event boundaries; it does not establish that every literary scene must end where a measured event boundary falls. 3.6 The historical strand: the scene–summary ratio is a moving variable One qualification applies to every test in this chapter, and it is historical. The preference for dramatised scene over narrated report found in much contemporary craft advice is a period convention , not a technical requirement. The broad comparisons below illustrate tendencies in selected works and schools of advice; they are not measured proportions for whole centuries. Period Dominant proportion Characteristic instrument Eighteenth century Summary-dominant; scene used for climaxes Fielding’s narratorial essays and chapter headings; Richardson’s countervailing “writing to the moment” in the epistolary novel Nineteenth century (realist) Balanced, with heavy summary and descriptive pause Balzac’s inventories; Eliot’s analytic commentary; the omniscient narrator’s right to survey James, Lubbock, and after Scenic ideal codified The scenic method; the dramatised centre of consciousness; effacement of the narrator Modernism Scene expands; summary contracts; ellipsis grows enormous Proust’s dilated occasions; Woolf’s “Time Passes”; Joyce’s single day Mid-century to present, anglophone craft advice Strong preference for scene in many manuals and workshops “Show, don’t tell”; influence from film and television Fielding’s practice is not incompetence. Tom Jones (1749) opens each of its eighteen books with an essay by the narrator, summarises months in a paragraph, and reserves full dramatisation for a small number of occasions. The effect is not slackness but authority : the reader is in the hands of a historian of the action who can move at will between the general and the particular, and the rationing of scene makes the dramatised occasions land with a force a wholly scenic novel cannot achieve. A book in which everything is a scene has no way to say this one matters more . 3.7 The first principle, stated precisely — and qualified The value shift. A scene worth keeping moves some charged value — trust to suspicion, safety to danger, ignorance to knowledge, hope to despair, intimacy to distance — from one pole towards its opposite, so that something is true at its close which was not true at its opening. The term and the formulation are Robert McKee’s ( Story , 1997), and the attribution matters: it is a screenwriting concept, developed for feature-length scripts. McKee describes a typical feature-length Archplot as having roughly forty to sixty scenes, rather than a fixed scene count. His own account is more careful than its transmission: he insists that the shift be charged — that the value be one the story has established as mattering — which is what distinguishes a value shift from mere incident. First: the test measures charge , not size. A scene in which the only change is that a woman notices her husband has stopped asking about her day has shifted a value. A scene containing a car chase in which nothing is risked has not. Second: the shift need not be visible to any character. In the great scenes of interiority — The Portrait of a Lady chapter 42 is the chapter’s principal example, at §9.8 — the shift is entirely in the protagonist’s understanding and entirely invisible from outside the room. In the great scenes of dramatic irony, the shift is in the reader’s knowledge and invisible to everyone in the book. Third: some scenes resist a narrow application of the test and are indispensable. Melville’s “A Squeeze of the Hand” ( §8.1 ) shifts Ishmael’s feelings without advancing the plot; the iterative texture-scenes of Things Fall Apart and the whole class of scenes whose function is to establish the normal against which a later departure will register may need to be judged in relation to the book , not only the local plot. Woolf’s dinner in To the Lighthouse ( §8.10 ) has a subtle value shift of its own. This is why §7.0 insists that the output of a test is a sentence, not a verdict. Fourth: the test is a period instrument. It formalises the assumptions of a scenic tradition running from James through Hollywood to the contemporary workshop. Applied to Fielding, Sterne or Cervantes it produces nonsense — not because those writers were careless, but because they were not attempting the thing the test measures. The correct standing of the principle, then, is this: it is not a standard a scene must meet, but an instrument that makes a writer’s choice visible to the writer. A scene that fails it may be right as it stands; what matters is that its author should know that it fails, and be able to say why the book needs it anyway. The Coda ( §16 ) returns to this and states it as the chapter’s final position.

chapter: Chapter 1 · The Purposes of a Scene
title: 4. The Domains of Purpose
text: 4.0 The model and its status The value-shift test ( §3.7 ) asks whether something changed. It does not ask in what register . That second question is what the domain model answers. The four domains. A scene’s change of state occurs in one or more of four registers: plot (the action changes), character (the person changes, or is revealed), theme (the meaning changes), and texture (the experience changes). The model’s status should be stated plainly before it is used. It is a set of lenses, not a partition. The domains overlap heavily and are not mutually exclusive; a betrayal is at once a plot turn, a character revelation and a thematic statement. The model does not sort scenes into boxes. It supplies four questions to ask of the same scene. Its value is diagnostic and comparative. It converts the unhelpful instruction make this scene better into separable questions with separable remedies, and exposes the difference between a scene that serves a domain and one that merely occupies it. Its lineage is mixed, and worth knowing. The plot component descends from Aristotle and Freytag by way of Swain and McKee; the character component from the twentieth-century pedagogy of the arc; the theme component from Jamesian and New Critical assumptions; the texture component from the descriptive tradition Genette and Barthes analyse. The four are therefore not commensurable — plot and character are properties of the fabula , theme of the reader’s interpretation, texture of the discourse . A tidier model would also be less useful. Its characteristic misuse is the checklist. A writer who sets out to hit four domains per scene produces the overstuffed scene described at §5.4 . The domains are a revision instrument, not a composition target. §4.7 states the qualification formally. Each domain below is set out with its definition, why it matters, its textual carriers, a discussion of its harder cases, its characteristic under- and over-delivery, and illustrations from published fiction. §4.5 proposes a fifth; §4.6 summarises; §4.7 supplies the anti-checklist qualification. 4.1 The Plot Domain — the action changes Definition. A scene serves the plot domain when it alters the causal chain: what has happened, what can now happen, what must now happen. Why it matters. Plot is the domain in which a scene’s necessity is easiest to demonstrate and easiest to fake. It is easiest to demonstrate because a plot function is testable by deletion — remove the scene, and see whether a later scene becomes incomprehensible or unearned. It is easiest to fake because activity resembles consequence , and a scene can be crowded with incident while leaving the causal chain where it found it. This is the domain in which Chatman’s kernel/satellite distinction ( §3.4 ) does its sharpest work.
