Functions and their carriers Function What it does Textual carriers Advance Moves the chain one step towards or away from the story goal An action completed; a journey made; a document obtained; a question answered Complicate Introduces an obstacle, cost or constraint that narrows options A refusal; a deadline; a debt; a third party who now knows Escalate Raises the stakes attached to a conflict already running A threat made specific; a cost made personal; a witness added Turn Reverses direction — a reveal, a betrayal, an irreversible act Aristotle’s peripeteia ; often a single line of dialogue or a single gesture Resolve Answers a dramatic question the book has held open The confrontation held; the letter read; the body found Plant / pay off Places, or cashes, an object, capability or piece of information An object noticed in passing; a skill exercised for another purpose; a name overheard Discussion Plant and payoff are a single function distributed across two scenes , and they are the reason a scene’s plot value cannot always be assessed locally. A scene may be doing almost nothing visible and be indispensable because it places, unemphatically, the object a later scene requires. The corresponding hazard is the unredeemed plant — Rabinowitz’s rules of notice (Chapter 9, §3.2 ) mean that anything given prominence is read as a promise. This is why the extraction test ( §7.1 , test 4) must be run forwards as well as backwards : not only “what would the reader fail to know?” but “what later scene becomes unearned?” Under- and over-delivery Under: the errand. The scene moves a body from one place to another and calls the movement plot. See §8.6 . Over: the pile-up. Three reversals in nine hundred words. Each turn devalues the last, because a reversal is legible only against a stable expectation. Illustrations Dostoevsky, Crime and Punishment (1866), Part One, chapter 7. The murder of the pawnbroker is a plot turn of maximum force, but the structurally decisive event in the scene is the one Raskolnikov did not plan: Lizaveta comes home. A second, unintended killing converts a crime he had theorised into a crime he cannot narrate to himself, and every subsequent scene in the novel runs on the difference. The lesson is exact: the plot value of a scene often resides in its deviation from the character’s plan, not in the plan’s execution. Full analysis at §9.5 . 4.2 The Character Domain — the person changes, or is revealed Definition. A scene serves the character domain when it alters what the reader knows about a person, or alters the person, under conditions that make the alteration evidential rather than asserted. Why it matters. Plot without character shift produces the sensation of watching machinery; readers who abandon competent commercial novels most often report that they “stopped caring”, which is a character-domain failure reported as an interest failure. More technically: the reader’s model of a character is a predictive instrument, and a scene that revises it changes how every subsequent scene is read. This is the primacy effect (Chapter 9, §3.1 ) operating locally. Functions and their carriers Function What it does Textual carriers Reveal Exposes an existing trait through action under pressure A choice made quickly; what the character does with their hands; what they notice; whom they lie to Test Puts a stated belief or value under strain to see whether it holds An offer that costs something; a request from the wrong person; a chance to be cruel unobserved Develop Moves a character one measurable step along an arc A concession; a habit broken; a form of address changed Complicate sympathy Lets the reader like, doubt or reassess someone they had settled A cruelty from the sympathetic; a kindness from the disliked; a plausible self-justification Reveal the gap Shows the distance between a character’s self-account and their behaviour Free indirect style; a stated motive contradicted by a gesture in the same paragraph Discussion Revelation requires pressure, not opportunity. The commonest character-domain error is the scene in which a character is given a comfortable occasion to be themselves: a conversation with a confidant, a moment alone with a memory, an interviewer who asks the right question. Nothing is learned, because nothing is risked. Character is evidenced by cost — what a person is willing to lose, and what they will do to avoid losing it. A scene that reveals character without cost has produced testimony rather than evidence. Under- and over-delivery Under: the trait exhibition. A scene demonstrating a quality the reader has already accepted. Doubly wasteful, since it is also redundant ( §8.2 ). Over: the epiphany. A character understands themselves completely, in language they would not have, at a moment convenient to the chapter’s end. Illustrations Achebe, Things Fall Apart (1958), chapter 7. Okonkwo’s participation in the killing of Ikemefuna is a reveal and a test in one stroke, and Achebe supplies the motive in a sentence of seven words placed immediately after the act: he was afraid of being thought weak. Nothing about Okonkwo has changed; everything the reader understands about him has. Analysis at §9.6 . 4.3 The Theme Domain — the meaning changes Definition. A scene serves the theme domain when it stages the book’s governing question in a form that produces meaning the scene does not state. Why it matters. Theme is the domain most often either neglected or embarrassed, and both responses come from the same misunderstanding: that theme is a message , and that serving it means announcing it. A book’s theme is better understood as its repeated question — what does a person owe the dead? what is a marriage for? what does a system do to the people inside it? — and a scene serves the domain when it puts that question to a character in circumstances where an answer costs something. Functions and their carriers Function What it does Textual carriers Dramatise the argument Stages the governing question in miniature, uncommented A choice whose terms are the book’s terms; a small decision with the shape of the large one Test the thesis Lets a character choose in a way that could undercut what the book seems to argue A sympathetic character acting against the book’s apparent values, and being right Mirror or foil Juxtaposes two characters or events so their difference produces meaning Placement; parallel action; a repeated situation with a different outcome Produce irony Lets the reader know what a character does not, so the scene means two things Dramatic irony; counterpoint; a line whose second sense is available only to the reader Recur Returns a motif under changed conditions so its meaning shifts An object seen again; a phrase repeated by a different speaker; a ritual performed without belief Discussion Counterpoint is the strongest single instrument in the domain , and Flaubert’s agricultural show ( §5.2 , §9.2 ) is its definitive demonstration: two discourses running simultaneously, neither commenting on the other, and the meaning generated entirely in the gap. The technique is available at every scale, from a chapter-length structure to a single line of dialogue landing against the wrong background noise. Under- and over-delivery Under: the name-check. One line of dialogue in which a character says something that sounds like the book’s title. The domain is being decorated, not served. Over: the mouthpiece. A character who exists to articulate the theme. Readers detect this instantly, and the detection costs the character domain more than the theme domain gains. Illustrations Flaubert, Madame Bovary (1857), Part Two, chapter 8. The agricultural show intercuts Rodolphe’s seduction rhetoric with the announcement of agricultural prizes — manures, breeds, a silver medal for fifty-four years of servitude. Neither discourse comments on the other; the novel’s argument about the language of romance is produced entirely by adjacency. Analysis at §5.2 (sentence level) and §9.2 (structure). 4.4 The Texture Domain — the experience changes Definition. A scene serves the texture domain when it alters the reader’s sensory, tonal or temporal experience of the book: where they feel they are, what register they are in, how fast the book is moving. Why it matters. Texture is the domain most easily dismissed by structural analysis and most responsible for whether a book is a pleasure to read. It is also the domain in which the reader’s trust is maintained between kernels: the sense that the world continues to exist when nothing is happening in it. Barthes’s reality effect (Chapter 4, The Descriptive Detail ) is the theoretical account; Auerbach’s discussion in Mimesis of the fully illuminated Homeric foreground against the biblical background “fraught with background” is the historical one. Functions and their carriers Function What it does Textual carriers Establish setting Grounds the reader physically in a place and time Exact nouns; weather with a function; the light; what the room costs Set tone Calibrates the emotional register carried into what follows Sentence rhythm; the narrator’s stance towards suffering; what is found funny Control pace Supplies a breather after intensity, or a quickening before it Duration choices ( §6 ); paragraph length; density of incident Deliver a set piece Provides the spectacle the book has promised and now owes Scale; sustained attention; the accumulation of small precise actions Establish the normal Builds the baseline against which a later departure will register Iterative narration; habitual action; ritual Discussion The last function is the domain’s best defence. A scene of pure texture that establishes what is ordinary in this world is not inert: it is load-bearing for a later scene . Achebe spends chapters on the ordinary observances of Umuofia so that their disruption can be felt as a loss rather than reported as a fact. The corresponding diagnostic refinement is important: the extraction test must be run on the pair, not on the member. Remove a normal-establishing scene and the later scene loses its force — which is the answer the test is designed to elicit, and which a writer running the test only backwards will miss. Under- and over-delivery Under: generic setting. A room with a table in it. The reader is nowhere, and being nowhere costs more than being briefly somewhere unimportant. Over: the runaway set piece. Texture at spectacular volume with every other value sitting where it started. See §8.5 . Illustrations Melville, Moby-Dick (1851), chapter 94. “A Squeeze of the Hand” — Ishmael and his shipmates kneading lumps out of cooled spermaceti — advances no major plot value but changes Ishmael’s feelings: he forgets the crew’s oath and feels affection for his companions. It is a counterexample to a plot-only diagnosis of purpose, and is analysed at §8.1 . 4.5 A Proposed Fifth: The Relational Domain This section extends the four-domain model. The four-domain model has an awkwardness that becomes visible as soon as one tries to use it on literary fiction. Ask what changed in the Hunsford proposal ( §9.3 ), in the doorway exchange between two siblings over a key, in the last conversation between a dying man and the child who will not visit again, and the honest answer is rarely the plot and rarely the person . It is: what is between them . The four-domain model as usually taught accommodates this by placing “realign a relationship” inside the character domain, and the accommodation does not sit well. This chapter proposes promoting it. The relational domain. A scene serves the relational domain when it alters the state of a relationship — the distribution of trust, power, obligation, intimacy, debt or hostility between two or more people — such that subsequent interactions between them must proceed on different terms. Why the relational will not stay inside “character” Two arguments, the second the stronger. 1. Relations change while both parties stay the same. After Hunsford, neither Darcy nor Elizabeth is a different person; both are the same people, holding radically revised information about each other and about themselves. The character domain records what a scene reveals about a person considered singly. It has no vocabulary for a change that is located in neither party and is real in both. 2. The carriers are distinct, and they are not the character domain’s carriers. A person is characterised by what they notice, what they risk, what they conceal. A relation is carried by an almost entirely different repertoire: Carrier What it registers Forms of address Name, surname, nickname, title, no name at all; and any change between them Turn-taking and interruption Who begins, who yields, who is permitted to finish, who repeats themselves Physical distance and orientation Who sits, who stands, who faces away, who touches an object rather than a person Permitted silence Who may say nothing without being asked what is wrong Shared reference Jokes that still work; shorthand that no longer lands; a story one of them has stopped telling Asymmetries of knowledge Who knows what about whom, and who knows that the other knows The right to ask Which questions each may put to the other, and which have become unaskable The argument against The parsimony objection. A relation is not a third thing standing between two people; it is a pair of mental states, one in each. When trust is lost, what has changed is that A now believes something about B. That is a change in A — a character change — and giving it a domain of its own reifies a convenient abstraction into an entity. The four-domain model already handles it: the usual model’s “realign a relationship” is a character function, correctly placed. The proliferation objection. If the relational is promoted on the grounds that it is frequent and has distinct carriers, the same argument promotes several others. Knowledge has distinct carriers and is at least as frequent — the reader’s information state changes in almost every scene. So does situation : the character’s material circumstances, independent of plot causality. A model that admits every well-carried category ends with eleven domains and no diagnostic power. The virtue of four is that a writer can hold four in mind while reading a draft. The boundary objection. Relational shifts are almost always also plot shifts. When Elizabeth refuses Darcy, options close: that is complication in the plot domain. When one sibling stops trusting another, the range of possible future actions narrows: that is complication too. If every relational shift can be redescribed as a plot shift, the new domain is not carving nature at a joint; it is offering a second description of the same cut. The chapter’s position This chapter adopts the fifth domain for diagnostic purposes while conceding that the four capture the majority of revision problems. The practical justification is asymmetric: writers who audit for four domains routinely fail to notice when a relational shift has not occurred, whereas writers who audit for five rarely mistake a plot shift for a relational one. The cost of the extra category is small; the cost of the blind spot is a family novel in which nothing between anybody ever changes. 4.6 Summary table Domain Established chiefly by Under-delivery looks like Over-delivery looks like Plot A choice that closes options; a plant; an irreversible act The errand; recapitulation; advance only Reversal pile-up; visible mechanism Character Behaviour under cost; the gap between account and act Trait exhibition; assertion Epiphany; the confessional Theme Juxtaposition; recurrence; dramatic irony The name-check; unearned universality The mouthpiece; the closed argument Texture Exact nouns; rhythm; ritual; the established normal Generic setting; tone without stance The travelogue; the runaway set piece Relational (proposed) Address, turn-taking, permitted silence, the right to ask Symmetry; statement; the reset Every scene a renegotiation; relationship as sole subject 4.7 Must all the domains be served at once? No, and the model is misused when it is read that way. Two qualifications. 1. The realistic target is two, occasionally three. The common formulation — a scene serving one domain is doing amateur work, a scene serving two or three is doing a professional’s work in the same word count — is a good rule of thumb and a bad rule. §5 develops it properly. A scene straining to hit all five reads as overstuffed rather than efficient, and the strain is legible to readers as authorial anxiety. 2. Domain allocation varies by mode and by position. A thriller weights plot heavily and may serve character only through action; a novel of consciousness may run for pages on character and texture with the plot domain idle; the opening pages (Chapter 9) have additional obligations that displace domain work; a final scene (Chapter 16) is generally required to close in several domains at once, which is why endings are hard. The domains are constant; the allocation is a genre-inflected and position-inflected choice.

chapter: Chapter 1 · The Purposes of a Scene
title: 5. Multiplicity: The Economy of the Scene
section: Multiplicity — The Economy of the Scene
text: 5.1 The principle, stated as a constraint Multiplicity is the practice of making a single unit of text discharge several narrative functions at once. Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages ) treats it as an arithmetical necessity; at scene scale the pressure is lower, and the principle is best stated as an economic proposition. The constraint. A novel has a finite number of scenes. Every scene costs the reader time and the book length. A scene serving one domain has spent a scene’s worth of the reader’s attention to buy one function; a scene serving three has bought three at the same price. The instruction is not “add domains” but “notice which domains are already latent”. Almost every draft scene contains an unexploited second function. The pass looks for it rather than importing one. The discipline is selection, not addition. The writer is not looking for a way to make one scene do five jobs; they are looking for the version of this scene in which the material already present does two more jobs. 5.2 Anatomy: the Hunsford proposal, phrase by phrase The situation: Elizabeth Bennet is alone at the Collinses’ parsonage, having just learned that Darcy separated Bingley from her sister Jane. Darcy arrives unannounced, paces, sits, and says: In vain I have struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you. Four sentences, twenty-nine words. The anatomy: Textual element Functions discharged In vain Character — the declaration opens on the vocabulary of defeat, so the reader learns before anything else that this man experiences love as a failure of self-government. Relational — the first word of the most important speech in the novel is about him. I have struggled Character — pride, and self-regard, in two words. Plot — a struggle implies a duration; the reader retro-fits weeks of resistance and understands that the proposal has a history. Theme — the novel’s question about the relation of feeling to judgement is opened by a man who has treated his own feeling as an enemy. It will not do. Voice / Texture — an idiom of practical dismissal, the phrase one uses about an unsatisfactory arrangement, applied to a passion. Character — the register in which he thinks about his own heart is administrative. My feelings will not be repressed. Character — the passive construction removes him as agent; his feelings act, he does not. Relational — nothing has yet been said to or about her. You must allow me Relational — the first appearance of you , and it arrives as an instruction. Plot — permission is being demanded, not requested, which shapes the refusal that follows. how ardently Character — the one word in the speech in which feeling escapes control. Theme — the collision of ardently with it will not do is the whole man in one sentence. I admire and love you Plot — the proposal is on the table; the scene’s engine is running. Relational — the sequence admire before love preserves the hierarchy the rest of the speech will make explicit. Seven elements; four domains touched; not a word spent on a job another word could have done. Note what Austen has not done: no interiority is supplied, no gesture is described, and Elizabeth is not consulted. The reader’s understanding of Darcy’s condition is entirely a deduction from diction. The scene’s second half performs the same operation in reverse. Elizabeth’s refusal culminates in a sentence that is simultaneously a plot turn, a character revelation, a relational rupture and the novel’s title in dramatic form: …you could not have made me the offer of your hand in any possible way that would have tempted me to accept it. The clause in any possible way is the load-bearing one. Elizabeth is not refusing this proposal; she is refusing the class of all proposals from this man — which is the strongest available statement, and which the novel will spend two hundred pages falsifying. The sentence also closes off her own options, since a woman who has said this cannot later accept without a change so large that the rest of the book is required to produce it. A single subordinate clause has generated the second half of a novel. 5.3 Where the multiplying work actually lives Novice revision looks for multiplicity in metaphor , on the assumption that figurative language is where meanings stack. At scene scale that is almost never where the work is. Four humbler places account for most of it. 1. The physical business. What hands do while mouths talk. A character who goes on wrapping plates in newspaper during a confrontation is supplying texture (the domestic chore), character (the refusal to stop), relational information (he will not give her his attention), and plot (he is packing, which means he has already decided something). Choose the business, and four domains follow. This technique transfers most widely, since every scene has hands in it, and it is the reason experienced writers ask “what are they doing?” before “what are they saying?” 2. The object that changes hands. A key, a ledger or a plate passed, withheld or refused registers power between two people without a sentence of statement. When Dov gives Elena the new key in the doorway and keeps the reason (Chapter 3, The Dialogue Exchange ), the key does the relational work and the withheld reason does the plot work. 3. What a character declines to say or ask. An unasked question is the cheapest relational carrier available, because it costs no words at all. When one sibling does not ask another where he was in March, the omission does character, relational and plot work simultaneously, and the reader performs the inference unaided. The corresponding craft error is the character who asks everything, producing a scene in which all information is extracted and none is withheld. 4. Placement against the reader’s knowledge. A scene the reader enters knowing more than the characters means two things in every line, so dramatic irony multiplies functions without adding a word. Placing a scene after a disclosure rather than before it is therefore itself a decision about multiplicity. 5.4 The ceiling Multiplicity has an upper bound, and the failure at that bound is the overloaded scene. Four symptoms mark it. Symptom What the reader experiences Every line significant No rhythm, only effort; emphasis becomes impossible because emphasis requires contrast Simultaneous wants Four characters each pursuing a distinct objective in one room; the reader cannot tell whose scene this is Illegible primary action The reader can say what is being established but not what is happening Symbolic saturation Every object turns out to mean something, so the reader stops believing in the room The remedy is the counter-intuitive one Chapter 9 states for the opening page and which holds with equal force here: a novel needs scenes that are only doing one thing. They function as rests. A reader who is never allowed to relax cannot register emphasis, and a book in which every scene is a three-domain scene reads as relentless rather than rich. 5.5 Exercise: the domain audit A practical procedure, and the most reliable teaching instrument in this chapter. Take a chapter of the draft and divide it into scenes by the functional criterion at §2.2 — a scene ends when the value it was moving stops moving. For each scene, write one line in a table: its number, its length in words, and the letters of every domain it actively serves : P (plot), C (character), T (theme), X (texture), R (relational). Beside each letter, write the specific change in three or four words. Not character , but she stops defending him . A letter you cannot annotate is a domain the scene occupies rather than serves; strike it. Add a final column: what the scene costs in words. Interpretation: Pattern Diagnosis First move Most scenes carry one letter The draft is spending scenes serially. Length is being used where selection is needed Run the multiplicity pass (§5.3) on the three longest single-letter scenes Most scenes carry four or five Over-pressurised; the reader has no rests Identify two scenes to simplify deliberately A long scene carries X only The runaway set piece ( §8.5 ), or a normal-establishing scene ( §4.4 ) Ask which later scene it is load-bearing for. If none, compress

chapter: Chapter 1 · The Purposes of a Scene
title: 6. The Scene–Summary Continuum
text: 6.1 The decision that precedes all the others Before a writer asks what a scene is for, there is a prior question that most drafts never consciously ask: at what speed should this material be narrated? 6.2 The scholarly frame: Genette on duration The four canonical movements set out at §3.3 give the axis along which the taxonomy runs. Movement Relation of narrative time to story time Reader’s experience Ellipsis NT = 0 Time has passed; the reader infers what filled it Summary NT < ST Being told about a stretch of time Scene NT ≈ ST Present at an occasion Descriptive pause ST ≈ 0 Looking, while nothing moves Frequency. Genette’s third category (after order and duration) concerns how many times an event is narrated relative to how many times it occurred. Three of his four possibilities are in constant use: Singulative — narrating once what happened once. The default. Repeating — narrating several times what happened once. The instrument of The Good Soldier , Absalom, Absalom! and every novel of contested testimony (Chapter 7 treats it). Iterative — narrating once what happened many times. Every Sunday he counted the till twice. The indispensable instrument for rendering a life rather than an occasion, and the one most atrophied in contemporary practice. 6.3 Twelve modes of narrating an event # Mode Description Exemplar Buys Costs 1 Full scene Isochronous rendering, moment by moment, usually with dialogue The Hunsford proposal ( §9.3 ) Presence; the reader as witness; maximum value-shift legibility Length; the flattening of proportion if used everywhere 2 Compressed scene Scene texture with internal ellipses: the occasion is rendered, but with hours removed at the joins The agricultural show ( §9.2 ) Scenic force at a fraction of the word count Requires confident joins; a clumsy join reads as a lapse 3 Scene-within-summary A summarising passage that opens for a paragraph into a rendered moment, then closes again A brief, particular occasion embedded in an account of habitual life The specifying instance: proof that the summary is true Repeated instances can turn a summary into a sequence of scenes 4 Dramatised summary Narrative time well below story time, but written in concrete particulars rather than abstractions Eliot narrating months of the Casaubon marriage Duration and texture; the most under-used mode in contemporary fiction Demands a narrator with an evident stance; impossible in strict effacement 5 Singulative summary Plain report of a bounded stretch of story time For the next three weeks he did not leave the house Speed; proportion; the ability to say this mattered less Nothing is felt; overuse produces a synopsis 6 Iterative summary One narration of many occurrences: the habitual, the customary, the ritual The father’s eleven years of ledger-keeping; Achebe’s observances A life rather than an episode; the normal against which departure registers Suppresses agency; nobody chooses anything in the iterative 7 Pseudo-iterative Iterative grammar, singulative detail Proust’s Combray evenings The atmosphere of habit with the vividness of an occasion Logically incoherent if examined; depends on the reader not examining 8 Descriptive pause The text expands while story time stops The Maison Vauquer in Père Goriot ; Melville’s cetology Density of world; the material argument Modern readers’ patience is short; must be doing thematic work 9 Interiorised scene The occasion rendered as consciousness rather than as action; duration governed by thought The Portrait of a Lady , ch. 42 ( §9.8 ) Change of state at maximum depth with no external event Requires a mind worth two thousand words; fails absolutely without one 10 Tableau An arrested moment, several figures held in relation, described rather than enacted The opening of Bleak House ; the frozen instant before a blow Emphasis; the sense of a significant configuration Halts momentum; a tableau at the wrong moment reads as authorial posing 11 Ellipsis The event is not narrated at all; the reader infers it from its consequences “Time Passes” in To the Lighthouse (Chapter 5 analyses it fully) Enormous power; the reader supplies what the text withholds The reader must be able to reconstruct; an ellipsis over an unguessable event is a gap, not a device 12 Reported scene The event narrated by a character to another character, at a remove Nelly Dean’s narration in Wuthering Heights Reliability questions; a listener whose reaction is itself a scene Two removes from the event; the teller’s presence colours everything Two further modes sit outside the duration axis and are listed because they are so often overlooked as options: # Mode Description Exemplar Buys Costs 13 The subjunctive scene The scene that does not happen: imagined, feared, rehearsed, or explicitly denied Gerald Prince’s category of the disnarrated — what a narrative tells us did not occur Character (what a person imagines is characterising); tension without expenditure Cannot bear plot weight; a subjunctive scene changes no state in the world 14 The documentary rendering The event delivered as artefact — letter, ledger entry, transcript, report The father’s entries in the back of the ledger Authenticity; a value shift delivered without a narrator Voice must be plausible as the document type; no focalisation available Notes on the modes most often forgotten Iterative summary (6) deserves special defence. It is the mode in which a novel says this is how things were . A draft that relies on isolated scenes alone may struggle to convey elapsed time and habit. One Tuesday can illustrate a man’s careful ledger-keeping, but cannot by itself convey eleven years of it. 6.4 How to use the taxonomy: substitution testing The taxonomy’s purpose is not classification but substitution . Its use is procedural: take a scene that is not working, identify the mode it is currently in, rewrite the same material in two other modes chosen for maximum distance from the original, and do not judge until all three versions exist. Take a scene that is not working. Identify which mode it is currently in — almost always mode 1 or mode 2. Rewrite the same material in two other modes , chosen for maximum distance: if it is a full scene, try singulative summary (5) and reported scene (12); if it is a descriptive pause, try compressed scene (2) and ellipsis (11). Do not judge until all three exist. Three outcomes are possible. Outcome Diagnosis The summary version loses nothing The scene was a summary inflated into a scene. Restore the summary, keeping at most a fifty-word scenic instance The summary version loses something the writer cannot name The scene has a texture or relational function the writer had not identified. Name it, then strengthen it The summary version loses something the writer can name immediately The scene is doing its job. Return to it and cut whatever is not that 6.5 Historical drift, and a caution against universalising the present The table at §3.6 sets out how the proportions have moved. Two observations belong here, because they bear on how the taxonomy is used. The first is that the modes have not changed; the fashions in them have — every option above has always been available, and what varies by period is which are unmarked , usable without the reader noticing a technique. The second is that the costs of the default are specific and countable. A manuscript written entirely in mode 1 will exhibit a flattened sense of elapsed time; an inability to render habit, which impoverishes character; the dramatisation of transitional material as errand scenes ( §8.6 ); an even emphasis in which no occasion can be marked as more important than another; and a curious thinness in the depiction of work, illness, marriage and grief, all of which are durational experiences that resist being staged on a single afternoon. The properly critical position. Learn the current conventions well enough to break them deliberately, and read historically well enough to know that they are conventions. A student who can write a good paragraph of iterative summary has an instrument most of their contemporaries have lost. 6.6 A note on the sequel The unit that follows a scene — in Swain’s terminology, the sequel : reaction, dilemma, decision — is the subject of Chapter 2 ( Scene and Sequel ), which treats the model in full, including its origins in mid-century American commercial-fiction pedagogy and the reasons for scepticism about its universality. Only one point is needed here, and it is a point about diagnosis. The two half-beats fail differently: a manuscript with too little sequel reads as incident without consequence, so that things keep happening and nothing lands; a manuscript with too much reads as brooding without motion, feeling without a next move. A scene’s purpose is therefore not only which domains it serves but whether the story is currently due for an action beat or a reflective one , and supplying the wrong kind is an independent failure mode, however well the wrong kind is executed. This is the register test at §7.1 , test 10. For everything else — the six beats, their internal structure, their history and their limits — see Chapter 2.

chapter: Chapter 1 · The Purposes of a Scene
title: 7. Diagnostic Method
text: 7.0 How to use the protocol The ten tests below are for revision, not composition . Applied during drafting they induce paralysis, and they induce it in a particular way: the value-shift test asks a question that can only be answered by a finished scene, so a writer who asks it in the third paragraph will stop writing in the fourth. Applied to a completed draft, chapter by chapter, they are the most efficient triage instrument in this chapter. Two procedural notes. Record the answer, not the verdict. The output of a test is a sentence describing what the scene does, not a pass or a fail. A protocol run that produces ten ticks has taught the writer nothing; a run that produces ten sentences has produced a description of the scene, which is what revision needs. A failed test is a question, not a death sentence. Every one of these tests is failed by at least one scene discussed in this chapter, most of them by scenes that are among the finest in the European novel. The test’s function is to make a choice visible so that it can be confirmed as a choice. 7.1 The ten tests Test 1 — The want test State, in one sentence, what the viewpoint character wants in this scene, right now. Interpretation. A missing want is the most common single fault in draft scenes and the one that most reliably explains a vague sense of flatness. But note the legitimate exceptions: scenes of pure reception, in which something is done to a character who wanted nothing (the arrival of bad news); and scenes in which the absence of a want is characterising, as with Camus’s Meursault (Chapter 9, §9.4 ). In both cases the writer should be able to say which exception applies. Test 2 — The resistance test Complete the sentence: “___ wants ___, and ___ is in the way.” Interpretation. An unresisted want produces activity rather than scene, and the resulting passage tends to be short, pleasant and forgettable. The most frequent draft error is nominal resistance: an obstacle exists but is overcome without cost, so the scene has the shape of conflict and none of its consequences. The follow-up question is therefore: what did getting it cost? If the answer is nothing, the resistance was ornamental. Failure pattern §8.8 treats this at length, together with the important counter-case in which a want is granted immediately and the granting is itself the disaster. Test 3 — The value-shift test Name what is true at the scene’s start and what is no longer true at its close. Procedure. Write two sentences in parallel, in the same grammatical form. Start: Nadia believes the ledger stopped when her father did. End: Nadia knows someone continued it, and has not asked who. Interpretation. Name the value being moved — trust, safety, knowledge, hope, standing, belonging — and its direction. A scene that moves a value the book has not established as charged has produced a change without consequence; McKee’s insistence on charged values ( §3.7 ) is this point. And note the class of scenes for which the test is inapplicable rather than failed: normal-establishing scenes ( §4.4 ), whose function is to make a later shift legible. For these, run the test on the pair. Test 4 — The extraction test Remove the scene entirely. What would the reader now fail to learn, feel or anticipate — and what later scene becomes unearned? Interpretation. “Nothing” means the scene is a satellite that has been given kernel resources ( §3.4 ). The available remedies, in order of preference: compress into a paragraph of summary; fuse with a neighbouring scene that does have a job; relocate the one load-bearing element into a scene that already exists; cut . Note that cutting is last. Most purposeless scenes contain one sentence that matters, and the efficient revision extracts the sentence rather than mourning the scene. Test 5 — The domain-count test Which of the five domains does this scene actively serve, as opposed to merely occupying? Interpretation. A scene marked with only one letter is thin unless it is short, is a deliberate rest, or is establishing a normal. Two is the working standard. Three is efficient. Four or five in a scene of ordinary length is a warning rather than an achievement ( §5.4 ). The most useful output of this test is usually not the count but the identification of the latent domain — the second function the scene could serve without additional length ( §5.3 ). Test 6 — The redundancy test Has the reader already received this value shift? Interpretation. Redundancy is the failure pattern most invisible from inside the draft, because each scene was written on a different day and felt new at the time. It is also the fault that most reliably produces the reader complaint that a book “sags in the middle”: the middle of a novel is where redundant scenes accumulate, since it is the region with the least structural pressure. The remedy is almost never to improve the second scene. It is to ask which of the two is better placed and delete the other. Test 7 — The summary-substitution test Rewrite the scene as three sentences of summary. What is lost? Interpretation. Three outcomes, tabulated at §6.4 . The crucial discrimination is between lost and merely absent : a scene’s atmosphere is always absent from its summary, and that is not by itself an argument for the scene. The question is whether the book needs that atmosphere at that point. This is the test that most often produces the answer a writer does not want, and it is the reason the protocol is placed in the revision sequence rather than the drafting one. Test 8 — The entry-and-exit test Does the scene start as late as it can and end as early as it can? Interpretation. Late entry and early exit are the cheapest revisions available, because they need no new writing. A scene that opens before the want is in operation spends its first page on arrival; a scene that continues past its last movement muffles its own shift, usually by explaining it. The exception is the slow entry that builds the normal the scene will break: the first chapter of Suzanne Collins’s The Hunger Games (2008) spends most of its length on the morning of the reaping before the draw. Where the opening pages do that work, run test 3 on the pair. Test 9 — The pressure test Does the information in this scene arrive under pressure, or is it being delivered? Interpretation. This is the diagnostic for the expository scene in disguise ( §8.3 ). Information delivered under pressure is retained, because it is bound to a transaction — the situation-model account ( §3.5 ) supplies the mechanism: facts attached to a person in a situation have somewhere to be stored. Information delivered as briefing is not retained, which means the info-dump does not even achieve its own stated purpose. The remedy is rarely to remove the information; it is to make someone reluctant to give it. Test 10 — The register test Is the story currently due for an action beat or a reflective one, and which is this? Interpretation. Four consecutive action scenes produce incident without consequence: things keep happening and nothing lands, because the reader has not been given the space in which landing occurs. Four consecutive reflective scenes produce brooding without motion. The register test catches a failure that is invisible at scene level and severe at book level, and it is the point at which this chapter hands over to Chapter 2 ( Scene and Sequel ), which treats the rhythm as its subject. 7.2 The reverse outline: the protocol at manuscript scale The tests above examine one scene. The instrument that examines a book is the reverse outline , and it is worth separating because it is a different operation with a different output. Procedure. Go through the finished draft and write one line per scene , in order, in a single document. Write each line in the language of consequence, not of event. Not “Elena and Dov talk in the doorway” but “Elena gets the key and not the reason, and stops believing her brother is protecting their mother.” Add, for each line, the scene’s length and its domain letters. Read the resulting document straight through, as a text in its own right. What the reverse outline exposes that scene-level testing cannot: Symptom in the outline Diagnosis A line that will only come out event-shaped That scene has not earned a consequence-shaped summary; it is a satellite Two lines that say substantially the same thing Redundancy ( §8.2 ), now visible where it was not before A run of six lines with no R or no P A domain has gone dark for a stretch of the book A stretch where every line begins “X learns…” The middle has become an information-delivery sequence Lines getting longer as the book proceeds Scenes are accreting functions rather than being chosen The last line of Act One arriving at 40 per cent A proportion problem invisible from inside 7.3 Reading the results Failed tests Likely diagnosis First move 1 and 2 No engine. The passage is an occasion, not a scene Find the want, or convert to summary ( §6.4 ) 3 alone, with 1 and 2 passing The scene has an engine that idles: a want is pursued and the situation is unchanged Make the pursuit cost something, or let the character succeed and discover the cost 4 alone A satellite at kernel length Compress, fuse, relocate the load-bearing sentence, then cut 5 alone (one domain) Under-served real estate Run the multiplicity pass ( §5.3 ) 6 alone Redundancy Choose the better-placed of the two scenes; delete the other 7 alone Mode error: summary inflated into scene Restore the summary; keep at most a fifty-word scenic instance 8 alone Entry and exit slack Cut to the first operative moment and the last moving one 9 alone Exposition in disguise Give the information to someone reluctant to part with it 10 alone Register mismatch Move the scene, or convert it to the other register 3, 4 and 6 together The scene is a fossil of discovery drafting Cut without ceremony; extract any usable sentence 1, 2 and 3 pass; 5 gives four or five Overstuffed ( §5.4 ) Simplify deliberately; the scene needs less, not more A warning about test 3. When a scene fails the value-shift test, the instinctive remedy is to add an event — a phone call, an arrival, a revelation. This is almost always the wrong move, because it treats a structural absence as a content shortage. The stronger remedy is to find the shift that is already latent in the scene and remove whatever prevents the reader from registering it. Most inert scenes contain a value shift the writer has muffled by continuing past it (test 8) or by having a character announce it ( §4.5 , “statement”).

chapter: Chapter 1 · The Purposes of a Scene
title: 8. Failure Patterns
text: Each pattern below is presented with its symptom , its mechanism (what actually goes wrong, as distinct from what the surface looks like), its remedy , and — most importantly — its exception : a published scene that commits the error and succeeds. 8.1 The Purposeless Scene Symptom. The scene occupies page time and shifts no value in any domain. It is usually pleasant, often well observed, and impossible to summarise in the language of consequence. Mechanism. A satellite has been given kernel resources ( §3.4 ). The scene exists because it was written, and it was written because the writer needed it: discovery drafting requires passages that find the story, and those passages are apparatus rather than narrative. The writer needed to write it to find the story; the reader does not need to read it to receive the story. Remedy. Test 4, run in both directions, then the ladder at §7.3 : compress, fuse, relocate the one load-bearing sentence, cut. The apparent exception: Melville, Moby-Dick (1851), chapter 94. “A Squeeze of the Hand” describes Ishmael and his shipmates squeezing lumps of spermaceti back into fluid, until Ishmael finds himself squeezing his companions’ hands and imagining universal fellow-feeling — let us squeeze ourselves universally into the very milk and sperm of kindness . No major plot event follows from the work in the tub. But Ishmael explicitly says he forgets the crew’s terrible oath and feels free of ill will. His emotional state changes, and he reaches towards his companions. The chapter therefore fails a plot-only test, not a test broad enough to include character, relation and theme. It is also indispensable to this reading of the book. Here, texture carries an argument. Moby-Dick accumulates ways of attending to the whale and the work around it; the cetology chapters, the chapter on whiteness, the chapter on the mast-head and the chapter on the spermaceti offer more than plot information. Remove the squeezing and the novel loses a position as well as a felt change in Ishmael: his alternative to Ahab’s monomania. The extraction test must ask about that change rather than looking only for a new step in the hunt. 8.2 The Redundant Scene Symptom. A second scene establishing something the reader already knows: another demonstration of the villain’s cruelty, another quarrel on the same terms, another refusal to answer the same question. Mechanism. The value shift has already been banked. Once a reader has registered a change of state, the state is changed; a scene that re-performs the change is asking the reader to learn something twice, and readers experience this as the book losing confidence. Remedy. Choose the better-placed of the two — usually the earlier, unless the later one is better executed — and delete the other. Do not attempt to differentiate them; a redundant scene made more interesting is a more interesting redundant scene. The exception: Kafka, The Trial (1925), chapter 5. Josef K. opens a lumber-room door in the bank and finds two warders being flogged by a man in a leather costume, on account of K.’s own complaint about them. He intervenes ineffectually and leaves. The following evening he opens the same door and finds the same scene, unchanged: the same men, the same posture, the same beginning of the same cry. He shuts the door. The same configuration recurs, though Kafka does not repeat the earlier passage verbatim. It is also one of the most frightening moments in the novel, and it works because repetition is part of the novel’s argument . In a world where progress is uncertain and the court’s reach is diffuse, the recurrence is a structural statement: K. confronts a punishment that seems not to have advanced since yesterday. 8.3 The Expository Scene in Disguise Symptom. The scene has all the furniture of drama — a room, two people, dialogue, someone getting up to pour a drink — and exists solely to deliver information to the reader. Characters ask questions they would already know the answers to; one of them explains the situation with unusual fluency. Mechanism. Information is being supplied rather than transacted . Per §7.1 , test 9, facts arrive without cost to the person parting with them, which means the scene has no engine, which means no want, which means Chatman’s kernel is absent and the scene is a briefing wearing a satellite’s clothes. The secondary damage is to the character domain: a person who exists to explain becomes an instrument, and instruments are not believed. Remedy. Give the information to someone who does not want to give it, in front of someone who should not hear it. The three components are: reluctance, an audience, and a cost. Any two will usually do. The exception: Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov (1880), Book Five. The Grand Inquisitor chapter is a scene in which one character recites to another a story he has composed, containing a long speech by a figure who explains, at length and without interruption, an entire theory of freedom, authority and human nature. It is exposition of the most undisguised kind: a monologue, delivered to a silent auditor, in a tavern, with no external action whatsoever. It succeeds for three reasons, and each is transferable. First, the exposition is the crisis : Ivan is not informing Alyosha, he is attempting to break him, and the ideas are the weapon. Second, the listener is at risk , so the reader watches a person rather than an argument; Alyosha’s silence and his final kiss are the scene’s actual events. Third, the speaker is exposed by what he says — the poem is a confession, and the reader learns more about Ivan than about the Inquisitor. 8.4 The One-Note Scene Symptom. The scene serves one domain only, competently, and nothing else. It is not wrong; it is under-used real estate. Mechanism. No mechanism, strictly — this is a pattern of inefficiency rather than of failure, and it is included because at book scale inefficiency becomes a structural problem. Twenty single-domain scenes in a novel of sixty produce a book that is a third longer than it needs to be, and length spent without return is the commonest reason a competent manuscript is refused. Remedy. The multiplicity pass at §5.3 . Look for the latent second function in material already present: the object in the room, the question not asked, the physical business. The exception: Tolstoy, Anna Karenina (1878), Part Three, chapters 4–5. Levin mows a meadow with his peasants for a full day. The scene serves one domain — texture — with total commitment: the rhythm of the scythe, the shifting of the line of mowers, the loss of self in labour, the moments when the work does itself and the moments when it does not. The plot does not move. Nobody’s relationship alters. No thesis is stated. It earns its sustained attention by duration and by conviction . The chapter is long enough that the reader stops waiting for it to become about something else and begins to inhabit it, which is its subject: the experience of work that is not instrumental. It is also positioned against Anna’s chapters, giving the labour a thematic role at the level of the book . Unlike Melville’s chapter at §8.1, its most obvious movement is experiential rather than an explicit change of feeling. 8.5 The Runaway Set Piece Symptom. A battle, a storm, a party, a chase, executed at spectacular volume, at great length, with every plot, character and relational value sitting where it started. Thrilling on its own; inert as soon as the reader turns the page. Mechanism. Texture at maximum, everything else idle. The set piece has a specific seduction: it is the material a writer most wants to write, it demonstrates capability, and it produces a strong local reading experience that conceals the absence of consequence. The diagnostic is brutal and simple — could the following chapter be written without it? Remedy. Put a kernel inside it. The standard technique is to give one character a small, specific, resisted want within the spectacle — get to the door, keep hold of the child, avoid being seen by a particular person — so that the reader has something to track. The spectacle then becomes the resistance rather than the subject. The exception: Hugo, Les Misérables (1862), Part Two, Book One. Nineteen chapters on the battle of Waterloo, in a novel about a paroled convict in Paris, arriving before the plot resumes. It is the most notorious digression in the nineteenth-century novel and has been cut from abridgements for a hundred and fifty years. It works — for readers who let it — by two devices. First, there is a kernel buried in it : in the final chapters, a scavenger robbing the dead on the field pulls a wounded officer from under a corpse, and the officer is Marius’s father, and the scavenger is Thénardier. Sixty pages of history exist to place one man in one debt. Second, the digression is the novel’s method rather than an interruption of it : Les Misérables is a book that argues history and individual life are the same substance at different scales, and it demonstrates this by refusing to distinguish them typographically. 8.6 The Errand Scene This pattern is added to the original five. Symptom. A character goes somewhere in order to do something, and the going is dramatised: the drive, the walk to the office, the queue, the arrival, the waiting room, the receptionist. The scene’s actual content occupies its last fifth. Mechanism. Transitional material has been mistaken for scene because it is chronologically continuous with a scene. The plot function is advance , which is the one function summary performs better than scene ( §4.1 ). The errand scene is the purest form of mode error ( §6.1 ): correct material, wrong speed. Remedy. Modes 5 and 11 ( §6.3 ). She drove to the shop. Or nothing at all — cut from the decision to the arrival, and let the reader supply the road. The exception: Woolf, Mrs Dalloway (1925). Clarissa walks from Westminster to Mulberry’s the florist to buy flowers, and the walk occupies a substantial part of the novel’s opening movement. It is an errand, dramatised at length, and it is one of the great passages in modernist fiction. The mechanism of its success is exact: the errand is not the subject, it is the occasion. What is being narrated is a consciousness, and the street furnishes the stimuli — the squeak of the hinges, Hugh Whitbread, the memory of Bourton — that let a mind be exhibited. The motor car stops outside Mulberry’s as Clarissa is choosing flowers; the aeroplane sequence follows and moves among other observers. The value shifts during Clarissa’s walk are interior, and the walk is the mode of their delivery. Chapter 5 ( The Transition ) analyses Woolf’s use of the motor car and the aeroplane as connective tissue between consciousnesses; the scene-level lesson is that an errand becomes a scene when the interior is the event , and remains an errand when it is not. 8.7 The Meeting-to-Decide Scene Added. Symptom. Three or more characters convene to determine what to do next. They review what has happened, canvass options, disagree mildly, and reach a decision. The scene is often placed at the start of the second act. Mechanism. Two failures compounded. First, the scene’s content is deliberation , which is a sequel function (reaction–dilemma–decision) staged as a scene; Chapter 2 ( Scene and Sequel ) explains why the two half-beats have different requirements. Second, and worse, the deliberation is generally between characters who all want the same thing, so the resistance is nominal — they are solving a problem, not opposing each other, and problem-solving is the least dramatic activity available to a group. Remedy. Three, in order of preference. Give the decision to one person , made alone and imperfectly, and let the others find out. Make the meeting a fight about something else — the plan may be agreed while an unrelated betrayal is being conducted under the table. Or summarise it : by the time they had finished arguing it was two o’clock and they had agreed on the only thing they could have agreed on. The exception: Stoker, Dracula (1897). The novel is substantially made of meetings. Van Helsing convenes the group repeatedly; documents are read aloud; typewritten transcripts are collated; plans are formed by consensus. By the diagnosis above the second half of the book should be inert. It is not, for a reason specific to its form. Dracula is an epistolary and documentary novel, and its meetings are scenes about the assembly of knowledge in a book whose antagonist is defined by what cannot be known about him. The convening is the action: each conference visibly converts scattered private records into a shared account, and the reader watches a group of people build, out of diaries and phonograph cylinders, the only weapon available against a creature that leaves no reflection. The meetings also carry a continuous relational charge — Mina is admitted, then excluded, then admitted again, and her exclusion is what allows the Count to reach her. 8.8 The Unresisted Want Added. Symptom. The viewpoint character wants something specific and gets it, at no cost, from someone who has no reason to refuse. The scene passes test 1 and fails test 2. Mechanism. Want without resistance produces activity, not scene. The reader’s engagement in a scene is a function of uncertainty about the outcome, and an unresisted want has no outcome to be uncertain about. The scene is therefore experienced as administration : something is arranged, and the book proceeds. Remedy. Three genuine options. Relocate the resistance inside the character — she gets the key, and the asking costs her something she was not prepared to spend. Change what is wanted : she came for the key and leaves wanting to know why he would not look at her. Or grant the want and make the granting the disaster , which is the strongest of the three and leads directly to the exception. The exception: Dickens, Great Expectations (1861), chapter 18. Jaggers finds Pip and Joe at the Three Jolly Bargemen, then speaks with them in the parlour. He informs Pip that he is to inherit a handsome property and be brought up as a gentleman. Pip wants this, and Jaggers does not oppose that wish. The transaction nevertheless has conditions, and Joe resists Jaggers’s manner and refuses payment for releasing Pip from his apprenticeship. The scene is one of the pivots of the novel: receiving what he wants begins Pip’s estrangement from Joe and the forge. Dickens registers the cost in Pip’s response to the news and in Joe’s exchange with Jaggers. Biddy’s pointed silence belongs to a later conversation with Pip in the same chapter. The resistance is partly in the transaction and partly in what the reader can foresee of its cost. 8.9 The Scene That Resolves at Its Own Climax Added. Symptom. The scene builds to a confrontation, the confrontation occurs, the matter is settled, and the scene closes on the settlement. Everything the scene raised, the scene answers. The reader has no reason to turn the page. Mechanism. The scene has been treated as a complete narrative rather than as a unit of a larger one. Its value shift is real, but it discharges rather than generates: the dramatic question is closed at the same moment it is answered, so no forward pressure is transmitted to the next unit. Swain’s insistence that a scene should end worse than it began (Chapter 2) is a crude version of this observation, and it is crude because “worse” is not the requirement — continuation is. A scene may end in triumph and still transmit pressure, provided the triumph creates a new problem. Remedy. Test 8’s exit half. Locate the moment the question is answered, and then ask what the answer makes possible or necessary . Frequently the correct exit is one line later than the resolution, and consists of a small fact that reopens it: the person who was not supposed to be listening, the object that is missing, the concession made too easily. The exception: Flaubert, Madame Bovary (1857), Part Three, chapter 8. Emma’s death is narrated at length and closes her own story. It leaves consequences for others unresolved: three chapters follow, in which Charles discovers the letters, deteriorates and dies, and Homais receives the croix d’honneur . The scene works as a close to Emma’s story near the end of the book because its resolution opens the question of what follows her death . Emma’s story ends; the novel’s does not, because the novel’s subject was never only Emma. Flaubert’s structure makes the point the diagnosis needs: a scene may resolve completely, provided the book has a question larger than the scene’s. Where a draft’s scene resolves completely and the book has no larger question, the fault is not in the scene. 8.10 The Second-Draft Scene Added. Symptom. A scene that is very well written, that every reader compliments, and that does nothing. It has usually been revised more than any other scene in the manuscript. The prose is the best in the book. Mechanism. Revision has been applied at sentence level to a structural problem, with the result that the scene’s inertness has been polished into invisibility . The better the prose, the harder the fault is to see — and the more expensive the fault becomes, since a beautifully written inert scene is the last thing a writer will agree to cut. Remedy. Test 7, applied ruthlessly, and then test 4 run forwards. Ask the question that sentence-level revision cannot answer: if this scene were merely adequate, would I still keep it? If the answer is no, the prose is holding up a scene rather than the scene supporting the prose. The exception: Woolf, To the Lighthouse (1927), Part One. The dinner at which the boeuf en daube is served has no plot function that could not be summarised in a line, contains no confrontation, and is composed almost entirely of surfaces: candles lit, a dish uncovered, awkwardness managed, Lily Briscoe deciding not to say what she thinks, Mrs Ramsay conducting the table. It is also the most heavily worked passage in the novel and one of the most celebrated in English fiction. It is not inert, and the discrimination matters. What the scene produces is a momentary coherence — Mrs Ramsay’s sense that here, now, something has been made that will outlast the evening — and the whole of the rest of the book is the loss and partial recovery of that coherence. The value shift is real, is registered by one consciousness, and is stated with great precision at the moment of leaving the room, when the scene has already become the past. Chapter 4 ( The Descriptive Detail ) analyses the dish; the scene-level point is that Woolf’s dinner passes test 3 while appearing not to. 8.11 Summary: symptom to mechanism Pattern Underlying mechanism Domains damaged Purposeless Satellite given kernel resources All Redundant A shift the reader has already banked P, C, R Expository in disguise Information supplied rather than transacted P, C One-note Inefficiency; unexploited latent domains — (cumulative, at book scale) Runaway set piece Texture at volume, all other values idle P, C, R Errand Transitional material dramatised; mode error P, X Meeting-to-decide Deliberation staged as scene; agency transferred to a committee P, C Unresisted want Want without cost produces activity, not scene P, R Resolves at its own climax Value discharged rather than transmitted P Second-draft Sentence-level revision applied to a structural fault All

chapter: Chapter 1 · The Purposes of a Scene
title: 9. Worked Analyses
text: Eight close readings and a revision case. The analytical apparatus is the same throughout: identify the engine (want, resistance), name the value shift, count the domains, and locate the entry and exit points. Where a work is read in translation, the translator is named, and structural claims are separated from texture claims. 9.1 Eliot, Middlemarch (1871–72), chapters 20–21 — the scene in which nothing happens twice The situation. Dorothea Brooke, six weeks married, sits weeping in her lodgings in the Via Sistina in Rome. Her husband Casaubon is at the Vatican library. She does not know why she is crying. The engine. Dorothea’s want is unusually hard to state, which is the scene’s subject rather than its defect: she wants to be given something to do — to be admitted to her husband’s work, to be of use, to have her devotion accepted. The resistance is Casaubon’s temperament, and the scene’s genius is that the resistance is not opposition. He does not refuse her. He fails to notice that anything is being offered. The value shift. At the start of chapter 20 Dorothea believes her disappointment is her own fault and a failure of understanding on her part. By the end of chapter 21 she has said the unsayable thing aloud — she asks him when he will begin to write the book — and has been answered with a coldness that converts a private unease into a public fact between them. What was a feeling has become a condition of the marriage . What the chapter is doing that the model cannot name. Eliot inserts, between Dorothea’s tears and the quarrel, a narratorial intervention of the kind Lubbock’s scenic ideal ( §3.2 ) exists to eliminate: the famous passage about the roar on the other side of silence, and the observation that we are all of us born in moral stupidity, taking the world as an udder to feed our supreme selves. Both are commentary; both interrupt the scene’s isochrony; both are essential. What the commentary does is perform the complication of sympathy for Casaubon that no dramatised action could achieve, because it is a matter of the reader’s interpretive stance rather than of any event. The narrator turns and asks the reader to consider that Casaubon also has an inside. 9.2 Flaubert, Madame Bovary (1857), Part Two, chapter 8 — the agricultural show Read in English; the translations most used are Eleanor Marx Aveling (1886), Francis Steegmuller (1957), Geoffrey Wall (1992) and Lydia Davis (2010). The structural analysis below survives all of them; claims about Flaubert’s rhythm and diction do not. The situation. The agricultural fair has come to Yonville. In the upper room of the town hall, Rodolphe Boulanger conducts the first serious stage of Emma’s seduction. Below in the square, a government official delivers a speech, and prizes are announced for livestock and manure. The device. Flaubert intercuts the two discourses without narratorial comment, so that Rodolphe’s declarations arrive punctuated by the announcements from the square. Seventy francs. Manures. Nothing else in the scene is asked to carry meaning; the meaning is generated entirely by the adjacency, and the reader performs the entire operation unaided. The value shift. Emma passes from a woman who is being approached to a woman who has permitted the approach. Nothing is consummated and nothing is refused. The change is that a boundary has been crossed silently, and the silence is what makes it irreversible. Domains — this is the definitive multi-domain scene. Domain What the scene does Plot Advances the affair by exactly one stage and establishes Rodolphe’s method, which the novel will use twice more Character Rodolphe is exposed by his fluency — a man who has said this before; Emma by what she is prepared to hear Relational The pair pass from acquaintance to complicity; the shared secret of the interrupted speech is their first possession in common Theme The novel’s central argument — that romantic language is a manufactured commodity indistinguishable from other agricultural produce — is made without a word of statement Texture The provincial world at its fullest: crowds, dung, brass, officials, and the ordinary boredom that makes Emma’s hunger comprehensible 9.3 Austen, Pride and Prejudice (1813), chapter 34 — the Hunsford proposal §5.2 anatomises this scene’s sentences. This section analyses its architecture. Entry. Austen begins with Elizabeth re-reading Jane’s letters and thinking about Darcy’s part in Jane’s distress. The doorbell rings later in the opening paragraph, and Darcy enters in the next. The brief preparation gives Elizabeth’s refusal a motive before the confrontation begins. The engine. Darcy wants to be accepted, and expects to be. Elizabeth wants him gone, and — more importantly — wants to make him answer for Bingley and for Wickham. The resistance is mutual and total, which is why the scene generates more heat per word than anything else in Austen. The structure. The scene has three movements, and the reader can feel each turn: Movement What happens The shift 1. The declaration Darcy proposes, at length, dwelling on the objections he has overcome Elizabeth passes from astonishment to anger 2. The refusal Elizabeth refuses, then names Jane and Wickham Darcy passes from confidence to incomprehension to fury 3. The exchange of charges Each accuses the other of a failure of manners and of justice Both pass from certainty to a wound they cannot yet name The value shift. Stated flatly: at the start, each believes their view of the other is correct and complete. At the end, each has been told, by the only person whose opinion they cannot dismiss, that it is not. Nothing is resolved. Both are wrong about most of it. The scene’s shift is from certainty to injury, and the injury is what makes the rest of the novel possible. Why it is the standing example for the relational domain ( §4.5 ). Ask the character-domain question — has either person changed? — and the honest answer is no. Ask the relational question and the answer is that everything has. A model without a relational category is obliged to describe the most consequential scene in the novel as a scene in which nothing happened to anybody. 9.4 Tolstoy, Anna Karenina (1878), Part Two — the steeplechase Translations in common use: Constance Garnett (1901), Louise and Aylmer Maude (1918), Rosamund Bartlett (2014), Marian Schwartz (2014), Richard Pevear and Larissa Volokhonsky (2000). Structural claims survive; the famous plainness of Tolstoy’s Russian does not survive uniformly. The situation. Vronsky rides his mare Frou-Frou in an officers’ steeplechase. Anna watches from the stand, beside her husband. At the last obstacle Vronsky makes an ill-timed movement in the saddle, comes down badly, breaks the mare’s back, and she is destroyed. Anna’s reaction in the stand is visible. Karenin observes it, and observes that others have observed it. On the drive home, Anna tells him she is Vronsky’s mistress. The double structure — the scene’s principal lesson. Tolstoy narrates the race twice: once from Vronsky’s side, as an experience of speed, judgement, and a physical error; and once from Karenin’s side, as a social occasion during which he watches his wife’s face. The two narrations are of the same minutes and are entirely different scenes. Narration Focaliser Want Resistance Value shift The race Vronsky To win The course; the horse; his own body Confidence → a shame he cannot discharge The stand Karenin To prevent a public scene Anna’s face; the presence of society Suspicion → certainty, and then the requirement to act on it Domains. Plot (turn — the confession follows directly and irreversibly). Character (Vronsky’s carelessness is exhibited in the one domain where he is competent, which is far more damaging than a scene of social carelessness would have been). Relational (two relations move in opposite directions in the same ten minutes). Theme (mirror: a man destroys a beautiful creature that trusted him, by a moment’s misjudgement, and receives sympathy for his distress). 9.5 Dostoevsky, Crime and Punishment (1866), Part One, chapter 7 — the murder Read here in Constance Garnett’s translation (1914); Pevear and Volokhonsky (1992), David McDuff (1991) and Oliver Ready (2014) are also in common use. Structural claims survive translation; the celebrated feverishness of the Russian syntax does not survive it evenly. The engine. Raskolnikov wants to carry out a plan. The resistance is almost entirely material and procedural: a door that must be got through, a woman who must be got past, a bolt, an axe under a coat, the interval before someone comes upstairs. Dostoevsky’s decision to make the resistance practical rather than moral is the scene’s central technical choice, and it is why the chapter reads faster than anything else in the novel. The value shift, and why it is not the obvious one. The obvious answer — he was not a murderer, and now he is — is true and insufficient. The scene’s operative shift is that the crime he committed is not the crime he planned . Lizaveta is the pawnbroker’s harmless half-sister; she walks in; he kills her because she is there. The theory that authorised the first killing has no account of the second, and Raskolnikov spends the rest of the novel unable to tell himself a story in which he is the man he intended to be. 9.6 Achebe, Things Fall Apart (1958), chapter 7 — the killing of Ikemefuna The situation. Ikemefuna, a boy who has lived in Okonkwo’s household for three years and calls him father, is taken out of the village to be killed, in accordance with an oracle’s decision. Okonkwo has been warned by an elder to have no hand in it. He walks with the party. The engine. The scene’s want belongs to Ikemefuna, and this is Achebe’s crucial choice: for most of the walk the reader is with the boy, who is thinking about his mother, wondering whether she is still alive, and playing a childhood game in his head with the rhythm of his own footsteps. He wants to get home. The resistance is invisible to him and known to everybody else, including the reader. The mechanism: dramatic irony as the engine. The scene generates almost unbearable pressure with no conflict whatever, because the reader holds information the focaliser does not. Nothing needs to be dramatised except walking. This is the strongest available refutation of the belief that a scene requires opposed wants; here there is one want, no opposition, and the resistance is the reader’s knowledge . The value shift. Two, in three lines. Ikemefuna passes from alive to dead. And Okonkwo passes from a man who has been told not to do a thing to a man who has done it — and Achebe supplies the reason immediately and without commentary: hearing the boy call him father and run to him, he cut him down, because he was afraid of being thought weak. Domains. Character (reveal and test, in a single act). Theme (the novel’s argument about the cost of a masculinity defined negatively — as the absence of everything the father was — is made in one clause). Plot (turn: the act is the origin of Okonkwo’s decline). Relational (a father-son relation is destroyed by the person who held it, which is why it registers as more than a killing). 9.7 Fitzgerald, The Great Gatsby (1925), chapter 5 — the reunion at Nick’s cottage The situation. Gatsby has arranged, through Nick, for Daisy to come to tea. It is raining. Gatsby has had the lawn cut and sent flowers. He waits. The engine. Gatsby wants an outcome he has spent five years and an enormous fortune constructing. The resistance is, of all things, embarrassment — his own. The scene’s daring is that its obstacle is not Daisy, not Tom, not the class barrier, but the fact that a man of formidable competence cannot get through the first ten minutes of the thing he has organised his life around. The clock. It is the best single object in any scene discussed in this chapter, and it earns its place by not being a symbol first . It is a physical accident, produced by a man leaning too far back, and it is funny. Only afterwards does the reader register that a man attempting to reverse five years has knocked over a stopped clock and caught it before it fell. Chapter 4 ( The Descriptive Detail ) treats the general principle; the scene-level lesson is that an object multiplies when its literal function is complete . The value shift. Gatsby passes from anticipation to possession, and Fitzgerald’s decisive move is to make this a loss . Nick’s observation near the chapter’s end — that there must have been moments even that afternoon when Daisy tumbled short of his dreams, not through her own fault but because of the colossal vitality of his illusion — converts a scene of fulfilment into the novel’s first statement of its thesis. 9.8 James, The Portrait of a Lady (1881), chapter 42 — the vigil Why this scene is the chapter’s central example. It has no dialogue, no second character, no physical action and no external event. A woman sits down by a dying fire and does not get up until dawn. By every surface criterion the workshop would apply, it is not a scene at all. It passes every test in §7 . The situation. Isabel Archer, having discovered Madame Merle and her husband in a room together — Osmond seated, Madame Merle standing, a configuration whose impropriety is entirely a matter of familiarity — sits alone after the guests have gone, and thinks. James on the chapter. In the preface to the New York Edition, James identified this chapter as one of the best things in the book, and described it as a representation simply of her motionlessly seeing , an attempt to make the still lucidity of her act as interesting as the surprise of a caravan or the identification of a pirate. He noted that it was designed to have all the vivacity of incident and all the economy of picture, and claimed that it throws the action forward further than twenty incidents would have done. This is the most useful single statement by a novelist about the scene of pure interiority, and it should be read alongside Lubbock ( §3.2 ), whose whole system was built out of James’s practice and which has no comfortable place for this chapter. The engine. Isabel wants to understand what she saw . The resistance is her own resistance: the understanding is unbearable, and the chapter proceeds by her repeated approach to and retreat from it. This is the purest available case of resistance located inside the focaliser (test 2), and it is why the chapter has more forward pressure than most chases. The value shift, stated in the required form. Start: Isabel believes her marriage is a private failure of feeling, and that her choices were her own.
