End: Isabel knows her husband hates her, that the hatred is settled and will not change, and suspects that her freest act was arranged for her. Duration. In Genette’s terms ( §3.3 , §6.3 ) this is the interiorised scene , mode 9: story time is a few hours, narrative time is a chapter, and the isochrony is maintained not by dialogue but by the pace of thought. James’s achievement is to make consciousness move at a legible rate — the chapter has stages, each with its own recognition, so that the reader experiences progression rather than accumulation. A draft that attempts the interiorised scene and fails almost always fails here: the thought does not advance, it circles. The chapter’s use in this textbook. It is the standing refutation of every mechanical reading of the model. A student who has concluded that scenes require dialogue, opposition, movement, event or a second person should be sent to chapter 42 and asked to explain what is missing. Everything the model requires is present; only its usual carriers are absent. The distinction between a function and its carrier is the distinction on which this chapter’s tests rest, and §9.8 is where it can be seen most clearly. 9.9 A revision case: the ledger scene A note on placement. In the household novel the ledger is first planted as an object in Chapter 4 ( The Descriptive Detail ), and Elena discovers its changed handwriting in the register drawer at a chapter break in Chapter 6 ( The Chapter Break ). The scene worked below imagines a later confrontation, in which Nadia, told of the discovery by Elena, confronts Dov at the shop. It is an exercise and not part of the novel’s sequence, and nothing in it binds the novel. Version A (draft) Nadia had been at the shop since nine. She had counted the receipts in the drawer twice, which took a while because the drawer stuck on the K and only came free on the third try, the way it always had. Dov arrived at eleven with a roll of bin bags and started on the shelves. Elena had found the ledger the previous week and rung her about it. Their father had kept it for eleven years, in his careful slanting hand with the crossed sevens — prices and repairs and the ordinary arithmetic of keeping a small shop alive. But after the ninth of March the writing changed. It was looser, and it was not his. Nadia had thought about this a great deal. She had known for some time that her relationship with her brother was not what it had been. Since their father’s death, things had been difficult between all three of them, and she found it hard to trust Dov the way she once had. “You’ve been writing in it,” she said at last. “Haven’t you.” Dov admitted that he had. He explained that he had not wanted to worry her or Elena, and that he had only been keeping up the accounts because somebody had to. Nadia said she understood. They finished the shelves together and went out for lunch, and neither of them mentioned it again that day. Diagnosis Test Result 1 — Want Fails. Nadia is at the shop; she is not trying to get anything. The passage never states an objective, and the scene begins two hours before anything is at issue 2 — Resistance Fails. Dov concedes immediately and explains himself fully. Nothing is in the way 3 — Value shift Marginal. Start: Nadia suspects Dov continued the ledger. End: Nadia knows Dov continued the ledger. A suspicion is confirmed, which is the weakest available shift, and it is confirmed by his simply saying so 4 — Extraction Backwards: the reader loses one fact, already available from the changed handwriting. Forwards: nothing later becomes unearned 5 — Domain count X only, and thinly. Character is asserted, not evidenced; the relational shift is stated (“she found it hard to trust Dov”), which is the domain’s characteristic under-delivery ( §4.5 ) 6 — Redundancy Fails. The reader learned that the hand changed after March the ninth at the chapter break; this scene re-delivers it 7 — Summary substitution Nadia asked Dov about the ledger. He said he had not wanted to worry them. Nothing is lost 8 — Entry and exit Fails both. Enters at nine in the morning with a receipt count; exits after lunch 9 — Pressure Fails. Every fact is delivered as briefing: eleven years, the crossed sevens, the date, the state of the siblings’ relations. No one is reluctant to say anything 10 — Register Reflective, in a position that calls for action — Patterns present: the errand scene ( §8.6 ) at the opening; the expository scene in disguise ( §8.3 ) in paragraph two; the unresisted want ( §8.8 ); the second-draft scene in embryo ( §8.10 ) — the prose is not bad, which is why the fault is hard to see Version B (revision) The ledger was in the register drawer, open at the ninth of March. Nadia took it out and held it up. “You’ve been writing in it.” Dov went on wrapping the shelf stock in newspaper, not looking up. “Somebody had to. I knew something was wrong.” He held out his hand for it. She watched his hands, steady, too steady, and put the ledger back in the drawer and shut it, and kept her palm flat on the wood. He didn’t argue. That was the part that frightened her. Eighty-nine words. The domain audit: Domain What the scene does Plot Opens a question (what did Dov see on the ninth of March that told him something was wrong?) which the novel answers only in Dov’s own chapter (Chapter 13, The Viewpoint Shift ). A plant, placed without emphasis Character Dov is revealed by a physical tell rather than by report: hands that are steady when they should not be, and a man who goes on working through an accusation. Nadia is revealed by what she does with the ledger rather than by what she says Theme If the novel’s question is what the living owe the dead’s silences, the scene stages it: two people negotiating over a document neither will read aloud Texture The domestic chore — wrapping stock in newspaper — sets a register of ordinary business interrupted, not of melodrama Relational The scene’s principal transaction. The outstretched hand is refused, and the ledger goes back into the drawer under Nadia’s palm. Afterwards neither of them holds it, and the right to it is open between them in a way neither would have predicted a week earlier Apply the value-shift test in the required form: Start: Nadia believes Dov’s silence is evasion, and expects him to deny it. End: Nadia knows he will neither deny it nor explain it, has kept the ledger from him, and has discovered that his not arguing frightens her more than a lie would have. What the revision did, procedurally Entered at the last possible moment (test 8). The receipt count, the arrival, the bin bags, the two hours of shelving are gone. The scene begins with the ledger already open in the drawer and the accusation already formed. Made the concession the problem. Version A’s fatal move is Dov’s full explanation. Version B gives him one sentence that concedes the small fact and withholds the large one — Somebody had to. I knew something was wrong — so that what he says increases the reader’s uncertainty rather than resolving it. This is the pressure test (test 9) satisfied by making the speaker reluctant. Replaced a stated relation with a transacted one. “She found it hard to trust Dov” becomes an outstretched hand and a refusal. The relational shift is now an event with a location in the room. This move transfers most readily to other scenes. Converted exposition into physical business ( §5.3 ). The wrapping of stock does character, texture, relational and plot work simultaneously — a man packing a shop is a man who has already decided to sell it — without an expository sentence. Exited on the last moving beat. Version A continues through lunch. Version B stops on that was the part that frightened her , which is the moment the value stops moving, and leaves the sequel — Nadia alone with the ledger — to the next unit (Chapter 2, Scene and Sequel ). What Version B has not solved First, it is too tidy. Eighty-nine words containing five domains, a plant, a physical tell and a closing line of interpretation is close to the density ceiling ( §5.4 ), and the last sentence — that was the part that frightened her — is the narration telling the reader how to read the preceding gesture. A more confident version would end on He didn’t argue , and trust the reader. Whether the interpretive line is a weakness or a legitimate act of narration is arguable; a workshop should argue it. Second, the redundancy is unresolved. If Chapter 6 has already given the reader the changed handwriting, then Version B’s value shift is not Nadia learns Dov continued the ledger but Nadia learns that Dov will not defend himself . That is a real shift, but it is a narrower one than the scene’s staging implies, and the scene should probably be rewritten so that the accusation is not about the handwriting at all.

chapter: Chapter 1 · The Purposes of a Scene
title: 10. The Scene Across Forms
text: The domain model was developed for the novel. It transfers to adjacent forms with adjustments that need stating, because students frequently import novel-scene habits into forms that punish them. 10.1 The short story The story’s characteristic difference is one of ratio : a scene may constitute a third of the whole. The ratio leaves no room for normal-establishing scenes, so the normal must be established inside the scene that breaks it, usually by iterative clauses (clauses of habit, telling what used to happen every day) embedded in scenic narration. 10.2 The novella The novella’s scene problem is that it is written by novelists. It has a novel’s tonal range and a fraction of its length, so a three-thousand-word scene consumes a twentieth of the book. The form’s characteristic solution is the compressed scene (mode 2): the occasion is rendered scenically but with aggressive internal ellipsis, so that the reader receives the texture of full dramatisation at half the cost. The Death of Ivan Ilyich is the model — Tolstoy dramatises perhaps a dozen occasions across a whole life, and summarises the rest without apology. 10.3 The screen comparison, and what does not transfer Contemporary craft advice imports heavily from screenwriting — “enter late, leave early”, “every scene must turn”, “a scene occupies continuous time and space”. Each transfers to prose to a different degree. Screen principle Transfers? Why Enter late, leave early Yes The mechanism is identical: attention is finite and the audience reconstructs the approach without help Every scene turns on a value Partly McKee’s formulation ( §3.7 ) was written for feature-length film; he describes roughly forty to sixty scenes in a typical Archplot. A novel can also make room for scenes whose effect emerges across a larger span A scene is a unit of continuous time and place Partly Screenwriting scenes are often organised around more or less continuous time and space, though a film scene may contain many cuts. Prose may also shift location, elide time or move between minds within a larger dramatic unit One further asymmetry is worth teaching. Film can summarise through montage, voice-over, transitions and ellipsis. These devices make compression differently perceptible from a prose sentence such as Three years passed . Prose can move into summary without a separate visual device; overlooking that option can produce the errand scene ( §8.6 ). 10.4 Translated fiction Structural claims survive translation. The counterpoint in Flaubert’s agricultural show, the double focalisation of Tolstoy’s steeplechase, the deviation from plan in Dostoevsky’s murder chapter and the interior progression of James’s chapter 42 are all present in every competent version, because they are properties of arrangement rather than of wording. 10.5 Concordance: concept to scene Concept Best displayed by Section The value shift at maximum clarity Pride and Prejudice , the Hunsford proposal §5.2 , §9.3 Multiplicity, organised density Madame Bovary , the agricultural show §9.2 The relational domain, in its purest form Pride and Prejudice , ch. 34 §4.5 , §9.3 Focalisation as a scene-defining choice Anna Karenina , the steeplechase §9.4 The want granted as disaster Great Expectations , ch. 18; The Great Gatsby , ch. 5 §8.8 , §9.7 The interiorised scene; pure consciousness The Portrait of a Lady , ch. 42 §6.3 , §9.8

chapter: Chapter 1 · The Purposes of a Scene
title: 11. Revision Checklist
text: Run each scene in a draft against this list before deciding it stays as written. Each item corresponds to a test in §7 or a pattern in §8 . Engine I can state in one sentence what the viewpoint character wants in this scene, right now. Something is in the way, and getting past it costs something I can name. Change I can write the two parallel sentences: what was true at the start, what is no longer true at the end. This is not a shift the reader has already been given elsewhere. Domains I can name which domains — plot, character, theme, texture, relational — the scene actively serves, and annotate each with the specific change. The scene serves at least two, or I have a specific reason it needs only one. Mode I have asked whether this material should be a scene at all, and tried it in at least one other mode ( §6.4 ). Habitual material is told iteratively rather than dramatised as a single day. Execution The scene begins at the first moment the want is in operation. It ends on the last moment the value moves, not on its explanation. Book scale Removing this scene would cost the reader something identifiable, and would leave a later scene unearned. The scene is in the register — action or reflection — that this point in the book requires.

chapter: Chapter 1 · The Purposes of a Scene
title: 12. Studio Work
text: 12.1 Practical exercises Exercise 1 — The domain audit. Apply §5.5 to one chapter of your draft. Produce the table, with each domain letter annotated in four words. Write 250 words on what the distribution reveals about your habits rather than about the chapter. Exercise 2 — Mode substitution. Take one scene and rewrite the same material in two other modes from §6.3 , chosen for maximum distance from the original. Do not judge until all three exist. Write 300 words on what each buys and costs. Exercise 3 — The iterative paragraph. Write 200 words of iterative summary (mode 6) conveying two years of a character’s habitual life. No scene, no dialogue, no single occasion. Then write the pseudo-iterative version (mode 7) and note what the added specificity gains and what it makes impossible. Exercise 4 — Entry and exit. Take a scene and delete its first paragraph; read. Delete the first two; read. Continue until deletion causes real loss. Repeat from the end. Record where the scene actually begins and ends, and write 150 words on why the deleted material felt necessary while drafting. Exercise 5 — The four-sentence scene. Write a complete scene in four sentences: a want, a resistance, a reversal and a consequence. Then write the same scene in eight hundred words. Compare which value shift is more legible. Exercise 6 — The unresisted want, three ways. Write a scene in which a character asks for something and receives it immediately. Then rewrite it twice: once relocating the resistance inside the asker, once making the granting a disaster in the manner of §8.8 . Identify which version your novel needs. Exercise 7 — The interiorised scene. Write 800 words in which one character, alone, understands something. No dialogue, no second person, no external event. The thought must advance rather than circle — mark the stages in the margin. Compare against §9.8 . Exercise 8 — The reverse outline. Reverse-outline an entire draft, or 40,000 words of one, per §7.2 . One line per scene, in the language of consequence. Submit the outline, not the draft, with 400 words on what it exposed. Exercise 9 — Counterpoint. Following Flaubert ( §9.2 ), write a scene in which two discourses run simultaneously and neither comments on the other — a private conversation against a public one, an argument against an announcement, a confession against a piece of routine business. The rule: no narratorial commentary of any kind. 12.2 Seminar questions Does the value-shift test describe narrative, or a period? §3.6 contrasts selected historical practices with a scenic preference in much modern craft advice. Test the claim by applying the protocol in §7 to three scenes from Tom Jones and three from a novel published in the last decade. What does the test measure in each case, and does it measure the same thing? Four domains or five? Argue for or against admitting the relational domain ( §4.5 ) as a separate category. Use the Hunsford proposal as your principal evidence, and answer the parsimony objection: if a relation is only a pair of mental states, what is left for the domain to name? What shifts in Melville’s “A Squeeze of the Hand”? See §8.1 . It has a place, a duration and a viewpoint, but little conventional plot movement. Ishmael says that his feelings toward the crew and their oath change. Does the chapter’s value-shift test capture that movement, or does it still understate what the passage contributes to the book? Whose conventions? The failure patterns in §8 are drawn from an Anglo-American workshop tradition of the last sixty years. Examine the scene construction of The Tale of Genji , Dream of the Red Chamber or a novel from a strong oral-narrative tradition, and determine which of §8 ’s prohibitions describe narrative and which describe a local literary culture. Eliot’s intervention. In Middlemarch chapters 20–21 the narrator interrupts a scene to instruct the reader in how to feel about Casaubon ( §9.1 ). Lubbock’s scenic ideal ( §3.2 ) would remove it; Booth would defend it. Which is right, and what would the chapter lose? Extend the question: is there a contemporary novel that could do this without being thought clumsy, and if not, why not? The ethics of the extraction test. A test that asks what a reader would lose treats the reader’s experience as the measure of a scene’s worth. Are there scenes whose value lies in something other than the reader’s gain — an obligation to a subject, an act of witness, a refusal to be efficient? Consider Hugo’s Waterloo ( §8.5 ) and the iterative chapters of Things Fall Apart . 12.3 Assessment rubric For a submitted scene (1,500–2,500 words) with a 750-word critical commentary. Band Craft (60%) Commentary (40%) Distinction A legible want under real resistance; a value shift that is charged and locatable; two or more domains actively served without strain; entry and exit chosen; information transacted rather than delivered; the mode is evidently a choice Names the scene’s mode and defends it against alternatives; identifies the scene’s own risks and what it has not solved; engages at least two theoretical sources critically rather than decoratively Merit Want and resistance present; a real but under-charged shift; two domains, one of them thin; entry or exit slack Accurate self-analysis; some theoretical engagement; risks acknowledged if not resolved Pass A scene exists; a want is discernible; one domain served competently; prose adequate Describes the scene accurately; theory referenced but not applied Fail No engine; no locatable shift; one or more failure patterns unrecognised Description without analysis; no engagement with the model

chapter: Chapter 1 · The Purposes of a Scene
title: 13. Glossary
text: Disnarrated — Gerald Prince’s term for what a narrative reports as not having happened: the imagined, feared, rehearsed or explicitly denied event. The basis of the subjunctive scene. §6.3 (mode 13). Dramatisation — Rendering an occurrence such that narrative time approximates story time. Defined here by duration rather than by the presence of dialogue, action or sensory detail. §3.3 . Extraction test — Removing a scene to determine what the reader would fail to learn, feel or anticipate, and which later scene becomes unearned. §7.1 , test 4. Focalisation — Bal’s and Genette’s term for the perspective through which narrative material is perceived, distinguished from the voice that narrates it. Determines whose scene a scene is. §3.4 . Interiorised scene — A scene whose duration is governed by the pace of thought rather than of action; consciousness rendered at scene speed. §6.3 (mode 9), §9.8 . Kernel / satellite — Chatman’s terms (after Barthes’s noyaux and catalysers) for events that branch the story and events that amplify a path already taken. §3.4 . Proairetic code — Barthes’s code of actions: the reader’s recognition of a sequence of gestures as a nameable action with a knowable completion. The mechanism of scene-level expectation. §3.4 . Pseudo-iterative — Genette’s term for passages narrated in the iterative whose detail is too particular to have recurred. §6.2 , §6.3 (mode 7). Relational domain — This chapter’s proposed fifth domain: the state of a relationship — trust, power, obligation, intimacy, debt, hostility — considered as an independently shiftable value. §4.5 . Scene — A unit of story in which a character pursues a concrete immediate objective against resistance, rendered in approximately real time, such that the state of the story is different at its close. §2.1 . Sequel — In Swain’s model, the reflective unit following a scene: reaction, dilemma, decision. Treated in full in Chapter 2 ( Scene and Sequel ). §6.6 . Situation model — In discourse psychology, the reader’s mental representation of the state of affairs a text describes, tracked across dimensions of protagonist, space, time, causality and intentionality. §3.5 . Value shift — McKee’s term for the movement of a charged value from one pole towards its opposite across a scene. The chapter’s central diagnostic. §3.7 .

title: 15. Further Reading
text: Annotated, grouped by what each source is good for . Starred items are the recommended first three. 15.1 On duration, and on what a scene is ★ Genette, Gérard. Narrative Discourse (1972; Eng. 1980). The indispensable book for this chapter. Chapter 2 on duration and chapter 3 on frequency contain everything §§3.3 , 6.2 and 6.3 are built from, and the analysis of Proust’s ratios is the best available demonstration that scene and summary are historical variables. Formidable in idiom, and worth the effort. ★ Lubbock, Percy. The Craft of Fiction (1921). Read for an influential formulation of the vocabulary rather than for its conclusions. The scene/picture distinction is developed here in a careful form. Read the chapters on Madame Bovary and The Ambassadors . 15.2 On why a part must answer to a whole Aristotle, Poetics , chapters 6–11. Twenty pages. The removability test, the necessary-or-probable connection, and the criticism of episodic plot are all here, and every craft manual since is a gloss on them. Sternberg, Meir. Expositional Modes and Temporal Ordering in Fiction (1978). The suspense/curiosity distinction reorganises how a writer thinks about what a scene may withhold. Demanding, formalist, unrivalled. 15.3 On showing, telling, and the limits of the scenic ideal ★ Booth, Wayne C. The Rhetoric of Fiction (1961/1983). The necessary corrective to “show, don’t tell”. Booth demonstrates that authorial effacement is a rhetoric with costs, not a neutral advance, and his account of distance is directly applicable to the scene. Long; the chapters on telling and showing and on the author’s voice are the relevant ones. 15.4 Cognitive work Zwaan and Radvansky (1998). A review article, and the clearest statement of the dimensions readers track. Directly relevant to what a value shift consists of. 15.5 Craft manuals, used critically McKee, Robert. Story (1997). The source of the value shift. Written for screenwriters, magisterial in tone, and best read as a rigorous articulation of one tradition rather than as a description of narrative. Its account of the scene, and of what McKee calls the “turning point”, is the sharpest in the craft literature. Swain, Dwight V. Techniques of the Selling Writer (1965) and Bickham, Jack M. Scene & Structure (1993). The scene–sequel model in its original and its clearest expositions. Mechanistic, dated in idiom, structurally sound. Chapter 2 ( Scene and Sequel ) treats them at length. 15.6 Within this textbook Chapter 2 ( Scene and Sequel ) — the rhythm this chapter defers: goal–conflict–disaster, reaction–dilemma–decision, and the causal chain. Chapter 3 ( The Dialogue Exchange ) — the domain model applied one level down, with its own relational fifth. Chapter 13 ( The Viewpoint Shift ) — focalisation as a structural choice; the answer to “whose scene is this?” Chapter 14 ( The Subplot ) — the attention tax: this chapter’s argument about the cost of a scene, applied to page space across plots. Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages ) — the scene with five additional contracts falling due at once. Chapter 16 ( The Ending ) — the scene whose value shift must be the book’s.

chapter: Chapter 1 · The Purposes of a Scene
title: 16. Coda: Against Mechanical Application
text: Everything in this chapter is an instrument for noticing. None of it is a rule, and the evidence for that is contained in the chapter itself. Consider what the model, mechanically applied, would remove. A plot-only reading would remove “A Squeeze of the Hand”, overlooking Ishmael’s change of feeling. A blanket rule against repetition would remove the second flogging in The Trial . A length rule would remove nineteen chapters of Waterloo. A ban on commentary would remove Eliot’s narratorial intervention in the Rome chapters. A two-domain minimum would remove Levin’s day in the meadow. A demand for external action would compress chapter 42 of The Portrait of a Lady into a paragraph, although James thought it the best thing in the book and said it threw the action forward further than twenty incidents would have done. A model that rules out that list has not identified defects in those scenes. It has identified its own limits. But the sharpest version of the argument is not that great scenes fail the test. It is that the test was never a test. A test has a pass mark and a consequence for failure. What §7 actually offers is a set of questions that convert an unusable dissatisfaction into a usable one. This scene isn’t working becomes: the want belongs to the wrong character ; or this is a satellite at kernel length ; or the reader banked this shift eighty pages ago ; or this is summary that has been inflated into dialogue because I only know how to write scenes . The first sentence can only be worried at. The others can be acted on. The value-shift test’s function is not to identify which scenes are good. It is to make a writer’s choices visible to the writer. A scene that fails a particular test may be the finest thing in the book. What matters diagnostically is whether the writer can explain what the book gains from it. The examples of Melville, Kafka and Hugo show several kinds of gain that a local plot test can miss. In revision, a writer who cannot yet answer the question may need to examine the scene’s relation to the whole book before deciding what to keep. There is a deeper reason the scene resists formula, and it belongs at the end. The instruments in this chapter all measure change , because change is what can be measured. But the experience of reading a scene is not an experience of registering alterations in a state vector. It is the experience of being somewhere, with someone, while something is at stake — and the sensation that the writer knows how much attention this occasion is worth and is spending neither more nor less. Every test in §7 is an oblique way of detecting that judgement in someone else’s manuscript, and in one’s own. Which suggests the last and least mechanical question, to be asked after the other ten: If I read this scene in a book I admired, would I feel that the writer had chosen to spend these pages here? If the answer is yes, the scene has a job, whether or not the chapter can name it.

title: Scene and Sequel
text: The Six-Beat Engine, the Causal Chain, and the Limits of a Mid-Century Model The Craft Behind the Story (Second Edition), Reference — Chapter 2. Part I: The Scene and Its Materials. A companion to Chapter 1 ( The Purposes of a Scene ), whose note on the sequel (§6.6) this chapter expands, and to Chapter 5 ( The Transition ), Chapter 6 ( The Chapter Break ), Chapter 14 ( The Subplot ) and Chapter 16 ( The Ending ). All illustrative passages are quoted briefly for the purposes of criticism and study; full citations appear in §14 . Where a work is read in translation the translator is named, and structural claims are distinguished from claims about texture. Contents On this page: Chapter Abstract · Learning Outcomes · Key Terms · How to Use This Chapter Introduction: The Two Halves of Narrative Motion Definitions and Boundaries Why Causality Carries the Weight The Six Beats — and a Proposed Seventh The Principle of Compression Interruption, Deferral, and the Shapes of the Chain Diagnostic Method — the ten tests Failure Patterns — with their counterexamples Worked Analyses — eight close readings and a revision case Scene and Sequel Across Forms · Concordance: concept to novel Revision Checklist Studio Work — exercises, seminar questions, assessment rubric Glossary Sources Cited Further Reading Coda: What the Engine Cannot Tell You Chapter Abstract Chapter 1 ( The Purposes of a Scene ) treated the scene as a unit of purpose and asked what each one is for . This chapter treats the join between units and asks a different question: what makes one unit follow another necessarily rather than merely next. Its spine is a six-beat model inherited from Dwight V. Swain’s Techniques of the Selling Writer (1965): a scene built from Goal, Conflict, Disaster , followed by a sequel built from Reaction, Dilemma, Decision , whose Decision becomes the following scene’s Goal. The model is compact, teachable and unusually durable. Swain codified it in a mid-century American writing manual informed by his experience in commercial fiction, and later trade manuals helped transmit it. The chapter presents it as what it is: a heuristic with a specific provenance, real explanatory power, and limits that exclude a great deal of admired fiction. The argument proceeds in four movements. Theory ( §3 ) — the grounding of the chapter’s first principle in Aristotle’s distinction between events that follow one another and events that follow from one another; in Peter Brooks’s account of narrative desire as a dynamic of delay and discharge; in Barthes’s proairetic code, Todorov’s equilibrium schema and Propp’s functions; in the discourse-psychology finding that causally connected events are better recalled than merely sequential ones; and in the institutional history of the model itself. Taxonomy ( §4 ) — the six beats anatomised individually, each with its textual carriers, its under- and over-delivery, its published illustrations, and — a question the usual account leaves open — what it looks like when compressed to nothing. A seventh unit is then proposed: the Hinge , the point at which a character’s criterion for choosing changes, which is where arc actually happens and which the six-beat model cannot name. Method ( §§5–7 ) — the principle of compression ; a taxonomy of twelve chain structures , from the clean chain to the chain deliberately broken; and a ten-test diagnostic protocol for revision. Application ( §§8–9 ) — twelve failure patterns, each paired with a published work that commits the fault and succeeds; eight close readings; and a revision case worked on the textbook’s running example. The chapter’s governing claim is this: A story is not a sequence of things that happened. It is a chain of things that had to happen next — and “had to” is a relation the reader constructs, not a property the text possesses. The second half of that sentence is the chapter’s contribution and its principal qualification. Causal necessity is an effect ; it can be produced by beat structure, and it can be produced by other means, and it can be deliberately refused. A model that treats it as a checklist has mistaken one route for the destination. A note on the examples. The illustrative passages are drawn chiefly from the European and anglophone novel; the Core chapter adds post-2000 fiction and screen cases, listed in §14.5. A concordance mapping each concept to the novel that best displays it appears at §10.6 . Where a work outside those lists demonstrates something they cannot, it is used and marked. Learning Outcomes By the end of this chapter, a student should be able to: Distinguish scene from sequel in Swain’s narrow sense, and both from the loose sense of “scene” used in Chapter 1 and in most workshop conversation. Identify each of the six beats in a published passage, name its textual carriers, and say what the passage buys by expanding or compressing it. Explain , with reference to at least three theoretical sources, why causal connection between narrative units produces effects that mere sequence does not — and where that account comes from historically. Trace a causal chain backwards through several scene–sequel pairs and locate the exact link at which necessity fails. Apply the ten-test diagnostic protocol to a draft and produce a prioritised revision plan. Diagnose the recurring failure patterns by mechanism rather than by surface feature, and state the conditions under which each “failure” is the correct choice. Evaluate the six-beat model’s provenance and limits, including the extent to which its prohibitions describe narrative and the extent to which they describe a commercial genre preference. Analyse at least one novel that runs on a different engine entirely, and account for how it generates momentum without the chain. Key Terms Scene (narrow sense) · sequel · goal · conflict · disaster · reaction · dilemma · decision · the hinge · the causal chain · propter hoc · proairetic code · narrative desire · dilatory space · deferred decision · compression · beat weight · motivation-reaction unit · equilibrium schema · function (Propp) · chain structure · the escalation treadmill Full definitions appear in the Glossary ( §13 ). Terms are bolded on first substantive use. How to Use This Chapter Reader Route Purpose Student in a seminar §§1–4 in order, then §6 and §9 ; §12.2 for discussion Conceptual grounding, then demonstration on real texts Writer in revision §7 (tests) → §8 (failures) → §5.5 (the beat-weight audit) → §11 (checklist) Fast triage of a live draft, in that order Teacher or workshop leader §4 , 6, 8, 9 for material; §12.1 for assignments; §12.3 for the rubric Ready-made teaching sequence with worked models and six seminar questions A caution before beginning is more necessary in this chapter than in most. The six-beat model is the most mechanisable instrument in this textbook, because it alone tells a writer what to write next. It can be turned into a template and filled in; drafts produced that way have a recognisable flatness: correct in structure, dead on the page. The model’s proper use is retrospective . It describes what a working chain looks like from the outside; it does not tell a writer what should happen next, and a writer who asks it to will get a plausible answer and a mediocre book.

title: 1. Introduction: The Two Halves of Narrative Motion
section: Introduction — The Two Halves of Narrative Motion
text: 1.1 One complaint, two opposite diseases A common complaint about an unsuccessful manuscript is that nothing is happening . It is also one of the least useful complaints, because two structurally opposite conditions produce it, and the remedy for each is the remedy that worsens the other. Consider two drafts. Draft One is full of incident. In eighty pages there is an arrest, a flood, a confession and a fire. Each is competently written and each is over within four pages, at which point the next chapter opens somewhere else with someone doing something new. A reader reports that the book is busy and that nothing is happening. What they mean is that nothing lands : events arrive at a rate that exceeds the reader’s capacity to convert them into consequence, and consequence is the only currency in which events are stored. Draft Two is full of interiority. Its protagonist has suffered a real catastrophe on page nine and has been considering it ever since. The prose is fine, the psychology is credible, the sentences are the best in the writer’s portfolio. A reader reports that the book is beautiful and that nothing is happening. What they mean is that nothing is due : the character has been weighing without committing, and a weighing that never terminates in a choice is not deliberation but scenery with a mind in it. Both drafts fail the same reader test and require opposite interventions. Draft One needs its catastrophes to be absorbed; Draft Two needs its absorption to terminate in a decision. A vocabulary that calls both “pacing problems” cannot tell them apart. This chapter’s vocabulary can. The asymmetry runs deeper than diagnosis. Craft language for the active half of narrative is rich and old: conflict, obstacle, stakes, reversal, climax. Craft language for the reactive half is thin, and where it exists, it is faintly pejorative — “reflection”, “downtime”, “the quiet bit”, “the breather”. The imbalance is not neutral. It encourages writers to treat aftermath as the space between the interesting parts, when in fact the aftermath is where a novel does most of its character work, most of its thematic work, and all of its work of converting event into motive. 1.2 The claim in its strong form A story is not a sequence of things that happened. It is a chain of things that had to happen next. That sentence is the chapter’s first principle, and it will be argued from four independent directions in §3 . What it does and does not claim needs stating carefully. It does claim that readers experience narrative units as connected or unconnected, that the difference is detectable, and that connection is produced principally by the pursuit and frustration of goals. It does claim that a unit which neither descends from what precedes it nor generates what follows is structurally free, however good its prose, and that structural freedom is felt by readers as inconsequence. It does not claim that causal necessity is a property of the text. “Had to” is a relation the reader constructs across a gap, and readers construct it very readily — often on evidence a logician would refuse. §3.7 develops this, and it is the chapter’s principal qualification. It does not claim that fiction organised on other principles is defective. The picaresque, the episodic satire, the novel of consciousness and the novel of static condition are all major forms in which the chain is loose, broken or absent by design. §6 and §8 catalogue them. It does not claim that the six beats are the only route to necessity. Thematic rhyme, formal pattern, image repetition and prosody all produce a sense of inevitability without a single goal being stated. What the six beats offer is the most teachable route, not the only one. 1.3 Where this chapter sits in the series Chapter 1 ( The Purposes of a Scene ) asked what a scene is for and answered in terms of the value shift — what is true at the end that was not true at the start — and the domains in which a shift can occur: plot, character, theme and texture, to which Chapter 1 adds a fifth, the relational. That chapter used “scene” in the loose, working sense: any stretch of dramatised action. This chapter narrows the term and adds the missing half. Where Chapter 1 asks does this unit do a job? , Chapter 2 asks does this unit’s job arise from the last one’s, and does it create the next one’s? The two tests are independent. A scene can pass the value-shift test and still be causally free — a magnificently executed episode that could be moved fifty pages in either direction without damage. Chapter 1 would keep it; this chapter asks what holds it in place. Three further dependencies run forward from here, and each is named where it arises: Chapter 5 ( The Transition ) handles how the gap between two units is crossed. This chapter handles what must be true on either side of it for the crossing to feel necessary. A transition can be technically flawless and still read as arbitrary if the chain is broken underneath it. Chapter 6 ( The Chapter Break ) handles where the gap is placed . The deferred decision analysed at §6.4 is a chapter-break technique before it is anything else, and the two chapters should be read together. Chapter 16 ( The Ending ) inherits the causal chain wholesale. An ending feels earned — Chapter 16’s central term — largely to the degree that it is the terminus of a chain the reader can trace backwards. §6.13 and §16 both point forward to this. One symmetry, named here at the outset, organises §6 . Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages ) works with no accumulated context; Chapter 16 ( The Ending ) works with nothing but accumulated context. The scene–sequel pair is the mechanism by which context accumulates in between. It is, in the plainest sense, the engine that carries a book from the first of those conditions to the second.

title: 2. Definitions and Boundaries
text: The vocabulary of this chapter is unusually treacherous, for a specific reason: two of its central terms — scene and sequel — already have widely used meanings that are not the ones intended here. A student who does not distinguish the senses early may conflate them throughout §§4–9 . 2.1 Working definitions Scene (narrow sense). A unit of dramatised action in which a point-of-view character pursues a concrete, immediate goal , meets conflict , and ends in disaster — a state materially worse than the one in which the unit began, or a success whose cost exceeds its value. Sequel. The unit that follows a scene, in which the same character registers the disaster emotionally ( reaction ), weighs a set of options none of which is good ( dilemma ), and commits to a new concrete objective ( decision ) — which becomes the following scene’s goal. Four elements of those definitions carry weight. “Point-of-view character.” The model is focalised. It describes the experience of one consciousness at a time, which is why multi-viewpoint novels run several chains in parallel ( §6.5 ) and why the model has little to say about narration that is not anchored in a person ( §8.7 ). “Concrete, immediate.” The goal is scene-sized, not book-sized. Get the key back before he changes his mind is a goal; understand my father is a theme. “Materially worse.” The disaster is defined by its structural function — it must generate a sequel — and not by its magnitude. A disaster can be a raised eyebrow. “Becomes the following scene’s goal.” This is the load-bearing clause and the whole reason the model exists. Without it, the six beats are a description of one unit; with it, they are an account of how units connect. 2.2 Scale and extent Neither half has a characteristic length, and one of the more damaging misreadings of the model is that a sequel is a chapter type . Unit Shortest observed Longest observed Note Scene A sentence A hundred pages (the Waterloo chapters of Vanity Fair ; the ball in Anna Karenina extended across several chapters) Length tracks the density of resistance, not the importance of the goal Sequel A single clause — she did not wait to see whether he would follow Five of the six parts of Crime and Punishment See §9.1 A complete pair A paragraph A volume Serial fiction often runs one pair per instalment Two consequences follow. First, the beats are functions, not paragraphs : a beat is a job done, and the job may be done in a subordinate clause. Second, the model does not predict chapter architecture. A chapter may contain three complete pairs, half a pair, or a sequel alone. Where the breaks fall is Chapter 6’s subject, and the two decisions — where the beats fall, where the breaks fall — are independent variables that a great many drafts confuse. 2.3 The term most often confused: “scene” The word “scene” is used in at least four distinct senses in ordinary craft conversation, and the differences matter. Sense Meaning Used in Loose / workshop Any continuous stretch of dramatised action, rendered moment by moment Chapter 1, and most of this series Narrow / Swain Specifically the goal–conflict–disaster half of the pair This chapter, §§4–9 Genettean A relation of duration — narrative time approximately equal to story time, as against summary, ellipsis and pause Chapter 5 ( The Transition ) Dramaturgical A division of an act, marked by entrance and exit Screen and stage practice; §10.4 This chapter uses the narrow sense throughout and signals the loose sense explicitly where it is needed. The Genettean sense is the one to keep most carefully separate, because it is a claim about rate rather than about function : a Swain scene may contain summary, and a Genettean scene may contain no goal at all. A second, cruder confusion is worth disposing of at once. “Sequel” here has nothing to do with a follow-up volume. Swain’s usage is idiosyncratic and, in retrospect, unfortunate; some later manuals substitute “aftermath” or “reflective unit”. This chapter retains “sequel” because it is the term in which the model is transmitted and because the alternatives are worse — “aftermath” implies passivity, and the sequel’s job is to produce a decision . 2.4 Adjacent terms Term Meaning Relation to this chapter’s units Beat Smallest unit of dramatic change; in screen usage, an exchange in which the transaction between characters turns A Swain beat is one of six named functions, which is narrower and more specific Motivation-reaction unit (MRU) Swain’s sentence-level unit: an external motivating stimulus, then the character’s response in the fixed order feeling, action, speech The same causal principle at paragraph scale; see §4.0 Kernel / satellite Chatman’s distinction between events that open alternatives and events that elaborate without branching A disaster is nearly always a kernel; reaction is usually satellite material Function Propp’s unit: an act defined by its significance for the course of the action An earlier analogue of a “beat”; see §3.4 Proairetic code Barthes’s code of actions — the reader’s naming of a sequence in progress The reader-side description of what a scene is; §3.3 Peripeteia Aristotle’s reversal: a change of fortune arising from the action itself The classical ancestor of “disaster”; §3.1 Turning point Loose critical term for any structurally consequential moment Overlaps disaster and decision without distinguishing them Obligatory scene The confrontation a plot has promised and must deliver A scene the chain has made necessary far in advance; see Chapter 16 Dénouement The unwinding after the climax Structurally, an extended terminal sequel; §6.9 Dilatory space Brooks’s term for the middle of a narrative, which resists the end it desires The theoretical form of the deferral techniques in §6 2.5 What this chapter excludes What a scene is for — the value shift, the five domains and the principle of multiplicity are the subject of Chapter 1 ( The Purposes of a Scene ), and are used here as established equipment. How the gap between units is crossed — Chapter 5 ( The Transition ). Where the gaps are placed, and what a break does to a deferred decision — Chapter 6 ( The Chapter Break ). Whose chain the reader is following after a shift — Chapter 13 ( The Viewpoint Shift ). Chains that run in the past — analepsis, and the cost of interrupting a chain to visit its antecedents, are Chapter 7’s ( Backstory and Flashback ). Parallel and subordinate chains — Chapter 14 ( The Subplot ). Braiding is treated here only as a deferral device ( §6.5 ); how a second chain earns its page space is Chapter 14’s question. The chain’s two boundaries — Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages ) and Chapter 16 ( The Ending ).

title: 3. Why Causality Carries the Weight
text: The causal chain is usually asserted and left there. It can be argued, and from several independent directions — classical poetics, psychoanalytic narratology, structuralist analysis, discourse psychology and institutional history. This section assembles the case, and then, in §3.7, takes most of it back — or rather, states the precise sense in which the principle is true, which is narrower and more interesting than the assertion. 3.1 Aristotle: because of this , not after this The distinction on which this chapter rests is the oldest in the field, and it is worth recovering in its original form rather than in the version craft manuals inherit. In the Poetics , Aristotle ranks plots. The worst, he says in chapter 9, are episodic — those in which the episodes follow one another with neither probability nor necessity. The best are those in which events occur contrary to expectation and yet on account of one another : the Greek is δι’ ἄλληλα ( di’ allēla ), “through one another”, and the phrase does the work this chapter’s “had to happen next” does, two and a half millennia earlier. Two refinements matter for practice. Aristotle’s criterion is probability or necessity, not certainty. The events must seem to arise from one another as this kind of person, in this situation, would act . This is a plausibility standard, not a logical one — which is why the model is a craft instrument rather than a proof procedure. Two of his structural devices illuminate the disaster beat. Peripeteia , the reversal, is a change to the opposite state of affairs arising out of the action itself; anagnorisis , recognition, is a shift from ignorance to knowledge. Either can turn a unit by changing a situation or a character’s knowledge; neither necessarily leaves the character worse off. The “yes, but” disaster of §4.3 is a peripeteia in miniature, and the “got what they wanted and discovered it was not what they needed” variant is anagnorisis domesticated. The Latin tag usually attached to this — post hoc against propter hoc , “after this” against “because of this” — comes from logic rather than from poetics, where it names a fallacy: the error of inferring causation from succession. Its migration into narrative theory involves a small and instructive irony. In logic, treating succession as causation is a mistake. In narrative it is a competence. Readers do it constantly, automatically and with very little evidence, and the entire art of the causal chain consists in supplying enough of that evidence to make the inference feel earned rather than imposed. §3.7 returns to this. E. M. Forster’s Aspects of the Novel (1927) supplies the formulation every student already half-knows: “The king died and then the queen died,” is a story. “The king died, and then the queen died of grief” is a plot. Two words — of grief — convert sequence into consequence. Forster’s example is worth pressing further than he presses it, because it demonstrates how cheap the conversion is. He does not dramatise the queen’s grief, motivate it, or show it. He asserts a causal relation in a prepositional phrase, and the reader accepts it. This is the mechanism the “and so / but” test ( §7.1 , test 6) exploits. 3.2 Brooks: narrative desire, delay and discharge The most sustained modern theorisation of what the goal–disaster engine actually does to a reader is Peter Brooks’s Reading for the Plot (1984), and it is the scholarly counterpart to the whole of §4 . Brooks’s argument begins by refusing the structuralist habit of describing plot as a static configuration. Plot, for Brooks, is dynamic : it is the “logic of the dis course” as it unfolds in time, and its motor is narrative desire — the reader’s want, produced by the text and sustained across it, for the end that will confer meaning on everything before it. Reading is the experience of being pulled towards a conclusion whose arrival will retrospectively organise the middle. Two consequences follow that bear directly on the six beats. First, the middle exists to resist the end it desires. Brooks, reading Freud’s Beyond the Pleasure Principle , describes the narrative middle as a dilatory space — an “arabesque” of detour, delay and repetition whose function is to prevent the short circuit, the “improper end” reached too quickly. A story that discharged its desire immediately would be no story. The disaster beat is the structural device that prevents the short circuit : every time a goal is nearly reached and then converted into a worse problem, the discharge is deferred and the desire renewed. This is the theoretical reason the “clean win” is a structural fault ( §8.2 ) rather than merely a missed opportunity. A clean win is a small death of desire. Second, plot is bound up with mortality. Brooks’s most quoted formulation describes plot as the “internal logic of the discourse of mortality” — narrative as the form in which a life, which is merely sequential while it is lived, becomes shapely by being read from its end. The relevance to the sequel half is exact. The Reaction beat is where a character registers that something is irreversible; the Dilemma beat is where the narrowing of remaining options is felt; the Decision beat is where a finite quantity of remaining life is spent on one course rather than another. A sequel is a small rehearsal of the fact that choices cannot be unmade — which is why the reversibility test ( §7.1 , test 9) catches so much weak material. Brooks also supplies the vocabulary for §6 . The techniques of interruption and deferral are not tricks appended to a plot; they are the plot’s own resistance to its ending, made visible. 3.3 The structuralist description: Barthes, Todorov, Propp Three structuralist accounts describe, from three directions, what the six beats formalise. None was written with craft pedagogy in view, and their independence from it is what makes the convergence worth noticing. Barthes’s proairetic code. In S/Z (1970), Roland Barthes distinguishes five codes by which a reader processes a narrative text. The proairetic — from proairesis , the rational determination of the result of an action — is the code of actions : the reader’s running capacity to recognise a sequence in progress and give it a name. Barthes’s own examples are gestures like Stroll , Murder , Rendezvous . The point is that the sequence is constituted by the naming : an action becomes legible as a unit because the reader can title it, and titling it involves projecting its completion. This is what a legible goal does. A goal is a licence to name the sequence. A character who wants the key allows the reader to open a file called getting the key , into which subsequent sentences are filed and against which they are measured. The goal may be stated or inferred from action. Flatness arises when the reader cannot discern a purpose and has no title under which to file the events , so files them separately, as a list. Barthes’s hermeneutic code — the posing and delaying of enigmas — is the proairetic code’s partner and is treated in Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages ). The distinction is useful here: the hermeneutic code makes the reader want to know ; the proairetic code makes the reader want to see what happens . Suspense in Meir Sternberg’s sense is proairetic; curiosity is hermeneutic. Most strong scenes run both. Todorov’s equilibrium schema. Tzvetan Todorov, in The Poetics of Prose (1971; Eng. 1977), proposes that the minimal complete plot moves from an initial equilibrium , through a force that disrupts it, through a recognition of the disruption and an attempt to repair it, to a new equilibrium which is not the old one restored but a second state of the same kind. The schema operates at the scale of the whole narrative; the six beats operate at the scale of the chapter. But they have the same shape, and a scene–sequel pair is legible as a Todorovian cycle in miniature: the goal presupposes an equilibrium worth defending or improving, the disaster disrupts, the sequel recognises and repairs, and the decision establishes a new state from which the next disruption can be launched. Two things follow. Todorov’s model explains why the model nests : the same structure describes a paragraph, a chapter and a novel, which is why a well-made book feels self-similar at several scales. And his insistence that the final equilibrium differs from the first is the theoretical form of Chapter 1’s value shift. Propp’s functions. Vladimir Propp’s Morphology of the Folktale (1928; Eng. 1958) analysed a hundred Russian wonder tales into thirty-one functions — units defined not by who performs them or how, but by their significance for the course of the action . This is the definitional move that makes a “beat” a beat: a function is a job, and the same job may be carried by any content. Three of Propp’s functions map onto the model with uncomfortable precision: Propp Swain VIII / VIIIa — Villainy, or Lack: the villain causes harm, or something is found to be missing Disaster IX — Mediation: the misfortune is made known and the hero is dispatched or allowed to go The bridge from disaster into reaction X — Beginning counteraction: the seeker agrees to, or decides upon, counteraction Decision Propp’s function X is a decision beat named as such, thirty-seven years before Techniques of the Selling Writer . The convergence is not evidence that Swain read Propp — there is no reason to think he did, and the first English translation appeared only seven years before his book. It is evidence that both were describing the same thing: a strongly conventionalised narrative grammar, one from the outside as an analyst, one from the inside as a working professional. That two such different projects arrive at the same units is the best available argument that the units are real. It is also, as §3.6 argues, an argument that they are real for a particular family of narratives . 3.4 Burke: form as appetite One further theoretical strand is worth adding because it names the mechanism the others describe. Kenneth Burke, in Counter-Statement (1931), offers the most economical definition of narrative form in the literature: Form is the creation of an appetite in the mind of the auditor, and the adequate satisfying of that appetite. Two words carry the load. “Appetite” makes form a condition of the reader rather than a property of the artefact — the same move Brooks makes fifty years later. “Adequate” concedes that satisfaction admits of degree, and that the relation between the appetite created and the satisfaction supplied is the whole art. Applied to the six beats, Burke’s formula produces the clearest statement of what each half is for. The scene creates the appetite — a goal is an appetite installed in the reader, and a disaster is an appetite denied and thereby intensified. The sequel converts an unsatisfied appetite into a new one , which is why a sequel without a decision ( §8.8 ) leaves a reader with a hunger and no dish coming. Burke’s later Grammar of Motives (1945) supplies a second instrument, less often applied to fiction than it should be: the pentad of act, scene, agent, agency and purpose, and the analysis of motive through the ratios between them. A scene–sequel pair can be described as the working-out of an agent–purpose ratio under pressure from scene and agency: the character wants X (purpose) and the situation (scene) will not permit the means (agency) they have. Where a draft’s motivation feels thin, Burke’s question — which term of the pentad is the narrative pretending is not there? — is frequently more productive than asking what the character wants. 3.5 The cognitive evidence: causal networks and what readers retain The strongest empirical support for the chapter’s first principle comes from discourse psychology, and it says something narrower and more useful than “causality is good”. Situation models. Rolf Zwaan and Gabriel Radvansky’s synthesis (1998) holds that readers do not store sentences but construct a situation model — a representation of the state of affairs described — indexed on a small number of dimensions. Two of the five are this chapter’s business: Dimension Reader’s implicit question Beat that supplies it Intentionality What does someone want, and is it being achieved? Goal , and its frustration at Disaster Causality What is making things happen? The chain as a whole; the descent of goal from decision The model’s central prediction is that readers pay a measurable processing cost whenever an index shifts without warning. A new scene whose goal does not descend from the previous decision is, in these terms, an unsignalled shift on the intentionality and causality dimensions simultaneously — which is a precise cognitive description of the “free goal” failure ( §8.1 ) and explains why it registers as effortful rather than merely as odd . Causal connection and recall. More directly to the point, a body of work associated with Tom Trabasso and colleagues models a narrative as a causal network — events linked by relations of necessity in the circumstances — and finds two robust effects. First, events that lie on the causal chain connecting the opening to the outcome are recalled better, judged more important, and included more often in summaries than events that lie off it, even when the off-chain events are equally prominent on the page. Second, the number of causal connections an event has predicts how well it is remembered. Events with many links are recalled at rates substantially above events with few, independent of their position in the text. Alan Graesser, Murray Singer and Trabasso’s constructionist account (1994) adds the mechanism: readers engage in a search after meaning , generating causal antecedent inferences as a matter of course — asking, in effect, why is this happening now? — while generating predictive inferences about what will happen next only weakly and inconsistently. That asymmetry is the most practically useful finding in this section, and it has two consequences that cut against intuition. Readers will work hard to connect a new event backwards. A chain that is there does not need to be underlined. The reader is already looking for the antecedent. Readers predict future events less consistently than they infer antecedents, but they can infer character goals. Experiments find that readers infer some unstated goals during comprehension, particularly larger goals that organise a sequence (Long, Golding and Graesser 1992). This is the empirical case for making a goal legible before the conflict begins, whether through a statement or through action whose purpose the reader can discern; it does not require a sentence of stated intention. The goal test ( §7.1 , test 1) asks whether the reader can name that purpose. A caution, stated plainly. These findings describe comprehension and memory , not literary value. They demonstrate that causally connected material is easier to retain and more likely to be judged important. They do not demonstrate that easily retained narratives are better ones, and a great deal of ambitious fiction deliberately makes retention difficult. The correct inference is modest: the chain is a device for making a narrative cheap to process , and cheapness of processing is a resource a writer may spend or decline to spend. 3.6 The provenance of the model A university textbook has an obligation the trade manuals do not: to say where its instruments come from. The six-beat model has a specific and traceable history, and knowing it changes how the model should be used. Dwight V. Swain (1915–1992) wrote for the American all-fiction magazines and produced category fiction before becoming a professor of professional writing at the University of Oklahoma. Techniques of the Selling Writer (University of Oklahoma Press, 1965) is the codification of a commercial practice, and its title is exact about its purpose. It is not a poetics. It is a manual for producing publishable copy in a market that paid by the word and bought reliably shaped stories in volume. The following parallels are an interpretation of how the model suited commercial writing, not a documented account of how each feature originated: Commercial-writing condition Corresponding feature of the model Payment by the word, high output, short deadlines A generative template — the model tells a writer what to write next, which criticism never does Magazine and paperback readers reading in short sessions Units sized to a sitting; each unit must end in a state that motivates the next Editorial demand for legible forward motion The prohibition on the clean win; the insistence that every scene end worse A genre readership with strong formal expectations Goals that are concrete and external; protagonists who act Swain also gives the model a second, smaller unit, which most restatements omit and which deserves rescuing: the motivation-reaction unit . At sentence and paragraph scale, Swain argues, narrative alternates between an external motivating stimulus (something happens, presented objectively) and the character’s reaction to it, rendered in a fixed order — feeling, then action, then speech. Later craft accounts distinguish involuntary reflex from rational action within that middle step. Whatever one thinks of the prescribed order, the MRU makes explicit what the six beats imply: the causal principle is meant to operate all the way down , from the paragraph to the book. §4.0 returns to it. Transmission. The model reached its present ubiquity chiefly through Jack M. Bickham , Swain’s colleague at Oklahoma, whose Scene & Structure (Writer’s Digest Books, 1993) restated the six beats for a new generation in the widely distributed Elements of Fiction Writing series. From there the model passed into the online craft ecosystem — writing blogs, plotting software, self-publishing pedagogy — where it now circulates in a highly simplified form, frequently without attribution and frequently without the qualifications Swain himself supplies. Much of what a contemporary writer encounters as timeless craft wisdom about “scene and sequel” is a fourth-generation copy of a 1965 trade manual. The historical coincidence. Swain’s book appears at the height of the American programme era — Mark McGurl’s term, in The Program Era (2009), for the period in which creative writing became an institutionalised university discipline and the dominant patron of American literary fiction. Two pedagogies were therefore being built at once, and they taught nearly opposite lessons: The university workshop The commercial manual Central unit The image, the sentence, the moment of perception The scene, the beat, the chain Prized effect Epiphany; the revelatory close Escalation; the unresolved close Model author Chekhov, Joyce, Hemingway, Flannery O’Connor Erle Stanley Gardner, John D. MacDonald Attitude to plot Suspicion; plot as vulgarity or as given Plot as the whole craft What counts as failure Sentimentality; inauthenticity Inertia; the reader who stops The two traditions were, for decades, almost hermetically separated, and the separation is the reason the six-beat model can still feel like a discovery to writers trained in literary programmes. It is also the reason the model carries assumptions that are worth surfacing. Its prized virtues — agency, escalation, forward motion, external goals — are the virtues of one tradition, historically situated. They are not neutral descriptions of narrative. §8.7 examines the sharpest case: the prohibition on the passive protagonist, which is very close to a genre preference wearing the clothes of a structural principle. The honest verdict is double, and students should be able to hold both halves. The model is a commercial pedagogy, and its provenance shows. It is also, demonstrably, a good description of how an enormous range of narrative actually works, including a great deal of fiction its author would not have read and would not have enjoyed. Provenance is a reason for care, not for dismissal. 3.7 The first principle, restated and qualified We can now state the principle. The causal chain. A scene’s disaster is the specific event the following sequel reacts to; that sequel’s decision is the specific goal the following scene pursues. Where both links hold, units read as consequences of one another; where either fails, units read as items on a list. And now the qualification, which is the more valuable half. Causality in narrative is conferred, not contained. Roland Barthes made the point with characteristic sharpness in “Introduction to the Structural Analysis of Narratives” (1966): everything suggests that the mainspring of narrative activity is precisely the confusion of consequence and chronological succession — what comes after being read as what comes because . Forster’s queen dies of grief only because Forster says so; and, more disturbingly for the model, she would die of grief in most readers’ minds even if he did not, provided the two deaths were adjacent and the marriage had been mentioned. Three practical consequences follow, and they are the reason §7 insists that a failed test is a question rather than a verdict. Adjacency does much of the work the model attributes to structure. A reader will read a sequel as caused by the disaster that precedes it with very little help. This is a resource: it means the causal signalling can usually be lighter than a writer fears, and that heavy signposting ( because of what had happened in the barn, she now had to decide whether… ) is nearly always a symptom of insufficient trust. The chain can therefore be simulated, and it can be faked. A draft can pass the chain test at the level of stated motive and still feel arbitrary, because the causality is asserted in the connective tissue rather than dramatised in the beats. The chain test ( §7.1 , test 5) is designed to be run on events , not on the sentences that link them, for this reason. Refusing the chain is a legitimate and well-populated option. The picaresque runs on succession by design; Don Quixote and Tristram Shandy make the arbitrariness of sequence part of the joke; Catch-22 makes the absence of causal logic its central argument ( §9.6 ); and a large body of modernist and postmodern fiction treats causal plotting as a nineteenth-century convention to be dismantled. A model that classifies these as failures has misunderstood its own status. The principle, then, is not a law of narrative. It is a description of the dominant mode, an account of the cheapest available route to felt necessity, and — most usefully — a diagnostic instrument that tells a writer what kind of book they are currently writing . That last formulation is the chapter’s real position, and §16 returns to it.

title: 4. The Six Beats — and a Proposed Seventh
section: The Six Beats — and a Proposed Seventh
text: 4.0 The model and its status The six beats are a functional taxonomy. Each names a job, not a quantity of prose; the same beat may occupy four pages or four words, and a single sentence may discharge two beats at once. What the taxonomy provides is a set of separable questions with separable remedies, which is what converts the useless instruction make this chapter better into something a writer can act on. Its characteristic misuse is as a composition template . Filled in beat by beat, it produces a recognisable species of competent, inert prose: the goal announced in the first paragraph, the conflict duly encountered, the disaster arriving on schedule, the reaction rendered in the approved physical vocabulary, the dilemma laid out in two balanced sentences, the decision closing the chapter. Everything is in place and nothing is alive. The reason is that the model describes the skeleton of a working scene, and a skeleton assembled first and clothed afterwards has the proportions of a diagram. Two protections against this, both used throughout §§4.1–4.6. Read the model backwards. Its proper use is on a completed draft, to find out what is already there and what is missing. Swain’s own book is a manual of composition; this chapter converts it into an instrument of revision, which is a change in kind. Attend to the compressed cases. For each beat, §§4.1–4.6 ask not only what full delivery looks like but what the beat looks like compressed to nothing — because in accomplished fiction that is what it usually looks like, and a student who has only seen the expanded version will not recognise the beat when it is doing its work invisibly. One further piece of Swain’s apparatus is worth carrying into the taxonomy, since it explains what the beats are made of. The motivation-reaction unit (MRU) is his sentence-level pattern: an external, objectively presented stimulus, followed by the viewpoint character’s response. Swain’s prescribed internal order for the response — feeling, action, speech — is too rigid to be adopted as a rule, and reads today as a period style. Later accounts distinguish involuntary reflex from deliberate action within his middle step. But the principle underneath it is sound and is the same principle as the chain: nothing in a narrative should arrive without a visible cause immediately preceding it, at whatever scale one is working. The MRU is the causal chain at the scale of the paragraph; the six beats are the same chain at the scale of the chapter; the plot is the same chain at the scale of the book. Each of the six sections below follows the same pattern: definition · what it buys · textual carriers · discussion · under- and over-delivery · illustrations · compressed to nothing. 4.1 Goal Definition. A concrete, immediate objective which the point-of-view character pursues within the unit, legible to the reader before the resistance begins, and specific enough that the reader can tell whether it has been achieved. What it buys. A yardstick. Without a goal there is no measure against which any subsequent event counts as progress or setback, and therefore — per Barthes ( §3.3 ) — no title under which the reader can file what happens. Tension is not produced by danger; it is produced by an outcome the reader can score. This is why a fight between two strangers is merely fast, and a conversation in which someone is trying not to cry is tense. Textual carriers Carrier Example of the form Note Direct statement of intention She had come to get the key and she was not leaving without it. Cheapest, bluntest; suits commercial registers and first-person retrospect A stated deadline or condition before he changed his mind Converts a goal into a goal with a clock , doubling its yield An action already in progress A character who is knocking on a door has a goal The most economical form; see “compressed to nothing” below A question the character asks Interrogation implies an objective Especially efficient in dialogue-led scenes; see Chapter 3 ( The Dialogue Exchange ) Descent from the prior decision The reader already knows what she resolved to do The strongest form: the goal arrives pre-motivated Selected detail What the character notices is what the character is looking for Characterisation and goal in one operation; the multiplicity principle of Chapter 1 Discussion The distinction that does the most work in revision is between the scene goal and the story goal . Find out what my father was hiding is a story goal; it cannot be pursued in a room. Get Dov to say why the locks were changed is a scene goal: it has an addressee, an occasion and a criterion of success. Drafts that feel unfocused very often have a perfectly clear story goal and no scene goals at all, and the resulting prose has the odd quality of being about something urgent while nothing urgent is happening. The second distinction is between a goal and a wish . A goal is something the character is doing something about now. A wish is a state of affairs they would prefer. Wishes are not scene engines, and a draft in which the protagonist wishes for a great deal and pursues nothing is the passive-protagonist problem ( §8.7 ) in its purest form. A third point, easily missed: the goal need not be admirable, achievable, or even conscious to the character , but it must be legible to the reader. A character who is manifestly trying not to know something has a goal, and it is a good one. Under- and over-delivery Under: the illegible goal . The scene has an engine the writer can name and the reader cannot. Diagnosed by the goal test ( §7.1 , test 1) and remedied not by adding a sentence of explanation but by giving the character an action whose object is visible. Under, second form: the diffuse goal — “she wanted things to be better between them”. Nothing can count as failure, so nothing can count as disaster. Over: the announced goal , in which a character states an objective the situation has already made obvious, usually in dialogue and usually to someone who does not need telling. The reader experiences this as being managed. Over, second form: the over-motivated goal , where a paragraph of justification precedes a small objective. Motivation is the sequel’s job, and importing it into the goal beat is the commonest way of stalling a scene’s opening. Illustrations Herbert, Dune (1965). Paul’s goal in the gom jabbar scene is stated as a physical instruction and could not be more concrete: keep his hand inside the box while the Reverend Mother holds a poisoned needle at his neck. He must not withdraw. The scene’s entire tension derives from the fact that success and failure are visible from outside — the hand is in the box or it is not — while the experience being resisted is invisible. §9.4 analyses the full sequence. Dostoevsky, Crime and Punishment (1866). Raskolnikov’s goal at the opening of Part One is a masterclass in the goal held just below the surface: he is conducting what he calls a rehearsal, and the reader is permitted to know that an objective exists, and its rough shape, long before its content is named. The scene remains taut because the criterion is legible — he is finding out whether he can — even while the object is withheld. Dickens, Great Expectations (1861). Pip’s goal in Chapter 1 is almost nothing: he is looking at his parents’ gravestones and trying to work out from the lettering what they were like. It is the smallest possible objective, and it is sufficient, because it is specific and because the convict’s arrival converts it instantly into a different one — survive this man — which is smaller still and completely legible. Compressed to nothing The goal beat compresses further than any other, because an action in progress implies its own objective . A character picking a lock has a goal; no sentence is required. Fiction of high accomplishment routinely opens units this way, and the apparent absence of a goal beat is in fact a goal beat carried by a verb. The test for whether the compression has succeeded is simple: ask what the character would count as success in the next ninety seconds . If the reader could answer, the beat is present. If only the writer could, it is missing. 4.2 Conflict Definition. The resistance the goal meets: an opposing person, a physical obstacle, a competing obligation, a rule, an absence, or the character’s own reluctance. Its job is to change the shape of the goal, not merely to postpone its achievement. What it buys. Duration with meaning. Conflict is what allows a scene to occupy pages without the reader feeling that time is being filled, because each encounter with resistance yields information — about the obstacle, about the character, about the cost of continuing.
