Five parts and an epilogue remain. Nothing in those five parts is a scene in the narrow sense that terminates the chain. Raskolnikov forms goals — evade Porfiry, find out what Razumikhin knows, discover what Svidrigailov overheard, get Sonya to read the Lazarus passage — and every one of them is a goal generated by his reaction to the murder rather than by a decision that closed a completed sequel. The book is one enormous Sequel with scenes inside it. Why this does not stall. Apply the test at §5.4 : does the expansion yield? Each of the five parts introduces a new consideration into the same dilemma. Part New consideration entering the sequel Two The body will not obey the theory; illness as refutation Three Porfiry: the theory stated aloud, in public, as an article Four Sonya, and the possibility that suffering is not a defeat Five Katerina Ivanovna’s death; the spectacle of another’s ruin Six Svidrigailov as the theory lived out to its conclusion, and his suicide Five parts, five new terms. The dilemma — confess or persist — is stable throughout, and it is never re-weighed in the same words twice, because each part changes what confession would mean . The hinge, and where it is. The decision to confess arrives at the end of Part Six. But the criterion change ( §4.7 ) does not happen there; it happens earlier and by degrees, and locating it is a genuine critical problem worth setting to students. The candidates are Sonya’s reading of the raising of Lazarus, the confession to Sonya, and — the strongest case — Svidrigailov’s suicide, which shows Raskolnikov the only other available future. What is not in doubt is that the confession is made on grounds Raskolnikov would have rejected in Part One, and that the epilogue insists the real change occurs after the novel ends. The verdict. Crime and Punishment does not break the model; it runs one iteration of it across six hundred pages. Every beat is present, correctly ordered, and correctly caused. What the novel demonstrates is that the six beats say nothing whatever about duration — that a structure devised to organise a magazine story will describe, without modification, one of the least commercial novels ever written, provided one abandons the assumption that a sequel is a chapter. It also demonstrates the model’s limit. What the six beats cannot tell you is why five hundred pages of a stable dilemma are gripping rather than tedious. For that one needs Brooks on desire and delay ( §3.2 ), or Bakhtin on the unfinalised consciousness, or simply the observation that the prose is doing something the diagram cannot record. Structural claims here survive translation; the texture claims do not. Readers working from Garnett, Pevear and Volokhonsky, or Katz will find the same chain and three different Raskolnikovs. 9.2 Brontë, Jane Eyre (1847) — the interrupted wedding Goal: to be married, that morning. Conflict: none, until Chapter 26, when a solicitor and a stranger interrupt the service. Disaster: the compounded failure, reaching backwards — the marriage is prevented, the household’s year of strangeness acquires an explanation, and Jane’s understanding of her own position is retrospectively rewritten. What follows is a model sequel of unusual proportions. Reaction occupies the remainder of Chapter 26 and is rendered almost entirely as sensory withdrawal — the room, the light, the physical incapacity — and by a shift into a register of dissociation. Dilemma occupies most of Chapter 27, and Brontë does the thing most drafts will not: she gives the wrong option the better speeches. Rochester’s case is materially sound and emotionally overwhelming, and the novel lets it run for pages. The hinge is Jane’s declaration that she cares for herself, and that the more friendless and unsustained she is, the more she will respect herself. This is not a decision; it is the criterion from which a decision can be derived, stated in the open. Decision is executed rather than announced: she leaves before dawn, with almost nothing, and the concreteness of the leaving — the road, the coach fare, the parcel left behind — is what makes it irreversible. The pair is a demonstration of §4.7 ’s argument in miniature. Remove the criterion sentence and the beats are all still present, correctly formed; what disappears is any reason to regard the departure as an arc rather than an event. 9.3 Dickens, Great Expectations (1861) — the convict on the marshes The opening chapters provide a compact scene–sequel sequence, and the first chapter is a teaching text for the smallness of a legitimate goal. Goal: Pip, in the churchyard, is trying to work out from the shape of the lettering what his dead parents were like. It is an objective of almost no magnitude, and it is sufficient, because it is specific. Conflict and disaster arrive together, in a voice — “Hold your noise!” — and a man among the graves who takes the child by the throat and threatens, in the novel’s most quoted line of dialogue, to cut it. The disaster is not the threat; it is the demand : a file and wittles, by morning, or the young man who is hidden with him will find Pip out. The sequel is chiefly in Chapter 2 , with terror rendered in Pip’s dream of the gibbet and his guilty perception of the pantry. His dilemma is real and both options are costly: steal from Mrs Joe, or fail the convict. His decision is executed physically, in the pantry, in the dark, with a pork pie. His guilt continues to colour his perception in Chapter 3, when the cattle seem to accuse him on the marshes. Two lessons. First, the goal beat may be nearly weightless if the disaster is not . Second, and more useful in revision: much of the sequel is carried by objects — the file, the pie, the brandy — and there is not one sentence of abstract deliberation in it. 9.4 Herbert, Dune (1965) — the goal made physical The gom jabbar scene is the model’s clearest illustration in twentieth-century fiction, and it repays study because it is so mechanically clean. Beat Realisation Goal Keep the hand in the box. Stated as an instruction, with a stated penalty; success is externally visible Conflict Pain, and the needle at the neck. The resistance is escalating and cannot be negotiated with Disaster The poisoned success ( §4.3 ). Paul passes, and passing identifies him as what the Bene Gesserit have been breeding for Reaction Physical: the hand examined and found unmarked, which is more disturbing than injury Dilemma Not Paul’s, initially, but Jessica’s — and the split is instructive Decision Compressed almost to nothing, and carried by the departure for Arrakis The scene’s efficiency comes from a decision made much earlier in the composition: the goal is physical, binary and observable , which allows Herbert to spend the entire unit on unexplained vocabulary and metaphysical exposition without the reader losing the thread. This is the general principle worth extracting: the more difficult the material, the simpler the goal beat must be. A reader who knows what would count as failure will tolerate a great deal of strangeness around it. 9.5 Dumas, The Count of Monte Cristo (1844–46) — the clean chain The novel is the purest surviving demonstration of structure 1 in §6.3 , and it earns its place in a university syllabus by being unembarrassed about it. The opening pair is exemplary. Goal: Dantès, newly promoted, is to be married that afternoon. Conflict: three men with reasons to prevent it. Disaster: arrest at his own betrothal feast. Sequel: the Château d’If, where the reaction beat is expanded to years, the dilemma is despair against endurance, and the decision — supplied by Faria — is to survive, learn, and escape. That decision is the next scene’s goal, as the model requires. Two features deserve comment. The engine’s visibility is a virtue here, not a defect. The feuilleton appeared in Le Journal des débats in several runs from August 1844 to January 1846; a reader returning after an interruption needs the goal-state to be recoverable in a sentence. The clean chain is a solution to a distribution problem before it is an aesthetic. The novel outgrows its own machinery. The last movement introduces dilemmas the revenge engine cannot price — whether the children of the guilty are legitimate targets — and it is at this point that the clean chain stops being sufficient and the book becomes serious. The lesson for a student is the reverse of the one usually drawn: the engine is not what makes the novel good; it is what makes the novel legible for long enough that its one hinge can land. 9.6 Heller, Catch-22 (1961) — the chain broken as argument Heller’s novel is the strongest counterexample in this chapter, because it fails almost every test in §7 and is not defective. The chapters are numbered and often titled for characters; events are narrated out of order, repeated with variation, and returned to with new information; the causal relation between units is frequently unavailable. The novel’s governing device is the regulation itself — there is only one catch, and it is Catch-22 — which is a causal loop : a rule whose application produces the condition that makes the rule apply. Where the model asks for descent, Heller supplies circularity. Three observations. The broken chain is the thesis. The book argues that the institution destroys causal reason, and a novel that proceeded by therefore would refute its own case in its form. Something replaces the chain. Not nothing — that would be incoherence. Heller substitutes two other engines: the escalating mission quota , which supplies a crude but genuine forward pressure, and the progressive disclosure of Snowden’s death , a curiosity structure ( §6.1 ) in which the same event is returned to and each return supplies a further detail, until the final telling. The chain is therefore only apparently absent. The Snowden material is a chain run backwards ( §6.3 , structure 11), embedded in a novel whose forward chain is deliberately jammed. Heller has not abandoned causal structure; he has moved it into the past, where his subject requires it. 9.7 Atwood, The Handmaid’s Tale (1985) — the sequel-dominant novel Offred’s narration is very largely reaction and dilemma. Scenes occur — the Ceremony, the shopping expeditions, the Commander’s office, the birth, Jezebel’s — but they are short, and they are frequently reported rather than enacted. The bulk of the text is a consciousness processing what it cannot act on. The reason is structural rather than stylistic. The decision beat is unavailable to a person without options , and Gilead has removed them. Atwood does not compensate by inventing agency; she builds the book on the absence. Two devices help sustain momentum, while a third reframes what the reader has encountered: Curiosity rather than suspense — the withheld past (the daughter, Luke, the escape attempt), distributed across the novel in Sternberg’s delayed mode. The formal frame — the “Historical Notes”, which appear after Offred’s account and reveal retrospectively that it has survived as a document with a provenance. Chapter 10 ( The Prologue ) treats this device as the prologue’s structural inverse. The small recovered agencies — Scrabble, butter as hand cream, the message in the cupboard. Each is a decision beat scaled to what remains possible. The lesson for the model is exact: a beat may be structurally unavailable, and a novel must then pay for it with another engine. What it cannot do is omit it and supply nothing. 9.8 Steinbeck, The Grapes of Wrath (1939) — the collective sequel Steinbeck alternates the Joads’ narrative with sixteen intercalary chapters that contain no continuing characters: the turtle crossing the highway, the tractors, the used-car lots, the roadside diner, the growing wrath in the eyes of the hungry. Read as description, they are digressions. Read structurally, they are the reaction beat given to a population . The Joads suffer a disaster; the intercalary chapter that follows registers it at the scale of a class, in a different register and with a different narrator. The private beat is priced socially, and the two chains — the family’s and the migration’s — are braided so that neither has to carry the other’s work. Two costs need naming. The chapters interrupt identification with the Joads, and some readers find that interruption frustrating; the collective sequel is a demanding structure rather than a free upgrade. The technique also requires a narrator willing to speak in a register the character chapters do not use, which is a formal contract that must be declared early — Steinbeck declares it in Chapter 1, before any Joad appears. 9.9 A revision case: the household The textbook’s running example — three siblings, a dead father’s shop, a mother who changed the locks in March — supplies the material. The pair follows directly from the doorway exchange analysed in Chapter 3 ( The Dialogue Exchange ): Elena learns there that the locks were changed and leaves wanting to know why; Dov gives her the key and withholds the reason. Version A (draft) Elena left with the key. She was angry with Dov, but there was no point arguing with him when he got like that, and anyway she had what she’d come for. She got into the truck and drove across town to the shop, thinking about what her mother might say if she asked her directly. She decided it wasn’t worth it. Better to look for herself. She parked outside, let herself in, and started with the register drawer. Diagnosis Test Result 1 — Goal Present in the previous scene; fine 3 — Disaster Weakened. “She had what she’d come for” prices the scene as a win. The cost — she trusts her brother less — is asserted (“angry”) and not spent 4 — Cost Fails. No currency is named 5 — Chain Technically intact and entirely carried by connectives: but , anyway , better to 7 — Dilemma False. One option is dismissed in six words on grounds of convenience (“wasn’t worth it”) 10 — Beat weight Reaction: five words, all of them a named emotion. Dilemma: twenty-three. Decision: a subordinate clause — Patterns present: skipped sequel ( §8.3 ), false dilemma ( §8.4 ), named emotion ( §8.12 ) Version A contains every necessary item . Its failure is arrangement: the sequel has been summarised rather than performed, so the decision that closes it is a matter of logistics rather than of character. Version B (the revision) Reaction — She didn’t cry in the truck, is what she’d tell people later, though she also couldn’t say what she’d done instead: some effortful blank thing with her hands on the wheel, the key already leaving a mark in her palm because she hadn’t unclenched. Dilemma — She could call their mother and ask outright, and get the same answer Dov had given her, or worse, the silence that meant she’d asked something true. Or she could go through the ledger herself, quietly, and risk finding out Dov’s silence in the doorway hadn’t been protecting their mother. It might have been protecting her. Decision — She didn’t call. She drove to the shop instead, let herself in with the key, and went straight for the register drawer that stuck on the K. What the revision did, procedurally Restored the reaction beat, and rendered it physically. The named emotion (“angry”) is replaced by an unclenched hand and a mark in a palm — §4.4 ’s rule, and §8.12 ’s remedy. Note the second move inside it: is what she’d tell people later installs a retrospective narrator who can see what Elena cannot, which is the reliability protocol for the rest of the book. Priced both options. Calling costs the possibility of the answer; investigating costs the possibility that the silence was protective. Neither is cheap, and — the test at §7.1 , test 7 — a sympathetic reader could reasonably prefer either. Located the real disaster. Version A treats the withheld reason as the cost. Version B locates it in the interpretation of the withholding: Dov may have been protecting Elena, which is worse than obstruction. The costed success of Version A has become the third shape, the poisoned success — the goal achieved and revealed to have been the wrong goal ( §4.3 ). Made the decision physical and generating. She drove to the shop is the decision and its execution at once ( §4.6 , “compressed to nothing”), and the register drawer that sticks on the K — planted in Chapter 10 ( The Prologue ) — supplies the next scene’s opening move without a sentence of setup. Set the beat weights deliberately. Reaction 44 words, Dilemma 56, Decision 27, against a moderate disaster. Chapter 14’s material — Dov’s sale of the shop — will require a heavier ratio, and the register has now been established at a level that leaves room above it ( §5.5 ). What Version B has not solved Three things, and they need stating because the model cannot see any of them. The decision is reversible. Elena could stop at the door, and nothing in the text forecloses calling her mother later. By §7.1 , test 9, the beat is weaker than it appears; the passage is carried by momentum rather than by irreversibility. There is no hinge. Elena’s criterion — find out for yourself, do not ask people who will lie — is the criterion she held in the doorway. This is correct for an early chapter, but the sequence is not doing any arc work, and a book made of pairs like this one would produce the treadmill diagnosis at §8.9 . The dilemma’s second option is more interesting than its first , which risks the asymmetry the false-dilemma test warns against. Whether It might have been protecting her is a devastating turn or a thumb on the scale is a legitimate editorial disagreement, and a good one to stage in a workshop.

title: 10. Scene and Sequel Across Forms
text: 10.1 The short story The story usually contains one pair , and frequently only its second half. Because there is no room to establish a chain, the causal work must be done by implication: the disaster is often prior to the text, and the story is the sequel. Two structural consequences. The decision beat carries disproportionate weight , because it is where the form’s characteristic ending lives — either taken and made irreversible, or refused and left visible (Hemingway’s withheld decision, §8.10 ). And the goal may be entirely retrospective : a story may be the account of a pursuit already concluded, in which case the beats survive but the reader’s relation to them inverts, as in §6.3 ’s structure 11. 10.2 The novella The novella’s characteristic structure is one disaster and a long sequel, which is why the form is so hospitable to the recursive structure ( §6.3 , structure 9) and why The Death of Ivan Ilyich is its exemplary case. The characteristic failure is a novel’s chain compressed into a novella’s length, producing pairs that are all scene and no absorption. 10.3 The series and the long novel Series fiction has a specific problem the model names: the volume-terminal decision . Each instalment must close a chain and open another, and the temptation is to end on a deferred decision ( §6.2 ) that the next volume will pay. This works once. Repeated across a series, it produces the reader’s sense of being managed, because the deferral is visibly a commercial device rather than a structural one. The stronger solution is to close the volume’s chain honestly and let the new goal be the hook. Long braided novels face the inverse problem: a chain interrupted for two hundred pages must be re-established when it resumes, and readers do not retain goal-states across that distance. Nineteenth-century practice solved this by restating the goal at each resumption, a convention modern readers often find clumsy and modern writers often under-supply. 10.4 Screen comparison The scene–sequel model transfers to screen with one large distortion and one useful import. The distortion: film has no cheap interiority. The reaction beat, which prose renders in a sentence, requires a held shot, a performance, or a scene of displacement activity — all expensive in screen time. Screen narrative therefore compresses sequels far harder than prose, and this is the principal reason craft advice imported from screenwriting under-values the sequel. A prose writer who adopts screen ratios will produce the skipped sequel ( §8.3 ) as a house style. The import: the act break . Commercial television’s act structure institutionalises the deferred decision — the break falls on a dilemma, and the audience is held across the interruption. It is the cleanest available demonstration that deferral is a taxable asset ( §6.1 ), and it is the origin of much contemporary chapter-break practice, as Chapter 6 ( The Chapter Break ) discusses. The “but / therefore” heuristic ( §7.1 , test 6) is itself a screen import, and should be handled as such: a good instrument, developed for a form with twenty-two minutes and no interiority, applied to a form that has neither constraint. 10.5 Translated fiction The series’ standing distinction applies with unusual clarity here. Structural claims survive translation; texture claims do not. The chain in Crime and Punishment is identical in Garnett, in Pevear and Volokhonsky, and in Katz: the murder ends Part One in all of them, and the confession closes Part Six. What differs is the reaction beat’s texture — the register of the delirium, the rhythm of the free indirect passages — which is the material on which any claim about compression depends. The practical rule for a student writing about a translated novel: beat analysis is safe; beat-weight analysis remains useful at the level of proportions; claims about how a reaction is rendered require naming the translator and, ideally, comparing two versions. 10.6 Concordance: concept to novel Concept Best displayed by Section Goal made physical and binary Dune (the gom jabbar) §4.1 , §9.4 Goal of near-zero magnitude, sufficient Great Expectations (the churchyard) §4.1 , §9.3 Conflict entering from another chain Jane Eyre (the interruption) §4.2 , §9.2 Disaster — the costed success The Grapes of Wrath (work found) §4.3 Disaster — the poisoned success Dune §4.3 , §9.4 Disaster reaching backwards Jane Eyre §4.3 , §9.2 Reaction as disordered perception Great Expectations (chapters 1–2) §4.4 , §9.3 Reaction expanded into the book’s subject Crime and Punishment §4.4 , §9.1 Reaction named, and rightly Great Expectations (the retrospective narrator) §8.12 Dilemma with symmetrical costs Huckleberry Finn (the letter) §4.5 , §5.2 Dilemma given the wrong side’s best speeches Jane Eyre (chapter 27) §4.5 , §9.2 Decision executed rather than announced Jane Eyre (the departure) §4.6 , §9.2 Decision deferred across five parts Crime and Punishment §4.6 , §9.1 The hinge — criterion named Jane Eyre ; Pride and Prejudice (the letter) §4.7 The hinge — criterion outranked, not refuted Huckleberry Finn §4.7 , §5.2 Compression — a decisive turn in a paragraph Huckleberry Finn §5.2 The clean chain The Count of Monte Cristo §6.3 , §9.5 The deferred decision, serially Great Expectations ; The Count of Monte Cristo §6.2 , §6.5 The braided chain Anna Karenina ; Bleak House §6.3 The displaced sequel Mrs Dalloway (Septimus and Clarissa) §6.3 The sequel-dominant novel The Handmaid’s Tale ; The Remains of the Day §6.3 , §9.7 The collective sequel The Grapes of Wrath §6.3 , §9.8 The recursive sequel Crime and Punishment §6.3 , §9.1 The broken chain as argument Catch-22 §6.3 , §9.6 The chain run backwards The Death of Ivan Ilyich §6.3 The refused decision The Stranger §6.3 , §8.7 Free goals by design Don Quixote §8.1 Clean wins sustained The Count of Monte Cristo §8.2 , §9.5 Escalation as satire Catch-22 §8.9 , §9.6 Passivity as the argument The Stranger ; title: 11. Revision Checklist
text: Run each scene–sequel pair against this list before deciding it stays as written. Each item derives from a test in §7 or a pattern in §8 . The scene I can state the point-of-view character’s goal in one sentence containing a verb of pursuit and a specific object. That goal descends from the decision that closed the previous sequel, and I can point to the sentence. The resistance changes the shape of the goal rather than merely postponing it. The unit does not end in a clean, costless win. I can name what the character paid, and in what currency. The disaster arises from the pursuit rather than arriving from outside it. The sequel The disaster produces a reaction on the page, not an immediate jump to the next goal. The reaction is carried by the body and by what the attention selects, not by emotional vocabulary — or the naming is being done by a narrator with a stake in it. Both of the dilemma’s options are costly, and I can state each cost in one sentence. A sympathetic reader could reasonably prefer either option. The decision is concrete enough to become the next scene’s goal. The decision forecloses something; it is not a preference the character could quietly abandon. The chain Tracing backwards three links, each is caused by the one before it and not merely followed by it. Reverse-outlined with only and then / but / therefore , there is no run of three “and then”s. Any compressed or skipped sequel is a pacing decision I can defend, not an oversight. Any deferred decision has a page number on which it is paid. The page-space given to each beat tracks its weight in the story rather than my default register. The book There is at least one decision in this manuscript that the protagonist’s earlier self would not have made, and I can say what changed. Where a beat is structurally unavailable to this character, another engine supplies what it would have supplied.

title: 12. Studio Work
text: 12.1 Practical exercises Exercise 1 — The beat annotation. Take three consecutive chapters of your draft and mark every beat in the margin: G, C, D, R, Di, De. Write 200 words on what the distribution shows. Exercise 2 — The chain trace. Reverse-outline twenty consecutive units using only and then , but and therefore . Mark every “and then”. Rewrite the disaster preceding the first one so that it forces the goal that follows. Exercise 3 — The beat-weight audit. Run the procedure at §5.5 over ten pairs and produce the plot of sequel length against disaster weight. Write 300 words interpreting it against the table there. Exercise 4 — Compression ladder. Take one full sequel of about 600 words and rewrite it in 200 words, then 50 words, then one clause. Identify the point at which the chain becomes illegible ( §5.4 ), and say what was carrying it at the last legible stage. Exercise 5 — The costed dilemma. For a dilemma in your draft, write the two costs first, in one sentence each, without looking at the passage. Then rewrite the beat from the costs. Compare. Exercise 6 — Structure substitution. Take a sequence that is not working and rewrite it as a different chain structure from §6.3 — a braided chain as a clean one, a clean chain with one deferred decision, a private sequel as a collective one. Do not judge until all versions exist. Exercise 7 — The hinge hunt. Identify the one decision in your manuscript that your protagonist’s opening-chapter self would not have made. Write 400 words on what changed and where. If you cannot find one, that is the exercise’s result. Exercise 8 — Displacement. Take a disaster that happens to your protagonist and give the reaction beat to another character, in another scene. Assess what the event gains and loses ( §6.3 , structure 6). Exercise 9 — The published pair. Choose any twenty pages of a published novel and produce a full beat analysis, including compression ratios. Write 600 words on what the analysis cannot capture. 12.2 Seminar questions Does Crime and Punishment break the model or complete it? §9.1 argues that the novel runs one iteration of the six beats across six hundred pages. Argue the opposite case: that a “sequel” of five parts is a different kind of object, and that calling it a sequel is a category error that saves the model by emptying it. Is the Hinge a beat, a property, or a category error? Argue for or against admitting the criterion change as a distinct unit ( §4.7 ), using Jane Eyre , Crime and Punishment and one novel in which no criterion ever changes. Is the prohibition on the passive protagonist a structural principle or a genre preference? §8.7 concedes that it is close to the latter. Test the claim against The Stranger , Oblomov and The Remains of the Day , and consider what value system the prohibition encodes. What replaces causality in Catch-22 ? §9.6 argues that Heller substitutes an escalating quota and a backwards-running disclosure. Is that enough, or does the novel simply exchange one chain for another and thereby concede the principle it attacks? Do the intercalary chapters of The Grapes of Wrath earn their place? Some readers find them interruptive. Is the collective sequel a structural achievement or a rhetorical intrusion — and does the answer depend on the reader or on the book? Whose chain? The model was codified in a mid-century American commercial market ( §3.6 ). Examine a narrative tradition organised on other principles — the frame-tale sequence, the episodic picaresque, the modernist novel of a single day — and say which of this chapter’s prohibitions describe narrative and which describe a local literary culture. 12.3 Assessment rubric The following rubric is for a submitted scene–sequel pair (1,500–2,000 words) with a 750-word critical commentary. Band Craft (60%) Commentary (40%) Distinction Goal legible and descended; resistance that alters the goal’s shape; a disaster with a nameable currency; a reaction carried by body and attention; a dilemma whose costs a reader could weigh either way; a decision that forecloses. Beat weights deliberately set Names its chain structure and defends it against alternatives; identifies its own unsolved problems; engages at least two theoretical sources critically Merit All beats present; the chain holds; one beat under-delivered or mis-weighted Accurate self-analysis; theory applied rather than cited; risks acknowledged Pass A pair exists; goal and disaster present; sequel thin or summarised Describes the work accurately; theory referenced but not applied Fail No disaster, or no sequel; the chain cannot be traced Description without analysis; failure patterns unrecognised

title: 13. Glossary
text: Beat — One of the six named functions of the scene–sequel pair. A job done, not a quantity of prose; a beat may occupy a page or a subordinate clause. §2.4 , §4 . Causal chain — The relation by which a scene’s disaster produces the following sequel’s reaction, and that sequel’s decision produces the following scene’s goal. §3.7 . Chain structure — A recognisable arrangement of scene–sequel pairs across a narrative, with characteristic benefits and costs. Twelve are tabulated at §6.3 . Compression — The setting of page-space against story-weight for a given beat. The principle is that the two should track each other; the failure is a default register applied regardless. §5.1 . Conflict — The resistance a goal meets, whose function is to change the goal’s shape rather than merely to postpone its achievement. §4.2 . Decision — The sequel’s terminal beat: a commitment to a new concrete objective, which becomes the following scene’s goal. §4.6 . Deferred decision — A sequel whose reaction and dilemma are shown but whose decision is withheld past a break, and later paid. §6.2 . Dilatory space — Brooks’s term for the narrative middle, which resists the ending it desires. The theoretical form of deferral. §3.2 . Dilemma — The weighing of options each of which carries a real cost, none obviously correct. §4.5 . Disaster — The scene’s terminal state: worse off, or a success whose cost exceeds its value, or a success revealed to have been the wrong goal. §4.3 . Displaced sequel — A structure in which the disaster belongs to one character and the reaction to another. §6.3 . Free goal — A scene goal with no origin in any prior decision. §8.1 . Function — Propp’s unit: an act defined by its significance for the course of the action, irrespective of who performs it. An earlier analogue of the beat. §3.3 . Goal — A concrete, immediate objective, legible before the resistance begins, specific enough that success can be scored. §4.1 . Hinge — This chapter’s proposed addition: the point between dilemma and decision at which the character’s criterion for choosing changes. Where arc happens. §4.7 . Motivation-reaction unit (MRU) — Swain’s sentence-level pattern of external stimulus followed by internal response; the causal chain at paragraph scale. §4.0 . Narrative desire — Brooks’s term for the reader’s want, produced and sustained by the text, for the end that will confer meaning on the middle. §3.2 . Proairetic code — Barthes’s code of actions: the reader’s capacity to recognise and name a sequence in progress. A goal is a licence to name the sequence. §3.3 . Propter hoc — “Because of this”, as against post hoc , “after this”. In logic, treating succession as causation is a fallacy; in narrative it is a competence. §3.1 . Reaction — The character’s registration of the disaster, which converts an external event into the internal state a decision can issue from. §4.4 . Recursive sequel — A sequel containing scenes within itself, each generating further reaction rather than resolution. §6.3 , §9.1 . Scene (narrow sense) — The goal–conflict–disaster half of the pair. Distinguished throughout from the loose workshop sense used in Chapter 1, and from Genette’s sense of a duration relation. §2.3 . Sequel — The reaction–dilemma–decision half of the pair. Nothing to do with a follow-up volume. §2.1 . Stalled sequel — A sequel expanded past the point at which new considerations arrive; repetition mistaken for depth. §8.5 .

title: 14. Sources Cited
text: 14.1 Criticism, narratology and theory Aristotle. Poetics . c. 335 BCE. Available in Classical Literary Criticism , translated by Penelope Murray and T. S. Dorsch. London: Penguin, 2000. Bakhtin, Mikhail. Problems of Dostoevsky’s Poetics . Translated by Caryl Emerson. Minneapolis: University of Minnesota Press, 1984. Barthes, Roland. S/Z . Translated by Richard Miller. title: 15. Further Reading
text: Annotated and grouped by what each source is good for . Starred items are the recommended first three. 15.1 On plot as a dynamic ★ Brooks, Peter. Reading for the Plot (1984). The indispensable modern book on why plots move readers rather than merely organising events. The chapters “Reading for the Plot” and “Freud’s Masterplot” are the ones that bear on this chapter, and they supply what no craft manual can: an account of desire rather than of mechanism. Shklovsky, Viktor. Theory of Prose (1925; Eng. 1990). For retardation, stepped construction and the argument that impediment is the substance of narrative rather than an obstacle to it. Sternberg, Meir. Expositional Modes and Temporal Ordering in Fiction (1978). For the suspense / curiosity distinction, which tells a writer which kind of deferral they are performing. Kermode, Frank. The Sense of an Ending (1967). For why chains want termini. Read alongside Chapter 16 ( The Ending ). 15.2 On the structuralist description ★ Barthes, Roland. S/Z (1970). The proairetic and hermeneutic codes, demonstrated at exhausting length on a single Balzac novella. Read the methodological sections and sample the analysis. Propp, Vladimir. Morphology of the Folktale (1928). Short, dry, and startlingly modern. The definition of a function is the best available explanation of what a “beat” is. Todorov, Tzvetan. The Poetics of Prose (1977). For the equilibrium schema and for the argument that narrative grammar is a grammar in the full sense. Chatman, Seymour. Story and Discourse (1978). For kernels and satellites — the precise vocabulary for which events open alternatives and which elaborate. 15.3 On motive and form Burke, Kenneth. Counter-Statement (1931) and A Grammar of Motives (1945). The “psychology of form” is three pages and worth a term’s study; the pentad is the best available instrument for diagnosing thin motivation. Aristotle. Poetics . Chapters 6–11 and 13–14. An hour’s reading, and the origin of nearly everything in §3.1 . 15.4 Cognitive work Zwaan and Radvansky (1998). The clearest statement of the dimensions readers track, including causality and intentionality. Trabasso and van den Broek (1985); Graesser, Singer and Trabasso (1994). For the empirical basis of the claim that causally connected events are better recalled, and for the finding that readers infer backwards more readily than forwards — the strongest single result in this chapter’s evidence base. 15.5 The craft literature, read critically ★ Swain, Dwight V. Techniques of the Selling Writer (1965). The source. Read it as a historical document of a commercial practice as well as an instrument: the idiom is dated, the confidence is total, and the model is sound. Note the motivation-reaction unit, which most secondary accounts omit. Bickham, Jack M. Scene & Structure (1993). The transmission text, and clearer than Swain on the mechanics of the join. Also the point at which the model begins to harden into doctrine. McKee, Robert. Story (1997). For the value shift (Chapter 1’s term) and for a screen-derived account of the same architecture. Use the vocabulary; discount the prescription. Yorke, John. Into the Woods (2013). The most intelligent recent synthesis of the structural tradition, and unusually honest about where its own model is a convention. Forster, E. M. Aspects of the Novel (1927). For the king-and-queen formulation, and for a definition of plot as causality that predates every manual in this list. 15.6 Within this textbook Chapter 1 ( The Purposes of a Scene ) — the value shift, the five domains and the principle of multiplicity, on which §§4–5 depend. Chapter 3 ( The Dialogue Exchange ) — the doorway exchange from which §9.9 ’s pair descends; subtext as a carrier of resistance. Chapter 4 ( The Descriptive Detail ) — the compressed disaster is nearly always carried by an object. Chapter 5 ( The Transition ) — how the gap between two units is crossed once the chain is sound. Chapter 6 ( The Chapter Break ) — where the gap is placed, and the deferred decision as a break technique. Chapter 14 ( The Subplot ) — the attention tax, and what a second chain must earn. Chapter 16 ( The Ending ) — what “earned” means, and why it is largely a function of a traceable chain.

title: 16. Coda: What the Engine Cannot Tell You
section: Coda — What the Engine Cannot Tell You
text: Everything in this chapter is an instrument for noticing. None of it is a rule, and the evidence for that claim is in the chapter itself. Don Quixote proceeds by free goals. The Count of Monte Cristo runs on clean wins for hundreds of pages. The Remains of the Day is a stalled sequel four hundred pages long, built on false dilemmas, narrated by a man who never forms a goal of his own. Catch-22 breaks the chain deliberately, and the breaking is the argument. The Stranger refuses the decision beat. The Handmaid’s Tale cannot supply it. Crime and Punishment commits, on a mechanical reading, the gravest fault the model recognises — a sequel that swallows five-sixths of the book — and is among the two or three most powerful novels ever written. A model that rules these out has not identified defects in them. It has identified its own boundaries, which is the most useful thing a model can do. Three points follow from that list. First, the six beats describe one way of building momentum, not the thing itself. They are dominant in commercial fiction, common in literary fiction, and absent from a great deal of admired writing — the episodic, the meditative, the polyphonic, the encyclopaedic, the novel of a single day. Momentum can also be produced by curiosity about the past, by formal pattern, by rhythm, by image, by the accumulating pressure of a voice. The chain is the cheapest route and the most teachable. It is not the only one, and a writer who believes it is will produce books that move well and mean little. Second, the model’s provenance is not a scandal but a specification. Swain codified it in his 1965 manual, informed by his experience in commercial fiction. Its emphasis on agency, escalation, external goals, and decisions that foreclose suits stories built around legible forward motion. That fit suggests where the model may be useful; it does not establish how or when Swain devised each part of it. Its assumptions about what a person can do to the world are not universal, and §8.7 concedes the sharpest case. Knowing an instrument’s context helps you judge what it will measure well and what it will measure badly. Third, and most usefully: the model’s real value in revision is diagnostic rather than corrective. It does not tell a writer what to do. It tells them what they have made. A draft that fails the disaster test in every chapter is not a broken thriller; it may be a novel of consciousness that has not yet admitted what it is. A draft in which no criterion ever changes is not necessarily deficient; it may be a satire, in which the refusal of change is the point, and which needs to be rewritten towards that rather than away from it. The most common productive outcome of running §7 ’s protocol is not a repaired chain. It is the writer discovering, sometimes with relief and sometimes with dismay, what kind of book they have been writing . Which suggests a final question, to be asked after the ten tests and in preference to any of them: If this book does not run on the chain, what does it run on — and is that engine actually running? A book that can answer needs nothing else in this chapter. A book that cannot has found the real problem, and it was never a problem of beats.

title: The Dialogue Exchange
text: Speech as Structure: What a Passage of Dialogue Must Do, and How to Test It The Craft Behind the Story (Second Edition), Reference — Chapter 3. Part I: The Scene and Its Materials. This chapter is a companion to Chapter 1 ( The Purposes of a Scene ), whose domains of purpose (including its proposed relational domain) and value-shift test it inherits and extends. It is also a companion to Chapter 4 ( The Descriptive Detail ), whose denotation/connotation pair is the descriptive analogue of the text/subtext distinction developed here. All illustrative passages are quoted briefly for the purposes of criticism and study; full citations appear in §14 . Where a work is read in translation, the translator is named, and the chapter observes the series’ standing distinction: structural claims survive translation, texture claims do not. Contents On this page: Chapter Abstract · Learning Outcomes · Key Terms · How to Use This Chapter Introduction: The Transcript Problem Definitions and Boundaries Why Dialogue Is Not Speech — the theory section The Domains of Purpose — five inherited, and a proposed sixth Multiplicity: The Economy of the Exchange Text and Subtext: The Two Channels Diagnostic Method — the ten tests Failure Patterns — with their exceptions Worked Analyses — eight close readings and a revision case Dialogue Across Forms · Concordance: concept to novel Revision Checklist Studio Work — exercises, seminar questions, assessment rubric Glossary Sources Cited Further Reading Coda: Against Mechanical Application Chapter Abstract Dialogue is the only unit of fiction with a rigorous empirical science attached to it. Linguists have been recording, transcribing and analysing actual human conversation for fifty years, and have established with considerable precision how turn-taking works, how meaning is generated by not saying things, how refusals are marked, and how status is negotiated in talk. Almost none of that has reached creative-writing pedagogy, which continues to teach dialogue by ear and by prohibition. This chapter takes the empirical literature seriously, and finds that it confirms the craft tradition’s intuitions while explaining them far better than the craft tradition can. It proceeds in four movements: Theory — why a passage of dialogue is not a transcript, grounded in H. P. Grice’s account of conversational implicature , in the conversation-analytic findings on turn-taking and preference organisation , in Erving Goffman’s work on footing and face , and in Bakhtin’s account of the novel as the form that stages competing social languages. A historical strand traces the contingency of quotation convention itself, and an empirical strand establishes the chapter’s principal negative claim: transcribed conversation and novelistic dialogue are different objects , and literary dialogue is a stylised convention that reads as real rather than a record of the real. Taxonomy — the five domains of purpose (plot, character, relational, theme, texture), each anatomised in terms of its textual carriers and its characteristic under- and over-delivery. The relational is the fifth domain proposed in Chapter 1 ( The Purposes of a Scene ) and adopted here because dialogue makes it load-bearing. A sixth is then proposed: the Silence domain , covering what is not said, who does not speak, and who is not in the room. Method — the principle of multiplicity applied to the exchange; a full account of the two channels of text and subtext, with a taxonomy of twelve named subtext mechanisms; and a ten-test diagnostic protocol for revision. Application — twelve failure patterns, each with a published counterexample; eight close readings; a revision case worked on the household example that runs through this series; and an apparatus of exercises, glossary, sources and further reading. The chapter’s governing claim is that a dialogue exchange is a transcript with an engine under it : two or more parties pursuing incompatible wants through speech, in which the balance of information, standing or feeling is measurably different at the end than at the start. One of its central contributions is to show how conversational implicature explains an important kind of subtext , while other kinds emerge through action, narration and the organisation of turns. A character who answers a direct question by changing the subject may invite the reader to infer an unstated meaning. Naming that correspondence gives writers one procedure for making subtext legible. A note on the examples. The close readings are drawn chiefly from the European and anglophone novel, with one short story, Hemingway’s “Hills Like White Elephants”, used because it isolates the variable more cleanly than any novel can; the Core chapter adds post-2000 fiction and screen cases, listed in §14.6. A concordance mapping each concept to the novel that best displays it appears at §10.6 . A note on quotation. Dialogue is the element of fiction most damaged by being quoted at length out of context, because its effects are cumulative: a line lands because of the eleven lines before it. Passages here are therefore short, and are frequently described rather than quoted. Where the description does the analytical work as well as the quotation would, description is preferred, and students should read the surrounding pages before accepting any judgement made here. Learning Outcomes By the end of this chapter, a student should be able to: Distinguish a dialogue exchange from adjacent units — the speech, the conversation, reported speech, the interview, the monologue — and explain why the distinctions matter in revision. Explain , with reference to Grice, to conversation analysis and to Goffman, why meaning in dialogue is generated as much by what is withheld and how it is withheld as by what is stated. Identify the six domains of purpose in any published exchange, and mark which lines discharge which. Analyse the relation between the two channels of text and subtext, and name which of the twelve mechanisms in §6.4 a given line is using. Apply the ten-test diagnostic protocol to a draft exchange and produce a prioritised revision plan. Diagnose the recurring failure patterns by mechanism rather than by surface feature, and articulate the conditions under which each “failure” is the correct choice. Evaluate the historical and cultural specificity of the chapter’s own prohibitions, in particular the twentieth-century Anglo-American preference for compressed, indirect, subtext-heavy speech. Assess the ethics and the craft of phonetically rendered dialect, and the uneven history of the prohibition against it. Key Terms Dialogue exchange · the two channels · text · subtext · conversational implicature · the Cooperative Principle · flouting · adjacency pair · preference organisation · dispreferred response · turn-taking · repair · footing · participation framework · face-work · heteroglossia · polyphony · the relational domain · the silence domain · attribution · said-bookism · literary dialect · the gap-closing move Full definitions appear in the Glossary ( §13 ). Terms are bolded on first substantive use. How to Use This Chapter Reader Route Purpose Student in a seminar §§1–6 in order, then §12 exercises Conceptual grounding, then guided practice Writer in revision §7 (diagnostics) → §8 (failures) → §11 (checklist) Fast triage of a live draft Teacher or workshop leader §4 , 6, 8, 9 for material; §12.1 for assignments; §12.3 rubric A ready-made teaching sequence with worked models A caution before beginning. This chapter contains taxonomies, tests and checklists. None of them is a formula. They are instruments for noticing, and their proper output is a question, not a verdict. A protocol that returns the answer this exchange fails test seven has done nothing until the writer asks why the book might want it to. Every test in §7 is failed by at least one of the novels analysed in §9 , and in several cases the failure is the reason the exchange is famous.

title: 1. Introduction: The Transcript Problem
text: 1.1 An asymmetry between accuracy and function Set two passages side by side. For the first, imagine a verbatim transcript of ninety seconds of conversation between two people who know each other well. Depending on the recording, it might contain overlapping speech, false starts, fillers such as um and you know , a self-correction, brief responses from the listener, or a topic raised and dropped. The transcript would faithfully record those features. On the page, however, they might distract from the speakers’ wants and from what changes between them. The second is a passage of novelistic dialogue, containing almost none of those features. Its speakers do not overlap. They finish their sentences, or break off at points the writer has chosen for effect rather than for the reasons real speakers break off. Every turn advances something. It is, by any empirical standard, an inaccurate representation of how people talk — and readers experience it as lifelike. That asymmetry is the chapter’s starting point. In no other domain of fiction is the gap between the represented thing and the representation so wide while the illusion of fidelity remains so strong. Descriptions of rooms are not required to be accurate inventories, and no reader expects them to be. Dialogue alone is habitually defended on the grounds that people really do talk this way . They do. They also produce, in life, enormous quantities of talk that would sink a manuscript: greeting rituals, weather, scheduling, agreement, repetition, the negotiation of who speaks next. Transcribed accuracy is not the standard. What a reader registers as realism in dialogue is not fidelity to the acoustic record but fidelity to a set of social facts about talk — that people want things from each other, that they do not say so directly, that saying and meaning come apart, that every turn positions its speaker relative to the last. Novelistic dialogue is a stylised convention that reproduces those social facts while discarding almost all the surface features of actual speech. §3.6 gives the empirical detail; the practical consequence can be stated at once. The realism of dialogue is a realism of pressure , not of transcription . A reader who says an exchange “sounds real” is reporting that the wants underneath it are legible, not that the words match a recording. 1.2 The claim in its strong form Two characters trading lines are a transcript. A dialogue exchange is a transcript with an engine under it: each speaker wants something from the other, wants it now, and the words are the instrument each is using to get it. The metaphor of the engine will be used throughout, and what it does and does not claim needs stating carefully. It does claim that a passage of speech without a want on at least one side is inert regardless of how good the individual lines are, and that this is testable ( §7.1 , test 1). It does not claim that the want must be large. I want you to admit you were wrong. I want to get out of this room without answering. I want you to say my name. These are sufficient. Chapter 1 ( The Purposes of a Scene ) makes the same point about scene goals, and the argument transfers unchanged: the goal must be legible and resisted, not important. It does not claim that the want must be conscious. A speaker may not know what they are after; the reader must be able to infer it. Indeed the gap between what a character is pursuing and what they think they are pursuing is one of the richest resources in the form, and §6 is largely about how it is engineered. It does not claim that all speech in a novel must be an exchange in this sense. Ritual talk, phatic exchange and small talk have legitimate structural uses — establishing register, marking the passage of time, providing the neutral ground against which a deviation registers. What they cannot do is carry a scene. 1.3 Where this chapter sits in the series Chapter 1 ( The Purposes of a Scene ) established the value-shift test — the demand that something charged be measurably different at a unit’s close than at its open — and the domains of plot, character, theme and texture in which such a shift can occur, to which it proposed a fifth. This chapter applies the test at a smaller scale and adopts that fifth domain, the relational : the negotiation of standing between speakers, which the usual four-domain model folds into character and which dialogue makes too load-bearing to leave there. §4.6 then proposes a sixth. Three relations to neighbouring chapters should be held in view: Dialogue is a mode of scene, not an alternative to it. Everything in Chapter 1 ( The Purposes of a Scene ) applies. An exchange that fails the value-shift test fails it for the same reasons a scene does, and the remedies — cut, compress to summary, fuse with a neighbouring unit — are the same. Dialogue’s two channels have a descriptive analogue. Chapter 4 ( The Descriptive Detail ) develops the pair denotation and connotation : what a detail names, and what it means. Text and subtext are the same structure in the speech channel, and the two chapters should be read together by any student who finds either pair abstract. Who reports the speech is a viewpoint question. All dialogue in a novel reaches the reader through a narrator, and the narrator’s position determines what the reader is permitted to know about the gap between saying and meaning. Chapter 13 ( The Viewpoint Shift ) handles the machinery; §9.5 below, on Wuthering Heights , shows what happens when dialogue arrives at two removes.

title: 2. Definitions and Boundaries
text: Craft discussion of dialogue is prone to a specific terminological collapse: the word dialogue is used indiscriminately for the material inside quotation marks, for the technique of representing speech, and for the structural unit. These are three different things with three different failure modes, and the chapter begins by separating them. 2.1 The unit under study Working definition. A dialogue exchange is a passage of spoken interaction between two or more characters, each pursuing a want through what they say, in which the balance of information, power or feeling between the speakers is measurably different at the end than at the start. Four elements of that definition carry weight. “Spoken interaction.” The unit is the interaction , not the speech. A page of one character talking at another who does not respond is a speech , not an exchange, and it obeys different rules — see §2.3 and, for the limit case, the analysis of the Grand Inquisitor at §9.3 . “Each pursuing a want.” Both sides. An exchange in which only one party wants something is an interrogation or a briefing; those are legitimate forms, but they are one-engined, and the diagnostic protocol will find them. “Through what they say.” The want is pursued by means of the talk. If the talk is incidental to how the want is pursued — two people negotiating while the real action is that one of them is stealing something — the exchange is a texture layer over a different unit. “Measurably different.” The value-shift test from Chapter 1 ( The Purposes of a Scene ), at the smaller scale. What has changed may be small: a fact has passed, a claim has been conceded, a form of address has altered. 2.2 Scale and extent There is no principled length for the unit, and any number given is a convention rather than a discovery. Three ways of delimiting it are in circulation, and they answer different questions. Delimitation Extent Answers the question The turn One speaker’s uninterrupted contribution What does this line do that the last one did not? The exchange A bounded stretch of turns on one matter, with a beginning and an outcome Has anything moved? The dialogue scene An entire scene whose action is talk Does this scene earn its page count? This chapter treats the middle delimitation as primary, because it is the unit at which purpose becomes visible. A single turn is too small to shift a value; a whole scene is large enough that a failing exchange inside it can hide behind a functioning one elsewhere. In practice an exchange in the sense used here runs from roughly six to sixty turns, and its boundaries are marked by a change of topic, a change of participants, or the arrival of the outcome that the exchange was pursuing. A useful rule of thumb for revision: the exchange begins at the first turn that could not be cut without loss, and ends at the last one. Most drafted exchanges have three or four turns of approach at the front and two of retreat at the back; both are the writer’s runway, not the reader’s requirement. The equivalent observation about openings appears in Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages ), where it is called throat-clearing. 2.3 The term most often confused with this one: conversation The distinction a reviser most needs is between conversation and exchange . Conversation is a social activity whose primary function is frequently the maintenance of the relationship rather than the transfer of anything. Much of it is what Malinowski called phatic communion : talk whose content is nearly irrelevant to its purpose, which is to establish and confirm that the channel is open and the relationship is intact. Greetings, weather, the ritual enquiry after health, the closing sequence — these are enormously important socially and almost inert narratively. An exchange, by contrast, is conversation under load. The distinction is not a matter of subject: two people can discuss the weather in an exchange and their own divorce in a conversation. It is a matter of whether anything is being contested. Conversation Exchange Primary function Maintain the channel and the relationship Pursue incompatible wants Ends when The participants are done Someone gets something, or is refused Value at stake None, or the relationship as a standing condition A specific value in a specific domain ( §4 ) Narrative use Establishing register; marking time; providing the baseline against which deviation registers Carrying a scene Diagnostic Removable, with only texture lost Removable only at identifiable cost Novels use both, and the error is not writing conversation; it is mistaking conversation for exchange — which is the dialogue-specific form of the error Chapter 1 ( The Purposes of a Scene ) identifies when it distinguishes a scene from scenery. 2.4 Adjacent terms Term Meaning Relation to the dialogue exchange Turn One speaker’s contribution, bounded by the transitions on either side The exchange’s smallest constituent; the unit of conversation analysis ( §3.2 ) Adjacency pair A two-turn sequence in which the first makes a particular second relevant — question/answer, offer/acceptance, greeting/greeting The mechanism by which a missing second turn becomes meaningful; the technical basis of the evasion mechanisms in §6.4 Speech (as a unit) Extended uninterrupted talk by one character Not an exchange, though it may sit inside one; §9.3 Monologue Sustained speech, addressed or unaddressed Distinct: Cohn’s quoted monologue is interior, not spoken Reported speech Speech rendered by the narrator rather than quoted — she said she would not come A compression option, and the alternative any removal test must consider ( §7.1 ) Free indirect speech Speech or thought rendered in the narrator’s grammar and the character’s diction, unquoted The boundary case; see Chapter 13 ( The Viewpoint Shift ) and §9.4 Attribution / tag he said , she asked — the identification of a speaker A technical apparatus with its own history; §3.5 , §7.1 test 9 Action beat An action inserted between turns in place of a tag (called simply a beat in the first edition; this edition keeps beat for Chapters 1 and 2) Carries the relational domain more often than writers notice; §4.3 Subtext What is wanted, feared or withheld beneath the line The chapter’s central mechanism; §6 2.5 What this chapter excludes Interior monologue and the representation of thought — Cohn’s territory, and Chapter 13 ( The Viewpoint Shift ). This chapter treats thought only where it interacts with speech, chiefly as the narrator’s licence to expose the gap between the two channels. Prose rhythm and sentence craft in the narration — the surrounding prose, as distinct from the speech, belongs to the study of voice. Dramatic dialogue as such. Plays and screenplays are discussed comparatively at §10.4 , but the chapter’s model is built for prose fiction, where a narrator stands between speaker and reader. That narrator is the single largest formal difference between novelistic and dramatic dialogue, and most craft advice imported from screenwriting mislays it. Dialect and sociolinguistic variation as a linguistic subject. §3.4 and §8.9 treat its representation as a craft and ethical problem; the linguistics of variation is a field of its own. The chapter break placed inside an exchange — a real technique, and the property of Chapter 6 ( The Chapter Break ).

title: 3. Why Dialogue Is Not Speech
text: Craft literature on dialogue is thin in theory and rich in prohibitions. Students are told to avoid as you know, Bob , to use said , to cut greetings, to avoid phonetic dialect, and to write on the slant rather than on the nose. Almost none of this is explained; nearly all of it is correct where it is correct; and the reason it works is available, in detail, in a body of empirical linguistics that the workshop tradition has never absorbed. This section assembles that case: four theoretical strands — Grice on implicature, conversation analysis on the machinery of turns, Goffman on footing and face, Bakhtin on the novel’s plurality of languages — followed by a historical strand on the contingency of the conventions and an empirical strand on what transcribed talk actually looks like. 3.1 Grice: meaning generated by breaking the rules The body of theory a writer of dialogue can least do without, because it accounts for subtext, is H. P. Grice’s account of conversational meaning, presented in Harvard’s William James series in 1967 and published as “Logic and Conversation” in 1975. Grice’s problem was that speakers routinely mean more than they say and hearers reliably recover the surplus. His solution posits that conversation is a cooperative activity governed by a general principle and four attendant maxims . The Cooperative Principle. Make your conversational contribution such as is required, at the stage at which it occurs, by the accepted purpose or direction of the talk exchange in which you are engaged. Maxim What it enjoins Craft translation Quantity Be as informative as required; no more Answer the question asked; no paragraph where a word will serve Quality Do not say what you believe false Tell the truth Relation Be relevant Answer this question, not a neighbouring one Manner Avoid obscurity and ambiguity; be brief and orderly Say it plainly So far this describes ideal, transparent talk — the dialogue of the maximally cooperative and therefore maximally boring interlocutor. Grice’s decisive move is what comes next. A speaker may violate a maxim quietly; a lie violates Quality. But a speaker may also flout a maxim — breach it openly, in a way the hearer cannot fail to notice — and when they do, the hearer does not conclude that cooperation has broken down. The hearer assumes cooperation is being maintained at a deeper level and therefore computes an additional meaning that would restore it. Grice calls this a conversational implicature . His classic example is a reference letter for a philosophy post which says only that the candidate’s English is excellent and his attendance regular: nothing false is stated, Quantity is conspicuously flouted, and the reader computes that the referee has nothing to say about the candidate’s philosophy. One useful correspondence follows: Conversational implicature is one way to produce subtext. When a character conspicuously departs from what an exchange calls for, the reader may infer an unstated meaning while still treating the character as cooperative. Other subtext arises through action, narration, and turn structure without such a departure. The correspondence is useful in revision. Grice’s maxims give a generative account of one set of subtext effects: conspicuous departures from what is expected can prompt characteristic inferences. Conversational implicature can also arise when speakers observe the maxims, and the mechanisms below do not exhaust subtext. Maxim flouted What the character does What the reader computes Named mechanism ( §6.4 ) Relation Answers a question by changing the subject The answer is unbearable, or damaging The Changed Subject; the Question Answered With a Question Quantity (too little) Answers in a monosyllable where more was due Refusal, contempt, or self-control Evasion; the Ritual Formula Quantity (too much) Supplies far more than was asked Anxiety, guilt, the manufacture of an alibi Over-answering; the Too-Precise Reply Quality Says what both know to be false Irony, or a shared fiction maintained The False Agreement Manner Answers with conspicuous circumlocution Something is being protected The Third-Person Deflection; the Unfinished Sentence What matters is the shape of the claim: the reader’s work in reading dialogue is often inferential, and a shared assumption of cooperation can license the inference even when the character appears to strain it. A direct line may still generate an implicature through what it selects or leaves unsaid in context; conspicuous flouting is one especially visible way to prompt the reader’s inference. Two qualifications should be carried. The maxims are culturally variable. Grice presented them as features of rational cooperative behaviour, but comparative work since — Elinor Ochs Keenan’s fieldwork on Malagasy speakers who systematically withhold information without generating the implicatures an English speaker would compute, and the wider tradition of cross-cultural pragmatics — establishes that their weighting differs across speech communities. A novelist representing a community whose norms of directness differ from the reader’s must establish the local baseline before deviation from it can signify. Implicature requires a norm, and the novelist must supply the norm before flouting it. Politeness competes with informativeness. Penelope Brown and Stephen Levinson’s Politeness (1987) argues that much apparent inefficiency in talk — hedging, indirection, circumlocution before a request — is the rational management of face , and is therefore not a flouting but the observance of a different imperative. A character who hedges may be concealing (implicature) or may be being polite (face-work), and the two produce different reader experiences. §3.3 develops the face side. 3.2 Conversation analysis: the machinery of turns Grice describes what talk means; conversation analysis describes how it is built. The founding paper is Harvey Sacks, Emanuel Schegloff and Gail Jefferson’s “A Simplest Systematics for the Organization of Turn-Taking for Conversation” ( Language , 1974), and its findings are among the most robust in the human sciences — derived from recordings, replicated across languages, specific enough to be falsifiable. Four bear directly on writing. 1. Turn-taking is locally managed and precise. Speakers do not wait for a pause; they project the end of the current turn and begin at or just before it. Overlap is common but brief; gaps are measured in fractions of a second. The implication for fiction is negative but useful: the rhythm of real conversation is far faster and more interlocking than alternating paragraphs suggest, so a writer wanting speed must produce it by other means — shorter turns, dropped attributions, interruption marked typographically. 2. The adjacency pair is the basic sequence. Certain first turns make a particular second conditionally relevant : a question makes an answer relevant, an invitation an acceptance or refusal. Conditional relevance is the key concept, because it means the absence of the expected second turn is itself an event — a noticeable absence , heard as meaning something. This is the machinery underlying every evasion in fiction, and it is why a character’s failure to answer is among the most economical moves in the form: nothing has to be written for a great deal to be communicated. 3. Preference organisation: refusals are marked, and the marking is regular. This is the finding that should most alter how writers draft. Anita Pomerantz’s work on assessments, and the wider conversation-analytic literature, establishes that the two possible seconds of an adjacency pair are not symmetrical. Preferred responses — acceptances, agreements — come immediately, briefly and without explanation. Dispreferred responses come with a characteristic package: a delay; a hesitation marker ( Well — ); a token agreement ( That’s a lovely idea, but ); an account offered without being asked for; mitigation ( I don’t think I can, quite ); and often no outright refusal at all ( I’ll see ). This package is how skilled novelists write reluctance. The delayed, hedged “no” that a reader registers as psychologically acute is not an intuition of the writer’s; it is a documented feature of talk the good writer has absorbed by ear. Conversely, a draft in which characters refuse each other flatly — “No.” “Then I’ll go alone.” — reads as stylised or hostile, and writers rarely know why: they are producing preferred-format turns with dispreferred content. The teaching move follows. A character who agrees instantly is agreeing; a character who agrees after a pause and an account has refused something. 4. Repair. Speakers correct themselves and each other continuously, and repair has a strong preference for self -correction: given the chance, speakers fix their own errors, and hearers give them that chance. Other-correction is rare and socially marked — which is why correcting another character’s name, title, date or word choice is one of the sharpest status moves available in dialogue, and one of the cheapest to write. A caution. Conversation analysis is a descriptive science of naturally occurring talk. The claim here is not that novelists should reproduce these structures — §3.6 argues emphatically that they should not — but that these structures are what readers have internalised, and therefore constitute the grammar against which a novelist’s stylisations are read. 3.3 Goffman: footing, participation, and face If Grice supplies the mechanism of subtext and conversation analysis the mechanism of sequence, Erving Goffman supplies the scholarly form of what this chapter calls the relational domain ( §4.3 ). Face-work. In The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life (1959) and “On Face-Work” (in Interaction Ritual , 1967), Goffman describes interaction as the mutual maintenance of face — the social value a person claims by the line others assume they are taking. Interaction is organised to protect the face of all participants, including that of the person one is opposing, which explains the elaborate mitigation, the offering of exits, and the willingness to accept a transparently false excuse. It also identifies the moment an exchange turns. An exchange turns when one party stops protecting the other’s face. That formulation gives a writer something to look for. In most drafted arguments the escalation is a matter of volume; in most published arguments that work, it is a matter of face — a name used in full, an excuse refused, a euphemism replaced by the accurate word, a courtesy withheld. Footing. In Forms of Talk (1981), Goffman dismantles the two-role model of speaker and hearer. A speaker may be the animator (producing the sounds), the author (composing the words), or the principal (whose position the words express), and these come apart: a clerk delivering a company’s refusal is animator but not principal. Footing is Goffman’s term for a speaker’s alignment to what is said, to the other participants and to their own role — and for the fact that it shifts, often within a single turn. A character who moves from I think to people say to she always used to say has changed footing twice, and each change alters who is answerable. This is not a subtle literary effect but something people do continuously, and one of the most under-exploited resources in draft dialogue. The Third-Person Deflection ( §6.4 ) is a footing shift used to shed accountability. The participation framework. Goffman’s third contribution is that talk has more parties than the two speaking. He distinguishes ratified participants — those the talk is officially addressed to, whether addressed or unaddressed — from bystanders : overhearers , known to be present, and eavesdroppers , not. Every utterance is designed with reference to the whole framework. The literary application is large enough that §4.6 builds a proposed domain on it. Consider how much great dialogue is designed for a third party: Elizabeth Bennet speaking to Darcy in a room containing Miss Bingley; Nelly Dean listening to Catherine while Heathcliff sits unseen; any exchange conducted in a servant’s presence, where the servant’s status as unratified participant is what makes the room usable. Who is in the room but not in the conversation is a structural fact about the exchange, not a detail of the setting. 3.4 Bakhtin: the novel as a contest of languages Bakhtin supplies the largest frame, and the one that underwrites the prohibition against characters who all sound the same. His argument, developed across The Dialogic Imagination (English translation 1981) and Problems of Dostoevsky’s Poetics (English translation 1984), is that the novel is constitutively different from poetry and epic in its relation to language. Poetry aspires to a unitary language; the novel is built out of heteroglossia — the actual stratification of a national language into the discourses of professions, generations, classes, regions and genres, each carrying its own evaluative charge. The novelist does not write in a language but orchestrates languages, and the book’s meaning arises from the friction between them. This is the scholarly ground for voice differentiation. The craft instruction that characters must sound different is usually justified on grounds of clarity. Bakhtin’s justification is stronger: a character’s speech carries a whole social position — the words they reach for, the register they default to, what they consider sayable, the authorities they cite. Two characters who sound the same occupy the same social world, and a novel in which everyone occupies the same social world has forfeited the form’s central resource. This is the argument against the ventriloquist exchange ( §8.2 ) in its strongest form, and it does not depend on realism at all. Polyphony. In the Dostoevsky book Bakhtin distinguishes the monologic novel, where all voices are finally subordinated to the author’s evaluative position, from the polyphonic novel, where characters’ ideological positions retain real independence. Ivan Karamazov’s argument against God is not defeated by the narrator; it is answered, if at all, by another character’s life. This is the basis for the theme domain’s requirement ( §4.4 ) that a staged dialectic be open — both positions given their best case, the narration declining to arbitrate. Bakhtin also supplies a term for something writers produce without naming: the character zone , the field around a character in which the narration itself becomes contaminated by that character’s speech habits, so that the boundary between narration and speech goes porous. Anglo-American criticism approaches the same phenomenon through free indirect style, which is why §2.4 lists free indirect speech as a boundary case rather than an exclusion. 3.5 The historical strand: quotation is a convention with a date Students routinely receive the contemporary conventions of dialogue presentation as though they were properties of narrative. They are properties of a period. Period or context Characteristic practice Pre-1700 No settled convention; speech marked by quoth , by said he , by formulae inherited from classical and biblical narrative; typographic marking sporadic and printer-driven 18th century Quotation marks spreading but unstable; speech frequently subordinated to reported forms; the epistolary novel sidesteps the problem Early 19th century (Austen) Direct speech used sparingly and at moments of consequence; much social interaction handled in reported and free indirect form; attribution minimal Mid-to-late 19th century Direct speech dominant; expressive attribution common ( returned , rejoined , expostulated ); adverbial modification routine; dialect rendered phonetically and at length Modernist period Convention becomes a subject: Joyce’s dashes in place of “perverted commas”; Woolf’s dissolution of the speech/thought boundary; Hemingway’s stripped attribution Recent craft instruction Said often preferred; attribution minimised; adverbs discouraged; action beats offered as alternatives to tags; dialect often signalled lexically rather than orthographically Contemporary experimental Quotation marks optional or abolished — Saramago, McCarthy, and a substantial strand of contemporary literary fiction Four observations follow, each a caution against universalising the present. 1. The typographic apparatus is not old. M. B. Parkes’s history of punctuation, Pause and Effect (1993), traces the slow emergence of the marks now used to signal quotation, which stabilise into their modern function only in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. A convention two centuries old is not a law of the form. 2. The preference for said is a convention, not a timeless rule. The nineteenth-century novel is full of rejoined , ventured and expostulated , used by writers of the first rank without embarrassment.
