Modern advice, familiar from Elmore Leonard’s 2001 rules, rests on the premise that attribution should be unobtrusive so the reader’s attention rests on the speech. That premise is defensible and this chapter largely endorses it ( §7.1 , test 9). A student who reads he expostulated as an error rather than a period convention has mistaken a fashion for a fault. 3. Austen’s practice would fail a contemporary workshop. Much of Pride and Prejudice ’s social interaction is not rendered as dialogue at all but as summary, indirect report and free indirect discourse, with direct speech reserved for what matters. Norman Page’s Speech in the English Novel (1973) — the standard study, and the most useful single book for a student of this chapter — documents how varied and deliberate the nineteenth-century handling of the speech/report boundary was. Contemporary practice over-uses direct speech, because it has been taught that showing beats telling. Austen’s ratio is a technique, not an archaism ; §9.1 shows what it buys. 4. The abolition of quotation marks is a formal contract, not a tic. Saramago’s Blindness (1995; trans. Giovanni Pontiero) runs dialogue into continuous paragraphs, marking speaker changes with a comma and a capital letter. Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages ) treats this as a formal contract declared on page one. What this chapter adds is that the device has a semantic consequence: without the visual separation of quotation marks, speech loses its ontological privilege over narration, and the reader stops experiencing speech as a distinct kind of material. In a novel about a society dissolving into undifferentiated crisis, that is not a typographic preference. §9.6 develops the reading. 3.6 The empirical caution: transcribed talk is not dialogue Work in discourse analysis and corpus linguistics documents features of spontaneous conversation that novelists may retain, omit, or stylise. Their frequency varies with the speakers, setting, and method of transcription. Feature of real talk In conversation In novelistic dialogue Overlap and simultaneous speech Occurs, usually in brief stretches Can be represented through interruptions or other typographic choices False starts and self-repair Occur as speakers plan and revise what they say Can be selected for characterisation or dramatic pressure Filled pauses ( um , er ) Occur at rates that vary by speaker and setting Can be included selectively Minimal responses ( mm , yeah ) Can signal attention or encourage a speaker to continue Can be retained when they affect the exchange Discourse markers ( well , you know ) Help speakers manage turns and meaning Can be selected to establish voice Syntactically incomplete turns Occur; their meaning may still be clear in context Can convey hesitation, interruption, or an established voice Topic drift and abandonment Can leave a topic unresolved Can suggest avoidance or a shift in attention Phatic sequences (greetings, closings) Occur where the social situation calls for them Can be compressed unless the ritual matters to the scene The conclusion is not that novelists are inaccurate. It is that literary dialogue is a stylised convention that reads as real , in the way stage lighting reads as daylight. The illusion is produced not by reproducing surface features but by retaining a small number of structural ones — the preference organisation of refusals, the conditional relevance of adjacency pairs, shifts of footing, the flouting of maxims — which are the features that carry social meaning. A writer who imports the surface features instead produces something that sounds less real, because disfluencies signify differently on the page: on a recording um is invisible; on a page it is a mark, and per the rules of notice discussed in Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages ) every mark on a page is read as intended. Deborah Tannen’s Talking Voices (1989) supplies the final turn of the argument. Studying how speakers report others’ speech in ordinary conversation, Tannen found such reports are rarely verbatim: speakers invent, compress and dramatise, producing what she calls constructed dialogue . The stylisation novelists perform on speech is a stylisation ordinary speakers also perform on speech. The novelist’s dialogue is not a departure from how people talk but a formalisation of what people already do when they retell talk. 3.7 The first principle, restated and qualified A dialogue exchange earns its place when speech is doing something that could not be done otherwise: when the words are the instrument of a want, when the balance of information, standing or feeling differs at the close from the open, and when what is said and what is meant do not entirely coincide. Four qualifications, each of which the rest of the chapter honours. Not every exchange must run on two channels. The gap between text and subtext is a resource with a limit, and §6.5 argues that closing it is a climactic move spendable once. A book in which every line is oblique is as monotonous as one in which every line is direct, and more irritating. The subtext requirement is culturally and historically local — a twentieth-century Anglo-American ideal, shaped by Chekhov’s reception, by Hemingway, and by the workshop system that codified them. §16 develops this at length and should be read as part of the argument, not as a disclaimer appended to it. The tests are diagnostic, not evaluative. The protocol in §7 identifies what an exchange is doing, not whether it is good. A writer who converts its outputs into verdicts will cut the most interesting material in the draft, because the most interesting material is where the conventions are being strained. Realism is not the standard, but plausibility is a constraint. Rejecting transcriptional accuracy does not license dialogue no human register would produce. What must remain true is the social grammar: that speakers manage face, that refusals are marked, that people design their utterances for everyone in the room. A character may speak in perfect epigrams — Wilde’s do — provided the epigrams still do the social work talk does.

title: 4. The Domains of Purpose
text: 4.0 The model and its status Chapter 1 ( The Purposes of a Scene ) established four domains of purpose — plot, character, theme and texture — as lenses for asking what a stretch of prose is actually for. The model’s virtue is that it converts the unusable instruction make this scene better into a set of separable questions with separable remedies. Dialogue inherits all four and adopts the fifth that Chapter 1 proposes. The relational domain — the negotiation of standing between speakers — could in principle be filed under character, and the usual four-domain model files it there, as realign a relationship . Chapter 1 argues for separating it; in dialogue it will not stay filed. Speech is the primary medium through which humans conduct status, and an exchange can leave both characters unchanged as individuals while permanently altering what each may say to the other. That is a value shift, it is invisible to the four-domain model, and it is what a very large proportion of memorable dialogue is actually doing. Goffman’s face-work and footing ( §3.3 ) are its scholarly form. Five domains are set out below, followed in §4.6 by a proposed sixth. For each: a definition, why it matters, the textual carriers through which it is realised, a discussion, the characteristic under- and over-delivery, and illustrations from published fiction. Two warnings about the model before it is used. It is a diagnostic instrument, not a specification. Its correct use is retrospective: applied to a drafted exchange to discover what it is doing. Applied prospectively — this exchange will serve plot and theme — it produces the overstuffed, visibly purposeful dialogue described at §8.11 . The domains overlap by design. A single line frequently serves three of them, and the point of §5 is that the best lines always do. Categorising a line is not the goal; noticing what a passage is systematically failing to do is. 4.1 Plot — information and decisions change hands Definition. The exchange moves the causal chain: a fact passes, a commitment is made, a plan is set or broken, a turn occurs. Why it matters. Dialogue is the novel’s most efficient mechanism for transferring information between characters, and therefore the mechanism most likely to be abused. Almost every failure pattern in §8 is a plot-domain failure in disguise: the writer needed the reader to know something and used two characters as a delivery system. Carriers Carrier Description Signal on the page Information under pressure A fact arrives because someone is forced to give it up The speaker’s reluctance is visible; the fact costs something to say The forced decision A character commits to something on the page, in front of a witness A future-tense first-person sentence with a named consequence Negotiation Terms offered, refused, countered Explicit conditionals; the vocabulary of exchange The turn Confession, exposure, a lie caught Usually a single short turn after a long one The revised plan Characters agree, disagree, or alter what happens next Specificity sufficient to bind: a time, a place, a name Discussion The plot domain’s central craft problem is that information is most needed by the reader at the moments when it is least plausible for a character to supply it. The solution the whole tradition converges on is not to remove the information but to make it cost something , and the mechanism has three parts: Give the fact to someone who does not want to say it. Reluctance converts transmission into an event. Give the need to someone who already suspects part of it. A listener who is testing rather than receiving changes the exchange from a briefing into an interrogation, and the reader watches a contest instead of overhearing a summary. Let the fact arrive incomplete. Information delivered in full is spent; information delivered as a fragment that raises a further question is, in Sternberg’s terms, converted from an expense into an asset — the same economy Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages ) applies to exposition. Note that none of this alters the information. What changes is that a relational value moves at the same time (§4.3), a character is revealed by what the disclosure costs them (§4.2), and the reader has been made to work. A second, less discussed plot function is the binding commitment . A decision made in a character’s head can be revised silently; a decision made aloud to another character has a witness, and the witness is what makes it structural. This is why the dialogue exchange is the natural site for the Decision beat that closes a sequel in the model treated in Chapter 2 ( Scene and Sequel ): saying it aloud is what converts a resolution into an obligation. Under- and over-delivery Under: the exchange in which nothing passes. Two characters discuss a situation both fully understand, and the reader learns only what they already knew. Diagnosed by test 1 ( §7.1 ). Over: the briefing. Every turn carries a fact; nobody resists; the reader is being brought up to date. This is the As-You-Know-Bob exchange ( §8.1 ) and the Expository Scene in Disguise identified in Chapter 1 ( The Purposes of a Scene ). Illustrations 1. Austen, Pride and Prejudice (1813) — the fact extracted by an antagonist. Lady Catherine de Bourgh arrives at Longbourn to demand that Elizabeth deny an engagement to Darcy. The plot information at issue — whether an engagement exists — is a fact Elizabeth does not possess; what she possesses is a refusal to promise. The scene’s plot work is therefore performed by an absence : Elizabeth declines to give the assurance demanded, Lady Catherine carries the refusal to Darcy, and Darcy reads it as encouragement. A fact is created by a conversation that transmits no facts. It is the most elegant piece of plot machinery in the novel, and it works entirely through what one character will not say. 2. Ishiguro, The Remains of the Day (1989) — information delivered as a weapon. When Miss Kenton informs Stevens of her engagement, the plot content is a single fact with a date attached. Its function is not informational but tactical: the announcement is made in order to be responded to, and Stevens’s failure to respond is the event. The plot domain and the relational domain are here the same act seen from two sides, which is the normal condition of good dialogue rather than an unusual achievement. 4.2 Character — the speaker is revealed Definition. The exchange discloses who is speaking: through diction, through what they avoid, through what they claim about themselves, and through the distance between the claim and the evidence. Why it matters. Speech is the most concentrated characterisation the novel possesses, because it is the only element in which the character rather than the narrator selects the words. Everything else in a novel is filtered; dialogue is, by convention, unfiltered — which is why a false note is so much more damaging in speech than in narration. Carriers Carrier Description Signal on the page Differentiated diction Vocabulary, register, syntax specific to this speaker The line misfits in any other mouth ( §7.1 , test 8) Characteristic sentence shape Length, subordination, whether the speaker finishes Consistent across scenes; the most reliable single marker Evasion What the speaker deflects, minimises or declines A question left unanswered; an adjacency pair left open The tested value A stated belief put under direct pressure by another speaker An assertion in one scene; a choice under it in another Self-description The speaker’s account of themselves, measurable against the evidence Any sentence beginning I’m not the sort of person who The register shift A change in how a character speaks when the audience changes Same character, two scenes, two idioms Discussion The last carrier is the most under-used and the most powerful. A character who speaks one way to a superior and another way to a subordinate has been characterised twice over: once by each register, and a third time by the fact of the switch. Goffman’s footing ( §3.3 ) is the formal account; the craft observation is simply that a single consistent voice per character is a beginner’s target, and the professional target is a consistent repertoire . The reader who notices that a character’s sentences get shorter in a particular person’s presence has been told something no description could supply. Evasion deserves separate emphasis because it inverts the intuitive relation between speech and disclosure. What a character will not say is more characterising than what they will, for the structural reason set out at §3.2 : a question makes an answer conditionally relevant, so a non-answer is a noticeable absence and the reader is licensed to interpret it. This is the character domain and the silence domain (§4.6) meeting, and it is why the silence test ( §7.1 , test 5) is among the most productive in the protocol. The self-description carrier is the character domain’s cheapest reliable effect and its most easily overplayed one. A character who says I’ve never been any good at this has supplied the reader with a claim, and the reader will spend the rest of the book measuring it. The cost is that the claim must then be measured: an unexamined self-description is a wasted line, and a self-description the book endorses without testing is a character speaking the author’s notes aloud. Under- and over-delivery Under: the interchangeable line. Grammatically clean, plausibly spoken, attributable to any of six characters. This is the ventriloquist exchange ( §8.2 ), and it is a common defect in drafted dialogue. Over: the tic. A character marked by a repeated verbal signature — a catchphrase, a dialect spelling, a habitual oath — which substitutes a label for a person. Dickens is the great exponent and the great cautionary case: Mrs Micawber’s I will never desert Mr Micawber is a triumph of comic characterisation and a demonstration of how little such a device can be made to yield in a serious register. Illustrations 1. Hurston, Their Eyes Were Watching God (1937) — character established by what a speaker forbids. When Janie is called on to make a speech at the lighting of the lamp, Joe Starks answers for her: his wife knows nothing about speech-making, he never married her for anything like that, and her place is in the home. Three short clauses characterise Jody completely — the proprietary mah wife , the retrospective justification, the appeal to a general principle — and characterise Janie by the silence they impose. The domain of character and the domain of relation are indistinguishable in the line, and the silence domain (§4.6) is doing at least as much work as either. 2. James, The Portrait of a Lady (1881) — self-description as a philosophical position. Madame Merle’s account of the self to Isabel — that there is no isolated person, that the self overflows into the house one lives in, the clothes one wears, the company one keeps — is simultaneously a worldly woman’s practical creed and the novel’s central question posed as social observation. Isabel’s reply insists on the opposite: that nothing belonging to her is any measure of her. Neither woman is stating a position for the reader’s benefit; each is defending a way of living against the other. That is the difference between a philosophical exchange and an essay read aloud by two speakers, and it is a difference of want , not of content. 3. Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov (1880; trans. Constance Garnett) — the value tested by its own advocate. Ivan tells Alyosha that he accepts God but returns the ticket — that no future harmony can justify the suffering of one tortured child. The passage is character work rather than theme work in the first instance, because what it reveals is a man who has constructed an unanswerable argument and cannot live inside it. Alyosha’s response is not a counter-argument; it is a question about who Ivan is. The theme domain is served because the character domain is served first. 4.3 Relational — the standing between speakers changes This chapter adopts the fifth domain proposed in Chapter 1 ( The Purposes of a Scene ). Definition. The exchange alters the balance of power, intimacy, obligation or permission between the speakers — what each may now say to the other, and on what terms. Why it matters. Status is transacted in talk more than anywhere else, and the transactions are minutely observable: who initiates, who yields the floor, who is permitted to change the subject, who apologises, who is corrected, who uses whose first name. A reader tracks these continuously and unconsciously, which means a writer who manages them deliberately is operating on a channel the reader is already monitoring. Carriers Carrier Description Signal on the page Address and naming Titles, first names, diminutives, full names, the refusal to use any A change in form of address mid-scene is always an event Turn-allocation Who speaks next, who interrupts, who is permitted to finish Interruption marked by dash; overlap; a turn abandoned The floor Who holds it, who takes it, who gives it up Long turns versus short; the length ratio across the exchange Question rights Who is permitted to ask, and who must answer Sustained one-way questioning is a status structure Correction Other-correction of a fact, a word, a title Rare in real talk ( §3.2 ); therefore aggressive on the page Physical position Standing, sitting, in a doorway, behind a desk The action beat , which carries relational value far more often than writers notice Permission and deference Asking versus assuming; the granting or withholding of an exit May I against I’m going to Shared reference Private shorthand, allusion, the pointed exclusion of a third party An unglossed reference is a claim of intimacy Discussion The relational domain is the reason the doorway is the most useful piece of furniture in fiction. A character who stands in a doorway controls access; a character who must ask to pass has already lost something. Physical arrangement is not setting, in an exchange; it is the diagram of the status relation, and moving a character across the room is a relational move that costs no dialogue at all. Three practical principles. 1. Status is a change , not a state. An exchange in which the powerful character is powerful throughout has not served this domain; it has illustrated a fact already established. What the domain requires is a movement, or a movement resisted under visible pressure. The status test ( §7.1 , test 3) exists to catch this. 2. Partial shifts are more interesting than total ones. A character who yields the ground but keeps the one thing that mattered has produced a more legible and more useful shift than one who capitulates. The worked example at §9.9 turns entirely on this: Dov surrenders the doorway and the key and retains the reason. 3. The strongest relational moves are the smallest. A shift from surname to first name; the withholding of a courtesy that has been given in every previous scene; an unanswered greeting; an answer addressed to a third party instead of to the questioner. These outperform declarations because they are acts rather than statements , and because they engage the reader’s inferential machinery ( §3.1 ) rather than reporting a conclusion to it. Under- and over-delivery Under: the static-status exchange ( §8.4 ). Competently voiced, well paced, and going nowhere, because the same person holds the upper hand at the last line as at the first and nothing has been contested. Over: the status contest as sole content. Two characters engaged in visible dominance display, with no plot fact and no relational history underneath — a dialogue that reads as posturing, common in genre pastiche and in workshop exercises written to demonstrate the concept. Illustrations 1. Austen, Pride and Prejudice (1813) — status inverted inside a proposal. Darcy’s proposal at Hunsford opens from a position of total assumed advantage: he has come to confer something, and the manner of the conferring is itself an assertion of rank. Elizabeth’s refusal removes it. The exchange is analysed in full at §9.1 ; what matters here is the mechanism, which is that the relational shift is produced by the form of Elizabeth’s reply as much as its content. She answers his declaration with a remark about what is customary on such occasions — meeting a claim of feeling with a point of etiquette, which refuses the frame he has offered before refusing the offer inside it. 2. Brontë, Wuthering Heights (1847) — relation determined by an unratified participant. Catherine’s confession to Nelly Dean that it would degrade her to marry Heathcliff, and that she is Heathcliff nonetheless, is a two-person exchange with a third party present whom one of the two speakers does not know is there. Every relational value in the novel is set by this arrangement. The point is developed at §9.5 ; here it exemplifies Goffman’s participation framework ( §3.3 ) doing structural rather than decorative work. 3. Ishiguro, The Remains of the Day (1989) — status maintained at ruinous cost. Stevens’s professional register is a status instrument: the formality is what allows him to decline every intimacy Miss Kenton offers without ever refusing one. The relational value that shifts across the novel is not power — Stevens’s position is secure — but permission : what Miss Kenton may say to him narrows, scene by scene, until the exchange in which she tells him she is to be married is the last one in which she tries. 4.4 Theme — the argument changes Definition. The exchange stages the book’s governing question, either by voicing competing positions or by generating irony between what a speaker means and what the reader hears. Why it matters. Dialogue is the only place in a novel where a proposition can be advanced by someone the author is not answerable for. This is Bakhtin’s polyphony ( §3.4 ) in its practical form: a novel can hold two incompatible positions in genuine suspension because two characters hold them, and the narration is not obliged to adjudicate. Carriers Carrier Description Signal on the page The staged dialectic Two positions the book is weighing, voiced by two speakers in real tension Neither speaker is a straw figure; both have their best case The thesis under pressure A character argues for what the book seems to believe, and might lose The narration does not intervene to help Dramatic irony A speaker’s words mean more, or other, to the reader than to the speaker The reader knows something the speaker does not The unremarked question The book’s central question posed in miniature and never named Neither speaker notices what the exchange is about The uncorrected error A false claim allowed to stand The narration’s silence is the comment Discussion The theme domain has the highest failure rate of the five, because its failure mode is so attractive. A writer with something to say gives it to a character; the character says it; the domain is served. What has actually happened is that the book has stopped and a position has been announced, which is the difference Bakhtin draws between the monologic and the polyphonic. The discriminating question is not does someone say the thematic thing? but does the exchange put the thematic thing at risk? A staged dialectic requires that the position the author holds might lose the argument on the page, and that the reader can feel it might. Three tests of whether a dialectic is real: Is the opposing case made in its strongest form? If the opponent’s argument is one a competent adherent would disown, no dialectic is occurring. Does the narration refrain from arbitrating? A narrator who tags one speaker’s contributions with he said reasonably and the other’s with she snapped has decided the question. Does either speaker want something other than to win the argument? Pure argument is essay; the exchange becomes fiction when the argument is instrumental — when one of them is arguing in order to be forgiven, or to postpone, or to make the other stay in the room. The third is the one workshops most often miss. Ivan Karamazov’s argument with Alyosha is unbearable not because the philosophy is powerful — though it is — but because Ivan is a man trying to make his brother agree with him, and Alyosha is a man trying not to lose his brother. Under- and over-delivery Under: thematic decoration. A single line that name-checks the book’s subject in an exchange doing other work, which Chapter 1 ( The Purposes of a Scene ) correctly refuses to count as serving the domain at all. Over: the therapeutic exchange ( §8.10 ) and the mouthpiece. Characters articulating the book’s argument, or their own psychology, in terms the book has provided rather than terms they would have found. Illustrations 1. Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov (1880; trans. Garnett) — the dialectic staged and left open. The Grand Inquisitor chapter is the extreme case in the European novel, and it tests this chapter’s model to destruction; it is analysed at §9.3 . 2. Achebe, Things Fall Apart (1958) — the argument conducted in the vocabulary of the culture that is being argued about. After the killing of Ikemefuna — a scene which Chapter 1 ( The Purposes of a Scene ) analyses as a scene — Okonkwo and Obierika discuss what was done. Obierika’s position is that the act, though sanctioned by the Oracle, is the kind of thing for which the earth punishes whole families; Okonkwo’s is that a man does not question what the Oracle requires. Neither speaks the language of the novel’s eventual reader. The dialectic is entirely internal to Umuofia, which is what makes it a dialectic rather than an anticipation of the colonial judgement the book will later refuse to endorse. A staged dialectic is strongest when both positions are indigenous to the world. 3. Ishiguro, The Remains of the Day (1989) — theme produced entirely by irony. Stevens’s disquisitions on dignity are advanced with total sincerity and heard by the reader as a diagnosis. No opposing position is stated in the novel’s dialogue; the opposition is supplied by the reader from the evidence Stevens supplies against himself. The theme domain is served without a dialectic, by irony alone, which demonstrates that the two carriers are independent. 4.5 Texture — the experience changes Definition. The exchange calibrates how the passage feels: its tone, its pace, its register, and the reader’s sense of where and among whom they are. Why it matters. Dialogue changes the visual density and rhythm of a page. Short turns and paragraph breaks can make an exchange feel brisk, while longer turns can slow it. This makes texture a pacing choice in every exchange: the question is whether its rhythm serves the book at that point. Carriers Carrier Description Signal on the page Turn length and rhythm Short exchanges accelerate; long turns decelerate The visual shape of the page, before a word is read Register Formal, demotic, technical, ritual Vocabulary and syntax, not orthography White space The proportion of page given to speech A structural rather than a stylistic decision Attribution density Frequency and elaboration of tags Heavy tagging slows; stripped attribution accelerates and destabilises Comic relief A warm or funny moment set against surrounding tension A shift in register, usually by one speaker only World signal Dialect, jargon, idiom, terms of address Tells the reader where and among whom they are without narration Discussion The most consequential and least discussed carrier is white space . Short dialogue turns break up the page and can create an impression of speed and immediacy. They can also make the passage feel more like scene in Genette’s sense — narrative time approximating story time, the closest fiction comes to isochrony. A writer can use dialogue as a pacing instrument independently of its content and ask whether a tonally heavy passage needs a change in rhythm. Register as world signal is the texture domain’s largest resource and its most fraught. The register a community speaks in tells a reader where they are more efficiently than any description — the courtesies, the ellipses, the technical vocabulary handled without explanation, what is treated as unsayable. It is fraught because the most obvious way to signal register is orthographic — spelling speech as it sounds — and that technique has a difficult history, treated at §8.9 and §9.4 . The general principle comes first: dialect is carried by syntax, idiom and lexicon far more reliably than by spelling. A character who says I don’t have but the one has been placed regionally and socially without a single apostrophe of elision. Under- and over-delivery Under: register-neutral speech. Everyone speaks a mild contemporary standard, and the reader learns nothing about the world from how it talks. This is the ventriloquist exchange ( §8.2 ) seen from the texture side. Over: the dialect showcase, in which orthographic representation becomes so dense that reading slows to decipherment, and the technique starts to signal the writer’s ethnographic effort rather than the speaker’s speech. Illustrations 1. Saramago, Blindness (1995; trans. Giovanni Pontiero) — texture produced by the removal of an apparatus. Running dialogue into unbroken paragraphs, with speaker changes marked only by capitalisation, produces a specific reading experience: speech becomes continuous with narration, individual voices become hard to separate, and the reader must actively work to attribute each turn. In a novel about the collapse of individual distinctness under catastrophe, the texture is the argument. §9.6 develops this. 2. Brontë, Wuthering Heights (1847) — dialect as world signal and as barrier. Joseph’s speech is rendered in a dense Yorkshire orthography that many readers cannot parse without effort, and Emily Brontë’s editors have periodically softened it. The unreadability is not incidental: Joseph is a figure of obstruction, and the reader’s difficulty with him is the same difficulty every character has. This is the strongest available defence of the dialect showcase, and it is a defence available only where the opacity is doing work. 3. Hemingway, “Hills Like White Elephants” (1927) — texture as the whole of the technique. Short turns, minimal attribution, no interiority, and a rhythm of question and deflection produce a surface so uniform that the reader is forced to attend to the small deviations from it. The story is discussed at §9.8 . 4.6 A Proposed Sixth: The Silence Domain This section extends the five-domain model. The five domains above all describe things that speech does. But a great deal of what a dialogue exchange accomplishes is accomplished by speech that does not occur, and the five-domain model can only describe such effects as a technique within one of the other domains — evasion as character work, interruption as relational work, the unspeakable as theme. This chapter proposes that the category is large enough, structurally distinct enough and consequential enough to be named. The silence domain. The exchange does its work through what is not said: through refusals to answer, through interruption and its prevention, through pause and delay, through characters who are present and do not speak, and through characters who are excluded from the exchange altogether. Carriers Carrier Description Signal on the page The unanswered question A first pair-part left without its second The next paragraph belongs to a different topic, or to an action The pause A measured delay before a turn An action beat, a paragraph break, an explicit notation of silence Interruption A turn terminated by another speaker The dash; the abandoned clause The refusal An explicit refusal to speak I’m not going to answer that — the marked case, and the weakest The silent participant A ratified participant present throughout who never speaks Their presence is stated at the start and not mentioned again The unratified participant Someone who hears the exchange without being party to it The overhearer, the eavesdropper, the servant The absent party Someone discussed and not present, or excluded from a conversation about them Third-person reference sustained across an exchange The unspeakable A matter the exchange organises itself around and cannot approach Repeated approaches and swerves; circumlocution The argument for the domain Three arguments, in increasing order of strength. 1. Its effects are not reducible to the other domains. A character who is in the room and does not speak for eight pages of dialogue is producing an effect that is not characterisation (we learn nothing about them), not relation (they are transacting nothing), not plot and not theme. It is a structural effect: it makes the exchange a performance with an audience, and everything said in it is designed for that audience. Goffman’s participation framework ( §3.3 ) names this, and no other domain has the vocabulary for it. 2. It has its own failure modes and its own remedies. The over-explaining exchange, in which every character says outright what they think, is a silence-domain failure: the diagnosis is not too much characterisation or too much plot but nothing is being withheld , and the remedy is specific. The silence test ( §7.1 , test 5) exists because the failure is not visible from within the other five. 3. It is where a great deal of the novel’s most serious content lives. What cannot be said in a given society, by a given person, to a given hearer is a description of that society’s structure. Morrison’s Beloved organises an entire novel around a matter its characters cannot approach directly. Ishiguro’s Stevens is constituted by the sentences he does not complete. The exclusion of women, servants and children from conversations that determine their lives is not a theme of the nineteenth-century novel; it is a dialogue structure the nineteenth-century novel repeatedly builds scenes out of. To treat these as instances of “character revealed through evasion” is to describe a cathedral as a load-bearing wall. The argument against It should be given its full force, because it is a good argument. Silence is a technique, not a purpose. The five domains answer the question what value has changed? — a plot value, a character value, a relational value, a thematic value, a textural value. Silence answers a different question: by what means? And the means is available to all five. An unanswered question shifts a relational value; an interruption shifts a relational value; an excluded party is a fact about the plot or the world. On this account the proposed sixth domain is a category error: it belongs in §6 with the other mechanisms, alongside evasion and the changed subject, and elevating it to a domain confuses the taxonomy of ends with the taxonomy of means . There is a second, subtler objection. A domain, in the model inherited from Chapter 1 ( The Purposes of a Scene ), is a register in which something can change . It is not obvious what a silence-domain value shift would look like. If the answer is “what may now be said between these people has narrowed”, that is a relational value; if it is “the reader now knows what cannot be spoken of”, that is theme. The chapter’s position This chapter adopts the sixth domain for diagnostic purposes while conceding that the objection has not been answered. The pragmatic justification is that writers do not look for what is absent unless they are prompted to , and a taxonomy that files silence inside five domains of presence will not prompt them. The theoretical justification is weaker and rests on the participation framework: the composition of the room — who may speak, who may hear, who is excluded — is a fact about the exchange’s structure that the other five domains cannot express, whatever may be true of the other carriers. Seminar question 2 ( §12.2 ) puts the disagreement to the class, and it is a real disagreement rather than a comprehension check. Illustrations 1. Brontë, Wuthering Heights (1847). Heathcliff leaves the kitchen before Catherine says I am Heathcliff . Nelly notices his departure and tells Catherine to hush, but withholds a clear account of what he heard. Two silences — one a departure, one a withholding — determine the novel’s entire subsequent plot. Neither is speech; both are dialogue. 2. Hurston, Their Eyes Were Watching God (1937). Janie’s exclusion from the store-porch talk is enforced by Jody, and her eventual entry into it — the moment she speaks in the store, in public, against him — is the novel’s central reversal. The exchanges Janie is not in are structurally necessary for the exchange she finally enters. 3. Hemingway, “Hills Like White Elephants” (1927). The story’s subject is never named by either speaker. The exchange is organised around a hole, and the reader’s construction of that hole is the entire reading experience. 4.7 Summary: the six domains Domain Chief carriers Under-delivery Over-delivery Plot Information under pressure; forced decisions; negotiation; the turn Nothing passes; both parties already know everything The briefing; every turn a fact, nobody resisting Character Differentiated diction; sentence shape; evasion; register shift; self-description The interchangeable line The verbal tic; a label for a person Relational Address; turn-allocation; the floor; question rights; correction; position Static status; nothing contested Dominance display with nothing underneath Theme Staged dialectic; thesis under pressure; dramatic irony; the unremarked question Thematic decoration; a single name-checking line The mouthpiece; the therapeutic exchange Texture Turn length; register; white space; attribution density; world signal Register-neutral speech The dialect showcase; decipherment Silence (proposed) Unanswered questions; pause; interruption; the silent, unratified and absent Everyone says everything they think Portentous withholding; coyness (see Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages )) 4.8 Must all six be served at once? No, and the model is misused when read that way. Four qualifications. One domain served fully outperforms five gestured at. The Hemingway story serves texture and silence at maximum and the other four thinly; it is a masterpiece. What the model catches is not the number of domains but the case where the honest answer is none . Exchanges have a primary domain, and it should be identifiable. In revision the useful question is not how many? but which one is this exchange for, and is that domain actually moving? Domains have a natural sequence across a novel. Early exchanges lean on character and texture, because the reader needs the voices before the contests. Late exchanges lean on relation and theme, because the accumulated history is what makes a small move legible. An exchange that serves the wrong domain for its position reads as misplaced even when it is well written — the dialogue equivalent of the register mismatch treated in Chapter 2 ( Scene and Sequel ). The domains are lenses, not slots. A line that does three things does not do them separately. Jody Starks’s refusal on Janie’s behalf is one act, and calling it character, relational and silence work is three descriptions of it, not three components of it.

title: 5. Multiplicity: The Economy of the Exchange
section: Multiplicity — The Economy of the Exchange
text: 5.1 The principle, stated as a constraint Multiplicity — the practice of making a single unit of text discharge several narrative functions at once — is introduced in Chapter 1 ( The Purposes of a Scene ) as a general virtue and is reused, in some form, by every chapter of this book. In dialogue it takes a particular shape, because dialogue’s constraint is unlike any other unit’s. The constraint is this. A line of dialogue has only one channel of production and two channels of meaning. Everything a novelist wants an exchange to accomplish must be routed through sentences that a specific person, with a specific history, in a specific mood, would plausibly utter aloud to a specific hearer for a reason of their own. Narration can address the reader directly; description can dwell; interiority can explain. Speech can do none of these without breaking. It must serve the book while appearing to serve only the speaker. This is why the classic failure of drafted dialogue is single-domain service. Two characters trade the facts the reader needs, and nothing else is riding on the trade. The exchange is legible , the information arrives , and the passage is inert — because the only thing happening in it is a thing that happens for the reader’s benefit rather than for the characters’. The fix is never to remove the information. It is to make the information cost something. Give the fact to a character who does not want to say it. Give the need to a character who already suspects part of it and is testing rather than receiving. Now the same facts arrive, but a relational value has moved ( §4.3 ), a character has been revealed by what the disclosure cost them ( §4.2 ), and the reader has watched two people negotiate instead of being briefed by two mouthpieces. Nothing about the plot information has changed; everything about what the exchange is doing has. Note the difference from the account of multiplicity given in Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages ), which is arithmetical — too few words, too many obligations. Dialogue’s multiplicity is not arithmetical but motivational . The constraint is not space. It is that every function must be discharged by a sentence someone had a reason to say. 5.2 Anatomy of an exchange, line by line A much-taught exchange in twentieth-century fiction comes near the opening of Hemingway’s “Hills Like White Elephants” (1927; a short story, used here because it isolates the variable more cleanly than any novel can). A man and a young woman wait at a Spanish railway station, drinking, and later discuss an operation without naming its nature — an abortion. Early on, looking at a line of hills across the valley, she says they look like white elephants; he says he has never seen one; she says no, he wouldn’t have; he objects that her saying so does not prove anything. Four turns. Nothing has happened. The exchange is one of the most efficient in the language. Turn Text Functions discharged 1 They look like white elephants Character (she makes images; she is the one still trying to play) · Relational (an offer — a bid for shared attention) · Texture (the landscape enters through her, not through narration) · Theme (a white elephant can be an unwanted, burdensome possession — a possible resonance for the situation, without either speaker glossing it) 2 I’ve never seen one Character (a literal man answering a figurative remark) · Relational (the bid declined; he answers the sentence rather than the invitation) · Silence (an adjacency pair completed in form and refused in substance) 3 No, you wouldn’t have Relational (retaliation; the status move of the exchange) · Character (she is quicker than he is, and knows it) · Plot (the first evidence that the pressure is on and the courtesies are going) 4 I might have. Just because you say I wouldn’t have doesn’t prove anything Character (defensiveness; a man arguing a point nobody made) · Relational (the escalation he cannot afford, because he needs something from her) · Theme (proof, evidence and reasonableness are about to be his entire rhetorical repertoire on the real subject) Several things are worth extracting from the table. Every turn serves at least three domains, and none announces any of them. The reader experiences four short remarks about scenery. The thematic content is carried by an idiom neither speaker glosses. A white elephant is conventionally an unwanted or burdensome possession, often costly to keep and difficult to dispose of. Neither character says this; the phrase is doing it. This is multiplicity’s cheapest and highest-yielding move — see §5.3. The relational contest is conducted entirely in the second channel. Turn 2 is a perfectly cooperative answer to the literal question and a flat refusal of the offer that was actually made. Grice supplies the mechanism ( §3.1 ): the man observes the maxim of relation with respect to the words and flouts it with respect to the act, and the reader computes the implicature. Nothing changes, and the exchange is not static. No fact passes; no decision is made. What moves is permission : after turn 3 the two of them are no longer able to talk about the hills. That is a relational value shift, and it is the only shift the passage needs. 5.3 Where multiplicity actually lives Novice revision looks for multiplicity in the content of what characters say, on the assumption that a line does more work when it means more. In practice, dialogue’s multiplying work is done in four much humbler places. 1. The choice of noun and idiom. Not the hills look strange but white elephants . A specific noun or a live idiom carries thematic and social freight that a general one would have to state. The best dialogue lines in fiction are usually the most concrete, and their concreteness is the mechanism. 2. The form of address. Whether a character is called by first name, surname, title, diminutive, nothing at all, or something they have not been called before. This single variable carries relational value on every line where it appears, at a cost of one word, and most drafts leave it constant across a whole novel. 3. What the answer does to the question. Whether the second pair-part is delivered, delayed, partially delivered, over-delivered or refused. This is the conversation-analytic machinery of §3.2 used as a compositional resource, and it is where the silence and relational domains are almost always available for free. 4. The action beat placed between turns. A gesture inserted in place of an attribution — turning a key over between two fingers, refilling a glass, not looking up — discharges texture, relation and character in a clause, while performing the tag’s practical function of telling the reader who is speaking. The action beat is the most under-used instrument in draft dialogue, and it is the one that most reliably converts a one-domain exchange into a three-domain one. Note what is absent from that list. Elaborate figurative language in the mouths of characters is the highest-risk instrument in dialogue , because a metaphor that misses draws attention to the author rather than to the speaker, and because most people do not talk in extended figures. Hemingway’s white elephant works because it is a dead idiom being used literally, which is the kind of figure real speakers produce. 5.4 The ceiling, and the limit case Multiplicity has an upper bound in dialogue as everywhere else, and its symptoms are specific. Symptom What the reader experiences Every line is quotable The exchange reads as a script for an audition; nobody is talking, everybody is performing No line is casual Without unstressed turns there is no rhythm, and without rhythm no emphasis Both speakers are equally articulate Wit distributed evenly signals a single author rather than two people The subtext is uniformly present If every line is oblique, obliquity stops signifying The remedy is counter-intuitive and best stated as a rule: an exchange needs turns that are only doing one thing. Ritual openings, a genuine agreement, a question answered plainly. These function as the neutral ground against which a deviation registers — the point §3.1 makes about implicature requiring a norm, restated as a compositional instruction. The limit case in the other direction is instructive. The exchange with the lowest multiplicity in serious fiction is often the most powerful: a single flat sentence, arriving after a hundred pages of obliquity, that does one thing only. §6.5 is about that move and why it can only be made once or twice in a book. 5.5 Exercise: the domain audit A procedure, and one of the more reliable teaching instruments in this chapter. Print one exchange from the draft, double-spaced, with the attributions removed. In the margin beside each turn , write the letters of every domain it serves: P, C, R, Th, Tx, S (plot, character, relational, theme, texture, silence). Count. Interpretation: Pattern Diagnosis Most turns carry P alone The exchange is a briefing. Find who does not want to speak, and give them the facts. Most turns carry C alone Voices are being displayed rather than used. Nothing is being contested; check test 3. R never appears Status is fixed. Either the exchange is over before it begins, or a shift is available and unwritten. S never appears Everybody is saying everything they think. Run test 5 and §6.4 . Most turns carry four or more Over-pressurised. Find a turn to let breathe. One turn carries most letters That is the exchange’s spine. Consider whether the surrounding turns are earning their place beside it. The instruction to strip the attributions before beginning is not incidental. It converts the audit into the transcript test ( §7.1 , test 7) at the same time, and it prevents the writer from reading a domain into a line that the tag rather than the speech supplied.

title: 6. Text and Subtext: The Two Channels
section: Text and Subtext — The Two Channels
text: 6.1 The mechanism Every line of working dialogue runs on two channels at once. Working mechanism — the two channels. Text — the literal content of the line: the words a court reporter would transcribe. Subtext — the want, fear or withheld fact driving the line, legible to the reader through context, contradiction or omission, but rarely stated by the speaker. The distance between the two channels is where dialogue does most of its actual work, and where a flat exchange most reliably reveals its flatness, because in a flat exchange the two channels have collapsed into one. Two clarifications are needed at once, because the term is used loosely in workshops. Subtext is not ambiguity. An ambiguous line is one whose meaning the reader cannot determine. A line with subtext is one whose surface meaning the reader determines easily and whose real meaning they also determine, and the two do not match. Subtext is a doubling of certainty, not a subtraction of it. This is the discrimination that separates the technique from the coyness Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages ) calls the withholding tease: the reader must be able to compute the second meaning, or nothing has happened. Subtext is not the same as concealment. A character may be perfectly aware of what they mean and perfectly aware that their hearer knows it; the indirection is then a courtesy, a formality, or a way of leaving both parties an exit. Goffman’s face-work ( §3.3 ) covers a great deal of what is loosely called subtext, and the two are worth distinguishing in revision, because they produce different effects: concealment generates suspense, face-work generates poignancy. 6.2 The Gricean account, formalised §3.1 established the correspondence; this section puts one part of it to work. Conversational implicature can produce subtext. When a character visibly flouts a maxim while remaining cooperative at a deeper level, the reader may infer an unstated meaning. Subtext can also arise without flouting, through the organisation of turns, action, and narration. The value of this correspondence is that it turns one intuition into a generative procedure. Grice’s four categories of maxims provide several ways a writer can make an apparent departure from cooperative talk meaningful: Ask And you get What if the character answered a different question? A flouting of relation What if they said much less than was due? A flouting of quantity, downward What if they said far more than was due? A flouting of quantity, upward What if they said something both parties know is false? A flouting of quality What if they said it in the most roundabout way available? A flouting of manner Each produces a distinct effect, and each is realised by one or more of the named mechanisms in §6.4. One refinement matters for fiction specifically. In conversation, an implicature is computed by the hearer . In fiction there are two hearers — the character addressed and the reader — and they need not compute the same thing. Three configurations are available, and choosing between them is one of the more consequential decisions in an exchange: Configuration Character computes Reader computes Effect Shared Yes Yes Complicity; two people managing a subject neither will name Reader-only No Yes Dramatic irony; the reader is ahead Character-only Yes Not yet Suspense; the reader knows something has passed but not what The reader-only configuration is the theme domain’s dramatic-irony carrier ( §4.4 ). The character-only configuration is rarer, harder, and the source of much of the pleasure of rereading: an exchange whose second meaning is available only once the book has supplied the missing premise. 6.3 What the narrator adds Prose fiction has a resource drama does not, and most craft advice on dialogue — imported wholesale from screenwriting — ignores it. A novel has a narrator standing between the speech and the reader , and that narrator can do four things a stage cannot: Withhold interiority , so that the reader is in the same position as the other character. This is the dramatic mode, and it is what Hemingway’s story does. Supply interiority selectively , exposing one speaker’s subtext and not the other’s. This is the ordinary condition of the third-person novel, and it converts an exchange into an asymmetry: the reader is inside one player’s hand. Contradict the speech , by reporting an action, a physical detail or a thought that the words deny. A character who says take your time while checking the clock has been contradicted by the narration, not by another speaker. Refuse to arbitrate , which is a positive act in the presence of the other three. A narrator who could tell the reader what a character means and does not has produced a silence of the narration, distinct from the silence of the character. The third of these is the workhorse, and it deserves a name because it is the most transferable technique in the chapter: the contradicting action beat . It is cheap, it is invisible, it discharges texture and relation while doing it, and it is available on any line. A great deal of the difference between drafted and published dialogue is that published dialogue puts the counter-evidence in the room. 6.4 A taxonomy of subtext mechanisms Twelve named strategies. Each is a way of producing a gap between the channels; each has a characteristic effect, and a characteristic cost. The middle column names the Gricean flouting where one is clearly involved. # Mechanism Flouts Description 1 Evasion Quantity ↓ The question is acknowledged and not answered; the turn is delivered and is empty 2 The Changed Subject Relation The answer belongs to a different topic; the swerve is the content 3 The Question Answered With a Question Relation The second pair-part is replaced by a new first pair-part; the burden is returned 4 Over-answering Quantity ↑ Far more is supplied than was asked for 5 The Too-Precise Reply Quantity ↑ / Manner Unnecessary exactitude — times, sums, names — where an approximation was due 6 The Delayed Agreement — (preference) Agreement arrives, but late and hedged, in the format of a refusal 7 The False Agreement Quality Assent given to end the exchange, which both parties know is not assent 8 The Third-Person Deflection Manner The speaker’s own position is attributed to someone absent, or to people in general 9 The Ritual Formula Quantity ↓ A courtesy or set phrase supplied where a real answer was owed 10 The Interrupted Concession — (turn-taking) A speaker begins to yield and is cut off, so the concession never becomes binding 11 The Significant Repetition Manner A word or phrase from the other’s turn is repeated back, unchanged, without comment 12 The Unfinished Sentence Manner The turn stops before its point; the hearer, and the reader, complete it Each is developed below with an exemplar, what it buys, and what it costs. 1. Evasion. The question is heard, its relevance is acknowledged — often explicitly, I know what you’re asking — and the turn produced does not contain an answer. It is the purest form of the mechanism, and the one most dependent on the surrounding norm: it registers only where an answer was clearly due. Exemplar. Stevens, in The Remains of the Day , asked about matters touching his father, his employer’s politics or his own feelings, produces turns of impeccable length and total emptiness. Buys: characterisation and relational value simultaneously, since a refused answer is a status act. Costs: it becomes exhausting when sustained; a character who evades everything becomes unreadable rather than opaque, which is a real risk in Ishiguro’s novel and one he manages by varying the register of the evasions. 2. The Changed Subject. The most cited and least analysed of the mechanisms. A character asked a direct question replies about something else, and the reader computes the implicature: the true answer is unbearable, or damaging, or would concede too much. Exemplar. Hemingway’s man and girl swerve between the drinks, the beaded curtain, the hills and the train, and every swerve is legible as a swerve. Buys: the maximum implicature for the minimum text; it is the technique’s cleanest instance. Costs: it can read as authorial evasion rather than character evasion if the reader cannot tell what is being avoided. The rule is that the reader must know what question was dodged , or the swerve is noise. 3. The Question Answered With a Question. A variant sharp enough to warrant separate listing, because its relational meaning is different: it does not merely decline the answer, it transfers the obligation. Where were you? — Why does it matter? Exemplar. Elizabeth Bennet uses it repeatedly against Darcy and against Lady Catherine, and it is the mechanism by which she keeps footing against social superiors. Buys: status, immediately and visibly. Costs: it is combative, and two characters using it alternately produce a tennis match ( §8.5 ). 4. Over-answering. A character supplies substantially more than was asked for. The implicature is anxiety, guilt, or the construction of an alibi — the disproportion signals that the question mattered more than it should have. Exemplar. This is the mechanism of the guilty explanation in every detective novel worth reading, and Dostoevsky uses it at length in Crime and Punishment ’s interview scenes, where Raskolnikov’s compulsive elaboration is the evidence against him. Buys: an unmistakable signal at no cost to plausibility. Costs: it lengthens the page, and it is close to self-announcing; readers spot it easily. 5. The Too-Precise Reply. A specialised over-answer: exactitude where approximation was due. Asked when he last saw her, a character gives the date and the hour. The implicature is that the matter has been thought about a great deal. Exemplar. Stevens’s habit of dating and locating his own recollections with unnecessary precision, in a novel whose subject is the unreliability of his recollection, is the definitive case. Buys: interiority without interiority; the reader learns what the character has been dwelling on. Costs: almost none, which is why it is the most under-used mechanism on this list. 6. The Delayed Agreement. Assent arrives, but in the packaging that conversation analysis identifies as belonging to refusals ( §3.2 ): a pause, a hesitation marker, a token agreement, an account, mitigation. The reader registers that a refusal was intended and defeated. Exemplar. Miss Kenton grants Stevens’s professional requests in this format throughout; the agreements are technically complete and audibly reluctant. Buys: the most efficient rendering of reluctance available in the language, and one grounded in a documented feature of talk rather than in an intuition. Costs: it requires the writer to trust the reader to hear format rather than content, which drafts often do not. 7. The False Agreement. Assent given in bad faith to close the exchange, which both speakers know is not assent. A flouting of quality where the flouting is licensed and mutual. Exemplar. Countless marital exchanges in James and in Eliot end this way, and it is the standard closing move of an argument that neither party can win. Buys: a way to end an exchange without resolving it, which is structurally invaluable, since unresolved exchanges are what generate subsequent ones. Costs: it can read as a fudge if the reader is not shown, later, that the agreement was hollow. A false agreement must be cashed. 8. The Third-Person Deflection. The speaker attributes their own position to an absent party, to a general practice, or to an institution: people are saying ; Ma said you’d ask that ; it’s not done . Goffman’s footing ( §3.3 ) is the exact account — the speaker is animating a position while declining principalship of it. Exemplar. Dov’s line in the household exchange at §9.9 — She said you’d ask that. She didn’t say I had to answer — is a double deflection, first to the mother and then to the absence of an instruction. Buys: deniability, which is a relational asset, and a great deal of information about who the speaker is protecting. Costs: it can flatten a character into a functionary if used as their only register. 9. The Ritual Formula. A courtesy, condolence or set phrase supplied where a substantive answer was owed. I’m sorry for your loss. That’s very kind. These things happen. The formula is unimpeachable and empty, and its emptiness is the message. Exemplar. The condolences offered to Stevens on his father’s death, and Stevens’s own thanks for them, are a sustained instance; so is nearly every exchange in a nineteenth-century drawing room where the real subject is money. Buys: an enormous amount of relational information at no cost to decorum, and it is the mechanism that makes polite society legible in fiction. Costs: the reader must know the formula is a formula, which is a problem across cultural and historical distance — a real difficulty in teaching Austen to students who cannot hear which of her civilities are dead. 10. The Interrupted Concession. A speaker begins to yield — You’re right, I should have — and is cut off before the concession completes, so that it never becomes binding. The interruption may be hostile, may be a rescue, or may be the interrupter’s inability to hear a concession they had not expected. Exemplar. The mechanism recurs throughout Wuthering Heights , where Nelly’s narration repeatedly reports speech broken off, and in James, where the interruption is often the more delicate of the two speakers preventing the other from saying something irrevocable. Buys: the appearance of movement without the fact of it, which is what a mid-book exchange often needs. Costs: it is a delaying device, and a reader who notices the delay twice will notice it every time thereafter. 11. The Significant Repetition. A word from the other speaker’s turn is returned, unchanged and uncommented. Did she. Not this key. Fine. The repetition performs receipt without agreement, and its flatness is the flouting of manner. Exemplar. Elena’s Did she at §9.9 . Hemingway’s characters do it continually; so, in a different register, do Pinter’s. Buys: the shortest possible turn that is nonetheless an act, and a way of marking that a word has landed hard. Costs: it is stylistically conspicuous, and in quantity it stops reading as speech and starts reading as technique. 12. The Unfinished Sentence. The turn stops before its point, and the hearer — and the reader — complete it. Distinct from interruption, in that no one else has done anything: the speaker has stopped. Exemplar. Stevens’s sentences do this at the crises of The Remains of the Day , and the novel’s most famous effects are produced by his declining to complete a thought about Miss Kenton. Buys: the reader’s participation, which is the deepest form of investment; the sentence the reader finishes is a sentence the reader has written. Costs: it is the most easily overplayed device on the list, and the ellipsis is the most overused punctuation mark in draft fiction. Use it where the character cannot continue, not where the writer wishes to imply depth. How to use the taxonomy: substitution testing The taxonomy’s purpose is not classification but substitution . A flat exchange is very often the right material in the wrong mechanism. The productive exercise is to take one turn — usually the most on-the-nose one — and rewrite it four times, once each as an evasion, a changed subject, a too-precise reply and a delayed agreement. The four versions will differ in what they imply about the speaker, and the choice between them is a characterisation decision the writer did not previously know they were making. Three practical notes on selection: Mechanisms are not interchangeable in status terms. Evasion and the changed subject are defensive; the question-for-a-question and the significant repetition are aggressive; the ritual formula and the third-person deflection are institutional, and characterise a speaker as someone with a position to protect. Mechanisms should vary between characters. If both speakers evade in the same way, they are the same person ( §8.2 ). A useful assignment in revision is to give each major character a default mechanism and one they never use. Mechanisms should vary across a novel. A character whose evasions become predictable has stopped being evasive and started being a habit. 6.5 The gap-closing move Everything above concerns widening the gap between the channels, which is the right move through most of the body of a book. The chapter’s central structural claim concerns the opposite operation. Closing the gap — letting text and subtext finally say the same thing — is a climactic move. It is available once, perhaps twice, in a novel, and it is spent the moment it is used. The mechanism is simple once stated. A reader who has learned across three hundred pages that this character deflects, hedges and does not finish sentences has been trained to expect the gap. When the gap closes — when the character says what they mean, plainly, once — the plainness is legible as an event, because the reader has a baseline against which to measure it. The line need not be eloquent. It generally should not be. Its power is positional. This is why the prohibition on on-the-nose dialogue is not a rule against direct speech. It is a rule against direct speech everywhere , which spends the technique’s one great effect before the story has earned it. A novel in which characters routinely say what they mean has no gap-closing move available at its climax, because there is no gap to close, and writers in this position typically reach instead for volume, event or a declaration that the reader has no reason to find remarkable. Three published instances, chosen because they are structurally identical and tonally unlike each other: Novel The gap-closing move What makes it land Pride and Prejudice Darcy’s second proposal: his affections and wishes are unchanged, and one word from her will silence him on the subject for ever A man whose first proposal was an essay in self-justification now speaks in short, unqualified clauses and offers her the power to end it The Remains of the Day Miss Kenton, at the end, telling Stevens plainly what she has thought about the life she might have had The one moment in the novel when one of the two says the thing; Stevens’s response is to keep his own gap open, which is the tragedy Their Eyes Were Watching God Janie’s public reply to Jody in the store A woman who has not been permitted to speak in that room speaks, and what she says is unanswerable Note that in two of the three the gap is closed by one party while the other keeps theirs shut. That asymmetry is the more useful lesson: the move does not require mutual disclosure, and is frequently stronger without it. A corollary for revision. If a draft’s climactic exchange is not landing, the first thing to check is not the climax but the two hundred pages before it. The move requires a trained reader, and the training is done in exchanges that seem, individually, to be doing very little. 6.6 Historical drift, and a caution The two-channel model presented here is not a description of dialogue as such. It is a description of a particular and datable ideal. Period Dominant relation between the channels 18th century Largely single-channel; characters declare intentions, and irony operates at the level of the narrator rather than between speakers Austen and the early 19th century A two-channel practice conducted in the vocabulary of manners; the gap is social (what may be said in this room) more than psychological Mid-to-late 19th century Expansion of the psychological gap; James makes the unstated content of an exchange the exchange’s subject Chekhov and after The gap becomes the primary technique; the “indirect” scene is codified in drama and exported to fiction Hemingway and the modernist story The narration withdraws entirely, leaving the reader to compute the subtext unaided; the “iceberg” formulation Mid-20th-century workshop practice to present Subtext-heavy dialogue becomes the taught default and the mark of literary seriousness Concurrent counter-tradition The novel of ideas, the comic novel of wit, the polemical novel and the philosophical dialogue continue single-channel and unembarrassed Two inferences follow, pulling in different directions, which is the point. The subtext ideal is a real technical achievement and worth teaching. It engages the reader’s inferential capacity, it produces characterisation without assertion, and it is the reason a great deal of twentieth-century fiction rereads well. It is a preference, not a law, and its dominance is a fact about a literary culture. Dostoevsky’s characters say outright what they think, at enormous length, and are among the most powerful in the form. Wilde’s say things nobody has ever said aloud. Compton-Burnett’s say outright what they mean in a syntax no one has ever spoken. §16 develops the argument; it is stated here so that the taxonomy above is not mistaken for a specification.

title: 7. Diagnostic Method — the ten tests
text: 7.0 How to use the protocol The ten tests below are for revision, not composition . Applied during drafting they produce paralysis and self-conscious dialogue, which is the worst kind. Applied to a finished exchange they are the most efficient triage instrument in this chapter. Four procedural notes. Run them in order. Tests 1–4 are structural, and a failure there invalidates the rest: there is no point tuning the attribution of an exchange that has no engine. Record the answer, not the verdict. The output of a test is a sentence describing what the exchange does. Dov holds the upper hand at the start and holds a diminished version of it at the end is useful. Fails test 3 is not. A failed test is a question. Every test below is failed by at least one exchange analysed in §9 , and in three cases the failure is the reason the exchange is famous. Test one exchange at a time. The unit is the exchange as defined at §2.2 , not the scene and not the chapter. Applying the protocol to a whole dialogue scene will produce an average, and averages conceal the passage that needs work. 7.1 The ten tests Test 1 — The removal test Cut the exchange and replace it with a single line of summary. What is lost that the summary cannot carry? Write the summary line out. Literally write it: She accused him of lying; he did not deny it. Then ask what the exchange had that the sentence does not. The honest answers fall into a small set — a fact the reader needed to see arrive rather than be told about; a status shift the summary flattens; a voice the reader needs more exposure to; a texture or pace the passage was providing. If the answer is nothing , the summary is the better version and should replace the exchange. This is not a hypothetical outcome. A substantial proportion of drafted dialogue is a scene the writer wrote in order to find out what happened in it, and summary is the correct final form. The refinement worth adding: compare the summary against the exchange for length as well as content. An exchange of nine hundred words that a nineteen-word summary fully replaces is not merely redundant; it is expensive, and it has spent the reader’s attention on a transaction that did not require it. Test 2 — The want test State, in one sentence each, what each speaker wants from the other in this exchange, right now. Both speakers. If one sentence will not come, the exchange has one engine and is an interview, an interrogation or a briefing — legitimate forms, but the writer should know which one they have written. If neither will come, there is no exchange, whatever is happening on the page. Two disciplines make the test sharper. The want must be directed at the other speaker — I want to understand the situation is a want, but it is not a want from a person. And it must be immediate : not the story goal but the thing wanted before this conversation ends. I want him to admit he knew. I want her out of the doorway. I want to leave without answering. Test 3 — The status test Name who holds the upper hand at the first line and who holds it at the last. If the answer does not change, ask the follow-up, which is the part of the test that does the work: was it contested? A status relation that is tested under real pressure and holds is a legitimate outcome, and frequently a more interesting one than a reversal. A status relation that nobody contests is a static-status exchange ( §8.4 ). The productive form of the test names the currency : who holds the information, who holds the physical position, who holds the right to end the conversation, who is asking and who is answering. These can move in opposite directions inside one exchange, and an exchange in which a character gains one and loses another is doing better relational work than one in which everything moves together. Test 4 — The cost test What does each significant disclosure cost the person making it? Take every fact that passes from one character to another and name the cost of saying it. If a disclosure costs nothing — if the speaker is glad to say it, or indifferent — ask why it is in dialogue rather than in narration. This is the plot domain’s specific test, and it is the one that catches the As-You-Know-Bob exchange ( §8.1 ) at the level of mechanism rather than surface. A character can be given entirely plausible motivation for a briefing and the passage will still read as a briefing, because plausibility is not the missing ingredient. Cost is. Test 5 — The silence test Name what each speaker chooses not to say. If the answer for either speaker is nothing — if every character says outright what they think and feel — the exchange is over-explaining itself, and the remedy is in §6.4 . The strong form of the test adds a second question: who else is in the room, and are they speaking? A ratified participant present throughout an exchange and silent throughout it is either doing structural work ( §4.6 ) or is a character the writer has forgotten about, and the two are easy to tell apart once the question has been asked. Test 6 — The implicature test For each turn, ask: is this exactly what was called for, given what preceded it? If not, what does the deviation imply? This is Grice ( §3.1 , §6.2 ) used as an instrument. Go through the exchange turn by turn with the four maxims in view. Mark any conspicuous flouting and write down the implicature it invites. For a cooperative turn — the expected contribution, in the expected quantity, on the expected topic, in plain terms — ask whether its choice of words or information nonetheless conveys something beyond what it says. Interpretation needs context. An exchange of twelve apparently cooperative turns may still convey more than the speakers say outright. An exchange in which every turn conspicuously flouts a maxim may exhaust the effect. Instead of aiming for a fixed proportion, look at where those departures occur: a turn at the exchange’s crisis can carry more force when the surrounding turns have established a baseline. Test 7 — The transcript test Strip every attribution, tag and action beat. Read the remaining lines aloud in sequence. Can you tell who is speaking? The most brutal test in the protocol and the most informative. It isolates the speech from everything the narration was doing to prop it up. Three outcomes: Outcome Diagnosis Speakers are immediately distinguishable The character domain is being served by the speech itself Speakers are distinguishable only by content Voices are undifferentiated; the reader is tracking who knows what, not who is talking Speakers are not distinguishable at all The ventriloquist exchange ( §8.2 ) The second outcome is the common one and the one writers misread as a pass. Content-based identification means the exchange would collapse if the two characters knew the same things, which is what happens in the second half of most novels. Reading aloud is not an ornament to this test. Silent reading recovers the attributions from memory; the voice does not. Test 8 — The substitution test Take the exchange’s three best lines. Could another named character in the manuscript plausibly say them? Where test 7 asks whether two speakers differ from each other, test 8 asks whether a speaker differs from the cast.
