It is the harder standard, and it is the one that catches the novel in which two characters are well differentiated and the other nine are the author. The practical procedure: type the line, then write beside it the names of the three characters most likely to be able to say it. If the list is long, the line is not doing character work; if the list is empty except for its owner, the line has been earned. Test 9 — The attribution test Count the tags. Read them in isolation. What proportion are said or asked, and what are the others doing? Three sub-questions. Density. How many turns carry an attribution? In contemporary practice the answer in a two-hander is usually well under half after the speakers are established, and an exchange tagged on every turn is being slowed for no reason. Verb. Every attribution that is not said , asked , replied or a near-neighbour should be justifiable. Expostulated , ventured , hissed and their kin describe the line instead of letting it perform, and their proscription — historically local, per §3.5 — rests on the sound principle that a line requiring an adverb to specify its tone has not been written yet. Action beats. Where an action stands in for a tag, ask what else it is doing. An action beat that only identifies the speaker is a tag with extra words. An action beat that identifies the speaker and carries relational or textural value is the most efficient object in an exchange ( §5.3 ). The test’s most useful output is usually a list of tags to delete rather than to change. Test 10 — The interruption audit Mark every point at which one speaker takes the floor from another, and every point at which a speaker yields it. Then ask three questions. Who interrupts? If the same character interrupts throughout, the exchange has a fixed status structure, which may be correct or may be a failure of test 3. If nobody interrupts, the exchange is a formal alternation, and formal alternation is the rhythm of a committee meeting. Where do interruptions cluster? They should cluster at the exchange’s crisis. Interruptions distributed evenly across an exchange read as a stylistic habit rather than as pressure. Are any interruptions structural? An interrupted concession ( §6.4 , mechanism 10) is a plot event: something was about to be conceded and was not. Marking these reveals how many of a draft’s unresolved threads are held open by a device rather than by a reason. 7.2 Reading the results Failed tests Likely diagnosis First move 1 alone The exchange is a scene the writer needed and the reader does not Replace with the summary line already written 2 and 4 A briefing wearing dialogue’s clothes Give the facts to someone who does not want to say them 3 alone Static status; nothing contested Find what one of them could concede, and make the other reach for it 5 and 6 On-the-nose; one channel Apply §6.4 to the three most direct turns 7 and 8 The ventriloquist exchange Rewrite each speaker’s turns in a different sentence length and a different vocabulary; do not attempt to make them “distinctive” 6 alone, with 1–5 passing Competent but flat; the material is there and the surface is transparent Substitution testing, per §6.4 9 alone Over-tagged or over-decorated; the exchange is being narrated at Delete tags; convert the survivors to action beats that carry a second function 10 alone Formal alternation; a committee rather than a contest Let one speaker take the floor from the other at the crisis All of 1–5 This is not an exchange Cut it, or find the want that would make it one A warning about test 7. When a draft fails the transcript test, the instinct is to make each character more distinctive by adding verbal tics, catchphrases and idiosyncratic vocabulary. This produces the over-delivery described at §4.2 — a label instead of a person. The reliable route to differentiation is structural rather than lexical: give each character a different average sentence length, a different relation to questions, and a different default subtext mechanism. Those three variables produce distinguishable speakers without a single quirk.

title: 8. Failure Patterns
text: Each pattern is presented with its symptom , its mechanism (what actually goes wrong, as distinct from what the surface looks like), its persistence (why competent writers keep producing it), its remedy , and — mandatorily — its exception : a published work that commits the error and succeeds. The exceptions are the intellectual point of the section. A pedagogy of prohibitions produces writers who can avoid faults and cannot make choices. In every case the pattern fails because of a mechanism, not because of a surface feature, and where the mechanism is absent the surface feature is harmless. 8.1 The As-You-Know-Bob Exchange Symptom. Characters tell each other things they would both already know, so that the reader can overhear them. As you know, Bob, our father left the shop to the three of us. Mechanism. The line gives more information than the speaker has a reason to supply. With no motive available in the fiction, the reader notices the author’s need to convey the fact rather than inferring an intention on the character’s part. The illusion that the characters exist independently of the book collapses at that point, and it is expensive to rebuild. Note that the failure is not informational. The information may be necessary and the reader may need it. What fails is the delivery mechanism: a briefing wearing dialogue’s clothes. Persistence. Dialogue is the most vivid available channel, and writers reasonably prefer to deliver in it. The prohibition is also easy to evade at the surface without addressing the mechanism, by adding a plausible reason for the conversation. Plausibility is not the missing ingredient; cost is ( §7.1 , test 4). Remedy. Three moves, in order of reliability. Give the fact to someone who does not want to say it. Give the need to someone who already suspects part of it , so that the exchange is a test rather than a transfer. Deliver the fact incompletely , so that what arrives is a fragment raising a further question. Where none of the three is available, the information belongs in narration, where no one has to pretend. The exception. The naive listener convention, which the novel inherited from drama and has used continuously for three centuries. Wuthering Heights is a major case: Lockwood knows little of the household, has been ill, and asks; Nelly Dean knows much of its history and has a captive audience and her own reasons for shaping the account. Her account to Lockwood supplies much of the novel’s exposition, though Lockwood’s own narration supplies some too. Frankenstein also places extended accounts inside a frame of listeners and speakers. Dracula uses a different solution: an assembly of journals, letters and other documents. The discrimination is exact. As-You-Know-Bob fails because the listener already knows. The naive listener does not, and the convention is not a loophole but the correct solution — with the standing cost that the writer must then make the listener interesting, which Emily Brontë does by making Lockwood a fool whose misreadings the reader can measure. 8.2 The Ventriloquist Exchange Symptom. Every character reasons, jokes and phrases things the same way — the author’s way. The exchange passes the eye and fails the transcript test ( §7.1 , test 7) on every line. Mechanism. The novel’s central resource, in Bakhtin’s account ( §3.4 ), is heteroglossia: the staging of the actual stratification of a language into competing social discourses. A novel in which every character speaks one idiolect has not merely made its speakers hard to distinguish; it has collapsed the social world into a single position and forfeited what the form is for. The practical mechanism is simpler. Writers hear dialogue in their own inner voice, and the inner voice has one vocabulary, one rhythm and one relation to a joke. Persistence. It is invisible from inside, because each line individually sounds right — it sounds right to the person who thinks in that idiom . It also survives line-editing indefinitely, since the fault is not in any line. Remedy. Structural, not lexical (see the warning at §7.2 ). Assign each principal a different average sentence length, a different relation to questions (who asks, who answers, who deflects), and a different default subtext mechanism from §6.4 . Then run the transcript test again. The exception, and it is a serious one. Ivy Compton-Burnett wrote twenty novels in which every character — parents, children, servants, tyrants and victims — speaks the same impossibly lucid, epigrammatic, syntactically formal English, at length, saying outright what they mean about matters no one would say aloud. The novels are almost entirely dialogue. They are not a failure of the technique; they are a different technique, in which the uniform register functions as a convention of the form , like verse in a Racine tragedy, and the differences between characters are carried by what they are willing to say rather than by how they say it. Within a page the reader accepts the convention and stops noticing it. Wilde is the second case and the more familiar one. In The Importance of Being Earnest everyone is witty in the same way, and the uniformity is the joke: a society in which the capacity for epigram is universal and moral seriousness is not. The exception generalises to a principle: an undifferentiated register is a failure when it is unintended and a style when it is declared. The test is whether the reader is invited to notice. 8.3 The On-the-Nose Exchange Symptom. Text and subtext say the same thing throughout. I’m angry that you lied to me. I know. I’m afraid of losing you. Emotionally legible, dramatically inert. Mechanism. A line that states a character’s feeling directly can foreclose the exchange instead of opening it. There may be nowhere for the reader to look, nothing further to infer, and no pressure left for the next line to apply. A cooperative utterance can still generate an implicature; the problem here is a passage that supplies its own interpretation before the reader has had to make one ( §6.2 ). Reader investment is often strengthened by reader work. There is a second and less obvious cost, developed at §6.5 : on-the-nose dialogue everywhere destroys the gap-closing move, because a book with no gap has no climactic plainness available to it. Persistence. It is what characters would say if they were being helpful, and writers instinctively make characters helpful. It is also encouraged by a misreading of the instruction to write clearly: clarity is a property of the prose, not of the characters’ self-knowledge. Remedy. §6.4 , applied to the three most direct turns. Substitution testing rather than deletion: the feeling stays, the statement of it goes. The exception, in two forms. First, the climactic declaration. The gap-closing move ( §6.5 ) is an on-the-nose line, and it is the strongest single move in the repertoire. Darcy’s second proposal states his position without qualification; Janie answers Jody in public in terms nobody could mistake. These are not exceptions to the rule so much as the reason for it: the rule exists to keep the move in reserve. Second, and more radically, Dostoevsky. The characters of The Brothers Karamazov and Crime and Punishment say outright what they think, at enormous length, including things about themselves that no one in life would articulate. Ivan states his theological position in full. Marmeladov delivers his own moral autopsy to a stranger in a tavern. Raskolnikov confesses. There is very little subtext in the ordinary sense, and the novels are among the most psychologically penetrating ever written. The reason needs stating with care, because it is the section’s most useful discrimination. Dostoevsky’s characters state their positions fully and are still not transparent , because what they say is not the truth about them : it is their most powerful self-account, offered in bad faith, under pressure, to a hearer they are trying to affect. The gap in Dostoevsky is not between what is said and what is meant. It is between what is said and what is the case . That is a different two-channel structure, it is at least as productive as the Chekhovian one, and a pedagogy that recognises only the second will misread half the European novel. 8.4 The Static-Status Exchange Symptom. Competently voiced, well paced, and going nowhere: the same person holds the upper hand at the last line as at the first, and nothing was contested. Mechanism. The relational domain ( §4.3 ) is untouched. Because status is what readers track most continuously and least consciously, an exchange in which it does not move produces a specific sensation — the reader feels that the passage was pleasant and cannot say what happened. Persistence. Status is invisible to writers in a way it is not to actors and directors, who are trained to play it. Nothing in the sentence-level craft of dialogue draws attention to it, and an exchange can be excellent line by line while failing entirely at this level. Remedy. Identify the currency ( §7.1 , test 3) and make one unit of it change hands. Usually the cheapest available move is physical: someone sits, someone stands, someone leaves the doorway. The exception. Beckett built a body of work on exchanges in which status is structurally incapable of moving, and the impossibility is the subject. So, in a quieter register, does the whole tradition of the ritual exchange — the liturgical, the ceremonial, the formulaic greeting — where fixity is the point and any movement would be a scandal. There is also a common and legitimate local use: an exchange in which status is contested hard and holds, which passes the test’s second question and is frequently more interesting than a reversal. The failure is not stasis; it is stasis that nobody tried to disturb. 8.5 The Tennis Match Symptom. Rapid, clever back-and-forth with real energy at the sentence level and no throughline. Entertaining in isolation, forgettable a page later, because no domain in §4 actually moved. Mechanism. Multiplicity is present at the level of wit and absent at the level of function. Each turn is doing one thing — being good — and the exchange’s shape is a flat oscillation rather than a trajectory. The characteristic signature is that the turns are interchangeable in order: if an exchange can be reshuffled without loss, nothing is accumulating. Persistence. It is the most enjoyable dialogue to write, it demonstrates fluency, and it is what writers produce when the scene is going well and they do not want to stop. Remedy. The reshuffle test — move three turns and see whether anything breaks. Then cut to the two turns that could not be moved and rebuild around them. The exception. Wilde, again, and the whole tradition of the comedy of manners: exchanges whose sole business is display, in books whose subject is a society organised around display. Austen’s Netherfield conversations run on the same principle with a difference that repays study — Elizabeth and Darcy’s sparring is a tennis match, and it is also the mechanism by which two people who cannot court each other openly conduct a courtship. The tennis match becomes structural the moment the reader can see what the players are actually playing for. 8.6 The Maid-and-Butler Opening Symptom. A novel or scene opens with two minor characters — servants, colleagues, guards — discussing the principals for the reader’s benefit. Nobody’s seen her since the funeral, and the brother’s been in and out of that shop every day. Mechanism. A specialised As-You-Know-Bob with an additional fault: the reader’s first exposure to the world is mediated by people who do not matter. Per the rules of notice discussed in Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages ), characters introduced early are read as significant, so the device makes a promise about two people it intends to discard. Persistence. It is a genuine inheritance from the drama, where the convention is ancient and where the practical problem it solves — how to orient an audience with no narrator available — is real. Prose fiction has a narrator and does not have the problem. Remedy. Ask what the servants know that the principals do not. If the answer is nothing, give the material to the narration. If the answer is something , the exchange is not a maid-and-butler opening at all; it is a scene about servants, and should be written as one. The exception. The Portrait of a Lady opens with three men on a lawn at Gardencourt discussing, among other things, the American cousin who is about to arrive. It is, structurally, a maid-and-butler opening. It succeeds because the three men are not minor: Ralph Touchett, his father and Lord Warburton are principals, their conversation establishes the terms — money, illness, marriage, English and American manners — on which the whole novel will run, and Isabel’s arrival into a room that has been discussing her is the novel’s governing situation in miniature. The device fails when the speakers are instruments and succeeds when they are stakeholders. The wider exception is the servants’ hall in the nineteenth-century novel generally, where servants discussing employers is not an exposition device but a representation of the actual information economy of a household — and where, as §4.6 notes, the servant’s position as unratified participant is a structural fact rather than a convenience. 8.7 The Name in Every Line Symptom. Characters address each other by name in nearly every turn. I don’t know, Elena. Then find out, Dov. Mechanism. Vocatives in real conversation are rare and marked: people use a name to summon attention, to claim intimacy, to warn, to reprimand, or to establish a relationship for a third party’s benefit. Because they are marked, each one is read as doing something, and an exchange in which every line is marked is an exchange in which nothing is. The device also solves a problem the writer has — telling the reader who is speaking — by giving a line to a character who has no reason to say it, which is the As-You-Know-Bob mechanism in miniature. Persistence. It is the easiest available substitute for attribution, and it feels warmer than a tag. Remedy. Delete all of them, then restore the two that were doing work. Solve the attribution problem with action beats ( §5.3 ) instead. The exception. The Remains of the Day , where Stevens addresses Miss Kenton as “Miss Kenton” with a frequency that in any other novel would be a fault, and where the frequency is the characterisation. The name is a barrier: it is deployed at the moments when a first name would be possible, and its repetition across decades is the record of a refusal. The device also functions in institutional and military registers, where terms of address are obligatory and their omission is the marked case — in a novel about a hierarchy, counting the vocatives is a way of reading the hierarchy. 8.8 The Attribution Fault Symptom. Speech tags that describe the line instead of letting it perform: he expostulated ; she hissed ; he said angrily ; she laughed , attached to a sentence one cannot laugh. Mechanism. Two distinct faults. Redundancy : the tag states what the line has already achieved, so the reader is told a thing they have just experienced, which retroactively converts an experience into an assertion. Compensation : the tag supplies a tone the line does not carry, which means the line has not been written yet, and the adverb is a note to self left in the manuscript. Persistence. Nineteenth-century models are full of expressive attribution ( §3.5 ), and a reader who has absorbed Dickens by osmosis will produce it. It also feels like variety, and repetition of said feels like poverty until one notices that said is invisible. Remedy. Test 9 ( §7.1 ). Delete tags to the minimum required for tracking; convert survivors to said or to action beats that carry a second function. The exception. The whole of the nineteenth century, which is a large exception. Dickens’s expressive attribution is part of a narrating voice that is continuously present, evaluative and comic; a narrator who is supposed to be invisible cannot afford rejoined , and a narrator who is a performer can afford anything. The rule is therefore conditional on a narrative stance, not universal: transparent narration requires transparent attribution; a foregrounded narrator may attribute as expressively as it likes. Contemporary novels with strongly voiced narrators — comic, retrospective, oral — recover the licence at once. 8.9 Phonetic Dialect Symptom. Non-standard speech rendered by respelling: apostrophes for dropped consonants, eye-dialect ( wuz , sez , woz ) that records no actual difference of pronunciation, and dense orthographic representation sustained over pages. This pattern requires more care than the others, because the prohibition against it has a real history of being applied unevenly, and a student is owed the history along with the advice. Mechanism, stated technically. Three distinct problems, which are usually conflated. Processing cost. Respelled speech is read more slowly, because the reader must convert orthography to sound to sense rather than orthography to sense. Sustained across pages this converts reading into decipherment, and a reader working that hard is not absorbed. Eye-dialect can mark a speaker without marking a distinctive sound. Sez represents an ordinary pronunciation of says ; wuz can represent a common reduced pronunciation of was . Neither spelling, by itself, establishes a distinctive accent. Used for one group while another retains standard spelling, such forms can make the marked speakers look less educated on the page. Asymmetry of marking. In a novel where one group’s speech is respelled and another’s is not, the unmarked group is thereby positioned as speaking language itself, and the marked group as speaking a departure from it. Every reader registers this, and it is a claim about who is central. The uneven history. The third problem is where the prohibition acquires its ethical weight, and where its enforcement has been least even. English novels have for two centuries rendered working-class, regional, Black, Irish, Scots and colonised speech phonetically while rendering the speech of the educated and metropolitan in standard orthography — including in books whose narrators are not otherwise unsympathetic. The received rule against phonetic dialect grew, in part, out of a correct perception that this practice was doing social work. But the rule has often been applied so as to fall hardest on writers representing their own communities, while the historical canon that established the practice is taught without comment. A student should be able to hold two facts together: that the technique has been used condescendingly for a very long time, and that a blanket prohibition disproportionately restricts the writers with the strongest claim to use it. Persistence. It is the most obvious way to signal register, and it feels like fidelity. Remedy. In the general case: carry dialect in syntax, idiom and lexicon rather than in spelling. Word order, tense and aspect systems, characteristic idioms, forms of address and what a speaker treats as sayable will place a speaker socially and regionally with complete precision and no orthographic cost. A single light orthographic marker, used sparingly, can then signal that a fuller representation is being withheld rather than that no difference exists. The exceptions, which are major. Their Eyes Were Watching God (1937). Hurston renders Black southern speech densely and phonetically, and the novel is one of the great achievements of American prose. Three features distinguish it from the condescending practice. The speech is celebrated rather than exhibited : the store-porch talk is the novel’s centre of value, its speakers are its wits and philosophers, and the reader is positioned inside the community rather than visiting it. The narration meets the speech halfway : Hurston’s free indirect passages move between a lyrical standard and the characters’ idiom, so the marked/unmarked asymmetry described above is dissolved rather than enforced. And Hurston was a trained anthropologist recording a language she spoke , which is not an aesthetic argument but is relevant to what the representation is for . It is worth teaching that the novel was attacked on this ground at the time — Richard Wright’s hostile review in New Masses (1937) accused it of catering to a white audience’s appetite for minstrel pleasure — and that the judgement has been comprehensively reversed. The reversal is itself instructive: a technique’s meaning is not fixed by its surface, and the same orthography can be a caricature or a claim depending on who holds the centre of value in the book. Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884). Twain prefixed an explanatory note claiming to distinguish several dialects, rendered by ear rather than by guesswork. The vernacular is the novel’s narrating voice, not merely its dialogue, which removes the asymmetry problem at a stroke: there is no standard register in the book against which Huck’s is a departure. Jim’s speech, however, is marked relative to Huck’s, and the novel’s handling of that difference remains contested among critics — a live disagreement rather than a settled one, and one worth setting as a seminar question ( §12.2 ). Wuthering Heights (1847). Joseph’s Yorkshire is nearly impenetrable, and editors have periodically softened it. The difficulty is functional ( §4.5 ): Joseph exists to obstruct, and the reader’s struggle with him replicates every character’s. This is the narrowest of the three defences and the most easily abused. The generalisable rule. Phonetic dialect fails when it marks a speaker as a deviation from a standard the book itself embodies. It succeeds when the book’s centre of value sits inside the marked speech, when the narration does not stand above it, and when the representation is doing something a lexical and syntactic rendering could not. 8.10 The Therapeutic Exchange Symptom. Characters articulating their own psychology in terms the book has supplied. I think I keep pushing you away because of what happened with our father. Mechanism. A double failure. The character has been given the author’s analysis, which they have no way of possessing; and the analysis, once stated, is closed to the reader, who now has a conclusion instead of evidence. It is on-the-nose dialogue with an additional layer of anachronism, since the vocabulary of self-diagnosis is a specific and recent register that most characters, in most settings, do not have access to. Persistence. Contemporary readers and writers live inside a therapeutic vocabulary, and it is how many people now speak. That makes the register plausible; it does not make it dramatic. Remedy. Give the analysis to a different character, as an accusation, which the first can then refuse. A diagnosis offered by an enemy is contestable; the same diagnosis offered by its subject is a verdict. The exception. Dostoevsky again, and this time more sharply. Raskolnikov’s confession to Sonya, Ivan’s account of his own position, Marmeladov’s tavern monologue: all are characters articulating their own psychology at length and with precision. They work because — as §8.3 argued — the self-analysis is itself an act with a motive. Raskolnikov confesses at Sonya, to make her carry it. The therapeutic exchange fails not because characters explain themselves but because, in the failing version, the explanation is disinterested. Self-analysis is dramatic when it is a move; it is inert when it is a report. The second exception is the novel that takes psychoanalysis as its explicit subject or its explicit setting, where the vocabulary is the world’s rather than the author’s. 8.11 The Speech That Answers a Question Nobody Asked Symptom. A character delivers a paragraph, or a page, in response to a prompt that did not call for it: a short question, a passing remark, or nothing at all. Mechanism. The exchange has stopped being an exchange. The second speaker has become an audience, and the passage is a monologue with an interlocutor attached for decency’s sake — usually signalled by that interlocutor’s contributions dwindling to Go on and I don’t understand . The reader detects the shift immediately, because the conditional relevance of adjacency pairs ( §3.2 ) has been suspended: the second speaker is no longer a person with obligations in the conversation. Persistence. The writer has something to deliver and has decided which character will deliver it. The prompting question is then reverse-engineered, which is why prompting questions in drafts are so often flat. Remedy. Interrupt it. Any of the three standard interventions works: let the listener object, let the listener leave, or let the listener ask the wrong question — the last being the most productive, since it forces the speaker to restate and reveals what they think the point was. The exception. The set speech has a long and distinguished life in the novel, and §9.3 analyses the greatest instance: Ivan’s Grand Inquisitor, in which one character speaks for many pages and the other is entirely silent. It works — and this is the whole of the discrimination — because the silence of the listener is the exchange’s content . Alyosha’s not answering is what the passage is about, and his eventual response is an act rather than a rebuttal. Where a listener’s silence is meaningful the set speech is an exchange by other means; where it is merely a convenience, it is not. The other standing exception is the sermon, the trial speech, the public address and the deathbed testament — set-piece forms with their own conventions, which the novel absorbs whole and which readers accept as generically licensed. 8.12 The One-Engined Exchange Symptom. One character wants something and the other does not want anything. The exchange proceeds by question and answer until the first character has what they came for. Mechanism. The definition at §2.1 requires a want on both sides. Where only one exists, the exchange has no resistance and therefore no shape: it terminates when the questioner runs out of questions rather than when something is decided. This is the structural fault underneath a great deal of dialogue that readers describe as “flat” without being able to say why, and it is distinct from static status — status may even move, in an interview, without the exchange acquiring an engine. Persistence. It is the natural shape of a scene in which a protagonist needs to find something out, which is a very common scene. Remedy. Give the answerer a want. It need not relate to the questioner’s: I want this over ; I want to know why you are asking ; I want you to think better of me than you do . A single sentence of motive on the answering side converts an interview into an exchange without altering the information that passes. The exception. The detective interview, which is one-engined by generic design and which readers accept because the pleasure on offer is inferential rather than dramatic — the reader is working alongside the detective, and the suspect’s flatness is data. The deposition, the interrogation and the frame-narrative enquiry (Lockwood questioning Nelly) all work the same way. In each, the genre has supplied the second engine outside the exchange: the reader’s own want. 8.13 Summary: symptom to mechanism Pattern Underlying mechanism Domains damaged As-You-Know-Bob The reader notices authorial exposition instead of a character’s motive P, C, R Ventriloquist Heteroglossia collapsed to one idiolect C, Tx On-the-nose Interpretation supplied too soon; the gap-closing move spent early C, Th, S Static status The relational domain untouched R Tennis match Wit without trajectory; turns reshuffleable P, R, Th Maid-and-butler Exposition delivered by non-stakeholders; a promise made about discardable characters P, C Name in every line A marked form used unmarkedly; attribution solved by giving a character a line they have no reason to say R, Tx Attribution fault Tag asserts what the line should perform, or compensates for what it fails to Tx, C Phonetic dialect Asymmetric marking; processing cost; eye-dialect that records only deviance Tx, C, and the book’s centre of value Therapeutic exchange The author’s analysis given to the character; evidence replaced by conclusion C, Th, S Speech answering nothing Conditional relevance suspended; the listener ceases to be a party R, S One-engined No resistance; terminates by exhaustion rather than decision P, R

title: 9. Worked Analyses
text: Eight close readings and a revision case. The apparatus is the same throughout: identify the primary domain ( §4 ), audit the two channels ( §6 ), and apply the tests that bear ( §7 ). 9.1 Austen, Pride and Prejudice (1813) — the Hunsford proposal Darcy arrives at the Collinses’ parsonage and, after a silence, declares himself: In vain I have struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you. Four sentences, and every one of them is about him. The declaration proper occupies the last; the first three are an account of an internal contest he has lost. Elizabeth is the occasion of the sentence, not its subject. Austen then compounds this by summarising what follows rather than quoting it — Darcy’s dwelling on her family’s inferiority, on the degradation of the connection, on the obstacles his judgement had opposed to his inclination — and by noting that the warmth with which he pressed these points seemed due to the rank he was wounding and was unlikely to recommend his suit. The technique to notice is the switch to report. The most damaging material in the proposal is not quoted . Austen gives the reader Darcy’s opening in direct speech, then withdraws to indirect summary for the offence, then returns to direct speech for the confrontation. This is the nineteenth-century speech/report boundary ( §3.5 ) used with complete deliberation: direct speech for what must be experienced, report for what would be tedious to endure at length and is more damning in summary. Elizabeth’s refusal answers a declaration of feeling with a point of form — the established mode on such occasions being to express a sense of obligation, however unequally the sentiments are returned. The move is the relational one described at §4.3 : she declines the frame before declining the offer. He has spoken as a man conferring; she replies as a woman receiving a social communication, and the mismatch strips the proposal of its assumed standing. Domain What the exchange does Plot The refusal, and the accusation about Wickham and Bingley, which produce the letter and therefore the second half of the novel Character Darcy revealed by the syntax of his self-account; Elizabeth by her instant recourse to form under provocation Relational Total inversion: he begins conferring and ends demanding an explanation for a refusal he had not conceived of Theme The novel’s question — whether judgement can be corrected — staged as an argument neither party wins Texture Alternation of direct speech and report; the deliberate withholding of the worst material from quotation Silence What Elizabeth does not yet know about Wickham, and cannot; what Darcy does not say about Bingley until asked Where it strains a test, and why that matters. The exchange relies less on conspicuous flouting than test 6’s first pass might lead a writer to expect: both parties state much of what they mean, fully and at length. This is the on-the-nose exchange as a deliberate structure. Its force comes from the surrounding novel, in which characters often speak through manners, and the Hunsford scene is a place where the pressure becomes too great for that machinery to contain. The gap-closing move ( §6.5 ) is being used here in the middle of the book, by two people simultaneously, and it costs both of them. 9.2 Austen, Pride and Prejudice (1813) — the Pemberley exchanges The Pemberley scenes are the structural answer to Hunsford, and they are conducted almost entirely in ritual formulae. Elizabeth, having toured the house believing Darcy absent, meets him in the grounds. What follows is a sequence of exchanges about how long she has been in Derbyshire, when she left Longbourn, whether the Gardiners are well, and whether he may be permitted to introduce his sister. Nothing of consequence is said. Both parties are visibly unable to complete their sentences; Austen notes their confusion, their repetitions, their asking of questions already answered. This is the ritual formula ( §6.4 , mechanism 9) at maximum load. The content of the exchange is null by design: what is being transacted is entirely in the second channel, and the reader computes it from three signals — the disproportion between the occasion and the parties’ agitation, the repetitions (which flout the maxim of manner), and the single substantive act buried in the phatic material, which is Darcy’s request to introduce Georgiana. In a novel governed by the rules of introduction, that request is a declaration; nothing else in the scene needs to be. Together, the Hunsford and Pemberley exchanges form the chapter’s clearest available demonstration of the two-channel principle: Hunsford Pemberley Channels One: both say outright what they mean Two: nothing meant is said Status Inverted violently Renegotiated by mutual deference Mechanism Direct declaration; direct refusal Ritual formula; unfinished sentences; a single formal act Reader’s work Judgement Inference Effect Rupture Repair The lesson for a writer is that the second scene is only legible because of the first. Austen has trained the reader across four hundred pages to read civility as a code, and at Pemberley she can therefore write an entire reconciliation out of enquiries about the weather in Derbyshire. 9.3 Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov (1880; trans. Constance Garnett) — the Grand Inquisitor Ivan recites to Alyosha a “poem” he has composed: Christ returns to Seville during the Inquisition, is recognised, is arrested, and is visited in his cell by the Grand Inquisitor, who explains at length why the Church has corrected his work — that men cannot bear freedom, that they will exchange it for bread, mystery and authority, and that Christ’s refusal to give them these was an act of contempt for human weakness. Christ says nothing throughout. At the end he kisses the old man; the Inquisitor releases him and tells him never to return. This passage tests the chapter’s model harder than any other passage discussed here, and it is worth being explicit about where the model bends. It is a speech, not an exchange, by the definition at §2.1 . The Inquisitor’s addressee never speaks. By test 2, half the want-test fails; by test 3, no status moves within the speech; by test 10, there are no interruptions. By §8.11 it is the failure pattern of the speech answering a question nobody asked, at a length no workshop would tolerate. And it works, for four reasons the model can articulate. It is embedded in an exchange that is running. The Inquisitor speaks to Christ; Ivan speaks to Alyosha, and that outer exchange has two engines. Ivan wants his brother’s agreement, or his brother’s horror; Alyosha wants not to lose his brother. Everything the model asks for is present at the outer level, and the inner speech is the instrument by which the outer want is pursued. The set speech is a move in a conversation happening one frame out. The listener’s silence is the content. Christ’s not answering is the passage’s argument. A reply would concede that the Inquisitor’s terms were the terms; silence refuses the frame, and the kiss is a response in a register the speech cannot reach. This is the silence domain ( §4.6 ) carrying the entire thematic burden of a chapter in which one character does all the talking. The dialectic is left open. The Inquisitor’s case is made in its strongest form — this is the requirement at §4.4 — and the narration does not arbitrate. Bakhtin’s account of polyphony ( §3.4 ) is built substantially on this chapter, and the standard critical observation is that Dostoevsky, an Orthodox Christian, wrote the most powerful case against his own position in the language. Alyosha’s objection, when it comes, is not a refutation; it is the claim that the poem praises what it means to blame. The two channels are present, but relocated. There is no subtext in the ordinary sense: the Inquisitor states his position completely. The gap is between what Ivan says and what Ivan is — a man constructing an unanswerable argument in order to find out whether he can live inside it, and using his brother as the test. This is the Dostoevskian two-channel structure identified at §8.3 , and it is why the chapter is character work of the first order despite containing no characterisation in the usual sense. What the model learns from the case. The requirement of two engines holds; it simply does not have to be satisfied at the level of the quoted speech. A sustained monologue is an exchange whenever the frame around it is contested — which is the same principle that licenses Nelly Dean (§9.5) and the naive-listener convention ( §8.1 ), arriving from the opposite direction. 9.4 Hurston, Their Eyes Were Watching God (1937) — vernacular, free indirect, and the right to speak Two moments carry the novel’s dialogue argument. The first: at the lighting of the street lamp in Eatonville, the crowd calls for a speech from Janie, and Joe Starks refuses on her behalf — his wife knows nothing about speech-making, he never married her for anything like that, her place is in the home. The exchange is four lines long and settles the terms of a marriage. The second, years later, in the store: Jody mocks Janie’s body in public, and Janie answers in public, telling him that when he pulls down his britches he looks like the change of life. The store falls silent. He never recovers. Why the second lands is entirely a matter of the first. The novel has established the porch as a space Janie is excluded from — the silence domain ( §4.6 ) operating structurally rather than locally, across two hundred pages. The fact about the retort that matters most is not its content but its venue . It is spoken where she has not been permitted to speak, in the register of the place, and it is unanswerable in that register. This is the gap-closing move ( §6.5 ) executed in the relational domain rather than the emotional one: what closes is not the distance between saying and meaning but the distance between Janie and the floor. On the phonetic rendering. §8.9 argues the general case; the specific point here is technical. Hurston’s narration is not standard prose against which the speech is a deviation. It moves continuously between a high lyrical register and the characters’ idiom, frequently within a sentence, so that the boundary between narration and speech is porous in Bakhtin’s sense — the character zone ( §3.4 ) rather than the quotation mark. A reader cannot locate a neutral position in the novel from which the dialect would read as marked, because the novel does not contain one. That is the structural answer to the charge of exhibition, and it can be stated as a general principle: the asymmetry that makes phonetic dialect condescending is an asymmetry between narration and speech, not a property of the spelling. Close the gap between the two and the problem dissolves. A note on translation and on texture. This is the clearest case in the chapter of a text whose effects do not survive paraphrase, let alone translation. The structural claims made here — the exclusion, the venue, the reversal — transfer to any language. The texture claims do not transfer at all. 9.5 Brontë, Wuthering Heights (1847) — dialogue at two removes The novel’s central exchange is Catherine’s confession to Nelly Dean that she has accepted Edgar Linton, that it would degrade her to marry Heathcliff, and that she is Heathcliff nonetheless — whatever their souls are made of, his and hers are the same. Heathcliff is in the kitchen, unseen behind the settle. He leaves after hearing that marrying him would degrade her and before the rest. Nelly notices his departure and tells Catherine to hush, but does not plainly tell her what he heard. The passage is a small anthology of everything in this chapter. Feature What is happening Participation framework ( §3.3 ) Three parties: two ratified, one an unratified overhearer whose presence one speaker knows of and the other does not The silence domain ( §4.6 ) Two silences — Heathcliff’s departure and Nelly’s withholding — determine the entire remaining plot Relational Nelly holds, throughout, the only complete information in the room, and uses it by omission Plot The novel’s causal engine is set by a conversation from which its principal participant walked out early Mediation The whole thing reaches the reader through Nelly’s retrospective narration to Lockwood, who is transcribing Dialogue at two removes. Everything a reader has of Catherine’s speech has passed through Nelly’s memory, Nelly’s interests, and Lockwood’s transcription — and Lockwood is a fool. The chain is: Catherine speaks → Nelly hears and later reports → Lockwood records → the reader reads. Every link is an opportunity for distortion, and the novel exploits all of them. This is worth teaching because it inverts the usual assumption about dialogue. §4.2 claims that speech is the novel’s least filtered material, the only element in which the character rather than the narrator selects the words. Wuthering Heights demonstrates that the claim is a convention , not a fact: a novel can foreground the reporting chain, and when it does, quoted speech becomes the least reliable material in the book rather than the most. Chapter 13 ( The Viewpoint Shift ) treats the machinery; Chapter 7 ( Backstory and Flashback ) treats the nested retrospection. What this chapter takes from it is a caution about test 7 — the transcript test assumes a transparent reporter, and where the reporter is not transparent, the test is measuring the reporter. The under-taught point. Nelly is not a neutral conduit and is not a fully unreliable one either; she is an interested party with a servant’s precise knowledge of a household and a servant’s exclusion from its decisions. Her position as an unratified participant in the family’s life is what makes her a total witness to it — the structural fact §4.6 argues the five-domain model cannot express. 9.6 Saramago, Blindness (1995; trans. Giovanni Pontiero) — dialogue without the apparatus Saramago abolishes quotation marks, paragraph breaks between speakers, and — largely — attribution. Speech runs on inside narrative paragraphs, marked by a comma and a capital letter where a new speaker begins. Characters have no names, only designations: the doctor’s wife, the first blind man, the girl with dark glasses. The effects are precise and worth separating. 1. Speech loses its ontological privilege. In conventional presentation, quotation marks assert that these words were actually said , in a way the surrounding narration is not. Removing them dissolves the boundary: speech and narration become the same substance, and the reader stops experiencing dialogue as a distinct kind of evidence. In a novel about an epidemic that removes the ability to see who is speaking, this is not a typographic preference. 2. Attribution becomes the reader’s labour. Because speakers are rarely tagged, the reader must attribute turns by inference — from content, from register, from position in a sequence. This makes the transcript test ( §7.1 , test 7) into the reading experience itself: a reader of Blindness is continuously performing test 7, and the novel is only legible because Saramago’s voices are in fact differentiated. The device is a demonstration that the test measures something real. 3. Pace accelerates and orientation degrades. White space is the texture domain’s largest carrier ( §4.5 ), and removing it produces long undifferentiated blocks that read fast and hold poorly. Readers report losing track of who is present — which is the represented experience. 4. The absence of names removes the vocative entirely. With no names, none of the relational work described at §8.7 is available. Saramago compensates by loading the relational domain onto the designations themselves: the doctor’s wife is defined by a relation, and the novel’s central irony is that the one person who can see is identified only by her marriage. Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages ) reads the same feature as a formal contract declared on page one. The addition here is that the device is semantic as well as formal: it alters what quoted speech means in the book, not merely how it looks. A translation caution. Pontiero’s English retains Saramago’s punctuation practice, and the structural claims above hold across the languages. Claims about the specific rhythm of the run-on sentences do not. 9.7 James, The Portrait of a Lady (1881) — negotiation as the whole of the action James’s dialogue is the most technically demanding in English fiction, and the reason is that almost every exchange is a negotiation in which the terms are never stated. Take the exchange in which Madame Merle sets out her view of the self to Isabel: that no one is isolated, that the self overflows into everything belonging to it — the house, the clothes, the books, the company. Isabel resists: nothing that belongs to her is any measure of her; everything that belongs to her is on the contrary a limit and a barrier, and an arbitrary one. What makes this dialogue rather than philosophy. Three things. Both women want something. Madame Merle wants to know what Isabel is, and how far she can be shaped; Isabel wants to be understood as she understands herself. The abstraction is instrumental. The reader’s information is asymmetric on rereading. Madame Merle is at this point already engaged in the project the novel will eventually disclose, and every abstract proposition she advances is, on a second reading, a piece of practical planning. This is the character-only implicature configuration described at §6.2 , and it is the reason the novel improves so much on rereading. Neither position is defeated. The novel’s plot arguably vindicates Madame Merle — Isabel is caught by the very material web she disclaims — and its moral sense is with Isabel throughout. Bakhtin’s polyphony ( §3.4 ) applies in full: the argument is not adjudicated by the narration. The technical signature. James’s characters conduct these negotiations through a set of moves that map onto §6.4 almost item for item: the question answered with a question; the too-precise reply; the significant repetition of the other’s word, held up for inspection; the unfinished sentence completed by the hearer. What distinguishes James is density — several mechanisms in a single turn — and the fact that his narration frequently reports the computation of implicature as an event: characters are shown working out what has just been meant, which is the theory of §6.2 dramatised. Where it fails a test. The transcript test ( §7.1 , test 7) is a genuine problem in late James, where the principals share a register so completely that stripping attributions makes attribution hard. This is a real limitation, argued about by critics, and it is not obvious that it is a fault: the shared register is itself a representation of a milieu in which everyone has been trained to speak the same way. 9.8 Hemingway, “Hills Like White Elephants” (1927) The canonical teaching case, and it earns the position. A man and a girl wait for a train at a Spanish station and conduct, in short turns and almost without attribution, a conversation about an operation whose nature — an abortion — is never named. He assures her it is simple, that it is not really an operation at all, that they will be fine afterwards. She asks what happens afterwards. Eventually she asks him, seven times over in one sentence, to please stop talking. Four features make it teachable. The narration withholds all interiority , so the reader computes implicatures from the same evidence the characters have. The subject is a hole in the text , so every turn is a swerve and the reader constructs the centre from the swerves. The repetitions are the pressure gauge — the man’s really and simple , her please — and the story’s climax is a flouting of manner rather than an event. And status inverts once : at the outset he is managing her, and after the sevenfold please he is not. The story can be analysed in a page, with every mechanism in §6.4 present except the ritual formula. Its influence is also worth flagging as a hazard. The story is the origin of a great deal of the mid-century workshop orthodoxy that §16 questions, and students who take it as a model rather than as a case tend to produce dialogue in which nothing is named because the writer has not decided what it is. 9.9 A revision case: the doorway exchange The chapter’s own worked example, using the household that runs through this series: a small shop, a father dead in March who kept its ledger for eleven years, a mother who changed the locks, and three adult siblings reconstructing what was withheld from them. Elena has driven across town to Dov’s front door; she does not yet know that the shop’s locks have been changed. Dov is in the doorway. The canonical facts in play are established elsewhere in the series: the register drawer that sticks on the K, and the good pen the father used for the ledger only, are planted in Chapter 10 ( The Prologue ); the ledger is first seen, as an unremarked object, in Chapter 4 ( The Descriptive Detail ), and the changed handwriting after 9 March is discovered in Chapter 6 ( The Chapter Break ). This exchange plants the changed locks. The key in it is the new key to the shop door. Version A — the on-the-nose draft Dov stood in the doorway. “I know you want the shop key,” he said. “I’ve been dreading this conversation.” “I’ve had a key to this shop since I was twelve,” Elena said. “It’s humiliating to be offered one by you.” “It won’t fit any more. Ma changed the locks in March, right after the funeral. I’ve felt caught in the middle ever since — I don’t want to betray her, but I don’t want to lie to you either.” “Why would she do that? Doesn’t she trust me?” “She said you’d ask that. She knew you’d take it personally, and I do think she’s right that you take things personally. But she asked me not to explain, and I feel I have to respect that, even though I know it’s hurting you.” He stepped back from the door. “I’m sorry. I really am.” Diagnosis Test Result 1 — Removal Fails. The summary line — Dov gave her the key and would not say why the locks had been changed — carries everything the exchange carries 2 — Want Passes on the surface. Elena wants the key; Dov wants to give it without explaining. But both wants are stated , which removes the reader’s work 3 — Status Fails. Dov concedes the doorway, the key, the fact of the locks, his own conflicted position and an apology. Nothing is contested, because nothing is withheld 4 — Cost Fails. Every disclosure is volunteered. Nothing costs anything 5 — Silence Fails absolutely. Neither speaker withholds a single thing, including their feelings about withholding 6 — Implicature Fails. Every turn is fully cooperative. There is nothing to compute 7 — Transcript Fails. Strip the tags and the two speakers are one person, both fluent in the same emotionally literate register 9 — Attribution Marginal. Two tags for five turns is defensible; the fault is elsewhere — Patterns present: on-the-nose ( §8.3 ); therapeutic exchange ( §8.10 ) — caught in the middle , take things personally ; As-You-Know-Bob ( §8.1 ) — right after the funeral , which Elena knows; ventriloquist ( §8.2 ) Note that Version A contains all the necessary information , and is not badly written at the sentence level. Its failure is entirely one of channel : it runs on one, and it therefore has nothing for a reader to do. Note also that Version A is more emotionally explicit than Version B and communicates less emotion — which is the chapter’s central claim in a single comparison. Version B “You’ll want the shop key,” Dov said, not moving from the doorway. Elena held out her hand. “I’ve had a key since I was twelve.” “Not this key.” He turned it over once between two fingers before he set it in her palm, face down, like he was folding a hand of cards. “Ma changed the locks in March.” “Did she.” Elena closed her fist around it. “Did she say why.” “She said you’d ask that.” Dov stepped back into the hall. “She didn’t say I had to answer.” Audit Domain What the exchange does Plot The locks were changed in March — a fact with a consequence Elena has not yet worked out, which is that she has been shut out for four months without knowing it Character Dov’s controlled, almost ritual handling of the key reveals a man managing a loyalty he has not resolved; Elena’s clipped, unpunctuated questions reveal that she already suspects more than she has been told Relational Dov opens holding the doorway and the key. He yields the object, keeps the one thing that mattered — the reason — and ends the conversation by withdrawing into his own hall. The shift is real and partial, which is the pattern §4.3 recommends Theme What family members owe each other in the way of truth, staged in miniature and named by neither speaker Texture Short unfinished sentences; a doorway; one extended simile in an action beat rather than in speech Silence Dov’s refusal; the mother’s absence from a conversation entirely about her; the question mark Elena does not use What the revision did, procedurally Converted every statement of feeling into an act. I’ve been dreading this conversation becomes not moving from the doorway . It’s humiliating to be offered one becomes an outstretched hand. The relational domain is carried by physical position throughout ( §4.3 ), which costs no dialogue at all. Applied the third-person deflection ( §6.4 , mechanism 8). Dov’s I feel I have to respect that becomes She didn’t say I had to answer — the same refusal, with principalship shifted to an absent party. He is now animating someone else’s instruction, which is both a shield and a disclosure: a man who needs the instruction to be someone else’s. Applied the significant repetition ( §6.4 , mechanism 11). Did she. Did she say why. Elena returns Dov’s own verb, twice, flat. The missing question marks are not a typographic affectation; they mark utterances that are not requests for information, because she has already drawn her conclusion. Made the information cost something ( §7.1 , test 4). The locks fact arrives inside a correction — Not this key — so that Elena is contradicted before she is informed, and the contradiction is what makes the information land. Added the contradicting action beat ( §6.3 ). Turning the key over like he was folding a hand of cards supplies the reader with counter-evidence to Dov’s compliance: a man who is conceding does not handle the concession that carefully. Deleted the apology. Version A’s I’m sorry. I really am closes the exchange. Version B’s last line opens one, because it announces that a reason exists and is being withheld — the distinction between planting and withholding that Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages ) draws for the stakes contract. Differentiated the registers. Dov’s turns are declarative and complete; Elena’s are two and three words long and structurally interrogative without being questions. Two variables, per §7.2 — sentence length and relation to questions — and no verbal tics. What Version B has not solved Three things, and they should be said plainly. It is conspicuously written. The card simile and the missing question marks are visible technique, and a reader alert to the contemporary literary register will recognise the moves. Version B passes test 7 against Version A and does less well against the shelf it sits on — the same qualification Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages ) makes of its own revision case. It leans hard on one mechanism. Three of the five turns run on deflection or repetition. A novel in which every exchange is built this way would be exhausting, and Dov in particular is at risk of becoming a man who only ever declines — which is the over-delivery described at §6.4 , mechanism 1. It does not serve the theme domain except by implication. The claim in the audit table — that the exchange stages what family members owe each other — is available to a reader who has the rest of the book. In isolation it is thin, and a writer should be honest about which domains an exchange serves in situ and which it serves only in the analysis. And one thing it does that Version A could not. Version B leaves a gap that a later exchange can close ( §6.5 ). Dov’s reason is now a withheld object with a location in the book. Version A spent it.

title: 10. Dialogue Across Forms
text: The model was developed for the novel. It transfers with adjustments that need stating, because students routinely import novel-dialogue habits into forms that punish them. 10.1 The short story The story has proportionally less room and a different relation to its own exposition, and four consequences follow. Difference Consequence for dialogue No room for a baseline Subtext must be legible from the first exchange, because there is no time to train the reader in a character’s habits Voices need not be many Two speakers is the norm; a story with five differentiated voices has spent its length on differentiation The gap-closing move is structural In a novel it is a climax; in a story it is often the ending itself Ritual and phatic talk cannot be afforded The approach turns described at §2.2 are cut entirely The important asymmetry is the first. A novel can teach the reader that a character deflects and then, three hundred pages later, cash the training. A story must produce the same effect by convention — the reader arrives already knowing that in a literary short story, a conversation about hills is not about hills. This is a real dependency on genre expectation, and it is why the form’s dialogue reads as mannered when transplanted. 10.2 The novella and the long novel The two long forms fail in opposite directions. The novella’s characteristic dialogue problem is that it is written by novelists: an exchange that takes four pages to arrive at its turn has spent a fiftieth of the book on approach. The novella wants exchanges that begin at the second or third turn — the discipline of §2.2 applied ruthlessly. The long novel’s problem is the inverse and less often named. Over eight hundred pages, a subtext-heavy dialogue practice becomes monotonous, and the great long novels do not sustain one. War and Peace , Middlemarch and The Brothers Karamazov all alternate between exchanges of extreme obliquity and exchanges in which characters simply argue at length. The alternation is what makes the oblique passages readable. A book’s dialogue practice must vary across its length for the same reason a page’s density must vary across a page — emphasis is relational, a point Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages ) makes about the density ceiling and which applies here without modification. 10.3 Series and sequence Series dialogue faces a specific hazard: the relational domain is the series’ principal accumulating asset, and it is the one most easily squandered. What makes a fourth-volume exchange between two recurring characters land is three volumes of history, and the temptation is to spend that history in every book by having the characters refer to it. Three principles. Re-establish the voices completely and the history not at all. Readers who finished the previous volume eighteen months ago retain the sound of a character and almost none of the plot. Recap in the relational channel, not the informational one. Not after what happened in Prague , but two people behaving towards each other in a way that only a shared history explains. Ration the gap-closing move across the whole sequence, not per volume. A series in which each book ends with a character finally saying what they mean has trained the reader that they always will. 10.4 The screen comparison, and a caution about borrowing Contemporary craft advice on dialogue is imported heavily from screenwriting, and most of it imports badly, for one structural reason: the screenplay has no narrator and the novel does. Resource Screen Prose Subtext carrier Performance — face, pause, the actor’s choice The narration: interiority, action beats, contradiction ( §6.3 ) Attribution Free; the viewer sees who speaks Costs a clause; a craft problem in its own right ( §7.1 , test 9) Silence Genuinely available; a held shot is a duration Must be written , and therefore ceases to be silence Overlap Reproducible Requires typographic stylisation Register and dialect Carried by the voice; no orthography required The problem of §8.9 Pace Fixed by the cut Set by turn length and white space Two specific mis-imports need naming. “Enter late, leave early” transfers cleanly and is among the best advice in the craft literature; it is the discipline of §2.2 . “Let the subtext play” does not transfer, because on screen an actor supplies what the line withholds, and on the page nothing supplies it unless the prose does. A novelist who writes a bare exchange expecting the reader to feel what an actor would have shown has written a screenplay without a cast. The third and least noticed difference is that screen dialogue is heard and prose dialogue is read , which is why disfluencies work in one and not the other ( §3.6 ): an um is inaudible in performance and conspicuous in print. 10.5 Translated fiction The series’ standing distinction applies with unusual force here. Structural claims about dialogue survive translation; texture claims do not, and register claims survive only partially. What transfers: The sequence of turns, and therefore every adjacency-pair and preference-organisation effect ( §3.2 ). Who evades, who deflects, who is interrupted, who is silent — the whole of §4.6 and most of §6.4 . Status moves realised through acts : correction, interruption, refusal, the granting or withholding of an exit. What does not: Idiolect and the transcript test. A translator produces the dialogue in their own language’s registers, and voice differentiation is remade rather than transferred. Garnett’s Dostoevsky, Pevear and Volokhonsky’s Dostoevsky and the intervening versions differ substantially in how alike the brothers Karamazov sound. Dialect, wholly. There is no equivalence between a regional English and a regional Russian, and translators’ solutions — invented dialects, class-marked English registers, standardisation — are all lossy, and are all interpretations. Address systems. Languages with a T/V distinction carry a relational value in every second-person pronoun that English cannot render without an added clause. The move from vous to tu is a relational event of the kind §4.3 describes, and in English it must be replaced by something else or lost. The practical instruction for a student: when analysing translated dialogue, run tests 1–6 and 10 with confidence, and run tests 7, 8 and 9 only with the translator’s name attached to the finding. 10.6 Concordance: concept to novel A study aid: each concept with the work that displays it best, and the section that treats it. Concept Best displayed by Section The engine — two wants, incompatible Pride and Prejudice (Hunsford) §9.1 Direct speech and report, alternated deliberately Pride and Prejudice §3.5 , §9.1 The ritual formula carrying everything Pride and Prejudice (Pemberley) §9.2 Subtext at maximum The Remains of the Day §4.3 , §6.4 The name as barrier The Remains of the Day §8.7 The too-precise reply The Remains of the Day §6.4 The staged dialectic, left open The Brothers Karamazov §4.4 , §9.3 The set speech inside a running exchange The Brothers Karamazov §8.11 , §9.3 On-the-nose dialogue that works The Brothers Karamazov ; Crime and Punishment §8.3 , §8.10 Vernacular as the book’s centre of value Their Eyes Were Watching God §8.9 , §9.4 The character zone; narration meeting speech Their Eyes Were Watching God §3.4 , §9.4 Exclusion from the exchange as structure Their Eyes Were Watching God §4.6 , §9.4 The participation framework; the unratified overhearer Wuthering Heights §3.3 , §9.5 Dialogue at two removes; the interested reporter Wuthering Heights §9.5 The naive-listener exposition convention Wuthering Heights ; Frankenstein §8.1 Dialect as functional obstruction Wuthering Heights (Joseph) §4.5 , §8.9 Dialogue without quotation marks Blindness §3.5 , §9.6 White space as a texture instrument Blindness §4.5 , §9.6 Negotiation with unstated terms The Portrait of a Lady §9.7 The maid-and-butler opening that works The Portrait of a Lady §8.6 Implicature reported as an event The Portrait of a Lady §6.2 , §9.7 The gap closed at the climax Pride and Prejudice ; Their Eyes Were Watching God §6.5 Undifferentiated register as a declared style Compton-Burnett; Wilde §8.2 Subtext with the narration withdrawn “Hills Like White Elephants” §5.2 , §9.8 Phonetic dialect, the contested case Adventures of Huckleberry Finn §8.9 The unspeakable organising an exchange Beloved ; “Hills Like White Elephants” §4.6

title: 11. Revision Checklist
text: Run each significant exchange against this list before deciding it stays as written. Each item derives from a test in §7 or a pattern in §8 . The engine I can state, in one sentence each, what both speakers want from the other in this exchange. Both wants are directed at the other person, and both are immediate rather than story-scale. The balance of information, power or feeling is different at the end than at the start — or has been contested and held. Removing the exchange would cost the reader something the summary line cannot carry. Domains I can name which domains — plot, character, relational, theme, texture, silence — this exchange actually serves, rather than merely touches. The relational domain is doing something; status is not simply fixed by default. Any information delivered here comes at a cost to the speaker, not a courtesy to the reader. No character says something purely so that the reader can learn it. The two channels Text and subtext are not identical for at least the key turns. I can name which mechanism from §6.4 each oblique turn is using. The exchange has some cooperative turns, so that the flouting ones register. I have not spent the gap-closing move here unless this is the place for it. Silence At least one speaker is withholding, deflecting or declining to answer something. I know who else is in the room, and whether their silence is doing work or is an oversight. I know who is being discussed and is not present. Voice With the tags stripped and the lines read aloud, I can tell who is speaking without relying on content. I could not move this exchange’s best lines into another character’s mouth without loss. Each principal has a different average turn length, a different relation to questions, and a different default evasion. Surface Every attribution that is not said or asked is justified; no adverb is compensating for a line that has not been written. Action beats between turns carry a second function, and are not tags with extra words. Names are used in the vocative only where the vocative is doing something. Dialect is carried by syntax, idiom and lexicon rather than by spelling — or, where it is not, I can defend the choice on the grounds set out at §8.9 . Shape The exchange begins at the first turn that could not be cut and ends at the last. Interruptions cluster at the crisis rather than being distributed evenly. The turns cannot be reshuffled without loss.

title: 12. Studio Work
text: 12.1 Practical exercises Exercise 1 — The domain audit. Annotate one drafted exchange per §5.5 , with the attributions stripped. Produce a table of turns against domains. Write 200 words on what the distribution reveals, paying particular attention to any empty column. Exercise 2 — Mechanism substitution. Take the most on-the-nose turn in a draft and rewrite it four times, once each as an evasion, a changed subject, a too-precise reply and a delayed agreement ( §6.4 ). Do not judge which is best until all four exist. Write 300 words on what each implies about the speaker. Exercise 3 — The transcript test, run properly. Strip every tag and action beat from a two-page exchange. Give the bare lines to a reader who does not know the book, and ask them to mark where the speaker changes and to describe each speaker in two adjectives. Record the answers verbatim without correcting them. Exercise 4 — The preference-organisation drill. Write an exchange in which one character refuses another, and produce the refusal in the full dispreferred format described at §3.2 : delay, hesitation, token agreement, account, mitigation, and a refusal that is never stated outright. Then write the same refusal as a flat no . Compare what each does to the relational domain. Exercise 5 — The maxim drill. Write one short exchange four times. In each version, one speaker flouts a different Gricean maxim at the same point in the sequence. Identify the implicature a reader computes in each case, and write it out in a phrase. Exercise 6 — Report and quotation. Take a drafted exchange of two pages and rewrite it in Austen’s proportions ( §3.5 , §9.1 ): direct speech for the two turns that must be experienced, indirect report for everything else. Compare the length and the effect. Exercise 7 — The silent third. Rewrite a two-hander with a third character present throughout who never speaks and is mentioned twice. Change nothing else. Write 200 words on what happens to the exchange. Exercise 8 — The gap-closing move. Locate the moment in your draft where a character says outright what they mean for the first time. If there is none, write it. If there are three, decide which one the book has actually earned, and convert the other two. Exercise 9 — Dialect without spelling. Take a passage of speech you have rendered phonetically and rewrite it so that syntax, idiom, lexicon and forms of address carry the same register, with no respelling. Then write 300 words on what has been lost and whether the loss is real ( §8.9 ). 12.2 Seminar questions Is subtext a technique or a period style? §6.6 argues that the two-channel ideal is a datable Anglo-American preference. Test the claim against Dostoevsky, Wilde and Compton-Burnett. Does the chapter’s model describe dialogue, or a fashion in dialogue? Five domains or six? Argue for or against admitting the silence domain ( §4.6 ) as a separate category, given the objection stated there — that silence is a means rather than an end, and that its value shifts are always relational or thematic on inspection. Use Wuthering Heights or Their Eyes Were Watching God as evidence. Does the Grand Inquisitor break the model? §9.3 argues that a set speech is an exchange when the frame around it is contested. Is that a genuine defence of the model, or a redescription that makes it unfalsifiable? What would a passage look like that the model could not accommodate? Phonetic dialect: whose rule, applied to whom? §8.9 argues that the prohibition has been applied unevenly by race and class. Read Hurston alongside a nineteenth-century English novel’s rendering of working-class speech. Is the difference one of technique, of position, or of the critic’s ear? Jim’s speech in Huckleberry Finn . Critics have disagreed for a century about whether Twain’s rendering of Jim is a sympathetic representation, a minstrel inheritance, or both at once, and the disagreement is live rather than settled. Set out the strongest version of each position before deciding. Is James’s dialogue a failure of test 7? In late James the principals share a register so completely that stripping attribution makes attribution difficult ( §9.7 ). Is this a defect the chapter’s protocol correctly identifies, or a representation of a milieu that the protocol is too crude to recognise? 12.3 Assessment rubric The following rubric is for a submitted dialogue exchange (1,000–1,500 words) with a 750-word critical commentary. Band Craft (60%) Commentary (40%) Distinction Two legible, incompatible, immediate wants; a status movement that is earned and partial; speakers distinguishable with tags stripped; subtext produced by identifiable mechanisms rather than by vagueness; silence used structurally Names its mechanisms and defends them against alternatives; identifies its own risks; engages at least two theoretical sources critically rather than decoratively; historicises its own choices Merit Both wants present, one under-resisted; status moves; voices distinct but occasionally converging; subtext present but reliant on one mechanism Accurate self-analysis; some theoretical engagement; risks acknowledged if not resolved Pass An engine exists; some domain movement; competent but interchangeable voices; subtext gestured at Describes the exchange accurately; theory referenced but not applied Fail No want on one or both sides; nothing contested; one channel throughout; failure patterns unrecognised Description without analysis; no engagement with the model

title: 13. Glossary
text: Action beat — An action inserted between turns in place of an attribution; called simply a beat in the first edition. The most efficient object in an exchange when it carries a second function, and a tag with extra words when it does not. §5.3 . Adjacency pair — A two-turn sequence in which the first part makes a particular second part conditionally relevant: question/answer, greeting/greeting, offer/acceptance-or-refusal. Schegloff and Sacks developed the account in “Opening Up Closings” (1973). Its importance for fiction is that the absence of the expected second part is itself an event. §3.2 . Animator / author / principal — Goffman’s decomposition of the “speaker” role: the one producing the sounds, the one who composed the words, and the one whose position the words express. These can come apart, and a character who separates them is deflecting responsibility. §3.3 . Attribution (tag) — The identification of a speaker: he said , she asked . Its density, its verbs and its replacement by action beats are all craft variables with a documented history. §3.5 , §7.1 test 9. Character zone — Bakhtin’s term for the field around a character in which the narration itself becomes contaminated by that character’s speech habits, so that the boundary between narration and quoted speech becomes porous. §3.4 , §9.4 . Conversational implicature — Grice’s term for meaning conveyed beyond what is said, inferred by the hearer using the context and an assumption of cooperation. It can arise when a maxim is conspicuously flouted or when the maxims are observed. This chapter’s claim: conversational implicature explains one important kind of subtext. §3.1 , §6.2 . Cooperative Principle — Grice’s general principle: make your conversational contribution such as is required, at the stage at which it occurs, by the accepted purpose of the exchange. Its four attendant categories of maxims are quantity, quality, relation and manner. §3.1 .
