The feeling is unease Carries: a woman on a stool with a book she cannot put down, and a dead man’s handwriting turning into someone else’s. The feeling is dread with an object 5 — Placement Strategy 1 (mid-scene cut) — the scene is interrupted before its own discovery Strategy 5, approximately (after the decision) — Elena has decided to read, and the next unit is pre-oriented 6 — Proportion Ends the chapter two sentences after the scene break, so its only event at the shop is two sentences long The chapter gains its discovery 7 — Variety The doorway closed on a withheld reason, and the scene before the drawer (Chapter 2’s sequel) ended on an unexecuted decision. A third unresolved exit in a few pages Contrast with the open exits before it 8 — Re-entry The next chapter must either resume this scene at once, or cut away and leave the alarm ringing The next chapter is free to go anywhere, because nothing is physically pending 9 — Container One chapter, very short One chapter, complete 10 — Architecture A short, sharp unit; reads as a jolt in the book’s structure A substantial unit; reads as the discovery the first act was for Ending type Cliffhanger Pivot , compounded with a recasting close — the last paragraph reframes the chapter from break-in to inheritance The verdict, and why it depends on the neighbours Neither option is correct in the abstract, and a student who concludes that Option B is “better writing” has missed the point of the exercise. The right cut is determined by what the chapters on either side do, and in this book they are known. What comes before: the doorway exchange (Chapter 3’s material), which closes on a withheld reason; then, in this chapter, Elena’s sequel in the truck, ending at a scene break on a decision she carries out immediately (Chapter 2), then the hard cut into the shop (Chapter 5). The reader has just been given a scene that ended on an unexecuted intention and a transition that opened on a disturbance. Two costly exits have been offered in quick succession. What comes after: Dov’s thread — the sale, the deadline, the papers signed without telling his sisters (Chapter 14’s material). This settles it, and the reasoning runs as follows. Option A’s cliffhanger would be answered by adjacency. If the chapter ends on someone has been in this drawer and the next chapter opens in Dov’s thread, the placement itself supplies the answer. The reader does not need to be told; they will infer it from the cut. A cliffhanger whose next chapter names the culprit by juxtaposition is not a cliffhanger; it is a delayed caption. Option B converts the same information into dramatic irony. With the changed hand already on the page, the cut to Dov is no longer a reveal but a view of the person the reader now suspects , going about his business. Everything he does in that chapter is read twice. This is a straight application of Sternberg’s distinction: A runs on suspense, which the following chapter deflates; B runs on curiosity, which the following chapter feeds. The variety test is against A. Three consecutive unresolved exits is the beginning of cliffhanger fatigue ( §8.2 ) in a novel whose register is domestic and whose whole effect depends on quietness. A book of this kind can spend an expensive exit perhaps five times, by this case’s estimate. The re-entry cost is against A. Ending mid-discovery obliges the following chapter either to resume the scene — which forfeits the handoff to Dov and the whole subplot architecture — or to abandon it, which leaves the reader impatient through a chapter they should be reading closely. The payoff map is for B. The series’ ending requires the changed handwriting to have been planted early and lived with for a long time, so that when all three siblings finally read the ledger the reader has been holding the fact for two hundred pages. Option A defers the plant by a chapter and reduces the time it has to work. Verdict: Option B , on the grounds of what precedes and follows it — not on the grounds that a partial resolution is intrinsically better than a full withholding. The condition under which A becomes right. If this chapter were the last chapter of Part One, A is the better cut, and by some distance. A Part boundary can carry an expensive exit that an ordinary chapter break cannot, because the reader is being told to expect a change and will accept a long-held question across it; and the next Part could then open in Dov’s thread without the juxtaposition reading as an answer, because a Part boundary licenses discontinuity. The same two sentences are a mistake at one structural position and the best available choice at another. That is the whole content of this chapter, in one comparison. The substitution test, run once more §6.5 requires the break to be tried a beat earlier and a beat later. Both are instructive. A beat earlier , ending on the leather faintly warm : an echo close. The chapter would end on a physical sensation with an unstated implication — someone’s arm, an hour ago — and no information at all. It is the most atmospheric of the three and the least useful, because the proposition would be raised twice and paid off never. A beat later , ending after Elena has read the first of the changed entries: the pivot becomes a disclosure, and the chapter acquires a second proposition it cannot pay off. This is the chapter that is really two ( §8.7 ). Three positions, three legitimate chapters, one right answer given the neighbours. The exercise is not about finding the good sentence; it is about discovering that the sentence was never the variable. What Option B has not solved Four things, and a workshop should say them. It resolves a question the novel might have wanted open longer. Once the reader knows a second hand continued the ledger, the field of suspects is small and domestic, and a good deal of the book’s remaining mystery is transferred from who to why . That is the right trade for this novel, whose subject is withholding rather than crime — but it is a trade, and a version of the book that wanted to sustain uncertainty about Dov for another hundred pages should choose A and accept the costs listed above. The last sentence is doing a great deal at once. She sat down on the stool because her legs asked her to, turned back to the first page, eleven years back, and started from the beginning carries a physical reaction, a characterisation, a decision and a structural handoff. It is close to the density ceiling that Chapter 1 ( The Purposes of a Scene ) §5 warns about, and read aloud it is slightly crowded. The restraint is convenient. She did not read any of it asks the reader to accept an investigator’s restraint at the moment she has most reason to look. It is motivated, since Elena means to know the ledger in order, from its first page; but it also protects the ending, in which the illness entries and the list near the end of the father’s pages must reach all three siblings at once (canon C10). The book does not return to Elena’s reading until the ledger has left her hands, which Chapter 14 ( The Subplot ) arranges. A sceptical reader may still see the author’s hand in her patience. The chapter’s proposition is inherited rather than raised. Elena arrives at the shop with a question given to her by the previous chapter. That is legitimate — propositions frequently carry across breaks — but it means this chapter cannot be assessed in isolation, and it is therefore a poor model for a stand-alone exercise. A chapter ending is not a portable skill. It is a decision about a position in a particular sequence.

title: 10. The Chapter Break Across Forms
text: The model in §§3–8 was developed for the novel. It transfers to adjacent forms with adjustments that need stating, because writers routinely import novel-scale segmentation habits into forms that punish them. 10.1 The short story A story rarely has chapters and often has sections. The difference is not one of scale alone. Difference Consequence No permission to stop is needed The reader will finish in one sitting. The exit is not being priced, because it will not be taken The break’s job is therefore purely structural It marks an ellipsis, a turn, or a change of vantage — not an offer The proportion principle inverts In a story, a long section reads as slow and a short one as abrupt, and there is no baseline to establish the contrast against Numbered sections are a genre signal A story divided into numbered parts announces a formal seriousness; an undivided one announces continuity The practical inference: a story’s section breaks should be justified by what happens across them, never by the reader’s comfort. The white space in a story of four thousand words is not a rest; it is a cut, and Chapter 5 ( The Transition ) governs it entirely. 10.2 The novella The novella’s segmentation problem is that it is usually written by novelists. It has a novel’s tonal amplitude and a fraction of its length, and a novelist’s chapter of five thousand words is an eighth of the book. Two solutions are in common use and both are respectable. The first is many very short chapters , which gives the novella the pulse of a long poem and lets the form’s characteristic compression become visible. The second is no chapters at all — a single continuous movement, sometimes with section breaks — which is how a substantial proportion of the canonical novellas are built, and which suits a form whose subject is very often a single unbroken pressure. What does not work is the middle: five or six chapters of novel length, which give the reader neither the pulse of segmentation nor the pressure of continuity, and which make a short book feel like an abbreviated long one. 10.3 The long novel, the series and the volume break Three effects operate at scale. The long novel can establish a segmentation grammar. By page two hundred, a reader knows what a section break means in this book and what a chapter break means, and thereafter the marks themselves carry information. This is a real asset, squandered by inconsistency, and it is the strongest practical argument for deciding early what each of a book’s signals is going to mean. Chapter 5 §10.3 makes the same point about transitions. The multi-volume work has a boundary stronger than any Part. The end of a volume in a series is the only break in fiction whose price is set partly by the calendar: a reader who finishes volume two waits for volume three, and the wait may be years. This is the modern survival of the Victorian number-ending, and it should be designed with the same care — which in practice means resisting the two commonest errors, the total cliffhanger (which converts a book into half a book, and which readers increasingly resent) and the total resolution (which removes any reason to return). The series volume-opening inherits the recap problem described at §8.9 and, unlike a chapter opening, is entitled to solve it. Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages ) §10.4 gives the principles. 10.4 Serial and instalment publication, then and now The conditions that produced the devices in §§4 and 6 have returned. Web serials, subscription-newsletter fiction, instalment platforms and serialised audio can restore a scheduled interval between releases, occurring in the reader’s life rather than on the page. What changes when the interval is real: Variable Codex Instalment Price of the exit Set entirely by the ending Set by the ending and by the enforced wait Recap A fault ( §8.9 ) A courtesy, and often a requirement Frequency of expensive exits Must be rationed; fatigue sets in fast Naturally rationed by the schedule Unit length The writer’s choice Constrained by the slot, as in the weekly serial Reader’s memory Continuous Degraded; anything not re-established is lost Feedback None until publication Continuous, and historically it has changed novels in progress Hughes and Lund’s The Victorian Serial (1991) is more useful to a writer publishing in instalments than any contemporary novel-structure manual, because the manuals are calibrated for a delivery format with no gap in it. The one modern difference to name is that the digital serial’s readers can and do read in bulk, catching up on twenty instalments at once — so the writer is designing simultaneously for a monthly rhythm and a codex rhythm, which is a problem the Victorians did not have and to which there is no elegant solution. 10.5 The screen comparison Contemporary craft advice imports heavily from television, and here the analogy is unusually good — better than it is for transitions — because the episode boundary and the chapter break are the same kind of object: a segmentation imposed by a delivery technology and subsequently exploited as an artistic resource. Three transfers that work: The act break. Broadcast television’s act structure exists because of advertising, and it produced a durable formal repertoire of small closes at fixed intervals. It is the closest available analogue to the number-ending: a commercial constraint that became a craft. The cold open. Beginning the next unit before the previous one has been resolved. In prose this is placement strategy 1 seen from the far side. The season finale. The exact analogue of the Victorian number-ending and the modern volume break, and subject to the same two errors. Two that do not transfer: The recap sequence. Television can deliver “previously on” outside the fiction, in a form the viewer can ignore. Prose has no such register; a recap in a novel is inside the narration and costs the reader attention whether they need it or not. The fixed slot. A television act is a duration; a chapter is a word count experienced at variable speed. Writers who reason about pacing in minutes are reasoning about a quantity prose does not control. A recent change runs the other way. Streaming’s automatic next-episode countdown has removed the exit : since Netflix introduced its Post-Play feature in 2012, the viewer must act to stop rather than to continue, and a controlled study found that participants with autoplay disabled watched in sessions about 17.6 minutes shorter (Schaffner et al., 2024; §14.5). That the change has made episode endings less conclusive, because the format no longer needs to survive a week, is this chapter’s conjecture. The equivalent in fiction is the e-reader’s seamless page turn, and the parallel is close: when the exit becomes harder to take, the ending has less work to do, and the craft of the boundary atrophies. 10.6 Children’s fiction, and the read-aloud chapter Middle-grade and younger children’s fiction often uses chapter length to suit reading sessions, including read-aloud sessions, and it shows how the chapter can be treated as a unit of time as well as story ( §3.2 ). A chapter intended for a seven-year-old may be calibrated to a bedtime reading, perhaps a ten-minute session; its word count depends on the reader and the text. This produces an inversion of everything §4 assumes. The reader — the adult doing the reading — wants a free exit , because the chapter has to end at the point where the child can be persuaded to sleep. Children’s writers are consequently expert at a manoeuvre the adult novel rarely needs: the ending that satisfies one reader and frustrates another, closing the immediate movement while leaving a small forward pull. The soft landing with a hook is the house style of an entire literature, and adult novelists could learn a great deal from it. Young-adult fiction inverts the inversion, and its convention — short chapters, frequent cliffhangers, alternating viewpoints — is closer to that of the short-chapter thriller ( §5.5 ). 10.7 The device: audiobooks and the displayed chapter Two modern reading technologies have altered the chapter’s function in ways that need naming because they are recent enough to be invisible. The audiobook. Chapter markers are navigation, restored to their original purpose ( §3.1 ) after two centuries of experiential use. But listening changes the ending’s operation in a specific way: the listener frequently does not know a chapter is ending until it has ended, because there is no visible white space approaching. The anticipatory half-second in which a print reader sees the page running out — and prepares to be released — does not exist. An ending that depends on the reader seeing it coming will not work in audio , which affects the soft landing more than the cliffhanger. The displayed chapter. The Kindle’s optional display of the time left in the chapter, estimated from the reader’s own speed (§14.5), has made the chapter a unit of time budgeting on the page. This chapter conjectures that the consequences are not small: that readers start chapters they have time for and decline chapters they do not; a long chapter is now visibly long before it is begun, and can be refused. This is a new constraint on the very long chapter and a new argument for varied lengths, since a reader offered a mixture will always find one that fits the interval they have. 10.8 Translated fiction The distinction the series maintains applies here with unusual clarity. Chapter structure often survives translation, but it must be checked against the edition used. Translators and editors may retain, rename, renumber or regroup divisions. Structural analysis of Dumas, Cervantes and García Márquez therefore needs an identified edition and, where the argument depends on an exact cut, comparison with the original. Intertitles do not survive. A chapter title is a piece of writing, and translators vary widely in how they render one — particularly where the original heading is comic, archaic or idiomatic, as in Don Quixote . Students comparing Rutherford and Grossman will find the headings differ in register far more than the narrative does. Editions intervene more than readers expect. Chapter divisions have been altered in translation and in reprinting: instalments merged for volume publication, chapters renumbered, Parts introduced or removed by editors. The nineteenth-century French serial novel is especially prone to this, and the number of chapters in an English Monte Cristo is not guaranteed to match a French one. Before making an argument about a translated novel’s segmentation, check that the segmentation is the author’s. 10.9 Concordance: concept to novel A study aid mapping each concept to the novel that best displays it. Concept Best displayed by Section The number as the unit of design Bleak House §9.1 The weekly slot and its shorter chapters Great Expectations §9.2 The labelled structural boundary Great Expectations (the Stages) §5.2 , §9.2 The feuilleton instalment boundary The Count of Monte Cristo §4.1 , §9.3 Cliffhanger frequency as a function of format The Count of Monte Cristo §8.2 , §9.3 Books and Part titles as thesis statements Middlemarch §6.6 , §9.4 The epigraph as counterpoint Middlemarch ; Dune §8.11 , §9.4 The soft landing as the dominant mode Middlemarch ; Pride and Prejudice §4.2 , §9.4 Chapter titles as narratorial performance Vanity Fair §3.4 , §9.5 The chapter-length silence (the unnarrated event) Vanity Fair (Waterloo) §6.4 , §9.5 The pivot delivered in a subordinate clause Vanity Fair Ch. 32 §4.3 , §9.5 Headings that summarise and mock Don Quixote §6.1 , §9.6 The false cliffhanger redeemed Don Quixote I.8–9 §8.8 , §9.6 Segmentation as method; the encyclopaedic chapter Moby-Dick §8.3 , §9.7 Variance that becomes rhythm Moby-Dick §9.7 Chapters named for people, defeating chronology Catch-22 §9.8 Curiosity rather than suspense as the engine Catch-22 ; The Trial §4.5 , §9.8 The chapter as a joke about chapters Tristram Shandy §8.1 , §9.9 The arbitrary cut made legible Tristram Shandy §8.1 The pivot as an eight-word sentence Bleak House Ch. 59 §4.3 , §9.1 The echo close, moral rather than lyric Bleak House Ch. 47 §4.4 , §9.1 The echo close, image planted for the ending The Great Gatsby Ch. 1 §4.4 The recasting close, narrator’s self-description The Great Gatsby Ch. 3 §4.6 The recasting close, Nwoye’s delayed reaction Things Fall Apart Ch. 7 §4.3 , §4.6 Parts contracting as an argument Things Fall Apart ; title: 11. Revision Checklist
text: Run a draft against this list once the manuscript is complete. The first four groups are applied chapter by chapter; the last two are applied to the whole book, and are the ones most often skipped and most often decisive. Proposition and payoff I can state, in one sentence, the question or tension this chapter raised near its start. I can write the chapter’s eighteenth-century heading: *In which ___*. The ending resolves, escalates, holds open, re-interprets or exchanges that proposition — and I can name which. The chapter’s first page and last paragraph, read consecutively, are audibly related. The exit I have decided whether stopping here should be free, moderate or expensive, and I can say why in terms of the chapters on either side. A reader who closed the book here and returned in three days would carry what I intend them to carry. Any cliffhanger is attached to a situation the reader already has a stake in. Any unresolved danger is one the next chapter honours; nothing is dispelled trivially on the following page. Placement I have tried the break one beat earlier and one beat later, and can say why the current position is right. I know which of the twelve placement strategies this cut uses. Any reveal or turn sits at the chapter’s close, unless it is deliberately buried and the burial is attributable to the narration. The chapter does not continue past the point at which its own question was answered. The next chapter does not have to re-establish anything the reader already had. Proportion This chapter’s length matches its weight in the book, not a habitual target. Its length is not within a few hundred words of every other chapter’s by default. Nothing has been added to reach a size. The sequence (whole manuscript) I have made the four-column table — number, length, ending type, price — and read it without the manuscript. Ending types vary deliberately; the column does not repeat one word. There are genuine soft landings, placed at the ends of movements, so the expensive exits keep their value. The chapter-length sequence has a shape I can describe in one sentence. No stretch of five consecutive chapters has interchangeable final sentences. The architecture (whole manuscript) Chapter numbering and titling are consistent from the first chapter to the last. If there are Parts, each boundary marks a real change and I can name it. If there are epigraphs, each is in tension with its chapter rather than a caption for it. Reading only the headings and the first and last sentences, the shape of the book is legible. The last chapter’s ending is not the fifteenth time this book has performed a full close.

title: 12. Studio Work
text: 12.1 Practical exercises Exercise 1 — The eighteenth-century contents page. Write a summarising heading, in the manner of Fielding or Thackeray, for every chapter of your draft. *In which ___.* Produce the whole list on one page. Chapters that resist the formula have no proposition ( §6.1 , §7.1 test 1). Write 200 words on what the list revealed. Exercise 2 — Six endings for one chapter. Take a single chapter and write six different final paragraphs, one for each type in §4 : cliffhanger, soft landing, pivot, echo, question, recasting. Do not judge until all six exist. Then write 400 words on what each version does to the chapter that follows. Exercise 3 — The substitution test. Choose the three chapter endings in your draft that feel weakest. For each, move the break one beat earlier and one beat later without rewriting a sentence ( §6.5 ). Record all three versions and state which you keep and why. Exercise 4 — The stopped reader. Give a reader four consecutive chapters of your draft and ask them to stop at each break, put the manuscript down for ten minutes, and write one sentence: what I want to happen next . Collect the four sentences verbatim. Do not explain, correct or discuss until all four are written. Exercise 5 — The chapter-length audit, on a published novel. Count the words in every chapter of a novel you know well. Plot them in order. Write 500 words on the shape of the curve, what it corresponds to in the novel’s action, and whether the mean or the variance is the more informative statistic ( §5.4 ). Exercise 6 — The four-column table. Produce the audit at §5.6 for your own manuscript. Bring the table, not the manuscript, to the seminar, and be prepared to have the book diagnosed from it. Exercise 7 — Re-segmenting. Take twenty pages of a novel that uses long chapters and re-break them into six short ones. Then take twenty pages of a thriller and merge them into two. Read both aloud. Write 300 words on what changed when nothing changed. Exercise 8 — The instalment rewrite. Take four consecutive chapters of your draft and re-plan them as a single monthly number in the Victorian manner: decide which effects fall where, and which chapter has to carry the ending that survives a month. Write the number plan as Dickens wrote his — a list of topics, characters and deferrals — and then say what the exercise changed about your ordering ( §3.3 , §9.1 ). Exercise 9 — The unnarrated chapter. Identify the event in your draft that matters most and is currently narrated. Remove it, place a chapter break where it would have been, and rewrite the chapters on either side so that the event is present only in its approach and its consequence ( §6.4 , strategy 12). Write 400 words on whether the novel survived, and on what would have to be true for it to survive. 12.2 Seminar questions Is the chapter a technology or a form? Dames argues that the chapter is an inherited technology of segmentation rather than a natural unit of narrative. If that is right, does it follow that any placement is as good as any other, or does the argument leave the craft of placement untouched? Test the claim against Tristram Shandy and against a contemporary thriller. Five ending types or six? Argue for or against admitting the recasting close ( §4.6 ) as a category distinct from the pivot. Use Things Fall Apart Chapter 7, The Great Gatsby Chapter 3, and Vanity Fair Chapter 32 as evidence. Ask which endings recast earlier material and which also pivot; distinguish Okonkwo’s motive, given within Achebe’s chapter, from Nwoye’s reaction at its close. Was the cliffhanger a commercial device that became a craft, or a craft device that the market happened to reward? The Count of Monte Cristo and Bleak House were both shaped by delivery formats with real intervals. Does knowing this change how the endings should be evaluated? Whose conventions? The failure patterns in §8 are drawn from Anglo-American trade practice since roughly 1960. Examine the segmentation of a novel from another tradition — the zhanghui chapters of classical Chinese vernacular fiction, or the divisions of The Tale of Genji , or a novel translated from a language whose publishing conventions differ — and identify which of §8 ’s prohibitions describe narrative and which describe a local literary culture. Does the digital exit change the craft? Streaming has removed the act of stopping from television; the e-reader has made the chapter a displayed quantity of time. If the reader no longer has to decide to continue, does the chapter ending still have work to do — and is the answer different for literary and commercial fiction? Should a novel be readable in any order? Catch-22 and Moby-Dick both use segmentation to weaken sequence; Hopscotch and The Dictionary of the Khazars go further. Is a chapter’s position in a sequence a property of the chapter, or only of the book? What would a novel lose if its chapters could be read in any order? 12.3 Assessment rubric For a submitted sequence of three consecutive chapters (4,000–7,000 words total) with a 1,000-word critical commentary. Band Craft (60%) Commentary (40%) Distinction Each chapter has a statable proposition and an identifiable payoff; the three endings differ in type and in price, and the differences are motivated by the sequence; lengths are proportionate to weight; at least one break is placed somewhere other than the obvious joint, defensibly Names each ending type and placement strategy and defends them against the alternatives it tried; identifies its own risks; engages Dames or the serial history critically rather than decoratively; assesses what the sequence does that no single chapter does Merit Propositions present; payoffs identifiable; some variety of ending type; lengths broadly proportionate; placements defensible if conventional Accurate self-analysis; substitution alternatives considered; some engagement with theory; risks acknowledged if not resolved Pass Chapters are complete units; endings are competent; variety limited; placements fall at the obvious joints throughout Describes the endings accurately; theory referenced but not applied; no evidence of alternatives having been tried Fail No statable proposition; endings arbitrary or uniformly cliffhung; length uniform by default; one or more failure patterns unrecognised Description without analysis; no engagement with the model; the sequence is not treated as an object

title: 13. Glossary
text: Articulated time — This chapter’s term for an experience the chapter can produce: reading divided into intervals with edges, so that a life or a history is felt as a sequence of episodes. §3.1 . Capitulum / kephalaion — Latin and Greek for a “little head”: terms for textual divisions and headings used, among other purposes, as finding aids. The chapter’s ancestor. §3.1 . Chapter architecture — The pattern a book’s breaks and larger divisions make as a whole, considered as an object of design. §6.6 . Chapter break — A structural boundary placed deliberately within the stream of scenes and sequels, whose position determines what a reader carries with them if they stop. §2.1 . Cliffhanger — An ending on visibly unresolved danger or crisis. The most expensive exit available and the fastest to fatigue. §4.1 . Closural allusion — Herrnstein Smith’s term for content that signals ending by association: night, sleep, departure, death, silence. Free closure, and dangerous for that reason. §3.5 , §8.10 . Echo close — An ending on a resonant image, gesture or line, carrying thematic rather than plot charge. §4.4 . Event boundary — In cognitive psychology, the point at which a perceiver segments continuous experience into a new event; marked by a measurable processing cost. §3.6 . Feuilleton — A serial novel printed in a French newspaper, often in a lower-page section. Its instalment breaks may differ from its chapter breaks. §3.3 , §9.3 . Intertitle — Genette’s term for the title of an internal division: a chapter or Part title. §3.4 . Number (part-issue) — A physical instalment of a serially published Victorian novel, typically thirty-two pages and three or four chapters. Often the real unit of design. §3.3 , §9.1 . Number plan (the “mems”) — Dickens’s surviving working notes for each monthly number, showing chapter allocation and scheduled withholding. §3.3 , §9.1 . Offered exit — This chapter’s term for the chapter break considered functionally: an opportunity to stop, whose price the writer sets. §2.1 , §3.7 . Payoff — What a chapter’s ending does with its proposition: resolve, escalate, hold open, re-interpret, or exchange. Inherited by Chapter 16 ( The Ending ). §6.3 . Permission to stop — The chapter’s first principle: every break offers the reader an exit, and the final sentence sets its price. §3.7 . Pivot — An ending on a reveal or turn that sends the reader forward with new urgency. §4.3 . Placement strategy — Where a cut falls relative to the six beats of scene and sequel. Twelve are tabulated at §6.4 . Principle of proportion — Chapter length, relative to neighbouring chapters, is read as a claim about tempo. §5.1 . Proposition — The question, tension or intention a chapter raises at or near its start. §6.3 . Question close — An ending that raises a statable question without the danger a cliffhanger implies; a curiosity instrument rather than a suspense one. §4.5 . Recasting close — Proposed in this chapter. An ending whose final sentence changes the meaning of the chapter just concluded rather than pointing forward, so that the reader looks back. §4.6 . Segmentation — The division of a continuous text into units. Dames’s central category, and the chapter’s subject. §3.1 . Soft landing — An ending on a settled, resolved beat, making the exit free. The type that makes the others legible. §4.2 . Zeigarnik effect — The finding that interrupted tasks are recalled better than completed ones; the usual psychological explanation of the cliffhanger, with a mixed replication record and heavy moderation by motivation. §3.6 .

title: 15. Further Reading
text: Annotated and grouped by what each source is good for . Starred items are the recommended first three. 15.1 On the chapter itself ★ Dames, Nicholas. The Chapter: A Segmented History from Antiquity to the Twenty-First Century (2023). A major book-length study of the subject and a foundation for this chapter. Read it for the argument that segmentation is a technology with a history, and for its attention to what happens to a reader in the interval between units. Its literary chapters — on Fielding, Sterne, Austen, Dickens, Eliot, Tolstoy and their twentieth-century successors — are also the best available anthology of chapter endings analysed as chapter endings. Not a craft book, and better for it. Dames, Nicholas. “The Chapter: A History” ( The New Yorker , 2014). The argument in a few thousand words. The right thing to assign undergraduates before the book. Genette, Gérard. Paratexts (1997). The chapter on intertitles is short and indispensable. Read it with a contents page of Vanity Fair open beside it. 15.2 On serial publication and the commercial shaping of form ★ Hughes, Linda K., and Michael Lund. The Victorian Serial (1991). The standard account, and the most directly useful book on this list for anyone publishing in instalments. Its central move — treating the interval between parts as part of the work rather than as an interruption of it — is the one modern craft writing has failed to absorb. Butt, John, and Kathleen Tillotson. Dickens at Work (1957). Old, unsurpassed, and built on the number plans. Read the chapters on Dombey and Son and Bleak House for what a working novelist’s structural planning actually looked like. Stone, Harry, ed. Dickens’ Working Notes for His Novels (1987). The documents themselves. Worth an hour with a facsimile page simply to see how little of it is prose and how much is scheduling. Patten, Robert L. Charles Dickens and His Publishers (1978). The commercial history. Useful as a corrective to any account that treats the serial format as an artistic choice. 15.3 On closure and the shape of endings ★ Smith, Barbara Herrnstein. Poetic Closure (1968). About poems, and the best available account of how endings work at any scale. The concepts of closural allusion and terminal modification are directly usable on chapter endings and are used throughout §4 . Kermode, Frank. The Sense of an Ending (1967). For the tick-tock, and for the argument that readers impose shape on duration. Short and permanently in print for a reason. Brooks, Peter. Reading for the Plot (1984). For narrative desire and the dilatory space. The chapters on plot’s dynamics explain what a break is doing to a reader’s want better than any craft manual. Torgovnick, Marianna. Closure in the Novel (1981). Chapter 16’s principal source, and worth reading alongside this chapter for the typology of closural strategies, which applies at chapter scale with almost no adjustment. 15.4 On what readers do at a boundary Zacks, Jeffrey M., et al. “Event Perception: A Mind-Brain Perspective” (2007). The clearest statement of event segmentation theory. Technical, but the first ten pages are readable by anyone and change how you think about where to cut. Zwaan, Rolf A., and Gabriel A. Radvansky. “Situation Models in Language Comprehension and Memory” (1998). The dimensions readers track, and the costs of shifting them. Used throughout Part II of this textbook. Emmott, Catherine. Narrative Comprehension (1997). Contextual frames; the best account of what a reader releases at a break and has to rebuild afterwards. On the Zeigarnik effect , read Zeigarnik’s 1927 paper in translation alongside Van Bergen’s Task Interruption (1968). The pairing is a good lesson in how a psychological finding becomes a craft slogan. 15.5 On counting Moretti, Franco. Graphs, Maps, Trees (2005). The case for quantitative literary history, and the licence for §5.4 . Short, argumentative, and worth reading even if the conclusions do not persuade. The Stanford Literary Lab pamphlets. Freely available, uneven, and occasionally revelatory. A good model for the kind of small empirical study a student can run on chapter lengths in an afternoon. 15.6 Craft manuals, used critically Swain, Dwight V. Techniques of the Selling Writer (1965) and Bickham, Jack M. Scene & Structure (1993). The source of the six-beat model on which the placement taxonomy at §6.4 depends. Mechanistic and dated in idiom; structurally sound, and the only craft writing that treats the relation between scene shape and cut placement seriously. Forster, E. M. Aspects of the Novel (1927). For pattern and rhythm — the closest the older criticism comes to what §5 calls proportion. Yorke, John. Into the Woods (2013). For act structure and its relation to segmentation, from a television perspective; useful for §10.5 . 15.7 Within this textbook Chapter 1 ( The Purposes of a Scene ) — the value shift, and the principle of multiplicity applied to the final sentence. Chapter 2 ( Scene and Sequel ) — the six beats that the placement taxonomy at §6.4 uses as coordinates. Read §6.4 with Chapter 2 open. Chapter 5 ( The Transition ) — how the gap is crossed. This chapter’s test 8 hands over to it directly, and its §6.6 tabulates the typographic marks. Chapter 13 ( The Viewpoint Shift ) — placement strategy 11 considered as a focalisation decision rather than as a cut. Chapter 14 ( The Subplot ) — the alternation of threads across breaks, and the attention tax that alternation spends. Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages ) — the first chapter break is where the opening’s contracts get their first test. Chapter 10 ( The Prologue ) — the prologue as a segmentation decision. Chapter 16 ( The Ending ) — which inherits proposition and payoff, and for which every chapter ending in the book has been a rehearsal.

title: 16. Coda: Against Mechanical Application
text: Everything in this chapter is an instrument for noticing. None of it is a rule, and the chapter contains its own evidence for that claim. Middlemarch ends almost every chapter softly and would fail the variety test in most of its Books. Moby-Dick violates the proportion principle so comprehensively that a manuscript following its practice would be returned unread, and is one of the great segmented works in the language. The Count of Monte Cristo uses many unresolved turns, though their effect changes with reading schedule. One Hundred Years of Solitude has no architecture for a reader to hold on to and is architecturally perfect. Don Quixote contains the most flagrant false cliffhanger ever printed. Tristram Shandy is a four-hundred-page demonstration that the whole apparatus is a convention. A model that rules these out has not found a defect in them; it has found its own edges. But the deeper argument of this chapter is not the usual one about exceptions. It is historical, and it is stated plainly here at the end. The chapter is roughly two thousand years old, and it has meant several different things. It has early uses as a retrieval device, helping a reader find passages in long texts. Some divisions were made by editors, scribes and scholars; others were authorial. Headings sometimes summarised what followed. Only in the last three centuries, and decisively in the last two, has it become what a contemporary novelist assumes it to be: an instrument for shaping a reader’s experience of time, a place to leave someone hanging, a unit of tempo, an offered exit with a price. Even that recent meaning is not one thing. The chapter of the monthly part-issue and the chapter of the paperback thriller share a name and almost nothing else. A monthly instalment ending had to sustain interest across a publication gap; a chapter ending inside that instalment did not have the same job. The paperback thriller can be read without a scheduled wait. Both are called chapters. Both are printed the same way. They are different tools. The practical consequence for a writer is exact: A novelist who treats the current form of the chapter as natural has mistaken a technology for a fact — and will therefore use it at only one of its settings. The whole repertoire is available. Titled chapters, summarising headings, mottoes, Parts with names, chapters of a paragraph, chapters of nine thousand words, chapters that are lists, chapters that are dialogue, blocks of chapters designed together as a number, and the refusal of chapters altogether. Every one of these has been used well by somebody, and every one of them is presently unfashionable enough to be nearly unused. A writer who knows the history has more instruments than a writer who knows the convention. What the model in §§4–8 does reliably is convert a vague dissatisfaction into a specific question. This chapter doesn’t land becomes: there is no proposition here , or the payoff resolves what should have been held , or this is the fourth expensive exit in a row and the reader has stopped believing me , or the real boundary was two pages ago . Specific questions can be answered. Vague ones can only be worried at. And beneath all of it is a fact about reading that no taxonomy reaches. A chapter break is the point at which a book stops being something the reader is inside and becomes an object in their hands that they may set down. Everything a novelist does at that boundary is an attempt to make the setting-down matter — to ensure that the interval, however long, is time in which the book continues to exist. Which suggests one last test, to be applied after the other ten: What is this book doing while it is closed? If the answer is nothing , the ending was free and should have been. If the answer is waiting, in the reader’s head, with something unfinished in it , the price was set deliberately, and the writer knows what they are doing.

title: Backstory and Flashback
text: Earning the Cutaway: The Past Inside the Present Narrative — Theory, Analysis and Practice The Craft Behind the Story (Second Edition), Reference — Chapter 7. Part II: The Joins. The third chapter of Part II. A companion to the chapters on the scene, the sequel, dialogue, detail, the transition, the chapter break, the opening pages, the prologue, the viewpoint shift and the ending. All illustrative passages are quoted briefly for the purposes of criticism and study; full citations appear in §14 . Where a work is discussed in translation, the translator is named. Both structural details and verbal texture should be checked against the edition used; translations can preserve broad sequence while changing emphasis and rhythm. Contents On this page: Chapter Abstract · Learning Outcomes · Key Terms · How to Use This Chapter Introduction: The Cost of Leaving the Present Definitions and Boundaries Why the Past Is Expensive — the theory section The Domains of Purpose — five, and a proposed sixth Multiplicity: The Economy of the Cutaway Choosing the Register of the Past Diagnostic Method — the ten tests Failure Patterns — with their exceptions Worked Analyses — eight close readings and a revision case The Cutaway Across Forms · Concordance: concept to novel Revision Checklist Studio Work — exercises, seminar questions, assessment rubric Glossary Sources Cited Further Reading Coda: Against the Tyranny of Forward Motion Chapter Abstract A narrative that leaves its present moment to visit an earlier one performs the most conspicuous manoeuvre available to prose fiction. It suspends a question the reader wanted answered, asks them to hold that question in memory, transports them backwards across a temporal gap, and then requires them to return. Every part of that sequence costs something. This chapter formalises the cost, names what can be bought with it, and sets out the choices available once the decision to leave has been made. It proceeds in four movements: Theory — when a backward movement in narrative time can create structural and cognitive demands, drawing on Gérard Genette’s analysis of anachrony (the chapter’s spine), Meir Sternberg’s account of expositional distribution and of curiosity as distinct from suspense , Paul Ricoeur’s and A. A. Mendilow’s treatments of narrative time, the psychology of temporal shift in discourse comprehension, contested trauma-studies accounts of a past resistant to sequential narration, and the distinct histories of literary retrospection and film flashback conventions. Taxonomy — the five domains a cutaway can serve (plot, character, theme, texture, reader knowledge), each anatomised in terms of its textual carriers and its characteristic under- and over-delivery, together with a proposed sixth: the structural domain , in which the cutaway is used as an architectural device rather than for its content. Method — the principle of multiplicity applied to the past; the backstory/flashback fork and the one-sentence compression check that resolves it; a taxonomy of fourteen registers of the past , from the single subordinate clause of implication to the reconstructed testimony of Absalom, Absalom! ; a taxonomy of triggers and returns; and a ten-test diagnostic protocol for revision. Application — twelve failure patterns, each paired with a published work that commits the fault and succeeds; eight close readings of published cutaways; a full revision case worked on the series’ running example; and an apparatus of exercises, glossary, sources and further reading. The chapter’s governing claim is stated as a debt: Every cutaway begins in deficit. Leaving a present-tense question spends interest the narrative has already accumulated, and the past material must buy that interest back — not merely be interesting in itself. The claim is deliberately harsh, and §3.9 and §16 both qualify it, because it assumes that the present-tense question is the primary source of a reader’s engagement. That assumption is accurate for most plot-driven fiction and false for a substantial tradition of admired writing — Proust, Faulkner, Ford, Morrison, Ishiguro — in which the past is not an interruption of the story but its subject. A chapter that cannot say so has mistaken a local convention for a law. A note on the examples. The illustrative works are chosen for what they demonstrate. A concordance mapping each concept to the novel that best displays it appears at §10.6 . The Core chapter adds post-2000 fiction and screen cases, listed in §14.6. Learning Outcomes By the end of this chapter, a student should be able to: Distinguish backstory from flashback as two registers of the same material, and explain why the choice between them is felt by readers who could not name it. Apply Genette’s apparatus of anachrony — analepsis and prolepsis, reach and extent, external, internal and mixed, completing and repeating — to any passage of retrospective narration, and explain what each distinction predicts about cost. Explain , with reference to at least three theoretical or empirical sources, why a backward movement in narrative time imposes a processing cost that a forward movement does not. Identify which of the five domains a given cutaway serves, assess whether it serves more than one, and argue for or against the proposed sixth. Select an appropriate register of the past from the fourteen tabulated in §6.4 , and defend the choice against at least two alternatives by substitution. Diagnose a draft cutaway using the ten-test protocol, producing a prioritised revision plan rather than a verdict. Recognise the failure patterns by mechanism rather than by surface feature, and articulate the conditions under which each supposed fault is the correct choice. Evaluate the limits of the deficit model, including its assumption that forward motion is the default state of narrative, and the traditions of fiction for which that assumption is inverted. Key Terms Cutaway · backstory · flashback · anachrony · analepsis · prolepsis · reach · extent · first narrative · external / internal / mixed analepsis · completing analepsis · repeating analepsis · ellipsis · paralipsis · iterative narration · the interest deficit · delayed and distributed exposition · curiosity (as distinct from suspense) · involuntary memory · rememory · belatedness · trigger · return · register of the past · the structural domain Full definitions appear in the Glossary ( §13 ). Terms are bolded on first substantive use. How to Use This Chapter Reader Route Purpose Student in a seminar §§1–6 in order, then §9 , then §12 Conceptual grounding, worked demonstration, guided practice Writer in revision §6.3 (the fork) → §7 (diagnostics) → §8 (failures) → §11 (checklist) Fast triage of a live cutaway Teacher or workshop leader §4 , 6.4, 8, 9 for material; §12.1 for assignments; §12.3 rubric Ready-made teaching sequence with published models A caution before beginning, and it matters more in this chapter than in most. The instruments below — six domains, fourteen registers, ten tests, twelve failure patterns — are calibrated against a particular craft convention: the scene-based flashback with a motivated trigger and a clean return. Film has developed related conventions, but a direct origin in cinema has not been established ( §3.8 ). Applied to In Search of Lost Time , to Absalom, Absalom! , or to the interpolated tale in Don Quixote , most of them return the answer fail . That is information about the instruments, not about the books. The proper output of every test in this chapter is a question, not a verdict.

title: 1. Introduction: The Cost of Leaving the Present
section: Introduction — The Cost of Leaving the Present
text: 1.1 Two temporal movements Consider two movements in narrative time, each of one paragraph’s length, in the same novel. In the first, the narrative moves forward : a scene ends, white space intervenes, and the next paragraph begins three weeks later. The reader adjusts to a new time and may have to update the situation model; pending questions can remain open, be answered, or lose their urgency. In the second, the narrative moves backward : mid-scene, with a question hanging — will she open the drawer, will he answer, does the key fit — the paragraph steps eleven years into the past. Now the reader must do three things at once. They must suspend the pending question rather than resolve it, holding it in memory at some cost. They must build a second situation — a different place, different ages, different people present — while the first remains live. And they must file the new material against the old, since past material acquires its meaning only in relation to the present it explains. These movements can create different narrative obligations, depending on what each passage interrupts and promises. A backward cutaway may suspend one situation and open another before returning; a forward jump can also require substantial reorientation. Call the craft question of managing that interruption the cutaway problem . Backstory and flashback need a chapter of their own because they offer distinct ways to present antecedents, not because a general cognitive ranking of backward and forward shifts has been established. There is also a useful revision question. A cutaway to 1971 invites the reader to ask why this earlier material matters here. A forward gap can invite a comparable question when it skips an event the reader expected to see. In either direction, the placement should reward the attention it asks for. 1.2 The claim in its strong form Every cutaway starts in debt. Leaving a present-tense question spends the interest the narrative has accumulated, and the past has to buy it back. Being interesting is not the same as being owed. The metaphor of interest as an account will be used throughout, and it is worth being exact about what it does and does not claim. It does claim that reader attention at any given moment is a finite quantity, unevenly distributed across a book, and that its local supply is a function of the questions currently open. It does claim that the debt is positional as well as qualitative . The same past material, moved to a lower-pressure moment in the present timeline, may cost almost nothing. A great deal of what is diagnosed in workshops as a bad flashback is a well-made flashback in the wrong place. This is the model’s most useful practical consequence, because it turns a rewrite into a move, and it is developed as test 8 in §7.1 . It does not claim that the past is unwelcome, or that fiction should minimise it. Some of the most durable novels in the language are almost entirely retrospective. It does not claim that the debt must be repaid immediately . A cutaway may run a deficit for pages, and settle it in one line on the return; a novel may run a deficit for its whole length and settle it in the last chapter. It does not apply at all in the form stated to books whose present timeline is deliberately the thinner of the two. For those, the metaphor inverts, and §3.9 and §16 say how. 1.3 Where this chapter sits in the series Three neighbouring chapters share a border with this one, and the borders need marking, since the commonest error in teaching this material is to run all three together. Chapter Owns This chapter owns Chapter 5 ( The Transition ) How a gap is crossed and the reader re-anchored: the orientation budget, hard cut and time-stamp, anchor and drift Whether to leave the present at all , and which register the past is delivered in once you have Chapter 6 ( The Chapter Break ) Where the gap is placed in the book’s segmentation The internal architecture of the material on the far side of a backward gap Chapter 10 ( The Prologue ) A separated unit before the main narrative, held to a higher bar because it precedes investment A separated passage inside the main narrative, held to a different bar because it interrupts investment The relation to Chapter 5 is the one students most often blur. A flashback requires a transition into it and a transition out of it, and both of those are Chapter 5’s material: the anchor after the gap, the drift when the anchor is deliberately delayed, the orientation budget spent on getting the reader from one side to the other. This chapter begins one step earlier and ends one step later. It asks whether the crossing should be attempted, what the far side should look like when you get there, and what condition the present must be in when you come back. The relation to Chapter 10 is a formal symmetry. A prologue and a flashback often contain the same material — an earlier event, dramatised, in another time. The difference is entirely positional, and the costs invert. A prologue arrives before the reader has invested in anything, and must therefore be interesting without accumulated context, as Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages ) describes. A flashback arrives after the reader has invested, and must therefore be worth more than the accumulated context it interrupts. The same two pages, moved from the front of the book into chapter nine, change from a unit that must generate interest to a unit that must justify spending it. This is why the manoeuvre catalogued at §8.11 — cutting a prologue on advice and reinserting it later as a flashback, unchanged — fails so reliably: the material has been moved across a boundary where the criteria reverse. Two further dependencies carry forward from earlier chapters: A flashback is a scene, and Chapter 1 ( The Purposes of a Scene ) still applies to it in full. Someone wants something, meets resistance, and the situation is different at the end. A cutaway that is called a flashback but contains no want, no resistance and no change is not a flashback; it is backstory with scenery, and §6.3 will show how to detect this in one operation. The four domains of Chapter 1 — plot, character, theme, texture — are the base taxonomy of this book , and Chapter 1 proposes a fifth, the relational domain. Chapter 3 ( The Dialogue Exchange ) adopts it; Chapter 4 ( The Descriptive Detail ) adds the world and audits relations under character, as this chapter also does; this chapter adds reader knowledge , because the cutaway’s most distinctive power is control over what the reader knows and when .

title: 2. Definitions and Boundaries
text: Craft discussion in this territory is unusually loose. “Flashback” is applied indifferently to a two-page dramatised scene, to a sentence in the past perfect, to a character’s spoken reminiscence, and to a whole novel’s retrospective design. Since these have different lengths, different costs and different failure modes, the chapter begins by separating them. 2.1 The unit under study Working definition. A cutaway is any passage in which the narrative leaves the temporal position of its present action to present material from an earlier point in the story’s chronology. It has two principal registers. Backstory is the past told — conveyed by summary, implication, report or dialogue, without the reader being required to live through it. Flashback is the past dramatised — a scene in its own right, rendered moment by moment, and subject to every rule that governs a scene. Four elements of that definition need emphasis. “The temporal position of its present action.” Genette’s term for this is the first narrative ( §3.1 ), and the chapter uses it throughout. Everything called past here is past relative to that reference point, not relative to the reader or to history. “Register.” The distinction between backstory and flashback is not a distinction between two kinds of content. It is a distinction between two ways of delivering the same content, and it is the chapter’s central craft decision ( §6 ). “Earlier point in the story’s chronology.” Movements in the other direction — prolepsis , the flash-forward — are the cutaway’s formal mirror, and are treated at §3.3 and as register 14 in §6.4 , but they are not this chapter’s main subject. “Any passage.” The definition deliberately includes the single subordinate clause. A great deal of a novel’s past is delivered in units too small to be noticed as cutaways at all, and one of this chapter’s practical arguments is that those units are usually underused ( §6.4 , registers 1–4). 2.2 Scale and extent Cutaways range over four orders of magnitude, and advice calibrated to one scale is frequently misapplied to another. Scale Typical length Reader’s experience Governing question The implication A clause; a phrase Barely registered as a departure Is the fact needed here ? The report A sentence to a paragraph A brief change of pitch Told or shown? ( §6.3 ) The scene 300–3,000 words A full temporal relocation Does it earn the suspension? The structure A whole strand of the book The past as a second timeline Is the architecture declared? ( §4.6 ) The chapter treats the third scale as primary, because it is where the craft decisions carry the most weight and where drafts most often go wrong. But the arithmetic of the other three matters. A novel that delivers its past exclusively at the third scale has, in effect, decided that everything the reader needs about the past deserves a scene — which is almost never true, and produces the bloat diagnosed at §8.4 . A useful rule of thumb, offered as a starting position and not a law: the past should be delivered at the smallest scale that does the job, and the burden of proof rises with the scale. A clause needs no justification. A paragraph needs to be the right paragraph. A scene needs an argument. A second timeline needs a structural reason ( §4.6 ). 2.3 The term most often confused: exposition Backstory and flashback are frequently equated with exposition , and the equation causes trouble in both directions. Exposition, in Sternberg’s precise usage ( §3.4 ), is the category of information a narrative must convey about its antecedents in order for the present action to be intelligible: who these people are, what the situation is, what has already happened. It is a category of content, distributed across a book, and it is not confined to the past — exposition can concern a present state of affairs (the layout of the house, the rules of the world) that no cutaway is needed to convey. Backstory and flashback are two of the several delivery mechanisms available for expositional content. The others include dialogue, description, the character’s habitual behaviour, documents, and the reader’s inference from an unexplained detail — this last being the mechanism Chapter 9 §4.4 calls normalisation . The practical consequence can be stated as a rule, because it removes a great deal of confusion in revision: Not all exposition is backstory, and not all backstory is exposition. A cutaway can deliver material the plot does not require at all — an ironic rhyme, a change of texture, a recalibration of sympathy — and much of the past a reader needs is best delivered without any cutaway whatsoever. The second half of that rule is the more useful. Writers who have been told their backstory is heavy typically respond by compressing it, when the more effective move is often to relocate it out of the cutaway register entirely: into an object, a habit, a way of speaking, an unremarked assumption. Chapter 4 ( The Descriptive Detail ) treats this at length under the heading of connotation; the ledger in the series’ running example carries eleven years of a man’s history without a single sentence of retrospect. 2.4 Adjacent terms Term Meaning Relation to the cutaway Anachrony Genette’s general term for any discordance between the order of the story and the order of the telling The genus; analepsis and prolepsis are its two species Analepsis Narration, after the fact, of an event earlier than the present point of the narrative The formal name for what this chapter calls a cutaway Prolepsis Narration in advance of an event that will occur later The mirror manoeuvre; §6.4 , register 14 Ellipsis A stretch of story time passed over in silence What a completing analepsis later fills ( §3.3 ) Paralipsis The omission of information a narrative’s own vantage should have supplied A lateral gap rather than a temporal one; typically the material of a late revelation Frame narrative A first narrative whose principal function is to occasion and contain another The limit case of the embedded tale ( §6.4 , register 6); see also Chapter 10 Retrospective narration A whole narrative told from a position after its events Not a cutaway: the past is the first narrative here Memory A character’s mental act of recalling A frequent motivation for a cutaway, and not a synonym for one Exposition Information about antecedents needed for the present to be intelligible A category of content; the cutaway is one delivery mechanism (§2.3) Flashforward Popular term for prolepsis Avoid in analysis; it obscures the reach/extent distinction Two of these deserve a further sentence. Retrospective narration is the case that most often confuses students. Great Expectations , The Remains of the Day and The Good Soldier are all narrated from a position later than most of their events; but in Great Expectations the childhood is the first narrative and the older Pip’s vantage is a layer of commentary upon it, whereas in The Remains of the Day the 1956 motoring trip is the first narrative and the 1920s and 1930s are analepses within it. The distinction is not a technicality. It determines what counts as an interruption of what, and therefore where the deficit falls. Memory is the other. A character remembering is a psychological event that a narrative may report; it is not the same as the narrative departing to render the remembered thing. A novel can say she remembered the argument about the pen — an event in the present, taking one clause — or it can leave the present and stage the argument. The first is backstory about a memory; the second is a flashback. Conflating them is the source of the drafting habit whereby every cutaway must be introduced by a character visibly remembering, which §6.6 identifies as the weakest available trigger. 2.5 What this chapter excludes The mechanics of crossing the gap — the anchor, the drift, the orientation budget, the technique-fit question — belong to Chapter 5 ( The Transition ), and this chapter cross-refers rather than duplicating. §6.6 handles only what is specific to a backward crossing: what motivates it, and what state the present must be in on return. Separated units preceding the main narrative belong to Chapter 10 ( The Prologue ). §8.11 treats only the failure that occurs when such a unit is relocated inside the narrative without being rewritten. Shifts of viewpoint belong to Chapter 13 ( The Viewpoint Shift ). A cutaway to a past scene the present viewpoint character did not witness is doing two things at once, and the viewpoint half of the problem is Chapter 13’s. Whole retrospective structures at book scale — the frame narrative, the memoir novel — are treated here only insofar as they bear on the question of the first narrative ( §3.1 ) and on the structural domain ( §4.6 ). Endings that reinterpret the past belong to Chapter 16 ( The Ending ). The line quoted in the series’ running example is planted in Chapter 10’s material and lands in Chapter 16’s; this chapter owns the middle term.

title: 3. Why the Past Is Expensive
text: Section 1 asserts that a cutaway begins in debt. The assertion is correct, but it is a metaphor, and a metaphor is not an argument. This section assembles the argument from six directions — formal, rhetorical, philosophical, cognitive, psychoanalytic and historical — because a writer who understands why a backward movement costs revises it more intelligently than one who has merely been told that it does. The section ends by restating the deficit principle and then qualifying it, since the qualification is where the more interesting teaching lies. 3.1 Genette: the first narrative, and the measurement of anachrony The indispensable apparatus is Gérard Genette’s, set out in Narrative Discourse (1972; English translation by Jane E. Lewin, 1980) — the work of narratology this chapter draws on most, and the one whose vocabulary craft teaching reproduces in a rough and unacknowledged form. Genette’s opening move is to separate the order in which events occur in the story from the order in which the narrative presents them. Any discordance between the two he calls anachrony . Anachrony is not an occasional ornament; it is, as Genette observes, so nearly universal in Western narrative that a strictly chronological telling is the marked case rather than the default. The Iliad opens in the tenth year of the war. The Odyssey opens with Telemachus, reaches Odysseus in Book V, and has him narrate Books IX to XII himself, in the past, at a feast. The decisive concept for a writer, and the one most often skipped in craft summaries, is the first narrative ( récit premier ). Anachrony is not measured against absolute chronology, or against the reader’s clock. It is measured against the temporal level the narrative has established as its principal one — the level to which the telling returns and against which everything else is felt as a departure. Without a first narrative there is no anachrony, only a sequence. Three consequences follow immediately, and all three are practical. A narrative must have a stable first level before a cutaway can be felt as a cutaway. This is the mechanism underlying the failure pattern at §8.6 : a flashback in chapter two arrives before the reader has consolidated a first narrative to depart from, so the departure is not registered as a departure. It reads instead as the book still deciding what it is. What counts as a departure depends on where the narrative has said its home is. In The Remains of the Day the home is a six-day motoring holiday in July 1956; in Great Expectations the home is Pip’s life from childhood forward. Identical retrospective material occupies opposite structural positions in the two books. A narrative can change its first level, and this is a large structural decision rather than a local one. Wuthering Heights effectively transfers its first narrative from Lockwood’s residence at Thrushcross Grange to Nelly’s chronicle, and then transfers it back for the ending ( §9.2 ). The transfer is what makes the novel’s shape unusual, and it is invisible to any analysis that treats the whole book as a single flat sequence. Genette’s two species of anachrony are analepsis — the evocation, after the fact, of an event earlier than the point in the story at which we currently stand — and prolepsis — narration in advance of an event that will come later. The term flashback nowhere appears in Genette’s system, and its absence is not fastidiousness. Analepsis names a relation between two positions in a narrative; flashback names a device with a particular twentieth-century shape (§3.8). The wider term catches things the narrower one misses: the single clause in the pluperfect, the parenthetical aside, the reference in dialogue to something that happened before the book began. 3.2 Reach and extent Genette’s two measurements of an anachrony are the most immediately usable part of his apparatus, and they are the part craft pedagogy most conspicuously lacks. Reach ( portée ) is how far the anachrony goes from the present moment of the first narrative — the size of the leap. Extent ( amplitude ) is how much story time the anachrony itself covers — the size of the visited territory. The two are independent, and every combination has a different profile. Short extent Long extent Short reach The recent single moment: yesterday’s argument, dramatised. Cheap; often the best available option, and underused Recent history summarised: the last six months of a marriage. Cheap but flattening; the natural home of summary Long reach The distant single moment: one afternoon, thirty years ago. The most expensive unit in the repertoire , and the one requiring the strongest justification The distant era: a childhood, a war, a family’s founding. Structurally a second book; usually requires the architecture of §4.6 Two observations that a working writer can use at once. The distant single moment is the costly case, and it is the one drafts reach for by reflex. A long reach requires the reader to build a whole context — different ages, a vanished place, a superseded set of relations — and a short extent gives them only one scene’s worth of material to build it from. The context is expensive and immediately discarded. This is the arithmetic behind the widespread and otherwise mysterious workshop suspicion of the childhood flashback ( §8.9 ). The suspicion is not about childhood; it is about the ratio of construction cost to occupancy. Reach can change during an anachrony, and the direction it changes in is a structural signal. An analepsis with a long reach and a long extent shortens its own reach as it proceeds, since it moves forward while the first narrative waits. Nelly Dean’s narrative in Wuthering Heights begins about thirty years before Lockwood’s present and closes the distance until it merges with it. A reader feels this as approach , and the feeling is one of the most reliable sources of momentum available inside a long cutaway — the past visibly coming to meet the present. Its absence is one reason a static, non-progressing flashback drags: nothing is closing. 3.3 The three distinctions that determine cost Genette subdivides analepsis further, and three of the subdivisions do real diagnostic work. First: external, internal and mixed. Type Definition What it can do External analepsis Lies entirely before the starting point of the first narrative Supplies antecedents. May still revise earlier reports or assumptions about this period Internal analepsis Falls inside the span of the first narrative Fills or revises material the narrative has already passed through. Risks redundancy, and can produce interference with what was already told Mixed analepsis Begins before the first narrative and continues into it The characteristic shape of the long embedded chronicle; must manage the overlap The distinction is not academic. An external analepsis covers time before the main action, but it can still challenge a prior account of that time. An internal analepsis works in time the main action has already crossed and may repeat or revise what the reader was shown. A writer should know which kind they are writing and what the reader already believes about the period. Second, and within the internal case: completing versus repeating. A completing analepsis fills a gap — an ellipsis — that the narrative previously left open. It supplies something the reader knew was missing. A repeating analepsis returns to material the narrative has already covered, in order to recolour it. This distinction is the sharpest instrument in the chapter, and craft teaching rarely has a name for it. A completing analepsis is met by a reader who already has a slot for it. The question what happened in the eleven years between them? has been open; the material arrives as an answer. The deficit is small, because the reader was already carrying the question. In Sternberg’s terms (§3.4), the narrative has been generating curiosity and is now discharging it. A repeating analepsis has no slot waiting. The reader has been told this already, and is being asked to accept a second telling — which is only worth their time if the second telling differs : a new vantage, a new fact, a new emotional weight, a revealed lie. The deficit here is large, and the payment must be visible. The practical form of the distinction is test 9 in §7.1 . Its diagnostic value is high because it converts a vague complaint — this flashback feels redundant — into a determinate question with a determinate remedy. If the cutaway is completing, the remedy for a flat one is usually placement: bring it closer to the moment the reader most feels the gap. If it is repeating, the remedy is difference: identify what the second pass adds, and if nothing does, cut it. It also names the achievement of the two most ambitious novels in this chapter’s allocation. The Good Soldier and Beloved are both built almost entirely of repeating analepses — the same events returned to again and again — and both survive the enormous deficit that implies, because each return supplies a visibly different colouring. Ford’s Dowell revisits the Ashburnhams’ history a dozen times and each revisit corrects the last; Morrison’s narrative approaches the events at 124 repeatedly, from different consciousnesses, at different distances, and never twice in the same terms. Repetition is the most expensive structure in this chapter and the one that produces its greatest novels — which should be enough to warn any student against reading the cost model as a prohibition. Third: prolepsis, and its asymmetry with analepsis. Prolepsis is formally the mirror of analepsis. It can create a question about how a foreseen event will occur, just as an analepsis can answer a question about the past. Neither direction has a guaranteed advantage in attention or comprehension. García Márquez’s opening sentence in One Hundred Years of Solitude (trans. Gregory Rabassa) invokes a later firing squad and generates a question about how the narrative will reach it. An advance reference to a later event can open a question that a subsequent passage answers. Tolstoy achieves a related effect by a different structure in The Death of Ivan Ilyich : Chapter I begins after Ivan’s death, and Chapter II turns back to his life. Relative to the funeral frame, that long retrospect is an analepsis, not a prolepsis ( §9.8 ). 3.4 Sternberg: distribution, and curiosity as an engine Meir Sternberg’s Expositional Modes and Temporal Ordering in Fiction (1978) is the second pillar. Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages ) uses Sternberg at its own §6.2 to argue that exposition is a distribution problem rather than a location; this chapter takes the argument further into the territory Sternberg himself was most interested in. Sternberg’s three modes — preliminary (antecedents delivered up front), delayed (action first, antecedents later), and distributed (antecedents dispersed throughout, never gathered) — describe where a book’s expositional mass sits. The cutaway is the primary instrument of the second and third. The concept that matters most here is Sternberg’s distinction between the interests a narrative can generate: Interest Uncertainty about Generated by Discharged by Suspense The future An open situation moving towards outcome The outcome arriving Curiosity The past A visible gap in what the reader has been told Exposition supplied Surprise The past, retroactively A gap the reader did not know existed The gap opened and filled at once The consequence for this chapter is fundamental and reframes the whole deficit model: A well-placed cutaway does not merely spend interest. It discharges an interest of a different kind — one the narrative deliberately created earlier by withholding. This is why the deficit metaphor, taken alone, is too pessimistic. It treats the past as a pure cost against a present-tense credit. Sternberg’s account shows that a novel can manufacture the appetite its cutaway will satisfy, so that the cutaway arrives as payment rather than interruption. The reader who has been wondering since the drawer, half a book earlier, why a looser hand takes over the ledger on 9 March is not being interrupted when Dov’s chapter finally goes back to that evening; they are being paid. Three operational rules follow, and they are among the most useful in the chapter. Open the gap before you fill it. The cheapest cutaway in any novel is the one the reader has already asked for. A single earlier sentence establishing that something happened, without saying what, converts a later analepsis from an imposition into a discharge. Backstory withheld is an asset; backstory delivered is an expense. Chapter 9 states this rule for openings. Applied to the whole book, it becomes a scheduling principle: the question is not how much past a novel contains but when it spends it . Curiosity and suspense can be run simultaneously, and the strongest cutaways do. A flashback that answers a standing question about the past while raising a new question about the present is generating both interests at once. The worked example in §9.9 is of this kind: a four-line cutaway that answers why does she care about this pen and opens what did he think anyone would need to check . 3.5 Ricoeur and Mendilow: configured time and the novel’s discovery of it Genette describes the mechanism and Sternberg the economy. Paul Ricoeur’s Time and Narrative (three volumes, 1983–85; English translation by Kathleen McLaughlin and David Pellauer) supplies the reason the mechanism exists at all. Ricoeur’s argument, in the form relevant here, is that narrative is the mode in which human time becomes intelligible.
