A trigger that is too neatly apt — the woman looks at a broken clock and remembers the day time stopped for her — announces the machinery. The best triggers are slightly oblique: the object is connected to the memory by something private to the character, and the reader infers the connection rather than being handed it. The return The return is the least revised part of a cutaway and the one that settles its debt, and its requirement can be stated as a single rule. The present must be changed by the time the narrative comes back to it. Not merely resumed — changed, in a way the reader can locate. There are four kinds of change, and they are not equally strong. Kind of change Description Strength Changed knowledge The reader now knows something that recolours the present scene Weakest on its own; the change is in the reader, not the story Changed understanding The viewpoint character now understands something they did not Stronger; the character has moved Changed question The present scene now has a different question in it from the one it had before Strong; converts the cutaway from a pause into a turn Changed action The character does something different from what they were about to do Strongest; the cutaway has altered the plot The changed question is the most generally available of the four and the most underused. It requires nothing dramatic: the character simply comes back to the present with a question they did not have, which the present scene now has to carry. In the worked example at §9.9 , Nadia returns from four lines of the past holding a question about her father — what did he think anyone would need to check — that the scene in the flat did not contain before she went. Nothing has happened; everything has changed. On re-anchoring , and to avoid duplicating Chapter 5 ( The Transition ): the return needs an anchor as any transition does, and the anchor should generally be an element of the present the reader already has — the coat, the doorway, the object still in the hand. What is specific to the backward crossing is that the anchor may need to do less work than after a forward gap, because the reader never lost the present; they were holding it in suspension. Over-anchoring on the return — a full re-establishment of a scene the reader was in two pages ago — is the temporal equivalent of the throat-clearing bridge in Chapter 5 ( The Transition ), and it is common because writers correctly sense that a return needs marking and incorrectly conclude that it needs explaining. 6.7 Historical drift, and a caution against universalising the present The conventions governing the past in fiction have moved substantially, and a student should be able to historicise the advice in this chapter rather than receive it as timeless. Period Dominant handling of the past Classical epic The excursus and the character’s recital; the past fully illuminated, no suspended background (Auerbach, §3.8 ) Early modern prose The interpolated tale; the found manuscript; formal detachability taken for granted ( Don Quixote ) 18th century Documentary frames; the editorial apparatus; the biography-from-birth as the default shape ( Tom Jones , Tristram Shandy satirising it) 19th century Preliminary and summarised exposition; the narrator’s authority to supply antecedents directly; the long oral chronicle ( Wuthering Heights ); the genealogical opening Modernist Chronology dissolved; memory as psychological rather than calendrical (Proust, Ford, Faulkner, Woolf); Mendilow’s subject Mid-century to present Screen flashbacks and prose retrospection use varied conventions; marked entrances and returns are common in some forms Contemporary The braided dual timeline, common in commercial and literary fiction alike ( The Forgotten Garden , 2008; Where the Crawdads Sing , 2018); the past as a second book Two inferences follow, and they pull in different directions, which is the point. The prohibitions in §8 describe a craft convention. The requirement of a motivated trigger, the suspicion of nesting, the demand for a changed return and the hostility to the long recital are useful questions for some contemporary fiction. They are not facts about all narrative, and their precise genealogy in workshop and screen practice is not established here. And the works that violate them are not tolerated exceptions. Wuthering Heights nests several narrative levels. In Search of Lost Time uses a taste to recover an extended recollection of Combray. Absalom, Absalom! is largely reconstruction by people who were not there. The Remains of the Day makes its present timeline deliberately the thinner of the two. These books make their handling of the past central to their design. The properly critical position is therefore double, and identical in form to the one Chapter 9 reaches about openings: learn the current conventions well enough to break them deliberately, and read historically well enough to know that they are conventions.

title: 7. Diagnostic Method — the ten tests
text: 7.0 How to use the protocol The ten tests below are for revision, not composition . Applied during drafting they produce a writer who cannot put anything in the past without a permit; applied to a finished draft they are the most efficient triage instrument in this chapter. Five procedural notes, one of them specific to this chapter and important. Establish first whether the protocol applies to your book. §3.9 sets out the condition: the deficit model assumes the present timeline carries the engine. If your novel’s present is deliberately thin — a drive west, a night’s conversation, a man dying in a room — then tests 1, 3 and 8 will return failures that are not defects. Decide this once, before you begin, rather than discovering it test by test. A writer who applies the protocol to The Remains of the Day and concludes that it should be cut has not found a fault in the book. Run them in order. Tests 1–4 are structural; their answers determine whether the later tests are worth running. There is no point tuning a trigger on a cutaway that should be a sentence. Record the answer, not the verdict. The output of a test is a sentence describing what the cutaway does, not a pass or a fail. Run tests on the manuscript, not on the passage. Five of the ten (3, 7, 8, 9 and 10) cannot be answered by looking at the cutaway alone, which is the chief way this protocol differs from the one in Chapter 9. A failed test is a question. Every one of these tests is failed by at least one novel discussed in this chapter, most of them by several. 7.1 The ten tests Test 1 — The momentum test What present-tense question is the reader in the middle of wanting answered when this cutaway begins? Name it in a sentence. If no such question can be named, the timing is arbitrary rather than chosen. Note carefully what this test does and does not detect. It does not detect that the cutaway is badly placed; it detects that the placement was not a decision. A cutaway arriving at a moment of no present-tense pressure may be perfectly placed — that is often where a cutaway should go — but a writer who cannot say what the present question was has not chosen anything. The refinement that makes this test useful: rate the pressure of the named question on a three-point scale — low, moderate, at peak. Then compare with test 5. A cutaway interrupting a peak question needs a return proportionate to what it interrupted; a cutaway placed at a low-pressure moment is cheap and may be doing more than the writer credits. Test 2 — The register test Run the one-sentence compression check from §6.3 . Does this need to be felt, or only known? Write the compressed sentence out. Place it in the manuscript. Read forward two pages. The three possible answers are keep the scene , keep the sentence , and keep neither — and the third is the most common outcome in first drafts. Test 3 — The removal test Cut the cutaway entirely. Read the surrounding twenty pages. What is lost, and in which domain? The answer must name a domain from §4 and must be specific. “The reader wouldn’t understand her” is not an answer; “the reader would not know that she had asked him about the pen and been given an answer she did not understand at the time” is. If the loss cannot be located in any domain, the passage is decorative and the removal is the revision. A refinement worth adopting: perform the removal on paper , and leave it removed for a day before reading. Writers reading a passage they have just deleted supply it from memory. Test 4 — The trigger test Is the cutaway motivated by something concrete in the present scene — an object, a phrase, a sensation, a question asked, a place, a silence — or does it arrive as an unmotivated authorial jump? Consult the table at §6.6 . Then ask the second half of the test, which is the half that matters: if there is no trigger, is the narration of a kind that can afford to do without one? Confident omniscient narration and retrospective first-person narration can move into the past without motivation; close third-person narration usually cannot, because it has promised to stay inside a consciousness. An untriggered cutaway in close third is not breaking a rule about flashbacks; it is breaking the narration’s own contract. Test 5 — The return test Does the story return to the present changed, or does the present scene simply resume? Identify which of the four changes at §6.6 has occurred: changed knowledge, changed understanding, changed question, or changed action. If the answer is changed knowledge alone, the change is in the reader rather than in the story, and the cutaway is doing less than it appears to. The mechanical form of this test: cover the cutaway with a sheet of paper and read the last sentence before it against the first sentence after it. If they read continuously — if the second follows from the first as though nothing had intervened — the cutaway is untethered ( §8.5 ). Test 6 — The reach-and-extent test How far back does this go, and how much time does it cover? Are the two proportionate to what it delivers? The apparatus is at §3.2 . Record two numbers — years back, and story time covered — and place the cutaway in the four-cell table. The cell to interrogate is long reach, short extent : the distant single moment, which requires the reader to build a whole vanished context and then immediately discard it. A cutaway in that cell must be delivering something that could not have been delivered by a nearer moment. Very often the same character point is available from a memory five years old rather than thirty, at a fraction of the construction cost. Also record whether the reach shortens during the cutaway. A long analepsis that moves forward, closing the distance to the present, generates its own momentum; one that stays at a fixed distance does not, and will need to find momentum elsewhere. Test 7 — The chronology test Could a careful reader, at this point in the book, write out the story’s events in the order in which they occurred? This is the test built on Ohtsuka and Brewer’s finding ( §3.6 ) that readers reconstruct an underlying chronology from a non-chronological telling, and that they pay for the reconstruction. The procedure is literal: take a reader who has read to this point and ask them to produce a timeline. Then compare it with yours. Three outcomes, with three different diagnoses: Outcome Diagnosis The reader’s timeline matches yours The anachrony is legible; proceed The reader’s timeline has gaps in the places you intended Working as designed — those are Sternberg’s open questions The reader’s timeline has gaps you did not intend , or events in the wrong order The book has confused rather than withheld, and the two feel identical from inside the manuscript The third outcome is the one no amount of self-reading will reveal, which is why this test requires another person. Test 8 — The placement test Would this cutaway cost less thirty pages later? Or thirty pages earlier? The most productive single test in the protocol, and the one that most often produces a large improvement for a small edit. The deficit is positional ( §3.9 ): the same material at a different point in the present timeline may cost a fraction as much and pay considerably more. The procedure is to name three alternative locations and, for each, answer two questions: what present-tense question would be interrupted there, and what would the cutaway be able to recolour that it currently cannot? A cutaway placed after the present behaviour it explains recolours that behaviour; the same cutaway placed before it merely prepares for it. Consult the three-position table at §4.5 . A related and slightly brutal version of the test: would this material be better as a later revelation than as a present cutaway? Much of what drafts deliver as flashback in the second act is more valuable withheld until the third. Test 9 — The completing-versus-repeating test Is this cutaway filling a gap the reader knew was there, or returning to material already narrated? The apparatus is at §3.3 . The two answers carry different burdens. Completing. The reader had an open question. Check that the question was actually opened — that some earlier sentence marked the gap — and check the interval. A gap opened four hundred pages ago and filled now may have gone cold. Repeating. The reader has been here before. Name, in one sentence, what this pass adds that the previous one lacked : a new fact, a new vantage, a new emotional weight, a revealed lie. If nothing can be named, the passage is redundant ( §8.2 ). If something can, the pass is legitimate however many have preceded it. The test also catches a third case that neither category covers: a cutaway that is neither completing nor repeating because the reader had no relation to the material at all — no open question, no prior account. This is the pure informational cutaway, and it is almost always a candidate for compression (test 2). Test 10 — The proportion test Across the manuscript, how much of the book is in the past, and does the book’s shape acknowledge it? Run on the audit sheet from §5.5 . Count the pages. The number is not a verdict — there is no correct proportion. The bands below are prompts invented for this revision exercise, not ranges established by a study or rules for classifying novels . Ask whether the book’s declared structure makes sense of the amount of past material. Proportion of past material Question it raises Under 5% Is enough antecedent material available for the reader to understand the characters? 5–20% Does each return to the past serve the book’s present design? 20–40% Is a second temporal strand emerging, and is its role clear ( §4.6 )? Over 40% Would a more openly retrospective or dual-timeline structure serve this book better? A manuscript with a large proportion of past material may benefit from an openly retrospective or dual-timeline structure. That is a question to test against the manuscript, not a consequence of crossing a numerical threshold. The Remains of the Day shows one possible retrospective design. 7.2 Reading the results Failed tests Likely diagnosis First move 2 alone Over-dramatised backstory Compress to the sentence you wrote; check what the freed space allows 1 and 4 The cutaway is on the writer’s schedule, not the reader’s Test 8: find the placement where a present question already exists 3 alone Decorative past Cut. Do not attempt to add a function to material that has none 5 alone The untethered return ( §8.5 ) Rewrite the return sentence for a changed question, not a re-anchoring 6 alone Long reach, short extent; construction cost exceeds occupancy Find a nearer memory that makes the same point 7 alone Confusion mistaken for withholding Supply one date, or one clause of orientation. Usually a very small edit 8 alone Right material, wrong place Move it. This is the cheapest large improvement available 9 alone, repeating Redundancy Name the difference or cut the pass 10 alone The book’s proportions and its declared structure disagree Change the structure, not the proportions 1, 3 and 5 together The cutaway is not connected to the book Consider whether the material belongs to a different novel A warning about test 8. When a cutaway is not working, writers instinctively revise the cutaway , because it is the object in front of them. The passage is usually not the problem. In many of the cases this protocol catches (an estimate from drafts read, not a count), the material is sound and its position is wrong — and moving four hundred words is a smaller operation than rewriting them, with a larger effect.

title: 8. Failure Patterns
text: Each pattern below is presented with its symptom , its mechanism (what actually goes wrong, as distinct from what the surface looks like), its persistence (why competent writers keep producing it), its remedy , and — importantly — the exception : a published work that commits the fault and succeeds. The exceptions are not decorative. A pedagogy of prohibitions produces writers who can avoid faults and not writers who can make choices. Every pattern below fails because of a mechanism, not because of a surface feature, and where the mechanism is absent the surface feature is harmless. One exception in this section is unusually strong: Absalom, Absalom! builds a major part of its design from the apparently reductive childhood origin described in pattern 8.9. The madeleine episode in In Search of Lost Time is discussed under 8.1 because it clarifies the distinction between an involuntary memory and an absence of a trigger. 8.1 The Unmotivated Cutaway Symptom. The flashback simply starts. Nothing in the present scene occasioned it; the reader can locate no object, phrase, sensation or question that opened the door. Mechanism. The departure is legible as an authorial act rather than a narrative one. In close third-person or first-person narration this is a breach of the narration’s own contract, which has promised to remain inside a consciousness; a consciousness does not relocate to 1994 because the manuscript needs a fact delivered on page 112. The reader does not usually formulate the objection in these terms. They experience it as a loss of confidence — the sudden visibility of a writer making arrangements. Persistence. The information really is needed, and the writer really has reached the point where the reader needs it. The diagnosis is right and the prescription is wrong: the need is expositional, and the response is a scene. Remedy. Either supply a trigger ( §6.6 ) or move the cutaway to a location where a trigger already exists. Test 8. In practice the second is more often correct, because a trigger invented to justify a placement tends to be over-apt ( §5.4 ). The exception. In Search of Lost Time (1913–27) does not lack a trigger. The taste of a madeleine dipped in tea recalls a taste the narrator knew as a child at Combray. He cannot at first identify what the sensation is offering him and tries to recover it. The useful exception is narrower: a concrete sensory cue can occasion a memory without the character willing the recollection or knowing its meaning in advance. Involuntary memory differs from deliberate recollection, not from triggered recollection ( §9.1 ). The general principle the exception establishes: the trigger requirement is a device for keeping a close, character-bound narration honest. Where a narration has other sources of authority — a philosophical first person, a confident omniscience, a declared retrospective frame — the requirement lapses. Tolstoy needs no trigger; neither does Eliot; neither does the narrator of The Death of Ivan Ilyich , who simply announces that the life had been most ordinary and proceeds. 8.2 The Redundant Flashback Symptom. A dramatised past scene that tells the reader something they already knew, or could have inferred without difficulty. Mechanism. The passage delivers no new information and no new feeling, so the deficit is incurred against nothing. Note the “or new feeling”: a scene that confirms what the reader inferred can still be worth its place if it supplies weight the inference lacked. The failure is not repetition as such; it is repetition without difference ( §3.3 ). Persistence. Writers write the flashback before they write the present material that makes it redundant, and then cannot see the redundancy because they wrote the scene first and it feels foundational. This is the same mechanism as Chapter 9’s throat-clearing: composition apparatus retained in the finished text. Remedy. Test 9. If the cutaway is repeating, name what the second pass adds. If nothing can be named in one sentence, cut. If something can, ensure it is visible — the difference must be perceptible on a single reading. The exception. The Good Soldier (1915). Ford’s Dowell returns to the same handful of events — the visits to Nauheim, Florence’s behaviour, Edward’s affairs, the four-day sequence in which everything collapses — a dozen times or more. Almost every return is formally redundant: the reader has been told. The novel survives because each return is differently wrong . Dowell revises, retracts, discovers he has misunderstood, and lets slip something he had previously suppressed. The material is constant and the narrator is not , which converts repetition from waste into the book’s principal instrument ( §9.3 ). 8.3 The Momentum Killer Symptom. The cutaway arrives at the story’s most tense present moment and stops it, with a payoff that does not match the interruption. Mechanism. Tension is not preserved during an interruption; it is replaced . A reader given six pages of other material does not spend those pages holding the previous tension in reserve — they build a new engagement with the new material, and the old tension has to be restarted from a lower level on return. The suspension described at §3.6 is a cognitive fact about the frame, not an emotional fact about anticipation. Persistence. The technique of cutting away at peak tension to intensify it is real, taught, and works — at the right length. Chapter 2 ( Scene and Sequel ) and Chapter 5 ( The Transition ) both treat deferral as a legitimate device. The failure is a misjudgement of scale rather than of kind. Remedy. At peak tension, measure the interruption in sentences, not pages . If the material requires more than that, it is in the wrong place: test 8. The exception. The scar of Odysseus, Odyssey XIX. Eurycleia’s hand is on the scar; the recognition is a heartbeat away; Homer breaks off for some seventy lines to narrate the boar hunt that made it. This is the most conspicuous momentum killer in European literature, and Auerbach’s reading in Mimesis (1946; trans. Willard Trask, 1953) argues that it is not a suspense device at all — that Homer’s world has no background, that the excursus is fully illuminated rather than held in shadow, and that nothing is suspended while it runs. The exception therefore establishes something stronger than a licensed deviation: the momentum test presupposes a narrative mode in which foreground and background exist , and in a mode that lacks the distinction, the test has no object. A second and more modern exception: Hugo’s Waterloo in Les Misérables (1862), which opens the novel’s second part, in the middle of Jean Valjean’s story, with an extended historical account and is defensible on the ground that the book’s subject is the relation between individual lives and historical forces. Chapter 14 ( The Subplot ) treats the Hugolian digression as the limit case of its own device; considered here, it is a reminder that a book may decide its interruptions are its argument. 8.4 The Info-Dump Backstory Symptom. Paragraphs or pages of compressed history with no scene-level engine, read as a report rather than felt as consequence. A particular risk wherever worldbuilding or family history tempts a writer to deliver a whole system at once. Mechanism. Two failures, usually simultaneous, and both are the same as Chapter 9 §8.3 diagnoses for openings. First, per Sternberg ( §3.4 ), delivering exposition early spends an asset that would have generated curiosity. Second, information is not memorable without a container : a reader given a family’s four generations before they care about anyone in it has nowhere to store the material and will retain almost none of it, so the dump fails even on its own terms. Persistence. The writer knows the history intimately and fears the reader will be lost without it. The fear is real; the remedy is misdirected. The reader does not need to know the history; they need to believe the writer knows it, which is achieved by confident specificity rather than by explanation. Remedy. Convert into implication. Ask of each expository sentence: which character would say this, to whom, and why? Then attempt the material at registers 1 and 4 ( §6.4 ) — the clause of implication and the iterative habitual — before allowing it any more space. The exception. Père Goriot (1835). Balzac’s long accounts of the Maison Vauquer, of the pension’s economics, of each lodger’s antecedents, are info-dumps by any contemporary standard, and they are causal rather than decorative: the novel’s argument is that the lodgers are what the rent makes them, so the rent must be specified before the people can be understood. Chapter 9 §4.4 reads the same material as world-building in an opening; considered as backstory, it demonstrates that a novel with a determinist thesis needs the determinants on the page. Moby-Dick (1851) supplies the more extreme case. The cetology chapters are expositional mass with no scene-level engine whatever, placed at intervals through a chase narrative, and they are the reason the book is what it is rather than an adventure story. 8.5 The Untethered Return Symptom. The cutaway ends and the present scene resumes as though nothing had happened — no acknowledgement, no consequence, no visible change in what the character does next. Mechanism. The deficit is never discharged. The reader has paid the cost of the departure and receives nothing at the point where the payment was due. Note that the cutaway may have been perfectly good: an untethered return can follow an excellent flashback, and the fault lies entirely in one sentence. Persistence. The return is written last, when the writer’s attention has already moved to the next scene, and it is treated as a re-entry problem rather than as the cutaway’s payoff. Chapter 5’s vocabulary makes this worse rather than better: a writer thinking about anchors will produce a competent anchor and stop. Remedy. Test 5. Rewrite the first sentence after the cutaway to carry one of the four changes at §6.6 — preferably a changed question, which is available in nearly every case and requires no plot event. The exception. “El curioso impertinente”, the interpolated novella in Don Quixote , Part I. A complete separate story, read aloud at the inn, occupying three chapters, and returning the narrative to the state it was in — nothing in Don Quixote’s situation is altered by it. Cervantes was criticised for the interpolations in his own lifetime, replied to the criticism inside Part II, and largely abandoned the practice there. The case is instructive because it is contested: the untethered return was a recognised convention that ceased to be one , and Cervantes’s own change of practice is the clearest available evidence that this prohibition is historical rather than structural. 8.6 The Second-Chapter Flashback This pattern is added to the original five. Symptom. The novel leaves its present for an extended visit to the past before the end of the second chapter. Mechanism. Per §3.1 , anachrony is measured against a first narrative , and a first narrative that has not been consolidated cannot be departed from. The reader has not yet formed the model that the cutaway would interrupt, so the departure does not register as a departure — it registers as the book not having decided what it is. Worse, the reader has no basis for evaluating the past material, since its whole function is to bear on a present they do not yet possess. Persistence. The writer knows the past material is essential and delivers it at the first opportunity. This is also an artefact of drafting order: a writer who wrote the backstory first to understand their characters tends to place it early. Remedy. Delay. As a rule of thumb, the first substantial cutaway should follow the point at which the reader could describe the book’s present situation in a sentence. That is usually later than it feels. The exception. The Death of Ivan Ilyich (1886). Chapter I is the funeral; Chapter II opens the retrospect and the retrospect is the rest of the novella. The pattern is committed in its most extreme available form and the book is a masterpiece, for a reason that can be stated: Tolstoy consolidates the first narrative in a single chapter by making it complete. The funeral has a beginning, a middle and an end, a protagonist in Peter Ivanovich, a want (to get away to his card game), and a conclusion. There is a first narrative to depart from because Chapter I is a finished thing. Compare the usual draft version of this pattern, in which chapter one is an unfinished fragment of a scene and chapter two goes back — and note that the difference is not the location of the cutaway but the completeness of what precedes it ( §9.8 ). 8.7 The Nested Flashback Added. Symptom. A cutaway inside a cutaway: a character in a flashback remembers an earlier thing, which is dramatised. Mechanism. The reader must track two nested temporal levels ( §3.6 ) and eventually return through both. This can become confusing if the intermediate level is not established clearly before another begins. A possible symptom is that the return from the inner cutaway goes unnoticed and the reader mislocates the following passage. No measured “worse than double” cost is established here. Persistence. Nesting arises naturally from association: one memory produces another. The writer, who knows where they are, does not feel the load. Remedy. Flatten. Nearly all nested material can be delivered as a single-level cutaway, or as a clause of implication (register 1) inside the outer one. If both levels must be dramatised, mark the layers structurally — a section break, a change of register — rather than relying on tense alone, since the pluperfect cannot go deeper than one step in English without becoming unreadable. The exception. Wuthering Heights (1847) nests three and sometimes four deep: Lockwood’s diary contains Nelly’s chronicle, which contains Isabella’s letter and Zillah’s report, which contain further reported speech. Frankenstein (1818) does the same — Walton’s letters contain Victor’s narrative, which contains the creature’s, which contains the creature’s account of the De Lacey family’s history. Both are among the most durable novels in English. The mechanism of their success is identifiable and teachable: each layer is marked by a change of voice. Nelly does not sound like Lockwood; the creature does not sound like Victor. The reader tracks the level by the diction rather than by the tense, which removes the load entirely. This is a general lesson worth extracting: nesting fails when the layers are indistinguishable, not when they are numerous ( §9.2 ). 8.8 The Better Past Added. Symptom. The flashbacks are more vivid, more urgent and more interesting than the present timeline. Readers report that they liked the book but skimmed the modern sections. Mechanism. The writer’s imaginative investment is in the past material — which is often where the novel’s originating idea lived — and the present has been constructed as a delivery mechanism for it. Two consequences follow. Every cutaway now pays a positive return, so the diagnostic protocol reports success while the book fails. And the reader, having learned that the past is where the value is, begins reading the present as an obstacle. Persistence. It is invisible from inside, because each individual cutaway tests well. This is the failure the domain model is least able to detect, and the reason test 10 exists. Remedy. Two options, and they are two different books. Either strengthen the present until it can carry the book — which usually means giving the present timeline its own value shifts rather than only its own occasions for remembering — or accept the diagnosis and restructure : make the past the first narrative, and let the present become an explicit frame. The exception. The Remains of the Day (1989). Ishiguro’s present timeline is deliberately the thinner of the two, and its thinness is the point. Six days in July 1956 contain a broken radiator, a walk up a hill, a misunderstanding about a butler’s identity, a parting from Miss Kenton at a bus stop in the rain, and an evening on a pier — set against Lord Darlington’s appeasement, the dismissal of the Jewish maids, the death of Stevens’s father during a conference, and twenty years of a refused attachment. The disproportion is the novel’s argument: a life spent in service to another man’s importance has very little present left in it. The book is the definitive counter-case to this pattern, and the discriminating question it establishes is not is the present thinner? but does the book know it, and is the thinness saying something? ( §9.6 ). Wuthering Heights is the second case, and cruder: Lockwood is a fool, and his fatuousness in the frame exists so that the passion in the chronicle can be measured against it. 8.9 The Childhood-Explains-Everything Cutaway Added. Symptom. A single childhood scene, usually of humiliation, loss or a parental failure, offered as the origin of an adult character’s defining trait. Mechanism. Three faults at once. Structurally , it is the expensive cell of §3.2 — long reach, short extent — requiring the reader to build a whole vanished context for one scene’s occupancy. Psychologically , it proposes a hydraulic model of personality that readers do not believe, because it does not match their experience of anyone including themselves. And narratively , an explained character is a closed question: once the reader has the key, the lock stops being interesting. Persistence. It is what the craft phrase character motivation is usually taken to mean, and it is reinforced by a century of popular psychology and by screen conventions in which a single traumatic memory is the standard shorthand for interiority. Remedy. Prefer illumination to explanation ( §4.2 ). Move the material nearer: a recent memory usually makes the same point at a fraction of the construction cost, and does not carry the determinist implication. Where the childhood material must stay, deliver it in a register that does not claim causal authority — the iterative (register 4), which describes what was normal, or the clause of implication (register 1). The exception. Absalom, Absalom! (1936). Thomas Sutpen’s whole design — the land, the house, the sons, the ruthlessness — is traced to a single childhood scene in which a boy sent to the front door of a Virginia plantation is told by a liveried slave to go round to the back. This is the childhood-explains-everything cutaway in its purest and most schematic form, and the novel is one of the twentieth century’s great achievements. Two features make the difference, and both are transferable. The origin is reported, not narrated : it comes to the reader through Sutpen’s account to General Compson, relayed through Mr Compson to Quentin and thence to Shreve, so that what the reader receives is not the boy at the door but a man’s explanation of himself , at four removes, from people with reasons to believe it. And the novel treats the explanation’s very neatness as evidence — a design so completely accounted for by one afternoon is itself a symptom. Faulkner makes the reductiveness of the device the device’s subject , which is the only reliable way to use it. 8.10 The Italicised Memory Added. Symptom. Cutaways marked by typography rather than by construction: italics, indentation, a different font, a row of asterisks — for material that is otherwise indistinguishable from the surrounding narration. Mechanism. The typography is doing work the prose declined to do. Two costs follow. The reader is trained to recognise a category of passage rather than to feel a change in the narrative, which converts the past from an experience into a labelled section; and sustained italics are physically harder to read, so the marked passages are the ones the eye learns to skip. There is a third cost, subtler: typographic marking removes the writer’s incentive to solve the transition, so the entrances and exits go unwritten. Persistence. It is easy, it is unambiguous, and it looks like design. It is also common in published fiction, which supplies the writer with precedent. Remedy. Attempt the passage with the marking removed. If it is then unclear where the past begins, the prose has a real problem which the italics were concealing; solve it with tense, with a shift of register, or with a trigger. Restore the typography afterwards only if it is doing something the prose cannot. The exception. The Sound and the Fury (1929). Faulkner’s Benjy section uses italics among its cues for shifts between periods that Benjy experiences without a stable chronology. Typography helps the reader distinguish layers; it is not literally the only available signal, since scene content and recurring people also orient the reader. The useful craft question is whether the marking helps the reader follow a viewpoint whose temporal associations differ from the narrator’s. Beloved offers the more radical alternative: Morrison marks her deepest temporal and vocal shifts largely by changes in syntax and diction rather than by typography, and the shift is unmistakable without a single italic. 8.11 The Prologue Relocated Added. Symptom. A dramatised past scene, usually of two to four thousand words, sitting between chapters in the first third of the book, self-contained and tonally distinct — and identifiable, once you know to look, as a prologue that was moved. Mechanism. §1.3 sets out the reason. A prologue and a flashback can contain identical material and are governed by inverse criteria. A prologue must generate interest without accumulated context; a flashback must be worth more than the accumulated context it interrupts. Material written to satisfy the first criterion has been optimised for the wrong thing: it is self-sufficient, which means it does not connect; it establishes rather than recolours; and it has no trigger, because it never needed one. Persistence. The advice to cut a prologue is common and often correct, and a writer who has been given it reasonably concludes that the material should be preserved elsewhere. The move is made without rewriting because the passage is finished, and finished prose resists revision. Remedy. Do not move a prologue. Rewrite it as a cutaway , which usually means shortening it by two thirds, attaching it to a present-tense trigger, and changing its ending so that it hands something to the scene it is interrupting rather than concluding on its own. The exception. Season of Migration to the North (1966; trans. Denys Johnson-Davies). Mustafa Sa’eed’s life story — Khartoum, Cairo, London, the women, the killing, the trial, the prison years — is in effect a complete separate novel, and it is delivered not at the front of the book but into the middle of it, as a night-long confession to the narrator. Structurally it is a prologue relocated: self-contained, tonally distinct, longer than any surrounding unit. It works because the relocation is motivated by the present . The narrator has already been made curious; Mustafa has a reason for telling and chooses his moment; the telling is an event in the frame narrative, with consequences for the man who hears it. The general rule the exception establishes is that relocated material must be given an occasion inside the present — which is what a prologue, by definition, does not have ( §9.7 ). 8.12 The Undeveloped Repeat Added. Symptom. The novel returns several times to the same past period, and the returns are the same beat told again: the same tone, the same relationship, the same information at slightly different lengths. Mechanism. Distinct from §8.2 in that no single return is redundant — each supplies something — but the sequence has no direction. A reader who has been to a past period three times expects the fourth visit to go further, and a fourth visit that does not is felt as the book marking time. The underlying error is treating the past as a place to be revisited rather than as a sequence to be advanced. Persistence. Writers develop a strong relationship with one past period and return to it because it is where they are comfortable. The audit at §5.5 catches this in the reach column: a uniform reach across a manuscript means one era is doing all the work. Remedy. Order the returns and give the sequence a direction — chronological approach, escalating disclosure, or increasing proximity to a withheld centre. Then check that each successive return is closer to something than the last. The exception. Beloved (1987). Morrison returns to the events at 124 and to Sweet Home repeatedly, from Sethe, from Paul D, from Denver, from Stamp Paid, from Baby Suggs, at varying distances and in varying registers. The novel is built almost entirely from this manoeuvre. It works because the returns converge : each approach comes nearer to the centre than the last, so that the reader experiences a spiral rather than a circle, and the final full account arrives as the completion of a movement the whole book has been making. The distinction between a spiral and a circle is the whole of this pattern , and it is assessable in one operation: list the returns in order and ask whether they get closer to anything ( §9.5 ). 8.13 Summary: symptom to mechanism Pattern Underlying mechanism Domains damaged Test that catches it Unmotivated cutaway Departure legible as authorial rather than narrative All; the narration’s authority most of all 4 Redundant flashback Repetition without difference Reader knowledge; plot 9 Momentum killer Tension replaced rather than preserved Texture; plot 1, 10 Info-dump backstory Information delivered without a container Plot; character; texture 2, 3 Untethered return Deficit never discharged All 5 Second-chapter flashback No consolidated first narrative to depart from Structure; reader knowledge 1, 6 Nested flashback Two frames suspended; the middle one unstable Reader knowledge; texture 7 The better past Present constructed as a delivery mechanism Structure 10 Childhood explains everything Long reach, short extent; the closed question Character 6 The italicised memory Typography substituting for construction Texture; reader knowledge 4 The prologue relocated Material optimised for inverse criteria Structure; reader knowledge 5, 8 The undeveloped repeat A circle mistaken for a spiral Structure; theme 9, 10

title: 9. Worked Analyses
text: Eight close readings and one revision case. The analytical apparatus is the same throughout: identify the register ( §6.4 ), measure the reach and extent ( §3.2 ), classify the analepsis ( §3.3 ), audit the domains ( §4 ), and assess the return ( §6.6 ). The eight are arranged in an order that is itself an argument. The first four are individual cutaways of increasing ambition; the last four are novels in which the cutaway has become the structure, and for which the deficit model has progressively less to say. 9.1 Proust, In Search of Lost Time (1913–27) — the involuntary sensory trigger Register: 8 (involuntary memory). Reach: from the narrator’s adult present back to childhood; an exact number of years is not specified here. Extent: the initial recollection opens onto an extended account of Combray; the whole novel is not a single cutaway. Type: external analepsis relative to the adult frame. The passage is the most cited cutaway in European fiction and among the least accurately taught. The narrator, an adult, is given tea and a small shell-shaped cake by his mother on a winter afternoon. The taste produces an overwhelming and unidentifiable joy. He drinks again, and the effect diminishes; he attempts to recover it by concentration and fails; and only when he stops trying does the source arrive — the same taste, offered by his aunt Léonie on Sunday mornings at Combray — and with it the town, the church, the streets, the gardens, the whole of a period he had believed lost. Four features deserve attention, and the third is the one this chapter exists to make. The reach is long, and the recollection opens an extended section on Combray. The madeleine episode gives the narrator access to material that voluntary recall had not supplied. Subsequent volumes contain other remembered episodes, narrative levels and present moments; they should not be counted as the extent of this one analepsis. The narrator’s effort is part of the mechanism. He initially cannot identify what the taste is offering, and repeated attempts to recover the sensation do not immediately reveal its source. The recollection is involuntary in its onset, although he then actively seeks to understand it. An involuntary memory can have a clear sensory cause. Proust uses the workshop’s sensory-trigger category while changing its effect. The madeleine’s taste matches the cake and tea once offered by Aunt Léonie. The present sensation has a specific relation to the recovered memory, but its significance is initially unknown to the narrator. The passage distinguishes an unbidden recollection from a deliberately searched-for one; it does not show that the memory lacks a trigger. The consequence for the trigger rule. §6.6 and §8.1 treat triggers as craft choices, not laws. Proust’s passage shows that a sensory cue can be unmistakable while the connection it reveals remains surprising and involuntary. On translation. The passage’s rhythm and diction change across Scott Moncrieff’s version, the Kilmartin and Enright revision, and Lydia Davis’s Swann’s Way (2002). The broad movement from sensation to recollection is recognisable across them, but close claims about wording or temporal cues require an identified edition. 9.2 Brontë, Wuthering Heights (1847) — nested retrospection, measured Register: 6 (embedded oral tale), containing 7 (found document) and further nesting. Type: mixed analepsis — it begins before the first narrative and continues into it. The novel’s temporal architecture repays exact description, because it is usually described loosely. The first narrative is Lockwood’s residence in the neighbourhood, beginning with his opening diary entry dated 1801 and his visit to his landlord. Within a few chapters Lockwood falls ill and asks Nelly Dean to tell him the history of the house. Nelly’s chronicle then occupies the great majority of the book. Measurement Value Consequence Reach About thirty years at the outset Long: an entire vanished generation must be constructed Extent About thirty years, narrated nearly continuously Long: the reader occupies the constructed context for hundreds of pages, so the construction cost is amortised Direction of reach Shortening throughout The chronicle moves forward while the frame waits; the reader feels approach Type Mixed; the analepsis eventually meets and merges with the first narrative The join is the novel’s structural climax as much as any event is The shortening reach is the feature to teach. This is the case §3.2 identifies as the source of momentum inside a long cutaway: the past is visibly coming to meet the present, and the reader can feel the distance closing. It is also what distinguishes the long chronicle from the static flashback, and it is available to any novel willing to let its retrospect progress . The nesting. Lockwood’s diary contains Nelly’s spoken chronicle, which contains Isabella’s letter (quoted at length), Zillah’s report, and a great deal of reported speech at further removes. By the count at §8.7 this is a fourfold nesting, and the reader is never lost. The mechanism is voice: Lockwood is fastidious, self-regarding and literary; Nelly is practical, moralising and partial; Isabella’s letter is frightened and immediate. Changes in diction help the reader track the layers , alongside the diary frame, quoted letters and changes of speaker. Chapter 13 ( The Viewpoint Shift ) treats the reliability consequences; the point here is purely structural. On the frame’s return. The novel does not simply exhaust Nelly’s chronicle and stop. Lockwood departs, returns some months later, receives the remainder of the story, and closes the book at the three graves. The frame is used , which is what distinguishes it from the frames that open and are forgotten. Chapter 10 ( The Prologue ) analyses Lockwood’s arrival as a functional prologue; considered from this chapter’s side, the same material is the container that makes a thirty-year analepsis structurally legible. Where the chapter’s model fails here. By test 1, Nelly’s chronicle begins at a moment of no present-tense pressure whatever — a bored, ill man asks a housekeeper for gossip. By test 10, the past occupies perhaps ninety per cent of the book. The novel is a demonstration that when the proportion is that extreme, the correct move is not to reduce the past but to build a frame adequate to containing it, which is the recommendation at §7.1 , test 10. 9.3 Ford, The Good Soldier (1915) — chronology destroyed and reassembled Register: 9 (repeating analepsis) and 11 (reconstruction), in combination. Type: internal and external analepses in unsignalled alternation. Dowell narrates his acquaintance with the Ashburnhams from a position after everything has happened, and he narrates it out of order — not artfully out of order, but in the order in which things occur to him, with corrections, retractions, digressions and returns. The novel’s most quoted structural remark is his own account of his method: he imagines himself telling the story aloud, at intervals, to a silent listener by a fire, saying things as they come to him. Chapter 9 §4.1 analyses the first sentence for its reliability signal; the concern here is the temporal architecture that sentence introduces. What the reader is actually doing. Ohtsuka and Brewer’s experiment ( §3.6 ) found lower accuracy on event-order questions for several noncanonical arrangements than for a canonical one. It does not measure the experience of reading The Good Soldier , but suggests a useful question about reconstructing its chronology. The reader is assembling a timeline — the meeting at Nauheim, the years of the affair, the sequence of the deaths, the recurrence of the fourth of August — from fragments delivered in an order determined by a narrator’s associations and evasions. The two functions of “I don’t know.” Dowell’s celebrated admissions of ignorance are usually taught as a reliability signal, and they are; but structurally they do something else. Each is a marked gap — an explicit statement that something is missing — and per Sternberg ( §3.4 ) an explicit gap generates curiosity where a silent one would generate nothing. Dowell’s ignorance is the mechanism by which the novel opens the slots that its later repeating analepses fill. He is not merely an unreliable narrator; he is a narrator who continuously announces where his account is defective , which is a technique of exposition as much as of characterisation. Repetition with difference. The events are told many times. The test at §7.1 (test 9) asks what each pass adds, and in Ford’s case the answer is always the same kind of thing and never the same instance: a fact Dowell withheld, a judgement he has revised, a motive he now attributes differently, a sympathy that has shifted. The material is constant and the narrator is not. This is the model for any writer contemplating a repeating structure: the second pass must be the same events seen by a changed person , and the change must be visible. Where the model fails. By test 7, the chronology test, the book fails comprehensively on a single reading and is designed to. By test 5, most of Dowell’s returns leave the present — the act of telling — entirely unchanged, because the present is a man in a chair. The novel demonstrates that when reconstruction is the reader’s activity, the return test measures the wrong thing. 9.4 Faulkner, Absalom, Absalom! (1936) — a past partly witnessed and repeatedly reconstructed Register: 11 (reconstruction), sustained for a whole novel. Reach: up to a century. Type: external analepsis; the first narrative is 1909–10. The first narrative is thin and sharply located: Quentin Compson in Rosa Coldfield’s parlour in September 1909, then in his father’s presence, then in a Harvard dormitory in January 1910 with his Canadian roommate Shreve. Much of the Sutpen history lies between 1807 and 1869. Rosa knew Sutpen and witnessed some events firsthand ; other decisive events, including Charles Bon’s death, reach the narrators through reports and conjecture. The novel’s method is reconstruction, and reconstruction of a specific and demanding kind. Rosa has a version, shaped by grievance. Mr Compson has another, shaped by the fatalism of a man who has inherited a defeated culture and a taste for irony. Quentin has fragments from his grandfather. Shreve has only what Quentin has told him, and no stake at all — and it is Shreve, the outsider, who does much of the imaginative work. The decisive scenes, including the confrontation at the gate between Henry Sutpen and Charles Bon, are constructed collaboratively by two young men in a cold room a thousand miles and forty years away, in the subjunctive: maybe , perhaps , it must have been . What this does to the chapter’s apparatus. Every measurement returns an anomaly. Test Result What it means 1 — Momentum No present-tense question of any pressure The present exists to occasion the reconstruction 4 — Trigger Triggered continuously, by conversation The trigger is the entire first narrative 6 — Reach and extent A century of reach, a century of extent The most expensive possible configuration 7 — Chronology Reconstructible only with effort; a chronology and genealogy appear in the novel’s appendices Faulkner prepared supplementary aids, and the published chronology itself contains dates later editors corrected 9 — Completing or repeating Both, continuously; the same events are told by successive narrators The friction between versions is the content The appended chronology is worth a seminar’s discussion. A novel that ships with a timeline in the back matter has conceded that its temporal architecture exceeds ordinary comprehension. Two readings are available and both are defensible: that the apparatus is a courtesy, or that it is an admission. The more interesting question is whether a reader who consults it is reading the book Faulkner wrote — since the difficulty of assembling the chronology is a substantial part of the represented experience. What the novel establishes for this chapter. The deficit model assumes that the past is being visited in order to explain a present. Here the present has no content to explain: Quentin’s situation is exhausted by his relation to the story he is telling. The cutaway is not a detour from the story; it is the story , and what the book is about is the impossibility of settling what happened. The formal name for this in Genette’s system is that the first narrative has been reduced to a bare occasion — a structure of which Wuthering Heights is the polite Victorian version and this is the extreme. 9.5 Morrison, Beloved (1987) — rememory, and the past that arrives as a person Register: 9 (repeating analepsis) and 12 (the unreachable past), in combination. The novel interweaves memory and the action at 124 without a regular alternation of two declared strands. Type: external and internal analepses, converging. The novel’s present is 1873 at 124 Bluestone Road, outside Cincinnati; its past is Sweet Home, the escape, and the events of 1855 in the woodshed. Chapter 9 §9.5 analyses the opening sentence for its withheld referent; the concern here is the temporal architecture the novel builds on it. Rememory. Sethe’s term, offered to Denver in an explanation that is also the novel’s theory of time: a thing that happened does not go away when it is over. The place where it happened persists; the picture of it is still there, outside her head, and someone else can walk into it. This is not metaphor within the novel’s terms — Denver is warned, in practical terms, against going to certain places. The formal consequence is that the past does not stay behind to be visited; it occupies space and can be entered . A narrative operating on that premise cannot organise its retrospects around a present-tense character choosing to remember, because remembering is not the mechanism. The past intrudes. The novel’s departures are therefore not departures at all in the sense §1.1 describes, and the deficit model has, in the most literal way, misidentified which term is the interruption. Caruth applied, and its limits. The account of traumatic experience at §3.7 — an event not fully registered when it occurred, returning belatedly, resistant to sequence — describes the novel’s form with unusual precision. The events in the shed are approached and veered away from repeatedly before being narrated; the approach is made by different consciousnesses at different distances; the full account arrives late, and even then partly through a newspaper clipping that Paul D cannot read. That is the shape Caruth’s model predicts. The chapter’s caution at §3.7 applies here too, and a student should hold both halves. Caruth’s literalist account of traumatic memory has been contested — by Ruth Leys on its clinical and theoretical foundations, by Stef Craps on its Eurocentric assumptions, by Dominick LaCapra on its tendency to collapse working-through into acting-out. It is possible to hold that Morrison’s form is a precise representation of traumatic memory, and possible to hold that it is a magnificent set of literary conventions for representing it, and the choice between those positions is not settled by the novel. What is not in doubt is the formal fact: the fragmentation is the subject and not a defect of construction. The spiral, not the circle. §8.12 sets the discriminating question for repeated returns: do they converge? Here they do, and the convergence is designed. Each approach to 1855 is nearer than the last — in information, in proximity of viewpoint, in the willingness of the narration to remain in the room. The final full account lands as the completion of a movement the entire book has been making, which is why the repetition, which by the arithmetic of §3.3 should be the most expensive structure in the chapter, reads as inevitability. And the past arriving as a person. The novel’s most radical formal act is to convert an analepsis into a character. Beloved is the past, embodied, walking up out of the water and into the house — which means the novel can dramatise the return of what is past in the present tense , without any cutaway at all. This is the limit case of the whole chapter, and it is worth a seminar’s attention: a book that can put its past on the page as a present-tense character has abolished the interest deficit by abolishing the departure. 9.6 Ishiguro, The Remains of the Day (1989) — the whole novel as motivated recollection Register: 5 (dramatised flashback) and 4 (iterative habitual), inside a frame that is itself register 7 (a day-by-day record). Type: external analepsis. First narrative: six days in July 1956. The novel’s design is the cleanest available demonstration that a thin present can be a structural asset rather than a defect. The frame. Stevens, an ageing butler, drives from Oxfordshire to the West Country in his employer’s car, ostensibly on an errand to a former colleague. The present timeline’s events, entire: he sets out; he worries about his motoring clothes; he mismanages the petrol; the radiator overheats; he is mistaken for a gentleman in a village; he walks up a hill and looks at a view; he meets Miss Kenton; he sits on a pier at dusk. Nothing in that list would sustain a chapter on its own. The mechanism. Each day of the drive is a chapter with a place-name heading, and each generates recollection by an entirely conventional means: the landscape, the errand, the meetings, the conversations, the physical fact of leaving a house he has not left in decades. The past supplies Lord Darlington’s political career, the 1923 conference at which Stevens’s father died upstairs while he continued serving, the dismissal of two Jewish maids at Darlington’s instruction, and the twenty-year non-relationship with Miss Kenton. Why the thin present works. Three reasons, all transferable. The journey supplies a structure with a destination , so the present has direction even without incident. The reader knows where the car is going and that something will be said when it arrives. The proportion is an argument. A life given entirely to another man’s household has very little present in it, and the disproportion between the two timelines states that without a word of commentary. §8.8 ’s discriminating question — does the book know it, and is the thinness saying something? — is answered affirmatively. The present is not inert; it is a slow reveal of the frame narrator’s condition. The bantering Stevens cannot manage, the professional dignity he keeps redefining, the confusion about who he is when he is not at Darlington Hall: the present timeline is where the reader watches the cost of the past being paid. The iterative. Ishiguro’s most underappreciated technical instrument here is register 4. Large stretches of the past are delivered not as scenes but as habitual practice — how the staff plan was drawn up, what the servants’ hall did in the evenings, what the great houses of that period expected — and the iterative is what establishes the normal against which the dramatised scenes register as exceptional. A student can learn more about the iterative from twenty pages of this novel than from any theoretical account of it. The return that never happens. The novel’s most sophisticated move, from this chapter’s point of view, is that Stevens’s cutaways frequently fail test 5. He returns from a devastating recollection to the present unchanged, and comments on the excellence of the English landscape. The failure is the characterisation: a man who can go back to the night his father died and return with a reflection on professional standards has told the reader everything. Where the untethered return is the represented condition, §8.5 measures the technique and misses the point. 9.7 Salih, Season of Migration to the North (1966) — the embedded life story Register: 6 (embedded oral tale), containing 7 (documents in the locked room). Type: external analepsis, delivered as speech. The unnamed narrator returns to his village on the Nile after seven years of study in Europe, addressing his account to a listening group. In the village he finds a newcomer, Mustafa Sa’eed, who is unaccountably reserved about his own history, and who one night, drunk, recites English poetry. The narrator’s curiosity is aroused; some time later Mustafa tells him his life — Khartoum, Cairo, London, the English women, the killing of his wife, the trial, the prison years — in a single long night’s confession. Why the embedded tale is the right register here, and not merely the traditional one. The teller has a motive, and it is withheld. Mustafa chooses to tell, chooses this listener, and the reader is not told why until much later. A dramatised flashback would have supplied the same events with none of that pressure. The listener is changed by hearing. This is the requirement §8.11 identifies for relocated material, and it is met continuously: the narrator’s own return from Europe becomes unstable in the light of Mustafa’s, and by the end he can no longer keep the two stories separate. The tale is not a container of information but an event in the frame narrative with consequences that run to the last page. The oral register carries the novel’s politics. The narrator addresses an audience; the story is being told in a village, in a tradition of telling, about a man whose formation was European. The form itself stages the encounter the book is about. The locked room. After Mustafa’s disappearance the narrator eventually enters the room he kept locked, and finds it furnished as an English study, with books, papers and a portrait. This is register 7 arriving after register 6: the spoken account is followed by documentary evidence, and the evidence does not simply confirm the speech. A novel that delivers its past twice, in two registers, has made the relation between the two registers into content — which is the substitution exercise at §6.5 performed inside the book rather than in the writer’s notebook. On translation. Denys Johnson-Davies’s 1969 English version is used here. Broad structural observations can be tested in that version, but claims about the texture of the narrator’s address or the relation between Arabic and English require comparison with the Arabic original. 9.8 Tolstoy, The Death of Ivan Ilyich (1886) — analepsis as the whole design Register: 3 (summary) modulating into 5 (dramatised scene). Reach: forty-five years, shortening to nothing. Type: external analepsis with a first narrative of one chapter. Translation: Louise and Aylmer Maude. The novella’s structure is the clearest teaching case in this chapter, because it is simple, extreme, and entirely successful. Chapter I is the first narrative , and it is complete. Ivan Ilyich’s colleagues learn of his death from a newspaper in their chambers, and each immediately calculates what it means for his own promotion. Peter Ivanovich attends the funeral, is trapped by the widow into a conversation about her pension, is unnerved by the corpse’s expression, and escapes to a game of cards. The chapter has a protagonist, a want, an obstacle, an ending. It is a scene, not a prologue , which is why Chapter II can leave it ( §8.6 ). Chapter II opens the analepsis with the sentence anatomised at §5.2 , and the remaining ten chapters are that analepsis, moving forward through the career, the marriage, the house, the illness, the doctors, the lie everyone maintains, the peasant Gerasim, and the final three days — until the retrospect arrives at the death the reader was told about on the first page. The frame-and-retrospect structure, and what it buys. Chapter I establishes a narrative present at the funeral. Relative to that level, Chapter II’s account of Ivan’s earlier life is an analepsis , not a prolepsis ( §3.3 ). The reader already knows Ivan will die and can ask how did a life arrive here — a question of Sternberg’s curiosity rather than suspense about the fact of death ( §3.4 ). There is a second and less obvious return on the design. Because the reader has met Ivan Ilyich’s colleagues before meeting Ivan Ilyich, they read the whole retrospect knowing what his death will mean to the people around him: an inconvenience, a vacancy, an occasion for calculation. The judgement the novella is going to deliver has been demonstrated before the case is heard. The domains, in a single structure. Domain How served Plot The causal history of a death; the illness traced to a fall while hanging curtains Character A man built entirely out of propriety, shown becoming that man decision by decision Theme The stated argument of §5.2 ’s sentence, tested over forty-five years Texture The accelerating rhythm: decades in paragraphs at the start, three days in chapters at the end Reader knowledge The verdict supplied before the evidence; the colleagues met before the man Structure The retrospect is the book; the frame is one chapter, and the design is declared in it The accelerating rhythm deserves separate notice , because it is the feature of the design that transfers most readily to other books. The analepsis begins in register 3 — years compressed into paragraphs, the iterative and the summary — and progressively slows, until the final chapters are approximately scene-rate and the last hours occupy pages. The reach shortens; the pace slows; the two together produce the sensation of arrival that a long retrospect otherwise lacks. This is the technique §3.2 describes abstractly, executed as well as it has ever been. 9.9 A revision case: the same material in two registers The following applies the protocol to the series’ running example — the invented contemporary novel about three siblings and their dead father’s shop. The scene under revision is the one in which Nadia, at the door of the flat above the shop, puts her hand into the pocket of her father’s coat, still on its hook, and finds the good pen. The canonical placement matters and should be stated before the versions. The good pen was planted in Chapter 10’s material ( The Prologue ), where the father pockets it on the last ordinary day instead of leaving it by the till. The line he speaks in the cutaway is quoted verbatim at the novel’s close, in Chapter 16’s material ( The Ending ). The prologue carries a fragment of the line, In case , as the father’s unfinished reason when he pockets the pen (Chapter 10’s revision case); this cutaway is therefore partly a repeating analepsis, and what the second pass adds is the rest of the line, the occasion, the listener and Nadia’s misreading. This cutaway therefore sits in the middle of a three-point structure: an object planted, a meaning supplied, a line returning. Everything below should be read against that. Version A (draft) When Nadia was nine her father let her help with the stock count for the first time. It was a Sunday in November and the shop was closed and the radiator by the door made its noise like something clearing its throat. He had set out two chairs at the counter and a mug of tea for each of them, and he showed her how to make the marks in fives, four strokes and one across, and how to cross a seven so it could not be mistaken for a one. “You have to be able to read it in ten years,” he said. She had asked him then why he was using the good pen. She had known even at nine that the good pen was for the ledger, that it lived by the till in its case, that Ma had had to buy a new nib for it twice that year because he kept losing it. She asked him whether he was going to lose it again, and whether Ma would be cross. He put the cap on the pen and set it down on the counter between them, and he looked at her over his glasses in the way he had when she had caught him out at something. Outside, a bus went past and the window shook the way it always shook. “Because someone should write it down properly,” he said. “In case anyone ever needs to check.” She had not understood what he meant. She had thought he meant the shop — the stock, the prices, the ordinary arithmetic of it, the things a shop had to be able to prove. She had gone back to her column of fives. He had gone back to the shelves, calling out the numbers, and she had written them down in her nine-year-old’s hand while he stood with his thumb hooked in his cuff and read the labels out to her one after another until the light went. (Approximately 320 words, and in the drafts this is modelled on it runs to two pages.) Diagnosis Test Result 1 — Momentum No present-tense question is named at the point of departure, because there is no present at the point of departure. The cutaway is not entered from a scene; it begins the section. Fail 2 — Register Compresses to: He had once told her, when she asked why a stock count needed the good pen, that someone should write it down properly, in case anyone ever needed to check. Nothing of consequence is lost. Fail 3 — Removal Removing it costs the reader the father’s line, which is load-bearing for Chapter 16’s ending. The material must stay in some form; the scene need not 4 — Trigger None. The narrative simply goes, in a close third-person narration that has no authority to do so ( §8.1 ). Fail 5 — Return There is no return; the section ends inside the past, on the light going. Fail 6 — Reach and extent Reach around twenty-five years; extent one afternoon. The expensive cell ( §3.2 ), and the whole context — the radiator, the bus, the two chairs — is built and immediately discarded 7 — Chronology Introduces a contradiction. The canon establishes that the father lost the pen twice that year and that Nadia questioned him on the second occasion. Relocating the exchange to her ninth year silently rewrites a recent, adult conversation into a formative childhood one 8 — Placement The material’s whole value is its bearing on the pen Nadia is holding four months after his death. It is not placed there 9 — Completing or repeating Completing — but the gap has not been opened. The reader has been given no reason to wonder about the pen 10 — Proportion One instance; but a manuscript with several of these is a childhood novel wearing a present-tense frame Patterns present: the unmotivated cutaway ( §8.1 ); the childhood-explains-everything cutaway ( §8.9 ); the untethered return ( §8.5 ), in its most complete form, since there is no return at all. What is worth noticing about Version A. It is not badly written. The radiator clearing its throat, the crossed seven, the marks in fives, the thumb hooked in the cuff — these are exact and characterising, and a workshop would praise several of them. The failure is entirely one of register, placement and motivation , and this is the general case: draft cutaways are far more often well-written and misplaced than they are badly written. Two further faults are worth isolating because they are invisible from inside. Version A converts an illumination into an explanation ( §4.2 ). By placing the exchange in Nadia’s childhood, it proposes that this is where she learned something about her father — that the moment is formative . The canonical exchange is not formative; it is an ordinary conversation between adults, half-forgotten, whose meaning changes retrospectively. The difference is the whole of the effect. Version A spends the line. The father’s sentence appears here, at leisure, in a scene that has been building towards it for three hundred words, cushioned by tea and radiators and a bus. The line carries the novel’s ending, where it is quoted again. Delivered like this, it has been used up. Version B (revision) Nadia found the pen in his coat pocket, right where she remembered him keeping it — except it wasn’t the register pen, the plain black one. It was the good pen, the fountain one he only used for the ledger, the one he wasn’t supposed to carry loose because he’d lose it. He’d lost it twice that year already, and made Ma buy a new nib. She had asked him about it once, the second time. Why he needed the good pen for a stock count nobody was going to read twice. He’d looked at her over his glasses like she’d caught him at something. “Because someone should write it down properly,” he said. “In case anyone ever needs to check.” At the time she’d thought he meant the shop. She had not thought, until just now, standing by the door with her hand in the pocket of a coat still on its hook, to ask him what he’d actually thought anyone might need to check. Audit Domain What the cutaway does Plot Reframes a detail the reader already has from Chapter 10’s material — the good pen carried loose on the last ordinary day — from an absent-minded habit into a deliberate choice, recasting present-timeline evidence without adding a fact Character The father’s habit of unstated caution; and Nadia’s habit, established in Chapter 4’s material as counting and not touching, of noticing only afterwards what she failed to ask at the time Theme “In case anyone ever needs to check” opens the novel’s argument about records outliving the people who keep them — the ledger, the misspelled doctor’s name, the changed hand after March the ninth Texture A change of register from grief at the door of the flat to an ordinary remembered exchange, and back, in four lines — pace controlled without the present scene being suspended for long Reader knowledge Recalibrates the irony Chapter 10’s material set up: the reader who watched him pocket the pen now understands why finding it lands on Nadia as it does Structure The middle term of a three-point architecture: object planted (Ch 10’s material), meaning supplied (here), line returning (Ch 16’s material) Measurements. Register 5 at minimum length, entered through register 1. Reach: months, not decades. Extent: one exchange. Type: completing — and the gap was opened by the prologue material, where the reader saw the pen pocketed and did not know why. Trigger: the object , the strongest available ( §6.6 ), and one that remains in her hand after the return. What the revision did, procedurally Changed the register, not the content. The same information; a scene of 320 words becomes an exchange of four lines. The compression check ( §6.3 ) was run and returned keep the sentence , and the sentence turned out to be the father’s own. Attached the cutaway to an object already load-bearing. The pen was planted two hundred pages earlier and is in Nadia’s hand at the moment of departure. The trigger did not have to be invented; it had to be found ( §5.3 ). Moved the exchange out of childhood. Restoring it to the recent past — the second time he lost the pen — removes the determinist implication, respects the canon, and makes the point sharper: this was an ordinary conversation, recently, which she did not understand at the time and understands now. Shortened the reach from twenty-five years to a few months. The construction cost collapses. No radiator, no bus, no two chairs: the reader already knows this shop. Rewrote the return as a changed question. Version A ends inside the past. Version B’s last sentence returns Nadia to the door of the flat holding a question she did not have when she reached into the pocket — what did he think anyone would need to check — which the present scene now has to carry. This is the changed question at §6.6 , and it converts the cutaway from a pause into a turn. Declined the explanatory sentence. Nothing states that the father knew he was ill, or that the pen was a signal. The reader assembles it, which is why it holds ( §5.3 ). What Version B has not solved An honest account has to include this, and four things are outstanding. The last sentence is doing a great deal of work and may be doing too much. She had not thought, until just now, to ask him what he’d actually thought anyone might need to check is the return, the changed question, the thematic statement and the emotional beat in a single construction. It is close to the density ceiling described at §5.4 , and a reasonable editor would ask whether the reader could get there with less — whether the clause at the time she’d thought he meant the shop has not already done the work, leaving the last sentence to say something plainer. The trigger is very apt. The object is the pen; the pen is the point; the memory is about the pen. §5.4 warns that an over-motivated trigger shows the machinery. The defence is that the aptness was established two hundred pages earlier by a different chapter and is therefore inherited rather than manufactured — but the defence depends on the prologue material existing, and a reader encountering this scene in isolation would find it neat.
