The register is the contemporary literary default. Wry, precise close third, with the past folded into the present through the pluperfect and a fragment of remembered dialogue. It is a well-made instance of a very common thing. Chapter 9 §9.8 makes the same concession about the same character’s opening paragraph, and the concession is worth repeating here for the same reason: the revision has solved the structural problem, and has not made the prose distinctive against its own shelf. The scene before has to motivate the hand. Nadia has learned not to touch the coat (Chapter 4’s material), and in this version the coat stays on its hook and only her hand goes into the pocket. Whatever moves her to do even that, months after March, has to be supplied by the scene this cutaway sits in, and Version B does not supply it. One thing Version B does not attempt, and might have. The material could have been delivered at register 6 — Nadia telling Elena about the exchange, in the present, in dialogue — which would have supplied a listener, a motive for telling, and the possibility of Elena disagreeing about what their father meant. That version does not exist, and the substitution exercise at §6.5 exists in order to make writers produce it before deciding.

title: 10. The Cutaway Across Forms
text: The apparatus above was developed for the novel. It transfers to adjacent forms with adjustments that need stating, because writers frequently import novel-scale habits into forms that punish them. 10.1 The short story The story has proportionally less room and a much less forgiving arithmetic. Two consequences follow directly from §3.9 . The deficit does not amortise. In a novel, an expensive cutaway can be paid off over the following fifty pages. A story has no following fifty pages, which means the return must arrive almost immediately — usually within the same paragraph as the cutaway itself. The dramatised flashback is often unaffordable. A story of four thousand words that spends eight hundred on a past scene has given a fifth of itself to material that is not the present situation. The registers that suit the form are 1, 2, 4 and 13 — the clause of implication, the participial aside, the iterative, and the corrected assumption — because all four deliver a past without stopping the story. Difference from the novel Consequence No room to amortise a deficit The return must be immediate A single situation, often a single scene Cutaways are usually internal analepses within a short span The reader holds the whole text in memory A repeating analepsis is more visible, and therefore more expensive The ending recolours everything The corrected assumption (register 13) is disproportionately powerful The last row is one possible advantage of short form: a final revelation about the past can recolour much of what preceded it while the text is still readily recallable. Novels can also produce large retrospective revisions. This is one reason to test whether a story’s past is strongest at the end rather than in the middle. 10.2 The novella The novella has a novel’s tonal amplitude and a story’s word count, and its characteristic problem in this territory is proportion. A single dramatised flashback in a thirty-thousand-word text is a structural event, not a passage. The form’s distinctive solution is the one Tolstoy uses ( §9.8 ): make the retrospect the whole design rather than an interruption of it. A novella can afford to be almost entirely analepsis in a way a novel usually cannot, because the reader’s investment in the first narrative has not had time to become the thing they are protecting. Where a novel that leaves its present for two hundred pages has abandoned something, a novella that leaves its present after twenty has simply declared its shape. 10.3 Series and sequels Series fiction faces a version of the problem that no other form has: the past is a previous book , and the reader may or may not have read it. Three principles, all of which are versions of the rules already stated. Recap is backstory, and the compression check applies to it. A returning reader needs a clause; a new reader needs a paragraph; neither needs a scene. A dramatised flashback to the previous volume’s climax is the form’s characteristic error, and it is worse than it looks: it is redundant for one audience and unearned for the other. Deliver the past as present-tense consequence rather than as summary — a character behaving in a way the previous volume explains and this one demonstrates. Chapter 9 §10.4 states the same rule for series openings. The iterative is the series writer’s best instrument. They had been doing this for two years now, and it had stopped being remarkable delivers a whole prior volume’s worth of relationship in a sentence, and characterises while doing it. 10.4 The screen comparison, and where it misleads Film and prose both tell stories out of chronological order, but a direct derivation of the prose cutaway from film has not been established ( §3.8 ). The comparison helps identify what each medium can signal readily. What film can signal visually. Entry cues. A dissolve, colour change or change of aspect ratio can mark a move into the past quickly. Such cues are optional, and viewers may still need to infer when and where a scene occurs. Visible context. A frame can show clothing, setting and apparent age together. It does not automatically specify a date, social position or the relation of the new scene to the previous one; prose can also establish several facts in a phrase. Return cues. A cut back to a familiar face can re-anchor a viewer, but the return’s meaning still has to be earned by the film, just as it does in prose. What prose can signal grammatically. Grammatical tense. English can place an event earlier with an auxiliary verb inside an ongoing sentence. Film usually uses editing, dialogue, voice-over or other cues to convey the same relation. The iterative. Prose can write every Sunday in two words. Film can convey repetition through montage, recurring scenes, narration or a calendar cue. Uncertainty about the past. Prose can say perhaps or it must have been . Film can also present incompatible or unreliable accounts: Kurosawa’s Rashomon (1950) dramatises conflicting versions of one event in flashback. The practical warning. A writer accustomed to dramatised screen flashbacks may reach first for register 5. The shorter prose registers are also available, and comparing them in revision can reveal a more fitting way to tell the past. 10.5 Translated fiction Two observations, both of which follow the series’ standing distinction between structural and textural claims. Broad structural claims often survive translation. The order of large narrative sections and the placement of major cutaways are usually retained, but temporal cues, sentence boundaries and local emphasis can change. Claims about reach, extent and type should be checked against the particular edition used, especially where they depend on a short passage. The grammatical marking of the past can change in translation. This is a sharper problem here than in most chapters, because English often marks a cutaway by tense , and tense systems differ. English can use the past perfect to signal a step behind the narrative past. One prose convention is to open a retrospect with past-perfect forms and then use simple past once its temporal position is clear. Other languages also have ways to mark anteriority; their conventions need checking case by case. Languages with grammatical aspect can distribute the work differently; Russian, for example, marks habituality and completion through aspect as well as tense, which an English translator may render with lexical cues such as would or used to . Languages without an obligatory pluperfect may signal the shift by adverbials, by particles, or by nothing at all, leaving the reader to infer the temporal relation from context. The consequence for a student: a claim about how conspicuous a cutaway feels is a claim about the language it is read in. The observation at §8.10 , that italics substitute for construction, is a claim about a typographic convention in anglophone publishing. The observation at §5.3 , that tense is the cheapest carrier available, is a claim about English. 10.6 Concordance: concept to novel A study aid: each concept with the work that best displays it. Concept Best displayed by Section The first narrative, and its reduction to a bare occasion Absalom, Absalom! §3.1 , §9.4 Reach and extent, both long, reach shortening Wuthering Heights §3.2 , §9.2 Long reach, short extent — the expensive cell Absalom, Absalom! (Sutpen at the door) §3.2 , §8.9 External analepsis with a one-chapter first narrative The Death of Ivan Ilyich §3.3 , §9.8 Completing analepsis, gap opened in advance Great Expectations (Magwitch’s account) §3.3 , §4.5 Repeating analepsis sustained for a novel The Good Soldier ; Beloved §3.3 , §9.3 , §9.5 Prolepsis opening a question about a later event One Hundred Years of Solitude §3.3 Curiosity as the engine rather than suspense The Good Soldier §3.4 , §9.3 The pre-Homeric alternative: no suspended background Odyssey XIX, via Auerbach §3.8 , §8.3 Trauma and the unavailable past Beloved §3.7 , §9.5 Plot: the origin, offered at four removes Absalom, Absalom! §4.1 Character: illumination without explanation The Remains of the Day §4.2 , §9.6 Theme: the retrospect as sustained argument The Death of Ivan Ilyich §4.3 , §9.8 Texture: the past as sensation In Search of Lost Time §4.4 , §9.1 Reader knowledge: the corrected assumption at book scale Great Expectations §4.5 The structural domain: the returning frame Wuthering Heights ; Season of Migration to the North §4.6 The structural domain: the recurring approach Beloved §4.6 , §8.12 Multiplicity in one sentence The Death of Ivan Ilyich (Ch. II’s first line) §5.2 Register 4, the iterative, used systematically The Remains of the Day ; Proust’s Combray §6.4 , §9.6 Register 6, the embedded oral tale Season of Migration to the North ; Wuthering Heights §6.4 , §9.7 Register 8, involuntary memory In Search of Lost Time §6.4 , §9.1 Register 11, reconstruction Absalom, Absalom! §6.4 , §9.4 Register 12, the unreachable past Beloved ; The Sound and the Fury §6.4 A sensory trigger whose meaning is initially unknown; an untriggered framed retrospect In Search of Lost Time ; The Death of Ivan Ilyich §6.6 , §8.1 Nesting that works, by voice Wuthering Heights ; Frankenstein §8.7 , §9.2 The deliberately thinner present The Remains of the Day §8.8 , §9.6 Italics as one cue for temporal shifts The Sound and the Fury §8.10 The untethered interpolation, historically licensed Don Quixote (“El curioso impertinente”) §8.5 Relocated material given an occasion Season of Migration to the North §8.11 , §9.7 The past embodied as a present-tense character Beloved §9.5

title: 11. Revision Checklist
text: Run each cutaway against this list before deciding it stays as written. Each item derives from a test in §7 or a pattern in §8 . Before you begin I know whether my present timeline carries this book’s engine, or whether the past does — and I have applied the protocol accordingly ( §7.0 ). The decision to leave I can name, in a sentence, the present-tense question the reader was holding when this cutaway began. I can name the concrete trigger — object, sensation, phrase, question, place, silence, date, document, resemblance — or I can say why this narration does not need one. I have asked whether this cutaway would cost less, or pay more, thirty pages later or earlier. The cutaway does not land at the story’s single most costly present-tense moment unless the payoff matches, and unless the interruption is measured in sentences. The register I have written out the one-sentence compressed version and read it in place. The material survives that check as a flashback rather than as backstory — or it has been demoted, or cut. If it is a flashback, the past scene has a want, a resistance and a change, as any scene must. I have attempted this material in at least one other register from §6.4 , including one shorter than the version I have kept. Backstory delivered as summary is a fact to know, not a moment that needed to be felt. Reach, extent and type I know how far back this goes and how much time it covers, and the two are proportionate to what it delivers. If the reach is long and the extent short, I have asked whether a nearer memory would make the same point. I know whether this analepsis is completing or repeating; if repeating, I can name in one sentence what this pass adds. If the same past period is visited more than twice, the visits converge on something rather than circling it. The return The present is changed on return — in knowledge, understanding, question or action — and I can say which. The return sentence performs that change rather than merely re-anchoring the reader. Covered up, the sentence before the cutaway and the sentence after it do not read continuously. I have not added the sentence that explains what the cutaway meant. Across the manuscript I have made the audit sheet ( §5.5 ) and read it as a whole rather than cutaway by cutaway. The manuscript does not deliver its past in a single register. The reach column is not uniform; the book’s past is not all in one era by default. I know what proportion of the book is past material, and the book’s declared structure acknowledges it. No cutaway repeats what the reader could already infer without gaining something by the repetition. No dramatised past scene is more vivid than the present timeline it serves — unless that disproportion is the book’s argument. Nothing is marked as past by typography alone.

title: 12. Studio Work
text: 12.1 Practical exercises Exercise 1 — The audit sheet. Produce the audit described at §5.5 for a complete draft: every cutaway, with page, reach, extent, register, domains and the open present-tense question. Do not revise anything. Write 300 words on what the sheet reveals that reading the manuscript did not. Exercise 2 — The compression ladder. Take one dramatised flashback and write it at four lengths: the full version, one page, one paragraph, one sentence. Place each in the manuscript and read forward two pages. Record at which length something is first lost, and what it is. Exercise 3 — Register substitution. Take one cutaway and rewrite it in three other registers from §6.4 , at least one shorter and one longer than the original. Do not evaluate until all four exist. Write 400 words comparing what each buys and costs. Exercise 4 — The spoken test. Convert a piece of backstory into something one character says aloud to another, for a reason, at a moment. If no character in the book has a motive to raise it, write 200 words on why the reader is being told. Exercise 5 — The iterative drill. Write a paragraph of past material three times: once as a dramatised scene, once as summary, once in the iterative ( every Sunday he would… ). Identify which the material actually wanted, and what the iterative version made available that the other two did not. Exercise 6 — Trigger inventory. List every cutaway in the draft and its trigger, using the table at §6.6 . Count the categories. If more than half share one category — most often the place entered, or a photograph — rewrite three of them onto different triggers. Exercise 7 — The relocation test. Take a cutaway that tests well and move it: thirty pages earlier, thirty pages later, and into the final chapter. Read all three in place. Write 300 words on what each placement makes the material mean, using the three-position table at §4.5 . Exercise 8 — The return rewrite. Take the first sentence after each of five cutaways in a draft. Rewrite each so that it performs a changed question rather than a re-anchoring. Compare the before and after with the cutaway itself unaltered. Exercise 9 — Reconstruction. Write a 1,000-word passage in register 11: an event narrated by two people, neither of whom witnessed it, who disagree. The event must be reconstructible by the reader and must not be settled by the text. Then write 300 words on what the disagreement supplied that a single reliable account could not. 12.2 Seminar questions Is the interest deficit a description of narrative, or of a market? §3.9 concedes that the model assumes the present-tense question is the primary source of engagement. Test the model against one novel written before 1900 and one written since 2000, and consider whether what it measures is the structure of narrative or the reading habits of a particular period. Five domains or six? Argue for or against admitting the structural domain ( §4.6 ) as a separate category rather than as texture or reader knowledge observed at book scale. Use Beloved or a contemporary braided-timeline novel as evidence. Was Cervantes wrong to yield? “El curioso impertinente” was criticised as an irrelevant interpolation, and Cervantes largely abandoned the practice in Part II. Was that a gain in craft or a loss of a form? What does the answer imply about the requirement, at §6.6 , that the present be changed on return? Does the trauma model describe memory or a convention? §3.7 sets out Caruth’s account of belatedness and the critiques by Leys, LaCapra and Craps. Reading Beloved alongside the disagreement, consider whether the novel’s fragmented approach to 1855 is evidence about how traumatic memory works, or a set of literary conventions for representing it — and whether the distinction matters to a writer. What kind of trigger is Proust’s madeleine? §6.6 lists sensation as a concrete trigger. Proust’s narrator tastes something associated with childhood but cannot at first identify the memory. What does the passage show about the difference between a trigger the reader can locate and a recollection the character cannot summon at will? Whose conventions? The prohibitions in §8 are drawn from an Anglo-American workshop tradition. Examine the handling of the past in Season of Migration to the North , One Hundred Years of Solitude or a classical Arabic or Chinese narrative, and decide which of §8 ’s twelve patterns describe narrative and which describe a local literary culture. 12.3 Assessment rubric For a submitted passage (1,500–2,500 words) containing at least one cutaway, with a 750-word critical commentary. Band Craft (60%) Commentary (40%) Distinction The register is demonstrably the right one and can be defended against alternatives; the trigger is present and not over-apt, or its absence is licensed by the narration; the reach and extent are proportionate; the return changes the present in a way the reader can locate; two or more domains served without strain Names its register and defends it against at least two alternatives it has actually written; measures its own reach, extent and type; identifies its own risks; engages at least two theoretical sources critically rather than decoratively Merit Register appropriate; trigger present; the return changes something, if only the reader’s knowledge; more than one domain served Accurate self-analysis; the apparatus applied correctly; risks acknowledged if not resolved Pass The cutaway is intelligible and connected to the present; one domain clearly served; the reader knows where they are Describes the cutaway accurately; theory referenced but not applied to the writer’s own decisions Fail No discernible relation to the present scene; register mismatched to material; the present resumes unchanged; failure patterns unrecognised Description without analysis; no engagement with the model

title: 13. Glossary
text: Analepsis — Genette’s term for narration, after the fact, of an event earlier than the point in the story at which the narrative currently stands. The formal name for what this chapter calls a cutaway. §3.1 . Anachrony — Any discordance between the order in which events occur in the story and the order in which the narrative presents them. The genus of which analepsis and prolepsis are the species. §3.1 . Backstory — The past told : conveyed by summary, implication, report or dialogue, without the reader living through it. One of the two registers into which the fork at §6.2 divides. Belatedness — In trauma theory, the property by which an overwhelming event is not fully registered at the time of its occurrence and returns afterwards, intrusively and out of sequence. Caruth (1996); contested. §3.7 . Completing analepsis — An analepsis that fills a gap the narrative previously left open; it arrives into a slot the reader already has. Contrasted with the repeating analepsis. §3.3 . Curiosity — Sternberg’s term for the interest generated by uncertainty about the past , as distinct from suspense (the future) and surprise (a past gap the reader did not know existed). §3.4 . Cutaway — This chapter’s cover term for any passage in which the narrative leaves the temporal position of its present action for earlier material, in either register. §2.1 . Distributed exposition — Sternberg’s mode in which antecedents are dispersed throughout a narrative and never gathered. §3.4 . Ellipsis — A stretch of story time passed over in silence. What a completing analepsis later fills. §2.4 . Extent ( amplitude ) — How much story time an anachrony itself covers. Independent of reach. §3.2 . External analepsis — An analepsis lying entirely before the starting point of the first narrative. §3.3 . First narrative ( récit premier ) — Genette’s term for the temporal level a narrative establishes as its principal one, against which all anachrony is measured. Without one, there is no anachrony, only a sequence. §3.1 . Flashback — In this chapter’s working vocabulary, the past dramatised as a scene, moment by moment: the second register of the fork. The term has a twentieth-century film history, but literary retrospective scenes predate cinema. §2.1 , §3.8 . Interest deficit — This chapter’s first principle: at the moment a cutaway begins, the reader is holding an open present-tense question, and the costs of suspension, frame-holding and chronology-tracking are incurred before the past material delivers anything. Originates here; used in Chapter 5 and Chapter 14. §3.9 . Internal analepsis — An analepsis falling inside the span of the first narrative, and therefore working in territory the reader already occupies. §3.3 . Involuntary memory — Proust’s mémoire involontaire : the past recovered by sensation rather than by the intellect, and not reachable by intention. Register 8. §6.4 , §9.1 . Iterative — In Genette’s analysis of frequency, telling once what happened many times: every Sunday he would… . Register 4, and the most underused instrument in the taxonomy. §6.4 . Mixed analepsis — An analepsis beginning before the first narrative and continuing into it. §3.3 . Paralipsis — The omission of information the narrative’s own vantage should have supplied; a lateral rather than a temporal gap. §2.4 . Prolepsis — Narration in advance of an event later than the established temporal level. Formally the mirror of analepsis; it can open a question about how that later event will occur. §3.3 . Reach ( portée ) — How far an anachrony goes from the present moment of the first narrative: the size of the leap. §3.2 . Register of the past — This chapter’s term for a recognisable way of putting past material on the page. Fourteen are tabulated at §6.4 . Rememory — Sethe’s term in Beloved for a past that persists as a place in the world, which another person can enter. §3.7 , §9.5 . Repeating analepsis — An analepsis returning to material the narrative has already covered, in order to recolour it. The most expensive structure in the chapter and the one that produces several of its greatest novels. §3.3 . Return — The point at which a cutaway ends and the first narrative resumes. This chapter’s requirement is that the present be changed , in knowledge, understanding, question or action. §6.6 . Structural domain — The proposed sixth domain: a cutaway used as an architectural device rather than for its content, to control the shape of the whole book. §4.6 . Trigger — The element in the present scene that motivates a cutaway. Ten kinds are tabulated at §6.6 ; the requirement of one is a consequence of narrative distance rather than an independent rule.

title: 15. Further Reading
text: Annotated, grouped by what each source is good for . Starred items are the recommended first three. 15.1 On narrative time and order ★ Genette, Gérard. Narrative Discourse (1972; Eng. 1980). The indispensable book for this chapter and the one whose apparatus underlies almost everything in §3 and §6 . The chapter on Order is short, demanding and worth reading twice; reach, extent, and the completing/repeating distinction are all set out there. Genette’s corpus is Proust throughout, which makes it double as a critical study of the novel §9.1 discusses. ★ Sternberg, Meir. Expositional Modes and Temporal Ordering in Fiction (1978). Formidable and unrivalled. The suspense/curiosity/surprise triad alone reorganises how a writer thinks about withholding. Read chapters 1–3 if not the whole. Ricoeur, Paul. Time and Narrative (1983–85; Eng. 1984–88). Philosophical rather than technical, and slow going. Read the first volume’s treatment of Augustine and of emplotment for the argument that narrative is how time becomes intelligible — the deepest available answer to the question of why fiction rearranges chronology at all. Mendilow, A. A. Time and the Novel (1952). The earliest systematic English treatment, and still a useful historical survey. Dated in its critical vocabulary; valuable for its account of the fictive present and of the novel’s changing relation to chronology. Bal, Mieke. Narratology (4th ed., 2017). The most usable classroom systematisation of Genette’s apparatus, with clearer terminology and worked examples. The book to put in front of a student who has bounced off Narrative Discourse . 15.2 On the flashback as a form with a history ★ Turim, Maureen. Flashbacks in Film: Memory and History (1989). A major study of the device in cinema. Its discussion of marked entry and exit offers useful comparisons for prose; it does not by itself establish that prose flashbacks originated in film. Auerbach, Erich. Mimesis (1946; Eng. 1953), chapter 1. Twenty pages on the scar of Odysseus and the sacrifice of Isaac that establish the distinction between a narrative with background and one without. Outside Genette, the reading that does most for this chapter, because it shows that the suspended background has a history. Chatman, Seymour. Story and Discourse (1978). Useful for the story/discourse distinction in its clearest English form, and for the treatment of gaps. 15.3 On trauma and the unavailable past Caruth, Cathy. Unclaimed Experience (1996). Short, influential, and the source of the belatedness model. Read it with its critics rather than alone. Leys, Ruth. Trauma: A Genealogy (2000). The major critique. Rigorous, historical, and unsparing about the theoretical foundations of the literalist account. LaCapra, Dominick. Writing History, Writing Trauma (2001). The acting-out / working-through distinction, and a more historically careful account than Caruth’s. Craps, Stef. Postcolonial Witnessing (2013). Argues that the canonical paradigm is Eurocentric and inadequate to collective and continuing traumas. The necessary corrective for anyone applying this literature to Beloved . 15.4 On the reader Emmott, Catherine. Narrative Comprehension (1997). Contextual frames, frame switching and frame recall — the best available account of what a reader is actually doing when a narrative relocates. Zwaan and Radvansky (1998). The review article; the clearest statement of the dimensions readers monitor and the costs of shifting them. Ohtsuka and Brewer (1992). An experiment comparing comprehension of event order across five narrated arrangements. Canonical order performed best and flash-forward worst in its temporal-order questions; useful evidence for testing chronology, not for a universal backward-shift penalty ( §7.1 ). Brooks, Peter. Reading for the Plot (1984). For the argument that narrative desire is a dynamic of delay and discharge — the theoretical relative of the interest deficit, arrived at from psychoanalysis rather than from economics. 15.5 Craft literature, used critically Lubbock, Percy. The Craft of Fiction (1921). An influential English discussion of scene and picture that §6.1 adapts for the backstory/flashback fork. Read for the terms; examine the hierarchy critically. James, Henry. The Art of the Novel (1934). The prefaces, especially on the “foreshortening” of antecedents — James’s own name for the problem this chapter calls the register of the past. Burroway, Janet. Writing Fiction . The standard university textbook; useful for exercises and for a wide range of quoted examples. 15.6 Within this textbook Chapter 1 ( The Purposes of a Scene ) — the base four domains, and the standard any flashback must meet once it becomes a scene. Chapter 4 ( The Descriptive Detail ) — denotation and connotation; the alternative to the cutaway for delivering a past through objects. Chapter 5 ( The Transition ) — the mechanics of crossing the gap this chapter decides whether to cross: the orientation budget, the anchor, the drift. Chapter 6 ( The Chapter Break ) — where gaps are placed in a book’s segmentation; proposition and payoff. Chapter 13 ( The Viewpoint Shift ) — for cutaways to material the present viewpoint did not witness. Chapter 14 ( The Subplot ) — the braided structure in the present; the attention tax, of which the interest deficit is the temporal form. Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages ) — §6.2 there, on Sternberg and the distribution of exposition, is this chapter’s direct predecessor. Chapter 10 ( The Prologue ) — the separated unit before the narrative; the inverse criteria described at §1.3 and §8.11 . Chapter 16 ( The Ending ) — where a novel’s past is finally settled, or refused.

title: 16. Coda: Against the Tyranny of Forward Motion
section: Coda — Against the Tyranny of Forward Motion
text: Everything in this chapter is an instrument for noticing. None of it is a rule, and one of its central instruments is more local than it looks. The interest deficit assumes that forward motion is the default state of a narrative and that the past is an interruption of it. That assumption is buried so deep in contemporary craft pedagogy that it is rarely stated, and it produces the whole vocabulary of this territory: earning the cutaway, justifying the flashback, paying back what leaving the present cost. The vocabulary is useful. It is also a description of one kind of novel. For a whole tradition of fiction the assumption runs backwards. Proust’s subject is the recovery of the past , and the present of his narrator is a device for making the recovery possible. To ask whether the madeleine earns the cutaway is to ask whether the novel earns itself. Ford’s Dowell has no present to speak of. A man in a chair, telling a story to nobody, over several evenings. The forward motion of The Good Soldier is not the motion of its events, which are over, but the motion of a mind failing to settle what they were. Faulkner’s Quentin and Shreve sit in a cold room and invent a scene neither of them saw. The present narrative contains two young men, a fire, and some talking; the book is about 1833, and about the impossibility of knowing 1833, and the thinness of 1910 is the condition under which that impossibility becomes visible. Morrison’s past is not behind Sethe. It is in the house, and then in the kitchen, and then at the table eating. The novel’s most radical formal act is to make the past a character, and a model that treats the past as a place a narrative visits cannot describe a book in which the past comes to the narrative. Ishiguro’s present is six days of driving and a broken radiator , and the disproportion is not a flaw the book overcomes but the sentence it passes on its narrator’s life. None of these is a marginal case. They are among the most consequential novels in the tradition this textbook teaches, and every one of them fails the protocol at §7 comprehensively. That is not a licence for weak work — the failure patterns at §8 catch real faults, and a draft in which the past arrives untriggered, unearned and unreturned is usually a draft with a problem. It is a reminder that the protocol measures a book’s relation to its own present , and that some books have decided their present is not where the interest lives. The honest formulation of the chapter’s principle is therefore double, and a student should carry both halves. If your book’s engine is in the present, then every departure from it is a debt, and the tests in §7 will tell you whether you are paying. If your book’s engine is in the past, then the present is a frame, and it should be designed as one — thin on purpose, shaped to occasion the retrospect, and honest with the reader about what it is. The unforgivable case is neither of these. It is the book that has not decided: a present timeline with an engine it does not trust, interrupted by a past it will not commit to, so that each is used to excuse the weakness of the other. That book fails every test in this chapter, and it fails them for a reason no test can state — not because it leaves its present too often, but because it never established one worth leaving. Which suggests a last question, to be asked after the other ten: Which of these two timelines is this book actually about — and does its shape know?

title: Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture
text: Order, Strands and the Meeting of Times: The Full Treatment The Craft Behind the Story (Second Edition), Reference — Chapter 8. Part II: The Joins. This chapter is new in the second edition, so its Reference layer is this single file rather than a corrected original. It extends the reader’s version in Core, Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture , and can be read without it: the definitions it relies on are restated in section 1. Illustrative passages are quoted briefly for the purposes of criticism and study, and full citations appear in section 10. Where a work is read in translation, the translator is named. The analyses disclose the endings of the works they discuss. Contents Scope and working definitions The theory at length: the two orders; Genette’s anachronies; primacy and recency; suspense, curiosity and surprise; unnatural times; the evidence The extended catalogue of architectures: the five of the Core chapter; the reset, the retold and the single day; a summary table; four rulings The extended catalogue of failure patterns The diagnostic procedures, with the order chart and the strand table Further analyses: Cloud Atlas , Hamnet , The Time Traveler’s Wife , Dunkirk The household arrangement in full The limits of the model Glossary of the chapter’s terms Sources 1. Scope and working definitions Story order is the sequence in which events happen in the world of a book; text order is the sequence in which the book presents them. Any discrepancy between them is an anachrony . A book is non-linear when its anachronies form a pattern at the scale of the book, so that the reader learns to expect them, rather than a scatter of local departures. It is multi-timeline when the pattern is organised as two or more strands : lines of the telling, each set in one time and continuous within itself, which the book leaves and resumes. Each continuous run of a strand is an instalment ; each passage between strands is a switch ; the distance in story time between strands at a given point is their interval ; the story time a strand covers per page is its rate ; and the point where strands meet is a convergence , which may be of times (one strand catches up with another), by cause (an act in one produces the situation in another) or by identity (a person or object is found in both). An orientation marker is anything that tells the reader which time she is in. The governing claim is that a book told out of chronological order earns the departure when the order does work that chronology could not: each strand runs on a question of its own, the reader always knows which time she is in and how far it stands from the others, and the meeting of the strands changes what at least one of them meant. The claim concerns use, not difficulty. A book may be hard to follow and justified, as Faulkner’s are, or easy to follow and unjustified, as a draft with dated chapters and no reason for them is. The boundary that matters most in revision is between a strand and a run of cutaways. A cutaway , in Chapter 7 , is a single departure into the past that ends where it began; it answers to the present it interrupts. A strand recurs, advances in its own time between instalments and runs on a question of its own. Material that recurs without a question of its own lies at the threshold between them (section 3.4). The chapter leaves the single cutaway to Chapter 7 , the withholding of truths for their own sake to Chapter 15 , the prologue as a unit to Chapter 10 , threads in one time to Chapter 14 , the duties of a middle to Chapter 11 , and the order of volumes in a series to Chapter 17, Series and Genre . 2. The theory at length 2.1 The two orders The Russian Formalists made the distinction that every later account of narrative time uses. Viktor Shklovsky, in essays of the 1920s, treated the arrangement of a story’s events as one of the devices by which art makes the familiar strange, and Boris Tomashevsky’s “Thematics” (1925; translated by Lee T. Lemon and Marion J. Reis, 1965) defined the fabula as the events in their causal-temporal order and the syuzhet as the same events in the order and manner the work presents them. The distinction tells a writer what she controls when she rearranges: not what happened, but when the reader meets it, and so what the reader knows at each point. It also tells her what she cannot change by rearrangement. A book whose events lack causal pressure in sequence will lack it in any order, since order can redistribute suspense but not create stakes. 2.2 Genette’s anachronies Gérard Genette’s Narrative Discourse (1972; translated by Jane E. Lewin, 1980) gave the comparison its working vocabulary. An analepsis goes back to an event earlier than the present of the narrative; a prolepsis goes forward to a later one. Each has a reach , its distance in time from the present it leaves, and an extent , the story time it covers. An analepsis is external when its whole extent lies before the start of the main narrative, internal when it lies within it, and mixed when it begins before and runs into it. Genette also named achrony , an event whose position in story time cannot be fixed, and syllepsis , the grouping of events by some kinship other than time, of place or theme, which is the principle of the mosaic. Genette’s notation numbers the positions of units in story order and writes them in text order. The household novel, charted in section 7, is 2–4[1]–3–4: the prologue (story position 2), the July present (4), within which Nadia’s memory of the pen (1) is an internal cutaway, Dov’s evening of 9 March (3), and July again. The formula shows at once that the book has one sizeable anachrony at its centre of gravity, the move to position 3 at about 78 per cent, and that its prologue is the first instalment of a strand whose second instalment is that chapter. A writer who charts a draft in this way usually finds either that the arrangement is simpler than she thought or that it has no pattern at all. 2.3 Primacy and recency Menakhem Perry’s “Literary Dynamics: How the Order of a Text Creates Its Meanings” ( Poetics Today , 1979) argued that readers form a frame from the first material they meet and interpret later material through it, the primacy effect , until accumulated evidence forces a change, after which the latest frame governs, the recency effect. Meir Sternberg’s Expositional Modes and Temporal Ordering in Fiction (1978) made the parallel argument for exposition: the placement of antecedent facts decides which the reader takes as normal. For a non-linear book the consequence is direct. Every arrangement installs some frame first, and the frame governs the reading of everything until it is overturned. Opening on the end of a story, as an anchored order does, makes the reader read every scene as a step towards it; opening on a strand set in the past makes her read the present as its consequence. Neither is neutral, and the writer’s choice of first strand is a choice of frame. 2.4 Suspense, curiosity and surprise William Brewer and Edward Lichtenstein’s structural-affect theory (“Stories Are to Entertain: A Structural-Affect Theory of Stories”, Journal of Pragmatics 6, 1982) derived three affects from the relation between event order and discourse order. Suspense follows when the text presents an initiating event and delays its outcome; curiosity when it omits a significant earlier event and the reader knows something is missing; surprise when it omits one without the reader knowing and discloses it later. Their readers judged texts more story-like when the order produced one of these structures and the outcome was resolved. The theory makes a braided book’s switch legible: it is a delay of outcome in one strand, which produces suspense only if the strand left behind holds an initiating event without its outcome. It also accounts for the anchored order, which converts the suspense of what will happen into the curiosity of how did it come to happen , and for the reverse order, which is curiosity at every step. 2.5 Unnatural times Brian Richardson (“Beyond Story and Discourse: Narrative Time in Postmodern and Nonmimetic Fiction”, 2002) and other writers on what they call unnatural narrative have described temporalities that no single story order can reconcile: times that loop, run backwards in causation as well as telling, contradict themselves, or move at different rates for different characters in one world. Virginia Woolf’s Orlando (1928), whose hero lives for more than three centuries and ages about twenty years, is a familiar case of the last. Most revision problems involve reconcilable times, and the chapter’s tools assume them; a book whose times contradict each other on purpose is judged by whether the contradiction is declared and used, which is test 1’s question in another form. 2.6 The evidence The empirical work on time in reading comes from the study of situation models, the mental representations readers build of the world a text describes. Rolf Zwaan, Mark Langston and Arthur Graesser’s event-indexing model ( Psychological Science , 1995) proposed that readers index events on five dimensions, time, space, causation, intentionality and protagonist, and update the model when any changes. Zwaan’s “Processing Narrative Time Shifts” ( Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition , 1996) found that sentences beginning An hour later or A day later took longer to read than those beginning A moment later , and that events from before a larger shift were recognised more slowly afterwards, though the distance in words was the same: a shift in story time makes earlier material less accessible. Keisuke Ohtsuka and William Brewer (“Discourse Organization in the Comprehension of Temporal Order in Narrative Texts”, Discourse Processes 15, 1992) reported poorer comprehension of the order of events when texts departed from chronological order; the chapter relies on the published summary rather than the paper for this finding. These studies use short texts, mostly invented, read once in a laboratory, and none measures a novel. They support one inference, that every switch of time imposes a cost the reader pays in updating, and they say nothing about the pleasures that justify the cost, which Brewer and Lichtenstein’s theory describes and which no study cited here measures at book length. 3. The extended catalogue of architectures 3.1 The five of the Core chapter Core classifies non-linear books by what governs their order. The braid alternates strands, each chronological within itself; in a converging braid the interval shortens until the strands meet in time ( Where the Crawdads Sing , 2018), and in a parallel braid it holds and the strands meet by cause or identity ( The Forgotten Garden , 2008; Station Eleven , 2014). The anchored order shows or announces an event early and tells the book towards it ( Chronicle of a Death Foretold , 1981, translated by Gregory Rabassa, 1982). The reverse order tells events backwards (Pinter’s Betrayal , 1978; Amis’s Time’s Arrow , 1991). The mosaic orders by association ( Slaughterhouse-Five , 1969; A Visit from the Goon Squad , 2010). The nested order opens times inside each other and closes them in reverse ( Wuthering Heights , 1847; Cloud Atlas , 2004). 3.2 The reset The reset tells one span of time more than once, each telling starting again from the same point and diverging. Ken Grimwood’s Replay (1986) returns its hero, who dies at forty-three, to his college years again each time he dies, so that the reader meets the same decades many times with variations, and the film Groundhog Day (1993), which Chapter 11 reads as a middle, repeats one day. The reset’s strands are versions, not times, and its orientation problem is to tell the reader which version she is in; the usual solution is a fixed point of restart that the reader learns to recognise, and a difference in the hero’s knowledge from one version to the next. Its question is what changes between versions and why, and it fails when the variations are arbitrary. 3.3 The retold The retold order tells one event several times from several vantages, each a strand of one event. Akira Kurosawa’s Rashomon (1950) gives four incompatible accounts of a killing; the first season of The Affair , which Chapter 13 reads for its allocation, tells each episode twice. The retold order is a viewpoint arrangement as much as a temporal one, and Chapter 13’s epistemological domain, adopted by Chapter 15 at the scale of a book as the plural-vantage form of the declined reveal, is its usual purpose: to show that no account suffices. 3.4 The single day in several lives A braid whose strands each cover one day, often in different years, is common enough to name. Virginia Woolf’s Mrs Dalloway (1925) is one day in one year with many minds; Michael Cunningham’s The Hours (1998) takes three days, in 1923, 1949 and the end of the century, linked by Woolf’s novel. The form’s rates are equal by design, and it must supply its variation by the strands’ differing stakes and by a convergence of identity (in The Hours , Laura Brown is the mother of Clarissa’s friend Richard). 3.5 Summary table The table summarises what each architecture does to the reader and what it risks. Architecture What governs order What the reader holds Typical convergence Chief risk Converging braid Two chronologies, interval shortening Suspense in each strand; the approach of the meeting Of times A strand skimmed Parallel braid Two chronologies, interval fixed A question in each strand; the expected link By cause or identity Convergence by coincidence Anchored order An event shown first Curiosity about how and why The anchor reached The anchor answers the book’s question Reverse order Story order inverted Curiosity at every step The first event, shown last Monotony of cause Mosaic Association or theme Assembly An event the fragments circle Achrony without purpose Nested order Frames The inner time judged by the outer The frame closed A frame left open Reset Versions of one span Comparison The final version Arbitrary variation Retold Vantages on one event Comparison of accounts A reconciliation, or none Repetition Single day One day in each strand Juxtaposition By identity Lockstep The rows combine. Memento (2000) is a reverse order braided with a forward strand that converges with it in time; Cloud Atlas is a nested order whose strands meet by reading; the household novel is an anchored order whose anchor, the prologue, is also the first instalment of a two-instalment strand. 3.6 Four rulings Four earlier chapters proposed categories and left this chapter to adopt or reject them at the scale of a book, because time at that scale is its material. The structural domain (Chapter 7): rejected as a domain of the cutaway; kept as the threshold of a strand. Chapter 7 proposed that a cutaway serves a structural domain when its function is architectural, establishing, maintaining or completing a pattern in the book’s design (the braided timeline, the returning frame, the recurring approach), and adopted it for diagnosis on condition that the pattern be declared and the claim checked. It conceded that the domain might be texture or reader knowledge seen at book scale, and that it mixed what does this deliver here? with what does this do for the book? Its test cases were The Forgotten Garden and Where the Crawdads Sing . At the scale of a book, both cases are strands, not runs of cutaways: each instalment of their past strands advances a question of its own (who left the child on the wharf, and why; how Kya becomes the woman the town suspects), and neither is justified by architecture alone. What Chapter 7 named is therefore the threshold of a strand , the point at which recurring material from another time acquires a question of its own and passes from Chapter 7’s tests to this chapter’s. The mixing of questions that Chapter 7 conceded is resolved by the threshold: what does this deliver here? is asked of a cutaway, what does this do for the book? of a strand. The first objection is upheld in part, since material that recurs in a pattern without a question of its own is texture at book scale, and fails as the explaining strand (section 4.1). Chapter 7’s two conditions survive as test 2 and as the rule that a strand be declared early. Temporal counterpoint (Chapter 14): adopted at the scale of a book, as a property of the arrangement. Chapter 14 proposed temporal counterpoint, a subplot on a different clock from the main plot’s, and adopted it on condition that a thread claiming it also show a chain, conceding that it might be a property of the telling, that it rarely appears without thematic counterpoint, and, as unanswered, that it gives every slow, inert thread a defence. This chapter accepts the first objection and turns it into the ruling: a difference of rate is made by the arrangement, and it works only where a crossing sets one strand’s time against another’s. That answers the third objection, because the claim is checked at the crossings, where it can be seen, rather than asserted of a thread; a slow strand that never meets a fast one where the difference shows has no counterpoint to claim. Dunkirk (2017) and Hamnet (2020) are the test cases (sections 6.2 and 6.4). The second objection stands: in both, the counterpoint carries the theme. For threads in one time, Chapter 14’s condition stands unchanged. The temporal domain (Chapter 4): adopted at the scale of a book, as the domain of orientation. Chapter 4 proposed that a detail belongs to a temporal domain when its work is to establish duration, sequence, decay, repurposing, season or interruption, with carriers in aspect, wear, residue and maintenance; it adopted the domain for diagnosis, conceding the parsimony objection, and left its fate at larger scales to this chapter. In a multi-timeline book the same places and objects appear in several times, and temporal detail is the only material that tells a reader which time a passage is in without a heading. That answers, at this scale, the objection that time is a feature of details rather than a kind: a detail may be chosen for the time it places a passage in and for nothing else, and such details are what orientation is made of. Jon McGregor’s Reservoir 13 (2017), which Chapter 4 used, is confirmed as the test case: its thirteen chapters, one a year, are oriented by the calendar of a village. The parsimony objection stands for the single detail, where Chapter 4 left it. The domain’s failure at this scale is the undated strand. The bridging object (Chapter 5): adopted at the scale of a book, as a means of convergence by identity, with a condition. Chapter 5 proposed the bridging object, a physical thing on both sides of a gap whose presence anchors the new unit by identity rather than resemblance, and adopted it for revision, conceding as unanswered that identity and resemblance may not differ for the reader. Its test cases were Station Eleven ’s paperweight and the household ledger. Both pass at book scale on one condition, which this chapter makes part of the definition: the object’s condition or custody must change between its appearances, so that the change measures the interval. Under that condition identity and resemblance do differ for the reader, because a resembling object carries no history and an identical one carries the time between. The paperweight’s changes of custody across twenty years and the ledger’s change of hand on 9 March each tell the reader how much time has passed and through whose hands. Without a change, the conceded objection stands, and the object is a match-cut. 4. The extended catalogue of failure patterns 4.1 The five patterns of the Core chapter The arbitrary arrangement departs from story order for interest the departure does not produce; it fails test 1, and its exception is Catch-22 (1961), whose scatter is a recurring approach to Snowden’s death. The lost reader is a failure of orientation, test 3; its exception is The Sound and the Fury (1929), whose first section makes disorientation its narrator’s condition. The explaining strand recurs like a strand and works like a cutaway, accounting for the present without a question of its own; it fails tests 2 and 6, and its exception is Citizen Kane (1941), whose flashbacks borrow the frame’s question. The lockstep braid runs its strands at one rate, failing test 5; its exception is The Hours (1998), whose equal days are its argument. The convergence by coincidence joins strands by a link that changes nothing, failing test 7; its exception is Cloud Atlas (2004), whose birthmark is idle and whose real link is reading. 4.2 The premature convergence Symptom. The second half of the book feels like an epilogue; readers say it lost its tension once the timelines met. Mechanism. A converging braid whose strands meet before the book has a question for the merged line. The meeting answers both strands’ questions at once, and nothing replaces them; it fails test 7 on the side of timing, and Chapter 15 ’s successor test. Remedy. Move the meeting later, or let it raise a question that only the merged line can answer, and make that the second half’s engine. Exception. Gillian Flynn’s Gone Girl (2012), whose diary strand meets the present at the start of Part Two, about halfway, and whose second half runs on the stronger question the meeting creates: what Amy will do next. 4.3 The frame left open Symptom. Readers reach the end and ask what became of the people in the opening. Mechanism. A nested order whose outer frame is opened and never closed, so the inner time is never judged by the outer; it fails test 7, since one convergence is missing. Remedy. Close the frame, however briefly, or cut it, unless its openness is the point and the book shows that it is. Exception. Henry James’s The Turn of the Screw (1898), which opens with Douglas and his listeners round a fire and never goes back to them; the open frame leaves the governess’s account without the judgement a closing would supply, which is the book’s ambiguity. 4.4 The over-labelled book Symptom. Readers report no confusion and little immersion; they read the headings more attentively than the prose. Mechanism. Orientation carried entirely by headings and time-stamps, so that the strands’ own material does no placing and the reader is told rather than shown which time she is in; it passes test 3 at the cost of the temporal domain’s work. Remedy. Remove the headings from one strand in a test copy and see whether its instalments still place themselves; supply the details that would let them, then keep only the headings that still earn their place. Exception. Audrey Niffenegger’s The Time Traveler’s Wife (2003), which heads its sections with a date and the lovers’ ages, and succeeds because its hero’s condition puts him in two times at once, where no detail could place the reader as quickly (section 6.3). 4.5 The strand that outgrows the book Symptom. Readers prefer the strand the writer meant as secondary, and the book’s ending, which resolves the other, disappoints them. Mechanism. A strand given a stronger question than the main line, so that the arrangement’s weight falls where the book’s resolution does not; it is the explaining strand’s opposite. Remedy. Either make the stronger strand the main line and resolve the book there, or weaken its question so that it serves the other. Exception. The Godfather Part II (Francis Ford Coppola, 1974), whose strand of the young Vito’s rise in the 1910s and 1920s many viewers prefer to Michael’s story in the 1950s; it succeeds because the film is built on the counterpoint, the father gaining a family as the son loses his, so neither strand is secondary. 5. The diagnostic procedures The tests use two documents. The order chart numbers every unit of the book (chapter or scene) by its place in story order and lists the numbers in text order, with each unit’s position in the book as a percentage; Genette’s notation (section 2.2) is a compressed form of it. The strand table gives each strand a row and seven columns: its question, its span of story time, its page count, its rate (span divided by pages), its viewpoint, its orientation markers, and the point and kind of its meeting with the others. Draft both before revising. Test 1, necessity. Retell the book in story order in a page. List what a reader of the arrangement knows, wants or fears at the quarter, the middle and three-quarters that a reader of the retelling would not. Fewer than two items in all is a failure; one item is a design to rebuild around. Test 2, strand question. Write each strand’s question in a line. Read the other strands for its answer; a question answered elsewhere before the strand reaches it is no question. For a strand set in the past, check especially that the present does not show its outcome. Test 3, orientation. Copy the first two sentences of every instalment onto one page and mark those that place the reader in time. Classify each marker as viewpoint, tense, detail, object or heading; a strand placed by headings alone is the undated strand. Test 4, interval. Plot each strand’s story time against text position. Lines that converge show a clock; parallel lines need a reason, usually a meeting by cause or identity; lines the reader cannot plot, because the text never says how far apart the times are, are a failure unless the book’s design is achronic. Test 5, rate. Read the rate column. Strands within a factor of two of each other run in lockstep unless a crossing shows a difference of another kind. For strands of different rate, find the crossing where the difference shows; if none exists, the counterpoint is claimed, not made. Test 6, switch. For every switch, note the open question left behind and the first thing that happens in the instalment entered. An instalment whose first page could be cut without loss is an entry that does not pay. Test 7, convergence. Name each meeting and its kind, then write what at least one strand means after it that it did not mean before. A blank is the convergence by coincidence; a meeting before the last third needs a successor question. Test 8, withholding. List each fact the arrangement delays. For each, ask whether a character could have told it earlier and why she did not; apply Chapter 15 ’s test for a withholder. 6. Further analyses 6.1 Cloud Atlas (David Mitchell, 2004): a nested order joined by reading Six stories, from a nineteenth-century Pacific journal (Adam Ewing’s) through letters of 1931 (Robert Frobisher’s), a thriller set in 1975 (Luisa Rey’s), a present-day comedy (Timothy Cavendish’s) and a twenty-second-century testimony (Sonmi-451’s), to an account of a far future after a collapse (Zachry’s), are told in nested order: the first five break off, the sixth is told whole at the centre, and the five resume in reverse, ending where the book began. Each later narrator encounters the earlier story as a text or a film: Frobisher finds half of Ewing’s journal, Luisa reads Frobisher’s letters, Cavendish is sent Luisa’s story as a manuscript, Sonmi watches a film of Cavendish’s, and Zachry’s people revere Sonmi. The strand questions are each story’s own, and the nested order adds a second question to each, how its story will be read later, which the next story answers. The book’s rates differ by centuries, and the counterpoint shows at every break, where a story is cut off and becomes, in the next, a document someone finds incomplete. The convergence is by identity, of a kind the chapter’s condition anticipates: the text changes custody and condition between strands (half a journal, a manuscript, a film), and each change measures the interval. The comet-shaped birthmark several protagonists share is the idle link (section 4.1); the reading is the working one. The nested order’s containment does the book’s argument: each age is judged by the next, which reads it as a fragment, and the book closes on the earliest voice, Ewing’s, resolving to oppose the predation the later stories have shown. 6.2 Hamnet (Maggie O’Farrell, 2020): counterpoint of a day and fifteen years The first part braids two strands. One covers a single day in 1596 in Stratford, when Judith, one of the twins, falls ill and her brother Hamnet runs from house to house looking for help; the other begins about fifteen years earlier, with the courtship of Agnes and a young Latin tutor whose name the novel never uses, and runs through their marriage, the children’s births and his departure for London. The second part follows the family after Hamnet’s death, to Agnes’s journey to London and a play that bears her son’s name. The two strands of the first part run at rates differing by a factor of thousands, and the arrangement makes the difference felt. Each instalment of the long strand ends at a choice whose cost the short strand is paying: Agnes’s decision to stay in Stratford when her husband goes to London is read against a day on which the father is absent and the mother is away from the house. This is temporal counterpoint as section 3.6 rules it, a property of the arrangement checked at the crossings, and it carries the book’s theme, the price of the life the marriage chose, which the second objection to the domain predicts. The strands converge in time when the long strand reaches 1596 and the day’s end, which is Hamnet’s death, and the second part changes the arrangement to a single chronological line, which is itself a change of rate after the meeting. 6.3 The Time Traveler’s Wife (Audrey Niffenegger, 2003): orientation as structure Henry DeTamble has a genetic condition that moves him involuntarily through time; Clare Abshire meets him first when she is six and he is thirty-six, visiting her childhood from his future, and he meets her first when he is twenty-eight and she is twenty, in a library in Chicago, when he has never seen her before. The novel alternates their first-person narratives, and each section is headed with a date and both of their ages. The arrangement is a braid of two lives in one chronology, Clare’s, with Henry’s instalments scattered through his own. The orientation problem is the hardest in the chapter: the same man appears at different ages in one scene, and a reader must know which Henry she is meeting. The headings solve it, and they are the over-labelled book’s exception (section 4.4). The questions are distinct for each narrator, Clare’s how to live with a man who comes and goes, Henry’s whether he can change what he has already seen, and the convergence is the one the opening implies, the meeting in which both are their own age. 6.4 Dunkirk (Christopher Nolan, 2017): three rates in one rescue The film braids three strands, titled at their first appearance: the mole, one week, following soldiers on the beach waiting for evacuation; the sea, one day, following a civilian boat, the Moonstone , crossing the Channel; the air, one hour, following Spitfire pilots covering the evacuation. They are intercut as though simultaneous, so that night falls in one strand while another is in daylight, and they cross at the rescues: a pilot shot down is picked up by the Moonstone , and men in the water are saved by the boat and covered by the pilot whose hour ends on the beach. The arrangement is temporal counterpoint at its purest, since the three rates are the design and the crossings are where they show: an event first seen in the hour-long strand is seen again from the day-long one, later in the film and earlier in its own strand’s day, so the viewer feels the same moment as an hour’s urgency and as a day’s labour. The questions are the strands’ own, whether these men get home. Orientation is carried by the title cards and by each strand’s own material, the beach, the boat, the cockpit, the cheapest markers in film. The convergence changes little in what the strands meant and much in what they feel like, which is the exception to test 7: the film’s argument is that the rescue was made of different durations that met. 7. The household arrangement in full 7.1 The draft strand The draft in Core’s “The Problem” braids six chapters in the father’s viewpoint through the first three-quarters of the book, each headed with a date. Charted, they fall at about 10, 22, 35, 48, 60 and 75 per cent: a scene of the second loss of the good pen, in February, with his line to Nadia; a day at the shop with a letter he does not open in front of anyone; the stock count and the till counted twice; a Sunday with Ma, who names his habit with the cuff; the prologue’s day retold at length; and the evening of 9 March up to the entry breaking off. The last would sit three per cent before Dov’s chapter of the same evening. The draft passes test 3 and fails tests 2, 5, 7 and 8, as Core records. Section 2.4 shows why test 6 fails as well: every switch into the strand leaves the sisters’ July on an open question and enters a time whose outcome the reader knows, so the switch converts suspense into nothing. Two chapters also retell what the book already has, the prologue’s day and the pen conversation, the first by duplicating a unit and the second by moving Nadia’s memory, with its misreading, into the father’s mind, where it cannot be a misreading. And the strand grants a viewpoint the allocation of Chapter 13 does not include. 7.2 The order chart Without the strand, the book’s story positions are: 1, the second loss of the pen, in the year of the father’s death; 2, the last ordinary day, early March, three days before he stopped answering the phone; 3, the evening of 9 March; 4, July. In Genette’s notation the text order is 2–4[1]–3–4. Position 1 is an internal cutaway within position 4, at about two-thirds, through Nadia’s memory; position 3 is a full chapter at about 78 per cent. The prologue and Dov’s chapter are the two instalments of a March strand. 7.3 The strand table Strand Question Span Share of book Viewpoint Markers Meeting March In case of what? (the prologue’s) A few days, from the last ordinary day to the evening of 9 March Two chapters, about 4 per cent The father; then Dov The label Prologue ; the date heading 9 March (proposed); the good pen in its place, the ballpoint, the ledger in one hand In the reading: the record of March read in July July What did the father leave, and what do the three do with it? A few weeks About 96 per cent Elena and Nadia The dust on the coat, the sign reading OPEN since March, the drawer, the ledger in two hands The convergence and the reading Measured across the gap between its instalments, the March strand covers a few days in about 4 per cent of the book and the July strand a few weeks in the rest, so the rates differ by a factor of about four, March the faster. The difference shows at one crossing, the ledger page on which eleven years of one hand stop and four months of another begin: the reader meets it in July at a quarter, and enters its first evening at 78 per cent. 7.4 The revision Version B cuts the draft strand and heads Dov’s chapter 9 March , written as the date stands in the ledger. It is the only dated heading in the book, and it uses the bridging object as an orientation marker: the reader has seen the date on the page where the hand changes, at about 25 per cent, and the heading places her by recognition rather than by a calendar. The chapter’s text is unchanged, including the two sentences that Chapter 15 adds to it. 7.5 What the revision settles, and what it does not The revision settles that the household novel is an anchored order with a two-instalment March strand, that the father has no strand of his own, and that the ledger is the object joining the times, under the condition of section 3.6, since it changes hands and hand between them. It does not settle the interval between the prologue’s day and 9 March, which the prologue measures from the day the father stopped answering the phone and the canon does not date; whether that day was the ninth is left to the author. It does not answer the early reader’s complaint that the father is a ghost, which the book’s subject defends and a reader may still reject. It assumes that no other chapter of the book carries a heading that would make a dated one unremarkable. And Nadia’s memory of the pen, the book’s one cutaway into a third time, must carry its marker, the second time he lost the pen , in its first sentence. 8. The limits of the model The model assumes a reader who reads once, in order, and assembles a story order as she goes, and a book whose times can be reconciled into one chronology. It fits the braided commercial novel, the anchored mystery and most literary arrangements well, and fits less well the books that unsettle chronology on purpose, whose times loop or contradict each other (section 2.5), and the rereader, who holds the whole story order from the first page and reads an arrangement as a set of juxtapositions rather than a sequence of disclosures. It also treats a strand as defined by its time, when some strands are defined as much by a viewpoint or a document, as the retold order shows; the chapter’s boundary with Chapter 13 is drawn for convenience, not on principle. And the evidence in section 2.6 measures the costs of a change of time and not its pleasures, so the model’s claim that an arrangement must earn its costs rests on argument rather than measurement. 9. Glossary of the chapter’s terms The definitions below are for the consolidated glossary. Achrony. Genette’s term for an event whose position in story time cannot be fixed from the text. Anachrony. Any discrepancy between story order and text order (Genette). Analepsis. An anachrony that goes back to an event earlier than the present of the narrative; external, internal or mixed according to whether its extent lies before, within or across the start of the main narrative (Genette). Anchored order. An architecture that shows or announces one event early and tells the book towards it. Arbitrary arrangement. A failure pattern: a departure from story order for interest the departure does not produce. Braid. An architecture that alternates two or more strands, each chronological within itself; converging when the interval shortens until the strands meet in time, parallel when it holds. Bridging object. At the scale of a book, an object present in two strands whose changed condition or custody measures the interval between them; a means of convergence by identity (proposed in Chapter 5, adopted at this scale with that condition in Chapter 8). Convergence. The point at which strands meet: of times, when one strand catches up with another; by cause, when an act in one produces the situation in another; by identity, when a person or object is found in both. Convergence by coincidence. A failure pattern: strands joined by a link that carries no cause and changes no meaning. Explaining strand. A failure pattern: material from another time that recurs like a strand but only accounts for the present, with no question of its own. Extent. The story time an anachrony covers (Genette). Instalment. One continuous run of a strand. Interval. The distance in story time between two strands at a given point. Lockstep braid. A failure pattern: strands at one rate, with crossings that produce no variation. Lost reader. A failure pattern: instalments that do not tell the reader which time she is in. Mosaic. An architecture whose units are ordered by association, theme or memory rather than by time. Multi-timeline. Of a non-linear book whose anachronies are organised as two or more strands. Nested order. An architecture that opens one time inside another and closes them in reverse. Non-linear. Of a book whose anachronies form a pattern at the scale of the book. Order chart. A list of a book’s units in text order, each numbered by its place in story order and placed by percentage. Orientation marker. Anything that tells the reader which time she is in: viewpoint, tense, period or wear, an object, a heading or a time-stamp. Over-labelled book. A failure pattern: orientation carried by headings alone, at the cost of the strands’ own placing. Premature convergence. A failure pattern: strands that meet before the book has a question for the merged line. Prolepsis. An anachrony that goes forward to a later event (Genette). Rate. The story time a strand covers per page. Reset. An architecture that tells one span of time more than once, each version starting again from the same point. Retold order. An architecture that tells one event several times from several vantages. Reverse order. An architecture that tells events backwards, unit by unit. Story order and text order. The sequence of events in the world of a book, and the sequence in which the book presents them (the Formalists’ fabula and syuzhet ). Strand. A line of the telling set in one time, continuous within itself, that the book leaves and resumes, and that runs on a question of its own. Strand table. A table giving each strand its question, span, page count, rate, viewpoint, markers and meeting. Switch. A passage from one strand to another. Syllepsis. Genette’s term for the grouping of events by a kinship other than time, of place or theme. Temporal counterpoint. At the scale of a book, a difference of rate between strands that a crossing makes visible; a property of the arrangement (proposed in Chapter 14 for threads, adopted at this scale in Chapter 8). Temporal domain. The work a detail does in establishing duration, sequence, decay, repurposing, season or interruption; at the scale of a book, the domain of orientation (proposed in Chapter 4, adopted at this scale in Chapter 8). Threshold of a strand. The point at which recurring material from another time acquires a question of its own and becomes a strand; what Chapter 7’s proposed structural domain named (rejected as a domain of the cutaway in Chapter 8). Undated strand. A strand whose instalments are placed in time by headings alone. 10. Sources Brewer, William F., and Edward H. Lichtenstein, “Stories Are to Entertain: A Structural-Affect Theory of Stories”, Journal of Pragmatics 6 (1982), 473–486. Genette, Gérard, Narrative Discourse: An Essay in Method (1972), translated by Jane E. Lewin (Ithaca: Cornell University Press, 1980). Ohtsuka, Keisuke, and William F. Brewer, “Discourse Organization in the Comprehension of Temporal Order in Narrative Texts”, Discourse Processes 15 (1992). Perry, Menakhem, “Literary Dynamics: How the Order of a Text Creates Its Meanings”, Poetics Today 1 (1979). Richardson, Brian, “Beyond Story and Discourse: Narrative Time in Postmodern and Nonmimetic Fiction”, in Narrative Dynamics: Essays on Time, Plot, Closure, and Frames , edited by Brian Richardson (Columbus: Ohio State University Press, 2002). Sternberg, Meir, Expositional Modes and Temporal Ordering in Fiction (Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press, 1978). Tomashevsky, Boris, “Thematics” (1925), in Russian Formalist Criticism: Four Essays , translated by Lee T. Lemon and Marion J. Reis (Lincoln: University of Nebraska Press, 1965). Zwaan, Rolf A., “Processing Narrative Time Shifts”, Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition 22 (1996). Zwaan, Rolf A., Mark C. Langston and Arthur C. title: The Opening Pages
text: The Beginning of the Main Narrative: Theory, Analysis and Practice The Craft Behind the Story (Second Edition), Reference — Chapter 9. Part III: The Architecture of the Whole. The first chapter of Part III, and the formal inverse of Chapter 16 ( The Ending ): the opening works with no accumulated context, the ending with nothing but. Builds on Chapter 1 ( The Purposes of a Scene ); its §4.6 formal contract is closed by Chapter 16 §4.6 , and its §8.4 borrowed hook is Chapter One’s version of the false advertising treated in Chapter 10 ( The Prologue ) §8.2 . All illustrative passages are quoted briefly for the purposes of criticism and study; full citations appear in §14 . Contents On this page: Chapter Abstract · Learning Outcomes · Key Terms · How to Use This Chapter Introduction: The Threshold Problem Definitions and Boundaries Why Beginnings Carry Disproportionate Weight The Contracts — voice, genre, character, world, stakes, and a proposed sixth Multiplicity: The Economy of the Opening The Attack: In Medias Res , Orientation, and the Repertoire of Gambits Diagnostic Method — the ten tests Failure Patterns — with their exceptions Worked Analyses — seven close readings and a revision case Openings Across Forms · Concordance: concept to novel Revision Checklist Studio Work — exercises, seminar questions, assessment rubric Glossary Sources Cited Further Reading Coda: Against Mechanical Application Chapter Abstract The opening pages of a novel are the only stretch of narrative that must perform every one of fiction’s core functions simultaneously and without credit . Every later scene draws on trust the book has already accumulated; the opening pages must generate that trust from nothing. This chapter formalises that intuition into a teachable model. It proceeds in four movements: Theory — why beginnings carry disproportionate interpretive and cognitive weight, drawing on the psychology of primacy effects, situation-model theory, reader-response criticism and reception aesthetics. Taxonomy — the five contracts (voice, genre, character, world, stakes), expanded here with a proposed sixth (the formal contract ), each anatomised in terms of its textual carriers and characteristic failure modes. Method — the principle of multiplicity , the historical tension between in medias res and orientation, a taxonomy of opening gambits , and a ten-test diagnostic protocol for revision. Application — expanded failure patterns with counterexamples, an anthology of close readings of published openings, notes on openings across forms, and a full apparatus of exercises, glossary, sources and further reading.
