title: Arc and Theme
text: Choice, Change and the Argument of a Book: The Full Treatment The Craft Behind the Story (Second Edition), Reference — Chapter 12. Part III: The Architecture of the Whole. This chapter is new in the second edition, so its Reference layer is this single file rather than a corrected original. It extends the reader’s version in Core, Arc and Theme , and can be read without it: the definitions it relies on are restated in section 1. Illustrative passages are quoted briefly for the purposes of criticism and study, and full citations appear in section 10. Where a work is read in translation, the translator is named. Contents Scope and working definitions The theory at length: Aristotle on character and choice; Forster’s flat and round; Egri’s premise and its descendants; the arc models compared; theme as a question; the evidence The extended catalogue of arcs: the disillusionment arc, arcs across an ensemble, the arc held across a series, and a summary table The extended catalogue of failure patterns The diagnostic procedures, with a blank criterion log and answer map Further analyses: Project Hail Mary , The Kite Runner , Paddington 2 The household arcs in full The limits of the model Glossary of the chapter’s terms Sources 1. Scope and working definitions A character’s arc is the course, across a whole book, of the rule by which that character resolves dilemmas. The rule is the criterion , a term from Chapter 2 : a rule about which cost is more bearable, applied whenever a character must choose between two options each of which costs something. Most decisions are made on a criterion the character already holds. The hinge , also Chapter 2’s term, is the decision at which a dilemma is resolved on a criterion the character did not hold before; the old rule is usually outranked rather than refuted. An arc is therefore read by setting a character’s largest decisions side by side and comparing the rules behind them. A theme is a question a book tests rather than a proposition it asserts, as Chapter 16 puts it for the ending. It differs from a topic, which names what the book is about, and from a thesis, which is one answer. Read from the other side, each character’s criterion is that character’s answer to the book’s question, and the book argues by arranging the answers and by where the protagonist’s hinge places the protagonist among them. The governing claim is that arc and theme are one structure. An arc exists only at a decision that costs something the old rule valued, and a theme is argued by setting one character’s choice beside the others’ rather than by saying what it means; a change that is announced, or a meaning that is spoken, is an arc or a theme in description only. The claim is about where change and meaning are made, in decisions, and not about how much change a book should contain. A book whose protagonist does not change can satisfy it, provided the refusal or the steadfastness is itself chosen under pressure. The chapter does not treat the single decision and its dilemma ( Chapter 2 ), the allocation of minds through which an arc can be shown from inside ( Chapter 13 ), thematic counterpoint between plot lines ( Chapter 14 ), the completion of arcs and the closure of themes at the last pages ( Chapter 16 ), the midpoint’s change of mode or knowledge ( Chapter 11 ), the reader’s change of understanding at a revelation ( Chapter 15, The Reveal ) or the arc of a character carried across several volumes ( Chapter 17, Series and Genre ). 2. The theory at length 2.1 Aristotle: character in choice The Poetics is the oldest source for the idea that character is shown in choice. In S. H. Butcher’s translation: “Character is that which reveals moral purpose, showing what kind of things a man chooses or avoids.” The words are ēthos and prohairesis , and the second means deliberate choice, a decision taken with a view to an end. The consequence Aristotle draws, that plot ranks above character, follows from the definition: a person is known by what they do, and what they do is plot. A speech in which a character says nothing about what they would choose, Aristotle adds in the same chapter, does not express character at all. The Poetics also supplies a term the chapter uses at one remove. Its recognition , anagnorisis , is a change from ignorance to knowledge, and in the best tragedies it coincides with a reversal of fortune. Recognition is not an arc in this chapter’s sense, since it changes what a character knows rather than the rule by which they choose. But the commonest staged arc in the novel puts a recognition before the hinge, and the refused arc ends on a recognition with no hinge after it, so the relation between the two is the axis on which several of the arcs in section 3 differ. 2.2 Forster’s flat and round E. M. Forster’s Aspects of the Novel (1927) gives the most quoted account of which characters change. Flat characters are “constructed round a single idea or quality”; round characters are “capable of surprising in a convincing way”. Forster defends flat characters, which are easy to recognise and remember, and reserves only tragedy of any length for the round. His test of roundness has two halves, and the chapter’s conditions for a change divide between them. Surprise is what the seed must not spoil and the scheduled arc loses; conviction is what the seed, the price and the enactment supply. A change that meets only the first half reads as the author’s convenience, and one that meets only the second reads as a plan. Forster’s division has a corollary that the arc models in section 2.4 tend to forget. A flat character can be the agent of another character’s change, and a book can have a round protagonist who does not change. Neither is a failure in his terms. 2.3 Egri’s premise and its descendants Lajos Egri’s The Art of Dramatic Writing (1946), written for playwrights, begins from the premise , “a proposition antecedently supposed or proved; a basis of argument”, and gives Macbeth ’s as “Ruthless ambition leads to its own destruction”. A play is the proof of its premise, carried out by characters whom conflict forces to change, and the writer who knows the premise knows what kind of person can carry it to its conclusion. Egri’s book was written for the theatre and was taken up by screenwriting teachers, and the manuals that followed turned his proof into a sequence of stages. Robert McKee’s Story (1997) separates characterisation , the observable sum of a person’s traits, from true character, which “is revealed in the choices a human being makes under pressure – the greater the pressure, the deeper the revelation, the truer the choice to the character’s essential nature”. He restates the premise as the controlling idea, a value and the cause by which it is won or lost, and sets it against a counter-idea that the story must give its due. John Truby’s The Anatomy of Story (2007) gives the hero a weakness and a need, a desire, an opponent and a self-revelation, and calls the story a moral argument, conducted through the hero’s and the opponent’s actions rather than through statement. K. M. Weiland’s Creating Character Arcs (2016) builds the arc on the lie the character believes, and names five arcs by what happens to it: the positive change arc, in which the character gives up the lie for a truth; the flat arc, in which the character already holds the truth and changes the world; and three negative arcs, disillusionment, in which the character learns a painful truth, fall, in which a character who knew the truth abandons it, and corruption, in which the character is gradually enslaved by lies. James Scott Bell’s mirror moment , discussed in Chapter 11 , places at the centre of the book the scene in which the protagonist looks at what they have become. 2.4 The arc models compared The table sets the main models against the chapter’s terms. It is introduced here because the models use different words for overlapping things, and a writer moving between manuals can mistake a difference of vocabulary for a difference of method. Source What changes Where it changes This chapter’s term Aristotle, Poetics Fortune and knowledge (recognition) At the turning point Recognition, which may precede a hinge Forster, Aspects of the Novel (1927) Whether a character can surprise convincingly Not placed The two halves of the conditions for a change Egri, The Art of Dramatic Writing (1946) The character, as the premise is proved Across the play Theme stated as a proposition McKee, Story (1997) True character, revealed and changed by choice under pressure At the climax The hinge; the controlling idea as statement Truby, The Anatomy of Story (2007) Weakness and need, resolved at the self-revelation Late, near the climax Need as a criterion not yet held; self-revelation as the recognition before a hinge Weiland, Creating Character Arcs (2016) The lie the character believes Across three acts, with a turn at the middle The old criterion; her five arcs mapped in section 3.4 Bell, Write Your Novel From the Middle (2014) Self-knowledge At the centre The mirror moment The models agree that change is made visible by choice under pressure and that its cause should be planted early. They differ on whether the change is in knowledge (Truby’s self-revelation) or in choice (McKee’s), and the chapter sides with choice: a self-revelation that is not followed by a decision is the announced arc. They also share the assumption that change is the value a story serves, which section 8 takes up. 2.5 Theme as a question The manuals state themes as propositions: Egri’s premise, McKee’s controlling idea. This chapter states them as questions, for a practical reason. A proposition written down before drafting tends to produce characters who illustrate it, and the opposition becomes a figure the book exists to defeat. A question can be answered differently by several characters, and McKee’s counter-idea and Truby’s moral argument both require that it should be. The proposition remains useful as the answer a book reaches, found in revision by reading the decisions, and the answer map in section 5 is a way of finding it. Four carriers of theme are distinguished in the Core chapter. The decision at the hinge is the book’s verdict, persuasive because the reader has weighed its cost. Variation , other characters answering the same question differently, is the argument the verdict is tested against. The motif , a recurring object or image, shows that the question persists and where its weight lies but cannot argue alone. Statement , a character or narrator saying what the book means, is the most explicit and the weakest as argument, and at the ending it borrows the authority of the last position that Chapter 16 calls privileged. The order runs from strongest to weakest as argument, on the reasoning that a carrier argues to the degree that the reader has felt a cost attached to it. 2.6 The evidence Melanie Green and Timothy Brock (2000) ran four experiments on transportation , the reader’s absorption into a narrative world. Readers who were more transported held more story-consistent beliefs afterwards and judged the protagonists more favourably, and labelling the story as fact or as fiction made little difference to either. The finding supports the claim that a story’s events can move a reader’s beliefs. It does not test the difference between stated and enacted themes, and the chapter’s preference for enactment rests on the conjecture, consistent with the finding, that statement addressed to the reader interrupts the absorption through which the effect works. 3. The extended catalogue of arcs 3.1 The five arcs in brief The Core chapter names five arcs by what happens to the criterion. In the conversion arc the criterion changes once, at a single priced decision, usually late. In the staged arc it changes in steps, or is recognised at one point and acted on at another. In the falling arc it is replaced by a worse one, usually through decisions each of which is defensible on the old rule. In the steadfast arc it holds under pressure designed to break it, and the change happens to others. In the refused arc the character reaches the hinge, sees the decision the new rule would make, and chooses by the old one. The Core chapter also rules on Chapter 2 ’s proposal of the hinge as a seventh beat: the hinge is adopted at the scale of the book, as the point where an arc is located, and rejected as a beat, since most decisions have none, it is inferred by comparison rather than seen, and two of the five arcs have none by design. The ruling concedes that arcs of erosion, such as Lydgate’s in Middlemarch , may have no hinge a reader can find. 3.2 The disillusionment arc Weiland’s disillusionment arc, in which the character learns that what they believed is false, is a sixth form that the Core chapter folds into the staged and refused arcs. What changes in it is knowledge about the world, and the criterion may survive the change or break under it. Flaubert’s Madame Bovary (1857) is the classic case of a criterion that survives: Emma Bovary’s belief in the romance of novels is disproved by each lover in turn, and she goes on choosing by it until her debts close every move. The disillusionment arc is useful as a diagnosis when a draft’s protagonist learns a great deal and decides nothing differently. The writer must then choose: let the knowledge reach a decision, which makes the arc staged, or make the failure to decide differently the subject, which makes it refused. 3.3 Arcs across an ensemble A book with several principal characters usually gives them arcs that answer one question in different ways, and the arcs are variations in the sense of section 2.5. Pride and Prejudice gives Darcy a counter-arc to Elizabeth’s: she learns that her judgement was prejudiced, he that his manner was proud, and each changes in a way the other’s change makes visible. The Godfather sets Kay’s arc against Michael’s, and her last position, outside the closing door, is the film’s measure of his fall. The ensemble’s risk is the arc for everyone in section 4.4: if every principal changes towards the same rule, the variation collapses into a single answer, and the cast has nothing unchanged against which to read the change. 3.4 The arc held across a series A series hero’s criterion must survive into the next volume, so the series usually gives its hero a steadfast arc and moves the changes to the people each book introduces. Lee Child’s Jack Reacher, whose Make Me (2015) Chapter 3 reads, is a clear case: each novel puts his rule under pressure in a new town, and the town changes. Some series give the hero a slow staged arc across volumes, with each book completing a smaller arc of its own. The arrangement is Chapter 17 ’s subject. 3.5 Summary table The table summarises the catalogue, including the disillusionment arc, so that a writer can find the form a draft’s protagonist has and the risk that comes with it. Arc What happens to the criterion Hinge Typical position of the hinge Main risk Example Conversion Changes once One At or just before the climax Free or scheduled Small Things Like These , Gilead Staged Changes in steps, or recognition precedes action Several Recognition near the middle, action later Spent too fast Emma , Project Hail Mary Falling Replaced by a worse rule One or none (erosion) Early, so the fall can unfold Reads as fate The Godfather , Macbeth Steadfast Holds under pressure; others change None by design — Untested virtue Paddington 2 , the Reacher novels Refused Recognised and kept None by design Recognition at the climax Unseen refusal reads as stasis The Remains of the Day , Manchester by the Sea Disillusionment Knowledge reverses; the rule may survive Optional Across the book Learning without deciding Madame Bovary Weiland’s five arcs map onto the table as follows: her positive change arc is the conversion or staged arc; her flat arc is the steadfast arc; her fall and corruption arcs are both falling arcs, distinguished by whether the character once held a better rule; her disillusionment arc is the last row. The refused arc has no place in her scheme. 4. The extended catalogue of failure patterns 4.1 The five patterns of the Core chapter The announced arc substitutes a realisation for a decision (exception: The Great Gatsby , where the retrospective narrator’s telling is the change). The free hinge changes the criterion after the plot has removed its cost (exception: Jane Eyre , whose return to Rochester is free and whose departure was paid in full). The scheduled arc is predicted from the first chapters and delivered on time (exception: The Kite Runner , section 6.2). The revoked arc returns to the old rule after the hinge because the plot needs it (exception: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn , whose Evasion Leo Marx argued in 1953 jeopardises the novel’s significance). The sermon removes variation and leaves the theme to statement (exception: Uncle Tom’s Cabin ). The patterns below extend the catalogue, each with the same four parts. 4.2 Replacement Symptom. The character at the end is a different person: different manner, different wants, different voice. Readers say the change is total and unconvincing. Mechanism. No constant survives, so the reader cannot read a development against anything. Replacement usually comes from revising the end of a draft without revising its beginning, so that two versions of a character meet in one book. Remedy. Test 5. Keep one thing unaltered and visible in the decision that confirms the change: the want, a habit of attention, a way of speaking. Exception. Oscar Wilde’s The Picture of Dorian Gray (1890–91), in which the change is moved off the character altogether. Dorian’s face stays young and beautiful while the portrait records each act, so the constant is the face and the arc is in the painting. The device makes replacement visible as the subject. 4.3 The drifting theme Symptom. The question the opening poses is not the one the ending answers. Readers find the ending satisfying in itself and unrelated to the book they began. Mechanism. The writer discovered the book’s real question while drafting, and revised the ending to answer it without revising the opening to pose it. The hinge is then a verdict on a question the reader was never asked. Remedy. Tests 7 and 8. Write the question the ending answers, and revise the opening and the answer map to pose it. Exception. Herman Melville’s Moby-Dick (1851), which opens as Ishmael’s account of going to sea to cure his low spirits and becomes Ahab’s tragedy, with Ishmael’s own question left behind until the epilogue returns him, floating on a coffin. The drift is part of the book’s encyclopaedic form, and readers who expect a single question are told early that they will not get one. 4.4 The arc for everyone Symptom. Every principal character learns something by the end, usually the same thing. Mechanism. The variation that should carry the theme collapses into a single answer, and the cast has no constant among it. The book becomes a sermon delivered by its whole cast. Remedy. Test 8. Let at least one principal keep the old answer, at a cost the book acknowledges. Exception. Richard Curtis’s film Love Actually (2003), whose ten linked stories mostly converge on one answer, that love should be declared. It holds partly because two strands do not: Sarah gives up a declared love for her brother’s sake, and Karen stays in a marriage she now knows is damaged. The film keeps two unconverted answers, and its own answer is tested against them. 4.5 The decorative motif Symptom. A recurring object or image is noticed by readers and discussed by the writer, and it is never present at a decision. Mechanism. The motif carries the theme without arguing it, since it is attached to nothing chosen. It becomes ornament, and the writer, sensing that the theme is not landing, adds more of it. Remedy. Put the motif in the room at the hinge, so that the decision is taken with it or about it. Exception. Virginia Woolf’s Mrs Dalloway (1925), in which the striking of Big Ben marks the hours across many minds and attaches to no decision. The book is about consciousness in time rather than choice, and the motif carries what the book argues: that the hours are shared and the minds are not. 4.6 The untested steadfast arc Symptom. The protagonist’s rule holds throughout, and the book never makes holding it cost anything. Readers find the hero admirable and the book inert. Mechanism. A steadfast arc depends on pressure. Without temptation or loss the criterion is not held but merely possessed, and the change transferred to others has no cause the reader can see. Remedy. Test 1, read as a steadfast arc. Offer the protagonist the world’s terms, with something to lose by refusing them. Exception. Paddington 2 (2017), section 6.3, whose bear is never tempted to be anything but kind. The film puts the cost into suffering rather than temptation, wrongful imprisonment and a near drowning, and its comedy’s contract does not ask for more. 5. The diagnostic procedures The eight tests in the Core chapter run on two documents. The criterion log has one row for each of the five to eight largest decisions a character makes, in book order, and five columns: position, as a percentage of the book; the options; the choice; the rule, as a short imperative in the character’s idiom; and the cost. Fill the rule column last, from the choice and the cost rather than from the writer’s intention. Then read down it. Tests 1 and 2 read the column for change and for the decision at which it occurs; test 3 reads the cost column at the hinge and the rows before it; test 4 looks for the new rule in other characters’ logs before the hinge; test 5 compares the first and last rows for what stays the same; test 6 looks after the hinge for a situation from an earlier row repeated and answered differently. Position Options Choice Rule Cost The answer map has the thematic question at the top, written as a question with at least two possible answers, and one row for each major character: the character, their rule from the criterion log, and the rule rewritten as an answer to the question. Test 7 checks that the question can be answered differently; test 8 checks that the opposition’s answer succeeds or costs something somewhere in the book. The protagonist’s hinge is then located on the map: the new rule adopts another character’s answer, combines two, or finds one no character held. Character Rule Answer to the question A last procedure helps with test 6. List every situation in the first third of the book that a character meets and could meet again: a call not made, a question not asked, a door not opened, an object not touched. These are the available enactments, and a strong hinge is usually confirmed by one of them. 6. Further analyses 6.1 Project Hail Mary : the hinge after the recognition Andy Weir’s Project Hail Mary (2021) opens with its narrator waking alone on a spacecraft with no memory of who he is, and his memories return in fragments throughout the book. Ryland Grace, a former scientist turned schoolteacher, believes for most of it that he volunteered for a mission to save Earth from a microbe dimming the sun. Late in the book a returning memory tells him otherwise: he refused, out of fear, and was sedated and sent. The recognition changes his knowledge of his own criterion, self-preservation, and the hinge follows it. Having found the organism that can save Earth and launched it home, Grace learns that it will also destroy the fuel aboard the ship of Rocky, the alien engineer who has become his friend, and he turns back to save him, giving up his own return. The epilogue finds him years later on Rocky’s planet, teaching its young science. Weir has said of the late revelation that Grace “resisted the call, but the call overcame his resistance. He didn’t choose to go.” The book is a staged arc in which the recognition comes almost at the hinge, so that the reader learns the old rule’s full cost only when the new one is about to be chosen. The constant is the teacher, who is a teacher at the end. 6.2 The Kite Runner : the scheduled arc at full price Khaled Hosseini’s The Kite Runner (2003) is the Core chapter’s exception to the scheduled arc, and it repays a longer look. The first chapter, set in 2001, has Amir receive a telephone call from Rahim Khan, his father’s friend, which ends: “There is a way to be good again.” The novel then returns to Kabul in the 1970s, where Amir, a wealthy boy, fails to defend his friend and servant Hassan from an assault by Assef, an older boy, and then drives Hassan and his father from the house. The arc is set from the first page: the wrong, the years of guilt in America, the call, and the return. When Amir goes back to Taliban-ruled Kabul to rescue Hassan’s son Sohrab, the man holding the boy is Assef, who beats Amir badly, and Sohrab stops him with a slingshot, as Hassan once threatened to. The symmetries are visible to any reader, and they meet Forster’s condition of conviction and give up surprise. What keeps the arc from the scheduled arc’s usual failure is the price. Amir’s hinge, choosing to go back at the risk of his life when his old rule was always to save himself, is paid in his body, and the aftermath withholds the cure the design seems to promise, since the rescued boy remains withdrawn and nearly silent through the last chapters, until a kite and Hassan’s phrase for you, a thousand times over on the last page. 6.3 Paddington 2 : the steadfast arc Paul King’s Paddington 2 (2017) is a steadfast arc on screen. Paddington, a bear from Peru living with the Brown family in London, is wrongly convicted of stealing a pop-up book and sent to prison for ten years. His rule, to be polite and to see the best in people, does not change; the prison does. He shares his marmalade sandwiches with the prison’s feared cook, Knuckles McGinty, and the kitchen and its prisoners are transformed around him; at the climax Knuckles and two other prisoners help to rescue him from a sinking brake van, and Paddington is cleared. The change has been transferred from the protagonist to the people he meets. As section 4.6 notes, the film’s cost is in suffering rather than temptation, since Paddington is never tempted to be other than he is, and the comedy’s contract does not ask for temptation. The answer map is simple and unambiguous: the question is whether kindness survives an unkind world, and the film gives the opposing answer to its villain, the actor Phoenix Buchanan, whose vanity is the only rule in the film that does not change. 7. The household arcs in full 7.1 The draft The draft ending, quoted in the Core chapter’s opening, adds two paragraphs after the reading: Elena’s realisation that some things a family could only know together , and Nadia’s line “He was protecting us. That’s what this family does. We protect each other by not saying.” The paragraphs are recorded in Editorial/Canon.md as not canon. The early reader’s notes, that Elena finishes the book as she began it and that the last pages tell the reader what to think, are the announced arc and the stated theme. 7.2 Criterion logs The logs below are built from decisions the earlier chapters have fixed, with the two decisions this chapter adds. Positions are estimates, as in Chapter 11 , whose positions for the middle this chapter adopts. Elena’s log shows one rule from the doorway to the convergence and a change at the convergence. Position Decision Rule Cost Before the drawer In Dov’s doorway, asks why the locks were changed, is refused, leaves with the key (Ch 3) Ask directly, once Shut out without a reason After the doorway Decides not to telephone her mother; drives to the shop (Ch 2) Find out for yourself Her mother left unasked 25% Reads the ledger alone, from the first page (Ch 6) Find out for yourself None yet 38% At the empty drawer, decides not to ask Dov who took the ledger; turns the sign to CLOSED (Ch 11) Do not ask people who will not tell you Dov closed as a witness 54% (new) Tells Nadia she does not know why Dov wants the flat cleared, and that she would tell her if she knew anything Keep what you know until you know all of it Her sister deceived; the mirror moment Convergence (new) Does not open the ledger; rings Nadia, tells her to come and why, and waits What concerns the three of them is read by the three of them The ledger she has wanted since the drawer, deferred Nadia’s log shows a staged arc completed at the ending, with her counting as the constant. Position Decision Rule Cost Opening Lets Dov’s calls ring out; counts receipts (Ch 9) Count; do not touch what cannot be counted Dov unanswered Before the drawer In the flat, watches the dust on the coat without brushing it (Ch 4) Do not touch The coat left to someone else’s care 50% Plays Dov’s message, counts its thirteen words (Ch 11) Count The reason not asked for 54% (new) Asks Elena whether she knows why; accepts I’d tell you Expect to be told Deceived without knowing it 66% Clearing the flat, puts her hand into the pocket of the coat on its hook, finds the pen (Ch 7) Do what has to be done, and no more The first touch Convergence (new) Answers Elena’s call at once Answer when asked None Ending Takes the coat down and puts it on, gathering the sleeves (Ch 16) Wear it The coat no longer a thing kept Dov’s log is a falling arc halted. He protects by withholding throughout, as his father did, and at the convergence he discloses. Position Decision Rule Cost 9 March, evening Finds his father’s broken entry; writes the date and the count beneath it, and goes on (Ch 13) Keep the form His father’s pages unread Before the drawer Gives Elena the new key and withholds the reason (Ch 3) Give what is needed, not why Elena’s trust 30%–38% Accepts the buyer’s deadline; clears the register drawer and takes the ledger home (Ch 14, Ch 11) Protect by withholding Elena’s reading 50% Asks his sisters to clear the flat, without saying why (Ch 11) Protect by withholding Nadia’s question 58% Signs without telling his sisters (Ch 14) Protect by withholding The shop Convergence Produces the ledger, which he held back from the sale, and says the looser hand is his (Ch 14) Show them His silence 7.3 The answer map The question is the one Chapter 3 first phrased: what do the members of a family owe each other in the way of truth? The other thematic statements the chapters have made (what the living owe the dead’s silences, ritual as a way of not quite facing loss, records outliving the people who keep them, counting set against unmeasured time) are aspects of it, and each is carried by one of the answers below. Character Rule Answer The father Write it down properly, in case anyone ever needs to check The truth is owed, but later, and to a record rather than a person Ma Change the locks and say nothing Unknown: the answer the book declines to test Dov Keep the form; give what is needed, not why The form of the truth without its content Nadia Count; do not touch; expect to be told Not asked for, and assumed Elena, to the convergence Find out for yourself; do not ask people who will not tell you The truth is something to be got, alone Elena, at the convergence What concerns the three of them is read by the three of them The truth is owed now, to each other, in one room The ending’s arrangement, three people reading one record, answers the question without stating it, and the map shows why the answer can be rejected: the father’s answer, the record kept alone, is the one the ledger embodies, and it is the reason the three can read anything at all. The book’s verdict is that his answer was right about the record and wrong about the timing. The mother’s row is empty by design, as Editorial/Canon.md requires, and the book’s refusal to fill it is what keeps the verdict from becoming a sermon. 7.4 The two passages The first passage is a mirror moment at about 54 per cent, between the midpoint request at 50 and the signing at 58. Elena helps Nadia begin to clear the flat, and keeps her suspicion of Dov: “Do you know why he wants it cleared?” Nadia was folding the tea towels into thirds and counting them as she went. Elena had a box of receipts on her knees and the empty drawer in her head. “No,” she said, which was true. “You’d tell me, though. If you knew anything.” “I’d tell you.” She would remember, later, how easily it had come. It supplies the scene that Chapter 11 recorded as needed, in which Elena keeps her suspicion from Nadia and it costs her something, and it plants the new rule in Nadia’s mouth. The second is the hinge, at the convergence after Dov’s chapter. Dov brings the ledger to the shop, where Elena is: Dov put the ledger on the counter and took his hand off it. “It’s all there,” he said. “From March, it’s mine.” She had wanted it since the drawer. She laid her palm on the cover, and the leather was warm from his arm, and she did not open it. “Ring Nadia,” she said. “She doesn’t answer me.” “She’ll answer me.” She rang, and Nadia answered, and Elena told her to come to the shop, and why. The reading in Chapter 16 ’s Version B follows, unchanged: They read it together, in the end — Elena at the register, Nadia on the stool, Dov standing because he said he’d rather. 7.5 What the revision settles, and what it does not The revision answers the complaint in Chapter 16’s case that Elena “completes by presence rather than act”. Her act now comes a page before the reading, and the reading’s first sentence, They read it together, in the end , records it. The decisions it adds are proposed as canon item C22, for the author to confirm: the scene in the flat at about 54 per cent; Dov’s bringing the ledger to the shop; Elena’s declining to open it, ringing Nadia and telling her why. Neither passage changes an earlier chapter’s text, and neither lets either sister read the illness entries before the ending, so C10 holds. Five things remain unsolved. The convergence, which Chapter 14 already found crowded with four discharges, now carries Elena’s hinge as well, and a reader may feel the architecture. Nadia’s answering at once, after a book in which she lets Dov’s calls ring out, may read as arranged. Elena’s new rule stops at the three siblings, and the book leaves open whether it would reach their mother: that keeps the mother’s silence unresolved, as the canon requires, and leaves Elena’s change visibly partial. The mirror moment depends on a retrospective sentence that may read as the narration underlining. And the warm leather is the third warmth the ledger has had (Chapter 6, Chapter 13, here), which may tip an echo into a tic; the sentence survives without it. 8. The limits of the model The model describes books in which change is the value a character’s story serves, and it describes them well. It describes less well three kinds of book. The picaresque and its descendants send a hero through a world that changes around them and do not ask the hero to change, and the criterion log will report a steadfast arc without pressure. Much modernist fiction observes a consciousness rather than trying it, and the decisions the log needs may not be on the page at all, since the book’s interest is in perception. And long-running series, and the genres built on them, need a hero whose rule survives, so that the arc is suspended or spread across volumes. In each case the tools report the model’s assumption, and the exceptions in the catalogue show what such books put in the arc’s place: a constant that is itself the subject, a recognition that is the climax, or a world that changes instead. A second limit concerns the theme. The answer map assumes that a book’s question can be stated in a sentence and that its characters’ rules are answers to it. Some books are built on several questions that do not reduce to one, and some on a question the writer cannot state without spoiling it. The map is still useful in such books, as a way of seeing which answers are present, but its verdict on whether the theme is argued should be weighed against the reader’s experience rather than taken as final. 9. Glossary of the chapter’s terms The definitions below are for the consolidated glossary. Announced arc. A failure pattern: a change reported as a realisation rather than shown in a decision. Answer map. The chapter’s tool for theme: the book’s question, and each major character’s criterion rewritten as an answer to it. Arc. The course, across a whole book, of the rule by which a character resolves dilemmas. Characterisation. The observable sum of a character’s traits, as distinct from the character revealed in choice (McKee). Constant. Something visibly unchanged in a character against which a change can be read (from Chapter 16). Controlling idea. McKee’s term for a theme stated as a value and the cause by which it is won or lost. Conversion arc. An arc in which the criterion changes once, at a single priced decision. Criterion log. The chapter’s tool for arc: a character’s largest decisions in order, with the options, the choice, the rule and the cost. Decision (carrier of theme). The choice at the hinge, read as the book’s verdict on its question. Enactment. The confirmation of a new criterion by a situation the book has shown before, answered differently. Falling arc. An arc in which the criterion is replaced by a worse one, usually through decisions each defensible on the old rule. Flat and round characters. Forster’s terms: a character “constructed round a single idea or quality”, and one “capable of surprising in a convincing way”. Free hinge. A failure pattern: a change of criterion made after the plot has removed its cost. Lie, the. Weiland’s term for the false belief a character holds at the start of an arc. Mirror moment. Bell’s term for the scene at the centre in which the protagonist sees what they have become; in arc terms, where the old criterion is seen to cost. Moral argument. Truby’s term for a story’s argument about how to live, conducted through the actions of the hero and the opponent. Motif. A recurring object, image or phrase that carries a theme by returning in changed contexts. Premise. Egri’s term for a theme stated as a proposition the play proves. Recognition. Aristotle’s anagnorisis : a change from ignorance to knowledge, which may precede a hinge. Refused arc. An arc in which the character reaches the hinge, sees the new rule’s decision, and chooses by the old. Revoked arc. A failure pattern: a return to the old criterion after the hinge, because the plot needs it. Scheduled arc. A failure pattern: a change predicted from the first chapters and delivered on time. Seed. The appearance of the new criterion before the hinge, usually in another character. Self-revelation. Truby’s term for the moment the hero sees the truth about themselves. Sermon. A failure pattern: a theme answered one way by every character and left to statement. Staged arc. An arc in which the criterion changes in steps, or is recognised at one point and acted on at another. Statement (carrier of theme). A character or narrator saying what the book means. Steadfast arc. An arc in which the protagonist’s criterion holds under pressure and the change happens to others. Theme. A question a book tests rather than a proposition it asserts. Transportation. Green and Brock’s term for a reader’s absorption into a narrative world. Variation (carrier of theme). Other characters answering the book’s question differently. Want and need. What a character consciously pursues, and, in the manuals, what they must change; in this chapter the need is a criterion not yet held. 10. Sources Aristotle, Poetics , translated by S. H. Butcher, in Aristotle’s Theory of Poetry and Fine Art (London: Macmillan, 1895); chapters 6 and 11. Bell, James Scott, Write Your Novel From the Middle (Compendium Press, 2014). Egri, Lajos, The Art of Dramatic Writing: Its Basis in the Creative Interpretation of Human Motives (New York: Simon and Schuster, 1946). Forster, E. M., Aspects of the Novel (London: Edward Arnold, 1927). Green, Melanie C., and Timothy C. Brock, “The role of transportation in the persuasiveness of public narratives”, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 79 (2000), 701–721. Marx, Leo, “Mr. Eliot, Mr. Trilling, and Huckleberry Finn ”, The American Scholar 22 (1953). McKee, Robert, Story: Substance, Structure, Style, and the Principles of Screenwriting (New York: ReganBooks, 1997). Truby, John, The Anatomy of Story: 22 Steps to Becoming a Master Storyteller (New York: Faber and Faber, 2007). Weiland, K. M., Creating Character Arcs (PenForASword, 2016). Films: The Godfather (Francis Ford Coppola, 1972); Love Actually (Richard Curtis, 2003); Manchester by the Sea (Kenneth Lonergan, 2016); Paddington 2 (Paul King, 2017). title: The Viewpoint Shift
text: Who Gets a Head, How Many, and When: The Architecture of Narrative Vantage The Craft Behind the Story (Second Edition), Reference — Chapter 13. Part III: The Architecture of the Whole. A companion to the chapters on the scene, the transition, the chapter break, the opening pages, the prologue and the subplot — Chapters 1, 5, 6, 9, 10 and 14. All illustrative passages are quoted briefly for the purposes of criticism and study; full citations appear in §14 . Where a novel is discussed in translation, the translator is named, and the chapter observes the distinction stated in this book’s Introduction: structural claims survive translation, texture claims do not. Contents On this page: Chapter Abstract · Learning Outcomes · Key Terms · How to Use This Chapter Introduction: The Allocation Problem Definitions and Boundaries Why Viewpoint Allocation Is a Structural Decision The Domains of Purpose — access, irony, contrast (viewpoint domain), sympathy, pacing, and a proposed sixth Multiplicity: The Economy of the Grant The Grant — a taxonomy of viewpoint architectures Diagnostic Method — the ten tests Failure Patterns — with their exceptions Worked Analyses — eight close readings and a revision case The Viewpoint Shift Across Forms · Concordance of concepts to works Revision Checklist Studio Work — exercises, seminar questions, assessment rubric Glossary Sources Cited Further Reading Coda: Against Mechanical Application Chapter Abstract A viewpoint shift is a change in whose consciousness the narration is filtered through. The mechanics of executing any single crossing — the handoff, the anchor, the cost of a frame switch — belong to Chapter 5 ( The Transition ). This chapter sits a level above them and asks the prior question: who is granted a consciousness at all, how many such grants a book can carry, and when in the book each is made. It proceeds in four movements: Theory — four independent bodies of work that together convert a craft intuition into an analytic. Genette’s separation of who speaks from who perceives , refined by Bal, Stanzel, Cohn and Booth, supplies the vocabulary. Alex Woloch’s account of character-space and the character-system supplies the rigour: narrative attention is a scarce, distributed resource, and the distribution is itself a formal and a political fact. The cognitive literature on theory of mind and situation models supplies the processing account, and Suzanne Keen’s scepticism supplies the necessary corrective to it. A historical strand establishes that the single limited third person is a recent and local dominance. Taxonomy — the five domains a viewpoint grant can serve (access, dramatic irony, contrast, sympathy engineering, structural pacing), each anatomised in terms of its textual carriers and its characteristic under- and over-delivery, expanded here with a proposed sixth, the epistemological domain : a vantage granted not to show what happened but to demonstrate that no single vantage can know it. Method — the principle of multiplicity applied to viewpoint allocation across a whole book; a taxonomy of thirteen viewpoint architectures ; the distinction between the first grant and the later grant ; and a ten-test diagnostic protocol. Application — twelve failure patterns, each with a published counterexample; eight close readings; a revision case drawn from the household narrative that runs through this book; notes on other forms; and a full apparatus. The chapter’s governing claim is that viewpoint is an allocation, not a technique — a distribution of a finite resource across a cast, whose shape is legible, arguable, and revisable. Its principal corrective is historical: what contemporary workshops call head-hopping names the violation of a convention that Fielding, Eliot and Tolstoy did not hold. And its principal extension is Woloch’s: the question is not only who receives a viewpoint, but what happens to the people who do not. A note on the examples. The novels analysed here are chosen because each displays a mechanism clearly. A concordance mapping each concept to the novel that best displays it appears at §10.6 . Learning Outcomes By the end of this chapter, a student should be able to: Distinguish a structural viewpoint shift from head-hopping, from a change of narrator, from a change of narrative distance, and from a transition, and explain why the distinctions carry different remedies. Deploy the vocabulary of focalisation accurately — zero, internal and external; fixed, variable and multiple — and say what it can describe that “point of view” cannot. Analyse a novel’s character-system in Woloch’s terms, identifying which characters are granted space, which are compressed, and what the compression produces. Identify which of the six domains a given viewpoint grant serves, and diagnose grants that serve none. Classify a novel’s viewpoint architecture against the thirteen-part taxonomy at §6.3 , and conduct substitution tests against the alternatives. Apply the ten-test diagnostic protocol to a draft and produce a prioritised revision plan, including a page-share audit. Historicise the prohibition on head-hopping, and state which of this chapter’s cautions describe narrative and which describe Anglo-American workshop practice since roughly 1960. Evaluate the empathy-budget metaphor itself, including the scarcity assumption it imports and the cases in which the assumption is false. Key Terms Viewpoint shift · head-hopping · structural shift · focalisation (zero, internal, external) · focaliser · the empathy budget · character-space · character-system · the first grant · the later grant · the bounded grant · the knowledge boundary · viewpoint architecture · the epistemological domain · page-share · character compression · reflector · free indirect style · narrative distance · theory of mind · narrative empathy Full definitions appear in the Glossary ( §13 ). Terms are bolded on first substantive use. How to Use This Chapter Reader Route Purpose Student in a seminar §§1–6 in order, then §9 , then §12 exercises Conceptual grounding, worked demonstration, guided practice Writer in revision §7 (diagnostics) → §8 (failures) → §11 (checklist), returning to §6.3 when the architecture itself is in question Fast triage of a live manuscript Teacher or workshop leader §3.3 , 3.5, 8.1 and 9 for material; §12.1 for assignments; §12.3 rubric A teaching sequence built around the chapter’s two arguments: allocation, and the historicity of the head-hopping rule A caution before beginning. This chapter contains taxonomies, tests and checklists. None of them is a formula. They are instruments for noticing, and their proper output is a question, not a verdict. The chapter’s own §16 argues against its central metaphor. A student who finishes able to apply the ten tests but unable to say why Middlemarch fails nearly all of them and is nonetheless the chapter’s central authority has read the apparatus and missed the argument.

title: 1. Introduction: The Allocation Problem
text: 1.1 An asymmetry between coverage and depth Consider two manuscripts of identical length, both about a family of four after a death. The first is told entirely through the eldest daughter. Everything the reader learns, they learn because she learned it — by being present, by being told, by inferring, by being lied to. Whole regions of the story are unavailable: the brother’s negotiations, the mother’s reasons, the father’s last months. The book is, in an obvious sense, badly informed. It is also, at the end of four hundred pages, in possession of one person so thoroughly that the reader can predict what she will notice in a room before she notices it. The second is told through all four in rotation. Nothing is unavailable. The brother’s negotiations are dramatised; the mother’s reasons are supplied; the father speaks for himself in a section set before his death. The book is comprehensively informed. It is also, at the end of four hundred pages, in possession of four people to one quarter of that depth each — and, if the rotation was governed by fairness rather than by need, possibly to less, because a reader who has been moved four times has been asked four times to begin again. Neither manuscript is better by construction. What separates them is not craft but allocation : a decision about how a finite quantity of reader attention and reader identification is to be distributed across a cast. That decision is made once, structurally, at the level of the whole book — and then honoured or violated at every scene boundary in it. This is the allocation problem , and it is different in kind from the problem Chapter 5 ( The Transition ) solves. Chapter 5 asks how a reader is carried across a gap; it assumes the far side has already been chosen. This chapter asks who is standing there. The asymmetry can be stated in its sharpest form, because it is what makes viewpoint a structural rather than a local decision: Coverage is additive. Each new viewpoint character adds the scenes that character can attend. Two viewpoints see roughly twice as much of the story as one. Depth is divisive. Each new viewpoint character divides the same finite quantity of pages, of remembered detail, of accumulated familiarity. Two viewpoints are known, on average, half as well as one. A book cannot buy coverage without spending depth, and cannot preserve depth without accepting blindness. Every viewpoint architecture in §6.3 is a particular settlement of that trade, and the settlements are not interchangeable. 1.2 The claim in its strong form Granting a character viewpoint is the largest single act of trust a novel asks of its reader — and the trust is drawn from a pool that does not grow when the cast does. The metaphor of a budget will be used throughout, and — since §16 will argue against it — it is worth being exact about what it does and does not claim. It does claim that reader identification is a resource with an upper bound in any given book, and that the bound is set principally by length, by the reader’s working memory for persons, and by the number of times a reader can be asked to reorient before reorientation becomes the dominant experience of reading. It does claim that the distribution of that resource is a formal feature of the book, as analysable as its chapter lengths or its handling of time, and that it can be audited ( §5.5 , §7.1 test 5). It does not claim that fewer viewpoints are better. As I Lay Dying has fifteen narrators in a very short novel and is not diluted. The claim is about the relation between number and available page count, not about number. It does not claim that identification is the only thing a viewpoint delivers. A viewpoint can be granted for irony, for information, for rhythm, or — §4.6 — to demonstrate that no vantage suffices. Several of those uses require the reader not to identify. It does not claim that the pool is fixed by nature. It is fixed by the book’s own construction, and a book that constructs its cast well can enlarge what it can carry. This is the qualification §3.6 develops and §16 presses hardest. The corresponding claim about the people who are not granted viewpoint is less obvious and, following Alex Woloch, more consequential: The characters who receive no viewpoint are not merely absent from the allocation. They are shaped by it. A character seen only from outside, in a book whose other characters are seen from inside, is not neutral in the reader’s model; they are compressed, and this character compression produces a specific and legible distortion — the type, the eccentric, the villain, the saint. That is the argument of §3.3 , and it is what raises this chapter above a discussion of technique. The allocation of viewpoint is the allocation of interiority, and the allocation of interiority is, in a novel, very nearly the allocation of personhood. 1.3 Where this chapter sits in the book Three chapters divide a single problem between them (Chapters 5 and 6 in Part II, The Joins , and this chapter in Part III), and each is incomplete without the others: Chapter Question Owns Chapter 5 ( The Transition ) How is the gap crossed? The handoff, the anchor, the orientation budget, drift, the cost of a frame switch Chapter 6 ( The Chapter Break ) Where is the gap placed? Segmentation, proposition and payoff, the cliffhanger, proportion Chapter 13 (this chapter) Who is on the other side? The grant, the architecture, the domains, the character-system The division is not merely administrative. It corresponds to three separable failures, with three separable remedies. A reader who cannot tell whose head they have entered has suffered an anchoring failure, and the fix is a proper noun in the first clause (Chapter 5 §4.5 ). A reader who resents being pulled away has suffered a placement failure, and the fix is to move the break (Chapter 6). A reader who does not care whose head they have entered has suffered an allocation failure, and no amount of anchoring or moving the break will fix it; the character should probably not have viewpoint at all. Four further dependencies are load-bearing here. Chapter 1 ( The Purposes of a Scene ) supplies the domains model — the practice of asking what a unit of narrative is for , and requiring more than one answer. §4 is that model transposed from the scene to the viewpoint grant. Chapter 14 ( The Subplot ) supplies the attention tax : the cost, in reader patience, of any material that pulls focus from the main line. The empathy budget is the attention tax narrowed to its most expensive form. A reader will tolerate a subplot that occasionally takes the page; being asked to become six different people is a larger request, made of a scarcer faculty. The two chapters share a single theoretical source in Woloch, and the book treats them as one argument applied at two scales. Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages ) supplies, at its §4.6 , the formal contract : the requirement that a book declare its structural rules — including whether narration is single or plural — before the reader has invested in a single thread. That chapter states the requirement and gives the reason. This chapter owns the requirement in depth: §6.5 anatomises how a viewpoint change is signalled, §6.6 formalises the cost curve that makes early declaration cheap and late declaration expensive, and §7.1 test 6 converts it into a diagnostic. Chapter 9 says declare early . This chapter says what declaring consists of, what it costs not to, and — at §8.4 and §9.5 — when a book should decline the advice. Chapter 10 ( The Prologue ) supplies the bounded grant in its most familiar form: one unit given to a consciousness that will not hold the reader again. §6.3 , architecture 6, generalises it.

title: 2. Definitions and Boundaries
text: Craft discussion of viewpoint is unusually prone to conflation. “Point of view” is made to carry person (first, third), distance (close, far), reliability, focalisation, narrative voice and the identity of the narrating agent, all at once, with the result that four different problems receive the same diagnosis. This section separates them before the argument begins. 2.1 The unit under study Working definition. A viewpoint shift is a deliberate change in the consciousness through which the narration is filtered, made at a structural boundary, in a book built to support more than one vantage. The decision underlying it — the grant — is the allocation to a particular character of access to the reader’s identification: how much, and beginning when. Three elements of that definition deserve emphasis. “Deliberate … at a structural boundary.” This excludes the uncontrolled mid-scene change treated at §2.3 — not because that change is always wrong (it very often is not; see §8.1 ) but because it is a different object with different consequences. “The consciousness through which the narration is filtered.” Not the person speaking. A first-person retrospective narrator speaks throughout while filtering the narration through her much younger self; the speaker has not changed and the filter has. Genette’s separation of voice from focalisation ( §3.1 ) exists to make this sayable. “The grant.” The chapter’s central object is not the shift but the decision it expresses. A shift is an event in the text; a grant is a structural commitment. One grant may produce forty shifts, or one. 2.2 Scale and extent Viewpoint decisions are made at four scales, and the chapter treats them differently. Scale The decision Where treated The sentence Whose judgement is in this adjective? §5.3 ; largely a matter of free indirect style The scene Whose consciousness holds this unit? §7.1 test 9; Chapter 1 The chapter or section Whose turn is this, and for how long? §6.5 ; Chapter 6 The book Who has viewpoint at all, how many, in what proportion? §5 , §6.3 — the chapter’s primary scale The primary scale is the last, and this is the chapter’s principal departure from most craft treatments of viewpoint, which operate at the first two. A manuscript can be flawless at sentence and scene level and still be structurally wrong: five well-executed viewpoints, each anchored cleanly, each internally consistent, can constitute a book that has spread itself so thin that no one in it is known. Extent — how long a grant is held — is a separate variable from number, and one that drafts routinely fail to consider. A book may grant viewpoint to six characters and yet be a single-viewpoint novel in every practical sense, if five of the grants are one chapter each. §6.3 treats extent as a defining feature of architecture rather than as a detail of execution. 2.3 The term most often confused: head-hopping Head-hopping is a change of focalisation within a scene, without a structural boundary, such that the reader’s access moves from one character’s interiority to another’s in the course of continuous action. The distinction between head-hopping and a structural shift is standardly drawn as follows: Head-hopping Structural viewpoint shift Location Mid-scene, mid-paragraph, sometimes mid-sentence At a scene, section or chapter boundary Signal None White space, chapter heading, an anchoring first clause Reader experience (as usually described) Momentary uncertainty about whose perceptions are being reported A managed reorientation Diagnosis in workshop practice An error A design decision The chapter reproduces this table because a student must know the convention. It then spends §3.5 and §8.1 arguing that the bottom row is wrong as stated, and that the table describes a local literary convention of roughly the last century , not a property of narrative. The case in short: Middlemarch , Anna Karenina , War and Peace , Vanity Fair and Tom Jones move between minds inside a single continuous scene constantly, deliberately and to enormous effect. What a contemporary workshop calls head-hopping is, in these books, simply omniscience — a narrator with free access to any consciousness, exercising it. The prohibition dates from the codification of Jamesian practice by Percy Lubbock and his successors, and it is a prohibition on an effect (unintentional wobble in an otherwise limited narration) that has been mistaken for a prohibition on a technique . The operative discrimination is therefore not where the change happens but whether the narration has a stable governing convention that the change belongs to : A mid-scene change of mind is head-hopping when the book has established a limited narration and then leaks. It is omniscience when the book has established a mobile narration and then moves. The reader’s uncertainty is produced by the mismatch, not by the movement. This is developed at length at §8.1 , which the chapter treats as its intellectual centre. 2.4 Adjacent terms Term Meaning Relation to the viewpoint shift Focalisation Genette’s term for the regulation of narrative information according to a perceiving position; who perceives , as distinct from who speaks The precise term for what a viewpoint shift changes Focaliser Bal’s term for the subject of focalisation — the agent whose perception organises what is presented The character receiving a grant Narrator The agent who speaks the narrative May be unchanged across a viewpoint shift, and often is Reflector / centre of consciousness James’s terms for a character through whom the narration is refracted without their narrating The single-fixed-internal architecture ( §6.3 , no. 1) Filter and slant Chatman’s pair: filter is the character’s perceptual and conceptual mediation; slant is the narrator’s attitudinal colouring Useful for separating a character’s seeing from a narrator’s judging within one sentence Free indirect style Third-person narration whose diction and judgement are contaminated by the character’s The chief carrier of internal focalisation in the modern novel; see §5.3 Narrative distance How close the narration stands to the focaliser’s consciousness A within-grant variable; a book may change distance without changing viewpoint. Chapter 9 §4.1 Person First, second, third Independent of focalisation: a first-person narrative may be externally focalised, a third-person one internally Character-space Woloch: the delimited position a character occupies within the narrative as a whole The scholarly form of what a grant confers, and of what its absence costs Character-system Woloch: the arrangement of many character-spaces into a structure of distributed attention The scholarly form of a book’s viewpoint architecture Head-hopping Mid-scene change of focalisation in a book with limited narration §2.3, §8.1 Omniscience Zero focalisation: narration not restricted to any character’s knowledge §3.5 , §6.3 no. 10 Two of these pairings cause most of the confusion in practice, and are worth isolating. Person is not focalisation. The Great Gatsby is first person and largely externally focalised on Gatsby: Nick reports what he sees and infers, and the interior of the man the book is about is closed to him. Mrs Dalloway is third person and internally focalised at extremely close range on a succession of consciousnesses. A student who believes “first person” means “close” and “third person” means “distant” will misdescribe both. Distance is not viewpoint. A book may move from She crossed the yard to Gravel. Not the grass, not today without changing whose consciousness it occupies. That is a change of narrative distance, treated in Chapter 9 §4.1 . It feels to an inexperienced reader like a viewpoint change, and it is diagnosed and remedied differently: distance drift is a prose problem, viewpoint drift is a structural one. 2.5 What this chapter excludes The mechanics of crossing. How a reader is anchored on the far side of a viewpoint change — the proper name in the first clause, the register shift, the shared object — belongs to Chapter 5 ( The Transition ) , §4.5 and §6.3 . This chapter cross-refers and does not duplicate. Where the break falls. The placement of the boundary at which a shift occurs, and the pacing consequences of cutting away at a tense moment, belong to Chapter 6 ( The Chapter Break ) . The declaration requirement as an opening problem. That a multi-viewpoint structure must be declared early is established in Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages ) , §4.6 . §6.6 here supplies the mechanism and the cost curve; it does not restate the case. Unreliability. Whether a narrator is to be believed is a distinct axis, treated in Chapter 9 §4.1 and grounded in Booth. It intersects this chapter at §4.6 and §9.5 , where multiple unreliable vantages become an epistemological structure rather than a characterisation device. Voice differentiation at sentence level. How two narrators are made to sound different is a prose matter belonging to Chapter 3 ( The Dialogue Exchange ) and to Chapter 9 §4.1 . This chapter is concerned with whether they notice , want and know differently — §7.1 test 4. Retrospective narration and the past self. The relation between a narrating I and an experiencing I is a focalisation problem, and where it is a temporal one it belongs to Chapter 7 ( Backstory and Flashback ) .

title: 3. Why Viewpoint Allocation Is a Structural Decision
section: Why Viewpoint Allocation Is a Structural Decision
text: This chapter asserts that granting viewpoint is expensive. The assertion is correct, and it can be argued from four independent directions — narratological, socio-formal, cognitive and historical. The four do not merely corroborate one another; they disagree productively, and the disagreements are where the teaching is. 3.1 Focalisation: separating who speaks from who perceives The indispensable move was made by Gérard Genette in Narrative Discourse (1972; Eng. 1980), and it is the most useful distinction in this chapter, because every later term depends on it. Earlier criticism had run two questions together under the heading of “point of view”: Who speaks? — the question of voice , of the narrating agent. Who perceives? — the question Genette named focalisation , of the position from which narrative information is regulated. The two vary independently, and the failure to separate them is why so much craft advice about viewpoint is unusable. A narrator may speak in the first person while perceiving from a position not their own (Nick Carraway recounting Gatsby’s boyhood, or Michaelis’s testimony); a narrator may speak in an impersonal third person while perceiving strictly through a single character’s senses and knowledge (Kafka’s The Trial , which almost never departs from what Josef K. can register). Person is a fact about the speaker; focalisation is a fact about the distribution of knowledge. Genette’s tripartite scheme: Type Description Genette’s formula Typical realisation Zero focalisation Narrator has more knowledge than any character; no restriction Narrator > character The classic omniscient novel: Fielding, Eliot, Tolstoy Internal focalisation Narrator restricted to what one character knows Narrator = character The limited third; the retrospective first person External focalisation Narrator reports less than a character knows: behaviour without interiority Narrator < character The “camera eye”; hard-boiled crime; Hemingway’s “Hills Like White Elephants” Genette then subdivides internal focalisation by how it behaves across a text, and this is where the scheme becomes a tool for the present chapter rather than a taxonomy of sentences: Fixed — one focaliser throughout. The Remains of the Day ; What Maisie Knew . Variable — the focaliser changes, one at a time, across the text. Madame Bovary ; Mrs Dalloway ; most contemporary multi-viewpoint fiction. Multiple — the same events are focalised successively through different characters. The Sound and the Fury ; Rashōmon -type structures; the epistolary novel of contradictory testimony. The distinction between variable and multiple internal focalisation is the most under-used item in the whole narratological toolkit, and it maps onto a craft distinction this chapter needs. Variable focalisation buys coverage : each vantage sees different material, and the reader assembles a wider world. Multiple focalisation buys incommensurability : each vantage sees the same material, and the reader assembles a doubt. The first is the ordinary multi-viewpoint novel. The second is the epistemological structure proposed as a sixth domain at §4.6 . Two cautions about the scheme, which students should carry. First, Genette himself noted that focalisation is rarely constant for long, and that the categories describe dominants rather than absolutes. A novel in fixed internal focalisation will contain sentences no character could have produced. This is not a defect in the novels; it is a limit on the descriptive power of the categories. Second, the scheme describes restriction of information , not intimacy. A narrative can be internally focalised and cold ( The Trial ); externally focalised and unbearably intimate (Hemingway). Craft advice that equates “close third” with “internal focalisation” has collapsed a knowledge relation into a tonal one. 3.2 Four refinements: Stanzel, Bal, Cohn, Booth Genette’s scheme is a skeleton. Four further bodies of work put flesh on it, and each supplies something this chapter needs. Franz Stanzel’s typological circle ( A Theory of Narrative , 1984; Eng. trans. Charlotte Goedsche) organises narrative situations not as discrete boxes but as positions on a continuum that returns on itself. Stanzel proposes three narrative situations : Situation Mediating agency Characteristic Authorial A narrator external to the story world, visible as a personality Commentary, generalisation, address to the reader First-person A narrator who is a character in the world narrated Identity of narrating and experiencing selves; embodied limitation Figural No perceptible narrator; a reflector character through whom events appear The illusion of unmediated presentation The value of the circle for this chapter is that it is a circle . Stanzel’s point is that the situations shade into one another by degrees, so that a novel can drift from figural towards authorial without any identifiable sentence where the change occurs — which is the phenomenology of the failure pattern at §8.6 , the omniscient slip. A model with discrete boxes cannot describe a gradual leak; a model with a continuum can. Mieke Bal’s refinement ( Narratology , 1985; 4th ed. 2017) is the most consequential for practical analysis. Bal argues that focalisation is not a property of a narrator but a relation between a subject and an object : there is always a focaliser and a focalised , and the analytic question is always double — who sees and what is seen . This produces two gains. It makes non-character focalisation describable. A crowd, an institution, a camera position or an unspecified observer can occupy the focalising position. §6.3 ’s architectures 9, 11 and 13 need this. It makes the object of vision analysable. To say that a chapter is focalised through Nadia is only half a description; the other half is what Nadia is permitted to look at . A character granted viewpoint but pointed only at plot information is the information mule of §8.2 , and Bal’s formulation is why the fault is visible as a fault. Bal is also the source of the useful observation that focalisation is embedded : a character may focalise another character who is themselves focalising something. Wuthering Heights runs three deep — Lockwood focalising Nelly focalising Heathcliff — and the reader’s access to the innermost layer is filtered twice. Dorrit Cohn’s Transparent Minds (1978) supplies the vocabulary for what a grant of viewpoint actually delivers at sentence level. Cohn’s three modes for third-person contexts: Mode Description Example form Psycho-narration The narrator reports a character’s consciousness in the narrator’s language She had never trusted her brother’s silences. Narrated monologue (free indirect) The character’s own language, in third person and the tense of narration Her brother’s silences. What was she supposed to do with those? Quoted monologue The character’s thought in the first person and present tense I have no idea what he is not telling me. The distinction matters here because the three modes cost different amounts of empathy budget. Psycho-narration is cheap: it reports a mind without requiring the reader to inhabit it, and a book can afford it for a dozen characters. Narrated monologue is expensive: it requires the reader to adopt the character’s idiom and judgement, and it is the mode in which a viewpoint character is truly inhabited. Quoted monologue is more expensive still. A draft that “has five viewpoint characters” may in fact have one inhabited consciousness and four psycho-narrated ones, and the diagnosis is invisible until the modes are named. Wayne Booth’s The Rhetoric of Fiction (1961; 2nd ed. 1983) contributes the axis of distance and the reminder that it is plural. Booth insisted that distance operates between several pairs of positions at once — narrator and character, narrator and reader, implied author and narrator, reader and character — and that a change in any of them alters the reader’s judgement. His essay “Distance and Point-of-View” (1961) is the compact statement. Booth’s contribution to the present argument is a warning. He observed that inside views produce sympathy more or less mechanically: sustained access to a consciousness tends to align a reader with it, more or less regardless of what the consciousness contains. This is the mechanism this chapter calls sympathy engineering ( §4.4 ), and Booth’s point is that it is not optional. A writer who grants viewpoint to a character has already, by that act, argued for them. A novel that gives an abuser a hundred pages of interiority and expects the reader’s verdict to be unaffected has misunderstood the instrument. Two further sources should be named. Boris Uspensky’s A Poetics of Composition (Eng. 1973) analyses point of view on four separable planes — ideological, phraseological, spatio-temporal and psychological — the sharpest available account of how a narration can be inside a character on one plane and outside on another. Shlomith Rimmon-Kenan’s Narrative Fiction (1983) offers a compact synthesis with a similar three-facet division, and remains the most usable single-chapter introduction. Norman Friedman’s pre-Genette taxonomy is treated at §6.2 . 3.3 Woloch: character-space, the character-system, and the distribution of attention This chapter’s “empathy budget” is a serviceable metaphor. Alex Woloch’s The One vs. the Many: Minor Characters and the Space of the Protagonist in the Realist Novel (Princeton, 2003) is the rigorous instrument the metaphor gestures at, and it is this chapter’s principal source. Woloch begins from an observation that is obvious once stated and rarely pursued. A novel contains many implied human beings; it has room to attend to very few of them. Every character in a realist novel therefore stands in a relation of friction between the fullness of the person they are asked to imply and the limited textual room they are given. Woloch names that room character-space : Character-space — the particular and delimited position that a character occupies within the narrative as a whole; the relation between an implied human being and the space the narrative affords them. And he names the arrangement of many such spaces into a single structure the character-system : Character-system — the arrangement of multiple character-spaces into a unified narrative structure, in which the attention given to any one character is a function of the attention withheld from the others. Three consequences follow, and each converts a craft intuition into an analytic claim. First: attention is scarce, and scarcity is structural rather than incidental. A novel’s attention is not merely limited by length in the way a suitcase is limited by volume. It is distributed , and the distribution has a shape. Woloch’s insistence is that this shape is a formal feature of the work — as available to analysis as its plot or its imagery — and that criticism has systematically ignored it because it appears to be a mere consequence of the story rather than a construction in its own right. Second: minor characters are not small; they are compressed. This is Woloch’s most useful single claim for a writer. A minor character is an implied person subjected to a squeeze, and the squeeze registers in the character’s presentation as distortion . The flatness of the flat character is not an absence of depth but the visible mark of depth being excluded. Hence the characteristic forms minor characters take in the realist novel: the eccentric with one repeated gesture, the grotesque, the type, the walk-on defined by an occupation. Woloch reads such figures as bearing the pressure of their own exclusion, and the reading changes what a writer sees on their own page. A tic is not characterisation; it is what characterisation is compressed into. This book calls the effect character compression , to keep it apart from Chapter 2’s compression of page-space against story-weight. Third: the distribution is a political fact. Woloch’s title is not decorative. The realist novel’s formal problem — one protagonist, many others, finite pages — reproduces at the level of form a social problem about whose experience counts. He develops this most fully on Le Père Goriot and on the English realist tradition, and the argument does not require the reader to accept any particular politics to be usable: it requires only the recognition that deciding whose interiority the reader will inhabit is a decision about whose experience the book treats as fully human. In a novel about a strike, granting viewpoint to the mill owner and not to the workers is not a neutral craft decision. Neither is the reverse. Both are arguments, and the reader receives them as arguments whether or not the writer intended one. Woloch offers, memorably, the formulation that the minor character functions as something like the novel’s proletariat — labouring to produce a protagonist’s significance while being denied the space in which significance can be represented. The phrase is polemical, and it is the fastest route into the argument for a student who has been taught to think of viewpoint as a technical choice. What this gives the chapter that the empathy-budget metaphor does not. The metaphor says Woloch’s model adds Attention is finite Attention is distributed , and the distribution has a describable shape Adding viewpoints costs depth The cost lands somewhere specific, and can be located Some characters get less The characters who get less are deformed by getting less, in patterned ways Allocation is a craft decision Allocation is a formal structure and carries an argument The practical upshot is the test at §7.1 , no. 10 — the character-compression test — which asks not what the viewpoint characters gained but what happened to everyone else. It is the only test in the protocol that looks away from the page under revision, and it is, in this author’s experience of teaching the material, the one that most often changes a manuscript. A caution. Woloch’s book is about the nineteenth-century realist novel, and its claims are calibrated to a form with large casts, a strong protagonist convention and an omniscient narrative habit. Applying it to a two-hander, a modernist consciousness-novel or a genre thriller requires adjustment, and the adjustment is not always small. The chapter uses Woloch as an instrument for noticing distribution, not as a theory that predicts value. 3.4 The cognitive strand: minds, models, and the limits of the empathy claim Three empirical and cognitive literatures bear on viewpoint allocation.
