The first two support the chapter’s claims; the third substantially qualifies them, and reporting the qualification is more useful than suppressing it. Theory of mind and levels of intentionality. Lisa Zunshine’s Why We Read Fiction (2006) proposes that narrative fiction exercises the ordinary human capacity for theory of mind — attributing mental states to others — and that the pleasure of much fiction lies in the difficulty of the attributions it demands. Zunshine borrows from Robin Dunbar the notion of levels of intentionality : I believe is first order; I believe that she wants is second; I believe that she wants him to think that she does not know is fourth. Zunshine reports that ordinary readers manage roughly four levels comfortably and degrade beyond that, and she reads passages of Woolf and Richardson as deliberate exercises at the ceiling. The application to viewpoint is direct and is not usually drawn. A viewpoint grant changes the level of intentionality the reader must track for that character, and for everyone the character thinks about. Before a grant, a character is an object of attribution: the reader guesses at them from behaviour. After a grant, they become a subject , and the reader must now hold both what they think and what others think about them. Adding a viewpoint character therefore does not add one item to the reader’s load; it adds a new set of relations between that character and every other. The load grows faster than the cast does, which is a precise mechanism for what “dilution” feels like from inside. Fictional minds and the continuing-consciousness frame. Alan Palmer’s Fictional Minds (2004) argues that narratology’s traditional focus on techniques for presenting speech and thought has produced too narrow an account of how readers construct characters. Readers do not assemble a character out of quoted thoughts; they maintain what Palmer calls a continuing-consciousness frame — a running model of a whole mind that persists between appearances and is inferred from action, dialogue, physical description and report as much as from interiority. Palmer’s later work on social minds ( Social Minds in the Novel , 2010) extends this to intermental, group-level thought — the “we” of a village or a family that thinks collectively. Two consequences follow for this chapter, and they pull in useful directions. A character does not need viewpoint to have a mind. This is the strongest available argument against granting viewpoint reflexively. Readers construct rich fictional minds from external evidence; the question a writer must answer is not how else will the reader know he has an inner life? but what does the reader need that only direct access supplies? That is test 1, the necessity test. Collective focalisation is not a gimmick. Palmer’s social minds give theoretical standing to architecture 9 in §6.3 , the collective we , and to the intercalary chapters of The Grapes of Wrath . Situation models and the cost of a shift. Zwaan and Radvansky’s synthesis (1998) holds that readers build a situation model of the state of affairs described, tracking five dimensions — protagonist, space, time, causality, intentionality — and paying a measurable processing cost whenever one changes. Chapter 5 §3.3 uses this to price the transition. The point specific to this chapter, and this chapter’s inference rather than Zwaan and Radvansky’s finding, is that the protagonist dimension is plausibly the most expensive of the five , because it is the dimension to which the other four are indexed: a change of protagonist typically drags space, time and intentionality with it, whereas a change of space often leaves the others intact. This is the cognitive basis for the claim that a viewpoint change is among the most costly moves available, and for the finding that a legible pattern reduces the cost — Emmott’s contextual frames (1997) permit frame recall rather than frame construction, so that the twelfth alternation in a book with a declared architecture is cheaper than the first. The Deictic Shift Theory literature (Duchan, Bruder and Hewitt, eds., Deixis in Narrative , 1995) formalises the same phenomenon from a linguistic direction: readers adopt a deictic centre — a here, a now, a who — and a viewpoint change requires them to abandon it and construct another. And now the qualification, which matters. The empathy-budget metaphor invites a romantic corollary: that novels build empathy, that more viewpoints mean more empathy, and that the moral value of fiction lies in this. Suzanne Keen’s Empathy and the Novel (2007) is the necessary corrective, and the chapter reports it rather than suppressing it. Keen surveys the empirical literature and finds the popular claim — that novel-reading reliably produces real-world empathy and pro-social behaviour — substantially unsupported. Her findings, stated carefully: Narrative empathy is real as an in-reading phenomenon. Readers do feel with characters, and the feeling is measurable. It does not reliably transfer. The inference from felt empathy during reading to altered behaviour afterwards is not supported by the evidence; Keen notes that empathy may even be easier with fictional persons because they make no demands. Authors’ empathetic intentions frequently misfire. Keen distinguishes bounded strategic empathy (directed at an in-group who already share the author’s assumptions), ambassadorial (directed at a specific out-group audience for a specific end), and broadcast (aimed at all readers) — and observes that the third, the most morally ambitious, is the least reliable. Empathy and judgement are separable. A reader can feel with a character and still condemn them, which is what the strongest novels of interiority arrange. The point is reinforced by the fate of the best-known experimental finding in the area. Kidd and Castano’s 2013 report in Science that reading literary fiction improved performance on a theory-of-mind task was widely publicised; a large registered replication by Panero and colleagues (2016) failed to reproduce the effect. The honest summary for a textbook is that the relation between reading fiction and social cognition is real but small, unstable across studies, and much weaker than the cultural rhetoric around it. What survives, and what this chapter needs, is the narrower claim: inside views produce alignment within the world of the book. Booth’s mechanism holds. Whether it improves anyone is a separate question with a discouraging evidence base, and a chapter that sold viewpoint as a machine for producing moral improvement would be selling something the research does not support. 3.5 The historical strand: the prohibition is younger than the novel This is the chapter’s principal corrective, because it changes the status of every caution that follows, and it should be stated plainly. The dominance of the single limited third person is recent and local. For most of the novel’s history in English, French and Russian, the default narrative situation was a mobile narrator with free access to any consciousness in the book, exercising that access whenever the material called for it — including within a single continuous scene. A brief historical survey makes the point better than argument. Period Dominant viewpoint practice Mid-scene movement between minds 18th century Epistolary polyphony ( Clarissa , Pamela ); the intrusive authorial narrator ( Tom Jones , Tristram Shandy ) Routine in the authorial mode; structurally impossible in the epistolary Early–mid 19th century Zero focalisation with a commenting narrator; large casts; social panorama ( Vanity Fair , Bleak House , Le Père Goriot ) Routine, deliberate, and often the point High realism (1860s–1880s) The mobile narrator refined into an instrument of moral analysis ( Middlemarch , Anna Karenina , War and Peace ) Constant, and executed with a precision no later convention has surpassed James and after (1880s–1920s) The centre of consciousness ; restriction as an aesthetic principle Increasingly treated as a lapse Lubbock and the codifiers (1921–1950s) Restriction as doctrine; the “rules” of point of view Named as an error Mid-century to present (Anglo-American) Limited third or first, one viewpoint per scene; multi-viewpoint permitted at chapter boundaries Proscribed in workshop and editorial practice The turn is attributable to a small number of identifiable interventions. Henry James , in the prefaces later collected as The Art of the Novel (1934), developed the idea of the reflector or centre of consciousness — a character through whose registering intelligence the events of the novel are refracted — and argued that a novel gains in intensity what it loses in scope by such restriction. James’s famous image of the house of fiction with a million windows, at each of which a watcher with a unique field of vision stands, is a statement of the same principle: the aperture and the watcher together make the subject. Percy Lubbock’s The Craft of Fiction (1921) converted James’s practice into precept. Lubbock’s preference for the dramatic showing of the scene over the narrator’s picture , and his treatment of shifting vantage as a lapse of control, are the proximate origin of what a modern workshop teaches. It is worth noticing that Lubbock’s book is a work of Jamesian advocacy, not of neutral description, and that E. M. Forster’s Aspects of the Novel (1927) dissented almost immediately — Forster argued that the novelist’s right to shift vantage is a resource, and that what matters is not consistency but the reader’s confidence in the writer’s control. Forster’s position is essentially the one this chapter adopts at §8.1 . The conventional force of the prohibition then hardened through mid-century American creative-writing pedagogy, which needed teachable rules, and through the commercial editing practices of the second half of the century. By the time a contemporary student encounters “don’t head-hop”, it is presented as a fact about reading rather than as the residue of a specific aesthetic programme with a date and an address. Stated plainly: “head-hopping” names the violation of a convention that Fielding, Eliot and Tolstoy did not hold. They moved between minds within a single scene continually and masterfully, and any account of narrative that classifies their practice as an error has produced a false description of the art in order to preserve a rule of thumb. Two qualifications keep this from being an argument for anarchy. The convention is real, and readers have been trained in it. A contemporary reader of contemporary fiction does experience an unsignalled mid-scene change as a wobble, because their expectations were formed by a hundred years of books that did not do it. Conventions are not laws, but they are also not nothing: violating one has a cost that must be paid for. The nineteenth-century practice is not the same manoeuvre performed carelessly. What Eliot and Tolstoy do is governed. The narrator’s mobility is established from the first page, exercised consistently, and accompanied by a narrating voice strong enough to hold the transitions together. The reader is never uncertain whose narration this is, only which mind it has stepped into. The workshop error is not omniscience but an unstable narration that has not established the right it is exercising . §8.1 develops this at length; the discrimination it arrives at is that the fault is in the establishment , not in the movement. 3.6 The first principle, stated — and qualified We can now state the chapter’s first principle with more precision than the metaphor allows. The allocation principle. A novel’s viewpoint structure distributes a finite quantity of reader attention, identification and mind-modelling capacity across its cast. The distribution is a formal feature of the work; it determines what the book can witness and how well it can know anyone; and it deforms, in patterned and legible ways, every character it excludes. And now the qualifications, which are where the more interesting teaching lies. (1) The pool is not fixed by nature; it is fixed by construction. The budget metaphor implies a quantity given in advance, like a sum of money. It is nearer to a muscle: a book that trains its reader well can carry more than a book that does not. As I Lay Dying asks a reader to hold fifteen focalisers in about two hundred and fifty pages, and readers manage, because Faulkner has made each voice instantly identifiable by idiom, because the sections are short, and because the reader’s task is not to invest in fifteen people but to triangulate one event from fifteen positions. Change what the reader is asked to do with a viewpoint, and the arithmetic changes. (2) Not every grant asks for identification. The budget metaphor assumes a single currency. In fact a grant may be spent for irony (the reader is placed inside a mind in order to see past it), for dread (the reader is placed inside a mind about to be destroyed), for comedy, or for testimony. Several of these are cheaper than identification because they require less: a reader can occupy Jason Compson’s section without any wish to be him. (3) Depth is not proportional to page share. A single well-chosen chapter can produce more felt knowledge of a person than two hundred diffuse pages. The revision case at §9.9 turns on this, and it is the argument for the bounded grant ( §6.3 , no. 6). (4) The scarcity is culturally and formally specific. Woloch’s model is calibrated to the realist novel with its protagonist convention. Forms that do not have that convention — the collective narrative, the systems novel, the polyphonic epic, the oral epic — distribute attention differently and are not well described as spending a budget. §16 presses this hardest. (5) The principle describes tendencies in reading, not laws of literary value. Every empirical source in §3.4 measures comprehension and response, not merit. A book may impose costs the model calls prohibitive and be worth every one of them.

title: 4. The Domains of Purpose
text: 4.0 The model and its status Chapter 1 ( The Purposes of a Scene ) establishes this book’s central diagnostic habit: ask what a unit of narrative is for , require the answer to name a category rather than a feeling, and treat a unit that serves only one category as under-employed. §4 transposes that habit from the scene to the viewpoint grant. The question the model answers is not is this character interesting? — almost every character is interesting to their author — but what does direct access to this consciousness buy that no existing vantage could deliver? Five domains are set out below, followed at §4.6 by a proposed sixth. For each: a definition; why it matters; the textual carriers through which it is realised; discussion; the characteristic under- and over-delivery; and illustrations from published fiction. Two warnings about the model’s status, both developed at §4.8. It is a diagnostic, not a licence : naming a domain does not authorise a grant, only makes its purpose explicit so that the purpose can be weighed against the cost. And it is misused as a checklist : a viewpoint character constructed to tick five domains is a committee decision and reads like one. Its proper use is in revision, on a draft that already exists, to find out what a vantage is actually doing rather than what its author hoped. 4.1 Access — the reader witnesses what the primary vantage cannot Definition. A grant made so that the narrative can be present at events the existing focaliser cannot attend: another room, another city, another decade, a conversation held in their absence, a death they do not witness. Why it matters. Access is the domain that makes a certain kind of book possible at all. A novel of a war, a conspiracy, a family dispersed across continents, or an institution cannot be told from a single vantage without becoming a novel about not knowing , which may be an excellent novel but is a different one. Access is also the most frequently invoked and the least frequently examined justification for a grant, because it is the one a writer arrives at while solving a plot problem — which is why §5 treats it as insufficient on its own. Textual carriers Carrier What it does Note A scene the primary focaliser is not in The plain form: events witnessed first-hand rather than reported The cheapest to write and the easiest to overvalue A different geography Another front, another country, another house Often drags time and space shifts with it; see Chapter 5 §3.3 on additive cost A different social stratum Servants’ hall, boardroom, prison, ward Buys world as well as access; a natural multiplier A different temporal position A vantage in the past or the future of the main line Overlaps Chapter 7 ( Backstory and Flashback ); a grant is a heavy way to deliver an analepsis A different order of being A ghost, an animal, a machine, the dead The limit case; see §4.6 and §8.8 Discussion The domain’s characteristic weakness is that its work can nearly always be done more cheaply. This is the central argument of §5 and it is worth previewing here in its practical form. Before granting viewpoint for access, a writer has at least five cheaper instruments available: Report. Someone tells the focaliser what happened. Inference. The focaliser deduces it from evidence — a smell of fresh ink in a drawer nobody has opened. Reassignment. The scene is rewritten so that the existing focaliser can plausibly be present. Document. A letter, a ledger, a recording, a message. Ellipsis. The event is not narrated at all, and its consequences carry it. The discipline is not to avoid access grants but to be able to say why the cheaper instrument was rejected. There is a good answer, and it is usually the same one: report can state a fact; only dramatisation can make a decision felt as it is made. A reader can be told that a man chose to go on writing in his father’s ledger. The reader cannot experience the choosing except from inside. Access is also the domain most vulnerable to genre inflation. Multi-viewpoint structure in commercial thrillers and epic fantasy is often weighted towards access — George R. R. Martin’s named-chapter rotation in A Song of Ice and Fire , whose vantages between them cover a continent, is the familiar case — and the form’s readers accept it because coverage of a large world is part of what they came for. Nothing is wrong with this; but a literary novel that imports the habit without the genre’s compensating pleasures acquires the cost without the return. Under- and over-delivery Under-delivery: the vantage attends a scene that turns out not to require attendance. A viewpoint chapter whose content could be compressed into one line of reported speech in the following chapter is an access grant that has bought nothing. Over-delivery: the book becomes a map rather than a story. Every location acquires a resident consciousness; the reader is fully informed and attached to no one. This is the diluted ensemble ( §8.3 ). Illustrations Tolstoy, War and Peace (1869). The largest access structure in the nineteenth-century novel, and the clearest demonstration that access alone would not have sufficed. Tolstoy needs a vantage at Austerlitz, at Borodino, in Moscow under occupation, in the Rostov household, at court and among the peasantry. But almost every one of those vantages is also a contrast: Pierre at Borodino is a civilian who does not understand what he is looking at, which is the book’s argument about history in miniature. Where Tolstoy grants access without a second domain — as with some of the staff-officer material — the pages are the ones readers skip. Stoker, Dracula (1897). Access as the whole architecture. The novel’s method is the assembly of documents from vantages that could not have met, and the plot is unavailable from any single one of them. §9.6 anatomises the system; the point here is that Stoker’s most celebrated access grant, the log of the Demeter ’s captain, belongs to a man who appears once, delivers a horror the other narrators cannot witness, and dies lashed to his wheel. It is an access grant in its purest form and one of the finest passages in the book. Dickens, Bleak House (1853). The anonymous narrator exists because Esther cannot be in Chancery, in Chesney Wold, in Tom-all-Alone’s and at the rag-and-bottle shop. But the access is inseparable from the vantage’s character : a present-tense, unattached, morally appalled intelligence with the whole country in view. Access supplied by a voice that is itself an argument is access that has been made to multiply ( §5 ). 4.2 Dramatic Irony — the reader knows what a character does not Definition. A grant made so that the reader acquires knowledge ahead of, or apart from, another character — most classically the antagonist’s vantage, which lets the reader see the trap being set. Why it matters. Dramatic irony is one of the two great engines of suspense, and it works by an asymmetry that only viewpoint allocation can create. Meir Sternberg’s distinction (Chapter 5 §3.4 ; Expositional Modes , 1978) is the precise instrument: suspense is uncertainty about the future, curiosity is uncertainty about the past, and surprise is the discovery that one’s model was wrong. A viewpoint grant that supplies the reader with knowledge the protagonist lacks converts curiosity into suspense — the reader stops wondering what is happening and starts dreading what will. Textual carriers Carrier What it does Note The antagonist’s plan, seen from inside Creates dread on the protagonist’s behalf The standard commercial use; also the standard failure ( §8.10 ) A character’s private knowledge of another’s error Makes an ordinary conversation unbearable The cheapest and most under-used form Simultaneity Two vantages, same hour, incompatible beliefs Requires the reader to hold both; see Chapter 5 §8.10 A confession the other characters never hear The reader is made a sole confidant Powerful; ends the possibility of surprise on that point The retrospective narrator’s foreknowledge I did not know then that… Chapter 7’s territory; a within-vantage irony rather than a cross-vantage one Discussion The domain has a paradox at its centre that drafts routinely mishandle: the irony grant spends a mystery to buy a dread, and the exchange is not always favourable. A crime novel that gives the killer viewpoint chapters has traded the question who did it? for the question will they be caught, and what will it cost? That is a real trade and a defensible one — it produces the “inverted” detective story, a form with an honourable history — but it is a trade, and a draft that makes it accidentally, in order to enjoy the villain’s company, has spent its principal asset without noticing. The most instructive form of the domain is also the quietest. Irony does not require an antagonist; it requires only that two vantages hold incompatible beliefs about the same situation and that the reader hold both. A novel in which a wife knows what a husband does not, and the reader has been inside both, converts every subsequent domestic exchange into a scene with two floors. The requirement that is easy to miss: dramatic irony demands that the two vantages meet again . Knowledge asymmetry is only an engine if the ignorant party keeps acting on their ignorance in the reader’s presence. A book that reveals the trap and then leaves the victim off-page has bought dread and spent it on nothing. Under- and over-delivery Under-delivery: the reader learns something the protagonist does not know, and it makes no difference to how any subsequent scene reads. The asymmetry is inert. Over-delivery: every question is pre-answered. A book that grants viewpoint to everyone with a secret has abolished mystery altogether; the reader watches characters be wrong for four hundred pages, which is a comic structure whether or not the book is a comedy. Illustrations Dostoevsky, Crime and Punishment (1866). The reader knows from the first chapter who committed the murder, and Dostoevsky’s whole engine is the resulting asymmetry: every scene with Porfiry Petrovich is legible on two levels at once, and the suspense is not who but when, and what it will do to him . The novel is the standard demonstration that surrendering curiosity can buy more than it costs. Tolstoy, Anna Karenina (1878). The finest quiet example in the canon. Because the reader has been inside Karenin — his humiliations, his religiosity, his procedural mind — the scenes in which Anna and Vronsky discuss him are unbearable in a way they could not be if he were only a husband seen from outside. Tolstoy uses viewpoint to withdraw the option of contempt. §9.4 . Stoker, Dracula (1897) — by refusal. Stoker grants viewpoint to seven or eight characters and pointedly not to the Count. The consequence is that the novel has almost no dramatic irony of the standard kind: the reader is as ignorant as the hunters, and the book runs on curiosity and dread rather than on foreknowledge. It is the clearest available demonstration that withholding a viewpoint is as much a design decision as granting one. 4.3 Contrast (viewpoint domain) — the reader inhabits a different value system Definition. A grant made so that the reader can occupy a materially different way of seeing — a different class, culture, generation, temperament, moral framework or cognitive condition — widening the book’s thematic range the way a subplot widens its plot range. (This edition names the domain contrast (viewpoint domain) , to distinguish it from Chapter 14’s contrast between plot lines.) Why it matters. Contrast is the domain that makes multi-viewpoint structure a thematic rather than a merely informational device. Chapter 14 ( The Subplot ) argues that a second plot line earns its place by commenting on the first; contrast is the same argument at the level of consciousness. A book with two viewpoints that see the same world in the same way has two cameras. A book with two viewpoints that value differently has an argument. Textual carriers Carrier What it does Note Differential noticing The two vantages register different things in the same room The primary carrier; see §5.3 Differential naming What each calls the same person, place or act Extremely cheap and almost never exhausted Differential explanation What each treats as needing no explanation Chapter 9 §4.4 ’s normalisation, used comparatively Incompatible idiom Register, syntax, vocabulary of judgement Chapter 3’s territory at sentence level Different time-sense One vantage measures in seasons, another in hours Underused; instantly characterising Different theories of causation One sees God, one sees economics, one sees luck The deepest form; Uspensky’s ideological plane Discussion Contrast is the domain most often claimed and least often delivered , because the differences a draft supplies are usually differences of circumstance rather than of vision. Two characters with different jobs, different ages and different problems may still notice the same details in the same order and appraise them with the same vocabulary — in which case the book has two biographies and one consciousness. The operational test ( §7.1 , no. 4) is brutal and effective: take the contents of two viewpoint chapters, swap them between the two characters, and ask whether a reader could tell. If the paragraphs survive transplantation, the contrast is notional. The strongest contrasts are built on what a vantage cannot see . A character’s blind spots are more distinguishing than their perceptions, because two people looking at a room will list overlapping objects, while two people failing to notice things fail in entirely different directions. This is why contrast and the epistemological domain (§4.6) are neighbours, and why the argument for separating them requires care. A caution that needs stating early. Contrast has an ethical dimension that the other domains lack. To grant a vantage in order to represent a way of seeing not one’s own is to take on a representational responsibility, and the craft question (“is the contrast delivered?”) does not exhaust the critical one (“is the representation adequate, and who is it for?”). Keen’s distinction between bounded, ambassadorial and broadcast empathy ( §3.4 ) is the useful frame, and §9.5 puts the problem in its sharpest available form. Under- and over-delivery Under-delivery: the redundant vantage ( §8.5 ). Two interiorities distinguished by biography and nothing else. Over-delivery: contrast as caricature. A vantage so committed to being the other view that it becomes a position rather than a person — the pious one, the cynical one, the young one. Woloch’s character compression, applied to a character who was granted space and then not permitted to use it. Illustrations Faulkner, The Sound and the Fury (1929). The maximal case. Benjy, Quentin and Jason do not merely see different things; they inhabit different relations to time, to language and to causation. Benjy’s section has no chronology because he has none; Quentin’s is saturated with a past that will not stay past; Jason’s is a running ledger of grievance and money. The same family, three incommensurable orders of mind. §9.2 . Tolstoy, Anna Karenina (1878). Levin and Anna constitute the most celebrated contrast structure in the European novel, and it is a contrast of value rather than of information: work against passion, country against city, the making of a life against the consumption of one. The two threads barely intersect in plot and comment on each other constantly. Whether that constitutes structural convergence is a live critical disagreement, treated at §9.4 and set as a seminar question. Rhys, Wide Sargasso Sea (1966). Contrast at its most politically loaded. Part Two is largely focalised through the English husband, whose vocabulary of appraisal — what a cunning devil , the island as excess, the wife as contamination — is systematically incompatible with Antoinette’s. The novel’s argument is carried almost entirely by the difference between two ways of naming the same place. §9.5 . 4.4 Sympathy Engineering — interiority complicates a verdict Definition. A grant made to a character the reader would otherwise judge from outside, so that the judgement becomes harder, more informed, or impossible. Why it matters. This is the domain in which Booth’s mechanism ( §3.2 ) is deployed on purpose. Sustained inside access aligns a reader with a consciousness more or less automatically; a writer who understands this can use it to withdraw the reader’s right to a simple verdict. It is the most powerful moral instrument in the novelist’s kit and the one most easily misfired. Textual carriers Carrier What it does Note The motive the reader can recognise Supplies a reason the reader can recognise in themselves The engine of the domain The cost the character is paying Converts an act into a sacrifice or a compulsion Effective even when the act stays indefensible The self-justification the reader can see through Aligns and distances at once Booth’s dual distance; the most sophisticated form A private tenderness One unwitnessed kindness or grief Cheap, powerful, and easily cloying The withheld explanation The reader learns why a silence was kept The household case at §9.9 uses this A body Pain, hunger, cold, fear Bypasses judgement entirely; the oldest device in the form Discussion The domain has two distinct modes, and conflating them is the commonest error in drafts. Exculpatory sympathy supplies information that changes what the act was : the silence was protection, not betrayal; the theft was for someone else. The verdict changes because the facts changed. Non-exculpatory sympathy supplies no such information. The act remains what it was, and the reader is nevertheless made to inhabit the person who did it. Nothing is excused; the reader’s position simply becomes more uncomfortable. The second is the more valuable and the harder. A book that uses interiority only to exculpate has used a structural instrument to deliver a plot revelation, and once the revelation lands the vantage has nothing further to do — which is why so many “sympathetic antagonist” chapters feel spent after one appearance. A book that uses interiority non-exculpatorily has permanently altered the reader’s relation to the character, and the alteration survives the plot. The timing question is decisive and can be stated as a rule. Sympathy engineering placed before a character’s damaging act produces dread and complicity; placed after it produces re-evaluation and, if handled poorly, the sense of an author lobbying. The revision case at §9.9 turns on this: the bounded Dov chapter is placed before the ledger is read by his sisters, so that the reader carries knowledge into a scene the characters enter without it — which recruits the irony domain as well. Under- and over-delivery Under-delivery: the vantage humanises nobody, because the interiority supplied is generic. A character who is revealed to be tired, and worried about money, and to have loved his father, has been given the interiority of anyone. Over-delivery: special pleading. The reader detects an author arguing rather than a character living, and the effect is a hardening rather than a softening of judgement. Readers resist being told how to feel about a person more strongly than they resist almost anything else in fiction. Illustrations Tolstoy, Anna Karenina (1878). Karenin, again, is the canonical case, and the passage most often cited is his forgiveness at Anna’s sickbed — a moment in which a man the novel has arranged for the reader to despise becomes, briefly, the best person in the room, and knows it, and cannot sustain it. Nothing is excused. The reader simply loses the option of contempt. Nabokov, Lolita (1955). The limit case, and the reason the domain needs its ethical caveat. Chapter 9 §4.3 treats the opening’s seduction of the reader; the structural point here is that the novel grants viewpoint to one consciousness only, and that the exclusive grant is the book’s method: the reader is given no alternative vantage from which Dolores Haze could be seen, and the absence is the novel’s most devastating formal fact. Character compression, weaponised. Eliot, Middlemarch (1872). The most famous deliberate deployment of the domain in English, and the subject of §5.2 and §9.3 . Eliot interrupts her own narration to ask why the reader’s sympathy should always follow Dorothea, and turns the vantage on Casaubon — a man the novel has permitted the reader to find ridiculous — to insist that he too has an intense consciousness and is spiritually hungry like everyone else. The turn is not exculpatory. Casaubon remains what he is. What changes is the reader’s licence to dismiss him. 4.5 Structural Pacing — the shift itself as a rhythm instrument Definition. A grant made, or a shift timed, so that the alternation becomes a pacing device across the whole book — the deferral of one thread’s resolution by movement to another, the variation of tempo by variation of vantage, the management of a long novel’s rhythm through its viewpoint pattern. Why it matters. This is the domain that operates at book scale rather than scene scale, and it is the one most easily invisible to a writer working forward through a draft. A viewpoint pattern is a rhythm whether or not it was designed as one, and an undesigned rhythm is usually a metronome. Textual carriers Carrier What it does Note The deferral cut Leaving a thread at maximum tension Chapter 6 owns the placement decision; this chapter owns the choice of where to go next Variable interval Returning to a thread after two chapters or after eighty pages, according to its state The most under-used pacing instrument in multi-viewpoint fiction Tempo contrast between vantages A fast, external consciousness alternating with a slow, ruminative one Buys rhythm and contrast simultaneously Convergence Vantages that begin apart and are brought into the same room Structural payoff; Chapter 16’s territory at the ending Acceleration of the pattern Alternations accelerating towards the climax Very effective; almost never planned Suspension of the pattern A long stay in one vantage after regular alternation Signals crisis without stating it Discussion The instructive point is that the pattern of visits is itself expressive , and that most drafts squander it by regularity. A book that alternates A, B, A, B for four hundred pages has taught its reader that nothing about the sequence means anything; the alternation has become furniture. A book that alternates A, B, A, B, A, A, A has said something about A’s crisis without a word of commentary. Tolstoy’s practice in Anna Karenina is the model, and Chapter 5 §9.4 describes it from the transition side: the interval between returns to each thread varies with the state of that thread, and the returns are timed to comment. The allocation-side observation is different and belongs here: Tolstoy’s page-share between Anna and Levin shifts across the novel , with Levin’s share rising as Anna’s world contracts, so that the book’s proportions enact its argument. Part Eight has no Anna in it at all. The deferral cut deserves a boundary marker. Cutting away from a thread at its point of maximum tension is a chapter-break decision, and Chapter 6 owns it. What belongs here is the question the break decision cannot answer: where does the reader go instead? A deferral into a vantage the reader is glad to see costs little; a deferral into a vantage the reader has been tolerating converts suspense into irritation. The value of a cliffhanger is set by the quality of the destination. Under- and over-delivery Under-delivery: the metronome. Fixed-length alternation regardless of what each thread needs — the viewpoint-scale version of Chapter 5 §8.3 . Over-delivery: the whiplash (Chapter 5 §8.5 ). Cuts so frequent that no thread accumulates enough continuous time for tension to form. A novel that never stays anywhere for more than four pages has a rhythm and no pulse. Illustrations Dickens, Bleak House (1853). The alternation between the two narrations is irregular by design — sometimes a chapter each, sometimes four or five consecutive chapters of one — and the irregularity is what keeps a sixty-seven-chapter novel from settling into a pattern the reader can predict. Serial publication reinforced it: Dickens’s number plans show him distributing the two voices across each monthly part for variety within the part, not merely across the whole. Faulkner, As I Lay Dying (1930). Fifty-nine sections of wildly varying length, from several pages to a single line. The variation is the pacing: Vardaman’s five-word section arrives as a shock because the sections around it are long. Section length, in a rotating architecture, is a tempo instrument that a chapter-based architecture cannot access as finely. Stoker, Dracula (1897). The pacing use of documentary polyphony is the dating : entries overlap, repeat and lag, so that the reader repeatedly knows something before the character writing the next entry does. Stoker also uses telegrams and cuttings as short, fast units between long journal entries — a rhythm effect achieved entirely through choice of document type. 4.6 A Proposed Sixth: The Epistemological Domain The five domains above are all, in a specific sense, positive : each names something a vantage supplies — information, asymmetry, a value system, a mitigation, a rhythm. Each assumes that the vantage is reliable within its own limits, and that assembling vantages produces a fuller picture. A substantial body of novels grants viewpoint for the opposite reason. The epistemological domain. A vantage granted not to show what happened but to demonstrate that no single vantage can know what happened. The incompleteness of each account is the point; the reader’s task is not assembly but the experience of irresolution. The structural signature is Genette’s multiple internal focalisation ( §3.1 ): the same events focalised successively through different characters, so that the accounts do not merely differ in coverage but conflict in substance. What variable focalisation gives to a jigsaw, multiple focalisation gives to a contradiction. Why it is distinct from contrast The objection to admitting a sixth domain is that it collapses into the third, and the objection must be taken seriously. Both involve incompatible ways of seeing. The distinction is in what the incompatibility is for : Contrast (§4.3) Epistemological (§4.6) Status of each vantage Reliable within itself; limited in scope Unreliable about its own scope ; may be wrong, not merely partial What the reader assembles A wider world A doubt Relation between accounts Complementary; they add Competitive; they subtract The reader’s final position Better informed than any character Aware that no position is available Test for presence Do the vantages value differently? Would a reader who read only one vantage believe something the book denies? The last row is the operational test. In a contrast structure, a reader who read only Levin’s chapters would have an incomplete picture but no false one. In an epistemological structure, a reader who read only one vantage would come away misled , and the book knows it. Textual carriers Carrier What it does Note Direct contradiction of fact Two accounts of one event that cannot both be true The plainest form; risks reading as error unless framed Differential gaps Each account omits what another supplies, and the omissions are motivated Subtler and stronger Speculation presented as narration A vantage narrating what it could not have witnessed Absalom, Absalom! ’s method The unreachable centre The one consciousness that could resolve the matter is never granted vantage Dracula ’s Count; Wide Sargasso Sea ’s Antoinette in Part Two Documentary framing that undermines itself An apparatus asserting authenticity in a book that demonstrates its impossibility Dracula ’s prefatory note Refusal of closure at the join The book declines to adjudicate between accounts The domain’s defining move Illustrations Faulkner, Absalom, Absalom! (1936) is the pure case, and it belongs to Chapter 7 ( Backstory and Flashback ) for its reconstruction method; the viewpoint-side observation is that the novel’s tellers — Rosa Coldfield, Mr Compson, Quentin, Shreve — narrate a story none of them witnessed, increasingly openly inventing it, and that the invention is not a flaw in their testimony but the novel’s subject. The vantages are granted because they are inadequate. Faulkner, The Sound and the Fury (1929) is the domain’s most teachable instance because its four sections are graded. Benjy cannot interpret; Quentin cannot stop interpreting; Jason interprets everything wrongly and with total confidence; the fourth section stands outside all three without resolving them. Faulkner’s own remark, in interviews, that he wrote the story four times and still failed to tell it is the domain’s motto. Rhys, Wide Sargasso Sea (1966). Part One is Antoinette’s; Part Two is largely her husband’s, with an interpolated stretch of hers; Part Three opens in Grace Poole’s voice before returning to Antoinette in England. The reader is never given an adjudicating vantage, and the novel’s refusal is inseparable from its argument: a book written to answer Jane Eyre ’s confident account of a madwoman cannot itself offer a confident account without repeating the offence. Stoker, Dracula (1897). The documentary apparatus asserts evidentiary completeness — the note prefacing the novel insists the papers are placed in sequence so that the facts may stand for themselves — while the novel demonstrates that the one consciousness that could explain the events is the one no document contains. Mina’s compilation of the record is an act of epistemological faith the book does not fully underwrite. Lessing, The Golden Notebook (1962). The domain applied to a single consciousness rather than to several. Anna Wulf’s four notebooks divide one life into incommensurable accounts, and the “Free Women” sections narrate the same life as a conventional third-person novel that the notebooks expose as a simplification. §9.7 . The argument against admitting it Three objections, each with force. It is contrast with unreliability added, and unreliability is a separate axis (Booth; Chapter 9 §4.1 ). On this view the sixth domain is a compound of two things the model already has, and compounds should not be listed alongside primitives. It describes a genre rather than a domain. The examples cluster heavily in modernist and postmodernist fiction. A domain that is unavailable to most novels may be a period style rather than a category of purpose. It is not a purpose but an effect. The other five name what a grant buys for the story ; this one names what the structure means . Mixing levels weakens the model’s diagnostic edge. The reply. Objection 1 understates the difference: an unreliable single narrator produces a puzzle with a solution the reader can reach, whereas multiple focalisation without adjudication produces a structure with no solution available in principle. That is a difference in kind. Objection 2 is answered by pointing at Dracula , a popular novel of 1897, and at the whole epistolary tradition of contradictory testimony from Clarissa onward — this is not a modernist invention. Objection 3 is the strongest, and the chapter concedes half of it: the epistemological domain does operate at a different level from the others, and a student should know that it is being admitted for diagnostic usefulness rather than for taxonomic symmetry. The practical value of admitting it is that it names a purpose a draft can be failing to serve. A writer with three contradictory testimonies who does not know that irresolution is a legitimate destination will “fix” the contradictions and destroy the book. The domain exists in the model so that a manuscript can be diagnosed as epistemological but not yet committed — the commonest form of confusion in ambitious multi-viewpoint drafts. A ruling at the scale of a book. Chapter 15 ( The Reveal ), named to adopt or reject the domain at the scale of a book, adopts it as the plural-vantage form of the declined reveal, a book that keeps a question of fact visibly open to its end. At book scale contrast plus unreliability ends in a reveal that says which account to discount, and this domain ends without one, which answers objection 1; the objection that it names what a structure means rather than what a grant buys lapses, since what a structure means is a reveal’s own subject; and the objection that its examples cluster in modernist fiction stands in part. See the full treatment , section 3.5. The authority domain: a ruling Chapter 10 ( The Prologue ) proposes an authority domain for the separated unit: a prologue or note that tells the reader what kind of text follows and how far to trust it, as Life of Pi ’s Author’s Note does, or the note before Dracula asserting that the papers have been placed in sequence so that the facts may stand for themselves. Chapter 10 left it to this chapter to adopt or reject, since the epistemological domain is its nearest relative. The ruling: it is not added to the domains of the grant, and it stays in Chapter 10 as a domain of the separated unit. A grant made to establish standing is already one of two things this model contains: a witness’s access (the Demeter ’s log), or an epistemological structure in which the frame’s claim is tested ( Dracula ’s documents against its note; Life of Pi ’s second story against its Author’s Note). The two proposals are one pair seen from opposite sides. The authority domain claims that a vantage suffices; the epistemological domain demonstrates that none does. The first belongs to a book’s threshold, the second to the allocation inside it. Seminar question 2 ( §12.2 ) puts the disagreement to the class. 4.7 Summary table: the domains, their carriers and their failures Domain Chiefly carried by Under-delivery Over-delivery Access Presence at otherwise unreachable scenes; different geography, stratum, order of being The vantage attends a scene reportable in a line The book becomes a map; nobody is known Dramatic irony Knowledge asymmetry; the antagonist’s plan; simultaneity The asymmetry changes no later scene Every mystery pre-answered Contrast (viewpoint domain) Differential noticing, naming, explaining; incompatible idiom and causal theory Two biographies, one consciousness Contrast as caricature; a position, not a person Sympathy engineering Motive, cost, self-justification, body, withheld explanation Generic interiority; anyone’s inner life Special pleading; the author lobbying Structural pacing Deferral cuts, variable interval, tempo contrast, convergence The metronome The whiplash Epistemological (proposed) Contradiction, motivated gaps, speculation as narration, the unreachable centre Contradictions read as authorial error Irresolution without stakes; the reader stops caring which account is true 4.8 Must all the domains be served at once? No, and the model is misused when read that way. Four qualifications. (1) Two is the working threshold, not five. §5 argues that a grant serving only Access is under-employed. It does not argue that a grant must serve everything. The most common shape in accomplished fiction is two domains strongly served and a third incidentally: Karenin’s vantage in Anna Karenina serves sympathy and irony, and picks up contrast as a by-product of being a bureaucrat in a novel about passion. (2) The domains are unequally available to different architectures. A documentary polyphony ( §6.3 , no. 8) is structurally rich in access and epistemology and structurally poor in sympathy engineering, because a document is a performance for a reader and interiority in it is always partly self-presentation. A rotating ensemble is rich in contrast and pacing and poor in dramatic irony, because a reader who visits everyone knows everything. These are properties of the architecture, not defects of the draft. (3) A domain may be served across a book rather than within a chapter. The single Addie section in As I Lay Dying serves almost nothing on its own terms and reorganises the entire novel retroactively. Domains are properties of grants, and grants are book-scale objects. (4) The proportion varies by mode and by genre. As a tendency rather than a measured finding, epic fantasy and commercial thrillers weight access and pacing; literary family novels weight contrast and sympathy; the modernist novel of consciousness weights contrast and epistemology. The domains are constant; the allocation among them is a genre-inflected choice , and applying a literary weighting to a thriller produces a slow thriller rather than a good novel.

title: 5. Multiplicity: The Economy of the Grant
section: Multiplicity — The Economy of the Grant
text: 5.1 The principle, stated as a constraint Multiplicity — established in Chapter 1 and reused throughout this book — is the practice of making a single unit of narrative discharge several functions at once. At the scale of the sentence it is a virtue. At the scale of the viewpoint grant it becomes something harder: an admission requirement . The reasoning is a constraint problem with three terms. A viewpoint grant is the most expensive instrument in the novelist’s kit , because it commits the book’s scarcest resource (identification, mind-modelling capacity, page share) for the duration of the book rather than for the duration of a scene. Its commonest justification — access — is the one for which the cheapest substitutes exist. Report, inference, reassignment, document and ellipsis ( §4.1 ) can all deliver information, and four of the five cost almost nothing. Therefore a grant justified by access alone is, in nearly every case, an expensive solution to a cheap problem . Which yields the principle in its operational form: Full access to a mind is the costliest tool available. Spending it on plain information delivery rarely earns back what it cost. A grant should be able to name two domains, and one of them should not be access. The threshold of two is a working heuristic rather than a law, and §4.8 has already qualified it. What matters is the discipline it enforces: before granting viewpoint, the writer must be able to complete two sentences — This vantage gives the reader ______ that no existing vantage could deliver. The cheaper instruments I rejected are ______, and I rejected them because ______. A writer who cannot complete the second sentence has not made a decision; they have followed a convenience. The corollary, which is less obvious and more useful. Multiplicity in this chapter runs in both directions. A well-chosen grant does more than one job — but it should also be true that the character receiving it was already doing more than one job in the book . A vantage awarded to a character who exists only to occupy it will read as an appointment. The strongest grants in fiction go to characters who were structurally load-bearing before they were focalisers: Esther Summerson is the plot’s hidden centre; Levin is the novel’s thematic counterweight; Jason Compson is the family’s economic engine. The grant confirms an existing importance rather than manufacturing one. 5.2 Anatomy: a viewpoint reallocation dissected The most instructive single sentence in English fiction on this subject is George Eliot’s, at the opening of Chapter 29 of Middlemarch (1872): One morning, some weeks after her arrival at Lowick, Dorothea — but why always Dorothea? Was her point of view the only possible one with regard to this marriage? The sentence begins a chapter in the manner the novel has trained the reader to expect, breaks off mid-clause, interrogates its own procedure, and reallocates the reader’s attention to Casaubon — from whose interiority the following pages proceed. It performs, in twenty-eight words, the entire argument of this chapter. Textual element Functions discharged One morning, some weeks after her arrival at Lowick, The ordinary machinery of a chapter opening: time anchor, place anchor, continuity with the preceding narrative. It establishes a norm so that the break can register as a break (Chapter 5 §6.5 on drift; Chapter 6 on the expectations a chapter division sets) Dorothea Names the expected focaliser — the character the reader has been trained across twenty-eight chapters to follow. Woloch’s protagonist convention invoked so it can be suspended — but The syntactic pivot. A dash and a conjunction perform a viewpoint change that most novels would spend a section break on why always Dorothea? Converts an allocation from a habit into a question. The word always is doing the structural work: it identifies the reader’s expectation as cumulative , built by repetition, and therefore as something the narrator has been building on purpose Was her point of view Names the object under discussion in the reader’s own critical vocabulary. Eliot is not merely shifting focalisation; she is telling the reader that focalisation exists and is chosen the only possible one Establishes plurality as a fact about the world rather than a device of the book. There are other possible views because there are other people with regard to this marriage? Fixes the scope. Not about everything — about this marriage , the specific object on which two vantages will now be shown to differ. Bal’s subject–object relation ( §3.1 ) made explicit in the prose Six observations follow, and they are the substance of this section. (1) The grant is bounded and the boundary is announced. Eliot does not make Casaubon a rotating viewpoint character. She takes the reader inside him for a stretch, and returns. This is the bounded grant ( §6.3 , no. 6) executed at chapter scale, and it is the cheapest form of a later grant available. (2) The reallocation is performed by the narrator, not by the structure. No white space, no heading, no chapter break. This is possible only because the book’s architecture is the mobile omniscient narrator ( §6.3 , no. 10), which has held the right of free movement from its opening pages. A limited-third novel attempting the same move at Chapter 29 would be committing the omniscient slip ( §8.6 ). The same sentence is a masterstroke in one architecture and an error in another , which is the chapter’s recurring lesson. (3) The move is a sympathy grant, not an exculpation. Casaubon is not revealed to be secretly admirable. He is revealed to have an interior — to be, as the narrator goes on to insist, as intensely conscious and as spiritually hungry as anyone else. Nothing about the marriage improves. What is withdrawn is the reader’s licence to find him merely absurd. Compare §4.4 ’s distinction between exculpatory and non-exculpatory sympathy. (4) It multiplies. The sentence serves sympathy engineering (Casaubon acquires an inside), contrast (two incompatible readings of one marriage), and — by naming its own procedure — a thematic argument about the moral cost of attention that the novel pursues to its last page. (5) It is a lesson in what an established convention buys. Eliot can afford this because she has spent twenty-eight chapters establishing a narrator who generalises, addresses the reader, and moves. The move costs almost nothing here because it was paid for there . §6.6 ’s cost curve is this observation formalised. (6) It is the seed of the chapter’s Woloch material. “Why always Dorothea?” is, in a single clause, the question The One vs. the Many takes a book to ask. Eliot’s narrator notices that attention is finite, that its distribution is a choice, and that the choice has moral weight — and then acts on the noticing. The architecture in which this sentence sits is analysed at §9.3 ; the sentence is treated here for its allocation mechanics rather than for its place in the novel’s design. 5.3 Where the multiplying work actually lives Novice revision looks for viewpoint differentiation in voice — in dialect, in sentence rhythm, in a character’s verbal tics. Voice differentiation is real and Chapter 3 treats it. But it is the most expensive place to work, the easiest to overdo, and, in third-person narration, frequently unavailable: a novel with four close-third viewpoints in a single social class cannot make them sound different without making three of them affected. The multiplying work of a viewpoint grant lives in four humbler places. 1. Selection of detail — what this consciousness registers. Two people enter the shop. One notices that the register drawer sticks and that the stock has not moved; the other notices that the coat still hangs on the hook and that someone has been brushing it. Nothing has been said about either person, and they are now entirely distinct. This is the most reliable instrument in the chapter, because it costs no additional words: the sentences were going to describe something , and choosing which thing is free. Note that selection also carries the domains. Differential noticing is the primary carrier of contrast ( §4.3 ); the noticing of a clue nobody else registers is access; the noticing of a kindness is sympathy. 2. The idiom of judgement — what appraisal words leak into the narration. Free indirect style is not principally a matter of dialect; it is a matter of evaluation . When a third-person narration calls a room poky , or a decision typical , or a brother impossible , the judgement belongs to the focaliser, and the reader knows whose head they are in before any name appears. Cohn’s narrated monologue ( §3.2 ) is the technical name; the practical instruction is that the adjectives are the viewpoint . Two characters can share a vocabulary and differ entirely in what they are willing to appraise. One will not permit herself to evaluate her mother; another evaluates everyone. That asymmetry is characterisation performed by the narration itself. 3. The knowledge boundary — what this vantage cannot know, and whether the prose respects it. Every grant draws a line, and the line is a resource rather than a restriction. A chapter that observes its boundary strictly produces inference, misreading and dread; a chapter that leaks produces the failure at §8.7 . The instruction that follows is counter-intuitive: when a viewpoint chapter feels thin, the usual fault is that it has been allowed to know too much, not too little. Interiority is generated by uncertainty. A focaliser who understands the situation has nothing to do but report it. The boundary also carries irony ( §4.2 ) for free: a vantage that misreads a situation the reader has understood from elsewhere is a dramatic-irony engine that costs no additional structure. 4. Naming — what this vantage calls people, places and acts. The cheapest differentiator in the language and the least used. A sister who thinks of him as Dov , a sister who thinks of him as my brother , and a mother who thinks of him by a name nobody else uses have been distinguished at no cost in words. Naming carries relation, distance, era, class and grievance simultaneously, and it operates below the reader’s conscious notice, which is where the most durable effects live. The same applies to acts. One vantage calls it selling the shop ; another calls it what he did ; a third calls it the arrangement . Three nouns, three moral positions, no exposition. The synthesis. Voice differentiation makes viewpoints sound different. Selection, judgement, boundary and naming make them be different. A draft whose viewpoints fail the distinguishability test ( §7.1 , no. 4) should be repaired at these four levels before anyone attempts a dialect. 5.4 The ceiling: how many vantages a book can carry There is no correct number, and any figure offered is a convention rather than a discovery. What can be stated is the relation that governs the ceiling, and the symptoms of having exceeded it. The relation has four terms: Term Effect on the ceiling Available length Raises it, roughly linearly, and only if the length is distributed What the reader is asked to do with each vantage Raises it sharply if the task is triangulation; lowers it sharply if the task is investment Distinguishability Raises it; fifteen instantly identifiable voices are cheaper than four interchangeable ones Legibility of the pattern Raises it; a declared architecture converts frame construction into frame recall ( §3.4 ) The commonest miscalculation in ambitious drafts is to treat only the first term as a variable. A writer with a long book assumes they can afford many vantages, and produces the diluted ensemble ( §8.3 ) — because length distributed across too many centres does not deepen any of them, it merely delays the reader’s arrival at each. Three symptoms of the ceiling being exceeded: Symptom What the reader experiences Re-identification lag Each section opens with a beat of who is this again? , even when the anchor is correct — a failure of memory, not of anchoring Interchangeable response The reader cannot predict how any given vantage will react to news, because none has a settled temperament Relief at return The reader is pleased to get back to one particular vantage and tolerates the others. This is the strongest single diagnostic, and it identifies the book’s real protagonist ( §8.9 ) The limit case, and why it is not a counter-argument. As I Lay Dying has fifteen focalisers in fifty-nine sections and perhaps sixty thousand words. On the arithmetic of page share it is impossible: Vardaman’s total allocation would not fill a short story. It is not diluted, for three reasons that between them constitute the real rule. The reader’s task is triangulation, not investment. The book is an epistemological structure ( §4.6 ) whose subject is a corpse and a journey seen from fifteen angles. Nobody is asked to become Cash. The voices are instantly identifiable , by idiom, obsession and syntax. Vardaman’s fish, Cash’s list of thirteen reasons for the bevel, Darl’s uncanny fluency. Identification costs the reader nothing. The distribution is grossly unequal and the inequality is the design. Darl has nineteen of the fifty-nine sections; several characters have one. This is not an ensemble in which everyone is served; it is a hub with a large number of spokes, and the hub is a man who ends the novel insane and speaking of himself in the third person. §8.9 . The generalisable statement is therefore not how many but: A book can carry as many vantages as it can make instantly identifiable and as its reader’s task requires. What it cannot carry is many vantages all asking to be inhabited equally. 5.5 Exercise: the page-share audit A practical procedure, and the most reliable instrument in this chapter for diagnosing a structural problem that feels like a prose problem. Procedure. List every viewpoint character. For each, record: total word count of their sections; number of sections ; the page at which they first receive viewpoint ; the page at which they last hold it ; and the longest gap between two of their sections . Convert word counts to percentages of the whole. Plot the sections in book order as a strip — one letter per section — so the pattern is visible as a shape. Beside each name, write in one sentence the domains the grant serves ( §4 ). Interpretation. Pattern Diagnosis First move One vantage above 60%, others in single figures A single-viewpoint novel with decorations. Possibly correct — but the minor grants should be examined for necessity Convert the small grants to report, or make them bounded and deliberate ( §6.3 , no. 6) Shares approximately equal across five or more An ensemble governed by fairness rather than need. The commonest cause of dilution Identify the real protagonist by the “relief at return” test (§5.4) and rebuild the proportions around them A vantage whose first section falls after the 60% mark A late grant. May be right; must be defended §7.1 , test 7 A vantage with one long gap exceeding a quarter of the book The reader will re-enter as if to a stranger Either add a bridging section or accept the gap and re-anchor heavily (Chapter 5 §4.5 ) The strip is a strict alternation for the whole book The metronome ( §4.5 ). The pattern has stopped meaning anything Vary the interval according to each thread’s state A vantage that stops entirely two-thirds through Either an unannounced bounded grant or an abandoned thread Check whether the reader is left waiting; abandonment is felt even when the plot does not require the vantage The domains column repeats “access” The book’s viewpoint structure is a delivery mechanism §5.1 A refinement worth the extra hour. Repeat step 5 for the characters who have no viewpoint, recording for each: how many scenes they appear in, whether their motives are ever explained, and whether the explanation comes from them or from someone judging them. That is the character-compression test ( §7.1 , no. 10), and its output is the part of the audit most likely to change the book.

title: 6. The Grant: Architectures of Viewpoint
text: 6.1 The grant as a structural commitment A viewpoint shift is an event. A grant is a commitment, and it has four properties that a writer should be able to state for every viewpoint character in a manuscript: Property The question Why it matters Recipient Who holds it? §4 and §7.1 tests 1–3 Extent How much of the book? §5.5 ; determines whether this is a viewpoint character or a bounded grant Onset When does it begin? §6.6; the difference between a first and a later grant Termination Does it end, and does the reader know? An unannounced ending reads as abandonment ( §5.5 ) Most craft treatments handle only the first. The other three are where structural failure actually occurs, and they are properties of the whole book rather than of any scene, which is why they are invisible while drafting forward and obvious in an audit. The four properties combine into a small number of recurring shapes. Those shapes are what this section calls viewpoint architectures , and a manuscript almost always belongs to one of them whether or not its author chose it. 6.2 The scholarly treatment The idea that a novel’s handling of vantage constitutes a describable form rather than a series of local choices arrives with Henry James and is codified against him. §3.5 gives the history; what belongs here is what each party contributed to the description of whole-book shapes. James’s contribution is the reflector , or centre of consciousness. His best-known figure for it — the house of fiction with not one window but a million, at each of which a watcher with a distinct field and instrument stands — states the principle: the aperture and the watcher together constitute the subject, and a different watcher at a different window is looking at a different novel. Two features of his position are usually lost in transmission. He presents restriction as a gain in intensity purchased by a loss in scope , which is a trade rather than a rule; and his own practice is less austere than his advocacy, since the narrator of The Ambassadors generalises and stands back with some freedom even while remaining largely fixed on Strether. Lubbock turned the trade into a doctrine and Forster dissented within six years ( §3.5 ). Forster’s position — that shifting vantage is a resource, and that what governs its success is the reader’s confidence in the writer’s command rather than any consistency rule — is the one this chapter adopts. Norman Friedman’s “Point of View in Fiction” ( PMLA , 1955) produced the first systematic typology in English — editorial omniscience, neutral omniscience, I as witness, I as protagonist, multiple selective omniscience, selective omniscience, the dramatic mode, the camera. Friedman’s categories mix voice and focalisation, which is the confusion Genette resolved seventeen years later; but the ambition of the piece, to describe whole-book shapes rather than sentence-level effects, is the one this section inherits. Stanzel’s typological circle ( §3.2 ) supplies the crucial structural insight for a taxonomy: architectures are not discrete species but neighbouring positions, and books drift between them. Several entries below are best understood as adjacent regions rather than as boxes. 6.3 A taxonomy of thirteen viewpoint architectures The taxonomy describes whole-book shapes . It is not exhaustive, the categories are not mutually exclusive, and accomplished novels frequently braid two — Bleak House is an alternating dual whose second narration is a mobile omniscient, and Beloved is a hub-and-spokes that becomes an unattributed chorus for one movement. # Architecture Description Exemplar Buys Costs 1 Single fixed One focaliser for the whole book; the reader never leaves The Remains of the Day ; The Trial ; What Maisie Knew Maximum depth; the knowledge boundary as a permanent engine; unreliability made structural Everything off-stage must be reported or inferred; no dramatic irony except within the vantage 2 Single mobile (the roving third) Variable internal focalisation, one mind at a time, moving freely but never within a unit Mrs Dalloway ; To the Lighthouse ; Madame Bovary Coverage without the machinery of declared sections; contrast at close range Requires very strong differential noticing, or the vantages blur; readers may not perceive a pattern to rely on 3 Alternating dual Two vantages in regular or irregular alternation for the length of the book Bleak House ; Wide Sargasso Sea (sequential rather than alternating) Contrast at maximum clarity; a rhythm the reader can feel; irony as a structural default The reader nearly always prefers one; the weaker half is felt as an interruption ( §8.9 ) 4 Rotating ensemble Three or more vantages in a repeating cycle As I Lay Dying ; The Poisonwood Bible Coverage; a social rather than individual subject; polyphony in Bakhtin’s sense Dilution ( §8.3 ); the cycle becomes a metronome; late-arriving readers cannot locate the centre 5 Hub-and-spokes One dominant vantage, plus subordinate vantages used briefly and for specific purposes Mrs Dalloway (Clarissa and Septimus); Beloved ; Anna Karenina (a two-hub variant) Depth and coverage together; the proportions themselves say what the book is about Requires the writer to accept an unequal cast, which drafts resist on grounds of fairness 6 The bounded single grant One chapter or section given to a consciousness that never holds the reader again Addie’s section in As I Lay Dying ; Casaubon in Middlemarch ch. 29; the prologue device (Chapter 10) A late grant at a fraction of the price; a single decision dramatised rather than reported The reader may expect a return; the grant must be shaped as complete in itself 7 Frame narrator with embedded tellers An outer narrator receives and transmits accounts from inner ones Wuthering Heights ; Frankenstein ; Season of Migration to the North Reliability questions; distance; a listener whose reactions guide the reader Two openings to earn; the outer frame must justify its own existence ( §8.12 ) 8 Documentary polyphony The book is an assembly of letters, diaries, transcripts, cuttings Dracula ; The Woman in White ; The Color Purple Authenticity; access to incompatible vantages; epistemology built into the form Interiority is always performed for a reader, so sympathy is hard; voices tend to converge ( §8.5 ) 9 The collective “we” A group focaliser: a village, a class, a generation, a chorus The Grapes of Wrath (intercalary chapters); The Virgin Suicides ; the abandoned nous of Madame Bovary A social mind (Palmer, §3.4 ); a moral vantage no individual could hold Nobody in particular is known; sustained use exhausts quickly 10 The mobile omniscient narrator Zero focalisation: a narrating intelligence with free access, exercising it, including within scenes Middlemarch ; War and Peace ; Vanity Fair ; Tom Jones Everything: scope, irony, commentary, analysis, moral range Requires a narrator strong enough to hold it; reads as authorial intrusion to readers trained on limitation 11 The unattributed choral voice Consciousness rendered without assignment; the reader infers or is denied the speaker Beloved , Part Two; The Waves ; Blindness Effects unavailable to attributed narration: merging, possession, anonymity, the collective wound Very high comprehension cost; unusable for long stretches 12 The second person You as focaliser: the reader positioned as, or addressed as, the character If on a Winter’s Night a Traveller ; Bright Lights, Big City Immediate implication; estrangement; a formal argument about reading itself Novelty fatigue; ambiguity about whether you is the reader, a character, or the narrator addressing himself 13 External focalisation — the refused grant No interiority granted to anyone; behaviour and speech only “Hills Like White Elephants”; Jealousy ; and locally, Dracula himself throughout Stoker’s novel Maximum inference; the reader does the work; opacity as subject Sustains poorly at novel length; readers supply interiority anyway and may supply the wrong one Notes on the harder entries. On 2 versus 4. The difference between the roving third and the rotating ensemble is not the number of vantages but the presence of a declared pattern . Woolf moves between consciousnesses without announcement or regularity, and the reader learns to expect movement rather than to expect a sequence; a rotating ensemble teaches a cycle, and the cycle becomes a promise. The practical consequence is that a roving third can add or drop a vantage at any point without structural cost, while a rotating ensemble cannot: an ensemble that quietly stops visiting one of its members has broken a rule it taught. On 5. Hub-and-spokes is the architecture most drafts are actually writing and least often admit to. Its virtue is that it resolves the coverage–depth trade rather than choosing a side: the hub is inhabited, the spokes are visited. Its difficulty is entirely psychological — writers who have grown fond of a secondary character resist giving them three pages when they have imagined thirty. §8.9 addresses the inverse failure, the ensemble that is secretly a hub. On 6. The bounded grant is, in this chapter’s estimate, under-used in contemporary fiction, and it is the structure this chapter recommends most often in revision. Its logic is a discount: the cost of a later grant (§6.6) is largely a cost of disruption to an established pattern , and a grant that visibly closes behind itself disrupts the pattern only once. The shaping requirement is that the section must read as complete — a self-contained account with its own beginning and end — rather than as the first instalment of a thread the book then drops. On 9 and 11. These two are frequently confused. A collective we has a determinate, if plural, speaker: the boys of the neighbourhood, the townspeople, the migrants. An unattributed choral voice withholds the speaker, and the reader’s uncertainty is the effect. Morrison’s Part Two monologues in Beloved begin attributed and end unattributed, which is the movement from 9 to 11 performed inside a single sequence ( §9.8 ). On 13. External focalisation is included because a taxonomy of grants must include the decision not to grant. Its most instructive appearance is local rather than global: a novel otherwise rich in interiority that keeps one character resolutely outside. Dracula, Bertha Mason in Jane Eyre , and — in the household narrative running through this book — the mother are all instances, and each is a case where the refusal carries the book’s argument or its damage. 6.4 How to use the taxonomy: substitution testing The taxonomy’s purpose is not classification but substitution . A manuscript that is not working is very often the right material in the wrong architecture, and the fastest way to discover this is to specify the alternatives enough to compare. The procedure: Name the current architecture from §6.3. Most writers get this wrong on the first attempt: drafts that describe themselves as rotating ensembles are usually hubs with underfed spokes. Name two neighbours — the architectures immediately adjacent on the coverage–depth axis. For each neighbour, write two hundred words stating what the book would gain, what it would lose, and which scenes would have to be rewritten. Rewrite one chapter in the strongest neighbour. Some standard substitutions and what they typically reveal: From To What the test usually reveals Rotating ensemble (4) Hub-and-spokes (5) That one vantage was always the book’s centre, and that three others exist to cover the map Alternating dual (3) Single fixed (1) That the second vantage’s material is reportable, and that its removal produces suspense rather than confusion Single fixed (1) Bounded grant added (6) That only one off-stage decision needed dramatising, and that everything else was fine as inference Rotating ensemble (4) Documentary polyphony (8) That the voices were never differentiated by mind , and that giving each a genre of document does the work by other means Single mobile (2) Mobile omniscient (10) That the writer has been suppressing a narrator who wants to speak, and that the suppression was producing flatness Any multi-vantage form External focalisation (13) for one character That a character the draft was explaining is more powerful unexplained The last row is the most frequently productive and the least frequently attempted.
