A great deal of what a draft calls “developing” a difficult character consists of granting them interiority, and a great deal of what makes such characters powerful is its absence. 6.5 How a viewpoint change is signalled Chapter 5 ( The Transition ) owns the crossing — what carries the reader from one side of the gap to the other, and the anchoring that resolves who on arrival ( §4.5 , §6.3 there). This section owns the prior question: by what device does the book tell the reader that a change of vantage is the kind of thing that happens here? The distinction matters because the two operate at different scales. An anchor resolves one crossing. A signal establishes a convention , and once established it makes every subsequent crossing cheaper (Emmott’s frame recall, §3.4 ). Signal Where it operates Legibility Cost Note Chapter or section heading naming the focaliser Paratext Total Commits the book to the pattern for its whole length; consumes the heading as a resource As I Lay Dying ’s fifty-nine named sections; a common commercial convention Part or book divisions Paratext High Coarse; permits only a few changes Wide Sargasso Sea ; The Sound and the Fury ’s dated sections The proper name in the first clause Prose High Almost none The workhorse; Chapter 5 §4.5 Absolute register shift Prose High once learned, low at first occurrence Requires two voices with no shared features Bleak House : present-tense panorama against retrospective I Section break (white space) with no other marker Typography Low on its own None Signals a change, not which ; must be paired with a prose anchor Change of document type Form Total Commits the book to an epistolary or documentary architecture Dracula : journal, phonograph diary, telegram, cutting Change of person or tense Grammar Very high Very high if not sustained Rhys’s Part Three shift; risks reading as error Typographic differentiation (italics, no quotation marks, spacing) Typography High Fatigues; unusable for long stretches Morrison’s Part Two; Faulkner’s italics for time-shifts Explicit narratorial handover Prose Total Period-marked; declares a mobile-omniscient architecture Middlemarch §5.2 ; Vanity Fair Three principles govern the choice. (1) Signal the architecture once, at maximum strength; signal each crossing at minimum strength. The first viewpoint change in a book should be unmistakable — a heading, a part division, an absolute contrast of voice. The twentieth needs only a proper name. Books that reverse this (a quiet first change, heavy signposting thereafter) are the ones readers describe as confusing, even though the confusion occurred once, near the start, and coloured everything after it. (2) The declaration should precede the reader’s first deep investment. This is Chapter 9 §4.6 ’s formal contract, and §6.6 supplies its mechanism. In practice: the first viewpoint change should occur at the first chapter break, not at page ninety. (3) Naming headings are a commitment, not a convenience. A book whose chapters are headed with names has promised that every chapter belongs to a named vantage. It can no longer include an unattributed chapter, a chapter focalised through a minor character, or a chapter of pure omniscient panorama, without the reader experiencing the omission as a puzzle. Faulkner keeps the promise absolutely in As I Lay Dying , including for Addie, who is dead. Writers who adopt the convention for its convenience frequently discover in the third act that they have foreclosed the manoeuvre the book needs. 6.6 The first grant and the later grant The chapter’s central mechanism can now be stated with the theoretical apparatus behind it. First grant. Viewpoint established while the reader’s investment across the cast is still forming — in practice, within the first chapters. Cheap, because the reader has not yet committed and a new vantage simply joins the field. Later grant. Viewpoint introduced after the book has trained the reader to follow a smaller set of vantages. Expensive, because it withdraws attention from positions the reader has already paid into, and because it retroactively revises the book’s declared form. The cost of a later grant is not a single quantity. It is the sum of three distinct charges, and separating them explains why some late grants are ruinous and others are the best thing in the book. Charge What it is Reduced by Formal surprise The reader learns the book is a different shape than they thought Early signalling of the possibility of movement, even if not exercised Attention withdrawal Pages that would have gone to established vantages go elsewhere Boundedness — a short grant withdraws little Investment cold start The new vantage has no accumulated familiarity; the reader must build a model from zero at a point in the book where they are least willing Prior presence — the character has been on the page, observed from outside, for the whole novel The third charge is the one drafts most often mismanage, and it yields the most useful practical rule in this section: A later grant is cheap in proportion to how long the reader has already been curious about the recipient. A character observed from outside for three hundred pages, whose silence has been the book’s standing question, costs almost nothing to enter. A character introduced and granted viewpoint in the same chapter, at the two-thirds mark, costs everything. This is why the bounded grant (§6.3, no. 6) is the standard remedy. It pays the first charge once, the second charge trivially, and the third not at all if the recipient has been present throughout. The household case at §9.9 is this configuration, and so is Casaubon’s chapter in Middlemarch : a character the reader has watched from outside for twenty-eight chapters, entered once, and left. The declaration window. Combining Chapter 9 §4.6 with the charges above yields a rough scheduling principle rather than a rule: Grant onset Status Requirement First chapter First grant None beyond ordinary competence Within the opening movement (roughly the first fifth) First grant, late The pattern should be legible by the end of this movement Middle of the book Later grant Must be either bounded, or supported by a domain payoff that no report could deliver Final quarter Late later grant Bounded, or the book must be one whose subject is the insufficiency of its own vantages ( §4.6 ) Final pages Extreme Legitimate only as a formal argument. Wide Sargasso Sea ’s Grace Poole; The Sound and the Fury ’s fourth section The bottom two rows are the interesting ones, and §8.4 supplies their counterexamples. A very late grant is not an error; it is a manoeuvre with a narrow success condition, which is that the arrival of a new vantage must be legible as the book’s argument rather than as the author running out of alternatives. 6.7 Historical drift, and a caution against universalising the present §3.5 established that the prohibition on mid-scene movement is recent. This section makes the wider point about architectures , which have moved at least as much. The table is a sketch of tendencies drawn from the novels this chapter reads, not a measured survey. Period Dominant architectures Driver 18th century Documentary polyphony (8); frame with embedded tellers (7); mobile omniscient (10) The fiction of the found document; the novel’s need to claim factual standing Early–mid 19th century Mobile omniscient (10), with occasional dual (3) Serial publication’s need for many threads; the social-panoramic ambition Late 19th century Single fixed (1) and single mobile (2) rising; omniscience under attack James; the aesthetic of restriction; the rise of psychological realism Modernist Single mobile (2), rotating ensemble (4), unattributed chorus (11) Consciousness as subject; the loss of confidence in a governing vantage Mid-century Anglo-American Single fixed (1) dominant; multi-viewpoint at chapter boundaries only Workshop pedagogy; Lubbock’s codification; editorial practice Contemporary literary Alternating dual (3) and hub-and-spokes (5) The two-hander; the interest in structural contrast; the marketability of a “braided” novel Contemporary commercial Rotating ensemble (4) with named-chapter headings Series length; ensemble television; the demand for coverage of large worlds Three inferences, which pull in different directions. The advice in §§5 , 7 and 8 is calibrated to the last two rows. Its cautions about dilution, late grants and head-hopping describe how a reader trained on contemporary convention responds. That is a reason to know the cautions, and not a reason to mistake them for laws. The novels that violate them are not tolerated exceptions. Middlemarch moves between minds within a paragraph; War and Peace changes vantage at will and interrupts to discourse on historiography; Bleak House introduces its second narration in Chapter 3 with no announcement whatever. A pedagogy that can only say this would be edited out today has explained an industry and not a book. The drivers are material as often as aesthetic. The named-chapter heading is not a discovery about reading; it is, on this chapter’s reading, a solution to the problem of a very long fantasy novel with many viewpoint characters, and it plausibly spread because it worked for that problem. Serial publication produced the multi-thread nineteenth-century novel. Ensemble television has probably shaped the contemporary rotating ensemble, though the influence is conjecture. Knowing which of one’s convictions about viewpoint are aesthetic and which are inherited from a distribution format is part of a writer’s education. The properly critical position is double: learn the present conventions well enough to break them deliberately, and read historically well enough to know that they are conventions.

title: 7. Diagnostic Method
text: 7.0 How to use the protocol The ten tests below are for revision, not composition . Applied during drafting they produce paralysis of a particular kind — the writer stops before every scene to ask whose head it belongs in, which is the surest way to write nobody’s. Applied to a completed draft, they are the most efficient structural triage in this chapter. Four procedural notes. Run them in order, and stop when one fails badly. Tests 1 to 3 are about whether a grant should exist at all; tests 4 to 7 are about the shape of the allocation; tests 8 to 10 are about execution and consequence. There is no point tuning the knowledge boundary of a vantage that should not have been granted. Run them on grants, not on scenes. The unit under test is a viewpoint character across the whole manuscript. A test applied to a single chapter will return a local answer to a structural question. Record the answer, not the verdict. The output of each test is a sentence describing what the book does. “Dov’s vantage serves sympathy and contrast, and appears once, at 78%” is useful. “Fails test 7” is not. A failed test is a question. Every test below is failed by at least one novel discussed in this chapter, several of them by Middlemarch . The test’s function is to make a choice visible so that it can be confirmed as a choice. 7.1 The ten tests Test 1 — The necessity test Could an existing vantage deliver this material by report, inference, reassignment, document or ellipsis? Procedure. For each scene held by the vantage under test, name the cheapest instrument that could carry its content, and write the substitute in one sentence. Then read the substitutes as a set. Interpretation. If most of the scenes translate without loss, the grant is an access grant that should be reconsidered. The important refinement is that the test asks about loss , not about information : report can always convey a fact. What report cannot do is dramatise a decision as it is taken, render a misapprehension from inside, or make a silence feel like a choice rather than an absence. If the loss is one of those three, the necessity test is passed. Test 2 — The domain test Which of the six domains does this specific grant serve? Procedure. For each vantage, list the domains from §4 , and beside each write the specific textual evidence — the scene, the passage, the effect. Domains asserted without evidence do not count. Interpretation. A grant serving only access is under-employed and should be converted to a cheaper instrument or given more to do. A grant serving two or more, at least one of which is not access, is earning its seat. A grant serving none — which happens more often than writers expect, particularly with viewpoint characters inherited from an early draft — should be removed. A useful secondary output: tabulate the domains across all vantages. A book whose every grant serves access and pacing has a delivery mechanism rather than a design; a book whose every grant serves contrast may be an argument with characters attached. Test 3 — The investment test Has this character earned enough presence and interiority to justify holding the reader’s head, or do they read as a plot vehicle with a name? Procedure. Before the character’s first viewpoint section, count their appearances, and write down what the reader knows of their wants — not their function, not their relation to the protagonist, but what they are trying to get. Interpretation. A vantage whose recipient had no legible want before the grant will read as an appointment. The remedy is usually not to add interiority inside the grant but to add presence before it: the character should have been on the page, wanting something visibly, for some time. This is the “cold start” charge at §6.6 , and it is paid before the grant rather than during it. Test 4 — The distinguishability test Swap the contents of two viewpoint sections between their holders. Could a reader tell? Procedure. Take a passage of two hundred words from vantage A and a passage of two hundred from vantage B. Change only the proper nouns required to make each grammatically consistent with the other’s situation. Give both to a reader who knows the book. Interpretation. This is the most unforgiving test in the protocol and the most diagnostic. If the passages survive transplantation, the book has two cameras and one consciousness — the redundant vantage ( §8.5 ). The repair is at the four levels of §5.3 : what each notices, what each is willing to appraise and in what words, what each cannot know, and what each calls things. Note that the test is about mind , not about voice: two vantages may be perfectly distinguishable in idiom and still fail, if the idiom is the only difference. A weaker but faster version, usable alone: cover the chapter headings of a multi-viewpoint manuscript and read the first paragraph of each section. Count how many you can assign correctly. Test 5 — The page-share audit What proportion of the book does each vantage hold, and what shape does the distribution make? Procedure. §5.5 in full. At minimum: word count per vantage as a percentage, number of sections, onset page, longest gap. Interpretation. Per §5.5 ’s table. The two findings that most often force a structural decision are approximate equality across five or more vantages (an ensemble governed by fairness rather than by need) and a long gap (a vantage the reader must re-enter as a stranger). Neither is automatically wrong; both must be defended rather than inherited. The audit also answers a question writers cannot answer introspectively: which character is the book actually about? The answer is very often not the one on the synopsis. Test 6 — The first-grant timing test On what page does the reader learn that this book has more than one vantage? Procedure. Find the page. Then find the page at which the reader’s investment in the first vantage becomes substantial — in practice, the end of the first sustained scene in which that vantage wants something and is resisted. Interpretation. If the second is earlier than the first, the book has trained the reader to expect single narration and then contradicted the training. This is Chapter 9 §4.6 ’s formal contract, and the expected symptom is resistance rather than confusion: the reader understands perfectly and resents it. The remedy is rarely to move the second vantage’s material. It is to declare the possibility earlier — a short section, a heading convention, a part division — so that the eventual shift is a fulfilment rather than a surprise. Test 7 — The late-grant test If this vantage arrives after the book’s opening movement, does the payoff cover the disruption? Procedure. Name the three charges from §6.6 — formal surprise, attention withdrawal, investment cold start — and estimate each. Then name the domain payoff and ask whether it could have been delivered by report. Interpretation. Late grants pass when three conditions hold together: the recipient has been present and observed from outside for a long time; the grant is bounded; and the material dramatises a decision rather than delivering information. They fail when the recipient is new, the grant is open-ended, or the content is expository. A specific and common failure: a late grant introduced because the plot has become impossible to convey from existing vantages. That is a plot problem presenting as a viewpoint problem, and adding a vantage treats the symptom. Test 8 — The knowledge-boundary test Does this vantage know only what it could know? Procedure. Mark every sentence in a viewpoint section that reports a fact the focaliser could not have. Include: other characters’ thoughts and motives; events elsewhere; physical descriptions of the focaliser’s own face and expression; information the focaliser learns later in the book; and — the subtlest — judgements the character is not capable of forming. Interpretation. A handful of marks is normal and, in most architectures, invisible to readers. A steady scattering is the omniscient slip ( §8.6 ) and indicates that the book’s architecture is not what its author believes. A cluster around plot-critical moments is the vantage that knows too much ( §8.7 ), and it is usually the writer solving an information problem at the reader’s expense. The productive follow-up is not to delete the marked sentences but to ask what the vantage would have had instead : an inference, a misreading, a wrong guess. Those are more interesting than the facts they replace, which is why the test so often improves a chapter it was meant only to correct. Test 9 — The scene-integrity test Within a single continuous scene, does the narration stay with one consciousness — and if it does not, is the book’s architecture one that permits movement? Procedure. Take five continuous scenes at random. Mark each sentence with the initial of the mind whose perceptions or judgements it reports. Where a scene shows more than one initial, ask the second question. Interpretation. The two-part structure of this test is deliberate and is the practical form of §2.3 and §8.1 . Mixed initials in a book whose architecture is single fixed (1), single mobile (2), alternating dual (3) or rotating ensemble (4) constitute head-hopping: the narration is leaking outside the convention it has established. Mixed initials in a mobile omniscient architecture (10) are the architecture operating. The diagnostic question is therefore never did the narration move? but has this book established the right to move, and does it exercise it consistently or only when convenient? A narration that moves at moments of plot necessity and stays put elsewhere has not established a right; it has found a loophole, and readers detect the difference. Test 10 — The character-compression test What has happened to the characters who receive no viewpoint? Procedure. List every character with a name and more than two scenes who holds no vantage. For each, record: (a) how many scenes they appear in; (b) whether their motives are ever explained; (c) whether the explanation comes from them, from a viewpoint character’s inference, or from the narrator; (d) whether the reader could state what they want; and (e) whether they have acquired a repeated identifying tag — a gesture, a phrase, a physical feature — that stands in for characterisation. Interpretation. This is Woloch’s test ( §3.3 ), and it is the only one in the protocol that looks away from the material under revision. Item (e) is the key. A repeated tag is the visible mark of character compression: it is what a person becomes when a book needs them to be recognisable and has no room to make them knowable. Character compression is not a fault. Every novel compresses its minor characters, and must. What the test asks is whether the character compression is distributed as the book’s argument requires . Three findings to watch for: The unexamined antagonist. The only character whose motives are never available is the one the plot needs to be wrong. The book has arranged for its own verdict. The instrumental relative. A parent, a spouse or a child who appears in many scenes, is never explained, and exists to make a viewpoint character feel something. The compressed group. A whole class, profession, ethnicity or generation present in the book without a single interior. This is the finding with the largest consequences and the one most often invisible to the author, because absence is not salient. The output of the test is not a demand for more viewpoints. It is a demand that the writer be able to say why these people are outside, and be willing to own the argument the arrangement makes. 7.2 Reading the results Failed tests Likely diagnosis First move 1 and 2 together The grant is a delivery mechanism Convert to report, inference or document; reassign the scenes 2 alone (access only) Under-employed vantage Give it a want and a blind spot, or make it bounded 3 alone Cold start Add presence before the first grant, not interiority inside it 4 alone Redundant vantage Repair at §5.3 ’s four levels; if irreparable, merge the two characters 5 (equal shares, five-plus vantages) Ensemble by fairness Identify the real centre and rebuild as hub-and-spokes ( §6.3 , no. 5) 5 (long gap) Abandonment felt by the reader Bridge, or terminate the grant visibly 6 alone Undeclared architecture Declare earlier; move the first change to the first chapter break 7 alone Unearned late arrival Bound the grant, or convert the material to report 8, scattered Omniscient slip Decide the architecture, then enforce it 8, clustered at plot points Vantage knows too much Replace knowledge with inference; the scenes usually improve 9 in a limited architecture Head-hopping Either repair to the convention, or commit to a mobile narrator from page one — not both 10 Distorted character-system Not a repair; a decision. Ask what argument the distribution makes and whether it is the intended one A warning about test 5. When a page-share audit reveals that a beloved secondary vantage holds four per cent of the book, the instinct is to expand it. This is almost always the wrong direction. Four per cent is what the book has decided that character is worth; the productive question is whether those pages are the right four per cent, and whether they should be one bounded, unforgettable section rather than six thin ones.

title: 8. Failure Patterns
text: Each pattern below is presented with its symptom , its mechanism (what actually goes wrong, as distinct from what the surface looks like), its persistence (why competent writers keep producing it), its remedy , and — mandatorily — the exception : a published work that commits the “error” and succeeds. The exceptions are not decorative. A pedagogy of prohibitions produces writers who can avoid faults and not writers who can make choices. In every case the pattern fails because of a mechanism, not because of a surface feature, and where the mechanism is absent the surface feature is harmless. The first pattern is the clearest case in this textbook of a rule that names a convention rather than a mechanism, and it is treated at proportionate length. 8.1 Head-Hopping Symptom. Within a single continuous scene, the narration reports the interiority of more than one character — moving from what she thinks to what he thinks, sometimes across a paragraph break, sometimes within a sentence — without a structural boundary. Mechanism, as usually described. The reader, having bound their model of the scene to one consciousness, must rebuild it around another with no warning. In Emmott’s terms ( §3.4 ) the contextual frame’s viewpoint slot is silently overwritten; in Zwaan and Radvansky’s, the protagonist dimension shifts without a marker. The result is a beat of uncertainty about whose perceptions are being reported, and a diffuse loss of intimacy: a reader who has been in nobody’s head in particular has been in nobody’s head. Mechanism, more accurately. The description above is true of a specific configuration and false as a general account, and the difference is the discrimination this chapter depends on. What produces the reader’s uncertainty is not movement. It is mismatch between the narration’s behaviour and the convention the book has established . A novel that has spent eighty pages confined to one consciousness has taught the reader that confinement is the rule; the ninety-first page’s excursion into a second mind is therefore read as an accident, and the reader’s response is not confusion about whose thought it was but a small loss of confidence in the book. A novel that has established from its first page a narrating intelligence with the whole world in view has taught the reader something different, and the same excursion is read as that intelligence doing what it always does. Two further distinctions sharpen this. (1) Governed movement versus opportunistic movement. The nineteenth-century mobile narrator moves on a principle : to compare, to correct, to widen, to judge. The workshop error moves when the plot requires a fact the current focaliser cannot supply. Readers detect the difference without being able to name it, because opportunistic movement correlates with information delivery and governed movement correlates with meaning. The test at §7.1 , no. 9 formalises the distinction: does the narration move where it has something to say, or where it has something to convey? (2) The strength of the narrating voice. Free access requires a narrator substantial enough to be the reader’s constant. Eliot’s narrator, Tolstoy’s, Thackeray’s and Fielding’s are all continuously audible presences with a temperament, a vocabulary and a set of opinions. The reader’s stability comes from them , not from any character. A contemporary novel written in transparent, self-effacing close third has no such presence, and when its narration moves there is nothing for the reader to hold. Omniscience is not free access; it is free access underwritten by a narrator. A draft that has the access without the narrator has taken on the liability without the asset. Persistence. Three causes, of which only the first is a fault of skill. Information pressure. The scene needs the reader to know what the other character is feeling, and the fastest route is to say so. The writer’s own vantage. A writer knows what everyone in the room thinks and does not experience the restriction as a restriction. Limitation is an artificial discipline, which is why it must be taught and why it decays under pressure. Reading history. Writers who have read a great deal of nineteenth-century fiction have absorbed a mobile convention and reproduce it inside a limited one. This is a mismatch, not an incapacity, and it is repaired by choosing an architecture rather than by learning a rule. Remedy. Not “stay in one head”. The remedy is a decision at the level of architecture ( §6.3 ), enforced consistently: Decide the architecture — limited or mobile — and write it down. If limited , replace every marked sentence (test 8) with what the focaliser could observe or infer. The scenes almost always improve, because inference is dramatic and knowledge is not. If mobile , establish the right in the first pages and exercise it throughout, including where it is not needed. A narrator who only moves when convenient has not established a convention. Do not do both. The commonest live manuscript is one that is limited by default and mobile at crisis points, and it fails in both directions at once. The exception — and it is very large. Three of the novels this chapter relies on most move between minds inside a single scene constantly, deliberately, and to effects unavailable by any other means. Middlemarch (1872). Eliot’s narration moves within scenes as a matter of course. In the Lydgate and Rosamond marriage, the reader is handed the same exchange from both sides in consecutive paragraphs — his exasperation and her serene incomprehension, each entirely reasonable from inside — and the marriage’s tragedy is constituted by the reader’s ability to hold both. No sequence of alternating chapters could produce this, because the effect depends on simultaneity: the reader must know what each is thinking at the moment the other speaks . Eliot also theorises the practice. The pier-glass parable at the opening of Chapter 27 — a scratched mirror on which a candle produces the illusion of concentric circles, an illusion that moves with the candle — is a statement about focalisation offered as a parable about egoism. Every consciousness organises the same scratches around itself. A narration able to move the candle is a narration able to demonstrate that the circles are not there. This is not a novel that would be improved by discipline; it is a novel whose subject requires the mobility that a workshop would call an error. Anna Karenina (1878). Tolstoy’s mid-scene movement is more rapid than Eliot’s and less announced. At the races, the narration passes among Vronsky riding, Anna watching, and Karenin watching Anna being watched — a triangulation that is the whole social catastrophe in miniature, executed in a few pages, and impossible to construct from any single vantage. At Anna’s sickbed, the movement among Karenin, Vronsky and Anna produces a scene in which three people are simultaneously transformed and none of them can be sure what has happened. Cutting the scene into three chapters would destroy it: the transformation is mutual and instantaneous. Tolstoy’s most extreme instance is also the most instructive for a theory of focalisation. During the woodcock shooting, the narration enters the setter Laska — her scent-world, her impatience with the men’s slowness, her judgement of her master. Every definition offered in §3.1 is tested by the passage, and the reason it is not a stunt matters: the dog’s vantage is epistemically superior to the men’s on the only question the scene cares about, which is where the birds are. Tolstoy is not being whimsical. He is demonstrating that consciousness is not co-extensive with reason, which is the argument Levin spends the novel failing to articulate. ( §9.4 .) War and Peace (1869). The largest instance and the one that most clearly exposes the prohibition’s provinciality. Tolstoy moves within a single battlefield scene from a general’s calculation to a private’s confusion to a horse’s stumble to a narratorial disquisition on the impossibility of any of them knowing what is happening. That last move — from character consciousness to a narrator who exceeds every character — is the manoeuvre a modern editor would flag most confidently, and it is the book’s thesis. The novel argues that history is not made by the people who believe they are making it; a narration restricted to any participant could not make the argument, because every participant believes otherwise. The discrimination to carry away. What Eliot and Tolstoy do differs from workshop head-hopping in four respects, and a manuscript can be tested against all four: Nineteenth-century mobile narration Workshop head-hopping Establishment The right is declared on the first page and exercised throughout The narration is limited by default and moves under pressure A narrator A continuous, audible intelligence the reader can hold Transparent narration with nothing to hold Motive for each move Comparison, correction, irony, judgement Delivery of a fact Predictability The reader learns that movement is the book’s mode The reader cannot tell whether the next paragraph will move The rule as it should be taught. Not never change viewpoint within a scene , but: do not exercise a right the book has not established. The prohibition on head-hopping is a prohibition on inconsistency masquerading as a prohibition on a technique. 8.2 The Information Mule Symptom. A viewpoint character whose sections exist to deliver plot information the protagonist could not access — a colleague who overhears, a servant who witnesses, an official who has the file — and who has no independent want or complicating interiority. Mechanism. The most expensive instrument in the kit ( §5.1 ) applied to the cheapest problem. The reader is asked to enter a mind and finds it furnished only with the plot. Because inside access carries an implicit promise of significance (Rabinowitz’s rules of notice, Chapter 9 §3.2 ), the mule also generates an unredeemed promise: the reader assumes this person will matter and keeps a slot open for them. Persistence. It solves a real problem, quickly, at a stage of drafting when structural costs are invisible. It is also invisible in isolation: any single mule chapter reads acceptably. Remedy. Test 1, then one of three moves: reassign the scene to an existing vantage; convert the content to report, document or inference; or give the mule a want that the information costs them something to acquire, which converts an access grant into an access-plus-sympathy grant. The exception. Wilkie Collins’s The Woman in White (1860) is built almost entirely of information mules and is one of the great popular novels in English. Collins’s minor narrators — the housekeeper, the cook, the doctor, the lawyer’s clerk — appear once each, testify, and vanish. They have no arcs. The structure works because Collins has framed the whole book as a legal deposition in which each witness speaks only to what they can attest, so that narrowness is the form’s virtue rather than its defect : a witness with an independent emotional life would be a worse witness. The lesson generalises. An information mule fails in a novel of consciousness and succeeds in a novel of testimony, because in the second the reader has been told what a narrator is for. 8.3 The Diluted Ensemble Symptom. Five, six, eight viewpoint characters in a book without the length to develop any of them. Coverage is total; investment is nil. Readers report that the book is “hard to get into” and cannot say why. Mechanism. The coverage–depth trade ( §1.1 ) resolved by default rather than by decision. Each additional vantage adds not one item to the reader’s load but a new set of relations (Zunshine, §3.4 ), so the cost grows faster than the cast. The compounding symptom is re-identification lag ( §5.4 ): the reader spends the opening of each section remembering rather than reading. Persistence. Fairness. Writers who have imagined a family or a crew fully find it invidious to grant three of them interiority and not the rest, and the ensemble grows by conscience rather than by design. Genre convention reinforces it: readers of epic fantasy and large-cast thrillers expect coverage, and the habit migrates into books that cannot support it. Remedy. The page-share audit ( §5.5 ), then conversion to hub-and-spokes ( §6.3 , no. 5). Most diluted ensembles are hubs whose author will not admit the hub. The second remedy, less often considered, is to shorten the sections : an ensemble becomes tractable when each visit is two pages rather than twenty, because the reader is asked to sample rather than to settle. The exception. As I Lay Dying (1930): fifteen focalisers, fifty-nine sections, one short novel. §5.4 gives the three reasons it is not diluted — the reader’s task is triangulation rather than investment, the voices are instantly identifiable, and the distribution is grossly and deliberately unequal. The Grapes of Wrath (1939) is a second and different exception: Steinbeck alternates a family narrative with intercalary chapters focalised through a collective ( §6.3 , no. 9), so that the “ensemble” is not a set of individuals competing for attention but a relation between one family and a people. Both books show the same principle: an ensemble is dilute when its members compete for the same reader function, and robust when they perform different ones. 8.4 The Unearned Late Arrival Symptom. A new viewpoint character appears at the two-thirds mark or later, holds several chapters, and pulls attention from vantages the reader has invested in. Mechanism. The three charges of §6.6 incurred together: formal surprise, attention withdrawal, and an investment cold start at the point in the book where the reader is least willing to begin again. The reader’s response is characteristically not confusion but impatience — they skim to get back. Persistence. It is a plot solution. The third act requires information or presence that existing vantages cannot supply, and a new one is the fastest fix. Remedy. Bound the grant ( §6.3 , no. 6); or plant the vantage earlier, even briefly, so the arrival is a return; or solve the underlying plot problem, which is usually that the climax has been placed where the protagonist cannot reach it. The exception. Two, and they are among the most admired final movements in the modern novel. Wide Sargasso Sea (1966) opens its Part Three in the voice of Grace Poole — a servant who has not narrated before, who narrates for a couple of pages, and who never returns. By every criterion above this should fail catastrophically: a brand-new vantage in the closing movement of a very short book. It succeeds because it performs the novel’s argument formally. Rhys’s subject is who is permitted to speak about a madwoman, and the last thing the reader is given before Antoinette’s final section is the voice of her keeper — the person Jane Eyre used to explain her. The grant is legible as the book’s meaning rather than as its author’s convenience, which is §6.6 ’s success condition. The Sound and the Fury (1929) does something structurally comparable in reverse: after three first-person sections, the fourth abandons the device entirely for a third-person narration centred on Dilsey. A reader trained across three sections to expect an interior monologue is handed, at the end, an outside. The effect is of air entering a sealed room, and it is unavailable to any book that had not sealed itself first. Faulkner then added, seventeen years later, an Appendix in yet another mode — a genealogical register — which some editions print first and which reopens the question of where the novel’s authority resides. 8.5 The Redundant Vantage Symptom. Two viewpoint characters who notice, judge and process events so similarly that granting both adds coverage but no new information, irony or contrast — indistinguishable interiorities wearing different names. Mechanism. The distinguishability failure of §7.1 , test 4. Its deep cause is almost always that the two characters were differentiated by circumstance rather than by mind : different ages, jobs and problems, but the same attention, the same appraisal vocabulary, the same theory of causation. Persistence. Circumstantial difference feels like difference while writing. It is also the kind of difference a synopsis can record, so a draft can look varied on a plan and read uniform on the page. Remedy. §5.3 ’s four levels, in order: differential noticing first, because it is free. If the repair fails, the two characters should probably be one, and the merge is nearly always an improvement — a single character with two problems is more interesting than two characters with one each. The exception. Dracula (1897) is frequently and correctly criticised for the sameness of its narrators: Jonathan Harker, Mina, Dr Seward and Lucy write a common late-Victorian epistolary prose, and readers routinely lose track of which journal they are in. The novel is nonetheless a masterwork of viewpoint structure, and the redundancy is part of why. The book’s evidentiary logic requires corroboration, and corroboration requires witnesses who agree. Four sharply differentiated observers producing four idiosyncratic accounts would have produced doubt; four decent, similar, credible people producing convergent accounts produce a case. Stoker’s redundancy is doing the work that differentiation would have undone. The generalisable point: redundancy fails in a novel of consciousness and can succeed in a novel of testimony (compare §8.2). 8.6 The Omniscient Slip Symptom. A book that is otherwise limited produces, every twenty or thirty pages, a sentence no focaliser could have generated: a fact about a character’s future, a description of the focaliser’s own face, a generalisation in a register the character does not possess. Mechanism. Stanzel’s circle ( §3.2 ) in action. The narrative situations shade into one another, and a book drifts from figural towards authorial without any identifiable moment of change. The reader does not consciously notice individual instances; the cumulative effect is a slight loss of the sense that the book is inside anyone, which is usually misdiagnosed as a prose problem. Persistence. These sentences are frequently the best in the draft. The authorial register is where a writer’s intelligence is most comfortable, and suppressing it feels like suppressing quality. Remedy. Test 8, then a decision rather than a deletion. If the marked sentences are the book’s best, the book may want a mobile-omniscient architecture and be fighting it. That is a legitimate finding, and acting on it — establishing the narrator properly from page one — is a better outcome than sanding the sentences down. The exception. To the Lighthouse (1927), Part II, “Time Passes”. Woolf’s novel is otherwise the roving third at its most refined, moving among consciousnesses at close range. The middle section abandons human focalisation altogether: an empty house, ten years, the wind in the passages, and the deaths of three of the novel’s people delivered in square brackets as parenthetical announcements. It is the most extreme viewpoint slip imaginable — from inside minds to no mind at all — and it is the greatest thing in the book, because the subject of the section is the indifference of duration to consciousness. Chapter 5 §9.1 treats it as an ellipsis; the allocation-side observation is that Woolf withdraws the grant from everybody , and the withdrawal is the meaning. War and Peace supplies the second exception in its historiographical passages, where the narration lifts clear of every character to argue about causation. Modern editors have proposed cutting them since the book appeared. They are the reason the novel is about what it is about. 8.7 The Vantage That Knows Too Much Symptom. A viewpoint character reports events they did not witness, thoughts they could not have read, or dialogue they were not present for — usually at the moments the plot most needs conveying. Mechanism. A knowledge-boundary breach (test 8) clustered rather than scattered. Where the omniscient slip is a drift, this is a raid: the writer needs a fact delivered and borrows the vantage’s credibility to deliver it. The cost is specific and severe. The knowledge boundary is what makes a limited vantage dramatic — it generates inference, misreading and dread — and a boundary that yields under pressure yields where those effects were most available. Persistence. It is invisible from inside, because the writer knows the fact and the sentence reads smoothly. It is also encouraged by the retrospective first person, where a narrator may legitimately know things the experiencing self did not, and the licence is easily overdrawn. Remedy. Replace knowledge with its shadow — the inference, the wrong guess, the thing half-heard. Where the fact is indispensable, supply it by the cheap instruments of §4.1 rather than by narratorial fiat. The exception. The Great Gatsby (1925). Nick Carraway narrates, in intimate detail, scenes at which he was not present: Gatsby and Daisy’s first kiss five years before Nick met either of them; Wilson’s movements on the afternoon of the shooting; Gatsby’s boyhood as James Gatz. Fitzgerald partly covers the breach by attributing some of it to later testimony — Jordan’s account, Michaelis’s — but the coverage is patchy and the most famous passages are unattributable. Critics have argued about this since the 1940s, and the honest verdict is that the novel commits the fault and is unharmed. The reason appears to be that Nick’s project is explicitly the construction of Gatsby: he tells us on the first page that he has been turning something over ever since, and a narrator engaged in making a legend is licensed to imagine. Wuthering Heights (1847) supplies a second: Nelly Dean reports verbatim conversations from decades earlier, including scenes she cannot have attended, and Emily Brontë makes no serious attempt to cover it. The frame architecture ( §6.3 , no. 7) absorbs the strain, and readers who notice tend to file it under Nelly’s unreliability rather than under the author’s carelessness — which is itself a finding: a vantage with a known interest in the story can overreach more safely than a neutral one. 8.8 The Corpse’s-Eye View Symptom. A viewpoint that cannot exist within the book’s own rules: the dead narrating, a character reporting their own unconsciousness, a vantage that persists past the moment it was extinguished. Mechanism. A breach not of the knowledge boundary but of the ontological one. Where a knowledge breach costs credibility, an ontological breach costs the world’s rules — and the world’s rules are what a reader has been using to calibrate every threat in the book. If death does not end a vantage, the reader must ask what else the book’s stated conditions do not mean. Persistence. It solves the hardest access problem in fiction — the interiority of a death — and it is emotionally irresistible to write. Remedy. Establish the licence early or not at all. This is a formal-contract problem (Chapter 9 §4.6 ): a novel in which the dead speak must be a novel in which the dead speak from the beginning , or the first instance will read as a cheat. The exception. Three, and they exhaust the ways of doing it. As I Lay Dying (1930). Addie Bundren’s single section is placed roughly two-thirds through, long after her death, and is the pivot of the novel. Faulkner earns it by having established from the first pages a formal convention — named sections, no narratorial frame — that makes no claim about who may hold one, and by Vardaman’s refrain that his mother is a fish, which has already put the ontology of the corpse in question. The section is a bounded grant ( §6.3 , no. 6) to the one consciousness the book has been circling, and it retroactively reorganises everything. The Posthumous Memoirs of Brás Cubas (1881). Machado de Assis declares the device in the dedication and the first chapter: the narrator is a dead man writing. Nothing is breached because the rule was stated first. Pedro Páramo (1955). Juan Rulfo makes the reader’s discovery that the speakers are dead into the novel’s central experience. The ontological breach is not a licence taken but the plot itself. The discrimination: the corpse’s-eye view fails when it is an exemption and succeeds when it is a premise. 8.9 The Ensemble with a Secret Favourite Symptom. A book presented as an ensemble in which one vantage is manifestly the author’s, and the others are visibly waiting. Readers describe skimming to get back. Mechanism. A mismatch between declared and actual architecture. The book’s signals (named chapters, regular rotation) promise architecture 4; its page share, its density of interiority and its emotional investment deliver architecture 5. The reader has been asked to distribute attention that the book has already concentrated. Persistence. Writers rarely know which vantage is their favourite. The audit at §5.5 reveals it; introspection does not, and the “relief at return” symptom ( §5.4 ) is felt by readers long before it is admitted by authors. Remedy. Not to suppress the favourite. Either declare the hierarchy — convert to hub-and-spokes, and let the proportions be visible — or raise the others by giving them what the favourite has, which is a want the reader can feel and a knowledge boundary that generates trouble. The exception. As I Lay Dying again, from the other side. Darl holds nineteen of fifty-nine sections; several Bundrens hold one. The book is unambiguously a hub-and-spokes wearing an ensemble’s clothing, and the imbalance is its argument: Darl is the family member who sees, and the novel’s action is the family’s collective decision to have the seer committed. The favourite is secret to the characters and not to the form , which is the condition under which the pattern becomes a technique. Wide Sargasso Sea is the second and more troubling instance. The husband holds the largest share of a novel written to give Antoinette the vantage Jane Eyre denied her. Critics disagree about whether this is a flaw, a concession to the source text, or the book’s sharpest move — the demonstration that even a novel written to restore a voice must contend with the volume of the one that displaced it. It is set as a seminar question ( §12.2 ). 8.10 The Antagonist Chapter That Spoils Its Own Suspense Symptom. A book built on a mystery grants viewpoint to the person who holds its answer, and the reader is thereby told what the book was going to be about. Mechanism. The irony trade of §4.2 , made without noticing. Sternberg’s curiosity is converted into suspense, and the exchange rate is unfavourable when the book’s other machinery was built for curiosity: an investigation plot whose reader already knows the answer must find something else for its investigators to do, and frequently has not. Persistence. Antagonists are enjoyable to write and their chapters are dramatic in isolation. The cost is structural and therefore invisible at the scene level, which is where drafting attention lives. Remedy. Decide which engine the book runs on — curiosity or suspense — and allocate accordingly. If the antagonist’s vantage is retained, the book must supply a replacement question, and the replacement must be at least as strong: how will they be caught , what will it cost , what will the protagonist become . The exception. Crime and Punishment (1866). Dostoevsky discloses the murderer in the opening chapters and focalises the entire novel on him. The curiosity is spent immediately and completely, and what replaces it is larger than what was lost: not who but what is happening to this man , a question no whodunit can pose. The form has a name — the inverted detective story — and a hundred and fifty years of descendants. Anna Karenina offers a subtler version. Tolstoy grants Karenin, the character a lesser novel would keep outside as an obstacle, enough interiority that he cannot function as an antagonist at all. The “spoilage” here is not of a plot secret but of a moral convenience, and the book is made by the loss. 8.11 The Viewpoint Granted Only to Be Killed Symptom. A character receives viewpoint for one section and dies in it, or shortly after. The grant is a mechanism for extracting emotion from a death or for showing the reader a threat. Mechanism. Two failures, usually together. The first is transactional : the reader detects that the interiority was issued in order to be cancelled, and responds to the manipulation rather than the death. The second is structural : the grant creates an expectation of continuation (Rabinowitz’s rules of notice again), and the expectation’s abrupt termination reads as a trick rather than as a loss. Persistence. It works in the moment. A death from inside is more affecting than a death reported, and the effect is available cheaply and repeatedly, which is why series fiction leans on it hardest. Remedy. Ask what the section would be worth if the character survived. If the answer is “nothing”, the grant is an effect rather than a vantage, and the material should be delivered from a survivor’s position — where it will also carry consequence, which the dead cannot. The exception. Two, and they define the success condition. Dracula (1897): the log of the Demeter ’s captain. A man the reader has never met, in a document nobody survives to explain, recording the disappearance of his crew one by one and ending with his decision to lash himself to the wheel. It is a viewpoint granted solely to be extinguished, and it is the most frightening passage in the novel. It works because the vantage is not there to make the reader mourn; it is there to establish what the antagonist is , and a witness who survives could not establish it. The grant serves access and epistemology, not sympathy. War and Peace (1869): Petya Rostov. Tolstoy takes the reader inside the boy on the night before his death — the half-dream in which the sounds of the camp become an orchestra he is conducting — and kills him the next morning in a single sentence, reported from outside, without emphasis. The manoeuvre is the prohibited one, and it is devastating because Tolstoy declines the transaction: he does not focalise the death. The reader is given the interior and then denied the moment for which the interior was supposedly being prepared. The discrimination. A vantage granted to be killed fails when the death is the payoff, and succeeds when the death is not narrated from inside — or when the vantage exists to establish something the survivors could not. 8.12 The Eye Without a Mind Symptom. A viewpoint character who observes everything and wants nothing. Their sections are full of other people; they have no project, no error in progress, and no stake. Readers describe them as “a bit of a blank”. Mechanism. A grant of position without a grant of interiority . The book has placed a camera where a person should be. Because the reader has been given access, they expect a mind, and the expectation goes unmet in a way that is hard to articulate and easy to feel. Palmer’s continuing-consciousness frame ( §3.4 ) is the theoretical form: readers maintain a running model of a whole mind, and a focaliser who supplies only perceptions leaves the model unfurnished. Persistence. It is the natural shape of a witness-narrator, and witness-narrators are useful: they let a book be about a character more interesting than the person telling it. It is also the natural shape of an author-surrogate, who is by definition the person in the room with the fewest problems. Remedy. Give the observer a want that conflicts with observing. A witness who needs something from the subject — money, forgiveness, permission, a story — is a witness with a mind, and their reporting becomes evidence about them. The exception. The Great Gatsby (1925), which is the pattern’s most celebrated instance and its most complete answer. Nick Carraway spends much of the novel watching, and announces early that he is inclined to reserve judgement; the book’s continuing critical argument is about whether he is a moral centre or an evasion. What saves the vantage is that Fitzgerald supplies the conflicting want prescribed above: Nick is snobbish, susceptible, dishonest about his own attraction to money, and involved with Jordan Baker in a way that indicts him. The novel’s last pages are a judgement, delivered by a man who claimed he would not deliver one. Wuthering Heights ’s Lockwood is a second and more comic instance: an observer so vain and so wrong that his blankness becomes the joke and the frame’s justification. 8.13 Summary: symptom to mechanism Pattern Underlying mechanism Domains damaged Head-hopping Exercise of a right the book has not established All; principally sympathy and contrast Information mule Costliest instrument on the cheapest problem Access delivered; nothing else served Diluted ensemble Load grows faster than cast; investment cannot be allocated Sympathy, contrast Unearned late arrival Three charges of §6.6 incurred at once Sympathy, pacing Redundant vantage Differentiation by circumstance, not by mind Contrast, irony Omniscient slip Drift along Stanzel’s circle without decision Sympathy; the reader’s sense of being inside anyone Vantage that knows too much Knowledge boundary yields under plot pressure Irony, sympathy; the dramatic value of inference Corpse’s-eye view Ontological rule breached as an exemption Epistemology; the world’s calibration Ensemble with a secret favourite Declared architecture contradicts actual page share Pacing, contrast Antagonist chapter spoiling suspense Curiosity traded for suspense without a replacement question Irony (over-served); pacing Viewpoint granted only to be killed Interiority issued in order to be cancelled Sympathy Eye without a mind Position granted without interiority Sympathy, contrast

title: 9. Worked Analyses
text: Eight close readings and a revision case. The apparatus is the same throughout: identify the architecture ( §6.3 ), audit the domains ( §4 ), and assess the allocation ( §5 , §7 ). 9.1 Dickens, Bleak House (1853) — the dual narration as an architecture Architecture: alternating dual ( §6.3 , no. 3), in which one of the two vantages is itself a mobile omniscient (no. 10) and the other is a fixed retrospective first person (no. 1). Bleak House is discussed in Chapter 9 as an opening and in Chapter 5 as a transition system. The question here is different and prior to both: why does this book have two narrations at all, and what does the allocation between them do? The two vantages, as a pair of decisions. The anonymous narrator Esther Summerson Person and tense Third, present First, past Position in time Contemporaneous with the events; no hindsight Retrospective; the closing chapter places the writing at least seven years after Extent of knowledge Institutional, national, systemic; but not uniformly interior Strictly personal; often the last to understand what the reader has grasped Relation to judgement Judges constantly, at volume, in the second person and the imperative Declines to judge, conspicuously and to the reader’s discomfort Share Conventionally counted as thirty-four of the sixty-seven chapters Thirty-three Domains served Access, contrast, pacing, epistemology Sympathy, contrast, irony The allocation is the argument. Bleak House is a novel about a society whose parts cannot see that they are connected — a Chancery suit, an aristocratic marriage, a crossing-sweeper, a slum. Its formal problem is therefore that no available human vantage can perceive its own subject. Dickens solves this by refusing to solve it: he supplies a vantage that sees the connections and cannot feel them, and a vantage that feels everything and sees almost nothing. The reader is the only position in the book from which both are available , and the novel’s design is an argument that such a position requires an effort of assembly that no character in England is making. A frequently missed nuance. The anonymous narrator is not fully omniscient in Genette’s sense. He repeatedly declines interiority — describing Tulkinghorn from outside, speculating about what a face may mean, reporting rumour as rumour. Critics have noticed this for decades, and it matters for this chapter: the narrator’s restraint is what preserves the novel’s mysteries in a book that would otherwise have given them away. Zero focalisation is a licence, not an obligation , and a mobile narrator who declines to enter a mind has made a decision as consequential as one who enters. Esther’s grant is the harder of the two. Her narration is a sustained exercise in a character reporting praise of herself while disclaiming it, and readers have divided since 1853 about whether this is unbearable or exquisite. The structural point is that her modesty is a knowledge boundary made of character rather than of position : she is present at scenes whose meaning she cannot admit to herself, and the reader’s task in her chapters is to read past her. This is the sympathy domain and the irony domain operating through the same sentences. On the declaration problem. Esther arrives in Chapter 3 with no heading, no announcement and no bridge. By Chapter 9 §4.6 ’s criterion this is a late declaration; by the test at §7.1 , no. 6 it falls after the reader’s first substantial investment. It succeeds because the differentiation is absolute — the two narrations share no feature of person, tense, temper or syntax — and because the first narration is so plainly not a person’s that the reader has not yet formed an attachment to be interrupted. The case shows the criterion doing real work rather than merely licensing convention. 9.2 Faulkner, The Sound and the Fury (1929) and As I Lay Dying (1930) — polyphony declared Architectures: The Sound and the Fury , a four-part sequence of bounded grants ( §6.3 , no. 6) closing into third-person narration; As I Lay Dying , a rotating ensemble (no. 4) that is in practice a hub-and-spokes (no. 5). The two novels, written a year apart, are the best available paired demonstration that the same formal device serves different domains depending on the reader’s task. The Sound and the Fury . Four sections, three of them interior monologue, dated April Seventh 1928, June Second 1910, April Sixth 1928 and April Eighth 1928. The dates are the declaration: a reader who reads the section headings knows before the first sentence that the book is plural and non-chronological. The grants are graded by interpretive capacity , and the grading is the design: Section Focaliser Capacity What the reader must do I Benjy Perceives; cannot interpret, cannot order time Construct a chronology the narration does not have II Quentin Interprets compulsively; cannot stop Distinguish event from obsession III Jason Interprets confidently and wrongly Correct a narrator who is certain IV Third person, centred on Dilsey Reports from outside all three Notice that the outside was available all along The novel is the chapter’s clearest instance of the epistemological domain ( §4.6 ). The three interior sections narrate substantially the same family history, and they do not add up; the fourth does not adjudicate. Faulkner’s much-repeated account of the book — that he told the story once, failed, told it again, failed, and was still failing after four attempts — is the domain’s motto. Note what the fourth section costs and buys. By the criteria of §8.4 it is an unearned late arrival of the most extreme kind: a change not of focaliser but of narrative mode , in the final movement. It works because the reader has been sealed inside three consciousnesses for two hundred pages, and the sensation of an exterior is unavailable to any book that had not sealed itself first. As I Lay Dying . Fifteen focalisers, fifty-nine sections, one journey. Where The Sound and the Fury grades its vantages by capacity, As I Lay Dying distributes them by proximity : Bundrens and neighbours, insiders and observers, so that the family is described from within and surrounded at the same time. Three structural observations belong to this chapter. (1) The distribution is unequal by design. Darl holds nineteen sections; several characters hold one. §8.9 treats this as the counterexample to the secret-favourite pattern: the imbalance is legible, and its content is the novel’s plot, since Darl is the family member who sees and the family’s action is to have him committed. (2) Addie’s section is the chapter’s model bounded grant. One section, placed roughly two-thirds through, spoken by a woman who has been dead since the novel’s early pages, and it reorganises everything before it. §8.8 explains why the ontological breach reads as premise rather than exemption. What is worth adding here is the timing : had Addie spoken first, the novel would have been a story with an explanation attached. Speaking late, she converts the preceding two hundred pages retroactively — which is a use of viewpoint allocation as a structural reveal, and one of the few available. (3) Section length is a pacing instrument. Vardaman’s shortest section — five words asserting that his mother is a fish — arrives with the force it does because the sections around it are long. A chapter-based architecture cannot modulate at this resolution. §4.5 . 9.3 Eliot, Middlemarch (1872) — the mobile narrator, and “why always Dorothea?” Architecture: the mobile omniscient narrator ( §6.3 , no. 10), in its most refined English form. The sentence itself is anatomised at §5.2 . What belongs here is the architecture that makes it possible and the argument it serves. The narrator as the reader’s constant. Eliot’s narrator is a continuously audible intelligence: it generalises, it addresses the reader directly, it makes moral discriminations, and it can be quoted as a mind in its own right. This is what §8.1 identifies as the missing asset in modern head-hopping — the movement is safe because the narrator is stable . The reader never loses their footing, because their footing was never any character. The novel theorises its own focalisation. Twice, memorably. The pier-glass parable at the opening of Chapter 27 observes that a scratched mirror, held to a candle, arranges its random scratches into concentric circles around the flame — and that the circles move when the candle does. Every consciousness organises the same world around itself, and the arrangement feels like a discovery about the world rather than about the observer. This is a theory of egoism and, simultaneously, a description of internal focalisation. A narration able to move the candle can demonstrate that the circles are not there. The second is Chapter 20, where the narrator observes that if we had a keen vision and feeling of all ordinary human life, it would be like hearing the grass grow and the squirrel’s heart beat, and we should die of that roar which lies on the other side of silence. This is the empathy budget stated as a fact about consciousness rather than as a fact about books. Attention is finite because human beings are finite; the novel’s economy of attention is a model of a moral economy. It is the strongest available answer to §16 ’s objection that the budget metaphor is merely borrowed from economics. “Why always Dorothea?” as a Woloch demonstration. The turn to Casaubon at Chapter 29 does three things at once: It names the allocation as an allocation — the only major English novel to interrupt itself to do so. It executes a bounded grant to a character the reader has been permitted to find ridiculous, without exculpating him. It generalises : the narrator goes on to protest against the concentration of interest on the young and blooming, on the grounds that the older and more eating griefs are what such concentration neglects. That is Woloch’s thesis, one hundred and thirty years early, offered as a complaint about the reading habits of novel-readers. The limits of the case. Middlemarch fails almost every test in §7 . It head-hops constantly; its narrator knows what no one could know; its viewpoint allocation is not declared by any signal a modern reader would recognise; and it grants and withdraws vantages at will. It is also among the two or three most intelligent novels in English about the problem this chapter treats. The proper conclusion is not that the tests are worthless but that they describe a convention within which most contemporary novels operate , and that a book able to establish a different convention is not bound by them. 9.4 Tolstoy, Anna Karenina (1878) — two hubs, and a dog Architecture: a two-hub variant of hub-and-spokes ( §6.3 , no. 5) inside a mobile omniscient narration (no. 10). Anna Karenina is treated in Chapter 1 as a source of scenes, in Chapter 5 as a transition system and in Chapter 14 as a subplot structure. The allocation question is distinct: how does a novel with two centres distribute itself, and what does the distribution mean? The two-hub structure. Anna and Levin are both hubs, each with spokes — Vronsky, Karenin, Dolly and Kitty variously attach to one or the other, and Stiva Oblonsky functions as the bridge, being the only character with substantial business in both worlds. The book’s page share between the hubs is not constant: Levin’s share rises through the second half as Anna’s world contracts, and Part Eight, which follows Anna’s death, contains no Anna at all. The proportions enact the argument. A life that consumes itself ends; a life that is being made continues, unresolved, into an eighth part that many readers find anticlimactic and that Tolstoy plainly regarded as the point. Whether the two plots converge is a real and long-standing critical disagreement. They meet once, late and briefly. Tolstoy insisted the novel had an architecture and that its unity lay in an internal linkage rather than in plot. Readers have disagreed ever since about whether the linkage is structural or merely thematic. It is set as a seminar question ( §12.2 ), and Chapter 14 ( The Subplot ) treats it from the plot side. Karenin, and the withdrawal of contempt. §4.4 and §8.10 have already used him. The structural observation to add is that Karenin’s grants are small : he holds relatively few pages, and their effect is out of all proportion to their extent. This is the best available evidence for §3.6 ’s third qualification — depth is not proportional to page share — and it is the empirical basis for the argument at §9.9 that a single bounded chapter can do what a rotating grant could not. Laska. During the woodcock shooting in Part Six, the narration enters Levin’s setter: her scent-world, her impatience with the men’s blundering, her assessment of her master’s competence. The passage tests every definition offered in §3.1 , and it is worth being exact about what it demonstrates. It is internal focalisation in Genette’s sense, on a focaliser who has no language. The narration must therefore supply language for a wordless consciousness, which is what Cohn’s psycho-narration ( §3.2 ) is for: the narrator’s words, the character’s mind. It is not anthropomorphism , and the distinction is technical. Laska’s world is organised by scent, by degrees of certainty about scent, and by irritation at the humans’ slowness. She is not given human thoughts; she is given a human grammar for canine ones. It is epistemically motivated . On the only question the scene cares about — where the birds are — the dog knows and the men do not. The grant is made to the character who is right. It is a bounded grant of a few paragraphs , made in a book whose narrator has established free movement from its opening. §5.2 ’s point about architecture applies: this is a masterstroke in Tolstoy’s architecture and would be a catastrophe in a limited third. Tolstoy did this more than once. The novella Kholstomer ( Strider , 1886) is focalised largely through a horse, and it uses the animal vantage for defamiliarisation in Shklovsky’s sense — the horse cannot understand property, and the incomprehension is an argument. A translation note. The Laska passage exists in English in Garnett’s version (1901), the Maudes’, Pevear and Volokhonsky’s (2000), Bartlett’s and Schwartz’s (both 2014), and they differ in how far they permit the dog articulate thought — some render her impatience in near-human indirect discourse, others keep it closer to sensation. The structural claim survives all of them: the narration enters a non-human consciousness and is epistemically justified in doing so. The texture claim does not survive , and any student writing about the passage should name the version they used. 9.5 Rhys, Wide Sargasso Sea (1966) — allocation as argument Architecture: sequential rather than alternating dual ( §6.3 , no. 3), with a single-page grant to a third vantage in the final part. This is the chapter’s central case, because it is Woloch’s thesis dramatised: a novel that exists because a character in another novel was denied a vantage. The structure. Part Focaliser Approximate share Function One Antoinette, as a child in Jamaica Roughly a quarter Establishes the world the second part will misread Two The English husband, unnamed throughout, with an interpolated section by Antoinette Roughly half The appropriation performed in real time Three Grace Poole, then Antoinette in England The remainder The keeper’s voice, then the voice Jane Eyre silenced The argument carried by the allocation. In Jane Eyre , Bertha Mason has no vantage whatever. She is the compressed character at the limit: Woloch’s distortion in its purest form — a laugh, a face at a door, an animal noise — which is what a person becomes when a novel needs them present and has decided they are not a consciousness. Rhys’s novel grants her the vantage, and the grant is not a device but the entire reason the book exists. Two features complicate the simple version of that account, and both are essential to teach. (1) The husband holds the largest share. A novel written to restore Antoinette’s voice gives more of its pages to the man who takes it away. Critics disagree about whether this is a concession, a flaw, or the sharpest thing in the book — the demonstration that even a corrective must contend with the volume of the account it corrects. §8.9 treats it under the secret-favourite pattern; §12.2 sets it as a seminar question. The most defensible reading is that Rhys is dramatising the mechanism of character compression itself : the reader watches Antoinette being converted from a person into a case, from inside the consciousness doing the converting. (2) The husband is never named. Jane Eyre ’s Rochester is present in every structural particular and is denied the name. This is an exact inversion of the source novel’s allocation, and it is performed by withholding rather than by granting. A student who has understood §6.3 , no. 13 — external focalisation as the refused grant — will see that Rhys uses two opposite instruments on the same target: she gives the husband a vantage and withholds his name, so that he acquires interiority without acquiring identity. Grace Poole’s arrival. §8.4 treats it as the counterexample to the unearned late arrival. The additional point for this section is that Grace Poole is the Jane Eyre character whose account of Bertha the earlier novel accepts. Handing her a vantage, briefly, immediately before Antoinette’s final section, stages the competition of accounts that the whole novel is about. The critical context. Gayatri Spivak’s “Three Women’s Texts and a Critique of Imperialism” (1985) reads Jane Eyre and Wide Sargasso Sea together as evidence about the imperial conditions of English literary subjectivity, and remains the standard starting point. It should be read alongside the dissent: Kamau Brathwaite and other Caribbean critics have questioned whether a white creole figure can stand for the Caribbean at all, which is a disagreement about who is entitled to a vantage rather than about how vantages are distributed within a text. Both positions are arguments about allocation , and putting them side by side is the most useful thing a seminar can do with this novel. 9.6 Stoker, Dracula (1897) — documentary polyphony Architecture: documentary polyphony ( §6.3 , no. 8), with a refused grant (no. 13) at its centre. The novel is a compilation: Jonathan Harker’s shorthand journal, Mina’s journal and later typescript, Lucy Westenra’s letters and diary, Dr Seward’s phonograph diary, newspaper cuttings, telegrams, a ship’s log, Van Helsing’s memorandum. Chapter 10 treats the prefatory note as a threshold device; the allocation question here is what the architecture buys and what it costs. What the form buys. Access without omniscience. The plot spans Transylvania, Whitby, London and the Carpathians and cannot be assembled from any single vantage. The documents supply coverage while preserving each witness’s ignorance, which is what a novel of dread requires. A built-in knowledge boundary. Each document is limited by what its author knew when writing , and by what its author is willing to commit to paper. Seward’s phonograph confessions and Mina’s decorous journal have different boundaries, and the difference is characterisation. Pacing by document type. Long journal entries alternate with telegrams and cuttings; the rhythm is achieved by form rather than by scene construction ( §4.5 ). Epistemology as premise. The prefatory note asserts that the papers have been arranged so that the facts may stand for themselves. The novel then demonstrates that the facts do not stand for themselves at all — a point Stoker makes explicit in the closing note, where Harker observes that the mass of material contains hardly a single authentic document, only typescript. What the form costs. Two things, and the novel converts both into assets. Voice redundancy. §8.5 : the narrators write a common late-Victorian prose and are frequently hard to tell apart. The evidentiary logic requires it. Corroboration is produced by witnesses who agree. Sympathy is hard to generate. A document is a performance for a reader, so interiority in it is always partly self-presentation. Stoker’s solution is Seward’s phonograph — a recording medium with no reader in view, in which a man can be heard to be wretched. The refused grant is the novel’s most consequential decision. Dracula himself produces no document. He speaks at length in Harker’s journal, in Harker’s transcription, framed by Harker’s fear. The Count is therefore the only major figure in the book who is externally focalised throughout, and the refusal produces the character: a consciousness that cannot be entered is a consciousness that cannot be predicted, bargained with or pitied. Compare Rhys (§9.5), where the same instrument — withholding — is used on the character with the power rather than on the monster. The teaching point. Dracula is a popular novel of 1897 that runs a rotating ensemble of eight vantages, declares its architecture on the first page, sustains an epistemological structure, and makes its central allocation decision by refusal. Students who suppose polyphony to be a modernist invention should begin here. 9.7 Lessing, The Golden Notebook (1962) — one consciousness, divided Architecture: a formal hybrid — nested documentary ( §6.3 , no. 8) inside a frame (no. 7), all of it belonging to a single mind. The novel is the chapter’s most useful case for a specific reason: it applies the whole apparatus of multiple viewpoint to one person. The structure. A conventional short novel titled “Free Women”, about Anna Wulf and Molly, narrated in the third person and divided into five parts; between those parts, sections from four notebooks that Anna keeps — black (her time in Africa and the novel she wrote about it), red (politics and the Communist Party), yellow (fiction: a story about a woman called Ella, who is Anna at one remove), blue (a diary intended to record fact) — and finally a single golden notebook in which the divisions collapse. Why the divisions exist. Anna divides her notebooks because she believes that keeping the parts of a life separate will prevent a breakdown. The novel’s argument is that the division is the breakdown, and that the golden notebook’s fusion is the recovery. The formal device and the psychological subject are the same thing. What this demonstrates for the chapter. Multiple focalisation does not require multiple people.
