Genette’s category ( §3.1 ) is defined by the same events recurring from different positions, and Anna supplies four positions herself: the novelist’s, the militant’s, the fictionaliser’s and the diarist’s. The yellow notebook’s Ella is a focaliser who is and is not the focaliser of the blue. The epistemological domain ( §4.6 ) applied inwardly. The accounts do not reconcile. The “Free Women” sections, which look like the reliable outer novel, are exposed by the notebooks as the most simplified version of all — a conventional narrative Anna could write about herself because it leaves out what will not fit. The frame’s authority is destabilised rather than established. Compare Wuthering Heights , where the frame stabilises. Here the outermost layer is the least trustworthy, which inverts the usual expectation of architecture 7. A caution. Lessing’s 1971 preface complains that the book’s shape — which she describes as the argument — was widely ignored in favour of its content. It is a useful warning for a chapter of this kind: a viewpoint architecture is a statement, and readers routinely read past statements made in form. A writer who intends an architecture to carry an argument should assume that most readers will receive the argument only if the content supports it too. 9.8 Morrison, Beloved (1987) — the unattributed monologues Architecture: hub-and-spokes ( §6.3 , no. 5) that becomes, for one movement, an unattributed choral voice (no. 11). Chapter 9 treats the novel’s opening; Chapter 4 treats the chokecherry tree. The allocation question is what happens in Part Two. The sequence. After a novel largely centred on Sethe, with substantial access to Denver, Paul D and Baby Suggs, Part Two presents a run of monologues: Sethe’s, Denver’s, and then Beloved’s — the last unpunctuated, without conventional sentence boundaries, in a syntax that will not resolve into ordinary speech. The sequence then merges into an antiphonal passage in which the three voices interleave, claim one another, and become difficult to assign. What the architecture does. (1) It grants viewpoint to a being whose ontological status the novel has not settled. Beloved may be a revenant, a survivor of the Middle Passage, a delusion, or all three. Granting her a monologue does not resolve the question; the monologue’s form — a consciousness without punctuation, in which a face in dark water and a woman picking flowers occupy the same grammatical plane — is a claim that the question cannot be resolved from inside. Compare §8.8 : this is the corpse’s-eye view as premise, and the premise was declared in the novel’s opening sentences, where a house is spiteful and full of a baby’s venom. (2) It converts possession into a formal property. Beloved’s assertion of belonging — I am Beloved and she is mine — is repeated across the sequence with the pronouns exchanged, so that the reader cannot determine who is claiming whom. Where an attributed narration would have had to state that the three women are losing their separateness, the unattributed one performs it. This is the strongest available demonstration that an architecture can carry content no sentence in the book has to state. (3) It is bounded, and the boundedness is what makes it legible. The choral movement occupies a small fraction of the novel and is surrounded on both sides by attributed narration. §6.3 ’s note on architecture 11 applies: unattributed narration has a very high comprehension cost and is unusable for long stretches. Morrison’s placement — late, brief, after two hundred pages of ordinary access — is what allows the reader to understand what has happened to the grammar. (4) The novel’s compression is deliberate and painful. The character with the least interiority in Beloved is the one whose act the whole book turns on — not because Sethe lacks a vantage, but because the act itself is approached repeatedly and entered only obliquely, from the outside, through the eyes of the men who came for her. Morrison’s allocation withholds the one interior the reader most wants, and the withholding is an argument about what can be represented. 9.9 A revision case: should Dov ever hold viewpoint? The preceding readings analyse allocations already made. This case is a decision being taken, which is the form most useful in a workshop. The situation. In the household narrative that runs through this book, Dov has been observed only from outside. Elena sees him in the doorway, holding it, giving her the key and withholding the reason (Chapter 3, The Dialogue Exchange ). Nadia hears him in unanswered calls (Chapter 9, The Opening Pages ). His sale of the shop and his deadline reach the reader by report (Chapter 14, The Subplot ). The ledger is first seen as an object in Chapter 4 ( The Descriptive Detail ), and the looser hand that continues it after the father’s entry of March the ninth is discovered by Elena, without her reading it, in Chapter 6 ( The Chapter Break ): an object, not an act. The question is whether the book should grant him viewpoint, and if so, in what form. Version A: Dov as a rotating viewpoint character from page one The alternative this chapter rejects. Constructed here so that its failure can be diagnosed rather than asserted. Dov had been at the shop since seven, which was earlier than he needed to be and later than he wanted. The buyer’s agent was due at eleven. He had the papers in the folder on the passenger seat and had not told either of his sisters, and he told himself this was because Elena would want to argue about the valuation and Nadia would want to argue about everything else, and there was no version of that conversation that ended with the shop sold before another winter of standing orders and no stock moving. He went through into the back and put the kettle on and looked at the coat on the hook the way he looked at it every morning, which was quickly. Someone had to keep the place open. Someone had to answer the phone. He had been answering the phone since March and neither of them had asked him what it cost. Diagnosis. Test Result 1 — Necessity Fails. Every fact here is available by report or inference: the sale, the secrecy, the deadline, the resentment. The book already conveys all four from Elena’s and Nadia’s vantages. 2 — Domain Access (the shop before opening), and a thin sympathy (he is tired and unthanked). No contrast: Dov’s appraisal vocabulary — argue , valuation , standing orders — is a difference of subject matter, not of mind. No irony, since the reader learns nothing the sisters will not shortly learn. 3 — Investment Passes trivially at page one, where nobody has investment yet. This is the trap: a first grant always passes the investment test, which is why the test must be run together with tests 2 and 5. 4 — Distinguishability Fails on the decisive point. Swap this passage into Elena’s vantage and change three nouns, and it survives. All three siblings in this version audit, count and resent. 5 — Page-share Fails structurally. A third of the book to a character whose function in every other chapter of this book is to be the withheld reason. 10 — Character compression Fails, and this is the largest failure. Granting Dov a vantage from page one converts the mother from an unexplained silence into a reported one — because Dov knows what she said to him, and a focalised Dov must either think about it or be seen conspicuously not thinking about it. The book’s one deliberately open thread is closed by the allocation itself. The mechanism of the failure. Version A destroys the book’s engine, and the destruction is a viewpoint decision rather than a plot one. The household narrative is an investigation: two sisters reconstructing what was withheld from them. Its dramatic value depends entirely on the reader’s information being close to the investigators’. Granting the withholder a vantage converts a mystery into a study of a man who has a secret , and Version A does not supply a replacement question strong enough to cover the loss. This is §8.10 , arriving through the front door. Version A also commits the redundant vantage ( §8.5 ), and the reason is instructive: the three siblings were differentiated in this draft by circumstance — one drives, one counts, one sells — rather than by mind. §5.3 ’s four levels have not been applied. Version B: a single bounded chapter, near the climax This chapter’s conclusion, presented with the diagnostic behind it. The grant. One chapter. Placed after Nadia finds the good pen in the coat pocket (Chapter 7, Backstory and Flashback ) and before the three of them read the ledger together (Chapter 16, The Ending ). It dramatises one thing: the evening of March the ninth, and the decision to go on writing. The last entry in his father’s hand was three lines long and the third line stopped halfway, so that the doctor’s name — misspelled, then misspelled differently, then got right — trailed off into a scratch. The name meant nothing to him. Dov sat with it for a while. The leather was faintly warm from the lamp. He looked for the good pen where it was always kept, beside the till, and it was not there, and he did not think about that then; he thought about it for years afterwards. What he used was a ballpoint from the drawer that stuck. He wrote the date. He wrote the count. He did not write anything else, because his father had not written anything else on the ninth either, and it seemed to him that the ledger had a way of being written in, and that if he did it wrong someone would be able to tell. Diagnosis. Test Result 1 — Necessity Passes. No other vantage witnessed it, and report can state the fact — he kept the ledger going — but cannot dramatise the choosing. Note that the fact has already been stated by the object, about half the book earlier. What is unavailable by any other means is the making of the choice, which is a decision, not information. 2 — Domain Passes on three. Sympathy engineering : from outside, the continuation of the ledger reads as forgery or as the beginning of the sale; from inside, it is filial. Contrast : Dov’s instinct is to protect through concealment, mirroring his father, against his sisters’ instinct to expose. Dramatic irony : after this chapter the reader carries into the ledger scene a knowledge the sisters do not have. 3 — Investment Passes. Dov has been present continuously since the doorway (Chapter 3), wanting something legible (the sale, the silence held) and resisted. The cold-start charge ( §6.6 ) is nil, because the reader has been curious about him for the length of the book. 4 — Distinguishability Passes , and by the four instruments of §5.3 rather than by dialect. Noticing : he registers the pen’s absence and the warmth of the leather, where Nadia would have registered a count and Elena a lock. Judgement : he appraises the ledger’s manner of being written in, which is a category neither sister has. Boundary : he does not know why the locks were changed, and the chapter does not tell the reader. Naming : he thinks his father , where Nadia thinks in objects and Elena thinks in questions. 5 — Page-share Passes. One chapter of a book otherwise divided between two sisters. The proportion is the point: the smallest possible allocation, at the highest possible value. 7 — Late-grant Passes. The three charges of §6.6 are paid at their minimum. Formal surprise: once. Attention withdrawal: one chapter. Cold start: none. 8 — Knowledge boundary Passes, and is the chapter’s chief instrument. Dov does not know where the good pen is; he does not know his father was ill, since the name on the third line means nothing to him and in the four months he keeps the ledger he writes forward and never reads back, so that he learns of the illness only when the three of them read the ledger together (Chapter 16), and not before; he does not know why his mother changed the locks. The narration’s the doctor’s name belongs to its small retrospective gap ( he thought about it for years afterwards ), not to what Dov understood that evening. The chapter is made of what he cannot see. 10 — Character compression Passes, narrowly, and only because of the boundary. The mother remains unexplained, because the vantage granted is one that does not know. Had the chapter been Ma’s, the book’s open thread would have closed. What the revision did, procedurally. Reduced extent to the minimum that carries the payload. The conclusion — cheap because bounded — is §6.6 ’s cost curve applied. Moved the grant to the point of maximum prior curiosity , so that the cold-start charge falls to nothing. Selected a decision rather than a fact. The fact was already delivered by an object, about half the book earlier; the grant supplies only what an object cannot. Built distinguishability from noticing, judgement, boundary and naming rather than from voice ( §5.3 ). Used the knowledge boundary as the chapter’s engine. The absent pen is the chapter’s centre and Dov does not understand it; the reader, who has read the Prologue, does. This is dramatic irony generated for free by a restriction. Preserved a character compression deliberately. The mother is not explained, and cannot be, from this vantage. What Version B has not solved. Four things, and a workshop should be made to argue about all of them. The reader may want more. A single chapter that succeeds creates an appetite the book then refuses. Some readers will experience the refusal as discipline and others as a withheld pleasure, and this is not a defect that can be designed away — it is the cost of the bounded grant, and it is paid every time. It solves Dov and leaves the mother. The character-compression test passes for the vantage granted and fails for the household as a whole: Ma appears throughout, changes the locks, speaks once at a remove, and is never entered. That is a defensible allocation — the book treats her silence as its one open thread — but it is an allocation, and a reader entitled to ask why always the siblings? has Eliot’s authority for the question. The chapter risks the special-pleading failure ( §4.4 ). A vantage granted immediately before a scene in which the character is judged is a vantage that looks arranged. The defence is that the chapter exculpates nothing: Dov still sells the shop, still signs without telling his sisters, and the ledger entries after March the ninth are still, in the plainest description, someone else writing in his father’s book. The interiority makes the act harder to name, not easier to forgive. Dov’s never reading back needs a reason. The knowledge boundary rests on his writing forward for four months without turning back through his father’s pages. The ledger had a way of being written in begins to supply the reason, and the chapter may need a sentence more; a reader who doubts it will doubt the boundary, and with it the claim that none of the three knew of the illness before the end. A note on the hypothetical. Nothing above dramatises the mother’s vantage, and the specimen in this section should not be read as evidence that the book intends to grant her one. Her viewpoint is used here strictly as a test case for §7.1 , no. 10 — the character whose exclusion the allocation must be able to defend.

title: 10. The Viewpoint Shift Across Forms
text: The allocation model was developed for the novel, which is the form in which the coverage–depth trade is most acute because it is the form with enough room for the trade to be made in more than one way. It transfers to adjacent forms with adjustments that need stating, because students routinely import novel habits into forms that punish them. 10.1 The short story The short story’s default is the single fixed vantage ( §6.3 , no. 1), and the default is close to a requirement. Difference Consequence No room to pay a cold-start charge twice A second vantage consumes an investment the story cannot rebuild No room for a legible pattern Two shifts do not establish an architecture; they read as instability The knowledge boundary is the story’s engine A short story is very often about what one person cannot see Character compression is total Every character but one is a minor character, and the form accepts this The exceptions cluster in two places, and both are instructive. The first is the story that uses only two vantages in sequence, so that the second reframes the first — a structure that works because it is not a pattern but a reversal. The second is the story that opens or closes with a widened vantage: Joyce’s “The Dead” moves, in its final pages, from Gabriel Conroy’s mortified interiority outward to a snow falling over the whole of Ireland, and the widening is the story’s meaning. That move is the omniscient slip ( §8.6 ) used deliberately and once, and it is unavailable to a story that has not first been rigorously confined. Note what the form makes visible: in a story, allocation is nearly all character compression. Woloch’s model applies with unusual clarity, because the reader can see the whole character-system at once. 10.2 The novella The novella’s characteristic viewpoint problem is that it is written by novelists. It has a novel’s ambition and a story’s word count, and multi-viewpoint structures that would be modest in a four-hundred-page book consume it. Three vantages in thirty thousand words is a page share of ten thousand words each — the length of a long short story, which is not enough to build the familiarity that makes alternation cheap. The forms that work are the single fixed vantage and the frame ( §6.3 , no. 7), which is why so many canonical novellas are frames: Heart of Darkness , The Turn of the Screw , Season of Migration to the North . The frame gives a novella the effect of plurality — two positions, two moral registers, a listener — at the cost of only one additional vantage, and it supplies a reason for the story’s brevity: it is being told, by someone, to someone, in an evening. 10.3 The long novel, the series, and serial publication Length raises the ceiling ( §5.4 ), but not in the way writers expect. What length actually buys is not more vantages but longer stays , and a long novel that spends its extra room on additional viewpoint characters rather than on longer visits has bought nothing. Serial publication complicates this and is worth a note, because the nineteenth-century multi-plot novel is the product of a distribution format. A monthly part had to contain variety, which encouraged multiple threads; a nineteen-month run had to sustain memory across long gaps, which encouraged strongly typed characters and repeated identifying tags — the very character compression Woloch analyses. Dickens’s number plans, which survive, show him distributing his narrations and his plots across each part deliberately. Series fiction faces a specific and under-discussed pressure: viewpoint casts grow. A series that begins with two vantages often has more by its fourth volume (an observation, not a count), because the world has expanded and coverage is required, and because a returning reader’s affection for a secondary character is a commercial argument for promoting them. The consequences are predictable and are the diluted ensemble in slow motion. Three principles: A viewpoint granted in volume three is a later grant with respect to the series, not a first grant with respect to the volume. The reader’s investment is cumulative across books. Terminating a grant is harder in a series than in a novel , because readers experience a vanished vantage as a promise broken across years. The bounded grant scales badly. Readers who have been trained by a series to expect continuity will read a single-appearance vantage as a setup rather than as a closed structure. 10.4 The screen comparison, admitted and corrected Contemporary craft advice imports heavily from film and television, and viewpoint is where the import does most damage, because the two media have opposite defaults. Film’s default is external focalisation. A camera shows behaviour. Interiority must be constructed — by voice-over, by point-of-view shots, by performance, by score — and every instrument is expensive and conspicuous. Prose’s default is the opposite: the moment a novel reports what someone thought, it has granted interiority, and it costs nothing. Two consequences follow, and both correct common advice. “Show, don’t tell” has been reinforced by screen logic in a medium that has the opposite economy. The phrase descends from Lubbock’s preference for showing over telling (1921), which is older than the screenwriting manuals that now repeat it. In film, interiority is expensive and behaviour is free. In prose, interiority is free and behaviour must be described. A novel that renders everything behaviourally has voluntarily adopted film’s constraint without acquiring film’s compensations — the face, the pause, the actor. The “ensemble show” model does not transfer. Television can cut among eight characters cheaply because the viewer re-identifies each in a quarter of a second, by face. Prose re-identification requires a name and a paragraph. An eight-vantage novel is not the equivalent of an eight-hander drama; it is considerably more expensive. What does transfer is David Bordwell’s analysis of narration in Narration in the Fiction Film (1985), whose three variables — knowledgeability (how much the narration knows), communicativeness (how much of what it knows it discloses) and self-consciousness (how far it acknowledges addressing an audience) — are a cleaner instrument than “point of view” for describing what a novel’s narration is doing. Genette’s zero focalisation is high knowledgeability; Stoker’s Dracula is high communicativeness within severely limited knowledge; Eliot’s narrator is high on all three. A note on restricted narration. Hitchcock’s much-quoted account of suspense — the audience shown the bomb under the table that the characters cannot see — is dramatic irony ( §4.2 ) produced by an allocation of knowledge, and it is transferable. What is not transferable is the cheapness of the allocation: a film supplies the bomb in one shot; a novel must grant a vantage or contrive a report. 10.5 Translated fiction Viewpoint is one of the areas where this book’s standing distinction, stated in its Introduction — structural claims survive translation; texture claims do not — is most consequential, because the chief carrier of internal focalisation in the modern novel is free indirect style, and free indirect style is grammatically dependent. Four specific hazards. (1) Free indirect style depends on tense and pronoun systems that differ across languages. English marks it by backshifted tense and third-person pronouns; languages with different tense architectures mark it differently or leave it ambiguous. A passage that is unmistakably free indirect in Russian or French may become, in English, either plain psycho-narration or quoted thought, depending on the translator’s decision. The architecture of the novel is unaffected; the distance at any given moment is a translator’s choice. (2) Languages that do not require subject pronouns leave focalisation less explicitly marked. In Japanese, for instance, an unmarked sentence may not specify whose perception it reports, and the reader infers from honorifics, verb forms of giving and receiving, and context. Translation into English forces a choice that the original did not make. Structural claims about a novel’s allocation survive; claims about the precise point at which the reader knows whose head they are in do not. (3) Naming systems carry viewpoint information that translation flattens. Chapter 5 §9.4 makes the point about Russian patronymics and diminutives: which form of a name the narration uses signals the social frame the narration has currently adopted. In English the signal is largely lost, and with it a quantity of focalisation information the original reader receives free. (4) Animal and non-human focalisation is especially translation-sensitive. §9.4 ’s Laska passage differs measurably across English versions in how much articulate thought the dog is permitted. The structural fact — Tolstoy focalises a dog — is robust. Everything a student might want to say about how far inside the dog the narration goes is a fact about the translation. The teaching rule. A student writing about viewpoint in a translated novel should name the translation in the first footnote, restrict distance claims to that translation, and confine cross-linguistic claims to architecture: who has a vantage, how many, in what proportion, and when each begins. Those survive. 10.6 Concordance: concept to novel A study aid mapping each concept to the novel that best displays it. title: 11. Revision Checklist
text: Run each viewpoint character, and each individual grant, against this list before deciding the architecture stays as written. Each item corresponds to a test in §7 or a pattern in §8 . The architecture I can name this book’s viewpoint architecture from §6.3 , and it is the one I intended. I have written two hundred words on what the book would gain and lose in the two neighbouring architectures. The number of vantages is proportionate to the page count available to develop each. The book’s viewpoint pattern is declared before the reader has invested deeply in a single thread. Each grant I can state what this vantage provides that no existing vantage could deliver. I can name at least two domains it serves, and at least one of them is not access. I have named the cheaper instruments I rejected — report, inference, reassignment, document, ellipsis — and why. This character had a legible want, on the page, before the grant was made. I can state where the grant begins, how much of the book it holds, and whether it ends. I can defend, for each vantage, why the book needs their perception and not merely their information. Distinguishability Two hundred words swapped between any two vantages would not survive the transplant. The vantages differ in what they notice, not only in what happens to them. The vantages differ in what they are willing to appraise, and in the words they use to appraise it. The vantages differ in what they call people, places and acts. Each vantage has a knowledge boundary I could state in one sentence. Proportion and rhythm I have run a page-share audit and the distribution is the one the book’s argument requires. No vantage disappears for a stretch long enough that the reader re-enters as if to a stranger. The interval between returns varies with each thread’s state rather than by rule. Where I cut away at a tense moment, the destination is a vantage the reader is glad to reach. Execution No scene changes whose head we are in unless the book’s architecture has established that right and exercises it consistently. No vantage reports what it could not know, except where a frame or a retrospective position licenses it. No vantage persists past the ontological boundary the book has set, unless the crossing is a declared premise. No vantage exists chiefly to be extinguished. Consequence I have listed every named character with no vantage, and can say why each is outside. No character has been reduced to a repeated identifying tag that I mistook for characterisation. I know what argument my distribution of interiority makes, and it is the argument I intend to make.

title: 12. Studio Work
text: 12.1 Practical exercises Exercise 1 — The page-share audit. Run §5.5 on a completed draft, or on a published multi-viewpoint novel. Produce the table and the section strip. Write 300 words on what the distribution reveals that you did not know, including which character the book is actually about. Exercise 2 — Architecture substitution. Identify your draft’s architecture from §6.3 . Name the two neighbours. Rewrite one chapter in the strongest neighbour, then write 400 words comparing what each version buys and costs. Do not judge until both exist. Exercise 3 — The swap test. Take two hundred words from two of your viewpoint characters. Exchange their contents, altering only the proper nouns required for grammatical sense. Give both to a reader who knows the draft and record, verbatim, what they say. Exercise 4 — The boundary rewrite. Take one viewpoint chapter and mark every sentence reporting something the focaliser could not know (test 8). Replace each with an inference, a misreading or a wrong guess. Do not add compensating information elsewhere. Assess whether the chapter is worse. Exercise 5 — Four levels of differentiation. Write the same three-hundred-word scene twice, from two different characters, changing nothing except (a) what is noticed, (b) the vocabulary of appraisal, (c) what each cannot know, and (d) what each calls the people and objects present. Do not change the prose rhythm or the dialect. §5.3 . Exercise 6 — The bounded grant. Identify one off-stage decision in your draft that is currently delivered by report. Write it as a single self-contained chapter from the vantage of the person who made it, at no more than 2,000 words, shaped so that the reader does not expect a return. Then decide whether the book is better with it. Exercise 7 — The compression audit. List every named character in your draft who has no vantage. For each, record the five items at §7.1 , no. 10. Write 500 words on the argument your distribution makes, whether or not you intended to make it. Exercise 8 — Head-hopping, historically. Take a scene of two to three pages from Middlemarch , Anna Karenina or War and Peace in which the narration moves among minds. Rewrite it in a strict single limited third. Then write 500 words on what is lost, and on whether any of it could be recovered by other means. Exercise 9 — The refused grant. Take the character in your draft you most want to explain and remove all interiority from them for the whole book, so that they are known only by behaviour, speech and other people’s inferences. Rewrite two of their scenes accordingly. Assess whether they have become weaker or more powerful, and say why. 12.2 Seminar questions Is “head-hopping” a defect or a convention? §3.5 and §8.1 argue that the prohibition dates from the codification of Jamesian practice and describes a local literary culture rather than a property of narrative. Test the claim against a scene from Middlemarch and a contemporary multi-viewpoint novel. If it is a convention, what obligations does a writer have towards it? Five domains or six? Argue for or against admitting the epistemological domain ( §4.6 ) as a separate category rather than as contrast plus unreliability. Use The Sound and the Fury , Dracula or The Golden Notebook as evidence, and address the objection that the sixth domain describes an effect rather than a purpose. The husband’s share in Wide Sargasso Sea . A novel written to give Bertha Mason the vantage Jane Eyre denied her allocates its largest share to the man who takes it away. Is this a concession to the source text, a structural flaw, or the book’s sharpest argument? Critics disagree, and the disagreement is not resolvable by appeal to the text alone. Do the two plots of Anna Karenina converge? Tolstoy insisted on the novel’s unity; readers have argued about it since 1878. Frame the question as one about allocation rather than plot: does the shifting page share between the two hubs constitute a structure, or merely an alternation? Is the empathy budget a description or an ideology? §16 argues that the metaphor is borrowed from economics and naturalises scarcity. Examine a novel that spends recklessly — War and Peace , As I Lay Dying , The Grapes of Wrath — and consider whether the model can accommodate it or must treat it as an exception. Who is entitled to a vantage? Woloch’s claim ( §3.3 ) is that the distribution of interiority is a political fact. Consider the two positions staged at §9.5 : Spivak’s reading of Wide Sargasso Sea as a critique of imperial subject-formation, and the Caribbean critical objection that a white creole figure cannot stand for the Caribbean. Is “who gets a viewpoint” a question internal to craft, external to it, or a case where the distinction fails? 12.3 Assessment rubric For a submitted multi-viewpoint sequence (2,500–3,500 words: at least two vantages, one of which must be a bounded grant) with a 1,000-word critical commentary. Band Craft (60%) Commentary (40%) Distinction Each grant serves two or more domains; the vantages survive the swap test on mind rather than idiom; knowledge boundaries are strict and generative; the architecture is declared and its proportions are expressive; the character compression of unfocalised characters is visibly deliberate Names the architecture and defends it against the two neighbours; identifies its own risks; engages at least two theoretical sources critically rather than decoratively; addresses what the allocation excludes Merit Grants are justified; vantages are distinguishable, chiefly by voice; boundaries mostly respected; the architecture is legible if not fully exploited Accurate self-analysis; some critical engagement with theory; risks acknowledged if not resolved Pass Two vantages exist and are anchored; domains can be named for at least one; boundaries occasionally breached Describes the structure accurately; theory referenced but not applied Fail Vantages are interchangeable or unmotivated; boundaries routinely breached; the architecture is accidental Description without analysis; no engagement with the model; failure patterns unrecognised

title: 13. Glossary
text: Access — The domain of purpose in which a grant buys presence at events the existing vantage cannot attend. §4.1 . Allocation problem — This chapter’s term for the structural decision about how a finite quantity of reader attention and identification is distributed across a cast. §1.1 . Bounded grant — A viewpoint grant held for one chapter or section, with no return. The cheapest form of a later grant. §6.3 no. 6, §6.6 . Character compression — Woloch’s account of the effect of restricted character-space on a character’s presentation: flatness, the type, the repeated identifying tag. Not an absence of depth but the visible mark of depth excluded. §3.3 , §7.1 no. 10. Named so in this edition to keep it apart from Chapter 2’s compression of page-space against story-weight. Character-space — Woloch’s term for the particular and delimited position a character occupies within a narrative, and the friction between an implied person and the room afforded them. §3.3 . Character-system — Woloch’s term for the arrangement of many character-spaces into one structure of distributed attention. §3.3 . Contrast (viewpoint domain) — The domain in which a grant buys access to a materially different way of seeing. §4.3 . Distinguishability test — The diagnostic that exchanges the contents of two viewpoint sections and asks whether a reader could tell. §7.1 no. 4. Dramatic irony — The domain in which a grant buys the reader knowledge a character lacks. §4.2 . Empathy budget — The chapter’s working metaphor: reader identification as a finite pool divided among viewpoint characters. Formalised by Woloch’s character-system ( §3.3 ) and criticised at §16 . Epistemological domain — This chapter’s proposed sixth domain: a vantage granted to demonstrate that no single vantage can know the events. §4.6 . Chapter 10’s authority domain is its counterpart at a book’s threshold and is not a domain of the grant (§4.6, the ruling). External focalisation — Genette’s category in which the narration reports less than a character knows: behaviour and speech without interiority. §3.1 , §6.3 no. 13. First grant — Viewpoint established while the reader’s investment across the cast is still forming. Cheap. §6.6 . Focalisation — Genette’s term for the regulation of narrative information according to a perceiving position; who perceives , as distinct from who speaks . §3.1 . Focaliser — Bal’s term for the subject of focalisation. §3.1 . Free indirect style — Third-person narration whose diction and judgement are the character’s; Cohn’s narrated monologue . §3.2 , §5.3 . Head-hopping — A change of focalisation within a scene in a book whose established narration is limited. Distinguished from omniscience, which is the same movement in a book that has established the right. §2.3 , §8.1 . Internal focalisation — Genette’s category in which narration is restricted to what one character knows. Subdivided as fixed, variable and multiple. §3.1 . Knowledge boundary — The limit of what a vantage can know; a generative resource rather than a restriction. §5.3 , §7.1 no. 8. Later grant — Viewpoint introduced after the book has trained the reader to follow a smaller set of vantages. Expensive, in three separable charges. §6.6 . Multiple focalisation — Genette’s category in which the same events are focalised successively through different characters. The structural signature of the epistemological domain. §3.1 , §4.6 . Omniscience — Zero focalisation: narration not restricted to any character’s knowledge. §3.1 , §6.3 no. 10. Page-share audit — The procedure at §5.5 for measuring the proportions of a book’s viewpoint allocation. Psycho-narration — Cohn’s term for a narrator’s report of a character’s consciousness in the narrator’s own language. Cheaper in empathy budget than narrated or quoted monologue. §3.2 . Reflector — James’s term for a character through whose registering intelligence events are refracted without their narrating. §6.2 . Structural pacing — The domain in which the alternation of vantages is itself a rhythm instrument. §4.5 . Structural shift — A deliberate change of focaliser at a scene, section or chapter boundary. §2.1 . Sympathy engineering — The domain in which a grant complicates a verdict the reader would otherwise reach from outside. §4.4 . Viewpoint architecture — A whole-book shape of viewpoint allocation. Thirteen are tabulated at §6.3 . Viewpoint grant — The allocation to a character of access to the reader’s identification: to whom, how much, beginning when, ending when. §6.1 . Zero focalisation — See omniscience .

title: 15. Further Reading
text: Annotated, grouped by what each source is good for . Starred items are the recommended first three. 15.1 On the distribution of attention ★ Woloch, Alex. The One vs. the Many (2003). The indispensable book for this chapter and the one that converts its central metaphor into an analytic. Demanding but lucid; the introduction and the chapter on Le Père Goriot are sufficient for most purposes. Read it for the claim that minor characters are compressed rather than small, and that the character compression is legible on the page. Levin, Richard. The Multiple Plot in English Renaissance Drama (1971) and Empson, William. Some Versions of Pastoral (1935), ch. 2. The prehistory of the same problem in drama, where attention is distributed across plots rather than across interiorities. Chapter 14 ( The Subplot ) uses both. Moretti, Franco. On form and quantity; useful for students who want to see character-systems measured rather than described. 15.2 On focalisation and its vocabulary ★ Genette, Gérard. Narrative Discourse (1980). The separation of voice from focalisation, and the tripartite scheme. Read the chapter on mood; the rest of the book belongs to Chapters 5 and 7 of this textbook. Bal, Mieke. Narratology (4th ed., 2017). The most usable elaboration of focalisation as a subject–object relation, and the best account of embedded focalisation. Consult rather than read straight through. Rimmon-Kenan, Shlomith. Narrative Fiction (1983). The clearest short synthesis in English; the chapter on focalisation is the single best introduction for a student meeting the term for the first time. Stanzel, Franz K. A Theory of Narrative (1984). The typological circle. Harder going than Genette, and worth it for the insight that narrative situations shade into one another rather than dividing. Uspensky, Boris. A Poetics of Composition (1973). The four planes of point of view. Underread, and the sharpest instrument available for analysing a narration that is inside a character on one plane and outside on another. 15.3 On consciousness in fiction ★ Cohn, Dorrit. Transparent Minds (1978). The systematic taxonomy of consciousness-rendering, and the source of the psycho-narration / narrated monologue / quoted monologue distinction that §3.2 uses to price the empathy budget. Precise, and the vocabulary is worth acquiring permanently. Palmer, Alan. Fictional Minds (2004). The argument that readers build whole minds from evidence far wider than quoted thought. The best available corrective to the belief that a character needs viewpoint in order to have an interior. Banfield, Ann. Unspeakable Sentences (1982). The linguistic account of represented speech and thought. Technical; for students with a grammar background. Wood, James. How Fiction Works (2008). Free indirect style, accessibly, with excellent examples. Short. 15.4 On empathy, and its limits Keen, Suzanne. Empathy and the Novel (2007). Essential, and essential specifically as a corrective. Read it before writing anything that claims fiction makes people better; the chapter on empathy’s unreliable transfer is the one that matters. Zunshine, Lisa. Why We Read Fiction (2006). Theory of mind and levels of intentionality; lively and full of readings. Use the intentionality material to think about what a viewpoint grant costs a reader. Kidd and Castano (2013); Panero et al. (2016). Read as a pair. The clearest available lesson in how a widely reported finding about fiction and social cognition fares under replication. 15.5 On the historical argument Lubbock, Percy. The Craft of Fiction (1921). Read as a period document and an advocacy, not as a manual. It is the origin of most of what a workshop teaches about viewpoint, and reading it cures the belief that the rules are natural law. James, Henry. The Art of the Novel (1934). The prefaces. Difficult, self-delighting, and the source of the reflector and of the house-of-fiction image. Forster, E. M. Aspects of the Novel (1927). The immediate dissent from Lubbock, and the position this chapter adopts. Also the origin of flat and round characters, which Woloch’s model substantially improves on. 15.6 Within this textbook Chapter 1 ( The Purposes of a Scene ) — the domains model, of which §4 is the viewpoint-side transposition. Chapter 3 ( The Dialogue Exchange ) — voice differentiation at sentence level, the complement to §5.3 . Chapter 5 ( The Transition ) — the mechanics of the crossing, the anchor, and the cost of a frame switch. Read §4.5 and §6.3 there alongside §6.5 here. Chapter 6 ( The Chapter Break ) — where the boundary falls, and the deferral cut. Chapter 7 ( Backstory and Flashback ) — retrospective narration and the relation between a narrating and an experiencing self. Chapter 14 ( The Subplot ) — the attention tax; the same argument as the empathy budget, applied to page space rather than to identification. Woloch is the shared source. Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages ) — §4.6 there, on the formal contract and the requirement to declare multi-viewpoint structure early. §6.6 here supplies the mechanism. Chapter 10 ( The Prologue ) — the bounded grant in its most familiar form.

title: 16. Coda: Against Mechanical Application
text: Everything in this chapter is an instrument for noticing. None of it is a rule, and the chapter’s central metaphor is the part most in need of scepticism. The empathy budget is borrowed from economics, and like all such metaphors it naturalises scarcity. A budget presupposes a fixed sum, competing claims and the necessity of trade-offs; it makes the allocation of interiority look like the allocation of money, which is to say like a problem with a correct answer and an unavoidable arithmetic. That framing has real diagnostic power — §5.5 and §7.1 could not exist without it — and it smuggles in an assumption that a great deal of fiction refutes. Consider what the model must say about the novels this chapter most admires. War and Peace has upwards of five hundred named characters and grants interiority, briefly or at length, to a startling number of them, including a boy whose interiority we briefly enter before his death. On the budget model this is profligacy: attention divided until nothing is left. On the page it produces the opposite of thinness — a sense, unmatched in the form, that the world is full of people whose insides are as crowded as the reader’s own. Tolstoy does not divide a fixed sum. He enlarges what the reader can hold , by demonstrating repeatedly that another person’s interior is available if one looks, until looking becomes the book’s habit and the reader’s. As I Lay Dying runs the same argument at the opposite scale. Fifteen consciousnesses in a very short book ought to be impossible. It is not impossible, because Faulkner has changed what a reader is being asked to do — and the budget model, which prices only one transaction, cannot register the change. Middlemarch ends by observing that the good of the world depends partly on unhistoric acts, and on the number of people who lived faithfully hidden lives and rest in unvisited tombs. That sentence is a claim about the character-system as much as about morality. A novel whose closing gesture is towards the people it did not have room for has understood the scarcity better than the model does — and has also declined to accept it as final. Three specific limits, then, on everything above. (1) The scarcity is a property of a form, not of narrative. The realist novel has a protagonist convention, and Woloch’s model describes what that convention does to everyone else. Forms without the convention — the oral epic, the chronicle, the collective narrative, the systems novel — distribute attention on other principles and are not well described as spending. A student who applies the model outside its range will find every one of those forms defective, which is a fact about the model. (2) Attention is not conserved. The economic metaphor implies that what one character gains another loses. Reading does not work like this. A reader who has been shown that Casaubon has an inside does not thereby care less about Dorothea; they care about her differently, and with finer discrimination. Interiority granted to a minor figure can increase the interest of a major one , because it changes what the major one is standing next to. Any model that cannot represent this is missing something the novels do routinely. (3) The model measures cost and cannot measure worth. Every empirical source in §3.4 measures comprehension, response and processing load. None measures value. A book may impose costs the model calls prohibitive — fifteen narrators, a corpse’s monologue, a hundred-page excursus, a narration that moves between minds inside a sentence — and be worth every one of them. Some novels spend recklessly and are the better for it , and a pedagogy that can only price the spending has taught economy and not literature. What the model does reliably is convert a vague dissatisfaction into a specific question. This book feels thin becomes: five vantages hold equal shares and none has a knowledge boundary , or this grant serves access only , or the only character whose motives are never available is the one the plot needs to be wrong . Specific questions can be answered. Vague ones can only be worried at. And there is a last question, less mechanical than the ten in §7 , which belongs at the end because it cannot be answered by an audit. Every allocation of viewpoint makes an argument about whose experience the book treats as fully real. Most writers make that argument without noticing, by following convenience, convention or affection. The chapter’s whole apparatus exists to make the argument visible, and having made it visible, it has nothing further to say about which argument to make. So the last test is this: If a reader could see only the shape of your allocation — who is inside, who is outside, and in what proportion — what would they conclude the book believes? If the answer is the book you meant to write, the architecture is right, whatever the tests say. If it is not, no amount of anchoring will repair it.

title: The Subplot
text: The Secondary Chain and the Distribution of Narrative Attention: Theory, Analysis and Practice The Craft Behind the Story (Second Edition), Reference — Chapter 14. Part III: The Architecture of the Whole. All illustrative passages are quoted briefly for the purposes of criticism and study; full citations appear in §14 . Where a work is discussed in translation, the translator is named, and the chapter observes the distinction this book’s Introduction draws: structural claims survive translation, texture claims do not. Contents On this page: Chapter Abstract · Learning Outcomes · Key Terms · How to Use This Chapter Introduction: The Second Story Definitions and Boundaries Why a Second Chain Costs — the theory section The Domains of Purpose — five, and a proposed sixth Multiplicity at Book Scale Braiding and Convergence — the mechanism section Diagnostic Method — the ten tests Failure Patterns — with their exceptions Worked Analyses — eight close readings and a revision case The Subplot Across Forms · Concordance: concept to novel Revision Checklist Studio Work — exercises, seminar questions, assessment rubric Glossary Sources Cited Further Reading Coda: Against the Pruned Novel Chapter Abstract A subplot is the largest optional unit in the novel. A scene can be cut in an afternoon; a subplot may occupy eighty pages, six chapters and a third of a book’s emotional weather, and cutting it is a structural operation rather than an edit. That scale is what makes the subplot the hardest unit in this textbook to teach, and the one on which the most confident craft advice is the least reliable. This chapter formalises the problem in four movements. Theory — six independent bodies of work that convert a craft intuition into an analytic. Aristotle’s unity of action supplies the oldest objection and E. M. Forster’s pattern the oldest defence. Richard Levin’s The Multiple Plot in English Renaissance Drama (1971) supplies the vocabulary of plot relation — analogy, contrast, direct linkage — and the crucial argument that a thematic relation can integrate a work whose plots never physically meet. William Empson’s “Double Plots” (1935) supplies the strongest available defence of the second chain: that the relation between two plots generates meaning that neither carries alone. Seymour Chatman’s kernels and satellites (1978) supply the sharpest single instrument in the chapter. Alex Woloch’s character-system, approached here from the plot side rather than the character side, supplies the political dimension. A historical strand establishes that the multi-plot novel is period-specific and materially conditioned, and a cognitive strand establishes that braiding rhythm is not a free variable. Taxonomy — the five domains a subplot can serve (thematic counterpoint, character testing ground, pacing relief, structural convergence, world expansion), each anatomised in terms of its textual carriers and its characteristic under- and over-delivery, together with a proposed sixth: temporal counterpoint , the subplot running on a different clock. Method — multiplicity applied at book scale; a taxonomy of fourteen braiding and convergence structures with their exemplars, purchases and costs; an account of braiding rhythm — how long a thread may be left dormant and what its resumption costs; and a ten-test diagnostic protocol for revision. Application — thirteen failure patterns, each paired with a published work that commits the fault and succeeds; eight close readings; a full revision case worked on this book’s running example; and an apparatus of exercises, glossary, sources and further reading. The chapter’s governing claim is stated as a levy: Every scene spent on a subplot is a scene not spent advancing the reader’s primary investment. A subplot earns that tax only by supplying something the main plot structurally cannot supply on its own. The claim is deliberately harsh, and §3.8 and §16 both qualify it, because the tax metaphor presupposes a single primary investment . That presupposition is accurate for most commercial narrative and false for the tradition that produced Middlemarch , Bleak House , War and Peace and Vanity Fair , in which no thread is the plot and the others are not deductions from it. Middlemarch does not have a subplot in the sense this chapter defines. It has four plots, and the relation between them is the novel. A note on the examples. The illustrative works are chiefly novels likely to remain in print and in discussion, with two plays where the theory of the double plot was built on the stage. A concordance mapping each concept to the work that best displays it appears at §10.6 . The second edition’s post-2000 and screen cases are listed at §14.5 . A note on drama. This is a chapter about novels, but the theory of multiple plots was built on the Renaissance stage, and two of its three principal sources (Levin, Empson) are studies of plays. King Lear is therefore analysed at §9.8 as the origin of the critical discussion rather than as a novel-substitute, and the chapter states plainly where the transfer from stage to page requires adjustment. Learning Outcomes By the end of this chapter, a student should be able to: Distinguish a subplot from the units most often confused with it — the recurring character, the episode, the digression, the frame, the parallel plot and the motif — and explain why presence is not a plot . Trace a secondary thread’s own goal–conflict–disaster chain in the terms established by Chapter 2 ( Scene and Sequel ), and identify where its causal links break. Apply Chatman’s distinction between kernels and satellites to determine what a given thread is doing inside its own system and inside the main plot’s. Classify the relation between two plots using Levin’s categories of analogy, contrast and direct linkage, and defend the classification from the text. Identify which of the six domains a subplot serves, and diagnose under- and over-delivery in each. Select a braiding and convergence structure from the fourteen tabulated at §6.4 , and state what the choice buys and costs. Audit a manuscript’s braiding rhythm, calculating dormancy intervals and estimating reinstatement cost. Evaluate the limits of the attention-tax model itself, including its dependence on a single-investment assumption and its origin in a particular publishing economy. Key Terms Subplot · secondary chain · the attention tax · presence is not a plot · kernel · satellite · character-system · plot-system · analogy · contrast (Levin) · direct linkage · double plot · braiding · braiding rhythm · dormancy interval · reinstatement cost · convergence (literal and thematic) · the promotion question · page-share · digression · multiplicity · crossing character · temporal counterpoint Full definitions appear in the Glossary ( §13 ). Terms are bolded on first substantive use. How to Use This Chapter Reader Route Purpose Student in a seminar §§1–6 in order, then §9 , then §12 Conceptual grounding, worked demonstrations, guided practice Writer in revision §7 (diagnostics) → §8 (failures) → §6.6 (braiding rhythm) → §11 (checklist) Triage of a live manuscript at structural scale Teacher or workshop leader §4 , 6.4, 8 for material; §9 for close-reading models; §12.1 for assignments; §12.3 rubric A ready-made teaching sequence with counterexamples built in Three cautions before beginning. First, this chapter’s instruments operate at a scale where mistakes are expensive. A diagnosis that a scene is not working costs an afternoon to act on. A diagnosis that a subplot is not working costs a rewrite. The protocol at §7 is therefore designed to produce descriptions rather than verdicts, and the chapter recommends running it twice, several weeks apart, before acting on it. Second, the chapter’s central metaphor is contestable and the chapter says so. The attention tax is a good instrument for the book that has one main plot. Applied to the multi-plot novel it produces confident nonsense — that Middlemarch should have cut Lydgate, that War and Peace should have chosen a family. §3.8 , §5.4 and §16 return to this. Third, none of the taxonomies here is a formula. They are instruments for noticing, and their proper output is a question. A model that answers “this subplot fails test four” has done nothing until the writer asks why the book might want it to.

title: 1. Introduction: The Second Story
text: 1.1 A structural asymmetry, stated concretely Consider two chapters of the same novel, adjacent in the printed book. Chapter 14 belongs to the main plot. A reader arriving at it has three hundred pages of accumulated investment behind them, a question they want answered, and a character whose fortunes they have been tracking since page one. The chapter can be slow, oblique, even inconclusive, and the reader will stay, because staying is what they were already doing. Chapter 15 belongs to a secondary thread. The reader arriving at it must do four things that Chapter 14 did not ask of them. They must suspend the question Chapter 14 raised. They must reinstate a set of characters, locations and stakes they last encountered forty pages ago. They must re-establish why this material matters. And they must do all of it while a live question is being held unanswered somewhere behind them, which is a cognitive load in itself. None of this is fatal, and thousands of novels perform the manoeuvre routinely. But the asymmetry is real, and it is not a matter of the second chapter being less well written. The two chapters are held to different standards by the reader, and the difference is structural. Chapter 14 is spending trust; Chapter 15 is asking for a fresh appropriation. Two further features make the subplot the hardest unit in this textbook. It is large. The units treated in Parts I and II are measured in paragraphs, pages or, at most, a chapter. A subplot is measured in chapters — sometimes in a quarter or a third of a book. When a subplot is wrong, the error is not local, and it cannot be corrected by revision at sentence level. This is why the diagnostic protocol in §7 belongs to structural editing rather than to line editing, and why it is best applied to a completed draft. It is optional in a way no other unit is. Every novel has an opening, an ending, transitions, scenes and, if it has more than one character, dialogue. Not every novel has a subplot, and many excellent ones do not. The Stranger , The Death of Ivan Ilyich , The Remains of the Day and Things Fall Apart run one line each — the last with an ensemble around it, but not a second chain. The subplot is thus the one large unit whose presence must be argued for , and the argument is what this chapter supplies. 1.2 The claim in its strong form A subplot is not free because it is good. It is taxed against the story the reader actually came for, and the tax has to be worth paying. The metaphor of a levy on attention will be used throughout, and it should be clear what it does and does not claim. It does claim that reader attention is finite and rivalrous — that a page given to one thread is not available to another, and that the reader’s willingness to be redirected is a resource with a floor. It does claim that the standard a subplot must clear is comparative, not absolute. The question is never is this good? but is this better than what the same forty pages could have done for the main line? It does not claim that subplots are suspect. The tax is a standard, not a prohibition. Most of the greatest novels in the European tradition pay it many times over. It does not claim that the main plot is more important than the subplot in some literary hierarchy. It claims only that the reader arrives with an investment already formed, and that a second thread must build its own. It does not apply, or applies only with heavy adjustment, where there is no single primary investment. This is the qualification developed at §3.8 , and it is the qualification on which the rest of the chapter depends. The attention tax is the same argument that Chapter 13 ( The Viewpoint Shift ) makes about identification under the name of the empathy budget . The two chapters share a theoretical source in Alex Woloch and should be read as one argument applied at two scales: Chapter 13 asks who the reader is permitted to become ; this chapter asks whose story the reader is asked to follow . A reader will tolerate a great deal of the second. The first is a scarcer faculty and a larger request. 1.3 Where this chapter sits in the book It belongs to Part III, The Architecture of the Whole , whose chapters take the whole book rather than a unit within it as their object. Its dependencies run backwards through the book and are load-bearing rather than decorative. Concept Chapter of origin How this chapter uses it Goal–conflict–disaster; reaction–dilemma–decision Chapter 2 ( Scene and Sequel ) The definition of a subplot depends on it entirely. A secondary thread is a chain in Swain’s sense, or it is not a subplot The causal chain (“had to happen next”) Chapter 2 The engine test ( §7.1 , test 1) is the chain test applied to a whole thread The principle of multiplicity Chapter 1 ( The Purposes of a Scene ) Restated at book scale in §5 The orientation budget; anchor and drift Chapter 5 ( The Transition ) Every braid crossing is a transition, and pays a transition’s costs Proposition and payoff Chapter 6 ( The Chapter Break ) Braiding is executed at chapter breaks; §6.2 depends on it The empathy budget Chapter 13 ( The Viewpoint Shift ) The attention tax is the same claim about page space The interest deficit Chapter 7 ( Backstory and Flashback ) A braid crossing opens a deficit in the same way a cutaway does, and the repayment mechanism is the same Earned and unearned Chapter 16 ( The Ending ) Convergence is the subplot’s version of earning; §6.4 is a taxonomy of ways to earn it Two relations deserve to be stated rather than tabulated. The relation to Chapter 2 is definitional. This chapter’s entire definition of a subplot — a chain , not a presence — is borrowed from the six-beat engine. A character who recurs without a goal, meets no resistance and suffers no reversal has no chain and therefore no subplot, however often they appear. Everything in §2 follows from that borrowing, and a student who has not read Chapter 2 should read it before this one. The relation to Chapter 5 is mechanical. Every crossing from one thread to another is a transition , and it incurs the orientation costs Chapter 5 sets out: the reader must be re-anchored in time, place, viewpoint and stake. Chapter 5 handles how the gap is crossed; Chapter 6 handles where the break is placed ; Chapter 13 handles who is on the other side . This chapter handles the fourth question those three leave open — whether the thing on the other side deserves to exist at all.

title: 2. Definitions and Boundaries
text: Craft discussion of subplots is unusually loose, and the looseness is not innocent. “Subplot” is routinely used for four different things — a secondary chain, a recurring minor character, a thematic motif, and any material that is not the main line — with the result that the advice attaching to it is incoherent. A writer told to “cut the subplots” and a writer told to “add a subplot for texture” are being told to operate on different objects. 2.1 The unit under study Working definition. A subplot is a secondary chain of causally linked scenes possessing its own goal, conflict and consequence, distinct from the main plot’s, running alongside it in story time, usually sharing characters or world with it, and competing with it for the same finite page count and the same finite reader attention. Four elements of that definition carry weight. “Chain.” The requirement is causal linkage in the sense established in Chapter 2 ( Scene and Sequel ): each unit descends from the one before it, so that the thread reads as things that had to happen next rather than things that also happened . This is the whole of the distinction between a subplot and a recurring character, and it is developed at §2.3. “Its own goal, conflict and consequence.” A subplot is not a smaller version of the main plot’s engine; it is a separate instance of the same engine. Its goal belongs to its own characters and is measured against its own stakes. A thread whose only goal is help the protagonist is not a subplot; it is main-plot machinery distributed across other people. “Alongside it in story time.” A subplot runs concurrently. Material set entirely in the past is treated in Chapter 7 ( Backstory and Flashback ) as analepsis, not here — though §4.6 proposes a genuine borderline case, the subplot running on a different clock, and argues that it belongs to this chapter. “Competing for the same finite page count.” The competitive relation is definitional rather than incidental. It is what generates the attention tax, and it is why the removal test ( §7.1 , test 9) is the chapter’s most brutal and most useful instrument. 2.2 Scale: how much of a book is a subplot? There is no principled threshold, and any number is a convention rather than a discovery. But the ranges below are stable enough across the tradition to be useful in diagnosis, and a manuscript that falls outside them is usually doing something it has not decided to do. Extent (share of total pages) What the reader experiences Typical designation Under 3% A recurring detail or a runner; no chain is legible Motif; running gag; texture 3–8% A thread the reader tracks but does not weigh Minor subplot; the “C-plot” of screen practice 8–20% A second story with its own stakes and its own arc Subplot proper; the classic “B-plot” 20–35% A co-plot; the reader is not certain which line is primary The double plot; Vanity Fair , Bleak House Three or more threads of 15–35% each No thread is primary; the relation between them is the subject The multi-plot novel; Middlemarch , War and Peace Two inferences follow from the table. The 8–20% band is where the attention tax bites hardest , because it is large enough for the reader to notice the diversion and too small for the book to have declared itself a multi-plot novel. In this chapter’s estimate, most diagnosable subplot failure occurs here. The bottom two rows are not larger subplots; they are a different form. A book in which four threads each take a quarter has not multiplied its subplots; it has abolished the category. This is the qualification §3.8 develops, and it is the reason this chapter’s title is faintly misleading about a third of the novels it discusses. 2.3 Presence is not a plot A frequent error in manuscript diagnosis is to mistake a recurring character for a subplot. The distinction is exact and can be settled in one operation. Test. Write down the character’s goal at their first appearance and at their last. If the two are the same goal in an unchanged state — or if there is no goal to write down — there is no chain. There is a person who keeps arriving. Both configurations are legitimate. A recurring character with no chain of their own may be doing indispensable work: supplying information, embodying a social world, providing the friction against which the protagonist is defined, carrying a motif. What such a character cannot do is discharge the domains at §4 that require a chain — structural convergence in particular, which has nothing to converge. The confusion persists because the surface features are similar. Both produce scenes away from the protagonist’s central pursuit; both recur; both feel, in draft, like a second story. The difference is invisible at scene level and obvious at book level, which is why the diagnosis belongs here rather than in Chapter 1. A corollary for revision. A recurring character who is nearly a subplot is one of the most economical opportunities in a manuscript. The scenes already exist and are already paid for. Supplying the character with a goal, an obstacle and a reversal — converting presence into chain — frequently costs a few hundred words and converts inert page-share into a functioning thread. §7.1 , test 1 is designed to find these. 2.4 Adjacent terms Term Meaning Relation to the subplot Main plot The chain carrying the reader’s primary investment The subplot’s competitor for attention, and usually its eventual destination Double plot Two chains of comparable weight, neither clearly subordinate Empson’s and Levin’s object; a subplot that has grown into a co-plot (§2.2) Underplot Older English term, especially in Renaissance drama criticism, for a socially “lower” second action Levin’s material; often but not always comic Counterplot A second chain constructed as the inversion of the first Contrast (Levin) as a whole design; §6.4 , structure 8 B-plot / C-plot Screen-writing terms for secondary and tertiary lines within an episode Useful for proportion; misleading in prose because they presuppose episode-length resolution ( §10.4 ) Episode A single self-contained incident that does not recur or build Fails the chain requirement; a detour, not a subplot Digression Non-narrative material — essay, history, catalogue — inserted into the narrative Has no chain at all; treated as the subplot’s limit case at §6.4 , structure 14, and §9.6 Frame narrative An enclosing story within which the main narrative is told Structurally outside rather than beside; see Chapter 10 ( The Prologue ) and §6.4 , structure 10 Parallel plot Two chains that never intersect A subplot that has failed to converge, or a deliberate structure; §8.1 Intercalary chapter A chapter of general or collective material alternating with the narrative The Grapes of Wrath ; a braid one of whose strands is not a chain ( §8.12 ) Runner A repeated small piece of business, comic or otherwise, with no chain Texture; below the subplot threshold (§2.2) Motif A recurring image, object or phrase Carries thematic relation without narrative causality; see Chapter 4 ( The Descriptive Detail ) Foil A character constructed to contrast with another A relation between characters ; a subplot is a relation between chains Kernel / satellite Chatman’s distinction between events that open alternatives and events that do not The chapter’s sharpest instrument; §3.4 2.5 What this chapter excludes Backstory and flashback. Material set before the present narrative is analepsis and belongs to Chapter 7 ( Backstory and Flashback ), and the arrangement of several timelines across a whole book to Chapter 8 ( Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture ). The borderline case — a second thread running in an earlier period as a concurrent narrative line — is claimed for this chapter and defended at §4.6 . Prologues and frames. A separated preliminary unit is treated in Chapter 10 ( The Prologue ). Where a frame converges by revelation it appears here as a braiding structure ( §6.4 , structure 10), but the frame’s own justification is Chapter 10’s problem. Viewpoint allocation. Which character narrates a thread is Chapter 13’s ( The Viewpoint Shift ) question. This chapter assumes the allocation and asks what the thread does. The two questions are near-inseparable in practice, and §9.3 on Bleak House is where they are treated together. Transitions between threads. The mechanics of the crossing itself — how a reader is carried from one line to another without disorientation — belong to Chapter 5 ( The Transition ). This chapter is concerned with the rhythm of the crossings ( §6.6 ), not their execution. Series instalments and series arcs. A plot line spanning several volumes is discussed at §10.3 ; the structural problems of the series as a form belong to Chapter 17 ( Series and Genre ). Ensemble narrative without chains. A novel that distributes attention across many characters without giving any of them a secondary chain — much of Mrs Dalloway , much of Ulysses — is not a multi-plot novel in this chapter’s sense. §10 returns to this.

title: 3. Why a Second Chain Costs
text: The attention tax is usually asserted in craft literature and rarely argued. It can be argued, and — more interestingly — it can be argued against , from within the same critical tradition. This section assembles both cases, because a writer who understands why a second chain is expensive prunes more intelligently, and a writer who understands why the expense is sometimes the point prunes less. Seven strands follow: the classical objection and its oldest answer; Levin on the relations between plots; Empson on juxtaposition as a machine for meaning; Chatman on kernels and satellites; Woloch on the distribution of narrative attention, approached from the plot side; the historical conditions that produced the multi-plot novel and then withdrew them; and the cognitive literature on tracking interleaved threads. The section closes by restating the chapter’s first principle and immediately qualifying it. 3.1 Unity of action: the oldest objection, and Forster’s answer The case against the subplot is as old as poetics. Aristotle’s Poetics (c. 335 BCE) makes unity of action the organising requirement of tragedy: the plot must imitate one action, complete and whole, and its parts must be so connected that the removal or displacement of any one of them disjoints the whole. The negative formulation is more useful for present purposes than the positive one. Aristotle names the episodic plot — the plot in which episodes succeed one another without probability or necessity — as the worst kind, and his objection is the one the attention tax formalises: material that does not participate in the causal structure of the action does not belong to it. Two clarifications prevent the standard misuse of this authority. First, Aristotle’s “double plot” is not a subplot. In Poetics chapter 13 he discusses tragedies with a double ending — the good rewarded and the bad punished — and judges the structure second-best, granting it its popularity only through the weakness of audiences. This is a claim about closure , not about secondary chains, and citing it against subplots is a mistranslation of the argument. Second, Aristotle permits in epic what he restricts in tragedy. The epic, being longer, may take on epeisodia — episodes that extend the work without belonging to the central action — and he treats this as a formal property of the longer form rather than as a licence for incoherence. The distinction matters for the novel, which is generically epic in scale and dramatic in its inherited critical vocabulary. Much bad advice about subplots consists of applying tragedy’s unity requirement to a form Aristotle would have classed with epic. The oldest answer to the objection is E. M. Forster’s, in Aspects of the Novel (1927). Forster’s late chapters on pattern and rhythm propose that a novel may be organised by relations other than causality: by shape (his examples include the hour-glass structure of The Ambassadors , in which two characters exchange positions), and by rhythm — repetition with variation, the recurrence of a motif whose reappearance carries an accumulated charge, for which his example is the little phrase of Vinteuil in Proust. Forster’s contribution to this chapter is a permission: a novel may be unified by pattern rather than by plot , and a second chain may be integrated by rhyme rather than by consequence. Forster also supplies the corresponding caution, and it is honest. He notes that pattern, pursued rigorously, tends to constrain what the novel can contain — that the beautifully shaped book pays for its shape in life. A subplot admitted for pattern alone is subject to this risk, and §8.13 names the resulting failure. 3.2 Levin: the relations between plots Richard Levin’s The Multiple Plot in English Renaissance Drama (University of Chicago Press, 1971) is the definitive study of how secondary actions relate to primary ones, and it remains the source of the most useful vocabulary available for the problem. Levin’s material is the English stage between roughly 1580 and 1640, a body of drama in which multiple plots were the norm rather than the exception; his method is to ask, of each play, what kind of relation the actions bear to one another, and to resist the assumption that the relation must be causal to be real. Three of Levin’s categories are load-bearing for this chapter. Direct linkage. The secondary action affects the primary one causally: its events change what is possible in the main plot, and the two are connected at the level of what happens. Analogy. The secondary action repeats the primary action’s pattern in a different key — a different social level, a different register, a different set of persons — so that the two illuminate each other by resemblance. Contrast (Levin). The secondary action inverts the primary one: the same situation resolved the other way, the same choice made differently, the same pressure producing the opposite result. Levin’s central and most useful argument is that analogical relation can integrate a play whose plots never physically meet. A secondary action that shares no character and no event with the main action may nonetheless be structurally integral, because the relation between the two is the play’s argument . He develops the point against a critical tradition — descending through Dryden and Johnson to the nineteenth century — that treated multiple action as a native English vice, an offence against unity to be excused rather than analysed. Two refinements of Levin’s model are worth carrying into novel criticism. The three-level play. Levin observes that Renaissance dramatists frequently constructed three actions rather than two, arranged on descending social levels — courtly, gentle, plebeian — with the relations of analogy running down the ladder. The structure survives in the multi-plot novel: Bleak House has its aristocratic Dedlocks, its professional and middling Chancery suitors, and its Tom-all-Alone’s, and the argument of the book is carried by the fact that a single secret runs through all three. Relations may be mixed and may change. A thread may begin in analogy and end in direct linkage; the change is itself an event, and in the novel it is usually the event called convergence . This gives the chapter a precise way to say what convergence does: it converts an analogical relation into a causal one , and the reader’s experience of a well-managed convergence is the retrospective recognition that the rhyme was also a mechanism. A caution about the transfer. Levin’s plays are two to three hours long and their plots are held in a single sitting. A novel’s threads are separated by days of reading. Analogy that is instantly perceptible across an interval of twenty minutes on stage may be imperceptible across an interval of eighty pages, and the novelist must therefore mark analogies that a dramatist could leave implicit. §6.6 gives the mechanism. 3.3 Empson: the double plot as a machine for meaning William Empson’s essay “Double Plots” — the second chapter of Some Versions of Pastoral (1935) — is the strongest available defence of the second chain, and it argues on grounds the attention tax cannot reach. Empson’s subject is the Elizabethan and Jacobean habit of running a “low” comic action beside a “high” tragic or heroic one, and his claim is that the pairing is not a concession to the groundlings but a device for producing meaning .
