The two actions are set beside each other so that each is read through the other; the comic action’s coarse version of the heroic action’s dilemma is a comment on it, and the heroic action’s elevation is a comment on the comic one. Neither comment is stated. Both are produced by juxtaposition, and — this is Empson’s essential move — the meaning generated belongs to neither plot alone. The consequences for this chapter are large enough to state as a list. The double plot generates a surplus. If the relation between two actions yields something neither carries by itself, then the second chain is not simply a deduction from the first’s page budget. It is an investment that pays in a currency the single-plot novel does not have. This is the most serious argument against the attention tax available in the critical literature, and the chapter accepts it. The “low” plot is not decorative. Empson’s reading of the Falstaff material in the Henry IV plays makes the tavern action a sustained interrogation of the honour the main action asserts. The comic thread is not relief from the argument; it is the other half of it. §8.7 builds its failure pattern on the difference between these two things. Juxtaposition is a technique with its own craft. Meaning by proximity requires the proximity to be managed : the two actions must be near enough in the reader’s memory for the comparison to occur. Empson’s dramatists could rely on a single sitting; the novelist cannot, and §6.6 converts this into a rule about dormancy. The relation may be felt without being formulable. Empson is careful that the effect works below the level of paraphrase — that an audience feels the two actions commenting on one another without being able to say what the comment is. Craft advice that demands a subplot’s thematic contribution be statable in a sentence is therefore demanding something the mechanism does not require. §7.1 , test 4 is worded to allow for this. Where Empson is vulnerable. His readings are frankly ingenious, and it is possible to construct an Empsonian defence of almost any two things placed side by side — a fact his critics have not been slow to observe. The defence “these threads comment on each other” is therefore unfalsifiable as stated , and a writer using it should be required to say what the comment is doing that a single plot could not do. That requirement is the whole content of §8.13 , the thematic alibi . 3.4 Chatman: kernels, satellites, and what a subplot is The sharpest instrument in this chapter comes from Seymour Chatman’s Story and Discourse (1978), and it is worth setting out with care because it converts several of the chapter’s intuitions into something that can be checked. Chatman, developing Barthes’s distinction between cardinal functions and catalyses , divides narrative events into two classes. Kernel. A narrative moment that raises and answers a question about the direction of events — a branching point. Kernels cannot be deleted without destroying the narrative logic: remove one and the story’s causal structure fails. Satellite. A narrative moment that does not open an alternative. It elaborates, delays, textures or amplifies. Satellites can be deleted without destroying the logic, though the discourse is impoverished by the deletion. Chatman is explicit that satellites are not worthless. Their deletion damages the aesthetic of the narrative while leaving its skeleton intact; a novel consisting only of kernels would be a synopsis. The distinction is between two kinds of necessity, not between the necessary and the disposable. Applied to the subplot, the distinction yields the most precise definition this chapter can offer, and it is worth setting out as a proposition. A subplot is a chain of events that are kernels within its own system and satellites within the main plot’s — until convergence, which is the moment its kernels become the main plot’s kernels too. Unpack the proposition in three parts. Kernels within its own system. This is the chain requirement of §2.1 restated formally. Inside the subplot, its turning points must be branching points: this thread must be capable of going one way or another, and its scenes must be the moments where that is settled. A thread whose “turning points” are all satellites even inside its own system is not a subplot at all — it is texture. This is what §7.1 , test 2 measures. Satellites within the main plot’s. This is the attention tax, formalised. Before convergence, the subplot’s events can be deleted from the main plot’s causal structure without breaking it. That is what makes them cost something: they are, from the primary line’s point of view, elaboration. Until convergence. And this is why convergence is the pivot of the whole chapter. Convergence is the moment at which the subplot’s kernels are promoted into the main plot’s kernel set — the moment when deleting the thread would break the main story’s logic and not merely thin it. Before that moment the removal test ( §7.1 , test 9) is a question about impoverishment. After it, the removal test is a question about coherence. Three practical uses follow immediately. Use Procedure What it reveals Locating convergence Find the earliest point at which deleting the thread breaks the main plot’s causal logic Where convergence actually is, as opposed to where the writer believes it is Diagnosing the vestigial thread Ask whether the thread’s own turning points are kernels inside it A thread of pure satellites has no chain and cannot converge Measuring the tax Count the pages spent on main-plot satellites before convergence The exact size of the loan the convergence must repay A caution. Chatman’s categories are cleaner in theory than in application, and the boundary between kernel and satellite is frequently arguable — a fact he acknowledges. Two competent readers can disagree about whether a given scene opens an alternative. The instrument is therefore diagnostic rather than decisive: its value is in forcing the question what would break if this were gone? , which is a question drafts are rarely asked. 3.5 Woloch from the plot side: which lives get plots Chapter 13 ( The Viewpoint Shift ) uses Alex Woloch’s The One vs. the Many (2003) to theorise the empathy budget, working from the character side: character-space, the compression of the minor character, and the distortion that compression produces. That material is not repeated here. What follows approaches the same book from the other direction, and the direction changes what the theory says. Woloch’s core claim is that a novel’s characters form a character-system — an arrangement of delimited character-spaces in which attention given to one is attention withheld from another. The claim this chapter takes up is a corollary Woloch does not need to state, because his object is characterisation: A character-system is also a plot-system. The same finitude that determines how much space a character receives determines whether they receive a chain . Some characters are granted goals, obstacles and reversals; others are granted appearances. The distribution of chains across a cast is a formal structure in the same sense that the distribution of interiority is. Three consequences follow, and they are the reason this chapter needs Woloch as well as Levin and Empson. First: having a plot is a stronger grant than having a viewpoint. A character may be focalised for a chapter and still have no chain — the reader inhabits them and learns nothing about what they want. Conversely, a character never focalised may possess a complete chain that the reader reconstructs from outside: Dov, in this book’s running example, is observed only from outside until a single bounded chapter near the climax, and has a full goal–conflict–disaster chain throughout. Viewpoint confers access; a plot confers consequence. The second is the scarcer and the more consequential grant, and it is not tracked by the vocabulary of viewpoint at all. Second: the distribution of chains carries an argument. Woloch’s insistence that the character-system is a political fact transfers directly and, arguably, more sharply. To give a character a plot is to say that their wanting produces effects in the world — that their life has causal weight. To deny them one is to say that their life is a condition rather than a story. A novel in which the servants appear constantly and never want anything is making a claim about servants, whether or not its author intended one. A novel about a strike in which the owners have a plot and the workers have a crowd is making a claim about who acts. Third: the tax and the grant are the same fact seen from two sides. The attention tax says: this thread costs the main line. Woloch’s model says: the main line’s centrality is produced by what the other threads are denied. The protagonist is not naturally central; centrality is manufactured out of the compression of everyone else. Held together, the two claims produce the chapter’s least comfortable question, which is set as a seminar topic at §12.2 and asked as a diagnostic at §7.1 , test 10: The promotion question. If this thread were the main plot, would the book be better? A writer who cannot answer that question has not decided which book they are writing. A writer who answers yes has learned something a hundred pages of line-editing would not have told them. A caution. Woloch’s model is calibrated to the nineteenth-century realist novel — large casts, a strong protagonist convention, an omniscient habit. It describes the multi-plot novel superbly and a two-hander poorly. Chapter 13 §3.3 enters the same caveat from the character side, and it applies here with equal force. 3.6 The historical strand: what produced the multi-plot novel, and what withdrew it Contemporary suspicion of subplots is presented in craft literature as a discovery about narrative. It is substantially an artefact of book length, and book length is an artefact of the market. Establishing this is not a debunking exercise; it is the difference between knowing a convention and mistaking it for a law. The Renaissance stage. Multiple plotting was the English theatrical norm for two generations, and Levin’s study documents the extent: double and triple actions in the majority of surviving plays. The conditions were a repertory system, a mixed audience, and an aesthetic with no allegiance to the neoclassical unities — an allegiance that arrived later, in the Restoration and through French influence, and brought with it the critical embarrassment about Shakespeare’s double actions that Levin’s book was written to dispel. The Victorian three-decker and the monthly number. The nineteenth-century English multi-plot novel was underwritten by two material arrangements that no longer exist. Condition Mechanism Effect on plot structure Serial publication in parts Novels issued in monthly (or weekly) instalments over one to two years Each part had to contain variety; alternation between threads was the simplest way to supply it The circulating library Mudie’s and its rivals bought in bulk and lent by subscription, and preferred the three-volume format because three volumes could be lent to three subscribers Length was commercially favoured rather than penalised; expansiveness was an asset Sale by the volume, not the reader’s hour A publisher’s revenue was tied to a physical format The economic pressure ran towards more pages, not fewer Slow reading, long runs A novel might occupy its readers for eighteen months Threads could be left dormant for a month and reinstated by the part’s own recapitulative habits The consequences are visible in the books. Vanity Fair (1847–48) and Bleak House (1852–53) were each issued in twenty monthly numbers. Middlemarch (1871–72) appeared in eight parts, a format Eliot and her publisher devised for it. War and Peace began serial publication in the Russian Messenger under a different title before being completed as a book. Anna Karenina was serialised in the same journal between 1875 and 1877, and its final part appeared separately after the editor declined to print Tolstoy’s treatment of the Serbian war — a fact that matters here, because it means the novel’s most disputed structural decision was also a publishing event. The withdrawal. The three-decker collapsed in the 1890s when the circulating libraries refused to sustain its price, and the single-volume novel became standard. The modernist novel then narrowed the field further, for reasons internal to its ambitions rather than commercial: a form organised around consciousness rather than around action has less use for a second chain of actions. Mrs Dalloway and To the Lighthouse have many lives in them and very few plots. The present. The contemporary literary novel is conventionally between eighty and a hundred and ten thousand words — roughly a third of Middlemarch . At that length, a subplot occupying twenty per cent of the book is sixteen to twenty-two thousand words, and the arithmetic of the attention tax becomes severe in a way it was not for Dickens. Meanwhile the braided structure survived, and thrives, in the places where length survived: epic fantasy, the multi-generational saga, the historical sequence, and — most vigorously — long-form television, which reinvented the monthly number as the season and rediscovered the A/B/C plot as an industrial method ( §10.4 ). The inference to draw. The contemporary suspicion of subplots is not a discovery about how narrative works. It is what a two-hundred-year decline in the average length of a novel looks like when it is restated as craft advice. Learn it as a convention of the present market, and read historically enough to know that it is one. Franco Moretti’s quantitative work — Graphs, Maps, Trees (2005) and the later essays on plot as network — is the natural place to pursue this, because it insists that formal change in the novel is legible as a function of quantity and market rather than only of intention. 3.7 The cognitive strand: what interleaving costs a reader The claim that braiding has a cost is empirically supported, though the support is indirect and the chapter should not overstate it. Two literatures bear on it. Situation models and updating. Rolf Zwaan and Gabriel Radvansky’s synthesis (1998) holds that readers construct a situation model of the state of affairs a text describes, tracking a small number of dimensions — protagonist, space, time, causality, intentionality — and incurring a measurable processing cost whenever one of them shifts. A crossing from one plot thread to another typically shifts all five simultaneously : different people, elsewhere, at a different point, pursuing different causes, wanting different things. This is the largest single update a narrative can ask for short of a change of narrator, and it is why Chapter 5 ( The Transition ) treats thread crossings as the most expensive transitions in the repertoire. Frame recall. Catherine Emmott’s Narrative Comprehension (1997) supplies the mechanism the writer actually needs. Emmott’s contextual frames are the reader’s running record of who is present in a scene and where; a frame that is left is not deleted but primed — held in a recoverable state — and reactivated when the narrative returns to it. Her account of frame switching and frame recall gives braiding its precise cognitive description: a thread is not re-read on resumption; it is recalled. The reader’s ability to resume depends on the frame being recoverable, and recoverability decays. Three inferences for the writer, stated as claims about tendency rather than as laws: Reinstatement is cheap when the frame is warm and expensive when it is cold. A thread resumed after twenty pages costs a clause of re-anchoring. A thread resumed after two hundred costs a scene of re-establishment — which the reader experiences as the book explaining itself. Cost is a function of interval and of distinctiveness together. A thread with a strongly individuated cast, setting and register decays more slowly, because fewer cues are needed to recall it. This is the cognitive justification for the old practical advice to make secondary threads look and sound different . The reader’s felt experience of a cold resumption is not confusion but resentment. They do not usually fail to reconstruct the thread; they resent being asked to. This is why the late-arriving and long-dormant thread ( §8.5 ) registers as a pacing complaint rather than a comprehension complaint, and why writers misdiagnose it. §6.6 converts these into working intervals and a dormancy audit. The chapter states plainly that the intervals there are conventions derived from practice, calibrated by the cognitive literature rather than derived from it. No experiment has established how many pages a novel’s B-plot may lie dormant, and any source that claims otherwise should be distrusted. 3.8 The attention tax, restated — and qualified The chapter’s first principle can now be stated in full. The attention tax. Every scene given to a secondary chain is a scene not given to the chain carrying the reader’s primary investment. A subplot therefore does not clear its cost by being well written; it clears its cost by supplying something the main plot structurally cannot supply on its own, and by eventually converting its own kernels into the main plot’s (§3.4). And now the qualification, which is where the more interesting teaching lies. The tax metaphor presupposes a single primary investment. It assumes there is a story the reader “came for”, against which everything else is measured. That assumption is accurate for most commercial narrative, for genre fiction of nearly every kind, for the well-made play, for the screenplay, and for the great majority of manuscripts a workshop will see. It is false for the multi-plot novel. Middlemarch does not have a subplot. It has four plots — Dorothea and Casaubon; Lydgate and Rosamond; Fred Vincy and Mary Garth; Bulstrode — and they are not ranked. The novel’s own account of its method is a web , not a trunk with branches: the narrator, pausing in Chapter 15, says that all the light at her command must be concentrated on this particular web and not dispersed over that tempting range of relevancies called the universe. A web has no main strand. Ask which of the four is “the” plot and the question does not resolve; ask what the relation between them is, and the novel answers at length. The same is true, with variations, of War and Peace , Bleak House , Vanity Fair and The Brothers Karamazov . In each case, applying the attention tax mechanically produces a confident absurdity: that Eliot should have cut Lydgate, that Tolstoy should have chosen a family, that Dickens should have decided between Chancery and Chesney Wold. Why, then, teach the tax at all? Because it is a stress test, not a description. Like the zero-context test in Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages ) §3.7 , its value lies in its austerity. A thread that survives the tax has a demonstrable function. A thread that fails it may be a co-plot in a multi-plot novel — but the writer must then say so , and accept the obligations that come with it, which are set out at §5.4 . In this chapter’s judgement, the commonest structural failure in ambitious manuscripts is not the presence of a second plot. It is a book that has half-declared itself a multi-plot novel and half-retained a hierarchy, so that the reader cannot tell whether the second thread is a co-plot to be weighed or a subplot to be tolerated. The double position to hold. For a book with one primary investment, the tax is the correct standard and should be applied without mercy. For a book without one, the tax is the wrong instrument, and the right question is Levin’s and Empson’s: what does the relation between these plots produce that neither produces alone? The rest of the chapter is written to serve both cases. §4 assumes a hierarchy; §5.4 and §6.4 do not.

title: 4. The Domains of Purpose
text: 4.0 The model and its status The domain model asks a single question of a secondary chain: what does this thread supply that the main plot, by its own nature, cannot? It is the operational form of the attention tax. A subplot that cannot answer has not failed aesthetically; it has failed to justify its page-share, which is a different and more tractable complaint. The model’s value is diagnostic. It converts this subplot feels like filler into a set of separable questions with separable remedies: the thread is doing pacing relief and nothing else; the thread is doing thematic counterpoint but the counterpoint duplicates rather than opposes; the thread is doing structural convergence but the convergence arrives before the reader has invested. Its dangers are two, and both should be named before the taxonomy begins. The retrospective alibi. Any thread can be described, after the fact, as serving some domain. “It’s thematic counterpoint” is the universal solvent of workshop discussion, and it is unfalsifiable as usually deployed. §8.13 is built on this failure, and §7.1 , test 4 is worded to close the loophole: the requirement is not that the thread has a thematic relation but that a reader can say what the relation asserts and what would be lost if it were not asserted . The checklist reflex. A writer who learns six domains will attempt to serve six. The result is the over-freighted subplot — a thread carrying so many declared functions that it has no shape of its own. §4.8 addresses this directly. Five domains follow, then a proposed sixth at §4.6. Each is set out with: what it supplies; its carriers — the structural features that realise it; discussion; characteristic under- and over-delivery ; and illustrations from published fiction. 4.1 Thematic Counterpoint What it supplies: a second treatment of the book’s governing question, conducted by other people under other conditions, so that the main plot’s answer is legible as an answer rather than as the only one available. Carriers Carrier What it looks like in the text Levin’s category The parallel dilemma A secondary character faces a structurally similar choice at a different social level or in a different register Analogy The road not taken A character does what the protagonist refused, or refuses what the protagonist did Contrast The inverted outcome The same pressure produces the opposite result — the marriage that works beside the one that fails Contrast The differently-priced success A character achieves what the protagonist wants and finds it costs more, or less, than expected Analogy with variation The shared object or institution A single thing — a lawsuit, a shop, a will, a house — that both threads must deal with, differently Analogy made concrete The rhyming phrase or gesture A repeated verbal or physical figure appearing in both threads Forster’s rhythm ( §3.1 ) Discussion Thematic counterpoint is the domain the tradition values most highly and the domain most often claimed without being delivered. The distinction that separates delivery from claim is the distinction Levin gives us between analogy and duplication . An analogical relation restates the main plot’s question in different terms , so that the difference in terms is itself informative. A duplicative relation restates it in the same terms, so that the reader learns that the book believes what it already said. The first produces the effect Empson describes — a meaning belonging to neither thread alone. The second produces §8.4 , the redundant mirror. The practical test is a subtraction. Ask: what does the book assert with this thread that it could not assert without it? If the answer is “the same thing, again, about someone else”, the thread is duplicative. If the answer names a qualification, a cost, an alternative or a limit, the thread is counterpoint. A second discrimination worth having. Counterpoint may operate at the level of outcome or at the level of terms . Outcome-counterpoint gives two characters the same problem and different endings; it is the easier form and the more visible. Terms-counterpoint gives two characters the same ending reached by incompatible routes, or the same route to incompatible ends, and it is where the domain does its finest work — because it prevents the reader from converting the book into a proposition. Under- and over-delivery Under-delivery: the decorative rhyme. The thread resembles the main plot without asserting anything about it. A reader notices the resemblance, waits for it to mean something, and is not repaid. Symptom: the writer can point to the parallel but cannot say what it argues. Under-delivery: the unmarked analogy. The counterpoint is present and the reader misses it, because eighty pages separate the two halves of the comparison. This is a braiding-rhythm failure ( §6.6 ) masquerading as a thematic one, and it is far commoner in novels than in plays for the reason given at §3.2 . Over-delivery: the thesis thread. A thread that exists visibly to make a point, populated by people who are positions. The reader experiences this as being lectured by the architecture. Symptom: the thread’s characters have no wants that are not illustrative. Over-delivery: the underlined rhyme. The book states the parallel — a character notices that their situation resembles someone else’s, or the narrator points it out. Occasionally superb (Eliot does it deliberately and with irony); usually a confession that the writer does not trust the structure. Illustrations Tolstoy, Anna Karenina (1875–77). The definitive case, analysed in full at §9.2 . Two chains — Anna and Vronsky; Levin and Kitty — treat one question: what is a life organised around love actually worth, and what does it cost to want the truth about it? The threads are joined causally at the start (Vronsky’s pursuit of Anna releases Kitty, whom Levin eventually marries) and touch once, late, to no consequence. Everything else that connects them is counterpoint, and it is the most sustained example of the domain in the European novel. Shakespeare, King Lear (c. 1606). The Gloucester action repeats the Lear action in a different key: a father who misjudges his children, is betrayed by the one he trusts, and is redeemed by the one he cast out. Levin’s analogy in its purest form; the play is discussed at §9.8 because the entire modern theory of the double plot was built on it. Eliot, Middlemarch (1871–72). Four treatments of vocation and its compromise: Dorothea’s thwarted desire for a life of consequence, Lydgate’s medical ambition destroyed by domestic economy, Fred Vincy’s slow acquisition of a usable trade, Bulstrode’s piety financed by a concealed fortune. The counterpoint is at the level of terms : each character discovers a different relation between what they wanted and what a provincial society will fund. See §9.1 . Thackeray, Vanity Fair (1847–48). Becky and Amelia are set as contrast in its most schematic available form — the adventuress and the sentimentalist — and the novel’s achievement is that the schema does not hold. See §9.5 . 4.2 Character Testing Ground What it supplies: pressure of a kind the main plot cannot apply, revealing facets of a character that the primary conflict has no occasion to reveal. Carriers Carrier What it looks like in the text What it reveals A different register of pressure Money where the main plot has love; family where the main plot has war; the body where the main plot has the mind How the character behaves when the stakes are of a kind they have not rehearsed A relationship the main plot has no room for A sibling, a subordinate, a child, an old friend Behaviour unobserved by the people the main plot cares about Command or responsibility The character is put in charge of something What they do with power, which the main plot may only let them seek A smaller failure A defeat with low stakes, early A rehearsal that lets the reader calibrate the character before the large defeat A situation with no audience The character acts where no one who matters is watching The gap between performance and conduct — Chapter 3 ( The Dialogue Exchange ) supplies the vocabulary Discussion The main plot tests a character in the terms of its own conflict, and those terms are necessarily narrow: a novel about a murder tests its protagonist’s capacity for concealment and its detective’s capacity for attention, and has little occasion to discover whether either is kind to their mother. A subplot can apply a pressure of a different kind, and the value of the different kind is that it produces information the main plot cannot fake . There is a structural point underneath this that is easy to miss. In the main plot, a character’s behaviour is always partly explicable by the stakes: they lied because their life depended on it. Under the smaller stakes of a subplot, behaviour is unexcused , and unexcused behaviour is the most efficient characterisation available to prose. A man who is brave under fire has told the reader about the fire. A man who cannot tell his sisters he has sold a shop has told the reader about himself. The domain’s structural requirement. For a testing-ground thread to pay its tax, the trait it reveals must be load-bearing later . A thread that reveals an interesting but inconsequential facet has delivered characterisation without consequence, which is texture at subplot prices. The revealed trait should be the trait on which a main-plot decision eventually turns. Under- and over-delivery Under-delivery: the anecdote. The thread reveals something and nothing is done with it. Symptom: the character’s behaviour in the subplot could be reversed without altering a single main-plot scene. Under-delivery: redundant testing. The subplot applies the same pressure as the main plot at lower stakes, so the reader learns what they already knew. This is the redundant mirror ( §8.4 ) in its character-domain form. Over-delivery: the personality showcase. A thread constructed so obviously to exhibit a quality that the exhibition becomes the thread’s only content. Frequently identifiable by the absence of a real reversal: the character is tested and passes, which is a demonstration rather than a test. Over-delivery: fragmentation. So many different pressures applied that the character reads as inconsistent rather than as complex. Chapter 13 ( The Viewpoint Shift ) treats the viewpoint version of this problem; the plot version is that a character with three subplots has no centre. Illustrations Tolstoy, War and Peace (1865–69). Nikolai Rostov’s card game with Dolokhov is the model instance. The war has tested Nikolai’s courage and found it real; the card table tests something the war cannot reach — his relation to his family’s money, his shame, and his inability to say no to a man he admires. He loses an enormous sum to a man who has just been refused by Sonya, and must go home and tell his father. Nothing in a battle chapter could have produced the scene in which the old count says he will find the money. Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov (1880). The Ilyusha thread — Alyosha and the schoolboys — puts Alyosha under a pressure the parricide plot cannot apply. In the main action he is a mediator among adults whose positions are fixed; among the boys he must actually do something, and the novel’s argument about active love is tested where it can fail. Discussed at §9.7 . Cervantes, Don Quixote (1605, 1615). Sancho’s governorship of Barataria is a testing ground in the purest sense: a comic subplot that takes the novel’s least reliable judge of reality and gives him authority. He governs well. The main action could not have discovered this, because the main action is organised around his subordination. Dickens, Bleak House (1852–53). Richard Carstone’s slow ruin is a testing ground for John Jarndyce as much as for Richard: the reader learns what Jarndyce’s benevolence can and cannot do, and learns it under a pressure the Esther plot never applies to him. 4.3 Pacing Relief What it supplies: a change of register, rhythm or stake that allows the main plot’s tension to be sustained without the narrative stalling — and, more narrowly, that allows the reader to be released without the story being suspended. Carriers Carrier What it looks like in the text Effect Lower stakes The subplot’s worst outcome is survivable Permits the reader to relax without abandoning the book A different tonal register Comic beside tragic, domestic beside political, warm beside cold Restores the reader’s capacity to feel the main register A different tempo Slower scenes, longer sequels, more description Chapter 5 ( The Transition ) and Genette on duration supply the vocabulary Deferral across a break The main plot is left mid-crisis while the secondary thread runs Converts relief into suspense; see Chapter 6 ( The Chapter Break ) A different social world Servants, children, animals, strangers Relief by change of company as well as change of stake Discussion Pacing relief is the domain that most often appears alone, and a thread serving only this domain is the shape readers correctly identify as filler. But the domain itself is not disreputable, and the reason should be stated carefully, because craft advice tends either to dismiss it or to over-credit it. Tension is a relational quantity. A narrative held at maximum pressure for two hundred pages does not read as unbearable; it reads as monotonous, because the reader loses the contrast against which pressure is felt. This is the same argument the model chapter makes about density at the sentence level in Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages ) §5.4 : emphasis requires unstressed material around it. At book scale, relief is what supplies the unstressed material. Relief is not the same as pause. A descriptive pause, a digression or a chapter of exposition also lowers the pressure, but does so by stopping the story. A subplot lowers the pressure while a story continues to run , which is why the domain exists at all. The reader is released from one anxiety into another, smaller one, rather than into nothing. The interruption dividend. There is a second and less obvious mechanism. Cutting away from the main plot at a moment of maximum pressure and running a secondary thread converts the relief into suspense : the reader wants to return, and the wanting is a form of tension that the main plot could not have generated by continuing. This is the braided version of the deferred decision from Chapter 2 ( Scene and Sequel ) §6.2 , and it is the most efficient available use of the domain — but it depends entirely on the interruption being short. §6.6 gives the interval. Under- and over-delivery Under-delivery: the holiday. The thread is pleasant, undemanding and unconnected. The reader relaxes so completely that returning to the main plot requires effort. Symptom: the reader can skip the thread and lose nothing they can name. Under-delivery: relief without a chain. Material that lowers the pressure but has no goal, conflict or consequence of its own. This is a digression ( §2.4 ) and should be judged as one. Over-delivery: the tonal breach. Relief so far from the main register that the book appears to have changed genre. A comic thread inside a grief novel is not automatically wrong — but the reader must be able to hold both, and the test is whether the comedy knows about the grief. Over-delivery: relief as the dominant experience. The reader begins to prefer the relief. This is one route into the main-plot hijack ( §8.3 ), and the more insidious one, because it is produced by a domain the writer believed to be modest. Illustrations Dickens, Bleak House . The Bagnet household — the old soldier, his wife, the birthday dinner at which the meat is always overcooked — is pacing relief performed by a master, and it is instructive that it is not only relief. The Bagnets stand surety for George, which converts a warm domestic runner into a mechanism by which Chancery-like debt reaches the one household in the novel that seemed safe from it. Relief that turns out to be plot is the domain at its highest value. Tolstoy, War and Peace . The alternation of the title is, at one level, a pacing structure: the domestic Rostov chapters exist so that the campaign chapters can be felt. What prevents this from being mere alternation is that the peace chapters carry the novel’s argument about where life actually happens, so the relief is also the thesis. See §9.4 . Shakespeare, Henry IV . The tavern scenes are the canonical instance of comic relief that is not relief, and Empson’s reading ( §3.3 ) is the reason the phrase “comic relief” should be used with care. See §8.7 . 4.4 Structural Convergence What it supplies: an eventual intersection with the main plot — the subplot’s chain complicating, obstructing, accelerating or resolving the primary one — so that the reader’s separate investment is repaid by integration rather than left stranded. Carriers Carrier What it looks like in the text Chatman’s terms ( §3.4 ) The supplied object The subplot possesses a thing the main plot needs — a document, a key, a witness, a name The subplot’s kernels become the main plot’s The supplied constraint The subplot imposes a deadline, a cost or a prohibition on the main plot Direct linkage in Levin’s sense The supplied person A character formed in the subplot enters the main plot changed Convergence by transfer The shared secret One fact belongs to both chains and its exposure resolves both Bleak House ’s method The collision The two chains’ goals turn out to be incompatible The strongest form; convergence as conflict The revealed identity A person in one thread turns out to be a person in the other Powerful, and the most easily abused ( §8.9 ) Discussion Structural convergence is the only domain of the six that is inherently obligatory in a hierarchical book: some form of convergence is required, or the subplot is a second story running in parallel. This chapter accepts the requirement and immediately loosens it in three directions. First, convergence may be thematic rather than literal. This is Levin’s central contribution ( §3.2 ): a relation of analogy can integrate a work whose actions never meet. A thread that never touches the main plot in event but is inseparable from it in argument has converged, in the only sense that matters to a reader’s sense of unity. Anna Karenina is the great demonstration, and §9.2 argues that its refusal of literal convergence is a positive achievement rather than a defect tolerated. Second, convergence is not a moment but a gradient . Threads converge by degrees: a shared minor character, then a shared location, then a shared consequence, then a shared crisis. Manuscripts that treat convergence as a single late event usually have a braiding problem rather than a convergence problem — the thread has not been touching the main plot at all, and then touches it decisively, which reads as contrivance however well prepared the contrivance is. Third, the timing of convergence is a design variable, not a rule. Early convergence lets the subplot feed the main plot’s machinery for the rest of the book; late convergence generates a larger payoff and requires a larger investment to have been paid in. §6.4 tabulates both, with their costs. Under- and over-delivery Under-delivery: the parallel line. No convergence of any kind, literal or thematic. §8.1 . Under-delivery: convergence by proximity. The threads end up in the same room, and this is treated as convergence. Nothing about either chain has changed; the characters have merely met. §8.10 . Over-delivery: the mechanism thread. A subplot that exists solely to deliver a plot component — the key, the letter, the witness. Everything it does is instrumental; nobody in it wants anything for themselves. Symptom: the thread ends the moment it has handed over the object. Over-delivery: total convergence. Every thread resolving into one, at one time, in one place, with everyone present. The nineteenth century did this routinely and got away with it; contemporary readers have a lower tolerance, and the effect is of a form closing rather than a story ending. Chapter 16 ( The Ending ) treats the general problem. Illustrations Dickens, Bleak House . The convergence apparatus of English fiction, and unsurpassed. Three chains — the Chancery suit, the Dedlock marriage, Esther’s search for her origin — converge on a single fact: that Esther is Lady Dedlock’s daughter by the law-writer whose handwriting Lady Dedlock recognises, in one shiver, in Chapter 2. The recognition is planted before the reader knows there is anything to recognise, and every subsequent thread runs towards it. See §9.3 . Dickens, Great Expectations (1861). Magwitch is the textbook case of the deferred convergence: a thread apparently closed in the first fifty pages returns to reveal that it was the main plot all along. The structure is discussed as a braiding option at §6.4 , structure 9. Thackeray, Vanity Fair . Becky’s production of George Osborne’s letter to Amelia — a note written years earlier, kept, and finally used — is a convergence that resolves Amelia’s chain using an object generated by Becky’s. It is also, characteristically, an act of cruelty performed as a kindness. See §9.5 . 4.5 World Expansion What it supplies: access to territory — social, geographical, institutional, historical — that the main plot’s protagonist and goal have no occasion to visit, delivering scope without diverting the primary chain. Carriers Carrier What it looks like in the text Risk A different class or caste The thread’s characters occupy a social position the protagonist does not Condescension; the picturesque poor A different institution Court, hospital, army, church, market, school The thread becoming an essay about the institution A different place Another city, another country, the road between Travelogue A different faction The antagonists’ side, seen from inside Sympathy leakage; see §8.3 A different scale of event The national, the historical, the geological, against the domestic The historiographical digression ( §9.6 ) A different species of knowledge Trade, craft, law, medicine, whaling Research displayed rather than used Discussion World expansion is the domain most associated with genre fiction and most maligned in literary craft advice, and the association is a historical accident rather than a principle. The nineteenth-century social novel used it constantly and for serious purposes: a novel arguing that a society is a single connected system requires the reader to see more of the system than one life touches. Dickens’s method is unintelligible without it. The domain’s structural difficulty is that it is the only one of the six that can be served without a chain . A writer wanting scope can simply describe the other territory, and the describing will be a digression rather than a subplot. This is why world expansion is the domain most often served by material that fails §2.1 ’s definition — and why §9.6 treats Les Misérables as the limit case of the whole chapter. The discrimination that makes the domain usable. Ask whether the new territory is entered by someone who wants something there . A thread that visits a hospital because a character needs a hospital expands the world as a by-product of pursuing a goal. A thread that visits a hospital so that the reader may see one has left narrative for exposition, and should be judged by the standards Chapter 7 ( Backstory and Flashback ) applies to expository material. Under- and over-delivery Under-delivery: the tour. The reader is shown a new part of the world and nothing happens in it. Symptom: the thread has a setting and no reversal. Under-delivery: the isolated territory. The new world never affects the old one. Scope without consequence, which reads as padding at the moment the writer feels most expansive. Over-delivery: the world eats the book. The expansion is more interesting than the main line, and the reader begins to resent returning. See §8.3 . Over-delivery: research on parade. The thread exists to carry what the writer learned. The diagnostic is Chekhovian: if the material would be equally at home in a different novel, it is research rather than world. Illustrations Dickens, Bleak House . Jo the crossing-sweeper and Tom-all-Alone’s exist so that the novel’s argument — that Chancery’s corruption is continuous with the slum’s contagion — can be made as narrative rather than as assertion. Jo has a chain: he wants to be let alone and to move on, is prevented, and dies of it. The world expansion and the thematic counterpoint are the same material. Tolstoy, War and Peace . The most ambitious use of the domain in the tradition, and the one that most tests its limits, because Tolstoy’s expansion eventually leaves narrative altogether for historiography. §9.4 separates the two operations. Melville, Moby-Dick (1851). The crew of the Pequod — Queequeg, Stubb, Flask, Pip, the try-works, the mates’ watches — supplies world without supplying a second chain, and the cetology chapters supply world with no narrative at all. Discussed as digression at §8.11 . Hugo, Les Misérables (1862). The Friends of the ABC and the barricade are world expansion that becomes structural convergence: a political thread introduced for scope turns out to be the mechanism by which Valjean’s chain and Marius’s chain are resolved together. See §9.6 . 4.6 A Proposed Sixth: Temporal Counterpoint The five domains above are all defined by content — theme, character, register, structure, world. There is a sixth relation available between two chains that none of them names, because it is a relation of rate rather than of substance. Temporal counterpoint. A subplot running on a clock different from the main plot’s — slower, faster, or located in another period — whose function is to make the main plot’s pace legible by contrast, and to let the book represent a duration it could not otherwise contain. The argument for admitting it First: pace is invisible without a comparison. A novel whose events all move at one rate has no way to tell the reader that they are moving fast, or slowly, because the reader has nothing to measure against. Introduce a second chain running at a different rate and both become perceptible at once. Chapter 5 ( The Transition ) establishes that duration is a manipulable variable at the level of the join; temporal counterpoint is the same variable operated at the level of the book. Second: it lets a novel hold two durations at once. Some subjects require a long clock and some require a short one, and a single chain must choose. A novel about a family across three generations cannot also render three days in detail; a novel about three days cannot also render three generations. A second thread on a different clock is the only structure that lets a book do both without leaving narrative for summary. This is what the domain supplies in the strict sense the model requires: it is a capacity the main plot structurally cannot have, because a chain has one rate. Third: it is already in the tradition, unnamed. Bleak House runs Esther’s months against Jarndyce and Jarndyce’s generations, and the discrepancy is the novel’s argument about institutional time. Wuthering Heights runs two generations against each other, so that the second is read as a slowed and survivable version of the first. Contemporary dual-period fiction — Possession and The Hours are familiar instances — is built entirely on this relation, and the standard craft account of it, which treats the earlier period as backstory, misdescribes it: the past-period thread is a concurrent narrative line with its own chain, not an analepsis serving the present one. Fourth: it explains a common failure the other five domains cannot. Manuscripts frequently contain a secondary thread that is competently constructed, thematically related and properly converged, and still reads as inert. A recurring cause is that both threads run at the same rate, so the braid produces no rhythmic variation and the crossings feel arbitrary. That diagnosis is unavailable without the domain. Carriers Carrier Realisation Different scene-to-summary ratio One thread rendered scenically, the other in summary; Genette’s duration, applied thread by thread Different elapsed time per page The main plot covering days, the secondary thread covering years Different period A concurrent chain set in another era, braided rather than flashed back to Different event density Many small reversals against few large ones A clock the reader can see A deadline in one thread and an open horizon in the other; a lawsuit, a pregnancy, a season, a decline Under- and over-delivery Under-delivery: the rates differ but nothing is made of the difference; the reader registers unevenness rather than counterpoint. Under-delivery: the slow thread is slow because it lacks a chain, and “different clock” is being used to excuse an absent engine. This is the domain’s own version of the thematic alibi ( §8.13 ), and it is the strongest argument against admitting the domain at all. Over-delivery: the discrepancy becomes the book’s whole content, and the two threads stop being stories about people. Over-delivery: the slow thread’s rate makes it unreadable in isolation, so it survives only as an idea about structure. The argument against admitting it The case against is serious and should be put at full strength. It may be a mode rather than a domain. The other five name things a subplot supplies to the reader . Temporal counterpoint names a property of the telling . One could argue it belongs with the braiding structures of §6.4 — a way of executing a thread — rather than with the reasons for having one. It rarely appears alone. Every example above also serves thematic counterpoint. If a domain never occurs unaccompanied, it may be an aspect of other domains rather than a domain in its own right. It licenses a bad thread. Admitting a domain defined by rate gives every slow, inert secondary line a defence. The alibi risk is higher here than for any other domain in the taxonomy. The dual-period novel may be a genre, not a structure. If temporal counterpoint is really the description of a fashionable form, elevating it to a domain confuses a period style with a narrative capacity. The chapter’s own position is that (1) and (2) are answerable and (3) is not. The domain is admitted, with the standing requirement that a thread claiming it must also demonstrate a chain — and the reader should treat §4.6 as this chapter’s most contestable paragraphs rather than as settled doctrine. Chapter 8 ( Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture ) adopts the domain at the scale of the whole book as a property of the arrangement, claimed only where a crossing shows the difference of rate, which answers the objection this section could not; for threads in one time, the condition above stands (its Full Treatment, section 3.6). It adopts Chapter 4’s proposed temporal domain at the same scale. Seminar question. Is temporal counterpoint a sixth domain of purpose or a braiding technique misfiled? Argue the case using Bleak House ’s Chancery clock, Wuthering Heights ’ two generations, and one contemporary dual-period novel of your choosing. A strong answer will consider whether the same argument would force the admission of spatial counterpoint as a seventh domain — and if not, why not. 4.7 Summary: the six domains Domain Principal carriers Under-delivery Over-delivery Thematic counterpoint Parallel dilemma; inverted outcome; shared object; rhyming gesture Decorative rhyme; unmarked analogy Thesis thread; underlined rhyme Character testing ground Different register of pressure; relationship the main plot lacks; unexcused behaviour Anecdote; redundant testing Personality showcase; fragmentation Pacing relief Lower stakes; different tonal register; deferral across a break The holiday; relief without a chain Tonal breach; relief as dominant experience Structural convergence Supplied object, constraint or person; shared secret; collision Parallel line; convergence by proximity Mechanism thread; total convergence World expansion Different class, institution, place, faction or knowledge The tour; isolated territory The world eats the book; research on parade Temporal counterpoint (proposed) Different scene/summary ratio; different period; visible clock Unexploited unevenness; absent engine excused by rate Structure as content; unreadable slow thread 4.8 Must a subplot serve all six? No, and the attempt is a recognisable pathology. The domains are not a checklist but a budget , in the sense Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages ) uses for its contracts. What is required is not that all six be served but that the total be worth the page-share — and that at least one domain be served in a way the main plot could not have served itself. Three working propositions, offered as rules of thumb and marked as such. One domain alone is rarely enough , and the domain that most often appears alone is pacing relief. This chapter endorses the claim in its practical form: a thread that can only claim relief is a candidate for trimming, or — better — for being given the second job it could do in the page count it already occupies. Two domains is the working minimum, and thematic counterpoint plus structural convergence is the most durable pair. It is the combination readers describe as “essential” rather than “tolerated”, because the thread means something and does something. More than three declared domains usually indicates a co-plot, not a subplot. A thread doing four jobs is not an efficient subplot; it is a second novel that has not been recognised as one. When the audit at §5.5 returns four or more domains, the right question is §7.1 , test 10 — the promotion question — rather than a further round of tightening. And the anti-checklist qualification, which should be stated as firmly as the model itself: A subplot that serves one domain magnificently beats a subplot that serves four adequately. The domains describe what a thread can do, not how much it must do. The Ilyusha thread in The Brothers Karamazov would score poorly on a mechanical audit of world expansion and pacing; it closes the novel.

title: 5. Multiplicity at Book Scale
text: 5.1 The principle, stated as a constraint Multiplicity — the practice of making one unit of text discharge several narrative functions at once — is introduced in Chapter 1 ( The Purposes of a Scene ) and reappears in every chapter of this textbook. At the scale of the subplot it changes character, and the change should be stated. At sentence scale, multiplicity is an economy: a well-chosen noun does the work of a clause of explanation. At book scale, multiplicity is a survival condition , because the unit under discussion is too large to be justified by any single function. No writer would defend forty pages on the ground that they supply pacing relief. Forty pages must be doing several things, and the several things must be inseparable — which is a stronger requirement than doing several things in succession. The constraint can be stated arithmetically. A subplot occupying 15% of a 100,000-word novel costs 15,000 words . Those 15,000 words are drawn from a budget in which the main plot’s own chain, its sequels, its transitions and its ending are already competing. The reader’s tolerance for diversion is not proportional to the book’s length: it is roughly constant, and is spent per crossing rather than per page. From which the operative rule: The discipline is not to give the subplot more jobs. It is to find the version of the subplot in which the jobs are the same act. A thread that supplies thematic counterpoint in chapter 9 and structural convergence in chapter 27 is doing two things. A thread whose convergence is its counterpoint — where the object it hands the main plot is the object the comparison was about — is doing one thing that means two. This is the book-scale form of the distinction Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages ) §5.1 draws between compression and selection. Compression stacks functions; selection finds the material that already carries them. 5.2 Anatomy of a multiplying beat Multiplicity at this scale cannot be demonstrated on a sentence. It can be demonstrated on a single beat of a subplot, dissected element by element. The instance is the chaplaincy election in Middlemarch (Book Two, chapter 18). Lydgate — whose thread is nominally the novel’s second plot — must cast the deciding vote for the chaplaincy of the new fever hospital. Bulstrode, who funds the hospital, supports Tyke. Lydgate prefers Farebrother, who is poor, likeable, and needs the forty pounds. Lydgate votes for Tyke. Element of the beat Functions discharged The hospital needs Bulstrode’s money Subplot chain (Lydgate’s goal is medical reform); World expansion (provincial philanthropy and its conditions); Thematic counterpoint (Dorothea’s fortune, in the other thread, is also trying to buy a good) The vote is small, public, and procedural Character testing ground (an unexcused choice: nothing forces him); Pacing relief (a committee, after Dorothea’s Rome) Farebrother is likeable and needs the salary World expansion (the economics of the provincial clergy); Thematic counterpoint (a third version of vocation compromised by money) Lydgate votes for Tyke Subplot chain (the disaster is deferred and its interest begins to run); Character test (the first surrender, from which the rest follow); Structural convergence, prospectively (this is the debt to Bulstrode that Bulstrode will later call in) The narrator’s commentary on the pressure of a petty medium Thematic counterpoint made explicit; Temporal counterpoint (the slow accumulating clock of provincial compromise, against Dorothea’s clock of crisis) Five domains, one committee meeting, and not one of them is served by a passage inserted to serve it. Two features of the beat are worth extracting for teaching. The convergence is planted inside the counterpoint. Lydgate’s vote is simultaneously the novel’s argument about how vocations are bought and the specific mechanism by which Bulstrode will later acquire a hold over him. The thematic relation and the causal relation are the same event , which is the condition §5.1 names. The beat is small. It is a vote at a meeting. This is the characteristic form of book-scale multiplicity: not a large scene doing many things, but a small, ordinary, structurally exact one placed where several lines of force cross. Writers looking for multiplicity in their own subplots tend to look at the big scenes. It is nearly always in the small ones. 5.3 Where the work actually lives Novice revision looks for subplot integration in theme — in a stated resemblance, or an image repeated across threads. In practice, the integrating work is done in four humbler places, none of them figurative. A shared object or institution. A lawsuit, a house, a will, a hospital, a ledger. A reliable integrator, because it gives both chains something to do to the same thing, and because a reader’s memory holds objects better than it holds parallels. Bleak House has Jarndyce and Jarndyce; Middlemarch has the hospital and Featherstone’s will; the running example in §9.9 has a shop and a ledger. A crossing character who belongs to both chains. Someone with business in each thread, whose crossings are motivated rather than convenient. Stiva Oblonsky does almost nothing in Anna Karenina except connect; Inspector Bucket does it in Bleak House ; Farebrother does it in Middlemarch . The crossing character is what makes braiding feel like one world rather than two books, and a manuscript that lacks one usually reads as parallel play ( §8.1 ) whatever its thematic ambitions. A repeated decision-shape. Not a repeated image but a repeated kind of choice : in this book, people keep having to decide whether to say a true thing that will cost them. When the same shape of dilemma recurs across threads, the reader perceives unity without any statement being made — and the perception survives the long intervals that defeat imagery. The placement of the crossing. Which chapter break the braid is cut on is a structural decision that does integrating work by itself: a cut from the subplot’s small betrayal to the main plot’s large one asserts a relation that no sentence has to assert. Chapter 6 ( The Chapter Break ) supplies the mechanics under the names proposition and payoff ; this chapter supplies the reason to care. Imagery can integrate — Forster’s rhythm ( §3.1 ) is this — but it is the highest-risk instrument at book scale, because a figure repeated across a hundred pages is either missed or heard as authorial insistence, and the margin between the two is narrow. 5.4 The ceiling: how many chains can a book run? There is a limit, and it is not where writers expect it to be. The naive assumption is that the limit is a thread count — three threads good, five threads too many. The tradition falsifies this immediately: War and Peace carries four families and something close to a dozen traceable chains; Bleak House carries three systems and perhaps a dozen sub-chains within them. Neither is confusing to read. The actual constraint is a product of three variables. Variable What it does Consequence Crossing frequency How often the narrative changes thread High frequency keeps frames warm ( §3.7 ) but fragments each chain’s momentum Cast distinctiveness How easily a thread is recognised from a sentence Strongly individuated threads survive long dormancy; interchangeable ones do not Dormancy interval How long a thread is absent Beyond a certain interval, resumption costs a re-establishing scene ( §6.6 ) The ceiling is reached when the product of these exceeds the reader’s capacity to hold the threads as chains rather than as a sequence of episodes. Two failure signatures mark it: The reader can name the characters but not the questions. They know who everyone is and cannot say what any thread is trying to achieve. The chains have degraded into a cast. The reader stops preferring. A healthy braided novel produces preferences: readers of Bleak House skip ahead to Esther or to the Dedlocks. When a reader has no preference among threads, the threads have stopped being distinct enough to compete, which is the same fact as their having stopped being legible. The limit case: War and Peace . Tolstoy exceeds every convention this chapter states and the book is not confusing, and the reasons are instructive rather than magical. The threads are anchored to families , which are the most memorable unit of organisation available in a realist novel — the reader holds the Rostovs as one object even when six Rostovs are in play. The crossing characters are numerous and motivated. Pierre has business with the Bolkonskys, the Kuragins and the Rostovs; the network has no isolated nodes. The crossings are frequent and short. Tolstoy rarely leaves a family dormant for the length that would require reinstatement. The threads are differentiated by register — Bolkonsky austerity, Rostov warmth, Kuragin appetite — so that a paragraph identifies its thread before a name appears. That is the honest account of the ceiling: it can be raised, and the means of raising it are technical rather than inspired. §6.6 and §7.1 , test 8 make them operational. The obligation that comes with exceeding the hierarchy. A book that runs three or more chains without a primary one has become a multi-plot novel and inherits three duties it cannot decline: It must declare itself early , so that the reader does not spend fifty pages deciding which thread is the real one. Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages ) §4.6 makes the same point about the formal contract; a multi-plot novel that opens like a single-plot novel has mis-promised. It must make the relations between threads carry the argument , since it has surrendered the unifying effect of a single pursuit. It must converge or rhyme at the end , because a form organised by relation is judged by whether the relation resolves. Chapter 16 ( The Ending ) treats what resolution can consist of. 5.5 Exercise: the page-share and domain audit A practical procedure for a completed draft, and the most reliable single instrument in this chapter. List every thread in the manuscript, including ones you have not thought of as threads. For each, write the goal, the obstacle and the consequence in one sentence each. Threads for which you cannot complete all three go on a separate list marked presence, not plot ( §2.3 ). Count pages. For each thread, total the pages in which it is the primary business of the scene. Convert to a percentage of the whole. Mark domains. Beside each thread write the letters of every domain it serves: T (thematic counterpoint), C (character testing), P (pacing relief), S (structural convergence), W (world expansion), X (temporal counterpoint). Mark convergence. For each thread, note the page at which deleting it would break the main plot’s causal logic ( §3.4 ). If there is no such page, write none . Mark dormancy. For each thread, note the longest interval in pages between consecutive appearances. Then read the table. Pattern in the audit Diagnosis First move A thread with one domain letter and more than 8% page-share Filler at subplot prices Find the second job it could do in the space it already occupies, before considering cuts A thread with only P Pacing relief alone ( §4.3 ) Give it a chain, or fold its function into an existing thread A thread with convergence: none Parallel play ( §8.1 ), unless the book is a multi-plot novel Establish thematic convergence deliberately, or accept the structure and declare it (§5.4) A thread with four or more domain letters and over 20% share A co-plot in a book that has not admitted it Run the promotion test ( §7.1 , test 10) Longest dormancy exceeding 15% of the book Reinstatement cost will be paid at resumption See §6.6 ; insert a short crossing or accept a re-establishing scene Page-share high, convergence very late A large loan repaid at the last moment Check that the braid has paid in consistently ( §8.5 ) Two threads with identical domain letters Redundancy; they are doing the same job ( §8.4 ) Differentiate their relation to the main plot, or merge them No thread above 40% and no thread with none under convergence A functioning multi-plot novel Stop applying the attention tax and apply §5.4’s three duties instead The audit takes an afternoon for a full manuscript and is worth running twice, several weeks apart, because the first run is contaminated by what the writer intended and the second is closer to what is on the page.

title: 6. Braiding and Convergence
text: 6.1 Two clocks, one spine A book has one spine. Two chains running concurrently in story time must nonetheless be delivered to the reader in sequence, and the sequencing is a design problem with no natural solution — because nothing in the story determines where the cuts fall. Two operations are involved, and craft discussion routinely conflates them. Braiding — the interleaving of two or more chains in discourse time: how often the narrative changes thread, at what points, and in what proportions. Convergence — the relation the chains eventually bear to one another: whether, when and how the secondary chain intersects with, complicates, or resolves into the primary one. Convergence may be literal (the chains meet in event) or thematic (they never touch, and comment on one another by juxtaposition). Braiding is a question about the reading experience ; convergence is a question about the story’s architecture . A book can braid beautifully and converge not at all ( §8.1 ), or converge decisively after a braid so sparse that the convergence is unearned ( §8.5 ). The two must be designed together, and §6.6 is where the chapter says how. One further distinction, borrowed from Genette, prevents a common confusion. Narrative cannot represent simultaneity; it can only alternate, and the alternation is a property of the discourse , not of the story. Two threads that a reader experiences as running “at the same time” are in fact being read one after another, and every device that produces the impression of simultaneity — the cut at a moment of suspension, the overlapping clock, the shared event seen twice — is a discourse technique with a cost. Chapter 5 ( The Transition ) treats the costs; this chapter treats the pattern. 6.2 Historical grounding: where braiding came from Braided narrative is old and was not invented by the novel. Interlace. Medieval romance, particularly the French prose cycles and their English inheritors, used a technique the scholarship calls entrelacement : the narrative follows one knight until a point of suspension, leaves him, follows another, and returns, with the abandonment signalled by an explicit formula — now the tale leaves off speaking of X and returns to Y . Malory’s Morte Darthur preserves the formulas. Two features of the medieval practice bear directly on modern craft. The transitions are announced , which removes the orientation cost entirely at the price of the illusion of continuity. And the threads are held together by a shared quest object rather than by causal linkage — the Grail integrates threads that never meet. The Renaissance stage. Levin’s material ( §3.2 ). The theatre’s braiding constraint was the scene, and its integrating devices were analogy and social hierarchy rather than causality. The serial novel. The nineteenth-century monthly number is the form in which braiding became an industrial technique. A part had to contain variety, end at a point of suspension, and remind readers of threads last seen a month ago. Dickens’s surviving number plans — the working notes in which he allocated threads and chapters across each part — show the allocation being made deliberately, thread by thread, and they are the best documentary evidence available for how a braided novel was actually managed. Chapter 6 ( The Chapter Break ) treats the number plans in detail. The twentieth century and after. The modernist novel largely abandoned braided plots while intensifying braided consciousnesses : Mrs Dalloway alternates minds without alternating chains. The braided plot survived in genre, in the saga, and in the historical sequence, and returned to cultural dominance through long-form television, where the A/B/C structure is a production requirement ( §10.4 ). 6.3 What the scholarship gives the writer Three of the theoretical sources in §3 convert directly into design instruments. From Levin: a classification of the relation. Every pair of chains stands in a relation of analogy, contrast, direct linkage, or some combination. Naming the relation is the first design decision, and it is prior to any decision about braiding, because the relation determines how visible the crossings must be. Direct linkage can survive long dormancy, because the causal connection reasserts itself on resumption. Analogy cannot, because analogy exists only in the reader’s active memory. From Empson: the requirement of proximity. If meaning is produced by juxtaposition, the two terms must be juxtaposed — which in a novel is a fact about page distance , not about thematic relation. This is the strongest theoretical argument for tight braiding in analogically related books, and it is not usually stated in craft literature. From Chatman: a definition of the convergence point. The moment at which the subplot’s kernels become the main plot’s kernels ( §3.4 ). This gives the writer something to look for: not “where do they meet?” but “where does deleting this break the main story?” 6.4 A taxonomy of braiding and convergence structures Braiding and convergence are often treated as a single mechanism with one timing variable. What follows is a working repertoire of fourteen structures, each with characteristic purchases and costs. They are not mutually exclusive; most long novels use four or five, and the more interesting books use them in patterned sequence. # Structure Description Exemplar Buys Costs 1 The alternating braid Regular alternation between threads, usually at chapter breaks Bleak House ; Anna Karenina Frames stay warm; rhythm becomes a formal contract Predictability; a thread may be cut away from at a moment it needed 2 The block structure Long uninterrupted runs of one thread, then another Les Misérables ; The Sound and the Fury ; 2666 Immersion; each thread keeps its own momentum Maximum reinstatement cost; the reader may not want to leave 3 Early convergence The chains intersect in the first third and run entangled thereafter Great Expectations (Jaggers); The Brothers Karamazov Unity established cheaply; the subplot feeds the main machinery Sacrifices the pleasure of separateness; less late payoff available 4 Late convergence The chains meet at or near the climax Bleak House (Bucket’s pursuit); Vanity Fair (the letter) Large payoff; the reader’s two investments discharged at once Requires consistent braiding to be earned ( §8.5 ); risks contrivance 5 The repeated intersection The chains touch briefly and often, separating each time Middlemarch ; War and Peace Unity without resolution; each touch recolours both threads No single climactic discharge; can read as diffuse 6 The convergent cascade Threads converge in sequence, not together — one, then another, then a third Bleak House ; Our Mutual Friend Sustained late-book acceleration; each convergence raises the stakes for the next Requires a large cast and a long book; hard to control 7 Thematic-only convergence The chains never meet in event; the relation is analogy (Levin) Anna Karenina ; The Grapes of Wrath The largest possible thematic surplus; no contrivance The hardest to earn; readers trained on plot may register it as failure 8 The inverting subplot The secondary chain is constructed as the main plot’s contrast (Levin) King Lear ; Vanity Fair Instant legibility; the comparison does the argument Schematism; the inversion may exhaust its interest early 9 Promotion: the subplot becomes the main plot A secondary chain is revealed to have been primary Great Expectations (Magwitch); Wuthering Heights (the second generation) Structural reversal; retrospective recolouring of the whole book The reader’s investment must survive the transfer; hijack if unplanned ( §8.3 ) 10 The frame that converges by revelation An enclosing narrative turns out to be causally implicated in the enclosed one Wuthering Heights ; Frankenstein ; The Handmaid’s Tale (the Historical Notes) Reframes everything at once; very cheap in pages One use only; can feel like a trick if the frame was inert 11 The nested subplot A chain contained inside another character’s telling, or inside a document Don Quixote (the interpolated tales); Wuthering Heights Formal richness; distance; a second narrator’s judgement The nesting must be motivated; the reader may resent the second remove 12 Convergence resolved off-page The subplot’s outcome is reported rather than dramatised Middlemarch ’s Finale; War and Peace ’s First Epilogue Enormous compression; a wide social sweep in few pages Feels like abandonment if the thread had been braided as major ( §8.2 ) 13 The dropped thread A chain introduced and deliberately not resumed Moby-Dick (Bulkington); Vanity Fair ’s minor lines Realism of a world larger than the plot; refusal of tidiness Almost always reads as an error unless the dropping is marked 14 The digression proper Non-narrative material — history, essay, catalogue — occupying a subplot’s page-share Les Misérables (Waterloo, the sewers); Moby-Dick (cetology); War and Peace (the historiography) Scale, authority, an argument the narrative cannot make Fails every test in §7 ; survives on other grounds entirely ( §8.11 ) Seven of the fourteen require discussion beyond the table. 1. The alternating braid. Regular alternation is the safest structure and the one most likely to become invisible, which is both its virtue and its risk. Its underrated property is that regularity becomes a formal contract in the sense of Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages ) §4.6 : once a reader has learned that this book alternates, a departure from the pattern is legible as emphasis. Novels that establish a strict braid and then break it at the climax — running four consecutive chapters in one thread — are using the pattern as a rhythmic instrument, and the effect is unavailable to a book that never established one. 2. The block structure. The block is the highest-risk structure in the table and the source of the most common large-scale reading complaint, which is not confusion but reluctance . A reader two hundred pages into one thread does not want to leave it, and the transition is felt as a demand rather than as a variation. The books that succeed with blocks nearly always compensate by making each block generically distinct — a different voice, a different period, a different apparatus — so that the change reads as a new movement rather than as an interruption. 5. The repeated intersection. This is the characteristic structure of the great multi-plot novels and the least discussed in craft literature, because it has no climactic shape. Threads touch, affect each other by a degree, and separate: Lydgate treats Casaubon; Dorothea visits Rosamond; Farebrother carries a message. No single intersection resolves anything. The cumulative effect is a world in which everything is connected weakly rather than a plot in which two things are connected strongly, and that is a claim about society, not just a technique. Eliot’s web ( §3.8 ) is the theory of it. 7. Thematic-only convergence. The structure usually treated as merely permissible, and treated here as one of the tradition’s summits. Its requirements are strict: the analogy must be marked often enough to survive the intervals (§6.6); the threads must share enough world for the comparison to be legitimate rather than authorial; and the ending must place them in relation without forcing a meeting. §9.2 gives the definitive case. 9. Promotion. The structure most likely to be mistaken for an error, because it is indistinguishable in the middle of the book from a hijack ( §8.3 ). The difference is entirely one of design: in a promotion the transfer of primacy is the book’s argument , and the earlier main plot is revealed as having been a misunderstanding — Pip’s expectations were about Magwitch all along, and the reader’s misplaced investment is the novel’s subject. In a hijack the transfer is an accident of the writer’s interest, and the book’s centre of gravity moves without the book noticing. 13. The dropped thread. Almost always a failure, and included because the exception is so instructive. Melville introduces Bulkington in a page and then explicitly refuses to develop him, calling the short chapter his stoneless grave — a dropping that is announced, mourned and thematically loaded. The rule the exception yields: a thread may be dropped if the dropping is a narrative event. A thread that merely stops has not been dropped; it has been forgotten. 14. The digression proper. The digression has no chain, no goal and no convergence, and therefore fails the chapter’s definition at §2.1 outright. It is included because the greatest novels in the tradition contain a great deal of it, and because a chapter that could not say why Les Misérables is not ruined by Waterloo would have described a convention rather than a mechanism. §8.11 and §9.6 carry the argument. 6.5 How to use the taxonomy: substitution testing The taxonomy’s purpose is not classification but substitution .
