A subplot that is not working is very often the right material in the wrong structure, and the fastest diagnostic is to ask what the same thread would be under a different arrangement. Four substitutions worth running on any troubled thread: If the thread is currently Try What the substitution usually reveals A block the reader resists returning from An alternating braid Whether the resistance was to the thread or to the interruption A late convergence that feels contrived A repeated intersection Whether the chains had any business with each other before the ending A thematic-only relation the reader misses One or two literal intersections Whether the analogy was ever legible, or only intended A thread that keeps growing in revision Promotion Whether you are writing the wrong book ( §7.1 , test 10) The exercise is cheap because it is done on an outline rather than on prose. Re-chart the manuscript’s thread allocation on a single page — one row per chapter, one column per thread, a mark where each is active — and then redraw the marks under a different structure. Most structural problems are visible on that chart within a minute, and invisible in the manuscript for months. 6.6 Braiding rhythm: dormancy and reinstatement A subplot braided in once or twice and then absent for two hundred pages cannot cash in a climactic convergence. That is a commonplace of craft advice, and the cognitive literature ( §3.7 ) explains why, but the formulation leaves the writer without a working quantity. This subsection supplies one, with an explicit warning about its status. The mechanism When a narrative leaves a thread, the reader does not delete it. Emmott’s account ( §3.7 ) is that the contextual frame is primed — held in a recoverable state — and reactivated on return. Reinstatement is therefore a recall operation, and recall has three properties the writer can act on: It decays with interval. The longer the gap, the more cues are required. It is cheaper for distinctive frames. A thread with an individuated cast, setting and register is recalled from fewer cues. It is cheaper when the suspension left a question open. An unresolved question is an active memory item; a thread left at rest must be reconstructed from scratch. The third property is the writer’s most powerful lever and the one most often wasted. Leaving a thread mid-question costs nothing and sharply reduces the reinstatement bill. (The size of the reduction is an inference from the frame research, not a measurement.) This is the braided form of the deferred decision from Chapter 2 ( Scene and Sequel ) and the proposition–payoff mechanism from Chapter 6 ( The Chapter Break ). Working intervals The table below states conventions derived from practice and calibrated against the cognitive literature. They are not experimental findings. No study has established how many pages a novel’s secondary thread may lie dormant, and any source claiming a number should be distrusted, this one included. What the table offers is a scale on which a manuscript’s behaviour can be described. Dormancy interval (as % of the whole book) What resumption costs Typical handling Under 5% Nothing; the frame is warm Resume in the first clause: a name and an action 5–10% A cue One sentence re-anchoring person, place and the open question 10–20% A paragraph Re-establish the stake before the scene begins; the reader has the people but not the pressure 20–30% A scene The thread must be restarted, which the reader experiences as the book explaining itself Over 30% Effectively a new introduction The reader has lost the chain; the thread will read as late-arriving ( §8.5 ) however early it began Three refinements. The interval that matters is the longest one, not the average. A thread appearing in chapters 3, 5, 7 and 34 has an average interval that looks healthy and a single gap that destroys it. The audit at §5.5 , step 5 measures the maximum for this reason. Distinctiveness buys interval. A thread whose cast, place and register are strongly individuated can survive roughly one band longer than the table suggests. This is the operational form of §5.4 ’s second variable, and it is the reason the standard advice to differentiate secondary threads is correct for a reason rarely given: not for variety, but because distinctiveness is a memory subsidy . A convergence must be paid into, and the payments must be recent. The rule of thumb the chapter offers, and marks as a rule of thumb: a thread that converges at the climax should have appeared in the quarter of the book immediately preceding it. A convergence prepared entirely in the first half and executed in the last chapter is a promise the reader has stopped holding. The rhythm of the crossings themselves Beyond dormancy, the pattern of crossings carries meaning, and four patterns can be named. Pattern Description Effect Even Regular alternation throughout Formal contract; predictability; safe Accelerating Crossings become more frequent towards the climax The braid tightens; the reader feels convergence approaching before it arrives Decelerating Crossings become rarer as the book proceeds Threads settle into their own momentum; suits a book ending in separation Interrupted Regular, then a long single-thread run The break is emphasis; effective only where regularity was established first Accelerating is the default for a book with a literal convergence , and it is a technique writers rediscover rather than plan. It works because increasing crossing frequency raises the reader’s expectation of contact without any statement of it; the form is doing the foreshadowing. 6.7 Historical drift, and a caution against universalising the present The conventions governing subplots have moved further than those governing any other unit in this textbook, and a student should be able to historicise the advice rather than receive it as timeless. Period Dominant practice Typical relation between plots Medieval romance Interlace, with announced transitions Integration by shared quest object Renaissance drama Double and triple actions on descending social levels Analogy and contrast; frequently no causal link 18th-century novel Interpolated tales; the picaresque episode; the inset history Loose; integration by narrator and by moral commentary 19th-century multi-plot novel Braided plots at comparable weight; serial part-issue Repeated intersection and late convergent cascade Modernist novel Braided consciousnesses rather than braided chains Simultaneity; juxtaposition; frequently no second chain at all Mid-century to present, literary One chain, tightly held; subplots small and convergent Direct linkage strongly preferred; analogy distrusted Contemporary genre and saga Multi-viewpoint braiding at large scale Alternating braid; convergent cascade; promotion Long-form television A/B/C plots per episode over a season arc Industrialised braiding; convergence per season Two inferences follow, and they pull against each other, which is the point. The advice in §§4 , 7 and 8 is calibrated to the contemporary literary and commercial novel , whose length is a market fact ( §3.6 ) and whose preference for tight causal linkage is a period style rather than a discovery. Applied to a nineteenth-century novel it produces confident errors; applied to a saga or a television season it produces the wrong arithmetic entirely. The historical structures that violate it are not tolerated exceptions. Bleak House would fail a modern structural edit on at least four counts — cast size, thread count, coincidence, digressive social commentary — and it is widely ranked among the most formally accomplished novels in English. A pedagogy that can only say “an editor would cut this today” has described a market and not a book. The double position to hold. Learn the present conventions well enough to break them deliberately; read historically enough to know that they are conventions, and that the form’s greatest achievements were built when they did not hold.

title: 7. Diagnostic Method — the ten tests
text: 7.0 How to use the protocol The ten tests below are for revision, not composition . Applied during drafting they produce paralysis at a scale from which manuscripts do not recover; applied to a completed draft they are the most efficient structural triage available. Five procedural notes, one more than the other chapters in this book require, because the stakes are larger. Run them in order. Tests 1 and 2 are definitional: a thread that is not a chain cannot be assessed for tax, convergence or proportion, because the categories do not apply to it. Tests 3 to 5 are functional. Tests 6 to 8 are quantitative. Tests 9 and 10 are the ones that change books, and they are last because they should be asked only of a thread that has survived the others. Record the answer, not the verdict. The output of each test is a sentence describing what the thread does. “Fails test 4” is not usable information; “converges only at the party in chapter 31, and nothing before chapter 27 prepares it” is. A failed test is a question. Every test here is failed by at least one novel discussed in this chapter, and §8 supplies the counterexamples deliberately. The test’s job is to make a choice visible so that it can be confirmed as a choice. Run the protocol twice, weeks apart. At this scale the first run reports the writer’s intentions and the second reports the text. The discrepancy between the two is itself diagnostic. Apply the protocol to every thread, including the main plot. Several of the tests — the kernel test, the page-share audit, the promotion test — only produce information comparatively. A main plot that fails the kernel test is a discovery worth an entire redraft. 7.1 The ten tests Test 1 — The engine test Can I state this thread’s own goal, its conflict, and its consequence, in three sentences, without mentioning the protagonist’s goal? The chain requirement of §2.1 , in its operational form. Write the three sentences. If the goal sentence has to be phrased as helps the protagonist to… or makes it harder for the protagonist to… , the thread has no goal of its own and is main-plot machinery distributed across other people — which may be perfectly good writing and is not a subplot. If there is no goal at all, the diagnosis is presence, not plot ( §2.3 ), and the remedy is usually cheap: the scenes exist; supplying a want and a reversal converts inert page-share into a functioning thread. Interpretation. This test has three outcomes rather than two. Chain present proceeds to test 2. Chain absent, scenes valuable proceeds to a decision about whether to build a chain or reclassify the material as texture. Chain absent, scenes not valuable proceeds directly to test 9. Test 2 — The kernel test Are this thread’s turning points kernels within its own system — moments that open an alternative — or are they satellites even there? Chatman’s instrument ( §3.4 ). List the thread’s four or five chief moments. For each, ask: at this point, could the thread have gone another way? A kernel is a branching point. If every listed moment is elaboration — a further illustration of a condition already established, a further instance of a character being what they already were — the thread is a sequence of satellites and has no internal causality, whatever its page-share. Interpretation. The commonest result in a failing manuscript is a thread whose first moment is a kernel and whose remaining moments are satellites: something happens, and then the thread simply persists in the state that something produced. The remedy is not more incident. It is a second branching point, ideally one that reverses the first. Test 3 — The tax test What does this thread supply that the main plot structurally cannot supply on its own? The chapter’s first principle, asked directly. Name the domain or domains from §4 . The word structurally is load-bearing and is the whole difficulty of the test: the answer must be something the main plot could not do by its own nature , not something it merely happens not to do. Two answers that do not count: It shows another side of the protagonist. The main plot can do that, by applying different pressure within itself. It’s interesting. Interest is a precondition, not a function. Interpretation. If the honest answer names only pacing relief, apply §4.8 ’s first proposition: look for the second job the thread could do in the space it already occupies, before considering a cut. If the honest answer is nothing , the thread has failed the chapter’s central standard and the remaining tests are formalities — with one exception, which is that a book without a single primary investment ( §3.8 ) is exempt from this test and should be assessed at §5.4 instead. Test 4 — The analogy test What does this thread say about the main plot, and what would be lost if it were not said? Levin’s relation ( §3.2 ), asked as a demand for content. The test is not whether a relation exists — one always can be constructed — but whether the relation asserts something. Complete this sentence: Because this thread exists, the reader understands that the main plot’s [situation] is [qualified / inverted / costed / limited] in the following way: … Three failure signatures: The sentence comes out as Diagnosis …is also true of other people Duplication, not counterpoint ( §8.4 ) …could have gone differently — with no account of how Decorative rhyme ( §4.1 ) Any sentence the writer can produce but no reader has Unmarked analogy: a braiding-rhythm failure ( §6.6 ), not a thematic one Interpretation. Empson’s caution ( §3.3 ) applies: the relation may work below the level of paraphrase, and a thread that produces a strong effect the writer cannot formulate is not thereby condemned. But the writer should then be able to name where the effect is produced — which pair of scenes, in what order — and if they cannot, the effect is probably an intention rather than a fact. Test 5 — The convergence test At what page would deleting this thread break the main plot’s causal logic — as opposed to merely thinning it? Chatman again, and the convergence test in its sharpest form. Do not ask where the threads meet. Ask where the main plot would stop making sense without this one. If the answer is a page number, that is the convergence point, and everything before it is a loan. If the answer is nowhere , the convergence is thematic at best, and test 4 becomes the only justification available. If the answer is a page number in the final ten per cent, check test 8 immediately: a very late convergence requires very consistent payment ( §8.5 ). Interpretation. Writers routinely believe convergence occurs earlier than it does, because they are counting the points at which the threads touch rather than the points at which they depend . A thread whose characters appear in the main plot’s scenes for two hundred pages and whose deletion would break nothing has not converged; it has been visiting. Test 6 — The proportion test Is the space this thread occupies proportional to its contribution — and, separately, to its position in the book’s hierarchy? Two questions in one, and they come apart usefully. Contribution proportion. Compare the thread’s page-share against the domains it serves. A thread serving one domain and taking a fifth of the book is disproportionate whatever its quality. Hierarchical proportion. Compare the thread’s page-share against its emotional weight in the reader’s experience. The dangerous configurations are the two mismatches: a thread with high page-share and low weight (padding), and a thread with low page-share and high weight (an under-served co-plot, which is a commoner and more interesting fault). Interpretation. The second mismatch is the one most worth acting on, because the remedy is expansion rather than deletion, and expansion is what writers in structural revision least often consider. Test 7 — The page-share audit What percentage of the book does each thread actually occupy, and does the distribution match the book I think I have written? The quantitative instrument, run as described at §5.5 . Count pages in which each thread is the primary business of the scene; convert to percentages; compare against the bands at §2.2 . Three distributions and what they indicate: Distribution Indicates One thread above 60%, others under 10% A single-plot novel with minor subplots; the attention tax applies with full force One thread 40–55%, one 20–35% A double-plot novel; Empson’s and Levin’s questions apply, and §4 ’s hierarchy is only half-true Three or more threads between 15% and 35% A multi-plot novel; §5.4 ’s three duties replace the attention tax Interpretation. The value of the count is that it is frequently a surprise. Writers systematically overestimate the page-share of threads they enjoyed writing and underestimate the share of threads that grew during drafting. The number is not a verdict; it is a correction to the writer’s model of their own book. Test 8 — The dormancy audit What is the longest interval between consecutive appearances of this thread, and what does the resumption cost? Run as described at §6.6 . Note the maximum interval, not the average. Then look at what the manuscript actually does on resumption: count the words spent re-establishing before the scene begins. Interpretation. A resumption that requires more than a paragraph of re-establishment has revealed its own dormancy problem, and the re-establishing paragraph is the symptom rather than the remedy. Two remedies, in order of preference: insert a short crossing in the gap, which is cheap; or move the thread’s material so that the gap does not occur, which is not. A second reading of the same data: check whether the thread was left mid-question . A thread suspended at rest costs more to reinstate than one suspended at an open question (roughly twice, by this chapter’s estimate rather than any measurement), and the fix is free. Test 9 — The removal test Cut the thread entirely. What is lost, in what domain, and does the loss exceed the pages recovered? The most brutal instrument in the chapter. Three procedural requirements make it usable rather than merely painful. Perform the cut on the outline, not the prose. Delete the thread’s rows from the chapter chart described at §6.5 , and read the resulting book’s shape. Name the loss in domain terms. “It would be worse” is not a result. “The book would then contain no instance of a person choosing money over a person, so Lydgate’s choice would carry the whole argument alone” is. Then ask the harder question: could the loss be supplied more cheaply? Frequently a thread’s entire contribution is one relation that a single scene elsewhere could carry. This is the most common productive outcome of the test, and it is the outcome writers most resist, because it converts eighty pages into one scene. Interpretation. If the honest answer is that nothing identifiable is lost, the thread should go, and the writer should expect the cut to be far more painful than the diagnosis suggests. If the answer is that the book’s logic fails — not its richness, its logic — the thread has converged and the test is over. Test 10 — The promotion test Would the book be better if this thread were the main plot? Woloch’s question, asked of a manuscript ( §3.5 ). It is placed last because it is the only test that can invalidate the answers to all the others, and because it should be asked of a thread that has already been shown to work. The test is answered comparatively, in four parts: Which thread has the most at stake for the person inside it? Which thread’s ending would cost the reader more to lose? Which thread has been growing across drafts? Which thread do you re-read? Interpretation. Three outcomes. The main plot wins. Proceed; the book’s hierarchy is correct and the subplot’s role is confirmed. The subplot wins on one or two counts. The likely diagnosis is an under-served co-plot (test 6), and the remedy is proportional rather than structural. The subplot wins on all four. This is the discovery the protocol exists to produce, and it is uncomfortable. Two responses are legitimate and one is not. Legitimate: promote the thread and restructure the book around it ( §6.4 , structure 9). Legitimate: recognise that the book is a double-plot novel and stop ranking. Not legitimate: leave the arrangement as it stands and hope the reader’s investment follows the writer’s intention rather than the writer’s interest. It rarely does; the result is §8.3 . 7.2 Reading the results Failed tests Likely diagnosis First move 1 alone Presence, not plot ( §2.3 ) Supply a goal and a reversal, using scenes that already exist 1 and 2 Texture wearing a subplot’s page-share Reclassify as motif or runner; cut to the size of what it is 2 alone A chain with one branching point and a long tail of consequence Add a second reversal, ideally inverting the first 3 alone The thread is competent and functionless Look for the second domain before cutting ( §4.8 ) 3 and 4 Filler; the thread neither does nor says anything Cut, and check whether its one useful relation can be supplied in a scene 4 alone Relation intended, not delivered Usually a braiding problem: bring the compared scenes nearer ( §6.6 ) 5 alone Parallel play ( §8.1 ) Establish thematic convergence deliberately, or admit the multi-plot structure 5 and 8 Late convergence unpaid for ( §8.5 ) Braid the thread into the preceding quarter, or move the convergence earlier 6 and 7 Proportion mismatch If share is high and weight low, cut; if share low and weight high, expand 8 alone Dormancy Insert a short crossing; leave the thread mid-question next time 9 alone Nothing is lost by removal Cut, and expect to grieve 10 The wrong book has been written Promote, or re-conceive as a double plot; do not leave as is A warning about test 10. When the promotion test returns an uncomfortable answer, writers instinctively defend the existing hierarchy — because the main plot is the more finished object, has been outlined longest, and is what the book was pitched as. In this chapter’s judgement it is usually the wrong instinct. The subplot that keeps growing is information. It is the manuscript telling the writer where its energy is, and the energy is not usually wrong.

title: 8. Failure Patterns
text: Each pattern below is presented with its symptom , its mechanism (what actually goes wrong, as distinct from what the surface looks like), its persistence (why competent writers keep producing it), its remedy , and — indispensably — its exception : a published work that commits the fault and succeeds. The exceptions are the intellectual heart of the section. A pedagogy of prohibitions produces writers who can avoid faults and not writers who can make choices. In every case the pattern fails because of a mechanism, not because of a surface feature, and where the mechanism is absent the surface feature is harmless. At this scale the exceptions are unusually distinguished, which is itself an argument. Of the thirteen patterns below, the counterexamples include several novels widely ranked among the greatest in their languages. That is not an accident of selection. It is evidence that the rules describe a contemporary commercial norm with unusual precision and describe the novel as a form rather badly. 8.1 The Parallel Play Symptom. Two chains run the length of the book without ever intersecting causally or commenting on one another. The reader experiences two books stapled together and reads one of them impatiently. Mechanism. No convergence of either kind ( §4.4 ). The second chain’s kernels never become the main plot’s ( §3.4 ), and no relation of analogy or contrast is established ( §3.2 ), so the reader has no way to convert the diversion into meaning. The failure is not that the threads do not meet; it is that nothing about either thread changes because the other exists . Persistence. It is produced by a specific and very common drafting history: the writer had two ideas and could not choose. It also survives revision unusually well, because each thread is individually satisfying, and revision at scene level cannot see the problem. Remedy. Two, and the cheaper one is nearly always right. Either establish a thematic relation and mark it — bring the compared scenes into proximity ( §6.6 ), give the threads a shared object or decision-shape ( §5.3 ), let one thread’s characters know the other’s exist. Or accept that there is no relation, and cut the weaker chain to a novella. The exception. Tolstoy, Anna Karenina (1875–77). The Levin thread never converges with Anna’s in any plot sense, and the novel is the greater for it. The two chains are joined causally at the start — Vronsky’s pursuit of Anna releases Kitty, whom Levin marries — and thereafter touch only once, when Stiva takes Levin to Anna’s house late in Part Seven. Levin is enchanted for an evening. Nothing follows. It is a meeting without convergence , which is a structure a model requiring intersection cannot describe: the chains occupy the same room and remain causally independent. What holds the novel together is Richard Levin’s category of analogy (the critic’s, not the character’s), sustained over eight parts and marked constantly: two people who want to live truthfully, one destroyed by the attempt and one not; two households; two forms of jealousy; two confrontations with death; two ways of failing to be understood by the person one loves. Tolstoy himself insisted, in a well-known letter defending the book’s architecture, that the connection lay not in the plot or in the characters’ relations but in an inner one, and he compared the novel’s construction to a vault whose keystone cannot be located. This is the counterexample the chapter takes most seriously , and it is analysed at length at §9.2 . It breaks the rule that a subplot must meet the main plot, and is better for it. The rule is therefore restated in this chapter as a rule about relation , not about intersection — and a student who leaves the chapter believing subplots must meet the main plot has learned the wrong thing. 8.2 The Vestigial Subplot Symptom. A thread introduced early with apparent weight — a named character, a stated goal, several scenes — that is abandoned, or resolved in a line of reported summary a hundred pages later. Mechanism. A breach of the promise made by placement. Per Rabinowitz’s rules of notice, material given early prominence is read as load-bearing (Chapter 9, The Opening Pages , §3.2 ), and a reader who has allocated attention to a thread does not silently deallocate it. The abandoned thread does not vanish from the reading experience; it persists as an unredeemed promise, and unredeemed promises accumulate as a sense that the book is not in control of itself. Persistence. Drafting. Threads are begun to see where they go; some do not go anywhere; the opening scenes are good and survive the cut that should have removed them. Vestigial subplots are the fossil record of a book’s abandoned intentions. Remedy. Cut backwards. The instinct is to supply the missing resolution, which costs pages the thread has already shown it does not deserve. The cheaper operation is to remove the thread’s early prominence — demote the character, delete the stated goal, convert two scenes into one — so that no promise is made. The exception. Melville, Moby-Dick (1851). Bulkington appears at the Spouter-Inn as a figure of extraordinary promise: a tall, deep-eyed sailor around whom the narration visibly gathers. He reappears at the helm, receives a chapter of his own — a short one — and is then explicitly abandoned. Melville calls the chapter Bulkington’s stoneless grave and declines to say more. Why does this succeed where a thousand vestigial threads fail? Because the dropping is a narrative event. Melville does not forget Bulkington; he mourns him on the page, and the refusal to develop him becomes an argument about the sea’s indifference to the men it takes. The exception yields the rule in its usable form: a thread may be dropped if the drop is marked, and cannot be dropped if it merely stops. Compare §6.4 , structure 13. 8.3 The Main-Plot Hijack Symptom. The secondary thread becomes more compelling than the primary one. Readers report skipping ahead to it; reviewers describe the book as being “really about” the subplot; the writer notices that the subplot chapters are the ones they enjoy writing. Mechanism. The book’s centre of gravity has moved and the book’s structure has not. The reader’s investment follows interest, not outline, so the main plot’s climax arrives to a reader who has stopped caring about it — and a climax landing on an investment that has migrated elsewhere produces the flattest effect in fiction: an event of maximum significance and minimum feeling. Persistence. Two causes, both benign in origin. Secondary threads are written with less anxiety, because less is riding on them, and unanxious writing is often better. And a subplot is usually the newer idea, so it has the writer’s current enthusiasm while the main plot has their commitment. Remedy. Test 10 ( §7.1 ), honestly answered. Then promote, restructure as a double plot, or — least often correct but sometimes right — deliberately reduce the subplot’s page-share and interest. What cannot be done is nothing. The exception. Thackeray, Vanity Fair (1847–48). Amelia Sedley is the novel’s nominal sentimental heroine, and Becky Sharp is the thread that eats the book. Thackeray’s own attention visibly follows Becky; so does the reader’s; so does the critical tradition, which has spent a hundred and seventy years discussing Becky and finding Amelia trying. The novel survives — thrives — because the hijack is converted into the book’s argument . The subtitle is A Novel without a Hero , and the narrator’s ironic management of the reader’s preferences is a sustained demonstration that we would rather watch an adventuress than a good woman, and that our preference is not to our credit. Thackeray makes the reader’s own hijack the subject. This is the discrimination the pattern requires: a hijack the book knows about is a structure; a hijack the book has not noticed is a fault. See §9.5 . 8.4 The Redundant Mirror Symptom. The subplot restates the main plot’s thematic point so closely that a reader can predict its every beat from the main plot’s, and learns nothing from the repetition. Mechanism. Levin’s analogy collapsed into duplication ( §4.1 ). The double plot’s whole value is that the second treatment is in a different key ; where the key is the same, no comparison is possible, and juxtaposition produces emphasis rather than meaning. The reader experiences it as being told twice. Persistence. It is the failure mode of good advice. A writer told that subplots should “echo the theme” will construct an echo, and an echo is by definition the same sound. Remedy. Change one variable and only one. Give the second thread the same dilemma at a different social level, or the same choice with a different outcome, or the same outcome reached by an incompatible route. Contrast is easier to execute than analogy and is the safer default in a short book. The exception. Shakespeare, King Lear (c. 1606). The Gloucester plot is the most literal mirror in the canon: a father misjudges his children, trusts the false one, casts out the true one, and is destroyed and partly redeemed. Levin and Empson both build on it, and the doubling is so exact that Samuel Johnson’s admirers and detractors have argued about it for two hundred and fifty years — A. C. Bradley judged the double action a defect in dramatic clarity while conceding that it produces the play’s impression of universality. The reason the mirror is not redundant is that the two actions differ in every variable except their shape. Lear’s suffering is metaphysical and expressed in language of cosmic scale; Gloucester’s is physical, and its central event is an atrocity performed on stage. Lear goes mad and sees; Gloucester is blinded and sees. Where Lear’s plot asks what a king is when stripped of kingship, Gloucester’s asks what a body is when stripped of eyes. The doubling generalises the argument from a family to a world — which is the Empsonian surplus ( §3.3 ) — and it does so by keeping the pattern and changing the register. The mirror fails when it repeats the key, not when it repeats the tune. 8.5 The Late-Arriving Thread Symptom. A subplot introduced in the second half, or braided in twice early and then absent for two hundred pages, which converges decisively at the climax. The convergence lands on weight the book has not built. Mechanism. Reinstatement failure ( §3.7 , §6.6 ) compounded by an investment shortfall. The reader is asked to feel a payoff proportional to an investment they were never given the opportunity to make. The felt experience is not confusion — readers reconstruct the thread easily enough — but a specific flatness at the moment of maximum intended effect. Persistence. Late threads are frequently the solution to a plotting problem discovered in draft three, and solutions arrive at the point in the writing where the problem was noticed rather than at the point in the book where they must be planted. Writers then plant retroactively and under-plant, because the material feels obvious to them. Remedy. Braid backwards. The rule of thumb at §6.6 : a thread converging at the climax should appear in the quarter immediately preceding it, and should have been established in the first third. Two short crossings in the dormant stretch are usually sufficient and cost a few hundred words. The exception. Tolstoy, War and Peace (1865–69). Platon Karataev enters the novel in its fourth volume, has no prior existence whatever, occupies a modest number of pages, and carries a substantial share of the book’s moral resolution: Pierre’s transformation in the prisoners’ shed is the answer the previous thousand pages have been failing to find. By every rule in this chapter he arrives far too late. He succeeds because of a distinction the pattern must accommodate. Karataev is not a thread; he is a term. He has no chain, no goal and no reversal — he is a condition Pierre encounters, and what converges is not a plot but an idea the novel has been circling since Pierre’s first conversation about freemasonry. The reader’s investment is not in Karataev, whom they have just met; it is in Pierre’s question, which they have held for three volumes. A late arrival can pay off an early investment provided the investment was in the question rather than in the thread. That is the discrimination writers most often miss when defending a late thread, and it is a demanding one: the question must be live in the reader’s mind and must still be unanswered. 8.6 The Romance Bolted On Symptom. A love story runs beside a plot to which it is unrelated: the detective’s relationship, the soldier’s sweetheart, the scientist’s marriage. Its beats are generic, its obstacles are misunderstandings, and its outcome could be reversed without altering a scene elsewhere. Mechanism. Test 1 passes and test 3 fails. The thread has a chain — romance plots are easy to construct correctly, because their shape is culturally over-determined — and supplies nothing the main plot could not supply, because it is not about anything the main plot is about. The generic availability of the form is what makes it inert: a reader recognises the shape immediately and therefore attends to nothing. Persistence. Commercial expectation in several genres; the writer’s sense that a protagonist needs a private life; and the fact that a familiar shape is quick to supply when a manuscript needs more pages. Remedy. Make the relationship about the same thing the main plot is about , which usually means making it a site of the same conflict rather than a refuge from it. A romance whose obstacle is the main plot’s central value — the thing the protagonist will not give up — stops being bolted on and becomes the character testing ground of §4.2 . The exception. Eliot, Middlemarch (1871–72), the Fred Vincy and Mary Garth thread. It presents as the most bolted-on element in the novel: a courtship comedy, with an idle young man, a sensible young woman, and an obstacle (he must find a respectable occupation) that would be at home in a much slighter book. It occupies a substantial share of the pages and touches Dorothea’s story hardly at all. It succeeds because it is the novel’s control case on vocation . Dorothea wants a life of consequence and is denied one; Lydgate wants a life of consequence and destroys it; Bulstrode buys one with concealed money; and Fred — the least serious person in the book — is the only character who actually acquires a usable trade, by being taught it, slowly, by a man who keeps accounts. The romance is the mechanism: Mary’s refusal is what forces the training. Reverse the courtship’s outcome and the novel’s argument about work changes. A romance is bolted on when its outcome is thematically inert, and integral when its outcome is one of the book’s answers. 8.7 The Comic-Relief Thread Symptom. A humorous secondary line — the comic servant, the eccentric neighbour, the workplace banter — that lowers the pressure and does nothing else. Mechanism. Pacing relief alone ( §4.3 ), the single-domain thread that §4.8 names as the commonest justification failure. There is a second and subtler mechanism: comedy that does not know about the book’s seriousness reads as a breach of register rather than as relief, and the reader’s tonal frame is damaged rather than rested. Persistence. The phrase “comic relief” is itself the culprit. It names the function as relief, which invites the writer to supply nothing further, and it carries the authority of long usage. Remedy. Require the comic thread to know what the book knows. The test: could this thread exist unchanged in a book with a different subject? If yes, it is imported. The strongest comic subplots are the ones that treat the main plot’s central value irreverently — which makes them thematic counterpoint, and pays the tax twice. The exception. Shakespeare, Henry IV , Parts 1 and 2 (c. 1597–98). The Falstaff material is the origin of the phrase “comic relief” and its permanent refutation. Empson’s reading in “Double Plots” ( §3.3 ) is the argument in full: the tavern is not a rest from the play’s concern with honour but a sustained assault on it. Falstaff’s catechism on honour is the counter-thesis to Hotspur’s, and the two are set beside each other so that neither can be simply believed. The comic action is therefore not relief but the other half of an argument the serious action cannot make about itself. The pattern’s proper statement follows: comic relief fails when it is only relief. Falstaff is also the exception to §8.3, since he hijacks the plays so completely that Shakespeare had to kill him offstage in Henry V rather than let him near a king. 8.8 The Occupational Subplot Symptom. A thread that exists to give a character something to do. Usually a secondary character the writer likes, or a viewpoint character stranded between their main-plot appearances, supplied with a small pursuit to occupy the intervening chapters. Mechanism. The thread is constructed from the outside in: the requirement was pages for this person , and a goal was reverse-engineered to fill them. Such threads fail test 2 characteristically — their turning points are satellites, because nothing depends on the outcome, and nothing depends on the outcome because the outcome was not the reason for the thread. Persistence. Multi-viewpoint structures generate it mechanically. A book that alternates six viewpoints must give each viewpoint something to narrate, and the sixth character may have nothing to want. Chapter 13 ( The Viewpoint Shift ) treats the allocation problem; this is its plot-side consequence. Remedy. Reduce the character’s viewpoint share rather than inventing business for them. A character who appears in three chapters wanting something is stronger than one who appears in nine wanting nothing much. The exception. Tolstoy, Anna Karenina , the Oblonsky thread. Stiva has, after Part One, almost no plot: he wants a better-paid post, he sells a forest badly, he arranges dinners, he owes money. It is a set of small pursuits invented to keep a character in motion, and it occupies a real share of a very long novel. It works for two reasons that convert an occupational thread into a functional one. First, Stiva is the novel’s crossing character ( §5.3 ): he is Anna’s brother, Dolly’s husband, Kitty’s brother-in-law and Levin’s friend, and almost every crossing between the two great chains passes through him. His small business is the connective tissue the novel’s structure requires. Second, his small business is the novel’s economic argument : the forest sold below value to a merchant, the sinecure sought through connections, the debts that Dolly’s household absorbs. Levin’s agricultural chapters state the case about land and work directly; Stiva’s dinners embody its opposite. An occupational thread is redeemed when the occupation is the point. 8.9 Convergence by Coincidence Symptom. The threads join because of an improbability: the two characters turn out to be related, or to have been at the same place years earlier, or to arrive at the same door on the same night. Mechanism. A violation of the causal standard the book has taught the reader to apply. Chapter 2 ( Scene and Sequel ) establishes that a story is a chain of things that had to happen next; a coincidence is by definition a thing that did not have to happen, and placing one at the load-bearing joint is placing the weakest available material where the most weight falls. The reader’s objection is rarely to the improbability itself — real life is full of them — but to the convenience : the coincidence serves the author, and its serving the author is visible. Persistence. Convergence is hard and coincidence is easy. It also frequently enters late, as the repair for a structural problem discovered in revision. Remedy. Two, in order of preference. Move the coincidence earlier : an improbability at the beginning is a premise and costs nothing, while the same improbability at the climax is a cheat. And make the coincidence caused by character : if the two threads meet because both people wanted something that made them go to that place, the meeting is motivated even if its timing is lucky. The exception. Dickens, Bleak House (1852–53). The novel runs on coincidence at a density no contemporary editor would permit. Esther is the illegitimate daughter of the woman whose portrait she happens to resemble; the law-writer whose hand Lady Dedlock recognises is Esther’s father; Jo carries smallpox from the graveyard to the girl who is the dead man’s daughter; Guppy, Krook, Nemo, Miss Flite and the Jellybys are all connected. The coincidences are not defects excused by genius. They are the novel’s thesis in structural form : that a society which believes itself divided into separate compartments — Chesney Wold and Tom-all-Alone’s, Chancery and the brickmakers’ cottages — is in fact one connected system in which infection, guilt and money travel freely. Dickens states the argument explicitly when he asks what connexion there can be between the place in Lincolnshire and the outcast sweeper, and the plot’s improbabilities are the answer. Coincidence is a fault when it is a convenience and a technique when it is a claim about the world. The lesser exception is instructive for the opposite reason. Charlotte Brontë’s Jane Eyre has Jane collapse, starving and anonymous, at the door of her own cousins — one of the most notorious coincidences in English fiction, and one Brontë neither disguised nor justified. It survives because the novel’s mode is providential and the coincidence is legible as providence rather than as convenience. The genre licenses it. A realist novel of the same period could not have done it. 8.10 Convergence by Encounter Symptom. The threads converge because the characters meet. They are in the same room at the end; they are introduced; they speak. Nothing else changes. Mechanism. A meeting is not a convergence. Applying test 5 ( §7.1 ), the meeting does not break the main plot’s logic if removed — one could delete the encounter and both chains would proceed unaltered. This is the commonest false positive in the whole protocol, because the meeting looks like the thing convergence is supposed to be, and writers mark it on their outlines as the point where the threads join. Persistence. The visual convention of screen narrative, where the convergence of storylines is very often literalised as an encounter and where the actors’ shared frame does real work. Prose has no shared frame; a meeting must produce a consequence or it has produced an image. Remedy. Ask what each character wants from the other, and make the wants incompatible. Convergence is conflict, not contact. If neither party wants anything from the other, the encounter is a curtain call and belongs at the end, if anywhere. The exception. Joyce, Ulysses (1922). The whole book runs towards the meeting of Bloom and Stephen, and when the meeting arrives it is deliberately, almost aggressively inconsequential: two tired men, cocoa, a conversation at cross purposes, an offer of a bed declined, urination in a garden, and a parting. Nothing follows. Stephen does not become Bloom’s son and Bloom does not become Stephen’s father, except in the sense that the reader supplies. This is not a failed convergence but an anti-convergence, and it works because the novel has spent seven hundred pages establishing that contact between human beings is this partial. The two chains have been converging thematically all day — the Odyssey structure, the paternity motif, the parallel exclusions — so that the encounter’s emptiness is felt against a convergence that has already happened elsewhere. An encounter can be the convergence when the emptiness of the encounter is the point, and only then. 8.11 The Digression Symptom. A long passage of non-narrative material — history, technical exposition, essay, catalogue — occupying the page-share of a subplot. No chain, no goal, no reversal. Mechanism. It fails §2.1 outright and every test in §7 by definition, since the tests assume a chain. The reader’s experience is of the book stopping, and Chapter 7 ( Backstory and Flashback ) describes the resulting interest deficit : an open question is suspended and nothing narrative is offered in exchange. Persistence. Research; conviction; the writer’s belief that the reader needs this to understand. All three are frequently correct about the need and wrong about the delivery. Remedy. The standard one is to distribute the material through scenes. It is the right advice for most manuscripts and it is worth noticing what it costs: distributed exposition cannot make an argument, because an argument requires continuity. A writer who actually has an argument to make may reasonably decline the remedy. The exception, or rather the two exceptions, which are among the largest in the tradition. Hugo, Les Misérables (1862). The Waterloo digression occupies a substantial book of the novel and describes a battle at which none of the principals is present. The essay on the Paris sewers, the history of the convent, the disquisition on argot — all fail every test in this chapter. And Hugo does something with Waterloo that repays close study: at the very end of the digression, in its last pages, Thénardier robs the dead on the battlefield and in doing so appears to save the life of Marius’s father, which creates the obligation that governs Marius’s entire relation to the Thénardiers. The digression terminates in a kernel. A hundred pages of history are converted, in a paragraph, into the load-bearing joint of a subplot. Whether that redeems the hundred pages is a legitimate critical disagreement and is set as a seminar question at §12.2 . The sewer digression works differently: it precedes Valjean’s carrying of Marius through those sewers, so that the reader traverses the described space with him. It is a descriptive pause functioning as preparation, and it is the clearest case in the tradition of a digression paid for by what follows it. Melville, Moby-Dick (1851). The cetology chapters are more radical, because they are not preparation for anything. They are an attempt to know a whale by classification, measurement, drawing, history and dissection, conducted at length, and their function is to fail : the accumulation of knowledge that does not produce understanding is the novel’s argument, and the argument cannot be made in three pages because its subject is exhaustiveness. A digression can be justified by being unbearable , which is a defence no craft protocol can accommodate and which a chapter that suppressed it would be dishonest. See §9.6 for the full treatment, and §16 . 8.12 The Metronome Braid Symptom. The threads alternate on a fixed schedule — every chapter, or every other chapter — regardless of what either thread needs. Crossings occur where the pattern says rather than where the material says. Mechanism. The braid has become a container rather than a rhythm. Two costs follow. Threads are cut away from at the wrong moments: a scene reaching its disaster is interrupted because the rotation demands it, and a thread with nothing to report is visited because its turn has come. And the reader learns the pattern, which converts every crossing into an expected event and eliminates the emphasis a departure from pattern could have carried ( §6.4 , structure 1). Persistence. Regular alternation is easy to plan, easy to hold in the head during a long draft, and reassuring. It is also the structure most likely to survive from an outline into a finished book unexamined. Remedy. Vary the interval by need, and reserve regularity for stretches where it can be broken to effect. A practical procedure: mark on the chapter chart ( §6.5 ) every crossing that occurred because the material demanded it; if fewer than half are marked, the braid is a metronome. The exception. Steinbeck, The Grapes of Wrath (1939). The intercalary chapters alternate with the Joad narrative on something very close to a fixed schedule, and one strand of the braid is not a chain at all — the general chapters have no continuing characters, no goal and no reversal. By this chapter’s definitions the structure should be inert twice over. It succeeds because the regularity is the form’s argument . The alternation asserts that the Joads’ particular journey and the general migration are the same event at two magnitudes, and a regular alternation makes the assertion continuously without ever stating it. Vary the interval and the claim weakens. Chapter 2 ( Scene and Sequel ) reads the intercalary chapters as collective sequel; the structural point here is complementary — a metronome braid is a fault when the regularity means nothing and a technique when the regularity is the claim. 8.13 The Thematic Alibi This is the failure the domain model itself generates. Symptom. A thread defended, in workshop or in the writer’s own head, on the ground that it “explores the same themes”. No other justification is offered, and none is available. Mechanism. The Empsonian defence deployed without the Empsonian mechanism ( §3.3 ). Any two narratives placed side by side can be described as commenting on each other; the description is unfalsifiable and therefore worthless as a justification. The alibi is dangerous because it is true — the thread does share the book’s themes — while being irrelevant, since sharing a theme is a property of almost everything a writer writes. Persistence. It is the only defence available for a thread the writer cannot bear to cut, and it is socially unanswerable in a workshop, where disputing it looks like a failure of subtlety. Remedy. Test 4 ( §7.1 ), applied strictly. Require the writer to complete the sentence because this thread exists, the reader understands that the main plot’s situation is qualified in the following way… and to name the two scenes between which the understanding is produced. A thread that cannot survive this has an alibi rather than a function. The exception. Tolstoy, Anna Karenina , the Koznyshev and Varenka episode. In Part Six, Levin’s half-brother Sergey Koznyshev goes mushroom-picking with Varenka intending to propose. Both know it. He begins to speak, cannot, and says something about the difference between two kinds of mushroom; she answers; the moment passes, and neither ever refers to it again. The episode occupies two short chapters, has no consequence for any chain in the novel, and exists — by any structural account — to rhyme. Its rhyme is with the novel’s other proposal scenes: Levin’s first, humiliating refusal; Levin’s second proposal, conducted in chalk initials, in which two people understand each other perfectly without completing a word; Vronsky’s approach to Anna, which is not a proposal and cannot be. Set beside these, Koznyshev’s failure asserts something the other scenes cannot: that the capacity to say the thing is not distributed according to merit, intelligence or even desire, and that a life can be decided by two minutes in a wood. It is thematic counterpoint doing everything and nothing else, and it is among the finest passages Tolstoy wrote. The discrimination. The alibi fails when the thread’s thematic relation is asserted ; it succeeds when the relation is executed — when the reader, without being told, holds two scenes together and something occurs. The difference is not in the defence but in whether the book has done the work of proximity, marking and contrast that makes the comparison happen. §6.6 is that work. 8.14 Summary: symptom to mechanism Pattern Underlying mechanism Domains damaged Tests that catch it Parallel play No convergence of either kind S, T 5, 4 Vestigial subplot Promise made by placement, not redeemed S 2, 5 Main-plot hijack Centre of gravity moved; structure did not All 10, 6 Redundant mirror Analogy collapsed into duplication T 4 Late-arriving thread Payoff exceeds investment; reinstatement failure S 8, 5 Romance bolted on Chain present, function absent T, C 3, 4 Comic-relief thread Single-domain thread; register unattached P, T 3 Occupational subplot Thread reverse-engineered from a page requirement C 1, 2 Convergence by coincidence Weakest material at the load-bearing joint S 5 Convergence by encounter Contact mistaken for consequence S 5 The digression No chain at all — 1 Metronome braid Regularity without meaning; crossings misplaced P, X 8 Thematic alibi Unfalsifiable relation offered as function T 4

title: 9. Worked Analyses
text: Eight close readings and a revision case. The analytical apparatus is the same throughout: name the relation between the chains in Levin’s terms ( §3.2 ); audit the domains served ( §4 ); locate the convergence point by the kernel test ( §3.4 , §7.1 test 5); and describe the braiding structure and rhythm ( §6.4 , §6.6 ). Where a work is read in translation the translator is named, and the distinction stated in this book’s Introduction holds: structural claims survive translation, texture claims do not. Everything argued below about plot architecture would be argued from any competent translation. Nothing argued below depends on a sentence’s rhythm. 9.1 Eliot, Middlemarch (1871–72) — the web, and the definitive case The threads. Four, none of them subordinate: Dorothea Brooke and Casaubon, and later Ladislaw; Tertius Lydgate and Rosamond Vincy; Fred Vincy and Mary Garth; Nicholas Bulstrode and his concealed past. A fifth, the Featherstone inheritance, functions as a shared machine rather than as a chain of its own. A fact of composition that settles the theoretical question. The Lydgate material and the Dorothea material began as separate works . Eliot was writing a novel about a provincial town, with a young doctor at its centre, and separately began a story called “Miss Brooke”; she fused them, and the fusion is the novel. This is the strongest available evidence for the chapter’s central claim about relation: the two chains were not derived from one another, they were set beside one another, and everything that makes Middlemarch one book was constructed after the decision to combine. Levin’s relation: analogy, at the level of terms. The chains are not causally dependent. Dorothea’s marriage would proceed unchanged if Lydgate’s did not exist, and the reverse. What binds them is a question posed four times with four different answers: what happens to a person who wants their life to be of consequence, in a place that will not fund it? Thread The want What the town does to it The answer produced Dorothea To be of use through devotion to a great work Marries the work’s custodian and finds no work Consequence is displaced into private acts nobody records Lydgate To do original medical research in a provincial practice Marries a woman whose expectations require an income he cannot earn honestly Consequence is destroyed by domestic economy, in instalments Fred Nothing, initially Requires him to acquire a trade before he can marry Consequence is small, learned, and achieved Bulstrode To be an instrument of providence Requires the concealment of how the money was made Consequence purchased is consequence forfeited Domains served by the Lydgate thread. Thematic counterpoint at maximum (it is the novel’s second and harshest answer to its own question); character testing ground for the town rather than for a person — Lydgate is the instrument by which Middlemarch is tested; world expansion (the medical profession, hospital politics, the economics of provincial reform); temporal counterpoint (Lydgate’s ruin is slow , accumulating in small debts and small compromises, against the sharper crises of Dorothea’s marriage); and structural convergence, which arrives late and at a single point. Convergence, located by the kernel test. Apply test 5: where would deleting the Lydgate thread break the main plot’s causal logic? The answer is Chapter 81 , when Dorothea goes to Rosamond to plead Lydgate’s innocence and Rosamond, unexpectedly, tells her the truth about Ladislaw. Dorothea’s marriage to Ladislaw depends on that conversation, and that conversation depends on the Lydgate thread having produced a scandal, a wife and a reason for the visit. Everything before it is analogy; at Chapter 81 the second chain’s kernels become the first’s. Note what this means arithmetically. The Lydgate thread occupies something close to a third of the novel and converges causally on one afternoon. No modern structural edit would permit that ratio, and the ratio is the novel. Braiding. The repeated intersection ( §6.4 , structure 5) executed with unusual density. The threads touch constantly and lightly: Lydgate attends Casaubon and delivers the diagnosis that shapes Dorothea’s marriage; Farebrother carries messages between the Vincy and Garth chains; Bulstrode’s money touches everyone; Featherstone’s will draws four families to one house. None of these touches resolves anything. Their cumulative effect is a world in which everything is connected weakly — which is the argument. Eliot’s own theory. The narrator’s account of her method in Chapter 15 is the best short statement of multi-plot form in English: she says that she has so much to do in unravelling certain human lots, and seeing how they were woven and interwoven, that all the light at her command must be concentrated on this particular web, and not dispersed over that tempting range of relevancies called the universe. Three things follow from the figure, and they are the reason this passage is quoted in every serious discussion of the multi-plot novel. A web has no trunk. The image excludes hierarchy. There is no main strand and no subordinate ones; there are crossings, and the crossings are where the material is. The web is a limit , not an expansion. The sentence’s rhetorical work is renunciation: this web and not the universe. Eliot is describing a multi-plot novel as an act of exclusion, which is the opposite of the way expansive nineteenth-century structures are usually characterised. The metaphor is a theory of the attention tax with the sign reversed. Attention concentrated on the relations between lots, rather than distributed across separate lots, is what makes the concentration affordable. The Finale, and off-page convergence. Eliot resolves several threads by report ( §6.4 , structure 12), and the compression is deliberate: the Finale’s business is to place each life in a duration longer than the novel, which is temporal counterpoint ( §4.6 ) executed in the last four pages. Chapter 16 ( The Ending ) treats the Finale in full. 9.2 Tolstoy, Anna Karenina (1875–77) — the convergence that is refused Read in Constance Garnett’s translation; the structural account holds across Garnett, the Maudes, Pevear and Volokhonsky, Bartlett and Schwartz. This is the chapter’s central example , because it breaks the rule that a subplot must meet the main plot, and is better for it. The threads. Two, of comparable weight: Anna, Vronsky and Karenin; Levin and Kitty. Around them a third, weaker chain — Stiva and Dolly — which functions as connective tissue ( §8.8 ). What actually connects them, stated accurately. Craft accounts of this novel routinely assert that the two plots never touch. That is not true, and the truth is more instructive. Connection Where What it does to the chains A causal link at the start Part One Vronsky’s pursuit of Anna causes Kitty’s humiliation and illness, which releases her to Levin. The chains are causally joined once, at the beginning Continuous social contiguity Throughout Stiva is Anna’s brother and Levin’s friend; Dolly is Kitty’s sister and visits Anna; the two worlds share a city and a class One meeting Part Seven Stiva takes Levin to Anna’s house. Levin is charmed, goes home, is ashamed. Nothing follows No further causal linkage — After Part One, no event in one chain changes what is possible in the other The Part Seven visit is the detail that repays attention, because it is a meeting without convergence — a structure that a model requiring intersection has no name for. The two protagonists occupy the same room for an evening, and the novel’s causal architecture is entirely unaffected. Tolstoy engineers the encounter and then declines to use it, which is a far stronger statement than keeping them apart would have been: he demonstrates that contact is not the same as connection. The relation: analogy, sustained over eight parts. The chains ask one question — what does it cost to want to live truthfully? — and answer it twice. Anna’s chain Levin’s chain The demand To love openly and not lie about it To live honestly and know why he is alive The society’s answer Exclusion, then destruction Tolerance, mild ridicule, and no help The confrontation with death Her own, chosen, under a train His brother Nikolai’s, attended, in a provincial hotel The experience of jealousy Terminal; the last chapters are a mind consuming itself Recurrent and survivable; the wedding-day panic, the visit to Anna The ending Part Seven Part Eight, which the novel is structured to reach after What is understood That the truth she demanded cannot be had on any available terms Something he cannot articulate, about living for the soul, arrived at in a field Domains. Thematic counterpoint, unambiguously and at the highest level available to the form. Temporal counterpoint ( §4.6 ): Anna’s chain accelerates towards catastrophe while Levin’s proceeds at the rate of harvests, a wedding, a birth, a death, a haymaking — two clocks, and the difference in clock is a large part of the difference in fate. Character testing ground, in the sense that each chain tests what the other’s premises would produce. Structural convergence: none after Part One , and this is the point. The critical disagreement, presented rather than resolved. Whether the two plots are unified has been argued for a century and a half, and competent critics still disagree. The case that it fails. The chains are causally independent after Part One; the novel could be published as two books; the Levin material’s agricultural and philosophical passages digress from any plot at all; the reader’s investment is repeatedly interrupted at the worst possible moments. Contemporary reviewers, including some sympathetic ones, made versions of this complaint. The case that it succeeds. The unity is thematic in Levin’s exact sense ( §3.2 ) — analogy carried by an enormous number of small rhymes, marked so persistently that no reader can miss the comparison even while being unable to state it. Tolstoy himself, in a well-known letter responding to this criticism, insisted that the connection lay not in plot or in the relations of the characters but in an inner one, and compared the book’s construction to a vault whose keystone cannot be identified. A third position worth putting to a seminar. That the question is malformed, because it applies a unity criterion derived from drama to a form Tolstoy was deliberately constructing against drama. He denied that the book was a novel in the European sense; the refusal of convergence may be a refusal of the whole apparatus that makes convergence seem necessary. Braiding. Alternating, at part and chapter scale, with the crossings distributed evenly enough that neither thread goes dormant beyond §6.6 ’s second band. This is what makes the analogy work: Empson’s requirement of proximity ( §3.3 ) is met continuously, so that the comparison is always live in the reader’s memory. A novel with this convergence structure and War and Peace ’s block braiding would fail. The thematic-only relation is affordable only because the braid is tight. The lesson for the chapter. The usual rule requires convergence and permits it to be thematic. Anna Karenina shows that thematic convergence is not a lesser option granted on sufferance but a structure with its own demands — dense braiding, marked analogy, shared world, and a willingness to let a meeting happen and produce nothing. The rule is not converge . The rule is relate, and pay for the relation in the currency it takes. 9.3 Dickens, Bleak House (1852–53) — three systems and one secret The threads. Three, and they are systems rather than storylines, which is what makes the novel the most instructive convergence structure in English. Chancery. Jarndyce and Jarndyce; Richard, Ada, Miss Flite, Gridley, Krook, Vholes. A suit that consumes lives and finally consumes itself in costs. Chesney Wold. Sir Leicester and Lady Dedlock, Tulkinghorn, Hortense, Rouncewell. A marriage built over a concealment. Esther. Her origin, her illness, her face, her marriage; and Jo, Charley, the brickmakers, Tom-all-Alone’s, which belong to her narrative and are the novel’s third social level. Levin’s three-level structure, in full ( §3.2 ). Aristocratic, professional-middling, destitute — with the relations of analogy running down the ladder, and one secret running through all three. Levin’s Renaissance dramatists could not have asked for a cleaner instance. The convergence apparatus. Everything runs on one fact: Esther is the daughter of Lady Dedlock and the law-writer known as Nemo. The mechanism by which it is planted is the finest single piece of construction in Dickens. In Chapter 2, Tulkinghorn brings an affidavit to Chesney Wold. Lady Dedlock asks who copied it; the question is the merest social nothing; and she nearly faints. A reader has, at that moment, no idea there is anything to recognise. Handwriting is the plant, and it is planted before the existence of the secret is known — which is why the convergence, when it arrives four hundred pages later, feels discovered rather than arranged. Compare §8.9 : the coincidences that follow are enormous, and they are underwritten by this one act of preparation. Convergence by cascade ( §6.4 , structure 6). The threads do not converge together. They converge in sequence, and the sequence accelerates: Stage What converges Effect Guppy’s discovery Esther’s face, the portrait, the name The reader converges before the characters do Jo’s journey The graveyard, the infection, Esther’s face Chancery’s contagion reaches the Esther thread physically Tulkinghorn’s investigation Chesney Wold and the law The Dedlock thread is captured by the Chancery thread’s instruments Tulkinghorn’s murder All three A crime that requires all three systems to solve Bucket’s pursuit Esther and her mother, in a night Literal convergence at maximum velocity The costs consume the estate Chancery closes itself Resolution by exhaustion rather than by judgement Domains. All six, which is what a novel of this length permits. World expansion is the most conspicuous — Jo and Tom-all-Alone’s exist so that a claim about social connection can be made as narrative. Temporal counterpoint ( §4.6 ) is the least noticed and structurally the most interesting: Jarndyce and Jarndyce runs on a generational clock — it began before the novel and has consumed a lifetime — while Esther’s narrative runs on months. The suit’s slowness is not a background fact; it is the second clock against which every human urgency in the book is measured, and it is why the novel’s argument about institutions can be made without an argument being stated. Viewpoint and thread together. This is the one close reading in the chapter where the allocation of viewpoint and the allocation of plot cannot be separated. Esther narrates her thread in the first person and in retrospect; the other two are given to a present-tense panoramic narrator who can be in Lincolnshire and in Chancery in the same paragraph. The two narrations are themselves a double plot: an inside and an outside, a person and a system. Chapter 13 ( The Viewpoint Shift ) treats the dual narration as a viewpoint structure; the point here is that the viewpoint division and the thread division are the same division, and that this is why Bleak House can hold three systems without confusion. 9.4 Tolstoy, War and Peace (1865–69) — braiding at maximum scale Read in the Maude translation; the structural account is translation-independent. The threads. Four families — Bolkonsky, Rostov, Bezukhov, Kuragin — carrying perhaps a dozen traceable chains, plus the historical narrative of the campaigns of 1805 and 1812, plus a non-narrative strand of historiographical argument that expands until it occupies the Second Epilogue entirely. Why it is not confusing. §5.4 gives the general answer; the particulars are worth listing, because they are the transferable craft. Threads are anchored to families , which readers hold as single objects. The crossing characters are numerous. Pierre has business with all four families; Andrei with three; the network has no isolated nodes and therefore no thread that can be forgotten. Crossings are frequent and short , keeping every frame warm ( §6.6 ). Threads are differentiated by register. A paragraph of Bolkonsky austerity, Rostov warmth or Kuragin appetite identifies its thread before a name appears — the memory subsidy of §6.6 . The relation between the two halves of the title. War and peace are not main plot and subplot. They are a temporal counterpoint ( §4.6 ) organised as a moral argument: the war chapters run on the clock of a campaign, in which everything is decided in hours by people who do not know what is happening, and the peace chapters run on the clock of a life, in which everything is decided over years by people who also do not know what is happening. The rhyme between the two is the novel’s thesis about historical causation, and it is made by the alternation rather than by the essays. Where the essays fail and why they are there. The historiographical passages have no chain, no goal and no convergence, and by §2.1 they are digression ( §8.11 ). Tolstoy’s own justification is that the novel’s narrative demonstrates something the discipline of history cannot state, and that the statement must therefore be made directly. This is the honest position for a chapter like this one to take: the essays fail every structural test and are not thereby shown to be wrong , only to be doing something narrative does not do. Readers have disagreed about them since the first serial instalments, and the disagreement is set as a seminar question at §12.2 . The exception this novel supplies to the chapter’s own rules. Platon Karataev, discussed at §8.5 , arrives in the fourth volume and carries the resolution. The general principle extracted there: a late arrival can discharge an early investment when the investment was in a question rather than in a thread. 9.5 Thackeray, Vanity Fair (1847–48) — convergence by contrast The threads. Two, established in the first chapter as a matched pair and never allowed to separate for long: Becky Sharp, who has nothing and wants everything; Amelia Sedley, who has everything and wants one thing that is not worth having. Levin’s relation: contrast, executed as a formal system. The two chains are constructed as inversions at every level — origin, temperament, marriage, motherhood, relation to money, relation to truth. This is the most schematic use of a double plot in nineteenth-century English fiction, and the novel’s achievement is that the schema breaks under its own operation. Variable Becky Amelia What the pairing produces Origin An artist’s daughter, unprovided A merchant’s daughter, provided Fortune as an accident, not a desert Marriage Marries for position, manages the man Marries for love, is not loved Sentiment is not rewarded and cynicism is not punished Motherhood Neglects Rawdon minor, who loves her Idolises Georgy, who leaves her The novel’s least comfortable rhyme Relation to truth Lies fluently and to purpose Believes what is comfortable Self-deception is put on the same footing as deception Fate Survives, diminished, respectable-ish Marries Dobbin, ten years late Neither is rewarded; both are merely finished with Domains. Thematic counterpoint at the level of outcome and of terms simultaneously; world expansion (Becky’s chain reaches into places Amelia’s cannot — the Continent, the gaming table, the court, the demi-monde); character testing ground reciprocally, since each woman is the pressure applied to the other; and one decisive structural convergence. The convergence. Located by test 5: near the end, at Pumpernickel, Becky produces the note George Osborne wrote to her years earlier, proposing that they run away together, and gives it to Amelia. Amelia’s idolatry of her dead husband collapses; she is released to marry Dobbin. Delete the Becky thread and Amelia’s chain cannot resolve — she has no other route out of the sentiment that has held her for six hundred pages. That is the kernel test returning a page number, and it is a beautiful piece of construction: the object that converges the plots is a piece of paper generated by the subplot, kept for twenty years, and deployed as an act of malice that functions as a rescue. The hijack, converted. §8.3 treats this novel as the great counterexample to the main-plot hijack. The structural note to add here is that the hijack is managed by the narrator . Thackeray’s showman-narrator continually draws attention to the reader’s own preference for Becky, and the novel’s subtitle — A Novel without a Hero — is the formal declaration that neither chain will be permitted to be the moral centre. A double plot with no primary thread is a structure that requires a narrator willing to say so. 9.6 Hugo, Les Misérables (1862) — the subplot’s limit case Read in the Denny and Donougher translations; the structural account is translation-independent, and the digressions are complete in Donougher and abridged in some earlier English versions — a fact students should check before arguing about proportions. Why it is here. Because a chapter that could not explain Les Misérables would have described a convention rather than a mechanism. The novel contains at least four kinds of secondary material, and they need to be separated before anything useful can be said. Material Type Chain? Converges? Marius and the Thénardiers Subplot proper Yes Yes, repeatedly and decisively The Friends of the ABC and the barricade Subplot, entering as world expansion Yes Yes — it is where three chains meet Waterloo Digression No In one paragraph, at its very end The convent; argot; the sewers Digression No The sewers, by preparation; the others, not at all Waterloo, and the paragraph that changes the argument. The Waterloo book occupies a substantial stretch of Part Two and describes a battle at which no principal character is present. It fails test 1 (no chain), test 2 (no kernels), test 3 (nothing the narrative could not supply), test 5 (deleting it breaks nothing) and test 8 (it is a single uninterrupted block). And then, in its closing pages, a man moves across the field robbing the dead, lifts an officer clear of a heap of bodies in the course of stealing from him, and is thanked. The officer is Marius’s father; the thief is Thénardier; and the obligation created by that misunderstanding governs Marius’s entire relation to the Thénardiers for the rest of the novel, including his refusal to see what they are. A hundred pages of history are converted, in a paragraph, into the load-bearing joint of a subplot. Whether that redeems the hundred pages is a real disagreement, and the chapter declines to settle it. Two positions: It does not. A single kernel does not justify a proportion of the book; the same kernel could have been planted in two pages, and the digression’s actual function is authorial — Hugo wished to write about Waterloo. It does, and the terminal placement is the argument. The point of the digression is that the great historical event and the squalid theft are the same event seen at two magnitudes, and that the private consequence of Waterloo, for this novel, is a lie told by a thief. Compress the history and the disproportion — which is the meaning — disappears. The sewers work differently and more defensibly. The disquisition on the sewers of Paris precedes Valjean’s carrying of the unconscious Marius through them. It is a descriptive pause functioning as preparation: the reader traverses the described space before traversing it with him, and the passage’s exhaustiveness becomes duration. This is the clearest case in the tradition of a digression paid for by what follows. The general principle the novel yields. A digression is not a subplot and cannot be assessed as one. It is judged on whether the book has an argument that narrative cannot make, and on whether the writer is one of the small number who can hold a reader through an argument. The tests in §7 will condemn every digression ever written; that is a fact about the tests, and §16 says so. 9.7 Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov (1880) — the thread that takes the ending Read in the Pevear and Volokhonsky translation; also available in Garnett, McDuff and Avsey. The thread. Ilyusha Snegiryov, his father the disgraced captain, and the schoolboys — Kolya Krasotkin above all. It occupies several books of a very long novel and appears, on a first reading, to be the least connected material in it. Its causal origin, which is exact. Dmitri, in a rage, drags Captain Snegiryov out of a tavern by his beard in front of his son. Ilyusha, humiliated on his father’s behalf, bites Alyosha’s finger to the bone — Alyosha being the only Karamazov available.
