The subplot begins as a consequence of the main plot’s central conflict , which is early convergence ( §6.4 , structure 3) in its most economical form: the thread is causally generated rather than introduced. Domains. Character testing ground, primarily and superbly ( §4.2 ): the parricide plot gives Alyosha nothing to do — he mediates among adults whose positions are fixed — while the boys give him a situation in which his elder’s instruction about active love can be attempted and can fail. Thematic counterpoint: the novel’s great question is whether suffering can be justified, asked most famously by Ivan in the form of a tortured child; the Ilyusha thread answers it not with an argument but with a dying child and the people around him. World expansion: the town’s poor, its schoolboys, its doctors and its shame. The convergence, which is the novel’s last chapter. The Brothers Karamazov ends not with the trial, not with Dmitri’s sentence, not with Ivan’s illness or Alyosha’s vocation, but at a stone outside town after Ilyusha’s funeral, with Alyosha telling the boys that one good memory from childhood may be the thing that saves a person, and the boys shouting for Karamazov. Consider what that placement claims. The subplot has been given the privileged position — Rabinowitz’s term, treated in Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages ) §3.2 and inverted in Chapter 16 ( The Ending ) — which is the strongest structural statement a novel can make about what it thinks it is about. Everything in the main plot is left partly unresolved (Dmitri’s escape is a plan, Ivan’s recovery is uncertain, Grushenka’s future is open) and the secondary thread receives the closing chord. The lesson. The domain audit at §5.5 would give this thread three domains and a moderate page-share, and would not predict that it ends the book. Position is a resource the domain model does not measure. A subplot placed last is asserting that the book’s answer lives there, and the assertion is available at almost no cost in pages. It is, in this chapter’s judgement, among the most under-used structural moves in contemporary fiction. 9.8 Shakespeare, King Lear (c. 1606) — where the theory came from Included, though a play, because Levin’s and Empson’s arguments were built on plays of this kind. The threads. Lear and his three daughters; Gloucester and his two sons. Shakespeare took the second from a story in Sidney’s Arcadia — the blind Paphlagonian king — and grafted it onto the Lear legend, which had no subplot. Levin’s relation: analogy in the strong form, with contrast at the level of register. A father misjudges his children; trusts the false; casts out the true; is stripped, exposed, and partly redeemed by the child he wronged. The pattern is the same twice, and the novelty is what is changed: Lear Gloucester Nature of the error Demands a declaration of love and mistakes rhetoric for feeling Believes a forged letter Register of suffering Metaphysical; storm, madness, the heath Physical; an atrocity performed on stage The organ of the plot Speech — what can and cannot be said Sight — what can and cannot be seen The redeeming child Cordelia, who returns with an army and is hanged Edgar, who disguises himself and stays The end Cannot survive knowledge Dies of joy and grief together, offstage Why it is the origin of the modern discussion. Two positions, still live: The double action is a defect. A. C. Bradley judged the second plot to overload the play and to blur its dramatic clarity, while conceding that it produces an impression of universality unmatched elsewhere in Shakespeare. Earlier neoclassical criticism made the objection more bluntly, and it is the objection the attention tax formalises. The double action is the play. Levin’s argument, and Empson’s method. The doubling generalises: what happens to Lear is not a story about a foolish king but a fact about the world, and the only way to assert that in a play is to have it happen twice, to different men, in different registers. This is the Empsonian surplus ( §3.3 ): the meaning belongs to neither action alone. What the transfer to the novel costs. Two adjustments must be made before this example can be used in a fiction workshop, and both point back to §3.2 . A play is held in a single sitting. The analogy between Lear’s plot and Gloucester’s is perceptible across twenty minutes. In a novel the same analogy across eighty pages requires marking. What Shakespeare could leave implicit, a novelist must braid. The stage supplies simultaneity that prose cannot. Edgar leads his blinded father across the same heath on which his king went mad, and the audience sees the space. A novel must construct the connection in language, which is why §5.3 recommends the shared object over the shared image. 9.9 A revision case: Dov’s thread The following applies the diagnostic protocol to this book’s running example — a contemporary literary novel about three adult siblings, Elena, Nadia and Dov, reconstructing what their father withheld from them in the months before his death. The main plot is the sisters’ reconstruction: Elena wanting to know why their mother changed the locks in March, a question the book leaves open, and Nadia and Elena working out what the ledger in the shop records. Dov’s thread is the novel’s subplot. Two versions follow. Version A — the thread as recurring texture In this version, Dov’s financial situation is present throughout the novel as atmosphere. It has no chain of its own. Its appearances are: Chapter Appearance What the reader learns 3 Dov mentions, in the doorway exchange, that the shop is losing money The shop is in trouble 7 Elena notices unopened envelopes from the bank on the counter The shop is in trouble 12 A neighbour asks Nadia whether the family is selling The shop is in trouble 19 Dov is short with Nadia on the phone about “sorting things out” The shop is in trouble 24 Dov does not come to the flat because he is “seeing someone about the lease” The shop is in trouble 31 All three siblings are in the shop at the same time; Dov says he has been dealing with an offer; the ledger is on the counter and they read it together The shop was in trouble, and here is the ledger A representative passage, from chapter 12: The woman from the hardware place two doors down asked her, in the tone people used for asking about illnesses, whether they’d decided anything about the shop. Nadia said they hadn’t decided anything about anything. The woman nodded as though that were an answer, and went back in, and Nadia stood on the pavement a while and counted the shutters that were down along the row. Four, out of eleven. It had been two, in March. The writing is not the problem. The paragraph does several things well: it locates the shop in a declining row, it gives Nadia something to count, which is her established habit, and it sets a private grief against an economic one. Diagnosis Test Result 1 — Engine Fails. The goal sentence cannot be written without the protagonists. Dov does not want anything with a stated object; he is in difficulty , which is a condition, not a goal. There is no conflict beyond circumstance and no consequence beyond continuation 2 — Kernel Fails. Six appearances, no branching points. At no moment could the thread have gone another way. Every appearance is a satellite: a further illustration of a state already established in chapter 3 3 — Tax Partially passes. World expansion (the declining row) and a thin pacing relief. No domain the main plot could not supply 4 — Analogy Fails. The sentence because this thread exists, the reader understands that… completes only as …the family is also under financial pressure . That is information, not relation 5 — Convergence Fails. Delete the thread entirely and the main plot’s causal logic is untouched. The siblings still find the ledger; the ledger still says what it says 6 — Proportion Share is low, weight is low; formally proportional, which is why the fault is invisible in a read-through 7 — Page-share Roughly 4%. Below the subplot threshold at §2.2 — a runner , not a subplot, though the manuscript treats it as one 8 — Dormancy Longest interval about 18% of the book. Would matter if there were a chain to reinstate 9 — Removal Cutting the thread costs the book one motif and nothing else. The row of shutters could be given to a single paragraph elsewhere 10 — Promotion Not applicable; there is nothing to promote Patterns present: presence, not plot ( §2.3 ); the occupational subplot ( §8.8 ), since the material exists to give Dov something to be doing between his appearances; convergence by encounter ( §8.10 ), because chapter 31’s convergence is the three of them happening to be in the same room ; and the thematic alibi ( §8.13 ) in embryo, since the thread’s defence — “it’s about what the family is losing” — is true and functionless. The central observation. Version A contains all the necessary information . Its failure is not of content but of structure : Dov is doing things, and none of the things is a decision. A reader finishing this novel would be able to say what Dov’s situation was and unable to say what Dov did. Version B — the thread as a chain This is the version the book uses. The same character, the same shop, the same financial pressure, arranged as a goal–conflict–disaster chain in the sense of Chapter 2 ( Scene and Sequel ), with a convergence column. Beat Dov’s chain Convergence with the main plot Chatman ( §3.4 ) Goal Sell the shop before another season of losses None yet; runs parallel to Elena and Nadia’s investigation Kernel in his system; satellite in theirs Complication A buyer demands the building, shop and flat, emptied by the end of the month The deadline collides with Elena’s reading of the ledger. Dov clears the register drawer before telling anyone and takes the ledger home, so that Elena, coming back to finish what she began, finds the drawer empty; then he asks his sisters to clear the flat by the month’s end, without saying why. The main plot’s urgency now has an external cause A kernel in his system; in theirs, the first touch, though nobody in the main plot yet knows its cause Disaster Dov signs the papers without telling his sisters Registers as a betrayal inside the main plot too, sharpening the dilemma Elena weighed in her sequel in the truck (Chapter 2’s worked example) The first main-plot kernel: her options change Decision / Reveal Dov produces the one thing he held back from the sale — the ledger — and admits that the looser handwriting after March the ninth is his own Full convergence: the subplot resolves by handing the main plot its central piece of evidence, and recolours every earlier scene in which the ledger was mentioned The subplot’s kernels become the main plot’s; deleting the thread now breaks the book Domain audit. Two domains, stacked, which is §4.8 ’s working minimum and its most durable pair. Thematic counterpoint. Dov’s instinct to protect by silence is his father’s instinct: a man who documented his illness in the back of a ledger and told nobody, and a son who sells a building and tells nobody. The rhyme is not stated. It is produced by the reader holding two withholdings together, which is Empson’s mechanism ( §3.3 ) and Levin’s analogy ( §3.2 ). What the thread asserts is a qualification the main plot cannot make about itself: the sisters are investigating a concealment, and their brother is concealing in the same way, for the same reason, and believes he is being kind. Structural convergence. He supplies the evidence. The convergence is literal, late, and — this is the part that matters — the object that converges the plots is the object the counterpoint was about. The ledger is both the proof and the parallel. This is the condition §5.1 names: the two jobs are one act. A third domain is served more quietly. Character testing ground: the sale applies a pressure the investigation cannot, because the investigation tests what Dov will say and the sale tests what he will do when nobody is watching. The signature is unexcused behaviour ( §4.2 ): nothing forces him to sign in secret. What the revision did, procedurally Converted a condition into a goal. The shop is losing money became sell the shop before another season of losses . This is the whole of test 1, and it is the most transferable move in the case: a thread acquires a chain the moment its character wants something with an object and a deadline. Supplied a branching point. The buyer’s demand that the building be emptied by month’s end is a kernel: the thread can now go two ways. Version A had no moment at which anything could have gone otherwise. Made the subplot’s clock the main plot’s clock. The deadline is the mechanism by which a parallel thread starts exerting force before it converges. This is the supplied constraint carrier at §4.4 , and it is why the middle of the book stops feeling like two activities. The deadline reaches Elena as an empty register drawer and Nadia as Dov’s request that the flat be cleared by the month’s end, made without the reason; the second gives Nadia a motive for putting her hand into the pocket of the coat, since a coat’s pockets are checked before it goes, while the coat itself stays on its hook (Chapter 7). Made the disaster a betrayal in both systems. Signing in secret is Dov’s disaster inside his own chain (he has committed himself and cannot now retreat) and an event inside the main plot (it changes what Elena’s investigation is about). One action, two systems — the multiplicity condition of §5.1 . Placed the convergence on an object already planted. The ledger is first seen as an object in Chapter 4 ( The Descriptive Detail ), named once in a clause about where the father wore his coat, and the looser hand after March the ninth is Elena’s discovery at the chapter break that Chapter 6 ( The Chapter Break ) works; Dov’s chapter (Chapter 13) has by then shown the reader whose hand it is. Version B does not introduce a new object at the convergence; it explains to the sisters one the reader has been carrying for about half the book. Compare the handwriting plant in Bleak House (§9.3): the strongest convergences are recognitions. Withheld viewpoint until near the climax. Dov is observed from outside for most of the book, and receives a single bounded viewpoint chapter near the climax — the structure Chapter 13 ( The Viewpoint Shift ) analyses. The plot-side consequence is that his chain is reconstructed by the reader from evidence, which makes the thread’s kernels inferences rather than reports, and does a substantial part of the work of the subplot’s suspense without a single scene of concealment. Braiding and rhythm Feature Version A Version B Structure ( §6.4 ) Runner; convergence by encounter Repeated intersection, accelerating, with a late literal convergence Page-share ~4% ~12% Longest dormancy ~18% ~9%, with a crossing inserted in the second-act gap Convergence point (test 5) None The chapter in which he produces the ledger Domains W, weak P T, S, C What Version B has not solved Four problems remain, and a workshop that declared the revision finished would have taught the wrong lesson. First, the convergence carries a great deal of weight for a single scene. Dov’s reveal must simultaneously resolve his chain, deliver the main plot’s evidence, retrospectively explain the handwriting, and land the thematic rhyme with the father. Chapter 16 ( The Ending ) treats overloaded final scenes; the risk here is that the reader receives four discharges at once and feels the architecture. Second, the thread now risks the redundant mirror ( §8.4 ). Dov protects by silence as his father did, and the closeness of the match is the danger. Levin’s analogy requires a change of key, and the current change — a son concealing a sale, a father concealing an illness — may be too small a variation to prevent the rhyme reading as restatement. The available correction is to make the two silences differently motivated. The father kept the record so that someone could check it — that is what the good pen was for; Chapter 7 ( Backstory and Flashback ) gives the reason in his own words, and the prologue (Chapter 10) plants its first two words. Dov keeps the same ledger in the same book, and enters only the date and the count: nothing about the buyer or the deadline. He continues the form of his father’s honesty and empties it of its content. That is a change of key rather than a repetition, and it costs a paragraph. Third, the promotion test ( §7.1 , test 10) returns an uncomfortable answer. Dov has the most at stake of the three siblings, is the only one who acts irreversibly, and is the only one whose chain has a deadline. On three of the test’s four criteria his thread is stronger than the investigation it serves. This book has decided that the novel is Nadia and Elena’s and that Dov’s opacity is a large part of the reason the ending works — but that is a decision, not a fact, and a different novelist would write the other book. The right outcome of a diagnostic protocol is frequently a defensible choice rather than a repair. Fourth, the empty drawer opens a question the book must manage. Elena now wants to know who took the ledger, and the book must keep her from putting the question to Dov until the convergence, or the convergence arrives early. That she might suspect their mother, who changed the locks, would hold the question open without explaining the mother’s silence; whether it can do so without reading as contrivance is for a later draft to test.

title: 10. The Subplot Across Forms
text: The domain model and the attention tax were developed for the novel. They transfer to adjacent forms with adjustments that should be stated, because writers routinely import subplot habits into forms that punish them. 10.1 The short story The short story is the form in which the subplot is nearly always wrong, and the reason is arithmetical rather than aesthetic. Difference Consequence Total length 2,000–8,000 words A subplot at 15% is 300–1,200 words: too little for a chain, too much for a motif No room for dormancy Any interval long enough to feel like braiding is long enough to fracture a story One value shift is usually the whole design A second chain implies a second shift, which competes for the ending The reader’s investment is single by default The attention tax applies at full force and without qualification What stories use instead is the compressed analogy : a second situation glimpsed rather than narrated — a neighbour’s marriage overheard, a parallel case mentioned once, a story told inside the story. It supplies Empson’s juxtaposition at a cost of a paragraph. The nested subplot ( §6.4 , structure 11) is the only structure from the taxonomy that transfers to the story intact, and it transfers because nesting requires no braiding. The exception is the linked collection , in which each story is a thread and the book is the braid. There the relations are Levin’s — analogy and contrast, almost never direct linkage — and the convergence, when it occurs, is thematic by necessity. 10.2 The novella The novella’s characteristic subplot problem is that it is written by novelists. It has a novel’s tonal amplitude and a story’s page count, and a thread that would be modest in a 120,000-word book occupies a quarter of a 30,000-word one. The form’s usual solution is the single-scene subplot : a secondary chain whose entire existence is one scene early and one scene late, with the middle inferred. The Death of Ivan Ilyich uses a version of it — the colleagues’ reaction to the death at the beginning, and the household’s arrangements at the end, frame a life told with almost no second chain at all. The general rule: in the novella, prefer a second chain that is two scenes long over one that is six scenes long. The reader will construct the intervening chain, and the construction costs the book nothing. 10.3 Series and sequences The series introduces a structure the single novel does not have: a thread that is a subplot in one volume and the main plot in another . This is promotion ( §6.4 , structure 9) distributed across books, and it is the form’s chief structural pleasure. Three principles: A volume must be legible as a whole. A thread that only makes sense in book four has failed inside book two, whatever its eventual payoff. The convergence test applies per volume as well as across the sequence. Dormancy intervals should be calculated across the sequence, not within a volume. A thread absent for a whole book has been dormant for a year of the reader’s life, and §6.6 ’s final band applies with force. Series writers systematically underestimate this. Promotion must be prepared in the volume before it happens, not merely in the volume where it began. The reader’s memory is of the last book they read. Chapter 17 ( Series and Genre ) treats the series as a form, and the dormancy of threads across volumes. 10.4 The screen comparison, and what does not transfer Long-form television is the current home of braided narrative, and its vocabulary — A-plot, B-plot, C-plot , the season arc, the “runner” — has entered prose craft discussion wholesale. Two features transfer and three do not. What transfers. Per-unit resolution. The discipline of giving each episode’s B-plot a small completed shape is a good discipline for chapters, and Chapter 6 ( The Chapter Break ) makes the case. The accelerating braid. Television’s tightening of cross-cutting towards a finale is the pattern §6.6 recommends, arrived at independently. What does not. Involuntary reinstatement. A returning thread on screen re-establishes itself the instant a face appears. Prose has no faces; every resumption is paid for in words. This is the single largest difference between the media and the reason television can sustain dormancy intervals that would destroy a novel. Actor-driven page-share. Television allocates screen time partly for contractual and production reasons, which produces the occupational subplot ( §8.8 ) as an industrial by-product. Novels have no such excuse and should not imitate the result. The obligation to continue. A season must generate next season’s threads, which produces deliberate non-convergence. A novel that leaves threads open for a series instalment it may never write has borrowed a structural habit from an economy it does not share. 10.5 Translated fiction Four of this chapter’s eight close readings were written in Russian or French, and the reliance is not accidental: the multi-plot novel’s greatest achievements are largely continental, and an anglophone student meets them in a translator’s English. The distinction this book’s Introduction draws between structural and textural claims applies with unusual clarity here, and to the chapter’s advantage. Plot architecture is the most translation-stable feature of a novel. Braiding intervals, page-share, convergence points, the relation between chains — all are properties of the story’s arrangement, and all survive intact into any competent translation. A student can argue about the structure of Anna Karenina from Garnett, from the Maudes, from Pevear and Volokhonsky or from Bartlett, and the argument will be the same. Two cautions: Abridgement is a structural intervention. Several nineteenth-century French and Russian novels circulate in English in abridged or “reader’s” editions from which the digressions have been removed. A student arguing about the proportion of Les Misérables occupied by Waterloo must first establish which text they are holding. Volume divisions and part titles are frequently editorial. Where an argument depends on where a book’s Parts fall — and several arguments in §6 do — the division should be checked against the original publication rather than against a paperback’s table of contents. 10.6 Concordance: concept to novel A study aid. Each entry names the work that most clearly displays the concept. Concept Best displayed by Section The multi-plot novel; the web as a theory of form Middlemarch §3.8 , §9.1 Analogy sustained without causal convergence Anna Karenina §8.1 , §9.2 A meeting that is not a convergence Anna Karenina (Levin’s visit to Anna) §9.2 Levin’s three-level structure Bleak House §3.2 , §9.3 Convergence by cascade Bleak House §6.4 , §9.3 The plant that precedes the secret Bleak House (the handwriting, ch. 2) §9.3 Coincidence as a claim about society Bleak House §8.9 Coincidence licensed by genre Jane Eyre (the Rivers cousins) §8.9 Braiding at maximum scale War and Peace §5.4 , §9.4 Temporal counterpoint as moral argument War and Peace (war against peace) §4.6 , §9.4 Temporal counterpoint by institutional clock Bleak House (Jarndyce and Jarndyce) §4.6 , §9.3 A late arrival paying off an early question War and Peace (Karataev) §8.5 Contrast as a formal system Vanity Fair §4.1 , §9.5 The hijack converted into the book’s argument Vanity Fair (Becky) §8.3 , §9.5 Convergence by an object generated in the subplot Vanity Fair (George’s letter) §4.4 , §9.5 The digression, and its terminal kernel Les Misérables (Waterloo) §8.11 , §9.6 The digression as preparation Les Misérables (the sewers) §9.6 The digression that refuses to converge Moby-Dick (cetology) §8.11 The dropped thread, marked Moby-Dick (Bulkington) §8.2 , §6.4 The subplot given the ending The Brothers Karamazov (Ilyusha) §4.2 , §9.7 A subplot causally generated by the main plot The Brothers Karamazov §9.7 The analogical double plot, at its origin King Lear (Gloucester) §8.4 , §9.8 Comic relief that is not relief Henry IV (Falstaff) §8.7 The crossing character as connective tissue Anna Karenina (Oblonsky) §5.3 , §8.8 Thematic counterpoint with no other function Anna Karenina (Koznyshev and Varenka) §8.13 Promotion: the subplot revealed as the main plot Great Expectations (Magwitch) §4.4 , §6.4 The frame converging by revelation Wuthering Heights ; title: 11. Revision Checklist
text: Run each secondary thread in a completed draft against this list. Each item corresponds to a test in §7 or a pattern in §8 . Is it a plot at all? I can state this thread’s goal, conflict and consequence in three sentences without mentioning the protagonist. The thread has at least two branching points — moments at which it could have gone another way. Every one of its scenes descends causally from the one before it; I can trace the chain without a broken link. If it is a recurring character rather than a chain, I have said so and sized it accordingly. What it supplies I can name the domain or domains it serves, and the naming survives a sceptical reader. At least one of those domains is something the main plot could not supply by its own nature. If the only domain is pacing relief, I have looked for the second job it could do in the space it already occupies. I can complete: “Because this thread exists, the reader understands that the main plot’s situation is qualified in the following way: …” The thread does not restate the main plot’s point in the same key. Convergence I can name the page at which deleting this thread would break the main plot’s causal logic — or I have accepted that the convergence is thematic and paid for it with dense braiding. The convergence is a consequence, not a coincidence, and not merely a meeting. The object or fact that converges the threads was planted before the reader knew there was anything to recognise. Anything introduced with apparent weight is paid off, or its abandonment is itself a narrative event. Proportion and rhythm I have counted the page-share of every thread, and the distribution matches the book I think I have written. The longest dormancy interval is one the resumption can afford; where it is not, I have inserted a crossing rather than a re-establishing scene. The thread is left mid-question whenever it is suspended. A thread converging at the climax appears in the quarter immediately preceding it. Crossings occur where the material requires them, not where the rotation demands them. Hierarchy The thread does not structurally outshine the main plot — or, if it does, I have promoted it or declared the book a double plot. I have asked the promotion question honestly, and recorded the answer rather than the verdict. If the book has three or more co-equal chains, it declares that fact in its opening pages and accepts the three duties at §5.4 . Removal I have cut the thread on the outline and read what remains. I can name what is lost in domain terms, not in feelings. I have asked whether the loss could be supplied more cheaply in a single scene elsewhere.

title: 12. Studio Work
text: 12.1 Practical exercises Exercise 1 — The thread chart. Produce the chart described at §6.5 for a completed draft or for a published novel: one row per chapter, one column per thread, a mark where each is active. Do not annotate it. Then write 300 words on what the shape alone reveals — where the braid tightens, where a thread disappears, whether the crossings accelerate. Exercise 2 — The page-share and domain audit. Run the full procedure at §5.5 on a draft. Produce the table. Write 400 words on the two largest discrepancies between the audit and your prior sense of the book. Exercise 3 — The engine conversion. Find a recurring character in your draft who has no chain. Give them a goal with an object and a deadline, one obstacle, and one reversal, using only scenes that already exist. Write the three sentences of test 1. Then write 200 words on what the conversion cost in new material — the answer is usually startlingly little. Exercise 4 — Substitution testing. Take one troubled thread and re-chart it under three different structures from §6.4 — for example a block, an alternating braid, and a repeated intersection. Do not write prose. Write 400 words comparing what each arrangement buys and costs for this particular material. Exercise 5 — The convergence hunt. For a published multi-plot novel of your choice, locate the exact point at which each secondary thread’s kernels become the main plot’s ( §3.4 ). Give page references. Then write 300 words on how the author prepared each convergence, and how far in advance. Exercise 6 — The analogy sentence. For every thread in your draft, complete the sentence at §7.1 , test 4, and name the two scenes between which the understanding is produced. Any thread for which you cannot name the two scenes has a braiding problem; propose the crossing that would fix it. Exercise 7 — The dormancy repair. Identify your draft’s longest dormancy interval. Write the 200-word crossing that would halve it — a scene, not a summary — and place it. Then compare the resumption as originally written with the resumption after the insertion. Exercise 8 — Levin’s classification. Take a novel with two clear chains and classify their relation as analogy, contrast, direct linkage, or a mixture, giving textual evidence for the classification and identifying the point at which the relation changes. 600 words. Strong answers will find a novel whose relation changes more than once. Exercise 9 — The removal, performed. Cut your draft’s largest subplot on the outline. Write the resulting book’s synopsis in 500 words. Then answer, in writing: what is lost, in which domain, and could it be supplied in one scene? Keep the answer; do not act on it for a month. 12.2 Seminar questions Does Anna Karenina converge? §9.2 sets out three positions: that the plots are causally independent and the novel therefore fails a unity criterion; that Levin’s analogy is a sufficient form of unity; and that the unity question is malformed because it imports a dramatic criterion into a form built against drama. Take a position and defend it against the other two. Tolstoy’s own defence of the book’s architecture may be used as evidence but not as authority. Is temporal counterpoint a domain? §4.6 proposes a sixth domain and states four objections to it. Argue for or against admission, using Bleak House ’s Chancery clock, Wuthering Heights ’ two generations and one contemporary dual-period novel. A strong answer will address whether the same argument would force the admission of a spatial counterpoint as a seventh. Does the terminal kernel redeem Waterloo? §9.6 puts two positions on the Waterloo digression in Les Misérables . Is a hundred pages of history justified by the paragraph in which Thénardier robs Marius’s father, or is the justification a critical courtesy extended to a writer we have decided to admire? What would settle the question? Whose lives get plots? §3.5 argues that the distribution of chains across a cast carries an argument about whose experience is consequential. Test the claim against two novels of your choosing in which a large group of people appears constantly and is never given a chain. Is the absence a formal necessity, an ideological fact, or both — and does the distinction survive examination? Is the attention tax a description of narrative or of a market? §3.6 argues that contemporary suspicion of subplots is partly an artefact of book length, and book length is an artefact of publishing economics. If that is right, what remains of the tax as a narrative principle? Test the model against one novel from before 1900 and one from after 1990. Should the main plot always win? §7.1 , test 10 asks whether the book would be better with the subplot promoted. Consider Vanity Fair , in which the subordinate thread takes the book and the novel is improved, and one contemporary novel in which the same thing happens and the novel is not. What distinguishes the two cases — design, management, or something the reader supplies? 12.3 Assessment rubric For a submitted structural analysis of a braided narrative (2,000–2,500 words) accompanied by a thread chart, or for a portfolio of two subplot chapters (3,000–4,000 words) with a 1,000-word critical commentary. Band Craft / analysis (60%) Commentary (40%) Distinction The thread has a chain with at least two kernels; domains served are plural and inseparable; convergence is located by page and is a consequence rather than a coincidence or an encounter; braiding rhythm is designed and the dormancy intervals are affordable; the relation between chains asserts something the main plot cannot assert about itself Names the relation in Levin’s terms and defends the classification from the text; identifies the thread’s own risks, including the promotion question; engages at least two theoretical sources critically rather than decoratively; distinguishes what the model shows from what it cannot see Merit A chain is present with a clear reversal; two domains served, though the second is thinner; convergence located and prepared; braiding competent, with one avoidable dormancy Accurate self-analysis; theory applied rather than cited; risks acknowledged if not resolved Pass A chain exists; one domain served; convergence present but late or lightly prepared; braiding regular but unexamined Describes the structure accurately; theory referenced but not applied Fail No chain — presence mistaken for plot; no convergence of either kind; page-share unrelated to contribution; one or more failure patterns unrecognised Description without analysis; the thematic alibi offered as justification

title: 13. Glossary
text: Analogy (Levin) — A relation between plots in which the secondary action repeats the primary action’s pattern in a different key. §3.2 . Attention tax — This chapter’s term for the cost, in reader attention, of any material that diverts from the chain carrying the reader’s primary investment. The formal counterpart of Chapter 13’s empathy budget. §1.2 , §3.8 . Braiding — The interleaving of two or more chains in discourse time: how often the narrative changes thread, at what points, and in what proportions. §6.1 . Braiding rhythm — The pattern of crossings across a whole book: even, accelerating, decelerating or interrupted. §6.6 . Chain — A sequence of scenes linked by causality in the sense established by Chapter 2 ( Scene and Sequel ), such that each descends from the one before. The defining requirement of a subplot. §2.1 . Character-system / plot-system — Woloch’s term for the arrangement of character-spaces into one structure of distributed attention; this chapter’s extension of it to the distribution of chains across a cast. §3.5 . Contrast (Levin) — A relation between plots in which the secondary action inverts the primary one. §3.2 . Convergence — The relation a secondary chain eventually bears to the primary one. Literal convergence is intersection in event; thematic convergence is relation without intersection. §6.1 . Convergence point — The page at which deleting a thread would break the main plot’s causal logic; the moment at which the subplot’s kernels become the main plot’s. §3.4 , §7.1 test 5. Crossing character — A character with business in two or more chains, whose crossings are motivated rather than convenient. §5.3 . Called the hinge character in the first edition; renamed because Chapter 2 keeps hinge for its own term. Digression — Non-narrative material occupying a subplot’s page-share; has no chain and cannot be assessed by this chapter’s tests. §2.4 , §8.11 . Direct linkage (Levin) — A relation between plots in which the secondary action affects the primary one causally. §3.2 . Dormancy interval — The number of pages between consecutive appearances of a thread. The maximum interval, not the average, is diagnostic. §6.6 . Double plot — Two chains of comparable weight, neither clearly subordinate; the object of Empson’s and Levin’s studies. §2.4 . Entrelacement (interlace) — The medieval romance technique of following one thread to a point of suspension, announcing the departure, and taking up another. §6.2 . Kernel — Chatman’s term for a narrative moment that opens an alternative and cannot be deleted without destroying the narrative’s logic. §3.4 . Page-share — The percentage of a book in which a given thread is the primary business of the scene. §5.5 , §7.1 test 7. Presence is not a plot — The chapter’s shorthand for the distinction between a recurring character and a subplot: recurrence without a chain is not a secondary plot. §2.3 . Promotion — The structure in which a thread introduced as secondary is revealed to have been primary; and, in revision, the decision to restructure a book around a subplot. §6.4 , §7.1 test 10. Reinstatement cost — What a reader must expend to resume a dormant thread; a function of interval, distinctiveness, and whether the thread was suspended mid-question. §3.7 , §6.6 . Satellite — Chatman’s term for a narrative moment that does not open an alternative and can be deleted without destroying the narrative’s logic, though the discourse is impoverished. §3.4 . Subplot — A secondary chain of causally linked scenes with its own goal, conflict and consequence, running alongside the main plot and competing with it for page count and attention. §2.1 . Temporal counterpoint — This chapter’s proposed sixth domain: a thread running on a different clock, whose function is to make the main plot’s pace legible and to let the book hold a duration it could not otherwise contain. §4.6 . Thematic alibi — The unfalsifiable defence of a functionless thread on the ground that it “explores the same themes”. §8.13 .

title: 15. Further Reading
text: Annotated, grouped by what each source is good for . Starred items are the recommended first three. 15.1 On multiple plots specifically ★ Levin, Richard. The Multiple Plot in English Renaissance Drama (1971). The indispensable book for this chapter and still without a rival on its subject. Read it for the categories — analogy, contrast, direct linkage — and for the sustained argument that thematic relation is a form of integration rather than a substitute for one. Its examples are plays; the transfer to the novel requires the adjustments set out at §3.2 and §9.8 . ★ Empson, William. Some Versions of Pastoral (1935), chapter 2, “Double Plots”. Forty pages that changed how the double plot is discussed. Read it for the argument that juxtaposition generates meaning belonging to neither term. Empson is allusive and assumes his examples; read the Henry IV material first. Bradley, A. C. Shakespearean Tragedy (1904). For the opposing case, honestly made: the chapters on King Lear treat the double action as a defect of dramatic clarity while conceding what it gains. Useful because Bradley is not a fool and is not persuaded. 15.2 On the distribution of narrative attention ★ Woloch, Alex. The One vs. the Many (2003). The book that converts a craft metaphor into an analytic. Chapter 13 ( The Viewpoint Shift ) uses it for character; this chapter uses it for plot. The introduction and the chapter on Le Père Goriot are sufficient for most purposes. Chatman, Seymour. Story and Discourse (1978). For the kernel/satellite distinction, which is the sharpest single instrument in this chapter. The relevant discussion is short and can be read in an hour. Moretti, Franco. Graphs, Maps, Trees (2005) , and his later work treating plots as networks. For the argument that formal change in the novel is legible as a function of quantity and market. Contested, and worth arguing with. 15.3 On plot, causality and desire Brooks, Peter. Reading for the Plot (1984). For why readers want the main plot to continue, which is the psychological basis of the attention tax. The chapters on the dilatory space of the middle bear directly on §4.3 . Forster, E. M. Aspects of the Novel (1927). The chapters on pattern and rhythm are the oldest usable defence of a novel unified by shape rather than by causality — and, in the same pages, the most honest account of what such unity costs. Aristotle, Poetics . Short, and worth reading in full rather than in quotation, chiefly to discover how little of what is attributed to it is there. 15.4 Cognitive work relevant to braiding Emmott, Catherine. Narrative Comprehension (1997). The best available account of how readers hold and resume suspended narrative frames. Directly underwrites §6.6 , and the only cognitive source in this chapter that a writer will find immediately usable. Zwaan and Radvansky, “Situation Models in Language Comprehension and Memory” (1998). A review article; the clearest statement of the dimensions readers track and the costs incurred when they shift. A thread crossing shifts all of them at once. 15.5 Craft manuals, used critically Swain, Dwight V. Techniques of the Selling Writer (1965). The origin of the goal–conflict–disaster engine on which this chapter’s definition of a subplot depends. Mid-century American commercial pedagogy; mechanistic in idiom, structurally sound, and honest about its own purposes. McKee, Robert. Story (1997). For the screen tradition’s account of subplot function, which is the source of much prose craft advice on the subject and should be read as such. Its assumption of a single primary investment is the assumption §3.8 qualifies. Yorke, John. Into the Woods (2013). The clearest popular statement of the view that subplots must mirror the main plot thematically. Read it beside §8.4 and decide whether the mirror it recommends is Levin’s analogy or the redundancy the chapter warns against. 15.6 Within this textbook Chapter 2 ( Scene and Sequel ) — the goal–conflict–disaster engine and the causal chain, on which this chapter’s definition entirely depends. Chapter 5 ( The Transition ) — the mechanics of every crossing between threads, and the orientation costs they incur. Chapter 6 ( The Chapter Break ) — where the crossings are placed, and the proposition–payoff mechanism that makes suspension productive. Chapter 13 ( The Viewpoint Shift ) — the empathy budget; the same argument as the attention tax, applied to identification rather than to page space. Woloch is the shared source. Chapter 7 ( Backstory and Flashback ) — the interest deficit, and the distinction between a concurrent thread and an analepsis. Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages ) — the formal contract, which a multi-plot novel must open early ( §5.4 ). Chapter 16 ( The Ending ) — what convergence must finally deliver, and the problem of the overloaded final scene.

title: 16. Coda: Against the Pruned Novel
text: Everything in this chapter is an instrument for noticing. None of it is a rule. The evidence is in the chapter itself. Anna Karenina fails the convergence test. Middlemarch ’s second plot occupies a third of the book and converges causally on one afternoon. Bleak House runs on coincidences no contemporary editor would permit and is the finest convergence structure in English. Moby-Dick drops a thread it introduced with enormous weight, and interrupts its own narrative for hundreds of pages to classify whales. Les Misérables contains a hundred pages about a battle at which nobody in the novel is present. Vanity Fair ’s subordinate thread eats the book. Every one of these is a failure by the protocol at §7 , and the protocol is not thereby shown to be wrong — only to be an instrument calibrated for a particular kind of book. That kind of book is real, and most manuscripts are it. A novel with one primary investment, ninety thousand words, and a secondary thread that has grown without supervision is a common object, and the attention tax will diagnose it accurately every time. A writer who runs the ten tests on such a book will find the answer, and the answer will usually be that the thread has no chain, or supplies nothing, or converges by encounter. The model works. That is not in question. What is in question is the inference writers draw from its working — which is that a leaner book is a better one, and that the discipline of pruning is the discipline of the novel. It is not. It is the discipline of a form under length constraint, in a market that has been shortening books for a century, taught by a pedagogy that developed alongside that market and mistook its conditions for principles. The tests in §7 have no vocabulary for a book that wants to hold four lives at once and rank none of them. Applied to Middlemarch , the protocol asks which of the four plots is the main one, and the novel’s answer — that the question is the mistake, that the light must be concentrated on the web and not on any strand — is unavailable to a model built on hierarchy. A form that can hold four plots at once is not a form that has failed to prune. It is a form doing something a single plot cannot do: representing a society as a set of relations rather than a protagonist as a set of obstacles. Levin’s analogy and Empson’s juxtaposition are not consolation prizes awarded to novels that could not manage a convergence. They are the mechanisms by which a book says something about how lives stand to one another — which is a subject, and arguably the novel’s largest one. Two closing propositions, offered in the order in which a writer should hold them. First: run the protocol. Most subplot problems are the ordinary problems, and the ordinary problems have ordinary solutions. A thread with no goal, no reversal and no convergence is not a multi-plot novel in embryo; it is a thread with no goal, no reversal and no convergence, and the fact that Tolstoy did something superficially similar is not a defence. The counterexamples in §8 are not permissions. Each of them succeeds by a mechanism that the chapter has tried to name, and none of them succeeds by accident. Second: know what the protocol cannot see. It cannot see position, and a subplot placed last can assert what a subplot given twice the pages cannot ( §9.7 ). It cannot see the surplus Empson describes, which is produced between threads and belongs to neither. It cannot see a writer’s conviction that the world contains more than one story, which is a conviction the greatest novels in the tradition were written to act on. Which suggests the last and least mechanical question, to be asked after the other ten: Does this book contain more life because this thread is in it, or only more pages? The tests exist to make that question askable. They do not answer it, and a writer who wants them to has misunderstood what an instrument is for.

title: The Reveal
text: Disclosure, Withholding and the Second Reading: The Full Treatment The Craft Behind the Story (Second Edition), Reference — Chapter 15. Part III: The Architecture of the Whole. This chapter is new in the second edition, so its Reference layer is this single file rather than a corrected original. It extends the reader’s version in Core, The Reveal , and can be read without it: the definitions it relies on are restated in section 1. Illustrative passages are quoted briefly for the purposes of criticism and study, and full citations appear in section 10. Where a work is read in translation, the translator is named. The analyses disclose the endings of the works they discuss. Scope and working definitions A reveal is a disclosure of a fact the reader lacked that changes the reader’s understanding of what she has already read. The first half of the definition separates it from new information, which changes only what will happen; the second makes it retrospective. Every passage that bears on a reveal is read twice: the first reading is the one the reader made at the time, and the second reading the one the reveal makes. The movement between them is the double reading , and a reveal is prepared when the passages before it support both. A recognition , Aristotle’s anagnorisis , is a character’s change from ignorance to knowledge, the reveal received on the page. The two often coincide and need not: a reader can learn alone, and a character can learn what the reader already knew. The governing claim is that a reveal is earned when the pages before it bear two readings and when something inside the book, a character who does not know or a teller with a reason not to say, explains why the truth came when it did; and that it may reinterpret whatever the double reading reaches and falsify only what a teller in the book could have shaped. The claim is about preparation and authority, not about how surprising a reveal should be. A reveal the reader half expects can satisfy it, and so can a reveal disclosed in the first quarter. The chapter does not treat the mechanics of narrating the past once a reveal has made it necessary, which belong to Chapter 7 ; the arrangement of timelines that withholds by structure, which belongs to Chapter 8, Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture ; the prologue that discloses its ending in advance ( Chapter 10 ); the placing of a midpoint in the book’s shape ( Chapter 11 ); the character’s change of rule, as distinct from the reader’s change of understanding ( Chapter 12 ); the allocation of minds, which decides who can know what ( Chapter 13 ); the ending’s other duties ( Chapter 16 ); or the reveal held across a series and the genres that require one ( Chapter 17, Series and Genre ). 2. The theory at length 2.1 Aristotle’s recognitions The Poetics (S. H. Butcher’s translation) defines recognition in chapter 11 as “a change from ignorance to knowledge, producing love or hate between the persons destined by the poet for good or bad fortune”, and calls the finest recognition one attended by a reversal, as in the Oedipus . Chapter 16 ranks the kinds. Lowest are recognitions by signs, birthmarks, scars, necklaces, the “least artistic” because they need no plot. Next are recognitions invented at will by the poet, as when Orestes simply declares himself. Third is recognition by memory, when a sight or a song awakens a feeling, and fourth by reasoning, as in the Choephori : “Some one resembling me has come: no one resembles me but Orestes: therefore Orestes has come.” A fifth, which Aristotle calls composite, turns on a false inference by one of the characters. Best of all is the recognition that “arises from the incidents themselves, where the startling discovery is made by natural means”. The ranking anticipates two of this chapter’s tests. A recognition by token or by the poet’s fiat is a reveal from outside (test 8), because nothing in the chain of events produces it; the recognition from the incidents is the reveal whose source is the book’s own causal system. And the pairing of recognition with reversal is the earliest statement of consequence (test 6): the discovery is finest when it changes the discoverer’s fortune in the same movement. 2.2 Sternberg’s three interests and Barthes’s hermeneutic code Meir Sternberg’s Expositional Modes and Temporal Ordering in Fiction (1978), and his later essays in Poetics Today under the title “Telling in Time”, derive narrative interest from the relation between the order of events and the order of telling. Suspense is uncertainty about the future of the story; curiosity is uncertainty about a past the reader knows to be missing; surprise is the discovery of a gap the reader did not know existed. The three are produced by arrangement, and a single fact can generate any of them depending on when the reader learns that she lacks it. A reveal answers curiosity or produces surprise, which gives the chapter its curiosity reveal and surprise reveal . The distinction matters in revision because the two are prepared differently. A curiosity reveal is prepared by keeping the question alive, and readers are expected to guess at it; a surprise reveal is prepared by double readings that do not announce themselves, and a guess spoils it. Roland Barthes’s S/Z (1970; translated by Richard Miller, 1974), a reading of Balzac’s novella Sarrasine , names the code by which a text poses enigmas and delays their answers the hermeneutic code , and lists its devices: the thematisation and proposal of the enigma, its formulation, the promise of an answer, the snare (a deliberate evasion of the truth), the equivocation (a mixture of truth and snare), jamming (an acknowledgement that the enigma is insoluble), the suspended answer, the partial answer, and the disclosure. The list is a repertoire for the space between a question and its answer, and two of its items, the snare and the equivocation, are what section 5 calls the decoy reading and the equivocation. Barthes’s jamming is the declined reveal seen from inside a sentence. 2.3 Hitchcock’s bomb In his interviews with François Truffaut ( Hitchcock , 1966; English edition 1967) Alfred Hitchcock distinguished surprise from suspense with a bomb under a table. Unannounced, its explosion gives the audience fifteen seconds of surprise; shown in advance, with a clock set for one o’clock, it turns an ordinary conversation into fifteen minutes of suspense. The lesson concerns alignment , whether the audience learns a fact with a character, ahead, or after. Hitchcock applied it to Vertigo (1958), whose deception is shown to the audience two-thirds through, before the hero learns it; he told Truffaut that nearly everyone around him had been against the change. The trade is not always made in suspense’s favour: Hitchcock himself made Psycho (1960) on surprise. The principle is that the writer chooses it. 2.4 The fair-play codes The golden-age detective story made explicit what a reveal owes the reader. S. S. Van Dine’s “Twenty Rules for Writing Detective Stories” ( The American Magazine , 1928) and Ronald Knox’s “Decalogue”, the preface to The Best Detective Stories of 1928–29 (1929), require among other things that every clue be presented to the reader, that the culprit be introduced early, and, in Knox’s words, that the criminal not be “anyone whose thoughts the reader has been allowed to follow”, and that the Watson “not conceal any thoughts which pass through his mind”. Agatha Christie’s The Murder of Roger Ackroyd (1926), narrated by its murderer, was attacked for breaking such rules and defended, then and since, on the ground that its narrator states nothing untrue (section 6.1). The codes are a period convention for one genre’s contract, and they are not applied literally outside it. Their principle survives in two parts: the reader must have been able in principle to reach the second reading, which is the double reading; and no mind the reader shares may hide a thought without a reason the book can show, which is the withholder of section 5. 2.5 The unreliable narrator and paralipsis Wayne C. Booth’s The Rhetoric of Fiction (1961) called a narrator unreliable “when he does not speak for or act in accordance with the norms of the work”, and reliable when he does; the reader of an unreliable narrator reads past the narration to an implied author’s norms. Gérard Genette’s Narrative Discourse (1972; translated by Jane E. Lewin, 1980) adds two terms for departures from a narration’s chosen focalisation: paralipsis , giving less information than the focalisation would supply, and paralepsis , giving more. A withheld fact in a narration that follows the mind which knows it is a paralipsis, and the fair-play codes forbid it unless it is motivated. The two theories together give the teller rule of section 3.6. Booth’s unreliability belongs to a teller, a narrator with a character and norms of his own, and a reveal can expose it. A narration that has declared no teller cannot be unreliable in Booth’s sense, because there is nobody whose norms differ from the work’s; a reveal that requires it to have stated an untruth makes the work, not a teller, the liar. 2.6 The evidence The evidence is experimental and drawn from short texts. Hans Hoeken and Mario van Vliet ( Poetics , 2000) varied the discourse structure of one story and found that a version containing an unexpected event was rated higher and recalled better than one without, and attributed the difference to readers reassessing preceding events, which is the double reading measured. They also found suspense where readers knew the outcome, which supports Hitchcock’s trade. Jonathan Leavitt and Nicholas Christenfeld ( Psychological Science , 2011) gave readers short stories, among them ironic-twist stories and mysteries, with and without a paragraph disclosing the outcome, and found the spoiled versions rated more enjoyable. Benjamin Johnson and Judith Rosenbaum ( Communication Research , 2015), with longer stories, found the reverse: unspoiled readers reported more suspense and more enjoyment. Thomas Daniel and Jeffrey Katz ( Psychological Reports , 2019) found spoilers reduced the enjoyment of television episodes but not of short stories. The results disagree on whether knowing an outcome reduces pleasure, and agree that it changes the kind of interest a reader takes. A conjecture consistent with all four is that a reveal’s value lies less in surprise than in the rereading it prompts, which is the claim of this chapter on other grounds. 3. The extended catalogue of reveals 3.1 The four objects, and the reveal of world Core classifies reveals by what they change. The reveal of event discloses what happened ( Rebecca , 1938, where Maxim’s confession recasts every silence the narrator read as grief). The reveal of identity discloses who someone is (Magwitch in Great Expectations ; the dead psychologist in The Sixth Sense ). The reveal of motive discloses why an act the reader watched was done (Okonkwo’s fear at chapter scale, in Chapter 6 ; the father’s illness in the household novel). The reveal of telling discloses something about the text itself: its author, its purpose, or its untruth ( The Murder of Roger Ackroyd , Gone Girl , Atonement ). A fifth object, which Core folds into the others, is the reveal of world : a disclosure about the rules of the story’s world, which recasts the meaning of every ordinary scene at once. Kazuo Ishiguro’s Never Let Me Go (2005) discloses, gradually and then plainly, that its students were created to provide organs, and every scene of school life becomes a scene in an institution with a purpose. It differs from the others in range, recasting the world rather than particular passages. 3.2 The gradual reveal Not every reveal has a moment. In the gradual reveal the truth is disclosed in increments, each confirming what the reader has begun to infer, so that the double reading is performed progressively rather than at once. Never Let Me Go is the model: Miss Lucy’s statement to the students is a disclosure the reader has half anticipated, and the book’s interest moves from what is true to how the characters live with it. A gradual reveal fails if one increment is so much larger than the others that it reads as a twist the earlier increments gave away; it succeeds when the reader’s inference and the characters’ acknowledgement advance together. 3.3 The false reveal A false reveal is a disclosure presented as the truth and later shown to be wrong, so that the book contains two reveals, the second correcting the first. Its legitimate form gives the false disclosure a source the book can blame, a lying witness or a character’s mistaken inference, and lets the true one reinterpret it rather than void it. Its illegitimate form is the narration announcing a solution and then retracting it, which teaches the reader to believe nothing the book states. Knives Out (section 6.3) contains a false reveal of the legitimate kind. 3.4 The serial reveal A serial reveal is a chain of disclosures, each recasting the last. The chain works when each reveal reinterprets the previous one and the reader can hold all of them at the end; it fails, as the serial reveal of section 4.3, when each voids the previous one, since the reader stops investing in any reading at all. 3.5 The declined reveal: a ruling Chapter 13 proposed the epistemological domain, a grant of viewpoint made to show that no single vantage can know what happened, and adopted it for diagnosis while conceding three objections: that it may be contrast plus unreliability; that its examples cluster in modernist fiction; and that it names what a structure means rather than what a grant buys. It left this chapter to adopt or reject it at the scale of a book. This chapter adopts it at the scale of a book, as the plural-vantage form of the declined reveal : a book that holds a question of fact open to its end and shows the reader that it is doing so. The ruling meets the objections in turn. The first is answered at this scale because the scale supplies the test that Chapter 13 lacked: contrast plus unreliability ends in a reveal that tells the reader which account to discount, while the epistemological domain ends without one, so that a reader who adopted any single account would believe something the book will not confirm. The third lapses, since what a structure means is a reveal’s own subject; a domain that names meaning is out of place among the purposes of a grant and in place among the outcomes of a book. The second stands in part. The declined reveal is commoner in literary fiction, though The Affair ’s first season keeps its lovers’ memories unreconciled on screen, and Yann Martel’s Life of Pi (2001) ends by offering one teller’s two accounts and asking which the listener prefers, the same refusal made by a single voice. The declined reveal is wider than the epistemological domain. It includes the single teller’s refusal ( Life of Pi ) and the plain silence, a fact the book does not give and no account disputes, which is the household’s mother. Its condition is visibility: the question must be kept before the reader and the book’s other questions closed around it, as Chapter 16 required of the mother’s reason for changing the locks. A declined reveal the reader can no longer see is an abandoned thread. Barthes’s jamming is its signature in the sentence: an acknowledgement, in the text, that the answer will not come. 3.6 The teller rule and range Chapter 6 proposed the recasting close, a chapter ending that changes the meaning of the chapter it closes, and noted that over-delivered it voids the chapter. Chapter 16 ruled that the category stops discriminating at a book’s last line and passed on the question it leaves, how far a close may recast a whole book, from the parallel that adds a layer to the retrospective reframe that changes what the book was. The answer distinguishes reinterpretation from falsification. A closing reveal reinterprets a passage when it gives it a second meaning while its first remains a true description of what the reader was shown; it falsifies a passage when it declares that what the reader was shown did not happen. The range of a reveal is the set of passages it recasts in either way; the term is distinct from Chapter 7’s reach , Genette’s measure of how far an anachrony leaps from the present. Reinterpretation may extend as far as the double reading holds. Falsification is governed by the teller rule : a reveal may falsify only passages that a teller in the book could have shaped, and only if the reveal identifies the teller and the book gives the teller a reason. Atonement falsifies its Balham reunion within Briony’s authorship and gives her motive; Gone Girl falsifies Amy’s diary within Amy’s authorship and gives hers; The Usual Suspects falsifies its flashbacks within Verbal Kint’s telling. The Murder of Roger Ackroyd and The Sixth Sense falsify nothing and recast their whole length by reinterpretation alone, which is the safest way to a range of the whole book. A close that falsifies passages the narration vouched for on its own authority, the dream ending, the simulation nobody in the book was running, voids the book as the over-delivered recasting close voids its chapter. The recasting close therefore needs no separate category at book scale: a close may recast a whole book when every passage it recasts survives the double reading or lies within a teller’s account. The teller rule is a reader’s contract rather than a law, and section 8 notes the books it does not fit. 3.7 Summary table The table summarises the objects and positions by what each recasts and what it typically leaves the reader holding. The extended catalogue of failure patterns 4.1 The five patterns of the Core chapter Core gives five: the cheat, the giveaway, the reported reveal, the idle reveal and the reveal from outside, defined in section 9. The patterns below extend the catalogue. 4.2 The coy narrator Symptom. The narration keeps announcing that it is withholding: if she had known then , it would be years before he understood , had she looked more closely . Readers grow impatient, and the reveal, when it comes, has been anticipated so often that it lands as a relief rather than a surprise. Mechanism. The coy narrator turns curiosity into irritation by advertising a gap without feeding it. Each announcement is a promise the narration does not keep until the end, and promises without increments read as manipulation. It is a form of the giveaway, since it tells the reader there is something to give away. Remedy. Cut every announcement but one, and make that one carry information: a clue that bears both readings, not a statement that a clue exists. Exception. Markus Zusak’s The Book Thief (2005), whose narrator, Death, announces deaths in advance as a matter of style. It succeeds because the announcements disclose rather than withhold: the reader is told what will happen and left wondering how, so the coyness is converted into dread, as Chapter 10 discusses for its prologue. 4.3 The serial reveal that voids Symptom. The last act stacks twist on twist, each overturning the last, and readers end unsure what was true and uninterested in deciding. Mechanism. Each reveal in the chain falsifies its predecessor rather than reinterpreting it, so that no reading survives. The reader, taught that every disclosure will be retracted, stops investing in any. It fails the teller rule repeatedly, or passes it only by naming a new teller at every step. Remedy. Order the chain so that each reveal recasts the last without voiding it, and so that ranges shrink as the chain goes. Cut any reveal that exists only to overturn the one before. Exception. The Usual Suspects , which stacks reveals in its last minutes and succeeds because they all collapse into one, the identity of the teller, so that the chain resolves into a single double reading of the whole film. 4.4 The red herring that eats the book Symptom. A false trail occupies so much of the book that, when it is abandoned, a large part of what the reader invested in turns out to have been for nothing. Mechanism. A red herring is a passage built to support a false second reading. When it grows into a thread, with its own scenes and characters, its abandonment voids the thread, and the reader experiences the reveal as a loss of the book she was reading. It fails test 6 in reverse: the reveal’s consequence is to make much of the book idle. Remedy. Keep red herrings at the scale of a passage. If a false trail must be large, give it a second job, a character’s arc or a thematic variation, so that it is reinterpreted rather than voided when it is abandoned. Exception. Wilkie Collins’s The Moonstone (1868), in which suspicion of Rosanna Spearman and of Rachel Verinder occupies much of the book and is abandoned, and the book succeeds because both trails are reinterpreted rather than voided: Rosanna’s actions were real and had a motive, love for the man who took the diamond, and Rachel’s silence protected him. 4.5 The withholding viewpoint Symptom. A viewpoint character turns out to have known the truth all along, and readers who have spent chapters in her mind feel that her thoughts were edited. Mechanism. Paralipsis without a reason: the narration follows a mind that holds the fact, and the fact does not appear. Knox’s rule against hiding the Watson’s thoughts describes it. In close third person it is harder to excuse than in first, because the first-person narrator has a motive the reveal can disclose, while the close-third narration has no teller to blame. Remedy. Either show where the character’s attention is, so that the fact is plausibly not in her thoughts in the scenes the reader shares; or give the narration a teller, a retrospective frame, so that the withholding belongs to someone; or move the viewpoint away from the knowing character in the scenes where the fact would surface. Exception. The household novel’s prologue ( Chapter 10 ), which follows the father on a day when he knows he is ill and does not name the illness. It holds, for most readers, because his attention is shown to be elsewhere, on the till, the boy, the pen, and because the one sentence that touches his knowledge, he could not have said in case of what , is an equivocation (section 7.2). It is the book’s nearest approach to the pattern. 5. The diagnostic procedures The tests use two documents. The double-reading table lists every passage bearing on one reveal, in book order, with its position as a percentage, its first reading and its second. The disclosure map has a row for each withheld fact and a column for the reader and for each major character, with the position at which each learns it; a cell may say never . Draft both before revising. Test 1, double reading. Read down the table and mark rows with one reading. A row with only a first reading is a candidate cheat; check it against test 2. A row with only a second is a giveaway; give it a first reading or cut it. Then look at the spread: more than half the rows in the last fifth of the book is an approach, and a reader will feel the reveal coming. Test 2, teller. For each passage the reveal falsifies, write who could have shaped it. If the answer is the narration , and the book has no declared narrator with a character of his own, the passage must be rewritten or reassigned. Test 3, withholder. Name the withholder of each reveal: a vantage that does not know, a teller with a motive, or an arrangement. For a vantage, write the reason for its ignorance and the place the reader sees it; for a teller, the motive and the place it is disclosed; for an arrangement, the convention that makes it acceptable. A reveal with no name in this column is the withholding viewpoint or the cheat. Test 4, alignment. For each row of the disclosure map, compare the reader’s column with the characters’. Where the reader is ahead, check that the gap is used as suspense; where she is level, check that the recognition is staged; where she is behind a character she follows, apply test 3. Test 5, successor. For each reveal before the last fifth, write the question it answers and the question it leaves, and compare them. If the second is weaker, move the reveal or find the decision it forces. Test 6, consequence. For each reveal, list the characters who act differently because of it and what the ending means because of it. An empty list is the idle reveal. Test 7, recognition. Find the scene in which each reveal is received. Mark whether the truth is found or told, and whether the finder does something on the page. Test 8, source. Trace each disclosure to its source and the source to its first appearance. A source first seen within a chapter of the reveal fails unless the genre’s contract allows it. 6. Further analyses 6.1 The Murder of Roger Ackroyd (1926): the range of the whole book without a falsehood Dr James Sheppard, a village doctor, narrates the investigation of the murder of Roger Ackroyd, conducted by Hercule Poirot, who has retired next door to grow vegetable marrows. Sheppard acts as Poirot’s companion and records the case. In the last chapters Poirot shows that Sheppard is the murderer, and the final chapter, “Apologia”, is Sheppard’s confession, written as he prepares to take his own life. He explains that he had begun the manuscript as an account of Poirot’s failure. The reveal is of identity and of telling at once, and its range is the whole book by reinterpretation alone. Sheppard’s narration omits but does not state an untruth. At the point where he removed the dictaphone and moved the chair after the murder he writes that he did what little had to be done, which is true under both readings, an equivocation in the sense of Core’s mechanism. The withholder is a teller with a motive, invisible until the end, which is why the book fails test 3 at the moment of reading and passes it in retrospect; it is Core’s exception to that test. The fair-play objection, that a narrator the reader follows hid his thoughts, is answered by the teller rule: Sheppard is a teller, his manuscript has a purpose the last chapter discloses, and the concealment belongs to him. A close-third version of the same plot, with no manuscript and no teller, would have been the withholding viewpoint of section 4.5. 6.2 The Silent Patient (2019): withholding by arrangement Alex Michaelides’s thriller is narrated by Theo Faber, a psychotherapist who takes a post at a secure unit in order to treat Alicia Berenson, a painter who shot her husband, Gabriel, and has not spoken since. Theo’s account of the treatment is interleaved with his account of discovering his wife Kathy’s affair, and with Alicia’s diary from before the killing. The reader takes the two strands of Theo’s life to run together. The reveal is that they do not: the affair belongs to years earlier, Kathy’s lover was Gabriel, and Theo, following him, became the masked man who held Alicia and Gabriel captive on the night of the shooting. Alicia’s diary, read in the last pages, tells the police so. The reveal is of telling, and its withholder is an arrangement inside a teller’s account. Theo never dates his two strands as simultaneous; the reader assumes it, because a narrator’s alternating strands usually run together. The book therefore passes the teller rule: nothing is falsified, and the reinterpretation reaches every scene of Theo’s marriage. It is also a case for Chapter 8, Non-linear and Multi-timeline Architecture , since the withholding is a timeline placed beside another without a stamp. Readers have divided over whether the arrangement plays fair. The double-reading table explains the division: the passages bear both readings, but few of them bear the second reading strongly enough for a reader to point to afterwards, which is the third property of a sound table in Core’s mechanism. 6.3 Knives Out (2019): a false reveal and a turn of alignment Rian Johnson’s film opens on the death of Harlan Thrombey, a crime novelist, at his birthday party. Early in its first act it shows the viewer what the detective, Benoit Blanc, does not know: Harlan’s nurse, Marta Cabrera, believes she gave him an overdose of morphine by mistaking his vials, and Harlan, to protect her, cut his own throat after coaching her in an alibi. Marta vomits when she lies, a trait the film establishes before it matters. From this point the viewer is ahead of the detective, and the whodunit has become a story of suspense about whether Marta will be caught. In the last act Blanc discloses that Marta made no mistake: Harlan’s grandson Ransom had swapped the vials’ contents, and Marta, by her nurse’s instinct, gave the right dose from the wrong labels. Ransom confesses when Marta tells him a witness has survived. The early disclosure is a false reveal of the legitimate kind (section 3.3). It was true as Marta perceived it, and the second reveal reinterprets rather than voids it: the flashback showed what she did and what the labels said, and never what the vials held. The film thus keeps the teller rule with a camera, since its images belong to Marta’s understanding of the night, an equivocation in pictures. The alignment turns twice, from level to ahead at the first disclosure and from ahead to level at the second, when the viewer learns the truth with Marta. The successor question at the turn, whether Marta will be found out, is stronger than the one it answered, and the closing reveal has consequence, since it frees Marta and gives her the house. 7. The household reveal in full 7.1 The draft In the draft convergence (Core, “The Problem”) Dov says that he took the ledger home, read it, and knows their father was ill and had seen a doctor since the autumn; these details are draft-only.
