From March, it’s mine.” , and adds two sentences to his chapter of the evening of 9 March, after he writes the date and the count: He did not turn back the page, then or in any of the months after. In eleven years he had never read a page of it; the ledger was for writing in, and reading it back had been his father’s business, and he did not start now. The sentences supply the reason for Dov’s ignorance that the case in Chapter 13 lacked. The reason is in character: Dov thinks of the dead man as his father , has just decided that the ledger has a way of being written in, and keeps the form of his father’s honesty without its content, as Chapter 14 proposes. The reason is visible before the reveal, so the withholder passes test 3, and it gives the convergence line its double reading. It also holds a thematic irony the book need not state: the father wrote in case anyone ever needs to check , and the one person who held the book for four months never checked. A rejected alternative placed the evidence outside Dov’s mind: Elena, at the convergence, would see a till receipt she had used to mark her place still standing out of the pages where she left it. It would have shown, from a sister’s viewpoint, that nobody had read on. It was rejected because it adds a plant to a scene that Chapter 12 and Chapter 14 already found crowded, and because it proves only that nobody moved a receipt. 7.5 What the revision settles, and what it does not It settles the withholder of the book’s largest reveal and the alignment of the ending: the illness reaches the reader and all three siblings at the reading, and the reader arrives at it half a step ahead, as a curiosity reveal rather than a surprise. It confirms the mother’s silence as a declined reveal, kept visible. It does not change the text of any earlier chapter; the two sentences are proposed for Dov’s chapter, for the author to confirm. Five things remain unsolved. The sentences state a motive rather than dramatise it. They use the narration’s retrospective gap a second time in a short chapter, which may read as underlining. Beside the doctor’s name they make the illness inferable at 78 per cent, which costs surprise. The prologue’s equivocation depends on one verb. And the convergence remains crowded for the sisters, so its sequence must let Elena receive the hand before Nadia arrives for the reading. 8. The limits of the model The model assumes a reader who reads forwards once and then looks back, and a book whose facts are stable enough to be disclosed. It fits the novel of secrets, the mystery and the thriller well, and the novel of consciousness less well, where what is withheld may be a feeling the character has not yet had rather than a fact anyone holds. It assumes too that a narration without a declared teller is authoritative, and the teller rule rests on that assumption. Some books unsettle it deliberately: metafiction that admits the author into the text, as John Fowles’s The French Lieutenant’s Woman (1969) does with its alternative endings, and the fantastic in which no frame decides between dream and event. In such books the teller rule describes what the reader expects in order to show what the book declines, and its failures are the book’s subject rather than its faults. The model also says little about the rereader, who reads every reveal ahead of the characters; section 2.6’s evidence is consistent with, but does not establish, the view that the double reading rather than the surprise is what a reveal contributes over time. 9. Glossary of the chapter’s terms The definitions below are for the consolidated glossary. Alignment. Whether the reader learns a withheld fact with a character, ahead of one, or after. Closing reveal. A reveal in the last part of a book, with no successor question inside it. Consequence. The property of a reveal that changes what a character does or what the ending means. Coy narrator. A failure pattern: a narration that announces its withholding without feeding it. Curiosity reveal. A reveal that answers a question the reader knew she had (after Sternberg’s curiosity). Decoy reading. A first reading supplied by a character with a reason to believe it, so that the reader’s error is attributable. Declined reveal. A book’s refusal, kept visible to its end, to disclose a fact or to adjudicate between accounts; at book scale, the form of Chapter 13’s epistemological domain. Disclosure map. The chapter’s tool for timing: a row for each withheld fact and a column for the reader and each character, recording when each learns it. Double reading. The reading of a passage twice, under the understanding before and after a reveal. Double-reading table. The chapter’s tool for preparation: every passage bearing on a reveal, with its first and second readings. Early reveal. A reveal in the first third of a book, which turns curiosity into consequence. Equivocation. A sentence true under both the first and the second reading. False reveal. A disclosure presented as true and later corrected by another. First reading; second reading. The understanding of a passage before a reveal, and after it. Giveaway. A failure pattern: preparation that supports only the second reading, or too densely supports both. Gradual reveal. A truth disclosed in increments, each confirming the reader’s inference. Idle reveal. A failure pattern: a reveal that changes nothing a character does or the ending means. Range. The set of passages a reveal recasts, by reinterpretation or falsification; distinct from Chapter 7’s reach . Recognition. A character’s change from ignorance to knowledge (Aristotle’s anagnorisis ); the reveal received on the page. Reported reveal. A failure pattern: the truth delivered as information by a character or the narration, rather than found. Reveal. A disclosure of a fact the reader lacked that changes her understanding of what she has already read. Reveal from outside. A failure pattern: a disclosure whose source lies outside the book’s causal system. Objects of a reveal. Event, identity, motive, telling and world: what happened, who someone is, why an act was done, what the text itself is, and the rules of the story’s world. Serial reveal. A chain of reveals, each recasting the last. Successor question. The question a reveal leaves the reader holding in place of the one it answers. Surprise reveal. A reveal of a gap the reader did not know existed (after Sternberg’s surprise). Teller rule. A reveal may falsify only passages a teller in the book could have shaped, and only if it names the teller and gives a reason. Cheat. A failure pattern: a passage before a reveal that supports only the first reading and is stated on the narration’s own authority. Turn reveal. A reveal near the middle that changes the book’s engine. Withholder. What keeps a truth from the reader until its disclosure: a vantage that does not know, a teller with a motive, or an arrangement. Withholding viewpoint. A failure pattern: paralipsis without a reason in a narration that follows a mind which knows the fact. 10. Sources Aristotle, Poetics , translated by S. H. Daniel, Thomas A., and Jeffrey S. Katz, “Spoilers Affect the Enjoyment of Television Episodes but Not Short Stories”, Psychological Reports (2019). Genette, Gérard, Narrative Discourse: An Essay in Method (1972), translated by Jane E. Lewin (Ithaca: Cornell University Press, 1980). title: The Ending
text: The Permanent Stopping Place: Theory, Analysis and Practice The Craft Behind the Story (Second Edition), Reference — Chapter 16. Part III: The Architecture of the Whole. A companion to the other chapters of this book and, in particular, the formal inverse of Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages ), whose argument this chapter completes from the other end of the book. All illustrative passages are quoted briefly for the purposes of criticism and study; full citations appear in §14 . Where a work is read in translation, the translator is named, and the chapter observes the book’s distinction: structural claims survive translation, texture claims do not. In the first edition this was the final chapter, and its coda, §16 , was written to close the book as well as the chapter; both are kept as written. In this edition Chapter 18 ( The Structural Edit ) closes the book, and this chapter closes Part III. Contents On this page: Chapter Abstract · Learning Outcomes · Key Terms · How to Use This Chapter Introduction: The Problem of the Last Page Definitions and Boundaries Why Endings Carry Disproportionate Weight The Domains of Purpose — plot, character, theme, catharsis, the final image, and a proposed sixth Multiplicity: The Economy of the Ending Earned and Unearned — the mechanism, and a taxonomy of sixteen closural strategies Diagnostic Method — the ten tests Failure Patterns — with their exceptions Worked Analyses — nine close readings and the capstone revision case Endings Across Forms · Concordance: concept to work Revision Checklist Studio Work — exercises, seminar questions, assessment rubric Glossary Sources Cited Further Reading Coda: Against Mechanical Application — and the End of the Book Chapter Abstract An ending is the only unit of a novel with no subsequent scene to correct it . Every other unit in this textbook operates inside a story still running, and can therefore be rescued by what follows: a slack chapter is redeemed by the one after it, a confusing transition is clarified two pages later, a scene whose point is invisible acquires one retrospectively. The ending has no such recourse. It is also the unit through which the reader re-reads everything that came before, so that its failures are not local but retroactive — they reach backwards and reassign meaning to four hundred pages that cannot answer back. This chapter formalises that asymmetry into a teachable model, and it does so in awareness of having been written as the last chapter of the first edition; in this edition it closes Part III, and two chapters follow it, on genre and series and on the structural edit. Every instrument the earlier chapters supplied — the value shift, the causal chain, proposition and payoff, the attention tax, closing the distance, the contracts — comes due here, in the way an ending’s plants come due. The chapter is therefore both an account of endings and a demonstration of one. It proceeds in four movements: Theory — nine strands establishing why the last pages carry disproportionate weight: Kermode on endings as fictions of concord ; Herrnstein Smith on the difference between closure and mere termination; Aristotle on necessity, probability and the unravelling; Brooks on the anticipation of retrospection; Torgovnick on congruence and the forms of the close; the cognitive literature on recency, privileged position and the peak–end rule; the history of the ending from the Victorian settlement to the contemporary open close; DuPlessis on whose endings were available to whom; and D. A. Miller’s argument that closure is always in some measure a betrayal of what made the book worth reading. Taxonomy — the five domains of an ending’s purpose (plot resolution, character-arc completion, thematic closure, emotional catharsis, the final image), each anatomised through its textual carriers, its under- and over-delivery, and published illustrations — expanded here with a proposed sixth, formal closure : the completion of the book’s own structural pattern rather than its story, which is what makes Nineteen Eighty-Four ’s Appendix and The Handmaid’s Tale ’s Historical Notes so disruptive. Method — the principle of multiplicity applied at the highest available stakes; the earned/unearned distinction, analysed as a claim about preparation and retrospective inevitability rather than about predictability; a taxonomy of sixteen closural strategies ; the proportion problem of climax and aftermath; and a ten-test diagnostic protocol for revision. Application — twelve failure patterns, each with a published counterexample that commits the error and succeeds; nine close readings, centred on the two endings of Great Expectations ; the ending across forms; a capstone revision case that audits the household narrative’s plants across the entire textbook, rerun across the second edition’s eighteen chapters in section 9.10.8; and a full apparatus of exercises, glossary, sources and further reading. The chapter’s governing claim is that an ending is not a stopping place but a retroactive lens — the unit through which the whole book is finally read — and that the practical consequence is a discipline of scarcity: an ending may spend only what the book has already earned the right to spend. The chapter’s governing caution is that this discipline assumes closure is desirable. A serious critical tradition holds that it is not — that the ending is where a novel domesticates the very instability that made it interesting. That objection is put at full strength in §3.9 and answered, partially and without evasion, in §6.1 and §16 . A note on the examples. The illustrative endings are drawn mostly from widely read novels. A concordance mapping each concept to the novel that best displays it appears at §10.7 . The second edition adds post-2000 and screen cases, listed in §14.5 , and treats several of them in the Core chapter. A note on spoilers. This chapter discusses the endings of some forty novels in detail, and cannot do otherwise. That is a real cost, and students should be warned before it is imposed on them. It is also a lesser cost than it appears: the argument of §6.2 is that a strong ending is not damaged by being known in advance, because inevitability and surprise are different properties. Whether the reader’s experience of Great Expectations survives knowing how it ends — twice — is one of the questions the chapter puts to the class. Learning Outcomes By the end of this chapter, a student should be able to: Distinguish the ending from the units nearest to it — the climax, the denouement, the epilogue, the coda, the last line — and explain why each distinction changes a revision decision. Separate resolution (the plot’s questions answered, or legibly declined) from closure (the felt sense of completion), and analyse the four possible combinations of the two. Explain , with reference to at least four theoretical sources, why the final pages of a narrative exert influence disproportionate to their length, and state accurately what the cognitive evidence does and does not support. Identify which of the six domains an ending serves, which it merely gestures towards, and which it deliberately declines. Analyse the earned/unearned distinction as a claim about preparation and retrospective inevitability, and demonstrate why an ending may be entirely unforeseen and still earned. Apply a taxonomy of sixteen closural strategies to a draft, and use substitution testing to discover which strategy the material actually wants. Conduct a whole-book plant audit: trace every element an ending relies on back to its planting, and identify anything load-bearing that arrives for the first time at the close. Diagnose the recurring failure patterns by mechanism rather than by surface feature, and argue for the conditions under which each “failure” is the correct choice. Evaluate the limits of the model itself — including the possibility, argued by D. A. Miller and by the whole tradition of the open ending, that the demand for an earned close is a demand the best novels are right to refuse. Key Terms Ending · climax · aftermath · denouement · resolution · closure · termination · the retroactive lens · the five domains · formal closure · earned and unearned · retrospective inevitability · the plant audit · closural strategy · closural allusion · terminal modification · fictions of concord · the narratable · anticipation of retrospection · peak–end rule · recency effect · privileged position · congruence · the proportion problem · the arrested ending · the double ending · the refused ending Full definitions appear in the Glossary ( §13 ). Terms are bolded on first substantive use. How to Use This Chapter Reader Route Purpose Student in a seminar §§1–6 in order, then §9.1 (the Great Expectations case), then §12 Conceptual grounding, the discipline’s best single case study, then guided practice Writer in revision §7 (diagnostics) → §8 (failures) → §6.4 (strategies) → §11 (checklist) Fast triage of a live ending, ending in a decision about strategy and proportion Teacher or workshop leader §§3.7–3.9 , 6.4, 8, 9 for material; §12.1 for assignments; §12.3 rubric A teaching sequence that includes the historical and political correctives, not only the craft rule A caution before beginning, in the same terms as Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages ) and Chapter 10 ( The Prologue ). This chapter contains taxonomies, tests and checklists. None of them is a formula. They are instruments for noticing, and their proper output is a question. A protocol that returns the answer “this ending fails test six” has done nothing until the writer asks whether the book wants it to. That caution carries more weight here than anywhere else in the textbook, for a reason that belongs at the outset. The instruments in this chapter are calibrated to endings that conclude . A substantial and distinguished body of fiction does not want to conclude, and the model will register its refusals as failures. When it does, the model is reporting on itself.

title: 1. Introduction: The Problem of the Last Page
section: Introduction — The Problem of the Last Page
text: 1.1 The inverse asymmetry Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages ) began by comparing page 3 with page 203. Page 203 arrives loaded, underwritten by two hundred pages of accumulated investment; page 3 has no account, and must secure every claim it makes out of its own resources. That asymmetry — the threshold problem — is the reason openings need a chapter of their own. This chapter begins from the same comparison, run in the other direction, and arrives at an asymmetry of the opposite shape. Consider page 403 of a four-hundred-and-four-page novel. By the standards of Chapter 9 it is the best-funded page in the book. Everything is available to it: every character the reader has come to know, every object the book has put on a shelf, every phrase it has repeated, every question it has raised, every register it has taught the reader to hear. Nothing has to be established. Nothing has to be explained. The account is not merely well funded; it is at its maximum balance, and it will never be topped up again. Which is the difficulty. Two constraints follow from that position, and they pull against each other. The first constraint is that the account cannot be added to. An ending may spend anything the book has already deposited and nothing it has not. A new character on page 403 is not a new character; it is a withdrawal against an account that was never opened. This is the structural fact underneath the whole folk vocabulary of endings that “cheat” — a vocabulary readers reach for immediately and reliably, whatever they know about narrative theory. What they have detected is an unfunded transaction. The second constraint is that there is no page 405. Every other unit in this textbook operates inside a story still running. A slack chapter can be redeemed by the one after it. A transition that loses the reader can be repaired two pages later, at the cost of a little goodwill. A scene whose purpose is invisible when it occurs can acquire one at the moment its plant pays off — Chapter 6 ( The Chapter Break ) calls this the relation of proposition and payoff , and the whole of Chapter 14 ( The Subplot ) depends on the reader’s willingness to wait for a thread to justify itself. The ending is the one unit for which waiting is not available. Whatever it does is what the book did. Put the two constraints together and a third fact emerges that is more consequential than either: The ending is read backwards. The reader’s last act of interpretation is not local to the last pages. It is an act of interpretation upon the whole , performed at the moment the whole first exists. Until the final page, a novel is an incomplete object about which the reader is still forming hypotheses; at the final page it becomes a completed object with a shape, and the shape is conferred from the end. This chapter calls it the retroactive lens , and it is the chapter’s first principle. It is also, as §3 will show, one of the most thoroughly theorised phenomena in twentieth-century criticism, under several different names. The practical consequence is a disproportion that every working novelist has felt and few can explain. A handful of unearned pages can flatten two hundred pages of careful work. Not obscure them — flatten them, retrospectively, so that scenes which were doing real work while the reader was inside them come to seem like machinery for a destination that did not deserve them. The reverse holds equally, and is the entire reason for taking the unit this seriously: an ending that lands can make a slack middle read as patience, an obscure early scene read as design, and a novel that was merely good read as inevitable. 1.2 The claim in its strong form Every earlier scene waits to find out what it was for. The ending is where they all find out at once. The metaphor of accumulated trust runs through this textbook, and here it reaches its terminus. Chapter 9 argued that the opening pages are where trust is minted . This chapter argues that the ending is where it is spent — spent completely, with no reserve held back, because there is nothing left to hold it for. The strong claim needs its limits stated. It does claim that a reader’s final judgement of a novel is disproportionately determined by its last pages, and that this judgement is applied retroactively to material the reader has already consumed and enjoyed. It does not claim that endings must resolve. Resolution is one option among several, and §2.3.2 and §6.4 spend some time separating it from the felt completion that readers actually respond to. A novel may leave every question open and close absolutely. It does not claim that endings must be positive, redemptive, consoling, or even satisfying in any ordinary sense. The Trial ends with a man knifed in a quarry and the observation that it is like the shame of it outliving him. Nobody finds this satisfying; almost everybody finds it complete. It does not claim that the ending is the part of a novel that matters most. It claims that the ending is the part with the least margin for error, which is a different and more modest proposition. A poor ending damages a great book. A great ending does not make a poor one. And it does not claim, though the craft literature routinely assumes it, that endings should be the last thing written . Many are the first. The evidence from working practice is mixed and the chapter takes no position on the composition order; what it insists on is that the ending must be revised last , because it is the only unit whose obligations cannot be known until the rest exists. There is one further qualification, and because it is a serious one it gets its own section rather than a bullet. The strong claim assumes the reader wants the book to end well. A large and distinguished tradition of criticism holds that the desire for a well-made ending is itself the problem — that closure is the moment a novel stops being interesting and starts being tidy, and that the demand for earned resolution is a demand for the extinction of what made the reader read. That argument is D. A. Miller’s, and it is put at full strength in §3.9 before this chapter attempts to answer it. 1.3 Where this chapter sits in the series Three placements matter, and each does work later in the chapter. First: the formal inverse of Chapter 9. The two boundary chapters of this textbook describe the same privileged position under opposite conditions. Chapter 9 §3.2 states the symmetry from its side, noting that both openings and endings are what Rabinowitz calls privileged positions , and that Kermode and Herrnstein Smith describe the ending’s work as “the retrospective conferral of shape” while the opening’s work is “the prospective creation of the conditions under which shape can later be conferred”. This chapter completes that argument from the other end. The formulation the two chapters share can be stated as a single line: The opening works with no accumulated context. The ending works with nothing but accumulated context. Every difference between the two units follows from that. The opening’s characteristic failure is default — a contract left unopened, a reader given nothing to hold. The ending’s characteristic failure is unfunded expenditure — a claim made on capital the book never deposited. The opening’s discipline is establishment ; the ending’s discipline is scarcity . And where Chapter 9’s zero-context test is an austere idealisation (readers do in fact arrive with a cover and a blurb), this chapter’s total-context assumption is close to literally true: a reader on the last page really does have the whole book behind them, and really does have nothing after it. Second: the terminus of the load-bearing concepts. This textbook is organised so that a small number of ideas recur and accumulate, and nearly all of them fall due in this chapter: Concept Introduced in What it becomes here The value shift (“what changed?”) Chapter 1 ( The Purposes of a Scene ) The final value shift, which is what an ending is at the level of the scene, and the reason a climax without aftermath can still be a complete scene and an incomplete ending ( §2.3.1 ) The causal chain (“had to happen next”) Chapter 2 ( Scene and Sequel ) Aristotle’s necessity-or-probability, and the mechanism of retrospective inevitability ( §6.3 ) Multiplicity Chapter 1 The single image that closes several accounts at once ( §5 ) Proposition and payoff Chapter 6 ( The Chapter Break ) The plant audit ( §7.1 , test 2), which is the instrument that closes the whole textbook The attention tax Chapter 14 ( The Subplot ) The proportion test: a thread’s resolution should be proportional to the page space it taxed ( §7.1 , test 6) The contracts Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages ) The tonal-match test ( §7.1 , test 8): the ending is where the genre contract is finally honoured or broken The formal contract Chapter 9 §4.6 Formal closure , this chapter’s proposed sixth domain ( §4.6 ) — the contract opened there is closed here Closing the distance Chapter 10 ( The Prologue ) The last and largest instalment of closing the distance; the prologue’s held note landing ( §4.6 , §9.10 ) Earned and unearned This chapter Originates here and is used retrospectively by Chapters 2, 4, 14 and 10, all of which invoke it before it is defined — which is itself a demonstration of the retroactive lens operating at the scale of a textbook Third: the last chapter. In the first edition this was the final unit of the book, and it laboured under the obligation it describes: a textbook whose final chapter is about endings and which ends badly has produced its own counter-example. In this edition Chapter 18 ( The Structural Edit ) closes the book, and this chapter closes Part III. §16 is written in that awareness, and the household narrative that runs through every chapter is concluded in §9.10 using nothing that has not already been planted — which is either the strongest available demonstration of the chapter’s thesis or a stunt, and the reader is entitled to decide which.

title: 2. Definitions and Boundaries
text: Craft discussion of endings is even more prone to terminological drift than discussion of beginnings, because the everyday words are all in use for several things at once. “The ending” names, variously: the last sentence, the last chapter, the last movement, the resolution of the plot, and the reader’s feeling on closing the book. These are five different objects with five different failure modes, and a revision note that does not say which is meant is unusable. The chapter therefore begins by separating them. 2.1 The unit under study Working definition. The ending is the final unit of a novel, distinguished from every other unit by two properties: it has no subsequent scene to correct, complicate or pay off what it delivers; and it is the material through which the reader retroactively re-reads everything that came before it. It comprises the climax and whatever aftermath the book requires in order to land. Four elements of that definition carry weight. “Final unit.” Not the final sentence. The ending is a stretch of narrative, and in most novels it is longer than writers assume — commonly the last chapter or two, sometimes the last movement of the book, occasionally (as in Anna Karenina ) an entire part. “No subsequent scene.” This is the constitutive property, and it is what makes the ending a kind of unit rather than merely a position . It is also why an epilogue does not escape the definition: an epilogue is not something after the ending, it is part of it. “Retroactively re-reads.” The ending is defined partly by an effect it has on other text. No other unit in this textbook is. “Climax and aftermath.” The composite structure is the source of most proportion errors, and §2.3.1 separates the two parts. Note what the definition does not mention: resolution, catharsis, satisfaction, or completion. Those are things endings often do, and §4 anatomises them. They are not what an ending is . An ending that resolves nothing is still an ending, and it is still subject to every constraint in this chapter. 2.2 How long is an ending? There is no principled answer, and any number offered is a convention. Four practical delimitations circulate, and — as with the opening (Chapter 9 §2.2 ) — they answer different questions. Delimitation Extent Answers the question The last sentence or paragraph 1–150 words What is the reader left holding? (the final image , §4.5 ) The last scene ~800–3,000 words Does the ending land as a scene , with its own value shift? The last chapter or movement ~3,000–12,000 words Is the aftermath proportionate, and are the domains delivered? ( §4 , §6.6 ) From the climax to the last word Highly variable; 5–20% of the book Is the structural shape of the close right? This chapter treats the third delimitation as primary — roughly the last chapter or movement — because that is the span across which the domains of §4 are actually discharged, and because it is the unit a revision decision usually operates on. Where a point applies specifically to the last line, or to the whole post-climactic stretch, the text says so. A rule of thumb worth carrying, and the inverse of Chapter 9’s: The opening’s contracts must be opened within two pages and honoured within the first chapter. The ending’s accounts must be closed within the last chapter and felt within the last page. The asymmetry in that formulation is deliberate. An opening can afford to work slowly because the reader has agreed to keep reading. An ending cannot, because the reader is leaving. 2.3 The two confusions Two distinctions do more work in this chapter than any others, and both are routinely collapsed in craft discussion. 2.3.1 Climax is not ending The climax is the last major confrontation or disaster — the peak of conflict, in the sense Chapter 2 ( Scene and Sequel ) gives the term, the final disaster beat of the final goal–conflict–disaster sequence. The ending is the climax plus whatever aftermath the book needs. The distinction matters because a book that stops at its climax and a book that lets its climax breathe into an aftermath are making two different structural choices, and choosing wrongly is one of the most common and most damaging errors in the repertoire ( §8.2 , §8.3 ). Aristotle already had the vocabulary: the desis , the tying of the knot, runs to the turning point; the lusis , the unravelling , runs from the turning point to the end. The lusis is not an appendix to the play. It is half the structure. Climax Aftermath Function Discharges the accumulated conflict Establishes what the discharge means Chapter 1’s terms The largest value shift in the book The reader’s opportunity to register that the value has shifted Chapter 2’s terms The final disaster The final sequel — reaction, dilemma, decision — for the whole novel Typical domains served Plot, catharsis Character, theme, the final image Failure if omitted The book has no engine The book has no meaning; §8.2 Failure if overlong Exhaustion; diminishing returns on violence Momentum death; §8.3 The most useful reframing here, because it turns a question of proportion into a structure the reader already knows, is to recognise the aftermath as the novel’s own sequel in Chapter 2’s technical sense. Every scene in that model is followed by a sequel in which the viewpoint character reacts, faces a dilemma and takes a decision; the aftermath of a novel is the same structure applied to the book. That is why an aftermath consisting only of reaction feels indulgent (a character grieving for thirty pages), and why an aftermath containing a decision — however small — feels complete. Nadia putting on the coat in §9.10 is a decision, not a reaction, and that is the whole reason it can end a novel. 2.3.2 Resolution is not closure The second confusion is more consequential and much less often named. Resolution is a property of the plot : the book’s dramatic questions are answered, or are legibly and deliberately left open. It is, in principle, checkable — one can list the questions and mark them. Closure is a property of the reader : the felt sense that the emotional and thematic arc is complete, that the book has arrived rather than stopped. It is not checkable, only reportable. These come apart in both directions, and all four combinations occur in published fiction. The 2×2 is the most useful diagnostic object in the chapter’s first half. Closure felt Closure absent Resolved The classical settlement. Jane Eyre ; Great Expectations (revised); Emma . Every question answered and the answering feels like arrival The hollow tidy ending. Every question answered and the reader feels nothing. This is the only one of the four that is a defect by default ( §8.5 ) Unresolved The open close that closes. The Handmaid’s Tale ; Blindness ; Beloved ; A Passage to India . Real ambiguity, complete feeling The deliberate refusal. The Castle (unfinished, and read as though not); parts of the nouveau roman . Legitimate, difficult, and much rarer than drafts imagine Three inferences follow, and they are the operative content of the distinction. Resolution is neither necessary nor sufficient for closure. A book can answer every question and feel unfinished; it can leave the central question open and feel absolutely done. Writers who diagnose a flat ending as a resolution problem and respond by answering more questions usually make it worse. Only one of the four quadrants is a default failure. Resolved-without-closure is the hollow ending, and it is a failure because the reader can see the work being done and cannot feel it. The other three are choices. The mechanisms that produce closure are largely formal, not informational. Herrnstein Smith’s whole book is about this: closure is produced by the arrangement of the last lines, not by the quantity of information they carry ( §3.2 ). This is why a novel can close on a sentence that answers nothing. The clearest single illustration is A Passage to India (1924). Its final page answers nothing: Aziz and Fielding cannot be friends, and the earth and the sky say, in the novel’s closing words, “No, not yet” and “No, not there”. No plot question is resolved by that. The reader nonetheless experiences complete closure, because the refusal is delivered in the book’s own governing terms — the failure of connection, which is the novel’s subject — and because the sentence is formally terminal: a negation, in the mouths of the landscape, with nothing possible after it. Resolution declines and closure arrives , in the same clause. 2.4 Adjacent terms Term Meaning Relation to the ending Climax The peak of conflict; the last major confrontation or disaster A part of the ending; §2.3.1 Denouement ( dénouement ) Literally “untying”; the unravelling of the complications after the climax The French inheritance of Aristotle’s lusis ; roughly synonymous with aftermath , with a stronger implication that facts are being disentangled Desis / lusis Aristotle’s tying and unravelling The two-part structure underlying §2.3.1 Resolution The answering of the plot’s dramatic questions A domain of the ending ( §4.1 ), not the ending Closure The felt sense of completion The effect an ending may or may not produce; §2.3.2 Termination Simply stopping Herrnstein Smith’s contrast term; the thing an ending must not merely be ( §3.2 , §7.1 test 7) Epilogue A separated final unit, usually displaced in time, voice or vantage The structural inverse of the prologue (Chapter 10); a strategy within the ending, not an alternative to it ( §6.4 , no. 7) Coda A short final movement in a different key, after the main structure is complete Musical borrowing; often synonymous with a brief epilogue, but implies tonal rather than temporal displacement Finale A last movement gathering the whole cast or theme Eliot’s own term for Middlemarch ’s last section ( §9.2 ) Aftermath Everything between climax and last word This chapter’s preferred neutral term, because it presupposes no shape Anticlimax A close deliberately smaller than the expectation it follows A strategy ( §6.4 , no. 11), not a defect, when chosen Last line The final sentence, considered as a citable unit The most privileged position in the book after the first line ( §3.6 ) Apparatus Appendices, notes, indexes and other paratext following the narrative The vehicle of several formal-closure effects ( §4.6 ); Genette’s territory Series hook A deliberate non-closure creating an appetite for a further volume (this edition keeps sequel for Chapter 2’s sense) A commercial strategy with a structural cost ( §8.11 ) Two of these deserve a note, because they are used loosely even in scholarship. Denouement and aftermath are not quite synonyms. Denouement carries the implication that something is being untied — that facts previously entangled are being separated, mysteries explained, identities revealed. That is a nineteenth-century plot’s characteristic aftermath. A modern novel’s aftermath frequently unties nothing and consists entirely of consequence. Using denouement for both smuggles in an assumption about what endings are for. Epilogue and coda are frequently conflated and should not be. An epilogue is displaced along an axis — time, voice, vantage — in the same way Chapter 10 ( The Prologue ) describes a prologue as displaced. A coda is not displaced at all; it is continuous, and merely changes key. The distinction matters in revision because the two have different costs: an epilogue must justify its exteriority, as a prologue must (Chapter 10 §1.2 ), while a coda need only justify its length. 2.5 What this chapter excludes For clarity of scope, the following lie outside it: Openings — see Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages ), the formal inverse, whose §4.6 formal contract this chapter’s §4.6 closes. Prologues, and the epilogue as a separated unit — Chapter 10 ( The Prologue ) treats separation as such, and its §8.9 and §9.8 deal directly with the epilogue that reframes. This chapter treats the epilogue only as one closural strategy among sixteen ( §6.4 ). Chapter endings — see Chapter 6 ( The Chapter Break ), which treats the temporary stopping place. The relation is exact: a chapter break offers the reader a place to stop; the ending offers the place they must. The structure of the climactic scene itself — see Chapter 1 ( The Purposes of a Scene ) and Chapter 2 ( Scene and Sequel ). This chapter takes the climax as given and asks what must follow it. Subplot convergence — see Chapter 14 ( The Subplot ), whose account of convergence and of the attention tax supplies this chapter’s proportion test ( §7.1 , test 6). Series endings as a commercial problem — touched in §10.3 ; Chapter 17 ( Series and Genre ) treats the series instalment, and the economics of multi-volume publication are outside scope. The unfinished novel — The Mystery of Edwin Drood , The Castle , The Man Without Qualities . These raise real questions about whether closure can be attributed posthumously, and The Castle appears twice below (§2.3.2, §6.4 ) as a limit case, but a text that has no ending cannot be analysed as having a bad one.

title: 3. Why Endings Carry Disproportionate Weight
text: The retroactive lens is asserted constantly in craft literature and almost never argued. It can be argued, and from an unusual number of independent directions — philosophical, formal, historical, political, cognitive. Endings have, in fact, the richest critical literature of any subject in this textbook, and a chapter that ignored it would be teaching intuitions that were rigorously theorised sixty years ago. Nine strands are assembled below. They are not variants of one another. Kermode is making a claim about human temporality; Herrnstein Smith about formal structure; Brooks about desire; Aristotle about probability; the cognitive literature about memory; DuPlessis about ideology; Miller about the whole enterprise. Where they agree, the agreement is evidence. Where they conflict — and Kermode and Miller conflict fundamentally — the conflict is the most useful thing in the section. 3.1 Kermode: endings as fictions of concord Frank Kermode’s The Sense of an Ending (1967) is the foundational modern text on the subject, and its central argument is not about novels at all. It is about why human beings need endings in the first place. Kermode begins from apocalypse. Western culture has spent two millennia predicting the end of the world, being wrong, and adjusting rather than abandoning the prediction. The pattern interests him because it exposes a general structure of thought: we are, all of us, in the middest — born after the beginning and dying before the end, with no access to either terminus of the story we are inside. To make sense of a middle, we posit ends. Kermode calls the resulting structures fictions of concord : imagined shapes that give a stretch of undifferentiated duration a beginning, a middle and an end, and thereby make it interpretable. His minimal model of this is the clock, and it is the most quoted image in the literature on endings. A clock, physically, makes an undifferentiated series of identical sounds. We do not hear it that way. We hear tick-tock — a tick that is a beginning and a tock that is an end, with an interval between them that the two sounds organise into a shape. Kermode’s point is that nothing in the acoustics licenses this. The distinction between tick and tock is supplied by the listener, who requires the interval to have a form. Tick is, in his phrase, a humble genesis; tock a feeble apocalypse. And the space between them — the interval that the ending makes into a duration rather than a mere succession — is where plot lives. Three consequences of Kermode’s argument bear directly on craft. (1) The ending is what converts succession into duration. Without a tock , a series of events is one thing after another. This is the theoretical form of the distinction Chapter 2 ( Scene and Sequel ) draws between a sequence of scenes and a causal chain : causality is a shape imposed retrospectively, and the point from which it is imposed is the end. A reader who cannot see how a book will end cannot yet know which of its events were causes. (2) Endings are impositions, and readers know it. Kermode is explicit that concord fictions are fictions — that the shape is not discovered in the material but supplied. Reality does not have tocks. Lives do not conclude, they stop; and even the deaths that end them are not endings in the formal sense, because they resolve nothing and confer no meaning on what preceded. (3) And we want them anyway. This is Kermode’s most valuable idea for this chapter, and it is the one most often lost in summary. He distinguishes between fictions that have hardened into myth — held to be literally true, no longer felt as constructions — and fictions held with what he calls a clerkly scepticism: known to be made, used regardless. Endings, he argues, belong in the second category for any sophisticated modern reader. We are entirely aware that novelistic endings are artificial impositions of shape on material that does not naturally have one. We want them all the same. The demand does not survive because it is naive; it survives because the need it answers is not defeated by knowing it is being answered artificially. Kermode’s principle, in the form this chapter uses it: endings are discredited but not abandoned . The reader who finishes a novel knows the shape was imposed and wants the imposition anyway. This is why the sophisticated open ending is not simply superior to the closed one, and why a novel that refuses shape on principle frequently disappoints readers who fully understand and endorse the principle. The rest of the chapter turns on that formulation. It permits the chapter to teach the craft of closure without claiming that closure is true, and to take the modernist and postmodern refusals seriously without concluding that the demand they refuse was stupid. Kermode also supplies a technical term this chapter will use in §6.2 . Borrowing from Aristotle, he treats peripeteia — the reversal, the falsification of expectation — as the mark of a sophisticated concord fiction rather than a naive one. A novel that fulfils its predicted shape to the letter is myth; a novel that disappoints the expectation it created, and then satisfies a better one the reader did not know they had, is doing what Kermode thinks fiction is for. The craft translation is direct: an ending should be inevitable in retrospect and unforeseen in prospect , and §6.2 argues that this is not a paradox but a description of how preparation actually works. 3.2 Herrnstein Smith: closure against termination If Kermode explains why we want endings, Barbara Herrnstein Smith’s Poetic Closure (1968) explains what an ending actually does to produce the feeling. It is a study of poems, which is why it is useful: because a poem is short enough to be analysed exhaustively, Herrnstein Smith is able to describe closural mechanisms at a level of formal precision no study of novels has matched. Her vocabulary remains the most exact available for what a last line does, and it transfers to prose with almost no loss. Her governing distinction is between closure and mere termination . A text terminates when it stops. A text achieves closure when the reader experiences the stopping as the appropriate and expected conclusion of the structure — when the final line produces “a sense of stable conclusiveness, finality, or ‘clinch’”. Every text terminates; not every text closes. The difference is entirely a matter of how the last lines are constructed, and Herrnstein Smith catalogues the constructions. Four of her mechanisms are directly usable in prose. Closural allusion. The final lines refer, at the level of content, to things that are themselves terminal: death, sleep, night, winter, silence, departure, stillness, the sea. The reference does not have to be structurally significant; the mere presence of a terminal referent at a terminal position produces a closural effect, because the reader’s sense of finality is reinforced by an image of finality. This is the cheapest closural device in the language, which is why it is also the most easily abused. A novel that ends with a character falling asleep, watching a train leave, or looking at snow is borrowing closure from the referent rather than earning it from the structure. It is also why so many endings feel right and audit badly: the allusion has done the work the domains were supposed to do. Terminal modification. A pattern established across the text is altered at its final instance — a line shortened, a refrain broken, a rhyme abandoned, a stanza truncated. The alteration signals that the pattern is not going to continue, and therefore that it is over. In prose the pattern in question is usually structural rather than metrical: a chapter shape, a section length, a habitual sentence rhythm, a recurring scene type. The last chapter that does not do what the previous forty did is a terminal modification , and readers register it as closure even when they cannot name the pattern that has been modified. §4.6 makes this the core of the proposed sixth domain. Failure of expectation, or the closural force of the unexpected. A conclusion may close by defeating the reader’s expectation rather than fulfilling it, provided the defeat is legible as final. This is Kermode’s peripeteia in formal dress, and it is the mechanism by which anticlimax ( §6.4 , no. 11) can close a book. Unqualified assertion. A final sentence in the declarative mood, without hedging, subordination or qualification, produces closure by grammar alone. Herrnstein Smith notes the special closural force of the epigram, the maxim and the proverb — utterances whose form claims general truth and therefore admits no continuation. Middlemarch ’s Finale ends this way; so, in a much stranger register, does Nineteen Eighty-Four . The prose version of the device is §6.4 ’s aphoristic close , and its risk is §8.6 ’s explained ending: an assertion that closes by telling the reader what the book meant has bought closure with the book’s own subtlety. Herrnstein Smith’s other lasting contribution is her treatment of anti-closure in modern poetry as a positive technique rather than an absence of technique. Poems that end without closural signals are not failing to close; they are using the absence of closure as a formal effect, and they can only do so because the closural conventions exist to be withheld. The consequence for this chapter is stated once and relied on throughout: An open ending is a closural strategy, not the absence of one. It works by withholding devices the reader knows are available, and it therefore depends on the reader’s competence in the conventions it declines. This is why an open ending in an otherwise conventional book reads as evasion, and the same ending in a book that has taught the reader to expect it reads as integrity. 3.3 Aristotle: necessity, probability, and the unravelling The Poetics (c. 335 BCE) supplies four things this chapter uses, and the third of them is the ancient form of its central craft term. The unity of action, and the definition of an end. Aristotle defines an end as that which naturally follows something else, either necessarily or as a rule, and has nothing following it. The definition matters because it contains both of the ending’s constitutive properties as this chapter states them in §2.1 : nothing after it, and a determinate relation to what precedes. Peripeteia and anagnorisis. The reversal (a change of the action into its opposite) and the recognition (a change from ignorance to knowledge) are, for Aristotle, the two most powerful devices of plot, and the finest tragedies combine them so that the recognition produces the reversal. This pairing is the analytic core of the classical climax, and it is the reason two of the strategies in §6.4 — the retrospective reframe and the anagnoristic close — are recognisably ancient rather than modern. Necessity or probability. Aristotle’s requirement that the events of a plot follow one another by necessity or probability is the oldest available statement of what this chapter calls earned . He is explicit that the incidents must arise out of the structure of the plot itself, so that they appear inevitable, and that a plot in which events follow one another merely after rather than because is inferior. Chapter 2 ( Scene and Sequel ) states the same requirement in modern craft terms as the causal chain — the test of whether each beat “had to happen next”. §6.3 shows that the two are the same test applied at different scales. The prohibition on the deus ex machina . Aristotle’s corollary is that the unravelling must arise from the plot itself and not from a contrivance — his examples are the machine in Medea and the business of the fleet in the Iliad . This is the direct ancestor of §8.1 , the unearned rescue. Two historical qualifications are essential and are set out in full at §8.1 : first, that the device is Euripides’ signature rather than his failure, and that Aristotle was expressing a preference against a living and popular practice; second, that a whole later tradition — Gay, Brecht — makes the arbitrariness of the rescue the point. One further Aristotelian term deserves rescue, because modern craft discussion has lost it. The Poetics divides a tragedy into the desis , the tying of the knot, and the lusis , the unravelling — and the division is not at the last scene but at the turning point. Everything after the peripeteia is lusis . On this account the aftermath is not a supplement to the structure; it is structurally half the play , and a drama that ends at its reversal has performed only one of its two movements. §6.6 ’s proportion problem is this observation converted into a working ratio. 3.4 Brooks: the anticipation of retrospection Peter Brooks’s Reading for the Plot (1984) provides the most direct theoretical grounding for the retroactive lens, and does so by way of an argument about desire. Brooks’s model of narrative is dynamic rather than structural. Plot, for him, is not a shape but a force — the desire that carries a reader forward, generated by an initial disequilibrium and discharged at the end. His key phrase for the reader’s state is the anticipation of retrospection : we read forwards in the expectation of a moment from which the whole will be retrospectively legible. We tolerate the middle because we expect an end that will explain what the middle was. Two consequences follow. The end is the point of legibility. Brooks argues that meaning in narrative is not distributed evenly along the sequence but conferred from the terminus. Until the end, every element is provisional — it might turn out to be a cause, a red herring, a theme, or nothing. The end fixes them. This is the retroactive lens, stated as a general property of narrative rather than as a craft observation, and it explains something the craft formulation does not: why an ending can make earlier material better without changing a word of it. The earlier material was always doing that work; the reader could not yet see which work it was. Plot seeks its own proper end. Brooks’s most contested move is his reading of Freud’s Beyond the Pleasure Principle as a model of narrative. The organism, in Freud’s account, seeks to return to quiescence but must do so by its own path — it insists on the correct death rather than a short-cut. Brooks transposes this: narrative desire seeks discharge, but a discharge that arrives too early or by the wrong route is unsatisfying. What he calls the short-circuit is the unearned ending: the right destination reached by an illegitimate path. The craft translation is exact, and it can be stated as a rule, because it explains an otherwise puzzling fact about reader response: Readers do not want the ending they want. They want the ending the book requires. A reader who spends four hundred pages hoping two characters will marry will nonetheless feel cheated by a marriage the book has not earned, and satisfied by a separation it has. The desire the ending answers is not the desire for a particular outcome; it is the desire for the right outcome, and rightness is a property of the path. This is the strongest available answer to the commercial instinct that endings should give readers what they want. It also explains why the two endings of Great Expectations ( §9.1 ) have been argued about for a century and a half: the disagreement is not about which outcome is nicer but about which one the book’s own path requires, and competent critics have reached opposite conclusions. 3.5 Torgovnick: congruence and the forms of the close Marianna Torgovnick’s Closure in the Novel (1981) remains the standard monograph on the subject and is the source of this chapter’s §6.4 taxonomy. Two of her contributions are load-bearing here. The typology of closural relations. Torgovnick classifies endings by their relation to the rest of the novel rather than by their content. Adapted, and with the vocabulary this chapter will use throughout: Relation The ending’s connection to the book Example of the type Circularity Returns to the beginning’s language, image or situation Wuthering Heights ; Finnegans Wake at the limit Parallelism Repeats a situation from earlier in the book, with the terms altered Great Expectations , revised (the garden, twice) Incompletion Deliberately leaves the pattern unfinished The Handmaid’s Tale ’s narrative proper Tangent Swerves to something apparently unrelated Nineteen Eighty-Four ’s Appendix; Madame Bovary ’s Homais Linkage Explicitly ties named threads together Bleak House ; most Victorian wind-up chapters The overt and the covert ending. Torgovnick separates endings that announce themselves as endings — an epilogue, a finale, a chapter headed “Conclusion”, a narrator stepping forward to sum up — from endings that arrive without announcement, the last scene being formally indistinguishable from any other. The distinction is useful in revision because the two carry different risks: an overt ending risks §8.6 (the explained ending) and §8.5 (the tidy-everything ending); a covert one risks §8.2 (climax without aftermath) and the failure of termination ( §7.1 , test 7). Congruence. Torgovnick’s evaluative criterion, and the one this chapter borrows most heavily, is whether an ending is congruent with the novel’s own logic — whether it emerges from the book’s established terms — or imposed on it from outside, by authorial preference, publisher’s pressure, generic obligation or fatigue. This is the scholarly form of the earned/unearned distinction, generalised beyond the question of plants: an ending can plant everything it uses and still be imposed, if what it does with the material contradicts the book’s own argument. §8.12 makes the imposed ending a failure pattern in its own right, and §9.1 shows the two endings of Great Expectations being argued about in these terms. 3.6 The cognitive strand: recency, position and the peak–end rule Chapter 9 grounded the opening’s disproportionate weight in Solomon Asch’s work on primacy . The ending’s counterpart is recency , and the empirical picture is both real and more limited than craft writing usually admits. This section states both. Serial position. The classic finding, established across decades of free-recall experiments and set out canonically in Murdock’s 1962 study, is the serial position curve : items at the beginning of a list (primacy) and at the end (recency) are recalled better than items in the middle. The curve is one of the most robust results in experimental psychology. Its application to narrative, however, must be made carefully. A novel is not a word list; readers do not recall novels by free recall; and the recency portion of the curve is a short-term memory effect that is substantially reduced by a filled delay after the list ends. What the serial position literature licenses is a general claim — positions at the boundaries of a sequence are privileged in memory — and not a specific one about how much of a novel’s ending a reader retains. Privileged position. Peter Rabinowitz’s Before Reading (1987) supplies the literary-critical form of the same claim, and it is the more directly usable. Readers operate with tacit rules of notice , and among the strongest are the rules of privileged position : titles, epigraphs, first and last sentences, and the openings and closes of chapters are automatically assigned interpretive weight. The last sentence of a novel is, on this account, the second most heavily weighted position in the book, and by some measures the first. It is read as a statement about the novel , whether or not it was written as one. This is the direct justification for the last-line test ( §7.1 , test 10) and for treating the final image as a domain in its own right ( §4.5 ). Note the difference between the two claims. Recency is about memory ; privileged position is about interpretation . The second is the more important for this chapter, because a novel’s ending does not need to be well remembered to be load-bearing. It needs to be treated as authoritative at the moment it is read. The peak–end rule. The most attractive empirical result in this area, and the one most frequently over-claimed, is the peak–end rule described by Daniel Kahneman and colleagues. In a series of studies of remembered discomfort — the cold-pressor experiments, and a much-cited study of patients undergoing colonoscopy with Redelmeier — participants’ retrospective evaluations of an unpleasant episode were predicted almost entirely by two data points: the most intense moment (the peak) and the final moment (the end). The duration of the episode contributed remarkably little, an effect known as duration neglect . In the most striking demonstration, an episode that was extended by an additional period of milder discomfort was remembered as less bad than the shorter episode it contained, because the added interval improved the end. The pull of this for a chapter on endings is obvious, and so is the temptation. The peak–end rule appears to be the empirical form of this chapter’s claim that a handful of unearned pages can flatten two hundred pages of careful work. It is worth being exact about how far that goes. What the peak–end rule supports: that retrospective evaluation of an experience is not an average of its moments, and that the final moments are weighted far out of proportion to their duration. What it does not support: any specific claim about novels. The studies concern brief affective episodes — minutes, at most an hour — of directly experienced physical discomfort, evaluated shortly afterwards. Reading a novel is a discontinuous experience spread over days or weeks, mediated by interpretation, memory consolidation, discussion, rereading and social context. The extension from the cold-pressor task to the four-hundred-page novel is an analogy, not a finding. The honest position is that the peak–end rule is a suggestive parallel that makes the craft intuition less surprising, not evidence for it. It is included here because students encounter it constantly in popular writing about storytelling, usually with the qualification removed, and should be able to state what it actually shows. The literary claim stands on its own evidence: the retroactive lens is supported by Brooks, by Kermode, by Rabinowitz’s rules of notice, and by the plain testimony of readers, and it does not need borrowed authority from a colonoscopy study. One further cognitive note, on the shape of the aftermath. Richard Gerrig’s work on transportation ( Experiencing Narrative Worlds , 1993), used in Chapter 9 to explain the opening’s start-up cost, has a symmetrical implication at the close: a transported reader must be returned , and return, like departure, has a cost. An ending that terminates at the peak of intensity leaves the reader in the fictional world with no exit; an ending that supplies aftermath is, among other things, providing a graduated descent. This is not a claim the experimental literature makes directly, and it is offered as a plausible extension rather than a finding — but it is the most economical explanation available for why a book that stops at its climax leaves readers feeling both satisfied and cheated at once ( §8.2 ). 3.7 The historical strand: from the settlement to the open close Endings have a history, and every prescription in this chapter is calibrated to a moment in it. A student who cannot historicise the advice will mistake a local convention for a discovery about narrative. Period Dominant closural practice What it assumed Classical and medieval Death, marriage, restoration of order, or the explicit moral. The envoi , the explicit , the narrator’s farewell That a story’s purpose is exemplary; the ending states what it exemplified 18th century The concluding chapter as settlement: fortunes distributed, marriages made, villains punished, the narrator addressing the reader directly ( Tom Jones ; Pamela ) That the narrator is a moral authority who may speak in his own person 19th century, English The marriage-and-inheritance settlement , delivered in a “wind-up” chapter: money, spouses, offspring, deaths and emigrations for the entire cast That the reader is owed an account of every named character’s subsequent life Serial publication Pressure towards tidiness and towards a legible conclusion, since the audience has waited eighteen months and the parts have been read separately That an ending must be recognisable as one, at speed Late 19th century Increasing resistance: the ironic settlement ( Madame Bovary ’s Homais), the withheld consolation ( The Mill on the Floss ), the ending that indicts the convention it uses That the settlement is a convention, and can be turned against itself Modernist The open ending : the arrested close, the final image without commentary, the refusal of the wind-up. Ulysses ; To the Lighthouse ; A Passage to India That the reader is competent to supply the meaning, and that stating it is vulgar Postmodern The refused ending : multiple endings, the ending that discloses its own arbitrariness, apparatus that displaces the close ( The French Lieutenant’s Woman ) That closure is an ideological imposition and should be exhibited as one Contemporary literary The unresolved close as house style: the final image, the ambiguous gesture, the sentence that declines to conclude That ambiguity signals seriousness The last row is the one that requires a plain statement, because it is the one students are living inside. The ambiguous ending is no longer brave. It is the house style of a genre. For roughly the last half-century, in Anglo-American literary fiction and in the workshop culture that supplies it, the unresolved close has been the default rather than the deviation. A novel that ends on a character standing at a window, a gesture left uncompleted, a sentence that trails, or a final image offered without commentary is not refusing a convention; it is observing one. This has three practical consequences that a writer should hold simultaneously. The open ending no longer carries its historical charge. When Joyce declined to conclude, he was declining something the reader expected. When a contemporary literary novel declines to conclude, it is meeting an expectation. The gesture is the same and its meaning has inverted. Ambiguity is therefore no longer self-justifying. It must now do the work any other strategy must do, and it must do it against the suspicion that it was chosen by default. This is why §8.9 ’s ambiguity-as-evasion is a live failure pattern now and would have been an incoherent complaint in 1925. The genre distribution is stark and should be named. Crime, romance, thriller and much science fiction retain strong resolution conventions; literary fiction has largely abandoned them. This is a fact about markets and readerships, not about narrative. A novel that resolves fully is not thereby commercial, and one that does not is not thereby serious. Two supplementary historical observations, both useful in seminar. On the wind-up chapter. The Victorian settlement is easy to mock and worth understanding. It served a real function under the conditions of serial publication: a novel issued in nineteen monthly parts over eighteen months is read by an audience whose memory of part four is dim, and the concluding survey of the cast is partly an act of retrieval . Chapter 6 ( The Chapter Break ) describes how the part-issue shaped segmentation; the same economics shaped the close. Trollope, in Barchester Towers , breaks off to remark on the awkwardness of the novelist’s final duty — the gathering of threads that must be done and cannot be made interesting — which is a nineteenth-century novelist telling us plainly that the convention was already felt as a chore. On Henry James, who saw it clearly. James’s essay “The Art of Fiction” (1884) contains the most quotable indictment of the settlement in the language: he objects to the expectation of a final “distribution at the last of prizes, pensions, husbands, wives, babies, millions, appended paragraphs and cheerful remarks”. And his preface to Roderick Hudson supplies the deepest single sentence written about endings by a practitioner: Really, universally, relations stop nowhere, and the exquisite problem of the artist is eternally but to draw, by a geometry of his own, the circle within which they shall happily appear to do so. That is Kermode’s argument, forty years early, from inside the workshop. Relations do not stop; the artist draws a circle within which they appear to. The ending is the circumference, and James’s word happily is doing a great deal — the appearance must be satisfying, not merely asserted. 3.8 DuPlessis: whose endings were available Rachel Blau DuPlessis’s Writing Beyond the Ending (1985) converts a craft problem into a historical and political one, and it belongs in this chapter as a matter of intellectual honesty rather than as decoration. Her argument begins from an observation about the nineteenth-century novel that is easy to verify and hard to unsee. For a female protagonist, the plot offered two endings : marriage, or death. A woman’s story concluded either in the social settlement that removed her from the narrative by absorbing her into a household, or in a death that removed her from it altogether. There were essentially no third options that the form recognised as endings. Elizabeth Bennet marries. Jane Eyre marries. Dorothea marries — twice, and the second marriage is treated by the Finale as a diminishment ( §9.2 ). Emma Bovary dies. Anna Karenina dies. Maggie Tulliver drowns. Edna Pontellier walks into the sea. Tess is hanged. DuPlessis’s term for this structure is the romance plot , and her claim is that it is not merely a recurring subject but a narrative ideology : a set of assumptions about what constitutes an ending at all, which determines what a female life can be represented as having been. A plot that can only conclude in marriage or death cannot represent a woman’s vocation, work, friendship, political life or intellectual development as terminal values, because it has no closural form for them. Her book is about the strategies twentieth-century women writers developed for writing beyond the ending — for continuing past the point at which the nineteenth-century plot would have stopped, and for inventing closural forms the tradition did not supply. The strategies she identifies include: displacing the romance plot with a plot of vocation; ending on the female protagonist’s relation to a community rather than to a husband; reparenting and the recovery of a maternal line; the collective or communal protagonist, which dissolves the individual settlement; and simply refusing the marriage-or-death alternative and closing elsewhere. Three things follow for this chapter. (1) The “mismatched final note” is sometimes a historical fact rather than a craft error. §8.4 treats a tonal mismatch at the close as a failure. DuPlessis’s work shows that some mismatches are the sound of a writer forcing available material into an unavailable shape. When a nineteenth-century novel’s heroine is married off in terms the preceding four hundred pages do not support, the diagnosis “the ending does not match the book” is correct, and the explanation is not incompetence. (2) Closural conventions encode assumptions about what a life is for. This generalises well beyond gender. An ending in which a colonised character’s story concludes with accommodation to the coloniser, or in which a working-class character’s story concludes with respectable advancement, is doing the same structural work. Things Fall Apart is the definitive demonstration: the novel ends by handing the last paragraph to the District Commissioner, who is contemplating the paragraph he will devote to Okonkwo in his book, The Pacification of the Primitive Tribes of the Lower Niger . Achebe closes his novel by showing the closural form that would have contained it, and the effect is to make the reader feel the violence of summary itself. (3) A writer choosing an ending is choosing among available forms, and the availability is historical. This is the point of the whole strand for a working novelist, and it is more useful than it sounds. When a draft’s ending feels wrong and every local repair fails, the diagnosis is frequently that the material is being poured into a closural shape it does not fit — usually one of two or three shapes the writer absorbed by reading. §6.5 ’s substitution testing is the practical remedy, and DuPlessis is the reason the exercise is worth doing at the level of the whole book rather than the last page. The seminar question this generates is set at §12.2 , no. 4, and it is a live one: whether the contemporary preference for the unresolved close is a liberation from the settlement, as its advocates hold, or merely the settlement’s successor convention, equally unexamined and equally likely to be seen through in fifty years. 3.9 Miller: the narratable, and the case against closure Everything above assumes that closure is desirable and that the craft problem is how to achieve it well. D. A. Miller’s Narrative and Its Discontents (1981) denies the assumption, and the chapter is obliged to put the denial at full strength before answering it — because it is the strongest available argument against the whole apparatus of earned resolution, and because a student who has not felt its force will apply this chapter’s instruments mechanically. Miller’s central concept is the narratable : the class of things that can be narrated , which he identifies with instability, deviance, insufficiency, transgression and unfulfilled desire. Narrative, on his account, arises from and consists of the narratable. What cannot be narrated is quiescence — the state in which nothing is lacking, nothing is deviant, nothing is in motion. The nonnarratable is not a subject but a silence. The consequence is structural and, once seen, difficult to dislodge: A novel exists because of its disequilibrium. Closure is the elimination of the disequilibrium. Therefore closure is the elimination of the novel’s own condition of existence. Miller works this through the nineteenth-century novel and finds, repeatedly, that the ending does not so much resolve the narratable as declare it over . The marriage at the end of an Austen novel does not answer the questions the novel raised about the relation between feeling and social form; it announces that those questions have stopped being asked. The settlements of Middlemarch do not reconcile Dorothea’s ardour with the world’s provision for it; they record that the ardour has been absorbed. On Miller’s reading, the traditional ending is characteristically thinner than the book it terminates — shorter, flatter, more schematic, written in a different and duller register — and this thinness is not a failure of execution but a structural necessity. The end must be less interesting than the middle, because interest is the narratable, and the end is where the narratable stops. Three of his subsidiary observations sharpen the argument and are stated separately here, because each has a direct craft consequence. The ending is where the novel’s language changes. Miller notices that closural passages frequently abandon the novel’s characteristic mode — free indirect access, scenic presentation, particularity — for summary, report and generalisation. The reader is moved from inside to outside. This is a real observation about real texts, and it is the mechanism underneath §8.5 ’s tidy-everything ending and §8.6 ’s explained ending: both are cases of a novel finishing in a register it did not use. Closure is retrospectively suspicious. Because the ending is where the novel becomes legible (Brooks), and because the ending is also where the novel’s disruptive energy is contained, the retroactive lens is not innocent. It reads the whole book from the position of its own containment . A reader who accepts an ending has, in a sense, agreed to interpret four hundred pages of instability as having been a detour on the way to stability. The demand for earned endings is therefore ideological, not technical. If closure is containment, then “earning” it means constructing the containment persuasively — making the reduction feel inevitable. The craft vocabulary of preparation, plant and payoff is, on this reading, a vocabulary for making the ending’s violence invisible. That is the case, and it should be allowed to stand for a moment without a rebuttal attached. Miller is not a sceptic on the margins; he is describing something readers routinely feel and rarely articulate — the flatness of last chapters, the sense that a book has become smaller in the act of finishing, the disappointment that follows even a competent conclusion. Three responses are available, and this chapter takes the third. The first response is refusal. Accept Miller entirely and conclude that novels should not close: that the open, the fragmentary and the interminable are the honest forms. This is a real position with real practitioners behind it, and its weakness is Kermode’s: readers who fully accept the argument continue to want endings, and a theory that describes the desire as false consciousness has not explained why it survives explanation (§3.1). The second response is dismissal. Note that Miller is describing the nineteenth-century novel specifically, that his examples are chosen for the argument, and that many endings are not thin. This is partly true and mostly evasive: the phenomenon Miller identifies is real in a very large number of books, including good ones. The third response, and this chapter’s, is to accept the diagnosis and dispute the prescription. Miller is right that closure ends the narratable and right that the ending is where a novel’s disruptive energy is contained. He is wrong that this makes the ending a betrayal, because he has assumed that the value of a novel is identical with its narratability. It is not. A novel is also an object with a shape , and the shape is available only from the end. The reader who reaches the last page loses the narratable and gains the whole — and the whole is not a consolation prize for the loss of instability; it is a different order of thing, unavailable at any earlier point. The chapter’s working position can therefore be stated as a concession and a claim in the same breath, and it is the qualification this chapter’s confident vocabulary most needs: Every ending is a loss. The craft question is not how to avoid the loss but what the reader is given in exchange for it. An ending that closes the narratable and offers nothing in return is the tidy ending ( §8.5 ), and Miller has described it accurately. An ending that closes the narratable and delivers, in exchange, a shape the reader could not previously see is what the rest of this chapter is about. This reframing has a practical yield, which is the test of whether it is more than a rhetorical escape.
