It predicts that the strongest endings will be those that preserve some narratable material while closing the book — that they will leave one thing running, one question live, one relation unsettled, not as evasion but as an acknowledgement that the containment is partial. That prediction is testable against the readings in §9 , and it holds: Middlemarch leaves Dorothea’s unspent ardour explicitly unaccounted for; Beloved leaves the question of what is to be done with the story unresolved by contradicting itself; Nineteen Eighty-Four ’s Appendix reopens the very despair its last line closes; and the household narrative in §9.10 deliberately leaves the mother unresolved. In each case the novel closes and something is still moving. 3.10 The retroactive lens, restated — and qualified The chapter’s first principle can now be stated in full. The retroactive lens. The ending is the position from which the whole book first becomes available as a whole, and the reader’s final act of interpretation is therefore performed upon everything, not only upon the last pages. Because there is no subsequent unit to correct it, the ending’s account of the book is the account that stands; and because meaning in narrative is conferred from the terminus rather than distributed along the sequence, the ending reaches backwards and determines, retroactively, what every earlier element was doing. Three corollaries, each of which generates an instrument later in the chapter. An ending may spend only what the book has already deposited. ( §6.1 ; test 2, the plant audit.) An ending’s failures are not local. A weak final chapter does not damage the final chapter; it damages the book. ( §1.1 ; test 1, the retroactive test.) The ending is the only unit whose obligations cannot be known until the rest exists. Hence: revise it last, whenever it was written. ( §7.0 .) And now the qualification, which is where the more interesting teaching lies and which the chapter will not withdraw. The retroactive lens describes a mechanism; it does not license a demand. The mechanism is real: endings do reach backwards, and readers do interpret from the terminus. But the inference usually drawn from it — that an ending must therefore be earned , in the sense of resolving what the book raised — smuggles in an evaluative premise the mechanism does not contain. It assumes that the retroactive act should produce coherence. Miller’s argument (§3.9) is that this assumption is the ideology of closure rather than a fact about narrative, and Kermode’s (§3.1) is that the coherence is in any case supplied by the reader rather than discovered in the material. The honest formulation, and the one on which the rest of the chapter proceeds: The demand that an ending be earned assumes that closure is the goal. A serious tradition holds that closure is what kills the book. This chapter teaches the craft of earned closure because it is teachable, because the great majority of failing drafts are failing at it, and because a writer who cannot do it cannot meaningfully decline to. It does not claim that the endings which refuse it are failing. Where the model and a great novel disagree, the model is reporting its own limits — and §§8 , 9 and 16 are constructed to make sure the student sees that happen at least a dozen times.

title: 4. The Domains of Purpose
text: 4.0 The model and its status The domain model treats an ending as owing the reader work in several distinct registers at once. It is the same analytical move Chapter 1 ( The Purposes of a Scene ) makes for the scene, Chapter 4 ( The Descriptive Detail ) for the detail and Chapter 10 ( The Prologue ) for the separated unit: a unit is anatomised by asking what kinds of work it can do, so that a vague dissatisfaction can be converted into a specific absence. Its value is diagnostic. “This ending isn’t working” is not actionable. “This ending delivers plot and catharsis, gestures at theme, and does nothing for character” is. Its danger is the one that the whole of §5 exists to counter: treating the domains as a sequence to be worked through. A book that stages an action climax and then appends a wrap-up chapter handling character, then theme, then feeling, has read the taxonomy as a schedule. The domains are registers in which an ending is heard , not tasks to be discharged in order, and the strongest endings sound several of them in a single image. Five domains are set out below, followed at §4.6 by a proposed sixth. For each: what it is, why it matters, the textual carriers through which it is realised, what under- and over-delivery look like, and illustrations from published fiction. One preliminary. The domains are not equally obligatory , and the inequality is a function of genre rather than of quality. A detective novel that fails plot resolution has failed; a lyric novel of consciousness may resolve nothing and be complete. §4.8 handles this properly; it is flagged here so that the tables below are not read as a bill. 4.1 Plot Resolution What the reader receives: answers to the dramatic questions the book raised — or a legible, deliberate refusal to answer them, which is a different thing from having forgotten that they were asked. Carriers Carrier The reader’s implicit question Where it lives The answered question Did she find out who kept writing in the ledger? The scene in which the information changes hands, or the moment a character acts on it The consequence enacted What follows from the answer? A decision, a departure, a transaction, a refusal The declined question, marked Is this being left open, or dropped? An explicit registration that the question remains — a character noting it, a narrator declining it The reallocated question Was I asking the wrong thing? A late redirection: the book answers a question the reader did not know was primary ( §8.7 ’s failure mode, used well) The irreversible act Can this be undone? Signature, death, sale, departure, confession, burning Discussion Plot resolution is the domain craft literature over-weights and theory under-weights, and both distortions produce errors. The over-weighting produces the belief that an ending’s job is to tie off . It is not. Its job is to reach a state in which the questions have stopped being live — which can be achieved by answering them, by making them unanswerable, or by making them no longer matter. Barthes’s hermeneutic code ( S/Z , 1970), invoked in Chapter 9 §4.5 as the mechanism by which an opening plants an enigma, closes here; and Barthes’s own account of the code includes not only the answer but the snare , the partial answer and the jammed enigma. A hermeneutic sequence can terminate without disclosure and still terminate. The under-weighting, more common in literary pedagogy, treats plot resolution as the vulgar domain — the one serious fiction rises above. This is a category error. A book that raised a question and then discarded it has not transcended plot; it has broken a contract , and readers feel it as carelessness rather than sophistication. The distinction the domain actually requires is between a question answered , a question declined on the page , and a question dropped . Only the third is a defect. The discrimination is worth a rule, because the rest of the domain depends on it: A declined question must be visibly declined. Somewhere in the ending, the text must register that the question exists and is not going to be answered. A character asks and is not told; a narrator notes the absence; a document is found to be incomplete. The registration costs a sentence and converts an oversight into a choice. The Handmaid’s Tale is the model. Offred’s fate is unresolved — but the Historical Notes stage an entire scholarly apparatus failing to determine it, which converts the gap from an omission into the novel’s subject. The reader is not left wondering whether Atwood forgot; they are shown people trying to find out and failing. A note on the plot question’s proper size. Chapter 14 ( The Subplot ) supplies the attention tax : every thread charges the reader page space and the novel owes a return proportionate to what it charged. The ending is where the bill arrives. A subplot that took eighty pages and receives one sentence of resolution has under-delivered; a subplot that took eight pages and receives a chapter has over-delivered, and the over-delivery is more damaging than it looks because it misrepresents the book’s own hierarchy. §7.1 ’s test 6 is this audit. Under- and over-delivery Under: the dropped thread . A character, a question or an object of evident significance is simply not mentioned again. Note that under-delivery is much more often caused by forgetting than by choice, and that the forgetting is invisible to the writer, who remembers everything. Over: the comprehensive settlement . Every named entity accounted for, in proportion to nothing. This is §8.5 , and its mechanism is that uniform resolution destroys hierarchy as uniform density destroys emphasis (Chapter 9 §5.4 ). Illustrations 1. Dickens, Bleak House (1853) — resolution as system. The novel’s plot resolution is famously total: Jarndyce and Jarndyce is consumed by its own costs, Lady Dedlock’s identity and death are settled, Esther’s parentage and marriage are settled, Tulkinghorn’s murder is solved, Krook’s shop and its papers are disposed of, and roughly two dozen minor figures receive a final position. It is worth teaching because it is the maximum case and it works — and the reason it works is that the resolutions are not distributed evenly but causally : nearly every thread terminates through Chancery, so the settlement is also the novel’s argument. Comprehensive resolution is safe when the comprehensiveness is itself thematic. 2. Flaubert, Madame Bovary (1857) — resolution by the wrong person. Emma dies; Charles dies; and Flaubert gives the novel’s final position not to either of them but to Homais, the pharmacist, who prospers and receives the cross of the Legion of Honour. The plot resolves and the resolution is an insult. This is Torgovnick’s tangent ( §3.5 ) used with maximum precision: the ending swerves to a minor character, and the swerve is the verdict, because the survival of Homais is what the book has been arguing all along. 3. Ishiguro, The Remains of the Day (1989) — resolution the character cannot register. The plot’s central question — whether Stevens will recognise what he gave up — is answered on the pier at Weymouth, where he does, briefly and devastatingly, and then turns immediately to the technical problem of bantering. The resolution is complete and the character walks away from it. This is a demonstration that plot resolution does not require a character to acknowledge the resolution , only that the reader be able to. 4.2 Character-Arc Completion What the reader receives: the final state of the change — or of the refusal to change — that the book has been tracking. Carriers Carrier The reader’s implicit question Note The act only this changed person could perform Would they have done that in chapter three? The strongest carrier available, and the most underused The repeated situation, answered differently What do they do the second time? Torgovnick’s parallelism ; the most reliable device for making change visible, since the reader makes the comparison The refused act What do they now decline to do? Change shown by omission; usually stronger than a performed act A change in what they notice Do they see the same things? Chapter 4’s territory: selection of detail as characterisation, used as an arc marker A change in address What do they call people now? Names, pronouns, forms of address; very cheap and very legible The unchanged element What survived? An arc requires a constant against which the change is measured Discussion The governing principle is that arcs are completed by behaviour, not by statement . A character who says they have changed has not demonstrated it; a character who does something they could not have done earlier has. This is the ending’s version of the oldest instruction in the craft literature, and it fails in drafts for a specific and identifiable reason: at the end of a book, the writer knows what the change was and is therefore able to name it, and naming is easier than staging. The strongest available device is the repeated situation . Put the character back in a circumstance the book has already shown, and let the difference in their behaviour carry the arc. It is efficient (it uses material already paid for), legible (the reader has the earlier instance to compare against), and unsentimental (nobody has to describe a feeling). It also produces closure by Torgovnick’s parallelism, so it discharges the character domain and a formal one at once. Two refinements matter in revision. First, the arc may complete as a refusal. Not every protagonist changes, and a book that tracks a failure to change owes the same completion. Stevens does not change; the ending shows him not changing, in full view of the opportunity. The novel is complete and the arc is complete, and it would be a poorer book if he had. Second, an arc requires a constant. Change is only perceptible against something stable. If everything about a character is different at the end, the reader registers replacement rather than development. The practical form: identify the one thing that has not changed and make sure it is visible in the final pages. Nadia in §9.10 puts on her father’s coat — a change — and gathers the sleeves so they do not drag , which is the same managing, measuring precision she has had since Chapter 9’s Version B. The constant is what makes the change legible. Under- and over-delivery Under: the unmarked arc . The character has changed and the ending gives the reader no occasion to see it. Frequently caused by an ending that is all plot: the protagonist is too busy resolving things to be observed. Over: the announced transformation . A character explaining what they have learned, or a narrator explaining it for them. See §8.6 ; it is the commonest single failure in student endings, and it is generated by anxiety that the reader will miss the point. Illustrations 1. Austen, Emma (1815) — the arc completed in an apology. Emma’s arc is a movement from confident misjudgement to accurate self-knowledge, and it completes not at her engagement but at Box Hill and afterwards, in her response to Mr Knightley’s rebuke. The novel’s ending confirms rather than performs the change. Worth noticing: the marriage is the plot resolution; the apology is the character resolution; they are separate events, several chapters apart, and the book is careful not to let one stand in for the other. 2. Achebe, Things Fall Apart (1958) — the arc completed by a refusal, and then annihilated. Okonkwo’s arc completes in his final act, which is the act his whole character has been driving towards and which his society can no longer contain. What Achebe then does is more radical: the last page removes the arc from the reader’s hands entirely and gives it to the District Commissioner, who is deciding how many paragraphs the matter deserves. The character domain is completed and then shown being erased , which is the novel’s argument about who writes endings. 3. Tolstoy, Anna Karenina (1878) — two arcs, completed at different distances. Anna’s arc completes in Part Seven; Levin’s completes in Part Eight, after her death, in a domain the novel has been building in parallel. The structural point, developed at §9.4 : a novel with two arcs cannot complete both at the climax , and the aftermath exists to complete the second. 4.3 Thematic Closure What the reader receives: the book’s final position — or its considered refusal of one — on the question it has been testing since its opening pages. Carriers Carrier The reader’s implicit question Note The recurring phrase, returned Where have I heard that? The most economical carrier available; see §5.3 The recurring object, reused What is it for now? Chapter 4’s motif economy, cashed The situation that answers the opening’s Is this where we started? Circularity; §6.4 , no. 1 The narrator’s generalisation What does the book think? Powerful and dangerous; §8.6 The parallel case Who else does this happen to? Theme carried by a secondary figure, which insulates it from the protagonist’s special pleading The withheld statement Why won’t it say? Refusal as position Discussion Thematic closure is the domain most often confused with the ending as a whole, and the confusion produces §8.6 . The confusion is understandable: theme is what a reader reports when asked what a book was about , and the ending is where they form the report. But theme is not a proposition the book asserts; it is a question the book has been testing , and the ending’s job is to conclude the test, not to publish the result. The distinction is operational. Compare two endings for the same novel: Version What the last page does Asserted theme A character says, in effect, we can never really know the people we love Concluded test Three people read a document that proves the person they loved kept something from them, and none of them says anything, and one of them puts on the dead man’s coat Both deliver the same theme. The first delivers it as a proposition the reader may agree or disagree with; the second delivers it as an experience the reader has just had. Only the second uses the book. This is the same discrimination Chapter 3 ( The Dialogue Exchange ) draws between text and subtext, and Chapter 4 ( The Descriptive Detail ) between denotation and connotation, applied at the largest available scale. Where the danger lies. Because the last pages carry privileged position ( §3.6 ), a generalisation placed there acquires enormous authority — it is read as the book speaking. This makes the narratorial generalisation the most powerful thematic carrier and the most easily abused. Eliot uses it magnificently ( §9.2 ) and could do so because the narrator has been generalising for eight hundred pages; a novel whose narrator has been effaced throughout cannot suddenly produce a maxim without the maxim reading as the author’s arrival. A narrator may state the theme at the end only if the narrator has been the kind of narrator who states things all along. Thematic assertion is a voice-contract question (Chapter 9 §4.1 ) before it is a thematic one. Under- and over-delivery Under: the unexamined close . The plot resolves and the book’s central question is simply not present in the final pages, so the reader closes it without a position on the thing it was about. Over: the thesis statement . See §8.6 . Also, in a subtler form, the ending that is only thematic — a final image so plainly symbolic that the characters have become its vehicles. Illustrations 1. Morrison, Beloved (1987) — theme closed by contradiction. The novel’s closing pages state, twice, that it was not a story to pass on — a phrase which in one idiom means not to be transmitted and in another means not to be declined , and which is printed in a book that is doing the transmitting the phrase forbids. Thematic closure here is achieved by an assertion that undoes itself; the reader is left holding a position the sentence will not let them settle. §9.6 analyses this in full. 2. Fitzgerald, The Great Gatsby (1925) — theme closed by widening. The last page leaves Gatsby entirely and moves to the Dutch sailors, the fresh green breast of the new world, and the general condition of a people borne backwards. The theme is completed by enlarging the frame until the individual case becomes an instance of something continental. §9.3 dissects the mechanism. 3. Camus, The Stranger (1942; trans. Ward, 1988) — theme closed by an assent the reader cannot share. Meursault’s final acceptance of “the gentle indifference of the world”, and his wish for a crowd of spectators greeting him with cries of hate, closes the novel’s argument about consciousness and meaning by having the protagonist arrive somewhere the reader is not invited to follow. Note the translation caution: the structural claim (the theme completes in an assent) survives every English version; the tonal claim (whether the assent is serene or defiant) does not, and differs measurably between Gilbert, Ward and Smith. 4.4 Emotional Catharsis What the reader receives: the specific felt release the book has been building — grief processed, tension discharged, dread confirmed, hope earned, anger permitted. Carriers Carrier The reader’s implicit question Note Physical proximity of characters kept apart Are they in the same room? The most reliable and least literary device on this list Silence after noise Has it stopped? Rhythm as feeling; the paragraph after the last shout The withheld gesture, performed Did they finally? Requires the withholding to have been established The permitted feeling Am I allowed to feel this? A character weeping, resting, sitting down, eating Rhythmic and syntactic release Do the sentences let go? Long sentence after short ones; a period after fragments The reader’s information advantage discharged Do they know what I know? Dramatic irony closed Discussion Catharsis is the domain most resistant to analysis and most damaged by the attempt, and this chapter treats it with corresponding brevity and a warning. The warning first. Catharsis is not an event the ending causes; it is a release of pressure the book has already created. No technique produces it in a book that has not built the pressure, and almost any competent technique produces it in a book that has. This is why the domain is the one most often “fixed” incorrectly: a writer who feels the ending is emotionally flat adds emotional material to the ending, when the deficiency is nearly always upstream. Chapter 13 ( The Viewpoint Shift ) supplies the relevant concept in the empathy budget : the reader’s capacity to feel for a character is a function of accumulated access, and an ending cannot spend what earlier chapters did not deposit. Aristotle’s katharsis is the source of the term and is less useful than its currency suggests, partly because what he meant by it — purgation, clarification, or something else — has been contested for two thousand years. What is transferable is the structural claim underneath: that a tragedy produces pity and fear through the arrangement of the incidents , not through appeals to feeling. Emotion is a product of structure. Walter Benjamin’s remark in “The Storyteller” (1936) is the more useful modern statement, and it is worth quoting because it explains why endings carry emotion disproportionately: the reader of a novel, he suggests, is drawn by the hope of warming their shivering life with a death they read about. What he is describing is the ending as the one place where a life becomes finished and therefore meaningful — an experience unavailable in life, since one’s own is never observed complete. The novel’s ending offers the reader a completed life to hold, and the emotional charge of endings is substantially the charge of that impossible perspective. Two practical notes. The physical is more reliable than the verbal. The most dependable catharsis carriers in prose are bodies: people in the same room who have not been, a hand taken, a person sitting down, a door opened, a meal eaten. This is not anti-intellectualism; it is a consequence of the fact that emotional release is registered somatically, and that a described physical event is the cheapest way for a text to produce a somatic response. Silence is the strongest instrument in the ending’s repertoire. Chapter 3 ( The Dialogue Exchange ) argues that what is not said carries the relational load; at an ending, a scene in which people who have been arguing for a book do not speak is worth any amount of dialogue. §9.10 ’s three siblings reading in silence is the household narrative’s entire cathartic payload, and it works because Chapter 3’s doorway exchange was adversarial and Chapter 9’s opening had Nadia declining to answer the phone. Under- and over-delivery Under: the cold close . Technically complete, emotionally inert. Diagnosable by asking what the reader is invited to feel on the last page and finding no answer. Over: the milked ending . Feeling extended past its discharge — a further page of weeping, a further paragraph of consolation. Its mechanism is that emotion decays under attention, so an ending that continues to solicit a feeling the reader has already had converts it into embarrassment. Illustrations 1. Steinbeck, The Grapes of Wrath (1939) — catharsis by an act that resolves no plot. The novel ends with Rose of Sharon, whose baby has been born dead, nursing a starving stranger in a barn. Nothing is resolved: the family’s situation is unchanged, the strike is unresolved, the road continues. The ending is nonetheless one of the most complete in American fiction, because the entire pressure of the book — the argument that survival is collective — is discharged in a single physical act. Catharsis without resolution, in one gesture. 2. Tolstoy, The Death of Ivan Ilyich (1886) — catharsis by the removal of the thing feared. The novella has spent its length inside a dying man’s terror; it ends with the terror gone and, in place of death, light. The release is proportionate to the pressure, and the pressure was built by a structure — the death announced first, then the life retraced — that guaranteed the reader would arrive at the deathbed with nothing to hope for. 3. Woolf, Mrs Dalloway (1925) — catharsis withheld and then granted in four words. The novel ends: For there she was. Nothing has been resolved; Septimus is dead; the party is a party. The release is produced by the sentence’s grammar — a stated existence, in the plainest possible words, after a book of hesitations — and by its being Peter Walsh’s perception rather than Clarissa’s, so that the reader is finally permitted to see her from outside and to find her present . Four words, and the whole book’s accumulated longing discharges. 4.5 The Final Image What the reader receives: the literal last thing the book shows them, which becomes the door they walk out through and the thing they will remember. Carriers Carrier The reader’s implicit question Note The object What am I looking at? Concrete, previously established, and not explained The gesture What are they doing? An action, preferably small and physical The grammatical form of the last sentence Does this stop? Herrnstein Smith’s territory; §3.2 The last word What is the final noise? Rabinowitz’s privileged position at maximum concentration The direction of attention Where am I looking — in, out, back, forward? The most underused variable in the domain The person of the last clause Who is present at the end? I , we , they , or nobody Discussion The final image is a domain rather than a decoration because of privileged position ( §3.6 ): whatever occupies the last sentence is read as a statement about the book. This has a consequence writers routinely underestimate. There is no neutral last sentence. A novel that ends on a character making tea has told the reader that tea is what the book was for. Sometimes that is right; the point is that it will be read that way regardless of intention. Four variables are worth isolating, because they can be manipulated independently and most drafts manipulate none of them deliberately. (1) Scale. Does the last image narrow to a detail or widen to a panorama? Beloved narrows to a single word. The Great Gatsby widens to a continent. Both close; they produce opposite after-images, and the choice should be made rather than inherited. (2) Direction in time. Does the final sentence look back, stay in the present, or project forward? The proleptic close ( §6.4 , no. 8) — narrating a future beyond the book’s action — is a distinct strategy with distinct costs, and its opposite, the arrested present-tense close, is another. (3) Grammatical closure. Herrnstein Smith’s unqualified assertion, applied. A last sentence that is short, declarative and unhedged closes harder than one that is long, subordinated and conditional; a last sentence ending on a strong stressed monosyllable closes harder than one ending on an unstressed syllable. These are not superstitions but observable regularities of English prosody, and they are why Bleak House ’s final unfinished sentence and Ulysses ’s final Yes feel so different in kind. (4) Who is present. A final image containing the protagonist, one containing another character looking at the protagonist, and one containing nobody are three different endings. The third — the ending that outlives its people — is a distinct and powerful device: Wuthering Heights ends with Lockwood at three graves and the moths and the heath, and the withdrawal of the human is the closure. Under- and over-delivery Under: the arbitrary stop . The last sentence is simply the next sentence, carrying no more weight than the one before it. Diagnosable by test 10 ( §7.1 ). Its symptom is that the reader turns the page expecting more. Over: the portentous image . A final image so heavily loaded that it announces its own significance — the symbol arriving with its explanation attached, or an image so composed that the prose visibly poses for a photograph. The rule is Chapter 4’s: an image can bear connotation only in proportion to the denotation it has established. Illustrations 1. Joyce, Ulysses (1922) — closure by affirmation and by punctuation. The novel ends with Molly Bloom’s yes I said yes I will Yes . Almost every closural device Herrnstein Smith catalogues is active at once: unqualified assertion; a terminal word that means assent; capitalisation as a terminal modification of a text that has been resisting capitals; and the closural allusion of memory and sleep. §9.7 develops this. 2. Orwell, Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949) — the final image as a defeat, and its reversal by apparatus. He loved Big Brother. Four words, a stated fact in the past tense, no qualification, no hope. It is one of the most complete final images in English — and it is followed by an Appendix that, by its grammar alone, arguably undoes it (§4.6, §9.5 ). 3. Saramago, Blindness (1995; trans. Giovanni Pontiero) — the image withheld at the last moment. The novel ends with the doctor’s wife looking up at the sky and then, in the book’s final movement, at the city, in a formulation that declines to give the reader the confirming vision they have been waiting three hundred pages for. §9.9 argues that the withholding is the novel’s ethical position rather than a coyness. 4. Brontë, Wuthering Heights (1847) — the image that removes the people. Lockwood at three headstones, wondering how anyone could imagine unquiet slumbers for the sleepers in that quiet earth. The closure is produced by the disappearance of everyone the book was about, by the transfer of the last word to its least reliable and least interested narrator, and by a question that is formally a question and functionally a full stop. 4.6 A Proposed Sixth: Formal Closure The five domains above are inherited from a broadly representational account of fiction: they concern the story — its questions, its people, its argument, its feeling, its last picture. But a reader arriving at the end of a novel is also completing something else. They are finishing an artefact : a physical and formal object with a pattern, and the pattern has its own terminus. Formal closure. The completion, breaking or fulfilment of the book’s own structural pattern, as distinct from its story: the frame that returns; the repeated chapter shape that alters at its last instance; the final section that answers the first; the suppressed narrator who reappears; the apparatus that displaces the narrative’s authority; the typographic or paratextual device that is finally explained or finally withdrawn. This is Chapter 9 §4.6 ’s formal contract falling due. That section argued that the opening pages teach the reader the book’s structural conventions — person and tense, temporal architecture, unit of division, plurality of narration, apparatus — and that a device introduced late reads as a gimmick because the contract was not declared. The contract opened there is closed here, and the closing has its own repertoire and its own failure modes. Carriers Carrier What is completed Example The returned frame A narrator or vantage established at the start reappears at the end Frankenstein ; Wuthering Heights ; Heart of Darkness The terminal modification of a repeated shape A pattern of chapters, sections or documents is altered at its last instance The Sound and the Fury ’s fourth section abandoning first person The answered first section The book’s last movement addresses its first directly Middlemarch ’s Prelude and Finale The suppressed narrator returning A voice withdrawn early comes back Madame Bovary ’s vanished nous — and the celebrated fact that it does not return The apparatus An appendix, note, index or editorial frame follows the narrative Nineteen Eighty-Four ; The Handmaid’s Tale ; Pale Fire The withdrawal of a device A typographic or formal constraint is released Saramago’s punctuation; Faulkner’s italics The completed count A numerical or sectional scheme reaches its designed end The seven-part structure of Anna Karenina answered by an eighth Why it is distinct from thematic closure The obvious objection is that formal closure is a species of thematic closure — that the form is an argument, and completing it completes the argument. The distinction the chapter maintains is this: Thematic closure operates on the book’s argument . Formal closure operates on the book’s artefact . They are frequently aligned and are not the same, and the clearest evidence is that formal closure can contradict thematic closure within a single book. Nineteen Eighty-Four is the demonstration, and it is the strongest single case for admitting the sixth domain. The narrative’s thematic closure is total and totally bleak: Winston is broken; the last line states that he loved Big Brother; the book’s argument about the survivability of the individual under total power is concluded in the negative. Then comes the Appendix, “The Principles of Newspeak” — and it is written in the past tense , by an evidently free scholar, for readers who are evidently not living in Oceania, in standard English, with footnoted reference to the narrative as a historical document. Nothing in the story changes. No plot question is reopened. No character is rescued. But the artefact now contains a vantage from which Oceania is over, and the reader who notices the tense has been handed a hope the narrative explicitly denied them. This is not thematic closure — the theme was closed four pages earlier — and it is not plot resolution. It is a formal operation on the book as an object, and it is powerful enough that a significant body of criticism regards the Appendix as reversing the novel’s despair. §9.5 examines the argument and does not settle it. The Handmaid’s Tale performs a related manoeuvre with the opposite valence. The Historical Notes place Offred’s account in an academic conference two centuries later, which formally guarantees Gilead’s fall — and simultaneously stages a male academic being facetious about a woman’s testimony, so that the formal consolation arrives inside a demonstration of how such testimony gets handled. Chapter 10 ( The Prologue ) analyses the Notes at §9.8 as a threshold arriving at the wrong end of the book; this chapter analyses the same device as a closural one. Both are true, which is why the device is so effective. Discussion: the three modes of formal closure (1) Completion. The pattern finishes as declared. A frame opened at the start closes at the end; a book in seven parts ends its seventh; an alternating structure alternates for the last time. Completion is the safest mode and the least remarked, because a satisfied formal expectation is invisible. Its value is nonetheless considerable: much of the sense of “rightness” readers report about endings they cannot analyse is formal completion doing its work below the level of notice. (2) Modification. The pattern alters at its last instance — Herrnstein Smith’s terminal modification ( §3.2 ). The Sound and the Fury runs three first-person sections and then, for the fourth, moves to third person and to Dilsey; the modification is the closure, and it is why the novel feels finished despite resolving very little. The mode’s danger is legibility: a modification the reader does not register as a modification is simply an inconsistency. (3) Disruption. The pattern is broken by something the book has not prepared — an apparatus, a voice, a document — which reframes the whole. This is the mode with the largest effects and the highest costs, and it is where the domain earns its keep as a separate category, because disruption cannot be described as thematic closure: it works by changing what kind of object the reader is holding. Under- and over-delivery Under: the unclosed form . A frame opened and never returned to; an epistolary novel that abandons letters; a book of alternating viewpoints that ends in one of them without acknowledgement. Chapter 10 §8.4 treats this as unresolved distance for prologues; the general case is the same. Note that under-delivery here is frequently invisible to the writer and perfectly visible to the reader as an unlocated dissatisfaction. Over: the formal flourish . A closural device with no relation to the book — an appendix because appendices are interesting, a coda in another voice because the writer wanted to write one. The test is whether the device answers something the book opened. The argument against a sixth domain The chapter is obliged to make the case against its own addition, and there is a respectable one. Position 1: five is enough, and the sixth is a category error. Formal closure is not a purpose an ending serves the reader; it is a means by which the other five are served. When Nineteen Eighty-Four ’s Appendix reverses the novel’s despair, what it has done is thematic — it has altered the book’s final position on whether the Party can be survived. That the alteration was accomplished by a formal device does not make it a separate domain, any more than a metaphor is a separate domain because it is a linguistic device. The five domains name what the reader gets ; formal closure names how . Admitting it confuses the model’s level of description, and a taxonomy that mixes ends and means loses its diagnostic value. Position 2: it is separately real, and the five-domain model cannot name its failures. The reply is that the objection proves too much. Every domain is served by means; the question is whether the reader experiences the completion as belonging to the story or to the object. And there is a decisive test case: a book can achieve full thematic closure and produce, in a reader, a distinct and locatable dissatisfaction whose content is the form did not finish . An epistolary novel that ends in ordinary narration has closed its theme and left something conspicuously open, and the five-domain model has no vocabulary for the residue. Formal closure has distinct carriers (frames, apparatus, section schemes), distinct failure modes (the unclosed frame, the abandoned device), and distinct remedies (return the frame, or remove it from the opening). Those are the criteria by which Chapter 9 admitted its own sixth contract, and they are met here. This chapter adopts the sixth for diagnostic purposes, while conceding that it sits at a different level of description from the other five and that a student who rejects it loses very little. Seminar question 2 ( §12.2 ) puts the disagreement to the class, with the Appendix to Nineteen Eighty-Four as the evidence. 4.7 Summary table: the domains, their carriers and their failures Domain Delivered chiefly by Under-delivery looks like Over-delivery looks like Plot resolution Answered questions; consequences enacted; irreversible acts The dropped thread; questions forgotten rather than declined The comprehensive settlement; resolution proportional to nothing Character arc The act only the changed person could perform; the repeated situation answered differently The unmarked arc; change asserted, never staged The announced transformation; a character explaining their growth Thematic closure Recurring phrase or object returned; the situation that answers the opening’s The unexamined close; the book’s question absent from its ending The thesis statement; characters as vehicles for a symbol Emotional catharsis Bodies in proximity; silence after noise; the withheld gesture performed The cold close; nothing to feel The milked ending; feeling solicited after discharge The final image An object, a gesture, the grammar of the last sentence The arbitrary stop; the reader turns the page The portentous image; the symbol arriving with its own gloss Formal closure (proposed) Frame returned; pattern modified; apparatus; section scheme completed The unclosed frame; the abandoned device The formal flourish; a coda answering nothing 4.8 Must all domains be served at once? No, and the model is misused when read that way. Four qualifications. 1. The domains are genre-weighted, and the weighting is not a hierarchy of merit. A crime novel that fails plot resolution has failed absolutely, because the genre’s contract is an epistemic one; a lyric novel of consciousness may resolve nothing at all. The following distribution is descriptive, not prescriptive, and it is worth putting in front of students who have absorbed literary-fiction defaults as universal law: Mode Load-bearing domains Frequently waived Detective / mystery Plot; formal (the solution’s disclosure structure) Character arc; catharsis Romance Plot; catharsis Formal; thematic Thriller Plot; catharsis Thematic; formal Literary realist Character; theme; final image Plot resolution, frequently Modernist / lyric Final image; formal; theme Plot; sometimes character Tragedy Character; catharsis; theme Plot resolution beyond the death Epic / systems fiction Thematic; formal Character arc for any single figure 2. A domain may be served by deliberate refusal, and refusal is not absence. The distinction is the one drawn at §4.1: a question declined on the page has been served; a question dropped has not. The same holds in every domain. An ending that refuses catharsis, visibly, has addressed the catharsis domain. 3. The domains are not equal in size, and an ending that serves two well beats one that serves six thinly. This is the direct consequence of §5 : multiplicity is the goal, and multiplicity means one carrier serving several domains, not several carriers each serving one. 4. The correct number of domains for a given ending is a question, not a target. The diagnostic form ( §7.1 , test 5) is not how many? but which, and did you choose? An ending serving three domains deliberately is in better condition than one serving five by accident. 4.9 Proposals from earlier chapters: rulings (second edition) Four chapters of this edition left a proposed category for this one to judge, and the formal closure proposed in §4.6 is itself left to a later chapter. Chapter 9’s formal contract: adopted at the scale of a book. Formal closure (§4.6) is the formal contract discharged. An unclosed frame, an abandoned device or an apparatus that answers nothing is a failure only where the opening declared a frame, a device or an apparatus, so the closing domain cannot be applied without the opening contract. The formal closure domain itself is adopted here for diagnosis, conceding that it sits at a different level of description from the other five; Chapter 18 ( The Structural Edit , section 3.4) rejects it as a domain of the ending and adopts it at the scale of the book as the form audit, a test of the book’s form on the second rung of its revision ladder: both test cases pass the audit, and in both the formal pattern carries while the payment lies in another domain (the Appendix’s past tense is received as hope, the Six Feet Under montage as the series’ theme), so the objection holds at the ending and the defence holds for the audit. Chapter 3’s silence domain: rejected as a domain of the ending, kept as a domain of the exchange. Its test case was to be the household mother’s unexplained silence. At the ending that silence is served by plot resolution, as a question visibly declined (§4.1): the reader is shown the three siblings reading a document that explains their father and says nothing of their mother. The siblings’ own silence as they read is a carrier of catharsis (§4.4). At this scale the objection Chapter 3 conceded, that silence is a means rather than a value that changes, holds; at the scale of a dialogue exchange, where a silent participant turns the exchange into a performance, the domain stands. Chapter 6’s recasting close: not a separate category at a book’s last line. The recasting close is defined against the chapter ending that points forward; at the last line nothing comes next, so every close looks back and the category no longer discriminates. It remains a type of chapter ending. The question it leaves, how far a close may recast the whole book, from the parallel that adds a layer (strategy 2) to the retrospective reframe that changes what the book was (strategy 13), passes to Chapter 15 ( The Reveal ), which answers it with the teller rule: a close may falsify only what a teller in the book could have shaped. Chapter 10’s last ordinary day: confirmed as a type of prologue. The household ending (§9.10) pays off the two objects of the father’s last ordinary day, the good pen and the unfinished In case , and leaves two of its details, the boy at the glass and the sign never turned to CLOSED, unredeemed. That is the type’s characteristic profit and its characteristic risk: a last ordinary day deposits more than an ending can spend.

title: 5. Multiplicity: The Economy of the Ending
section: Multiplicity — The Economy of the Ending
text: 5.1 The principle, stated as a constraint Multiplicity — the practice of making a single unit of text discharge several narrative functions at once — is introduced in Chapter 1 ( The Purposes of a Scene ) and recurs in every chapter of this textbook. At the ending it operates at its highest stakes, and for reasons opposite to those that govern the opening. Chapter 9 argued that multiplicity is an arithmetical necessity in the opening pages, because the opening has the fewest words, the most simultaneous obligations and the least reader patience. None of those constraints applies at the close. An ending may be long; the reader has already decided to finish; and the obligations, while numerous, could in principle be discharged serially across a final chapter of any length. The constraint at the ending is different in kind, and stating it correctly is the whole of this section: At the ending, multiplicity is not an economy of space. It is the difference between a conclusion the reader watches and one they undergo . An ending that works through the domains in sequence — the confrontation, then a chapter in which the protagonist reflects and is seen to have changed, then a passage in which the theme is stated, then a final image — is not too long. It is legible as a procedure . The reader can see the machinery, because the machinery has been laid out end to end where anyone can watch it operate. And the reader’s response to visible machinery at an ending is not boredom but something worse: the retroactive suspicion that the preceding four hundred pages were also machinery, which is the retroactive damage §1.1 describes. The usual form of this point is a warning against treating the five domains as a checklist. The stronger form of the claim, and the one this section argues: The strongest endings close several accounts in a single image rather than working through the domains in sequence — and the reason is not efficiency but simultaneity . When plot, character and theme resolve in the same gesture, the reader cannot separate them, and what they experience is not three resolutions but one meaning. This is why so many of the most admired endings in fiction are short . The last page of The Great Gatsby ; the last four words of Mrs Dalloway ; the last sentence of Things Fall Apart ; the last word of Beloved . It is not that brevity is a virtue at endings. It is that an ending which has found the single carrier does not need length, and one that has not cannot be rescued by it. A corollary for revision, which inverts the instinct: A long ending is usually a symptom, not a problem. When an aftermath sprawls, the cause is almost always that no single carrier has been found and the domains are being served one at a time. Cutting the aftermath does not fix this; it produces a short ending that still serves the domains serially. The fix is upstream: find the object, gesture or image capable of carrying more than one account, and let the others go. 5.2 Anatomy of a multiplying ending The clearest available demonstration in a single paragraph is the last movement of Achebe’s Things Fall Apart (1958). Okonkwo has hanged himself; his people cannot cut him down, since a man who takes his own life is an abomination; the District Commissioner arrives, listens, reflects on the book he is writing, and the novel closes: He had already chosen the title of the book, after much thought: The Pacification of the Primitive Tribes of the Lower Niger. The novel does not end with Okonkwo. It ends with the sentence in which a colonial administrator names his own book. Dissected: Textual element Domains discharged He — the last pronoun of the novel belongs to the Commissioner Formal (the vantage has been captured); thematic (whose account survives?) had already chosen — the decision precedes the events; the pluperfect Character (a man for whom Okonkwo’s death was material); plot (the outcome was settled before the encounter) after much thought Character (self-regard); catharsis — the reader’s fury has a target, which is the release the novel’s final movement has been withholding The Pacification Thematic (the word that converts destruction into administration) Primitive Tribes Thematic (the register that will replace the one the reader has spent the book inside) of the Lower Niger World / final image (the specific place, reduced to a geographical category); formal (a title inside a title) The paragraph’s scale — Okonkwo’s whole life is contemplated as a paragraph Plot (Okonkwo’s arc is closed by being summarised ); formal (the novel demonstrates the closural form that would have contained it) Every domain is touched, in one sentence, and the sentence performs no visible closural work at all: no summary, no reflection, no image of finality, no statement of theme. It is a man deciding on a title. Three observations for the classroom. (1) The multiplicity is achieved by a change of vantage, not by compression. Achebe has not packed six things into a sentence; he has found the one position from which one thing means six. This is the distinction Chapter 9 §5.1 draws between compression and selection , at the largest scale it can operate. (2) The domains are served in a way that would be impossible serially. Suppose Achebe had written the same content as four separate passages: Okonkwo’s death; a passage on the loss to the clan; a passage on the Commissioner’s indifference; a closing statement about colonial historiography. Every element would survive and the effect would be gone, because the effect depends on the reader discovering the four things simultaneously in a single flat sentence and having nowhere to put the resulting anger. (3) The multiplication is retrospective. None of this is legible in the sentence itself. It is legible only because the reader has spent two hundred pages inside the world the Commissioner is about to describe in a paragraph, and it is therefore an exact demonstration of the retroactive lens: the ending confers meaning on the preceding book, and the preceding book confers meaning on the ending, in one operation. 5.3 Where closural multiplicity actually lives Novice revision looks for multiplicity in symbol , on the assumption that the last page is where a book’s images should become significant. In practice, the multiplying work at an ending is done in four humbler places, none of them figurative. 1. The object already in the room. The most efficient closural carrier available is a physical thing the book has established, used, and left lying about. It carries plot (what it is), character (whose relation to it is at issue), theme (what it has come to mean) and image (what the reader is looking at) without a single word of explanation, because all four meanings were deposited earlier. The coat in §9.10 is this; so is Queequeg’s coffin in Moby-Dick ’s epilogue, which is a plot device, a character’s gift, a thematic statement about the uses of death, and the final picture, all at once, and which was built as a coffin in chapter 110, sixteen chapters before it is caulked as the ship’s life-buoy. 2. The gesture the book has shown before. A repeated action, performed differently, discharges character (the change), plot (the situation has altered), and formal closure (parallelism) simultaneously. It is the most reliable device in the repertoire because the comparison is done by the reader, which means the writer never has to state it. 3. Tense, aspect and person. The cheapest closural instrument in the language, and the most consistently overlooked. A shift from past to present, from present to past, from I to we , from a character’s name to a pronoun or from a pronoun to a name, will alter a final paragraph’s whole relation to time and to the reader without adding content. Nineteen Eighty-Four ’s Appendix is a formal reversal accomplished, in the last analysis, by a tense . Chapter 9 §5.3 makes the same observation about openings ( had once been ; was to remember ): grammar is the least expensive worldbuilding available, and it is also the least expensive closure. 4. Who is given the last position. The choice of which consciousness, or which voice, occupies the final paragraph is a structural decision that most drafts make by default and that the strongest endings make deliberately. Giving the close to the protagonist, to a witness, to a minor character, to a document, or to nobody produces five different books. Flaubert gives it to Homais; Achebe to the Commissioner; Brontë to Lockwood; Orwell to a lexicographer. In each case the assignment is the argument. Symbol can multiply — Rose of Sharon in The Grapes of Wrath does — but it is the highest-risk instrument available at a close, for the reason Chapter 4 ( The Descriptive Detail ) gives about connotation generally: an image that overreaches its established denotation draws attention to the author. At an ending, where every element is being read as a statement about the book, the attention is fatal. 5.4 The ceiling: the over-determined ending Multiplicity has an upper bound at the close as it does at the opening, and the failure at that bound has a distinct character. The opening’s ceiling failure is strain : too much information per sentence, no rests, no emphasis (Chapter 9 §5.4 ). The ending’s ceiling failure is different, and worse, because it is a failure of credibility rather than of comprehension. The over-determined ending is one in which every element visibly means something. The weather participates. The object is a symbol. The minor character returns to close a rhyme. The last line answers the first. Nothing is present that is not doing work. Three symptoms mark it: Symptom What the reader experiences No inert material Every noun in the final pages has been assigned a function; the world has stopped existing independently of the meaning Convergence without cause Threads arrive together because the ending requires it, not because anything made them The audible click The reader can hear the book locking shut, and the sound is the author’s The mechanism is the one Barthes identifies in “The Reality Effect” (1968), running in reverse. Barthes’s argument is that certain details signify nothing except reality itself, and that their apparent uselessness is what authenticates a fictional world. An ending in which nothing is useless has withdrawn that authentication at the exact moment the reader is deciding whether the book was true. The remedy is counter-intuitive, and it is stated here as a rule because it is the opposite of what a writer polishing an ending will instinctively do: An ending needs some material that means nothing. A bus going past. A radiator. The stool somebody sits on. These are not padding; they are the evidence that the world is not being operated. An ending assembled entirely from significant elements does not read as meaningful; it reads as arranged. The limit case is instructive. Middlemarch ’s Finale is, by any measure, an over-determined ending: it settles every major figure, generalises about human significance, and closes on a sentence of enormous rhetorical weight. It nonetheless does not read as arranged, and the reason is that Eliot has spent eight hundred pages establishing a narrator who does this all the time . Over-determination is a failure of consistency rather than of quantity. A book whose narration has been generalising throughout may end on a maxim; a book that has been rigorously scenic may not. 5.5 Exercise: the closural audit A practical procedure, and the most reliable teaching instrument in the chapter’s first half. It is deliberately mechanical, and its output is a distribution rather than a verdict. Print the last three pages of the draft, double-spaced. In the margin beside each sentence, write the letters of every domain it discharges: P (plot), C (character), T (theme), E (emotional catharsis), I (final image), F (formal). Mark, separately, every sentence that discharges nothing — the inert material of §5.4. Count. Interpretation: Pattern Diagnosis First move Most sentences carry one letter, and the letters appear in blocks The ending is serial . The domains are being worked through in sequence and the reader can see it Look for a single carrier — object, gesture, or vantage — that could take two of the blocks. Delete one block entirely and test whether it is missed One sentence or image carries four or more The spine has been found Build the close around it; consider moving it later; check that nothing after it is anticlimactic No inert sentences at all Over-determined (§5.4) Restore two or three sentences that mean nothing More than a third inert The aftermath is running on residual momentum Locate the last sentence that discharges a domain and test whether the book ends there A column is empty across all three pages A domain is unserved Deliberate refusal, or oversight? ( §7.1 , test 5) The letters are dense in the first of the three pages and thin in the last two The ending has already happened and the book is still going §8.3 ; consider whether the real last line has been passed The last row is the exercise’s most valuable single output. In student drafts, by this book’s estimate rather than any count, the true ending is often two to four pages before the printed one , and the audit locates it without argument.

title: 6. Earned and Unearned
text: 6.0 What this section covers “Earned” is the central term in craft discussion of endings and the least analysed. It is used as though its meaning were obvious, and it is not: writers apply it confidently to endings they like and cannot say what test they have run. This section takes the term apart. It proceeds in seven steps. §6.1 states what the earned/unearned distinction actually claims, which turns out to be two claims rather than one. §6.2 separates the claim from the thing it is most often confused with, predictability, and argues that the separation is the whole art. §6.3 grounds both in Aristotle and in the plant economy this textbook has been building since Chapter 6. §6.4 supplies a taxonomy of sixteen closural strategies. §6.5 shows how to use a taxonomy of strategies in revision, which is not by classification. §6.6 addresses the proportion problem of climax and aftermath. §6.7 historicises the whole apparatus and warns against universalising the present. 6.1 What “earned” claims The working distinction is the standard one: Earned — every element the ending relies on was planted or built earlier in the book, so that the resolution feels, in hindsight, like a culmination the reader could have anticipated even if they did not predict it. Unearned — the ending depends on something introduced at the last moment: new information, a sudden capability, an outside rescue, a fact withheld not for effect but for convenience. This is correct and incomplete. Unpacked, it contains two distinct claims , which have different evidence, different failure modes and different remedies, and which are conflated at some cost. Claim 1 is about preparation, and it is a fact about the text. Every element the ending uses as load-bearing must exist in the book before the ending. This is checkable, mechanically, by anyone with a copy: it is the plant audit ( §7.1 , test 2). Its failure mode is the unearned rescue ( §8.1 ). Its remedy is to plant the missing element earlier, which is nearly always a small edit — a sentence in chapter four — rather than a structural repair. Claim 2 is about retrospective inevitability, and it is a fact about the reader. The ending must produce, in hindsight, the sense that this was what the book was going towards. This is not checkable. It is a felt property, it can fail in books where every element is dutifully planted, and its remedy is not planting but pressure — the sense that the material was building towards something rather than merely accumulating. The distinction matters because the two failures look identical from inside a draft and require opposite responses. Claim 1 fails Claim 2 fails Symptom The reader says where did that come from? The reader says so what? Diagnosis An element is doing load-bearing work and was not deposited Every element was deposited and none of them was under pressure What is missing A plant A want , running through the book, that the ending answers Remedy Insert the plant, early and unremarked Strengthen the mid-book, not the ending Cost of the wrong remedy Adding pressure to an unplanted ending produces melodrama Adding plants to an unfelt ending produces a well-documented shrug The second failure is far more common in competent drafts and far less often correctly named. A writer who has been told to plant things will plant them; the resulting ending will be defensible, traceable, and inert. Claim 1 is a necessary condition and not a sufficient one , and a chapter that taught only the plant audit would produce endings that pass an audit and land on nothing. The full statement the chapter uses from here on: An ending is earned when everything it relies on was already in the book, and when what it does with that material answers a pressure the book has been building. The first is a matter of deposit; the second of interest accrued on it. A note on why this is the answer to Miller. §3.9 left the chapter with a concession: every ending is a loss, and the question is what the reader gets in exchange. Claim 2 is the answer. An ending that merely closes the narratable has taken something and given nothing; an ending that closes the narratable by answering a pressure the narratable itself generated has converted instability into shape. The exchange is real, and it is what “earned” names. Miller’s thin endings are thin because they satisfy Claim 1 and ignore Claim 2 — they dispose of the disequilibrium administratively. His diagnosis is right about the endings he examines, and the remedy is not to abandon closure but to stop treating it as disposal. 6.2 Inevitability is not predictability A damaging misunderstanding in this area, because it produces two opposite errors, is the belief that an earned ending is one the reader can see coming. It is not, and the confusion produces two opposite errors: writers who fear predictability and therefore withhold preparation, and writers who fear the accusation of cheating and therefore telegraph. The distinction: Predictability is a property of the reader’s state before the ending: they can say what will happen. Inevitability is a property of the reader’s state after it: they cannot imagine it having happened otherwise. These are independent. All four combinations exist: Felt inevitable afterwards Not felt inevitable Predicted beforehand The classical satisfaction. The reader sees the shape coming and is pleased to be right — the mode of tragedy, where the audience knows the myth, and of much romance and crime The tedious ending: predicted, arrived, meant nothing Not predicted The target. Unforeseen and, in retrospect, the only possible outcome. This is the whole art The cheat: unforeseen and arbitrary — §8.1 The top-left quadrant deserves emphasis, because contemporary craft discussion tends to treat predictability as a defect tout court . It is not. Greek tragedy is entirely predictable to its original audience; the pleasure is in watching the known outcome arrive by the particular route this dramatist has chosen. So is the marriage plot: nobody reading Pride and Prejudice is uncertain that Elizabeth will marry Darcy, and the novel is not damaged by it. Surprise is one source of satisfaction at an ending and not the principal one. What produces inevitability without predictability is a specific and teachable structure, and it needs naming because most drafts get it backwards: Plant the materials in plain sight; withhold the combination . The reader should be able, afterwards, to point at every component and say they saw it. What they could not do is assemble them, because the assembling required a piece of judgement — a decision by a character, a shift of vantage, a recognition — that only the ending supplies. This is Aristotle’s anagnorisis doing structural work. The recognition is not new information arriving; it is existing information reorganised. And it is why the strongest twist endings are also the most heavily planted: the elements were all present, in the open, doing other apparent jobs. Two practical consequences. (1) Plants should not look like plants. An element inserted so that the reader will notice it has been half-spent already. Genette’s term for the unemphatic advance notice is the amorce — a seed that passes as ordinary and becomes significant only retrospectively (Chapter 10 §6.2 uses the same term for the prologue’s fragments). The good pen going into the coat pocket in the household narrative’s prologue is an amorce : at the time it is a small oddity about a man’s habits. (2) The test for a plant is not “did the reader notice?” but “can the reader find it?” These are different questions with different answers, and the second is the one the earned/unearned distinction actually depends on. A reader who reaches the last page and cannot locate the preparation feels cheated. A reader who located it in advance feels clever. A reader who could not have located it in advance but can locate it now is having the intended experience. 6.3 Aristotle’s necessity or probability, and the plant economy The ancient form of the earned test is the requirement in the Poetics that the incidents of a plot follow one another by necessity or probability . Aristotle is precise about the alternative he is rejecting: a sequence in which events follow one another merely after rather than because . The distinction is the same one Chapter 2 ( Scene and Sequel ) makes with the causal chain — the test of whether each beat “had to happen next” — and applying it at the scale of the whole book gives the earned test its logical form. Two refinements from the Poetics are worth carrying into revision. “Or probability” is doing a great deal of work. Aristotle does not require that endings be necessary ; probable is enough. This is a lower bar than modern craft discussion usually assumes, and it licenses a good deal. An ending need not be the only possible outcome; it needs to be one that the established characters, in the established world, would plausibly produce. Chapter 14’s Levin-and-Anna problem is the standard case: nothing necessitates Levin’s arrival at faith, and the novel’s claim is only that a man like that, in that situation, might. The plot’s own structure is the source. Aristotle’s stipulation that the unravelling arise from the plot itself rather than from a contrivance is the ancestor of the whole modern prohibition on the deus ex machina , and it contains a discrimination that the modern version has lost. What Aristotle objects to is not implausibility but externality : an outcome produced by something outside the causal system the play has built. A wildly improbable event generated by the plot is acceptable; a probable one imported from outside is not. This is why coincidence at an ending is so much more damaging than coincidence at a beginning — a point worth teaching as a rule, since it explains a large asymmetry that puzzles students: Coincidence may start a story and may not end one. A chance meeting on page one is a premise; the same meeting on page four hundred is a contrivance. The reason is causal position: an opening coincidence generates the causal chain, and a closing one substitutes for it. The plant economy, formalised. This book has built the machinery for this in the chapters before this one and it can now be stated as a single system. Stage Chapter The operation Deposit Chapter 4 ( The Descriptive Detail ) An object, phrase or gesture is established with a denotative job, so that it is present without being flagged Maintenance Chapter 6 ( The Chapter Break ) Proposition and payoff : the element recurs at intervals, accruing connotation, so that the reader’s frame stays warm Instalment Chapter 10 ( The Prologue ) Closing the distance : partial closures are scheduled so the reader is periodically reassured the material is load-bearing Discharge This chapter The element is used, in the ending, to do work it could not have done at deposit The whole system has one purpose: to make the fourth stage possible without the reader detecting the first three as preparation. And it produces the chapter’s most testable single instruction: Nothing new and load-bearing arrives at the ending. Everything the ending uses was deposited, maintained, and instalment-paid; what the ending contributes is not material but combination . That instruction has a limit, and the limit should be stated because students over-apply the rule. It prohibits new load-bearing elements, not new elements. An ending may perfectly well contain a room the reader has not seen, a minor character who has not appeared, a sentence about a bus going past. What it may not do is rest on them. The test is substitution: if the element were removed, would the ending still work? If yes, it is furniture and is welcome. If no, it must have been planted. 6.4 A taxonomy of sixteen closural strategies The strategies below are adapted from Torgovnick’s typology of closural relations ( §3.5 ) and Herrnstein Smith’s account of closural devices ( §3.2 ), with additions from practice. They are not mutually exclusive — most strong endings braid two or three — and they are not ranked. Each is a shape the ending can take, with characteristic purchases and characteristic costs. # Strategy Description Exemplar Buys Costs 1 Circularity The close returns to the beginning’s language, image or situation Wuthering Heights (Lockwood on the moor, twice); One Hundred Years of Solitude Formal closure at maximum; the shape becomes visible Can imply nothing has changed; risks reading as a trick 2 Parallelism A situation from earlier recurs with its terms altered Great Expectations , revised (the ruined garden); Pride and Prejudice (the second proposal) Character arc made visible without statement; uses paid-for material Requires the earlier instance to be memorable; fails silently if it is not 3 Tangent The close swerves to something apparently unrelated Madame Bovary (Homais’s medal); Nineteen Eighty-Four (the Appendix) Verdict delivered without comment; escapes the protagonist’s special pleading Reads as evasion or as authorial whim if the relation is not inferable 4 Incompletion The pattern is deliberately left unfinished The Handmaid’s Tale ; Huckleberry Finn (lighting out) Honesty about what cannot be settled; preserves the narratable ( §3.9 ) Now the default of a genre (§6.7); must work against the suspicion of default 5 The frame closed A narrator or vantage established at the start reappears Frankenstein (Walton resumes); Heart of Darkness Perspective; the story is shown having been received Two endings to write; the outer one is often flatter than the inner 6 The coda or finale A short final movement in a changed key, after the structure is complete Middlemarch (“Finale”); War and Peace ’s epilogues Room for the character and theme domains after a plot-heavy climax The commonest site of §8.3 (endless aftermath) and §8.5 (tidiness) 7 The epilogue in another voice The close is delivered by a different speaker, register or document The Handmaid’s Tale (“Historical Notes”); Dracula (Harker’s note) Reframing power; the story is placed in a world larger than itself The reader has invested in the first voice and must be persuaded to accept a second 8 The proleptic close The future beyond the action is narrated Middlemarch ; Jane Eyre ’s final chapter Consequence made visible; the settlement’s classical instrument Forecloses the reader’s imagination; the most conventional strategy on the list 9 The terminal image The book ends on a picture, without commentary Blindness ; Wuthering Heights ; The Grapes of Wrath Maximum after-image; leaves interpretation with the reader Carries no information; fails if the image has not accrued meaning 10 The aphoristic close A generalisation, maxim or unqualified assertion Middlemarch (unvisited tombs); The Great Gatsby (boats against the current) Herrnstein Smith’s strongest formal device; portable, memorable Requires a narrator licensed to generalise; one step from §8.6 11 The deliberate anticlimax The close is smaller than the expectation it follows Vanity Fair (the puppets put back in the box); Madame Bovary Refuses false elevation; can be devastating Indistinguishable from failure unless the deflation is legible as chosen 12 The arrested ending The book stops mid-action, before the outcome The Handmaid’s Tale (the step into the van); The Grapes of Wrath Intensity; the reader completes the gesture The reader may experience it as the printer’s error; needs a strong formal signal 13 The retrospective reframe A late disclosure changes what the whole book was Atonement ; The Murder of Roger Ackroyd The retroactive lens weaponised; enormous force Spends the reader’s trust; a second reading must be better , not merely different 14 The appendix or apparatus Non-narrative matter follows the narrative Nineteen Eighty-Four ; Pale Fire Formal closure ( §4.6 ); can reverse the narrative’s own verdict Only available to books whose formal contract admits apparatus (Chapter 9 §4.6 ) 15 The double ending Two endings are given, or the choice between them is exhibited Great Expectations (two published states); The French Lieutenant’s Woman Makes the arbitrariness of closure visible without abandoning it Almost always reads as metafiction; rarely available to a realist book 16 The refused ending The text declines to conclude, and marks the refusal Villette ; A Passage to India ; The Castle Integrity where the material admits no settlement Cannot be distinguished from evasion by inspection; §8.9 Four clusters behave alike in revision. Strategies 1, 2 and 5 are return strategies. They close by revisiting. They are cheap (the material is paid for), reliable, and require nothing new. They are also the strategies most likely to be available in a draft that already has an ending problem, and the first place to look. Strategies 6, 7, 8 and 14 are displacement strategies. They close by moving — in time, voice or register — away from the narrative. They buy perspective and cost immediacy, and every one of them opens the question Chapter 10 asks of prologues: does this material require its exteriority? Strategies 9, 10, 11 and 12 are terminal strategies. They are decisions about the last page rather than the last chapter, and they can be substituted for one another almost freely without touching the structure. This makes them the cheapest thing to experiment with and the least likely to fix a structural problem. Strategies 3, 4, 13, 15 and 16 are disruptive . They close by refusing the expected relation between ending and book. They have the largest effects, the highest failure rate, and — this is the significant point — they are almost never available as a repair. A book either was always going to end this way or cannot be made to. 6.5 How to use the taxonomy: substitution testing The taxonomy’s purpose is not classification. Knowing that a draft ends with a proleptic close is worth nothing by itself. Its purpose is substitution testing , as with Chapter 9 §6.5 ’s opening gambits and Chapter 10 §6.4 ’s prologue types. The procedure: Name the strategy the draft currently uses. Most drafts use one without having chosen it, and the commonest unchosen default in contemporary literary fiction, as far as this book can judge without a count, is 9 (the terminal image) and in commercial fiction 8 (the proleptic close). Write the same ending in two other strategies , chosen from a different cluster. Not sketches — actual prose, at least a page each. Do not judge until all three exist. The finished draft always feels correct; that is a property of finish, not of fit. Ask what each version makes the book about. This is the diagnostic question, and it is more informative than asking which is best. An ending in strategy 6 makes a book about consequences; the same material in strategy 12 makes it about a moment; in strategy 3 about a world that continues regardless. The exercise is set formally at §12.1 , exercise 2. Its reliability is high enough to be worth a claim: in a workshop setting, by this book’s estimate rather than any measurement, roughly a third of endings that “aren’t working” are the right material in the wrong strategy, and the substitution locates the problem faster than any amount of line-editing. A specific and common finding is worth flagging. Drafts that feel too tidy are frequently strategy 6 or 8 material that wants to be 2 or 9 — a novel that has written a finale when it needed a parallel scene. And drafts that feel abrupt are frequently strategy 12 that wants to be 6: the writer, correctly wary of the endless aftermath, has stopped at the climax and left four domains unserved. 6.6 Climax and aftermath: the proportion problem The most consequential structural decision at an ending is not which strategy but how much aftermath . Both errors are severe and they are opposite ( §8.2 , §8.3 ), which means the correction for one produces the other, and drafts commonly oscillate. The framing that resolves the oscillation is Aristotle’s ( §3.3 ): the aftermath is not an appendage to the structure but the lusis , the second of two movements. The question is therefore not how much can I get away with? but what does the unravelling have to do?
