What only the aftermath can do: Task Why the climax cannot do it Show the consequences of the climax Consequences are, by definition, subsequent Complete a second arc Two arcs cannot peak in the same scene without one subordinating the other (Chapter 14’s kernel/satellite distinction) Let the reader register the value shift A shift occurring at maximum intensity is felt but not understood; understanding requires a beat of lower pressure Deliver catharsis Release requires the pressure to have stopped Provide descent from transportation ( §3.6 ) The reader must be returned Deliver the final image The image after the event outlasts the image of the event What the aftermath must not do: Prohibition Failure it produces Introduce a new question The book restarts and then stops Resolve threads in order of appearance rather than of weight §8.5 Continue past its own last decision §8.3 Explain what the climax meant §8.6 The operational rule the chapter offers on proportion: The aftermath ends at the last decision, not at the last consequence. Consequences are infinite; decisions are countable. Find the final decision any character takes — however small, and it may be as small as putting on a coat — and end within a page of it. This rule is Chapter 2’s ( Scene and Sequel ) sequel structure applied to the whole book ( §2.3.1 ): reaction, dilemma, decision . A book’s aftermath that stops at reaction feels indulgent; one that reaches a decision feels complete; one that continues past the decision into further consequence feels like a failure to notice that it had finished. How much do the traditions permit? The following is descriptive and approximate, derived from the works discussed in this chapter. It is offered as a corrective to the assumption that “short aftermath” is a rule rather than a period preference. Tradition Typical aftermath as % of the book Characteristic form Greek tragedy 10–20% The messenger speech and the chorus’s summation; the lusis is structurally substantial 18th-century novel 5–10% The concluding chapter; narrator’s direct address; distribution of fortunes Victorian, serialised 5–15% The wind-up chapter, sometimes a full number; every named character accounted for Tolstoyan Up to 12% An entire final part after the climax; a second arc completed ( Anna Karenina , Part Eight) Modernist 0–3% The terminal image; frequently no aftermath at all Contemporary literary 1–5% A short final scene or a single image; the coda is out of fashion Contemporary commercial 3–8% A short resolution chapter plus, frequently, a forward-looking beat Genre series 3–10% Resolution of the volume plus a series hook ( §8.11 ) Two things follow. First, the range is enormous, which means no absolute prescription can be right. Second, the contemporary literary norm is at the extreme low end of the historical distribution — which is worth knowing before concluding that a draft’s forty-page final movement is self-indulgent. It may be Victorian. 6.7 Historical drift, and a caution against universalising the present §3.7 laid out the history. This section states its consequence for the advice in this chapter, in the same terms Chapter 9 §6.7 and Chapter 10 use, because it is this book’s standing intellectual obligation. Almost every prescription in §§7 and 8 is calibrated to Anglo-American literary and commercial practice since roughly 1960. That is a real tradition with real standards, and a writer working inside it needs to know them. It is not narrative. Specifically: Prescription in this chapter Describes narrative Describes a local culture Nothing new and load-bearing at the close (§6.3) ✔ (Aristotle; nearly universal) An ending must be felt as well as resolved ( §2.3.2 ) ✔ Aftermath should be short ✔ (post-1920; the Victorian and Tolstoyan norms are three to five times longer) A character should not state the theme ( §8.6 ) ✔ (post-1900; the eighteenth- and nineteenth-century narrator does this as a matter of course) Ambiguity is a legitimate close ( §4.8 ) ✔ (post-1900, and now itself a default — §3.7 ) Every named character need not be accounted for ( §8.5 ) ✔ (the Victorian reader expected the opposite, and was not naive to expect it) Coincidence may not resolve (§6.3) ✔ (Aristotle) but the tolerance varies hugely by period and genre The series hook is a defect ( §8.11 ) ✔ (a judgement of the standalone literary novel; serial forms have always done it) The properly critical position is the same double one this book has maintained throughout: learn the current conventions well enough to break them deliberately, and read historically well enough to know they are conventions. A pedagogy that can only say “a modern editor would cut this” has explained the market and not the book — and at the ending, more than anywhere else, the market’s preferences have hardened into an aesthetic without anyone deciding that they should. One final observation, which §16 returns to. The contemporary preference for the unresolved close is frequently defended on the grounds that life does not resolve. This is true and is not an argument, for the reason Kermode gives ( §3.1 ): novels are not like life in any other respect either, and the demand for shape is not a demand for accuracy. A novel that refuses to conclude because life does not conclude has confused mimesis with form. The good reasons for an open ending are formal and thematic — that this book’s material admits no settlement, that the refusal is the argument — and they are available. The mimetic reason is not one of them.

title: 7. Diagnostic Method
text: 7.0 How to use the protocol The ten tests below are for revision, not composition . That instruction is standard across this textbook and it is more emphatic here, for a specific reason: the ending is the unit whose obligations cannot be known until the rest of the book exists. A writer who applies the plant audit while drafting will write a book made of plants. Five procedural notes, one more than the other chapters, because this protocol has a peculiarity the others do not. Run them in order. Tests 1–4 are about the ending’s relation to the book, and their failures invalidate the rest: there is no point tuning a last line in an ending that rests on an unplanted element. Record the answer, not the verdict. The output of a test is a sentence describing what the ending does, not a pass or fail. A failed test is a question. Every test below is failed by at least one novel discussed in this chapter, most of them by several. Several of these tests cannot be run on the ending alone. This is the peculiarity. Tests 1, 2, 6 and 9 require the whole book — which means the protocol takes days rather than hours, and which is why writers skip them and why skipping them is, in this book’s judgement, a common reason that unearned endings survive into print. Revise the ending last, whatever order it was written in. Many novelists write the ending first, and there is nothing wrong with that. But an ending written first is a hypothesis about the book , and the book that actually got written may have falsified it. A damaging revision error, and a frequent one, is the writer who protects an early-written ending and bends the last hundred pages towards it. Chapter 9 §7.2 gives the equivalent warning about openings and it applies with more force here: the ending is twenty pages; the book is four hundred. 7.1 The ten tests Test 1 — The retroactive test Reread the book’s earlier scenes with the ending in mind. Do they now read as intentional? Procedure. Take five scenes from the first two-thirds of the book, chosen at random rather than for convenience. Read each and ask what the ending has made of it. Write one sentence per scene: in the light of the ending, this scene was ___. Interpretation. Three outcomes. Every scene acquires a function: the ending is doing its retroactive work. Some scenes acquire a function and some are unchanged: normal and healthy. Not every scene need be retroactively transformed; most books have a great deal of good material that simply is what it was. Scenes are stranded — they now read as irrelevant, or worse, as belonging to a different book. This is the diagnostic result, and it points in two directions. Either the ending is wrong, or the scene is. The choice between those is the largest editorial decision in a revision, and it should be made explicitly rather than by default. The test’s characteristic false positive is worth flagging: a scene that seems stranded may be doing tonal or textural work that has no plot correlate. The refinement is to ask whether the reader would miss it, not whether it feeds the ending. Test 2 — The plant audit Trace every element the ending relies on back to its planting. Procedure. This is the most mechanical test in the chapter and the most reliable. It is also the test that closes this entire textbook, because every earlier chapter’s material comes due at it. List every element the ending uses as load-bearing — every object, fact, capability, relationship, phrase or piece of knowledge without which the ending would not work. Aim for eight to twenty items. If the list is under five, the ending may be under-built; if it is over thirty, the ending is probably doing too much. For each, record the page and chapter of first appearance , and the pages of any intermediate appearances. Mark any element whose first appearance is in the ending itself . Mark any element whose first appearance is early and which then disappears for more than a third of the book . Interpretation. Finding Diagnosis Move An element first appears in the ending Unearned in the strict sense ( §6.1 , Claim 1) Plant it earlier, unremarked. This is usually one sentence An element appears once, very early, and not again Planted but not maintained; the reader’s frame has gone cold Add one intermediate appearance (Chapter 10’s instalment schedule) Every element traces cleanly and the ending still feels flat Claim 1 satisfied, Claim 2 not ( §6.1 ) The problem is not here. Go to test 9 The list is dominated by information rather than by objects, relationships and decisions The ending is a disclosure rather than an event Consider whether the book’s climax is a revelation that ought to be an action The one-sentence version of this test , which is the form to remember: nothing new and load-bearing arrives on the last pages. Note the qualifier, per §6.3 : new material is fine, new load is not. Test 3 — The earned test Does the ending depend on a new element — new information, a sudden capability, an outside intervention? Procedure. Test 2 finds unplanted elements; this test asks whether the resolution mechanism itself is imported. Complete the sentence: “The situation is resolved because ___.” Then ask whether the thing in the blank was produced by the book’s own causal system or arrived from outside it ( §6.3 ). Interpretation. Three characteristic failures, in ascending order of severity: New information. A letter, a document, a confession that supplies a fact the reader could not have had. Sometimes legitimate — detective fiction is built on it — but only where the possibility of the fact was established. New capability. A character does something they have not been shown to be able to do. New agent. Someone or something not previously in the causal system intervenes. This is the deus ex machina proper ( §8.1 ), and it is the most reliably fatal of the three because it removes the protagonist from their own ending. Test 4 — The inevitability-versus-predictability test Could a reader have predicted this? Can a reader, now, imagine it otherwise? Procedure. The test requires two readers, or one reader and some patience. For predictability: stop a first-time reader thirty pages before the end and ask them to write, in two sentences, how the book will finish. Collect several such predictions. For inevitability: ask a reader who has finished to describe an alternative ending they would have accepted. Ask them to make the case for it. Interpretation. Map the results onto §6.2 ’s grid. Predictions accurate? Alternative easy to construct? Diagnosis No No — readers struggle to imagine another ending The target. Unforeseen and inevitable Yes No Classical satisfaction. Not a defect; check that the pleasure is in the route ( §6.2 ) No Yes — readers produce alternatives readily and find them as good The ending is arbitrary. It is one of several available outcomes and the book has not distinguished it Yes Yes The ending is inert. The book’s material never narrowed The third row is the important one and the hardest to accept, because it is the result an ending gets when it is fine . An ending that could have gone several ways with equal justice has not concluded the book; it has stopped it in one of its possible positions. Test 5 — The domain test Which of the six domains does the ending deliver, versus merely gesture towards? Procedure. Run the closural audit at §5.5 . Then, for each domain marked present, apply the delivery discrimination: is there a specific passage a reader could point to, or is the domain being credited on the strength of the writer’s intention? Gesture is the commonest form of self-deception in an ending, because the writer supplies the missing content from their own knowledge. Interpretation. Record which domains are delivered, which gestured, which refused, and which absent. Then ask, per §4.8 , whether the distribution matches the book’s mode. A literary novel that delivers plot and gestures at character has probably mis-weighted; a thriller that delivers plot and refuses theme has probably not. Test 6 — The proportion test Is the aftermath the right size, and is each thread’s resolution proportional to the weight it carried? Procedure. Two parts. (a) The climax-to-end ratio. Measure the distance from the climax to the last word as a percentage of the book. Compare against §6.6 ’s table for the tradition being worked in. A figure outside the range is not a verdict but a question. (b) The weight audit. List every subplot and major question. For each, record the approximate page space it occupied and the approximate page space its resolution receives. Chapter 14 ( The Subplot ) calls the first figure the attention tax ; this is the refund. Interpretation. Pattern Diagnosis Aftermath under 1% and four domains unserved §8.2 , climax without aftermath Aftermath over 10% in a contemporary literary novel Possibly §8.3 — but check the tradition first; it may be deliberate Every thread resolved at roughly equal length §8.5 , the tidy-everything ending. Uniform resolution destroys hierarchy A thread that took 80 pages resolved in one sentence Under-delivery; the reader will experience this as the book losing interest in its own material A thread that took 8 pages resolved in a chapter Over-delivery; usually a sign that the writer found this thread more interesting than the book did The operational rule from §6.6 : find the last decision any character takes and check how far the book runs past it. More than a page or two is usually consequence rather than ending. Test 7 — The termination test Has the book ended, or has it merely stopped? Procedure. Herrnstein Smith’s distinction ( §3.2 ), converted into a question a reader can answer. Give the last two pages to a reader who has read the book and ask a single question: “Is there anything after this?” Ask it neutrally. Then ask them to say what told them. Interpretation. The value of the test is in the second answer. A reader who says “yes, it’s over” and can name what told them — a returned image, a shortened sentence, a settled grammatical form, a pattern completed — is reporting a closural device operating. A reader who says “yes” and cannot say why is reporting an effect that may be coming from the page or from the physical fact that the pages have run out, and the distinction matters: a book that closes only because the paper stops has terminated, not ended. The reverse result is also informative and much more common than writers expect. A reader who says “no, I thought there was another chapter” has identified an ending that has not signalled itself, which is usually a formal problem ( §4.6 ) rather than a content one and is often fixed by a terminal modification rather than by new material. Test 8 — The tonal-match test Does the final note match the tone the book has actually earned? Procedure. Read the last page. Then read three passages from the middle third, chosen at random. Ask whether they belong to the same book — in register, in the narrator’s stance towards suffering, in what the prose finds important, and in what it permits itself to hope. This is Chapter 9’s promise test (test 6 there) run in reverse, and the two chapters name the same violation at opposite ends of the book. Chapter 10 §8.2 calls the entrance version false advertising ; this chapter calls the exit version the mismatched final note ( §8.4 ). The map of this textbook (see §1.3 ) records the symmetry deliberately. Interpretation. The characteristic failure is unearned uplift — a grim book closing on hope the material does not support — and its characteristic cause is not incompetence: the writer has spent two years inside a bleak book and wants, personally, to be let out. The inverse failure, the gratuitous darkening of a book that has earned warmth, is rarer and is usually an anxiety about seeming sentimental. The refinement. Tone is not the same as outcome. A book may end in disaster and in a warm tone, or in success and in a cold one. What must match is the narrator’s relation to the material , not the material’s valence. Test 9 — The reread test Is a second reading a different and better experience — and does the ending survive being known? Procedure. This test cannot be run quickly and is therefore the one most often omitted. Its cheap form: take three passages that the ending retroactively changes, and read them as a reader who knows how the book ends. Ask what they now yield. Interpretation. Three outcomes. The passages yield more. The ending has converted them into double-layered material — the reader who knows sees the preparation and the surface. This is the strongest available evidence of an earned ending, and it is the positive form of test 1. The passages yield the same. Neutral. Much good writing does this. The passages yield less. This is the significant result and it identifies a specific defect: an ending whose effect depended entirely on the reader not knowing. Strategy 13 ( §6.4 ), the retrospective reframe, is the highest-risk case, and the standard for it is exacting: a novel that reframes must be better on a second reading, not merely different, or the reframe was a trick. The test also catches a subtler problem. If the ending’s plants become obvious on rereading — if the seeded elements now look like seeds — the planting was too heavy ( §6.2 ). The target is preparation that remains invisible as preparation even when the reader is looking for it. Test 10 — The last-line test Read the final paragraph in isolation. Does it carry weight given the full context — or does it coast on it? Procedure. Copy the last paragraph onto a separate page. Read it cold. Then ask three questions: What is the reader looking at? (If the answer is “an abstraction”, the final image domain is unserved.) What does the last sentence do grammatically? (Assertion, question, fragment, subordinate clause; §4.5 .) What is the last word? (Rabinowitz’s privileged position at maximum concentration.) Interpretation. The important discrimination in this test separates it from Chapter 9’s voice test. An ending is allowed to depend on everything that came before it. That is its condition, not its failure. Unlike an opening, which must work with nothing, a last line may be incomprehensible in isolation and perfect in place. For there she was means nothing on its own. What it may not do is coast. A last line coasts when it borrows weight from the preceding book without adding any — when it is simply the next sentence, placed last, and could be exchanged for the sentence before it without loss. The practical form: take the last paragraph and the paragraph before it, and ask whether the book could end on the earlier one. If it could, and nothing is lost, the final paragraph is not doing work. This is the ending’s version of Chapter 9 §8.7 ’s deletion ladder, and it has a similar hit rate. 7.2 Reading the results Failed tests Likely diagnosis First move 2 and 3 Unearned in the strict sense; an element or agent is imported Plant it earlier — usually a sentence in the first third 4 (third row) alone The ending is arbitrary: one of several equally available outcomes The problem is in the middle of the book, not the end. Narrow the material 1 alone The ending strands earlier material Decide explicitly whether the ending or the scenes are wrong. Do not fix both 5 alone Domains mis-weighted for the mode Find one carrier that can take two of the unserved domains ( §5.3 ) 6(a) low, 5 failing Climax without aftermath ( §8.2 ) Add the lusis , not more climax 6(a) high Endless aftermath ( §8.3 ) Find the last decision and end within a page of it 6(b) uniform Tidy-everything ( §8.5 ) Cut resolutions, do not add them. Let two threads go unresolved and see what is lost 7 alone Termination without closure A formal device is missing: a terminal modification, a returned image, a settled last sentence 8 alone Mismatched final note Change the ending, not the book 9 alone The effect depended on ignorance If strategy 13, the reframe must add rather than replace. Otherwise reduce the surprise and increase the preparation 10 alone The last paragraph is not doing work Test whether the book ends a page earlier Everything passes and the ending is flat §6.1 ’s Claim 2: preparation without pressure Nothing in this section will help. The middle of the book has not built a want the ending answers A warning about the last row. It is the most common outcome of a competent revision, and the protocol cannot solve it, because the protocol audits the ending and the fault is elsewhere. An ending that satisfies every test and lands on nothing is reporting that the book was never about anything urgent enough to conclude. That is a real diagnosis, it is worth reaching, and it is why §16 argues that the last chapter is where a novel finds out what it was.

title: 8. Failure Patterns
text: Each pattern below is presented with its symptom , its mechanism (what actually goes wrong, as distinct from what the surface looks like), its persistence (why competent writers keep producing it), its remedy , and — importantly — its exception : a published work that commits the “error” and succeeds. The exceptions are not decorative, and in this chapter they carry an unusually heavy load. Endings are the site of the most durable critical disagreements in the discipline, and several of the “failures” below are committed by works whose endings are among the most admired in the language. In every case, the pattern fails because of a mechanism, not because of a surface feature, and where the mechanism is absent the surface feature is harmless. 8.1 The Unearned Rescue Symptom. Resolution arrives through an element the book never integrated: a sudden power, a stranger’s intervention, a document that appears, a fact withheld from the reader until the moment it is required. Mechanism. The ending’s causal chain is broken. Aristotle’s formulation ( §3.3 ) is exact and better than the modern one: the objection is not to improbability but to externality . The resolution is produced by something outside the causal system the book built, which means the preceding four hundred pages did not, in the end, determine the outcome. The retroactive damage is severe because it applies to the whole: if the ending did not follow from the book, the book was not going anywhere. A secondary and equally damaging effect is that the protagonist is removed from their own ending. A rescued character has not acted; and since character is legible chiefly through choice under pressure, an unearned rescue does not merely resolve the plot badly — it dissolves the character domain at the exact moment it was due. Persistence. Three causes, all structural rather than moral. The writer has painted the situation into a corner and the rescue is the only exit. The writer has fallen in love with a set-up whose logic produces an outcome they do not want. Or — most commonly — the writer has not noticed that the resolution requires a fact the reader does not have, because the writer has it. Remedy. Test 3. Complete the sentence *the situation is resolved because ___* and check whether the thing in the blank belongs to the book’s causal system. Where it does not, there are two moves, and the first is nearly always right: plant it earlier , unremarked, so that the intervention becomes the arrival of something the reader already knew existed; or change the outcome to one the existing system produces. The exception, and it is a large one. The deus ex machina is Euripides’ signature device, not his failure. Medea ends with Medea escaping in the chariot of the Sun; several other plays resolve by divine intervention. Aristotle disliked it and said so in the Poetics — but Aristotle was expressing a preference against a living, popular and deliberate practice, and later criticism has increasingly read Euripides’ machines as ironic rather than lazy: a god arrives to impose an order the human action has shown to be unavailable, and the visible artificiality of the arrival is the point. The line from there to modern practice is direct and explicit. John Gay’s The Beggar’s Opera (1728) halts before Macheath’s execution so that the Beggar and the Player can argue about the ending, the Player insisting that the audience requires a happy one — whereupon Macheath is reprieved. Brecht and Weill’s The Threepenny Opera (1928) makes the device explicit: a mounted messenger arrives with a royal pardon, and the text observes how seldom such riders come in reality. In both, the unearned rescue is the argument. The device is not a failure when the arbitrariness is the content. A third and different exception, from inside the realist novel: Jane Eyre (1847) resolves its central dilemma when Jane, on the point of accepting St John Rivers, hears Rochester’s voice calling her name across an impossible distance. This is supernatural intervention arriving at the precise moment of decision. It works — and generations of readers have found it the novel’s most powerful passage — because Brontë has spent the whole book establishing a world in which presentiment, dream and vision are operative, and because the voice does not decide for Jane; it interrupts a decision she then makes herself. The rescue is unearned in mechanism and earned in preparation , which is the discrimination the pattern requires. 8.2 The Climax Without Aftermath Symptom. The book ends at the peak of conflict. The plot concludes and stops; character, theme, catharsis and the final image are left technically unaddressed. Mechanism. Only half the structure has been executed. In Aristotle’s terms ( §3.3 ) the desis is complete and the lusis absent. The consequences are specific rather than general: a value shift occurring at maximum intensity is felt but not registered (Chapter 1’s terms), because registration requires a beat at lower pressure; catharsis cannot occur, because release requires the pressure to have stopped; and the reader, transported, is not returned ( §3.6 ). The characteristic reader response is diagnostic and peculiar: satisfaction and dissatisfaction at once. That was exciting. Is that it? Persistence. It is the correct fear applied at the wrong point. Writers are warned, rightly, against the endless aftermath (§8.3) and against the Victorian wind-up, and the contemporary literary norm for aftermath is the shortest in the historical range ( §6.6 ). A writer avoiding one error over-corrects into its opposite. It is also, more simply, a stamina problem: the climax is the most exciting thing to write and the aftermath the least, and drafts frequently stop where the writer’s energy did. Remedy. Not more climax. Ask what only the aftermath can do ( §6.6 ’s first table), and supply the minimum that does it. Very often this is one scene and sometimes one paragraph. The operational rule: find the last decision — the aftermath’s job is to reach one, and it may be very small. The exception. The Handmaid’s Tale (1985) ends its narrative proper with Offred stepping into the van, into the darkness within or else the light, with no aftermath whatever. It is a pure arrested ending ( §6.4 , no. 12) and the four unserved domains are left unserved — by the narrative . Atwood then supplies them at a two-hundred-year remove, in the Historical Notes, which deliver plot (Gilead fell), theme (the handling of women’s testimony), formal closure ( §4.6 ) and a bitter substitute for catharsis. The lesson is not that aftermath is dispensable but that it may be displaced : the domains are served, in another register, by a device the novel’s formal contract permits. The Grapes of Wrath (1939) is the cleaner case. It stops on Rose of Sharon’s gesture with no aftermath at all — no consequence, no future, no commentary — and it is complete, because the gesture is the aftermath: an act of consequence rather than an event of conflict. A climax that is itself a decision does not require a further beat to reach one. 8.3 The Endless Aftermath Symptom. So much material follows the climax that momentum dies. The reader’s attention is exhausted before the last page. Mechanism. Narrative interest is generated by unresolved tension; after the climax there is none, and the aftermath is therefore running on residual goodwill, which decays. The specific damage is that the actual final image arrives to a reader who has stopped attending, so the book’s most privileged position is spent on someone who is skimming. Chapter 7 ( Backstory and Flashback ) supplies the precise concept in the interest deficit : a passage that does not generate its own forward pull is borrowing against reader patience, and the debt compounds. An aftermath is by definition low-tension material, and long aftermaths are therefore the largest single interest deficit most novels run. Persistence. Two causes. The first is the writer’s reluctance to leave a world they have lived in for years — a real and sympathetic motive that produces real damage. The second is a misunderstanding of obligation: the belief that every thread must be accounted for (§8.5 is the same error at a different scale). Remedy. §6.6 ’s rule. Locate the last decision any character takes; end within a page or two of it. Then apply the §5.5 audit and check whether the final pages are discharging domains or merely continuing. The exception, and it is essential. Anna Karenina ’s Part Eight is an endless aftermath by any modern standard: an entire eighth part, after the death that ends the title character’s story, largely devoted to Levin’s spiritual crisis and its resolution, plus Vronsky’s departure for the Serbian war and a good deal of argument about Slavic questions. Readers and editors have complained about it since publication, and Tolstoy’s own publisher declined to print it in the serial. It is nonetheless indispensable, and §9.4 argues the case in detail. The short form: the novel has two arcs , and the second cannot complete at the first’s climax. A book that ended with Anna under the train would be a different and much smaller novel — one about a woman’s destruction rather than about two ways of living with the same problem. The general principle the exception establishes: An aftermath is not too long if it is completing an arc. It is too long if it is reporting consequences. War and Peace pushes the same principle to its limit with two epilogues, the second of which is not narrative at all but a treatise on historical causation. That one is harder to defend and is frequently skipped, which is a fair verdict — but note what it demonstrates: an aftermath can fail and leave a great novel undamaged, because a reader who abandons an epilogue has still read the book. 8.4 The Mismatched Final Note Symptom. The last image or line does not match the tone the book has earned — a grim novel closing on uplift, a comic one closing on unmotivated darkness, a quiet one closing on a flourish. Mechanism. A genre-contract violation at the exit. Chapter 9 §4.2 establishes that the opening pages contract with the reader about what kind of book this is; the ending is where that contract is finally honoured or broken. Because the ending occupies privileged position and is read retroactively, a mismatched note does not merely disappoint — it reassigns the book, and the reader leaves with an impression at odds with the four hundred pages they actually read. The symmetry with Chapter 10 is exact and is recorded in this textbook’s map: Chapter 10 §8.2 ’s false advertising and this chapter’s mismatched final note are the same violation at the two ends of the book. One promises a book the reader will not get; the other retracts a book the reader has already had. Persistence. The dominant cause is not craft failure but authorial fatigue and authorial mercy. A writer who has spent years inside a bleak book wants to be released from it, and grants the release on the last page. A secondary cause is external: editorial or market pressure towards a more consoling close, which is §8.12’s territory and is very old. Remedy. Test 8. Read the last page against three random middle passages and ask whether they belong to the same book. Where they do not, change the ending, not the book — the ending is twenty pages and the book is four hundred. The exception, and it is the one the chapter returns to most. The revised ending of Great Expectations (1861) is arguably a mismatched final note, and most readers prefer it. Dickens’s original ending has Pip and Estella meet briefly in a London street, exchange a few words, and part; the revised ending places them in the ruined garden at Satis House and closes on Pip seeing no shadow of another parting. On the tonal-match test, the case against the revision is strong: the novel has spent five hundred pages dismantling Pip’s expectations, and a close that grants him the one expectation he should have lost can be read as the book conceding what it argued. And yet the revision is the version nearly every reader has read, it is the version most editions print, and a great deal of serious criticism defends it as the better ending. §9.1 sets out the disagreement in full and declines to resolve it. What the case establishes here is a limit on the test: the tonal-match test is a strong instrument for detecting a change of register and a weak one for adjudicating it. A tonal shift at the close can be a failure of nerve or a final modulation the book has earned, and no mechanical procedure separates them. 8.5 The Tidy-Everything Ending Symptom. Every subplot and question resolved with equal, mechanical thoroughness, regardless of what mattered. Mechanism. Uniform resolution destroys hierarchy. Emphasis is relational: a thread’s resolution lands as significant because other threads’ resolutions are smaller or absent. An ending in which everything is settled to the same degree communicates that nothing was more important than anything else — which contradicts the weighting the book spent four hundred pages establishing. This is Chapter 9 §8.5 ’s overstuffed first page, at the other end of the book and with a different surface. There, uniform density destroyed emphasis; here, uniform resolution destroys hierarchy. The underlying principle is the same for both: significance is produced by difference, and a text in which everything is significant contains nothing significant. There is a second mechanism, which is D. A. Miller’s ( §3.9 ): the comprehensive settlement is where a novel most visibly administers its own material, and the register shift from scene to inventory is what makes last chapters read as thinner than the books they end. Persistence. A sense of obligation, and it is not baseless: readers do ask what happened to people. The obligation is real and the response is disproportionate. It is also, in genre fiction, an explicit convention that many readers want. Remedy. Cut resolutions; do not add them. The productive exercise is subtractive: remove the resolutions of the two least-weighted threads and read the ending again. Almost always, nothing is lost and the remaining resolutions gain force. Where something is lost, that thread was more load-bearing than the audit suggested and should be restored. The exception. Jane Eyre (1847) resolves everything, at length, in a final chapter that opens with the most famous settlement sentence in English — Reader, I married him — and proceeds to account for Adèle’s schooling, Diana and Mary’s marriages, Rochester’s partial recovery of sight, the birth of a son, and finally, in a passage occupying the novel’s last position, St John Rivers’s missionary death in India. By modern standards it is the tidy-everything ending in its pure form. It succeeds for two reasons that generalise. First, the resolutions are not uniform: they are graded, and the grading is a moral argument, culminating in the deliberate strangeness of giving the novel’s final words not to Jane’s happiness but to St John’s fatal self-denial. Second, and more fundamentally, the novel is a first-person retrospective narration by a woman explicitly addressing a reader — a form in which the accounting for everybody is what the narrator would do . The tidiness is in character. The general rule the exception yields: comprehensive resolution is safe when it is graded, and when the comprehensiveness is motivated by the narration rather than by the author’s sense of duty. 8.6 The Explained Ending Symptom. A character, or the narrator, summarises what the book has meant. Often in dialogue; often in a penultimate scene; often beginning I suppose what I’ve learned is . Mechanism. The book’s thematic work is transferred from the reader to the text. Theme, per §4.3 , is a question the novel tests; an explanation converts it into a proposition the reader may accept or reject, and either response is worse than the experience the novel could have produced. There is also a specific structural harm: an explanation is a resolution, so the ending’s most privileged position is spent on a paraphrase of the book rather than on the book. The second mechanism is a voice-contract violation (Chapter 9 §4.1 ). A novel that has been rigorously scenic and then, on its last pages, produces a narratorial generalisation has changed its terms at the moment it can least afford to. Persistence. Anxiety, and it is the most sympathetic motive in this section. The writer has spent years on a book whose meaning is subtle and cannot bear the thought that a reader might miss it. The explanation is insurance. It is also the case that explanations are easy to write at the end of a book, because by then the writer knows what it means. Remedy. Delete the explanation and read the ending without it. In most drafts, by this book’s estimate, nothing is lost. Where something is lost, the missing content should be converted into an act or an object per §4.3 , not restored as speech. The exception. Middlemarch (1871–72) ends with a Finale in which the narrator explains, in general terms and at some length, what the reader should conclude — about Dorothea, about the conditions of a woman’s ardour, and about the moral economy of unrecorded lives. It is one of the greatest endings in English ( §9.2 ). Two things license it. First, the narrator has been generalising for eight hundred pages: the explanatory register is not introduced at the close, it is the book’s native mode, and its arrival at the end is a formal completion rather than a rupture. Second — and this is the discrimination the pattern actually needs — Eliot’s generalisation does not paraphrase the novel; it extends it. The Finale does not tell the reader what Dorothea’s story meant; it tells them what cannot be known about lives like hers, and hands them a proposition the preceding book has made available but has not stated. The failure is not explanation as such. The failure is explanation that replaces the book with a summary of itself. Anna Karenina is the harder case and worth setting beside it: Tolstoy ends on Levin explicitly formulating what he has come to believe, in his own consciousness, at length. Whether this is thematic closure or authorial preaching is a live critical question, and it is set as a seminar question at §12.2 . 8.7 The Ending That Resolves the Wrong Question Symptom. The plot concludes, comprehensively and competently, and the reader closes the book with the sense that the thing they cared about was not the thing that got settled. Mechanism. A mismatch between the novel’s stated dramatic question and its operative one. Most novels raise a plot question early and then develop, over their length, a different and deeper interest — usually relational or moral. If the ending answers the first and ignores the second, every domain is technically served and the reader’s actual investment is unaddressed. This is a failure of the ending to notice what the book became, and it is closely related to §6.1 ’s Claim 2. It is also the pattern that most often produces the reader complaint it was fine, I don’t know, it just ended . Persistence. The stated question is the one in the outline, the synopsis and the pitch. The operative question emerged during drafting, is unrecorded, and is frequently invisible to the writer, who is still working to the plan. Remedy. Ask two readers, separately: what did you want to happen? Not what did you expect — what did they want. The answers identify the operative question, and they are frequently not the plot’s. The exception, which is the most contested ending in American literature. Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884) spends its length on a moral question — whether Huck will betray Jim — and answers it definitively in the celebrated passage in which Huck decides to go to hell rather than turn him in. The novel then continues for a dozen chapters at the Phelps farm, in which Tom Sawyer stages an elaborate and cruel pantomime of a rescue for a man who is, it emerges, already legally free. Hemingway’s verdict — that the book should be read up to the point where Jim is stolen and that the rest is cheating — is the standard indictment, and the standard version of this failure pattern: the novel resolves an adventure and abandons its moral question. But the defence is serious and long-standing. T. S. Eliot and Lionel Trilling both argued for the ending’s necessity; and a substantial modern reading holds that the Phelps farm sequence is the point rather than the evasion, since it dramatises what Jim’s freedom is worth in a society that will convert his liberation into a boy’s game. On that reading the novel does not resolve the wrong question; it answers the right one with a bleakness that readers have wanted to escape for a century and a quarter. The case is set as a seminar question at §12.2 . What it establishes here is a caution: the accusation that an ending resolves the wrong question is sometimes the reader refusing the question the book actually asked. 8.8 Death as Resolution Symptom. A central problem is resolved by the death of a character — usually the character posing the problem, occasionally the protagonist. Mechanism. Death is the most available terminal event in fiction and the most frequently substituted for a decision. Its structural attraction is its weakness: it is unarguable, it is final, and it requires nothing of anyone. When a novel resolves through a death that no character chose and none of the book’s forces produced, the ending has been outsourced to mortality. E. M. Forster’s remark in Aspects of the Novel (1927) that without death and marriage the novelist would scarcely know how to conclude is usually quoted as a joke, and it is a diagnosis: these are the two events the form treats as automatically terminal, which makes them the two most likely to be used as substitutes for structure. The specific harm is to the character domain. A character who dies has not chosen anything, and the reader’s accumulated investment in their capacity to choose is discharged into an event rather than an act. Persistence. It works, at the level of feeling, almost regardless of preparation, because readers respond to death. This makes it the most reliable way to produce an emotional effect at a close without having earned one, and therefore the most tempting. Remedy. Test 3 and the substitution question: if the character had lived, would the book’s central problem be resolved? If not, the death is doing structural work it should not be doing. The usual correction is to place the death before the ending, so that the ending contains a decision made in its light. The exception. The Death of Ivan Ilyich (1886) is a novella in which death is the entire content, announced in the first pages and arrived at in the last, and it is not a failure because the death is not a resolution — it is the situation the whole work examines, and what resolves is Ivan’s relation to it. The discrimination generalises: death fails as an ending when it resolves; it succeeds when it is the condition within which something else is resolved. Don Quixote (1605–1615) is the more interesting case and is treated in full at §9.8 . Cervantes ends by killing his protagonist — and Alonso Quixano’s death is not the end of a plot but the withdrawal of a capacity : he recovers his wits, renounces the books of chivalry, makes a will, and dies as a man who can no longer be Don Quixote. The death resolves nothing in the plot and everything in the book, because what dies is the possibility of further adventures. §9.8 argues that this is closure by ending the character’s availability , and that it is one of the very few endings in fiction designed to prevent other people from writing more. 8.9 Ambiguity Used as Evasion Symptom. The book declines to settle its central question, and the refusal reads as an absence of decision rather than as one. Mechanism. Per §3.2 , an open ending is a closural strategy that works by withholding devices the reader knows are available. It therefore requires the withholding to be legible. When the withholding is not legible — when there is no formal signal that the openness is chosen — the reader cannot distinguish it from the writer not knowing. The historical dimension ( §3.7 ) makes this worse than it used to be. In 1925, an unresolved close was a deviation from a strong convention and therefore self-marking. In the present, the unresolved close is itself the convention in literary fiction, which means it no longer signals anything by its mere presence. Ambiguity must now be specific — the reader must be able to say what is undetermined and why the book cannot determine it — or it reads as default. Persistence. It is the easiest ending to write, it is fashionable, and it is unfalsifiable: a writer challenged on it can always claim intention, and no reader can prove otherwise. Remedy. Two questions. What, in one sentence, is ambiguous? — an ambiguity the writer cannot state in one sentence is not a design. And what would resolving it cost the book? — if the answer is “nothing”, the ambiguity is not doing work. Where the ambiguity survives both, mark it: some formal signal, some registration that the question exists and is being left ( §4.1 ). The exceptions, and there are two kinds. The first is the ambiguity that is the subject. Blindness (1995) ends by withholding the confirmation the reader has been waiting three hundred pages for, and the withholding enacts the novel’s argument about seeing ( §9.9 ). Beloved ends by contradicting itself about whether the story should be passed on, and the contradiction is the only honest position available on its subject ( §9.6 ). In each, the reader can state what is unresolved. The second kind is more instructive because it is contested at source. Villette (1853) ends by declining to say whether M. Paul survives his voyage: Charlotte Brontë intended to drown him, her father wished for a happy ending, and the published close is a deliberate compromise which describes a storm, invites the “sunny imagination” to hope, and stops. It is an ambiguity produced by external pressure — the definition of §8.12’s imposed ending — and it is nonetheless one of the most admired closes in Victorian fiction, because the compromise happens to produce the refusal the novel’s material requires. The origin of an ending is not evidence about its quality , which is a point the Great Expectations case ( §9.1 ) makes at greater length. 8.10 The Last-Minute Reversal Symptom. A disclosure in the final pages changes the meaning of the whole book: the narrator was lying, the events did not occur, the protagonist is not who they appeared to be. Mechanism. The strategy is legitimate — it is no. 13 in §6.4 — and it fails in a specific and identifiable way: when the reversal replaces the reading experience rather than adding a layer to it. A reframe that invalidates everything before it converts four hundred pages into a set-up for a trick, and the reader who feels this has been given a worse book than the one they were reading. The diagnostic is test 9 (the reread test). A reframe must make the second reading better , not merely different. If the earlier chapters yield less on rereading, the reversal spent the book. A secondary failure is that a reversal is enormously expensive in trust: it teaches the reader that this narrator’s assertions need not be believed, at the exact moment the book most needs to be believed about its own conclusion. Persistence. The reversal is intoxicating to plan and produces, in the writer, a strong feeling of cleverness that does not survive contact with a reader. Remedy. Test 9, and the substitution question in its strongest form: would this book be worth reading if the reader knew the reversal from page one? Where the answer is no, the reversal is carrying the book. Where it is yes, the reversal is doing what it should. The exception. Atonement (2001) reverses in its final section: the novelist Briony discloses that the reunion of the lovers, which the reader has just read, did not happen, and that she has written it as a form of restitution. This is a maximum-strength retrospective reframe, and it survives test 9 outstandingly — the novel is substantially better on a second reading, because the reader now sees the earlier sections as a made thing and can watch the making. What makes it work is that the reframe is the book’s subject : the ethics of a novelist granting a consolation she cannot grant in fact. The reversal does not invalidate the reading; it interrogates it. Contrast The Murder of Roger Ackroyd (1926), where the reversal is a formal joke of the highest order and the reread yields the pleasure of watching the concealment operate — but where nothing thematic is added. Both are successful; they succeed at different things, and the difference is worth teaching. 8.11 The Series Hook This edition calls the pattern the series hook, since the book keeps sequel for the reaction, dilemma and decision of Chapter 2. Symptom. The book declines to close a major question in order to create an appetite for a further volume. A last-page arrival, a survivor revealed, an unopened letter, a returning threat. Mechanism. The strategy converts a structural position into a commercial one. The cost is precise: the ending’s most privileged position ( §3.6 ) is spent on a proposition rather than a payoff , which reverses the whole relation this chapter describes. Instead of closing accounts, the last page opens one — and because of the retroactive lens, the reader’s final act of interpretation is applied not to the book they read but to a book that does not yet exist. The secondary harm is to the formal domain ( §4.6 ). A hook declares that this artefact is not complete in itself, which retrospectively demotes it from a book to an instalment. Persistence. Commercial pressure, and it is real: series sell, and publishers ask for hooks. It also feels generous — the writer believes they are offering the reader more. Remedy. Distinguish an open question from a hook . A novel may end with things unresolved and be complete, provided the unresolved material is not the thing the book was about. The test: does the last page close the volume’s own central question? If yes, a further question may be raised. If no, the volume has not ended. The exception. Don Quixote , Part I (1605), ends with an explicit promise of a third sally and an invitation to whoever might write it. That invitation was accepted — by Avellaneda, whose spurious continuation appeared in 1614 — and Cervantes’ response in Part II is a celebrated reaction to a series hook ( §9.8 ). The episode is worth teaching because it shows the hook doing what a hook does: declaring the work incomplete, and thereby licensing others to complete it. The serial novel is the systematic exception. Dickens’s part-issues, documented in the number plans discussed in Chapter 6 ( The Chapter Break ), end on hooks by design, and the practice is not a defect but the form’s engine. What distinguishes the serial instalment from the failing standalone is that the serial’s reader has contracted for continuation. Chapter 9 §10.4 makes the same observation about series openings: the conventions of a form the reader has entered knowingly are not violations. 8.12 The Imposed Ending Symptom. The ending is congruent with something other than the book: a genre convention, a publisher’s preference, a reader’s expectation, an author’s fatigue, a moral requirement external to the material. Mechanism. This is Torgovnick’s category ( §3.5 ), and it is the most abstract failure in this section because it can coexist with technical competence. An imposed ending may plant everything it uses, serve all six domains, land its final image, and still be wrong — because what it does with the material contradicts the book’s own argument. It is worth distinguishing carefully from the unearned rescue. An unearned ending uses material the book did not supply. An imposed ending uses the book’s own material to reach a conclusion the book does not support. The first is a failure of preparation; the second a failure of congruence . Persistence. Every external pressure on a novel arrives at its ending, because the ending is where a book declares its position and positions are what publishers, readerships and censors care about. The pressure is frequently invisible in the finished text and legible only in the archive. Remedy. Test 1 and test 8 together. Where the ending strands earlier material and shifts register, imposition is the likely diagnosis. The corrective question is Torgovnick’s: whose logic does this ending obey? The exception, which is also this chapter’s centrepiece. The revised ending of Great Expectations is an imposed ending in the documentary sense: Dickens wrote one close, showed the proofs to Edward Bulwer-Lytton, who objected, and wrote another. The textual history is documented in the scholarly editions, and Dickens himself recorded his expectation that the alteration would make the story more acceptable. By the criterion above, that should settle it. It does not. The revised ending is the one nearly every reader has read, and a century and a half of criticism has failed to reach agreement on which is better — with distinguished advocates on both sides, including George Bernard Shaw, who printed the original in his own edition, and equally distinguished defenders of the revision. §9.1 sets the case out in full. The general principle, which qualifies every pattern in §8: The provenance of an ending is not evidence about its quality. An ending written under pressure may be the right one; an ending written in perfect freedom may be imposed by a convention the author never examined. Congruence is a property of the relation between ending and book, and it must be assessed by reading, not by biography. 8.13 Summary: symptom to mechanism Pattern Underlying mechanism Domains damaged Unearned rescue Resolution external to the book’s causal system Plot, character Climax without aftermath Only the desis executed; no lusis Character, theme, catharsis, final image Endless aftermath Interest deficit; residual goodwill exhausted Final image, catharsis Mismatched final note Genre contract broken at the exit Theme, catharsis, final image Tidy-everything Uniform resolution destroys hierarchy Plot, theme Explained ending Theme transferred from reader to text; voice contract broken Theme, catharsis Resolves the wrong question Operative question ≠ stated question Character, theme Death as resolution An event substituted for a decision Character, catharsis Ambiguity as evasion Withholding not legible as chosen Plot, theme, formal Last-minute reversal Reframe replaces rather than layers All, retroactively Series hook Privileged position spent on a proposition Formal, plot Imposed ending Congruent with something other than the book All

title: 9. Worked Analyses
text: Nine close readings of published endings, followed by the chapter’s capstone revision case. The analytical apparatus is the same throughout: identify the closural strategy or strategies ( §6.4 ), audit the domains ( §4 ), assess the multiplicity ( §5 ), and — where the case permits — name the critical disagreement rather than resolving it. The first reading is the longest, and deliberately. The two endings of Great Expectations constitute the best single case study available anywhere on this subject, because a major novelist wrote two endings for the same book, both survive, the circumstances of the change are documented, and a century and a half of competent criticism has failed to agree about which is better. Nothing else in the discipline lets a student watch the earned/unearned distinction, the congruence criterion, the tonal-match test and the imposed-ending question operate simultaneously on the same material. 9.1 Dickens, Great Expectations (1861) — the two endings The situation Great Expectations ran as a weekly serial in All the Year Round from December 1860 to August 1861. Pip, a blacksmith’s boy raised by hand, is given an anonymous fortune, believes it comes from Miss Havisham and is intended to secure him Estella, discovers that his benefactor is the convict Magwitch and that Estella is Magwitch’s daughter, loses the money, loses Estella to the brutal Bentley Drummle, nurses Magwitch to his death, is nursed in turn by Joe, and goes abroad to work in the merchant house of Clarriker. The novel then has to end, and there are two published endings. The original ending Dickens’s first close, which he wrote and set in proof, is brief. Pip has returned to England after some years. Walking in London with little Pip — Joe and Biddy’s son, named for him — he encounters Estella in the street. She is a widow: Drummle has died, following an accident with a horse he had ill-treated. She has remarried, to a Shropshire doctor who had attended her during her marriage and who is poor. She takes little Pip for Pip’s own child. They exchange a few words and part. Pip’s closing reflection is that he was glad afterwards to have seen her, because in her face and voice he could see that suffering had been stronger than Miss Havisham’s teaching, and had given her a heart to understand what his heart used to be. The intervention As the serial was completing, Dickens showed the proofs to Edward Bulwer-Lytton — a friend, a fellow novelist, and the author whose next work was to follow Great Expectations in All the Year Round . Bulwer-Lytton objected to the ending and urged a happier one. Dickens rewrote it. The textual history is documented in the scholarly editions, notably Edgar Rosenberg’s Norton Critical Edition, and Dickens’s own account survives in his correspondence with John Forster: he recorded that Bulwer-Lytton was strongly of that opinion, that he had made the change, and that he had no doubt the story would be more acceptable for it. Two further textual facts matter and are frequently omitted from teaching versions of this story. First, there are more than two states. The revised ending appeared in All the Year Round with the final sentence reading I saw the shadow of no parting from her . For the one-volume edition of 1862 Dickens altered it to I saw no shadow of another parting from her — a small change with a real semantic consequence, discussed below. A student who speaks of “the two endings” is simplifying a textual situation with at least three relevant states. Second, Forster preferred the original and printed it. John Forster reproduced the cancelled ending in his Life of Charles Dickens , which is why it survives at all in general circulation, and why the disagreement has been available to readers since the nineteenth century rather than being a discovery of modern textual scholarship. The revised ending Pip returns to England after eleven years. He goes to the site of Satis House, which has been demolished and sold; only the garden wall remains, and the garden. In the evening, in the mist, he finds Estella there. Drummle is dead; she has been “bent and broken, but — I hope — into a better shape”. They speak. She asks that they continue friends apart. They leave the ruined place together, and Pip closes: I took her hand in mine, and we went out of the ruined place; and, as the morning mists had risen long ago when I first left the forge, so the evening mists were rising now, and in all the broad expanse of tranquil light they showed to me, I saw no shadow of another parting from her. Structural comparison Original Revised Closural strategy ( §6.4 ) 3 (tangent) and 11 (anticlimax): a chance street meeting, deliberately small 2 (parallelism) and 1 (circularity): the garden returned to; the mists of the forge answered by the mists of Satis Location A London street; public, accidental Satis House garden; private, saturated Estella’s condition Remarried, to a poor doctor; suffering has softened her Widowed, unattached, “bent and broken” Contact A handshake, and parting Hands joined, and departure together Formal closure ( §4.6 ) None: the ending does not complete a pattern Strong: the mists frame the novel; the ruined garden answers the untouched one Plot resolution Complete and flat Complete, with one question left grammatically open Character arc Pip’s arc completes in his relief ; he wants nothing Pip’s arc completes in his taking a hand he was never permitted to take Thematic closure Expectations were false and are finished Contested — see below Final image Two people separating in a street Two figures leaving a ruin in mist The case for the original The case is Torgovnick’s congruence criterion ( §3.5 ) applied strictly, and it is strong. The novel is a systematic dismantling of the idea that Pip’s expectations were ever real. Its whole argument is that the fortune was a delusion, that gentility was a fraud, that Estella was manufactured as an instrument, and that the only durable goods in the book are Joe’s forge and Biddy’s plainness. An ending that grants Pip the one thing he wanted, in the very garden where he was taught to want it, gives back at the last minute what five hundred pages removed. The original ending, on this reading, is congruent and the revision is imposed. It leaves Pip with what the novel has actually earned him: work, a modest competence, an affection for another man’s child, and a moment of adult perception in which he can register Estella’s suffering without needing anything from her. It is also, formally, an anticlimax in the precise sense of §6.4 no. 11: the encounter is brief, accidental and unheightened, and the deflation is the point. The advocates are distinguished. John Forster, Dickens’s friend and first biographer, preferred the cancelled version and printed it. George Bernard Shaw preferred it too, and used it in the edition he prefaced, arguing that the revision falsified the book; a good deal of twentieth-century criticism followed him. The general form of the objection is §8.4 : a mismatched final note, produced by §8.12 ’s mechanism, external pressure. The case for the revision The case is subtler and, in the view of a good deal of modern criticism, stronger. (1) The revision is more heavily planted. Test 2 favours it decisively. The revised ending uses the garden at Satis House, the mists, the ruin, and the phrase-shape of Pip’s first departure — all material the novel established at length. The original uses a street the novel has not established, a Shropshire doctor who does not exist until this page, and a horse. On the plant audit, the original is the ending that introduces new elements, and the revision is the one that closes accounts. (2) The revision completes a formal pattern. The morning mists rose when Pip first left the forge; the evening mists rise now. This is textbook circularity and it is Herrnstein Smith’s terminal modification simultaneously: the same image at the opposite end of the day and of the book. The original completes no pattern at all. (3) The revision is not, on close reading, happy. This is the point most often lost. Satis House is demolished . The garden is a ruin. Estella describes herself as bent and broken. Nothing is restored; two damaged people meet in the wreckage of the place that damaged them. And the final sentence is grammatically careful in a way the paraphrase “they live happily ever after” cannot capture: I saw no shadow of another parting from her. Pip sees no shadow. He does not say there is none. The sentence reports the limits of his perception in a novel whose entire subject is a man perceiving wrongly — and Dickens’s 1862 alteration from the shadow of no parting to no shadow of another parting sharpens this, by moving the negation from the parting to the shadow and inserting another , which concedes that there has already been one. A reader who has attended to five hundred pages of Pip being confidently wrong has every reason to distrust the sentence, and many readers do. (4) The novel’s operative question may not be the one the original answers. Per §8.7 : a novel’s stated question and its operative question frequently differ. Great Expectations states a question about money and class. What it develops, over its length, is a question about whether a person made instrumental by another can recover the capacity for attachment — a question about Estella , not about Pip’s fortune. The original ending answers it in report (Pip observes that suffering has changed her). The revised ending answers it in action (she asks to be friends; she takes his hand). On this reading the revision resolves the operative question and the original resolves the stated one. What cannot be settled, and why the chapter refuses to settle it The disagreement is not a matter of one side having overlooked evidence. It turns on a prior question about what kind of book Great Expectations is, and competent readers answer it differently: If the novel is fundamentally… Then the congruent ending is… A satire on gentility and expectation The original: Pip must be left with nothing he expected A study of a damaged man learning to perceive Either, but the revision gives him something to perceive with A romance whose obstacles are social and psychological The revision: the obstacles are removed and the pair remain A tragedy of two people manufactured by others The revision, read pessimistically: two ruins in a ruin There is also a methodological point the case establishes better than any other in the chapter, and it can be stated as a general principle: The provenance of an ending is not evidence about its quality. That Bulwer-Lytton asked for the change tells us why the second ending exists. It tells us nothing about whether it is better. An ending written under pressure may be the one the book required, and an author’s first instinct may be a habit rather than a judgement. Congruence must be assessed by reading, not by biography. What the case teaches Test 2 and test 8 can disagree. The revision is better planted and more tonally suspect. When the plant audit and the tonal-match test conflict, no procedure resolves them; a judgement must be made about what the book is. A tonal shift at the close may be a modulation rather than a failure. §8.4 ’s exception is this case, and the limit it establishes on the test is real. Ambiguity can be produced by grammar rather than by content. I saw no shadow of another parting is a closed ending in its plot and an open one in its epistemology. Endings can be revised without being repaired. Both versions are competent; the second is not a correction of an error in the first. This is set as seminar question 1 at §12.2 , and it is the best available assessment task in the chapter, because a student can be required to argue either side from the same evidence and will find both arguable. 9.2 Eliot, Middlemarch (1871–72) — closure by widening Strategies: 6 (coda or finale), 8 (proleptic close), 10 (aphoristic close). The structure Middlemarch opens with a Prelude about Saint Theresa of Ávila and the difficulty faced by later women of ardent nature born into an age with no coherent social faith to give their ardour form. It closes with a section headed Finale , which reports the subsequent lives of the principal characters and then generalises. The Finale is, by the standards of §8.5 , an extreme tidy-everything ending. Fred and Mary are settled and their children accounted for. Lydgate acquires a prosperous practice, writes a treatise on gout, dies at fifty of diphtheria, and regards himself as a failure. Rosamond remarries, comfortably. Dorothea marries Will Ladislaw, bears a son, and is absorbed into the political life of a man of moderate distinction — an outcome the Finale describes without enthusiasm, noting that many who knew her thought it a pity that so substantial a nature should be known in a limited circle as a wife and mother. And then the last sentence: …for the growing good of the world is partly dependent on unhistoric acts; and that things are not so ill with you and me as they might have been, is half owing to the number who lived faithfully a hidden life, and rest in unvisited tombs. Why the ending does not close by tightening Nearly every ending discussed in this chapter closes by narrowing : to a gesture, an image, a word. Middlemarch closes by widening , and the widening is the mechanism. Movement What happens to the frame The individual settlements The frame is at its narrowest: named people, specific outcomes “Her finely-touched spirit had still its fine issues, though they were not widely visible” The frame lifts from the person to the category of person “the growing good of the world is partly dependent on unhistoric acts” The frame widens to history as such “things are not so ill with you and me” The frame includes the reader — the only place in the novel where you and me appears in this position “unvisited tombs” The frame closes on a place where nobody goes The final phrase is Herrnstein Smith’s closural allusion ( §3.2 ) at maximum strength — a tomb, unvisited, is about as terminal a referent as English possesses — and it arrives inside an unqualified general assertion, which is her other strongest device. Formally, this is one of the most heavily closed sentences in the language. The domains Domain How served Plot Comprehensively, and with graded weight: Lydgate’s failure gets more space than Fred’s contentment, because it cost more Character Dorothea’s arc completes as a diminishment that is not treated as one — the novel refuses both the triumph and the tragedy Theme The Prelude’s question is answered directly: there is no Saint Theresa available, and the ardour goes into unrecorded acts Catharsis Withheld from the characters and granted to the reader, in the last clause, by inclusion Final image An unvisited tomb: nobody present, nothing to see Formal Prelude answered by Finale. The book’s own structural frame closes ( §4.6 ) Two complications worth teaching (1) The Finale was itself revised. Eliot altered the Finale after the first edition, softening a passage that laid the blame for Dorothea’s circumscribed life more squarely on the society around her. This is a second instance of the Great Expectations problem in miniature — a great novelist adjusting the emphasis of her own close — and it is worth putting beside §9.1 to establish that authorial revision of endings is normal rather than scandalous. (2) The ending is D. A. Miller’s best evidence and its best refutation at once. On Miller’s reading ( §3.9 ), the Finale is the containment he describes: Dorothea’s narratable ardour is disposed of into a marriage, and the novel’s disruptive energy is administratively closed. That reading is available and is not perverse. But the Finale is also the strongest available counter-instance, because Eliot says so . The novel does not conceal the containment; it names it, regrets it, attributes it to “the conditions of an imperfect social state”, and closes on a sentence about lives whose value cannot be recorded. The narratable is not eliminated; it is declared to be unrecordable , which is a different operation. This is the pattern predicted at §3.9 : the strongest endings close the book while leaving something still moving. What remains moving in Middlemarch is the question of what Dorothea’s ardour was for, and the Finale’s achievement is to make the reader feel that the question survives the answer. 9.3 Fitzgerald, The Great Gatsby (1925) — the last page Strategies: 9 (terminal image), 10 (aphoristic close), 3 (tangent, mildly — the book leaves its subject entirely). The movement Gatsby is dead, the funeral has been attended by almost nobody, Tom and Daisy have retreated into their money, and Nick has closed up his affairs to go west. On the last night he goes down to the beach and lies on the sand. The final page performs a sequence of frame-shifts that repay being tabulated, because they are the mechanism. Stage Frame Nick on the beach; the houses melting away The present, one man The island as the Dutch sailors first saw it — the fresh, green breast of the new world Three centuries back; a continent The transitory enchanted moment, man face to face with something commensurate to his capacity for wonder Human capacity as such Gatsby’s green light at the end of Daisy’s dock Back to the novel’s own central image The orgastic future that year by year recedes Forward, indefinitely So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past. Everyone, always The last sentence is worth the same word-level attention §5.2 gives to Achebe: Element Function So Consequential; the sentence claims to follow from what precedes, which grants it the authority of a conclusion we The pronoun shifts from Gatsby, and from Nick, to the reader and the species. This is the single largest move on the page beat on Effortful, continuous, unrewarded; a verb of persistence rather than progress boats against the current The novel’s water imagery — the Sound, the dock, the rain at the reunion — cashed in a figure borne back Passive: the effort is real and the motion is backwards ceaselessly The one polysyllable in the sentence; it slows the line at the point where the meaning is “without end” into the past The last two words return the novel to its own subject — Gatsby’s attempt to repeat the past — and close on the noun the whole book has been arguing about Note the prosody, which is not decorative. The sentence ends on past — a single stressed syllable, a hard consonant cluster, a full stop. Herrnstein Smith’s account of closural force in verse applies directly: a terminal stress closes harder than a terminal unstressed syllable, and English readers register this without knowing they do. Compare an ending on into the past again and the difference in finality is immediate. The domains, and one instructive absence Domain How served Plot Served earlier, in the accounting of the funeral and of Tom and Daisy; the last page adds nothing Character Nick’s arc completes in his decision to go west, several pages before the close Theme Served entirely here, and by enlargement : Gatsby’s error becomes the national condition Catharsis Granted by the change of pronoun. The reader is invited into the sentence Final image Absolute Formal The green light returns; the novel’s controlling image closes The instructive absence is plot . The last page of The Great Gatsby resolves nothing whatever; every plot question was settled in the preceding chapter. This is the strongest available demonstration of §2.3.2 ’s distinction: resolution occurs earlier, closure occurs here, and the two are separable operations that the same book performs in different places. The risk it runs The page is a maximal instance of the aphoristic close , and it is worth teaching what licenses it, since a student attempting the same move will usually fail. Nick has been a generalising narrator from the novel’s first paragraph — his father’s advice, “reserving judgments is a matter of infinite hope” — and the book has established him as a man who thinks in propositions. Chapter 9 §4.5 analyses that opening as a retrospective promise : a narrator’s posture claiming that something happened which reorganised a life. The last page is that promise being honoured. A narrator who had not been established as a maker of general statements could not close this way; the aphorism would read as the author arriving. 9.4 Tolstoy, Anna Karenina (1878) — Part Eight Strategies: 6 (coda), 8 (proleptic elements), and — structurally — the aftermath as a full movement. The problem the ending solves Anna dies at the end of Part Seven. The novel then continues for an entire further part, beginning some two months later, in which: Koznyshev’s six years’ book is published to indifference; the Serbian war fever produces a train of volunteers; Vronsky, half-destroyed, boards a train for Serbia with a toothache; and Levin, at Pokrovskoe, passes through a crisis of meaning that resolves in an exchange with a peasant about living for the soul, a storm, a fright about his infant son, and a private, unannounced arrival at faith. The book ends inside Levin’s consciousness, on the recognition that his life has an unquestionable meaning of goodness which he has the power to put into it. By every contemporary standard this is §8.3 , the endless aftermath, and it has been criticised as such since publication; Tolstoy’s serial publisher declined to print Part Eight, which appeared separately. Why it is not a failure The novel has two arcs , and Chapter 14 ( The Subplot ) supplies the vocabulary for what follows. Levin’s thread is not a subplot in the satellite sense; it is a second kernel, and the two never converge at the level of plot — Levin and Anna meet once, late, and the meeting changes nothing. What links them is that both are testing the same proposition about how a person is to live once the available social forms have stopped answering. Two arcs cannot complete at the same climax. Anna’s completes at the station. If the book ended there, Levin’s thread would be a long, beautifully written appendage with no terminus, and the novel would collapse into what a century of abridgements have tried to make it: a book about an adulteress’s destruction.
