The general principle the case establishes, and it is one of the most useful in the chapter: An aftermath is not too long if it is completing an arc. It is too long if it is reporting consequences. Part Eight reports very few consequences of Anna’s death — that is what readers complain of — and completes an entire second arc, which is why it cannot be cut. The mechanism of the transfer What Tolstoy does structurally is a repeatable technique. Anna’s death is not the novel’s climax for Levin ; it barely registers in his section. What Part Eight does is transfer the reader’s accumulated grief into a thread where it can be discharged, since Anna’s own thread admits no consolation. The catharsis available at the end of Part Seven is horror. The catharsis available at the end of Part Eight is something else, and it is only available because the horror preceded it. Note also the deliberate coldness of the transfer. Vronsky’s last appearance is a man with toothache, going to be killed in someone else’s war, unable to think about anything. Tolstoy refuses the surviving lover any grandeur, and the refusal is what prevents Part Eight from reading as consolation. The live disagreement Whether the Levin thread converges is a real critical question and is set as seminar question 3 at §12.2 . Two positions: It converges thematically and not literally , which is the point: the novel’s argument is that these lives do not intersect, and the formal separation enacts it. It does not converge at all , and Part Eight is Tolstoy attaching a religious conclusion to a novel that did not require it. On this reading, Levin’s arrival at faith is §8.6 — the explained ending — in its purest form, since a character does in fact spend the last chapters formulating what the book means. The second position is stronger than students usually expect, and a seminar in which nobody argues it has not read Part Eight carefully. 9.5 Orwell, Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949) — the last line and the Appendix Strategies: 9 (terminal image) and 10 (aphoristic close) for the narrative; 14 (appendix) and 3 (tangent) for what follows. The narrative’s close Winston, released, sits in the Chestnut Tree Café with gin and a chess problem. He has met Julia; each has betrayed the other; there is nothing left. A telescreen announces a victory in Africa. Something breaks in him, and the novel ends: He loved Big Brother. Four words. Consider what is packed into their form rather than their content. It is an unqualified assertion in Herrnstein Smith’s exact sense: declarative, past tense, no hedge, no subordination, no adverb. It is monosyllabic apart from the name. It ends on the name of the thing that has destroyed him, so the last word of the book belongs to the Party. And it is a statement of fact by the narrator , not a report of Winston’s belief — the free indirect narration that has been inside Winston’s head for three hundred pages here delivers a verdict about him from outside, which is the grammatical form of a man’s inner life being annexed. By the domain audit: plot resolved (the Party wins), character arc completed as annihilation, theme closed in the negative, catharsis delivered as despair, final image absolute. Formal closure: none. And then the Appendix The novel is followed by “The Principles of Newspeak”, some twelve pages of expository prose on the structure and purpose of the language, its A, B and C vocabularies, and the intended completion of its adoption by 2050. It contains no narrative. It is written in standard English. And it is written in the past tense , by a scholar who quotes and analyses the Times of the period as a historical document, and who explains Newspeak’s principles to readers who evidently do not use it. Nothing in Winston’s story changes. But the artefact the reader is holding now contains a vantage from which Oceania is over — a free scholar, writing afterwards, in a language the Party was designing Newspeak to abolish. The argument that the Appendix therefore reverses the novel’s despair has been made in various forms by later novelists and critics, Margaret Atwood and Thomas Pynchon among them, and it is one of the strongest cases in fiction for §4.6 ’s contention that formal closure is a distinct domain , because the operation is performed on the object and not on the story. Three observations sharpen it. (1) The reversal is accomplished by a tense. No content is required. This is §5.3 ’s third carrier — grammar as the cheapest closural instrument available — operating at the scale of a whole novel’s meaning. (2) Orwell defended the Appendix’s presence. It is documented that his American book club asked him to cut the Appendix along with the Goldstein book, and that he refused, at a substantial commercial cost. Whatever he intended by it, he regarded it as load-bearing. (3) The reading is contested, and should be. The counter-argument is that the Appendix is a piece of worldbuilding apparatus, that its tense is the ordinary tense of an encyclopaedia article, and that reading a fall of the Party out of it is a modern reader’s need for consolation projected onto a footnote. This position has the merit of noticing that the Appendix is placed after the novel — that is, outside it — and that Orwell’s title for it is descriptive rather than framing. The chapter takes no side, but records the methodological point: the disagreement is possible only because formal closure and thematic closure are separable. If the two were the same domain, the Appendix could not contradict the last line, and the argument could not arise. Seminar question 2 ( §12.2 ) puts this to the class as the test case for the sixth domain. A note on the pairing with The Handmaid’s Tale Atwood’s Historical Notes perform the same structural operation with a different outcome, and the two make the best available paired teaching example. Nineteen Eighty-Four Appendix The Handmaid’s Tale Historical Notes Form Anonymous scholarly exposition A conference paper, with a named speaker and an audience Effect on the regime Implies its end, without saying so States its end explicitly Effect on the protagonist None; Winston is not mentioned Offred’s fate is investigated and cannot be determined Effect on the reader Consolation, arguable Consolation, immediately withdrawn: the scholar is facetious about the testimony Domain served Formal, contradicting thematic Formal, plot, thematic — and a bitter substitute for catharsis Chapter 10 ( The Prologue ) analyses the Historical Notes at its §9.8 as a threshold arriving at the wrong end of the book. That analysis and this one are compatible: the same device is a displaced prologue and a closural apparatus, and it is effective because it is both. 9.6 Morrison, Beloved (1987) — the phrase that contradicts itself Strategies: 4 (incompletion), 9 (terminal image), and a terminal modification ( §3.2 ) executed on a sentence. The close The novel’s last chapter withdraws from scene into a choral register. Beloved is gone; the neighbourhood forgets her; her footprints by the stream appear and disappear; the story is described as one that everyone deliberately puts down. And a sentence recurs: It was not a story to pass on. It appears, is repeated, and then — in its final occurrence — arrives with its tense altered to the present. The novel then closes on a single word standing alone: Beloved. The contradiction inside the phrase The line does at least three incompatible things at once, and the incompatibility is the point. Reading of pass on Meaning of the sentence What it does To transmit, hand down This story must not be told Forbids the book that contains it To decline, to refuse (as in cards) This story cannot be refused Requires the book that contains it To die, to pass away This story will not die Neither forbids nor requires; asserts persistence All three are current English. The sentence is therefore not ambiguous in the ordinary sense — it does not have a meaning the reader must guess — it is self-cancelling , and it is printed inside a four-hundred-page act of transmission that makes the first reading demonstrably false. The reader cannot settle it, and the inability to settle it is the closest a sentence can come to representing the novel’s subject: an event that must not be spoken about and must not be forgotten. Two formal operations The tense shift. The move from it was to this is is a terminal modification in Herrnstein Smith’s exact sense ( §3.2 ): a pattern established by repetition is altered at its last instance. It also does something specific to the reader’s position. It was not a story to pass on describes the characters’ relation to the past. This is not a story to pass on describes the reader’s relation to the book in their hands. In three words the novel steps out of its own frame and addresses the act of reading it — and does so without any of the announcements a metafictional gesture usually requires. The final word. The book ends on the name, alone, as a one-word paragraph. Consider what this does with the domains: it is simultaneously plot (the entity has been dispersed and the name survives), character (the unnamed baby finally has a word), theme (what remains of a person when the story is put down is the name on the headstone), catharsis (an address rather than a statement — the last thing the book does is speak to her), and final image (a word on a white page). It is also the novel’s title , which makes it a formal closure of the most economical kind available: the book ends by becoming its own name. Note that this is the same device analysed in Chapter 9 §9.5 , from the opposite end. Beloved opens with a number where a name should be — 124 was spiteful — and closes with a name and nothing else. The novel’s whole trajectory is legible in the movement from an address to a name, and the two privileged positions are doing it between them. The disagreement worth staging Beloved is the standard modern counter-instance to §8.9 , ambiguity as evasion — and a sceptic can put the opposite case, which is worth hearing. The objection: the sentence’s undecidability is produced by a lexical accident of English, the reader who notices it is performing a critic’s operation rather than a reader’s, and the choral last chapter is a register the novel has not otherwise used, arriving after the story is over to supply an effect the story did not produce. The reply, and it is strong: the choral register has been used — the unattributed monologues of the preceding section establish it — so the last chapter is a completion rather than an arrival; and the novel has been explicitly concerned with what can and cannot be said since its first page. But a seminar in which nobody puts the objection has not tested the ending. 9.7 Joyce, Ulysses (1922) — closure by affirmation Strategies: 10 (aphoristic close, in an unusual mode), 9 (terminal image), 1 (circularity, at the level of the whole day), 14 (apparatus, in the smallest possible form). The close The novel’s final episode, “Penelope”, is Molly Bloom’s unpunctuated interior monologue, conventionally divided into eight great sentences. It closes with a recollection of Howth Head and Bloom’s proposal, and ends: and yes I said yes I will Yes. Then, below it, in most editions: Trieste–Zurich–Paris, 1914–1921. Why this is the most technically interesting close in the chapter Almost every closural device Herrnstein Smith catalogues is operating at once, in a text that has spent seven hundred pages refusing them. Device How it operates here Unqualified assertion Yes is the shortest possible unhedged affirmative; there is no more assertive word in English Terminal modification The episode has run without capitals or full stops for forty pages. The final Yes is capitalised and followed by a full stop. The pattern is broken at its last instance, and the breaking is the closure Closural allusion Memory, dusk, a hillside, a proposal, sleep. The referents are all terminal Repetition with intensification yes… yes… Yes — the same word three times in eight words, rising Circularity The last word of the book is the first word of the episode; the day that began with Bloom’s breakfast ends in his wife’s assent to having married him And then the colophon. Trieste–Zurich–Paris, 1914–1921 is not part of the fiction; it is the author’s record of composition, and by long convention it is printed as though it were the last line. Its effect is a formal closure of the sixth-domain kind ( §4.6 ): the reader is moved, without transition, from Molly’s consciousness in 1904 to the fact of a book having been made across three cities and seven years of war. The novel’s last gesture is to become an object. The domain audit, and what is missing Domain How served Plot Barely. Nothing is resolved. Bloom has come home; Boylan has been; nobody has decided anything Character Molly’s arc, such as it is, completes in a memory rather than an action; Bloom’s completes in her assent to him, which he does not hear Theme Fully: the novel’s argument about ordinary life as sufficient subject is delivered by an unqualified affirmation of an ordinary marriage Catharsis Very high, and produced almost entirely by rhythm and repetition rather than by event Final image Howth, the rhododendrons, a proposal accepted Formal Maximal: the pattern breaks, the day closes, the book declares itself made Plot resolution is essentially absent, and Ulysses is nonetheless one of the most completely closed novels in English. It is the chapter’s cleanest single demonstration of §2.3.2 : resolution and closure are separable, and a book may have all of the second and none of the first. The caution The strategy is close to unavailable to most books, and the reason should be given rather than leaving students to attempt it. The final Yes works because seven hundred pages have established a texture of relentless qualification, irony, interruption and doubt. An unqualified affirmative closes hard in proportion to the qualification it terminates . In a book whose prose has been affirmative throughout, the same word closes nothing. This is the general form of the point made about Eliot at §8.6 and about Fitzgerald at §9.3: a closural device is licensed by what the book has been doing, not by its own properties. 9.8 Cervantes, Don Quixote (Part II, 1615) — ending the character’s availability Strategies: 8.8’s death (used as the exception it names), 5 (the frame closed), and a strategy no other book in this chapter attempts: closure as prohibition . Quotations follow Edith Grossman’s translation (2003); the structural claims survive translation, the texture claims do not. The close In the last chapter of Part II, Alonso Quixano returns home ill, sleeps, and wakes sane. He abjures the books of chivalry, declares that he is no longer Don Quixote de la Mancha but Alonso Quixano the Good, makes his will — including a clause disinheriting his niece if she marries a man who reads books of chivalry — receives the sacraments, and dies. Sancho, weeping, begs him to get up and go looking for adventures. Then the narrative apparatus takes over. The notary observes that he has never read of a knight errant dying so calmly and so Christianly in his bed. And Cide Hamete Benengeli, the fictional Arabic historian whose manuscript the whole novel purports to translate, addresses his own pen, hangs it up, and declares that for him alone Don Quixote was born and he for Don Quixote: the one to act and the other to write. He warns off the “false writer of Tordesillas” from disinterring the knight’s bones or attempting further adventures. What is being closed This is the only ending in the chapter that closes something other than a story. Consider what it actually accomplishes: Level What ends Plot Very little. The third sally has concluded; the plot has been episodic throughout and has no accumulating question to answer Character Alonso Quixano recovers his wits — which is to say the character of Don Quixote ceases to exist before its host does . The madness ends, then the man Theme The novel’s argument about reading and delusion completes: the cure is worse than the disease, and everyone present would rather have him mad Catharsis Sancho’s plea to get up and try again is the release, and it is placed in the mouth of the character who has spent the book being sceptical Formal The frame closes: the historian, the manuscript, the pen The book’s future Closed by decree The last row is the point. In 1614, between the two parts, a writer under the name Alonso Fernández de Avellaneda published a spurious continuation of Don Quixote . Cervantes’ Part II absorbs the insult into the fiction — his characters encounter people who have read the spurious continuation, and the itinerary is altered so that Don Quixote will not go where the counterfeit says he went — and the ending completes the operation. The character is killed, sanity is restored first so that no resurrection can be plausible, and the historian’s pen is hung up with an explicit prohibition attached. This is an ending designed to prevent further text . It is the exact inverse of §8.11 ’s series hook, and it can be named as a distinct closural operation: Closure by withdrawal of availability. The book ends not by resolving its questions but by removing the conditions under which more of it could be written. What is closed is not the plot but the character’s capacity to have further adventures. Why this is the strongest exception to §8.8 §8.8 holds that death fails as an ending when it substitutes for a decision. Here the death is preceded by a decision — Alonso Quixano’s renunciation — and the death itself is almost an afterthought, reported briskly, with the will given more textual space than the dying. What the ending stages is a man choosing to stop being someone, and the novel’s grief is not that he died but that he stopped first. The general principle: death closes a book when what dies is a possibility rather than a person. A note on Part I Part I (1605) ends with the opposite gesture: an explicit promise of a third sally and an invitation to whoever might write it. That invitation produced Avellaneda. The two endings of Don Quixote therefore constitute the discipline’s best natural experiment in the series hook ( §8.11 ): the same author, the same character, one open ending and one closed, with a documented consequence in between. It is set as an exercise at §12.1 . 9.9 Saramago, Blindness (1995) — the withheld confirmation Strategies: 9 (terminal image), 4 (incompletion), and the withholding of a payoff the novel has spent its length promising. Read in Giovanni Pontiero’s translation (1997). The structural claims below survive translation; the claims about the run-on syntax are claims about Pontiero as much as about Saramago, and the point is made in Chapter 9 §4.6 and again here. The close An unexplained epidemic of white blindness has emptied a city. Throughout, one character — the doctor’s wife — has retained her sight, concealed it, and used it to keep a small group alive at enormous personal cost. She has spent the novel expecting, sentence by sentence, to lose her sight too. At the end, as arbitrarily as it came, sight returns to the population. The group recovers. And the doctor’s wife goes to the window and looks up — and what she sees is white: the whiteness that has been the novel’s image of blindness throughout. Her own turn appears to have come. Then she lowers her eyes, and the city is there. Near this, in one of the novel’s most quoted exchanges, the characters agree that they do not think they went blind; they think they are blind, and always were: blind people who can see but do not look. The mechanism: a payoff withheld and then converted The novel has run on a single suspense: will she lose her sight? It is the book’s central pull-forward question, established early and maintained for three hundred pages. Every closural convention available says that this question must be answered. Saramago answers it and immediately makes the answer worthless. She looks up and sees white — and the white is the sky. The reader’s dread is triggered, held for a clause, and dissolved into weather. What was going to be the novel’s largest plot payoff is spent on an optical joke, and in its place the book substitutes a thematic proposition that reframes the entire epidemic: sight was never the issue. This is closure by substitution of question , and it is the constructive form of §8.7 . The ending resolves a different question from the one the plot posed — and it works, where §8.7 ’s failures do not, because the substituted question is one the novel has been building in parallel from the beginning, and because the reader is shown the substitution happening rather than having the original question quietly dropped. The domains Domain How served Plot Resolved perfunctorily and deliberately: sight returns, unexplained, as it left. The book refuses to make an event of it Character The doctor’s wife’s arc completes not in relief but in the discovery that her sight was never the privilege she took it for Theme Fully, and by explicit statement — the closest the novel comes to §8.6 , licensed by a narration that has been sententious throughout Catharsis Deliberately small. The book declines the release it has earned Final image A woman at a window; a city; whiteness that turns out to be sky Formal The typographic constraint — no quotation marks, no paragraphing of speech — is never released, which is itself a closural decision: the book does not return the reader to normal prose, because it does not think normality is available That last row is worth dwelling on. Chapter 9 §4.6 analyses Blindness ’s typography as a formal contract declared on the first page. The formal closure question is what happens to a declared constraint at the end, and Saramago’s answer is the least common one: nothing . The device is neither completed nor withdrawn. A book that has made its reader work for three hundred pages does not, at the close, hand the work back — and the refusal to release the constraint is the formal analogue of the refusal to grant the confirming vision. Why this is not §8.9 Ambiguity as evasion requires that the reader be unable to say what is unresolved. Here they can say it in one sentence: it is not known why the blindness came or went, and it is not known whether the recovery will last. Both gaps are marked in the text, both are consistent with a novel whose subject is the arbitrariness of catastrophe, and neither could be closed without converting a parable into a plot. 9.10 The capstone revision case: the household ending, and the audit of a whole textbook The nine readings above are of published fiction. What follows is the chapter’s own worked example, and it was also the first edition’s capstone: the household narrative that runs through every chapter, brought to its conclusion, with every element traced back to the chapter that planted it. The case is the capstone for a reason that is structural rather than sentimental. §7.1 ’s test 2 — the plant audit — is the only test in this book that requires the whole work, and it has therefore been impossible to demonstrate until now. The earlier chapters have been depositing material. This section is where the deposits are checked. 9.10.1 The situation A small shop. A father who kept its ledger in a careful, slanted hand with crossed sevens for eleven years — prices and repairs and the ordinary arithmetic of keeping a small shop alive. He died in March, after an illness he documented and told nobody about. Their mother changed the locks. Three adult children — Elena, who drives a truck and wants to know why; Nadia, who counts things and left the flat over the shop seventeen months ago for one with heating; and Dov, who held the doorway, gave Elena the key, withheld the reason, and has been quietly selling the shop — have spent the book reconstructing what happened from the objects he left. The novel’s climax is the bounded viewpoint chapter analysed in Chapter 13 ( The Viewpoint Shift ) §9.9 : the evening of March the ninth, Dov at the ledger, the good pen not where it should be, and the decision to go on writing. The ending follows it. 9.10.2 Version B: the ending the book has been building The working text, corrected in the second edition in one clause (see §9.10.7, item 4): They read it together, in the end — Elena at the register, Nadia on the stool, Dov standing because he said he’d rather. Their father’s hand ran clean and careful for eleven years of entries, prices and repairs and the ordinary arithmetic of keeping a small shop alive, and then, three pages from the end, a different kind of entry altogether: dates, a doctor’s name misspelled twice and corrected once, and beneath it, in the same careful hand as always, a list of what needed doing if he ran out of time to do it himself. He had known. He had not told them. He had, instead, done what he always did, which was write it down properly, in case anyone ever needed to check. Dov’s hand picked up where his father’s left off on March the ninth, looser at first and then not. He hadn’t known what else to do with a ledger that had stopped making sense the way ledgers were supposed to. It was Nadia who went up to the coat, in the end. It was hanging on the hook where nobody had moved it. She didn’t ask permission. She took it down, and after a moment, so the sleeves wouldn’t drag, she put it on. 9.10.3 The domain audit Domain How it is delivered Carrier Plot The father knew he was ill and documented it rather than telling anyone; Dov continued the ledger from the evening of 9 March The three pages from the end; the changed hand Character Nadia takes down and wears the coat she has spent the book refusing to touch; in Chapter 7 her hand went no further than its pocket The coat, and the gesture of gathering the sleeves Theme “In case anyone ever needs to check” recurs, now understood by everyone in the room including the reader The father’s own line, returned Catharsis All three siblings physically together, in silence, for the first time in the book Bodies in one room; nobody speaking Final image Nadia in a dead man’s coat, managing the sleeves The coat Formal The ledger, the object the novel has been reading in fragments, is read whole and in company; the reading that began alone (Chapter 6’s stool) is completed by three people The ledger as the book’s structural spine Six domains, three carriers. That ratio is the point of §5 : the coat serves character, final image and catharsis simultaneously; the ledger serves plot, theme and formal closure; and the room serves catharsis by itself. Nothing in the passage is doing only one job, and no domain has a scene of its own. The closural strategies ( §6.4 ) are 2 (parallelism) — the coat returned to, the doorway exchange answered by a room in which nobody argues — and 9 (the terminal image) . There is no coda, no epilogue, no proleptic close, and no explanation. The ending is covert in Torgovnick’s sense ( §3.5 ): the last scene is formally indistinguishable from any other scene in the book, and it closes anyway. 9.10.4 The plant audit, run across the whole textbook This is test 2 ( §7.1 ), performed properly. The ending contributes no material; it contributes a combination — three people, one room, one document read continuously — which is what §6.3 requires. Three plants are unredeemed (rows 15–17). One is deliberate and defended below. Two are honest debts, and a textbook that concealed them would be teaching the wrong lesson. Chapter 10 predicted the failure of row 16 in advance, which is a point in favour of the diagnostic protocol and not a defence of the ending. Row 5 deserves a note , because it looks like a violation and is not. Dov’s decision is deposited only one chapter before the ending. That would be fatal if the ending disclosed it — the reader would be receiving load-bearing information at the close (test 3). It does not. The reader already knows; what the ending supplies is the sisters finding out, and the effect is dramatic irony discharging rather than information arriving. The audit question is not “when was this deposited?” but “does the ending depend on the reader learning it here?” 9.10.5 Version A: an ending that resolves by a new element The following is a deliberately weak alternative, written to fail in an instructive way. It is a counterfactual and is not part of the household canon ; in particular, the mother’s account of herself given below is invented for the purpose of being rejected, and the household narrative does not contain it. The letter came on a Tuesday, forwarded twice, and it was Elena who opened it. Whitlock & Ames, Solicitors, regretted to inform the family of the late proprietor that the deeds to the premises had been placed in trust the previous February, and that a copy of the medical report lodged with them at that time was enclosed for the beneficiaries’ attention. She drove out to her mother’s that evening. Ma let her in without being asked and put the kettle on and stood with her back to it while Elena read the report aloud; and when it was finished she said that she had known since January, that he had made her promise, and that changing the locks had been the only way she could think of to stop the three of them getting into the ledger before she had decided what to tell them. She was sorry. She had not known how to say it. She was saying it now. Nadia came at nine and they told her, and Dov drove over at eleven, and by midnight there was nothing any of them did not know. Diagnosis. Test Result 1 — Retroactive Fails badly. The book’s reconstruction is retroactively converted into a delay before the post arrived. Elena’s investigation, Nadia’s counting, Dov’s silence and the whole business of the ledger become an elaborate way of not opening a letter 2 — Plant audit Fails. The solicitors, the trust, the medical report and the February date are four load-bearing elements deposited nowhere 3 — Earned Fails on all three of §7.1 ’s severities at once. New information (the report); new agent (the firm); and — worst — the resolution is delivered by someone outside the book’s causal system 4 — Inevitability Fails. A reader can construct six alternative endings of equal justice, because nothing in the material determines this one 5 — Domain Plot over-served; character unserved (nobody does anything; four people receive); theme stated by the mother rather than experienced; catharsis asserted (“she was sorry”); final image absent — the passage ends on a clause about information 6 — Proportion The mother, who has had no scene in the book, receives the largest speech in the book 7 — Termination The passage stops. Nothing formally closes 8 — Tonal match Fails. The register is procedural — forwarded twice , beneficiaries’ attention — in a book whose register is domestic and physical 10 — Last line “there was nothing any of them did not know” is an abstraction, and the last word is know — Patterns present: the unearned rescue ( §8.1 ); the explained ending ( §8.6 ); the tidy-everything ending ( §8.5 ); death-adjacent resolution by disclosure rather than decision ( §8.8 ); and, underlying all of them, the imposed ending ( §8.12 ) The mechanism. Version A commits a single error from which the rest follow: it makes the novel’s question what happened? rather than what do these three do with what they can reconstruct? Those are different books. The first is answerable by a document. The second is answerable only by the siblings, and only in each other’s presence. Once the question is misidentified, everything else is forced. If the answer can arrive in the post, the ledger is redundant. If the ledger is redundant, Dov’s continuation of it is a curiosity rather than a confession. If the mother explains herself, the family’s central silence is dissolved by exposition. And if everything is known by midnight, there is nothing left for anybody to do — which is why Version A cannot produce a final image: an ending needs an act, and Version A contains only receipt. Note also what Version A does to the material it does use. The changed locks, planted in Chapter 3 as an unexplained act of withholding, are converted into a practical measure with a stated purpose. The plant is not merely unredeemed; it is spent , in the way Chapter 10 §9.9 describes its own Version A spending the good pen. A wrong ending does not simply fail to pay its debts. It cancels them. 9.10.6 What the ending does, procedurally Set against Version A, the working ending can be described as a series of decisions rather than as an inspiration. It answers the operative question, not the stated one ( §8.7 ). The stated question — why were the locks changed — is not answered. The operative question — can these three be in a room together — is answered by putting them in one. It resolves by combination, not by material ( §6.3 ). Every element is old. What is new is that the ledger is read continuously , by all three , in the shop. The novel has shown the ledger four times and always in fragments, always alone. It uses a single carrier for three domains ( §5.3 , carrier 1: the object already in the room). The coat closes character, final image and catharsis. It completes the arc by a repeated situation with the terms altered ( §4.2 ). Nadia has stood in front of that coat since Chapter 4 and not taken it down; in Chapter 7 her hand goes no further than the pocket. She takes it down. Nobody says anything about it. It preserves the constant. So the sleeves wouldn’t drag is Nadia measuring, adjusting, managing — the behaviour that has characterised her since Chapter 9’s opening. The change is legible because the constant is visible in the same clause. It ends on a decision, not a consequence ( §6.6 ). Putting on the coat is the last decision anybody takes, and the passage stops within a sentence of it. It refuses to explain ( §8.6 ). “He had known. He had not told them.” Three facts, no interpretation. The reader performs the inference that a lesser ending would perform for them. It lets the father speak last, through a phrase, without a scene. Write it down properly, in case anyone ever needs to check is returned as the explanation of an act rather than as a moral, and it is the only generalisation in the passage — licensed because it is quoted from a dead man rather than asserted by a narrator. 9.10.7 What Version B has not solved Six reservations, offered because a capstone that ends in triumph would contradict everything in §16 . 1. The mother is unresolved, and this is a choice with a cost. She changed the locks in March and the novel never says why. She has no scene of her own in the book. The ending does not approach her; the three siblings read a document that explains their father and says nothing about their mother, and the book stops. The defence is that her silence is the novel’s last piece of narratable material, deliberately preserved — the pattern §3.9 predicts of endings that close a book while leaving something moving. The novel is about what a family withholds from itself; an ending that closed every withholding would have argued that withholding is a solvable problem, which is what the book denies. There is also a structural defence: the reader now possesses, from the ledger, an explanation of the father’s silence, and is therefore in a position to extend the same charity to the mother’s without being told to. The unexplained silence beside the explained one is the ending’s most economical thematic act. The cost is real and should be named. A reader may reasonably close the book feeling that the largest question has been sidestepped, and that the ending has resolved the tractable withholding and declined the intractable one. Chapter 13 §9.9 reached the same verdict from the viewpoint side — it solves Dov and leaves the mother — and a reader entitled to ask why always the siblings has Eliot’s authority for the question. The honest statement is that this is an allocation, not a discovery, and a different novelist would write the other book. 2. Two prologue plants are left on the table. The boy at the glass and the unflipped sign (rows 16 and 17) are deposited in a privileged position and never redeemed. Chapter 10 predicted the first would be fragile because a person is harder to recognise than an object. By the promise-inventory logic Chapter 9 applies to openings, these are unredeemed promises, and the remedy is either a second appearance earlier in the book or deletion from the prologue. Chapter 11 proposes the second appearance (see 9.10.8). 3. The passage may be over-determined ( §5.4 ). Every noun in it means something: the ledger, the hand, the dates, the doctor’s name, the coat, the sleeves. There is no inert material — no bus going past, no radiator — and the audit at §5.5 would return “no inert sentences at all”. Whether that reads as concentration or as arrangement is a legitimate editorial disagreement, and it is worth staging in a workshop. The available correction is a sentence that means nothing, placed between the ledger and the coat. 4. The move to the flat is made in a clause. The first edition read Nadia was the one who found the coat , which imported a discovery the situation does not contain, since she has known where the coat is for four months; the second edition reads It was Nadia who went up to the coat . The correction exposes a smaller problem: the three read in the shop and the coat hangs in the flat above it, so the last paragraph changes place in a single clause, and a reader may stumble on stairs the sentence does not mention. 5. Elena receives least. She is the investigator; she drove to the shop, opened the drawer, found the changed hand, and drove the book’s whole forward motion. In the ending she is at the register, reading. Her arc completes by presence rather than by act, which is the weakest form of completion in §4.2 ’s table. The defence is that she has already had her decision — in the truck, in Chapter 2’s sequel — and that a novel cannot give three characters a final act without diluting all three. The objection is that the reader has spent more time with her than with anyone. Chapter 12 proposes an act for her at the convergence (see 9.10.8). 6. The ending is covert, and covert endings fail test 7 more often than overt ones. There is no formal signal that this is the last scene: no coda, no time-shift, no change of register, no terminal modification. A reader may reach the last line and turn the page. The counter-argument is that the coat is the signal — that an object withheld for the length of a book, finally taken, is as strong a terminal marker as a formal device — and that the book’s whole method has been to let objects do the work that a more explicit novel would give to structure. But it is a risk, and it is the risk this ending takes. 9.10.8 The plant audit rerun across the second edition The audit in 9.10.4 was run against the first edition, whose twelve chapters were the only depositors. The second edition adds six chapters, and each of them did two things to the household material: it deposited new elements, and it proposed a way to pay a debt that the first audit had recorded. An audit of the ending that ignored them would certify a book that no longer exists, so this section runs test 2 ( §7.1 ) again, over every element any of the eighteen chapters deposits, and asks of each the question 9.10.4 ends on: does the ending depend on the reader learning it here? Two terms need fixing first. An element is paid where the book uses the load it carries, and maintained where the book returns to it before the payment without using it. A payment marked proposed rests on a revision that one of the new chapters makes in its household case and leaves for the author to confirm; nothing in an earlier chapter’s text is changed by it. The proposals are in the household cases of Chapter 8 (the arrangement of times), Chapter 11 (the middle), Chapter 12 (Elena’s arc), Chapter 15 (the reveal of the illness), Chapter 17 (the book’s genre) and Chapter 18 (the edit of the whole), each in section 7, and in the subplot case of Chapter 14 , section 9.9. proposed 32 Elena does not telephone her mother 2 11, 12 16 (the locks unanswered in view) A sign of the decline; proposed Findings. The thirty-two rows fall into four groups. Sixteen are paid in the working texts of the chapters (rows 1 to 9, 11, 13, 14, 17 and 23 to 25). Nine are paid only by a proposed revision (rows 15, 21, 22 and 26 to 31). Three belong to what the book declines rather than pays (rows 18, 20 and 32). Four carry no load: the cuff, which is present in the object and never named; the list, the one element that appears first in the ending; the stool; and the till counted twice, a seed that nothing grows from. The sum is 16 + 9 + 3 + 4 = 32. The first finding of 9.10.4 survives the rerun. Nothing load-bearing arrives for the first time in the ending, and the list (row 12) is still the only element that does, kept there because no earlier chapter could show it without a sister reading the illness entries or Dov reading back. The six new chapters deposited nine elements (rows 25 to 32 and the extension of row 18), and every one of them is paid at or before the reading, most of them at the convergence. None of them is spent in the ending’s three paragraphs, which 9.10.2 gives unchanged. The first audit’s three unredeemed plants have changed status. The changed locks (row 20) remain unredeemed by design, but the second edition gives the decline its signs, which the first edition lacked: Dov’s refusal in the doorway, and three decisions of Elena’s not to ask, in the truck (row 32), at the empty drawer (row 27) and at the convergence, where she rings Nadia rather than her mother. Chapter 17 argues that a book in the mystery mode may decline the mystery’s solution only if it declares the decline, and these are the declaration. The boy at the glass and the sign (rows 21 and 22), which 9.10.7 item 2 left as debts, are paid by the scene Chapter 11 proposes at the empty drawer; if the author rejects that scene, they return to the table, and the remedy remains deletion from the prologue. The rerun also finds a cost the first audit could not see. The convergence, Dov bringing the ledger to the shop, now pays five rows (25, 27, 28, 29 and 30) and the sale besides, in a scene that the first edition did not contain. The ending’s own passage is no more crowded than it was, but the scene before it is the most heavily loaded in the book, which is the over-determination that 9.10.7 item 3 found in the last paragraphs, moved one scene earlier. Chapter 12 records the crowding as unsolved, and the rerun agrees. The brushing of the coat (row 18) was the one element the first audit did not list at all, since the first edition’s ending does not use it. Under the mystery mode that Chapter 17 identifies, an unexplained weekly act on a dead man’s coat reads as a clue, and a clue never paid is a question of fact declined without a sign. Chapter 18 proposes the sign: Nadia says that Dov thinks she brushes the coat, she does not, and neither sister asks the next question. The row moves from debt to decline, at a price Chapter 18 names: the sign makes the person who brushes the coat inferable by elimination, and the inference points at the mother. Three objections of 9.10.7 are answered in part by the new chapters. Item 2, the two prologue details, is answered by Chapter 11’s scene, as above. Item 5, that Elena completes by presence, is answered by Chapter 12’s decision at the convergence: she lays her palm on the ledger, does not open it, and rings Nadia, so that her completion is an act, the change of her rule from find out for yourself to what concerns the three of them is read by the three of them . Item 6, the covert ending, is unchanged, and so are items 1 and 4: the mother stays unresolved, and the move from the shop to the flat is still made in a clause. If a proposal is rejected. Because nine payments rest on proposals, the audit is conditional, and a writer who declines one of them should know which rows it reopens. The table gives, for each proposal, the rows that return to the audit and the problem that comes back with them. Proposal Chapter Rows reopened What returns The request to clear the flat 14 9, 26 Nadia’s hand in the coat’s pocket in Chapter 7 has no motive in the scene before it The empty drawer, the second boy and the sign 11 21, 22, 27 The prologue’s two details are debts again, and Elena must be kept from asking Dov by other means Elena’s decision at the convergence 12 15, 28, 29 Item 5 of 9.10.7: Elena completes by presence Dov never reads back 15 30 Dov’s ignorance of the illness has no motive, and It’s all there loses its second reading The heading 9 March 8 31 The reader is oriented at about 78 per cent by the chapter’s text alone The book a standalone, the decline declared 17 32 The decline of the locks has one sign, Dov’s refusal, under a mode that reads silence as a clue The brushing declined with a sign 18 18 The row is a debt again, or the weekly brushing is cut from Chapter 4, at the cost of Nadia’s measure of the days between brushings The table shows why the audit has to be run on the whole book and run last. Each proposal was made in a chapter about one unit, the middle, an arc, a reveal, and each looks local there; the audit is the place where they are seen to support one another, so that rejecting one reopens rows that another chapter’s revision assumes. Chapter 18 calls this a reopened test, and places the plant audit on the third rung of its revision ladder, the shape, where it reads the deposits column of the book map backwards from the ending; it is the check that the book’s deposits and payments agree, and it has to be rerun after every repair that moves either.

title: 10. Endings Across Forms
text: The model above was built for the novel. It transfers to adjacent forms with adjustments that need stating, because students routinely import novel-ending habits into forms that punish them — and because two of the forms below invert the model’s economics entirely. 10.1 The short story The story’s ending is the most technically demanding in prose, and the reason is arithmetical. A novel’s ending can rely on four hundred pages of deposit; a story’s ending can rely on fifteen. The ratio of accumulated context to closural demand is the worst in the form , which is why so much of the twentieth century’s thinking about endings was done by story writers. Four differences. Difference Consequence Almost no aftermath is available The lusis is compressed into a paragraph or absent. Strategies 6, 7 and 8 ( §6.4 ) are effectively unavailable Plot resolution is frequently waived entirely The modern story’s characteristic close is the terminal image (9) or incompletion (4) The title is part of the ending As Chapter 9 §10.1 notes, a story’s title is a working part of the text. It is also, very often, the element the last line completes — the reader returns to it The last sentence carries a proportionally enormous share In a novel the last line is one of several closural devices; in a story it is frequently the only one The dominant modern convention deserves naming, because students absorb it without noticing. The epiphanic close — a moment of unspoken recognition, usually rendered as an image, arriving in the last paragraph — descends from Joyce’s Dubliners and became, through the American story of the mid-twentieth century, the default. It is now in the position §3.7 describes for the ambiguous novel ending: no longer a discovery, and no longer self-justifying. A story that closes on a character looking out of a window at snow is not concluding; it is signalling that stories conclude this way. The corrective is the same as for novels: the strategy must be chosen against alternatives ( §6.5 ), not inherited. 10.2 The novella The novella’s ending problem is the mirror of its opening problem (Chapter 9 §10.2 ). It has a novel’s tonal amplitude and a story’s word count, which means it can build a novel’s worth of pressure and has a story’s room in which to discharge it. Two consequences. The novella is the natural home of the arrested ending ( §6.4 , no. 12) and of death as a structural terminus ( §8.8 ). Both discharge maximum pressure in minimum space. Proportion is unforgiving. A three-page aftermath is under one per cent of a novel and five per cent of a novella. The §6.6 table’s percentages should be halved for the form. The Death of Ivan Ilyich remains the model, and the reason is that its structure solves the proportion problem in advance: by announcing the death first and then retracing the life, Tolstoy converts the entire novella into an aftermath, so that the ending has nothing left to do but arrive. 10.3 Series, serials and the volume ending The series inverts several of this chapter’s economics, and a writer working in one should know which. Variable Standalone novel Volume in a series Obligation to close the central question Absolute Applies to the volume’s question only Cost of the series hook High ( §8.11 ) Near zero, where the form has declared itself Available aftermath Constrained by momentum Larger: the reader is not leaving Retroactive lens Operates on this book Operates on the series so far, and is revised by every subsequent volume The last line’s privilege Maximum Diluted; the series’ last line is the privileged one The last row is the significant one and it produces a rule that many series writers discover too late: In a series, the retroactive lens is not fired until the final volume. Every earlier volume’s ending is provisional, and a later book can retroactively ruin an ending that worked. This is the structural reason that series conclusions disappoint so reliably: they must close the accumulated accounts of every previous volume, at a length calibrated for one. The serial — the work published in parts and read as a continuous whole — is a different case, and Chapter 6 ( The Chapter Break ) covers its instalment endings. What concerns this chapter is the pressure serialisation exerts on the final ending, described at §3.7 : an audience that has waited eighteen months requires a conclusion legible as one, at speed, which historically produced the wind-up chapter. Contemporary episodic television is under the same pressure and produces the same result, with the same complaints. 10.4 The screen comparison Three things transfer from screen endings to prose, and three do not. Transfers: The proportion problem is identical , and screen has a vocabulary for it: the “false ending”, the sequence of scenes each of which could have closed the film. The complaint made about the endings of long fantasy films is the pattern of §8.3 . Terminal modification works the same way. A film that has cut fast and cuts slowly at the last, or a series that drops its title sequence for a finale, is doing what a novel does when it alters a chapter shape. The retroactive reframe transfers completely , and screen exploits it more systematically than prose, because a visual medium can replay earlier images literally. Does not transfer: Screen has involuntary closural signals that prose lacks. Credits roll; music resolves; the image fades. A film cannot fail test 7 (termination) in the way a novel can, because the medium supplies the signal regardless of the storytelling. Prose has no fade to black, which is why the formal domain ( §4.6 ) has to be constructed rather than inherited. Duration is fixed and visible. A viewer with twelve minutes left knows the ending is coming; a reader with fifty pages left knows the same, and both facts shape expectation — but the film’s audience cannot skim, cannot stop, and cannot check. The reader’s awareness of the remaining page-block is a closural instrument no screen work possesses, and it is why an ending that arrives twenty pages before the physical end of a book is disquieting in a way no film can reproduce. Serial television’s economics reward non-closure in a way publishing does not, because renewal is decided after transmission. The result is a form structurally biased towards §8.11 , and craft advice imported from it should be treated accordingly. 10.5 Translated fiction The series’ standing distinction applies with particular force at endings: structural claims survive translation; texture claims do not. Three specific observations. 1. Last lines are the most translation-sensitive sentences in a book. Everything §4.5 says about grammatical closure — terminal stress, unqualified assertion, the last word — is a claim about a specific language’s prosody and syntax, and none of it survives. A translator who preserves the sense of a final sentence may lose the closural force entirely, and one who preserves the force may have to alter the sense. Compare the endings of The Stranger across Gilbert, Ward and Smith: the structural fact (Meursault arrives at an assent) is invariant; whether the assent sounds serene, defiant or flat differs measurably between them, and so does the reader’s final impression of the novel. 2. Word order determines what the last word can be. Languages with different default orders cannot place the same element last without distortion. A German or Latin sentence can end on a verb the English must move; a Japanese sentence’s final particle has no English equivalent. Any analysis that rests on “the last word of the novel is X” is, in translation, an analysis of the translator’s decision. 3. Apparatus is added and removed in translation. Afterwords, translator’s notes, glossaries and scholarly introductions accrete around translated novels, and they sit where a formal-closure device would sit ( §4.6 ). A student analysing whether a novel ends with apparatus must check the original’s contents page. Chapter 10 §10.6 makes the same point about front matter, and the two cautions are the same caution. The practical instruction for a seminar: when analysing a translated ending, state which claims are structural and which are textural, and — where the point is textural — name the translator in the sentence. 10.6 Interactive and multiple-ending forms A brief note, because the form falsifies one of the chapter’s assumptions and it is worth seeing which. Video games, hypertext fiction and branching narratives frequently offer several endings, selected by the reader’s choices. This is not the same as §6.4 ’s double ending (no. 15), which exhibits two endings to a reader who receives both; here the reader receives one and knows others exist. The consequence is that the retroactive lens fires differently . A player who reaches an ending knows it is one of several, which means the ending cannot claim that this is what the story was — only what it became. Kermode’s concord fiction ( §3.1 ) is weakened at the point where it does its work: a tock that could have been a different tock organises the interval less firmly. Two observations follow, and both are useful for prose writers. Multiple endings tend to produce weaker closure and stronger authorship-feeling. The reader’s awareness of the branch converts the ending from a discovery about the material into a record of their own choices. The forms that solve this do so by making the multiplicity thematic — by being about choice, determinism or replay. This is the same solution §6.4 no. 15 requires of the double ending in prose, and the same solution §8.9 requires of ambiguity: a structural device that draws attention to itself must be about something. 10.7 Concordance: concept to work A study aid. Each entry names the work whose ending most clearly displays the concept. Concept Best displayed by Section The two-endings problem; congruence contested Great Expectations §8.4 , §8.12 , §9.1 Closure by widening rather than tightening Middlemarch §9.2 The aphoristic close, licensed by a generalising narrator Middlemarch ; The Great Gatsby §6.4 , §8.6 , §9.3 Resolution and closure occurring in different places The Great Gatsby §2.3.2 , §9.3 Aftermath completing a second arc Anna Karenina , Part Eight §8.3 , §9.4 Formal closure contradicting thematic closure Nineteen Eighty-Four (the Appendix) §4.6 , §9.5 Apparatus as closural device Nineteen Eighty-Four ; The Handmaid’s Tale §4.6 , §6.4 , §9.5 Terminal modification of a repeated sentence Beloved §3.2 , §9.6 Ambiguity that is not evasion Beloved ; Blindness §8.9 , §9.6 , §9.9 Closure by unqualified affirmation Ulysses §4.5 , §9.7 The colophon as formal close Ulysses §9.7 Closure by withdrawal of the character’s availability Don Quixote , Part II §8.8 , §9.8 The series hook and its documented consequence Don Quixote , Part I §8.11 , §9.8 A payoff withheld and converted Blindness §9.9 The arrested ending The Handmaid’s Tale ; The Grapes of Wrath §6.4 , §8.2 Catharsis without resolution The Grapes of Wrath §4.4 Comprehensive resolution that works Bleak House ; Jane Eyre §4.1 , §8.5 The unearned rescue that succeeds Jane Eyre (the voice on the moor) §8.1 Resolution given to a minor character Madame Bovary (Homais) §4.1 , §6.4 The ending that erases its protagonist’s arc Things Fall Apart §4.2 , §5.2 Multiplicity at maximum in one sentence Things Fall Apart §5.2 The image that removes the people Wuthering Heights §4.5 The frame closed Frankenstein ; Wuthering Heights §6.4 Resolution the character cannot register The Remains of the Day §4.1 Closure by refusal A Passage to India §2.3.2 , §6.4 Death as the condition rather than the resolution The Death of Ivan Ilyich §8.8 , §10.2 The contested aftermath Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (the Phelps farm) §8.7 Catharsis in four words Mrs Dalloway §4.4 The terminal modification of a formal pattern The Sound and the Fury (the fourth section) §4.6 The politics of the available ending Middlemarch ; Anna Karenina ; The Awakening §3.8

title: 11. Revision Checklist
text: Run a draft ending against this list before deciding it is doing its job. Each item corresponds to a test in §7 or a pattern in §8 . The whole-book tests (these require the manuscript, not the last chapter) I can trace every element the ending relies on back to an earlier planting, with chapter and page. Nothing new and load-bearing arrives for the first time in the ending. (New material is permitted; new load is not.) Rereading five earlier scenes with the ending in mind, they read as intentional — or, where they do not, I have decided whether the ending or the scene is wrong. The ending answers a pressure the middle of the book built, not only a question it asked. A second reading of the book would yield more, not less. Climax and aftermath The book distinguishes its climax from its aftermath, and I can point to where one becomes the other. I can say what the aftermath does that the climax could not. The aftermath ends at the last decision , not at the last consequence. The proportion is a choice I can defend against the historical range, not an accident of stamina. Domains I can name which domains — plot, character, theme, catharsis, final image, form — the ending delivers, which it gestures at, and which it refuses. Each domain I claim is delivered has a passage a reader could point to. At least one carrier serves more than one domain. The distribution matches the book’s mode rather than a default. Resolution and closure Every question the book raised is answered, or visibly declined on the page — none is merely dropped. Each thread’s resolution is proportional to the space it occupied. Any deliberate ambiguity can be stated in one sentence, and I can say what resolving it would cost. The book has ended and not merely stopped: I can name the device that signals it. Tone and the last page The last page and three random middle passages belong to the same book. No character and no narrator explains what the book meant. The final paragraph does work the paragraph before it does not. I know what the last word is, and why it is that one. A reader closing the book on this line carries the feeling intended, not only the information. Deletion I have tried ending the book one paragraph, one scene and one chapter earlier, and read what remains.

title: 12. Studio Work
text: 12.1 Practical exercises Exercise 1 — The plant audit, in full. Take a completed draft. List every element the ending uses as load-bearing (aim for twelve to twenty). For each, record the chapter and page of first appearance and of every intermediate appearance. Produce the table in the form of §9.10.4 . Write 300 words on what the distribution shows — in particular, on any element that appears once and then not again for a third of the book. Exercise 2 — Strategy substitution. Take one draft ending and write three versions using three strategies from §6.4 , chosen from different clusters — for example 2 (parallelism), 7 (epilogue in another voice) and 12 (arrested). Write a page of each. Do not judge until all three exist. Then write 400 words on what each version makes the book about . Exercise 3 — The deletion ladder, from the other end. End the book one paragraph earlier; read. One scene earlier; read. One chapter earlier; read. Record where the ending actually is, and what the deleted material was doing for you rather than for the reader. This is Chapter 9 §12.1 ’s exercise 3 run in reverse, and it has a comparable hit rate. Exercise 4 — The last-line laboratory. Write ten different final sentences for the same ending: one aphoristic, one an image, one dialogue, one a single word, one interrogative, one very long, one very short, one in the future tense, one in the present, one that names an object. Read them aloud. Record which closes hardest, and which is right — they will not always be the same, and the difference is the exercise. Exercise 5 — The domain annotation. Run the §5.5 closural audit on the last three pages of a draft. Produce the letter distribution and the inert-sentence count. Write 200 words interpreting it against the table in §5.5 . Exercise 6 — The two endings. Following §9.1 , write two endings for the same story: one congruent with what the material implies, one congruent with what the reader wants. Do not label them. Give both to three readers and ask which is better and which is right . Record any case where a reader separates the two answers, and write 300 words on it. Exercise 7 — The counterfactual ending. Write a deliberately unearned ending for your own draft — one that resolves by a new element, in the manner of §9.10.5 — and then diagnose it against §7.1 . The exercise is not satirical: writing the failure deliberately is the most reliable way to see the mechanism, and students routinely discover that their real ending shares one of its defects. Exercise 8 — Climax and aftermath, measured. Take three published novels from different periods. For each, locate the climax and measure the aftermath as a percentage of the whole. Compare against §6.6 ’s table. Then do the same for your own draft and write 200 words on whether your proportion is a choice or an inheritance. Exercise 9 — The unavailable ending. Following §3.8 , take a nineteenth-century novel with a female protagonist and write the ending the form did not permit — the one in which she neither marries nor dies. Then write 400 words on what had to change earlier in the book to make your ending possible. The point of the exercise is in the second part: closural forms constrain plots, not only conclusions. 12.2 Seminar questions The two endings of Great Expectations . Read both (Forster’s Life and every scholarly edition print the cancelled version). Argue for one. You must address: the plant audit, which favours the revision; the congruence criterion, which is usually taken to favour the original; and the significance — if any — of Bulwer-Lytton’s intervention. A strong answer will explain why the disagreement has survived a century and a half rather than declaring it resolved. Five domains or six? Argue for or against admitting formal closure ( §4.6 ) as a domain distinct from thematic closure. Use the Appendix to Nineteen Eighty-Four as the test case, and address the objection at §4.6 that formal closure names a means rather than an end . Does Part Eight belong to Anna Karenina ? Is Levin’s conclusion a second arc completing ( §9.4 ) or an authorial conclusion appended ( §8.6 )? Tolstoy’s serial publisher declined to print it; readers have complained ever since. Make the case that they were right. Is the unresolved close a liberation or a successor convention? §3.7 argues that the ambiguous ending is now the house style of a genre and §3.8 that closural forms encode assumptions about what a life is for. Has contemporary literary fiction escaped the marriage-or-death binary, or exchanged it for a default of its own that will look equally unexamined in fifty years? Is Miller right? §3.9 puts the case that closure is a betrayal of the narratable and §6.1 attempts an answer. Test both against a single novel of your choosing. Is the ending of that novel a containment, an exchange, or something the distinction does not capture? The Phelps farm. Does the last quarter of Adventures of Huckleberry Finn resolve the wrong question ( §8.7 ), or does it answer the right one in a way readers have wanted to escape? Address Hemingway’s verdict and at least one defence of the ending. 12.3 Assessment rubric For a submitted ending (1,500–2,500 words, with a one-page summary of the preceding novel) and a 1,000-word critical commentary. Band Craft (60%) Commentary (40%) Distinction Every load-bearing element traceable to an earlier planting; at least one carrier serving three or more domains; proportion between climax and aftermath evidently chosen; a last line that does work the preceding paragraph does not; any ambiguity specific and defensible Names its closural strategy and defends it against two alternatives actually attempted; runs the plant audit on its own work and reports an unredeemed plant; engages at least three theoretical sources critically, including one that tells against the submission Merit Most elements planted; domains served but with one carrier per domain; proportion defensible; final image present and functional Accurate self-analysis; strategy identified; risks acknowledged if not resolved; theory applied rather than cited Pass An ending exists that closes the book’s central question; some domains served; nothing fatally unearned Describes the ending accurately; some engagement with the taxonomy; the plant audit attempted Fail The ending rests on an unplanted element; the book stops rather than ends; the final note contradicts the material without evident purpose Description without analysis; no plant audit; failure patterns present and unrecognised

title: 13. Glossary
text: Aftermath — Everything between the climax and the last word. This chapter’s neutral term, preferred to denouement because it presupposes no shape. §2.3.1 . Anagnorisis — Aristotle’s recognition : a change from ignorance to knowledge. At an ending, the mechanism by which existing information is reorganised rather than new information supplied. §3.3 , §6.2 . Arrested ending — A close that stops mid-action, before the outcome. Strategy 12 at §6.4 . Attention tax — Chapter 14’s term for the page space a subplot charges the reader. The ending is where the refund is due; §7.1 , test 6. Circularity — Closure by returning to the beginning’s language, image or situation. Torgovnick’s category; strategy 1 at §6.4 . Climax — The last major confrontation or disaster; the peak of conflict. A part of the ending, not a synonym for it. §2.3.1 . Closural allusion — Herrnstein Smith’s term for a final reference to something itself terminal — death, sleep, night, departure — which lends the close a borrowed finality. §3.2 . Closural strategy — A named shape an ending can take, with characteristic purchases and costs. Sixteen are tabulated at §6.4 . Closure — The reader’s felt sense that the book has arrived rather than stopped. Distinct from resolution , and separable from it in both directions. §2.3.2 . Coda — A short final movement in a changed key, continuous with the narrative. Distinguished from an epilogue, which is displaced. §2.4 . Congruence — Torgovnick’s criterion: whether an ending emerges from the novel’s own logic or is imposed on it from outside. §3.5 , §8.12 . Denouement — The untying; the classical aftermath, with the implication that entangled facts are being separated. §2.4 . Desis and lusis — Aristotle’s tying and unravelling. The division falls at the turning point, which makes the aftermath structurally half the work rather than an appendix. §3.3 , §6.6 . Domain (of an ending) — A register in which an ending does work: plot resolution, character-arc completion, thematic closure, emotional catharsis, the final image, and — proposed here — formal closure. §4 . Double ending — Two endings supplied, or the choice between them exhibited. Strategy 15 at §6.4 . Earned — Of an ending: resting only on material the book already deposited (Claim 1), and answering a pressure the book built (Claim 2). §6.1 . Ending — The final unit of a novel, distinguished by having no subsequent scene to correct it and by being the material through which the reader retroactively re-reads the whole. Comprises climax and aftermath. §2.1 . Fictions of concord — Kermode’s term for the imagined shapes by which we give an undifferentiated middle a beginning and an end. §3.1 . Final image — The literal last thing the book shows, considered as a domain rather than a decoration. §4.5 . Formal closure — This chapter’s proposed sixth domain: the completion, modification or disruption of the book’s own structural pattern, as distinct from its story. Closes the formal contract of Chapter 9 §4.6 . §4.6 . Imposed ending — An ending congruent with something other than the book: a convention, a publisher, a readership, an author’s fatigue. §8.12 . Inevitability (retrospective) — The reader’s post-hoc sense that the ending could not have been otherwise. Independent of predictability. §6.2 . Narratable, the — D. A. Miller’s term for the instability, deviance and desire from which narrative arises and which closure eliminates. §3.9 . Peak–end rule — Kahneman and colleagues’ finding that retrospective evaluation of a brief affective episode is dominated by its most intense moment and its final moment. Reported here with its limits: the extension to novel-length experience is an analogy, not a finding. §3.6 . Plant audit — The whole-book test: trace every element the ending relies on back to its planting. §7.1 , test 2; performed at §9.10.4 . Privileged position — Rabinowitz’s term for locations a reader automatically treats as significant. The last sentence is among the strongest. §3.6 . Proleptic close — An ending that narrates the future beyond the action. Strategy 8 at §6.4 . Proportion problem — The question of how much aftermath a book requires; the site of §8.2 and §8.3 , which are opposite errors. §6.6 . Recency effect — The better recall of items at the end of a sequence; the counterpart to primacy. Robust for lists, and applied to novels only as a general claim about the privilege of boundary positions. §3.6 . Refused ending — A text that declines to conclude and marks the refusal. Strategy 16 at §6.4 . Resolution — The answering, or legible declining, of the plot’s dramatic questions. A domain, not the ending. §2.3.2 , §4.1 . Retroactive lens — This chapter’s first principle: the ending is the position from which the whole book first becomes available as a whole, and the reader’s final interpretation is performed upon everything, not only the last pages. §1.1 , §3.10 . Retrospection, anticipation of — Brooks’s term for the reader’s forward motion in expectation of a moment from which the whole will be legible. §3.4 . Retrospective reframe — A late disclosure that changes what the whole book was. Strategy 13 at §6.4 ; §8.10 . Series hook — A deliberate non-closure creating appetite for a further volume; called the sequel hook in the first edition (this edition keeps sequel for Chapter 2’s sense). §8.11 . Tangent — Closure by swerving to something apparently unrelated. Torgovnick’s category; strategy 3 at §6.4 . Terminal modification — Herrnstein Smith’s device: a pattern established across the text is altered at its final instance, which signals that it will not continue. §3.2 , §4.6 . Termination — Simply stopping. Herrnstein Smith’s contrast term for what closure is not. §3.2 , §7.1 test 7. Tick-tock — Kermode’s minimal model of plot: the listener supplies a beginning and an end to an undifferentiated series, and the interval between them becomes a duration with a shape. §3.1 .
