title: 15. Further Reading
text: Annotated, grouped by what each source is good for . Starred items are the recommended first three. 15.1 On endings specifically ★ Kermode, Frank. The Sense of an Ending (1967). The indispensable book, and short. Read it for the tick-tock, for the argument that we hold our concord fictions sceptically, and for the deepest available account of why the demand for endings survives knowing that endings are imposed. The literary examples date; the argument does not. ★ Smith, Barbara Herrnstein. Poetic Closure (1968). The most precise formal analysis of closure in the language. It is about poems, which is why it works: closural mechanisms are visible in ten lines and invisible in four hundred pages. Every device in §3.2 and §4.5 is hers. ★ Torgovnick, Marianna. Closure in the Novel (1981). The standard monograph, and the only one that offers a working typology of novelistic closes. Read for the congruence criterion and for the overt/covert distinction, both of which are directly usable in revision. Miller, D. A. Narrative and Its Discontents (1981). The essential complication. Difficult, and worth it: the concept of the narratable will change how a reader experiences last chapters, and not always comfortably. Chapters on Austen, Eliot and Stendhal. DuPlessis, Rachel Blau. Writing Beyond the Ending (1985). The politics of closure. The historical argument — that a female protagonist’s plot could conclude in marriage or death and effectively nowhere else — is demonstrated rather than asserted, and the account of twentieth-century strategies for escaping it is the practical half. Carroll, Noël. “Narrative Closure.” Philosophical Studies 135 (2007). A short analytic-philosophy treatment arguing that closure is the answering of the questions a narrative has raised. Useful as a rigorous statement of the position this chapter’s §2.3.2 complicates. 15.2 On plot, desire and the shape of the whole Brooks, Peter. Reading for the Plot (1984). The dynamic account of narrative: plot as force rather than shape. The opening chapters and the essay on Freud’s masterplot are the relevant ones; the Freudian reading is contestable and the concept of the anticipation of retrospection is not. Aristotle. Poetics . Forty pages. The desis / lusis distinction, necessity or probability, peripeteia and anagnorisis, and the objection to the machine — four of this chapter’s load-bearing ideas, in a text a student can read in an evening. Genette, Gérard. Narrative Discourse (1980). For the amorce and for the vocabulary of prolepsis, which is what §6.4 ’s proleptic close actually is. Chatman, Seymour. Story and Discourse (1978). For kernels and satellites, the vocabulary in which §7.1 ’s proportion test is best stated. 15.3 On the reader Rabinowitz, Peter J. Before Reading (1987). The rules of notice, and the reason the last sentence of a novel is read as a statement about the novel. Underread and immediately practical. Gerrig, Richard J. Experiencing Narrative Worlds (1993). Transportation, and — relevant here — the psychology of leaving a narrative world as well as entering one. Genette, Gérard. Paratexts (1997). For appendices, afterwords and notes considered as thresholds. The systematic background to §4.6 ’s apparatus carrier. 15.4 Cognitive and empirical work, used carefully Kahneman et al. (1993); Redelmeier and Kahneman (1996). The peak–end studies. Read the originals rather than the popularisations, and note the duration and modality of the episodes studied. §3.6 explains why the extension to novels is an analogy. Murdock (1962). The serial position curve. A one-page result worth seeing in its original form, so that its distance from literary reading is visible. 15.5 On the Great Expectations case Rosenberg, Edgar, ed. Great Expectations , Norton Critical Edition. The textual history, both endings, the relevant correspondence, and a selection of the critical dispute. The single best classroom resource on this chapter’s subject. Forster, John. The Life of Charles Dickens (1872–74). Where the cancelled ending survives, and where Dickens’s own account of the change is recorded. 15.6 Craft literature, used critically James, Henry. The Art of the Novel (1934). The prefaces. Read the Roderick Hudson preface for the circle drawn by a geometry of one’s own; James’s essay “The Art of Fiction” (1884) contains the indictment of the distribution of prizes and babies. The best practitioner’s writing on this subject and not superseded. Forster, E. M. Aspects of the Novel (1927). Chatty, dated, and containing the sharpest joke in the field about death and marriage. The chapters on plot and on pattern are the relevant ones. 15.7 Within this textbook This chapter draws on, and completes, the following: Chapter 1 ( The Purposes of a Scene ) — the value shift, which is what an ending is at the level of the scene; the domain model’s original form. Chapter 2 ( Scene and Sequel ) — the causal chain, which is the earned test at the scale of the beat; and the sequel structure, which §2.3.1 applies to the aftermath of a whole novel. Chapter 3 ( The Dialogue Exchange ) — text and subtext; the doorway exchange against which §9.10 ’s silence is measured. Chapter 4 ( The Descriptive Detail ) — denotation and connotation; the object economy on which every closural plant depends. Chapter 5 ( The Transition ) — the orientation budget, and the hard cut that delivered the reader to the ledger. Chapter 6 ( The Chapter Break ) — proposition and payoff , which is the plant audit’s other half; and the temporary stopping place, of which the ending is the permanent one. Chapter 13 ( The Viewpoint Shift ) — the empathy budget, which determines what catharsis an ending can spend; and the bounded chapter that is this book’s climax. Chapter 7 ( Backstory and Flashback ) — the interest deficit, which is the mechanism of §8.3 . Chapter 14 ( The Subplot ) — the attention tax, which supplies §7.1 ’s proportion test; kernel and satellite. Chapter 9 ( The Opening Pages ) — the formal inverse. Its §3.2 states the symmetry; its §4.6 ’s formal contract is closed by this chapter’s §4.6 . Chapter 10 ( The Prologue ) — closing the distance; the held note that lands here; and the false-advertising failure of which §8.4 is the exit version.

title: 16. Coda: Against Mechanical Application — and the End of the Book
section: Coda — Against Mechanical Application — and the End of the Book
text: The evidence against the model is inside the model Everything in this chapter is an instrument for noticing. None of it is a rule, and the proof is in the chapter itself. Ulysses fails the plot-resolution test entirely and is one of the most completely closed novels in English. The Great Gatsby resolves nothing on its last page, having resolved everything on the page before. Anna Karenina runs an aftermath that would be cut by any contemporary editor and cannot survive without it. Jane Eyre is resolved by a supernatural voice across a moor and by a settlement so comprehensive it accounts for a French schoolgirl’s education. Middlemarch ends with a narrator explaining what the book meant. Beloved closes on a sentence that contradicts itself twice and then on a single word. Blindness spends three hundred pages promising a payoff and converts it into a joke about the colour of the sky. Don Quixote ends by forbidding further books. And Great Expectations — the case this chapter treats as its centrepiece — has two endings, written by the same man, one of which almost certainly fails the tonal-match test and is the one nearly everybody prefers. A model that ruled these out would not have identified a defect in them. It would have identified its own limits, which is what §3.10 said it would do and what §§8 and 9 were built to demonstrate a dozen times over. There is a stronger version of the caution, and this chapter has been carrying it since §3.9 . The whole apparatus of earned closure assumes that closure is worth having. D. A. Miller’s argument that closure eliminates what made a novel worth reading is not a marginal position, and this chapter’s answer to it — that the reader loses the narratable and gains a shape unavailable at any earlier point — is a defence rather than a refutation. It concedes the loss. Anyone who ends a book is choosing to stop something that was still alive. What the model does reliably What the instruments do, and it is not nothing, is convert a vague dissatisfaction into a specific question. This ending isn’t working becomes: four of the six domains are being served in sequence and the reader can watch the machinery ; or the resolution rests on a solicitor’s letter that arrives from outside the book ; or this is a coda and the material wants a parallel scene ; or every element is planted and none of them was ever under pressure . Specific questions can be answered. Vague ones can only be worried at, usually by rewriting the last page repeatedly, which is the least effective revision available because the last page is almost never where the problem is. The most useful result the protocol can return is also its most deflating, and it is worth restating at the end because students reach it more often than any other: an ending that passes every test and lands on nothing is reporting that the book was never about anything urgent enough to conclude. The instruments cannot fix that, and they are valuable partly because they can find it. A writer who discovers, at the end of a plant audit, that everything traces cleanly and nothing matters has learned something no amount of work on the final chapter would have taught them. Why the ending closes Part III There is an obvious reason and a better one. The obvious reason is symmetry. A textbook that treats the units of the novel from the scene outward has to reach the book’s second boundary last, having begun at the smallest thing that can stand alone and passed through the joins and the architecture on the way. Chapter 9 and Chapter 16 are the two edges, and putting them at either end of Part III is tidy. The two chapters after this one leave the single book’s units behind: Chapter 17 follows the ending’s promises out to the genre and the series, and Chapter 18 sets every test in the book, this chapter’s included, in the order in which a revision should run them. The better reason is that the ending is where a novel finds out what it was. That formulation is not mystical. It is a plain description of a mechanism this chapter has spent its whole length establishing. Until a book ends, its material is provisional: an element might turn out to be a cause, a theme, a red herring or a habit. Brooks’s account ( §3.4 ) is that meaning in narrative is conferred from the terminus rather than distributed along the sequence, and Kermode’s ( §3.1 ) is that the shape is supplied rather than discovered. Put them together and the consequence for a writer is exact and slightly alarming: you do not know what you have written until you have written the end of it. This is why the ending is the only unit whose obligations cannot be established in advance, why it must be revised last whatever order it was drafted in, and why the plant audit — the one test in this book that requires the whole manuscript — could not be demonstrated until §9.10 , after the chapters before it had deposited something to audit. It is also why writers so often report that the ending told them the book was about something other than what they intended. That is not a failure of planning. It is the retroactive lens operating on the person best placed to feel it. And it is why this chapter’s most-repeated instruction is not about endings at all. When the ending will not work, the fault is very often four hundred pages upstream, and the discipline the chapter actually teaches is the discipline of looking there. Trust minted, and trust spent Chapter 9 argued that the opening pages are where a book’s trust is minted: page 3 has no account, and every claim it makes must be secured out of its own resources. This chapter has argued the inverse. The ending has the fullest account in the book and cannot add to it. Everything it spends was deposited earlier, by scenes that did not know what they were depositing, in chapters that had their own business to attend to. The good pen went into a coat pocket on an ordinary afternoon because a man could not have explained why; it is worth what it is worth at the end because nobody made anything of it at the time. That is the relation between the two boundaries, and it is the sentence the first three Parts of this textbook have been building towards: The opening is where a novel asks to be trusted. The ending is where it finds out whether it should have been. Around them lie the chapters on how the trust is kept: what a scene is for, what follows a scene, how people talk, what a described thing is doing there, how the reader is carried across a gap, where the gap is placed, when the past may be entered, how more than one time is braided, what a book may put before itself, how a middle holds, how a character changes and a theme is argued, who stands on the other side of the gap, how a second story earns its space, and when a reveal may come. Every one of those chapters offered a taxonomy, a set of tests, a list of failures and a set of exceptions large enough to embarrass the taxonomy. That was deliberate. Every instrument in these chapters is a way of noticing, and every model in them is a heuristic that great books violate. A student who finishes this textbook able to recite the models has acquired less than one who finishes it able to say, of a particular book, which model it breaks and what it gets in exchange. What is left open This textbook runs a single invented novel through every chapter — a shop, a ledger, a coat on a hook, three siblings, and a mother who changed the locks in March and never said why. The chapters before this one planted; this one audits, and §9.10.8 reruns the audit across all eighteen. Nearly everything came due: the pen, the phrase, the changed hand, the silence, the coat. The mother did not. She has no scene of her own in any chapter, and the ending does not go to her. §9.10.7 defends that choice and concedes what it costs, and the concession is the right note on which to close a book about endings. A novel that closed every account would have argued that families are solvable. The one thing this one has consistently maintained is that they are not, and the ending’s last act of discipline is to leave the largest silence where it was. That is a decision, not a discovery. Someone else would write the other book. The last question Chapter 9’s coda ends with a question to ask of a first page: does this sound like someone who knows what they are doing? It works because an opening’s subject is competence — a stranger deciding, in two pages, whether to trust the person holding the pen. An ending’s subject is not competence, and the equivalent question cannot be about the writer. By the last page the reader has stopped assessing and started remembering. What they are doing, in the moment before they close the book, is finding out what all of it was. So the last question of this chapter is one a writer can actually ask, and can answer without self-deception, and will usually find uncomfortable: What did this book turn out to be about — and is that on the last page? If the two answers match, the ending is doing its work, whatever the protocol says. If they do not, the last page is not the problem and never was. And if the question cannot be answered at all, that is the most useful result available, and it arrives at the only point in the process where there is still time to do something about it: at the end, looking back, which — as every chapter of this book has argued in its own way — is where the shape of a thing finally becomes visible.

title: Series and Genre
text: Promises Inherited and Promises Deferred: The Full Treatment The Craft Behind the Story (Second Edition), Reference — Chapter 17. Part IV: Beyond the Book and Into Practice. This chapter is new in the second edition, so its Reference layer is this single file rather than a corrected original. It extends the reader’s version in Core, Series and Genre , and can be read without it: the definitions it relies on are restated in section 1. Illustrative passages are quoted briefly for the purposes of criticism and study, and full citations appear in section 10. Where a work is read in translation, the translator is named. The analyses disclose the endings of the works they discuss. Contents Scope and working definitions The theory at length: the horizon of expectations; kinds and modes; the detective story’s two stories; the romance’s elements; formula and the iterative scheme; semantics and syntax; series and saga; the evidence The extended catalogue: the five promises in detail; further series forms; a summary table; prequels and reading order; genres that expect a dual timeline The extended catalogue of failure patterns The diagnostic procedures, with the promise inventory and the volume table Further analyses: Bring Up the Bodies , Beach Read , 61 Hours , Twin Peaks The household case in full The limits of the model Glossary of the chapter’s terms Sources 1. Scope and working definitions A genre , for a writer, is the set of expectations a reader brings to a book she has identified as belonging to a group of works treated as alike. It is known by its conventions , which divide into semantic elements (places, objects, figures, kinds of event) and syntactic elements (the relations among them and the order of events), after Rick Altman. The core promise of a genre is the convention whose violation its readers treat as a breach of contract; an obligatory scene is a scene its readers expect and miss if it is absent. A mode is a genre’s character carried, as an adjective, into a work of another kind, borrowing conventions without, by default, the core promise. A hybrid makes two core promises and keeps both. A convention can be kept, varied or declined; a declared decline is one shown inside the book early enough to be believed, with a replacement promise that the book keeps, and with the declined question kept in view. A series is a sequence of separately published works that share characters, a world or a continuing story and invite reading as related. Each work is a volume ; this edition calls a later volume a series instalment and keeps sequel for the reaction, dilemma and decision that follow a scene in Chapter 2. A volume has a volume question , which it must close, and may carry a series question , closed if at all by the last volume. The series hook is Chapter 16’s: a volume that declines to close a major question in order to bring the reader to the next. Re-entry is the opening of a later volume, which must serve a returning reader and a new one; dormancy across volumes is the absence of a carried thread from one or more volumes. The governing claim is that a genre is a set of promises the reader brings to a book and a series a set she carries out of it, and that a book keeps faith with both when every convention it invokes is kept or visibly declined before the reader has staked much on it, and each volume closes its own question and leaves open only what it has shown to belong to the series. The claim concerns declarations, not compliance. A book that declines a genre’s central payment can satisfy that genre’s readers if it tells them in time; a book that pays everything can still fail them if it promised something else. The boundary that matters most in revision is between a series and a set of books that share a setting. A set of books by one writer in one town, each with its own cast and none carrying a question, is a series only in a bookseller’s sense; it makes no promise across volumes beyond the place and the voice, and the chapter’s series tests do not apply to it. The relay series (section 3.2) lies at the threshold: it carries a world and its people, and a reader rewarded for reading in order has been made a small promise. The chapter leaves the genre contract of the first pages to Chapter 9 , the prologue’s genre test to Chapter 10 , the serial’s chapter endings to Chapter 6 , the declined reveal to Chapter 15 , the last line and the series hook at a book’s end to Chapter 16 , and the arrangement of times within a volume to Chapter 8 . Market categories and publishing economics are outside its scope. 2. The theory at length 2.1 The horizon of expectations Hans Robert Jauss’s inaugural address at Konstanz in 1967, published as “Literary History as a Challenge to Literary Theory” and translated by Timothy Bahti in Toward an Aesthetic of Reception (1982), argued that a work is received against a horizon of expectations formed by the reader’s experience of earlier works of its kind, its themes and the difference between poetic and practical language. A new work confirms, varies or breaks that horizon, and Jauss measured a work’s aesthetic distance by how far it departs from it. For a novelist the theory’s use is narrower and practical. The horizon is formed before the book is opened, largely by genre, and the book is judged against it from the first page. A writer cannot choose a reader’s horizon, but she can correct it early, and a book that leaves an inherited horizon uncorrected will be judged by it to the end. 2.2 Kinds and modes Alastair Fowler’s Kinds of Literature (1982) argued that genres are better understood as families than as classes, linked by resemblances no single feature defines, and distinguished the kind , a genre with its full repertoire including its external form, from the mode, a selection of the kind’s features without its form, named by an adjective: comic, pastoral, gothic. The distinction answers a question writers ask often, whether a book that uses a genre’s furniture belongs to the genre. In Fowler’s terms it belongs to the mode, and the reader’s expectation of a core promise is the point at which mode and kind are confused. The household novel is a family novel in the mystery mode, and its draft jacket sold it as the kind. 2.3 The detective story’s two stories Tzvetan Todorov’s “The Typology of Detective Fiction” (1966; translated by Richard Howard in The Poetics of Prose , 1977) described the classic whodunit as two stories: the story of the crime, complete before the book begins and absent from it, and the story of the investigation, present but slight in itself, whose task is to recover the first. He contrasted it with the thriller, which fuses the two and tells the story of the crime as it happens, so that curiosity gives way to suspense. The account explains why the mystery’s core promise is structural. The investigation story is not complete until the crime story has been told in full, so a mystery that declines its solution has left its own second story unfinished, whatever else it achieves. A family novel in the mystery mode can borrow the investigation without committing to the crime story, provided the investigator’s question is shown to be one the book will not finish. 2.4 The romance’s elements The Romance Writers of America defined the genre by two elements, a central love story and an emotionally satisfying and optimistic ending, and added that a romance may have any tone or setting. Pamela Regis’s A Natural History of the Romance Novel (2003) described the form historically, from Samuel Richardson’s Pamela to the contemporary category romance, and found eight elements in it: a definition of the society the lovers must reform or leave, their meeting, the barrier between them, their attraction, the declaration, the point of ritual death at which the union seems impossible, the recognition that removes the barrier, and the betrothal. Regis’s list is the clearest available statement of a genre’s syntax, and it shows how much a romance can vary while keeping its promise: any element can be brief, displaced or ironised, so long as the betrothal, or its modern equivalent, arrives. 2.5 Formula and the iterative scheme John Cawelti’s Adventure, Mystery, and Romance: Formula Stories as Art and Popular Culture (1976) defined a formula as a conventional structure of narrative a culture’s readers know, and argued that formula stories balance convention, which gives the pleasure of the known, against invention, which keeps the known from going dead. Umberto Eco’s “The Myth of Superman” (1962; translated by Natalie Chilton, 1972) described the iterative scheme of the serial hero, whose stories each begin as if the last had not happened, so that he never ages or uses himself up; Eco called the effect an oblivion of consecutiveness. In “Innovation and Repetition: Between Modern and Post-Modern Aesthetics” (1985) he argued that serial forms please two readers at once, the naive reader who enjoys the story and the competent reader who enjoys the variations worked within the scheme. Between them the two accounts give the episodic series its theory: its readers pay for the scheme, and its craft lies in what each volume does inside it. 2.6 Semantics and syntax Rick Altman’s “A Semantic/Syntactic Approach to Film Genre” (1984) proposed that critics had defined genres either by lists of elements (the western’s horses, hats and frontier towns) or by structures of meaning (the western’s opposition of wilderness and civilisation), and that both were needed. Genres are most stable when a semantic set and a syntax coincide, and they change when one is carried over without the other. Altman’s later Film/Genre (1999) added that genres are made and remade by producers, critics and audiences using them, so a genre’s boundaries are always under negotiation. For the writer the semantic/syntactic distinction yields the chapter’s two common variations, new dress on an old syntax and an old dress on a new syntax, and its two common failures, the genre in costume (section 4.1) and the hybrid that keeps neither syntax. 2.7 Series and saga Eco’s essay of 1985 also offered a typology of serial forms: the retake, which continues a successful story; the remake, which retells it; the series, in which a fixed situation and a fixed set of characters recur and each story is complete; the saga, in which the characters age and history accumulates; and intertextual dialogue, in which a work quotes others. Jason Mittell’s Complex TV: The Poetics of Contemporary Television Storytelling (2015) described a mode of television that combines episodic and serial storytelling, closing a story each week while carrying arcs across seasons, and made the viewer’s knowledge of the form part of its pleasure. The chapter’s four forms of series (section 3.2) cut across both typologies: the episodic series is Eco’s series, the serial is his saga told as one story, and the running arc is Mittell’s combination. 2.8 The evidence Rolf Zwaan’s “Effect of Genre Expectations on Text Comprehension” (1994) gave participants the same texts with different instructions, telling some that they were reading literary stories and others that they were reading news. In the summaries the chapter has consulted, the first group read more slowly, kept more of the surface wording and built weaker models of the situations described; the expectation of a kind changed what readers attended to before any convention was kept or broken. The study used short texts and two broad categories, not genres of fiction, and the chapter takes from it only the modest conclusion that a reader’s belief about what she is reading governs how she reads it. Claims about how readers of one fiction genre treat another’s conventions, and about genres’ commercial shares, have not been measured here and are treated as impressions. 3. The extended catalogue 3.1 The five promises in detail The Core chapter sorts genres by five core promises. Each is set out here with its usual conventions, its obligatory scenes and the variations its readers accept, since a writer revising in a genre needs to know which conventions are load-bearing. The promise of solution. The mystery poses a question of fact, usually who committed a crime and how, and guarantees an answer from evidence the reader has been shown. Its conventions include the investigator, the closed circle of suspects, the clue, the false solution and the fair-play rule that the reader see what the detective sees, codified in Ronald Knox’s “Decalogue” (1929) and S. S. Van Dine’s twenty rules (1928). Its obligatory scenes are the discovery of the crime and the exposure. Its readers accept an unpunished culprit, a detective who fails at everything but the answer, and an exposure performed by someone other than the detective; they do not readily accept an unanswered question, unless the book has declared it. The promise of union. The romance guarantees that the lovers at its centre end together and that the ending is emotionally satisfying and optimistic. Its conventions are Regis’s eight elements and, in contemporary category romance, a narrow viewpoint allocation, often alternating between the lovers. Its readers accept a union that is a beginning rather than a marriage, a barrier that is internal, and a point of ritual death that is quiet; they do not accept a death or a parting at the end, which moves a book to another shelf, as Me Before You , the Core chapter’s exception to its test 2, shows. The promise of the threat met. The thriller, the horror novel and the adventure establish a danger and guarantee its direct confrontation. Their conventions include the clock, the escalation of stakes, the hero at the mercy of the threat and, in the thriller, a threat to many as well as to one. Their readers accept a hero’s death, a pyrrhic victory and a threat that survives in diminished form; they resist a threat that is never confronted, as the Core chapter’s exception to the undeclared decline, No Country for Old Men , shows at its cost. The promise of the kept rule. Science fiction and fantasy declare a world unlike ours and guarantee that it will obey its declared rules, so that problems are solved within the world’s terms. The critic Darko Suvin called science fiction’s effect cognitive estrangement, a world strange enough to be seen freshly and consistent enough to be reasoned about. The conventions include the novum, the new thing that makes the world differ, and the cost of the rule. Readers accept a rule never explained, and resist one broken to resolve a plot. The promise of significance. Literary fiction guarantees that its particulars will add up to more than a summary of its events could hold, and that the ending will alter the reader’s view of what preceded it. Its conventions include the open or partial ending, the domestic scale, the close attention to consciousness and the epiphany. Its readers accept the decline of any other genre’s payment, and resist an ending that pays a genre’s promise the book had not made, which they read as a concession: the novel that ends with a wedding nobody believed in, or a murder solved by a confession that arrives from nowhere. 3.2 Further series forms The Core chapter names four forms of series: episodic, with a running arc, serial and relay. Two more need naming. The anthology shares a premise, a title or a tone and nothing else: each volume has its own world and cast. Rod Serling’s The Twilight Zone (1959–64) is the classic screen case. It promises a kind of experience, not a continuity, and its volumes are judged as standalone works; its single convention across volumes is its frame, which is a formal contract in Chapter 9’s sense. The companion is a book set in a series’ world whose question is unrelated to the series question, often centred on a minor character. A companion is a relay volume that makes no promise to the series and asks nothing of it; it must stand as a book. 3.3 Summary table The table gives the six forms by what a single volume closes, what carries, and what the form promises the reader about the next volume. Form A volume closes What carries What the form promises of the next volume Episodic Everything The hero, the world, the hero’s rule The scheme again, varied Running arc The volume question One line, a step per volume The scheme, and the next step Serial A stage The story The story continued, in order Relay The volume question The world and its people A new centre, in a known world Anthology Everything A premise or a frame The kind of experience again Companion Everything The world Nothing The table’s last column is the practical one: a volume that breaks its form’s promise of the next, an episodic volume that ends on an open question or a serial volume that closes the story, has changed the contract and should say so. 3.4 Prequels and reading order A prequel is a volume set before the others in story time, usually written after them. It is an analepsis at the scale of the series in Chapter 8 ’s sense, and it inherits that chapter’s strand problem: its reader knows how its story ends, because the later volumes have told her, so its question cannot be what happens. It must run on a question the later volumes leave open, how or why or at what cost, or on a character the later volumes could not show. The order of reading is then a decision with consequences. C. S. Lewis’s The Magician’s Nephew (1955) was the sixth Narnia book published and is set first; later editions renumbered the series in story order, and readers who meet it first read as a creation story what readers in publication order read as an answer to questions the first book had raised. Neither order is wrong, but the writer should know which reader she is writing for. 3.5 Genres that expect a dual timeline Some genres take an arrangement of times as a convention. The dual-timeline mystery braids a present-day investigator, often a woman tracing her family, with a strand in the past, and its readers expect the strands to converge by identity: a person in the present found to descend from, or to be, a person in the past. Kate Morton’s The Forgotten Garden (2008) is an example. In such a book Chapter 8 ’s necessity test is answered by the genre before the book begins, and the convergence is the obligatory scene; the strand question test still applies, since a past strand that only explains the present fails readers of the genre as it fails anyone. The time-slip romance and the multi-generational family saga make similar promises, the first of a union across times, the second of a pattern completed in the youngest generation. 4. The extended catalogue of failure patterns 4.1 The five patterns of the Core chapter The Core chapter treats five patterns, each with its symptom, mechanism, remedy and an exception. The undeclared decline invokes a core promise and declines it at the end without a sign inside the book (exception: No Country for Old Men ). The genre in costume uses a genre’s semantic elements without its syntax, so readers apply a promise the book never makes (exception: The Buried Giant ). The volume that owes its question leaves its own question open at the last page to bring the reader back (exception: 61 Hours , section 6.3). The deferred answer holds a series question across volumes without advancing it (exception: the Harry Potter novels and Snape’s allegiance). The recap at the door opens a later volume with summary (exception: the television Previously on sequence). Four more follow. 4.2 The reset hero Symptom. A series hero who changed in one volume is found in the next as he was before, and readers complain that the previous book did not count. Mechanism. The reset hero has had a criterion changed, in Chapter 12 ‘s sense, and the change undone between volumes without a scene. It fails test 8. The cause is usually the episodic form reasserting itself over a running arc the writer did not mean to start. Remedy. Either show the reversal, as a scene in the new volume with its own price, or move the change in the earlier volume to another character, so that the hero’s criterion was never at stake. Exception. Seinfeld (1989–98), whose writers worked to Larry David’s rule “no hugging, no learning”. Its characters learn nothing because the series declared from the start that they would not; the reset is the form, and the comedy is the characters’ immunity to consequence. 4.3 The undone ending Symptom. A series ends a character or a story conclusively, and a later volume reverses the ending. Mechanism. The undone ending fires Chapter 16 ’s retroactive lens on a volume and then withdraws it, so that the reader’s final judgement of the earlier book is cancelled. It reduces every later ending’s authority, since the reader has learned that endings in this series can be revoked. Remedy. Avoid a conclusive ending that may need undoing; if one must be undone, make the reversal cost something in the story, and give the earlier ending a reading that survives it. Exception. Arthur Conan Doyle’s “The Final Problem” (1893), in which Holmes and Moriarty go over the Reichenbach Falls, and “The Adventure of the Empty House” (1903), in which Holmes returns. The public outcry at his death was long and loud, and The Strand Magazine lost subscribers; the return succeeds because Doyle gives it a story, Holmes’s years in hiding from Moriarty’s men, and because readers had wanted the ending undone. 4.4 The escalation ratchet Symptom. Each volume’s threat is larger than the last, until the series’ world can no longer contain it and the stakes stop meaning anything. Mechanism. The escalation ratchet treats Chapter 11 ’s rule that a middle must raise its prices as a rule across volumes, so that each volume must exceed the last. The threat met is a promise about confrontation, not scale, and scale has a ceiling. Remedy. Escalate by cost to the hero rather than by size of threat: a smaller danger that takes something the hero cannot spare raises the stakes without raising the ceiling. Exception. The Harry Potter novels, whose threat grows from a stolen stone to a war across seven volumes. The series commits the ratchet and succeeds because it pays each enlargement in cost to Harry, the deaths of people he loves, so that the stakes rise in him as well as in the world. 4.5 The overloaded last volume Symptom. The final volume of a long series is longer than the others, slower in its last third, and disappoints readers who loved the earlier volumes. Mechanism. The overloaded last volume must close the series question and every thread carried across the volumes, at a length calibrated for one book, and the retroactive lens judges the whole series by it, as Chapter 16 ’s treatment of series endings argues. The deferred answer (section 4.1) is its commonest cause. Remedy. Close carried threads in the volumes before the last, so that the last carries only the series question and the threads that the answer needs. Exception. The Lord of the Rings , whose last volume closes its main question with several chapters still to come and spends them on returns, a scouring of the Shire and departures, which readers have found too long and many have come to love for that reason. 5. The diagnostic procedures Test 1, shelf. Write two sentences of jacket copy from the first chapter alone and two from the last chapter alone, without reference to the rest. If they belong on different shelves, the book drifts; decide which shelf it is on and revise the other end. Test 2, core promise. Name the genre the opening declares and its core promise, from section 3.1. Find the page where the promise is kept. If there is none, the book has declined it, and test 3 applies. Test 3, declared decline. Draw up the promise inventory: a row for each convention the book invokes, with its genre, the percentage of the text at which it is first invoked, whether it is kept, varied or declined, and where that is shown. For each declined row, find the first sign of the decline inside the book; if it falls after the first quarter, move it or add one earlier. Then name the replacement promise and the page that keeps it. Test 4, variation. Mark the convention the book varies most. Ask whether the book’s meaning, as its ending states it, lies in that variation. A formula book may pass this test by declaring its scheme; record the choice. Test 5, volume question. Write the volume question in a line, find the scene that closes it and its percentage. If the scene is absent or falls after the last page, the volume owes its question. Test 6, series step. For each volume, write in a phrase the step it takes on the series question: a fact learned, a possibility removed, a cost paid. Two successive volumes with no step are stalled. Test 7, re-entry. Give the first chapter of a later volume to a reader who has not read the series, and ask her who the people are and what they want. Mark every sentence of summary; count the facts it delivers that the first chapter’s scenes need. Test 8, criterion across volumes. Write the hero’s criterion, in Chapter 12’s form, at the end of the previous volume and at the start of this one. If they differ, find the scene that shows the change. The volume table gathers tests 5 to 8: a row per volume, with columns for the volume question and where it closes, the series step, the threads carried and their dormancy in volumes, the hero’s criterion, the re-entry and the last page. 6. Further analyses 6.1 Bring Up the Bodies (Hilary Mantel, 2012): the middle volume of a serial with a known end Mantel’s trilogy follows Thomas Cromwell from the 1520s to his execution in 1540, and its reader knows the end from history. The series question cannot be whether he falls but how a man so able comes to it, and each volume takes a step on that question by closing a historical stage: Wolf Hall (2009) with Cromwell’s rise and the death of Thomas More, Bring Up the Bodies with the fall of Anne Boleyn in 1536, The Mirror & the Light (2020) with Cromwell’s own. The middle volume is the hardest position in a serial, since it neither begins nor ends the story, and Mantel’s book, which won the Booker Prize as its predecessor had, shows the solution: it is the most closed of the three. Its volume question, how Cromwell will rid the king of Anne, is posed early and closed by her execution, and its step on the series question is that Cromwell, in doing so, makes the enemies who will destroy him. Its re-entry is a scene, not a summary: His children are falling from the sky , the first sentence says, and the children are falcons named for his dead daughters, flying at Wolf Hall in September 1535 with the king. A new reader learns that Cromwell grieves and serves, and a returning reader is reminded of the daughters the first volume lost, without a line of recap. 6.2 Beach Read (Emily Henry, 2020): a romance about the romance’s promise Henry’s novel makes genre its subject and keeps its genre’s promise. January Andrews writes romances with happy endings and has stopped believing in them after her father’s death and what she learned about him afterwards; her neighbour for the summer, Augustus Everett, writes acclaimed literary fiction with dark endings. They agree to swap genres, each writing a novel in the other’s. The book’s syntax is Regis’s: the meeting, the attraction, the barrier (each lover’s distrust of the other’s kind of ending as well as of the other), the point of ritual death and the declaration. Its variation is that the lovers argue about the promise the book is keeping, so that the romance’s optimistic ending is earned against an objection the book has given its hero to make. It is a case of variation by making a convention the subject: the promise is kept and examined in the same pages, and readers of the genre were given what they came for. 6.3 61 Hours (Lee Child, 2010): a hook in an episodic series The Reacher novels are an episodic series of the purest kind: a drifter arrives in a place, finds an injustice, ends it and leaves, with the hero’s rule unchanged. 61 Hours , the fourteenth, sends Reacher to Bolton, South Dakota, in winter, where he agrees to protect Janet Salter, an elderly librarian who is the only witness willing to testify against a methamphetamine operation. She is shot dead by the town’s police chief, and Reacher kills the chief and the operation’s head in an underground facility; the book ends as the tunnels’ fuel ignites and Reacher runs for the stairs, while a military officer in Virginia, Susan Turner, watches the news of the explosion. The volume question, the witness and the operation, is closed; the hook is on the hero’s survival, the one thing an episodic series promises to carry. The next volume, Worth Dying For , appeared later the same year with Reacher alive in Nebraska. The hook is a departure from the form, and it costs little because the form is so plainly declared: no reader of the fourteenth volume believed the series had ended, so the hook asked only how. The hook’s cost depends on the form: in an episodic series it postpones nothing the volume owed. 6.4 Twin Peaks (ABC, 1990–91): a series question answered and not replaced David Lynch and Mark Frost’s series opens on the body of Laura Palmer and is organised around the question its first season made famous, who killed her. The question is the series question, and the show’s first season advanced it by steps while multiplying its town’s other mysteries. The answer came in the seventh episode of the second season, broadcast on 10 November 1990: Laura’s father, Leland, possessed by the spirit called BOB. The episode drew about 17.2 million households and the next about 13.3 million, and the series was cancelled the following year. The case is not that the answer was wrong; it was prepared and terrible. The series had no second question of equal force ready to take the first one’s place, so the answer closed the series question while the series continued, and the volume table, filled in for the second season, would show rows with no step. Lynch later said he had not wanted the question answered at all, which describes the alternative, a declared decline in the manner of The Leftovers . 7. The household case in full 7.1 The draft The household novel is a contemporary literary family novel, quiet and domestic in register, set in a small British town with a ring road. Four months after the father’s death in March his three adult children reconstruct what he left. The book poses in its first chapter the question why their mother changed the shop’s locks, and declines to answer it; the mother is never focalised and never gives an account of herself. The draft under revision adds two things at the request of the writer’s agent, who wants a second book: a last page, after Nadia puts on the coat, on which the mother rings the shop and Elena answers; and jacket copy that reads In March their father died, and their mother changed the locks. Four months later, one of his children is going to find out why. 7.2 The promise inventory The inventory below lists every convention the book invokes, with Version A’s two additions marked. A reader who holds the mystery’s promise treats every unexplained detail as a clue, so the coat’s weekly brushing, which Chapter 4 planted and no chapter uses, becomes a second question of fact; the book declines it without a sign, and under the mode it has chosen that is an undeclared decline, small but real. The boy at the glass and the sign would also be read as clues, and Chapter 11’s proposal pays them by rhyme, which a reader of the mode may find a thin answer. 7.3 The volume table for a second volume The agent’s second book can be drafted as a row of a volume table, and the row shows why the book cannot have one. Volume Volume question Series question and step Threads carried Criterion Re-entry Last page 1, the novel What these three do with what they can reconstruct; closed at the reading Why the locks; no step (declined) The mother’s silence; the sale Elena’s: what concerns the three of them is read by the three of them — Version A: hooks on the mother’s call 2, proposed Why the locks The same question; its only possible step is the mother’s account The mother Elena’s rule extended to her mother The call — The second row’s volume question is the first volume’s declined reveal, and its only step is the mother’s own account, which the first volume’s meaning depends on not having and which the canon forbids. A second volume on any other question would be a companion, which makes no promise across volumes and needs no hook. 7.4 The revision Version B removes the last page, so that the novel ends where it did, with Nadia, the coat and the silence kept in view, and proposes jacket copy that makes a promise the book keeps: Four months after their father’s death, Elena finds that her key no longer fits the shop, and that someone else has been writing in his ledger. The changed hand is a kept promise, answered for the reader at about 78 per cent and for the sisters at the convergence, and the locks appear as a fact, not a question. The text needs no new sign of the decline: the inventory shows the book declaring it by Dov’s refusal and by three decisions of Elena’s, in the truck, at the empty drawer and at the convergence, each choosing not to ask. 7.5 What the revision settles, and what it does not It settles the book as a standalone with no series question, and fixes the genre declaration in the text rather than in the paratext. It leaves four things open. The first sign of the decline, in the truck, is legible as a decline only in retrospect, so the declaration is cumulative and a reader with a mystery’s horizon may hold the question to the end. The jacket is not the writer’s, and nothing in the book can stop a publisher printing the question again. The coat’s weekly brushing is an undeclared decline under the mystery mode, which a later chapter, or the author, must either pay, give a sign, or cut. And the agent’s request is answered only negatively. 8. The limits of the model The model assumes a reader who arrives with one horizon and holds it, and readers bring several and change them as they read. It assumes that genres have core promises stable enough to name, and genres change: the romance’s optimistic ending is a definition its writers adopted, and the detective story’s fair play a set of rules written in the late 1920s; a writer in fifty years may find the five promises out of date. It treats the jacket as the paratext that matters, when readers also meet a book through reviews and recommendations. And it has nothing to say about why a reader chooses a genre, or about the readers who read across all of them, for whom a declined convention is a pleasure in itself. Its use is narrower: to let a writer see which promises her book makes, and to keep or decline each on purpose. 9. Glossary of the chapter’s terms The definitions below are for the consolidated glossary. Anthology. A series whose volumes share a premise, title or frame and nothing else. Companion. A book set in a series’ world whose question is unrelated to the series question; it makes no promise across volumes. Convention. A feature readers expect of a genre, semantic or syntactic. Core promise. The convention whose breach a genre’s readers treat as a breach of contract: solution, union, the threat met, the kept rule or significance. Declared decline. A convention declined with a sign inside the book early enough to be believed, a replacement promise that the book keeps, and the declined question kept in view. Declined convention. A convention a book invokes and does not pay. Deferred answer. The failure of a series that holds its question open across volumes without advancing it. Dormancy across volumes. The absence of a carried thread from one or more volumes, measured in volumes and in the reader’s months. Episodic series. A series whose volumes close everything and carry only the hero, his world and his rule. Formula. A conventional story structure a culture’s readers know (Cawelti). Genre. For a writer, the set of expectations a reader brings to a book she has identified as one of a group of works treated as alike. Genre in costume. The failure of a book that uses a genre’s semantic elements without its syntax. Horizon of expectations. The expectations, formed by earlier works, against which a reader receives a new one (Jauss). Hybrid. A book that makes two genres’ core promises and keeps both. Kind. A genre with its full repertoire of features, as distinct from a mode (Fowler). Mode. A genre’s character carried, as an adjective, into a work of another kind, borrowing conventions without, by default, the core promise (Fowler). Obligatory scene. A scene a genre’s readers expect and miss if it is absent (Coyne). Paratext. Everything that surrounds and presents a text: title, cover, jacket copy, epigraph, shelf (Genette). Prequel. A volume set before the others in story time; an analepsis at the scale of a series. Promise inventory. A table of the conventions a book invokes, with where each is first invoked, whether it is kept, varied or declined, and where that is shown. Re-entry. The opening of a later volume, which must serve a returning reader and a new one. Recap at the door. The failure of a later volume that opens with summary of the earlier ones. Relay series. A series that keeps a world and passes the centre to a new protagonist in each volume. Reset hero. A series hero whose change in one volume is undone in the next without a scene. Running arc. A line carried across an episodic series, advancing a step per volume while each volume closes its own question. Semantic and syntactic elements. A genre’s building blocks, and the relations and order among them (Altman). Serial. One story published in volumes, each closing a stage. Series. A sequence of separately published works sharing characters, a world or a continuing story, which invite reading as related. Series instalment. A later volume of a series; this edition’s term for what is elsewhere called a sequel. Series question. The question that runs across a series’ volumes and is closed, if at all, by the last. Undeclared decline. The failure of a book that invokes a core promise and declines it at the end without a sign inside the book. Undone ending. A conclusive ending in one volume reversed by a later one. Variation. Keeping a genre’s core promise while changing a convention: new semantics on an old syntax, a varied obligatory scene, or a scene performed by someone unexpected. Volume. One work of a series. Volume question. The question a volume is built on and must close. Volume table. A table with a row per volume of a series, recording its question and where it closes, its step on the series question, the threads carried, the hero’s criterion, the re-entry and the last page. Volume that owes its question. The failure of a volume that leaves its own question open at the last page to bring the reader back. 10.
